replies: Hi there — what do you need?
I don't know enough to answer that honestly. A search should sort you out quickly — and I'm happy to help with the rest of it.
I'm not sure about that one, sorry — I'd rather not guess. A quick search online will get you a solid answer, and I can help you make sense of what you find.
That's beyond what I know well, sorry. Searching for it will turn up better sources than I can offer; tell me what you find and I'll help you weigh it up.
You're {name}.
Nothing said yet for that to be: tell me the thing itself in a word or two and I'll take it from there.
Two ways to choose: the one that is best at the main thing, or the one that is decent at everything. Most people regret the second. What would it have to be good at?
I can't pick for you, but two questions settle most choices like this: which one you would still choose in a year, and which is cheaper to undo if it turns out wrong. Which way are you leaning?
Nice to meet you, {name}. What can I help with?
Go on - what's been happening?

Sound is a pressure wave travelling through air, water or a solid: something vibrates, pushes the particles next to it, and the push travels outwards. It cannot cross a vacuum, and it goes faster through water and solids than through air.
What do you need? I'll take it from there.
What would be most useful to sort out?
That is yours to weigh, and I don't have the details to weigh it for you. It comes down to what you would lose, how likely that is, and whether you could put it back. What would you lose at worst?

I can't say yes or no to that honestly. The test I would use is the worst that happens if it goes wrong, and how easily you could undo it. If both are small, it is worth a try - how bad is the worst case?
No verdict from me on this one - I would be guessing. Say what would make you change your mind, and if nothing would, that is your answer already. What would change it?

The Commons is the elected half of parliament: 650 MPs, one per constituency, and the party with a majority of those seats forms the government. MPs vote on the laws, question ministers - prime minister's questions is the Wednesday set-piece - and sit on select committees that go through a department's work line by line.
{name}, not {pname} — got it.

I don't know this one well enough to say why, and a made-up reason is worse than none. Cases like it usually have two or three causes, and the way to tell which is yours is what else happens at the same moment. What else have you noticed?

The record is the only place it is written down, and a name I got half right would stick, so I can't check one: Wikipedia has it with its sources and the official site will confirm it - tell me what you find and I'll help you make sense of it.
The Wikipedia page for it answers that in a line and cites where the line comes from, and I can't look it up from here: paste what it says and I'll help you weigh the rest.
I would be guessing at the reason. Whatever it is, it will have a before and after: what was different the first time it happened?
No cause I could name honestly. The reliable way to find one is to change a single thing at a time and see whether it goes away - two changes at once tells you nothing. What have you tried?

Name the thing they did, not the day in general: "Thank you for the lemon cake and for staying to help with the chairs, it made the afternoon easy." One line about a specific detail beats a paragraph of adjectives, and send it the same day, because thanks the next morning reads as an afterthought.
I can't give you a list without making it up. The useful question is what you would say no to: once that is settled there are usually only two or three options left. What is a no?
Nothing in front of me to suggest from. Tell me the two or three things that are fixed - where, when, how much - and I can say what sort of option fits them. Which is the one that cannot move?
I don't know it yet — you haven't said.

Give *Rumours* by Fleetwood Mac a go if you've never sat with it, *Blonde* by Frank Ocean for something slower, or *The Köln Concert* by Keith Jarrett if you want piano you can work to. Tell me what you already like and I'll narrow it down.

I have no list to hand you, and I would rather not invent one. What makes a shortlist worth anything is that the choices are actually different: one cheap, one that lasts, one that is least effort. Which of those three are you after?
Hi {name} — good to meet you. What's on your mind?
I'm listening — say more if it helps.

There is no right answer I can point you at. What every pick like this comes down to is what you will use most, and whether the cheaper one is good enough for that. What are you down to choosing between?
Hi {name} — still here. Where were we?

Test yourself instead of rereading: cover the page, say or write what you remember, then check. That one change does more than any technique. Then space it out - the same thing tomorrow, in three days, in a week - because the forgetting and the effort of getting it back is what makes it stay. Say it out loud or write it by hand rather than only reading, link a new fact to one you already know, and sleep on it: a night's sleep is when it gets filed.
Sure. What have you tried so far? That tells me where to start.
I can narrow it once I know what is on the table and what would make one of them useless to you. What is on the table?

Universal Credit is claimed online at gov.uk in one form for everything, and you can ask for an advance of the first payment on the same call - it is repaid slowly from later payments, so ask for it rather than borrowing. Have your bank details, housing costs and childcare costs ready, because the first payment takes about five weeks and the advance is what covers that gap. Child Benefit is a separate form (CH2) and is worth backdating: claim within three months of the birth or you lose the money. Citizens Advice will check what else you qualify for, free.

Work out how many nights you have first, then give each place at least three of them: a base with day trips beats a list of cities, because every move costs you half a day. Book the first two nights and the last night only, keep one day free in the middle, and sleep near the airport on the way home.
I don't know your car — you haven't said.
The useful part is what rules one out - money, timing, effort, or a line you will not cross. Tell me that and what you are choosing from.
The United States has 50 states, plus Washington DC, which is a federal district rather than a state. Alaska and Hawaii are the two outside the mainland.
Glad that helped.

Pick the one thing you would happily be bad at, and buy the cheapest version: a ten pound ukulele, a second-hand chess set, a supermarket sketchbook and pencils. Keep it in the room where you sit, and give it twenty minutes twice a week. The hobby that sticks is the one with the shortest walk to it, not the one you researched most.
A shortlist needs the thing you are starting from: what you are choosing between, and the one limit you cannot go past. Give me those two and I will put three or four in order.

The things that work: same wake-up time every day, no caffeine after early afternoon, not much alcohol in the evening (it wakes you in the second half of the night), a cool dark room, and getting out of bed if you're awake for more than 20 minutes. Screens off half an hour before bed and a short walk most days help more than any app. If you're worn out all day too, or it has gone on for weeks, ask a GP: they can check your bloods, and broken sleep plus no energy is worth ruling out.
Hi {name} — all good here. What's keeping you busy?

Try two or three taster sessions before choosing anything: the club matters far more than the sport. Pick one where the coach learns the children's names, keeps everyone playing, and the ratio of adults to children is decent — and for a shy child, a smaller club beats a big one with a waiting list. Ask if you can watch the first session from the side.
*Grand Designs* for the build, *Location, Location, Location* for the search and *The Great Interior Design Challenge* if you want the rooms. Grand Designs is the one with the arguments.
No record book here, sorry, and a half-remembered number would be wrong without saying so. The Wikipedia page for it keeps the list and dates it - tell me what it says and we can go from there.

I can't check the forecast from here, sorry - no live weather in me. A weather app has today's for your postcode, hour by hour, and for a trip later in the year the monthly averages are the useful thing.

Say what you do remember out loud - a scene, a voice, where you were when you saw it - and put that into a search or a forum; somebody always knows it. The name usually surfaces once you stop chasing it, and running the alphabet for the first letter shakes it loose. For a song, hum it into a song-finder app; for a book, the cover colour and the shop are as good as the title.
I can't check a record from here, sorry - the list moves when somebody breaks it. Wikipedia keeps it with the date each one was set; paste what it says and I'll help you weigh it up.
Happy to help — tell me what you've got so far and I'll add what I can.
If you want something easy and good tonight: *Groundhog Day* for comedy, *Knives Out* for a clever whodunnit, or *Arrival* if you'd rather think. All three work on a sofa with no planning.
No live weather from me, sorry. A forecast app or the national weather site has what is actually coming where you are, and the monthly averages for a trip months away.

A hutch the size of a small shed, not the one in the shop: a rabbit needs a run it can stand up in and stretch out in, plus a covered sleeping box, and it wants company - two rabbits, a neutered pair, is kinder than one. Hay all day, a handful of greens, a spoon of pellets, and water in a bottle rather than a bowl. Handle it every day from the start: a rabbit that is picked up rarely will scratch to get down.

In the first six months the shop has to prove the fault was not there when it sold it, so "you damaged it" is a claim it has to back up, not one you have to answer: put it in writing, say you are rejecting it as not of satisfactory quality, and ask for a full refund. Inside 30 days you can insist on the refund; after that they get one repair or replacement, and if that fails or drags on you can ask for the money back or a price reduction. Wear and tear is only a defence for something plainly used hard - a zip that went on a month-old coat is not that. Keep the receipt, the photos and the emails, and the small claims track is free online for anything under £10,000.

A degree passes at 40% in most UK universities (50% in Scotland, and 50% for a taught masters), and the class comes from your average, weighted by credits: 70% and up is a first, 60 to 69 a 2:1, 50 to 59 a 2:2 and 40 to 49 a third. Modules usually need 40% to count, a resit is often capped at the pass mark, and some courses need a pass in every year to carry credits forward, so check your course handbook.
Thanks for telling me — I'm here if you want to dig into any of that.

Three half-hour sessions a week is enough to feel different in a month, and you need no equipment: a walk or a jog for ten minutes to warm up, then squats or sit-to-stands, press-ups on the stairs or against the worktop, a hip hinge, and a plank, two rounds of each. Push into the last two or three of every set and add a rep each week, because that progression is what changes anything. Walk on the days between, and give it six weeks before you judge it.

Basketball is five a side over four quarters, and you score 2 points in the basket, 3 from behind the arc, and 1 from the free-throw line. You have to keep dribbling or pass — picking the ball up and walking with it is a travel.

A league is decided over a season: every team plays the others home and away, and the table decides who wins, so one bad afternoon only costs you three points. A cup is knockout: you play once, and losing means you are out, which is why a lower team can beat a big one on the day. That is how the same club can be top of the league and out of the cup in the same week.
What have you got so far, and what isn't working? That tells me which advice is worth having.

Most children lisp while they are learning their sounds and grow out of it on their own - the /s/ and /z/ sounds often take until about four and a half, and /r/ and /th/ until six or seven. Don't correct them or ask them to say it again: repeat the word back correctly in your own sentence and let it go. Ask the health visitor or the GP for a speech and language referral if the lisp is still there at four and a half, if strangers cannot understand them at three, if they are losing sounds they used to say, or if they are being teased or going quiet about it at nursery.
When two are close, what separates them is how they are in use rather than on paper. What will you use it for most?
*Happy Valley* for tense British crime, *The Bear* for short, intense episodes, or *Detectorists* if you want something gentle and funny. All three are easy to watch with a partner.

Fix the wake-up time first: the same hour every day, including after a bad night, and the rest tends to follow within a fortnight. Then the three that do most of the work - daylight and a walk in the first hour, no caffeine after lunch, and a screen-free half hour before bed - and only get into bed when you are sleepy rather than tired. Waking in the small hours is usually the mind, not a sleep problem: keep the room dark, don't check the clock, and after about twenty minutes get up and sit somewhere dim until you are sleepy, so the bed stops being the place you lie and argue with yourself. Still broken after six weeks of that is worth a word with a GP.
Got it. Is there anything you'd like a hand with?

Light is a form of energy that travels as a wave and also as particles called photons, at about 300,000 km a second in a vacuum. It carries colour, lets us see, and is only a tiny part of the electromagnetic spectrum.

Pick four dinners you already cook and plan the week on one list before you shop, then cook once for two nights: a big chilli or a tray of roast vegetables tonight, the rest in a pasta bake or wraps tomorrow, and one night that needs no cooking at all. Put one double batch in the freezer for the night you are late home, and keep two fallbacks in the cupboard - pasta and a tin of tomatoes, rice and eggs - for the night the plan falls apart.

I can't see tonight's listings, so here is what I would start instead: *Happy Valley* if you want tense, *The Detectorists* if you want gentle, or *Groundhog Day* if you want a film you can rely on. Tell me the mood and I'll narrow it.
What usually goes wrong? Start there, not with the whole list.

Count the people first, because it decides the room and the food: 8 to 12 is easy to cook for at home, 30 to 40 is about as many as a house takes, and a pub's back room or a restaurant takes 20 to 60 for a similar price to a hall. Pick the day and send one message with the date, time, place and whether it is a meal or drinks, because "let me know if you can make it" gets half-answers. Keep the food to things made the day before - a pie or a chilli kept warm, a baked ham, bread, two salads and a bought cake - and give two people one job each, drinks and cards and the speech, so you are not doing all of it. Send the invitations three to four weeks ahead, six for a big do or a date near Christmas, and ask for replies by a date a week before. Budget £10 to £15 a head for a buffet at home and £25 to £40 in a restaurant's back room, drink on top.
Decide it on the one thing it must do well for you and compare only on that; the rest of the difference rarely matters. What must it do well?
No honest number from me without knowing the size and who does it. If it is the simple version it is quick; if anything has to be taken out first it is not. What has to happen?

Start with the cheapest things and with what the car tells you: a misfire that shakes the whole car and puts the engine light on is usually a spark plug, a coil pack or a plug lead, and a garage reads the fault code for about 30 to 50 pounds and names which cylinder it is. A diesel that goes flat only when you ask for power is often a blocked fuel filter or a clogged particulate filter, and a petrol car that pulls less hard than it did but runs smoothly is usually a dirty air filter, a failing air-flow sensor or a sticking brake caliper. Check the tyre pressures first, because four soft tyres feel exactly like a sick engine, and if a warning light is on, have the codes read before replacing anything.
*Hades* is the one I'd hand you first: fast, short runs, and it never wastes your time. *Stardew Valley* if you want calm, and *The Last of Us* if you want a story to sit through.

For a book: *The Thursday Murder Club* (funny with short chapters, so it is easy to pick up and easy to put down), *Lessons in Chemistry* (funny and big-hearted, and everyone in a book group has an opinion on it) or *The Midnight Library* (gentle and hopeful, and readable in a few evenings). Tell me the last one you enjoyed and I'll match the next.

A football match is two halves of 45 minutes, with 11 a side including the keeper, and the clock keeps running — it does not stop for injuries or substitutions. The 90 minutes is why teams time-waste, and why added time at the end of each half can be long.

That is arithmetic more than a fact. Tell me the size of it, how many there are, and what it is per one, and I will work the total out with the steps shown so you can check them. Which of those do you have?
There are eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, which is why the number went down from nine.

I haven't got a figure for that, and guessing one would be worse than none. A number like this is worked out from two or three others rather than looked up - give me those and I will do the sums with you. What have you got to go on?

Buy the shop's own-label bottle from a named region rather than a brand at the same price: a £7 Côtes du Rhône, Rioja or Chianti from the supermarket's own range usually beats a £7 brand, because you are paying for the wine and not the label. On a red, look for the words reserva, crianza or a named village; for a white, Picpoul, Muscadet and an own-label Albariño are the safest cheap buys, and a screw cap keeps it fresher. Skip the half-price 'was £12' bottles - the plain £6 to £9 rows are where the value is. For fizz, the word Valdobbiadene on a prosecco, or a Crémant instead of champagne, gets you the same evening for a third of the price.
Good — that sounds like the right next step. Tell me how you get on.

A unit is 10ml of pure alcohol, which is a small glass of wine at 12 per cent, half a pint of ordinary lager or a single 25ml spirit - so you work it out as strength times volume. The UK guideline is no more than 14 units a week for men and women, spread over three days or more, and a 13 per cent bottle of wine is about nine or ten units, so a bottle most nights is over it.

Raw fruit and veg that make your mouth tingle, itch or come up in a rash is usually oral allergy syndrome: the proteins in apple, peach, kiwi, melon, tomato and strawberry are close enough to birch or grass pollen that your body treats them as pollen. The itch stays in the mouth and lips and settles within an hour. Most people find the cooked or peeled version is fine, because heat and peeling break the protein down, and an antihistamine from a pharmacy eases a bad day. See a GP if it happens with nuts or several fruits, or the rash spreads beyond the mouth. Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, a wheeze, or trouble breathing is 999 - that is a real allergy, not this.
Seasons come from the Earth's 23.5-degree tilt, not from how close it is to the sun. When your half of the planet leans towards the sun you get summer: longer days and more direct light.
I can't see the news from here, sorry. A news site or app will have the latest; tell me the story and I'll help you make sense of it.

I don't know the size of the job, so any time I gave you would be a guess. Most things like this are minutes for the small version and a day or more for the big one, and which one you have is the whole question. How big is it?

Fish and chips feeds a group for the least money and nobody argues about it. If tastes differ, Indian beats Chinese: more vegetarian mains, and the sides stretch, so two mains with one rice and one bread feeds three. With a fussy child or someone veggie, a Chinese with plain rice and a separate veg dish keeps everyone fed. And if it is the same order every week, add one dish you have never had rather than swapping the whole thing - that is how you find the next usual.

Get closer and hold the phone still: brace it against a wall, a table or your chest, and tap the screen on the person or thing you are shooting so the brightness is set for that and not for the sky behind. Wipe the lens on your sleeve first, because a smeared lens is what makes phone photos look flat and hazy. Take three and keep the sharpest - it costs nothing.

Go by energy and noise, not size: a whippet or greyhound sleeps most of the day and suits a flat, while a collie or terrier needs a job and will bark at every noise in the stairwell. A fostered rescue can tell you what the dog is like indoors, and a breeder cannot. Check your lease allows dogs in writing, and think about the stairs before you say yes to a big old dog you will end up carrying.

A pin-tumbler lock has pairs of pins resting across the plug and the barrel, and the key's ridges lift each pair until the break between them sits exactly at the line the plug turns on. Once every pair is level the plug can turn; the wrong key leaves one pin too high or too low, and that is what picking and bump keys attack.
That sounds sensible. Shout if it does not go to plan.

The sun evaporates water, it rises and cools into cloud droplets, and the droplets bump together until they're heavy enough to fall. Rain is just that water coming back down, usually after a cloud has grown thick and tall.
What's the thing you most want to get right? That's the part worth spending advice on.

Anything that gets you warm and out of breath counts, so pick the kind you will actually turn up for three times a week: brisk walking, cycling, swimming, stairs, dancing or a run-walk. Add two short strength sessions - squats or sit-to-stands, press-ups on the stairs or against the worktop, a row with a band or a loaded bag - because muscle is what keeps carrying and climbing easy. Three half-hours and two strength sessions a week is plenty to start, and adding five minutes or one rep a week beats changing everything at once.

Maths and the sciences are learned by doing, not reading: work through the examples with the book open, then close it and do them again, then do past papers with the mark scheme next to you. Mark them honestly and write down the topics that lost marks; those get redone three days later. Learn the formulas by using them in questions rather than copying them out ten times, and if a topic still will not work, ask a teacher or a classmate to watch you do one question.
No way for me to know that one: I wasn't in the room. What happened?

Pick one thing for two weeks, not five: a twenty-minute walk after a meal, a vegetable with every main meal, or water instead of the second fizzy drink. Any one of those is most of what "healthier" means, one that sticks beats three that don't, and two weeks is long enough to know whether it fits your week. Which of the three could you start tomorrow?

Pick the team someone you already watch with supports, or the one nearest to where you live — going to games matters more than the badge. Watch a few matches first and let it happen; supporting a team is mostly habit plus the people you watch it with. Nobody will test you on the history, whatever the internet says.

A base is the opposite of an acid: it takes hydrogen ions, turns red litmus blue, and reacts with an acid to make a salt and water. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water, such as baking soda or bleach.

Porridge with a spoon of peanut butter and a banana, eggs on toast, or yoghurt with fruit and oats: any of the three takes under ten minutes and keeps you going until lunch. If mornings are rushed, boil an egg the night before and take a piece of fruit with it.

Two truths and a lie: each of you says three things about yourself, two true and one made up, and the rest guess the lie - a point for each correct guess, and you tell them the answer before the next person goes. Three is the right number of players upwards, and the lies get better by the second round.

An apple and blackberry crumble: the fruit in a dish with a spoon of sugar, a crumble of 100g each of flour and butter rubbed together with 50g of sugar, 40 minutes at 180C (160C fan), and custard. It scales to any number, it is better made in the morning, and it is the pudding people are pleased to see.

Check the entry requirements on the university or college page for the exact course, because they differ more than people expect - most want five GCSEs at grade 4 or above including English and maths, and A-levels or a BTEC in a subject that fits. Pick the subjects that keep two doors open rather than one, and ask a teacher or someone doing the job now what they actually needed.

Half the plate vegetables or salad, a quarter protein (fish, chicken, beans, eggs), a quarter starchy carbohydrate, plus a thumb of fat and fruit for pudding. If most meals look roughly like that and you drink water rather than fizzy drinks, you do not need to count anything.
No number from me without the figures it comes from - that is what stops it being a guess. What numbers do you already have?

Take one at a time, a month at a time, and cancel when the series ends: almost every service sells monthly with no contract, so a year of switching costs far less than a year of all of them. Two are worth keeping at once at most - one for the family boxsets and one for what you watch live, football or the soaps. Check the service you already pay for through the TV or broadband bundle before adding another, because that is where the cheapest month usually hides.
I wasn't there, so you know better than I do. How was it?
I wasn't there, so I can't say - I only know what you tell me. How did it go?

Two or three sessions a week of five moves covers the whole body at home: squats or sit-to-stands for legs, press-ups (hands on a worktop if needed) for chest and arms, a row pulling a loaded bag or a band towards you for the back, glute bridges for hips, and a plank for the middle. Do two or three sets of eight to twelve, and add a little each week - more reps, a slower lower, a heavier bag - because muscle only grows when the last rep is hard. Two sessions a week beats five that you stop after a fortnight.

*The Thursday Murder Club* by Richard Osman is the safest pick: funny, short chapters, easy to pick up. For something darker, *The Silent Patient*; for a younger reader, *Wonder* by R. J. Palacio or *The Explorer* by Katherine Rundell. Tell me what you last enjoyed and I'll narrow it down.

Give the worry a time and a page: fifteen minutes in the evening when you write down everything on your mind, then ask of each one what you would actually do if it happened, and what the next step is. When it turns up at three in the afternoon, write one line to bring to the slot and go back to what you were doing - postponing is the part that trains it. Ten slow breaths out, longer than the in, settle the body enough to do that. If it is most days for six months or more, that is worth the GP and talking therapy, which works well on this.

Gravity pulls every part of a large body towards its centre, and over 4.5 billion years that has pulled the Earth into a ball. Its spin makes it bulge slightly at the equator, so it is a squashed sphere rather than a perfect one.
Nice one. Let me know how it goes.

Testing yourself is what makes things stick; rereading notes mostly feels productive without being so. Turn each topic into five questions and answer them with the book shut, then check, and redo the ones you got wrong tomorrow and again in a week. Reread only the bits you could not answer.
That depends on what somebody finds once they start, which is why nobody will give you a firm number before they look. Ask for the usual time and add half again. Who is doing it?
That's the lot I have on that one. Tell me which bit isn't landing and I'll try a different angle.
Wind is air moving from an area of high pressure to one of low pressure, and the sun creates those differences by heating land and sea unevenly. The bigger the pressure gap, the stronger the wind.

Cosmos, lavender, hardy geranium, sedum, verbena and pot marigold flower for months with nothing but deadheading, and daffodil and allium bulbs do the spring. Buy perennials rather than bedding: they come back every year, so the border fills itself instead of being replanted each May. Put the tallest at the back, water them in their first fortnight and leave them alone after that.

Donald Trump is the US president: he took office in January 2025 for a second term, after beating Kamala Harris in November 2024. JD Vance is vice president. A president serves four years and can be elected twice.
Hi {name} — still here, thanks — how are you getting on?

Pick the one task that slows you down most and learn just that: a 20-minute tutorial on the one thing, then use it on real work the same day. Ask your manager for the training budget by showing what it will save (a day a month, fewer errors); most budgets go unspent because nobody asks.

A modern screen is a grid of millions of pixels, each with red, green and blue lights under it, and the picture is just each one being told how bright to be for that frame. A new frame goes up 50 or 60 times a second, faster than your eye follows, which is what makes it look like smooth movement.

A touchdown is six points, the extra point kick after it is one more, a field goal is three, and a safety - tackled behind your own goal line - is two. That is the whole scoring system in American football.

A dry, breezy day dries a normal load outside in two to four hours, and a cold sunny day with wind is nearly as good as a warm one, so 8C and breezy beats 20C and still. Rain, fog and damp evening air put the water back, so bring it in before dusk. In winter, spin it an extra five minutes, then dry it indoors on an airer with a window open a crack: the water has to go somewhere, and an open window is cheaper than the heating.

Split your time in three: a few minutes going over yesterday's phrases out loud, most of it on new phrases said aloud and written down once, and a few minutes listening to something short at normal speed. Learn whole phrases you will use rather than grammar tables, and speak from the first week — even to yourself in the kitchen. One lesson or one conversation partner a week is what makes the rest work.

Test it outside the app first: press Windows key + R on Windows, or open Spotlight with Cmd + Space on a Mac. If the key does nothing there either it is the keyboard, and the usual cause is a stuck key or a spill, so unplug it or turn the laptop off and turn it upside down to dry. If the on-screen keyboard works, the built-in one has failed and a USB keyboard will do until it is fixed. Also check Filter Keys and Num Lock, which make the keyboard look broken.
That's a fair thing to have on your mind. What's the part that's weighing on you most?

The Roaring Twenties were the 1920s in America: jazz, cinemas, cars, radios and short skirts, on borrowed money and with drink banned by Prohibition. It ended with the Wall Street crash of October 1929 and the Depression that followed.

These turn on the exact wording and on your own dates rather than on the rule itself, and I cannot see either from here. Ask whoever decided it, in writing, to confirm it for your dates, and keep the reply: a free advice line will read it with you.

Twenty questions: one person thinks of a person, a place or a thing, the others ask questions that can only be answered yes or no, and twenty questions has to be enough. It works in a car, at a table, and with children from about six.
What settles these is fit rather than quality, so name the job it has to do and the limit you cannot go past - money, space or time. Which of those is tighter?
What would you do about it if you were sure?

Would you rather: one of you puts two bad options against each other and everybody has to pick one and say why in a sentence - 'would you rather be ten minutes late every day or an hour late once a week'. The reasons are the fun part, not the choice.

Ask once, in person, or with a short note through the door or under the wiper, that says what you want - 'this is my space, please leave it clear' - and date it. If it carries on, photograph the car in the space each time with the date, time and number plate, because that log is what gets acted on. On a public road nobody owns the space outside their house: only a marked bay, a dropped kerb or an obstruction is the council's business, so report a car across your dropped kerb to the council's parking line. On private land the landowner or the managing agent can warn them, and a permit scheme is what stops it coming back.

*Codenames* is the one to bring to a group: two teams, one word grid, and it works from four players up. *Wavelength* and *Just One* are the same idea for people who do not like arguing, and for a big party *Werewolf* or *Mafia* needs nothing but a deck of cards.

Check the price history before believing a sale: CamelCamelCamel does it for Amazon and Keepa for many shops, and a "was £200" tag that was £200 for one week tells you nothing. Compare the unit price (per kg or per wash) rather than the pack price.

Choose it for the space it will need in twenty years, not the one it needs now: the label gives a height and a spread, and most disappointment with trees is a tree planted at a third of its final width against a fence. Keep it well away from a house wall, the drains and the path, because roots go as wide as the branches, and check the soil and the light where it is going: a tree that wants acid soil sulks in chalk and one that wants sun goes thin in shade. Plant bare-root between November and March while it is dormant - it is cheaper, and it settles far better than a potted one in leaf. Dig a hole two or three times as wide as the roots and no deeper than the soil mark on the trunk, spread the roots, and put the stake in before the tree so the root ball is not speared. Firm it in, water it well, mulch round the base but leave a clear gap against the trunk, and give it a good soak every week or two through the first two summers, because that is what turns a stick into a tree.

Field hockey is 11 a side over four 15-minute quarters, so 60 minutes of play, and it has no offside rule - that was dropped in 1999, though you can only score from inside the shooting circle and only with the flat side of the stick. Ice hockey is a different game: six on the ice including the goalie, three 20-minute periods, and there the blue line does make an offside.

Get 16GB of RAM and a 512GB SSD if the budget stretches, 8GB and 256GB if it doesn't, and a 13 or 14 inch screen for carrying about. Don't pay for a graphics card unless you game or edit video; a good screen and keyboard matter far more day to day.

Most adults do best on seven to nine hours, but the number is a guide and the test that matters is how you are by mid-afternoon: yawning, reaching for coffee and losing the thread on six hours means you are short, whatever the chart says. The fix is usually a 30-minute earlier bedtime rather than a lie-in at the weekend, and keeping the wake-up time the same even after a bad night. Some people genuinely run fine on six and it runs in families; if your days are fine, the number is not a problem to solve.
Narendra Modi is the prime minister of India: in office since 2014, and in his third term since June 2024. The president, whose role is largely ceremonial, is Droupadi Murmu.

Plants make their own food by photosynthesis: they take carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil and use sunlight to turn them into sugar. The green chlorophyll in their leaves captures the light, and oxygen is released as a by-product.

Search for the sport plus your town and 'club', then email and ask about a taster session: most clubs have a beginners' or social night that costs a few pounds. Turn up to that rather than a match, and say you're new — clubs are used to it, and it's the fastest way to find people at your level.
The States: New York for a first trip. San Francisco and the coast for California. Chicago for food and the lake in summer.

Two things decide these: the exact wording of the rule, and your own dates. A general answer from me could be right about the rule and wrong about you. Whoever runs it - the office, the department, or the helpline that owns the rule (GOV.UK for most of these) - is the one that will confirm your own case, and a free advice line will read it with you.

Yes - five 80g portions of fruit and veg a day, which is about a handful each: a banana, an apple, three heaped spoons of peas, a cereal bowl of salad. Fresh, frozen, tinned and dried all count, potatoes do not, and juice or smoothies only count once a day however much you drink.

An ecosystem is a community of living things plus the non-living parts they depend on - soil, water, air and sunlight - interacting in one place. A pond, a woodland and a garden are ecosystems, and they work because energy flows through them and materials are recycled.

Attach it to something you already do every day - after the kettle boils, after you brush your teeth - because a new habit needs an old one to hang on. Make the first version almost too small to fail (one page, one glass, two minutes), keep it in the same place and time, and put a tick on a wall calendar: the streak is what carries it past the first fortnight, when the novelty has gone.

*Codenames* is the safest buy: two teams, one grid of words, five minutes to learn, and it works from four players up. *Ticket to Ride* if you want a proper board with a bit of thinking in it, and *Just One* if the table is mixed ages and nobody wants a rulebook. City for a week, countryside for a month. If I had to choose one for good it would be the countryside, with a town within reach.

Five minutes sitting still with your attention on your breathing is the whole of it: the mind wanders, you notice and come back, and the coming back is the exercise, not a failure. Same time each day, for two weeks before you judge it. The eight-week courses, MBSR and MBCT, are the ones that have been tested, for low mood and for anxiety, and an app like Headspace teaches the same thing.
Harry Potter is by JK Rowling.

Look for the places that sell a lot of one thing: a market hall or a food court, a bakery, a cafe at the back of a shop, a street food van in a regular spot, or the lunch board outside a restaurant that wants the office trade. Walk a street back from the station or the main road, where the rents are lower, and follow the queue of people who work nearby.
Nice of you to say - thank you.

A chord is three or more notes together, the key is the home note a song keeps returning to, and an octave is the same note higher or lower. The time signature says how many beats are in a bar. Ask about one and I'll give you its answer.

The Earth is layered: a thin rocky crust, a hot slow-flowing mantle, a liquid outer core of iron and nickel, and a solid inner core. The churning iron outer core is what makes the magnetic field that keeps the solar wind off us.

40-40 is deuce: from there you need two points in a row, and the first of them is advantage, so a game can go on a long time. At 6-6 in a set a tie-break decides it - first to seven points, two clear.

Answer the offer rather than the content: 'I'd rather you asked how it went than told me what to do' - once, and warmly, because most advice is love with nowhere to put it. Keep the decisions they would rewrite to yourself, and ask their view on one thing where it is genuinely welcome, because a person with a job to do gives less advice from the sidelines. With your children, give the rule rather than the argument: 'we do bedtime this way at ours'.

Ask for one interesting piece by name, rather than for fairness in general: "I'd like to own the migration in the next quarter; I've done the last two audits and want the stretch." Then agree it in your one-to-one, and offer a swap so nothing is left uncovered; managers respond to a plan, not a complaint.

Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon dioxide, which traps heat in the atmosphere instead of letting it escape to space. That extra heat raises average temperatures, melts ice and makes extreme weather more likely; the science is settled, though predicting any one storm is not.

Here is one, made up on the spot: It started with a small thing nobody in the house had planned for. The Tuesday came and went, and it was still there on the Wednesday. By Friday the whole street had an opinion, and no two of them matched. In the end they kept it, and it kept them.

Kids, about 15 minutes: pasta with butter and cheese, fish fingers or a small roast tray of chips and peas, or scrambled eggs on toast. Keep the sauce on the side and give them less than you think they want, then let them ask for more.

Match it to the age and the room rather than to the adverts. Under about ten, a Nintendo Switch is the safe first console: it comes with a game, works handheld or on the television, and Nintendo's free parent app sets a daily limit and turns it off at bedtime. For a teenager who plays with friends online, an Xbox Series S (about £250) or a PS5 is the one to look at, and each needs a paid plan on top - Game Pass Core or PS Plus, about £7 to £11 a month - before anyone can play online at all. Whichever you pick, set it up as a child account with your email and set the spending limit before the first game is opened, because that is what stops the £50 of extras.

Open a stocks and shares ISA and put a set amount a month into a global index tracker, which spreads the money over hundreds of companies for a fee of around 0.2%. £50 a month is plenty to start, and the money wants five years or more untouched, because the value will fall some years and you need the time to ride it out.

Outside is a little harder at the same pace, because of the wind, the cambers and the turns, so set the treadmill to 1% incline if you want the two to match: either gets you fit and the one you will actually do wins. Go outside when you can for the daylight and the changing ground, and use the treadmill when it is dark, icy, or you want an exact pace for intervals.

Pick something they would use every week and would not buy themselves: good coffee and a proper mug, woolly socks, a decent notebook, or a voucher for the thing they always say they will do. If you know what they are into, buy into it - a good knife for someone who cooks, a head torch for a runner, secateurs for a gardener - and put a real message in the card, which does half the work.

A short nap is worth having: 20 minutes, ideally before about 3pm, and set an alarm, because 90 minutes leaves you groggier than when you lay down. It helps most if you lost sleep the night before or you are driving later. Skip it if you already lie awake at night, and if you need one every afternoon for weeks, that is worth a word with the GP, especially with low mood, thirst or weight loss.

A steady half a kilo to a kilo a week comes from a deficit you can live with, not a crash: cut the drinks, the handfuls and the second helping - usually 300 to 500 calories a day - and eat the protein and vegetables first, because they fill you up longer than the same calories of bread. Walk 30 minutes most days and lift something twice a week, so what goes is fat, not muscle. You cannot choose where it comes off: belly fat goes when the total comes down, and the scales stalling for a week is normal.

A dog is bored because the day is short on sniffing and chewing, not because he needs more toys. One walk where he is allowed to stop and sniff does more than a long march, and a scatter of his dinner on the lawn or in a snuffle mat takes ten minutes off the clock. Add five minutes of training a day, something legal to chew and a game of tug, and break the day up rather than saving it all for the evening.

A lens focuses light onto a sensor covered in millions of tiny light counters, and each one records how much light landed on it. The sensor reads out those numbers, and the processing turns them into the picture - which is why a bigger sensor with bigger counters beats more of them on a small one when the light is poor.

A life cycle is the stages a living thing goes through from one generation to the next: a frog goes egg, tadpole, froglet, adult, and a butterfly goes egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly. A plant's is seed, seedling, flowering plant, then seed again. The adult stage is the one that makes the next generation, which is what closes the circle.

Shoes are decided by length and width, so buy for the longer foot and the wider one - the two are rarely the same - and try them late in the day when your feet are at their biggest, in the socks or tights you will wear. A thumb's width at the toe, the widest part of the shoe at the widest part of your foot, and no lift at the heel when you walk: if the heel slips, a smaller size will pinch the toe instead. Leather gives a little, so a leather shoe should be snug rather than roomy, and a synthetic one will not give at all.

Shut the windows and pull the curtains on the sunny side in the morning, then open everything wide once it is cooler outside than in, usually after 9pm. A fan in an open window pulling air through the flat beats one blowing at you. Keep the oven off and cook early, and put a bowl of water out if the air is dry.

Snow forms when water vapour freezes straight into ice crystals high in a cloud, and the crystals stick together as they fall. It only reaches the ground as snow if the air stays cold all the way down, which is why a cold snap often brings sleet instead.

Sunlight contains every colour, and air scatters the short blue wavelengths far more than the long red ones, so blue light reaches your eyes from all over the sky. That is also why the sky reddens at sunset: the light crosses more air, the blue is scattered away, and the reds come through.

Water when the top couple of centimetres of compost is dry, not on a fixed day, and let it drain away rather than sitting in water. Most houseplants die of too much water rather than too little: a pot with no drainage hole, or a saucer left full, rots the roots and the leaves go yellow and drop. If the compost smells sour, repot in fresh compost and water less; if it is bone dry and light, soak the pot in a bowl for ten minutes. Beyond that it is light - most want a bright spot out of direct sun - and a feed every few weeks in spring and summer only.
Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the surface while Michael Collins stayed in orbit; Armstrong's first step was the one everyone remembers.

Book a beginners' class rather than a video: most studios run a drop-in hatha or beginner class for about ten to fifteen pounds, and a teacher can see your back, which a video cannot. Wear something you can move in and borrow a mat - a cheap 6mm mat is the only thing worth buying - and go twice a week for a month before you judge it. Skip any pose that hurts and tell the teacher about a bad back or neck before you start.

Check for slime before you look at the colour: a yellow or floppy leaf is age rather than poison - light and time break the green down - so pick those out and use the rest. Slimy, sour-smelling or brown-and-soft leaves are not safe, and once one leaf is slimy the bag is best binned, because the slime is bacteria and rinsing does not take it off. Wilting on its own is only water loss, so 10 minutes in iced water brings the crunch back, and limp-but-dry leaves are perfect in a soup, a curry or a stir-fry. Keep the bag in the salad drawer with a piece of kitchen paper in it and eat it within 3 to 5 days of opening.

For cooking: *MasterChef: The Professionals* is the one about the cooking itself, *The Great British Bake Off* for baking and *Saturday Kitchen* for a lazy morning, all of them long-running and easy to start anywhere.

Go for protein plus fibre at about four in the afternoon, 150 to 250 calories: Greek yoghurt with berries, an apple with a spoon of peanut butter or a handful of nuts with a boiled egg. It holds you a couple of hours where a biscuit holds you twenty minutes, so you are not starving at dinner.

Pick one theme for the year rather than ten goals, then turn it into three actions with dates: "run 5k by June - book a race in January, run twice a week" does more than "get fit". Make each one small enough to start in ten minutes on a bad day, put the first step in the diary this week, and look at the list once a month rather than every day. Two things that raise the odds: write them down where you will see them, and tell one person.

Pick one language and one small thing you want to make - a page for a hobby, a script that renames files - and work through a beginner course in that language only. Python or JavaScript is the usual start; HTML and CSS first if you want to see a page you build in a browser. Code a little every day, typing examples out rather than reading them, and when you get stuck, read the error message out loud before searching for it.

A paragraph is one idea in three or four sentences, about 60 to 100 words: long enough to make the point and short enough to take in at a glance. Start a new one when you move to a new idea, and if one runs past a screenful, split it where the subject changes.

A food chain is the line of who eats whom, starting with a plant that makes its own food and ending with a predator. Energy is lost at every step, which is why top predators are few and a chain rarely has more than four or five links.

Reading on paper in low light is one of the better wind-downs there is, and a book you have read before is easier to put down than a new one. It is the backlit screen and the scrolling that delay sleep, so a phone or tablet story is the one to move; an e-reader on a warm setting is much closer to paper. If a book hooks you so hard you are still going at 2am, keep a dull one by the bed and save the page-turner for the daytime.

Speed is how fast you are going, distance over time: 100 miles in two hours is 50 mph. Velocity is that speed with a direction, so a car going round a roundabout at a steady 30 mph has a constant speed and a changing velocity. Average speed is the whole trip's distance over the whole time, which is why a two-hour journey with a stop does not average the speed you had on the motorway.

Start with something tiny today: open the past paper or the topic list and write down what you already know about one topic — ten minutes, that is the whole job. Then work backwards from the exam date and give each topic a day, in 25-minute blocks with a 5-minute break. The last week should be past papers under time, not reading notes.

The phone is a radio with a small computer in it: it finds the nearest mast, tells the network it is there, and every call or page is passed from mast to mast as you move. The aerial on a mast covers a few hundred metres in town, which is why the same phone works in one room and not the next.
The UK is four countries: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Great Britain is the island with the first three on it, which is why people mix the two up.
The figure comes from a quote or a listing, not from me: get the same description from two places, in writing, and check what each one includes - the parts, the labour, the call-out and the VAT.

Three sessions a week is the number to aim for, with a day off between them, and it is the same for running, the gym or swimming. The health guideline is 150 minutes of something that makes you breathe harder each week, which is three 50-minute sessions or five half hours. Two or three weeks in, that gets easier and you can add a session.

Three short lines: what it is about, what you want, and a thanks. "Hi Sam, could we talk about the rota this week? Thursday suits me best. Thanks." No apology paragraph at the front, and say who you are if they may not have your number - tell me who it is for and what you need and I will write yours.

Track two weeks of what actually leaves the account before you change anything: the subscriptions you forgot are usually where it went. Then pick an amount you will not miss, 10 to 20 per cent of what you take home, and move it on pay day into a separate account you carry no card for, so saving happens before the spending. Build towards three to six months of essential bills as the buffer, and raise the standing order by 10 pounds whenever a bill or a habit goes.

Twenty minutes a room on a timer, top to bottom, floor last: a bin bag for the rubbish and a basket for everything that lives somewhere else, then dust from the ceiling down (corners, the tops of pictures, lamp shades), then wipe the marks, then hoover. For a whole house, do the rooms visitors see in the order they see them - hall, loo, kitchen, sitting room - and shut the doors on the rest. How often: the kitchen and the bathroom twice a week for the loo, the basin and the worktops, bedding weekly, the rest when it looks like it needs it, and a deep clean - skirting boards, inside the windows, behind and under the furniture - once a season.

Two months out: check the passport has six months left on it, book what sells out, and take the insurance out the day you book, so a cancellation is covered. Two weeks out: repeat prescriptions, any jabs the country wants, and a card that works abroad; a week out, send copies of the passport and insurance to someone at home.

Two syllables with a hard sound in it is the rule - Biscuit, Otis, Poppy, Rufus - because a name you can shout across a park has to carry, and a long soft one gets shortened whether you like it or not. Say it out loud with 'come' and with 'no' before you commit: nothing that sounds like either, and nothing that a person or another animal in the house already answers to. A cat can be sillier - they learn the tone rather than the word, so a daft name does no harm - but a dog will hear it a few thousand times.

Water evaporates from the sea and land, rises and cools into clouds, falls as rain or snow, and runs back to the sea: the same water goes round and round. Sunlight drives it and gravity brings it back down.

You put your bag in a tray, take out laptops and liquids (100ml in a clear bag), and walk through a scanner, sometimes with a pat-down. It takes ten minutes and nobody minds how nervous you are, so just follow what the staff say and give yourself two hours before the flight.

Area is the amount of surface inside a shape, measured in square units: a room 4 m by 3 m has an area of 12 square metres. For a rectangle it is length times width, for a triangle half base times height, and for a circle pi times the radius squared.

*The Last Dance* is the one that grips people who do not follow basketball, *Sunderland 'Til I Die* for football and *Welcome to Wrexham* if you want to enjoy one. All three are about the people, not the scores.

Brown rice keeps the bran and the germ, so it has about three times the fibre of white and a slower rise in blood sugar; wholewheat pasta is the same idea against white pasta. White rice and pasta are not bad - they just give you less fibre and less staying power. Both keep their calories, around 130 to 150 per 100g cooked, so the swap is about fibre and fullness, not about weight.

Do one small thing you used to enjoy today, at half enthusiasm, because mood follows action more often than it arrives on its own: a walk to the shop, a phone call, ten minutes of a game you liked. Then stack the three things that lift a low mood most reliably - daylight within an hour of waking, 20 minutes of walking, and one person you really talk to rather than message - and keep bedtime and meals at the same time, because a sad week wrecks both and then feeds itself. Write one line a day about how it went, so you can see it is not all bad. If it is most days for two weeks, if the pleasure has gone out of everything, or if it is stopping you eating or working, take it to the GP: talking therapy works, and in most areas you can refer yourself.

Draw the same mug three times: once in one line without lifting the pen, once looking only at the mug and never at the paper, once in under a minute. Three bad drawings beat one careful blank page, and the second one usually surprises you.
Draw a house for the person sitting next to you: what is on the roof, what is behind the door. Ask them what is missing afterwards and let them add it in pen.

Eat where it is busy and freshly cooked, and have it hot: a queue and a hotplate are better signs than a clean table. Have bottled or filtered water and the ice made from it, peel your own fruit, and skip the raw salad that a kitchen has washed in tap water. Carry rehydration sachets and a hand gel, and check the vaccinations and malaria advice for that country about six weeks before you go.

Engineering wants A-level maths and physics, then an accredited MEng or BEng degree, and the accreditation is the part to check because it is what leads to chartership. The other route is a degree apprenticeship with an employer, which pays from day one and ends with the same qualification, or a technician apprenticeship if you would rather start with your hands.

Heating and hot water are most of the bill, so start there: on gas, turn the boiler flow temperature down to 55 to 60C and heat only the rooms someone is in; all electric, put the immersion and any room heaters on a timer for the hours you actually use. Then standby and lighting, which is about a quarter, so switch off at the wall. Ask your supplier in writing for the standing charge and unit rate of their cheapest tariff; a fixed deal usually beats the standard variable one.

Inflation is how much more things cost than a year ago, as a percentage: at 3% a £100 shop costs £103 next year, and £100 in a savings account at 2% buys less than it did. The Bank of England aims for 2% and moves interest rates to get back to it, which is why a mortgage or a savings rate changes when inflation does.
Japan: Tokyo for the city and the food. Kyoto for temples and old streets. Osaka for eating, with a rail pass once you visit more than one.

Meditation is paying attention to one thing on purpose - usually the breath - and coming back to it each time you notice you have drifted; an empty mind is not the aim, and the noticing is the skill. The tested versions are the eight-week courses, MBSR and MBCT, mainly for low mood and anxiety.

On a table: *Ticket to Ride* (trains, simple, satisfying), *Codenames* (two teams, one word grid) and *Azul* (tiles, quick, sharp). *Ticket to Ride* is the safest box for a household.

Pick something they'd use every week and wouldn't buy themselves: good coffee and a proper mug, woolly socks, nice soap, a book about something they care about. If you know what they do at the weekend, buy into that instead - a voucher for the pool, the cinema or a class. Something consumable and slightly better than usual is the safest bet for someone you don't know well.

A share is a piece of a company: you get a slice of its profit and its problems, and what it is worth moves with what buyers will pay that day. One share in one company can halve; a fund holding hundreds of companies spreads that risk, which is why most people should start with an index fund inside an ISA.

A bill is a draft law: it has to pass both Houses, then get royal assent from the monarch. In each House it goes through a first reading (just the title), a second reading where the principle is voted, then committee, report and third reading. The Lords can delay a bill for about a year, but not kill it.

A force is a push or a pull that can change an object's speed, direction or shape, measured in newtons. Gravity, friction and the push of a hand are all forces, and an object with no net force keeps doing what it was doing.

Potential energy is energy stored ready to be used: a ball held up high has potential energy, and it turns into kinetic energy as it falls, faster and faster. Kinetic energy is the energy something has because it is moving. Both are measured in joules. Potential is mass times gravity times height, so twice the height is twice the energy; kinetic is half the mass times the speed squared, so doubling the speed gives four times the energy.
Read the book first if you care about the story, watch the film first if you might not finish the book. An adaptation cuts, so the film rarely ruins a good novel — the other way round happens more.
Russia, at about 17 million square km, nearly twice the size of Canada in second place. China and the United States come next.
