Start with acrylics: they dry in minutes, clean up with water, and a starter set is under twenty pounds. If it is watercolour you want, the paper decides everything - cold-pressed 300gsm and no cheaper - and you work light to dark because you cannot paint white back in. Either way, paint the same simple thing - one mug, one window - five times instead of five different things, and work bigger than feels comfortable with one brush that holds a point.

Start with a teacher or a good app for the first month and ten or fifteen minutes a day on the basics: every instrument has its own awkward first fortnight, and one lesson early saves months of undoing. Pick one short piece you like as the target.

Sunlight bends as it enters raindrops, reflects off the back and bends again on the way out, which splits it into colours. You only see one with the sun behind you and rain in front, and the red band is always on the outside of the arc.

The clocks go back an hour at 2am on the last Sunday in October and forward an hour at 2am on the last Sunday in March. The point of it is the light: the hour is moved to the part of the day when most people are up and out, so summer evenings stay light and winter mornings are not dark until nine. Late October buys an extra hour in bed, and the evenings close in by about 5pm; late March hands the hour back.

Under an hour you do not need to carry anything: have 300-500ml in the hour before you go and take water at fountains or taps on the way. Past an hour, or on a hot day, carry 400-700ml and drink a few mouthfuls every 15-20 minutes rather than one big stop. To keep it cold, fill the bottle half full and freeze it the night before, top it up with cold water on the way out, and put it in a belt or vest rather than in your hand. Over 90 minutes take electrolytes, and drink to thirst - drinking lots of plain water on a long run can make you feel worse, not better.

Use the name out loud in the first minute - "Nice to meet you, Sarah" - and hang it on something physical: alliteration (Tall Tom), a rhyme, or a face feature. Repeating it twice early beats any trick later, and if it has gone, say so straight away: "Sorry, your name's gone" costs less than guessing.

Use a broad-spectrum sunscreen of at least SPF 30, with four or five stars for UVA, and use more than feels right: about two tablespoons for an adult in a costume, reapplied every two hours and after swimming or sweating. SPF 50 for children, and sunscreen adds to shade, a hat and a shirt rather than replacing them.

Weight is the pull of gravity on a mass, measured in newtons: a 60 kg person weighs about 600 N on Earth, about 100 N on the Moon and nothing at all in orbit. Mass is how much stuff is in something, measured in kilograms, and it is 60 kg in all three places. The scales in your bathroom measure weight and are marked in kilograms for the mass that goes with it here.

Yes, if your screen is below eye level: a stand or a pile of books brings the top of the screen to eye level, an external keyboard and mouse go at elbow height, and that is what stops the neck craning down all day. A laptop alone is always too low for long sessions, so the cheap version - box under the laptop, separate keyboard - does most of the job; buy the stand if you want it to look tidy or to swing up and down.

Anchor the wake-up time first and let the bedtime follow: get up at the same time every day, weekend included, and get outside into daylight within an hour of it, because morning light is what sets the clock. Then move bedtime fifteen minutes at a time, a couple of nights each, rather than an hour overnight. Keep naps under twenty minutes and early in the afternoon, skip caffeine after lunch while you shift it, and give it a week before it stops feeling like effort.

Ask once, cheerfully, once you have picked the thing - "is there anything you can do on the price?" - then stop talking and be ready to walk away: silence and a customer who will leave are what move a price. Take the display model or last season's colour, offer to pay in full today, check the online price so they can match it, and never say your maximum. At a market or car boot sale, offer about two thirds and settle in the middle.

Ask one open question about the thing you are both already in - the queue, the weather, how they know the host - and then ask a second question about their answer. People remember a good listener, not a clever line, so let a silence sit for a second rather than filling it yourself.
Charles III is the king: he became monarch in September 2022, when Elizabeth II died. Camilla is queen, and the heir is Prince William.
Citizens Advice covers this free, and a call beats searching. Tell me what they say and I'll help you weigh it up.

Clouds are tiny water droplets or ice crystals hanging on specks of dust, formed when rising damp air cools. They look white because the droplets scatter all colours of sunlight equally; they turn grey when they're thick enough to block the light.
Cold, if I can wrap up: you can always add a layer, and a cold walk ends with a hot drink. Heat is harder to escape from.
Dogs, by a whisker: daft, straightforward and pleased to see you. A cat is the kinder choice if you're out all day, though.

Emulsion for walls and ceilings: matt for a bedroom or a living room, and a washable matt or eggshell where it has to take scrubbing, such as a hallway, a kitchen or a kids' room. Woodwork wants eggshell or satinwood rather than gloss, because gloss shows up every lump and brush mark. Bare wood or metal gets a primer then an undercoat; plastic, melamine and old gloss need an adhesion primer first or the paint peels; anything that gets hot, like a radiator or a pipe, wants a heat-resistant paint made for metal. New plaster wants a mist coat - emulsion thinned by about a fifth with water, no vinyl - to soak in and seal the dust. Buy a sample pot before the big tin, because colour on a wall is not colour on a card.

Essay subjects are learned by writing answers, not by reading the notes again: get the mark scheme for your board, write three timed past questions a week and plan the other two in a spider diagram. Mark your own answer against the criteria and count what you missed - a point you did not make, a quote, the evaluation sentence at the end - because the marks are in the structure as much as the knowledge. Learn five specific examples or quotes per topic rather than twenty vague ones, and keep them on cards: one named case with a date beats a paragraph about 'many historians'.

Flowers, most of the time: go to a florist rather than a garage and ask for what is in season, and a mixed bunch is always safe. A plant lasts years and is the better present for someone who likes looking after things, but give an orchid or a houseplant only to a person who will remember to water it.

For tonight: *Groundhog Day* (funny), *Knives Out* (a clever whodunnit) or *Arrival* (if you want to think). On a series instead, *Happy Valley* is tense and *The Detectorists* is gentle. All easy picks with no homework needed.

For a rectangle, area = length × width; for a triangle, ½ × base × height; for a circle, π × radius². Keep all the measurements in the same unit. So a room 4m by 3m is 12 square metres, and an L-shaped floor is two rectangles added together.

Four things, all before you book: a passport each, because a child's lasts five years and takes a few weeks to arrive, so do not book flights until it is in your hand; a free GHIC card each for Europe, one per person; seats together, so ask when you book, since a child under 12 is meant to sit with their adult; and travel insurance that names every child. If you are crossing a border without the other parent, take a signed letter from them saying you have their permission. Photograph every passport and keep the pictures on your phone.
Glad to hear it — and thanks for coming back to say so.
Late spring for me: long evenings, everything green, and not hot enough to make excuses.

Milk is good for you: a 200ml glass has about 7g of protein and a third of an adult's daily calcium, and it is one of the cheapest ways to get both. Semi-skimmed is the sensible default for most adults - the same protein and calcium as whole milk with about half the fat. Whole milk is the right one for a child under two, and a fortified plant milk is the swap if you do not do dairy.

Most constant tiredness is dull rather than medical: too little sleep, a late screen, alcohol, caffeine after lunch, or no daylight. Give it two weeks of the basics before you assume anything else - the same bedtime and getting-up time every day, twenty minutes outside in the morning, no caffeine after two, and no phone in the bedroom. If it is still there after that, see a GP for a blood test: low iron, an underactive thyroid and low vitamin D are the usual finds, and iron is common and easy to treat, especially for anyone with heavy periods.

Naming places I have not been to would be guessing, so here is the shape of a day instead: one big thing in the morning, one long lunch, and nothing booked after it. Are you after coast and walking, or food and towns?

Open with the thing you found out, not with the background: "Cheap ovens lie about their temperature" gets read, "Many people own ovens" does not. One idea per post, 600 to 900 words, subheadings every few paragraphs, and end by telling the reader what to do next.

Pick two things and put them in the diary by Friday: one that gets you out of the house - a walk with a destination, a market on Saturday morning, a museum or gallery you keep meaning to visit - and one person to see or one thing waiting for you at home. The free ones that work are the walk, the park, a canal, a hill with a view, the library and a market on a Saturday morning. Two plans makes a good weekend; five makes a list you abandon by Saturday lunchtime. An evening is the same rule: one thing out and one thing in. Tell me the town and who is with you and I can suggest something specific.
A pharmacist or your GP can answer that today — that's the quickest route to a straight answer.

A rock is a solid piece of the earth made of one or more minerals: granite is mostly quartz and feldspar, and limestone is mostly calcite. Rocks come in three kinds - igneous from cooled magma, sedimentary from settled layers, and metamorphic changed by heat and pressure.

A wing is shaped so air moves faster over the top than underneath, and the pressure difference pushes the wing up; that force is called lift. Engines provide the forward thrust, and lift grows with speed until it beats the plane's weight.

A day that works most places is one big thing in the morning and nothing booked after it, though I don't know this place well enough to name the things: one worth the journey out, one long lunch, the rest loose. What do you usually enjoy doing?

A graduate job in the UK usually starts around £25,000 to £30,000, with London and the big finance, law and tech employers at £35,000 to £45,000, and small charities, media and museums nearer £22,000. Judge an offer on the whole package - pension match, paid training, travel, and the hours - and on what the first two years teach you, because that sets the salary after them. A lower start where someone senior actually trains you usually beats £2,000 more where nobody does.

Plan the week around what's already in the cupboard, shop with a list once a week, and buy own-brand staples (pasta, rice, tins, oats, frozen veg) where the difference is invisible. Cutting meat to two or three dinners a week is the biggest single saving for most households.

Play with a wand toy for five or ten minutes, two or three times a day, and let her stalk and pounce before you let her catch it, then give her a meal so the hunt has an end. The rest of the day wants things rather than toys: a food puzzle, a cardboard box, a paper bag, somewhere high to sit and a window to watch. Rotate the toys and put half of them away, because a basket she has seen for months is furniture.

Points go to the top ten: 25 for a win, then 18, 15, 12, 10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 1. The bonus point for the fastest lap only ran up to 2024 and has been dropped, so do not count on it. Sprint weekends pay points to the top eight, and the driver and the team with the most points at the end of the year are the champions.

Put the phone in another room — not face down, another room — and work in 25-minute blocks with a 5-minute break where you get up. Before each block, write the one thing you will finish on a scrap of paper so you do not have to decide where to start. Same desk, same time, same little ritual helps more than willpower.

Read the letter or the text reminder first, because it says what to do before this one and most appointments need nothing. Worth doing every time: write down the two or three things you want to raise, most worrying first, and take the list of medicines you are on, or the boxes themselves. Arrive ten minutes early for a place you have not been to, and ring if you cannot make it - a missed slot usually means a long wait for the next one.

Register as self-employed with HMRC as soon as you start, then file online by 31 January after the tax year ends; the deadline to register the first time is 5 October. Keep every invoice and receipt as you go, because expenses cut the bill, and put a quarter of each payment aside so January is no surprise. Side income under £1,000 a year needs no return.

Sell something before you register anything: one paying customer tells you more than a plan, and you can trade as a sole trader from the day you start. Then do three things in this order - register as a sole trader with HMRC (by 5 October after the end of your first tax year), open a second bank account so business money is not mixed with rent and shopping, and keep every receipt and invoice from day one, because the expenses are what cut the tax bill. Tell HMRC the date you started, not the date you got round to it. A name, a phone number and one clear service are enough to begin: a website and a logo can wait until someone is paying you.

Six to eight glasses a day, about 1.5 to 2 litres, is plenty, and more in heat or after exercise; tea, coffee, milk, squash and food all count towards it, and pale straw-coloured urine is the check that you are about right. If you forget, keep a filled bottle where you sit and drink a glass with every meal.

Start with very little: trainers or astro boots, shorts or leggings, a water bottle and, for football or hockey, shin pads. Clubs lend sticks, bats and bibs to beginners, so email and ask what they provide before you buy anything.

Tell me which key it is on and I will name it: the tall line on the left of the keyboard is the pipe (|), the mark over 2 is the at sign (@), over 3 the hash (#), and the wavy one on the left is a tilde (~). If you can paste it into a line, I can read it too.

That changes by the day and by the place, so anything I said would be yesterday's - the day and the place decide it. The place's own page has today's, one phone call confirms it, and a map listing carries the hours underneath the address.

The minimum is a front light of 500 lumens or more, a rear light, a gold-rated D-lock through the frame and a rack, a waterproof jacket and gloves. Plan a route on quieter roads or a cycle path, leave shoes and a change of clothes at work, and start with two days a week: six miles takes about half an hour at an easy pace.

The model number and the exact code on the display are what settle these - the number is on a sticker on the machine, or in the settings screen under About. Put the model number into the maker's own support page and it gives the manual and what that code means.

The side streets five to ten minutes further out are where the free and cheap spaces are: read the sign at the entrance, because a residents' bay or a one-hour limit is what the tickets come from. For a station or a town centre, the station car park or a park and ride is usually cheaper than the multi-storey, and the parking apps (RingGo, PayByPhone, JustPark) show the live price and let you top up from your phone. Photograph the bay number and the sign before you walk off.

The Grand Slams are the four biggest tournaments: the Australian Open in January, the French Open at Roland-Garros on clay, Wimbledon on grass, and the US Open. Winning all four in the same year is a calendar Grand Slam - Rod Laver did it in 1969 and Steffi Graf in 1988.
The date on a figure matters as much as the figure, and I can't check one I wasn't told: Wikipedia has that number with its source - tell me what it says and I'll help you make sense of it.

The headline rate is only half of it: an evening or weekend price, a day cap, a return or a longer booking often costs less than paying by the hour, and the operator's own page lists them all. Check today's figure there before you pay.
They're means 'they are', their means it belongs to them, and there is a place or 'there is'. So: they're late, their car, over there. In a hurry, ask what the word is doing: person, owner or place.

Traffic that crawls is a gap problem: count four seconds to the car in front and brake early and gently, so the person behind has time to do the same - most jams are made by that accordion, not by the crash. Stay in one lane where you can and watch the brake lights two cars ahead rather than the one in front. Add twenty minutes before you set off and plan a stop every two hours, which is what keeps the last hour the same as the first.

Treat 30C as the everyday setting: it is about 10p a load cheaper than 40C and gets shirts, jeans and normally-worn clothes just as clean, as long as the drum is not crammed and you use the full dose of detergent. Save 40 for heavy soiling, 60 for towels, bedding, underwear, socks and anything greasy or stained, and 90 only for illness or nappies.

Twice a day for two minutes with a fluoride toothpaste, spit rather than rinse so the fluoride stays on, and clean between the teeth once a day with floss or interdental brushes. Sugar between meals is what causes decay, so keep it to mealtimes, and a check-up every year or two keeps small problems cheap.

Walking counts, and brisk walking for 30 minutes most days does most of what a gentle gym session would for your heart and mood. Add two short strength sessions a week for muscle and bone, and pick up the pace until you are slightly out of breath.
What do you call a sleeping bull? A bulldozer.

You can get plenty without meat: eggs, milk, cheese and yogurt, a tin of beans or chickpeas (about 15g of protein), lentils (about 18g per 100g dry), tofu, nuts, seeds and wholegrains. Spread it over the day rather than one meal - beans at lunch, eggs or tofu at dinner, yogurt and nuts as a snack - and there is no need to count anything.

An apple and blackberry crumble is the easiest crowd-pleaser: fruit in a dish, a crumble of butter, flour and sugar on top, 35 minutes at 180C, and custard. Baked rice pudding and bread and butter pudding are just as easy and soft enough for anyone who finds chewing hard; Eton mess takes five minutes if you buy the meringues.

An electric car drives like an automatic with one difference: when you lift off the accelerator it slows itself down and puts charge back in the battery, so you brake with the right pedal for most stops and use the left one only for a hard stop. Treat the range as about 70% of the official figure in winter, charge to 80% for everyday use and 100% only before a long run, and check the car's own route planner for chargers rather than arriving on 5%.

Ancient Egyptians built them about 4,500 years ago, around 2560 BC for the Great Pyramid of Giza, as a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu. The workers were organised, paid labourers, not slaves, hauling stone on ramps and sledges.

Ask work first, then price the journey three ways before you buy anything: a season ticket only beats weekly or daily tickets above about three days a week, a flexi ticket or a carnet covers two or three days, and a railcard pays for itself in about a dozen trips if you qualify for one. If you drive, park and ride, a lift-share board or a parking space a ten-minute walk out usually undercuts the station car park, and asking whether your employer does a season ticket loan or a cycle-to-work scheme is free money in effect. Booking the next day's travel the night before is where the cheap fares go.

Batteries feed a motor that turns the wheels directly, so there is no gearbox to shift and full pull is there from a standstill. Lifting off turns the motor into a generator that pushes power back into the battery - that is the regenerative braking - and the brake pedal blends that with the real brakes so you rarely use them up.
*Paddington 2*: funny for the adults too, and nothing in it will scare an 8- or 11-year-old. *The Mitchells vs the Machines* or *Matilda* are good backups.
*Patchwork*, *Jaipur* and *Hive* are the three best two-player games that are quick to learn. For a card game with no kit, gin rummy works just fine.

*The Hobbit* is the easiest way in, *Mistborn* by Brandon Sanderson if you want a big magic system to learn, and *Piranesi* by Susanna Clarke if you'd rather have something short and strange. All three are fine for adults and teenagers.

Change a few things you can keep doing rather than going on a diet: fill half the plate with vegetables, put protein in every meal so you are not hungry an hour later, swap sugary drinks for water or squash, and walk for half an hour a day. Losing about 0.5 to 1kg a week is the rate that stays off, and the plan that works is the one you would still follow in a year. If you are hungry all the time, or the weight is going on without trying, see a GP.

Compound interest pays interest on the interest as well as on what you put in, so £1,000 at 5% is £1,050 after a year and £1,102.50 after two, because the second year pays 5% of £1,050. The rule of 72 is the shortcut: divide 72 by the rate to get the years it takes to double, so 5% doubles in about 14 years.

Cut the adverbs and put one thing a reader can see in every paragraph: not 'the kitchen was messy' but 'the bin was full of cereal boxes'. Then vary the sentence length - short where it is tense, longer where it is calm - and read it aloud, because the sentence you stumble on is the one to fix. That is three passes, and they fix most flat writing.

Decide in this order, because each one removes half the list: set a budget per head and a distance you will actually travel, then pick a place whose menu is short - eight good dishes beats forty average ones - and read the reviews from the last month, not the star average. If two are still level, choose the one you would be sorry to lose; if neither would bother you, the cheaper one is fine. Still stuck, book a table rather than a takeaway: a table settles it and you eat something that is not from a box.

Don't wear white or cream to a wedding unless the invitation says so: it's the couple's colour and reads as upstaging them. Anything else bright and comfortable works, and flat shoes are a kindness to yourself at an outdoor ceremony.
Draw the kitchen as a mouse would see it - everything enormous and books on the floor. One shape to start with stops the 'I don't know what to draw' that a blank page causes.

Dress for ten minutes in: a thin wicking base layer, a fleece over it and a windproof shell on top - waterproof rather than thick if it is wet - so you should feel slightly cold on the doorstep and warm by the first mile. Wind is what makes it cold, so keep it out at the neck, cuffs and ankles and cover the hands and ears, which is where it bites first. Take a layer you can tie round your waist or push in a pocket for the way home.

Each morning pick the one task that would make the day a good one, and do it before email. Then batch the small things (messages, approvals) into two set times, and keep a "later" list so you stop holding them in your head; most of the day's stress is unfinished small things, not hard ones.

Exchange rates move every day, so I cannot give you a figure that will still be right tomorrow: your bank's app or any currency converter has the rate this minute. What costs more than the rate is the fee on top of it - a normal debit card abroad often adds about 3% and hides a mark-up in the rate, while a travel card or a bank that uses the mid-market rate adds nothing on weekdays, and the kiosk at the airport is the worst rate you will find. For a purchase, pay in the local currency when the machine offers to convert for you, because that conversion is the seller's own and it is always worse than your bank's.

For most club golfers it is not the swing but the aim and the tempo: check that feet, hips and shoulders all point where you want the ball to start, then swing at eight out of ten with a smooth one-two count. Practise half-swings with a 7 iron and brush the grass - the divot should come after the ball. Two or three lessons with a pro filming you will save a season of guessing.
For the sheet: *The Long Shots*. Others that go down well: *The Night Owls* and *The Comeback Club*.

For two or three nights: one change of clothes plus a layer, one pair of comfortable walking shoes, toiletries in a bag, phone charger and any tickets. Roll clothes to fit more in, and leave the "just in case" outfit at home.

For an action film: *Die Hard* (132 minutes, still the best one, and it is a Christmas film too), *Mad Max: Fury Road* (120 minutes, one long chase, and it never drags), or *John Wick* (101 minutes, short, clean, and all about the fighting). Any of them is a good way in, and I can go shorter or pick one if you tell me the mood.

For a small business the bill is mostly hosting: a domain name is about £10 a year, a site builder or simple hosting is free to about £20 a month, and a developer charges £500 to £3,000 for a five-page site. Start with a free page on a builder and pay for the domain, because the name is the bit you keep; move to better hosting when the phone rings twice a week. A shop is the expensive part - card fees around 1.5% plus 20p an order, and Shopify from about £25 a month - so sell through an existing marketplace first and build the shop once you know what people buy.

For a film: *Paddington 2* (warm, funny, and good at any age), *Knives Out* (a whodunnit everyone can follow, with jokes all the way through) or *The King's Speech* (a true story that gives everyone something to talk about afterwards). Say the mood and I'll narrow it down.

For a machine, the maker's own sheet is written for your exact model: the sticker on the back or inside the door has the number, and the code on the display is the other half. The maker's support page with that model has the manual, the fault codes and the reset sequence.

Four short paragraphs: what you want and by when, the facts in date order, what you have already tried, and what happens next if nothing changes. Put your address, their name and address and the date at the top with a subject line saying what it is about, open with 'Dear Mr Smith' or 'Dear Sir or Madam' and close with 'Yours sincerely' or 'Yours faithfully', and keep the whole thing to one page.

George Washington was the first president of the United States, from 1789 to 1797. The first electoral college chose him unanimously and he stepped down after two terms, which set the pattern every later president followed.

Get into a building or a hard-topped car, away from windows, and stay there 30 minutes after the last thunder. If you're caught in the open, move off high ground and away from lone trees, water and metal fences, and crouch low on the balls of your feet.

Get it cold fast and split it now: cool it within an hour, keep what you will eat in the next 3 days in the fridge and freeze the rest flat in bags or tubs. Mash keeps a month frozen and stew, curry, soup or bolognese three, and a cake or a loaf freezes well sliced, three months; rice is the one to be strict with - fridge it within the hour and eat it within a day. Reheat once, until piping hot right through, and next time cook 75 to 100g of dry pasta or 60g of rice a head.
Good. Let me know how you get on.

Hold each one for 20 to 30 seconds, twice on each side, and do the set two or three times a week - daily works too but the gains come from doing it often, not from going deep. The five that matter for everyday life are the backs of the thighs, the hips and hip flexors, the calves, the chest and the upper back; warm up first with a few minutes of walking, and ease into the stretch rather than bouncing at the end of it.

John Logie Baird gave the first public demonstration of television in London in 1926, using a spinning disc. Philo Farnsworth's all-electronic system, shown in 1927, is the one every modern set works on.

Leaves look green because chlorophyll, the pigment that captures sunlight for photosynthesis, reflects green light and absorbs the reds and blues. In autumn the chlorophyll breaks down and the yellow and orange pigments underneath show through.

Litter tray and litter, two bowls, a scratching post, a carrier, a soft bed and food for its age, plus a vet visit booked for the first week. A second litter tray and a few toys save a lot of trouble, and nothing stringy or small enough to swallow.

Look for a roast date, not a best-before: beans are best from a few days to about six weeks after roasting, and supermarket bags with only a best-before are usually months old. Buy whole bean and grind per brew - fine for espresso, medium for a filter machine, coarse for a cafetiere - or ask the shop to grind it for the pot you use. A medium roast suits most brewing, and about 60g of coffee to a litre of water is the strength to start from. Keep the bag sealed and in a cupboard, not the fridge.

Look for a club that advertises a beginners' or "back to" session rather than a team trials night — most sports now run them, and the standard is friendly. Try three in a month before you judge, and go twice before deciding you are unfit for it, because the first session is always the worst one. Nobody at a casual session is watching you; they are all watching the ball.

Make the plan first and write the essay from it: list three or four points that answer the question, put one piece of evidence under each, and put them in the order that makes the argument grow. Then write the body paragraphs first and the introduction last, when you know what you argued. Two hours of planning saves a day of staring.

Mass is how much stuff is in something, measured in kilograms, and it does not change wherever you go. Weight is the pull of gravity on that mass, measured in newtons: a 60 kg person weighs about 600 N on Earth, about 100 N on the Moon and nothing at all in orbit, while their mass is 60 kg in all three places. So the scales in your bathroom measure weight and are marked in kilograms for the mass that goes with it here.

No first-hand knowledge of that one here, so no verdict from me. What it comes down to is how it works for the thing you actually want it for, how it holds up after a few months, and what it costs you if it is wrong. Recent reviews from people who wanted the same thing are the shortest way to all three.
Nothing so far — you haven't mentioned anything coming up. What have you got?

Parliament is the Commons, the Lords and the monarch, and it makes the law, votes the taxes and holds the government to account. The government is separate: the prime minister and about 20 ministers running the departments, sitting inside parliament - which is why a government with a majority usually gets its laws through.

Pick one shape and put a time on it, because a free day with no plan turns into the sofa. The ones that cost nothing: a walk with a destination (a park, a canal, a hill, a shop that sells something you like), a free museum or gallery - most have a permanent collection that costs nothing - and the library, which has events, papers and warmth. At home: a film nobody has seen, a bake with whatever is in the cupboard, a swap of clothes or books with friends, or a board game with a rule that the phones stay in another room. For a family, one outside thing in the morning and one quiet thing after lunch is plenty: children remember the day that had a walk and a picnic in it, not the one that cost forty pounds.

Pick something with a bit of movement, like a coffee and a walk or a gallery, so silences have scenery. Ask about what they would do with a free day and what they are into lately; questions about them beat clever lines every time.

Pick the one thing you would be sorry to miss and plan the day round that, though I can't recommend places I have not been to: it decides where you stay, when you eat and what you drop. What sort of thing do you like doing?

A mile is 20 minutes at a brisk walk - three miles an hour, and 1.6 km - or about 15 minutes if you are pushing it. Brisk means you are breathing a bit harder and can talk but not sing. Half an hour a day is the number that earns most of the benefit: about a mile and a half, or the seven to eight thousand steps people talk about. If you want a target, walk a mile at a pace that leaves you slightly warm rather than comfortable, three times a week, and time yourself - it is an easy number to watch come down. Are you walking for fitness or for a particular distance?

A bird is a warm-blooded animal with feathers, a beak and two wings, and it lays hard-shelled eggs. All birds have feathers and none has teeth, and most can fly - though ostriches, penguins and kiwi cannot.

A budget tyre fitted is about £55 to £80 a corner, mid-range £75 to £120 and premium £120 to £200, with fitting, balancing and disposal £15 to £25 of that. Read the size off the sidewall - 205/55 R16 - and ring two or three fitters with it: the same tyre can differ by £40. Two at a time is fine, new pair on the back, and change them at 3mm of tread.

A carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gas a person, a household or a product causes, counted in kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent over a year. For a household in the UK it is roughly 8 to 10 tonnes, and the weight is not where people think: heating and electricity and car travel are the bulk of it, while a flight is big in one hit and a plastic bag is almost nothing. The changes that move it most are the boring ones - a heat pump or good insulation, less red meat and dairy, fewer and shorter flights, a smaller car - and offsetting does not cancel them out.

A factor divides into a number exactly - 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12 for 12 - and a multiple is in its times table: 12, 24, 36. A prime factor is a factor that is also prime, so 12 is 2 x 2 x 3. Work out how many nights you have first, then give each place at least three of them: a base with day trips beats a list of cities, because every move costs you half a day. For Japan the window is Late March to April for the blossom, or October to November for the autumn colour. Book the first two nights and the last night only, keep one day free in the middle, and sleep near the airport on the way home.

Work down the list: a feed, a burp, a clean nappy, a swaddle, then a dark room with white noise and a steady shush. Long evening crying is normal in the first three months and peaks around six weeks - a sling, a walk or a warm bath often breaks it. Call 111 the same day if the cry is high or unusual, they will not feed, are floppy or hot, or if you feel close to shaking them: put them down and step out of the room.
World War Two ran from 1939 to 1945. Britain and France declared war on Germany after it invaded Poland, and it ended with Germany's surrender on 8 May 1945 and Japan's on 2 September.
Yes - in the kitchen a broccoli is a vegetable, but botanically it is a flower, not a fruit: the fruit is the part that holds the seeds.

You are comparing your unedited day with other people's edited highlights, so the comparison cannot come out fair: compare with yourself a year ago instead, and mute the three accounts that reliably leave you feeling behind. When the thought lands, name it plainly ("that is comparison, not fact") and answer it with one thing you can do this week that the person you were five years ago could not. If it is one person you keep measuring yourself against, spend less time in front of them and more on the thing you actually want to be better at.

Your contract is the place to look first: it sets your hours, your breaks and whether overtime is paid. On top of it the law gives you a 20-minute break on a shift over six hours, 11 hours between shifts, and an average 48-hour week unless you signed an opt-out. If something is not being followed, ask for it in writing - that is what an employment adviser or a union rep needs to help.

About two months, not the three weeks people quote: in the study that measured it the median was 66 days, and the easy ones (a glass of water with breakfast) settled in a few weeks while the hard ones took most of a year. Missing one day made no difference to how long it took, so a slip is not a restart - the rule is never miss twice.

Acne happens when hair follicles get blocked by oil and dead skin, and skin bacteria multiply in the blocked pore; hormones make the oil glands busier, which is why it peaks in the teens. Wash gently twice a day, do not pick, and a pharmacy treatment with benzoyl peroxide or salicylic acid is a reasonable first try; painful cysts or scarring deserve a GP.

Aim for about 150 minutes a week, which is around 20 minutes a day: anything that gets you warm and out of breath - five half-hours, or three twenty-minute sessions and some walking - plus two short strength sessions. Three or four sessions a week is plenty to start; consistency beats length.

Aim for a palm-sized portion of protein at each meal - eggs, milk or yoghurt at breakfast, beans, lentils or chicken at lunch, fish or mince at dinner - which lands most adults near the 0.75g per kilo of body weight they need. Greek yoghurt, cottage cheese, tinned fish, eggs, tofu and lentils are the cheapest ways to add it.

Alcohol is a group 1 carcinogen and there is no amount that is good for you: the risk starts with the first drink and rises with the total, which is why the guidance is about keeping it low rather than finding a safe level. The liver, the blood pressure and the risk of seven cancers - mouth, throat, oesophagus, liver, colon, and in women breast - all move the same way. A couple of drink-free days and staying under 14 units a week is what keeps the risk small.

Ask for the first appointment of the day and wait in the car until it is your turn, with a towel over the carrier. Leave the carrier out all week with a worn T-shirt in it and feed her beside it, so it is not the thing that only means the vet. Ring the desk before you go: a calming spray or a sedative is kinder than being held down for a jab.
Australia: Sydney for the harbour and the beaches. Melbourne for food, with the Great Ocean Road from there. Flying between the cities is normal.
Beer is brewed from grain, usually barley, with hops for bitterness and yeast for the alcohol.

Book the train as soon as the date is fixed: advance singles tied to one train are usually about half the walk-up fare, and they go on sale around 12 weeks ahead. A railcard pays for itself in one or two long journeys, and check the price of two singles as well as a return - two advances are often cheaper than one return.
Book the first two nights and the last night only, keep one day free in the middle, and sleep near the airport on the way home.

Book from the hotel's own site once you know the name, then check three things: the last two months of reviews only (owners change, and old praise is stale), the map for the walk to the station or the old town, and the small print for a city tax and the cancellation date. A room away from the lift or the road is worth asking for in the booking notes, and ring the desk for anything that matters - they answer faster than the site.

Buy one adjustable dumbbell or one kettlebell and nothing else to begin with: about 6 to 10 kg suits most beginners and 10 to 16 kg if you are already strong, and a used one goes for £40 to £80. Add a resistance band for about £10 and a step or a sturdy chair, and that covers squats, rows, presses and carries - a mat only if your floor is hard. Skip the bench and the multi-gym until you have trained for six months, because the routine is what makes the difference, not the rack.

Buy for the battery first: most smartwatches last a day or two, so one that lasts a week changes how you use it. A fitness band at £40 to £80 covers steps, sleep and notifications; pay £200 to £300 only if you want a screen and apps on your wrist, and expect the step and heart-rate numbers to be rough rather than medical. Is it for exercise, notifications, or looks?
Can't call that one for you, sorry. Say what you'd lose either way and I'll lay it out with you.
Canada: Toronto and Montreal for cities. Banff and Jasper for the Rockies. Vancouver if you want sea and mountains together.

Catch it and cut the power before anything else: a bucket under the drip, and turn off the light circuit for that room at the fuse board if water is near a fitting, because water and ceiling lights are the dangerous pair. Do not go up on a wet roof or into a loft with wet boards - a fall from a roof kills more people than a leak ever does. Absorb what you can, move furniture and photos, and photograph it all with the date: the ceiling may sag, so stay out of the room if the plaster bulges. If you rent, tell the landlord in writing now and keep the message, because a leak they were told about is theirs to fix. Then get a roofer out - most will tarp a live leak the same day - and check your insurance covers the escape of water.

Cheap party food people actually eat: a big pot of chilli or a pasta bake, garlic bread, and a bowl of crisps and dips. For standing-up food, sausage rolls, cheese straws and fruit on sticks go further than anything fiddly.
Citizens Advice covers this free, and a call beats searching — that's the quickest route to a straight answer.

Clip a tuner on the headstock and take the string order low to high: E, A, D, G, B, E - the sixth string is the thick one, and the top E is the thin one. Turn the peg slowly and always come up to the note from below, because slackening down to it leaves the string ready to slip. Ten seconds a string, and tune every time you pick it up; guitars move with the room.

Coaches are the cheapest way between two cities: booked two or three weeks ahead a long trip is often under 20 pounds when the train is over 60, and the overnight coach saves a hotel night as well. Book on the operator's own site or app, take the ticket on your phone, and put the big bag in the hold, which is included but has to be tagged. Arrive 15 minutes early: coaches leave on time and do not wait.

Cold and easy to carry: a frittata cut in wedges, sausage rolls, cheese with oatcakes or bread, tomatoes and a bag of grapes. Freeze a bottle of water the night before - it keeps the food cold and then it is your drink.

Colour the new growth every four to six weeks and leave the rest alone, because overlapping permanent dye on hair that already has it makes the ends darker and drier each time. For grey, go one shade lighter than you think you want, since grey takes colour cooler and darker than the swatch. A root spray or a wand made for it covers a few days of regrowth without a whole dye job.

Confidence comes from the route, not the traffic: ride the quiet-street version at a weekend, then take it on a weekday at a quieter hour, and repeat until the turns are automatic. Ride a door's width out from parked cars, take the middle of the lane at junctions so nobody squeezes past, and look back before you move over. Never go up the inside of a lorry or a bus: that is where the serious crashes happen.

Cook two big things on one day and portion them: a pot of chilli or bolognese and a tray of roast veg, then cook rice or pasta fresh on the day. Cool it within two hours, box it in the portions you will actually eat, and keep three days in the fridge or freeze the rest. Chop an onion, wash a bag of salad and grate some cheese while you are there and a weekday dinner takes ten minutes. Cooked rice is the one to freeze on the day, not the next.

Crocodiles have narrow, V-shaped snouts and their fourth tooth shows when the mouth is shut; alligators have broad, U-shaped snouts and it stays hidden. Crocodiles are also the ones that tolerate salt water.
Draw an animal wearing a hat it would never choose. Give them three minutes and no sharpener: the limit is what gets a drawing finished, and a finished silly one beats a perfect blank page.

Eat something with carbs an hour or two before if you can, and protein within a couple of hours after - a banana and yoghurt, or toast and eggs, is plenty. The order matters far less than the total: getting enough food and sleep is what makes the training work.

Electricity is the flow of electric charge, usually electrons pushed along a wire by a voltage. A circuit has to be a complete loop: the source pushes the charge, the wires carry it, and a device like a bulb uses the energy as it passes.

Falls are usually several small things adding up rather than one bit of clumsiness: leg strength and balance, eyesight, blood pressure that dips on standing, medicines, and the house itself - which is why the second one is worth acting on rather than waiting for the third. Ask the GP for a falls review: they check blood pressure lying and standing, go through the medicines, and can refer to a falls clinic or a strength and balance class, which is what actually cuts falls. Then take the house apart: grab rails on the stairs and by the loo, a night light, rugs lifted or taped down, cables out of the walkway, and a phone within reach from the floor. If they cannot get up or put weight on it, or knock their head - especially on a blood thinner - that is a same-day call.

For most of Europe the order is fixed: microchip first, then a rabies vaccination at least 21 days before you travel, then the paperwork - an EU pet passport or an animal health certificate from your own vet - and a tapeworm treatment for a dog on the way back from some countries. Check both countries' own rules, and the ferry or airline's, because each has its own kennel or cabin booking. Start six weeks out: the 21 days catches people, and nothing can be backdated.

For most people with a varied diet the only supplement worth taking is vitamin D in autumn and winter (10 micrograms a day), plus folic acid if you are pregnant or trying. A multivitamin mostly makes expensive urine; if you eat little fish, vegans should add B12.
For the sheet: *Second Wind*. Others that go down well: *The Wild Cards* and *The Early Birds*.
For Paris: April to June and September to early October: 18-24C and the parks at their best. July and August are hot and many small restaurants close, and November to February is grey and cool.

For a laugh: *Groundhog Day* is the funniest safe pick, *The Grand Budapest Hotel* if you want something stylish with the same warmth, and *Paddington 2* if you want to laugh from the first minute. All three are fine with anyone in the room.

Get a heavy pan properly hot, pat the steak dry, salt it and sear it 2 to 3 minutes a side for medium rare, turning once. Rest it 5 minutes under foil before cutting, which matters as much as the cooking.

Gin wants tonic about one to three with a big wedge of lemon or lime, and cucumber or a sprig of rosemary if you have it; vodka takes the same plus elderflower or ginger beer, dark rum wants ginger beer and a squeeze of lime, whisky wants soda or ginger ale, and tequila wants grapefruit soda and salt. Cheap tonic is fine but use plenty of ice and stir it, because a warm, flat G and T tastes of nothing.

Give every child a ball and keep them moving: ten minutes of a game with a ball each (dribble and freeze), fifteen of one skill in a small game (passing through gates, or 1v1 to a line), then twenty minutes of small-sided matches, four a side, no keepers. No queues, no laps, no long instructions — if they stand still for more than a minute you lose them. Finish with a game they already love and a quick handshake line.
Go off the room rather than the label - one notch up from what most people there will have on, and a layer to shed if you are the only one dressed up. Cold where you are?

Go bigger than feels right: in a living room the rug should reach under the front legs of the sofa, so about 160x230cm for a small room and 200x290cm behind a three-seater, and a bedroom rug wants to run at least 60cm past each side of the bed. Wool wears and cleans better than polyester and does not flatten as fast; a thick underlay makes a cheap rug feel expensive and stops it creeping. Take the size you are considering and tape it out on the floor before you buy, and check it can be washed or spot-cleaned.

Go by the forecast for the hours you will actually be out rather than for the whole day, and dress for the coldest and wettest of those hours. As a rule of thumb: under about 10 degrees a proper coat, between 10 and 18 a jumper with something windproof over it, over 18 no coat and loose cotton instead. Then one layer you can take off, and a hood or an umbrella if there is any rain in the forecast - being caught wet on the way home is what ruins a day, not the temperature.

In Japan: Sushi at a counter and a bowl of ramen in Tokyo, takoyaki and okonomiyaki in Osaka, tofu and kaiseki in Kyoto. Convenience-store food is genuinely good and cheap.

In London: pick one area a day rather than criss-crossing: South Bank, the museums in South Kensington, and the markets in the East End. The Tube is quickest; walking between central stops is often as fast.
In Amsterdam: the Jordaan on foot, the Rijksmuseum and a canal walk at dusk. Book Anne Frank House tickets online weeks ahead; they sell out completely.
In Paris: walk the Île de la Cité to the Marais, pick one big museum rather than three, and eat in a market street rather than by the Eiffel Tower. Book the Louvre or Orsay timed entry online.
In Chicago: the architecture boat tour, the Art Institute and the river walk, then deep dish once for the experience. The Loop is walkable and the trains from O'Hare run all night.

India became independent on 15 August 1947, and the country was split at the same time: Pakistan was created for Muslims, and the movement of people either way killed hundreds of thousands. Pakistan's own independence day is 14 August, a day earlier.

It turns on the thing itself and on what it is for - a trip, a form, a job and a pan of something all want different things. Tell me which it is and I will give you the short version, rather than the general one that fits none of them.

Jupiter is the biggest planet: about 143,000 km across, or 11 Earths side by side, and more than twice as massive as all the other planets put together. It is a gas giant with no solid surface to stand on.

Keep the book where you idle - beside the kettle, in your bag, by the bed - and read in the small gaps instead of waiting for a free evening. Quit a book at about 50 pages if it has not gripped you: forcing yourself to finish things you dislike is what stops the habit.

Keep a nap to 20 minutes and take it before 3pm, or you'll feel groggy and sleep worse that night; 30 to 60 minutes is where the grogginess lives, so set an alarm. Skip it if you already lie awake at night, and if you need one every afternoon for weeks, that is worth a word with the GP, especially with low mood, thirst or weight loss.

Keep it plain and fast: fish fingers or chicken strips with peas and oven chips, pasta with grated cheese and sweetcorn, or a cheese omelette with toast. Put something green on the plate and don't make a second dinner if they refuse it.

Layers and a waterproof: a thin base layer, a fleece over it, a waterproof jacket with the hood up in the wind, and over-trousers in the bag for the top of the hill. Wear boots with real tread and take a spare pair of socks, and keep cotton off your skin - it holds the water and makes a wet walk cold, where wool or a synthetic layer still keeps you warm.

Learn seven to ten words at a time, out loud, and test yourself instead of reading the list: cover the English side and say the word, then swap. Put each new word in a short sentence you would actually say, and go back over yesterday's words for two minutes before adding new ones — spacing is what makes them stay.

Leave at nap time or early if you can, plan a stop or a walk about every two hours, and pack snacks, water, sunshades and a tablet with films downloaded. A surprise bag of small new things to hand out one at a time is the trick for the last hour.

Lure him into it and name it once: a treat just above his nose moved back over his head drops his bottom into a sit, so say 'sit' the moment it lands and give the treat. The same hand carries on down to the floor for 'down', and a flat palm held up for 'stay', one step at a time. Three or four goes, several times a day, and stop while he is still enjoying it; never push his bottom down, let him work it out.

Make it small and scheduled: a set time, everything you need out and ready, and a session so short that skipping it feels sillier than doing it. Track the days you show up rather than the results, and do it with someone or book it like an appointment: habit carries you when motivation does not.
Mash 2 ripe bananas into 2 eggs and a spoon of flour, and fry small pancakes in butter for 2 minutes a side. Ripe bananas are the whole point, and they need no added sugar.

Meet on neutral ground, one walker each, and walk them side by side rather than face to face, then let them off lead only in a fenced space where the older dog can walk away. At home give the older dog his own bed, bowl and corner that the puppy cannot reach, feed them apart, and step in before the puppy hangs off his ears. Two weeks of short, supervised time together settles most pairs; guarding food or a hard stare needs a behaviourist.

Memory is not one store: short-term memory holds a handful of things for seconds, and long-term memory is a web of connections between neurons that gets stronger each time you recall it. Sleep and repetition file it away, and forgetting details is normal - the brain keeps the gist and drops the rest.

Most mountains are made by two plates of the earth's crust pushing together, which folds and crumples the rock into ranges like the Himalayas and the Alps. Others are volcanoes piled up by eruptions, or blocks of crust lifted along a fault, like the Sierra Nevada.

Motivation follows action, not the other way round: do ten minutes and decide after. Pick the subject you least dread but find easiest to start with, because a bad day is about getting one thing done, not all of it. If it has felt pointless for weeks, tell someone at school or work; that is a different problem from laziness.

Nearly all of it is the same leaf at different levels of oxidation: green tea is dried before it can darken and tastes grassy, black tea is fully oxidised and malty, and oolong sits between them, roasted and floral. White tea is the young leaf barely processed, light and sweet, and pu-erh is aged and earthy, an acquired taste. Peppermint, chamomile and rooibos are infusions of other plants rather than tea, so they have no caffeine and suit the evening. Everyday picks: English breakfast or Assam if you take milk, Earl Grey for the citrus, and a plain green or jasmine drunk without milk.

On a console: *Hades* for short, fast runs, *The Last of Us* if you want a story to sit through, and *Elden Ring* if you want a huge, hard world. *Hades* is the one I'd start with.

Once a year for a health check, and the yearly booster goes in at the same visit. Puppies and kittens: a course of two or three jabs two to four weeks apart, then the yearly one. Past about eight years old, twice a year is worth it. A rabbit needs its teeth checked once a year. The practice usually texts the reminder, so ask them to set one.

One pizza each and a garlic bread to share: a 12-inch is one hungry person and a 9-inch a light one, so a 12-inch between two plus a side is the cheaper way to feed a pair. A plain margherita and one with a topping beats two fully loaded ones, which are the ones left half eaten.

One team bats to score runs and the other bowls and fields to get them out; an over is six balls, and an innings ends when ten batters are out or the overs run out. You are out if the ball hits your stumps, if a fielder catches it before it bounces, if you are run out, or leg before wicket — hit on the pads by a ball that was going to hit the stumps.

One 20cm cook's knife does almost everything, so spend the money there - around 25 to 40 pounds on a forged one with a full tang gets an edge that holds - and add a serrated bread knife and a small paring knife when you need them, rather than buying a set of six cheap ones that none of them do a job well. Hold it before you buy it, because the handle has to fill your hand, and only buy something you can sharpen yourself with a steel or a stone.

Pick one regular thing and go every week: a running club, a pub quiz team, a choir or a class that runs for several weeks. Adult friendships come from repeated low-stakes time together, so choose something you would enjoy alone and say yes to the first drink after. Then be the one who suggests the next time: it is repetition rather than charm, and it takes about three months of turning up.

Pick one thing to say before you go in and write it in a sentence on the agenda or a note: a question, a number, or "I can take that". Say it in the first ten minutes if you can - the first thing is the hard one and the rest get easier - and open with the ask rather than the run-up. If you get talked over, use their name and finish the point once: "Sorry, Martin, I hadn't finished - the number is 40, not 14."

Pick the thing you cannot change - the floor, the tiles, the worktop, the sofa - and take the wall colour out of it in a paler version of itself. Then add one deeper tone from the same family for a rug or cushions and a wood or a metal to warm it: three colours, one of them a near-neutral. Paint a sample patch you can watch in the morning and again under the lamp before you buy a tin, because a colour on a small card lies.

A mortgage is a loan secured on the home, usually over 25 to 35 years: you put down a deposit of at least 5% (10% gets much better rates) and borrow the rest. Lenders usually cap the loan at about 4.5 times your income, so £30,000 a year plus a 10% deposit buys roughly £135,000. Most people fix the rate for two to five years, and a fee-free broker will compare the whole market for you, which is worth doing even if you think you know your bank.

A neuron is a nerve cell: a long strand that carries an electrical pulse from one end to the other and passes it on to the next cell through a tiny gap called a synapse, using a chemical. You have around 86 billion of them, and learning is the connections between them getting stronger with use.

A number I invented would be worse than none, and the year is half of it, so I would not guess: the Wikipedia page or the official site will have it, with the source; paste what it says and I'll help you weigh it up.
A round of golf is 18 holes, and a full round on foot takes about four hours - about two hours for nine. A group is up to four players, and the winner is whoever takes the fewest shots.

A solid has a fixed shape and a fixed volume: its particles are packed tightly together and vibrate in place, which is why a solid keeps its shape unless something pushes or breaks it. Ice, wood and rock are solids; melting turns a solid into a liquid.

A solution is a mixture where one substance dissolves in another: the dissolved substance is the solute and the liquid it goes into is the solvent. Salt water and sugar water are solutions, and the dissolved part cannot be filtered out.

A species is a group of living things that can breed together and produce fertile young: dogs are one species, and a horse and a donkey are different species because their mule offspring cannot have young. Members of a species share most of their genes.

A ukulele has four nylon strings, a much smaller body and the tuning G-C-E-A; a guitar has six steel or nylon strings in E-A-D-G-B-E and two and a half octaves more range. The ukulele is the easier first instrument by a wide margin - four strings, soft on the fingers, and most chords need two or three fingers - while a guitar can play bass lines and full chords. A baritone ukulele is the size of a small guitar and is tuned to the guitar's top four strings.
A Test match is up to five days, 90 overs a day; a one-day match is 50 overs a side; a T20 is 20 overs a side and takes about three hours. Same game, very different patience required.

A date like that is nearly always written down somewhere - a confirmation, an order page, a letter, an email - and that is where to look first: it carries a reference, the date they gave you, and what they promised. Then one short chase, quoting the reference and asking for a day rather than "soon", is what moves it. What is it you are waiting to hear about?
A dentist is the one to see, and most will fit an urgent case in — that's the quickest route to a straight answer.

A fan does not cool the air, it moves it: the air passing over your skin takes heat away and speeds up the sweat evaporating, so you feel cooler while a fan left running in an empty room changes nothing. Ceiling fans work best blowing down in summer and pulling up in winter, which stirs the warm air off the ceiling.

A hard surface wants lifting and wiping rather than blotting: take the worst off with a plastic scraper or the back of a knife held flat, then wipe with hot water and a drop of washing-up liquid, turning the cloth as it takes the colour up. Anything stronger gets tested on a hidden corner first, because acid eats limestone and concrete and bleach dulls a seal, and a cream cleaner on a damp cloth takes the last of the film off without either.

A healthy dinner is a palm of protein, a fist of potato, rice or pasta, and half the plate vegetables: 150g of chicken with 200g of new potatoes and a big pile of broccoli comes to about 400 calories, so a 500-calorie cap is easy to stay under, and a salmon fillet or a fist of chickpeas makes the same plate again. Grill or roast rather than fry, and measure the oil, because a tablespoon of it is 100 calories on its own.

A hyphen joins words into one (well-known, two-year-old) and has no spaces. A dash separates a phrase for emphasis — like this — and British style usually spaces an en dash. Word processors can turn two hyphens into a dash for you.

A jacket is decided by the shoulders and nothing else matters as much: the shoulder seam should end on your shoulder bone, and the padding should follow your own line rather than sit out past it, because a shoulder is the one thing a tailor cannot change much. Then check the chest - you should be able to slide a flat hand inside the buttoned jacket - the sleeve, which should end at the wrist bone and show about a centimetre of shirt cuff, and the seat, where the jacket should just cover it without flaring. Button the middle button only and sit down in it before you decide.

A mammal is a warm-blooded animal with a backbone that has hair or fur and feeds its young on milk. Almost all give birth to live young rather than laying eggs, and they keep a steady body temperature - which is why a whale is a mammal even though it lives in the sea, and a bat is one even though it flies.

A manual car goes because the clutch reaches the biting point before any gas: clutch down, first gear, then let the pedal up slowly until the bonnet lifts and the revs dip, hold it there, and add a little gas as you let it up the rest of the way. Practise finding that point five or ten times on a flat quiet road, because pulling away is only that point held while the car moves. Take your foot right off the pedal once you are moving - riding it is what wears a clutch out.

Porridge is the better everyday bowl: oats are wholegrain, and a 40g serving has about 4g of fibre and no added sugar, so it keeps you full until lunch. Plain cereal does the same job with less fibre; granola and crunchy clusters are the ones to watch, because a 50g serving can carry 12 to 15g of sugar. If you want cold cereal, pick a wholegrain one with under 10g of sugar per 100g.

Protein is a building material made of chains of amino acids: the body uses it to build and repair muscle, skin, hair and organs, and enzymes are proteins too. Meat, fish, eggs, milk, beans, lentils, nuts and tofu are good sources.

Put it in writing with the shape you want and the answer to their worry: "Could I do 8-4 instead of 9-5? I would still cover the 9am call, from home on Teams." Offer a three-month trial and fix the date you will review it - a trial is far easier to say yes to than a permanent change.
Quick: a tuna salad in 10, a bean stew in 25, or a sausage traybake if you have 45 minutes. Tell me what is in the fridge and I will pick properly.

Read what each axis is measured in first, including the units and the step between the numbers. To read a value, go up from the number you know to the line, then across to the other axis. A straight line means the same change each time; a curve means it changes faster or slower.

Roast chopped veg at 200C (180C fan) for 25 minutes with oil and salt, then stir it through pasta or rice; a fried egg on top makes it a meal. Frozen veg works too, straight into the pan for the last 5 minutes.

Roughly £10 to £15 covers a secret santa or a colleague, £20 to £30 a friend or a nephew, £30 to £60 a close friend or a sibling, and £50 to £100 a partner or a parent. Fix a total for the year before December and divide it per person, and agree a cap out loud with a group: the number is a budget line, not a measure of how much you like someone.

Same answer, and it covers this: Wind is air moving from an area of high pressure to one of low pressure, and the sun creates those differences by heating land and sea unevenly.

Send a short thank-you the same day: "Thank you for the conversation today — I'm even keener on the role after hearing about the new system. Happy to answer anything else." Chase once, a week after you applied: two lines, say you are still interested and one thing you would bring to the job, and ask if they need anything else from you. Then leave it - ring only if the advert gave a date and it has passed. Keep applying elsewhere in the meantime.

Something small and mostly carbohydrate, an hour or two before: a banana, a round of toast, a small bowl of porridge. Leave longer after a big meal - three hours - or you will feel it. For a short easy run first thing, plenty of people go out with nothing but water and are fine. The one rule is nothing new on the day of a race: try it in training first.

Something worth sitting down to, and hard to get wrong: chicken thighs roasted skin side up on a tray of potatoes, onion and peppers at 200C (180C fan) for 40 minutes, or a salmon fillet with the same tray for 15. Buy a good pudding and the whole thing feels like a dinner.
Sorry to hear that. What would help most right now?

Sort the transfer when you book the flight rather than the day before: check the airport's own site for the trains, buses and the official taxi rank, then pick the one that gets you there with slack. Aim to be at the airport two hours before a short-haul flight and three before a long-haul one, and add the walk from the drop-off to the terminal plus the queue at bag drop. If someone is driving you, find out the drop-off point and any charge first, because at most big airports you cannot be dropped at the door.

Spices are not bad for you: they are the cheapest way to make plain food taste of something, which is why a boring diet gets eaten less. Turmeric, cinnamon, garlic, ginger and black pepper do no harm in the amounts that go in cooking, and the salt and the heat are what to watch - a hot dish is painful rather than harmful. Watch the blends and the ready-made sauces, because they carry the salt.

Spider plant, snake plant, pothos and the ZZ plant are the ones to start with: they take low light, a missed watering and a radiator, and still look fine. Water them when the compost is dry rather than on a schedule, keep them out of the hottest sun, and they will outlive the ones that want fussing.

Start where you can already run 5km comfortably and build up over about sixteen weeks: three runs a week (one long, two short and easy), and add no more than 10% to the weekly total. Your longest run only needs to reach 32km, three weeks before the day, then taper — the last two weeks are much shorter on purpose. Do not do your longest run and your fastest in the same week.

Start with something short and gripping: *Of Mice and Men* (about 100 pages), *The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time*, or any *Reacher* book by Lee Child. Short chapters and a fast plot matter more than literary prizes when you're out of the habit.

Start with the airline, because cabin sizes differ: a 55x40x20cm case fits most paid cabin allowances, while the free underseat bag is around 40x20x25cm, and a bag outside the airline's own limit is the one thing that gets charged at the gate. Four wheels and a hard polycarbonate shell survive the hold better, soft bags give and squash into a car; either way check the empty weight against a 23kg allowance and buy from a brand that covers wheels and handles for years rather than months. A TSA lock matters only for the US. For a week away, 40 to 45 litres of cabin case is enough if you pack light and wash a shirt.

Start with two walks a week you could hold a conversation through, 20 minutes each, and add five minutes a week rather than a new plan: after years off, the first month is about the habit and the tendons, not the heart. Add two short strength sessions (sit to stand, a push, a pull) once the walking feels easy, and expect soreness for a day or two, not for a week. If you have a heart condition, joint trouble or are over 60 and have not exercised in years, a word with a GP first is sensible.

Start earlier and in smaller pieces than feels comfortable: the changes usually begin around nine or ten, and a first period comes about two years after the breasts start to develop, so the explaining has to be done before it happens. Use the proper words, keep it to a few minutes at a time in the car or at bedtime, and cover both sexes so a boy hears about periods and a girl about wet dreams. A good book left where they will find it does half the work, and "ask me anything, including the embarrassing bits" keeps the door open.
Stay in Le Marais for the centre and cafes, Saint-Germain for the classic postcard, or Canal Saint-Martin for cheaper nights and a younger crowd.

Stir 500g strong white flour, 325ml warm water, 7g yeast and 10g salt into a soft dough, knead it 8 minutes and leave it 1 to 2 hours until doubled. Stretch it thin, and bake as hot as your oven goes, 250C, for 10 to 12 minutes. With no yeast, use a flatbread base or add a teaspoon of baking powder and rest it 20 minutes.

Sudden bad pain in one testicle is an emergency - ring 999, or get to A&E - because a twist can only be saved in the first few hours. A dull ache that came on slowly, or a small lump, is usually a cyst, a varicocele or an infection and should be looked at by a GP within a few days rather than left. Do not wait to see if it settles.

Summer is hotter because the Sun is higher in the sky and stays up longer, so the same patch of ground gets more direct sunlight and more hours of it. The Earth is actually farthest from the Sun in July, which is why distance is not the explanation.

Take the train into the centre: parking runs twenty to thirty pounds for a day, the congestion charge is on top of that, and then you are still looking for a space. Drive only if you are heading somewhere outside the centre or carrying things - and then park at a Tube or rail station on the edge and finish by train. Book the train two or three weeks ahead and it is usually cheaper than the fuel plus parking.

Ten strokes a side on a steel brings a blunt edge back for a week; a whetstone, coarse side then fine, once a month is what actually sharpens it. Hold the blade at 20 degrees, keep the fingers of your other hand behind the edge, and wash and dry it by hand: a dishwasher blunts a knife and splits a wooden handle.

That is a published rate rather than a quote: whoever runs the place sets it, it moves with the day and the season, and a cap or a longer stay usually costs less per hour. Their own page or listing has today's, so ask what the whole stretch comes to rather than the headline figure.

That is happening where I cannot see it: no papers, no bulletins, nothing that reaches me. The body's own page or a news report has the outcome; say what it says and we can work out what it means for you.

That is hunting instinct, not a health problem, and it is worst at dusk and dawn, so keep him in then and put a bell on his collar. Teach a rock-solid "leave it" with treats and swap every carcass for something better: scolding him for bringing it to you only teaches him to eat it out of sight. Clear it up in gloves.

The routine matters less than the regularity: same time, lights down, screens off, and something calm for the last half hour, like a shower, a few pages of a book or the dishes. Keep the bed for sleeping, and if you are not asleep in 20 minutes get up and read somewhere dim until you are sleepy.

The Great Depression began with the Wall Street crash in October 1929 and lasted through the 1930s, with a third of American workers out of a job at its worst. Banks failed, prices fell, and trade shrank because every country tried to save itself alone.

The American Civil War ran from 1861 to 1865, when eleven southern states left the Union rather than accept limits on slavery. The north blocked the ports with its navy, the slaves along the Mississippi were freed, and the war ended in April 1865 with about 620,000 dead.
The Moon doesn't change shape; half of it is always lit by the sun, and we see a different slice of that lit half as it orbits the Earth. A full moon takes about 29.5 days to come round again.

The Moon is the Earth's only natural satellite, about 384,000 km away, and gravity holds it in orbit. It makes no light of its own - we see sunlight reflected from its surface - and its pull is the main cause of our tides. It takes about 27 days to go round the Earth and the same time to turn once, so we always see the same side.

The UK limit is 14 units a week for men and women, spread over three or more days, and a unit is a small glass of wine or half a pint of ordinary beer - so a bottle of wine is about nine. Cutting down works better with rules than willpower: no drink on two nights a week, no drink in the house, and a smaller glass.

The cheapest new work is the client you already have: go back to everyone you worked for in the last year with one specific offer - a set number of hours a month, or the service you did not offer them last time. A past client is far more likely to say yes than a stranger. Then ask each happy client for one name and for a review in writing, and put those words where people actually look. Pick one channel and be there consistently rather than on four occasionally, and put your prices up 10% on new work before you think about hiring anyone.

The easiest is WhatsApp: open the chat with the person, tap the camera icon at the top, and they get a ringing call. For an iPhone-to-iPhone call it is FaceTime in the same place. If they use Zoom, they send you a link - tap it at the time of the call, allow the camera and microphone, and you are in.

The filling that is made fresh, in a baguette or a sub rather than sliced bread, and ask for the salad on the side if it has to travel back to a desk: wet salad in the sandwich is what makes it collapse. A hot filling - meatballs, a toastie, a chicken escalope - is the one worth ordering out, because it is the one that will not be as good made at home.

The internet is millions of computers agreeing on one way to pass messages - your request is cut into small packets, each labelled with where it is going, and routers hand them on hop by hop until they reach the server. Long fibre cables under the sea carry it between countries, and the reply usually takes well under a tenth of a second.

There is no one price for it. What it comes to turns on the size, the seller and the day, so the useful thing is two quotes for the same thing with everything included. Tell me the two figures and I will work out what each leaves you.

Three rungs, in order. Save what you can each month first, then use a 0 per cent purchase credit card only if you can clear it inside the 0 per cent window, then a personal loan - the advertised rate starts around 6 per cent and is cheapest over 7,500 pounds, and only 51 per cent of accepted applicants have to get it. For a deposit, a lifetime ISA adds 25 per cent to up to 4,000 pounds a year and must be open a year before you buy, and a 5 per cent deposit is the usual minimum. Price any car finance as a total: the monthly payment hides the interest. No payday loans.
