Treat it as a work problem with a work rule, not a feelings problem: name the two behaviours you have seen, with dates, and set what has to happen on a shift (who answers the phone, who signs off what) so the job does not need them to like each other. See them together once, then separately, because each will tell you a different story and both are partly true. Anything that is bullying, threats or a refusal to work goes down in writing and up to HR or your own manager, because the longer it drifts, the more it is your problem rather than theirs.

Twenty minutes of brisk walking, cycling or stairs most days is plenty to build a base. Add one or two short sessions where you're a bit out of breath, and you get most of the benefit of longer workouts.

Use the official rank at the airport rather than anyone who approaches you inside, and check the app price or the posted fare before you get in. Insist on the meter, or agree the total first, and keep small notes so you are not waiting for change.

Use a shared album rather than sending them one by one: on an iPhone, Photos > Albums > + > New Shared Album and invite them; on Android, Google Photos > Sharing > Shared album. Everyone can add to it and it does not fill up anybody's messages.
Water boils at 100C (212F) at sea level, and the boiling point drops as you go up: about 95C in Denver or Mexico City, and 71C on the summit of Everest, which is why tea brews badly up there.

Water is wet because it clings to surfaces and spreads across them instead of beading up: its molecules stick to each other and to most things, so a thin film stays on your skin. Wetness is that film, not a property of the water on its own.

Wet your hands, then soap for twenty seconds - about as long as singing Happy Birthday twice - and cover the backs of the hands, between the fingers, the thumbs and the fingertips under the nails. Rinse and dry on a clean towel, because wet hands pick up germs again, and use hand gel only when there is no sink.

Whatever time you'll actually stick to is the best time: morning suits consistency, evening suits people who feel stiffer early. If you go in the evening, finish at least two hours before bed so it doesn't keep you awake.

Whether a dish holds you comes down to two things, and pasta or rice with a tomato sauce has neither: there is almost no protein in it and very little fat. Add a tin of chickpeas or beans, a boiled egg, a handful of grated cheese or a thick slice of bread and the same dish keeps you full for hours instead of one. The other half is the amount: a portion of dry pasta about the size of your closed fist is right for one person, and a tin of tomatoes counts as the vegetable, not the filling. The things that fill you up for least money are beans, lentils, potatoes, eggs, oats, yoghurt and wholemeal bread, and a soup or a green salad on its own rarely lasts past two hours.

Write down what comes in each month, then what goes out in two piles: the fixed ones (rent, bills, travel, debt) and the ones you decide week by week (food, going out, clothes). What is left is what you can save or throw at a debt, and if the piles add up to more than comes in, cut from the weekly ones first because that is where the slack is. The 50/30/20 shape - half on needs, a third on wants, a fifth on saving - is a starting point, not a rule, and a notes app you check every Sunday beats a clever spreadsheet you never open.

Write down five dinners, not seven: three you can cook without thinking, one new one and one night for leftovers or something from the freezer. Then shop once from that list, plus breakfast and lunch things, and buy the fresh veg you will use in the first three days. A plan you can move a night around is the one that survives; a strict seven-day plan usually gets abandoned by Wednesday.

240g of ground coffee makes 20 mugs, each mug holding about two level tablespoons, 12g, and 60g filling a litre jug. In a cafetiere, pour water a minute off the boil, leave it three to four minutes, then press and pour it all off the grounds, because coffee left standing on them goes on brewing and turns bitter. Go stronger for espresso, weaker with milk.

AI stands for artificial intelligence, and in use it means software that finds the pattern in a lot of examples instead of being told the rule. That is why it is good at sorting photographs and writing a first draft, and why it can state a wrong fact as confidently as a right one - the answer is fluent whether or not it is true.

About 5 minutes start to finish. Blend a banana, a handful of frozen berries, 200ml milk or yoghurt and a spoon of oats for about 30 seconds, adding liquid until it pours. Frozen fruit instead of ice is what keeps it thick and cold, and a spoon of oats makes it hold you until lunch.

About 20 minutes start to finish. Warm corn or wheat tortillas in a dry pan for 20 seconds a side and keep them in a tea towel, then fill them with something already cooked and cut small - spiced mince, shredded chicken, black beans, fried fish or roast vegetables - with raw onion, coriander and a squeeze of lime. Two fillings and something sharp is a better taco than four that all taste the same.
Admission and parking prices are set locally and move with the season, so the current one is on their website or through one call, and a map listing has the number.

An acid is a substance that releases hydrogen ions when it dissolves in water: it tastes sour, turns blue litmus red, and reacts with a base to make a salt and water. Vinegar, lemon juice and stomach acid are weak acids; car battery acid is strong.

An automatic has two pedals and no clutch, so your left foot does nothing at all - keep it on the floor and use only the right foot for go and stop, or you will ride the brake without knowing. Select D and the car creeps forward when you release the brake, which is what makes it easy in traffic; P is for parking, R for reverse, and N is almost never needed. Going down a long hill, drop to a lower gear (often marked L, 2 or a manual mode) to hold your speed back instead of braking all the way.

An earthquake is the ground shaking when two slabs of the Earth's crust slip past each other and the energy built up is released as waves. The slipping happens at a fault, and the shaking is strongest near it.

Answer the letter within 28 days and name who was driving: ignoring it is the expensive path, because it is six points and up to £1,000 instead of three and £100. If you were driving, take the speed awareness course where it is offered - no points, about £100 - and pay the fixed penalty if not. The notice has to reach the registered keeper within 14 days of the offence, so if it is much later than that, say so in your reply.

Ash, oak, beech, hawthorn, hornbeam and birch are the best firewood: dense, slow burning, low in tar, and ash burns well even when it is not fully dry. Pine and other softwoods burn hot and fast and leave creosote in the flue, so they are for kindling rather than a night's burn, and never burn painted or treated timber, plywood, chipboard or driftwood - the fumes are poisonous and the salt and preservative wreck the flue.

Ask one person you already get on with to get a coffee, and say yes to the first lunch or after-work drink even when you would rather go home. Work friendships come from small repeated things - the same coffee break, the same walk at lunch, a shared job - rather than one big effort, so pick one person and be the one who suggests it again next week.

Ask three questions and answer them honestly: who walks it twice a day in the rain, who pays, and where it goes when you are away. A puppy is about £1,500 to £2,000 in the first year and around £1,000 a year after that, with 30 to 60 minutes of walking a day, training classes, insurance and a vet, and it cannot be left more than a few hours for the first months. If you rent, get the landlord's yes in writing first. If all three answers are real, it is a good idea; if one of them is a hope, wait.

Before a week away, move the pots into shade, soak everything, and stand them on trays of water; a plastic bottle with a pinhole in the lid, upside down in the compost, keeps a big pot going for days. Anything precious is worth asking a neighbour to look in.
*Only Connect* is the cleverest thing on television, *Would I Lie to You?* is the funniest panel show and *University Challenge* the most tense. Start with Would I Lie to You? for a group.

*Paths of Glory* is the one to start with: Kubrick, the WWI trenches, 88 minutes. *Went the Day Well?* (92 minutes) is a British village invasion story from 1942, and *Journey's End* (107 minutes) stays in one dugout and never shows the battle. All three fit inside two hours, and *Full Metal Jacket* is 116 if you want the training half too.
*A Short History of Nearly Everything* by Bill Bryson is the one to start with: how we know what we know, and funny throughout. *The Selfish Gene* by Richard Dawkins if it is evolution you want.

Boil them 6 minutes for a runny yolk or 9 to 10 for hard boiled, lowering them into water that is already boiling and cooling them under the tap before you peel. Frying is butter in a hot pan, 2 to 3 minutes for a runny yolk, and scrambling is low heat and slow stirring, off the heat while it is still glossy.
Botanically a banana is a fruit, and in the kitchen too: it grows from the flower and holds its seeds. A vegetable is a different part of the plant - a root, a leaf or a stem.
Brasília, not Rio, and a planned city built in four years.

Bright but out of direct midday sun is what most houseplants want: an east window, or a metre or two back from a south or west one. Move it closer to the glass if the stems are pale and stretched with gaps between the leaves, and further back if the leaves have brown scorched patches on the side facing the window. Turn the pot a quarter turn each time you water so it grows evenly, and give it a few weeks to settle - a plant moved into suddenly stronger light can scorch before it adjusts.

Build stamina with easy, longer efforts rather than all-out ones: three sessions a week of 20 to 30 minutes at a pace where you can still talk in short sentences, adding five minutes a week. Once those feel comfortable, swap one for four minutes hard, two easy, repeated three or four times.

Butter both slices right to the edges before anything else - that is the barrier that keeps the bread from going soggy - then put the wet things against the butter and the cheese, ham or egg in the middle, and cut it in half so it holds together. A good sandwich is about 1cm of filling on bread cut no thicker than that; keep it to two fillings plus something sharp, and the wet filling goes in a separate box if the sandwich is built early. Fillings that work: cheddar with apple and mustard, tuna with celery and mayo drained well, ham with cucumber and piccalilli, or a leftover roast with something pickled. For a toastie, butter the outside of both slices and press them in a hot dry pan until they are golden on both sides.
Canberra, not Sydney: it was purpose-built as the compromise between Sydney and Melbourne.

Change them every one to three months of near-daily playing, or when they look dull or rusty and go out of tune within minutes - a set is six to ten pounds. A string that keeps breaking at the same place means a sharp edge on the saddle or the nut, or a burr in the tuning peg, so run a fingernail along each and file any catch smooth. Change one at a time so the neck keeps its tension, and stretch each new string by pulling it gently away from the board before you tune it up.

Charles Dickens (1812-1870) was the Victorian novelist who wrote Oliver Twist, A Christmas Carol, David Copperfield and Bleak House. He worked in a boot-polish factory as a boy, and that memory of child labour runs through his books, which were published in monthly parts and read aloud across the country.

Check the frame for cracks and dents around the welds, spin both wheels to see if they wobble, and test the brakes and gears on a ride. Ask for the frame number and check it against a stolen-bike register before you pay; a service costs £50 to £95, so leave room in the budget.

Christopher Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492, sailing for Spain, and thought he had found a route to Asia. He never set foot in North America itself; the Vikings had reached Newfoundland about 500 years earlier.

Claim child benefit as soon as the birth is registered: one parent claims for all the children, on the HMRC app or on form CH2, and it can be backdated three months. It pays about £26 a week for the first child and about £17 for each one after. Over £60,000 adjusted net income the high-income charge takes some of it back and by £80,000 it has taken all of it, but claim anyway: that is what gives you the National Insurance credits.
Coffee is the roasted and ground seed of a fruit, brewed with hot water.

Coming into the UK you can bring 4 litres of spirits, 18 litres of wine or 42 litres of beer, 200 cigarettes, and other goods - perfume and gifts count here - up to 390 pounds, all per person. Anything above that you declare in the red channel and pay duty on. Keep the receipts, and note that the person carrying it must own it.

Compost is plant waste that has rotted down into dark crumbly stuff that smells of earth: layer green things like grass, peelings and weeds with brown things like cardboard, dead leaves and twiggy prunings, keep it as damp as a wrung-out sponge, and turn it now and then. Six months to a year and it is ready to spread on beds or dig in, and it feeds the soil rather than the plant. Bagged potting compost is a different thing - sterilised, and made light enough for roots in a pot.
Cream the butter and sugar first, fold the flour in last, and chill the dough 20 minutes so they spread less. Leave 5cm between them on the tray.

Daylight hours swing with the Earth's tilt: your half leans away from the Sun in winter, so it rises later, climbs less high and sets earlier, and the day is short. In the UK that is about 7 hours 45 minutes of daylight around 21 December, against 16 hours 45 minutes in June.
Depends what it is for. Say the thing you are doing and I will tell you what it takes - and where a rule rather than common sense decides it, who to ask.

Do them out loud, in order, then shuffled, in two-minute bursts a few times a day - short and often beats long and rare. Learn the easy ones first (2s, 5s, 10s, then the squares) so more than half the table is familiar. The hard ones are 6x7, 7x8, 8x9; make up a silly rhyme for just those.

Dreaming happens mostly in REM sleep, when the brain is nearly as active as when awake. Scientists think it helps sort memories and practise threats and feelings; there is no good evidence that dreams predict the future.

Dry the leaves properly - a tea towel or a spinner - because water is what makes a dressing slide off them, then dress with 3 parts olive oil to 1 part vinegar and a teaspoon of mustard, and salt it at the table. A bowl of leaves becomes a dish with one crunchy thing (toasted seeds, croutons, a handful of nuts) and one sharp thing (pickled onion, a squeeze of lemon, a little grated cheese), and it wants dressing a minute before it is eaten, never hours.

Eggs are the second commonest source after chicken, and the germ is salmonella, which sits on the shell and sometimes in the egg. In Britain a British Lion-marked egg is fine raw or runny, even in pregnancy, because those flocks are vaccinated; an unmarked egg, a duck egg or anything from abroad is the one to cook through. Keep eggs cold, don't wash them, and bin one that is cracked and dirty. Cramps and diarrhoea come 12 to 72 hours later and usually pass in a few days; fluid is the thing that matters.

Every hole has a par, and you count the shots you take: one under is a birdie, two under an eagle, three under an albatross, and one over is a bogey, two over a double bogey. Add up the stroke count over 18 holes and the lowest total wins; your handicap is the number subtracted from your total so players of different ability can compete.

Explain it out loud to someone who does not know it, without notes. Where you stumble or reach for jargon is exactly what you do not understand yet, so go back to that bit and try again. Ten minutes of teaching yourself in the mirror is worth an hour of rereading.

Fifteen minutes a day keeps a house, and the daily fifteen is the same three things: make the bed, wipe the kitchen surfaces and put the dishes away. Then give one room a proper clean on a weekday rota - bathroom on Monday, kitchen on Wednesday, floors on Friday - and leave the weekends for bedding and towels, which is one wash each. Fit the monthly jobs (the oven, the windows, behind the sofa) to the first weekend of the month rather than to a mood, and do a ten-minute tidy before bed so the morning starts level.

Find what starts it and block that first: a curtain over the window he watches, or the post put through a box away from the door. Then reward the quiet - a treat the moment he stops - and don't shout, because to a dog shouting sounds like you joining in. If he barks for hours when he is left, that is the being-left problem rather than the barking one.

Fine, in the amounts anyone eats by accident: the pips and kernels of apples, pears, cherries, plums, peaches and apricots hold amygdalin, which releases a little cyanide when the pip is crushed and chewed - but you would have to chew a cupful at once to be in trouble. A pip swallowed whole comes out the other end intact, so a child who ate two or three is not an emergency; watch for a sore tummy and ring 111 if you are worried. The flesh is the part to eat, and the pips are best left in the core.

Five years after the 31 January filing deadline is the rule for anything a tax return touches: keep the invoices, receipts and bank statements that long, and 6 years if you run a limited company. Keep payslips, contracts and pension letters for as long as you are in the job and a year after, keep a receipt while the guarantee or warranty still runs, and shred anything with your name, address or account number on it before it goes in the bin.
Flour, water, salt and yeast, and time: a slow rise in the fridge overnight gives more flavour than anything you can add.

For puzzles: *Portal* (short, funny, brilliant), *The Witness* if you want to be stuck properly, or *Baba Is You* for something unlike anything else. *Monument Valley* on a phone if you only have ten minutes.

For an Indian film: *Lagaan* (a village cricket match against the British, and nearly four hours) or *Dangal* (a father, two daughters and wrestling, and it is a true story). Both are in Hindi with subtitles. Say the mood and I'll narrow it down.

For a proper scare: *Get Out* is the smart one and not gory, *A Quiet Place* is jumpy from the first minute, and *Hereditary* is the genuinely unnerving one. For an old-fashioned ghost story, *The Others*.

For a small used car, budget about £2,000-£3,000 a year all in: insurance around £500, fuel £80-£120 a month, road tax from £195, and £400-£600 for MOT, servicing and tyres. Get an insurance quote before you buy the car, because that one number can decide the whole budget.
For a laugh: *Groundhog Day* on film, *Schitt's Creek* on telly, or *The Thursday Murder Club* if you would rather read. Say which and I'll pick one.
France: Paris for the museums and the food. Lyon for the best eating in the country. Provence for small towns and markets, and don't rush it.

Fresh pasta is 100g of tipo 00 flour and one large egg per person, mixed to a stiff dough, kneaded 5 minutes and rested 30 minutes under a bowl, then rolled as thin as you can and cut. It cooks in 2 to 3 minutes in salted water, not the 10 a dried pasta takes. Semolina and water with no egg is the southern way, and it wants a rolling pin or a machine.

Fresh beans ground just before you brew, and a scale: 60g of coffee per litre for filter, or 18g in a double espresso. Stale grounds or a brew too weak to taste is what makes home coffee thin next to a cafe's.

Friction is the force between two surfaces that rub together, and it slows movement and turns the lost energy into heat. It is why brakes get hot and why oil and smooth surfaces make machines last longer.

Frozen and tinned are as good as fresh, and often better: vegetables are frozen within hours of picking, so their vitamins outlast a cabbage that has sat in the fridge all week, and tinned tomatoes are better than the pale ones flown in out of season. Frozen peas, sweetcorn, spinach and berries are the best buys, and tinned beans, chickpeas and sardines are cheap protein with nothing added. The tin or the bag is not the problem - read the label: brine, syrup, oil and sauces are where the salt and sugar come from. Frozen fish is fine too, thawed overnight in the fridge and cooked from there.
Fusilli, farfalle or penne, because the nooks and the flat middles catch the dressing, and none of them clump when they are cold.

GCSE grades run from 9 down to 1: 4 is a standard pass, 5 a strong one, and 7 to 9 are the top grades. Below 4 is not a pass yet, and English and maths can be retaken at college until you are 18. Tell me the grade and the subject and I will say what it opens up.

Garlic bread and a green salad with a sharp dressing, because the salad is what cuts through the sauce. Tear the bread, rub it with garlic, oil and salt and give it 8 minutes in a hot oven while the pasta cooks.
George RR Martin wrote A Game of Thrones.
Germany: Berlin for the history and the nightlife. Munich for beer gardens and the Alps. The Rhine and Mosel valleys for small wine towns.
Good thing to take on. What's the first step from where you are?
Good for you! That's really lovely news.
Grapes do not ripen after picking, so a sour bunch stays sour. Ripe grapes are firm and come away from the bunch easily, with a dusty bloom on the skin rather than a sticky one.
Green if you want less caffeine and drink it without milk; black if you take milk or want a proper cup in the morning. Green wants water just off the boil and two minutes, or it turns bitter.
Happy to help.

Homework earns its place in small doses: about ten minutes a night in the first years of primary, half an hour by the end of it and an hour or so at secondary, and the evidence for it is weakest for the youngest children. What makes it work is the same each night - a fixed time, a clear table, and you nearby without taking over. If it is regularly taking much longer than the school's own limit, or ending in tears, that is worth one short message to the teacher rather than a battle every evening.
How long that goes on for comes from what it is, and I do not know yet. Say what it refers to and I will tell you what usually happens.

In England and Wales the owner is on the title at HM Land Registry: use its Find a property service, pay about £3, and the title register gives you the owner's name, the price last paid and the boundaries on a map, without telling them you asked. Scotland is Registers of Scotland, and Northern Ireland is Land and Property Services. If the plot is unregistered, the deeds are with the owner or held by the Land Registry, and your council can help you find out who to ask.

In the Clock app, edit the alarm and tap Sound (iPhone) or the bell icon (Android) - on an iPhone the list ends with Pick a Song, which uses anything in your library, and on Android there is usually a plus sign to add a file. Start quiet and put the phone across the room: a gentle sound you have to get up to stop wakes you better than a loud one by the bed.
In France: A bakery lunch, steak-frites in Paris and a bouchon in Lyon, with cider and cream in Normandy. The fixed-price lunch menu is where the value is.

In San Francisco: the Golden Gate on foot or by bike, the ferry building, and one neighbourhood properly rather than five badly. Layers matter: the fog rolls in and the temperature drops ten degrees by the water.
In San Francisco: Tap a Clipper card or a phone on Muni: $2.50 buys 90 minutes on the buses and the metro. BART is a separate fare for the airport, and the hills are real, so take the cable car once.
In Boston: walk the Freedom Trail, eat in the North End, and cross to Cambridge for a half-day. The T is small and easy.

In a right-angled triangle the two shorter sides squared add up to the longest side squared: a squared + b squared = c squared. Sides of 3 and 4 give 9 + 16 = 25, so the longest side is 5; to find a shorter side, take one square away from the other instead.

In maths a term is one part of an expression, separated from the others by plus or minus signs: in 3x + 4y - 7 there are three terms, 3x, 4y and -7. Terms with the same letter part are like terms and can be added together, so 2x + 3x becomes 5x.
India: Delhi for the history. Jaipur and Jodhpur for Rajasthan. Kerala for the backwaters, and one region rather than criss-crossing the country.

It is about three weeks and 21 stages, and the winner is whoever finishes with the lowest total time — not the most stage wins. The yellow jersey goes to the overall leader each day, green is the points competition for sprinters, and the polka dot is for the best climber. Most of the overall lead is built in the mountain stages and the two time trials.
Jane Austen wrote Pride and Prejudice, Sense and Sensibility, Emma, Persuasion and Mansfield Park, among others.

Jars, pouches and ready-made pots are fine, and the rules on them are the same as on anything else: no salt, no sugar, no honey before one. Read the stage on the front against what they are managing now, decant it into a bowl rather than feeding from the pouch, and throw away what the spoon has been in. Warm it by standing the bowl in hot water, never in the pouch or the jar, and check it is not hot in the middle.

Julius Caesar (100-44 BC) was the Roman general who conquered Gaul, crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC and made himself dictator for life. A group of senators stabbed him to death on 15 March 44 BC, and the republic never recovered from it.

Keep serving one small piece of veg next to something they already like, without a fight or a reward: it can take ten tries before a toddler accepts a new one. Roasting carrots or broccoli in a little oil makes them sweeter, and a dip to dunk turns it into a game. Grated or blended into what they already eat - carrot in the bolognese, courgette in a muffin, spinach in a soup - gets the veg in without a standoff.

Kinetic energy is the energy something has because it is moving, and potential energy is energy stored ready to move: a ball held up high has potential energy, and it turns into kinetic energy as it falls, faster and faster. Both are measured in joules. Kinetic is half the mass times the speed squared, so doubling the speed gives four times the energy; potential is mass times gravity times height, so twice the height is twice the energy.
Kombucha is sweet tea fermented with a culture of yeast and bacteria, which turns the sugar into acid and a little alcohol.
Late spring. Everything is green and nobody has started complaining about the heat yet.

Log in to the router - the address is usually 192.168.0.1 or 192.168.1.1 and the password is on the sticker on the back - and open the page called Connected Devices, Attached Devices or DHCP Client List, which names every device on the network. Anything you do not recognise: change the wifi password there and it drops off, then join your own things again. Your phone's wifi settings will also show your own connection's details if the router has no such page.

Low sun sends its light through far more atmosphere, which scatters the blues away and leaves the reds and oranges to reach you. Dust and cloud make it stronger, which is why the best sunsets come after a clear, dusty day.

Magnesium has only a little evidence behind it, and only if you are short of it: the glycinate or citrate sorts, not the oxide. Valerian and the herbal teas do very little in trials. The gummies are usually a low dose of melatonin or an antihistamine. What beats them is a steady wake-up time, no caffeine after early afternoon, and getting up rather than lying there.

Make up the best bed and plan one shared outing a day, so the flat is mainly for sleeping and everyone gets a reason to leave it. Agree meal times on the first evening and keep one evening for yourself; the stay goes better when nobody is guessing.

Make it too small to fail: two minutes, one press-up, one page. Tie it to something you already do at the same time each day — after you brush your teeth, before you sit down with a coffee — so the day decides instead of your mood. Do one habit at a time for a month, and mark it off on a calendar you see, because seeing the chain is what keeps it going when the first enthusiasm runs out.

Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, about 58 million km out, and it goes round once every 88 Earth days. It is not the hottest, though: Venus is, because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps the heat.

Miles and minutes depend on the roads on the day, which is why a journey planner is the one to ask - I can't measure one from here: put the two places in and it gives the distance and the time in one go.

Money against value: if the quote is more than the car is worth, or more than half of it in one go on an old car, let it go. A 'dangerous' MOT item like brakes, steering or rust near a mounting is not worth fixing on a cheap car; tyres, a clutch or a cambelt on an otherwise sound car usually are. Scrap value is only £150 to £400.

Most throws, blankets and cushion covers go in the machine on a normal 30C or 40C cycle with the rest of the load, and a cover with a zip comes off the pad first. A throw you sit under every day wants a wash every few weeks, cushion covers about once a month, and anything a pet sleeps on far more often than that.

Most adults are told every six months, but if your teeth and gums are healthy a dentist may say twelve, and the NHS guidance is that the interval should be set by your risk - so ask them to write it down. Go sooner for bleeding gums, a tooth that hurts when you bite, or a mouth ulcer that has not healed in three weeks.
Mountains: you can always find shade and a view, and the walk earns the dinner. Beaches win with small children, though — sand keeps them busy for hours.

Move the charger out of the bedroom and put a cheap alarm clock in there, so the phone sleeps in the kitchen and the argument stops being about the hour. Agree it in daylight rather than at 2am, and make it a swap you both do for a week: phones down an hour before bed, both of you. If handing it over is too big a fight, set the router to switch the Wi-Fi off at a fixed time and blame the house.

Name the thing they did and what it changed for you, then stop: "Thank you for the meal on Saturday - I came home full and happy." One detail from the evening that only you would know beats a paragraph of adjectives, and anything you are actually going to do, say when.

Nightmares usually follow stress, late food, alcohol or a heavy film before bed, so start there. If the same one keeps coming back, write it down in the day and rehearse a different ending a few times: that is the technique that works. See a GP if they are waking you most nights or coming with flashbacks.

Nikola Tesla (1856-1943) was a Serbian-American engineer who designed the alternating-current motor and supply that power grids still use, and gave his name to the unit of magnetic field. He died poor in a New York hotel, and his claims about sending power through the air were never shown to work.
No strong view on that one, honestly. What's yours?

Nothing on my side can listen or play, sorry. Say what you noticed: how loud, how often, which room. Most house sounds have two or three usual causes and the answer narrows it.
On a Switch: *Animal Crossing: New Horizons* to wind down, *Mario Kart 8 Deluxe* for people in the room, and *The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild* for a big adventure.

One mug of rice to one and a half mugs of water, lid on, 10 to 12 minutes on the lowest heat, then 10 minutes off the heat with the lid still on before you fork it through. Rinse it until the water runs clear first. Don't stir it and don't drain it - that is what makes it gluey.

One room at a time, three bags on the floor — bin, donate, keep — and the donate bags go to the car the same day or they drift back. Ten minutes a day beats a lost weekend, and start with the room you walk through most, because clearing that one is what makes the rest of the house feel possible.

Open flowers in a garden drop when their flush is over, so deadhead down to the next bud and most plants come again in a few weeks. Buds that fall before they open are a shock rather than age: dry roots are the commonest - water deeply once and mulch - then a cold night, strong wind, or greenfly and caterpillars, which you find by opening one fallen bud. Put that one thing right before you feed anything.

Ordinary clothes plus one big shape, and nothing to sew: a black hoodie with ears on a headband is a cat, a cardboard box is a robot, a dressing gown and a towel round the head is a shepherd. Hats, ears and face paint do more than the outfit, and one prop - a cardboard sword, a wooden spoon, a stack of books - tells everyone who it is meant to be.

Par is the score a good player should take on the hole. One under par is a birdie, two under an eagle, three under an albatross, and one over is a bogey - two over is a double bogey. A handicap is about your average score over par, so 18 is a shot a hole over par; single figures is a strong club player and scratch is zero.

Pay the debts that keep a roof over your head first: rent or mortgage, council tax, energy and water, because those escalate fastest. Credit cards and loans come next, smallest balance first if you need momentum or highest interest first if you want to pay least. Before anything gets out of hand, one free call to StepChange or Citizens Advice is worth more than any spreadsheet.

Pick one stretch of daytime to sleep and guard it like a night: straight home, dark room, phone off, and the same hours seven days a week, including days off, so your body clock settles. Wear sunglasses on the way home and keep the bedroom cold, and take a short nap before the shift rather than a long one after it.
Pick the one thing that would make the day easier and give it a fixed slot; everything else can move around it. What is the thing you keep not getting to?

Pick by what you will actually use it for, not by which is easiest on paper: the language of the country you visit, or of the family you are marrying into, beats any ranking. With no reason to choose, Spanish is the usual bet - about 500 million speakers, spelling that matches the sound, and a lot of cheap material - and if you already have French or Italian, the other one of the pair is the cheapest start of all. The clock is the real cost: about 600 to 750 hours of class for Spanish, French or Italian, but roughly 2,200 for Arabic, Chinese, Japanese or Korean.

A mineral is a natural solid with a definite chemical make-up and a crystal structure, formed in the earth without anything living making it: quartz, calcite and iron ore are minerals. A rock is usually a mixture of minerals.
A noun names a person, place or thing - Jess, Leeds, table, kindness. If you can put 'the' in front of it, it is a noun.

A pharmacist will answer that one properly and for nothing, without an appointment - take the packet in and they will check it against whatever else you take. Tell me what they say and I'll help you with the next bit.

A pharmacy terbinafine or clotrimazole cream clears athlete's foot in two to four weeks - keep using it a fortnight after the skin looks fine - and dry between the toes properly, wear cotton socks and change shoes a day on, a day off. Wash socks hot and don't share towels.

A planet is a large round body that orbits a star and has cleared other objects out of its own orbit. There are eight in our solar system - Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune - and Pluto is a dwarf planet because it shares its orbit with other icy bodies.

A poem leans on sound as well as meaning: rhythm, rhyme if you want it, and the line breaks doing some of the work. No rules you have to follow - the two forms with rules are the haiku (three lines, 5-7-5) and the limerick (five lines, aabba). Ask me for either and I'll write one.
A scale is the ladder of notes a key is made of, up or down: do re mi fa sol la ti do. A major scale sounds bright and a minor one darker, and both are eight notes with the first repeated at the top.

A shop cannot refuse a refund for faulty goods, whatever the sign says: under the Consumer Rights Act you can reject it for a full refund within 30 days, then claim a repair or replacement. A credit note is an offer, not a right, and how you paid is no excuse either. If they still will not, ask your card provider for a chargeback and quote their refusal.

A sole trader is the simplest thing that works: you and the business are the same person, you file a self assessment, your accounts stay private, and if it goes wrong you are personally on the hook for the debts. A limited company is a separate legal person, so your own money is mostly protected, but you file accounts at Companies House where anyone can read them, pay corporation tax on profits (19% to 25%), and take money out as a salary through payroll and as dividends, which means an accountant is worth having. It costs about £50 to set one up and a few hundred a year to run. Most people start as a sole trader and move over when profits are steady, when they take on a contract with real risk, or when they hire someone.

A sticky, gritty red eye with crusty lashes in the morning is usually conjunctivitis: bathe it with cooled boiled water and a fresh cotton wool ball for each eye, and stop wearing lenses until it is better. A stye is a blocked lash follicle - a warm compress for 10 minutes several times a day brings it to a head; never squeeze it. Pain, light sensitivity or blurred vision is a same-day GP or optician visit.

A triangle is a flat shape with three straight sides and three corners, and its three angles always add up to 180 degrees. By its sides it is equilateral (all three equal), isosceles (two equal) or scalene (all different); by its angles it is acute, right-angled or obtuse.

A trip to Mars takes about seven months each way with current rockets, because the planets are so far apart. Missions wait for a launch window about every 26 months, when Earth and Mars are lined up best.

A unit trust pools money from thousands of savers into one fund and you buy units worth the fund's holdings, so £100 buys a slice of everything in it. An index fund is the same idea run by a computer following a market, for under 0.3% a year, where an actively run trust charges about 0.75% and has to beat the market to be worth it.
A weekend is one neighbourhood walked properly, not two cities. Book the first two nights and the last night only, keep one day free in the middle, and sleep near the airport on the way home.

A PhD is three to four years of full-time original research under a supervisor, ending in a thesis of about 60,000 to 80,000 words and a spoken exam called a viva: it trains you to produce new knowledge, and it is not required for most jobs outside research. Look for a funded place first - a studentship pays fees and a stipend, and the funded ones are advertised on FindAPhD and on university pages - because self-funding a PhD is expensive for the career it buys. Write to a named supervisor with a two-page proposal and ask what they have funding for, rather than applying to a department in general.

A car is decided by the trips you actually make, not the ones you imagine: mostly short local miles with charging at home, electric; a long motorway run every month, petrol or a hybrid. Put insurance, tax and a service into the first-year budget, then only look at cars under that. The reliable boring one beats the fun one you cannot afford to fix.

A cloth, not a bottle: a microfibre cloth just damp with water, wrung out, wiped over with the screen off, then a dry corner for the streaks. No sprays straight onto a screen, because the liquid runs into the edge; no vinegar, alcohol, glass cleaner or hand sanitiser, because they take the coating off and leave the smeary patch you are trying to clean.

A dog is pregnant for about 63 days, so nine weeks, and anything from 58 to 68 is normal - the date is a window, not a day. She is usually scanned or x-rayed around 55 days to count the pups, and she will want a quiet box a week before.

A driver is the small program that lets the system talk to one piece of hardware - a printer, a graphics card, a wifi chip. Windows and macOS bring most of them already, and a device that stops working after an update, or a printer that is suddenly offline, is often the driver rather than the thing itself: look on the maker's own site rather than a download site.

A fish is a cold-blooded animal with a backbone that lives in water and breathes through gills. It has fins to swim and usually scales, and most lay eggs; a whale or a dolphin is not a fish because it breathes air and feeds its young on milk.

A full-body session three times a week beats a body-part split for the first year: five moves - a squat, a push, a pull, a hinge and a carry - three sets of eight to twelve reps, and add a little weight once twelve feels easy. Monday, Wednesday and Friday (or Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday) with a walk between, five minutes of anything that gets you breathing before the first set, and a rest day between sessions, because that is when the muscle is built. Twenty minutes counts if that is the time you have; what changes the result is turning up three times a week for two months, not the perfect plan.

A galaxy is a huge group of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity; galaxies form as clouds of gas and dark matter pull together. Our Milky Way holds 100 to 400 billion stars and is about 100,000 light years across, and there are billions of galaxies beyond it, most with a supermassive black hole at the centre.
A gas has no fixed shape or volume: its particles are far apart and move freely, so a gas spreads out to fill whatever it is in. Air and steam are gases; cooling a gas enough turns it into a liquid.

A good 15-minute tomato sauce: soften sliced garlic in olive oil, add a tin of tomatoes and a pinch of salt, and simmer it while the pasta cooks. Tear in a few basil leaves at the end and loosen it with pasta water.
A haiku, then: Cold tap in the yard, the kettle ticks itself warm, morning starts again.

A home kit is a box you can use one-handed in the dark: plasters in a few sizes, sterile gauze and tape, a crepe bandage, small scissors, tweezers, disposable gloves, a thermometer, and children's paracetamol with the dose worked out by weight. Add an ice pack, antiseptic cream and the 111 number, then check it once a year and replace anything past its date.

A jet is a fan in a tube: the fan sucks air in, the compressor squeezes it, fuel is burned in that air and the hot gas blasts out of the back. The push comes from throwing that gas backwards, and the same shaft also drives the fan that keeps feeding it - which is why a jet works best at speed and high up, where the air is thin.

Plan the driving days rather than the hours: put the stops in first, every two hours and one proper stop a day, and don't book more than six hours of driving in a day. Book the first and last night's bed before you go, check the spare tyre, the oil and the breakdown cover, and keep the overnight bag on the back seat.

Prepare four stories in situation-task-action-result shape: a week you organised, a difficult customer or colleague, something you fixed, and a time you got it wrong and changed. Then write three questions for them about the team, the first six months and what good looks like. Say the answers out loud once - saying it is different from thinking it.

Prices move week to week and shop to shop, so a number from me would be out of date the moment I said it. The shop's own page has today's price, and a comparison site shows what the others are charging this week.

Put the ask in the subject line and in the first sentence: "Invoice 2144 - payment due" tells them what it is before they open it. Then three or four sentences - what you want, the one or two facts they need, and by when - and a plain sign-off with your name. If you want an answer, say what happens next: "If I do not hear back by Friday I will call."

Put the dates on a blank timeline you draw yourself, and group them around a few anchor events you already know. Then link each new date to a story or a person rather than a bare number, and test yourself by covering the dates and filling them in. Ten dates you can place beat fifty you half-remember.

Put the food in a slow feeder bowl or scatter it across a towel so he has to work for it, split the day's food into three or four small meals, and use bigger kibble if he is on dry food. A dog that gulps also swallows air: with a deep-chested breed, take him to the vet straight away if his belly is swollen and he is retching and can't settle, because that is bloat.

Put two hours in the morning in your own calendar as a meeting and move anything that lands on top of it: the work that needs thinking has to come before the day fills up. Then make the rest smaller: accept 30 minutes rather than an hour, ask for an agenda before you accept, and leave ten minutes between meetings so one cannot run into the next.

Quarter it round the core with a knife and cut the core out of each quarter at an angle, or push an apple corer straight down over the stalk. A peeled or cut apple browns in minutes, so toss it in a little lemon juice if it has to wait.
Reducing is simmering a sauce uncovered until water boils off and it thickens and tastes stronger. Watch it at the end - the last two minutes do most of the work.

Reviews beat anything I could say about place, which I have never been to: a map app or the town's visitor site will name the ones people rate - tell me what you want from it and I'll help you choose.
Reviews beat a guess from me about places, since I have never been to any of them: a map app or the local visitor site names the ones people rate - say what matters and I'll help you narrow it down.

Roughly: flattened card and paper, glass jars and bottles, tins and cans, plastic bottles and tubs, and clean foil - rinsed, loose rather than bagged, because a bag of the right things still goes to waste. Soft plastic (carrier bags, crisp packets, film lids) is not collected at the kerbside in most places: the big supermarkets take it in a bin by the door. For anything odd, the council's A to Z page has a line for it.

Rowing is legs, then body, then arms on the drive, and arms, body, then slide on the way back. Keep the handle level and pull it to the same spot at the bottom of the ribs every stroke, and rate 20 to 22 rather than thrashing at 30. Ten minutes of steady pieces with someone filming you side-on will show the timing errors faster than any coaching cue.

Salad leaves, cherry tomatoes, chillies, herbs, radishes and dwarf beans all do well in pots. Use containers at least 30cm deep with drainage holes, and water daily in summer, because pots dry out fast.

Same answer, and it covers this — A life cycle is the stages a living thing goes through from one generation to the next: a frog goes egg, tadpole, froglet, adult, and a butterfly goes egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly.
Same answer, and it covers this — Water evaporates from the sea and land, rises and cools into clouds, falls as rain or snow, and runs back to the sea: the same water goes round and round.
Same answer, and it covers this: A dog is bored because the day is short on sniffing and chewing, not because he needs more toys.
Same answer, and it covers this: A food chain is the line of who eats whom, starting with a plant that makes its own food and ending with a predator.
Same answer, and it covers this: Try two or three taster sessions before choosing anything: the club matters far more than the sport.

Say the rule before the trouble, not while it is happening, in one sentence: 'we do not hit; if you hit, the tablet goes away'. Then give the same consequence every time, because the sameness is what does the work, and keep the telling-off to about ten seconds with the reason inside it. And don't hit - it teaches that hitting works. If the same thing blows up every day, look for the pattern first: tired, hungry, right after school, or screens.

Separate them first and deal with it when everyone is calm; refereeing who started it teaches them to argue better, not less. Then give them one job to do together, like making pudding, so the row ends in cooperation instead of a winner. A turn-taking timer on the thing they both want does more than a telling-off.

Shorter days tell trees to stop making chlorophyll, the green stuff, and as it fades the yellow and orange pigments underneath show through; some trees also make red pigments. The tree then seals off each leaf and lets it drop, so it loses less water over winter.

Sizes are not measurements, so treat the number on the label as a shop's opinion: women's UK sizes have crept up about two steps in fifty years, so a 1970s 16 is roughly today's 12, and every chain runs its own chart, which is why you can be a 20 in one shop and a 24 in the next door. Measure yourself once with a tape - bust at the fullest point, waist at the narrowest bit above the navel, hips at the widest, about 20cm below the waist - write the numbers in cm and use that shop's own size guide for that garment. Then fit the widest part of you and have the rest taken in, which is £10 to £20 at a dry cleaner's, and look at the tall, petite and curve ranges, because they are cut on those same measurements rather than on a number. A bigger size is a fact about the pattern, not about you.

Slow down before the water, not in it: at 50mph a tyre has to shift a bucketful of water a second, and above about 60mph it can start to float, which is aquaplaning. Leave double the gap you would leave dry, put the lights on so the spray behind you shows up, and brake gently and earlier - a wet road takes much longer to stop on. If the steering goes light, ease off the accelerator and hold the wheel straight until the tyres grip again; do not brake hard. A road under water deeper than the tyre's tread is worth turning round for, and wet leaves at a junction are as slick as ice.

Sourdough is a starter, not dried yeast: 100g of fed starter to 500g strong flour and about 350ml water, mixed and left 4 to 6 hours with a fold every hour until it is puffy, then shaped and proved in the fridge overnight. Bake it at 250C in a lidded pot for 20 minutes with the lid on and 20 to 25 with it off. A starter takes about a week of feeding before it will raise a loaf, so this is a plan for next weekend rather than tonight.
Spain: Barcelona for a city and a beach in one trip. Seville for the Alcázar and the tapas. Madrid for the museums, with Toledo a short train ride away.

Spend the 20 minutes on speaking aloud and short listening, not on apps that only make you tap words: 10 minutes of a course with audio, 5 of vocabulary you will actually use, 5 of repeating phrases. Twenty minutes every day beats two hours on Sunday, and in six months you will manage the basics of a trip.

Split what actually lands in your account: fixed bills and food first, then move a set amount to savings the day you're paid, and treat what's left as the spending money. The 50/30/20 rule (half needs, a third wants, a fifth saved) is a starting point, not a law; paying yourself first is the part that works.

Split ends cannot be repaired, so a 1cm trim is the only fix: then keep them tidy with conditioner on the mid-lengths and ends, a wide-tooth comb on wet hair and a towel squeezed rather than rubbed. Heat styling and a tight band in the same spot are what split them again fastest.

Start when they can pull their own trousers down and tell you they are doing a poo: pick a week at home with no long trips, put them in pants and offer the potty every 30 minutes rather than asking. Praise the sitting, not only the result, and treat accidents as part of it.

Start with the bow and the open strings: long, slow bow strokes on one string are the first month, because a straight bow and a steady sound come before any tune. Ten minutes a day, and a teacher from the first week — this is the instrument where a bad habit is hardest to undo.

Start from the invitation: the dress code, the time and the venue settle nearly all of it, because a 2pm church wedding and a 6pm hotel one want different clothes. With no code, go one step up from your smartest everyday outfit - a mid-length dress or a tailored trouser suit in a dark or jewel colour, closed shoes that cope with grass, and a layer for the evening. Borrow or hire if it is one wear; nobody remembers a guest's outfit twice, and comfort is what you will notice on the day.

Take one bed, not the garden: strim or mow the lot so you can see it, then clear a single rectangle the size of a rug, dig it over and plant something in it, and cover the rest with cardboard weighted down with compost or old bricks to kill the weeds while you work through it. Half an hour a day on one bed beats a lost weekend on all of them.

Take the pedals off and drop the saddle until both feet reach the ground, then let them push along and coast with their feet up - a child who can balance for five seconds can ride, and an adult learning does the same on a bike with the saddle low. Hold the back of the saddle, not the handlebars, when they first pedal, and let go without saying so. Twenty minutes at a time beats an afternoon, and a flat, empty car park beats a narrow pavement.

Take the wheel off, unseat one side of the tyre with two levers, pull the tube out and find the hole by pumping it up and listening or dunking it in water. Patch it or fit a new tube, then run a finger round the inside of the tyre for the thorn or glass that made the hole, or the new tube goes the same way. One that keeps going flat usually still has the sharp thing in it, or a tube pinched under a lever.

Take the fear seriously without feeding it: check the room together with the light on, leave a small lamp or the door ajar, and give a boring, calm bedtime routine at the same time each night. Nightmares are normal at four to six and usually ease; if a child is terrified most nights for weeks, mention it to the health visitor or GP.

Take a notebook, a pen, your ID and the paperwork they asked for, and dress one notch smarter than you think you need to. Your only jobs on day one are names, where the kettle and toilet are, and writing down what you are told. Asking questions is not a weakness in week one - it is the whole job.
Tea is the leaf of one plant, Camellia sinensis, brewed in hot water; how it is processed decides whether it is black, green or white.
Tell me what you liked about the last film you enjoyed: the story, the jokes, or how tense it was. Name one and I'll suggest something close.

Tent with its pegs and a mallet, a sleeping bag and a mat - a foam or inflatable one, not just the tent floor - a head torch, a stove with fuel and a lighter, and a water container. Take warm layers and a waterproof even in summer, boots you can walk in, bin bags, a small first-aid kit with blister plasters, and food in a cool box. Book the pitch ahead and check the site's rules on fires, dogs and arrival time.
That one is yours to answer. What would make it better for you - more of something, or less of something?
That depends on the thing itself and what you are doing with it. Say which and I will tell you, rather than guess at it.

That is the place's own call, and it is usually written down: their own page lists it under visiting or facilities, and somewhere you are staying puts it in the booking terms. One phone call settles it either way.
That is live, sorry - timetables and listings change by the hour. The operator's or the venue's own app has the current one, today's included, and I'll help you plan around whatever it says.
That's a good place to be. Enjoy it.

The rule that works for most people is one full rest day a week plus an easy day between hard ones: never two hard sessions back to back. Muscle is built while you recover, not while you lift. If you want to move every day, make the in-between days walks, easy swimming or stretching rather than another full session.

The same tilt the other way: your half leans towards the Sun in summer, so it rises earlier, climbs higher and sets later, and the day is long. In the UK that is about 16 hours 45 minutes of daylight around 21 June, against 7 hours 45 minutes in December.

The same hour in the same order every night: screens off 45 minutes before bed, the lights down, and three small things done the same way - teeth, tomorrow's clothes out, ten minutes of a book. Keep the bedroom cool, dark and quiet, and put the phone on charge in another room, because the check at 11pm is what stretches the hour. If you are not asleep in about twenty minutes, get up and read somewhere dim until you are sleepy rather than lying there watching the clock.

The signs to act on are: not eating for a day, hiding away, breathing fast or with the mouth open, drinking or weeing far more than usual, a sudden weight loss, a coat that stops being groomed, or a pet that stops wanting its usual walks or its run about. Animals hide illness until it is advanced, so any of those in a pet that is normally lively is a vet call rather than a wait: ring the practice and say what has changed and when. A rabbit or a guinea pig that stops eating at all is a same-day call: neither can vomit, and a gut that stops moving is an emergency in hours.

The time you eat matters far less than how much you eat over the day, so a late dinner will not make you put on weight by itself - but food within two or three hours of lying down makes heartburn and a broken night more likely, and a heavy meal late can leave you waking at 3am. If late is the only time you can eat, keep it smaller and lighter: protein and vegetables rather than a takeaway and a pudding.

The American colonies declared independence from Britain on 4 July 1776, and won it after fighting until 1783. The Declaration's argument, that governments rule by the consent of the governed, is why the date still matters.

The Renaissance was the revival of art, learning and science in Europe from roughly 1400 to 1600, starting in the rich Italian city-states. It looked back to ancient Greece and Rome and put human experience, not just religion, at the centre.

The covid and flu boosters are offered each autumn to anyone 65 or over, pregnant, in a care home, or living with a condition like asthma, diabetes or a weak immune system, plus carers and health staff; the invitation comes to you, and failing that a pharmacy or the NHS app will book it. They are yearly because protection fades, and outside those groups a pharmacy gives the flu jab for about £15 to £20.

The first law says a thing keeps still, or keeps going in a straight line at the same speed, unless a force acts on it - which is why a passenger is thrown forward when a bus brakes, and why a seatbelt is the force that stops them. The second law is the useful one: force equals mass times acceleration, F = ma, so the same push moves a light thing quickly and a heavy one slowly, and a 1,000 kg car pushed with 2,000 N accelerates at 2 m/s each second. The third law says every force has an equal force back the other way: you push the ground and it pushes you forward, a rocket throws gas down and the gas throws the rocket up.
There are five oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. The Pacific is the biggest and deepest; its Mariana Trench goes down about 11 km, deeper than Everest is tall.
There is no microphone or speaker on this end, so I can't hear it. Describe it - a thud, a rattle, a drip, a hum - and where it comes from, and we can work it out from that.

They are not the same: baking soda is pure bicarbonate and needs an acid (buttermilk, yoghurt, lemon, treacle) to make things rise, while baking powder already has the acid in it. One way is easy and the other is not: in place of a teaspoon of soda use about three teaspoons of baking powder, and put the acid the recipe counted on in some other way or the tang is lost; in place of a teaspoon of baking powder use a quarter teaspoon of bicarbonate with a teaspoon of lemon juice or vinegar, and only in something that has the acid to meet.

Three things settle it, and none of them is the model year. If what you have still holds a charge to the evening, opens apps without a wait and still gets security updates, a new phone buys you a better camera and a nicer screen rather than a faster life, so waiting a year costs you nothing. Upgrade when the battery has gone (a service is £50 to £90 on most phones), when the updates have stopped, or when the repair costs more than the handset is worth. When you do buy, take last year's model outright: it is £250 to £400 instead of £800 to £1,200 for the same phone, with three or four years of updates still to come.

I can't see it from here, sorry - only the words you type reach me. A light that blinks on a machine is nearly always a code: count the flashes and note what it does before repeating, and the manual or the maker's app names that pattern. On a router, red usually means no internet at all, so check the provider's status page first.
I can't check live times, sorry. The operator's app (or the board at the stop) is the one that knows, and tell me the time and I'll work out the rest of the day with you.
I don't know *There* well enough to call it honestly. Tell me what you liked about the last thing you enjoyed and I'll say whether it's that kind.

Turn off the two things that actually feed it. Location: Settings > Privacy & Security > Location Services on an iPhone, Settings > Location > App permissions on Android, and set each app to While Using only - the apps that do not need it, set to Never, and turn off Precise Location for shopping and social apps. Ads: on an iPhone, Settings > Privacy & Security > Tracking and turn off Allow Apps to Request to Track, which resets everything to one opt-out; on Android, Settings > Privacy > Ads > Delete advertising ID. In a browser, turn on Prevent Cross-Site Tracking in Safari or block third-party cookies in Chrome - that is how most of it follows you from site to site. The phone is not quietly listening - the ad that follows a conversation comes from your location, your searches and the people you are near.

Two or three times a week is plenty for most adults, with a wash of the face, hands, feet, under the arms and the groin every day; the rest of the skin can wait. Five to ten minutes and lukewarm is enough for a whole shower, and long hot ones strip the oils out of dry skin, so moisturise while it is still damp. Wash more often in hot weather or after sport, because sweat and smell are what need washing off.

Two things decide these: the exact wording of the rule, and your own dates. A general answer from me could be right about the rule and wrong about you. Whoever runs it - the office named on the letter, the department, or the helpline that owns the rule (GOV.UK for most of these) - is the one that will confirm your own case, and a free advice line will read it with you.

Two things decide it: how long you have, and whether you want sun or a city. With a week and a wish for sun, the Canaries, Greece or southern Spain; with a long weekend, Lisbon, Porto, Prague or Edinburgh; with children, a short flight to Menorca or the Algarve. Tell me the month and I will be more use than that.

Two hours before departure is the safe rule. The bag drop closes 45 to 60 minutes before the flight and the gate 20 to 30, so the bag drop is the real deadline, not the departure time. Add half an hour at a big airport in the early morning or on a Friday.
Ugh, that's a lot to carry. What would make today a bit easier?

Under-fives usually travel free on local buses with a paying adult, and 5 to 15 pay a child fare, often about half: the operator's own page gives the age and the price for your area. Free travel to school is a council decision and it turns on distance - usually over 2 miles for a child under 8 and over 3 miles for an 8 to 16 year old going to the nearest suitable school, or closer if the route is unsafe to walk. Ask the council's school travel team; a 16 to 18 year old in full-time education usually needs a council or operator discount card instead.

Use the neck rule: a runny nose, sneezing or a mild sore throat above the neck is fine for easy exercise; a chesty cough, fever, aching or a stomach bug below it means rest until you are properly over it. Come back at half your usual effort for the first session, and do not count a hard session as something that clears it.

Use a six-digit passcode with Face ID or the fingerprint, not a four-digit PIN: a six-digit code is a million combinations and the thumb is faster than typing anyway. Turn on auto-lock at 30 seconds, and check in Settings that your photos and messages are backed up so a lost phone is an annoyance rather than a loss.

Vegetarian and still a proper dinner: a chickpea and spinach curry with rice, a lentil and mushroom lasagne, or a tray of roasted veg with feta and couscous. One dish everyone eats beats a meat main with something made separately.

Vincent van Gogh (1853-1890) was a Dutch painter whose The Starry Night, Sunflowers and self-portraits are among the most recognised pictures in the world. He sold almost nothing in his lifetime, cut off part of his own ear in 1888, and died at 37, with his fame arriving afterwards.

Visit two or three on a normal morning rather than an open day, and judge the walk: a 15-minute walk you can do twice a day for seven years beats a better school in traffic. Ask the head how they handle a child who is behind and what the classes are like on a bad day, and ask other parents about the playground and the office staff, not just the teaching. Ofsted tells you what the inspectors saw on one day, so read the last two reports for a trend and take the catchment distance from the council, which is what actually decides who gets a place.
Washington DC, not New York.

Water coming in from outside is not a stopcock: it stops taps, not rain or a rising water table. Stay out of a cellar with sockets in it, or switch the whole supply off at the consumer unit first, and pump or wet-vac the water out rather than mopping it about. Sandbags or a flood door across the doorway help tonight, photographs help the insurer, and a drain that backs up in a storm is the water company's to clear.
Water freezes at 0C (32F). Salt lowers that, which is why roads are gritted, and pressure lowers it too, which is why ice skates glide on a thin film of water.

Weather is what the air is doing today: rain, wind, sun, temperature. Climate is the long-run pattern of that weather over years and decades, so one cold week says nothing about climate change and one hot day is not proof of it.

Weather is chaotic: a tiny error in today's readings grows over days, so a forecast a week ahead is a good guess and tomorrow's is usually close. Showers are also small enough to miss your street while soaking the next town, which is why a 30% chance of rain still means a wet walk sometimes.
Who's that, then?

Wipe the strings and the back of the neck with a dry microfibre cloth every time you put it down - the sweat and skin oil is what makes a neck sticky and kills strings. Once or twice a year, take the strings off a rosewood or ebony board, scrape the grime off with a plastic card, and put a few drops of lemon oil on it; a lacquered maple board only needs the dry cloth, and never use furniture polish on the body.

World War One began in 1914 after the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, was assassinated in Sarajevo. Alliances then pulled the great powers in: Austria attacked Serbia, Russia mobilised, and Germany declared war on Russia and France.

World War Two began in Europe on 1 September 1939, when Germany invaded Poland; Britain and France declared war two days later. Japan had already been at war with China since 1937, and the United States joined in December 1941 after Pearl Harbor.

Write one to nine as words and 10 and up as figures, except when a number starts a sentence - then spell it out: "Twenty people came." Keep it consistent within a sentence, and use figures for money, times and measurements.

Write the date, then the one thing you would tell a friend about the day - what happened, and what you thought of it - in three or four lines and without tidying it up. Keep it where you will actually open it and write at a fixed time, because the habit is the hard part; a page of plain sentences beats a blank page waiting for a good day.
Write tomorrow down tonight — three things, one of them small — and do the smallest first, before the day fills up. Where does the time usually go?

Write down every purchase for a month, or let your banking app sort it into categories. The surprises are nearly always takeaways, subscriptions and small card taps, and seeing them once is what makes cutting them easy.

Write down every job and how long it takes, including the invisible half - knowing when the bin goes out, the school forms, the appointments - because that is most of the work and nobody counts it. Then split by whole areas rather than by tasks: one of you owns the kitchen and the bins, the other owns laundry and the bathroom. Owning means noticing when it needs doing, not waiting to be asked, so agree a standard rather than a method ("the kitchen is clear by bedtime" can be checked; "do it properly" cannot). Revisit it once a month while the system beds in, and say thank you out loud when you notice something, because a split that nobody mentions still feels unfair.

Write in your own words, in short lines, and do not try to transcribe: you are making a map to come back to, not a transcript. Leave a wide margin for questions after the lesson and add them the same evening, in five minutes, while it is still fresh. Handwriting beats typing for remembering, if it is a choice.

Yes, once, and make it easy to answer: something specific and short ('Saw this and thought of you - how did the interview go?') rather than a bare 'hey'. Then put the phone down and let the answer come or not; a second message chasing the first is what actually reads as too much, and the silence is information either way.

Yes: an easy hour on a bike burns roughly 300 to 400 calories and counts as the moderate activity the 150-minutes-a-week advice means, and the bike carries your weight so it is easier on the knees than running. A commute of twenty minutes each way gets you to the weekly target on its own. Push a little harder on two rides a week if you want fitness rather than just movement, and eat normally rather than eating back every calorie the ride burned.

Yes: it builds flexibility and balance and strengthens the muscles that hold you up, and it counts as exercise, though the heart and lungs get less from it than from a brisk walk. Two or three sessions a week is where the change shows, and a weekly class plus ten minutes at home most days is the usual way people keep it up.

Yes - *MasterChef: The Professionals* is the one about the cooking itself, *The Great British Bake Off* for baking and *Saturday Kitchen* for a lazy morning, all of them long-running and easy to start anywhere.

You do not have to tell your employer until 15 weeks before the baby is due, and it is worth knowing that once you do, you are protected from being treated worse because of it. Tell your manager in a short meeting, then confirm the date in writing: your due date, when you plan to start maternity leave, and how the work will be covered. Ask for a risk assessment of your role, and remember antenatal appointments are paid time off - you do not book them as holiday.
