£350 to £550 buys a new laptop that does everything most people need - browsing, email, video calls, streaming and office work - and £700 and up is where photo editing, big spreadsheets and gaming start to need it. Below about £250 new you are buying something that is already slow, so at that price buy a refurbished ex-business machine instead: three years old, grade A, with a warranty, for a third of new.
20 minutes.

350g self-raising flour, 2 teaspoons baking powder, 85g cold butter rubbed in, then 3 tablespoons of sugar and about 150ml milk to bring it together - handle it as little as you can. Cut into rounds, brush with milk and bake at 220C (200C fan) for 12 to 15 minutes, until risen and golden.

50g of oats to 300ml of milk or water per person, with a pinch of salt, stirred over a medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes. Take it off while it still looks a little loose, because it thickens as it stands, and stir in a splash more milk if it sets.

500g strong white flour, 7g dried yeast, 10g salt and 350ml warm water, kneaded for 10 minutes until smooth and stretched. Leave it somewhere warm for an hour until doubled, knock it back, shape it into a tin, leave it 45 minutes more, then bake at 220C (200C fan) for 30 minutes - it is done when it sounds hollow underneath.

About 20 minutes per 500g plus 20 minutes at 190C (170C fan), so a 2kg bird takes roughly 1 hour 40 minutes. Check the thigh reads 74C on a thermometer and the juices run clear, then rest it for 15 minutes before carving.

Above about 25C, slow down rather than stop: expect 20 to 30 seconds a kilometre slower for every 5C over 15C, and let the pace go. Run early or late, drink to thirst before and after, take walk breaks, and wear light, loose clothes. Stop and get into shade if you go dizzy, get a headache, feel sick or stop sweating. The first hot week is the worst one, and the body adapts in about ten days.

Affect is usually the verb and effect the noun: the rain affected the game, the rain had an effect on the game. The exception worth knowing is that you can "effect a change", meaning to bring it about.
Africa has 54 countries, or 55 if you count Western Sahara, which is disputed. Nigeria is the most populous and Algeria the largest by area.

Aim for two real conversations rather than working the room: ask what they are working on and what brought them there, then listen. Have one sentence ready about yourself and follow up with a two-line message the next day. People forget the pitch and remember who was easy to talk to.

'Do you speak english' in Spanish is ¿Habla inglés? — say it roughly "AB-la een-GLES". Learn it out loud a few times rather than reading it, and people will understand you even if the pronunciation is not perfect.

Aldi and Lidl are the cheapest of the big names for own-brand staples, around a fifth less than Tesco or Sainsbury's. Asda is usually the cheapest of the big four, Morrisons, Tesco and Sainsbury's come next and price-match Aldi on the basics, and Waitrose and M&S are the dearest. A convenience shop - the Co-op, a corner shop - costs more again, so it is for a top-up, not the weekly shop.

Algebra is arithmetic with letters standing in for numbers, so a rule works for every number at once: if a notebook costs n pounds, three cost 3n. The letters are called variables, and the usual job is to rearrange an equation until the letter is alone.
All good here. What's keeping you busy?

Almost always it is a website allowed to send notifications, or Chrome's own pop-ups: in the browser settings turn off Pop-ups and redirects, and in Site settings > Notifications remove the sites you do not recognise. Clearing browsing data once also stops the older kind. Nothing is being hacked, and you do not need any app that claims to clean it.
An African elephant is the biggest land animal: a big bull is about 3 metres at the shoulder and 6 tonnes, and a newborn calf is around 100 kg.
An adult butterfly usually lives only a few weeks, though a butterfly that overwinters as an adult can live many months.

An angioplasty is the same tube as an angiogram, with a tiny balloon on the end that is blown up to squash the narrowed artery open, and usually a mesh stent left in to hold it there. It takes 30 to 60 minutes, you are awake with numbing at the wrist or groin, and you are usually in for the day or one night. The stent is permanent and grows a layer of the artery's own lining over itself, so it is not something that needs changing.

An angle is the amount of turn between two lines that meet at a point, measured in degrees: a quarter turn is 90 degrees, a half turn 180 and a full turn 360. A right angle is exactly 90, an acute angle is less than that and an obtuse one is between 90 and 180.

An app is a program built for a phone or tablet, installed from the store that came with the device - the App Store on an iPhone, the Play Store on Android. It runs on the phone itself and keeps its own data, so an app and the website of the same name can hold different things, and deleting the app usually takes its data with it.

An asteroid about 10 km wide hit what is now Mexico 66 million years ago. The dust it threw up blocked the sun for years, plants and the animals that ate them collapsed, and the dinosaurs that could not fly died out; birds, which are their descendants, survived.

An electric car is worth it if you can charge at home and do under about 200 miles a week: home charging is roughly 3p a mile against 15p for petrol, and there is almost no servicing. Skip it if you cannot charge at home, or if you regularly do long motorway runs, where public charging costs nearly as much as fuel.

An engineer's day depends which engineer: a design engineer works in CAD and calculations, a site engineer sets out and checks work against drawings, and a maintenance engineer is called when a machine stops. All of them are solving a problem with a constraint, and the paperwork is the record that the thing is safe.

An enzyme is a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction in a living thing without being used up itself: amylase in saliva starts breaking down starch, and lactase splits milk sugar. Each enzyme fits only the substance it acts on, like a key in a lock.

An espresso is about 18g of finely ground coffee to a double shot of 60ml in 25-30 seconds. Grind fine, tamp level and firm, and if it runs much faster the grind is too coarse, if it dribbles the grind is too fine. Whole milk froths most easily and skimmed the least. With no steamer, heat the milk in a pan to just before it simmers and whisk hard for 20 seconds, or shake it in a lidded jar and give it 30 seconds in the microwave.

Answer three things in that order and keep it to a page: how you know them and for how long, one or two things they actually did with what came of it, and whether you would employ them again. Name the job they are going for and speak to that, give dates and job titles you would stand behind if the employer rang to check them, and say nothing you could not defend to the person's face. Warm but specific beats warm and vague.
Anything with a bit of swing to it. Loud is fine, clever is optional.

Apply on UCAS: one form, up to five courses, the personal statement and a reference, with 15 October for Oxford, Cambridge, medicine and veterinary science and mid-January for everything else. The statement is the part people worry about, and the rule is to start with the subject, not your childhood: what you have read, built or done that made you want it, then what you want to learn next. Two drafts and one reader who knows the subject beats five drafts alone.
Argentina have won the men's World Cup three times: 1978, 1986 and 2022.

Around 180C for most frying, 170C for chips so they cook through before they colour; with no thermometer a cube of day-old bread turns golden in about 30 seconds. Heat the oil with nothing in it and fry in small batches so it does not drop. Stay under the fat's smoke point: butter, or clarified butter about 150C; a plain or light olive oil about 200 to 240C; rapeseed, sunflower or vegetable oil about 220 to 230C.

Ask the vet for a nurse appointment and wait in the car until it's your turn, then feed him treats in the waiting room without letting other dogs crowd him. Ask them to crouch down and examine him on the floor, and go in for a free weigh-in every few weeks so most visits are boring: a dog who has been in four times for nothing is a much easier patient.

Ask them to show you the first step they'd try, then work one example together and let them do the next alone: that's the bit that teaches. If they're stuck on why, not how, draw it; almost every school maths idea has a picture (a bar for fractions, a graph for equations).

Ask two people who have had work done for a name, then check the trade body register before you call: Gas Safe for anything on gas, NICEIC or NAPIT for electrics, and the Federation of Master Builders for a bigger job. Get three written quotes that name a price, a start date and what is included, ask for the public liability insurance certificate, and pay a small deposit on a card rather than cash up front.

Ask what exactly feels scary, because 'school' usually means one thing: the bus, a particular lesson, or being picked for teams. Fix that one thing together (a practice bus ride, a word with the teacher, a friend to walk in with), and keep the mornings calm and predictable while it settles.

Ask your GP to refer you, and in England you can also send yourself to an NHS talking therapies service online without seeing a GP first. Say what you want help with and ask for it by name - CBT for anxiety or low mood, counselling, or a specific service - because a named referral gets a date and a vague one sits on a list, and ask how long the wait is and what you can do meanwhile. Private therapy runs about £40 to £70 a session: check the therapist is on the BACP, UKCP or BABCP register, and ask about a lower-cost first session or a trainee rate. If money is the block, ask a charity or a university training clinic about low-cost counselling.
Ask away, I'm listening. What's going on?

Ask before the deadline, say how much more time you need and what you'll deliver: "I'm not going to do this justice by Friday. Could I have until Tuesday? I'd then send the finished draft rather than a thin one." A specific new date does the work — no long explanation of why you're behind.

Ask for it in writing and do not sign the same day. Read the four clauses that cost people money: what you have to deliver and by when, how and when you get paid and what happens if they pay late, notice and termination, and who is liable for what. Mark up the ones you want changed, send the document back with your changes and a short note saying why, and get anything promised on the phone written in - an email saying they will cover it is worth more than a friendly call. For a lease, an employment contract or anything over a few thousand pounds, have someone who does this read it; a union checks an employment contract free, and Citizens Advice will look at most others.

Ask how long they've owned it and why they're selling, then check the MOT history online for gaps and advisories before you look at the paint. On the drive, listen for knocks over bumps and make sure every gear and switch works; pay for an inspection on anything over a couple of thousand, and never send a deposit before you've seen the car and the V5 in their name.

Ask in person after class with one specific thing ("I get the formula but I can't do the last question on the sheet"), and say what you've already tried. Teachers help far more often than students expect, and an email the same day saying thank you makes them remember you next time.
Back to it: Test it outside the app first: press Windows key + R on Windows, or open Spotlight with Cmd + Space on a Mac.

Bare-root trees and shrubs go in from November to March while they are dormant, and potted ones any time the ground is not frozen or waterlogged. Dig a square hole twice the width of the roots, keep the soil mark on the stem at the same level, firm it in well and water it through its first summer. Autumn planting beats spring: the roots work all winter.

Be specific about what you need and when, and agree the basics up front: bedtimes, treats and what to do if the child is ill. Grandparents usually want to help and hate guessing, so a short 'could you do Tuesdays, and we do baths' beats hinting.

Beat 2 or 3 eggs with a pinch of salt, melt a knob of butter in a pan over a low heat, pour them in and stir slowly with a spatula, pushing the set egg in from the edges. Take them off while they still look a little wet, after 2 or 3 minutes, and stir in a little more butter off the heat.

Beat 100g soft butter with 200g icing sugar, a spoonful at a time, then a splash of milk or vanilla until it is light and spreadable. That covers the top and middle of a 20cm cake; for chocolate, beat in 50g cooled melted dark chocolate.

Before paint you need filler for the holes, fine sandpaper, masking tape, a dust sheet, a roller and tray, a brush for edges and an old screwdriver to open the tin. One litre of emulsion covers about 12 square metres, so measure the walls and buy two coats' worth.
Berlin, since reunification in 1990.
*Codenames* (2 minutes to learn, works with any group), *Ticket to Ride* (simple, satisfying trains) and *Sushi Go!* (fast, small, cheap) are the three to start with. All are done in under an hour.

*Discovery* by Daft Punk for tunes, *Selected Ambient Works 85-92* by Aphex Twin for the quiet end, and The Chemical Brothers' *Dig Your Own Hole* for the big-beat one. Dance music is built to be heard whole, so let an album run.

*Dobble*, *UNO* and *Snakes and Ladders* work for a range of ages, and *Catan Junior* if they are ready for a proper board game. For a rainy afternoon, a treasure hunt round the house costs nothing and takes the longest.
*Educated* by Tara Westover, *Into the Wild* by Jon Krakauer or *The Diary of a Young Girl* by Anne Frank: all real, all hard to stop reading.

*Kind of Blue* by Miles Davis is the one to start with: quiet, unhurried, and every tune is a simple theme with the solos built on it. Then *Blue Train* by John Coltrane for something with more muscle, and *Ella and Louis* if you would rather hear a voice first. Play one album right through twice before you decide - jazz gives up its tune on the second listen.

*Live at Folsom Prison* by Johnny Cash is the doorway: no polish, all story. Then Dolly Parton's *Jolene* for the songwriting, and Chris Stapleton's *Traveller* if you want the modern, soul-tinged end of it. Country is story-first, so listen to the words before the twang.

*Saga* by Brian K. Vaughan is the usual first pick for an adult: a space story with a family at its centre and art that carries the plot. *Watchmen* if you want the one that changed what comics could do, *Persepolis* by Marjane Satrapi for a memoir told this way, and *Heartstopper* by Alice Oseman for a warm school romance. For manga, *Death Note* or *One Piece* is where most people start. Begin with a complete story rather than a forty-year superhero run, and a library will lend all of these.

*Think* by Simon Blackburn is written for someone who has never read any: a chapter a question, no jargon. *Sophie's World* by Jostein Gaarder tells the whole history of it as a novel if you want the story instead.
Bitter and acidic at once, with the roast on top: darker roasts taste of chocolate and toast, lighter ones of fruit and citrus, and the bitterness is the part that survives milk and sugar.

Bitter coffee is over-extracted: grind it coarser, let the water come off the boil for half a minute, and take it off the grounds sooner - about 4 minutes in a cafetiere, 25 to 30 seconds for an espresso. Sour is the same dial the other way and wants a finer grind, hotter water and a little longer. Stale beans and a dirty machine make both, and instant tastes bitter when it is made with boiling water - let the kettle rest first.

Blot up what you can with kitchen paper, then rinse the mark from the back of the fabric in cool water - pushing it out rather than through the cloth - and work in a drop of washing-up liquid or a little biological detergent. Leave it fifteen minutes, wash at the hottest the care label allows, and air-dry it: a mark that has been through a dryer is much harder to shift, so check it before it goes in.

Blot it with kitchen paper, then rinse it from the back in cold water before any soap touches it, and rub a little washing-up liquid in with your fingers. Wash it as hot as the label allows with a scoop of oxygen bleach: for whites that is the hottest wash it takes, for colours a 40C one. Do not tumble dry it until the mark has gone, because heat sets it for good.

Boil them in salted water: 10 to 12 minutes for small new potatoes, 15 to 20 for chunks, 20 to 25 for whole medium ones. A knife should slide in with no resistance at all, and drain them the moment it does, or they go watery. If they keep going mushy, it is usually the potato rather than the pan: floury ones (Maris Piper, King Edward, Desiree) break up in water and are for mashing and roasting, so boil the waxy ones (Charlotte, Nicola, any new potato) and keep the water at a gentle simmer rather than a rolling boil, and do not stir them.

Book the leg around their nap, feed or give a dummy at take-off and landing so their ears clear, and take a sling for the airport and a change of clothes in your hand luggage. Most airlines fly a baby from about two weeks old, on your lap or in a booked bassinet seat, and a pushchair goes free in the hold. In the car they need their own car seat, rear-facing until they are 15 months, and a stop every couple of hours.

Book boarding early, ask your vet for a recommendation, and visit before you book: clean, calm and willing to show you the runs tells you more than any website. A pet sitter at home suits cats far better than a cattery.

Book close to the middle of town and a street or two back from the main road: the station, the food and the evening are then walkable, and the rooms just off the front are quieter and cheaper. At the seaside that means a street back from the front rather than the front itself. Look at the map for a bar or a through road under the window, check the last bus or train if you will be out late, and book somewhere with free cancellation so you can move if the area is not what you hoped.
Boredom is a good excuse for a walk with a podcast — twenty minutes usually resets it.
Botanically an avocado is a fruit that grows from the flower and holds its seeds. Cooks call it a vegetable because it is savoury and goes in mains, but that is a kitchen word, not a plant one.
Botanically a tomato is a fruit that grows from the flower and holds its seeds. Cooks call it a vegetable because it is savoury and goes in mains, but that is a kitchen word, not a plant one.
Both: Australia is the smallest continent and the only country that is a whole continent. It is also the sixth largest country by area, and the only one that is both a country and a continent.

Both are about 100 calories a tablespoon, so the difference is small. Butter is saturated fat; the olive- and rapeseed-oil spreads are the healthier swap if you use a lot of it, and the ones with added plant sterols do lower cholesterol a little. If you use a scraping on toast, use whichever you like more.
Bramley for a crumble or a pie: it is sharp and collapses where an eater stays in lumps. One eater (Cox or Braeburn) to two Bramleys if you like a bit of bite left.
Brazil: Rio for the beaches and the views. The Pantanal for wildlife. Salvador for music and the old town.

Breakfast is not magic, and skipping it does not make you fat or thin on its own: what matters is the total day. If you are hungry in the morning, eat something with protein and fibre - eggs, porridge, yoghurt and fruit - because it makes the mid-morning biscuit much less likely. If you are genuinely not hungry, waiting until lunch is fine.

Brisket is a long cook, not a quick one: in the oven at 150C (130C fan), covered, for 3 to 4 hours, or about 1 hour per 500g, with a splash of stock in the tin, until a fork slides in with no pull. Season it heavily the night before if you can. It slices better after 20 minutes resting, and it is the one cut that is better the next day.

Brisket is low and slow: 110 to 120C at the lid, a couple of chunks of oak or hickory, and about 1.5 hours per kg - a 4kg joint is 9 to 11 hours - until it probes 93 to 95C inside. Wrap it in foil or butcher paper once the bark is dark and set, and rest it an hour before slicing.

Brown bananas are perfect for banana bread: mash 3 of them with 100g melted butter, 150g sugar, 2 eggs and 200g self-raising flour, and bake at 180C (160C fan) for about an hour. It keeps 4 days in a tin and freezes well.

Buoyancy is the upward push a liquid or gas gives anything in it, equal to the weight of the fluid it pushes aside. A steel ship floats because the air inside makes it push aside more water than the ship itself weighs, while a solid lump of steel cannot.

Buttercream or ganache keeps 3 to 4 days in a sealed tub in the fridge, or 2 months in the freezer: bring it back to room temperature and beat it again before you use it. The cake is better filled on the day.

Buy one and a half to twice the window width in fabric, or the curtains hang flat and let light round the edges, and measure the drop from the pole or track to where you want them to end - just below the sill, or to the floor for a longer look. A lined curtain keeps heat in and light out far better than an unlined one, and a thermal lining is worth it in a bedroom. Eyelet headings slide easily on a pole, pencil pleat gives a fuller look on a track; for anything over 2m wide, two panels rather than one.

Buy to the list the school sends, not to the supermarket display, and buy two of the things that get worn out: two jumpers with the badge, two or three polo shirts, two pairs of trousers or skirts, a PE kit in the school colours and plimsolls for indoors. A child starting in reception also needs a spare set of clothes in a bag for the first weeks and wellies if they play outside. Shoes with a closed toe, and Velcro if they cannot do laces yet. Name labels on everything, including the coat and the water bottle. Most schools sell good second-hand uniform and it is fine to ask, and two of each is enough for the first term because children grow out of the second set before they wear out the first.

Buy very little in advance: a car seat, a cot or Moses basket with a firm new mattress, a pram, six babygros in two sizes, nappies and whatever you're feeding with. Put the cot in your room, empty, with no bumpers or pillows, and pack the hospital bag at 36 weeks with snacks and a long phone charger — everyone forgets the charger.

Buy a used acoustic from a shop that sets it up for you, 80 to 150 pounds: a 30 pound supermarket one sits too high off the neck, hurts your fingers and is why people stop after a fortnight. Practise fifteen minutes a day, not an hour once a week, and learn G, C, D and Em, which is most of the songs you already like. An app is fine for a month; six lessons after that fix your hands before the habits set.

Buying at a distance gives you 14 days from the day it arrives to change your mind, for any reason and without giving one: tell them in writing, send it back within 14 days of that, and the refund comes within 14 days of the goods or your proof of posting, including the standard delivery cost. You pay the return postage unless their terms say otherwise, and personalised, perishable or opened hygiene items are the exceptions.

By law you need third-party cover, which pays for other people's injury and damage but not for your own car. Comprehensive usually costs only a little more over a year, so for anything but a very cheap car it is the better buy. Breakdown cover is separate, and declare any modification, because an undeclared one can void the policy.

Capitalise the first word of a sentence, names of people, places, days and months, and titles before a name: Nadia, Cardiff, Tuesday, Doctor Reid. Don't capitalise seasons, job titles on their own, or words in the middle of a sentence just because they feel important.

Carer's Allowance is for someone giving 35 hours a week or more of care to the same person: about £83 a week, and you can earn up to about £204 a week after tax and still get it (both figures move every April, so check this year's on gov.uk). The person you care for has to be getting a disability benefit - Attendance Allowance, the daily living part of PIP, or DLA middle or higher rate - their savings and income are not part of the test. Claim it even if you are unsure, since it also gives you National Insurance credits; over State Pension age the same care is paid through Pension Credit instead. On Universal Credit, tell them you are a carer as well - the carer element is separate.

Change one thing you do on autopilot - a different walk, a new lunch, saying yes to the first invitation - because a rut is a loop of the same cues. Put one thing in the diary this week that you are looking forward to: the lift comes from having something ahead more than from willpower.

Charity shops take toys only if they are complete and clean, so a nursery, a sure start centre or a refuge will take what a shop will not, and a free-ad site clears a box of lego in a day. Wash what you have and put the pieces back in their boxes first. A car seat or a cot is the exception: charity shops cannot take them, so it goes to the tip unless a friend wants it, and broken plastic is general waste.

Cheap weeks come from the same eight things: rice, pasta, tins of tomatoes, chickpeas or lentils, onions, carrots, frozen veg and eggs. Pick four dinners you already cook from those and put them on the fridge: a big chilli or bolognese stretched with lentils so it eats twice, a tray of roast vegetables with the rest in a pasta bake, a lentil dhal, and beans on toast. That is about 20 pounds a head for the week, and nothing in it goes off.

Check the airline's own allowance on your booking: a cabin bag is usually around 55 x 40 x 20 cm and 7 to 10 kg, and a checked bag around 20 to 23 kg. Weigh the bag at home, because excess weight at the airport is expensive and adding a bag online beforehand is much cheaper. On a connecting flight the strictest airline's limit applies.
Check they're breathing, put them on their side in the recovery position, and call 999 or 911; if they're not breathing, start CPR.

Chicken is cooked when the thickest part reaches 75C on a digital thermometer, pushed into the thigh without touching bone; 74C held for a minute is the same thing. The juices run clear and no pink is left. A whole bird at 190C (170C fan) takes 20 minutes per 500g plus 20.
China: Beijing for the Wall and the Forbidden City. Xi'an for the terracotta army. Shanghai for a city you can walk.

Churn double cream past whipped cream and it splits into butter and buttermilk: 300ml of double cream at room temperature, beaten in a food processor or shaken in a jar for 10 minutes, first goes thick, then grainy, then sloshes. Pour the buttermilk off, rinse the butter in ice-cold water and squeeze it dry with the back of a spoon, work in salt to taste, and it keeps 2 weeks in the fridge. The buttermilk is for scones or pancakes.

Chutney is fruit or veg with half its weight of sugar and enough vinegar to cover, simmered down until a spoon drawn across the pan leaves a trail - an hour or two - then potted in hot jars and left 3 to 4 weeks to mellow. The vinegar is what keeps it, so do not skimp on it.
Citizens Advice answers tenant questions free, and a call beats searching — that's the quickest route to a straight answer.
Citizens Advice answers tenant questions free, and a call beats searching. Tell me what they say and I'll help you weigh it up.

Clearing is how you get a place when you have no offer or your grades missed: from July to October, search the official UCAS Clearing service for courses with vacancies, then ring the university yourself with your UCAS personal ID, your grades and the course code - an offer made on that call is a real offer. Have the list and your grades in front of you, ring three or four in one morning, and add the one you want in UCAS Track before you relax. If you already have a place and want a better one, that is adjustment, which is the same search with a deadline of five days.
Clothes come down to the weather and how long you are standing about: a layer you can take off, and shoes you can spend the day in. Is it indoors or out?

Coeliac disease is an immune reaction to gluten that damages the lining of the gut - not an allergy, and it does not go away; the treatment is a strict gluten-free diet for life, and the gut heals over a few months of it. Strict, and that means being careful about the crumbs in a shared kitchen: a separate toaster, no knife going back in the butter or the jam, no chips from a fryer that has fried battered fish, oats only when the packet says gluten free, and a check on stock cubes, gravy, soy sauce and sausages. There is no cheat day: a little gluten keeps the gut inflamed even when you feel nothing, and the damage builds up quietly. Eating out works if you say coeliac when you book and ask what else goes in the fryer - restaurants that cook from scratch are easier than ones that assemble, and a takeaway with no answer is not worth it. Ask the GP for a dietitian once, and the pharmacist whether a tablet is safe. If it is a suspicion rather than a diagnosis, have the blood test before you cut gluten from your diet, because it only works while gluten is still in it.

Coffee that tastes wrong is nearly always the brew, not the bean: water just off the boil (about 90 to 95C rather than boiling), a slightly coarser grind and less time in the water, so 3 to 4 minutes in a cafetiere or 25 to 30 seconds for espresso. Bitter means too hot, too fine or too long; sour or thin means the other way, with a finer grind and a little longer. A tiny pinch of salt in the cup takes the edge off a bitter pot.

Cold first: a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a tea towel, ten minutes on and ten off, for the first day or two, then leave it alone. Keep your head up on two pillows at night so it drains, take paracetamol if you need it, and don't blow your nose for a few days - that pushes air into the lids. The colour fades over about two weeks. Get it looked at the same day if your sight changes or goes double, the eye itself is red or bloody, the pain is severe, or the blow was to the head and you have vomited or feel drowsy.

Come back at about half of what you used to do: run-walk to start, one minute of easy jogging to two of walking, twenty minutes, three times a week, and add a minute of running a week for six weeks before you think about pace. Keep every run slow enough to talk, take a day off between them, and expect the first fortnight to feel harder than the numbers say. Sort the shoes first if yours have been in a cupboard for years - worn-out cushioning is what makes a comeback hurt.

Compare the price per kilo or per 100g on the shelf label rather than the pack price: bigger packs are usually cheaper per unit, but not always, and only if you'll finish them. Food you throw away is the most expensive food in the kitchen.

Condensation is a gas turning back into a liquid when it cools. Warm air holds water vapour, and when it meets a cold surface the vapour loses heat and forms droplets - that is the mist on a bathroom mirror, the water on a cold glass, and the clouds in the sky.

Contact the seller first rather than the courier: the contract is with the shop, and it has to refund or replace a parcel that never arrived, even if the tracking says it was delivered. Check the photo, the safe place, the bins and the neighbours first, keep the tracking page, and ask in writing for a replacement or refund within 14 days. If they stall, charge it back on the card.

Cook the fruit with just enough water to stop it catching - apples and blackberries 20 minutes, redcurrants 10, mint as a strong vinegar infusion - then strain it through a muslin or a clean tea towel hung over a bowl and leave it overnight: squeeze it and the jelly goes cloudy. For every 600ml of juice weigh out 450g of sugar, warm them together until the sugar has gone, then boil hard to 104C (or until a drop on a cold plate wrinkles) and pot it hot. It sets in a day.

Cooked food keeps 3 to 4 days in the fridge, raw meat and fish 1 to 2 days, and milk, cheese and yogurt until the date on the pack, or a couple of days past it if they look and smell right. Cooked rice is the exception at 1 day, and anything left out for more than 2 hours goes in the bin: the bugs that make you ill have no smell.
Cooked leftovers keep 3 to 4 days in the fridge if they went in within 2 hours of cooking. Reheat them until piping hot all the way through, once only, and bin anything you're unsure about.

Cotton breathes, takes up water and gets softer with washing; polyester does not absorb water, so it dries fast and wicks sweat, but it holds body oils and smell, which is why a cheap polyester top pongs after one wear. A blend is the compromise most clothes are: 60/40 polycotton creases less and dries faster than pure cotton, and 5% elastane in a cotton shirt is what stops it losing its shape. For sheets and summer shirts, cotton; for sportswear and rain jackets, polyester.

Cut the crown off and score the skin down the ridges, then pull it apart over a big bowl of water: the seeds sink, the white pith floats, and nothing sprays your shirt. For a whole one in a hurry, hold a half cut-side down over a bowl and whack the back with a wooden spoon and the seeds drop out in a minute.

Cut the liquid sugar first, because it is the easiest to lose and the least filling: fizzy drinks, juice and squash swapped for water, sparkling water or tea. Then make the sweet thing a planned part of the day - a biscuit with the afternoon cup - instead of a thing you graze on, since grazing is what keeps the craving going. Protein and fibre at breakfast (eggs, porridge, yoghurt with nuts) takes the edge off the four o'clock search, and half a teaspoon less in the tea for a fortnight gets your taste down without noticing.

Cut vegetables into similar-sized pieces, toss them with oil and salt and roast at 200C (180C fan) for 30 to 40 minutes, turning once. Give them space on the tray; a crowded tray steams instead of roasting.

Cut dry hair, so you can see where it actually falls, and take less off than you think: small snips across the width, not one line, because hair springs up once it dries. For a fringe, comb a thin section down flat, hold it between two fingers and cut just under them, checking both sides sit level with the eyebrow. For length, part it down the middle, bring both sides forward under the chin and cut them together so they match. Sharp hairdressing scissors, about fifteen pounds, give a far cleaner line than kitchen ones.

Daniel Craig played James Bond in five films, Casino Royale (2006) to No Time to Die (2021). The next Bond has not been announced. Before Craig: Pierce Brosnan, Timothy Dalton, Roger Moore, George Lazenby and Sean Connery.

Density is how much mass is packed into a volume: a block of iron and a block of foam the same size have very different densities. Water has a density of about 1 kg per litre, which is why things less dense than water float.

Depression is low mood most of the day, most days, for two weeks or more, with the pleasure gone out of things you normally enjoy. At that point see a GP rather than wait it out: talking therapy is the first treatment and it works, and you can refer yourself for NHS talking therapy without going through a GP. Meanwhile daylight soon after waking, a twenty-minute walk and the same wake-up time every day help, and so does one person who knows how it is.

Digestion is how the body breaks food into pieces small enough to absorb: chewing and stomach acid start it, enzymes in the small intestine split carbohydrates into sugars, proteins into amino acids and fats into fatty acids, and the nutrients pass through the gut wall into the blood. The whole trip usually takes six to eight hours, and fibre and water keep it moving.

Do it yourself on the cosmetic jobs - painting, tiling a splashback, hanging a door, laying a floor - and pay a trade for anything on gas, the consumer unit or a new circuit, anything structural (a wall out, a lintel, a new opening), and full bathroom or kitchen plumbing, because those need a certificate, building control or both, and your buildings insurance will ask who did the work. Most trades charge £150 to £250 a day, so get three written quotes that name a price, a start date and what is included. The test is what a mistake costs: a repaint is a weekend, a leak through a ceiling or an unsigned gas job is not.

Dreams like that are usually the brain sorting the day out, and they come on strongest in a week with something on your mind. Writing it down in the morning is the usual trick for one that keeps coming back.

Ducks want a house to sleep in and water deep enough to dip a whole beak, so a tub they can climb out of does a pond's job. Layers' pellets and grit, bedding changed often because they are far messier than hens, and the same shutting in at dusk.

Dust it, then work a hard wax polish or a beeswax-and-oil mix into the grain with a soft cloth, along the grain, and buff it off after ten minutes. Little and often beats a thick coat, which goes sticky and picks up dust.

ETF stands for exchange-traded fund: a basket of shares that is bought and sold like a single share, so one purchase spreads the money over hundreds of companies. The charge is usually a fraction of a percent a year, and over decades that costs less than picking shares yourself - which is the whole argument for it.

Earache in an adult is usually a cold or a sore throat spreading to the middle ear, and it settles in a few days: paracetamol or ibuprofen at the dose on the pack, a warm flannel over it, and don't poke anything in. See a GP if it lasts more than three days, if there is discharge from the ear, or if you also have a high temperature or swelling behind the ear.
Early autumn: warm enough to sit outside, dark early enough to stay in, and no pressure to be doing something.

Either, and it does not matter much: a couple of minutes on a tight spot before you train loosens it enough to move better, and afterwards it feels good without doing much for soreness. What works is slow passes over the muscle, 30 to 60 seconds a spot, breathing out and stopping at a 6 or 7 out of 10 rather than gritting your teeth. It will not fix a tight muscle on its own - strength work and a bit of stretching do that - so treat it as the warm-up, not the cure.

Energy is the ability to make something happen - to move, heat, light or power something - and it is never used up, only changed from one form into another. Food stores chemical energy, a moving bike has kinetic energy, and a hot cup has thermal energy.

Evaporation is a liquid turning into a gas at its surface, without needing to reach boiling point. Water left in a glass disappears over days because the fastest molecules escape into the air; warmth, wind and a larger surface make it happen faster, which is why washing dries on a line.

Evening snacking is usually a habit loop rather than hunger: it starts with being tired, bored or in front of a screen, and it is the cue you have to change. Brush your teeth straight after dinner, keep food out of the living room, and make dinner big enough and with enough protein and fibre that you are not catching up at ten. If you know you will want something, plan it - a yoghurt or a bowl of cereal at nine, eaten sitting down, beats an unplanned raid at eleven.

Every claim that is not yours needs the author, the year and the page, and every source you used goes in the list at the end: author, year, title, publisher (or URL and the date you looked at it). Use the exact style your course asks for — Harvard, APA and MLA differ — and copy the format from your course guide rather than from memory. Quote sparingly and put the page number in, because a quote without one is the thing markers flag.

Fifteen to twenty minutes a day beats two hours on Sunday, and start with the hardest four bars rather than the beginning: play them slowly enough to get them right, four times in a row, then put them back in the piece. Use a metronome at a speed you can play cleanly and nudge it up two beats a minute, because sloppy and fast teaches sloppy. Scales and one technical exercise first warm the hands up, and finish on something you enjoy so you want to come back tomorrow.

Figures like that come from whoever counts them, and the year and the boundary change the answer: "the town" and "the wider area" are two different numbers. The official statistics page or the council's own figures have the current one, with the year it is for printed beside it.

Fill the sink with the hottest water you can bear and a squirt of washing-up liquid, then work in order: glasses and mugs first, plates and cutlery next, and the greasy pans last. Rinse in hot water and stand everything to air dry on a rack, and change the water the moment it goes greasy rather than adding more soap to it.

Fill up on protein and fibre first: eggs, beans, yoghurt, chicken, vegetables and whole grains keep you full on fewer calories. Eat slowly, drink water before meals, and aim for half a kilo a week rather than a crash diet, which is what makes hunger unbearable.

Find three things before you read the rest: who sent it, the date, and the line in bold that says what they want and by when. Copy the reference number at the top too, because it is the first thing they ask for when you ring. If a paragraph still makes no sense, ring the number printed on the letter and say it plainly - "I have your letter and I do not understand what you need me to do" - then ask them to email you the answer so you have it in writing. Ringing costs nothing and no deadline is ever hurt by asking, but the deadline itself does pass, so ring before it even if the only thing you say is that the letter is unclear. Citizens Advice will read it through with you for free, and for benefits or debt ask the council or them about a welfare rights worker.

Find flat, empty tarmac and a line to stand on, and learn to push and stop before you try anything else: front foot across the board at an angle, back foot on the ground, and three pushes then both feet on. Bend your knees and keep your weight over the board rather than leaning back, and look where you are going, not at your feet. A helmet and wrist guards cost less than an evening in A&E, and pads make you braver.

Fix a regular time and a clear table, and stay nearby without taking over; the point is the routine, not a perfect page. If a piece takes more than 20 minutes for a primary-aged child, write a note to the teacher rather than pushing through.

Flatten chicken breasts to an even thickness, season them and roast at 200C (180C fan) for 18 to 20 minutes, or until the middle is 74C. Resting them for 5 minutes keeps the juice in; slicing them straight from the oven is what dries them out.

For most club golfers the pace matters more than the line: pick a spot a foot past the hole on the high side and try to roll the ball over it, because a putt that finishes close is holed eventually and one that is hit too hard is not. Keep the wrists still and rock the shoulders, with the same length back and through. On long putts, aim to leave it inside a metre rather than to hole it.

For rain, a waterproof shell with taped seams (Gore-Tex or similar) at £150 to £250 outlasts three cheap ones: check the hood, the zip and the seams under the arms, and try it on over a jumper. A shower-resistant jacket is fine for a dash to the shops and no good for a wet walk.

For that age, one thing they will use every day beats a pile of toys: a scooter, duplo, sticker and activity books, or a decent football. Ask the parents what they already have too much of, and buy the batteries with it. Wrap it in something they can play with afterwards.

For the train: That one is a live departure, so the operator's app, or the board at the station, is where the next one and any delay or cancellation show up. A journey planner puts the whole trip together.

For Japan: Late March to April for the blossom, or October to November for the autumn colour. June is the rainy season, August is hot and humid, and the New Year week is the busiest travel period of the year.

For Usa: It depends where: May and September for the northeast, spring and autumn for the southwest, and June to September for the national parks and mountains. Avoid the July 4th week and Thanksgiving for flights.

For about 12 thin pancakes, whisk 100g plain flour, 2 eggs and 300ml milk with a pinch of salt, then let the batter rest 20 minutes. Cook them in a hot non-stick pan with a little butter, about a minute a side, until bubbles pop on top and the edges look dry. The rest is what stops them tearing; American ones want a teaspoon of baking powder and a thicker batter. Flat ones are a batter that was too thin, or an old raising agent.
For 25 people you want about 12.5kg of duck on the bone: seven birds of about 2kg each.

For a run: something around 160 to 170 beats per minute keeps the pace steady, so *Mr Brightside*, *Titanium* and *Don't Stop Me Now* all work, or a Daft Punk album run straight through if you would rather not think about it.

For a series with friends: *Ghosts* (silly and warm in 25-minute episodes, which is what a mixed room wants), *The Detectorists* (gentle and very funny, and nothing in it is upsetting) or *The Bear* (short, intense episodes that pull you through a whole series in a weekend). Say the mood and I'll narrow it down.

For a story: *The Last of Us* (grief and a road trip), *Red Dead Redemption 2* (a slow western with a lot of heart), or *Disco Elysium* if you would rather read. *The Last of Us* is the one people finish and then sit still for a while.

For a superhero film: *Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse* (117 minutes, the animation is worth it on its own), *The Incredibles* (115 minutes, works for adults and children in the same room), or *Guardians of the Galaxy* (121 minutes, funny first and superhero second). Any of them is a good way in, and I can go shorter or pick one if you tell me the mood.

For a warm week: light cotton tops and shorts, one long-sleeved layer and a light waterproof, plus swimwear, a hat, high-factor sun cream and shoes you can walk in. Take two pairs of shoes at most and one smarter outfit if you plan to eat out; everything else can be washed.

For a crowd, one big dish rather than plates: an apple and blackberry crumble (fruit in a dish, a crumble of 100g each of flour and butter with 50g of sugar, 40 minutes at 180C/160C fan, with custard), or a baked rice pudding, or a bread and butter pudding - all made in the morning, and all soft enough for anyone who finds chewing hard. An Eton mess takes five minutes if you buy the meringues.

For a drop goal, catch the pass and hold the ball out in front of you with its point down, then drop it and kick it off the ground as it starts to bounce - the ball has to touch the ground first, so the timing is the whole skill. Watch the ball rather than the posts, keep your head down, and strike through the bottom half so it goes up and over. Practise from ten metres until you can do it without looking at your feet.

For a joint or muscle that aches without a fall or a twist, keep it moving gently rather than resting it: a short walk, a warm bath and paracetamol or ibuprofen gel usually settle it in a week or two, and strength work on the muscles around it is what stops it coming back. See a GP or physio if it is swollen, locks or gives way, wakes you at night, or has not improved after two to three weeks.
For Chicago: May, June and September: 20-27C and the lakefront at its best. July and August are hot and humid, and January and February are brutal with the wind off the lake.
Four 15-minute quarters, so 60 minutes of play, but the clock stops on every incomplete pass and the whole game runs about three hours, and longer for the Super Bowl with its half-time show.

From about eight, twice a year is worth it: the vet can find the things old cats hide — kidney trouble, thyroid, arthritis, high blood pressure — before you see them. Weigh her monthly at home and ask for a blood and urine test at the annual visit. Don't wait for the check-up, though, if she loses weight, drinks more, hides away, stops grooming or goes off her food; those need the vet this week.

GPU stands for graphics processing unit: the chip that does the thousands of small arithmetic sums a picture is made of at once. That is why it draws games and video smoothly, and why the same chip does machine learning, which is the same kind of sum on a much bigger scale.

Gas is much the cheapest for heat: about 6 to 7p a unit (kWh) against about 24 to 25p for electricity, so the same heat costs roughly a quarter as much, and that is why a gas boiler is the cheap way to warm a house. The one electric thing that competes is a heat pump, because it moves heat instead of making it - three units of heat for one of electricity puts it near or below gas - while panel heaters, fan heaters and an immersion are the dearest, at about four times the gas price for the same warmth. Whatever the fuel, the cheapest heat is the heat you do not lose: loft and cavity insulation, and a boiler flow temperature of 55 to 60C, cut the bill more than switching fuel does.

Gas is the cheapest to run: a gas ring is roughly 10 to 15p an hour against 25 to 35p for a standard electric ring, and a gas oven is about half the cost of an electric one at the same heat. Induction is the one most people prefer in use - about 15 to 20p an hour, because it puts almost all the heat into the pan and boils a pan of water in around half the time, so the shorter cooking usually makes up the difference. The pan matters as much as the fuel: a flat base that covers the ring, and a lid on, save more than changing fuel does.

Gases in the air, mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour, let sunlight in but absorb the heat that bounces back off the ground, much like glass in a greenhouse. That keeps the Earth about 33C warmer than it would be. Burning coal, oil and gas adds more of those gases, so more heat is trapped and the planet warms.

Get the money apart quietly and early: open a current account in your own name and have your pay and any benefits go there, then list every joint account, loan, credit card and direct debit so nothing bounces in your name. Tell the bank you have separated, keep paying the mortgage or rent until a solicitor says otherwise, and book the free first session most family solicitors offer before you agree anything.

Get the chair right first and the rest is cheap: an adjustable one so your feet are flat and the arms sit at elbow height, the screen top at eye level, a stack of books or a riser under a laptop, and a lamp beside your writing hand rather than behind you. A separate keyboard and mouse are the other fix worth paying for.

Get three quotes on the same written scope, and don't start until you have the money for the whole job plus 15% for what the walls hide. Order the kitchen or bathroom six to eight weeks before you need it, because that is the delay everyone hits, and put the start date and the payment stages in a contract rather than agreeing them by text.

Give him somewhere he can get to that nobody reaches into - a covered crate, or the gap behind the sofa - and do not pull him out of it: a pet allowed to hide comes out sooner. Crouch down and turn side-on rather than leaning over him, talk quietly, and let him come to you; that is weeks of small steps rather than one good day. If it came on suddenly in an older animal, or he growls when he is cornered, have the vet look at him - pain and failing eyesight turn calm pets fearful.

Gluten free: potatoes, rice, corn, quinoa and lentils are all fine, so a chilli, a curry, a stir-fry or a tray of roast veg with rice needs nothing changed. For a bake, use a gluten-free plain flour blend with a quarter teaspoon of xanthan gum per 200g and let the batter stand 20 minutes; cornflour is for thickening a sauce. Watch the labels for wheat, barley, rye and 'may contain', use tamari in place of soy sauce, and check the sausages and the stock cubes.

Go to an indoor wall with hired shoes and a taster session first, about twenty pounds, and try bouldering: it needs no partner and the routes are the height of a room. Give it three visits before you buy shoes, and only then a pair that fits tightly. Outdoors comes later, with somebody who already knows how to belay.

Go at the time you would actually go, on a weekday evening if that is when you are free: a gym that is full at six is the one you stop using. Then check three things - the distance from home or work, because anything past fifteen minutes gets skipped, whether the classes you want are included in the price or cost extra, and the notice period on the contract, which is often a month and sometimes three. Ask for a day pass or a week trial before you sign, look at the changing rooms as well as the equipment, and work out the price per visit rather than per month: 40 a month is cheap at three visits a week and dear at one. The cheapest gym is the one you actually use.

Go by the fibre first: merino is the warmest for its weight and the softest against the neck, lambswool is thicker and cheaper, and a wool-rich blend of 80 per cent wool and 20 per cent nylon keeps its shape where a high-acrylic knit pills and holds damp. Buy it big enough to wear over a shirt, and treat a wool jumper as one you air rather than wash - that is what keeps it warm for years.

Gravity is the attraction between anything with mass: the Earth pulls you toward its centre, and you pull the Earth back by the same rule. Bigger mass means a stronger pull, which is why the Moon orbits the Earth and the Earth orbits the Sun.

Guests usually go smart: a dress or a shirt and trousers with closed shoes, and a layer, because gowns and halls are either freezing or stuffy. Flats or a wide heel are kinder if the photos are on grass.

Hair grows about 1 to 1.5cm a month, and nothing makes that much faster: the length is set by your genes and how long each follicle keeps growing before it sheds. What you can do is stop losing it to breakage - fewer hot washes and straighteners, a wide-tooth comb on wet hair, a loose band rather than a tight bobble - and keep the ends trimmed every two or three months so splits do not travel up and make the length look thin. If it is thinning as well as slow, get iron, ferritin, thyroid and vitamin D checked, because that is the one cause worth fixing.

Hard water, too much detergent and drying on a radiator are what make washed cloth stiff: use half the detergent, add a cup of white vinegar to the rinse, shake each piece out and dry it with airflow. Denim and thick cotton soften after a few wears, so give it a wash or two before you decide it has been ruined.
Hats, ears and face paint do more than the outfit, and one prop - a cardboard sword, a wooden spoon, a stack of books - tells everyone who it is meant to be.

Heat the room you are sitting in and shut the door: a 1kW electric radiator warms a small room for about 25p an hour, usually less than running the whole boiler for one person, and a heated throw costs about 3p an hour. Then stop the losses, a few pounds each: a brush strip on the door, a chimney balloon, foil behind the radiator. If the central heating is on, keep the flow at 55 to 60C and heat only the rooms you use.

Height is the whole thing: standing in their normal shoes, the top of the handle should sit at the crease of the wrist with the arm hanging relaxed - roughly the top of the hip crease - and most sticks adjust between about 75cm and 95cm, so get one with a pin or twist lock rather than a fixed length. It goes in the hand opposite the bad hip or knee, because that is the side that takes the weight while the bad leg steps. A single-point stick is for balance and a weak leg; a quad stick or a frame is steadier if both legs are weak or they need to stop and rest, and a four-wheel rollator with a seat and a basket is the one people actually keep using because it carries the shopping. Get it measured free by an NHS physiotherapist or occupational therapist, or a pharmacist will do it in two minutes; expect £10 to £25, and replace the rubber ferrule once it is worn or shiny.

Hibernation is a way of getting through a season with no food: the animal's temperature, heart rate and breathing drop, and it lives off the fat it laid down in autumn. A bear's heart can slow from 40 beats a minute to 8, and a hedgehog turns almost cold to the touch. A bat or a hedgehog woken in winter has spent a lot of energy for nothing, so leave one be.

Hot food wants to stay above 63C: a slow cooker on low, an oven on its lowest with the door ajar, or a lidded pan on a trivet, served in small batches so what is out gets eaten. Cold food wants to stay under 5C. Anything that has sat between the two for more than two hours is the food that makes people ill, so bin it.

Hunger is your body's signal that fuel is running low: the stomach releases a hormone called ghrelin, and blood sugar and habit both feed into it. Feeling hungry again soon after a meal is often a fast carbohydrate meal rather than a real shortage; protein, fibre and fat keep it down for longer.
I'd do a potato curry (30 minutes): fry onion with spices, add cubed potato and tomatoes with a splash of water and simmer 20 minutes. Something else that works is vegetable soup.

I'm really glad you told me, and you deserve help right now, not later. Please call a crisis line and stay with someone you trust: Samaritans 116 123 (UK, free, any time) or 988 (US); if you've taken something, call 999 or 911.

Iceland is cheap for frozen food: frozen and ready meals are cheap and everything else is dearer. It is one of the cheapest places to do a full shop, though the range of brands is smaller, so anything specific may need a second stop.

In England and Wales you need a rod licence from the Environment Agency for any freshwater fishing, even for a day, and it is separate from the permission to fish: the lake or club sells a day ticket on top. Buy it online or at a Post Office - about £7 for a day, £13 for eight days, £35 for a season, per rod, and under-13s free. Scotland needs none for coarse or trout, but salmon does. Fishing without one is a fine.

In the time you have, do a circuit: 40 seconds each of squats, press-ups (on your knees is fine), a plank and lunges, twice round, with a minute's rest. Bodyweight work like that keeps strength and gets your heart going without a gym.
In the USA: Go regional: barbecue in Texas or Kansas City, a po'boy in New Orleans, pizza by the slice in New York, tacos in Los Angeles.

In the bank's own app there is usually an 'Add to Apple Pay' or 'Add to Google Pay' button on the card, and it is the quickest way; otherwise open Wallet on the phone and add the card number by hand or with the camera. In Italy: Rome for cacio e pepe or carbonara, Naples for pizza and Bologna for ragù, with a coffee standing at the bar. Order the house wine; it is cheaper than water in some places.

In Los Angeles: pick two areas and expect to drive between them: Venice or Santa Monica, the Griffith observatory at sunset, and one studio tour if you want one. It is far bigger than it looks on a map.
In Mexico: Tacos al pastor from a stand, tamales for breakfast and mole in Oaxaca, with the salsa on the side so you choose the heat.

In coffee, oat is the plant milk that behaves best - the barista cartons are made not to split, and they foam. Soy is next and tastes slightly beany in a long black; almond is thin and can separate in hot coffee; coconut changes the taste of the cup. Whole milk foams the thickest and semi-skimmed is the usual for a flat white, and a splash of milk in black coffee takes the edge off without much milk at all.
In China: Go regional: dim sum in Guangzhou and Hong Kong, hand-pulled noodles in Xi'an and a Sichuan hotpot in Chengdu. Order several dishes and share them.

In maths a power tells you how many times to multiply a number by itself: 3 to the power 4 means 3 x 3 x 3 x 3, which is 81. The small raised number is the exponent and the number being multiplied is the base; a square is a power of 2 and a cube is a power of 3.
India has the most people, at about 1.45 billion, just ahead of China at about 1.41 billion since 2023. The United States is a distant third, at about 340 million.

It depends on the age: by two most children have around fifty words and join two together, and by three they say short sentences a stranger half understands. Below the age for that, a hearing test comes first - glue ear is the commonest and most fixable reason - and then a speech and language referral from the health visitor, because the waiting list is the thing to beat.

It is the comma before the last item in a list: milk, eggs, and bread. British writing usually leaves it out and American keeps it, and it earns its place when it stops a misreading - I'd like to thank my parents, Ayn Rand, and God. Keep to one habit through a document either way.

It's with an apostrophe always means 'it is' or 'it has': it's raining, it's been ages. Everything else is its, no apostrophe: the cat licked its paw. If you can swap in 'it is' and the sentence still works, use it's.
Italy: Rome for the ancient city and the Vatican. Florence for the art you can walk between. Naples and the Amalfi coast for pizza and sea.

Jeans are fitted by three numbers, so try a size either side of the one you think you are: the waist should sit snug with no gap at the back, the rise about an inch below your navel, and the hem break once on the shoe. Look for 98% cotton with a little elastane, which holds its shape without clinging, and a leg that is long enough not to ride up when you sit.

8GB of RAM is fine for browsing, email and word processing; 16GB is worth it if you keep a lot of tabs and apps open at once, or edit photos or video. On most thin laptops you cannot add it later, so buy the 16GB now if the budget stretches.

Keep a short diary for two weeks: date, time, what it was, how long. Then ring the council's environmental health team, who must look into a statutory nuisance and can serve an abatement notice. Builders are usually held to about 8am to 6pm on weekdays and Saturday mornings, so a 6am start is worth reporting.

Keep a list of the words you actually get wrong (not a generic list), and test yourself on those five at a time by writing them, saying them and covering them. For the ones that refuse to stick, break them into a silly phrase or find the small word inside the big one (there's "a rat" in separate).

Keep it to one minute and start when she is already sleepy, after a meal: let her sniff the brush and put it down beside her first, then do one stroke along her back, a treat, and stop while she is still happy. A soft rubber glove or a short-bristled brush hurts less than a metal comb on a short coat, and the belly, tail and legs are for the vet or the groomer, not for a cat who already hates it. Two or three of those minutes a week is plenty for most cats. If she used to be fine and has started to hate being touched, that is often pain - teeth, back, an over-sensitive patch - so have her looked at.

Knock two split pieces together: well seasoned wood cracks like a bat on a ball, and green wood thuds. The ends of a dry log are pale, cracked and often dark-ringed, and a cheap moisture meter pushed into a freshly split face should read under 20 per cent. Burning wet wood is why a fire smokes, spits and blacks the glass, and it gives around half the heat, because most of the flame's energy goes on boiling the water out of the log instead of heating the room.

Late March to early April, moving north as the season goes: Tokyo usually peaks around the end of March, Kyoto a few days later. Book accommodation months ahead, and be flexible, because a cold spring can delay it by a week or two.

Layers pellets or mash as the base, about 120 g a day per hen, plus grass, weeds, insects and vegetable scraps; grit and crushed oyster shell keep the eggshells hard. Bread and corn are treats rather than feed, and avocado, citrus peel, salt and anything mouldy are not for them at all.

Layers, a waterproof outer and boots with real tread: snow is fine, ice is what puts people on the ground, so a deep sole beats a smooth one and anything you can lean on beats a handbag. Cover the ears, hands and neck, and wear wool or a synthetic base layer rather than cotton, which holds the damp and chills you. Take the layers off indoors rather than sweating in them and then going back out.

Learn four shapes first - G, C, D and E minor - because those four are most of the songs you already know, and practise moving between two of them rather than holding one well. Ten minutes a day: one minute of slow changes with a metronome or a steady count, then play a song with the same two chords in it, and add a third only when the change is clean.

Leave the kitchen to the second-to-last day, because it is the room you still need, and keep one box open until the morning: kettle, two mugs, tea, a tea towel, washing-up liquid, a sharp knife, a tin opener and a corkscrew. Do it one cupboard at a time and set a box down on the counter as you empty it, so nothing gets carried across the room; plates and glasses go on edge in small boxes with a towel round them, never stacked flat. Anything out of date or never used goes in the bin bag rather than the van, the fridge wants emptied, defrosted and dried out a day before, and it travels upright. Write KITCHEN - OPEN FIRST on the boxes you will want that night, and put the food and the cleaning stuff in their own two boxes so you are not hunting for the bin bags.

Leave it somewhere around 25C for 1 to 2 hours, until the dough has doubled. Yeast eats the sugars in the flour and gives off gas, and the stretchy gluten holds it in bubbles, so warmth and time are the whole job. If it hasn't moved at all, the yeast is dead, so check the date and use water that's warm rather than hot.

Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519) was an Italian painter, engineer and anatomist: the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper on one side, notebooks of flying machines and dissected bodies on the other. Fewer than twenty of his paintings survive, and it is the range of his curiosity that made him famous.

Lights are the law between sunset and sunrise, and worth using in daylight as well: a flashing rear light is what makes a driver look twice in rain or at dusk. Use a steady front light bright enough to see the road by - 400 lumens is plenty in town - and a rear light at saddle height, not on your bag where a coat covers it. Charge them weekly; the light that dies halfway home is the one nobody sees.

Living things vary, and the ones whose variations suit their surroundings tend to survive and pass those variations on. Over many generations that selection changes the population: small changes accumulate into new species.

Look for the dot at the top of the screen: green means the camera is on, orange means the microphone, and it only appears while an app is using it. If it shows when you are not in any app, open Settings > Privacy > Camera (Permissions on Android, Privacy & security on a laptop) and turn off every app you do not trust, then restart the phone; a camera nobody can account for is worth a backup and a factory reset rather than a new phone.

Lower the temperature before you make the point: raise it when neither of you is tired, hungry or has had a drink, and bring one thing, not the three you have been saving up. Make the worktop boring and the floor worth being on. Feed her before you cook rather than while you eat, and never leave a chair pulled up against the counter. Make it safe, photograph it before you clear anything, and ring your insurer's claim line: a roof, a shed or a fence is usually on the buildings cover, a car on its own comprehensive policy. Tarpaulin over the hole, weighed down - not under it. Keep the debris and the receipts, and report it within a few days: the deadline is short. A neighbour's tree is an insurance claim too unless they were negligent, so tell them and keep the photos.

Make it look lived in and keep the signs of absence out of sight: a couple of plug-in lamp timers, a radio on a timer, post held at the sorting office and a bin put out by a neighbour, because piled post and a full bin are what tell a burglar the house is empty. Ask a neighbour to park on the drive, don't post the trip until you are home, and tell your insurer if it will be empty for more than 30 days.

Match the limit to the age: under two, video calls and the odd photo only; two to five, an hour of good programmes a day; older children, a set amount agreed in advance. Watch it with them when you can, keep screens away from meals and the hour before bed, and have one screen-free part of each day so it isn't a fight every time.

Measure the room, the door and the stairs before you fall for one, and keep 60cm of walking space past it. Then look at the build: a hardwood or beech frame screwed and glued, not stapled chipboard, and seat cushions of 30 to 35kg foam with a fibre wrap, or feather if you will plump them daily. Sit on it for ten minutes rather than three, and check the fabric's rub count - 25,000 for adults, 30,000 and up for children and pets. Made-to-order sofas take six to twelve weeks, so ask about the return policy before you pay.

Melatonin is a short-term sleep aid rather than a knock-out: 1 to 2 mg about an hour before bed shifts your body clock, so it suits jet lag or a bedtime that has drifted late, and it works best with a dark room and the same wake-up time. Ask a pharmacist first if you take blood thinners, epilepsy drugs or antidepressants. If sleep has been poor for weeks, see your GP - it is not a long-term fix.
Mexico: Mexico City for the food and the museums. Oaxaca for markets and mezcal. Tulum if you mainly want the beach.

Mohandas Gandhi (1869-1948) led India's independence movement through non-violent protest, most famously the 1930 Salt March, and India was free in 1947. He was assassinated in January 1948, before the new country had settled.

Most people need around 45 hours of lessons plus 20 hours of private practice before they pass, so two lessons a week gets you there in about six months at 40 just as at 18. Lessons run 25 to 40 pounds an hour, and a block with one instructor beats single lessons with three. Most rashes are contact or heat: a new soap or washing powder, a plant, sweat, or a viral thing that fades in a few days. Cool the skin, skip perfumed products, and an antihistamine at night helps the itch; a thin layer of 1% hydrocortisone cream twice a day for up to a week settles a very itchy patch, but keep it off the face. Two rashes are not wait-and-see - one that does not fade when you press a glass on it, and one with a fever or a swollen face or lips - so get those seen the same day.

Most training injuries come from a jump in load, not bad luck: add about a tenth a week at most, to the weight or to the miles. Warm up for five minutes, take a lighter first set, and keep the form good on the last set or drop the weight - a sloppy last rep is where most of them happen. Never train through a sharp pain. If an ache lasts more than two weeks, or a joint gives way, see a physio rather than resting it for a month.
