The creamier way is a custard - 4 yolks, 100g sugar and 500ml of milk and cream cooked to 80C - frozen in a tub and beaten every 30 minutes three times. Home-made ice cream wants eating within a fortnight.

Nobody was hurt, so this is a report and a claim rather than an emergency: ring 101 for a crime or incident number, photograph the damage before you clean or repair anything, and tell your insurer the same day even if you mean to pay for it yourself. Check the excess before you decide, because a wing mirror or a window often costs less than the claim would; if the car itself has gone, ring 999 while it is happening and give the insurer the crime number.

Nobody keeps that number in their head - it moves daily and the version printed next to it is the only one that counts. Read two offers rather than one, and add on the fee or the terms before you decide which is really cheaper.
North America has 23 countries, from Canada down to Panama; the Caribbean islands are counted separately as part of the region.
Not one I can call honestly, sorry. Name the last thing you enjoyed and I'll say whether this one is that kind of thing.

Nothing rhymes exactly with *orange*. The near ones are *sporange* (a spore case on a fern), *Blorenge* (a hill in Wales) and the two-word *door hinge*. If you need it for a poem, put *orange* at the end of a line that does not have to rhyme, and rhyme the line before it with something else.

Nothing in a dream is a warning - it is the day being filed, and a vivid one usually means a lot was going on. A pen by the bed and a few lines in the morning take the sting out of the ones that keep coming back.

Olive oil or rapeseed oil is a good everyday choice: both are high in unsaturated fat and fine for normal frying. Save the extra virgin olive oil for salads and low heat, and use a plain vegetable oil when you need a very hot pan.
On pizza, yes. Fruit and cheese is not the crime people make it out to be.

On a shift longer than six hours you are entitled to a 20-minute break, and to 11 hours' rest between shifts; under six hours there is no legal minimum, and the break can be unpaid. If your lunch is being cut short every day, put it in writing once - the rota and the times - and ask for the 20 minutes back.

One moist thing and one with a bit of crunch or sharpness, and it stops being a sad sandwich: cheddar with apple and pickle, tuna with celery and a little mayo (drained, or the bread goes), hummus with grated carrot and cucumber, or leftover roast chicken with lettuce and mustard. Butter both slices to the edges first so the bread does not go soggy, and keep tomato or cucumber in the middle. Egg with cress, brie with grape, or corned beef with a lot of mustard are the other three worth having in your pocket.

One person, one language works well - you always in one, your partner in the other - and the rule that matters is that each language gets real, daily use rather than lessons. Expect the school language to win once they start, so keep books, cartoons and relatives in the other one. Children who mix the two are not confused; it sorts itself out by about five.

One thing out of the house and one thing at home usually fills it. Out: a walk somewhere you have not been, a Saturday market, or a museum or gallery - most are free and good for an hour or two. Home: something to cook properly, a film, or a jigsaw with the radio on. Rain only moves the walk to a pool or a cinema. Is it just you, or is someone coming with you?

One thing out of the house and one long thing at home is what saves a wet day. Out: the swimming pool, the library, a free museum gallery, or a walk in proper waterproofs, because a wet park is empty. Home: something with a start and an end, a whole film, a proper cook, a board game, or the job you keep not doing. Decide both in the morning, or the afternoon goes to the sofa and a phone.
One kid, eight. What are they into at the moment?

Order the thing you would not cook at home, and get one more dish than there are people so there is something left cold for tomorrow: a shared starter, a main each, one side for two people. On a Chinese that is a soup or the salt and pepper ribs, two mains with rice between them, and a vegetable; on an Indian it is a dry dish and a wet one, a bread and a rice, not three curries; on a chippy it is one large chips for two. Collect it if you can - it arrives hot instead of steamed - and ask for sauces on the side.

Ordinary clothes plus one big shape, and nothing to sew: a black hoodie with ears on a headband is a cat, a cardboard box is a robot, a dressing gown and a towel round the head is a shepherd. Hats, ears and face paint do more than the outfit, and one prop - a cardboard sword, a wooden spoon, a stack of books - tells everyone who it is meant to be. Superhero: a plain t-shirt with a paper logo taped on, leggings, and a cape cut from an old sheet pinned at the shoulders - pinned, never tied round the neck.

Oxidation is a substance reacting with oxygen: iron rusts, a cut apple browns, a fire burns, and the cells in your body get energy the same way. It does not always need a flame; slow oxidation is what rust and browning are.

PIN stands for personal identification number, which is why "PIN number" says the word twice. It is checked by the card itself rather than by a computer anywhere else, so the number never leaves the machine you put the card in - and nothing legitimate ever asks you to type it into a phone call, a text or a website.

Panting is how a dog cools down, so on a warm night give him a cooler spot than the bedding he has, water within reach and a bowl in the shade; walk him early and late rather than in the heat of the day. A dog that pants hard while it is not hot, or has bright red gums, is a vet call rather than a cool room.

Paracetamol or ibuprofen, plenty to drink, honey in warm water and a salt-water gargle (half a teaspoon in a glass) all ease it, and most sore throats are viral and settle in three to five days. See a GP if it lasts more than a week, you cannot swallow fluids, or it comes with a high fever and a stiff neck.
Paris.

Pay over £100 on a credit card and the card company is jointly liable if the seller folds or the goods never turn up: that's Section 75, up to £30,000, and it works for deposits too. To claim, write to the card company saying you are claiming under Section 75, with the date, the amount, the seller and what went wrong; if they refuse, the Financial Ombudsman is free.
Pi (π) is about 3.14159: the circumference of any circle divided by its diameter. For most everyday sums, 3.14 is close enough.

Pick one wake-up time and keep it every day for two weeks, weekends included: the morning light is what sets the clock. Then move bedtime 15 minutes earlier every few nights, keep the room dark and cool, and take a short walk in daylight before noon. Melatonin half an hour before bed helps some people while the habit sets.

Pick the coat by the weather you are actually out in: a waterproof shell for rain, down or padded for cold and dry, wool for town. £80 to £150 buys a padded coat that lasts a decade, £150 to £250 a waterproof shell that does not leak at the shoulders.

Pick the course by where you want to be at the end of it: a job, a licence, or the habit of studying. Ask two people who finished it what they do now, and count the hours a week it really takes. If the point is interest rather than a qualification, a short evening course tells you whether you like it before you pay for three years.

Pick a route you already know on quiet streets, ride it once at a weekend so the turns are not a surprise, and start with two days a week rather than five. Leave a lock, a spare tube and a pair of shoes at work, so there is nothing to carry and nothing to forget. The first fortnight is the hard part and after that the ride is the easy part of the day. A waterproof and a rear light is all the kit you need.

A musty car is water: lift the mats and press a hand into both footwells and the boot floor, and check the spare-wheel well, because that is where a leak collects first. Clear the drains under the windscreen, check the door and sunroof seals and the boot seal for splits, and dry the car out with the heater on and a window open on a long drive, not with a bowl of vinegar. If the smell comes on when the blower runs, it is the air con: change the cabin filter, have the evaporator cared for by a garage, and run it for a few minutes every week so the drain does not stay damp.

A new fish needs the tank ready before it goes in: a filter running, water treated with a dechlorinator, and the tank cycled for four to six weeks so the bacteria that eat the fish's waste can grow. Feed only what it clears in two minutes, once or twice a day, and change about a quarter of the water every week. A goldfish needs 100 litres and a filter - a bowl is not a home for it.

A night runs in cycles of about ninety minutes: light sleep, then deeper sleep, then a stretch of REM where you dream, and round again. The deep sleep is heaviest in the first half of the night and the dream stretches get longer towards morning, which is why a 6am wake with a dream still in your head is normal and why the last hour feels so strange to be woken out of. Waking between cycles feels much better than waking in the middle of deep sleep, so count back in ninety-minute blocks from your alarm: five is seven and a half hours of sleep, which is why 11pm to 6.30am often feels better than 11pm to 6am.

A pair of 4mm needles and a ball of smooth aran wool is the whole kit, about ten pounds, and a plain square is the first project. Watch one slow video of knit and purl rather than reading about it, make a dishcloth, and only then start a scarf. Wool shops and libraries both run free sit-and-knit groups, which is how most people get past the first mess.

A phone will not fill the frame with the moon: zoom to 10x or more, rest the phone on a wall, a fence or a tripod, turn the flash off, then press and hold on the moon until the focus locks and drag the little sun slider down until the moon is a white disc and not a glowing blob. A full moon is the worst night for detail - at half you get the craters along the shadow line. For stars, put the phone on something solid, use night mode, and give it the full few seconds it asks for.

A postcode, a phone number and opening hours all change hands, so I can't hold them: a map app turns the name into the address, the postcode and the number, and the place's own page has today's hours.

A predator is an animal that hunts and eats other animals: a fox, an owl and a lion are predators, and the animals they eat are their prey. Predators keep prey numbers in check, which is why removing them can upset a whole habitat.
A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 that divides only by 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and so on. 1 is not prime, and 2 is the only even prime.

A puppy has two injections: the first at six to eight weeks, usually done by the breeder, and the second at ten to twelve weeks, and he can go out for walks a week after the second one - around twelve to thirteen weeks. Until then he can be carried outside, meet people and play on clean floors indoors, because the socialising window shuts around sixteen weeks and waiting for the last jab to start it is a mistake. Book the second one as soon as you get him home.

A puppy is about 800 to 3,000 pounds from a breeder depending on the breed, and 150 to 350 from a rescue, and the first year costs more than the puppy does: jabs and a microchip 60 to 100, neutering 150 to 300, insurance 20 to 40 a month, plus food, worming, a crate and a bed. Budget around 1,500 in the first year and keep a vet fund separately. Walk away from anyone who will not show you the mother.

A pyramid has a flat base and triangular faces that meet at a point above it; the base can be any polygon, and a square-based pyramid is the one people picture. Its volume is one third of the area of the base times the height.

A red lentil dhal is the dinner I would cook: lentils, an onion, garlic, cumin and a tin of tomatoes simmered 20 minutes, with rice or bread. Or chickpeas and spinach: fry onion, garlic and spices, add a tin of chickpeas and a tin of tomatoes, simmer 15 minutes and stir spinach through at the end.

A refurbished phone is a good way to save 30 to 50%: buy from a seller who grades the condition and gives a 12-month warranty, and check the battery health figure. Avoid anything sold as "for parts" or with an iCloud lock.

A rocket pushes gas out of the back at high speed, and the equal push forwards lifts it; it does not need air to push against. It has to reach about 28,000 km/h sideways to stay in orbit rather than fall back.

A satellite is anything that orbits a larger body: the Moon is Earth's natural satellite, and most people mean the machines we launch. They stay up by moving sideways fast enough that they keep falling around the Earth and missing it.
A sentence needs a subject and a verb and makes one complete point, starting with a capital and ending with a full stop: 'The bus was late.'
A short poem about cockney rhyming slang: I keep a little slang in mind, the sort of slang that's hard to find. It does not shout, it does not boast, and that's the slang I like the most.
A soft or shrivelled apple or pear has lost water: it is fine to eat, and it is at its best stewed, baked or in a crumble.

A solstice is the day the sun is highest or lowest in the sky, which is why it is the longest day (about 21 June in the north) or the shortest (about 21 December): the Earth's tilt is leaning that half of the planet most towards or away from the sun.

A spring stores energy by bending steel, and the steel gives it back only while it is strained within its elastic limit - pull a coil a little and it straightens and returns, pull it past that point and it stays stretched. That limit is why a spring is rated for a weight and sags once it is asked for more.

A stroke is the blood supply to part of the brain cut off, either by a clot or a bleed, and the test is FAST: Face - has one side dropped when they smile? Arms - can they lift both and hold them up? Speech - is it slurred or jumbled? Time - if any of those, ring 999 now and say the time it started, because clot-busting treatment works best in the first few hours. Give them nothing to eat or drink in case they cannot swallow. A TIA, the same signs passing in minutes, is still a 999 or same-day GP call, since it warns of a bigger one. Recovery is mostly physio and speech therapy in the first months, and the sooner it starts the more comes back.

A synonym is a word that means roughly the same as another: happy and glad, begin and start. Roughly is the important bit - glad fits "I'm glad you came" where happy would be too strong, so pick by the shade you want.
A two-layer chocolate or madeira sponge is the easy crowd-pleaser: bake it the day before, wrap it well and fill it with buttercream on the day. One 20cm tin serves 8 to 10 people generously.
A verb is the doing or being word: run, eat, seems, is. Every sentence needs one, and the verb changes with the time - I walk today, I walked yesterday.

A voucher is not a cop out - a vague one is. Make it specific: a card for somewhere they already go (the cinema, a bookshop, the garden centre, their favourite cafe), or for a thing rather than a shop, and write on the card what you would do with it. Cash is fine too, and nobody is insulted by it: 'I did not know which one you wanted, so put it towards it' is the whole note. What reads as lazy is the generic card for a shop they never go in, handed over with nothing written on it - and a small thing plus a voucher beats both.

A windproof outer layer is the whole trick: a shell over a jumper feels far warmer than a thick coat the wind goes straight through. Keep it done up at the neck and wrists, tie long hair back, and skip anything loose or long that flaps. A hat that covers the ears and a bag with a zip finish the job.

A year is 365 days because that is roughly how long the Earth takes to go round the Sun once: 365.24 days. The extra quarter day is why we add a leap day every four years, so the calendar stays in step with the seasons.

A bar is one group of beats, marked off by the bar lines on the page: in 4/4 that is four beats to a bar, which is why eight bars is the length of most pop verses. A bar and a measure are the same thing.

A bedroom around 16 to 18C suits most people for sleep: cool enough that you need a duvet, not so cold you wake up. Cracking a window for ten minutes before bed, a lighter duvet in summer and a hot water bottle rather than a hot room all help, and a warm bath an hour before bed sends you to sleep faster than a warm bedroom does.

A blender is a tall jug with blades in the base, for things that pour - smoothies, soup, sauces. A food processor is a wide bowl with a blade and discs, for chopping, slicing and grating solid food like onions, nuts or pastry. Thin and liquid, blender; chunky or grated, processor.

A block of scrap wood or the heel of a heavy shoe taps in panel pins and small tacks without marking the surface. For anything bigger than that, wait, or borrow one: a saucepan is heavier than it looks and dents both the pan and the wall.

A browser is the program you read websites in: Chrome, Safari, Edge and Firefox are the common four and they all do the same job. Anything you type in the address bar, any page you save a password for and any tab you leave open belongs to that one browser, which is why an account that works on your phone can look lost on a laptop until you sign in.

A bulleted list needs the same lead-in for every line and no full stops if the lines are fragments: 'Bring:' then 'milk', 'eggs', 'bread'. Capitalise each line or none, and keep the grammar parallel - all nouns or all verbs, not a mix.

A cell is the smallest unit of a living thing: a jelly-like space wrapped in a thin skin, with DNA inside and machinery that turns food into energy. Your body is made of about 30 trillion of them, and each kind is shaped for its job, from a nerve cell that carries signals to a red blood cell that carries oxygen.
A cheese omelette: beat 3 eggs, cook them in butter on a low heat for 2 minutes, fold the cheese in and slide it onto toast. Low heat is what keeps it soft rather than rubbery.

A chip is a small, low shot from just off the green, and the trick is to hit down on it rather than scoop it up: take a 7, 8 or 9 iron, put the ball back in your stance with your hands ahead of it and your weight on your front foot, and make the same small swing back and through so the club takes the ball first and the turf after. Land it about a third of the way onto the green and let it run out, and change club rather than swing harder for a longer chip - a 7 iron runs more, a wedge stops sooner. A pitch is the same idea with a fuller swing and more loft, so the ball flies most of the way and stops quickly. If you keep thinning or chunking them, you are trying to help the ball into the air: keep the hands ahead, don't flick the wrists, and brush the grass after the ball.

A click or clunk that keeps time with the steering is usually a CV joint on the driveshaft: the rubber boot splits, the grease comes out and the joint wears. Look behind the front wheels for a torn boot and grease sprayed round the inside of the arch. A garage replaces the joint or the shaft, an hour or two of work, and it is worth doing before it fails - a joint that lets go leaves the car with no drive. A single clunk on full lock can also be a top mount or a drop link, which is cheaper.

A comet is a lump of ice, dust and rock left over from the birth of the solar system. Near the Sun its ice turns to gas, and the solar wind blows that gas and dust into a long tail pointing away from the Sun.

A console is cheaper and simpler: it plays everything at good quality for years, no upgrades, and you can sell it on. A gaming PC costs more up front but gets cheaper games, higher settings and mods, and doubles as a work machine - so pick the console for a shared living room and the PC if you already sit at a desk with a monitor.

A cookie is a small file a website asks your browser to store: the note that keeps you signed in, the contents of your basket, or an ID that follows you between pages. It is not a program and it cannot read your files - the worst of them is tracking - and clearing them signs you out of most sites.

A covalent bond is two atoms sharing a pair of electrons, which is how most of the molecules around you are held together: water, oxygen, sugar, plastic. Sharing is what makes a molecule stay one thing, rather than the ions of an ionic bond.

A day is 24 hours - the time from one noon to the next. One full turn against the stars takes 23 hours 56 minutes; the extra four minutes are because the Earth has moved on along its orbit as it turned.

A dividend is the slice of its profit a company pays to shareholders, usually two to four times a year and often 2% to 4% of the share price over a year. It is not promised: a company can cut it, and a high yield is often the market saying it expects one. Outside an ISA, the first £500 of dividends a year is tax-free.

A dress is decided by the bust, the waist seam and the hips together, so try it on in the order the seams fall: the bust should sit inside the darts rather than above or below them, the waist seam should land on your natural waist, and the skirt should hang from the hip without pulling across the front. Then sit down, raise your arms and take a few steps: a dress that rides up when you sit or lifts when you reach will not get worn. Buy for the widest of the three and have the rest taken in, which is the cheap direction to alter.

A dripping tap is nearly always a worn washer or cartridge: turn the water off at the isolating valve under the sink, take the handle off, and take the old part to a hardware shop to match it. It's a 20-minute job and saves a lot of water.

A dry tablet keeps its strength for a long time past the date on the box, and paracetamol that has sat in a cupboard is usually still fine to take; a pharmacist will check any you take every day. What does not keep is anything wet: insulin, eye drops, opened liquids and cough syrup lose their strength and can grow bacteria, so replace those rather than use them. Never flush old medicines down the loo or put them in the bin - hand them in at any pharmacy, which takes them for free.
A female cat is a queen.

A fever, pus or a puffy face with a bad tooth or swollen gums is a spreading dental infection, so ring a dentist today - or 111 for the out-of-hours dental service - rather than waiting for it to settle. Take paracetamol or ibuprofen at the dose on the pack, keep drinking and keep the mouth clean. Go to A&E if the swelling closes your eye or spreads down your throat, or if you cannot swallow or breathe.

A fossil forms when a dead animal or plant is buried quickly and its hard parts are slowly replaced by minerals from the surrounding rock over thousands of years. Most living things rot away entirely, which is why fossils are rare.

A fraction is a part of a whole written as one number over another: the bottom says how many equal pieces the whole is cut into and the top says how many of those you have, so 3/4 is three pieces out of four. The one thing that trips people up is that the same amount has lots of names - 2/4 is 1/2, and 0.5 is 1/2 too - which is why you can simplify and compare them by putting them over the same bottom number.

A gear is a toothed wheel that turns another wheel, so turning one turns the other at a different speed or with more force: a small gear driving a big one gives slow, strong, and the other way round gives fast, weak, which is how a bike's gears work.

A good new phone is £250 to £500, a budget one £120 to £250, and a flagship £800 to £1,200; a grade-A refurb or last year's model is about half its launch price and does the same job. Buy the handset outright and pair it with a SIM-only plan at £8 to £15 a month, because a bundled contract usually costs more over two years.

A gym is worth it if the door is within ten minutes of you and you will go twice a week: the walk decides it, not the equipment. Skip it if the nearest one is a drive away, and pay monthly rather than a year up front. A £20 leisure-centre one you use beats a £60 one you dread.
A haiku is three lines counted in sounds: five, then seven, then five, usually about one moment rather than a story: Rain on the window, a hundred small taps, all night, and the garden drinks.

A hybrid or gravel bike with 32 to 40mm tyres, mudguard and rack mounts and disc brakes: those stop in the wet and take a pannier. £500 to £800 new, £200 to £350 secondhand. A road bike with 23mm tyres and no mounts fights a commute, and a step-through frame is easier in town clothes.

A javelin is thrown over the shoulder from a run: a straight run-up of about eight strides building through the last three, the arm back and high with the point level by your ear, then the front foot plants and the hips turn before the arm comes through. Let it go with the tip up and run through past the line, because the throw is measured where the tip lands. The length comes from the run-up and the hip turn, not from muscling it.

A jug blender is the tall jug with a blade in the base, for smoothies, soups, hummus and crushing ice: liquid in, smooth out. It needs enough liquid to keep the food moving, so a thick mix wants stirring or a little water; hot soup goes in a third at a time, with the lid held down, because steam lifts it off.

A letter or a card just needs the right stamp and the full address; a parcel needs a customs form, at the counter a CN22 (a CN23 once the value is over a few hundred pounds), naming what is inside, its weight and its value - that is what the receiving country works its duty and tax out from, so write the truth rather than gift. Price goes by weight band: a small parcel to Europe is roughly £10 to £20 and outside Europe more, so weigh it first and compare a courier once it is over 2kg. Nothing perishable, no loose lithium batteries by air, and alcohol and perfume only within the limits.
A lever is a bar that turns on a pivot, and it lets a small push move a big weight if the pivot sits close to the weight: a crowbar, a wheelbarrow, a see-saw and a bottle opener are all levers.

A marathon is 26.2 miles, or 42.2 kilometres — the odd 0.2 is there because the 1908 London course was extended to finish in front of the royal box. A half marathon is the obvious first step, and most training plans build up to it over about sixteen weeks.
Pitch is how high or low a note is, set by how fast the sound vibrates: a short string or a tight one vibrates faster and sounds higher.

Pizza is bread, cheese and topping, so the thin crust and the vegetable toppings are the good end of it and a stuffed crust with extra cheese is the other end. A whole 12-inch one is 1,000 to 1,200 calories, so half with a salad is a meal, and a takeaway one carries a lot of salt.
Plants need sunlight as the energy source for photosynthesis, the reaction that makes their food. Without enough light they cannot make sugar, so they stop growing and their leaves yellow and drop.
Pleased for you. Thanks for telling me how it went.

Plenty shifts a period by a few days - stress, a bug, a bad month of sleep, a change in weight, travel, the pill - so the useful next step is a test rather than a wait: from the day it was due, first pee of the morning, and again in three days if it is negative and nothing comes. Three months without a period, bleeding between periods or after sex, or a positive test with pain or bleeding is a GP appointment. If your cycles were always irregular, a few weeks late on its own is not alarming.

Plug in a USB keyboard: if that types, the laptop's own keyboard is the fault, and a restart plus the maker's keyboard driver from their support page fixes it more often than not. If the keys that fail are a block of them, look for a sticky key or a spill; on a Mac, check System Settings > Keyboard.

Press the microphone button on the speaker: on an Echo it is the circle with a line through it on top, and it glows red when the mics are off; a Google Home or Nest has a switch at the back. Nothing is recorded while it is off, and in the Alexa app, Settings > Alexa Privacy > Review Voice History lets you delete what it already has.

Press a clean cloth on it and keep pressing for ten minutes without lifting it to look; most small cuts stop by then. If the edges gape, it's deep, or it's still bleeding after twenty minutes of steady pressure, get it looked at.

Pressure is force spread over an area: the same push on a smaller area gives a higher pressure, which is why a knife cuts and a wide boot does not sink into snow. It is measured in pascals, and in a fluid it rises with depth.

Put the alarm across the room, and set it for the same time every day including weekends, because a lie-in on Sunday is what makes Monday impossible. Be in bed eight hours before it, and leave the book open at the page the night before so the first ten minutes need no decision. Then get up when it rings: negotiating with yourself is the part that fails.

Put the cursor under the column and press AutoSum (Alt and = in Excel; the sigma in the toolbar on Google Sheets): it writes =SUM(A1:A20) for the range it finds. If the total comes out short, look for a number typed with a space or an apostrophe in front - Excel reads those as text - and the little green triangle in the corner is how it tells you.

Put it in writing, a text or email is fine, and keep a copy. Name what is wrong and when it started, say what you want done and ask for a date, then keep the messages: landlords have to do most repairs in a reasonable time, and anything that came with the flat, appliances included, counts, while something you brought with you is yours to fix. If they ignore you, your council's environmental health team or Shelter can push it along.
Quick: tuna pasta in 15, chickpea curry in 25, or a lentil dhal if you have 30 minutes. Tell me what is in the fridge and I will pick properly.
Quick: tuna pasta in 15, a frittata in 20, or a potato curry if you have 30 minutes. Tell me what is in the fridge and I will pick properly.
Quick: tuna pasta in 15, a frittata in 20, or a chicken traybake if you have 40 minutes. Tell me what is in the fridge and I will pick properly.
Quick: tuna pasta in 15, macaroni cheese in 25, or a sausage traybake if you have 45 minutes. Tell me what is in the fridge and I will pick properly.
Quick: a tuna salad in 10, tomato pasta in 20, or a salmon traybake if you have 30 minutes. Tell me what is in the fridge and I will pick properly.
Quick: a chicken salad in 15, a fish foil bake in 25, or vegetable soup if you have 30 minutes. Tell me what is in the fridge and I will pick properly.
Quick: a chickpea salad in 10, spinach and chickpea curry in 25, or vegetable soup if you have 30 minutes. Tell me what is in the fridge and I will pick properly.

RAM stands for random access memory: the working space a computer keeps open programs in, wiped when it loses power. More of it helps when many tabs or programs are open at once; it does not make a single program faster, and a full disk is the more common reason a computer feels slow.

Read the labels on every packet you use, including the icing and the decorations, and keep the packets out so everyone can check them; cross-contamination is the usual slip, so use clean bowls and a fresh knife. A plain sponge with buttercream and a different fruit instead of the strawberry filling is the easy swap. Ask the parent of the allergic child what they avoid before you bake, not on the doorstep.

Register the birth within 42 days at the register office for the district where the baby was born, and book the appointment online: you need the date and place of birth, and both parents' names, places of birth and jobs. The short certificate is free; the full one, which is the one a passport application needs later, costs about £12.50.

Register free with the Telephone Preference Service (tps.org.uk) to cut marketing calls, and use the phone's own block list for the ones that keep coming: on an iPhone it is Settings > Phone > Silence Unknown Callers, on Android it is Caller ID and spam protection in the Phone app. Never press a number to "speak to someone" or reply to a silent call, because that proves the line is live; if the caller says they are your bank, hang up and ring the number on your card.

Rehearse the first sixty seconds out loud until you could say it half asleep, because that is the only part your nerves will attack. Then slow down and pause at the ends of sentences rather than filling the silence - a room reads a pause as confidence, and it gives you time to breathe.

Replace them once the midsole has gone flat or the heel is worn through: the cushioning is what has gone, no repair brings it back, and it starts to show as heel or knee pain. Buy at the end of the day in the socks you will wear them with, leave a thumb's width at the toe, and check the heel does not lift when you walk.

Replace walking boots every 800 to 1,000 miles, or sooner if the sole has gone thin under the ball of the foot: a boot is finished when the midsole has compressed and it no longer holds your foot over rough ground, which is why a leather upper in fine condition can still be a boot to throw away; a resole buys another few hundred miles.
Rest it, put an ice pack on for 15 minutes at a time, and wrap it snugly but not tight; keep it up when you sit down. If you can't put weight on it or it swells badly, get it checked.
Reviews beat anything I could say about city, which I have never been to: a map app or the town's visitor site will name the ones people rate - tell me what you want from it and I'll help you choose.
Reviews beat a guess from me on the beaches near you, which I have never been to: a map app's, sorted by what you need, is the honest way - say what matters and I'll help you narrow it down.
Reviews beat a guess from me about place, since I have never been to any of them: a map app or the local visitor site names the ones people rate - say what matters and I'll help you narrow it down.
Reviews from people who have been beat my guess on the restaurants near you, since I have never been to any of them: sort a map app's by what you need, and the count matters more than the score.
Rhythm is the pattern of the music in time - where the beats fall and which are strong. A drummer keeps it, and you can clap it without knowing any notes.

Ribs want low and slow: 2 to 2.5 hours covered at 150C (130C fan) with a splash of water in the tray, then 15 minutes uncovered at 220C (200C fan) with a glaze to sticky them up. In a slow cooker it is 6 to 8 hours on low, then 10 minutes under the grill. They are done when the meat has pulled back from the bone and a fork twists in it easily.

Rice burns when there is no water left under it: the heat is too high, so the pan dries out before the grain is cooked and the bottom scorches. One mug of rice to one and a half of water, bring it to the boil with the lid on, then turn it down to the lowest ring for 10 to 12 minutes without stirring - stirring rubs the starch off and makes it catch. A heavy pan and a lid that fits are most of the fix, and 5 minutes off the heat at the end finishes it.

Ring them rather than using the app if you can: say the day, the time and what it is for, and ask which card holds the booking and what a cancellation costs before you give the details. Get a text confirmation in writing. A table is usually held 15 minutes, so say if you will be late and mention anything that matters - a birthday, a highchair, a wheelchair; for a haircut or a viewing, ask for the quieter part of the week, when they can move you. For a table tonight, ring back at lunchtime, when tables come free.

Ring at the moment the lines open - 8am for most GP surgeries - and ask for the first appointment of the day: same-day slots go in the first half hour. Say in one sentence what it is for, because "I need it looked at today" books faster than "I was wondering", and ask to go on the cancellation list if the wait is weeks. Dentists are the same: say it hurts and ask what they have sooner, and 111 can find an urgent NHS dentist if yours cannot see you within a few days. If there is nothing at all, ask which day the next slots are released and whether the duty doctor can ring you back, and remember a pharmacist can treat a lot of everyday things the same day.

Run most of your miles slow enough to hold a conversation, then add one faster session a week: six 2-minute efforts with 2 minutes of easy jogging between them. Progress comes from that weekly session plus the easy miles, not from chasing every run.

Run a full scan with the built-in tool (Windows Security, or Malwarebytes free on a Mac), let it remove what it finds and restart. A popup saying you are infected is usually the scam itself, so close the tab and never ring the number on it. If you did install something, disconnect from the internet and change your passwords from another device.
Salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes, so ice on a road melts even when the air is below 0C. It only works down to about -6C, which is why councils grit before the coldest nights.

Same answer, and it covers this — The things that work: same wake-up time every day, no caffeine after early afternoon, not much alcohol in the evening (it wakes you in the second half of the night), a cool dark room, and getting out of bed if you're awake for more than 20 minutes.

Same answer, and it covers this — The things that work: same wake-up time every day, no caffeine after early afternoon, not much alcohol in the evening (it wakes you in the second half of the night), a cool dark room, and getting out of bed if you're awake for more than 20 minutes. Screens off half an hour before bed and a short walk most days help more than any app. If you're worn out all day too, or it has gone on for weeks, ask a GP: they can check your bloods, and broken sleep plus no energy is worth ruling out.
Same answer, and it covers this: *The Last Dance* is the one that grips people who do not follow basketball, *Sunderland 'Til I Die* for football and *Welcome to Wrexham* if you want to enjoy one.

Same answer, and it covers this: Keep it to one minute and start when she is already sleepy, after a meal: let her sniff the brush and put it down beside her first, then do one stroke along her back, a treat, and stop while she is still happy.

Same answer, and it covers this: Maths and the sciences are learned by doing, not reading: work through the examples with the book open, then close it and do them again, then do past papers with the mark scheme next to you.
Same answer, and it covers this: Put the dates on a blank timeline you draw yourself, and group them around a few anchor events you already know.
Same answer, and it covers this: Seasons come from the Earth's 23.5-degree tilt, not from how close it is to the sun.
Same answer, and it covers this: Snow forms when water vapour freezes straight into ice crystals high in a cloud, and the crystals stick together as they fall.
Same answer, and it covers this: A hybrid or gravel bike with 32 to 40mm tyres, mudguard and rack mounts and disc brakes: those stop in the wet and take a pannier.
Same answer, and it covers this: Testing yourself is what makes things stick; rereading notes mostly feels productive without being so.

Same answer, and it covers this: The things that work: same wake-up time every day, no caffeine after early afternoon, not much alcohol in the evening (it wakes you in the second half of the night), a cool dark room, and getting out of bed if you're awake for more than 20 minutes.
Same answer, and it covers this: Water evaporates from the sea and land, rises and cools into clouds, falls as rain or snow, and runs back to the sea: the same water goes round and round.

Same answer, and it covers this: Work out how many nights you have first, then give each place at least three of them: a base with day trips beats a list of cities, because every move costs you half a day.
Same answer, and it covers this: I can't check the forecast from here, sorry - no live weather in me.

Same answer, and it covers this: Check the price history before believing a sale: CamelCamelCamel does it for Amazon and Keepa for many shops, and a "was £200" tag that was £200 for one week tells you nothing.
San Francisco (SFO) is 21km south, and BART to the city is 30 minutes for about $10. Oakland (OAK) is across the bay and often cheaper.

Say what they did and what it was worth to you: "Thank you for the time you gave me over the summer - I still use the list you wrote." One sentence of detail, one of what it meant, then stop; people keep the short ones.

Say what you bought, how long you have used it and what it did well, then the one thing that went wrong, with a fact: "the handle bent on the fourth use". Two lines of that beats a star rating, and a fair review is far harder for a shop to dismiss than an angry one. Put it where people look and the business will see it - the order page for an online shop, Google Maps for a cafe or restaurant, TripAdvisor for a hotel - and keep the order number and any photos.

Second-hand furniture is the best value there is, and charity shops and Freecycle are the places to look. Check for woodworm holes, sagging cushions and smoke smell, and measure your door and stairs before you collect anything big.

Second hand, for anything that is not safety-critical: a new car loses 15 to 20% in the first year and 40% by three, a new bike or laptop a third in a year, and a four-year-old version of either does the same job for half the money. Buy new where the warranty is the point (a washing machine, a boiler, a helmet, a car seat) and second hand everywhere else, checking it works before you pay.

See the GP or health visitor rather than changing their food: a child who is losing weight or not growing needs the reason found, and the growth chart is what shows it. While you wait, add calories where they are cheap - full-fat milk, cheese, yoghurt, peanut butter on toast, eggs - and add an extra snack rather than bigger meals. Ask for an urgent appointment if they are also weeing a lot or very thirsty, or having loose stools, because that is not a phase.

Sell it on the photos and the price: every side and the inside, washed, and the mileage, year and MOT date in the first line, priced against what the same car is actually selling for. Take a bank transfer and wait until the money is in your account - a screenshot of a payment is not a payment - before you hand over the keys; nobody genuine overpays and asks for the difference back, and nobody genuine sends a courier. Sign the V5C/2 slip over to the buyer, keep the rest of the log book, and tell DVLA online the same day or the tax and any fines stay yours.

Send an agenda 24 hours before with the decision you need, and start with it. If there isn't a decision to make, it's an email; if it's only updates, make it a 10-minute stand-up. Ending on "who does what by when" is what stops the same meeting coming back next week.

Set the reminder the moment you think of it, while the phone is in your hand: "remind me to ring the dentist at nine tomorrow" into Siri or Google, or an alarm labelled with the job. Anything with a date - dentist, MOT, renewal, a birthday - goes in the calendar now, with an alert the day before and a yearly repeat for birthdays. A job that takes under two minutes is quicker done than remembered, so do it there and then; for the rest, leave the note where you will trip over it - the door keys, the kettle, the front door.

Set a small standing thing rather than relying on finding time: a Sunday call, a voice note when you think of them, or a shared series you watch in the same week. Friendships survive distance on rhythm, not on long letters.

Share it from the app you already message each other in, because then it is live and they can see you moving. WhatsApp: open the chat, tap the + or the paperclip, choose Location, then Share live location and pick 15 minutes, 1 hour or 8 hours. iPhone: in Messages tap the person's name at the top, then Share My Location, or use Find My > People > Share My Location. Android: Google Maps > your picture > Location sharing > New share. It keeps updating until you stop it, so stop it when you are there.

Shirts are decided by the collar and the shoulders, so check those two before anything else: with the top button done, two fingers should slide inside the collar, and the shoulder seam should end on your shoulder bone rather than hanging past it. A sleeve is a cheap alteration and a shoulder is not, so buy for the shoulder and shorten the sleeve to the wrist bone. In a shop, raise both arms: if the cuffs ride up past your wrist or the front buttons gape, it is a size too small.

Shooting is one repeatable motion: elbow under the ball, a small dip, and push up from the legs so the ball leaves your fingertips with backspin. Start a metre from the hoop and make 20 in a row before you step back, then finish every session with 20 free throws while you are tired, because that is when games are decided. Keep the guide hand off the ball and do not let the shooting elbow drift out.

Short and often: ten to twenty minutes a day, most days of the week, beats one long session at the weekend. Whatever is awkward in it gets the first five minutes, and stopping while it is still going well is what keeps you coming back to it.

Simmer it uncovered for 10 minutes to reduce it, or blend a ladleful and stir it back in for body without flour. A handful of red lentils thickens a soup or stew in 15 minutes; for a stew, take the lid off for the last half hour.

Skates want a firmer lace than shoes and nothing left trailing: lace from the bottom, keep the foot snug through the middle, then pull the top two tight at the ankle so the heel cannot lift, double knot it, and tuck the ends inside the top of the boot. Do them up with thin socks or warm feet, because tight laces on cold feet is how toes go numb, and loosen the top two before you take them off.

Sleep is when the brain files the day's memories and clears waste, and the body repairs muscle and releases growth hormone. Most adults need seven to nine hours; if you are short for weeks, mood, concentration and immunity suffer before you feel sleepy.

Slow to about two-thirds of your usual speed and finish the ends of words, which is most of what 'clear' means. Pause at the full stops instead of running the sentences together, drop your voice a little at the end of a sentence rather than letting it rise, and if you are on a call, stand up - it makes the voice carry.

Small scratches are fine to keep cooking on. Once it is scratched through to the metal, or the coating is flaking or peeling into the food, replace the pan: you do not want flakes of coating in a meal, and a worn pan stops being non-stick anyway. Until then, keep metal tools, scouring pads and an empty pan on high heat away from it, because those are what scratch it.

Smoking is the single biggest cause of cancer and heart disease you can remove yourself: the tar and the carbon monoxide damage the lungs and the arteries, and about half of lifelong smokers die early because of it. There is no safe number of cigarettes - one to four a day still multiplies the heart risk - and the gains start within days of stopping, which is why quitting at any age is worth it.

Soil holds a plant up and holds the two things it needs: water around the roots and the minerals it cannot make itself, like nitrogen for leaves and phosphorus for roots. Plants can grow without it only if someone feeds them those minerals in water, which is how hydroponics works.

Soil is crushed rock mixed with rotted plant and animal matter, plus air, water and a vast number of microbes. The rotted part, humus, is what holds water and feeds plants, and it takes hundreds of years to build up an inch of it. A handful of healthy soil has more living things in it than there are people on Earth.
Some people genuinely run fine on six and it runs in families; if your days are fine, the number is not a problem to solve.
Something cold: an Eton mess, a lemon posset, or affogato - a scoop of vanilla ice cream with a shot of hot espresso over it.
Something easy: *Paddington 2* on film, *The Detectorists* on telly, or *The Thursday Murder Club* to read. None of them asks anything of you.

Something floats when it is less dense than the water it pushes aside, and sinks when it is denser. That is why a steel ship floats: it is mostly air inside, so the whole thing weighs less than the water it displaces.

Speech goes in double quotation marks, and a quote inside a quote takes single ones: 'She said "I am coming" and left.' The full stop or comma goes inside the closing mark when it belongs to the speech, and every new speaker starts a new line. Do not close the marks and carry the same speech on after a comma.

Stand up and move for two minutes every half hour, drink water, and put a bright light on your face — sleepiness at a desk is often boredom plus warm air. Do the hardest thing first and leave the reading for when you are flagging. If you are falling asleep at 9pm you need sleep, not coffee: an early night and an hour in the morning beats two hours of fighting it.

Start on the home keys and do not look down: left hand on a s d f, right hand on j k l and the semicolon, thumbs on the space bar, and cover your hands with a cloth if you keep peeking. Ten to fifteen minutes a day on a free drill site, typing real sentences rather than random letters, is enough to build it. Accuracy first and speed second, because a wrong key costs more time than a slow one: most people go from about 30 to 50 words a minute in a month of daily practice, and the last stretch comes from typing your own messages rather than the drills.

Start with the right hand alone on a song you already know, one note at a time, and the left hand on two or three chords to go with it: hands separately for the first few weeks is not cheating, it is how everyone does it. Twenty minutes a day, and a teacher for the first month so your hand shape is right.

Start with the router your provider gave you: if the speed at the router is fine and only the far rooms are slow, a mesh two-pack (about £80 to £150) beats a single expensive router. Put the main unit high and central, not in a cupboard or beside the microwave, and wire the second one back to the first with a cable if the walls are thick. Wi-Fi 6 is worth having if your devices are new; a wired connection is still the fastest answer for a TV or a desk.

Start with the short, loud, famous pieces rather than a symphony: Vivaldi's *Four Seasons*, the first movement of Beethoven's fifth, and Holst's *The Planets*. Then sit with one symphony whole - Beethoven's seventh, or Dvorak's *New World* - because the point of the long form is how it carries you from the first minute to the last. Films are a good way in too: most film scores are classical music that already has your attention.

Start with the treble clef only: the five lines are E, G, B, D, F from the bottom up and the four spaces spell FACE, and ten minutes a day of naming notes off a page is how it sticks. Then the same for the bass clef (Good Boys Do Fine Always on the lines), then note lengths and rests; a beginner tutor book and a free app like Tenuto cover it, and playing each note on the instrument as you name it is the part that makes it real.

Start with what is on the floor: pick it all up into one basket, take the cups and plates out to the kitchen and bin the rubbish, because clothes, cups and paper are most of a mess and that alone makes a room look tidy. Then wipe the one surface you use most - the worktop, the table or the bedside - and give the rest one room a day rather than all of it in a panic.

Start with a plunger over the plughole with a little water in the bowl, then undo the trap underneath (bucket first) and pull the gunk out. A kettle of hot water with a spoonful of bicarbonate and vinegar clears the rest; chemical drain cleaner is the last resort, not the first.

Start at about half of what you think you can manage and go every other day for the first two weeks - 20 minutes of walking or easy cycling is plenty, and the aim is to finish feeling you could have done more. Add about a tenth a week after that, and expect the second day to be sorer than the first, which is normal, while a joint that hurts is a stop. Give it six weeks before you judge it, because the habit and the tendons come back more slowly than the muscle.

Start from the money you need, not from what feels cheeky: add up your yearly costs (tools, insurance, software, travel, a phone) and the income you want to take home, add about a third on top for tax and quiet weeks, then divide by the days you can actually bill - about 220 a year if you work full time, and far fewer if you spend half the week on admin and chasing work. That gives a day rate; an hourly rate is that divided by six or seven. Then check three people doing the same job and put yourself in the middle. Quote a fixed price for a fixed job, not hours, and take a deposit of a third or a half up front.
Stephen King wrote The Shining, Misery and Carrie.

Stop preparing your reply while they are still talking: most of us are half a sentence ahead, and people can hear it. Then say back what you heard in one line - "so the meeting went badly and your boss blamed you" - before you offer anything, and ask one follow-up question instead of topping up with your own story. Sit still and leave a second of silence after they stop; that gap is usually where the real thing gets said.

Sunlight knocks electrons loose in a layer of silicon, and the layers either side are treated so they push those electrons one way, making a current; an inverter then turns it into the mains electricity the house uses. Output falls sharply in shade rather than a little, because a shaded cell blocks the flow through the whole panel.
Suzanne Collins wrote The Hunger Games.

Swap rather than erase: a yoghurt with fruit instead of a yoghurt with sugar in it, two squares of dark chocolate instead of a bar of milk, nuts or cheese instead of biscuits, and sparkling water or squash instead of fizzy drinks. Keep one sweet thing you really like, at a set time, rather than cutting sugar out completely - the all-or-nothing version is the one that collapses in a fortnight.

Swimming shoulder is nearly always too much front crawl too soon: halve the distance for two weeks, keep the pull long and relaxed rather than yanking each stroke, and add ten minutes to a swim instead of a whole extra session. Sharp pain, or an arm that will not lift, is a physio's job.
Take something small for the house, ask them questions about themselves, and don't try to impress — be interested and easy. Offer to help with the washing up; it's the cheapest way to be liked.

Take the FA's free online Laws of the Game course first, then book the basic referee course through your county FA - about 20 hours, a theory exam and a practical run-out - and join a local league. Ask for a mentor for your first games, arrive an hour early and blow the whistle loud: players test a quiet one.

Take the insoles out, stuff the toes with newspaper and stand them somewhere warm and airy to dry slowly - never on a radiator, in an airing cupboard or in the tumble dryer, because heat cracks leather and shrinks trainers. Change the paper after an hour or so and give them a full day, since half-dry is what makes them smell next. To keep the rain out next time, wax leather boots while they are clean and dry and spray fabric ones with a proofer.

Take the letter or email with the address and time, a printed copy of your CV, a pen and a notepad, and the name of the person you are meeting. Photo ID for the building, and ask at the desk for them by name.

Take two cards from different banks and a little local cash, and always pay in the local currency when the terminal offers to convert you - the "pay in pounds" option adds 3 to 5%. Use a bank ATM rather than a currency kiosk, and tell your bank you are travelling if it still asks.

Take everything out and put back only what you wore last year, in one go, with a bag for the charity shop by your feet. Then group by what you put on together - work, weekend, gym - rather than by type, and hang the long things at one end so the space under them takes a box. Fold knitwear and jeans flat on a shelf (hangers stretch shoulders), keep one hanger style so nothing snags, and turn the rail so the season's clothes are at eye level. Shoes paired on the floor, and one in-one-out rule from then on.

Take it: being cold or wet for an hour costs you far more than carrying something you never put on, and it is the bright morning that catches people out. Read the forecast for the hours you will actually be out, because the day's high is at two in the afternoon and the cold and the showers come later; under it a thin layer you can take off is worth more than a thicker coat, and if you will be standing about after dark, that is the case for the warm one.
Tea, most of the time: it's a better excuse to stop for five minutes. Coffee when you actually need to be awake in a hurry.

Teaching wants GCSEs at grade 4 or above in English and maths, plus a science for primary, then a degree in a subject schools teach, then a PGCE or a school-based training place - or a teaching apprenticeship, where you are paid while you train. Primary teaching takes any degree but checks your curriculum subjects, and secondary wants the subject you will teach.

Teething is dribble, red cheeks, chewing on a fist and waking more at night, and it comes and goes for a few days at a time. A high fever, a sore bottom or a baby who is really unwell is not teething, so treat that as illness. Give them something cold and hard to chew - a chilled teething ring, a clean cold flannel, a stick of cucumber in a mesh feeder - and rub the gum with a clean finger; sugar-free teething gel helps some. If they are distressed, children's paracetamol at the dose on the pack by their weight is fine from three months, and ibuprofen from three months and over 5kg. The first tooth usually arrives around six months, but anywhere from four to twelve is normal.
Tell me what you already like and I'll narrow it down.
Ten minutes: an Eton mess, bananas with ice cream and butterscotch sauce, or yoghurt with honey and toasted nuts. A good shop-bought tart with cream is a proper pudding too, and no one minds.

Ten minutes a day, same time, and let them read the same book twice - the second read is where the fluency comes from. Take turns (you read a page, they read a page), run your finger under the words, and stop while it is still going well. Let them choose from three books you have already picked, so the choice isn't a battle.
Ten-minute dinners: pasta with garlic, chilli and olive oil; eggs on toast; or cold rice fried with frozen veg, an egg and soy sauce. Tell me what is in the fridge and I will pick one.

That number moves every year and it depends where the line is drawn, so the body that publishes it is the one to quote: the national statistics site has it with the year, and the local council publishes its own for the area it covers.
That is the retailer's or the maker's to say, sorry, and prices and stock move daily. The model number is the thing to search, and I'll help you weigh what you find against a repair.
That's such sad news, I'm sorry. Some days will be heavier than others — I'm here if you want to talk about it, or about anything else.
That's a heavy feeling, and it's fair to have it. Be kind to yourself today.
That's lovely news.

The numbers on a tape are centimetres with millimetres marked between them, and the hook at the end is loose on purpose - about a millimetre of play, so it works hooked over an edge and butted against one. For anything inside a frame or a recess, measure from the 100 mm mark instead and take 100 mm off the reading, and the hook never matters. On a ruler the zero is at the very end, so check a new ruler against a tape once: some are trimmed a millimetre short.

The observable universe is about 93 billion light years across, and that is wider than its 13.8 billion year age because space itself stretched while the light travelled. The whole universe may be far larger again, and we cannot see past that horizon.
The ostrich is the biggest bird, at up to 2.7 metres and 150 kg, and it cannot fly. The wandering albatross has the widest wingspan, about 3.5 metres.

The parts of a sentence, in the order they turn up: a noun names something, a verb is what it does or is, an adjective describes it, an adverb says how the doing happened, and a pronoun stands in for the noun. 'The tired dog slept badly' - dog is the noun, tired the adjective, slept the verb, badly the adverb.

The roads decide it rather than the map, so I can't give you the miles and the time myself: put the two places into a map app and it'll have both; say what you're planning and I'll help with the rest of it.

The router is the box that joins your home network to the line from your provider and gives every device in the house its own address, so they can find each other and the internet. A modem is the part that speaks to that line; most homes now have both in one box, which is why turning it off and on fixes so much.

The rule that keeps a habit alive is never miss twice: one missed day is a rest, two is how a habit ends, so the day after a slip you do the smallest version — one minute, one page — and the chain starts again. Plan that now, before the bad week, and cut the habit to a size that survives it rather than resetting to the version you could only do while life was calm. A streak you broke is not a score you lost: keep the total visible, mark today, and carry on from there instead of waiting for a fresh Monday.

The Earth spins because the cloud of dust and gas it formed from was already turning, and nothing has braked it much in 4.5 billion years. The Moon's tides are slowly slowing it, so the day grows about a second longer every 50,000 years or so.
The Earth turns on its axis about once every 24 hours, so the half facing the Sun is in daylight while the other half is in night. The Sun itself does not go anywhere.

The Earth is about 12,742 km across (12,756 km at the equator, 12,714 km from pole to pole) and 40,008 km round the poles, a little less than the 40,075 km round the equator because the spin bulges it out. It weighs about 6 billion trillion tonnes.

The simplest signs are dark yellow pee, a dry mouth, tiredness and a headache: aim for pale straw urine, which is about six to eight glasses a day for most adults. Water, squash, tea and milk all count. If someone is confused, dizzy on standing, or has not peed for half a day, especially in the heat or with a bug, that needs a GP.

The solar system is the Sun and everything held in orbit around it by its gravity: eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets such as Pluto, and billions of asteroids and comets. It formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a cloud of gas and dust, and the Sun holds 99.8% of its mass.

The two things that lift a park player fastest are a first touch that keeps the ball close and being able to pass with both feet: twenty minutes of wall passes a few times a week does both. Then add scanning - a look over your shoulder before the ball arrives - so you know your next pass before it reaches you.
The African elephant is the biggest land animal: a big bull is about 3 metres at the shoulder and 6 tonnes.

The Lords is the unelected half: about 800 members, mostly life peers appointed for their expertise, plus 26 bishops and a handful of hereditary peers. It revises bills line by line and sends them back to the Commons, but it can only delay one for about a year, and it cannot touch a money bill at all.

The Milky Way is the galaxy we live in: a flat spiral of 100 to 400 billion stars, with the Sun about 26,000 light years from the centre. The pale band you see on a dark night is us looking along the disc from inside it.

The Moon only looks as if it follows you: it is about 384,000 km away, so driving a few kilometres barely changes its angle against the stars. Nearby trees and houses rush past, which makes the Moon seem to keep pace.

The Moon's gravity pulls the sea towards it, making a bulge on the near side and a matching one on the far side, and the Earth turns through both. That gives two high tides roughly 12 hours 25 minutes apart, and the Sun's pull makes spring tides bigger at full and new moon.

The Reformation was the break-up of western Christianity in the 1500s. Martin Luther nailed his 95 complaints about the Church to a church door in Wittenberg in 1517, printing spread them across Europe, and the countries that followed him became Protestant. About 1 hour start to finish. Line a pie dish with shortcrust pastry, put in filling that has cooled (a hot filling steams the base), brush the rim with egg and lay a lid on, pressing it down. Cut a hole in the middle for the steam, brush the top with egg, and bake at 200C (180C fan) for 30 to 35 minutes until the pastry is golden.

About 1 hour 20 minutes start to finish. Brown 500g of lamb or chicken with a chopped onion, 2 garlic cloves, a tablespoon of garam masala and a cup of yoghurt, then simmer 25 minutes. Part-cook 300g of basmati for 5 minutes, layer it over the meat with saffron milk and fried onions, and steam it covered on the lowest heat for 20 minutes - the layering and the steam are what make it a biryani rather than rice with meat on top.

About 1 hour 30 minutes start to finish, most of it rising. 500g strong white flour, 7g yeast, 325ml water and 10g salt mixed and left an hour, then stretched thin on a floured tray and baked as hot as the oven goes, 240C or more, on a tray or stone heated for 20 minutes first, for 8 to 10 minutes. Tomato and cheese go on lightly, because a heavy topping steams the base instead of baking it.

About 2 hours start to finish for a 2kg chicken. Work backwards from the meat: 20 minutes per 500g plus 20 at 190C (170C fan), so a 2kg bird is 1 hour 40 and then rests 15 minutes. Potatoes go in at 200C for 45 minutes, so start them 20 minutes after the bird; stuffing and pigs in blankets 25 minutes; the veg 10 minutes before the end; and make the gravy in the roasting tin while the meat rests.

About 3 to 4 hours for a tray of ice cubes in a freezer set to -18C, two hours for a thin layer of water in a shallow tray, and overnight for a deep tub. Smaller, flatter and colder all freeze faster, so an empty freezer beats a full one.

About 3 hours start to finish, most of it waiting. Mix 500g strong white flour, 7g yeast, 10g salt and 325ml warm water into a soft dough, knead 10 minutes until it is smooth and springs back, leave it covered until it has doubled (about an hour), shape it into a tin and prove it another hour, then bake 30 to 35 minutes at 220C (200C fan). Knock it out of the tin and let it cool before you cut it, or the crumb goes gummy.

About 5 minutes: once a day for a long-haired cat, twice a week for a short-haired one. The two brushes worth having are a metal-toothed comb for long coats and a rubber curry brush for short ones. Brush along the way the fur lies, in sections on the back legs and under the belly where the tangles start, and keep it short and calm. A cat that hates it does better with a few minutes after a meal than one long session.

About 5,500C at the surface and around 15 million C at the core, hot enough to fuse hydrogen into helium. That reaction is what makes the heat: the Sun's own gravity squeezes the hydrogen together, and the energy crosses space as light.

About 10 minutes start to finish. Mash 2 ripe avocados with the juice of a lime and a good pinch of salt, then stir in half a small onion, a chilli and a handful of coriander, all chopped small. Lime, not the stone, is what keeps it green, so press cling film onto the surface if it is waiting.

About 15 minutes start to finish. Cut everything before you start and cook in a single layer over the highest heat: hard vegetables 2 minutes, then soft ones and the meat, then sauce off the heat. Two batches beat one full wok, because a crowded pan steams instead of frying, and soy sauce goes in at the end so it does not burn.

About 15 minutes start to finish. Trim them and cut a cross in the base, then boil 6 to 8 minutes in salted water until a knife goes in easily - no longer, or they go grey and sulphury. Halve and fry them in butter with bacon or chestnuts for the last 3 minutes, which is what turns them from a duty into something people go back for.

About 20 minutes start to finish. Shape 500g of minced beef into four patties with nothing but salt and pepper - work it as little as you can - and cook them in a very hot dry pan 2 to 3 minutes a side, pressing once. Rest them a minute, then build with cheese, lettuce, tomato and something sharp like pickles or mustard; salt inside the mix draws the water out and makes them dry.

About 20 minutes start to finish. Soak 200g of flat rice noodles in hot water for 10 minutes, then stir-fry prawns or tofu in a very hot wok, push them aside and scramble 2 eggs in the space, and add the drained noodles with 2 tablespoons of tamarind or lime juice, 2 of fish sauce and 1 of sugar. Toss for a minute with beansprouts and peanuts; the pan must be hot or the noodles steam instead of frying.

About 40 minutes start to finish. Make a roux from 40g butter and 40g flour, whisk in 500ml milk and let it thicken, then stir in 150g mature cheddar off the heat. Stir it through cooked macaroni, top with more cheese and breadcrumbs and bake 20 minutes at 200C (180C fan); mustard powder in the sauce is what stops it tasting flat.

About 40 minutes start to finish. Soften a chopped onion and a red pepper in olive oil in a wide pan, stir in 2 chopped garlic cloves, a teaspoon of smoked paprika and 300g of paella or bomba rice for a minute, then add 900ml of hot stock and your chicken or prawns and simmer 18 minutes without stirring. Rest it 5 minutes off the heat under a tea towel: the crust on the bottom is the point, and stirring it is what stops it forming.

About a litre a day for a toddler, six to eight small cups (1.2 litres) for a 4 to 8 year old, and milk plus the water in food count; under six months milk is the only drink. Leave a beaker where they can reach it, refill it without a word, and offer sips at every snack - juice or squash is one small glass with a meal, not the drink they carry all day. Pale yellow urine and a wet nappy or a trip to the loo every few hours mean they are getting enough, and no wet nappy for eight hours or a drowsy, sunken-eyed child is a call to 111.

About 600 hours of real study to hold a proper conversation in Italian - around 2 years at an hour a day, or three times that at twenty minutes a day, which is why a little every day beats a long weekend. A holiday and small talk come far sooner: about 100 hours, which a twice-weekly evening class reaches in a year.

About 70p a pint, so a two-pint bottle is £1.25 to £1.45 and a four-pint one £1.70 to £2. The filtered and the organic sorts cost half as much again, and a corner shop is dearer than a supermarket. Those are 2025 prices, and they are the sort of thing that moves.

About 75 minutes start to finish. Soften a chopped onion, carrot and celery in oil for 10 minutes, add 500g mince and brown it hard, then a glass of milk or wine, a tin of tomatoes and a spoon of tomato puree. Simmer it 45 minutes to an hour, as low as it will go; the long cook is the difference between mince in tomato and a ragu.

About £100 to £200 buys a decent one: adjustable height and armrests, a seat you can set to the right depth, and a five-year guarantee on the gas strut. Cheaper chairs lose their height and wobble within a year; a used Steelcase or Herman Miller for the same money is the better buy if you can sit in it first.

About £50 is the usual gift from a friend, £100 or more from a close friend or when the two of you go as a couple; what you can afford beats the table you are given. Check the registry next, since most couples list what they actually need, and a contribution to the honeymoon beats a guess. If there is no list, money in a card with a real note is never wrong, and one small thing for their home lands better than something big and impersonal. Say yes to the registry rather than worry about being original.

Abraham Lincoln (1809-1865) was the American president through the Civil War, who issued the Emancipation Proclamation freeing the slaves in the rebel states in 1863. He was shot at Ford's Theatre in Washington in April 1865, days after the war ended.

Abs are the muscle across the front of your middle, and everyone has them - what shows is the layer of fat in front, so training makes them bigger and only a steady calorie deficit makes them visible. Sit-ups alone will not do it: two 20-minute sessions a week of squats, press ups (from the knees is fine) and a row with a bag or band, plus walking, is the whole of what works.

Accountancy asks for no fixed subjects, though maths and a numerical subject help, and there are three ways in: A-levels then an AAT or ACCA/ACA training contract, a degree then the same exams, or an accountancy degree apprenticeship where the employer pays for the exams. The exams are the qualification either way, so the route with the least debt is usually the apprenticeship.
Add one or two short sessions where you're a bit out of breath, and you get most of the benefit of longer workouts.
Add some plants — fair enough. What's stopped it happening so far?

Add water to his food - a splash in the bowl, or soak the kibble 10 minutes - and put a second bowl down somewhere he passes, filled to the brim, washed daily. A splash of unsalted broth or the water from boiled chicken makes it worth drinking, and a dog that has been running or is on dry food in warm weather needs more than the same dog on wet food.

Add another cloth on top of the first and keep pressing for ten minutes without lifting it to look - lifting is what starts it again. If it still comes through, or they go pale or dizzy, that is 999 or 911; otherwise it needs seeing today, so ring 111 for the nearest walk-in or A&E.

Adolf Hitler (1889-1945) led Nazi Germany from 1933 to 1945, started the Second World War, and ordered the Holocaust, in which about six million Jews were murdered along with Roma, disabled people and others. He killed himself in Berlin in April 1945 as the Soviet army reached the city.
Adult lessons at your local pool are the fastest route.

Adult lessons at your local pool are the fastest route: most run classes for complete beginners, often in small groups, and every instructor has taught adults who are frightened of the water. Book a course rather than one lesson, start in the shallow end with floats, and ask for an instructor who is used to nervous beginners. Nobody in an adult class is watching anybody else.

Adults get two to four colds a year, and they cluster when you are short of sleep, stressed or run down - that is not a weak immune system, it is the usual pattern. Sleep seven to nine hours, eat properly, wash your hands and take vitamin D in winter; see a GP if you are getting infections that need antibiotics more than a few times a year.
Advice is the noun, advise is the verb: give advice, and I'd advise you to wait. Both are said with a soft 's' in advice and a 'z' sound in advise, which is the memory hook: advi-s-e, it doe-s.

Agree the end date at the start of the visit, out loud: 'It's been lovely having you - shall we say Sunday?' Then keep one afternoon or evening of the stay for yourself, out of the house if that is easier, and say what you are doing rather than asking to be excused.

Aim for 30g of fibre a day, and most people get half that. The easy sources are beans and lentils (7 to 8g a tin), wholegrain bread and pasta, porridge oats, and fruit with the skin on. Increase it slowly and drink more water, or you will feel bloated for a week.
Air fryer: chicken thighs 25 minutes at 190C, chips 20 at 200C after a shake in oil, salmon 10 at 190C. It is a small hot oven, so one layer and a shake halfway, or it steams instead of browning.
'Please' in French is S'il vous plaît — say it roughly "seel voo PLEH". Learn it out loud a few times rather than reading it, and people will understand you even if the pronunciation is not perfect.
'Thank you' in Spanish is Gracias — say it roughly "GRA-thee-as". Learn it out loud a few times rather than reading it, and people will understand you even if the pronunciation is not perfect.

Albert Einstein (1879-1955) was the German-born physicist whose theory of relativity rewrote how we think about space, time and gravity, and whose E=mc2 links mass and energy. He won the 1921 Nobel Prize for work on light and the photoelectric effect, and left Germany for the United States in 1933.

Aldi is the cheapest of the big names: own-brand staples run roughly a fifth less than at Tesco or Sainsbury's, on a smaller range with few named brands. It is one of the cheapest places to do a full shop, though the range of brands is smaller, so anything specific may need a second stop.

Alexander the Great (356-323 BC) was king of Macedon who conquered the Persian Empire by the age of 30, marching as far as the Indus. He died in Babylon at 32, and his generals split the empire between them.

Alexander Graham Bell is credited with inventing the telephone and got the key patent in 1876, though Antonio Meucci had demonstrated a working voice device years earlier. Bell's patent, and the company built on it, is why his name stuck.
Alliteration repeats the opening sound of nearby words: slippery slope, sweet sixteen, the wild wind. It is about the sound, not the letter - "know nothing" is alliteration and "cute cat" is not.

Allow up to ten weeks for a standard application, and treat that as the planning figure rather than a promise: check the current wait on your government's passport site, because it moves with the season. If you need it sooner, that site sells a faster service and a premium appointment - pay for it, keep the reference, and do not book anything you cannot move until the passport is in your hand.

Almost nothing goes in outdoors: garlic and broad beans in a mild spell, and everything else indoors. Sow tomatoes and chillies under cover from late winter, chit early potatoes on a windowsill after Christmas, and order the seed you want for the year.

Almost always yes: frozen vegetables cost less than fresh for the same weight, because nothing has to be sorted, shipped soft or thrown away, and tinned beans, chickpeas and tomatoes are cheaper still. Frozen also wastes nothing, since you pour out what you need and the bag goes back. The one thing worth paying for fresh is a vegetable you are going to eat raw, where the texture is the point.
Also from that answer: Move on to the next thing.
Also from that answer: Write down the two or three things you want to raise.
Also from that answer: Check that water runs away rather than down the wall.
Amsterdam, though the government sits in The Hague.
