An octave is the gap between a note and the same note higher or lower, eight notes up the scale. It sounds like the same note because the frequency exactly doubles: A is 440 vibrations a second, the A above it 880.

An optical alarm has a light and a sensor in a chamber, and smoke drifting in scatters the light onto the sensor, which sets it off. An ionisation one passes a tiny current through the air and smoke changes it. Optical ones catch smouldering fires sooner and ionisation ones catch flames, which is why both are sold.

An orbit is the curved path one object takes around another because gravity pulls it inward while its sideways speed carries it forward. The Moon orbits Earth about once a month, and Earth orbits the Sun once a year at about 30 kilometres a second.

An orchid drops its flowers when that show is over, not because it is dying: cut the bare spike an inch above the second node, keep it in bright light out of direct sun, and give it cooler nights - around 16 to 18C - because the drop in temperature is what sets new buds. It usually takes a couple of months, and the old spike left on often flowers again from the same stem.

An organ is a part of the body made of several tissues working together for one job: the heart pumps blood, the lungs take in oxygen and the liver cleans the blood. Your skin is the largest organ, and organs work together in systems.
An ostrich runs at about 70 km/h over a short distance, and 40 to 50 km/h for longer, which is the fastest of any bird on land.
An ounce is about 28.35g, and there are 16 ounces in a pound.

An IP address is the number that identifies a device on a network, a bit like a house number: your router has one on the internet and gives each phone and laptop inside the house its own. The one inside changes when you reconnect, and the one on the internet changes when the router restarts, which is why nothing important - an email account, a bank - is tied to an IP address.
An IPA is a heavily hopped pale ale; the hops were originally there to keep the beer on the voyage to India.
An adjective describes a noun: a red bus, a tired dog, an honest answer. It sits before the noun or after 'is' - the bus is red.

An adult dog chews for a reason and teeth are not it: boredom, a walk that is too short, or being left alone longer than it can take. Give it a proper sniffy walk before you go out, leave a stuffed Kong or a long-lasting chew, and block off the sofa for a fortnight while the habit breaks. If it has just started in a dog that never did it, get its teeth and gums checked, because a sore mouth makes a dog chew to soothe it.
An adverb says how, when or where something happened: she sang loudly, we left early, he waited outside. Many end in -ly, but not all do (soon, well, fast).

An air purifier is worth it in a bedroom if you have hay fever, a cat or a sealed window: a HEPA filter on low all night changes how you sleep. Skip it for damp, which needs a dehumidifier, and check the replacement filters are cheap before you buy.

An alpaca is the smaller of the two, with a short blunt face and upright, banana-shaped ears, and it is kept for its fine wool. A llama is taller, with a longer head and long ears that curve back, and it is used as a pack animal and as a guard for a flock. Llamas are more independent and will face a fox; alpacas are easily spooked.

An americano is a double espresso (about 60ml) with about 120ml of hot water added, never the other way round: the water goes in after the shot because brewing onto hot water scorches the coffee and it turns bitter. Whole milk froths most easily and skimmed the least. With no steamer, heat the milk in a pan to just before it simmers and whisk hard for 20 seconds, or shake it in a lidded jar and give it 30 seconds in the microwave.

An atom is the smallest unit of an element, with a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons. Atoms join into molecules, and everything you can touch is made of them; they are mostly empty space.

An early-rising adult dog is usually on a habit, not a need: push his last walk and last meal an hour later, then leave him and keep the greeting flat until the alarm goes, because getting up to let him out teaches him that 5am works. Blackout curtains help in summer, and if the waking is new, a dog that suddenly cannot last the night should see the vet.

An eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up. In a solar eclipse the Moon passes between us and the Sun and covers it; in a lunar eclipse the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, which turns a dull red.

An electric shock happens when your body becomes part of a circuit: touching something live lets current flow through you to the ground, and it is the current, not the voltage alone, that does the harm. Switch the power off at the mains before touching anyone who is still connected, and call the emergency services if they are unconscious or burned.

An electric circuit is a complete loop that charge can flow round: a source such as a battery pushes current out through a wire, through a component such as a bulb, and back to the source. Break the loop with a switch and the current stops; in a series circuit everything shares one path, and in a parallel circuit each branch has its own.

An electric current is the flow of electric charge: in a wire, electrons drift along and carry energy from the battery or the mains to whatever is using it. It is measured in amperes (amps), and a current only flows round a complete circuit.
An espresso is a small, strong shot of coffee forced through finely ground beans by a machine, about 25 to 30ml.

An espresso is a small, strong shot of coffee forced through finely ground beans by a machine, about 25 to 30ml. A cappuccino is an espresso with equal parts steamed milk and thick foam, usually in a smaller cup than a latte.

Ancient Egypt gave us the 365-day calendar, papyrus paper, hieroglyphic writing, glass and the water clock, and Egyptian surgeons were stitching wounds, setting broken bones and removing cataracts by about 2500 BC. Their maths was practical: fractions, a base of ten, and the 3-4-5 triangle for squaring a corner.

Android: Settings > Display > Screen timeout. iPhone: Settings > Display & Brightness > Auto-Lock. Anywhere from 30 seconds to five minutes works and a minute is the usual compromise; if you set it long, keep a passcode on, because the screen protects everything else. A phone that locks while you read is usually a screen protector confusing the sensor. Laptop: Power & battery > Screen and sleep on Windows, Lock Screen on a Mac.
Andy Serkis plays Gollum: the voice and the motion capture in The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit films. He also second-unit directed parts of the Hobbit trilogy.

Anger is the body's alarm at a threat or at a goal being blocked: adrenaline speeds your heart and tenses your muscles, and the emotional part of the brain reacts before the thinking part has caught up. It usually passes in minutes; slow breathing and naming what set it off help it pass sooner.

Animal hide, mostly cow, that has been tanned: the skin is cleaned, then treated with tannins or chromium so the protein stops rotting and stays soft. Suede is the same skin buffed on the inside face.

Ankles that puff up through the day and go down overnight are usually fluid pooling from sitting or standing a long time, hot weather or a long flight. Walk about every hour, put your feet up above hip height and cut back on salt. Ankles puffy on both sides can also come from a tablet or from the heart. Ring 111 today if an ankle is hot, red and spreading, or painful on just one side, and see a GP if it is one leg only, comes on suddenly, or comes with breathlessness.
Another one from it: Bring one thing.
Another one from it: Check it once a year and replace anything past its date.

Antarctica is technically the largest desert, because a desert is defined by how little it rains. The Sahara is the largest hot desert, at about 9 million square kilometres, roughly the size of the United States.
Antarctica is the coldest place on Earth: Vostok Station recorded -89.2C in 1983. The coldest place with people living in it is Oymyakon in Siberia, where winter temperatures reach about -50C.

Anwar Ibrahim is the prime minister of Malaysia: in office since November 2022, after decades in opposition. The king, whose crown rotates every five years between the state rulers, is the head of state.
Any one of those is most of what "healthier" means, one that sticks beats three that don't, and two weeks is long enough to know whether it fits your week.
Any time!

Anything with a plug, a battery or a cable is electrical waste and can't go in the bin. A shop that sells you a new one has to take the old one back, like for like, and the tip has a small-appliance skip. Wipe a phone or laptop and take the SIM and memory card out first; a charity shop or a repair cafe can make use of one that still works.
Anything without words works best for focus: lo-fi hip hop, film scores by Hans Zimmer or Ólafur Arnalds, or ambient Brian Eno. Words compete with reading in a way that instrumentals don't.

Apples are ready from August for the earlies and October for the keepers: cup one and twist - ripe fruit comes away with the stalk on and the pips inside are brown. Pick in dry weather, use the windfalls first, and store only perfect fruit, in a cool dark place, not touching.

Apply through your council's school admissions service, not to the school: the deadline is 31 October for a secondary place and 15 January for a primary or reception place, and you list several schools with the one you most want first. An application after the deadline is only looked at once everyone else has been placed, and if you are refused you appeal to the school's admission authority, which is usually the council.
Are you walking for fitness or for a particular distance?
Are dogs carnivores — that's the one I'd take, and either is fine.

Aristotle (384-322 BC) was a Greek philosopher who studied under Plato and taught Alexander the Great, and who set out logic, biology and politics in a way Europe used for 1,500 years. He taught that the Earth sat at the centre of the universe, which held astronomy back until Copernicus.

As a rough guide, an adult dog eats about 2% of his body weight a day: 400g of food for a 20kg dog, split into two meals. Use the bag or tin as a starting point, then go by condition: you should feel ribs easily but not see them, and see a waist from above. Puppies need more, and a vet can weigh him and give you an exact amount.

Ask the store, not the app: Apple and Google both refund accidental and unwanted purchases themselves, and the app can only point you back at them. Use the store's report-a-problem page, name the order and say whether a child made the purchase, and ask within 14 days. If the store says no, a card chargeback is the next step.

Ask to see their registration card before they start and check the number on the register yourself: Gas Safe for anything on gas, NICEIC or NAPIT for electrics, and the competent person scheme for a builder. On the Gas Safe card the photo and the licence number should match the person in front of you, and the card lists which work they are registered for - boilers, cookers and fires are separate tickets. A gas certificate signed by somebody who is not on the register is not worth the paper.

Ask what the first three months look like, why the last person in the role left, and what the team is like on a bad week. Then one for them: "What do you enjoy about working here?" It is the easiest question in the room and it changes the tone.

Ask your manager in writing for a private room with a lock, a chair and a socket - not the toilet - and breaks long enough to pump, roughly every three hours. In the UK you must not be treated worse for it, and your employer has to give you somewhere to rest. A double pump halves the time. No fridge? A cooler bag with two ice packs keeps milk cold to the end of a shift, and labelled bottles stop any mix-up.

Ask about the thing you are both already in the middle of - the queue at the kettle, the meeting you have just left, the weather on the walk in - then give one detail of your own, so it is a swap and not an interview. "Did the bike get fixed?" is worth more than any clever line, and leaving after a couple of minutes is normal.

Ask for one named job on a named day - "can you do bathtime on Tuesday and Thursday?" - rather than for more help in general, which is too vague to say yes to. Then count the work nobody sees: the appointments, the clothes that keep getting too small, the food that has to be thought about before it can be cooked. Write it down for a week and split it by whole areas, so one of you owns bedtime and the other owns food and washing. If your partner says the split is fair and the list says otherwise, the list is the thing to talk about rather than each other, and a few sessions with Relate can hold that conversation if it keeps going round.

Ask for one defined sum and say when you will pay it back, in a message rather than at the end of a meal: 'could you lend me £400 until the 28th, and I'll pay £100 a week'. Say what happens if you miss one, and ask whether they can afford it, because a loan between family is where the row starts. Put it in writing, and for a big sum sign a simple note with the amount, the date and the repayments: it protects both of you. Never borrow it for spending.

Ask for the list in order, in writing: "Which two of these are the priority this week, and which can wait?" Work the top one, and send a one-line note when a new ask pushes something down: "Taking this on, so the other thing moves to Friday." A manager who cannot name two priorities has told you something; keep that email.

Ask for it back in writing today, naming the amount and the date: "I paid the £400 invoice on Tuesday and sent it again on Thursday by mistake - please can you refund the second one." Most people and most trades refund or credit it once they are asked plainly, and the message is the date you can prove. If they will not, ask your bank to recall the payment while it is recent and a money claim online takes the rest; never pay anyone who offers to get it back for you.

Ask four or five people, not a crowd, and fix the next date before the first meeting ends - a club that meets every six weeks at a set day keeps going, one that waits for everyone to be free does not. Pick short books to begin with, let whoever chose it lead for ten minutes, and bring one question rather than a summary: "who did you believe?", "what would you have done?". Rotate who chooses, keep food simple, and let people come having only read half. To join one instead of starting one, ask at the library and the independent bookshop: both keep a list, and a group of five usually has room.

Ask it the weather, set a timer or an alarm, play the radio, add something to a shopping list, or put a question to it - say "Alexa" first, then the ask. To set one up, plug it in, open the Alexa app and sign in, and it finds the speaker and joins your wifi; the app's Things to Try lists the rest, and the button on top mutes the microphone.

At the first meeting, split the work in writing with names and dates, and pick one person to hold the whole thing together. Swap drafts before the deadline so no one is the bottleneck. If someone does nothing, tell them early what you need by when; chasing at the end is where the resentment comes from.

Athelstan, crowned in 927, is usually counted as the first king of a united England: he was a grandson of Alfred the Great and took York from the Vikings that year. Before him there were kings of Wessex, Mercia and Northumbria rather than of England.
Aubergine gluten-free pasta: fry cubed aubergine in plenty of olive oil for 10 minutes until soft, add garlic and a tin of tomatoes, simmer 10 minutes and toss with the gluten-free pasta.
Augusta, not Portland.

Augustus (63 BC-14 AD) was the first Roman emperor: Julius Caesar's adopted heir, who took the name Augustus when he came out on top of the civil wars in 27 BC and ruled for forty years. He kept the forms of the republic while holding the power of a king, and his reign opened the two centuries of peace Romans called the Pax Romana.
Austin, not Houston or Dallas.

Baby-led weaning means skipping spoon-fed purees and letting them pick up soft finger food themselves from about six months. It is safe at that age and no more of a choking risk than spoon feeding, and you do not have to choose: most people end up doing a mix of both.
Back to it: Find what starts it and block that first: a curtain over the window he watches, or the post put through a box away from the door.
Back to it: For Japan the window is Late March to April for the blossom, or October to November for the autumn colour.

Back to it: For cooking: *MasterChef: The Professionals* is the one about the cooking itself, *The Great British Bake Off* for baking and *Saturday Kitchen* for a lazy morning, all of them long-running and easy to start anywhere.
Back to it: Grandparents usually want to help and hate guessing, so a short 'could you do Tuesdays, and we do baths' beats hinting.
Back to it: Harmony is two or more notes sounding together, usually as the chords under the melody.
Back to it: Its wide loops move a lot of air, which a flat or a ball whisk does not, so it is the one for meringue; it is no good for a thick mixture - that is a wooden spoon's job.
Back to it: MPs vote on the laws, question ministers - prime minister's questions is the Wednesday set-piece - and sit on select committees that go through a department's work line by line.

Back to it: Magma cools to igneous rock such as granite or basalt; wind and water wear any rock into grains that settle, get squashed and cement into sedimentary rock such as limestone and sandstone; heat and pressure bake or squeeze rock into metamorphic rock such as marble.
Back to it: Our Milky Way holds 100 to 400 billion stars and is about 100,000 light years across, and there are billions of galaxies beyond it, most with a supermassive black hole at the centre.
Back to it: Read the questions before the passage, so you know what to look for.
Back to it: Screens off half an hour before bed and a short walk most days help more than any app.
Back to it: A mineral is a natural solid with a definite chemical make-up and a crystal structure, formed in the earth without anything living making it: quartz, calcite and iron ore are minerals.
Back to it: A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 that divides only by 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and so on.
Back to it: A tailor can usually save it.

Back to it: A car engine burns fuel in short bursts inside a cylinder: a piston slides down sucking in air and fuel, the spark or the heat of compression sets it alight, the bang drives the piston back, and the exhaust is pushed out before it starts.
Back to it: A fossil forms when a dead animal or plant is buried quickly and its hard parts are slowly replaced by minerals from the surrounding rock over thousands of years.

Back to it: A life cycle is the stages a living thing goes through from one generation to the next: a frog goes egg, tadpole, froglet, adult, and a butterfly goes egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly.
Back to it: A magnet is an object that produces a magnetic field, which pulls on iron, nickel and cobalt and pushes or pulls on other magnets.

Back to it: Ask for a day pass or a week trial before you sign, look at the changing rooms as well as the equipment, and work out the price per visit rather than per month: 40 a month is cheap at three visits a week and dear.
Back to it: Tell me what you already like and I'll narrow it down.
Back to it: The Earth turns on its axis about once every 24 hours, so the half facing the Sun is in daylight while the other half is in night.

Back to it: The things that work: same wake-up time every day, no caffeine after early afternoon, not much alcohol in the evening (it wakes you in the second half of the night), a cool dark room, and getting out of bed if you're awake for more than.

Back to it: Two truths and a lie: each of you says three things about yourself, two true and one made up, and the rest guess the lie - a point for each correct guess, and you tell them the answer before the next person goes.

Back to it: Waking in the small hours is usually the mind, not a sleep problem: keep the room dark, don't check the clock, and after about twenty minutes get up and sit somewhere dim until you are sleepy, so the bed stops being the place you lie.
Back to it: Warm company stops blue going cold: mustard, tan leather, brass, a warm white on the walls, and one wooden thing.
Back to it: Water evaporates from the sea and land, rises and cools into clouds, falls as rain or snow, and runs back to the sea: the same water goes round and round.

Back to it: Water left in a glass disappears over days because the fastest molecules escape into the air; warmth, wind and a larger surface make it happen faster, which is why washing dries on a line.
Back to it: Work out how many nights you have first, then give each place at least three of them: a base with day trips beats a list of cities, because every move costs you half a day.

Bacteria are single-celled living things, so small that millions fit on a pinhead. Most are harmless or useful, from the ones in yoghurt to the ones in your gut, and a few cause illness; unlike a virus, a bacterium can grow and divide on its own.
Bake a traybake the day before the party - chocolate or lemon, one tin feeds 15 in squares - then add fairy cakes, jam tarts and sausage rolls. That covers a birthday tea without any decorating.

Bake fillets at 200C (180C fan) for 12 to 15 minutes - done when the thickest part flakes into opaque white, so keep it a minute short rather than a minute long - or fry them skin side down in a hot pan for 4 minutes, then 2 on the other side.

Baking soda is pure bicarbonate of soda and needs an acid - buttermilk, lemon, yoghurt - to make something rise. Baking powder is bicarbonate with the acid already mixed in, so it works with plain liquid and is what most cake recipes mean. To swap them, use about three times as much baking powder as soda, and never the other way round.

Bank statements and utility bills count because they carry your name, address and a date, and most places want one from the last three months. A paper copy beats a phone screenshot. If everything is in someone else's name, ask the council for a council tax letter or order a certified copy of the electoral roll. Check the list that office accepts before you go.

Barking is usually the alarm going off, so find what starts it and block that first: a curtain over the window he watches, or the post put through a box away from the door. Then reward the quiet - a treat the moment he stops - and don't shout, because to a dog shouting sounds like you joining in. If he barks for hours when he is left, that is the being-left problem rather than the barking one.

Basil, mint, chives and parsley are the ones that work indoors: a sunny windowsill, away from the draught of a window you open, and water when the top of the soil is dry rather than to a schedule. Mint needs its own pot or it swamps everything next to it. The supermarket pot dies because it is several seedlings crammed into one small pot, so either split it into a bigger one or expect two or three weeks and buy small plants from a garden centre instead.

Bathe it with cool water or salt water, dry it and keep the dog from licking it, and get the vet to look today if it is deep, gaping, bleeding steadily or it will not put weight on it. Check between the toes and across the pad for glass or a grass seed, since those keep a small cut open. A nick that has stopped bleeding: bathe it twice a day, keep it dry and covered on walks, and ring the vet if it goes red, swollen or smelly.

Bathe it with cooled boiled water on cotton wool, one wipe per eye, working from the inside corner out, and use a fresh piece each time. A clear watery eye in an otherwise happy animal often settles in a day or two; yellow or green discharge, a squint, pawing at it or a cloudy eye needs the vet today - an ulcer gets worse fast and drops made for a human eye can make it worse still.
Bats are not blind: they see about as well as a cat in dim light. What makes them special is echolocation, squeaks too high to hear that bounce back and tell them where things are in the dark.

Be flexible on dates and airports and book eight to six weeks ahead for Europe, longer for long-haul. Tuesday and Wednesday flights are usually cheapest, and luggage fees often close the gap between budget and full-service airlines.

Beans are 10 to 16 weeks from seed, the dwarf sorts quickest. The others, from seed: salad leaves and radishes 4 to 6 weeks, beetroot 10 to 12, carrots and runner beans 12 to 16, peas 12 to 14, courgettes 10 to 12, sweetcorn 12 to 14, tomatoes 16 to 20 from sowing (12 to 16 from planting out), cabbages and broccoli 16 to 20, parsnips 22 to 24, and leeks or onions 20 to 24. Garlic takes about eight months from an autumn clove, and strawberries fruit the summer after planting. The seed packet is the tie-breaker, because a fortnight either way is normal.
Beijing.
Being on the same page means agreeing about what you are doing. Are you trying to get someone to agree with you?
Beloved is by Toni Morrison.
Ben Nevis is the highest, at 1,345 metres (4,413 ft).

*Animal Farm* by the same author first, because it is one evening's reading and the same argument. Then *Brave New World* by Aldous Huxley, and *Fahrenheit 451* by Ray Bradbury for the shortest of the three.
*Arrival* is the smartest one, *Apollo 13* the most tense, and *Interstellar* the biggest. For something lighter, *Galaxy Quest* is a lovely comedy about actors on a spaceship.
*Before Sunrise* (two people talking all night), *When Harry Met Sally* (the funny one) or *Pride & Prejudice* (2005) for the longing and the costumes.
*Free Solo* for one man on a cliff, *The Jinx* for a case that turns, and *Planet Earth II* for the pictures. None of the three needs any background to enjoy.

*How I Built This* has the founder of one company telling how it actually started, in an hour, and it is the most useful one if you are thinking of starting something. *The Bottom Line* puts three bosses in a room and asks them the same question, and *StartUp* follows one company from the first day, mistakes included.

*Illmatic* by Nas for words and storytelling, *The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill* for singing and soul, and *good kid, m.A.A.d city* by Kendrick Lamar for a whole album that tells one story. Read the words once on paper - rap is the one pop form where the writing rewards a second pass.
*Klara and the Sun* (what makes someone human), *The Remains of the Day* (a whole life looked back on) or *Sapiens* if you would rather have ideas than a story.

*Pink Moon* by Nick Drake for voice and guitar alone, *Blood on the Tracks* by Bob Dylan for words, and Fleet Foxes' first album if you want harmony. Folk is words and one instrument, so start with one person and a guitar.
*Rumours*, still. It is the one album where every song is the good one.
*Schitt's Creek* starts daft and gets warmer, *Derry Girls* is sharp and short, and *The Detectorists* is gentle comedy.
*Schitt's Creek* is the safe pick: short episodes, funny from the first series. *Derry Girls* if you want something sharper, or *Paddington 2* if it's a film tonight rather than a series.

*Serial* series one is where to start: one murder, a year of reporting, and the reason everyone else started making them. Then *Casefile* (calm, one case an episode), *Criminal* (short, strange cases, less grim) or *The Teacher's Pet* if you want one long story done properly.

*Song Exploder* takes one song and has the person who made it pull it apart, track by track, in 20 minutes. *Desert Island Discs* is the long interview with the music choices in it, and *All Songs Considered* is the weekly new-music one.

*Stardew Valley* is the one: farm, fish, befriend the village, nothing timed against you, and it runs on almost anything. *Hades* if you want ten-minute runs with a fight in them, or *Unpacking* for an evening of something quiet.

*The Daily* takes one story a day and reports it properly in 20 minutes, *Today in Focus* does the same from a British side, and *The Briefing Room* explains one running story with the people who know it. For business, *The Bottom Line* puts three chief executives in a room and asks them the same question.
*The Detectorists*, *Mortimer & Whitehouse: Gone Fishing* or *The Great British Bake Off*: all warm, low-stakes and easy to follow when you're tired. Nothing in them needs your full attention.
*The Flatshare* (funny and warm), *Beach Read* (a bit sharper) or *Pride and Prejudice* if you want the classic.
*The Haunting of Hill House* is creepy rather than gory, *Bird Box* is fast and tense, and *The Shining* if you want the classic.
*The Silent Patient* and *Gone Girl* both turn on a twist; *The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo* if you want the reveal to make you cry as well.
*The World at War* is the one people still cite, *Time Team* for digging and Lucy Worsley's series for the social side. All three are old and none of them feel dated.

*The Blade Itself* by Joe Abercrombie for the same grim humour with fewer characters to keep track of, *The Name of the Wind* for one voice telling its own story, or *The Priory of the Orange Tree* if you want dragons in a single volume.
*Wavelength* and *Just One* are the same idea for people who do not like arguing, and for a big party *Werewolf* or *Mafia* needs nothing but a deck of cards.

Bin anything already opened - flour, rice, oats, cereal, raisins, dried fruit - because the larvae come in the packet, and put the rest into airtight jars. Wipe the shelves with hot soapy water right into the corners and along the door seal, leave a bay leaf or a few cloves out, and do a second round a fortnight later to catch what hatched.

Birds head off in autumn because the insects, worms and berries they live on run out as the days shorten; the trip costs a lot of energy but beats starving. They find their way by the sun, the stars, landmarks and the Earth's magnetic field, and many come back to the same nest site.

Black smoke is too much fuel, blue smoke is burning oil, and thick white smoke that doesn't clear is coolant getting into the engine. A puff of white on a cold morning is just steam and is normal; the other three want a garage soon.

Black tie for a man means a dinner jacket, black trousers with a satin stripe, a white dress shirt with a proper bow tie, and black shoes; for a woman it means a long or cocktail dress, not a business suit. A dark suit with a normal tie is the fallback if you don't own the rest, and it's much better than staying home.

Bleach lifts your own colour out rather than adding blonde, so a dark head comes up orange first and needs a second session weeks later, or a toner, to finish it: a toner is a weak purple or blue dye that cancels the yellow and lasts a few weeks. Roots lift fastest in the scalp's heat, so check them at 20 minutes and never go past the packet time, with a strand test on a hidden piece before the rest. Never bleach over henna or a box dye with metallic salts, which can turn hair green and burn, and never bleach hair that is already lightened. For a full change or highlights, a salon costs less than the repair after a home job.

Bleeding when you brush is usually gum disease and it is fixable: brush all the way to the gum line for two minutes twice a day, clean between the teeth with floss or interdental brushes once a day, and use a soft brush rather than pressing harder. See a dentist or hygienist - a scale and polish plus that routine usually stops it in a few weeks. Left alone it is the main cause of lost teeth in adults.

Blocking stops them finding you, messaging you or seeing anything you post: open their profile, tap the ... menu, then Block. They are not told, and you can undo it in Settings > Blocked. Unfriending is the smaller step - Friends, then Unfriend - which stops the posts but still lets them message you.

Blot, don't rub, with kitchen paper, then dab with cool water and a drop of washing-up liquid from the outside in, and blot dry with a towel; repeat until nothing more comes up. Work in small patches and never soak it, or the backing and underlay stay damp and start to smell. Grease wants neat washing-up liquid first, and a stain that survives all that is a job for a carpet cleaner.

Blot it at once, don't rub, then run cold water through the back of the fabric so the mark comes out the way it went in. Work in a drop of washing-up liquid with your fingers, leave it five minutes and rinse. If it has dried in, soak it in oxygen bleach (whites and colourfast things only) and wash it at the hottest the label allows. No iron or tumble dryer until the mark has gone, because heat sets it.
Blueberries: stirred into pancake or muffin batter, or simmered 5 minutes with a spoon of sugar and a squeeze of lemon for a compote that keeps a week.

Boil it in unsalted water for 6 to 8 minutes - salt toughens it - or grill it, turning it now and then, for 10 to 12 minutes until the kernels start to char. In the microwave a cob takes 3 to 4 minutes on full power. Butter, salt and pepper, and it needs nothing else.

Bones in the leg take the longest: about 12 weeks for a shin or ankle, and a thigh bone can be four months or more. The cast usually comes off before the bone is fully strong - it is the X-ray at each clinic visit that decides - and the muscles and joint need a few weeks after that to feel normal, so build back slowly rather than testing it early.

Book the coach two or three weeks ahead: the cheapest seats are the first to go and a seat bought on the day can cost two or three times as much. Pick the seat when the site offers it, be at the stop 15 minutes early because coaches leave on time, and take the luggage rules seriously - one case in the hold is usual and anything extra is paid for at the stop.

Book as early as you can: advance singles usually go on sale about twelve weeks ahead and are the cheapest fares. Travelling off-peak (in the UK, after 9:30am) avoids the peak price, a railcard pays for itself in a couple of trips, and a split-ticket site can cut the fare further by buying the same journey as two shorter tickets.

Book a proper meeting and bring evidence: what you delivered this year, with numbers, and what the same job pays elsewhere. Then ask for a specific figure with the reason attached: "I'd like to move to 34,000, given I've taken on the reporting and the last two hires came in at that level." Ask when you will hear back, and follow up in writing.

Book a sight test: about twenty minutes, and the only thing that says whether you need glasses and what prescription - nothing you do at home settles it. The blur usually has a name: eyes that ache after a chapter in bed are the focusing muscles tired from close work and dim light, and a distance that has gone soft is short sight, which a pair from the test sorts. It is free on the NHS if you are under 16, over 60, diabetic or a close relative has glaucoma, and £25-£45 on the high street otherwise. Sudden blur in one eye, floaters, flashes or a curtain across the sight is an A&E or optician-today job.

Book a travel clinic or a pharmacy that does travel jabs four to six weeks before you fly: some courses are two or three doses a month apart, and most of them take a fortnight to work. Thailand and most of Asia, Africa and South America want hepatitis A and typhoid for almost any trip. Yellow fever is a certificate some countries in Africa and South America ask for on arrival, and malaria tablets are a separate decision about the risk in the area you are actually staying in. Check the country on the NHS Fit for Travel or the GOV.UK travel advice pages - that is the list that counts - and keep the record card with your passport.

Boredom is the brain asking for something engaging: with no clear goal it looks for novelty or meaning, and time feels slow because little is being laid down as a memory. It is not a flaw, and letting yourself be bored for a bit often restarts curiosity and ideas.

Both work for somebody, so it comes down to what you would miss if you had to give the other one back, and which of them fits the week you actually have. Write down what each one is for before you compare what they cost, and the one you have to keep justifying is usually the answer.

Both, and the food decides most of it: lift twice a week to keep the muscle you have while the fat comes off, and add cardio for the burn, so two of each beats either alone. If you can only keep one, keep the lifting, because muscle is what a diet takes first and it is what keeps you burning a little more all day.
Both are right: grey is the British spelling and gray the American one, and neither is a mistake. Pick the one your reader expects and keep it the same through a piece of writing.

Both are correct; just be consistent. British English uses colour, organise, centre and travelled, and American English uses color, organize, center and traveled. Most word processors can set the dictionary to the one you want.

Brambles come back from the crown and from any tip that roots where it touches the soil, so cutting the tops only makes them shrubby. Cut the stems to the ground, dig the crown out with a fork and pull up the tips that have rooted further out, and do it before they flower so nothing seeds. Then keep cutting the regrowth every few weeks through the season: a bramble starved of leaves runs out of root by the second year.
Bramley for cooking, Cox or Braeburn for eating: a Bramley is sharp and falls apart, and an eater stays in pieces. A bag of 'cooking apples' at the market is a Bramley.
Breaking the ice just means getting a first conversation going with someone you do not know well. Is this a new job, a date, or a room full of strangers?
Brian Cox's *The Planets* is the easy way into space, *Forces of Nature* for how the world works, and *Chemistry: A Volatile History* if you would rather have the story of the ideas.

Bricklaying mortar is 5:1 building sand to cement, or 4:1 for a wall that takes the weather, mixed soft and buttery rather than wet. A 25kg bag of cement with five bags of building sand lays roughly 150 bricks or 40 blocks, so measure the wall first - a 10m single-skin wall 1m high is about 600 bricks. Pointing and rendering are both a 4:1 mix, and a footing or a small concrete base is 6 parts ballast to 1 of cement.
Brilliant. Really pleased for you.

Bring something with protein and fibre in it - nuts, fruit, yoghurt, oatcakes, cheese - and keep it in your drawer or the office fridge, so the 3pm vending machine is not the decision. It is cheaper too: a £1.20 snack a day is about £250 a year. Water in a bottle on the desk covers most of what people mistake for hunger.

Bring the things that make the room theirs and give you something to do together: a framed photo, a small photo album, their own blanket or cardigan, a radio or a favourite mug, and a newspaper or a box of their usual sweets. Check what the room already has and what the home allows before you buy anything, and take one thing a visit rather than a car load - it is the visits, not the stuff, that make the room theirs.

Bring a pan of water to a bare simmer with a splash of vinegar, stir it into a gentle whirlpool and slide the egg in from a cup. 3 minutes gives a soft yolk; lift it out with a slotted spoon onto kitchen paper.

Brunch is one thing on the table people help themselves to: scrambled eggs on toast with tomatoes and something green, a frittata cut into wedges, or pancakes with fruit and yoghurt. For more than four, baked eggs in one dish with bread beside it - fried eggs for eight are cold before the last one is done.

Brush the dust off and wipe them with a barely damp cloth, then dry them away from a radiator, because heat cracks leather. Work a thin coat of cream polish in with a cloth in small circles, leave it ten minutes, brush it off and buff hard with a soft cloth - several thin coats beat one thick one. For boots that see rain, finish with a wax polish rather than a cream, and give them a fresh coat at the start of every winter.

Brush them, with a pet toothpaste and a finger brush, at the back first and only for a few seconds to start - human toothpaste is not for animals. Brown tartar and bad breath mean a vet check: a scale and polish is what stops gum disease, and chewing is not a substitute for it.

Budget for the deposit (five weeks' rent, and it has to be held in a protection scheme), the first month up front and the bills, then have ready: photo ID and proof of address, three months of payslips or a guarantor, and a reference from a previous landlord. In England most letting agent fees are banned, so you should only pay rent, the deposit and a holding deposit. Read the tenancy agreement before you sign it.

Build it from a want, a wall and a turn: what the character wants in the first scene, what stops them, and the one thing that changes the plan. A plot that sounds far-fetched is usually missing the practical steps - the key, the alibi, the person who noticed - so make the method vague and the aftermath exact: the cup half drunk, the dog still alive, the wrong person blamed. If you want a villain's plan to be believable, give them one small mistake a careful reader could spot on a second read, and let a minor character be the one who spots it.

Buildings insurance covers the structure and comes with the mortgage; contents covers what's inside and is optional but usually worth it. Insure for the cost of rebuilding or replacing, not the market value, and check the single-item limit before assuming a bike or laptop is covered. A machine that has simply worn out is not a claim - that is a repair - while accidental damage cover or a home emergency policy is what pays for a leak or a boiler that has packed in.
Business is busy-ness gone crooked: b-u-s-i-n-e-s-s.
Butter and sugar creamed first, then eggs a little at a time, then flour folded in gently, and a spoon of milk if the mix is stiff.
Buttercream or icing between the layers and on top is all a party cake needs: spread it warm, chill the cake first, and keep it plain or add a handful of fruit or sweets.
Buttercream is 100g soft butter to 200g icing sugar, beaten with a splash of milk.

Buy the size you are now, not the one you were: two pairs of trousers and three tops that fit at the shoulder and the waist cover most of a week, and a straight cut or a little stretch forgives more than a fitted one. Measure yourself once with a tape over what you wear underneath and buy to those numbers, because the label varies by shop by as much as two inches - try the two nearest sizes and keep the one that sits right. Restock one thing at a time, in colours that go with what you already have, and don't buy a whole wardrobe until your weight has been steady for a couple of months.

Buy the boring things that get used up: clothes in the three to six month size, a pack of muslins, a board book, or a voucher for a meal they do not have to cook. Skip newborn sizes (everyone buys them and the baby outgrows them in a fortnight), skip toys (a baby cannot hold one) and skip anything big, since they have no room. Offer to hold the baby while they sleep: that is the thing they actually want.

Buy the loaf that is still warm and one pastry to eat before you get home: a sourdough or a tin loaf keeps two days on the board and a week sliced in the freezer, and a cheese twist or a croissant is what a bakery is for. Ask which loaf is today's rather than yesterday's - it is the one question they are always happy to answer.

Buy this one rather than bake it: a gluten-free loaf needs a batter, not a dough, plus psyllium or xanthan to stand in for the stretch, and it is the one thing a shop does better. For a bun or a pizza base, a gluten-free bread flour blend with a teaspoon of xanthan per 500g and a wet dough, proved in the tin, gets there.

Buy a flat webbing lead about 2m long, in one piece rather than an extending one: a metal clip, a padded handle and a width of 20 to 25mm for a medium dog. Check the stitching at both ends and the clip before you use it, and replace a chewed lead rather than tying a knot in it.

Buying privately is buyer beware: the item only has to match its description, so there's no right to a refund when it later breaks. From a dealer or shop the full 30-day rejection right applies, and paying by card adds your bank as a route.

By hand in cool water with a wool wash or a little shampoo, squeeze rather than rub, rinse in water of the same temperature and roll it in a towel to take the water out. Dry a hat over an upturned bowl so it keeps its shape, lay gloves flat with the fingers straightened out, and keep all three off a radiator, which is what shrinks them.

By law a child under 12 and under 135cm tall needs the right car seat or booster, and it has to be the one made for their weight or height, fitted properly. A rear-facing seat goes in the back if there is an active airbag in front. Above 135cm or 12 years old they use the adult belt.

CEO stands for chief executive officer: the person who runs the company day to day and answers to the board. Their name is on the big decisions, not on the ordinary complaint - a refund or a wrong bill is still the customer service desk's job.

CV stands for curriculum vitae, Latin for the course of your life, and the name oversells what should be a page or two: the last two jobs with what you actually did in them, dates, qualifications, and a line at the top saying what you are after. Gaps are fine on a CV so long as the dates are honest.

Cacti and succulents want a sunny windowsill, gritty compost and far less water than they get: soak the pot, let it dry right through, and that is every two to three weeks in summer and barely at all from November to March. A Christmas cactus is the exception - it is a forest cactus - so give it bright light out of full sun, water when the top half of the pot is dry, and cool nights in autumn, which is what sets the buds.

Caffeine is still in your body hours later: about half of it is gone after five or six hours, so a 4pm coffee is still a quarter there at midnight. Have your last ordinary cup by early afternoon and switch to decaf, herbal tea or water after that. If you are sensitive, even one after 6pm can cost you the deep sleep that does the repairing.
Cake going stale: crumble it into a bowl with custard, or with fruit and cream for a trifle, and slices toasted in a hot pan with butter come back crisp. It also freezes well, wrapped whole.
California is eight hours behind the UK all year, so it is 6.16am there now and 2.16pm here.
Call 999 or 911 and keep them sitting upright; use their inhaler or adrenaline pen if they have one, and start CPR if they stop breathing normally.

Can't tell you whether a place is safe from here, and I won't guess at it. What changes the answer is the time of day you would be out, how busy the street is then, and whether you would be walking it alone. The police's own crime map for the postcode says more than any general view of a place does.
Canada borders the US. The border with the United States is the longest land border in the world, about 8,890 km.

Capers are the unopened flower buds of a Mediterranean shrub, pickled in brine or packed in salt, and used for a sour, salty hit in tartare sauce, with salmon, and in puttanesca. Rinse the salted ones before use, and chop rather than crush them. The bigger caperberries are the open fruit of the same plant and are eaten whole.

Capital gains tax is a tax on the profit when you sell something that has gone up in value - shares, a second home, a business, a painting - not on the money the sale brings in. Your own home is exempt, and in 2025-26 the first £3,000 of gains in a year is tax free; above that, gains on shares and property are taxed at 18% or 24% depending on your income.

Carbohydrates are one of the main food groups: sugars and starches that the body breaks down into glucose for energy. Bread, rice, pasta, potatoes, fruit and sugar are carbohydrates, and fibre is a carbohydrate the body cannot digest.
Carry rehydration sachets and a hand gel, and check the vaccinations and malaria advice for that country about six weeks before you go.

Carry it in your hand luggage, never the hold, in its original box with the pharmacy label on it. Liquids over 100ml, insulin and anything injected need a doctor's letter or a copy of the prescription to get through security, and insulin travels in a cool bag but never touching ice. Pack a few days extra in case you are delayed, and check the country's rules for controlled medicines a couple of weeks ahead.
Carson City, not Las Vegas.

Cash for anything you will need within five years, and a global index tracker inside a stocks and shares ISA for money you can leave longer: the tracker has grown more than cash over any twenty-year stretch, but it can be down 20% or 30% for a year or two, and that is fine only if you do not have to sell. A common split is three to six months of bills in an easy-access account, then everything above that in the tracker, added to every month rather than all at once.

Castling moves the king two squares towards a rook and puts that rook on the other side of it, and it is the one move where two pieces go at once. It takes one move, it is only legal if neither the king nor that rook has moved, nothing is between them, the king is not in check, and the king does not pass through or land on a square that is attacked. Do it early, usually within the first ten moves: it puts the king behind pawns and brings the rook into the game.

Catch a ladder straight away by dabbing clear nail polish on both ends, then wash tights in a net bag. Keeping your nails smooth, your feet smooth and putting them on with damp hands is what stops the next one.

Cats scratch to mark territory, so put a tall scratching post right next to the corner she uses, and make the sofa less appealing with a throw or double-sided tape for a few weeks. A post with height lets her do it properly.

Cats wash constantly, so licking is only a problem when it is aimed at one spot: a cat working at a paw for minutes at a time is sore, itchy or stressed. Turn the paw over and look between the toes for a thorn or a grass seed, and part the fur for tiny black specks of flea dirt - a flea allergy is the commonest cause and one flea is enough. A bald or red patch, a swollen toe or a cat who has stopped grooming the rest of herself needs the vet within a day or two. Feliway or a quiet room helps the stress kind, and a cat collar has to be a snap-release one.

Cats are pregnant for about nine weeks, 63 to 65 days, and the vet usually wants to see her about three weeks in to confirm it. Feed her kitten food from around four weeks in because she needs the extra, and put a box somewhere quiet and warm with towels in it so she has a den to choose; she will pick her own spot if you do not. A cat in season is not ill and not in pain - the calling and rolling is hormones - but she will get out of the door given the chance, and the litter arrives nine weeks later, so book the spay and keep her in until it is done.

Cats are sociable, but they hunt alone and sleep sixteen hours a day, so an adult cat does not need company the way a dog does: a clean tray, water, food and something to climb are enough for the hours you are out. Two cats that get on will often choose to be in the same room, so two is kinder than one if you are out long days - but get them together as kittens, or introduce an adult pair slowly. What does need a person about is a kitten: it wants feeding little and often for months.

Cats are crepuscular, which is why they will happily get you up at 5am: feed the last meal late, play hard for ten minutes before bed, and never get up to feed or play at night, or the routine sticks. An automatic feeder helps more than anything else.

Cats dig in bare, dry soil, so the reliable fix is to take that away: mulch the beds, lay chicken wire just under the surface, or plant through a membrane. Citrus peel, coffee grounds and a scattering of holly leaves or pine cones make the surface unpleasant, and a water pistol or a motion-triggered sprinkler teaches one cat to go elsewhere fast - renew it after rain, because scents fade.
Champagne is sparkling wine from the Champagne region of France, fermented a second time in the bottle, which is what the price pays for. Cava and cremant are made the same way elsewhere.

Change the password from a device you trust, then look at what the intruder set up: a recovery email, a forwarding rule, a connected app. Turn on two-factor with an app rather than a text, tell the contacts it messaged not to send money, and use the account's own report-a-hack page so it reviews the logins.

Charged particles from the sun hit gases high in the atmosphere and make them glow: green from oxygen, reds and purples from nitrogen. You need a dark, clear night and a high latitude, so northern Scotland, Iceland and Scandinavia are the usual spots.
Charity shops take toys only if they are complete and clean, so a nursery, a sure start centre or a refuge will take what a shop will not, and a free-ad site clears a box of lego in a day.

Charity shops, the clothes banks in car parks and the textile skip at the tip take anything wearable. Worn-out fabric still earns its place in a textile bank, where it becomes rags or stuffing, so a bag of split trousers is not waste. Wash it first, put shoes in pairs, and a duvet or pillow that is past it goes to the textile bank rather than the bin.

Cheap food that people finish and that travels: a big bowl of pasta salad, sausage rolls or sausages on sticks, cheese and crackers, and a tray of fairy cakes. Keep it to things you can make the day before, and buy the paper plates.

Check the router lights first: no light on the internet or WAN light means the problem is the line, so look up your provider's service status page on your phone - a postcode outage is the most common cause and needs waiting, not fiddling. If the lights are normal, unplug the router for 30 seconds and plug it back in, then try a cable; mobile data on the phone gets you back online while you wait.
Check the service you already pay for through the TV or broadband bundle before adding another, because that is where the cheapest month usually hides.

Check the soil before you water, not the calendar: push a finger in and water only when the top few centimetres are dry, then water until it runs out of the bottom. Plants in pots need it far more often than plants in a border, and in hot weather a big soak twice a week beats a sprinkle every day, because it gets water down to the roots.

Check the tyre pressures first, because one soft tyre pulls the car. If the pressures are right, it is the tracking or a worn suspension part: a four-wheel alignment is about £30 to £60 and stops the tyres scrubbing away.

Check the Recycle Bin on Windows or the Bin on a Mac first, and in Word or Excel open File > Info > Manage Document > Recover Unsaved Documents, which holds copies for a few days even when you never saved. If the file lived in OneDrive or Google Drive, right-click it and open Version history, or look in the drive's own bin: both keep deleted files for 30 days.

Check the bin first: on an iPhone it is Photos > Albums > Recently Deleted, where deleted photos sit for 30 days, and on Android it is Google Photos > Library > Bin, for 60 days. If they are gone from there, iCloud.com or Google Photos on a browser will show anything still in the cloud, and a backup from before the loss is the last resort.

Check the disk is not full (under 10% free slows Windows badly), then cut what starts with the machine: Task Manager > Startup, and turn off the things you do not need. If it has a spinning hard drive, swapping it for an SSD is the single best £40 you can spend; adding RAM helps if you always have many tabs open.

Check what is running first: Task Manager on Windows or Activity Monitor on a Mac shows the battery-hungry app, and browsers with many tabs are usually it. Turn the brightness down, and turn off Bluetooth and the keyboard backlight when you are out. A laptop battery is good for about 300 to 500 full charges, so in Settings > Battery (or the battery menu on a Mac) check its condition: below about 80% of new, a replacement is £40 to £80 and a shop fits it in an hour.

Check when the minimum term ends and what the early exit figure is, then ask for both in writing: in the UK the rest of the line rental is capped at what you still owe, and a network must give you a PAC or STAC code free if you are switching or cancelling. Bundled handsets are usually paid off in full; for a TV or broadband service the same notice and exit figure apply, and there is no code. If you are out of the minimum term you can simply give 30 days' notice; inside it, ask for the figure and compare it with staying to the end.

Check five job adverts for the role you want: if a master's is not listed as essential, a year in the job usually teaches more and costs less, and you can do the master's later, often with an employer paying part of it. Do it now if the career you want needs it to enter at all - teaching, law, clinical roles - or if you want the research year for its own sake.
Cheddar is the all-rounder for cooking and sandwiches, mozzarella for a pizza, parmesan for grating and feta for a salad. Gruyere is the one that melts smoothly for a rarebit.
Cheetahs live about 10 to 12 years in the wild.

Chicken, about 20 minutes: slice a breast thin, fry it hot for 5 or 6 minutes, then add a tin of tomatoes or a spoon of pesto and serve it with pasta or a wrap. Whole thighs take 35 minutes, so save those for a night with more time.

Children under 12 are better off with no caffeine at all: a small body clears it slowly, so a can of cola at lunch can still be keeping a seven-year-old awake at ten. Teenagers should stay under about 100mg a day - one coffee, or two cans of cola - and none after early afternoon. Energy drinks are the usual culprit and a big can is 160mg or more, so they are worth a firm no under 16, and none of it replaces sleep.

Chipping in is a shared cost split between the people it is for, so the fair default is the same amount from everybody: whoever is organising works out the total and how many people are covering it, and the rest pay that share. In practice that is a fiver or a tenner for an office collection, ten to twenty pounds for a wedding, a big birthday or a leaving do from people who know them well, and more than that is a personal choice, not an expectation. If you are the one collecting, ask for a contribution rather than name a figure for people, keep it private - a link or an envelope, no list of who gave what - and if the pot comes up short, buy smaller rather than chase the difference. It is always fine to say no, or to give less, without explaining why.
Chocolate: melted with butter and stirred into beaten eggs for a mousse, or baked into brownies - 150g chocolate, 100g butter, 2 eggs and 100g sugar, 25 minutes at 170C (150C fan).
Christopher Luxon is the prime minister of New Zealand: in office since November 2023, leading a National-led coalition. The head of state is King Charles III, represented by a governor-general.

Citrus does not ripen any further once it is picked, so a pale, dry one stays that way. An orange or a satsuma is ready when it feels heavy for its size, which is juice rather than thick skin, and smells sweet at the stem; the small thin-skinned ones are usually the sweeter.

Clear the surfaces, then work clockwise so you do not double back: hot soapy water on the surfaces and the sink, the hob while it is still warm, and the floor last so the crumbs you drop land on it. Daily is a wipe round, weekly is the hob and the sink, monthly is the oven and the inside of the fridge. Where grease has built up, hot water with a good squeeze of washing-up liquid lifts it and cold water only smears it, and a paste of bicarbonate on a cloth takes the film off tiles, the splashback and the top of the cupboards. Most of the work is not letting things dry on, because a wipe while the pan is still warm beats an hour of scrubbing.

Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt, from 51 BC until her death in 30 BC. She was Greek, not Egyptian, spoke Egyptian, and allied with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony to keep Egypt independent of Rome.
Coffee is the roasted and ground seed of a fruit, brewed with hot water. An espresso is a small, strong shot of coffee forced through finely ground beans by a machine, about 25 to 30ml.

Cold water through the back of the fabric and blot, don't rub. A drop of washing-up liquid, five minutes, then rinse. Still there once dry: oxygen bleach, then the hottest wash the label allows. No heat until it has gone.

Cold water first, straight away, and blot rather than rub. If the mark is still there when it has dried, a soak in oxygen bleach usually lifts it, and a dry cleaner can still save a delicate fabric if you get it there quickly.

Cold brew it: eight teabags to a litre of cold water in the fridge overnight, bags out in the morning, then lemon and sugar to taste, which has none of the bitterness of a hot brew cooled down. In a hurry, brew double strength in a mug of boiling water for four minutes, take the bags out, and pour it over a jug of ice.

College is further education: A-levels, BTECs, T-levels, apprenticeships and access courses, usually for 16 to 18 year olds and mostly free until 19. University is a degree, three or four years, with tuition loans and maintenance loans to pay for it. The route that works for most people is whichever gets you the qualification the job you want actually asks for: a trade, nursing or design can go straight from college into work, while law, medicine and teaching need the degree. College first is not a step down - an access or foundation year costs less than a wasted degree and keeps the university route open.

Collisions between ice and water drops in a storm cloud build up electric charge. When the difference gets big enough, the charge leaps through the air as a huge spark: lightning, which heats the air so fast it makes the bang of thunder.

Compare on a search site, then book on the airline's own site, because a booking agent's cheap fare usually costs more once its card fee and its no-changes rule are counted. Before you pay, add the baggage for each person and pick the seats: the headline fare often leaves both out, and that is where a cheap ticket stops being cheap. Pay by credit card if the fare is over £100, which gives you section 75 cover if the airline fails, and check every passenger's passport has six months left on it.
Congratulations — that's lovely news.

Congratulations. The first fortnight is mostly feeding and sleep: eight to twelve feeds in 24 hours, six or more wet nappies a day, and the midwife comes on day five for the heel-prick blood spot test. The cord drops off in about a week to a fortnight, and the birth weight, down by up to a tenth in the first days, is back by two weeks. Ring the midwife or 111 the same day if the baby is too sleepy to feed, has fewer wet nappies, or looks yellow.

Cook one big oven dish rather than several pans: a tray of chicken thighs or sausages with halved potatoes, peppers and onions at 200C (180C fan) for 45 minutes, which does four to six, so count the potatoes yourself. Allow about 200g of meat and a big potato each, add a loaf of bread and a bowl of salad, and write the times down so nothing needs the oven at once.

Cook one big oven dish rather than several pans: a tray of chicken thighs or sausages with halved potatoes, peppers and onions at 200C (180C fan) for 45 minutes, which does four to six, so count the potatoes yourself. Allow about 200g of meat and a big potato each, add a loaf of bread and a bowl of salad, and write the times down so nothing needs the oven at once. Anything that can be made that morning - a chilli, a stew, a lasagne - just gets reheated, which leaves the day free.

Cook two big pots on one afternoon and the week is half done: a chilli or bolognese and a curry or dhal, each cooled and split into portions, then frozen flat in bags so they thaw in minutes. Cook rice and pasta fresh while a portion reheats, label the bags with the date, and eat them within three months.

Cooked vegetables keep 3 days in the fridge in a covered box, and roast veg 3 to 4 days, because the oven has already taken the water out of them. Get them in there within 2 hours of coming off the heat, in a box rather than on a plate, and reheat once, piping hot. Cooked mushrooms and courgette go first, in 2 days, and anything slimy or sour goes in the bin, because the bugs that make you ill have no smell.

Cooked chicken or turkey keeps 3 days in the fridge in a covered box, and freezes for up to 3 months. Cool it within 2 hours of cooking, reheat it once until it is piping hot all through, and eat it cold only if it went straight into the fridge.

Cookies spread when the dough is warm or the butter is too soft: chill the dough 30 minutes and put it on a cool tray, and leave a good 5cm between them. Too much sugar or a greased tin makes them spread further, and a fan oven needs 20C less than the recipe.
Cooking, travel, money, work, gadgets, kids, feelings — everyday questions and plans. Ask away.
Cool showers, plenty of water and a loose cotton shirt are what help; leave blisters alone. If someone is shivery, dizzy or badly blistered, that needs a doctor.

Cool the room rather than the bed: open windows on both sides for a through draught, keep the curtains shut in the day, and put a bowl of ice in front of a fan. A lukewarm shower before bed, cotton sheets and a hot water bottle filled with cold water at your feet all help more than sleeping with no cover at all.

Cool it under cool running water for twenty minutes, then cover it loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy cloth. Don't use ice, butter or cream, and get it checked if it's bigger than your palm, on the face or hands, or blistered.

Cotton breathes, takes up water and gets softer with washing; polyester does not absorb water, so it dries fast and wicks sweat, but it holds body oils and smell, which is why a cheap polyester top pongs after one wear.

Count the screens that stream at once: one or two people on HD needs about 40Mbps, a house with four people streaming and gaming needs 100-200Mbps, and upload speed matters more than download if you are on video calls. Full fibre is worth it when it costs roughly what you pay now, because it uploads as fast as it downloads and the line is not shared; a cheaper part-fibre deal is fine if nobody is home all day.

Count back about eight hours from the time you have to get up, and keep that bedtime the same seven days a week: the regularity matters more than the exact hour. If you lie there awake, go to bed half an hour later rather than earlier, so bed means sleep again.

Courgettes, squashes and cucumbers carry male and female flowers on the same plant, and the female one has a tiny fruit behind the flower. If the little fruit goes yellow and drops off, the pollen never got to it - pick a male flower, peel the petals back and dab it into the middle of a female one early in the morning, when the flower is fresh. Cold nights under 10C and a very hot dry spell both stop the pollen working, and a plant fed hard on tomato feed grows leaves instead, so water at the base and wait for the weather to pass.

Cover tender plants when frost is forecast, which means a night at 2C or below at ground level: the forecast for the town is often two or three degrees warmer than the garden, so watch for a clear, still night. Fleece, an old sheet, a cloche or a bucket of water beside them is enough, and take it off in the morning. Bring pots and hanging baskets in, water before a frost rather than after, and lift any spuds still in the ground.

Crawling comes at 6 to 10 months, and bottom-shuffling instead of crawling is normal. Sitting comes at about 6 months, pulling up 9 to 12, walking 9 to 18, first words near 12. Your red book charts all of it and the health visitor reviews it; ask early if two or three are late together, if one side is used much more than the other, or if a skill is lost.

Crisp tofu: press a block, cube it, fry in hot oil until golden on most sides, then toss with soy sauce, honey and chilli. Tempeh: slice it, simmer 5 minutes to take the bitterness off, then fry it 3 minutes a side and glaze it with soy, honey and lime.

Cue games are won with the cue ball, not the pot: before every shot decide where the white has to finish for the next one, and hit it with the pace that leaves the easiest next shot rather than the hardest pot. Play the shot you can make nine times out of ten. Practise a straight pot up and down the table 50 times, stopping the cue ball dead, then following through and screwing back.

Cut the sugar you drink first, because liquid sugar does not fill you up at all, then make sure you are eating protein and fibre at meals: most evening sugar cravings are hunger from a lunch that was too small or too white. Keep the sweet thing out of the house rather than relying on willpower at nine at night, and expect three or four days of feeling deprived before it settles.
Cuts. If you were hoping I'd say "items for burns", then you've decided already.

Dairy free is easy to cook around: oat, soya or almond milk in place of milk, olive oil instead of butter, and a tin of coconut milk where a recipe wants cream. Watch the labels for whey, casein, milk powder and lactose, which sit in stock cubes, bread, biscuits and some crisps, and check the pesto and the chocolate too.
Daniel Radcliffe plays Harry Potter in all eight films (2001-2011). He was eleven when the first one was shot and twenty-one by the last.

Dark matter is the name for mass we cannot see but can measure: galaxies spin and bend light as if they hold far more matter than the stars show. Nobody yet knows what it is made of, which is why it is one of the big open questions.
Day trips from Los Angeles: Santa Monica and Malibu down the coast, Disneyland in Anaheim (an hour by car) and Catalina island by ferry from Long Beach. Almost all of it needs a car.
Day trips from New York: Beacon for Dia:Beacon (80 minutes on Metro-North), Philadelphia (90 minutes on Amtrak) and the Hamptons by the LIRR. The Jersey shore is a longer day.
Day trips from San Francisco: Muir Woods and Sausalito (ferry, then a shuttle you book ahead), Napa by car, and Santa Cruz over the hill. Yosemite is four hours, so it wants a night.
Days like that are easier when the shape is set rather than the plan: one thing out of the house, one meal, and the rest left loose. What kind of thing do you enjoy doing?

Deal with the trust, not the handset: say what the checking does to you - 'when you go through my phone I feel like I'm being investigated' - and ask what they are actually worried about, because there is usually one thing under it. Then agree a rule you both keep: passwords shared or not, but no checking in secret. If it carries on, that is a couples conversation, not a phone one.

Decide what you actually want from the conversation before you start it - an apology, a change, or just to be heard - and ask for that rather than for the whole history. Pick one recent thing and say it plainly: 'When you rearrange my plans without asking, I feel about ten years old.' Pick a short visit or a walk rather than a long sit-down, and leave the subjects that never move alone. If it turns into the same loop, going quiet for a week and then ringing about something ordinary often shifts more than another attempt to settle it.
Denver — nice. How long have you been there?
Denver.

Diana, Princess of Wales (1961-1997) married Prince Charles in 1981 and became one of the most photographed people in the world, known for her charity work on AIDS and landmines. She died in a car crash in Paris in August 1997.

Diesel only pays if you do long, steady runs: as a rule of thumb over 12,000 miles a year with most of it motorway, and fewer than that if the car is also doing short hops. Below that the diesel costs more to buy, more to service and its filter clogs on short trips, so a petrol car is the cheaper buy. Mostly town driving, cold starts and trips under twenty minutes are petrol, or a hybrid if the budget reaches one.

Dig the hole 250 to 300mm across and two foot (600mm) deep, stand the post on about 50mm of gravel so the cut end never sits in water, and get it plumb on two faces with a spirit level before anything goes in. One 20kg bag of Postcrete does one post: pour it dry around the post, water it as the bag says, brace the post and leave it a day before a panel goes on. A 100mm square or 75mm round post is right for a 1.8m panel; in soft soil, or on a windy corner, go deeper rather than wider.

Distillation is boiling a liquid off a mixture and condensing it back to a liquid somewhere cooler, which separates things that boil at different temperatures: spirit is distilled from a fermented mash, and distilled water is water with the minerals left behind.
Do not stop suddenly on your own: steroids, antidepressants, epilepsy tablets and anything for the heart or blood pressure can be dangerous to stop, even when they are the problem.

Do not click to find out: hover over the link or long-press it and read the real address, because scammers use lookalike domains like rnicrosoft.com. Check the address is exactly the company's own, with https and no extra words before the dot, and if you are still unsure, type the company's address into the browser yourself rather than using the link.

Do the one that is the point of the session first, because the second one gets the tired version of you: if you are there to get stronger, lift first and finish with ten minutes of cardio; if you are training for a run or a ride, do that first. Ten easy minutes on the bike before you lift is a warm-up, not cardio. The best order is the one you will keep doing twice a week.

Do the smallest possible first step, not the whole job: open the book at the page and write the title and today's date, or set a timer for five minutes and let yourself do it badly. Putting it off is mostly about the task feeling too big to start, and it shrinks as soon as you are in it. Decide tonight what tomorrow's first step is, so then it is an instruction to follow rather than a choice to make.

Do the three things they will actually notice, in this order: clear the floor into one basket and shut the doors on the rest, put out glasses and something to nibble, and cook one thing from what you already have - pasta, an oven tray of whatever vegetables and sausages are in, or bread, cheese and something cold from the fridge. Buy only the missing bit on the way home, and don't start a clean nobody will see: a drink in their hand and food within half an hour is the whole of it.
Do this one: Start with a free page on a builder and pay for the domain.

Do it wet and in sections, from the ends upwards: soak the hair with conditioner, hold it above the knot and work a wide-tooth comb through a couple of inches at a time rather than dragging a brush from the top. A leave-in detangler and a soft brush with flexible bristles make the same job much less of a fight, plait it or tie it loosely for bed so the knots cannot form overnight, and if every morning is still tears then a shoulder-length cut is a perfectly good answer rather than a defeat.

Do it in the app, not by deleting the icon: every app hides it under Settings > Account, usually as Deactivate (reversible) or Delete (permanent). Deactivating keeps your posts and your name; deleting does not, and most apps give you 30 days to log back in and change your mind.
Does anything ease it - rest, heat, or a painkiller?

Dogs dig out of boredom, heat or the smell of something buried, so give it a spot of its own — a sandpit with toys buried in it — and reward digging there. Cover the rest with stones or a mesh, keep it exercised and never shout when it's already dug.

Don't leave them alone, and ask them directly whether they are thinking about suicide. If they've taken anything or you're scared for them, that's 999 or 911; otherwise a crisis line (116 123 in the UK, 988 in the US) will talk to the two of you.
Draw something badly on purpose, and keep it. Being a beginner at something for an afternoon is good for you.
Dress for the coldest hour of it and the longest you will be on your feet: shoes decide more of a day than people expect. Are you inside or out?

Dried fruit keeps 6 months in a sealed jar and a year in the fridge, and past that it hardens rather than spoils. Bring it back in 10 minutes in a bowl of hot water, or leave a slice of bread in the jar overnight. White crystals on the outside are sugar, not mould.

Drop the dial about 20C for a fan oven, and check the real heat with a cheap oven thermometer hung in the middle: an oven that runs 25C hot browns the outside before the middle is set, which is the commonest reason a bake burns on the bottom and stays raw in the middle. Trust the thermometer over the dial, turn the tray round halfway through, and if yours runs hot by a fixed amount, note the number you actually use on a sticker inside the door.

Dry before wet, and top before bottom: hoover or sweep first, dust from the ceiling down so the floor catches what falls, and mop last - a mop over grit just pushes the mud about. On a wooden floor the dry mop goes over first and the wet one is barely damp. And clear the floor, the worktops and the shelves first: a broom cannot reach a floor that is still full, and a cloth cannot wipe a ledge with things still on it.

Dry everything, put a bowl under the trap and run the tap to see where the water appears. A drip at a plastic joint is nearly always a hand-tight nut: give it another quarter turn, no more, because overtightened plastic splits. If it's the trap, unscrew it, clean out the gunge, check the rubber washer is seated and put it back. Wrapping PTFE tape on a plastic thread makes it worse, not better.

Dry meat is overcooked meat, so keep it juicy with a thermometer and a rest rather than basting: chicken and pork come out of the oven at 74C, beef at 55C for medium rare or 65C for well done, and then sit on a warm board under foil for 10 to 20 minutes, which lets the juice settle back in instead of running onto the plate. A 2kg chicken wants 20 minutes per 500g plus 20 at 190C, started breast down so the white meat sits in the fat. Basting mostly costs oven heat and changes little.

Ducks float because their bodies are light and their feathers trap air, while a gland near the tail supplies oil that keeps the water out. Their bones are hollow too, so the whole bird is far less dense than the water it sits in.

Each kernel holds a little water inside a hard shell. Heat turns that water to steam, the pressure builds until the shell splits, and the starch inside puffs out and sets: the pop is the shell giving way, and a kernel that is too dry or has a cracked shell will not pop.
