Early morning, just after the kettle. Nobody wants anything from me yet.
Eat in a restaurant by yourself, with a book, once. Nobody is looking, and it is the most peaceful hour you can buy for the price of a lunch.

Eating to manage a feeling is very ordinary, and the feeling does not go away because you tell yourself off for it. The practical version: eat proper meals so hunger is not part of it, keep the triggering food out of the house, and put a ten-minute walk or a phone call between the urge and the cupboard - the urge usually passes. If it happens most days and you feel out of control, that is worth talking to a GP about; Beat's helpline (0808 801 0677) is free and does not judge.

Eggs are the fastest dinner there is: an omelette takes 2 minutes, a frittata with last night's vegetables 10 minutes, and eggs on gluten-free toast is a proper dinner if there is cheese in the fridge.
Egypt is in Africa. The Sinai peninsula, across the Suez Canal, is in Asia, which is why Egypt is sometimes called transcontinental.

Elastane - sold as Lycra or Spandex - is the rubber-like fibre that makes a fabric stretch and spring back: 2% in a shirt keeps the shape, 5% in jeans lets you sit down, and 20% is sportswear. It is what wears out first, because heat and chlorine break it down: wash it cool and never tumble dry it, and it will keep its stretch for years instead of going baggy at the knees.

Elements at the top, bottom or back heat the air, and a thermostat switches them on and off to hold the temperature on the dial. A fan oven blows that air around, so it browns more evenly and cooks about 20C cooler and a little faster than a conventional one; the dial is only an average, which is why an oven thermometer earns its place.
Elephants live 60 to 70 years in the wild, and a big bull can reach 70.

Eleven or twelve is when most children get their first phone, and the rules matter more than the model. Agree the amount in advance: about two hours a day of screens for fun at that age, and what happens when it runs out, because a rule made mid-argument is a fight. Charge it in the kitchen overnight with a cheap alarm clock in the bedroom, and set the phone's own downtime with a passcode they do not have. Taking it off them for a week over a bad mood only teaches them to hide it: keep confiscation for the things you said you would.
Elizabeth I reigned from 1558 to 1603, the last Tudor: she settled the church, saw off the Armada in 1588, and never married, which is why the succession went to her cousin James of Scotland.
1/2 as a decimal is 0.5.

Email the tutor today, before they mark it: the date you can deliver, what you have done so far, and the reason in one sentence. Universities cap late work rather than refusing it, so a complete essay handed in now usually beats a perfect one next month - and if the reason is illness or a bereavement, ask for the extenuating-circumstances form as well, because that can lift the cap.

Emmanuel Macron is the president of France: elected in 2017 and re-elected in 2022. A French president serves five years, so the next election is due in 2027, and the prime minister, who runs the day-to-day government, is appointed by the president.

Empty one cupboard at a time, wipe the shelves with hot soapy water and dry them before the tins go back, and leave a bay leaf or a few cloves in the corners to keep the musty smell down. The outsides want a wipe every couple of weeks, near the hob more often, and a twice-a-year clear-out is what stops food going out of date at the back.

Emulsion takes a second coat in 2 to 4 hours and is properly hard in about a day; undercoat and gloss want overnight, 16 to 24 hours, and longer in a cold room. A small hole of filler is hard in about an hour, so it can be sanded and painted the same day, but a deep fill wants overnight or it shrinks back and shows. Silicone has to be a paintable one - most sanitary silicones cannot be painted at all - and it wants 24 hours to cure before a brush goes near it.

Energy comes from sleep, daylight and food, in that order: the same bedtime and getting-up time every day, ten minutes outside in the morning light, and a lunch with protein and slow carbs rather than just a sandwich, so three o'clock does not flatten you. Water through the day and no caffeine after two help too. Still flat after two weeks, ask your GP for a blood test for iron and thyroid.
England: London for the museums and the markets. Bath for the Roman baths. The Lake District for hills and walking.
England have won the men's World Cup once: 1966.
Episodes beat films when the evening is short: *The Bear* is 25 minutes an episode, *Derry Girls* is 22, and *Inside No. 9* is half an hour with a twist.

Equity is the part you actually own. In a house it is the value minus the mortgage, so a flat worth £250,000 with £150,000 left to pay has £100,000 of equity, and it moves up and down with prices; in a company it means the shares, so equity there is a slice of the business and what it is worth.
Essay subjects are learned by writing answers, not by reading the notes again: get the mark scheme for your board, write three timed past questions a week and plan the other two in a spider diagram.
Europe has 44 countries, or about 50 if you count the transcontinental ones such as Russia and Turkey. The exact number depends on where you draw the eastern edge.

Eve's pudding is the one to know when the cupboard is thin: sliced apple or any fruit in a dish, then a sponge of 100g each of butter, sugar and self-raising flour with 2 eggs spread over the top, baked 40 minutes at 180C (160C fan). With no flour at all, halved bananas baked with butter, brown sugar and a pinch of cinnamon take 15 minutes.

Every one of these is quoted per person and moves with the day of the week, so one figure from one place says little on its own. The same count and the same extras asked of two places is the comparison - and the venue's own page has today's numbers.

Every six to eight weeks for short hair, eight to twelve for long, or whenever the ends start looking ragged. A trim does not make hair grow faster, but it stops the split ends travelling up the hair shaft, which is what makes long hair look thin. A dry cut on wavy or curly hair is more honest about how it falls than a wet one.

Every day is fine for most people: it is long hot showers and harsh soap that leave skin tight and itchy, not the water itself. A five-minute warm shower daily is plenty, and every other day is enough if you wash the face, armpits and groin in between, unless you have been sweating or it is hot. If your skin still feels dry, shorten the shower and turn the heat down before you cut one out.

Everybody's first is the worst one, and almost nobody does it as badly as they think. Practise it once, out loud and timed, and know that the beginning is the part to have ready. What would go wrong if it went wrong?
Expect the step and heart-rate numbers to be rough rather than medical.

Factor 30 or higher sun cream, a bottle of water each, a hat, and a windbreak or umbrella for shade, plus a towel each and one spare for the car. Take cash for parking and a bag for your rubbish, because bins on the sand are thin on the ground.

Fasting works for weight loss because it makes eating less happen almost by accident, not because it does anything special: 16:8 and 5:2 come out level with ordinary calorie cutting in the trials. Pick it only if skipping breakfast suits you - if it leaves you raiding the cupboard at nine at night, it will not work. Not for anyone pregnant, underweight or with a history of eating disorders.

Feeling like a fraud in a job you were hired for is close to universal, and it is not evidence of anything: the people around you are guessing too. The antidote is evidence, not reassurance - keep a running note of what you have actually delivered and looked up, and read it before a one-to-one. Ask a colleague you trust what they think you should worry about; their answer will be smaller and more specific than your own.

Feet about shoulder-width with the toes turned out slightly, chest up and eyes forward: sit back and down as if reaching for a chair, and let your knees travel forward over your toes while your back stays straight. Go as deep as you can with your heels down - hips below the knees is the usual aim - and practise onto a chair until it feels natural.

Fifteen to twenty minutes a day, five or six days a week, beats one long session at the weekend: the chord changes are what need repeating, and your fingertips need the odd rest day more than the extra minutes. Ten minutes is enough on a busy day - the streak matters more than the length.

Fill a wide-mouth flask with boiling water for five minutes, empty it, then put the food in steaming hot and it will still be warm at lunchtime; a tea towel round the flask adds an hour or two. The middle ground is the risky bit, because food between 5C and 63C grows bacteria, so reheat it until it is steaming just before it goes in and throw away what is left at the end of the day.

Fill a bottle in the morning and keep it where you sit, and put a glass by the kettle so every cup of tea comes with one. Drinking with meals and after every trip to the loo is the cheapest trigger. Squash, tea and milk count towards your fluids, so if you dislike plain water, flavour it with lemon or have a diluted squash instead.
Filter coffee is ground coffee steeped in hot water and then filtered out, through paper in a dripper or a metal mesh in a cafetiere.

Fireflies glow through a chemical reaction in their tail: luciferin reacts with oxygen and gives off light with almost no heat. They use it to attract mates, and each species has its own flash pattern.

First past the post means the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins the seat, even with only 35% of the vote, and it is how all 650 MPs are elected. It usually gives one party a working majority on well under half the national vote - which is why smaller parties argue for proportional representation, where seats match vote share.

Fish is done when it flakes at its thickest point and has turned from glassy to opaque all the way through, and a thermometer in the thickest part reads about 60C. Cod or haddock loins take 10 to 12 minutes at 200C, and a thin fillet 6 to 8. A fork should slide in with no resistance - if the middle still looks see-through, give it two more minutes rather than serving it early.

Fit first: try them on in the afternoon in the socks you will wear, with a thumb's width at the toe and no lift at the heel, because a boot will not stretch to fit. Then look at the sole - deep rubber tread, a waterproof upper - and at lacing that lets you tighten the ankle without pinching across the foot.

Fitted sheet first, corners over the corners of the mattress and the elastic under it, then the flat sheet if you use one, then the duvet shaken out so it hangs evenly on both sides. Pillows last, plumped and stood up against the headboard, or laid flat if the bed is only going to be slept in. Pull the duvet back a hand's width at the top so the sheet shows, and the bed looks made with the top edge straight.

Five players from each team take a penalty each, in turn, and the side that scores more wins; if it is still level after all ten, it goes to sudden death, one each until one side misses. Everyone else waits on the halfway line, the keeper has to keep one foot on the line, and the same player cannot take twice until everyone who can has taken one.
Five cats, Bulldogs, Poodles, Huskies, Collies and Shepherds — how long have they been with you?

Five a day is real, and it is about 400g of fruit and vegetables rather than five items: a portion is 80g, which is one apple, three heaped tablespoons of peas, or a handful of grapes. A smoothie counts once however much of it you drink, and so does a 150ml glass of juice, because the fibre is broken up and it goes down too fast - whole fruit is better. Potatoes, chips and crisps do not count: they are the carbohydrate on the plate.

Five hours is on the short side: most adults need seven to nine, and the shortfall shows as yawning, coffee and losing the thread by mid-afternoon. Half an hour earlier to bed, and the same wake-up time every day, is the fix - a long weekend lie-in is not.

Five is early for a name and nothing to worry about: the shoulder and hand are still building, so most children get a recognisable name somewhere between four and six. Give the hand other work first - threading, cutting, playdough, big chalk on the path - and practise the name in short bursts with a chunky pencil and a dotted version to trace, five minutes at a time and no more. Worth asking nursery or the reception teacher whether the grip is right, and worth a word with the health visitor if a child of six cannot hold a pencil or copy a circle at all.

Fix it with light and meals rather than willpower: get outside in the morning, keep the evening dim, eat at the new meal times and move bedtime 30 minutes a night rather than all at once. No long naps, and no caffeine after lunch while it settles.

Flavour comes from browning: roast the bones and the vegetables at 220C (200C fan) for 30 minutes before they go in the pot, and add a spoon of tomato puree or a few dried mushrooms. Don't let it boil, which drives the aroma off, and salt it only at the end. Reduce the strained stock by half and you have a stronger one for the freezer.

Floury potatoes (Maris Piper, King Edward, Rooster) for roast, mash and chips, waxy ones (Charlotte, Jersey Royal, Nicola) for salads and boiling whole. The bag says which on the front, so buy by that rather than by the price.

Fluids and paracetamol, and light clothes rather than a pile of blankets - a fever is the body doing its job, and the number matters less than how you feel. Get seen the same day if it comes with a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade under a glass, trouble breathing, or if it lasts more than three days.

Fly it in open ground away from trees and power lines, with the wind at your back. Let out ten or fifteen metres of line, have someone hold the kite up and walk back until the line is tight, then pull gently and let line run through your hands as it climbs. A steady 8-20 mph is the sweet spot: if it loops and dives, let out line, and if it will not rise at all, wait for more wind rather than running.
Folding is mixing gently with a big spoon, turning the bowl and cutting through, so you keep the air in whipped egg white or cream.

For most things a bank statement, a utility bill or a council tax bill from the last three months, with your name and the address on it, is exactly what they want; a driving licence counts for some and not others, so ask which two they accept, and a paper copy beats a phone screenshot. If nothing is in your own name, ask the council for your entry on the electoral roll, or your GP or landlord for a letter on headed paper.

For most adults with type 2 the target is 4 to 7 mmol/L before meals and under 8.5 two hours after, and an HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol, which is 6.5 per cent - your own team may set yours higher or lower, so it is worth knowing the numbers they wrote down for you. HbA1c is the average of the last two or three months rather than one day, which is why the annual blood test is judged on it. Testing at home is only needed for some people, so ask whether yours is one of them.

For most interviews, smart casual is the safe bet: a clean shirt or blouse, dark trousers or a skirt, and closed shoes; a suit only if the company is formal. Check the office on their website or LinkedIn and dress one step smarter than that.

For six people, pick three or four cheeses: something soft like brie, a hard one like a mature cheddar, a blue, and something goat's or sheep's for variety. Add crackers, grapes, chutney and nuts, and take them out of the fridge an hour before.

For someone into cooking: an apron and a decent wooden spoon (£15), a good olive oil and a nice tin (£20) or a decent chef's knife (£35). Buy the one they will actually use rather than three they might, and put a real message in the card.

For sport, polyester or a polyamide blend: it does not absorb sweat, so it dries fast and stays light, where cotton gets heavy and cold. Look for a mesh panel or a wicking finish, and wash it soon after - the smell that lingers in sports kit is oil trapped in the fibre, which a cool wash does not shift.

For that age, buy something they would use every week and would not buy themselves: good coffee or tea, a bottle of what they already drink, a voucher for a place they like, or a book by an author they follow. One useful thing beats a pile of small ones.

For the next bus: The next one is live, so nothing here can see it. The bus operator's app, or the timetable printed at the stop, has the time - text the stop's code where it has one - and a journey planner joins the trip up.
For the sheet: *The Early Birds*. Others that go down well: *The Underdogs* and *The Try Hards*.
For the sheet: *The Night Owls*. Others that go down well: *The Comeback Club* and *Second Wind*.
For the sheet: *The Underdogs*. Others that go down well: *The Try Hards* and *The Long Shots*.
For the sheet: *The Wild Cards*. Others that go down well: *The Early Birds* and *The Underdogs*.

For the first seven calendar days you need no note at all: fill in the self-certificate your employer gives you. After that a GP fit note covers you, and you can ask by phone or online rather than in an appointment; it can say you may be fit for work with reduced hours or lighter duties. Hospital doctors, nurses and physios can issue one too.

For the hamstring, sit or stand with one heel on a low step, keep that leg straight and hinge forward from the hips with a flat back until you feel the pull behind the thigh - hold 30 seconds, three times each side. No bouncing and no reaching for your toes with a round back. Do it after the run, when the muscle is warm.

For white, e4 or d4 - both free your pieces and give you a plan - and for black answer e4 with e5 or the Sicilian, and d4 with d5 or the King's Indian. Learn one opening each side by its ideas rather than its moves: what the pawns are doing, where the pieces belong, and which piece you are happy to trade. Ten moves you understand beat forty you cannot remember.
For India: October to March for most of the country: dry and cooler. April to June is brutally hot in the north, and the monsoon runs June to September.
For Italy: April, May, late September and October: warm, not crowded, everything open. July and August are hot and packed, and August in the cities means half the restaurants shut.
For Japan the window is Late March to April for the blossom, or October to November for the autumn colour.
For San Francisco: September and October: the warmest, clearest months at 18-24C. July and August are foggy and cool, and the rain comes November to March.

For an animated film: *Spirited Away* (125 minutes, the one that turns people who say they do not like animation), *The Mitchells vs the Machines* (114 minutes, fast, funny, and a robot apocalypse a family can watch), or *Toy Story* (81 minutes, short, and it still holds up). Any of them is a good way in, and I can go shorter or pick one if you tell me the mood.

For 25g of dark chocolate, use 3 level tablespoons of cocoa with a teaspoon of sugar and a teaspoon of butter or oil. Milk chocolate goes in at the same weight but is sweeter, so leave a spoonful of the recipe's sugar out.

For cooking: milk with a knob of butter and a teaspoon of cornflour thickens much like cream. Cold, or on the side: plain yoghurt, sour cream or creme fraiche. Stir those in off the heat, because cream and yoghurt split if they boil.

For curtains and cushions, weight and light matter more than the fibre: a lining makes any fabric hang better and keeps the light out, and a polycotton or a linen-look weave is cheaper and does not fade the way a printed cotton does. For a sofa that gets sat on, a tight weave in a blend beats a loose linen.

For damp shade: ferns, hostas, astilbe, hydrangea, brunnera and foxgloves all cope and look after themselves. Dry shade under a tree is the hard one - hardy geranium, epimedium, vinca, lungwort and ivy are the ones that survive it. Whatever you plant, dig in leaf mould or compost first: shade plants fail more often from thin dry soil than from the lack of sun.

For a musical: *Singin' in the Rain* (103 minutes, the one that makes people like musicals), *La La Land* (128 minutes, bright, sad at the end, and easy to follow), or *The Sound of Music* (174 minutes, long, which is what a wet Sunday wants). Any of them is a good way in, and I can go shorter or pick one if you tell me the mood.
For a patch, scrape it back to sound plaster, wet the edges, press filler in with a wide filling knife and scrape it flat while it is still soft, then sand it once dry.
For a soft one, 5 to 6 minutes: 5 leaves the yolk running, 6 gives a set white with a soft middle. Cool it under cold water the moment it comes out, or it carries on cooking in its own heat.

For a station or a town centre, the station car park or a park and ride is usually cheaper than the multi-storey, and the parking apps (RingGo, PayByPhone, JustPark) show the live price and let you top up from your phone.

For a sunny border: lavender, salvia, verbena, sedum, rudbeckia, cosmos and a grass or two give colour from June to October and take the heat. Plant in spring or early autumn and water them well through their first summer, because that is what makes them drought-proof later; after that, a mulch in spring is most of the work. Med-style plants want sharp drainage, so add grit to heavy soil rather than compost.

For a thriller: *Sicario* (121 minutes, cold and relentless, and it never lets you settle), *Prisoners* (153 minutes, a kidnapping and a father who will not stop looking), or *Gone Girl* (149 minutes, a marriage thriller that keeps turning on you). Any of them is a good way in, and I can go shorter or pick one if you tell me the mood.

For a toddler, one thing they will use every day beats a pile of toys: a set of chunky blocks, a ball, a book with flaps to lift, or a scooter they will still fit next year. Ask the parents what they already have too much of, and buy the batteries with it.

For a volcano: a bottle in a cone of foil and clay, then bicarbonate of soda with vinegar and a little washing-up liquid for the eruption (red food colouring helps). The part that earns marks is the write-up: label the bottle as the magma chamber, and explain that the gas is what pushes it out. It takes an afternoon and a tray.

For a week in a carry-on: two tops, one warm layer, one pair of trousers you can wear twice, and shoes you have already walked a mile in - then take a third of it out. Roll clothes instead of folding, take travel sizes, and plan to wash once. It also saves the wait at the belt.

For a weekend the travel time is the whole trip, so pick somewhere under two hours door to door: Bath, York, the Cotswolds or the Norfolk coast at home, or Bruges, Lille or Amsterdam by train. Two nights is the right length, the train three or four weeks ahead is the cheap fare, and a room in the middle beats one with a car park.

For a younger reader: *The Bolds* by Julian Clary (funny on every page), *The Worst Witch* (short chapters), *The Explorer* by Katherine Rundell for animals and adventure, or *Dog Man* if comics are easier. Start with *The Bolds* or *Dog Man*: jokes first, and no long descriptions to get through.

For a baby over six months, a consistent wind-down, dim lights and a fixed bedtime help more than any trick; feedings at night are normal for much longer than people expect. Ask your health visitor or GP if you're worried, and never use anything that promises a quick fix for a very young baby.

For a birthday tea, a big chocolate or lemon traybake cut into squares is the easy one: one tin feeds 15 and you bake it the day before. Then a batch of fairy cakes, some jam tarts and a plate of sausage rolls, and the table is done.

For a blocked ear, olive oil drops twice a day for a few days soften the wax, and swallowing or yawning clears the pressure after a cold or a flight. Don't put cotton buds in it. If hearing drops, there is pain or discharge, or it has lasted a week, a pharmacist can look and a GP can syringe it.
For a good cry: *Manchester by the Sea* on film, *Normal People* as a series, or *Never Let Me Go* if you would rather read.

For a journey by road that is a map app, and for one by train it is the operator's own planner: both give the miles or the connections for the hour you would actually go, which is the part a rough figure from anyone else gets wrong.

For a long drive, a narrator who can hold a voice for hours beats a famous book: *The Thursday Murder Club* (Lesley Manville, about 7 hours) is easy to follow with traffic about; *Project Hail Mary* (Ray Porter, about 16 hours) is the one people finish and start again; *Circe* (Perdita Weeks, about 13 hours) if they want something with a story to it. Pick something 8 hours or longer for a drive of that length, and listen to ten minutes of the sample before you commit.
For a long listen: *Rumours* by Fleetwood Mac, *Graceland* by Paul Simon, or *The Rest Is History* if you would rather hear talking. Tell me what the journey is and I'll make it specific.

For essays, video calls and Netflix, almost anything current works: 8GB RAM, a 256GB SSD and a 14 inch screen, around £400 to £550. A Chromebook is fine if everything lives in Google Docs, but avoid it for a course that needs Windows software.

For everyday cooking, olive oil and rapeseed oil are the best all-rounders: mostly unsaturated fat, and rapeseed has the most omega-3 of the ordinary oils. Extra virgin olive oil is fine for frying at normal pan heat. Coconut oil is the one to hold back on, because it is about 85 per cent saturated fat. Whichever you use it is still about 120 calories a tablespoon, so how much matters more than which.

For frying and roasting, melted butter or margarine works at the same amount; turn the heat down a little, because butter burns sooner than oil. In a cake, oil-for-butter is the other direction: use three-quarters of the weight of the butter the recipe asks for.

For funny, *The Thursday Murder Club* by Richard Osman is the easy pick: short chapters, a mystery that keeps moving, and jokes on every page. *Three Men in a Boat* if you want an old one that still makes people laugh out loud, or *Good Omens* by Pratchett and Gaiman for something daft and warm.

For funny: *No Such Thing as a Fish* (four people, one bizarre fact each, about half an hour), *The Adam Buxton Podcast* for long chats that wander, or *Off Menu* where guests order their dream meal. All easy to dip in and out of.
For laughs: *What We Do in the Shadows* (a daft vampire mockumentary), *The Nice Guys* (funny and twisty) or *Paddington 2*, which makes almost everyone laugh.
For £28: one month at £28 a month. Pick the rate your pay can carry and set the standing order for the day after payday, so you never have to decide again.
For £31: one month at £31 a month. Pick the rate your pay can carry and set the standing order for the day after payday, so you never have to decide again.

Force it off by holding the power button for ten seconds, unplug everything except the charger and start it again: a printer or a memory card is often what it is stuck on. If it still stops at the logo, start it in safe mode (hold Shift while it boots on Windows, or hold Shift on a Mac) and remove whatever you installed last; a machine that will not start at all needs a repair shop or the maker's recovery drive.

Forty-five minutes to an hour is the sweet spot: five minutes of warm-up, three or four exercises at three sets each, and a couple of minutes between sets. Past 90 minutes you are mostly resting and getting tired rather than stronger, so drop an exercise rather than the rest.
Four rabbits, Cows, Elephants, Lions and Wolves — how long have they been with you?

Four things stop a loaf rising, in the order worth checking. The yeast is dead - test it in warm water with a pinch of sugar and it should foam in ten minutes; water over about 45C, or a tin past its date, kills it. The water was too hot or too cold, so the dough never got going. The salt went in on top of the yeast and stalled it - keep them apart until the flour is in. Or it simply had not had long enough somewhere warm: doubling takes 1 to 2 hours at 25C and much longer in a cold kitchen. A dough that rose and then fell was left too long.

Four full days in Paris, not counting the day you arrive or the day you fly home: that covers the main sights at a normal pace, with time to sit down for lunch, and a day more if you want one of the day trips.

Four hours at a time is the usual comfortable limit for an adult dog, and puppies much less. Build it up in short chunks, leave something to chew and a radio on, and a dog-walker or a neighbour for longer days.

Fourteen days from the day it arrives on anything bought online, by phone or by post - no reason needed - and another 14 days to send it back, with the return postage at your cost unless the item is faulty. It does not cover personalised or perishable goods, sealed hygiene items once they are opened, or a service you asked them to start straight away, and in a shop there is no cooling-off right at all: only their own returns policy.
Free money advice covers this — MoneyHelper in the UK does it without charge — that's the quickest route to a straight answer.
Free money advice covers this — MoneyHelper in the UK does it without charge. Tell me what they say and I'll help you weigh it up.

Frequency is how many times something happens in a second, measured in hertz: 50 Hz is fifty times a second. A sound's frequency is its pitch - 440 Hz is the A above middle C, and the higher the number the higher the note - while a radio station's 100 MHz is a hundred million waves a second. It is the reciprocal of the period, so a wave that repeats every 0.02 seconds has a frequency of 50 Hz, and the wavelength is the speed divided by the frequency.

Fresh water boiled once, one teabag per mug, three to four minutes and then the bag out: that is the whole of a good cup, and the milk goes in last. Green tea wants cooler water, about 80C, for two to three minutes, and black tea wants it just off the boil, three to five. Bitter tea has steeped too long in water that was too hot, and a mug that tastes of the last one is a bag left sitting in it.

Friedrich Merz is the chancellor of Germany: in office since May 2025, after his CDU/CSU bloc won the February 2025 election. The president, whose job is mostly ceremonial, is Frank-Walter Steinmeier.

From outside the house it is usually roadworks, a boiler flue or a fan next door, or an animal - and if it keeps you awake, the council's noise team wants the times and days written down, which is what gets anything done. I can't hear any of it from here: which side of the house is it on?

From six months, two or three small goes a day at set times rather than all day long, and the best snacks are the ones they can hold: toast fingers, soft fruit, cooked veg sticks, plain yoghurt, a little cheese, oatcakes. Keep away from the choking shapes - whole grapes, whole nuts, popcorn - and sit them down while they eat. Two snacks a day between meals is right from one: fruit, plain yoghurt, toast, oatcakes, cheese, veg sticks. Keep them at set times rather than in the hand all afternoon, because a child who grazes does not sit down for the meal, and keep the choking shapes - whole grapes, whole nuts, popcorn - for later.

From the main station, take the metro, tram or airport-style express bus and leave the taxi for the cases and the late hour: in most European cities the ride from the main station to the centre is 2 to 5 euros and a taxi is 15 to 25. Buy the ticket at the machine or on the app before you board, walk to the official rank outside the main exit rather than taking an offer from someone inside, and have the address written down or on the phone screen.
From San Francisco Airport: BART to the city is 30 minutes for about $10. A taxi is 25 to 40 minutes and $50 or more.

From about a year they can have what the rest of the family eats, with two changes: take their portion out before the salt goes in, and cut it small - no whole grapes, whole nuts or popcorn before about four. Before one the food is practice, and milk is still the meal, so the family dinner is offered alongside it rather than instead of it.

From a dark place you can see about 2,000 to 3,000 stars at once, and the whole sky holds around 9,000 visible to the naked eye. The Milky Way alone has 100 to 400 billion, and the observable universe has more stars than there are grains of sand on Earth.

Front pads fitted are usually £100 to £200 and discs add £80 to £150 a pair, so a front set with discs is roughly £200 to £350; rears last longer and cost a bit less. Pads are a wear item, so this is normal upkeep rather than a fault, and any garage can quote you in five minutes.

Fry sliced onions for 10 minutes, add garlic, ginger and curry powder, then the chicken and a splash of stock, and simmer for 20 minutes. Yoghurt or tinned tomatoes stirred in at the end make the sauce.

Garlic bread, or aglio e olio: garlic warmed gently in butter or oil, never browned, which is what turns it bitter. Roast potatoes: parboiled 8 minutes, shaken in the pan with hot oil, then 40 minutes at 200C (180C fan).
Gases in the air.

Genghis Khan (about 1162-1227) was the Mongol leader who united the nomadic tribes and built the largest land empire in history, from China to eastern Europe. He was born Temujin, and his grandsons went on to take Baghdad and reach Hungary.
George Orwell wrote 1984, Animal Farm and Down and Out in Paris and London.
Germany: Berlin three full days, Munich two, so five days in all with the journey between them.

Get something that shows you noticed: a book by an author they mentioned, a better version of something they use every day, or an afternoon planned around their favourite thing. The best gifts are specific to one person, so start from what they talk about.

Get the pan properly hot with the oil already in it, then leave the food alone for the first minute: it releases itself once it has browned. For pasta, stir it for the first minute in a big pan of water; for rice, rinse it and don't stir it at all.

Get the root, not the leaves: dandelions and plantains come back from a finger of taproot, and bindweed, ground elder and nettles from any white root left in the soil, so dig them out with a grubber or fork before they seed. On a lawn, feed and mow it properly and thick grass crowds them out; on a patio, path or gravel, hoe or flame them young, or pour boiling water over them. Cardboard and mulch starve a whole bed of them in a season, and a weedkiller is the last resort, never on a windy day.

Get the station and the custody record number first, because that reference is what everyone else quotes from then on. Ask for the free duty solicitor: saying you want one is not an admission and it is the step most people skip. Note the time of the arrest as well, since the clock starts there - usually 24 hours before they have to charge or release.

Get them away from the other customers and let them finish the whole complaint before you say anything: most people wind down once they have been heard. Then say the problem back in their words, and give the one thing you can actually do and when - "I can't refund it today, but I can have the manager ring you before five." Don't argue about who is right, and don't take swearing or threats: end it, and get a colleague or the manager, because being shouted at is not part of the job.

Get up after 20 minutes of lying there awake and do something dull in low light until you feel sleepy, then go back: staying in bed teaches your brain that bed is where you lie awake. Keep the wake-up time the same every day, dim the lights an hour before, and park tomorrow's worries on paper before you get in.

Get your report free from Experian, Equifax or TransUnion, correct anything wrong on it, register on the electoral roll and set up a direct debit for at least the minimum on every card. Keeping card balances under about 30% of the limit and not applying for several things at once does most of the rest.

Get an 8kg drum for a family, a 1,400 spin speed and the best energy rating you can afford: the running cost over ten years beats the purchase price difference. Measure the gap and the door before you order, and check the warranty length.

Get clear before you confront: what you actually saw or found, not the feeling that something is off, because the conversation goes better when you are asking about a fact. Then ask once for the truth - 'I found this and I need you to tell me what it is' - rather than an accusation you then have to defend. Before you start, decide what you want out of it: the truth, a promise it stops, counselling, or time apart. A counsellor or Relate will hold that conversation with you if it keeps turning into a row, and a few sessions on your own help too.

Get a free UNiDAYS or Student Beans account with your college email, and Totum (the old NUS card, about £15 a year) if you want the ones that need a physical card; most big chains give 10%, and plenty give student prices only when you ask at the till, so ask every time. On top of those, a 16-25 Railcard takes a third off train fares and an 18+ Student Oyster takes 30% off London travelcards.

Get down to their level, say what they are upset about in a plain sentence, then hold the limit and wait it out; a toddler needs the calm more than the explanation. A snack and a two-minute warning before a change of scene ('we're leaving when the slide is done') prevents most of them, and a public meltdown is normal at this age, not a sign you are doing it wrong.

Give notice first: you each do it at your local register office at least 29 days before the wedding (in Scotland a marriage notice to the registrar), with a passport or birth certificate and proof of address. Book the venue and the registrar's slot, and find two witnesses. The 29 days is a legal minimum, not a booking window, so do not leave it late.
Give one room a proper clean on a weekday rota - bathroom on Monday, kitchen on Wednesday, floors on Friday - and leave the weekends for bedding and towels, which is one wash each.

Give one thing they do and one thing they own before you describe their face: a woman who counts the stairs as she climbs them and keeps her bus tickets in a tin is a person, and "tall, with brown hair" is a form. Two details, one of them slightly odd, and let the reader do the rest; people remember what a character does far longer than how they look.

Give the day a hard edge and keep it the same one: laptop shut and work phone in a drawer at a fixed time, then something physical - a walk, a shower, cooking - because the body changes gear more reliably than the mind. Tell your team the hours once, in writing: "I'm offline after 6 and I pick up messages at 9." If you work from the room you live in, put the laptop out of sight at the end of the day; a screen in the corner is a shift that never ends.

Give your role, your experience and one thing you care about, and leave out the adjectives: "Registered nurse, eight years in A&E, interested in how teams hand over at shift change." Two lines is about 25 words, so cut anything a stranger could not ask a follow-up question about - and keep the thing you want to talk about.

Give it in writing with a date and a figure: "From 1 April my rate is £X an hour, the same as new clients pay now." Go through the club's own site rather than a reseller: home tickets usually need a membership or a ballot first, and the club's official resale page is the only safe way to get a sold-out one at face value. Go to A&E today and say that one side is swollen or hard and when it started; if the pain came on suddenly it is a twisted testicle, which has only a few hours before it is lost. Ring 999 or 911 if the pain is severe, you are vomiting, or the scrotum looks discoloured.

Go back to the basics of toilet training: take him out every hour and after every meal, nap and play, wait five minutes and praise and treat him the moment he goes outside. A puppy can hold about an hour for every month of age - two hours at two months, four at four - and less when he is excited or has just drunk, so expect a night trip until he is four or five months old. Go by fit: try them on in the afternoon with match socks on, leave a thumb's width at the toe, and go half a size up for a child whose feet are still growing. Granola is oats with oil and sugar baked on, so a 50g serving usually carries about 11 to 15g of sugar, and a bowl of it with milk is closer to a pudding than to porridge. It is not a bad breakfast, it is a portion problem: measure 40g into a bowl rather than pouring from the bag, pick a bag with under 10g of sugar per 100g, and eat it with plain yoghurt and fruit, which is the fibre and the protein that make it last until lunch.

Grapes, crushed and left to ferment: the yeast on the skins eats the sugar in the juice and turns it into alcohol. Red wine spends its time with the skins and white is pressed off them first, which is where the colour comes from.

Great Britain is the island: England, Scotland and Wales. The UK is the country, which is that island plus Northern Ireland. So England is in Britain and in the UK, Northern Ireland is in the UK but not in Britain, and the British Isles is only geography - both islands, including the Republic of Ireland, which is a separate country.
Greece: Athens for the Acropolis and street food. Santorini for the view. Naxos for beaches and cheaper rooms.

Greenfly and blackfly are both aphids and get the same treatment: squash them by hand or spray the undersides of the leaves and the soft growing tips with soapy water - a teaspoon of washing-up liquid in a litre. Broad beans are the usual blackfly crop, and the tips are the first place to look: pinch the top few inches out once the flowers set. Ladybirds and their larvae will clear a lot for you, so leave a marigold or a poached egg plant nearby.
Greenland is the largest island, at about 2.2 million square kilometres. Australia is bigger but is counted as a continent rather than an island, which is the usual quiz gotcha.
Greens: 4 to 6 minutes shredded in boiling salted water, stalky bits first. They are done when they are tender but still green; drain them well and dress with butter or a little oil.

Grey or white walls with a cool blue somewhere, because orange dates fast in large amounts. Sample it before you buy with a patch on the wall or a cushion taken home, because orange changes with the light, and keep the rest of the room quiet so the one colour has somewhere to sit.

Gross is what you earned before anything is taken, net (or take-home) is what lands in the bank, and the difference is income tax, National Insurance and any pension you pay in. A pay figure is always quoted gross unless it says take-home, so a job advertised at £30,000 is about £2,000 a month in your hand on a standard code, and less if you pay into a pension. Check the tax code against your HMRC coding notice (1257L is the standard one): a wrong code is the usual reason a wage comes out short.

Gross is your pay before anything is taken out of it: the number in the job advert, on the contract and at the top of the payslip, before income tax, National Insurance and pension. What actually lands in your bank is net, or take-home, and the gap between them is those deductions - about a fifth of it on an ordinary wage. So a salary quoted at £30,000 is gross unless it says take-home.
Groups is the plural of group. Most words just add s: cat and cats, plan and plans, house and houses.

Grow what gives you a lot from a little: salad leaves, radishes, spring onions, dwarf beans, cherry tomatoes, chillies, one courgette plant, herbs in a pot by the door, and strawberries in a basket. Go upwards where you can - beans and cucumbers up a frame, tomatoes in a grow bag - and sow a few seeds every three weeks rather than everything at once, so you eat from June to October instead of facing a glut in August. On a balcony, weight the pots, keep the tall things against the wall out of the wind, and follow the sun before you buy: a south or west wall grows tomatoes and herbs, a north one wants leaves, mint and ferns.

Guarding food or a bone is ordinary dog behaviour that gets worse when it is punished, so stop taking things off him and teach a trade instead: hold a better treat out to one side, say "drop" as he leaves it, give the bone back, and hands coming near start to mean something good. Feed him where nobody walks past and leave him alone with a bone. If he has actually snapped at a child, ask the vet for a referral to a behaviourist rather than a trainer's quick fix.

HMRC gives a flat rate for a uniform you have to wear and wash: £60 a year for keeping it clean, £140 where it wears out quickly, and up to £18 a month for laundry if you wash a uniform with your employer's logo at home. Claim it on form P87 at gov.uk - it is free, takes about ten minutes, and you can go back four years, so the first claim is often a few hundred pounds.

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language: it is the set of tags that say what each part of a web page is - a heading, a paragraph, a link - and the browser turns those tags into the page you see. It is not a programming language and it cannot do arithmetic, which is what CSS and JavaScript are for.

Hair that comes out in handfuls for a few months is usually telogen effluvium: an illness, a stressful few months, a crash diet or having a baby pushes hair into its resting phase, and it grows back once the cause passes - iron and thyroid tests are worth asking for. A smooth round bald patch (alopecia areata) or a scalp that is scaly, itchy or sore is a GP appointment, and so is hair loss with no obvious trigger.

Half the fat to flour by weight: 250g plain flour and 125g cold butter rubbed in with a pinch of salt, then a few spoons of cold water to bring it together. Rest it in the fridge 30 minutes before rolling, and bake blind at 190C (170C fan) for 15 minutes for a flan case.

Halve it, scoop out the seeds and roast it cut side down at 200C for 35 to 40 minutes, until a knife goes into the flesh like butter; spaghetti squash wants 40 to 45, then fork it into strands. A whole one takes nearer an hour.

Hard cheese keeps 2 weeks in the fridge once opened and soft cheese about a week: wrap it in paper rather than cling film, which sweats it, and keep it in the vegetable drawer, which is the coldest part. Heartburn is a burning behind the breastbone that comes on after food or when you lie down, and an antacid settles it in minutes; a heart attack is a heaviness or tightness that can come on at rest, often spreads to the arm, jaw, neck or back, and comes with sweating, feeling sick or breathlessness. If the pain is new, crushing, or arrives with sweating, breathlessness or a spreading ache, treat it as the heart and ring 999 - an ambulance is the right price of being wrong.

Heat the oven as high as it goes with a heavy tray or a pizza stone inside, then slide the pizza onto the hot tray and give it 8 to 12 minutes, until the edge blisters and the underside is crisp: a thin base and a preheated surface do what an oven alone will not. Horatio Nelson (1758-1805) was the British admiral who beat the French fleet at the Nile in 1798 and the combined French and Spanish fleet at Trafalgar in 1805, where he was shot and died on his own ship. He lost an arm and an eye in earlier actions and is remembered for the signal 'England expects that every man will do his duty'.
Horseradish is hot in the nose, like mustard, and the burn lasts seconds rather than minutes. A teaspoon of the creamed sort is plenty for a plate of beef.

Hot sauce covers everything from 500 to 300,000 Scoville, so the bottle is the only way to know: Tabasco is about 2,500, sriracha about 2,000, and a scotch bonnet sauce can be a hundred times hotter. Taste a drop before you commit.

Hot steam lifts grease and kills most bacteria on tiles, grout, hard floors, the shower and the hob, with no chemicals - about four seconds with the head on one spot is what does it, so move slowly rather than scrubbing. Skip laminate, engineered and unsealed wood and anything with a gap the water can get under, because the heat lifts the surface; skip carpets and upholstery, where a hire machine once a year is cheaper; and keep it off cold glass, which can crack. Empty the tank after every go, and descale it every few months with half water, half white vinegar for 20 minutes.

Humidity is how much water vapour the air holds; relative humidity is that as a share of the most it could hold at that temperature. Warm air holds more, which is why a hot muggy day feels worse than the same heat in dry air.

Phone and tablet: Play Protect on Android and an iPhone need nothing else. Add a free Malwarebytes scan only if something is already misbehaving. The others stay easy, with one session of faster bursts if you have the energy. Nothing new on race day, and a first half is always better run a little slower than you think you can.

One vomit or one loose poo in a dog that is otherwise bright is usually nothing: withhold food for a few hours, then offer small amounts of plain chicken and rice, and keep the water down. Ring the vet if it repeats, if there's blood, if he is flat and not drinking, or if it is a puppy, an old dog or going on for more than a day.

One base and two or three day trips beats three cities in a week, because the day you move is a day you lose. For India the window is October to March for most of the country: dry and cooler. Book the first two nights and the last night only, keep one day free in the middle, and sleep near the airport on the way home.

One channel going funny is the aerial or the box, and every channel is the set: push the aerial lead and the HDMI lead back in at both ends, then press Source and pick the socket the box is in. A lost colour or a green or pink tint is the picture mode, so reset it in Settings > Picture and check Colour is not at zero. One folder or box for each thing you actually have to keep — tax, home, car, health — and one tray for this month. Shred anything with your name and an account number on it. Bank statements, bills and payslips you can download do not need keeping; keep the last six months at most, and anything you have not needed for a year goes in a labelled box in the loft rather than the drawer.

One heavy thing is the usual cause: a duvet or a bath mat balls up on one side and the machine refuses to spin, so shake it flat and run a spin only cycle. Still soaked? Clear the filter behind the kick plate, because a machine that can't drain won't spin. On an older machine the belt can slip off, which is a cheap part.

Onions want dry, dark and airy: a mesh bag or a string in a cupboard, never the fridge, where the damp makes them soft and mouldy, and not in the same bag as the potatoes, because each makes the other go off faster. They keep a month or more, and a cut half keeps 3 to 4 days wrapped in the fridge.

Open the Clock app, tap the plus sign (Alarm > Add on Android), pick the time and the days and save. Check the alarm volume is up, since most phones use a separate alarm volume, and leave the phone off silent mode if the alarm still does not sound.

Ordinary arthritis - osteoarthritis - is the wear-and-tear kind: it aches after years of use, is stiff first thing and eases as you move, and the treatment is using the joint rather than sparing it. Walking, swimming or cycling and a little strength work a few times a week keep the muscles that support the joint strong, and paracetamol with an ibuprofen gel handles a flare better than most tablets sold for arthritis. Glucosamine and cod liver oil have not held up in trials, no diet cures it, and cold, damp weather can make it ache more without damaging the joint; losing weight if you are carrying extra takes real load off knees and hips. Stiffness that lasts more than an hour in the morning, or a joint that is hot, red and swollen, is the inflammatory kind and wants a GP soon - ask about physiotherapy, and about a steroid injection for one joint that keeps flaring.

Osmosis is water moving through a thin membrane from where there is more of it to where there is less, until the two sides even out. A raisin plumps up in water and a slug shrivels in salt for the same reason: the water follows the salt. That is also how a plant's roots drink, and why a wilted lettuce leaf firms up in cold water.

Pack what you use least first - books, spare bedding, the cupboard under the stairs - and keep a 'first night' box out of the van: kettle, mugs, chargers, loo roll, bedding and a change of clothes. Paid overtime depends on your contract: if it says overtime is paid, they must pay it, but if it says nothing there is no legal right to extra pay for extra hours - only that your average pay still clears the minimum wage. Check the contract for the rate and when it starts, and put any change to your hours in writing so it is clear which ones were agreed.

Paint it all one pale colour, ceiling included, and put a mirror where it catches a window: the eye reads the reflection as another room. Hang the curtains at ceiling height rather than at the window, keep the floor visible, and use one rug that stops short of the walls rather than carpet that runs wall to wall.

Paprika is ground dried peppers - sweet, hot or smoked depending on which chilli was used, and the Hungarian sweet one is what people usually mean. Sweet paprika cannot take high heat: stir it in near the end, or bloom it in warm oil for a few seconds, or it turns bitter. Smoked paprika is for depth, in chorizo, beans and roast chicken.

Paracetamol or ibuprofen, a decongestant spray, tissues, honey and lemon, and a thermometer. Rest and plenty to drink do most of the work, and a cold clears in about a week without antibiotics - see a GP if you are short of breath, if a fever lasts more than five days, or if you are getting worse after day five rather than better.

Paris — no first-hand knowledge of the place, so no verdict from me. The things that settle it are how far the flight or the drive is, how hot it gets, and how much walking there is once you are there. Reviews from the last few months say what a place is like now rather than five years ago.

Peas or greens with butter, and bread and butter to mop the plate. A spoon of mustard or horseradish on the side cuts through a rich pie, and both take 5 minutes from frozen.
Penne, rigatoni or lasagne sheets, because a tube keeps its shape through the oven and the sauce gets inside it, where a long strand turns to one lump.

Pet insurance is worth it for a dog or a cat if you could not find £2,000 in a hurry: a broken leg or a blocked bladder runs to £1,500 and up. Take lifetime cover rather than the cheapest accident-only policy, because anything the vet has already treated is excluded for good, and a dog costs about £20 to £40 a month. If you would rather not pay monthly, keep £1,000 in a separate pot instead.
Pets are family, so treat it the way you would a family death for them: say you're sorry about the dog, and offer one concrete thing if you're close enough.

Phlegm that sits in the throat is usually a drip from the back of the nose - a cold, an allergy, a blocked nose, dry air, reflux or smoking - rather than your chest producing it. A salt water rinse (half a teaspoon in a glass of cooled boiled water) or a steroid nose spray for a fortnight is what shifts most of it, with plenty of water and the room not too dry. See a GP if it lasts more than three weeks, comes with weight loss or night sweats, or if the phlegm is bloodstained or green with a fever.

Photograph it straight away and ask for a refund the same day: you paid for the job done with reasonable care, and a botched one breaks that. Set a public target (100 to 500 pounds for a local run), say what the charity does in a sentence, and name the date. Pick one thing with a roof and one without, so a wet afternoon does not ruin the day: a museum with a hands-on gallery plus a park and a picnic is about 20 pounds for a family if the museum is free. Book only what sells out (a pool session, a train ride), pack lunch, and leave by three while everyone is still enjoying it. Free standbys worth checking near you: the library's holiday activities, a city farm, and the local nature reserve.

Pick or snip the spent flower off with its stalk, down to the next bud or strong shoot, and do it every few days through the summer. That is the whole trick: once a plant is allowed to set seed it stops making flower, so cutting the dead heads off is what keeps it going until the frost. Dahlias, cosmos, sweet peas, geraniums and petunias all want it twice a week in a hot spell, and sweet peas must not be left to make pods, because a pod turns the plant woody and it stops. Annuals that are nearly over can be cut back hard, to 15cm, and they come again.

Pick something real, small, and already being worked on: "I used to take everything on rather than ask for help, so now I list what is on my plate with my manager every Monday." Skip the humble-brag about perfectionism, and skip anything that is the core of the job you are applying for.

Pick the one thing they did that you noticed - the spare bed, the early start, the extra trip to the station - and say what it saved you: "Thank you for having me for the weekend - the lift on Sunday saved me the whole morning." Then say when you will have them back, if you mean it.

Pick the thing you cannot change - the sofa, the floor, the tiles - and pull one colour out of it for the walls in a paler version of itself, then one deeper tone for a rug or cushions and a wood or metal to warm it. Three colours, one of them a neutral, and a sample pot painted on a patch of wall you can see in the morning and at night: that is the whole trick.

Pick your corner before the run starts, keep it low and side-foot it inside the post, and do not change your mind on the last step: a firm, repeatable penalty beats a clever one. Practise ten to the same corner at the end of training so the run, the plant foot and the strike are one habit.

Pick a tie a shade darker than your shirt and darker than the suit, and let one bold thing carry it: a patterned tie with a plain shirt, or a patterned shirt with a plain tie. With a navy suit, most things work - burgundy, bottle green, a dark striped tie - and a tie the same colour as the suit is the one to skip.

Pick a class that runs a free taster and go with no partner - most salsa, swing and ceroc nights rotate partners anyway. Wear smooth soles and give it three weeks before deciding, because the first lesson is always clumsy. A weekly class beats a course of videos, since the whole thing is other people's timing.

Pick eight to ten short ones you can use for more than one theme, and learn them in fours to six words rather than whole speeches - "a plague o' both your houses" is learnable, a fifteen-line speech is not. Say each aloud, look away and say it, then write it from memory; do three a day and cycle back through the rest. Practise the sentence you will build around it, because the quote alone earns nothing without the two lines of analysis after it.

Pick four dinners you already cook and plan the week on one list before you shop, then cook once for two nights: a big chilli or a tray of roast vegetables tonight, the rest in a gluten-free pasta bake or wraps tomorrow, and one night that needs no cooking at all. Put one double batch in the freezer for the night you are late home, and keep two fallbacks in the cupboard - gluten-free pasta and a tin of tomatoes, rice and eggs - for the night the plan falls apart.

Pick four dinners you already cook and put them on the fridge, then shop for just those - one double batch goes in the freezer for the night you are late home. Keep one night loose for eggs on toast or a takeaway, and plan whatever spoils first for the day after you shop.

A metal is an element that conducts heat and electricity, is usually shiny, and can be bent or hammered into shape without breaking: iron, copper, aluminium and gold are metals. Most elements are metals, and they sit on the left and middle of the periodic table.

A microphone on the outside of the headphones listens to the noise and the headphones play the same sound inverted, so the two waves cancel where they meet your ear. It works best on steady low sound like engines and least on speech, which is why you still hear the person next to you.

A modem turns the signal on the line coming into your home - fibre, cable or the phone socket - into a network connection, and the router is what shares that connection round the house. Most home boxes do both jobs in one, which is why people use the two words for the same box; the modem is the half that talks to the street.

A molecule is two or more atoms joined together: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen make a water molecule, and DNA is a very long one. The atoms can be the same, as in oxygen gas, or different, as in water.

A narcissist is someone with an inflated sense of their own importance and little room for other people's feelings. The word is used loosely in ordinary talk; as a diagnosis it is a specific personality disorder, and only a professional can make it.

A new bathroom is usually £3,000 to £7,000 fitted, and £8,000 to £12,000 with the bath moved, the walls tiled and the plumbing changed. Tiling and moving the toilet or the bath account for most of the difference. Ask for the scope written down, including who makes good the walls, and agree what happens if the floor under the old suite is rotten.

A normal room is a day's work with two coats: an hour or two to cut in and roll, then about four hours before the second coat, so most people do the first coat in the evening and the second the next morning. A whole flat or house is roughly a day per room, plus a day for the ceilings and woodwork. A single door, a run of skirting or a radiator is a morning: an hour or two a coat, with overnight between the coats.

A normal body temperature is 36.1 to 37.2C (97 to 99F) in the mouth, up to half a degree higher in the evening. From 38C (100.4F) it is a fever, and 37.5 to 38 is a raised reading to watch rather than treat. A stiff neck, a rash that does not fade under a glass, or trouble breathing with a fever is a same-day call, and so is 38C in a baby under three months.

A nurse in the NHS starts on band 5, about £30,000, and goes up to about £36,500 with experience; a specialist or ward manager is £37,000 to £45,000. London adds about £5,000, and nights, weekends and overtime are on top of the basic pay.

A once-a-day non-drowsy antihistamine (cetirizine or loratadine) is the usual first step, and a steroid nasal spray from the pharmacy works better if your nose is the worst part, started a week or two before your season begins. Shower and change when you come in, keep windows shut in the morning and around midday when the count peaks, and dry washing indoors.

A pair of glasses is usually £100 to £300 with standard lenses, and varifocals or thin lenses push it to £300 to £500. The frame is where the money goes, and the two-for-one offers usually mean two pairs of a cheap lens. Ask what the lenses cost on their own, and ask for your prescription and pupillary distance so you can compare anywhere.

A pastry brush is the small brush for glazing and greasing: beaten egg on a pie lid, milk on a bun, melted butter in a tin, a wash of syrup on a warm cake. Silicone takes the heat and washes clean; a bristle brush gives a finer finish but sheds, so keep it for cool jobs.

A patch is a DIY job and a whole wall is not: for anything over a square metre get a plasterer, because the finish is all in the timing. For a patch, scrape it back to sound plaster, wet the edges, press filler in with a wide filling knife and scrape it flat while it is still soft, then sand it once dry. A skim is two coats of multi-finish about an hour apart, each 2 to 3mm, laid on with a trowel and flattened with a wider one, then polished with a wet trowel when it starts to set - and the whole wall wants PVA or a bonding agent first, or the new plaster dries too fast and crazes.

A percentage is a fraction of 100: 25% means 25 out of every 100, or a quarter, and 100% is the whole thing. To turn a fraction into a percentage, divide the top by the bottom and multiply by 100, so 3/5 is 60%.
A piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black, seven and a bit octaves from A0 to C8.
A plumber or electrician will spot it in minutes. Tell me what they say and I'll help you weigh it up.
A poem about lost friendship needs one real thing in it: give me a sound, a smell or a day from it and I'll build the poem round that.

A policy is decided by its own wording and its list of exclusions, not by the kind of claim it sounds like. Read the exclusions first, then ring the insurer to confirm your own case before you claim or pay for anything: they have to tell you, and that answer is the one that counts.

A polygon is a closed flat shape made only of straight sides that do not cross. A triangle has 3 sides, a quadrilateral 4, a pentagon 5 and a hexagon 6; a circle is not a polygon because its edge is curved.

A prism is a solid with the same cross-section all the way along, like a triangular prism or a long box. Its volume is the area of that cross-section times the length. A cube and a cuboid are prisms too.

A professional championship fight is twelve rounds of three minutes with a minute between, and most ordinary fights are four, six, eight or ten. Amateur bouts are usually three rounds of three. You win on points from the judges if it goes the distance, or by knockout, and a boxer who cannot continue loses.
A pronoun stands in for a noun so you are not repeating it: I, you, he, she, it, we, they, me, him, her, them. 'Sam lost Sam's keys' is why we have them.

A pulled thigh or calf muscle, or the ache that lands a day after squats, wants the same start: rest it, ice it for 20 minutes at a time for two days, then gentle stretching and a slow return to what you were doing, with the leg kept up when you sit. Calf pain with a hot, swollen leg, or a shin that hurts to touch after a knock, needs looking at.

A pulley is a wheel with a rope running over it: one changes the direction of a pull, so you pull down to lift a load up, and two together halve the force you need by doubling the rope. That is why a flagpole and a crane both use one.

A puppy is the other way round: about five minutes of walking for every month of age, twice a day, so a four-month-old gets two twenty-minute walks and no long hikes or stair runs until the growth plates close at a year.

A quick-release collar with a bell cuts the hunting down, and keeping her in from dusk until morning misses the hours most of it happens; a garden bird feeder on a pole away from cover helps too. She is bringing food to the household rather than being naughty, so take the bird away in gloves and don't scold her for it.

A rabbit is picked up with one hand under the chest and the other under the hindquarters, held against your body so the back legs cannot kick out - never by the ears, the scruff or the back of the neck, because a rabbit that kicks while nothing is holding its back end can break its own spine. Sit on the floor with him on your lap for a few minutes a day and a bit of food in your hand, and put him down before he starts to struggle, so being picked up stops being a surprise. A pet that squeals, flinches or struggles at being handled when he did not before needs a vet - a sore tooth, an injured back or mites is the usual reason and a rabbit that stops eating after it is worth ringing the vet the same day.

A rabbit is bored when it has nothing to chew and nowhere to dig: give it a run of a few hours a day outside a hutch, a box of hay to root through, willow or apple sticks to chew and something to hide under. A lone rabbit wants a rabbit friend more than it wants toys, and the two are happiest neutered and introduced slowly.
A ragu of mince, onion, carrot and tomato cooked down for at least an hour, a bechamel, and parmesan between and on top: the rest is layering.

A rap about work: Yo, the work is back and it is here to stay, I have been up since six and I am out all day. They said it was nothing, I said it was mine, so the work and me, we are doing just fine. Give me one real thing from it - a sound, a smell or a day - and I will write the rap round that.

A rat runs to 20 to 25 cm in the body, with a thick tail as long again, a blunt nose and small ears; a mouse is 7 to 10 cm, with a pointed nose, big ears and a thin tail about as long as its body. Rats travel the same run each night from drains, rubbish and walls; house mice live indoors in cupboards and under the floor.

A ratio compares two amounts by division, so a ratio of 2:3 means the second amount is one and a half times the first. A recipe using 2 cups of flour to 3 of milk is in the ratio 2:3, and scaling both numbers by the same amount keeps the ratio the same.
A red flag is a warning sign worth taking seriously: a deposit asked for before a viewing, or a new job with no contract.
A rhyme about moby dick: I keep a little dick in mind, the sort of dick that's hard to find. It does not shout, it does not boast, and that's the dick I like the most.
A rhyme about five words: I keep a little word in mind, the sort of word that's hard to find. It does not shout, it does not boast, and that's the word I like the most.

A roofer is who takes this one on: it is scaffold and two people, and the water from a job that fails costs more than the job. Ring two near you - a quote costs nothing, and it tells you whether this is a small job or a bigger one than it looks.

A room thermostat is a switch that reads the air - when the room reaches the set temperature it stops asking the boiler for heat, and it starts again a degree or two lower. Turning it up does not heat the room faster, only further - the boiler flow temperature and the size of the radiators set the speed.

A rough target is 25 times what you want to spend each year on top of the state pension: £10,000 a year beyond it wants a pot of about £250,000. The full new state pension is around £11,500 a year from 66 or 67, and you can take private pension money from 55 (57 from 2028), so check your forecast on the government's pension service before you decide anything.

A rug, a cool bag with a freezer block, plates and cups you do not mind losing, a bottle opener, napkins, a bin bag and water. Skip anything heavy with mayonnaise unless it is eaten within the hour: sausage rolls, cheese, fruit and a flask keep for hours.

A sandwich or wrap with something filling (cheese, tuna, ham, hummus), fruit, something crunchy and a drink is a packed lunch in five minutes; cook extra dinner and take the leftovers in a tub and it is quicker still. Keep anything with meat, fish, egg or dairy cold until you eat it.

A seat for carrying a child clamps to the frame, not to the seatpost, and it holds them until about 22kg: 20kg to 22kg is the usual limit, so check the seat's rating against your child's weight rather than their age. From about nine months, once they can sit up by themselves, a rear seat is the usual choice: it needs a harness, footwells and a helmet even for a short trip, a high-back seat gives the head some support, and it is the frame tubes the brackets bolt to. Never fit one to a bike with a carbon frame or a rear suspension, and take the child off before you fold or park the bike. Two children, or one under nine months, want a trailer instead: it sits behind and low, with a flag and lights on the back.

A shadow is the patch where an object blocks light: light travels in straight lines, so an opaque object stops the rays and leaves a dark shape behind it. The shadow is biggest when the light source is close to the object and the surface is far behind, and a point of light gives a sharper edge than a wide one.

A shooting star is a speck of dust or grit burning up high in the atmosphere, not a star falling. Most are the size of a grain of sand and vanish in a second; during a meteor shower you can see dozens an hour.

A shop service is £50 to £95 for the basic job - the bearings, the gears, the brakes and the wheels trued - or £120 to £200 for a full strip-down and rebuild. Once a year is the usual answer, sooner if you ride in the wet or cover a few thousand miles, and it is worth it when the gears skip or the brakes feel spongy. Check the chain, the cassette, the brake pads and the tyres yourself, and ask what the price covers before you book.

A short story about the american south: He had carried the south from one flat to another for eleven years. The morning he finally opened it, the kettle boiled and the phone rang at the same time. He let the kettle win, and the phone stopped. Then he sat at the table with the south and read the whole thing twice.

A short story about the first contact: The contact arrived in a box with no sender and no note. It sat in the hall for a week, and then it started to hum. She unscrewed one corner, looked inside, and sat down on the floor. "Well," she said to nobody at all, "that changes the week."

A short story about two cities: It started with a city nobody in the house had planned for. The Tuesday came and went, and it was still there on the Wednesday. By Friday the whole street had an opinion, and no two of them matched. In the end they kept it, and it kept them.

A short story about an inn staffed: The staffed arrived in a box with no sender and no note. It sat in the hall for a week, and then it started to hum. She unscrewed one corner, looked inside, and sat down on the floor. "Well," she said to nobody at all, "that changes the week."
