A short story about humans on mars: He had carried the mar from one flat to another for eleven years. The morning he finally opened it, the kettle boiled and the phone rang at the same time. He let the kettle win, and the phone stopped. Then he sat at the table with the mar and read the whole thing twice.
A short essay is usually 1,000–1,500 words, a university one 2,000–3,000, and coursework will state it. Aim for 10% under the limit; going over is the mistake markers mind.
A shower runs at about 10 litres a minute, so five minutes is 50 litres and ten is 100; a power shower can be twice that, and turning the tap off while you soap up is the free half of the saving.
A simile compares with like or as (her laugh was like a kettle), and a metaphor says it is the thing (her laugh was a kettle). Both make a picture; the metaphor just does it without the 'like'.

A smart thermostat is worth it if the house is empty in the day: about £50 to £100 a year off a gas bill, so £150 to £250 fitted pays back in two to three years. Skip it if someone is home all day, or if the heating is already set to come on only when you are in: turning the flow temperature down and putting thermostatic valves on the radiators gets much of the saving for a fraction of the price.

A smooth lump on the back of the wrist that comes and goes is usually a ganglion cyst: harmless, often smaller after a few weeks, and worth a GP look only if it is painful, growing fast or stops you using the hand - they can drain it, but a lot come back. A hard, fixed lump, or one anywhere else, gets checked by a GP within a couple of weeks.

A soggy waffle is a batter that is too thin or an iron that is not hot enough: make it thicker than pancake batter - it should plop off the ladle rather than pour - let it rest 10 minutes so the flour takes up the liquid, and heat the iron until a drop of water skitters on it. Fill it three-quarters so the steam can escape, and stand the cooked ones on a rack in a low oven rather than stacking them, because a stack steams itself soft.

A solicitor's day is files and clients: reading, advice, letters, negotiation, and time recorded in six-minute units. Conveyancing is volume, family and crime are court dates, and commercial work is documents. The pressure is deadlines and other people's money, and most of the job is writing clearly about what should happen next.

A song about most popular songs: Verse: It was a Tuesday, nothing much to say, I thought about the song and I walked away. Chorus: Oh, the song, the song, it comes back around, the song comes back around.
A song about simon: Verse: It was a Tuesday, nothing much to say, I thought about the simon and I walked away. Chorus: Oh, the simon, the simon, it comes back around, the simon comes back around.

A song about award winning songs: Verse: It was a Tuesday, nothing much to say, I thought about the song and I walked away. Chorus: Oh, the song, the song, it comes back around, the song comes back around.

A song about billboard right: Verse: It was a Tuesday, nothing much to say, I thought about the right and I walked away. Chorus: Oh, the right, the right, it comes back around, the right comes back around.

A sonnet is fourteen lines in iambic pentameter - ten syllables a line, stress on every second one. Shakespeare's kind rhymes in three quatrains and a closing couplet (abab cdcd efef gg) and turns at line nine; the Italian kind splits six and eight.
A spoonful means a level tablespoon, 15ml unless the recipe says heaped; a cupful is 250ml, filled level rather than heaped. Go by the recipe where it gives a weight.

A sports drink is water with sugar and salt, and it only earns its place in a long or hot session: over about an hour, or two sessions in a day, or a match in the heat. For an ordinary gym hour, a 5k or a swim, water is enough - a 500ml bottle of sports drink is about 30g of sugar, and the salt you lose is replaced by the next meal. A cheap version of the same thing is squash with a pinch of salt in a bottle of water, and a glass of milk does more for you after a hard session than most of the shelf does.

A square root is the number that times itself makes yours: the square root of 49 is 7 because 7 x 7 = 49. Learn the squares up to 12 x 12 and you can place anything between them by eye, and the root button gives the exact answer - so the square root of 50 is a little over 7.

A steady, even sound covers the small noises - a door, a stair, a cough - that wake a light sleeper, so it helps most in a shared or noisy room rather than instead of a bedtime routine. Keep it low: quieter than a shower, about the level of a quiet conversation, and an arm's length or more from the cot or the head of the bed. Leave it on at the same level all night rather than fading it out, but never loud enough to hide a cry or the smoke alarm. A fan, an untuned radio or a phone app all do the same job, and there is no good evidence that one colour of noise works better than another.

A stiff neck is usually muscular, from posture or sleeping awkwardly: heat, gentle stretches and a look at your screen height help, and a soft collar for a day or two is fine but not longer, because the muscles need to work. Get seen the same day if it comes with a fever, a bad headache, or light hurting your eyes.

A strimmer cuts grass and edges of a lawn with a nylon line on a spinning head, a hedge trimmer is a bar of blades for the flat sides and top of a hedge, a leaf blower is a fan in a tube, and a chainsaw is a loop of chain on a bar for timber. The strimmer is for grass, the trimmer for a hedge's shape, and the chainsaw only for wood - not for a hedge, where it chews the growth instead of cutting it clean.

A supermarket herb pot is a dozen seedlings crammed into one small pot, so it runs out of root room and food and starts going yellow within a fortnight. Split it into two or three pots with fresh compost now, keep it in good light, and water when the top dries out; leaving it crowded is what kills it, not your watering.

A tailor can usually save it. What they can change: a jacket taken in at the sides, the sleeves shortened, the hem let down an inch or two, and trousers let out about one size (2-4cm) if there is seam allowance left inside the waist. What nobody can fix is a jacket that is tight across the chest or whose shoulder seam sits past your shoulder bone - that is a size up, and no alteration makes it right. A local alterationist charges £15 to £40 for a jacket taken in and £10 to £25 for a hem, usually inside a week; ask them to pin it on you so you can see the fit before they cut.

A tailor can usually take a garment out by about one size, and a trouser waist by about 5cm, because what allows it is the seam allowance still inside: a waist or a hem is £20-40 and a jacket £40-80, done in a few days. Judge it on the shoulders - they can be taken in a little but never let out, so a jacket tight across the back is the one to pass on. Take the trousers with the jacket so the length is set with the shoes you will wear, and it is worth it on a suit whose cloth is decent, not on one that has gone shiny at the seat.

A tenth to a fifth of what you take home is the usual amount to put by: £200 to £400 a month on £2,000, in a separate account with a standing order for the day after payday so it leaves before you can spend it. If that is too much this month, take the fixed amount you would not miss and raise it by £5 whenever a bill drops.

A tick has to come out properly: fine-tipped tweezers as close to the skin as you can get, pull steadily straight out without twisting, then clean the spot. Do not burn it, smother it in oil or pull it with your fingers - that makes it more likely to leave mouth parts behind or pass infection on. Keep it in a sealed pot in case the vet asks, and check the animal over daily after walks in long grass. Ring the vet if the bite goes red or a rash spreads from it, if the animal goes off its food, or if there is a limp or a fever in the weeks after.

A time is a rate times a size: minutes per kilo, hours per coat, days a chapter. Whoever sets the rate - the recipe, the course, the trade - says what it is, and give me your size and I will do the multiplication.

A traybake: halve the potatoes, toss everything with oil, salt and lemon slices, and roast at 200C (180C fan) for 35 to 40 minutes, skin side up, until the skin is crisp and the juices run clear. Squeeze the roasted lemon over before serving.
A triangle is a flat shape with three straight sides and three corners.
A troll is someone who posts to wind people up rather than to argue in good faith. Answering them is the contact they wanted.

A tumble dryer is worth it if you would use it three times a week or more and it saves a job you dislike; skip it otherwise, because it takes up a cupboard. Buy the cheap one first, because most of these are replaced by a better model you only learn you wanted after a year of using the first.

A turkey is done when the thickest part of the thigh reads 74C and the juices run clear, not pink, where you pierce it; the breast reads about 70C by then and carries on cooking as it rests. Without a thermometer, the leg should move freely in its socket and the skin pull away easily - then rest it 30 minutes under foil.

A tyre holds air, and the air carries the car: the rubber only has to keep the shape, which is why the pressure in it decides how much tread stays on the road. Where the rubber touches, it grips by pressing into the surface and by the rubber squirming in the grooves, and water has to escape through the tread or the tyre rides up on it and aquaplanes.

A van up to 3.5 tonnes drives on an ordinary full licence and much like a big car, but it is wider, taller and has no rear window in most panel vans, so you drive it on the two side mirrors. Set both mirrors out a little further before you move, take corners wider than feels natural because the back wheels cut inside, and reverse slowly with a second person behind you if there is one. Remember the height: a standard van is often over two metres, so check the barrier or car-park limit before you drive in.
A violin has four strings, tuned G, D, A and E from the lowest up.
A walk-in centre today, as I said - no appointment, and they can look at it properly.
A warm bath an hour before bed sends you to sleep faster than a warm bedroom does.

A watch marked 5ATM or 50m is fine for a swim and a shower, 3ATM is a splash only, and IP68 means it survives a dunk rather than a swim. No watch likes hot water or soap, because steam and shampoo get past the seals, and the seals age - so a shower or a pool is fine, a hot bath or a dive is not.

A waterproof with a hood is the one thing that decides the day, with a thin layer underneath rather than a thick coat, because rain gear is warm once you move. Wear shoes that keep water out - leather or a waterproof boot rather than canvas, which soaks and stays wet - and take a second pair of socks. Cotton next to the skin is what makes a wet day cold, so a synthetic or wool base layer is worth more than an extra jumper.

A weight or a wound spring stores the energy, a gear train slows it down, and an escapement lets it out one tick at a time - that tick is what moves the hands at a steady rate. A pendulum or balance wheel sets the rhythm, which is why a grandfather clock keeps good time and a cheap watch drifts. A quartz watch swaps the pendulum for a crystal vibrating 32,768 times a second, which a chip counts down to one second.
A year on Mars lasts 687 Earth days, nearly two of ours, because Mars is further from the Sun and moves more slowly round it. A Martian day is only about 40 minutes longer than an Earth day.

A Lifetime ISA pays 25% on what you put in, up to £1,000 a year, and you can pay in until you are 50. The money has to go on a first home under £450,000 or wait for retirement at 60 - take it out for anything else and the 25% charge takes the bonus back, so it suits deposit money you will not touch for a year, not savings you might need sooner.

A 15-minute tomato pasta: soften sliced garlic in olive oil, add the tinned tomatoes and a pinch of salt, and simmer while the pasta cooks. Tear in a few basil leaves at the end and loosen it with a splash of pasta water so it clings.

A VPN encrypts the traffic between you and the internet, which is worth it on hotel and cafe wifi; it does not make you anonymous. For everyday home use you do not really need one, and the free ones usually make their money from your data, so pay a few pounds for Mullvad, Proton or similar if you want one.

A back that gives trouble on and off is usually muscular, and what keeps it quiet is strength and movement rather than rest: walk most days, and add two short sessions a week of a slow bridge lying down or sit-to-stand from a chair. Ask your GP about physio if it is stopping you sleep or work, and ring 111 the same day if you cannot pass urine, have numbness between your legs, or it came on after a fall.

A bald patch is usually fleas, a skin infection or an allergy, and sometimes a spot rubbed raw by licking or a harness. Have the vet look if it is spreading, scabby, itchy or the dog is unwell; flea treatment for every pet in the house and a hot wash of the bedding sorts the commonest cause.

A balloon whisk is the round, balloon-shaped wire one, for putting air in: egg whites to peaks, cream to soft folds, a batter smooth. Its wide loops move a lot of air, which a flat or a ball whisk does not, so it is the one for meringue; it is no good for a thick mixture - that is a wooden spoon's job. Use a big bowl and lift the whisk right out of the mixture each turn, and take the cream from the fridge cold.

A banana starts growing downwards, then turns and grows upwards towards the light, and the side facing the ground grows faster, so the fruit ends up curved. The bend is set by the time it is cut, which is why a bunch hangs like a hand of fingers.

A banana is about 100 calories with 3g of fibre and around 400mg of potassium, and the sugar in it (about 14g) comes with that fibre and water, so it is a snack rather than a problem - fresh fruit is not what the 30g free-sugar limit is aimed at. A greener one has more resistant starch, which is good for the gut; a spotted one is sweeter and easier to digest before a run. One or two a day is fine, and the same holds for apples, oranges and pears at 60 to 80 calories each.
A bass guitar has four strings, E, A, D and G - the same notes as the bottom four of a guitar, an octave lower.

A battery turns chemical energy into electricity: a reaction inside pushes electrons from one terminal to the other, and the circuit carries them round to do work. A rechargeable one reverses that reaction when you plug it in.

A bed it can stretch out flat in, two bowls, a collar and a lead, a harness for walks where it pulls, poo bags and food of the brand it is already on, plus a coat if it has a thin coat like a greyhound. A rescue usually comes with its own lead and a bag of food, so ask the centre what it has been eating and keep to that for the first fortnight, and budget about £1,500 to £2,000 a year for a dog before any vet bill.

A bee is furry, round and brownish or striped softly, and a honeybee dies after one sting because the sting stays in the skin; a wasp is smooth, bright yellow with black bands and a pinched waist, and it can sting over and over. Bees are after nectar and pollen and leave you alone; wasps hunt insects and in late summer want sugar, which is why they come for your drink. Flick a wasp away rather than swat it, and if a sting brings swelling of the face or trouble breathing, that is 999.

A bird's wing is curved on top, so air moving over it travels faster and presses less than the air underneath; the difference lifts the bird. Flapping provides thrust, and light, hollow bones keep the whole body easy to carry.

A birth weight between about 5lb 8oz and 8lb 13oz is normal, and the number on its own says very little: what matters is the line in the red book. A baby usually gets back to their birth weight by two weeks and then gains roughly 150 to 200g a week for the first few months, so the health visitor plotting it once is worth more than any single figure. Ask them to weigh the baby if you are unsure, and go sooner if the gain flattens off, if there are fewer than six wet nappies a day, or if the baby is too sleepy to feed.

A black hole is a place where matter is packed so tightly that its gravity pulls in everything, even light. Most form when a very massive star runs out of fuel and collapses; we spot them by the way their gravity moves and heats nearby gas.

A blender is worth it if you would use it three times a week or more and it saves a job you dislike; skip it otherwise, because it takes up a cupboard. Buy the cheap one first, because most of these are replaced by a better model you only learn you wanted after a year of using the first.

A blood moon is a lunar eclipse: the Earth sits between the Sun and the Moon, and the only sunlight reaching the Moon has passed through Earth's atmosphere, which scatters the blue away and leaves red. It is safe to look at, unlike a solar eclipse.

A blood test is a small sting and a vial or two, and there is nothing about having one to worry about - it is the number it comes back with that matters. If that comes back outside the range they will tell you, and it is usually repeated in a few weeks.

A 20cm sponge bakes at 180C (160C fan) for 25 to 30 minutes; a loaf tin needs 45 to 55. It's done when a skewer in the middle comes out clean, and it's worth checking 5 minutes early the first time. About an hour and a half start to finish, counting mixing and cooling.

A bruise is blood under the skin from a knock: it looks black at first, then fades through purple, green and yellow over one to two weeks. A cold pack for twenty minutes with a cloth round it, a few times in the first two days, eases it. Get it seen the same day if it swells hard and fast, the skin is broken, the part will not take your weight, or a patch goes black with no knock you can remember.
A bucket is about 10 litres, a mop bucket 5 to 15 depending on the size, which is the measure to count in when you are sizing a water butt: a 100 litre butt is ten buckets.
A bullet point is the dot that starts each item in a list. Keep every item to a line, start each one the same way, and leave the full stops off short items.

A cake takes three swaps: 60g of yoghurt or half a mashed banana, or a flax egg (a tablespoon of ground flaxseed and three of water, left five minutes), for each egg; unsweetened soya or oat milk for the milk; and a block margarine or 80g of neutral oil for every 100g of butter. Add an extra half teaspoon of baking powder, because the egg was doing some of the lifting, and give it five minutes longer in the oven. Soya milk browns best, and a sponge made this way keeps a day less.

A calorie is a unit of energy - the heat that raises 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius - and the calories on a food label are really kilocalories, a thousand of those each. Most adults need around 2,000 to 2,500 of them a day, and a pound of body fat holds about 3,500.

A cappuccino is a third espresso, a third steamed milk and a third foam: pull a double espresso (about 60ml), heat about 120ml of milk to 60-65C while letting plenty of air in so it doubles to a stiff foam, then pour the milk in and spoon the foam on top. Whole milk froths most easily and skimmed the least. With no steamer, heat the milk in a pan to just before it simmers and whisk hard for 20 seconds, or shake it in a lidded jar and give it 30 seconds in the microwave.

A car battery that keeps going flat is usually either old (they last 3 to 5 years) or being drained by something left on, a stuck boot light or a failing alternator. Get the battery and charging system tested free at most tyre or battery places; if it is the original battery and the car is five or more, replace it.

A car hangs on steel ropes that pass over a pulley at the top, and a counterweight on the other end weighs about the same as the car plus half a load, so the motor only has to shift the difference. A governor trips a brake that grips the guide rails if the car falls faster than it should, and the doors will not open unless the car is level with a floor.

A career in enterprise software — no first-hand knowledge of that one. The honest answer turns on the pay, the hours, and what the day actually looks like rather than what the job is called. The pay scales are published, and asking two people who do it now about a normal week settles more than any article.
A carnivore is an animal that eats other animals: a lion, a cat, a heron, a spider. Most have sharp teeth or a beak for tearing meat, and a short gut, because meat is easier to digest than plants.

A carpenter's day is either second fix in a finished house - doors, skirting, stairs, kitchens - or a workshop bench making what goes in. Site carpenters do more cutting and fitting, bench joiners do more setting out and jointing, and both need to read a drawing and work to a millimetre. Dust, noise and knees, and the good ones are never out of work.

A cat that keeps being sick needs the vet rather than a wait-and-see: repeated vomiting in a cat is often a swallowed blockage (string, a hairband, a toy) or a poison, and cats go downhill fast. Offer small amounts of water, no food for a few hours, and ring the vet; go straight away if there is blood, if she is retching with nothing coming up, or if she is flat and hiding.

A cat chews houseplants for the crunch and the water in the leaves, but some are dangerous: true lilies are deadly to cats, even a sniff of the pollen, and ivy, poinsettia and peace lily burn the mouth. Move those out of reach, put a tray of cat grass down instead, and ring the vet if she drools, vomits or looks wobbly.

A cat costs about £700 to £1,000 a year once insurance and a vet fund are in, and unlike a dog it does not need you home at lunchtime: an adult cat sleeps through a working day, which is why people who cannot have a dog often do well with a cat. Get an adult rather than a kitten if you are out, two if the house is empty all day, a litter tray each plus one, and settle the landlord and who looks after it when you go away before you fall for one.

A catalogue turns over every month with the rights, so typing the title into YouTube's own search is what says whether it is there today - I can't see it from here, and it says whether that is a rental or part of the subscription.
A catalogue turns over every month with the rights, so I can't hold the list: YouTube's own search settles it in seconds, and says whether the thing is included or to pay for.
A character has to tell a lie to somebody they love, on a day that is otherwise ordinary. Write the ten minutes before they do it and leave the lie out of the page.

A cheap electric brush with a timer cleans more evenly than most hands manage with a manual, and an expensive one is not twice as good, so pick one with a two-minute timer and a small round head. Change the head every three months. What matters more than the brush is a fluoride toothpaste and spitting rather than rinsing at the end.

A chemical reaction is when substances rearrange their atoms to make new ones: bonds break, new bonds form, and the starting materials are used up. Burning, rusting, baking and digestion are all reactions, and they usually give out or take in heat.
A chord is three or more notes played together: C major is C, E and G, all at once. Major chords sound settled and minor ones sound sad, which is most of why a song has a mood at all.

A 30g handful of nuts is about 175 calories and one of the better snacks you can buy: 6g of protein, 3g of fibre and fat that is mostly unsaturated, and people who eat them regularly tend to weigh less, not more, because they are satisfying. Walnuts are the one with omega-3 (plant ALA). Buy them unsalted and unsweetened, and count the handful out rather than eating from the bag.

A cold stays in the nose and throat: a runny nose, sneezing, a sore throat, and you can still get up and work. Flu comes on in hours with a fever, aching limbs and being flattened in bed, and the cough and the tiredness can drag on for two or three weeks. You can get flu more than once, because each season has different strains - that is why the jab changes every year - and a cold is a different family of viruses again.

A cold tap that runs warm is nearly always warm water getting into the cold pipe: a mixer tap or shower cartridge letting by, or a non-return valve that has failed, and in a house with a hot water cylinder a faulty mixing valve does the same. Feel the pipe under the sink - if it turns cold after a minute or two it is just the pipe run sitting warm in a cupboard, which is harmless; if it stays warm, have the check valve or cartridge replaced. If it is only the one tap, that tap is the culprit; if it is every cold tap, look at the cylinder, the mixing valve or the shared supply.

A cold usually peaks in two or three days and is gone in about a week, though a cough and a blocked nose can linger for two weeks and that is normal. Rest, plenty of fluid and paracetamol for the ache are the treatment; antibiotics do nothing for a virus. See a GP if it lasts more than three weeks, if you are breathless or wheezing, or if a child is drinking less and has a fever that will not come down.

A colon introduces what explains or follows: a list, an example, a quote. "Take three things: milk, eggs and bread." No capital after it unless a full sentence follows, and no colon straight after a verb - "the things I need are milk, eggs and bread", not "are: milk".
A concrete block is 440 by 215mm, so a square metre of single-skin wall is about 10 blocks. How big is the wall - length and height in metres?

A corner shop covers more of a dinner than people expect: rice, pasta, eggs, tinned beans and chickpeas, tinned tomatoes, frozen peas, onions, potatoes, milk, cheese and a curry powder or stock cubes. What it will not have is fresh herbs, good bread or anything unusual, so take the dried or tinned version rather than going without. Rice, eggs and frozen peas make fried rice in 15 minutes, and a tin of chickpeas with an onion and curry powder is a curry in 25.

A couple or a family of four spends about 70 to 80 pounds a week on food shopping, from about 55 for two cooking from scratch, and about 100 to 130 once lunches and a takeaway are in it. A list once a week is what keeps it there.

A credit card is worth having if you clear it in full every month: it builds a credit history and gives you protection on purchases over £100. Start with a card for bad or no credit history if that's you, set a direct debit for the full balance each month, and never use it for cash or to spend money you don't have.

A cube is a solid with six square faces of the same size, twelve edges and eight corners: a sugar lump and a die are cubes. Its volume is the side multiplied by itself three times, so a 2 cm cube holds 8 cm³, and its surface area is six times one face.

A damp cloth with a little washing-up liquid takes most of it, and a dab of toothpaste or a melamine sponge lifts what is left on paint, varnish, laminate or a worktop. Test a hidden patch first and keep the sponge light: too much rubbing takes the paint or the finish with it. Dried ink wants a drop of nail polish remover on a cloth, wiped off and rinsed. On a carpet, a rug or a sofa, blot with warm water and washing-up liquid instead of scrubbing, then rinse and dry it flat.

A 60 litre bag of compost covers about 1 square metre at 50mm, and a 145 litre bag about 2.5 square metres. Measure the area and work out the volume at the depth you want, then divide by what a bag holds, and order a tenth more than the sums say - a bag never spreads as far as the label claims. For a raised bed, fill the top 300mm with compost and the rest with rougher soil or rubble at the bottom; a bed one metre by two at 300mm deep takes about 6 bags of 60 litres.

A dead appliance is usually the plug, the fuse or a door switch: swap the fuse, try another socket, shut the door firmly and look the fault code up in the manual. If it stays dead, take the model number off the sticker and ask the maker or a local repairer for a fixed-price quote, because under six years old a repair is usually the cheaper way.

A debit card takes the money straight out of your own account as you pay, so you can only spend what is there; a credit card borrows from the card company and sends you a bill later, with interest if you do not clear it. A debit card costs nothing to use and cannot leave you in debt, while a credit card over £100 gives you the card company's protection if the seller goes bust or never delivers.

A decorator's merchant rather than a chain for the paint itself: the trade brands cover better, cost less and they will mix a colour to a sample. For one room, a DIY shop for the brushes, trays and sheets is fine, and cheap brushes are the false economy - they shed.

A diamond or a delta, about 1.2 to 1.5 metres across, is the usual first kite: it launches easily, flies in light wind and costs about fifteen to twenty-five pounds. Look for one with a long tail (it steadies the flight for a child) and a line of at least 30 metres on a winder. Skip the stunt kites and the two-line ones: they need more wind and a lot more practice. A cheap supermarket delta is fine to learn on - you can spend more when they ask for a second one.

A disabled person's bus pass is a council scheme and it costs nothing to apply. You qualify if you are blind or partially sighted, deaf, or cannot walk without help or can only walk a short way without severe pain, and also with a learning disability or if a driving licence was refused on medical grounds. Apply to your council with a photo, proof of address and evidence of the disability, and it gives free travel on local buses at any time rather than from 9.30am. In London it is the Freedom Pass, and a companion travels free with you on it if you cannot travel alone.

A dog shows pain by changing how he moves rather than by crying: stiff getting up, refusing the stairs or the sofa, lagging on walks, licking one spot, panting at rest or snapping when touched. Look at him from behind while he stands - a hunched back and a tucked belly is a sore middle. Anything that lasts more than a day is a vet visit, and a dog who cannot settle or is breathing fast needs one today.

A dog is usually done at about six months, and the bigger the breed the later: a large or giant dog is often left to nine or twelve months, a small one at five or six, and a bitch before her first season or three months after one ends rather than in the middle of it. It depends on the animal. A cat at four to six months, a female from about four, before her first litter. A rabbit at about four months for a buck and five or six for a doe, and both before they are bonded rather than after. There is no upper limit either, so an older animal can still be done and the vet will weigh the anaesthetic against the reason. Nothing says you must, so it is a choice as well as a date: ask your own vet what they would do for your animal, because the timing is a conversation, not a rule.

A doula is a trained companion who supports you through pregnancy, birth or the first weeks at home: she stays with you, helps you understand what is happening and what your choices are, and looks after the practical side. She is not a midwife and does no medical care - no examinations, no monitoring, no advice on the baby's health - so she is there alongside the midwife, not instead of her. Most charge a few hundred to about a thousand pounds for a birth, and finding one early matters, because good ones book up.

A dry mouth is usually mouth breathing - a blocked nose, a stuffy room, snoring - or a side effect of a medicine, and alcohol and caffeine late on make it worse. Water by the bed, a saline spray if your nose is blocked and less to drink in the evening sort most of it. If you are also thirsty and weeing a lot, or it never goes, ask a GP to check it.

A dull ache with no cause is more often a cyst, a varicocele or an infection than an emergency: supportive underwear and an anti-inflammatory help, and a GP should look at it within a couple of weeks rather than a wait and see. An ache that came on after a long ride, a run or a session in the gym is usually just the tubes being knocked about, and settles in a day or two. If it turns sudden and severe, or you are sick with it, that is the hospital the same day. In a boy or a teenager, ring 111 or the GP today rather than waiting the fortnight out: a child is the one who cannot afford to wait.

A fan pulls air out of the machine, so the pressure inside drops and the air outside pushes in through the nozzle, carrying dust with it. The bag or the cyclone lets the air through but not the dust; a full bag, a blocked hose or a clogged filter cuts the flow, which is why the suction fades.

A fan, for a British summer: it moves the air for a few pence an hour, and on the two or three nights that are unbearable it is enough to sleep. An air conditioner only earns several hundred pounds if you cannot sleep for weeks of heat - it uses as much electricity as a fridge and has to be vented out of a window.

A fan does not cool the air, it moves it, and moving air over your skin is enough to feel a few degrees cooler, so it is worth it for sleeping in a hot room: a tower or pedestal fan at £25 to £60 is much quieter than a cheap one, and it costs a penny or two an hour to run. Put it in the window at night to pull cool air in, and skip portable air conditioning unless the room is also humid, since that is the expensive way round.
A female dog is a bitch.

A fever is the immune system turning up the body's thermostat to make it harder for germs to multiply, so it is a response rather than the illness itself. It is common with infections and usually settles in a few days; in a baby under three months, or with a stiff neck, confusion, a rash that does not fade or trouble breathing, get medical help urgently.

A few pounds over a winter or a stressful stretch is normal, and what shifts it is not a diet but two or three swaps you can actually keep: a slightly smaller plate, water or squash instead of the sweet drink, fruit in place of the afternoon biscuit, and a walk after dinner. Weigh yourself once a week at the same time of day rather than daily, because water swings a kilo or two either way, and muscle and getting older move the scales without anything being wrong. See a GP if the weight has gone on quickly without your eating changing, or it comes with being very thirsty, very tired or short of breath.

A fixed rate is a price that cannot move for a set time: a fixed energy tariff for 12 or 24 months, or a fixed mortgage rate for two, five or ten years. You pay a little more than the variable rate for that certainty, and leaving a fixed mortgage early usually costs an early repayment charge, so check the exit fee before you sign.

A flapjack is oats held together with butter, syrup and sugar, so it is a biscuit with fibre in it: a shop one is 200 to 250 calories and 15g of sugar, and a cereal bar is often much the same. It is a better snack than a chocolate bar and it is not a healthy one; a handful of nuts or a yoghurt with fruit keeps you going longer for the same calories.

A flat while you are out: pull over somewhere safe, hazards on, and put the spare on (or use the sealant kit), keeping under 50mph to the nearest garage. If it is still up, drive slowly to a tyre place instead: a nail in the middle of the tread can be plugged for around £20 to £30, while sidewall damage cannot and needs a new tyre.
A flat white is a double shot of espresso under a thin layer of steamed milk, about 160ml in the cup.

A fridge moves heat out of the inside and dumps it at the back. A pump compresses a refrigerant gas, which releases heat, then lets it expand inside the fridge, where it absorbs heat and cools the air.

A full-size football pitch is about 105 metres by 68 metres, which is 115 by 74 yards and a bit under two acres; the laws allow 90 to 120 metres long and 45 to 90 wide, which is why pitches differ. The goal is 7.32 metres wide and 2.44 metres high.

A gene is a section of DNA that holds the instructions for making one thing the body needs, usually a protein: eye colour, blood type and how a muscle works all come from genes. You inherit half your genes from each parent, and they switch on and off depending on the cell.

A general election has to be held at least every five years, and the prime minister can call one sooner. All 650 seats are fought on one day, and under first past the post the most votes in a constituency wins it, even without a majority there. Whoever can command a majority of the Commons is then asked by the monarch to form a government. To vote you have to be 18, on the electoral register, and not a member of the Lords.

A gluten-free bake needs a blend, not one flour: a shop gluten-free plain flour blend with a quarter teaspoon of xanthan gum per 200g, and a splash more liquid than the recipe says, because there is no stretch in it to hold water. Let the batter stand 20 minutes before it goes in the oven and it stops tasting gritty. Expect it to brown faster, so drop the oven 10C and give it five minutes longer.

A goose is the bigger bird, with a long neck and legs set further back, and it grazes grass; a duck is smaller with a shorter neck, and it dabbles in water for insects and weed. Geese are louder, bolder and better guards, and ducks are calmer and easier in a small garden.

A grant is money you keep; a loan is money you pay back. A bursary or a scholarship is the same kind of thing as a grant - the university, the council or a charity gives it and it is not repaid - while a student loan comes out of your pay once you earn over the threshold. Grants for students are mostly from the university's own hardship fund, so ask the student advice service in your first week; outside college there are council welfare schemes, and charities that give one-off grants for a boiler, a bed or a course. Always ask whether a grant is means tested, what it can be spent on, and whether it counts against your benefits.
A group of turtles is a bale.
A group of cats is a clowder.
A guitar has six strings, E, A, D, G, B and E from the thickest up. A 12-string guitar has twelve, in six pairs.
A haiku about cats, 5-7-5: Cat on the warm sill, one eye on the garden birds, both ears fast asleep.

A hamster needs a deep bed of paper or wood-shaving bedding, a solid wheel and a sand bath, in a cage at least 80cm by 40cm on one level rather than tubes. Spot clean the wet corner daily, change the bedding every few weeks, and give a water bottle rather than a bowl. They are awake at night, so keep the cage out of the bedroom.

A hamster, gerbil, rat or mouse is cupped in both hands, one under the chest and one over the back, and never picked up by the tail or the scruff. Sit on the floor with him on your lap for a few minutes a day and a bit of food in your hand, and put him down before he starts to struggle, so being picked up stops being a surprise. A pet that squeals, flinches or struggles at being handled when he did not before needs a vet - a sore tooth, an injured back or mites is the usual reason.

A hand that locks, catches or will not straighten has something physically in the way, so it is worth being examined this week rather than waiting for it to settle: ring your GP and say which movement brings it on, whether it lets go on its own, and whether there was a twist or a knock before it started. A knee that locks is usually a torn cartilage or a loose piece of it catching in the joint, which a physio or doctor can tell apart by hand in one appointment, so keep off twisting sports and deep squats until then rather than testing it. Go to 111 the same day if the joint swells up, is hot, or you cannot put weight on it at all.

A handicap is how many shots you get: it is roughly your best scores, averaged, against the course rating, so a 20-handicapper gets a shot on the 18 hardest holes and plays the course as a scratch golfer would. It goes down when you score better than your handicap - you need a few rounds, not one - and it is why two players of different ability can have a fair match.

A herbivore is an animal that eats only plants: a cow, a rabbit, a deer, a caterpillar. Its teeth grind and its gut is long enough to break down plant fibre, which is why it spends much of the day eating.

A hernia is a piece of bowel or fat pushing out through a weak spot in the wall of muscle that is meant to hold it in - commonest in the groin, where the wall is thin already, and then at the belly button or along an old operation scar. It shows as a soft lump that is there when you stand and cough and gone when you lie down, and it is usually a dull ache rather than a pain. It will not mend itself, and it does not need a repair unless it is bothering you, but it does need to be looked at by a GP so the diagnosis is on your record. A hiatus hernia is different: the top of the stomach slides up through the diaphragm into the chest, which causes heartburn and is treated with the reflux advice and a tablet rather than an operation. Go to A&E the same day if a lump that used to go back in becomes hard and very tender, or comes with vomiting, a swollen belly or no wind - that is a hernia that has been trapped, and it needs a surgeon rather than a wait.

A hiccup is a sudden spasm of the diaphragm followed by your vocal cords snapping shut, which makes the 'hic' sound. It usually happens after a big meal, a fizzy drink or a laugh, when the stomach pushes up against the diaphragm, and it is harmless.

A hip that clicks or pops and does not hurt is almost always harmless: a tendon flicking over a bump, or gas coming out of the joint fluid, and it needs nothing doing. Keep the muscles around it working, because clicking that turns into pain is usually a strength problem rather than the noise. If it starts to hurt, swell or lock, have a physio or your GP look at it.
A horse lives 25 to 30 years, and ponies often reach 35. Teeth and feet decide the last third of that, so a yearly check of both is worth more than anything else.

A house survey is a surveyor's inspection of the structure of the house you are buying, and it comes in levels: a level 1 condition report is the basics only (about £300 to £500), a level 2 HomeBuyer report is the usual one for a modern house in reasonable order (£400 to £700), and a level 3 building survey is the one for an old, unusual or visibly tired house (£600 to £1,500). It looks at the roof, walls, damp, drains and electrics rather than the decoration, and it is not the mortgage lender's valuation.

A houseplant that will not flower is usually short of light or being fed too much: most of them need a bright spot with a few hours of sun a day to set buds, and a feed high in nitrogen grows leaves at the flowers' expense, so switch to a tomato feed with more potash in late summer. Peace lilies and Christmas cacti also want cooler nights and a slightly pot-bound root to be nudged into flower; African violets want the light and nothing else changed.

A houseplant flops over for one of three reasons: it has grown tall and thin reaching for light, the pot has become top-heavy for its roots, or the roots have rotted in soggy compost and let go. Move it somewhere brighter, put a cane or a hoop in and tie the stems loosely, and check the drainage holes before you water again - a pot standing in a full saucer is the usual cause.

A hybrid has a petrol engine and an electric motor and the car picks which to use: the motor pulls away from a stop and creeps in traffic, the engine takes over once you are moving, and braking turns the motor into a generator that refills the small battery. A self-charging one is never plugged in, so it holds only a mile or two of electric running and the saving is in town; a plug-in does 20 to 40 miles on electric before the engine starts.

A hybrid is worth it for town and stop-start driving and not for the motorway: the motor does the pulling away, the engine does the cruising, and the battery is refilled by braking, so the saving comes from the slow work where a petrol engine is thirstiest. Expect 15 to 25% less fuel in town and very little at a steady 70. A self-charging hybrid costs a few thousand more than the same petrol car, so count how many years of that saving it takes to pay the difference. A plug-in hybrid is a different bet: it only pays if your normal day fits inside its 20 to 40 miles of electric range and you plug it in at home, because one running on an empty battery is heavier than the petrol car it replaced.

A jeweller or watch shop fits a new strap while you wait, usually £10 to £25 for a leather or silicone one, and a broken strap is always replaced rather than mended. A metal bracelet is resized by taking links out for £5 to £15. If it is a smartwatch, buy the band yourself: most use a quick-release pin, and a new one is £8 to £20.

A joist is one of the beams under a floor or above a ceiling that carries the boards you walk on, usually timber, set about 400mm apart, with cables and pipes running through the gaps. You may notch one at the top edge near a support, never in the middle of the span, and never drill through the bottom edge where it is in tension. A joist that is soft, stained or sagging is a surveyor's or builder's question, not a DIY one, because the fix changes the structure.

A knee that gives trouble is helped most by the muscle above it: sit-to-stands from a chair, step-ups onto a low step and straight-leg raises, two or three times a week, which builds the thigh muscle that takes the load off the joint. Keep walking on the flat and skip deep squats and running downhill; a physio can set the pace. A knee that locks, gives way or swells hot needs a GP.

A knock that turns the nail black is blood trapped under it. Ice it for ten minutes at a time for the first day, keep the hand or foot up, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen for the ache. A small dark patch fades over weeks as the nail grows out. Get it seen the same day if it throbs hard, the nail is lifting, half of it is dark, or the finger will not bend properly: a doctor can let the blood out, and draining it at home can infect it.
A limerick about poems: There once was a poem I knew, whose stories were never quite true. They wandered the day, and took their own way, and honestly, what can you do?

A liquid has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container: its particles are close enough to stick together but free to slide past each other. Water, milk and oil are liquids; heating a liquid enough turns it into a gas.

A list inside a sentence takes commas, and semicolons when the items have commas of their own: 'we need flour, which is in the cupboard; eggs, which are in the fridge; and milk.' A colon introduces the list, and never after a verb: 'the things I need are milk, eggs and bread', not 'are: milk'.

A magnet and a coil push a cone in and out in time with the signal, and the moving cone moves the air, which is the sound. A small cone cannot shift much air, so it makes the high notes well and the bass not at all: that is why a speaker with a big cabinet and a port sounds fuller at the same volume.
A major scale sounds bright and a minor one darker, and both are eight notes with the first repeated at the top.
A male cat is a tom.
A male dog is a stud.
A male lion is about 190 kg and 1.2 metres at the shoulder, and the mane grows darker as he gets older.

A mattress lasts about eight to ten years if it is looked after: airing it and turning or rotating it every few months is what keeps it there. Replace it once it sags or the springs go, or you wake up stiff.

Place value is what a digit is worth because of where it sits: in 4,582 the 4 is four thousands, the 5 is five hundreds, the 8 is eight tens and the 2 is two ones. The same digit means different things in different columns, which is why 0.5 is five tenths and 0.05 is five hundredths.

Plain flour stands in at the same weight, and the loaf is a little softer for it, so knead two or three minutes longer to build the gluten back. A teaspoon of gluten powder per 500g gets closer, and for a pizza or a naan plain flour is all you need. Do not use self-raising: it is the wrong lift for bread.

Plan on hepatitis A and typhoid for India, and book a travel clinic or a pharmacy that does travel jabs four to six weeks before you fly: some courses are two or three doses a month apart, and most of them take a fortnight to work. Malaria tablets for India are a separate decision again - they depend on the area and the season you are going in. Check India on the NHS Fit for Travel page - that is the list that counts - and keep the record card with your passport.

Plan on hepatitis A and typhoid for South Africa, and book a travel clinic or a pharmacy that does travel jabs four to six weeks before you fly: some courses are two or three doses a month apart, and most of them take a fortnight to work. Check South Africa on the NHS Fit for Travel page - that is the list that counts - and keep the record card with your passport.

Plan a utility room round the machines and the water: the washing machine and the dryer want an outside wall for the vent and the plumbing, a sink close to the drain, and a worktop over the appliances at about 900mm so there is a surface to fold on. Leave 600mm clear in front of every door you have to open, put the boiler behind a cupboard you can still get into, and keep a shelf at eye height for powder, pegs and the iron - it is the walk-through clutter, not the size of the room, that makes a utility room useless.
Plant something you can eat and keep it alive to the plate. Herbs on a windowsill count, and one tomato plant teaches you more than a book does.

Plant bare-root roses from November to March, while they are dormant, or potted ones any month the ground is not frozen: a hole wide enough to spread the roots, the graft union an inch below soil level, firmed in hard. They want sun and rich soil, and a feed in March and again in July is what keeps them flowering.

Plantain is a cooking banana: bigger, starchier and meant to be cooked, never eaten raw. Green ones are savoury and firm, so slice them thin and fry them crisp; left until the skin is black they are sweet, and thick coins fried in butter go soft and caramelised. Either way they take salt, chilli or a bean stew.
Plants take up water through their roots, and it is pulled up narrow tubes in the stem by evaporation from the leaves. That is why a cut flower wilts and why overwatering drowns roots that need air.

Plants in pots need it far more often than plants in a border, and in hot weather a big soak twice a week beats a sprinkle every day, because it gets water down to the roots. Check the soil before you water, not the calendar: push a finger in and water only when the top few centimetres are dry, then water until it runs out of the bottom.
Play one album right through twice before you decide - jazz gives up its tune on the second listen.

Poach salmon in water that is trembling rather than bubbling, about 80C, for 6 to 8 minutes for a fillet, or 15 to 20 minutes for a whole side in a 120C oven. It is done when a knife goes into the thick end and the flakes just separate; milk, a bay leaf and a few peppercorns in the water are what a restaurant poach tastes of.

Polaris sits almost exactly above the Earth's north pole, so the rest of the sky turns around it while it stays put. Find it from the two stars at the end of the Big Dipper's bowl: follow the line through them about five times their gap. It is not the brightest star in the sky, just the one that marks north.

Ponds are small and shallow: light reaches the bottom across most of one, so plants grow right through the middle. A lake is deep enough to have open water in the middle, with its own wind-driven ripples and a shore where plants stop. There is no exact size that splits them, but a pond you could wade across is a pond.

Pork ribs take 110 to 120C for four to six hours, until the meat has pulled back from the bone and the rack bends without breaking. Rub them with salt, sugar and paprika the night before, and only sauce them in the last 20 minutes or the sugar burns.

Potatoes are 10 to 12 weeks from planting for earlies and 18 to 20 for maincrop. The others, from seed: salad leaves and radishes 4 to 6 weeks, beetroot 10 to 12, carrots and runner beans 12 to 16, peas 12 to 14, courgettes 10 to 12, sweetcorn 12 to 14, tomatoes 16 to 20 from sowing (12 to 16 from planting out), cabbages and broccoli 16 to 20, parsnips 22 to 24, and leeks or onions 20 to 24. Garlic takes about eight months from an autumn clove, and strawberries fruit the summer after planting. The seed packet is the tie-breaker, because a fortnight either way is normal.
Potential energy is energy stored ready to move.

Pre-book it: the price at the barrier is often two or three times the pre-booked price for the same space, and the cheapest of all is usually a park-and-ride a few minutes out with a shuttle. Compare the total against the alternatives before you choose, because a week of parking often costs about what a taxi costs each way, and for two or three days the taxi, the train or a lift from a friend usually wins. Check the drop-off charge too, since many airports now charge for the kiss-and-fly lane.

Precipitation is water falling out of the sky - rain, snow, sleet or hail - when droplets in a cloud join up until they are too heavy to stay up. It is one step of the water cycle, after evaporation and condensation.

Premenstrual symptoms usually start a week or two before a period and are at their worst in the five days before it, then ease within a day or two of bleeding starting. Track them for two or three cycles - the pattern is what tells you it is the cycle and not the week. If it is bad enough to wreck two weeks in four, or the mood change is severe, that is worth the GP: PMDD is real and treatable.

Prick a 250g potato all over, rub it with oil and salt and bake it at 200C (180C fan) for an hour to an hour and a quarter, straight on the oven shelf rather than in a dish, so the skin crisps all over. In a hurry, microwave it 8 minutes first and then give it 20 minutes in the hot oven for the skin. Cut a cross in the top and open it while it is hot, with the butter going in before the filling. About 1 hour 15 minutes start to finish.

Pull the drawer right out until it stops, press the release catch in the middle of the softener compartment, and take it to the sink. Lift out the cap and the siphon tube, soak everything in hot water with a little washing-up liquid or a dishwasher tablet for half an hour, then scrub the corners with an old toothbrush. Reach into the housing left in the machine and scrub the top and the back of it too, because that is where the black grows, and run an empty hot rinse before the next load. Use powder now and then and leave the drawer open between washes: softener is what feeds it.

Purring is not only happiness. Cats purr when they are content, but also when they are nervous, in pain or healing — the vibration seems to settle them. So read the rest of the cat: a loose body and slow blinks mean content, crouched and tight means worried. A cat that purrs but has stopped eating still needs the vet.

Push the probe into the thickest part, away from bone, fat and the tin, and wait for the number to stop climbing: 75C for chicken and pork, 63C for beef or lamb you want pink, and 60C for a joint that will rest, because it keeps rising as it sits. Chicken thighs want 80C if you have the patience, since that is where the connective tissue gives in. Check the thermometer itself by standing it in a glass of crushed ice and water, where it should read 0C, and wash the probe in hot soapy water between uses.

Push a bit of filler into the hole with a filling knife, leave it a little proud, and sand it flat once it is hard - two thin coats dry faster and sand better than one thick one. Anything bigger than a 50p piece, or a hole through plasterboard, wants a plasterboard patch stuck behind it and filled over before you paint. A crack wider than a couple of millimetres, or one that keeps coming back, is a builder's job rather than yours.

Push a finger about 2cm into the soil: water it if the soil is dry at that depth, and wait a day or two if it is still damp. A pot tells you by weight as well, because a light pot is a dry pot, and a thirsty plant droops and then perks up within a day of a drink. Water until it runs out of the drainage holes and empty the saucer, because roots left standing in water rot.
Put one double batch in the freezer for the night you are late home, and keep two fallbacks in the cupboard - pasta and a tin of tomatoes, rice and eggs - for the night the plan falls apart.
Put the stops in first, every two hours and one proper stop a day.

Put the ask in the subject line and in the first sentence: "A quick question about Thursday" tells them what it is before they open it. Then three or four sentences - what you want, the one or two facts they need, and by when - and a plain sign-off with your name. If you want an answer, say what happens next: "If I do not hear back by Friday I will call."

Put the child's name and class in the subject, say what you have noticed and what you would like: "Sam (5B) has been anxious about maths homework — could we talk for ten minutes this week?" Keep it to a few lines and ask for a specific next step.

Put the gap on the CV with a plain label - "Career break: caring for a parent, 2019-2021" - because an unexplained gap reads as bigger than it is. Add anything you did in it: a course, volunteering, freelance work, a language. Written down, it stops being the thing the interview is secretly about.

Put them where you already eat rather than on a separate pile: grated carrot or courgette in the mince, a handful of spinach stirred into pasta at the end, frozen peas straight into rice, beans or lentils bulking out a chilli. Frozen and tinned count, and so does a bag of mixed veg thrown into a tray bake. Aim for one extra portion at a meal you already have rather than a new meal you have to keep up.
Put 1 beside the other figure for the same job - what you were paying before, or what a friend was quoted - and then it means something. What have you got to compare it with?

Put away 10 to 20 percent of your take-home, and get three to six months of essential spending in place first: that keeps a lost job from becoming debt. A rough guide after that is one year's pay by 30, three by 40 and six by 50, so 30k a year means 30k at 30 and 90k at 40. Save on payday, not at month end.

Put a hard avocado in a paper bag with a banana and leave it on the counter for a day or two; the banana's gas speeds it up. Once it gives slightly at the stem end it's ready, and lemon juice stops a cut one going brown.

Put four columns on paper: the money after the real extras - the season ticket, childcare and the extra hours at what your time is worth, because a rise that adds ten hours a week is often a pay cut - what you would learn in two years, who you would work for, and what happens if it goes wrong. Then take the offer that keeps more doors open, and ask for 48 hours rather than deciding on the call.

Put it in this order. First clear any credit card, overdraft or pay-later debt, because that costs 20% or more a year and nothing safe pays that. Second, build three to six months of essential bills in an easy-access account - instant access, no notice, no card, so a broken boiler is an annoyance rather than a loan. Third, money you will not touch for five years goes into a global index tracker inside a stocks and shares ISA; anything you will need sooner stays in cash, where the rate is lower but the money is there. If it is for a first home, a Lifetime ISA adds 25% up to £1,000 a year, and that is the best return you will get for that goal.

Quick from seed: salad leaves and radishes in 4 to 6 weeks, spring onions 8, dwarf beans 10 to 12. Tomatoes, courgettes and chillies take 12 to 16 weeks from sowing, and new potatoes 10 to 12 from planting (maincrop 18 to 20). Check the seed packet for the variety, because a fortnight either way is normal, and sow a small row every three weeks so the crops arrive in a trickle rather than all at once.
Quinoa takes 12 to 15 minutes: one part quinoa to two of water, lid on, simmering, then 5 minutes off the heat and fork it through. Rinse it first, or it tastes soapy.

Radiation is energy travelling as waves or particles, and heat that reaches us from the Sun crosses empty space that way, with nothing to carry it. The word also covers the harmful ionising sort, from X-rays and nuclear material, which is why those have safety limits.

Rain rearranges a day out rather than cancelling it: keep the outdoor parts loose - a walk, a beach, a garden - and put one indoor thing into each day, a museum, a pool, a long lunch or a castle you can go round under cover. Book only what you can move and decide on the morning, when you can see the sky.

Rain wears minerals out of rocks and carries them to the sea, and when the water evaporates the salt stays behind. Rivers keep adding a little, so the sea has become salty over hundreds of millions of years.

Rap is the act - someone talking in time over a beat. Hip hop is the whole culture around it: the beat, the DJ, the dancing, the graffiti, the way people dress. So every rap record is hip hop, and a hip hop night can go hours without a rapper. For the words, start with *Illmatic*; for the sound, *The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill*.
Rasgulla originate. I'd take that and not think about it again.

Rates like that are set by whoever runs the place and they change with the season: their own site or one quick call has the figure they actually charge, and a map listing carries the number if there is no site.
Rather be tom Brady. I wouldn't spend another minute on it — both work.
Raw chicken keeps 1 to 2 days in the fridge, on the bottom shelf, and cooked chicken 3 days; both freeze well for up to 3 months. Go by the use-by date on the pack, which beats any general rule.

Raw eggs keep about three weeks past the date on the box if they have stayed cold, so the fridge is the place for them: in their carton on a shelf rather than in the door, where the temperature swings. Go by the date and by how they smell when you crack one.

Read the two- and three-star reviews first: they say what actually goes wrong, while five-star ones are often written the day the thing arrived. Then check whether the reviews are spread over months or all landed in one week (a burst is bought), look for the line that says the purchase was verified, and search the product name with "problem" or "broke" to find the complaints. A brand-new product with hundreds of glowing reviews is the one to distrust most.

Read a section, then close the book and say its three points out loud before going on - rereading feels like study but the recall is what sticks. Turn each heading into a question first ("what is a supply curve?") and answer it from memory, then write one line per page in your own words. Come back to those lines after ten minutes, the next day and a week later, and you keep most of it with far less total time.

Read it twice, all the way through, before you touch anything: what it serves, the prep time and the cooking time separately, the oven setting, and whether anything has to chill, soak or rest. Then get every ingredient out and cut up, which is what the French call mise en place - most recipes go wrong in the last five minutes because the onion was not chopped yet. Two phrases to know: 'divided' means the amount is split between stages (half the cheese in the sauce, half on top), and 'until' is a cue rather than a time - until golden, until it comes away from the pan. Times in a recipe are for that oven and that tin; trust your eyes and nose first. Check the tin size too, because a wrong-sized tin changes the depth and with it the time.

Reading in dim light does not damage your eyes - it tires them, and a tired eye feels sore, waters and gives you a headache. What helps is light that comes from the side or over your shoulder and lands on the page rather than from behind you onto the screen: a lamp at about 40 to 60cm, a little behind your shoulder, and a warm-white LED of 6 to 9 watts is plenty for a book. Keep the room light on too, so your eye is not looking from a bright page into a black room, and every 20 minutes look across the room at something far away for 20 seconds. If the print has to be very close or very bright before it is clear, that is worth an eye test.

Red meat, liver, lentils, beans, chickpeas, tofu, fortified cereal and dark green veg are the everyday sources, and a bowl of fortified cereal or a lentil curry is as good as a steak. Have vitamin C in the same meal - a glass of orange juice, peppers, tomatoes - because it can double how much you take up, and keep tea and coffee an hour away from the meal, since the tannins block it. A low a blood test has found is treated with tablets.

Redness like that is usually contact or heat and it settles on its own in a few days. Plain water rather than soap, leave it uncovered, and show a pharmacist if it is no better by the weekend or it is spreading. A fever with it, or red that does not blanch under a glass, is a same-day call rather than a wait. When did you first notice it?

Reflection is light bouncing off a surface: the ray hits the surface and leaves at the same angle on the other side of an imaginary line straight up from it. A smooth surface such as a mirror reflects the rays in one direction and gives a clear image; a rough surface scatters them and gives a duller, softer one.

Refraction is light bending as it crosses from one material into another at an angle, because it changes speed: that is why a straw looks broken in a glass of water, and how a lens or a pair of glasses focuses light.

Remote for the work that needs quiet, the office for the work that needs people. Two or three days in is the arrangement most people end up preferring, and it keeps you in the room when decisions get made.

Repair it if the phone is under four years old and the fault is the screen, the battery or the charging port: £50 to £120 at a local shop, far less than a new phone. Replace it when the water damage or the logic board is the problem, or when updates have stopped, since those repairs cost more than the handset is worth.

Repair it if it is under five years old and the fault is the battery, the drive, the screen or the fan: those are £50 to £150 and give you years more use. Replace it when the motherboard or the case is gone, or when it cannot run the software you need, because those repairs cost more than the machine is worth.

Repeat that a few times a week, never let dogs rush up nose to nose on the lead, and stay calm yourself because the lead tightens when you brace and that tells him there is something to fear. Start further away than you think you need to: a distance where he can see a dog and still take a treat, then let the other dog pass and walk on.

Replace a phone battery every two to three years, or about 500 full charges: the settings show the health: on an iPhone it is Settings, Battery, Battery Health, and anything under 80% is worn out. A phone that dies at 20%, shuts down in the cold or gets hot on charge is the same verdict, and a new battery is £30 to £70 fitted rather than a new handset.

Replace a smoke alarm every ten years, with a new battery every year: the sensor drifts with age and most modern ones are sealed, so the replace-by date stamped on the back is the one to go by, and it should be tested monthly.

Replace a helmet after any knock that put it between you and the ground, even with no crack you can see: the foam that absorbs the hit has already done its job once. With no crash, about five years is the usual advice, because sweat and sun harden the foam and the straps. It should sit level, two fingers above the eyebrows, with the strap snug enough that you can open your mouth wide and feel it pull down.

Reserve the seat when you book the ticket: on most trains a reservation is free with an advance ticket and a few pounds on a walk-up fare, and it is worth having on any long trip. Friday evening and Sunday afternoon trains are the busiest, so a booked seat there is the difference between sitting and standing.

Rest a muscle about 48 hours before training it hard again, so not the same one every day: two full-body sessions a week with a day between them, or an upper/lower split on back-to-back days so each muscle still gets its rest. Training the same muscle every day is how people end up sore, stale and not adding weight.

Restless legs feel like a crawl or a fizz in the legs in the evening that only moving eases. Ask a GP for a blood test first, because low iron is a common cause; cut caffeine and alcohol late, and try a warm bath and calf stretches before bed. If it is disturbing your sleep most nights, say so, because it is treatable.
Reviews beat anything I could say about spot, which I have never been to: a map app or the town's visitor site will name the ones people rate - tell me what you want from it and I'll help you choose.
Reviews beat a guess from me on the walks near you, which I have never been to: a map app's, sorted by what you need, is the honest way - say what matters and I'll help you narrow it down.
Reviews beat a guess from me about part, since I have never been to any of them: a map app or the local visitor site names the ones people rate - say what matters and I'll help you narrow it down.
Reviews from people who have been beat my guess on the cafes near you, since I have never been to any of them: sort a map app's by what you need, and the count matters more than the score.

Rice, pasta and boiled potatoes are much the same for you: about 130 to 150 calories per 100g cooked, so the portion is what matters - 75 to 100g dry of rice or pasta, or a potato the size of your fist. Pick whichever you will actually eat and fill half the plate with vegetables; the wholemeal versions are a small upgrade, not a different food.

Rice and beans together give all the amino acids the body cannot make itself, and so do beans on toast, lentils with rice, and hummus with bread. You do not have to pair them at the same meal, either: it is the day's food that counts, not one plate, so a peanut butter sandwich and a bean chilli on the same day is enough.

Ride less than you think: twenty to thirty minutes on a flat, quiet route, every other day, and add about ten minutes a week rather than going for the ride you used to do. Give the bike ten minutes first - tyres pumped hard, brakes that stop it, a chain with a drop of oil - and set the saddle so your knee is almost straight at the bottom of the pedal, because a saddle too low is what makes a first ride hurt. Stay in an easy gear and spin rather than push.
Right then. The bit that decides it is unchanged: if it was one of the bad list, ring the vet now rather than waiting for a symptom.
Right, no fixing from me then. What's on your mind?

Ring or log in and ask why it went up and from which date: it is usually the end of a fixed deal, a meter estimate instead of a reading, or a price rise the supplier has to tell you about in advance. Give an up-to-date reading, and if the tariff ended, switch rather than stay on the standard one - for a phone or broadband, ask for the retentions team and say you are leaving, which is where the discounts are.

Ring the number on the back of the card: a decline is usually a security check, a daily limit or a block the bank can lift in one call. A contactless tap over £100 needs the PIN, and a hold from a hotel or a petrol pump can freeze money for a few days.

Ring the supplier before the next bill, not after, and ask for a payment plan you can keep to: they have to offer one, and the letters stop while it runs. While you are on the phone, ask to go on the priority services register if anyone in the house is disabled, ill or under five, and ask about the Warm Home Discount (£150 off one winter bill) and any hardship fund the supplier runs. Your council's Household Support Fund covers bills and food, water's own scheme is WaterSure, and Citizens Advice will make the calls with you for free. Nothing gets cut off today: that takes a warrant.

Ring the ward before you set off: visiting hours are set ward by ward and change, many open late morning or early afternoon until about 8pm. Ward rounds, meals and handovers are usually closed, and two at the bedside at a time is the common limit. Don't visit with a cough, cold or stomach bug, use the hand gel both ways, and leave flowers at home: most wards ban them.

Ring the charity shop before you load the car: most take a bag or two of books and say no to a bootful, and a book bank at the tip or a supermarket car park takes as many as you have. Paperbacks go down well at a hospital, a care home or a phone box library, and a school fair clears children's books. Anything mouldy, damp or water-damaged goes in the paper recycling, not to a shop.

Ring the council's adult social care team and ask for a care needs assessment: it is free, anyone can ask for one, and it is the door to everything else - help with washing and dressing, a carer coming in, day centres, equipment, a pendant alarm, and the financial assessment that decides what is paid. The person has to agree to it, so ask them first and go with them, and write down the bad days rather than the good ones: what they cannot do without help, and what happens on a day nobody is there. The decision comes in writing, and if it says they do not qualify it can be challenged. Ask for a carer's assessment for yourself in the same call - it is separate, and it is your own support, not theirs.

Ring today rather than wait if the animal is struggling to breathe, straining to pee and passing nothing (a blocked cat can die in a day), has a hard swollen belly, is fitting, has eaten something poisonous, or cannot stand - say exactly what you see when you ring. For anything else the call is free: most practices triage on the phone and will tell you whether to come in, and a nurse appointment costs less than a consultation.

Ring your provider and ask for the retention or loyalty price, and say plainly that you are looking at leaving: the deal they offer on that call is usually 20 to 30% below the list price, and a two-year recontract is what buys it, so only take it if you are happy to stay. Out of contract, you are free to go with 30 days' notice and a PAC code, which is the strongest thing to say on the call. Check the bill lines first, though: phone insurance, extra data and an add-on nobody uses are the usual culprits. If money is tight, ask about the social tariff, which most big providers now offer quietly.

Ring your vet today and say how many and how long ago, even if a dog seems fine: grapes and raisins can shut down a dog's kidneys, and there is no amount known to be safe, so a small one and a handful is enough to treat. Treatment works much better started early, and the vet may make a dog sick or give fluids.

Ring your water company's sewer line: the public sewer, the manhole and the drains under the road are theirs, and they clear them free. Keep children and pets away, don't lift a manhole cover yourself, wash your hands after touching anything it reached, and photograph the mess before you clear up for an insurance claim. If it is only ever inside your own boundary it is your drain, and that is a drain company.

Ring as soon as you know, not on the morning: a day's notice lets the practice hand your slot to someone on its waiting list, and 24 hours is the notice most of them ask for. Use the text reminder or the NHS app if the practice has one, and rebook in the same call so you keep your place. For a hospital appointment ring the number printed on the letter rather than the main switchboard, and ask them to move it rather than cancel it. A missed hospital appointment costs the NHS about £120, and a surgery can take someone off its list after repeated no-shows.
Ring 999 or 911 straight away and tell them there is a gunshot wound. Keep pressing on it with something clean and don't stop to look, and let the ambulance crew move them.

Rinse the pond water off with a hose and dry him, especially between the toes, then keep him warm and quiet for the rest of the day. Either way keep him out of the water and do not let him drink from it: ponds and slow rivers carry leptospirosis from rats' urine, which is why the annual jab matters, and a pond with a green scum on it in summer is blue-green algae, which is an emergency - ring the vet at once and do not wait for a sign. Watch for coughing, fast or noisy breathing or a wobble over the next few hours, because that is water in the lungs and needs the vet that day.

Roast potatoes or mash, and something green with butter, plus a sauce made in the pan: splash in stock or wine, scrape the brown bits up and let it reduce for 2 minutes. That is a whole dinner from what is already on the hob.

Roast cauliflower: florets tossed in oil, cumin and salt at 200C (180C fan) for 25 minutes, until the edges are brown and crisp. Egg fried rice: cold rice fried hard, an egg scrambled into it with soy sauce and peas, 10 minutes.

Roast chicken thighs at 200C (180C fan) for 35 to 40 minutes, skin side up and salted first; the skin crisps and the juices run clear. Soft herbs - parsley, basil, coriander, dill, mint, chives - want the end of the cooking, not the start: chop them and stir them in off the heat. A handful blitzed with oil, lemon and garlic is a green sauce for fish, chicken or new potatoes, and the stems go in at the start of a soup.

Roll walnut-sized balls, space them well apart, and bake at 180C (160C fan) for 10 to 12 minutes - they firm up as they cool. 125g soft butter creamed with 100g sugar, an egg beaten in, then 200g plain flour and half a teaspoon of baking powder.
Romantic: *Before Sunrise* on film, *Starstruck* as a series, or *The Flatshare* to read.

Roots do three jobs: they hold the plant in the ground, they take up the water and minerals the leaves cannot make, and they store food for next year. The fine root hairs are what does the drinking, which is why a plant in a small pot dries out so fast.
Rosé is wine that spent a few hours with the red grape skins, enough for the colour and not for the tannin.
Rough one. A shower, something warm to eat and an early night usually resets it.

Round up, or ten percent on a fare: a couple of pounds on a twelve pound ride is plenty, and paying the meter exactly is fine too. Taxi drivers here are not paid on tips the way they are in the States.
