Same as before: An ecosystem is a community of living things plus the non-living parts they depend on - soil, water, air and sunlight - interacting in one place.
Same as before: On a table: *Ticket to Ride* (trains, simple, satisfying), *Codenames* (two teams, one word grid) and *Azul* (tiles, quick, sharp).
Same as before: Pick a route you already know on quiet streets, ride it once at a weekend so the turns are not a surprise, and start with two days a week rather than five.
Same as before: Play with a wand toy for five or ten minutes, two or three times a day, and let her stalk and pounce before you let her catch it, then give her a meal so the hunt has an end.
Same as before: Roast chopped veg at 200C (180C fan) for 25 minutes with oil and salt, then stir it through pasta or rice; a fried egg on top makes it a meal.
Same as before: Search for the sport plus your town and 'club', then email and ask about a taster session: most clubs have a beginners' or social night that costs a few pounds.

Same as before: Sleep apnoea is the airway at the back of the throat closing for ten seconds or more, many times a night, so breathing stops in short bursts and you wake just enough to start again - which is why the snoring breaks off and why eight hours leaves you flat.
Same as before: A ragu of mince, onion, carrot and tomato cooked down for at least an hour, a bechamel, and parmesan between and on top: the rest is layering.
Same as before: A short nap is worth having: 20 minutes, ideally before about 3pm, and set an alarm, because 90 minutes leaves you groggier than when you lay down.
Same as before: A waterproof with a hood is the one thing that decides the day, with a thin layer underneath rather than a thick coat, because rain gear is warm once you move.
Same as before: A cold usually peaks in two or three days and is gone in about a week, though a cough and a blocked nose can linger for two weeks and that is normal.
Same as before: A console is cheaper and simpler: it plays everything at good quality for years, no upgrades, and you can sell it on.
Same as before: Water coming in from outside is not a stopcock: it stops taps, not rain or a rising water table.
Same as before: Wear something you can stand in for hours and won't mind getting warm: jeans or a skirt, flat boots or trainers, and a layer you can tie round your waist.
Same as before: You haven't told me about your diet.
Same as before: Buildings insurance covers the structure and comes with the mortgage; contents covers what's inside and is optional but usually worth it.

Same as before: Check the entry requirements on the university or college page for the exact course, because they differ more than people expect - most want five GCSEs at grade 4 or above including English and maths, and A-levels or a BTEC in a subject that fits.
Same for my nighttime sleep: 20 minutes.

Same for my sleep: pick one stretch of daytime to sleep and guard it like a night: straight home, dark room, phone off, and the same hours seven days a week, including days off, so your body clock settles.
Same for the puzzle: the rest of the day wants things rather than toys: a food puzzle, a cardboard box, a paper bag, somewhere high to sit and a window to watch.
Same for the top: Energy is lost at every step, which is why top predators are few and a chain rarely has more than four or five links.
Same for the ball: potential energy is energy stored ready to be used: a ball held up high has potential energy, and it turns into kinetic energy as it falls, faster and faster.
Same for water: it travels faster in water and fastest in solids, and it cannot travel through a vacuum because there is nothing to vibrate.
Same for atoms: Atoms join into molecules, and everything you can touch is made of them; they are mostly empty space.
Same for a good football: *The Last Dance* is the one that grips people who do not follow basketball, *Sunderland 'Til I Die* for football and *Welcome to Wrexham* if you want to enjoy one.
Same for a great list, thanks: Pick the one thing you would happily be bad at.

Same for a grilled cheese: butter both slices right to the edges before anything else - that is the barrier that keeps the bread from going soggy - then put the wet things against the butter and the cheese, ham or egg in the middle, and cut it in half so it holds together.

Same for a lower price: ask once, cheerfully, once you have picked the thing - "is there anything you can do on the price?" - then stop talking and be ready to walk away: silence and a customer who will leave are what move a price.
Sanae Takaichi is the prime minister of Japan: in office since October 2025, and the first woman to hold the job. The head of state is the emperor, Naruhito.
Sandbags or a flood door across the doorway help tonight, photographs help the insurer, and a drain that backs up in a storm is the water company's to clear.

Santorini and the Amalfi coast are the postcard picks, and both are heaving in July and August: Italy's lakes or Puglia give you the same views and food with fewer people. For a beach honeymoon with guaranteed sun, the Maldives from January to April, or Zanzibar if you want something less built up.
Sausages in a tin with onions and apples, on a cold day. Nothing clever, and it works every time.
Savoury on a normal day — eggs, or toast with something salty — because it keeps you going until lunch. Sweet is for weekends and holidays.

Say the plain thing and stop there: "I'm sorry, that's a shock. How are you doing?" Let them name the illness and the treatment in their own time, and take your steer from how much they want to talk about it. No cures, no "my aunt had that and she's fine", no advice - and offer one specific, repeatable help, like lifts to appointments, then do it.

Say the plain thing and then be quiet: "I'm so sorry - I don't have words, but I'm here." Name the person who died if they have named them, say their name back, and offer one concrete thing instead of "let me know if you need anything": a lift, a meal on Thursday, sitting with them. Do not explain, compare it to your own loss, or look for the bright side; the comfort is in staying, and in being the one who is still there in three weeks.

Say the ask in the first line, the reason second, and keep it to four sentences: "Could you send the signed form by Friday? Finance needs it to pay the invoice this month." Read it once as if you were annoyed and take out anything that could be read that way, then send; the shorter the email, the less there is to misread.

Say the hard thing while they are still here rather than at the airport: one evening just the two of you, and tell them what they have been to you. Then put the contact in the diary before they go - a real time each week rather than 'we'll see'. The first month after is the quiet one, so have one thing in it that is only yours.
Say what happened, how it made you feel and what you want to change, once: "I felt left out when the plans changed". One topic at a time, no list of past grievances, and ask for their side.
Say which service and the mood and I'll narrow it down.

Say yes to the person and no to the timing: "I'd like to help with that; I'm on the audit until Thursday, so I can start Friday, or drop something else if it's urgent." That gives them a choice instead of a refusal, and it makes your workload visible.

Say yes to a term of cheap lessons before you buy anything: school lessons or a group class cost a fraction of one-to-one, and four to six weeks tells you whether it will stick. Borrow or rent the instrument for that first term - a second-hand keyboard or guitar is thirty or forty pounds - and only buy once they have kept it up. Ten to fifteen minutes a day at the same time beats one long weekend session, and sit in for the first few weeks, because most children stop at the point where practice turns into an argument. The same test works for a sport or coding: ask for a taster session before anyone pays a term's fees.
Say you're sorry, name them if you can, and offer something practical. "I'll bring dinner on Thursday" helps far more than "let me know if you need anything".
Say it out loud or write it by hand rather than only reading, link a new fact to one you already know, and sleep on it: a night's sleep is when it gets filed.

Say it out loud three times, standing up, with the slides in front of you: the first run finds the sentences that only looked fine on paper, the second is against a timer, and the third is to one person who will tell you where they lost the thread. Time it against the slot you were given and cut material rather than speed up. Write the opening sentence and the closing one out in full and keep everything between them to a few words per card, then practise stopping for a second after your last point instead of trailing off.

Say it plainly and early, in your own words, then stop: 'I'd have loved to, but I can't make that one' for a party, 'I can't do the weekend, but I could come on the Sunday' for family. What you can't do, one reason if you want to give one, and nothing dressed up. A made-up excuse is one you have to remember, and if you do want to see them, offer another day in the same breath.

Say it as your own feeling about one thing, not a list: 'When you said that in front of everyone, it stung and I have been thinking about it.' Then say what you would like instead - 'I would rather you told me on my own' - and leave it there; a question at the end, like 'did you mean it that way?', keeps the door open. Soon and in private beats saving it up, and face to face beats a text if you can manage it.

Say it as a preference and not as a rejection, once, warmly: 'I love that you think of me - could we do a coffee and a walk instead of a top? I only wear two of them.' Then make it easy for her by naming what you do want: a book, a plant, socks, or money towards something bigger. A specific wish list beats a general 'please stop', which sounds like the presents were the problem.

Say it at the table before you pay and ask for that dish to come off the bill; for a takeaway, ring the restaurant the same day rather than the app. Cold, raw or the wrong meal is not what you ordered, so photograph it and dispute that amount on the card if they will not take it off. Bad service gets the manager there and then and the service charge off; a hygiene problem goes to the council's environmental health team.
Scientists think it helps sort memories and practise threats and feelings; there is no good evidence that dreams predict the future.

Scrambled eggs: 3 eggs on a low heat with butter, taken off while still glossy, on toast in 5 minutes. Pancakes: 100g flour, 2 eggs and 300ml milk whisked and rested 20 minutes, then a minute a side in a hot buttered pan.
Screens off half an hour before bed and a short walk most days help more than any app.

Scrub it with hot water and a stiff brush or a handful of coarse salt while it is still warm, then dry it on the hob over a low heat: a little washing-up liquid is fine, but soaking it is what strips the seasoning. To season it, rub a thin film of oil over the inside and bake it upside down at 200C for an hour, then do it once more. If it rusts, scrub the rust off first and season it the same way afterwards. Keep it out of the dishwasher: the detergent strips the seasoning off and the pan comes out with rust spots. A wok wants exactly this care too.
Searing is browning meat hard in a hot pan, for flavour and colour, not for cooking it through. Pat it dry first and leave it alone until it releases by itself.

Seattle — no way of seeing a place I haven't been to, so no verdict from me. What decides it is the walk from the station or the bus, the light in the rooms, the noise at the time you would be home, and what the neighbours are like. A map app shows the walk and the streets, and one visit on a weekday evening tells you the noise.

Select the numbers and the header row, then Insert > Recommended Charts in Excel (or the chart button in Google Sheets) and take the simple one it offers: bars for comparing amounts, a line for change over time, a pie only for parts of one whole. If the chart comes out as one flat series or the labels are wrong, the header row was read as data - delete it and select again from the header down.
Self-raising flour for a sponge or a scone, or plain flour with 2 teaspoons of baking powder per 100g. Strong bread flour is the one to keep out of a cake, because the gluten makes it chewy.
Sergiy Korsunsky — that's the one I'd take, and either is fine.

Serve it with something wet — gravy, a spoon of yoghurt, a squeeze of lemon and oil — and next time take it out 5 minutes earlier and rest it under foil. Dry meat or fish is nearly always overcooked, and resting is what keeps the juice in.

Set the oven to 150C (130C fan, gas 2) for a slow roast: lower than that and the meat sits in the danger zone for hours, higher and the outside dries before the middle softens. A covered pot keeps it moist, and a shoulder of lamb or pork or a beef brisket wants 4 to 5 hours. It is ready when a fork twists easily in the middle.

Set a stop date in the next two weeks and use nicotine replacement or a prescription aid as well as willpower: on willpower alone most attempts fail, and patches, gum or a vape roughly double to triple your odds, with free help from a stop-smoking service adding more. Know your two triggers and plan the swap - a walk after meals, something in your hands on the phone - because a craving peaks in about five minutes and passes. Slips are normal, not the end of it: two failed tries still leave you far better off, and the health gains start within days.

Set it up in this order: the TV's own network settings first (Settings > Network, pick your wifi, type the password with the remote), then test with one built-in app. If the wifi list is empty on a smart TV, restart the router and the TV, and check the TV is on the 2.4GHz band, which older sets need; a Fire Stick or Roku plugged into the HDMI port is the cheap fix for a TV whose own apps have stopped working.

Settings > [your name] > iCloud > Manage Account Storage shows the list: photos and old device backups are almost always the top two, so delete the backups of phones you no longer own, then empty Recently Deleted. The 50GB plan is about 79p a month, and if you would rather not pay, keep photos only on the phone and turn on Optimise iPhone Storage.

Seven hours is inside the seven to nine most adults need, so there is nothing to fix if your days are fine. If you are yawning by mid-afternoon anyway, half an hour earlier to bed does more than a weekend lie-in.

Shade and water out all day, walk before ten and after five so the pavement is not burning his pads - if it is too hot for your hand for five seconds, it is too hot for his feet. Never leave him in a parked car, even with the windows down: it reaches 40C inside in ten minutes. A wet towel to lie on helps, and flat-faced, old and thick-coated dogs struggle most. Heavy panting with wobbling or collapsing is heatstroke, so cool him with wet towels and ring the vet on the way.
Shehbaz Sharif is the prime minister of Pakistan: in office since March 2024. The president is a ceremonial role; the prime minister runs the government, though the army has a large say.

Shop around about three weeks before renewal, comparing a few sites plus a couple of direct insurers: loyalty is punished. A higher voluntary excess, a named driver, paying annually instead of monthly and a black-box policy all bring the price down. A new driver pays £1,500 to £2,500 in the first year, so a telematics policy that scores your driving is usually the biggest saving there is.

Short, true and forward-looking: what the old job could not offer, then what you went looking for. "I had gone as far as I could there and wanted the design work to be the main part of the job, which is what this role is." Never blame a person and do not mention money first; if you were let go, one plain sentence and move on - "the team was restructured and my role went with it" - then say what you have done since. You need not volunteer it if the form does not ask, but never answer no to a direct question: a reference check can bring it out, and a quiet explanation beats being caught.

Shorten sentences, cut the warm-up, and put the ask first: "Could you send the file by Friday?" beats three lines of context before the point. Use the same word for the same thing throughout, and read it aloud — anything you stumble on, rewrite.

Show it once, let them do it badly without being corrected, then give them one thing to change next time. That order is what makes it stay. Say how old they are and what they can already manage, and I will make it concrete.

Shut it down and unplug it, tip it over and shake it gently, then use a soft brush or short bursts of compressed air held at an angle, not straight down. Wipe the keycaps with a cloth just damp with isopropyl alcohol - never spray anything onto it. A key that sticks needs a drop of alcohol round its edge and a few presses, not a soaking.

Sing along to something you can hear clearly and quietly - headphones at half volume - because most people cannot hear themselves and push too hard. Breathe low into the belly, keep the throat relaxed, warm up with lip trills or humming for two minutes, and record yourself on your phone once a week: the recording is the lesson. For range or a song that keeps going wrong, three or four lessons with a teacher do more than a year of videos.
Siri — that's the one I'd take, and either is fine.

Sit or lie down the moment it starts, with your feet up, and drink a glass of water: most spells are the blood pressure dipping, not enough to drink, a skipped meal, being too hot, or a passing virus, and they pass in a minute. Get up in stages from now on, and eat something if it has been hours. See a GP if it keeps happening, if your hearing changes or rings with it, or if it happens lying down too.

Sit closer to the router or use a cable, and shut the other heavy things on the laptop: a browser with twenty tabs is usually the cause of a freezing call. Turn the video off when the sound matters more, and in Zoom or Teams set the video to a lower quality - a still picture and clear sound beats a frozen face.

Sit deep and still: a long leg with the heel down and a soft hand that follows the horse's mouth does more than any amount of kicking. Learn to absorb the movement in your hips rather than your hands - walk and trot without stirrups, on the lunge if you can - and ride a well-schooled horse at a riding school for a term; the feel of a trained one teaches faster than a green horse will.
Six dogs, Frogs, Toads, Salamanders, Newts, Caecilians and Deer — how long have they been with you?
Six dogs, Monkeys, Whales, Turtles, Lizards, Crocodiles and Snakes. Who's in charge?
Six dogs, Beagle, Labrador, Siamese, Chihuahua, Parakeet and Persian. Who's in charge?

Six hours is on the short side: most adults need seven to nine, and the shortfall shows as yawning, coffee and losing the thread by mid-afternoon. Half an hour earlier to bed, and the same wake-up time every day, is the fix - a long weekend lie-in is not.

Size the nail to the job, not to the room: 40mm to 50mm lost-head or oval nails for skirting and architrave, 50mm to 65mm for a floorboard, 30mm for a 6mm batten, and thin panel pins for beading and a back panel. As a rule the nail wants to be about two and a half times as long as the piece it is holding, and the top third of it has to bite into something solid behind.

Size the screen to the distance you sit, not to the budget: for a 4K set that is about one and a half times the diagonal, so 50 inches at roughly 2 metres and 65 at 2.5, and a desk monitor sits an arm's length away, which suits 24 to 27 inches. Then spend the money on the panel rather than the badge - a mid-range OLED or mini-LED beats the biggest cheap set, and a good IPS monitor beats a cheap 4K one. Check the ports you actually need (three HDMI on a telly, USB-C and a height-adjustable stand on a monitor), and skip 8K and the shop's extended warranty, which a home insurance policy or a credit card often covers already.

Skipping breakfast is not harmful for most adults: what matters is the food you eat over the whole day, not the hour you start. Don't skip it if you are pregnant, on insulin or a diabetes tablet that can cause hypos, or a child - and eat something if you get shaky or headachy mid-morning.

Sleep talking is common and almost always harmless: it happens in light sleep, it runs in families, and most people never know they do it. Nothing needs treating - keep the last drink early, cut late caffeine and get enough sleep, because it gets worse when someone is overtired or feverish. Ask the GP about it if the talking comes with acting out dreams or violent movement, since that pairing is worth checking for a sleep disorder.

Sleep apnoea is the airway at the back of the throat closing for ten seconds or more, many times a night, so breathing stops in short bursts and you wake just enough to start again - which is why the snoring breaks off and why eight hours leaves you flat. The signs are loud snoring with silences, a gasp or a choke, a dry mouth and a morning headache, and nodding off in the day; extra weight, a thick neck, alcohol at night and sleeping on your back all make it worse. Ask a GP for a sleep study - it is done at home with a monitor on your finger - because a CPAP mask or a mouth splint fixes most cases and untreated it is hard on the heart.

Small amounts, with a lot of white or black: a red sofa wants pale walls and no second colour. Sample it before you buy with a patch on the wall or a cushion taken home, because red changes with the light, and keep the rest of the room quiet so the one colour has somewhere to sit.

Small and specific beats big and vague. Send one message today saying you have been thinking of them, then offer a fixed thing: "I'll bring dinner on Thursday" or "walk on Sunday?" rather than "let me know if you need anything". Ask whether they want company or quiet before you turn up, and do not tell them to cheer up - being told to feel better is the one thing that never works.

Smoked cannabis is harmful in a different way from tobacco: most joints are rolled with tobacco, so they carry the same tar and nicotine, a joint is held in longer, and the risk of psychosis and of anxiety is real and rises with heavy use and with high-THC skunk. It is not physically addictive like nicotine but the habit is hard to shift, and the damage is worse under about 25 while the brain is still developing. Vaping THC or eating it takes out the smoke, not the effects on the mind.
So about 160x230cm for a small room.

Soak the scaled part in half water, half white vinegar, or a spoonful of citric acid in water: boil it in the kettle and leave it an hour, or tie a bag of it round a shower head or tap for an hour. Rinse twice afterwards, and do it again whenever it furs up.

Soak in cool water with a cup of white vinegar for half an hour, then wash at 40C with biological powder and no fabric softener. The smell lives in bacteria left in the fibres, so an occasional 60C wash of the whole load is what keeps it away.
Soccer. I wouldn't spend another minute on it — both work.

Soft herbs - parsley, basil, coriander, dill, mint, chives - want the end of the cooking, not the start: chop them and stir them in off the heat. A handful blitzed with oil, lemon and garlic is a green sauce for fish, chicken or new potatoes, and the stems go in at the start of a soup. Stir a spoon of pesto through hot pasta with a splash of the cooking water, spread it over chicken or fish before baking, or loosen it with oil and lemon as a dressing for tomatoes or mozzarella.
Software product. I wouldn't spend another minute on it — both work.

Something sharp, something salty, something crunchy: olive oil and lemon or vinegar, then salt, then nuts, seeds or croutons. A dressing of 2 parts oil to 1 part vinegar with a spoon of mustard, shaken in a jar, keeps a week in the fridge.

Something starchy, something green, and something sharp or juicy: potatoes or rice or bread, a green vegetable with butter or oil on it, and a squeeze of lemon, a spoon of yoghurt, or a tomato salad. Keep it to one of each and it works with nearly anything - the sharp thing is what stops the plate tasting flat.

Something that makes a day in bed easier: a flask of soup with bread, a box of their favourite tea, a magazine or puzzle book, and a link to a film you know they like. Offer one specific thing at one specific time - "I'll leave soup on the step on Thursday" - because "let me know if you need anything" is the thing a poorly person never does. Skip flowers and skip food you do not know they can face.
Something to look forward to, then - what's the plan?
Something hopeful: *Hunt for the Wilderpeople* on film, *Ted Lasso* as a series, or *The Midnight Library* to read. All three leave you better than they found you.

Sooner is better than tidy: lift the plant by its base rather than by the stem, keep as much of the root ball as will hold together, and shake off only the compost that has already come loose. Stand it in fresh compost in a pot with drainage holes - the same size or one up, never a big jump - firm the compost round the roots, water until it runs out of the bottom, and keep it out of direct sun for a week. White firm roots are fine and brown mushy ones can be trimmed off. A cracked pot will hold for a while, but slip it inside another pot or repot it, because a break under the rim gives way all at once.

Sort the paperwork first: anywhere abroad, that is a passport with six months left on it when you come back, travel insurance taken out the day you book rather than the day you fly, and your booking, policy and passport photo page saved on your phone so they work with no signal.

Sort two things this week: a decision in principle from a lender, which says what they will lend, about four and a half times your income, and a solicitor who quotes a fixed fee, because the searches and the paperwork start as soon as an offer is accepted. Then book the survey before you exchange, and keep at least £2,000 back for it, the searches and the moving van, since those are spent whether or not the sale goes through.

Sort by colour, not by kind of garment: whites and light colours in one load, darks and brights in another. It is new dark and red items that bleed for their first few washes, so wash those alone or with other darks the first time, and cold water keeps both the colour and the size.

Sound that comes in from outside is most often work on the road, a neighbour's extractor or boiler, or an animal - and a log of times and days is what the council acts on. Nothing here can listen, so where in the house do you hear it clearest?

Sound is a pressure wave travelling through air, water or a solid: something vibrates, pushes the particles next to it, and the push travels outwards. That is what I can tell you; on whether to use social media analytics, the maker's support page will say.
Sounds alright. Anything good in it?
South America has 12 countries, from Colombia and Venezuela round to Argentina and Chile.

Sow tomatoes indoors in March or April and plant them out in early June, once nights stay above 10C: 45cm apart, or one to a grow bag, burying the stem up to its first leaves. Harden them off over a week first - a cold night sets a tomato back a month.

Space looks black because there is almost nothing there to scatter light into your eyes; light only reaches you if it comes straight from a star or a lit object. The sky is bright blue from Earth because our air scatters sunlight everywhere.

Spain — no way of seeing a place I haven't been to, so no verdict from me. What decides it is the walk from the station or the bus, the light in the rooms, the noise at the time you would be home, and what the neighbours are like. A map app shows the walk and the streets, and one visit on a weekday evening tells you the noise.

Sparkling water is water with carbon dioxide dissolved in it, so there is no sugar and no calories in it and it counts towards your fluids like still water. The fizz is a weak acid, which is why dentists say drink it with a meal rather than sip it all day, and it can leave you feeling bloated. The flavoured bottles are the ones to read: many of them carry sugar or sweetener.

Spend your budget on support, not springs: a medium-firm pocket-sprung or foam mattress suits most people, and you should lie on it for 15 minutes in the shop. Buy somewhere with a 100-night trial, and replace it every 8 to 10 years.

Spit in each lens, rub it round and rinse it out, or wipe a drop of baby shampoo over the inside and let it dry - both leave a film the water cannot bead on. Then keep the seal still: a mask that is too tight, or goggles pressed on with the strap under a swim cap, squeezes out the warm air and fogs faster. Anti-fog sprays work for a session or two.

Split what actually lands in your account: fixed bills and food first, then move a set amount to savings the day you're paid, and treat what's left as the spending money. On whether to use do that. thanks for your, the official page, gov.uk or your bank will know more than I can.

Split it, so one loss is not the whole trip: a card and a day's cash on you, a second card in the hotel safe or packed separately, and a note of both card numbers and your bank's lost-card number somewhere offline. Carry a small amount in a front pocket or a zipped bag rather than a back pocket, use bank ATMs in daylight, and a money belt only if you will really wear it. If a card goes, freeze it in the app and ring the bank straight away, and check the phone before you fly: roaming on, a roaming pass for that country, and the bank app logged in, because that is how most of us pay now.

Spoon it into the cup and level it rather than scooping from the bag, because a cup is a volume and how much it holds depends on how the ingredient went in. With no scales at all, use one mug for everything in the recipe - the proportions matter more than the exact weight.

St John's wort is a real drug and it argues with several: it makes the pill less reliable, it cuts the level of warfarin and of some heart and transplant drugs, and with an SSRI it can push serotonin too high. Leave it out if you are on any of those, and tell a pharmacist you take it before you start anything new - people forget it counts as a medicine.

Stand the round on a chopping block - a big flat stump - and bring the axe down through the middle, not at the edge: the ground swallows the force of a blow and the block gives it back. Knotty or wide rounds go with two steel wedges tapped in along the end grain, and a stubborn one is easier after a few weeks of drying. No axe at all means a wedge and a club hammer, or drill a line of holes down the face and hit the wood with a mallet.

Stand a fridge thermometer in a glass of water on the middle shelf and leave it overnight: the fridge wants 3 to 5C and the freezer -18C, and the dial's numbers are not degrees. A fridge that will not reach it wants the door seals checked - close the door on a sheet of paper and see if it slides out easily - and the coils at the back dusted. Don't overfill it either, because cold air needs space to move.

Standing all day is a load problem rather than a foot one, and the fixes are cheap: a rubber mat or a folded towel where you stand, shoes with a firm sole and a little heel rather than flat pumps or trainers, and sitting down for two minutes every hour even if it is only on a box. Shift your weight from foot to foot and rise onto the balls of your feet twenty times an hour - that pumps the calf and keeps blood moving, which is what stops the ache by the end of a shift. Compression socks help if your ankles swell. If the heel is worst on your first steps in the morning, that is plantar fasciitis rather than the standing, and it wants stretching rather than a mat.

Start pocket money at about six, a small fixed amount on the same day each week, and let them spend it badly while the sums are still small. Split it into spend, save and give jars so the saving is visible, and pay extra for jobs beyond the normal helping rather than docking the basics. Say prices out loud when you shop and name the choice you are making - "the small one is £3 or the big bag is £5, which is better value?" - and keep it about what money does rather than what it is: what we save for, what a bill is, and why the card is not free money.
Start quiet and put the phone across the room: a gentle sound you have to get up to stop wakes you better than a loud one by the bed.

Start with one square you can finish today: 5 mm needles and a smooth aran yarn, cast on about 30 stitches and knit every stitch of every row. That is garter stitch, it is flat and it does not curl, and 30 stitches is a scarf about 20 cm wide - two 100 g balls make one about 1.5 m long. Your tension evens out after ten rows, so the first rows looking uneven is not a mistake.

Start with one joint and one small thing - a box, a stool - using hand tools: a hardpoint saw, a chisel, a square and a bench hook will do more than a garage of machines. Men's sheds and community workshops hire out bench time and somebody to ask, which is worth more than the tools when you are starting.

Start with soft food they can hold themselves rather than something on a spoon: cooked carrot or broccoli, toast fingers, ripe pear, banana, avocado, or a spoon of plain yoghurt. One food at a time, a few days apart, so a reaction is easy to spot, and milk first so they are not too hungry to try. How much is a few spoonfuls or a few sticks at the start, half a fist by nine months and about a fist at a year. Around six months is the age, unless a health visitor has said otherwise.

Start with something they can eat: cut an apple into four, take one piece - that is one quarter. Then show that the bottom number is how many pieces the whole was cut into and the top is how many you have. Do halves, quarters and thirds with real objects before any writing, then move to drawing them as bars of chocolate.

Start with the mouth, not the tune: getting a clean sound out of the head joint is the first week, then long notes on a few fingerings. Ten minutes a day, and a teacher early, because the embouchure is the thing that is hard to fix yourself.

Start with the compilations rather than a single artist: a *Fabric* or *Global Underground* mix, then Jeff Mills' *The Occurrence* for how stripped back it can be. Techno is about the build over eight minutes, so give it time.
Start with this: Test it outside the app first: press Windows key + R on Windows, or open Spotlight with Cmd + Space on a Mac.
Start with this: Write down what is actually due this week.

Start with three 10-minute walks in a week you can keep, then add five minutes to one of them each week until you are walking 30 minutes on five days - that is the 150 minutes a week the guidelines ask for. Walk fast enough that you can talk but not sing, wear the shoes you already have, and put each walk in your diary like an appointment so it happens on the days you do not feel like it.

Start with what you can repeat three times a week: a 20 to 30 minute walk, two short strength sessions and some balance work, and add a little each week. Strength training twice a week matters more after 50 than a hard cardio session, because it is what keeps muscle and bone. Check with a GP first if you have a heart condition or you have not exercised in years.
Start with *Big Sunshine*; *Sir Rocket* and *Saint Sunshine* if it sticks. A nickname works best when it comes from something only you two know.
Start with *Doctor Nonsense*; *Big Chaos* and *Sir Nonsense* if it sticks. A nickname works best when it comes from something only you two know.

Start with *La Boheme* or *Carmen* - two or three hours, famous tunes, and a story you can follow without the plot notes. Watch a filmed production rather than listening only, because a lot of what happens is on the faces. Subtitles are normal, not cheating.
Start with *Saint Pockets*; *Tiny Trouble* and *Lady Pockets* if it sticks. A nickname works best when it comes from something only you two know.
Start with *Sir Biscuit*; *Saint Saturday* and *Tiny Biscuit* if it sticks. A nickname works best when it comes from something only you two know.

Start with *The Rest Is History* (two funny historians), *Desert Island Discs* for people talking about their lives, or *Casefile* if you want a true crime story told straight. Tell me what you usually listen to and I'll aim closer.

Start with a voice or a fact, not the weather: "My mother stole a car on her way to my christening" and "The rent was due on Friday and I had 40p" both make a reader ask a question. One sentence, something happening or someone talking, and no throat-clearing before it. Write ten, throw eight away - the tenth is usually the one you keep.

Start with a beginner mat class, not the reformer: a mat class is about ten to fifteen pounds, needs only a mat and a cushion, and a teacher who watches you is the point of it. The one thing to learn first is the breath - wide into the ribs on the effort, with the belly gently held, never sucked in hard. Twice a week for a month, and tell the teacher about any back or neck trouble beforehand.

Start with a free needs assessment from the council - it opens the door to home help, grab rails and a care package without you paying privately first. Then take the falls out of the house: rugs taped down, a light by the bed, a shower seat, a keysafe so help can get in. Frame it as what they want to keep doing, not what you have decided for them.

Start with Companies House, which is free: search the name or the number on their quote and you can see whether the company exists, when it was formed and whether the registered address is a real place rather than a mail drop - a limited company has to put its number and registered address on its website and its invoices. Then the trade checks: a written quote rather than a verbal one, proof of insurance, and for gas, oil or electrical work the registration number you can check yourself on the Gas Safe, OFTEC or NICEIC register. A neighbour who has used them beats any review site, and pay by card rather than bank transfer so there is a chargeback if it goes wrong. Never pay the whole price up front - a deposit for materials is normal, the rest when it is done.

State the order, the problem and what you want, in that order: "I ordered a lamp on 3 May (order 12345). It arrived cracked. Please send a replacement or refund the £40." Give a deadline of 14 days and mention your rights only if they say no.
State. I wouldn't spend another minute on it — both work.
Stay in Midtown for the sights and the noise, the Lower East Side for food and bars, or Brooklyn for cheaper rooms and 20 minutes on the train.
Steak: salt a thick one, 2 minutes a side in a smoking-hot pan, then rest it as long as it cooked. Thin strips are better stir-fried hard for 2 minutes with garlic and soy.

Stir in a splash more milk or plain yoghurt and a pinch of salt, because salt is what turns the sweetness down, and leave it a minute to loosen. If it is still too sweet, a handful of berries or a spoon of yoghurt does more than adding more oats. Next time, leave the sugar out of the pan or the jar and put it on the table: porridge takes very little, and the milk brings out the sweetness of the oats.

Stop resetting it - an immersion element that trips the breaker has gone electrically, and resetting it each time is how a fuse board gets hot. Leave the circuit off at the spur, and get it swapped: the tank is drained, the old element unscrewed and a new one fitted, an hour's work for a plumber or electrician. Until then the boiler or the back-up heating is what you have for hot water.

Stop waiting for a free evening and put a small, regular thing in the diary instead: a twenty-minute call every second Sunday, or a walk at the same time each month. Say why you are doing it - 'I miss you, and I am bad at this, so I am booking us in' lands better than a vague let's catch up. Voice notes between times keep the thread alive, and doing one small favour beats a grand plan you both cancel.

Stop, switch the engine off and put your hazards on, then check nobody is hurt and ring 999 if they are. Swap names, addresses, phone numbers, insurers and policy numbers with the other driver, and photograph the cars, the road and the damage. If you did not exchange details you must report it to the police within 24 hours, and tell your insurer the same day even if you are not claiming.

Stop arguing about the coat and argue about the temperature instead: 'It's four degrees - you can wear the thin one or the thick one, your pick.' Give two options you can live with, put everything by the door the night before, and let them be cold for one trip with the coat in your bag. The fight is usually about being told, not about the coat.

Stop bidding for the verdict: you will not win the argument about who is favoured, and a parent who has done it for thirty years will not suddenly see it. Say the one thing you want from them, once and plainly - "I'd like you to ask about my week too" - and put the effort into the relationship you can build with your brother or sister directly, rather than through your parents. Keep visits short enough to be pleasant, stop covering for the favourite, and take the comparison out of what you agree to: being the one they worry about less is not the same as being loved less.

Stop it at the setting, not with a telling-off: turn on Ask to Buy in Family Sharing, or set Settings > Face ID & Passcode > iTunes & App Store purchases to Always Require, so nothing is bought without you. Then ask Apple or Google for a refund on the last 90 days of charges - both have a form for exactly this, and they usually give it back the first time.

Strike it with the laces, not the toe: plant the standing foot beside the ball with the knee over it, keep the ankle locked and swing through the middle of the ball, then follow through where you want it to go. For a pass, use the inside of the foot with the ankle at a right angle - the toe is what makes it balloon.
Sucre is the constitutional capital; La Paz is where the government sits.

Sugar dissolves fastest in hot liquid: warm the water or milk first, stir until the liquid is clear rather than for a set time, and use about 200g of sugar to 100ml of water for a syrup. Caster sugar goes in quicker than granulated and icing sugar dissolves almost at once. A spoonful of lemon juice or golden syrup stops a syrup crystallising as it cools.
Sus means suspicious or not quite right, of a thing or a person: 'that email looks sus', 'he was acting sus all night'. It is short for suspicious.

Sushi is a good everyday choice: fish, rice and vegetables, with very little fat, and a supermarket box is usually 300 to 500 calories. The traps are the fried fillings, the mayonnaise-heavy boxes and the soy sauce, which is salty enough to matter if you pour in the whole sachet.

Swallows come back to Britain from mid-April, a few as early as March, and leave between late September and early October; swifts arrive in early May and are gone by mid-August. They winter in southern Africa. So an empty nest in early October is normal, not a sign that something went wrong.

Swap in pulses: red lentils for mince (a mug of them and a splash more stock, 20 minutes), or a tin of green lentils and chopped mushrooms for the texture, and chickpeas, tofu or big flat mushrooms where there was chicken. Season it the way you would the meat, with stock, soy or paprika, and the swap goes unnoticed.
Sweden: Stockholm for the islands and the museums. The archipelago in summer. Gothenburg for a second city.

Sweep or vacuum first, then mop with hot water and a squirt of washing-up liquid, wringing the mop out until it is barely damp, because standing water is what leaves the streaks. Give a sticky patch a second pass with a little more soap, then go over the whole floor once with clean water, since the soap film left behind is what dulls it and grabs the next lot of dirt. A greasy ring by the cooker comes off with a paste of bicarbonate of soda on a cloth.

Sweep it rather than wipe it: a brush and dustpan, then a torch held flat on the floor shows the bits the brush missed and a damp piece of kitchen paper picks up the dust. Wrap the glass in newspaper or an old tea towel and put it straight in the outside bin, not the kitchen one and not the recycling, and keep shoes on in there until the floor has had the torch over it. A cut from glass that will not stop bleeding after ten minutes of pressing needs looking at.
Sweetcorn fritters: a tin of drained corn, 2 eggs and 3 spoons of flour, fried 2 minutes a side. Egg fried rice: cold rice fried hard, an egg scrambled into it with soy sauce and peas, 10 minutes.

Sweeteners are safe at the amounts in drinks and yoghurts: aspartame, sucralose and stevia have been tested for decades, and the cancer alarm about aspartame is a hazard rating that would need something like twenty cans a day. The honest catch is that diet drinks do not seem to help people lose weight - they do not fill you up, and they keep a sweet tooth sweet. Water, tea or coffee is the cheaper swap.

Switch on Low Power Mode and the phone will last hours longer: Settings > Battery on an iPhone, or Battery saver in Android's settings. Turn the screen brightness down, drop 5G to 4G if that is a setting you have, and ask in the nearest cafe, library or shop to plug into a socket for fifteen minutes - a short top-up is fine for the battery.
Switzerland: Zurich or Lucerne as a base. The Bernese Oberland for the mountain trains. A rail pass pays off fast.

Symmetry is when a shape or object looks the same after a fold, turn or flip. A line of symmetry divides a shape into two halves that are mirror images - a square has four, a circle has infinitely many - and rotational symmetry is how many times it matches in a full turn.

Synthetic filaments for anything water-based - emulsion, water-based gloss and satin - and natural bristle for oil-based gloss, which holds the solvent and lays off flatter without leaving brushmarks. Width matters more than brand: a 2 inch angled sash brush for cutting in and for gloss on woodwork, a 3 or 4 inch brush for a wall, and cheap is fine for emulsion but not for gloss, where a shedding brush leaves hairs in the finish. Between coats, wrap a water-based brush in a damp cloth inside a bag rather than washing it out each time, and comb a bristle brush straight after cleaning so it dries in shape.
Take one night away on your own: a train, a cheap room, a book. It is a different kind of trip from a holiday with people, and easier than it sounds.

Take photo ID and proof of address dated within the last three months - a bank statement, utility bill or council letter - and you can usually open one online in ten minutes with a selfie and a photo of the ID. To move an existing account, use the free current account switch service: it moves your direct debits, standing orders and salary within seven working days and forwards stray payments for three years.

Take something that needs nothing from anyone else's kitchen: a big bowl of pasta salad, a tray of sausages or a quiche, cheese and crackers, or a traybake cut into squares. Nothing with cream in it if it will sit out, and take it in a dish you do not need back. If the host says not to bring anything, take a bottle or something for after - and ask what is already coming so you are not the third pasta bake.

Take the old door off its hinges and measure it, because a new one is trimmed to that, not the other way round: width, height, and the distance from the top edge to the hinge centres. Cut 2-3mm off the closing edge and 3mm off the bottom, plane a whisker of a chamfer on the closing side so it does not rub, and keep the hinge positions from the old door - about 125mm up from the top and 250mm from the bottom, so the door weight is carried at the top. Chisel the recesses no deeper than the hinge leaf, screw the hinge to the door first, hang it on the frame with one screw in each and check it swings before the rest go in. A door wants 2-3mm all round at the closing edge and 5mm or so off the floor over a carpet; if it swings itself open or shut, the frame is out of plumb, not the door.

Take the pressure off the night, not the work: the revision is done by then, so the job is a fixed stop time, the phone out of the room, and something that is not revision for the hour before bed. Keep the worry concrete - ask what they are most afraid of forgetting, write it down and leave it on the desk, because a written worry stops the circling. If the exams are weeks away and sleep is still gone, or they are not eating or cannot get to school, tell their tutor, because that is worth more than any technique.

Take the smallest real break first: a day off this week, and one week booked in the diary that nobody can move. Then bring the load to your manager as a list of what is due and what you can do, and ask which to drop - burnout is usually a staffing problem landing on one person. Tell your GP if you are not sleeping or eating properly, because a sick note is a normal thing to ask for and it protects your job.

Take the train or the coach between cities instead of flying, book a month or two ahead, and stay in hostels or travel out of season: May, June and late September cost about half what August does. Eat where people work - market stalls, bakeries, a supermarket lunch - and choose one small town over a second capital. Cheapest weeks are midweek city breaks, Tuesday to Thursday.

Take the cheapest money first. Paying customers, then a startup loan - the British Business Bank backs £500 to £25,000 at a fixed rate through accredited lenders - then grants and competitions, then angel investors, and an overdraft or invoice finance last because it costs the most. Raise for 12 to 18 months of runway and a milestone that makes the next round possible, and keep six months of costs untouched as reserve. Have three things ready before you talk to anyone: your last 12 months of figures, a one-page forecast, and how much of the business you are willing to give away.

Take the days you have booked as booked: your employer approved them, and leave that was agreed before the notice went in is normally still yours to take, or to be paid for if the last day falls before the holiday does. Check your contract or staff handbook for how much notice they want for leave - often twice the length of the holiday - and give it in writing. A full-time job is entitled to 28 days a year including bank holidays, so if you are offered less than that, that is the thing worth asking about. Days you have not taken when you leave are paid at your normal rate.

Take the edge off with fat and sweetness rather than more of anything sour: a knob of butter or a spoon of cream, a pinch of sugar, or a little bicarbonate of soda on the tip of a knife for a tomato sauce. If it is a stew or a curry, ten more minutes of simmering with the lid off softens the acid; if it is a salad dressing, add oil rather than more honey.

Take the free GHIC card for state healthcare in the EU and pair it with proper travel insurance: the card covers treatment, not getting you home. Buy insurance when you book so cancellation is included.

Take them to an optician: straightening an arm, tightening a screw and adjusting the bridge are free at almost every high-street optician, take a few minutes and need no appointment. The one job worth doing yourself is a loose screw, with a glasses screwdriver or the smallest one in a jeweller's kit, and a bent plastic arm can be eased straight after a dip in warm water - but never bend metal frames cold, because they snap. If the frame itself has cracked, ask them to put new lenses in a new frame rather than glue it, and keep your old pair as the spare.

Take your foot off the accelerator and off the brake, and steer gently where you want the front of the car to go: the tyres grip again by themselves, and pressing either pedal hard is what keeps a skid going. On ice, brake early and lightly in a straight line before the bend rather than in it, leave three or four times the usual gap, and pull away in second gear if the wheels spin. Anything under 7C and wet is worth slowing down for, because that is when ice forms without looking like it.

Take a dish that holds its heat and needs nothing at the last minute: a tray of roast vegetables, a big grain salad, or a chilli to plug in. Ask what is already coming first, so you are not the third pasta bake.

Take it off the heat and lift out the burnt bits rather than stirring them in, because the smoky taste spreads through everything. If it has gone all the way through, a splash of stock and something creamy hides a little of it, but a properly burnt sauce is better started again.

Take it to an Authorised Treatment Facility - a scrapyard that takes whole cars and gives you a Certificate of Destruction - because that certificate is the proof the car is gone. Hand over the V5C and the keys, keep the certificate, and tell DVLA yourself the same day so the tax, the insurance and any fines stop with you. Empty everything out first, and take a private plate off before it goes on the truck. Expect £150 to £400 for a small car, paid by weight.

Take it in this order. First clear any credit card, overdraft or pay-later debt, because that costs 20% or more a year and no savings account pays that. Second, put three to six months of essential spending in an easy-access account, so a broken boiler is an annoyance rather than a loan. Only then think about the long term, and for money you will not need for five years that usually means a global index tracker inside a stocks and shares ISA, or a bit more into your pension. A few thousand pounds is a cushion before it is an investment, so do not lock it into a fixed bond. If you claim means-tested benefits, check how a lump sum counts before you spend it.

Talk side by side rather than face to face: in the car, on a walk, or while washing up, and keep it to a couple of minutes. Ask about the small stuff and let them bring the big stuff when they are ready; a teenager who says nothing at seven often talks at ten.
Tallahassee, not Miami.

Tannin first: dry and slightly astringent, with the flavour of the leaf behind it, and it goes bitter if it is left in the water too long. Milk softens the tannin, which is why a strong tea takes milk and a delicate one does not.

Tap water in Japan is safe to drink: it is treated, the restaurants serve it, and a refillable bottle saves money all week. Bottled is only worth it if the plumbing in an old building makes the taste odd.
Tap a contactless card or phone on the turnstile: a subway ride is $2.90 whatever the distance and trains run all night.
Tbilisi - the country's capital. The US state of Georgia has Atlanta.

Tea and coffee cut how much iron you take up, and so do milk, cheese and calcium tablets; vitamin C does the opposite. Take the iron with water or a glass of orange juice, an hour before food or two hours after, and leave an hour between the tablet and a cup of tea.

Tea first, milk last, in a mug: you can see how strong the tea has got before you pour, and the leaves brew in water at full heat instead of water cooled by milk. Milk first is the old way with a pot and a thin china cup - a splash of milk stopped boiling water cracking the china, and it stretched a small amount of tea - so it is not wrong, just fussier, and the bottom of the cup ends up milky unless you stir.

Tea is fine: four or five cups of ordinary black tea is about half the caffeine of the same number of coffees, it counts towards your fluid, and the tea itself has no calories - the sugar and the biscuits are what add up. Herbal and green teas are caffeine-free or nearly, so they are not the ones to worry about in the evening. If you are anaemic or take iron tablets, keep the cup an hour away from a meal, because the tannins cut how much iron you take up.

Teenagers need eight to ten hours and their body clock runs late, so lights out between 8.30 and 10pm is right and 10pm is not late. Fix the wake-up time and keep it at weekends, get daylight early, and keep the phone out of the last half hour.

Tell your manager first, in person or on a call, and keep it short: "I've decided to move on. I'd like to give you four weeks' notice from today." Then hand over one written paragraph with your last day in it. You never have to say why, and it is rarely worth it.
Tempeh: slice it, simmer 5 minutes to take the bitterness off, then fry it 3 minutes a side and glaze it with soy, honey and lime.

Temperature measures how fast the particles in something are moving: faster particles mean a higher temperature and slower ones mean a lower one. It is not the same as how much heat is stored, which is why a cup of tea and a bath can be the same temperature but hold very different amounts of heat.

Ten minutes a day beats one big clean: pick a fixed time - before bed is the easy one - and do the surfaces in one room and the washing-up, so nothing piles up. Give everything a home, a box, a hook or a shelf, and anything without one goes out. One load of washing a day beats a mountain at the weekend, and a basket at the bottom of the stairs takes the things that belong in another room.

Ten minutes a game is plenty: musical statues, pass the parcel with a sweet in every layer, pin the tail on the donkey, and a treasure hunt of picture clues round the garden. Sleeping lions calms them down before food, and Simon Says fills the gap while the cake comes out. Tell me the age and I'll pitch it right.

Ten to twelve and a half percent is the norm, and check the bill first: if a service charge is already on it, that is the tip and you add nothing. If the service was poor, ask for it to come off before you pay.

Ten to fifteen minutes a day beats one long session a week: learn the four chords G, C, D and Em first, then play songs that use them, since songs keep you going where scales do not. Most people can strum through a simple song in two or three months that way; sore fingertips for the first fortnight are normal.

Test the speed on a cable or right next to the router first, because that tells you whether the problem is the broadband or the wifi. If it is the wifi, move closer, use 5GHz, and check how many devices are streaming; if the cabled speed is also low, it is your provider and worth a call.

Test them with a knife rather than a fork: it should slide in with no resistance at all and the potato should still hold its shape. Boiled, that is 10 to 12 minutes for small new potatoes, 15 to 20 for chunks and 20 to 25 for whole medium ones; a fork tells you too late, and a potato left a minute too long goes watery.
Thailand: Bangkok for temples and street food. Chiang Mai for the north. A flight south for the islands.

Thank them, say no plainly, and don't over-explain: "Thanks so much for thinking of me, but I can't make it. I hope it goes brilliantly." If you'd like to keep the door open, add one line about catching up another time.
Thanks - that helps. If it is in one spot and repeats, it is usually something fixed: a pipe, a board, a fitting. If it wanders round the house, it is air or water. Which is it?
That needs hands I haven't got, sorry. The words I can do: give me the message and I'll tidy it, shorten it or say it better.

That one is set by the council or the department, so I can't say it from here, sorry. The letter or the site with your address on it is the one that counts; bring me what it says and I'll help you fill it in.
That one is decided case by case rather than by a general rule, and the part that decides it is the part only you can see. Give me that detail and I will tell you what I would check first.
That sounds unsettling. Is there one thing you can check or ask about that would settle it?
That would get to me too. Do you want to work out what to say to them, or is it more a case of letting off steam?

That green or blue is harmless: the sulphur compounds in garlic and onions turn colour with acid, and with copper or unlined iron, and nothing else about the food changes, so eat it. It shows up in garlic dressed with lemon or vinegar, in pickle brines and in pickled onions. Blanching the cloves for 30 seconds before pickling, adding the acid at the end and using a stainless pan all stop it happening.

That is still the thing to do — Keep a short diary for two weeks: date, time, what it was, how long. Then ring the council's environmental health team, who must look into a statutory nuisance and can serve an abatement notice. Builders are usually held to about 8am to 6pm on weekdays and Saturday mornings, so a 6am start is worth reporting.

That is still the thing to do — Under-fives usually travel free on local buses with a paying adult, and 5 to 15 pay a child fare, often about half: the operator's own page gives the age and the price for your area.

That is still the thing to do — Water evaporates from the sea and land, rises and cools into clouds, falls as rain or snow, and runs back to the sea: the same water goes round and round. Sunlight drives it and gravity brings it back down.
That is still the thing to do: For a story: *The Last of Us* (grief and a road trip), *Red Dead Redemption 2* (a slow western with a lot of heart), or *Disco Elysium* if you would rather read.

That is still the thing to do: Get into a building or a hard-topped car, away from windows, and stay there 30 minutes after the last thunder. If you're caught in the open, move off high ground and away from lone trees, water and metal fences, and crouch low on the balls of your feet.

A £1,000 loan repaid over a year at 20% APR costs about £1,110 in total. A 0% on purchases card has no interest, but a cash withdrawal from it starts at about 25% APR from day one.

ASAP stands for as soon as possible, which in an email is a polite way of asking without giving a time. If somebody needs it by a date, the date is the useful thing to say back, because as soon as possible means something different to everyone.
Abdel Fattah el-Sisi is the president of Egypt: in office since 2014, after leading the 2013 takeover. The president holds most of the power, and the army is a large part of the economy.

About 5 days in the salad drawer; a whole unopened bag keeps a week longer. Wash and dry the leaves properly, keep them in a bag with a piece of kitchen paper and dress them only at the table, because wet leaves and early dressing are what make salad limp. Brown-edged or slimy leaves are past it, so pick those out before they spread.

About 7,000 to 8,000 steps a day is where most of the benefit is - the health gain levels off there rather than at 10,000, which came from a 1960s pedometer advert - so add a daily twenty minutes on top of what you already do rather than chasing a round number. If you are a long way off, two ten-minute walks beat one long one because they are easier to keep up, and the walking you do getting about counts.

About 10p a full charge, so a year of commuting is £15 to £25: a 500Wh battery is half a unit of electricity, and a unit is around 25p, which is why the electricity never shows up next to fuel. A 40-mile commute five days a week is roughly 100 charges a year - call it £10 to £20 - and the battery is the cost that matters, not the plug.

About 15p a wash at 30C in electricity, against 25p at 40C: heating the water is most of what a wash costs, so 30C is the cheapest cycle that still cleans everyday clothes, shirts and jeans properly with a modern detergent. Go to 40C for heavily soiled work clothes and 60C for towels, bedding and anything with a stomach bug or a cold, because that is about killing germs rather than shifting dirt. A cold or 20C cycle saves a few pence more but struggles with grease.

About an hour for a straightforward boiler, and up to ninety minutes if it is the first service in a while or the engineer has to check the flue and the safety devices. It is a set of checks rather than a strip-down: they run the boiler, test the flue and the gas pressure, clean what they can reach, and leave you the service record. Book it for late summer if you can, because the wait is longer once the cold weather starts.

About 200 calories per 100g as a side, nearer 300 if the tray is deep in oil - the potato itself is only about 90 before the fat goes on, so it is a carbohydrate like any other and the oil is what adds up. A thin film that just coats them, on a tray that is hot rather than swimming, is what keeps a roast potato an everyday thing.

About 25 to 45 minutes at a time, then a proper 5 to 10 minutes away from the desk: two or three hours of that is a good day, and four is a very long one. What counts is testing yourself in the block, not the hours you sat there. If you keep losing track, set a timer for the block and stop when it goes, even mid-sentence — stopping on a problem you can pick up again makes the next start easy.

About 250ml a mug and a splash more for what boils off, so roughly 600ml for two mugs - fill one mug and tip it in twice, then a little extra. Only boiling what you need is the quickest saving in the kitchen and it scales the kettle up more slowly, but don't go under the element's minimum or the kettle will click off before it boils.
About 384,400 km (238,900 miles) away on average, which is roughly 30 Earths side by side, and light takes 1.3 seconds to reach us from it. It is drifting about 4cm further away each year.

About 45 seconds for one mug and around 3 minutes for a full 1.7-litre kettle in a 3kW one, so boiling only what you are going to drink is both quicker and cheaper. A 2kW kettle takes roughly half as long again.

About 50 miles, or an hour at 50mph, which is enough for the trip to a tyre place and not a motorway run of a hundred miles: keep to 50mph, drive gently and go straight there. Check its pressure every few months, because they are often flat when you need them, and it does not count as a spare for a car with different size wheels at the front.

About a tablespoon (15ml) a head, made at 3 parts oil to 1 of vinegar or lemon: 45ml of oil and 15ml of vinegar dresses four, 70ml and 25ml dresses six, plus a teaspoon of mustard and a pinch of salt either way. Put the dressing in the bottom of the bowl and toss the leaves on top of it rather than pouring it over.

About a third of the post in the ground: 600mm (two foot) under a standard 1.8m panel, and 750 to 900mm on an exposed, windy corner or in sandy soil. Two foot is enough if the hole is about 250 to 300mm across and set in Postcrete or a 3:1 ballast and cement mix, with the concrete sloping away from the post so water runs off - check it plumb before the mix goes off, because a post only 300 to 400mm down leans within a winter.

About a week is a fair bet for a mixed bouquet: tulips and roses give you around seven days, daffodils and sweet peas five, carnations and lilies ten to fourteen, and a bouquet of gypsophila or dried stems longer than that. The stems seal over within a day or two, so an angled cut and clean water every couple of days is what buys the extra days.

About a litre of water for every 100g of pasta: a big pan filled about two thirds, at a rolling boil before the pasta goes in, and a teaspoon of salt per four litres. Keep it boiling and stir for the first minute so the pieces do not stick together - there is no need for oil in the water, which only makes the sauce slide off.

About 70 to 85 million people died in the Second World War, most of them civilians, which makes it the deadliest war ever fought. The Soviet Union lost around 27 million and China 15 to 20 million, and the Holocaust accounts for six million of the dead.

About 700 to 1,200C, or 1,300 to 2,200F, depending on the rock: basalt runs hottest and flows fastest, while the thick slow lava of a volcano like Etna is cooler. Steel melts at about 1,500C, so lava is hot enough to glow but not to melt steel.

About half an hour after a big meal, and no wait at all after a snack: the cramp rule comes from one small study and the evidence does not back it up. Keep out of deep water if you have been drinking, and don't swim on a stomach that feels too full.

About £10 to £20 at a bike shop for a puncture: most will fit a new inner tube and check the tyre for the thorn or glass that caused it for that, and a patch on its own is often cheaper or free if you bought the tube there. Doing it yourself is £5 to £8 for a tube, and the levers cost £3 to £5 once. A puncture that keeps coming back is usually the sharp thing still in the tyre, so ask them to run a finger round the inside, and a tyre with a cut or a thin patch is worth replacing at £15 to £35.

About £10 to £25 for a solid plate or a gas burner cap, and £25 to £50 for an induction zone's part, so it is worth fixing rather than replacing the cooker. Buy by the cooker's model number rather than by eye - the same size ring is not always the same fitting. An electric one is usually two screws and a spade connector; a gas ring has to be fitted by a Gas Safe engineer.

About £175 a year, in one go or by direct debit, and you need it for live TV on any channel or for BBC iPlayer, not for streaming like Netflix. It is free at 75 with Pension Credit, half price if you are blind. If it has run out, renew in the TV Licensing account before the letters start; if you no longer need it, cancel there and ask for a refund of unused months.

Above the neck and no temperature - a cold, a sore throat - and an easy run is fine once you feel up to it. Flu or a fever means a week of easy effort after the fever has gone, building back up over two or three weeks, because the fatigue outlasts the illness. For a strain or a niggle, walk pain-free first, then run and walk in alternate minutes, and add a little each week rather than starting where you left off.

Acacia leaves, browsed four to five metres up: a giraffe eats up to 45 kg of leaves a day with a 45 cm tongue and lips tough enough for the thorns, and it drinks only every few days because the leaves hold so much water. It spreads its front legs to reach a waterhole.

Acceleration is how quickly speed changes, measured in metres per second squared: 2 m/s squared means each second it goes 2 m/s faster. A car from 0 to 60 mph in 9 seconds is accelerating at about 3 m/s squared, and gravity pulls a falling thing at about 9.8. Slowing down is acceleration the other way, so a brake is not a different idea, just one that points backwards.

Acid rain forms when sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from burning coal and oil mix with water in the air and fall as weak acid. It harms trees and lakes; filters on power stations and cleaner fuel have cut it a lot since the 1980s.

Act fast: wash the ruined whites again straight away in cold water, and rewash with oxygen bleach if a wash cycle has already set the colour. Colour catcher sheets in the next few washes pull out what's left, and sort darks from lights from then on.

Add organic matter and let the worms do the rest: two or three barrowloads of garden compost or well-rotted manure per bed, spread on top in autumn and left for the worms to pull in. On clay, grit and compost together open it up; on sand, compost holds the water. Mulch every autumn, do not dig it in, and never walk on a wet bed - the compaction is what most soil problems actually are.

Add the parts of the ratio first, then divide the amount by that: sharing £50 in the ratio 2:3 is 5 parts, so each part is £10 and the shares are £20 and £30. To simplify a ratio, divide both numbers by the same thing, so 10:15 becomes 2:3.

Add weight when you can hit the top of your rep range on every set with clean form - usually every week or two when you are new. Take the smallest jump you have, 2.5kg on a bar or the next dumbbell up, and expect to lose a rep or two for a session or so; that is the new weight working, not a bad day.

Adult sizes, UK to EU to US. Women: UK 3 = EU 36 = US 5.5, UK 4 = 37 = 6.5, UK 5 = 38 = 7.5, UK 6 = 39 = 8.5, UK 7 = 40 = 9.5, UK 8 = 41 to 42 = 10.5. Men: UK 6 = EU 40 = US 7, UK 7 = 41 = 8, UK 8 = 42 = 9, UK 9 = 43 = 10, UK 10 = 44 = 11, UK 11 = 45 to 46 = 12. Half sizes and brands drift about a size either way, so use the brand's own chart when it has one, and measure your foot instead of guessing: stand on paper, mark the heel and the longest toe in socks, then add 1.5 to the centimetres and multiply by 1.5 - a 25 cm foot is an EU 40 - and try shoes on late in the day, when feet are at their biggest.
Affect is the verb and effect is the noun: the weather affects my mood, and the weather has an effect on my mood. A useful memory: 'cause and effect' is always the noun.

After a normal hard session, a day of easy walking or nothing at all is enough, and 48 hours is plenty before the same hard session again - soreness eases faster with gentle movement than with complete rest. Build back with two easy runs before your next hard one, and see a physio if pain is sharp, one-sided, or still there after two weeks.

After a big meal, blood flow shifts to the gut and the body clock dips in the early afternoon, so feeling sleepy is normal, especially with a lot of refined carbs or alcohol. A smaller lunch, a short walk and daylight help; see a GP if it happens after every meal with thirst, weight loss or falling asleep mid-conversation.
After a long walk or a big day that is normal, so let him sleep it off with water down and feed him later than usual. If he is still flat tomorrow, or will not eat or drink, that is a vet visit.

After every roast that leaves fat in it for the tray, rather than on a timetable, and the racks and shelves want a soak every couple of months, or as soon as the oven smells of last week's dinner: they lift out, soak in the bath with a couple of dishwasher tablets, and go back in dry. Tray bake tins rust if they are left to drip-dry, so they go back in dry too.

Agree the rule with your partner first and let them say it to their own parents: 'ring before you come, and we'll say yes most of the time.' Put the shape in place of the telling-off - a standing Sunday lunch, or a text when you set off - because a visit with a slot in it stops feeling like an ambush. If they have a key, ask for it back once, for the reason you can both live with: 'we've started locking up at night'.

Agree the rule before the bill lands, not over it: usually even thirds and the person who earns most offers to cover the drinks, or everyone pays for what they had. Say it as a rule rather than about a person - "shall we just split it three ways?" - and whoever holds the card takes transfers the same day, service charge included. The discomfort comes from not saying it, not from the amount.

Agree the boring things before the boxes: what each of you pays and into which account, who owns what, and what happens if it ends - a cohabitation agreement is a page and it saves the worst conversations. Then test the split before you commit to it: a month of alternating who cooks, cleans and shops shows you far more than a holiday does. Keep one evening a week that is yours alone, and say out loud now how you will both handle money arguments later.

Agree the length before you go, in the same breath as the date: two nights is plenty for most trips, and a day trip leaves you both glad to have seen each other. Take something for the table rather than a present, and book the way home before you arrive so the last hour is not the anxious one.

Agree to a limit instead of refusing the person: "I can cover tonight, but I can't do Fridays." Then keep it - a rule you stick to is kinder than a yes you resent. If it is most weeks, tell your manager what is happening without framing it as a complaint: "I've covered six of Priya's shifts this month; can we look at the rota?" Covering occasionally buys goodwill; covering always just moves the problem onto you.

Agree a rota that names the job, the day and the standard, written on the fridge: bins out Tuesday night, kitchen sides wiped after you cook, bathroom every other Sunday, clean dishes out of the rack before bed. Then say it once, in person, about the system rather than about them - 'the kitchen is getting on top of me, can we split it properly?' - and let whoever cannot do their week swap it rather than skip it. A cleaner for the bathroom every fortnight is about GBP 20 to 30 a head a month, and it is usually cheaper than the resentment.

Aim at the wake time, not the bedtime: get them up at the same time every day, weekends included, and open the curtains and put breakfast out straight away, because the body clock follows the morning light and the evening sorts itself out a week or two later. Take the phone and the charger out of the room, and let them stay up later rather than fight a 10pm battle a teenager's body cannot lose. If they are missing school most days for more than a couple of weeks, or sleeping through alarms and falling asleep in class, ring the school and ask the GP about their sleep - that is not laziness.

Aim at the work, not the person: "can we check the numbers before Friday?" rather than "that's wrong", then name the one thing you would change and stop. "No, that won't work" with nothing after it is what reads as defensive. It is worth asking once, without heat - "when I said that, what came across as defensive?" - because most managers will name a habit you can change, and a habit is easier to fix than a manner.

Aim for the six-yard box rather than the penalty spot: drive it inswinging and low with the inside of the foot, and send two players across the near post so the keeper has to decide. Practise one corner ten times - the ball you can repeat beats the clever one.

Aim for 15 to 25C by day: open the vents and the door at about 25C, and shut them again mid-afternoon so the heat is kept for the night, because a closed greenhouse is 5 to 10C warmer than the air outside. Tomatoes, cucumbers and peppers stop growing below about 12C and set no fruit below 15C, so a heater set to 10 to 12C keeps them alive rather than growing, and a max-min thermometer in the shade inside tells you what your own greenhouse is really doing.

Aim for about ten or fewer in a window, and treat more than about twenty as a sign the work has no shape rather than a memory emergency: each tab costs a few tens of megabytes, and it is worth closing them once the machine starts swapping to disk. Group what belongs together - tab groups or a second window per project - pin the two or three you use all day, and close everything you opened to read later into a bookmark folder or a read-later list. If you keep losing the same kind of page, that is the one to pin rather than to keep finding it again.

Air the room hard, wash the soft things (curtains, cushions, throws), and put bowls of white vinegar out overnight: the vinegar absorbs the smell and the room doesn't smell of vinegar by morning. Wipe hard surfaces; smoke clings to walls and furniture, not the air.

Air them before you wash them: hang them where a draught gets at them overnight, or in the bathroom while you shower, and a day's smell mostly goes.
