When you do wash them, turn them inside out, cold or 30, half the usual detergent and an extra rinse - the bacteria sit in the seams, and too much soap leaves a film that holds the smell. A cup of white vinegar in the rinse clears what is left, and skip the tumble dryer, which bakes it in.

Air thins and expands as it rises, so it holds less heat, and the ground gives its warmth up to the cold sky faster than thin air can hold it: the temperature drops about 6.5C for every kilometre you climb. The sunshine up high can still feel fierce while the air around you stays cold.

Air-fry potato chunks at 200C for 20 to 25 minutes, shaking the basket halfway: cut them to the same size, keep them in one layer and toss them in a little oil first. Parboiled ones take 12 to 15 minutes, and a whole jacket potato about 40 minutes at 190C.

Air-popped popcorn is a good snack: a big bowl is roughly 30 to 50 calories, it is whole grain, and the fibre and the chewing make it more filling than crisps. It is the butter, the salt and the toffee that turn it into a treat, so go easy on those rather than on the popcorn itself.

Air con loses a little gas every year, so if it is only cool, get it regassed: about £50 to £80 and best done by a garage. Run it for ten minutes a week all year to keep the seals from drying out. A musty smell means new cabin filter and an antibacterial clean.

Air it outside for a day first, then wash it if it can be washed - at the temperature on the label - with half the usual detergent and no softener, and dry it in the open air rather than on a radiator. Anything that cannot be washed - a wool coat, a blazer, a suit - goes in a steamy bathroom for twenty minutes, or in a bag with a saucer of bicarbonate of soda overnight, and then air. If it comes back after that, the smell is in what it is stored in, so wash the drawer or the wardrobe and let both dry out before the clothes go back.

Air it before you wash it: hang it outside, or in a room with a window open, for a day, because most of the smell sits on the surface and blows off. Then wash it at whatever the label allows - 30C for a washable coat, 40C for a jumper - with half the usual detergent and no softener. If it cannot be washed, hang it in a steamy bathroom for twenty minutes and air it again, or put it in a bag with a saucer of bicarbonate of soda overnight. Don't spray perfume on it; that makes smoke plus scent, and it clings harder.

'Kind regards' or 'Best wishes' are safe for almost anything work-related, and 'Thanks' works when you have asked for something. 'Yours sincerely' only when you started with Dear Mr or Ms, and 'Yours faithfully' when you started Dear Sir or Madam.

'I couldn't care less' is the one that means what it says - I care so little that I have no less to give. 'I could care less' says the opposite, though people use it that way anyway; in writing, use couldn't.
'Use by' is about safety: don't eat it after that date, and don't freeze it after it either. 'Best before' is about quality, so food is usually fine for a while after, using your eyes and nose.
Alan Rickman plays Severus Snape in all eight Harry Potter films (2001-2011).
Alcohol is poisonous to dogs and cats: even a small amount of beer or wine can make a small dog very ill. Keep glasses out of reach, and ring the vet with the pet's weight and how much it drank.

Alcohol is what takes a permanent marker off a hard surface: dab hand sanitiser, isopropyl alcohol or a little nail polish remover onto a cloth and wipe with the grain, changing the cloth as it lifts the ink, then wash the residue off with soapy water. On pale wood or laminate, try a soft eraser or a dab of toothpaste first, because alcohol can dull a varnished finish - test in a corner you will not see.

Alcohol leaves at about one unit an hour and nothing speeds that up - coffee, a cold shower and food only make you feel different, not soberer. A pint of normal-strength beer, a medium glass of wine or a single spirit is two to three units, so a heavy evening can still leave alcohol in your blood the next morning, which is why the morning-after drive is the one that catches people.
All right is the form to write: two words, as in "are you all right?" Alright is fine in a text or a line of dialogue and most people read it without noticing, so keep it for those.
All together means everyone in one place - we sang all together. Altogether means completely or in total - that's altogether different, ten pounds altogether.

Allow about 500g of turkey per person, a bit more if you want leftovers: 4kg feeds 8 comfortably, 5kg feeds 10. Check the label for the weight once it is stuffed, and buy the bird rather than a crown if you want the legs for a curry afterwards.
Allow about 75g of dry rice per person, or a mugful for two: it swells to two or three times its size, and leftover rice is better under- than over-estimated.

Allow 75 to 100g of dry pasta per person as a main, or 50g as a starter: a bunch of spaghetti as thick as a 10p coin is about 80g. Pasta roughly doubles in weight when cooked, so a 500g packet feeds four or five.
Allspice is warm and peppery, not hot - it tastes of cinnamon, clove and nutmeg at once, which is where the name comes from. A few berries in a stew or a cake, and no heat at all.

Almost always the top has grown wider than the base, so the bottom sits in its own shade and the light never gets to it: cut the sides back so they slope in towards the top, take the height down a little at the same time, and feed and water the base - that is what makes it shoot again. Privet, yew, beech and hornbeam come back from old wood; leylandii and most conifers do not, so on those you cut only into green growth and accept the bare patch. If the brown is patchy and spreading with no shape to it, check for box blight or a vine weevil in the soil before you feed anything.

Almost always it is not a virus but a pop-up advert: close the browser tab, clear the browser data and ignore any number it tells you to ring. If the phone really is behaving oddly, run the built-in scanner (Play Protect on Android) or a reputable free scanner once, then change the passwords you used on that device.

Almost always it's one specific thing, not a sacking: a project, a change, a bit of feedback. Before you go in, write the three things you've delivered lately and one question you want answered, and ask at the start what it's about; walking in with notes is what turns the panic into a normal conversation.

Almost anything, which is what an omnivore means: a pig eats 2 to 3 kg of feed a day, and roots for grubs, roots and fallen fruit with a nose built to dig. It cannot sweat, so it wallows to cool down. Kitchen scraps and any meat are illegal to feed to a pig in the UK, and that rule is what keeps swine fever out.

Almost anything, about 25 to 30g a day, plus water: grain, fruit, scraps, pet food, eggs, even soap and candles. That range is why rat baiting works with something they already like, and why the bin and the bird feeder are the two places they go first.

Almost anything, and mostly things we leave out: worms, beetles, slugs and grubs out of a lawn, small rodents, birds and their eggs, fruit and berries, and every kind of food waste - which is why a bin bag left out is the same meal, easier to reach. A cat is not on that list: an adult cat can look after itself and a fox backs off.

Almost every smart bulb only joins a 2.4GHz wifi network, so give the phone a 2.4GHz one while you set it up, and check the router has not got band steering hiding the two names. Then reset the bulb (usually five quick off-and-ons at the switch) until it flashes, and add it in its own app before anything else. A bulb that drops off every week is usually at the edge of the wifi.

Almost every airline carries a pushchair free, but it goes in the hold rather than the cabin: keep it until the aircraft door, where it is tagged and taken down the steps, and pick it up on the jetty or at the baggage belt at the other end. A car seat can fly with you if you bought it a seat, and a bag over the pushchair saves the fabric. Ask for the airline's own rule in writing if you are checking it in at the desk.

Almost everything is fine while you are breastfeeding, and there is no list of foods to avoid: cheese, sushi, runny eggs, spicy food and shellfish are all OK, and nothing you eat will upset your baby's stomach - the odd windy night is not the curry. The two that need care are alcohol, where you wait two to three hours after a drink before the next feed (or express first), and caffeine, which is about 200mg a day, roughly two mugs of instant. Eat and drink enough: you need about 500 extra calories a day, and a glass of water within reach of where you feed is the easiest way to get it.

Amelia Earhart (1897-1937) was the American pilot who flew the Atlantic alone in 1932 and vanished over the Pacific in 1937 trying to fly round the world. No wreck or body was ever confirmed, which is why the search for her plane goes on.
An omnivore eats both plants and animals: people, pigs, bears, crows and most gulls. That mix is why our teeth are partly sharp and partly flat, and why a varied diet suits us.

An open bag of frozen veg goes straight back in the freezer: press the air out, clip it, and use it within a month or two before it dries out or picks up ice. Re-freezing is the one with a rule: food that has fully thawed can be cooked and then frozen again, but not frozen raw a second time, because the thaw is when bacteria multiply and freezing does not kill them. Frozen peas that have half thawed in a warm kitchen are still peas - cook them now rather than put them back.

An open bottle keeps 3 to 5 days: stopper it and keep it in the fridge, reds too, and take a red out an hour before you drink it. A vacuum stopper or a squirt of inert gas buys another day or two, and after that the wine is still fine for cooking - wine that has turned vinegary is a good vinegar.

An opened tin of tuna keeps 2 days in the fridge, emptied into a bowl with a lid - left in the tin it tastes of metal. Eat it cold in a sandwich or flake it through a sauce, and do not freeze it, because it comes back dry and woolly.

An opened tin of coconut milk keeps 4 to 5 days in the fridge in a tub or a jug, and the thick cream separates to the top, so stir it back in. An unopened tin keeps a year in the cupboard. Freeze what is left in an ice-cube tray and drop the cubes into a curry.

An opened tin keeps 2 days in the fridge, and only once you have emptied it into a bowl or a lidded tub: leave food in the tin and the metal taints it and can make you ill. Cover it, keep it cold, and reheat it until it is piping hot. An unopened tin keeps for years in a cupboard, so trust the date stamped on it.

An opened box keeps 2 to 3 months in an airtight container and goes soft before it goes off, so taste rather than sniff it. The date on the box is for the sealed bag inside; stale cereal comes back crisp in a 150C oven for 5 minutes, spread out on a tray.

An ordinary full UK licence covers a van up to 3.5 tonnes, so a standard Transit or a short-wheelbase Luton is fine to hire. Anything heavier needs the C1 entitlement, which you get by passing a separate test; the hire firm will ask for your licence and a second proof of address.

An out-of-date blue inhaler is not dangerous, and it is not empty either: salbutamol keeps most of its strength well past the date on the canister, so if you are wheezy and it is the only one in the house, use it. Then order a replacement this week - the dose weakens with age and the propellant runs down. If it is a brown preventer past its date, replace that first, because it is the one doing the work every day. If you are reaching for the blue one more than three times a week, the thing to book is an asthma review rather than a new inhaler: a preventer that suits you should mean you hardly need it.

An oven clean by a professional is usually £50 to £90, and the hob and the extractor are often £15 to £30 extra each. It takes an hour or two and the difference is mostly how long since it was last done. Ask whether the price includes the shelves and the door glass, and whether they use a dip tank for the racks - the good ones do.

An oven door that is stiff or will not shut is nearly always the hinge: open it and look at the two arms at the bottom, because a bent arm or a hinge that has dropped makes the door rub on the frame. Check nothing inside has slipped forward first - a shelf or a tray stops the door a centimetre short - and wipe the burnt grease off the hinge area. If it still will not sit shut, hinges are a cheap part for most makes: take the model number off the sticker and order a pair.

An oven grill wants about five minutes preheating with the door shut, with the shelf 10cm or so below the element: the element should be glowing red across its whole length, and a drop of water flicked at the pan should sizzle. Food that browns in a minute and stays raw inside means the shelf is too high, not that the grill is too hot.

An over is six balls bowled by one bowler from one end, then someone else bowls from the other end. In a limited-overs game a bowler can bowl at most a fifth of the overs - 10 in a 50-over match, 4 in a T20.

An overactive thyroid is treated with carbimazole or propylthiouracil, sometimes with radioiodine or surgery, and the dose is set on blood tests every few weeks at first. Eat regularly rather than cutting back - it burns through energy, so weight loss is the thyroid, not the diet - and go back sooner if your heart races, your hands shake, or your eyes feel gritty or look different.

An overdraft is spending more than the current account holds. An arranged one is agreed with the bank and usually costs a set fee or a monthly rate; an unarranged one costs more and is reported to the credit file after a few weeks. Most banks now charge a flat monthly fee for an arranged overdraft, so ask for the fee per month, not the APR.

An overdraft is a loan from your bank that lets your balance go below zero. You agree a limit in advance and pay interest or a daily fee for the days you use it, so it is borrowed money rather than extra money, and it has to be paid back. Arranged means the limit was agreed with the bank and is the cheaper version; unarranged means you spent past it, which costs more, can bounce payments and is marked on your credit file. Some accounts give a small fee-free buffer, usually about £10 to £25, and the cheapest way to use one of these is to move money across at the start of the month and be back in credit before the deepest days.

An overnight soak does most of the work for you: warm water and a scoop of biological detergent, then wash it as normal in the morning. Keep wool, silk and anything with a dry-clean label out of it, keep brights away from whites, and do not leave a load more than a day or it starts to smell.

An oxymoron puts two words together that fight: deafening silence, living dead, bittersweet, a small crowd. It is a deliberate contradiction, and it is different from a plain contradiction because the clash is the point.

An underactive thyroid is treated with one levothyroxine tablet a day, on an empty stomach half an hour before breakfast, and the dose is set by a blood test six to eight weeks after you start and then once a year. Do not stop it because you feel better. Go back sooner if you get palpitations, lose weight without trying, or feel more tired on the same dose. A borderline result is usually retested before anyone treats it.

An unopened tub keeps about a week past the date on the lid, and once a spoon has been in it keep it 3 to 5 days - the date is for the sealed pot. Plain yoghurt that has separated with a little water on top is fine - stir it back in. Bin it if there is mould on the surface, or if it smells sour or fizzy rather than tangy.

An update is waiting and will keep asking until it is done: save your work, close what you are in and let it restart once, and give it twenty minutes without touching it. If it asks again the next day, the update is failing to install - free up disk space (updates need several gigabytes) and let it run with the charger plugged in.

An update is a new version of an app or of the phone's own system, and most of them close security holes rather than add features. Do them: on an iPhone it is Settings > General > Software Update, on Android Settings > Software update, and it is worth letting it happen overnight on wifi. The risk of skipping them is a known hole being used against you.

An LED is a sliver of material that gives out light when current flows through it, because electrons dropping across a gap release energy as photons. Almost none of the energy becomes heat, which is why a 9W LED matches an old 60W bulb, and white ones are blue LEDs with a yellow coating that mixes to white.

An MP's basic salary is £91,346 a year, set by the Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority rather than voted by MPs, and it goes up with public sector pay. Office costs, staff and travel are claimed separately against receipts and published, so the headline figure and the expenses are not the same pot. A minister or the prime minister gets extra on top for the job.

An RCD is the switch in the consumer unit that cuts the power when current leaks to earth - through a damaged cable, a wet socket, or a person - and it works in about 30 milliseconds, which is fast enough to save a life. It is different from the MCB, which protects the cable from overload, so a tripping RCD means something is leaking somewhere rather than using too much. Press the test button twice a year, and if it keeps tripping, unplug everything on that circuit, reset it, and add things back until it goes - a tripping RCD that will not reset is an electrician's visit.

An SSD has no moving parts, so the machine starts in seconds and apps open at once; a hard drive is a spinning disc and only wins on price for each gigabyte. For a laptop the SSD is the one upgrade that makes an old machine feel new - a 500GB one is cheap now and cloning the old disk across is a job a shop will do in an hour. Buy a big hard drive only for bulk storage and backups.

An SSD is storage with no moving parts, which is why a laptop with one starts in seconds and opens programs straight away. It is faster, quieter and more shock-proof than a spinning disk and dearer for the same size, which is why a desktop often has an SSD for the system and a big disk for the archive.

An abnormal result is usually a number a little outside the range, not a diagnosis: a slightly low vitamin D, or a liver figure up after a bug, is repeated in a few weeks and settles. Ask three things on the phone - which test it was, what your number was and what the normal range is - and then what the plan is. "They want to see you again" usually means a value worth a look rather than bad news, and you can ask for a copy of the result.

An abnormal smear means some cells looked a little different, not that you have cancer: the commonest results are borderline or mild changes and most clear up on their own. HPV found with normal cells usually means a repeat smear in a year; borderline or mild changes usually mean a colposcopy, a closer look at the cervix that takes about 15 minutes. Keep the appointment, and ask which of those results you have.

An adult needs roughly 2,000 to 2,500 calories a day, and the exact number depends on your size and how much you move: about 2,000 suits most women and 2,500 most men, with 1,500 to 1,800 for steady weight loss. Food labels count in kilocalories, so the "calories" on a packet are these numbers.

An adult passport is about £95 and a child's about £62, done on gov.uk, and about £12 more each if you post the paper form instead. Do it on gov.uk itself: the websites that charge £20 to fill the same form in for you are charging for a service the site gives away, and a Post Office check-and-send is about £16 on top for checking the photo. The fee goes up each April, and it usually takes about three weeks, longer in the summer.

An adult cat is fine on her own for a working day - food, water, a clean tray and somewhere warm to sleep - and most cope with a night too. Past 24 hours she needs someone to look in daily: cats get shut in cupboards and run out of water, and a weekend away is a visitor, not a big bowl. Crying at the door is usually boredom or a change in the house, so leave a window perch, somewhere to hide and a few minutes of play when you get in.

An adult cat is fine with a working day, and two cats are often happier than one because they keep each other company while you are out. A kitten is not: it wants feeding little and often and gets into trouble on its own. Leave a clean tray, water away from the food, a window to watch and something to climb, and ask a neighbour to look in on the longest days.
An adult has 206 bones; a baby is born with roughly 270, and many of those fuse together as you grow. The smallest are three tiny ones in each middle ear.

An advisory is not a fail, so you can keep driving while you sort it, but it is the garage telling you what will fail next year. Tyres, brakes and a leaking shock are worth doing in the next few weeks rather than at the last minute, and any garage will quote from the sheet.

An air source heat pump is usually £10,000 to £14,000 fitted, and the Boiler Upgrade Scheme takes £7,500 off, so most people pay £2,500 to £6,500. Running it costs less than gas for the same heat if the house is insulated and the radiators are big enough for the lower flow temperature, so a draughty house with small radiators eats the saving. Ask for two quotes, each with a heat loss survey of your own house, because that survey is what the price turns on.

An airbag is a cloth bag that a chemical charge fills with nitrogen in about a twentieth of a second: a sensor spots the sudden stop and fires it, then it deflates so you can get out. It only works with the belt, the strap that locks when a sprung weight catches on a ratchet.

An allergy is the immune system mistaking something harmless - pollen, pet dander, dust, a food - for a threat and releasing histamine, which causes the sneezing, itchy eyes or rash. Hay fever is that reaction to pollen; antihistamines block the histamine, and a pharmacist can advise on the best one for you.

An allergy is the immune system reacting to a food: it can come on within minutes and can be dangerous, with swelling or trouble breathing, so it means strict avoidance. An intolerance is the body struggling to digest something - uncomfortable, but not dangerous - and lactose is the common one.

An alloy is a metal mixed with another element to make it stronger or easier to work: steel is iron with carbon, brass is copper with zinc, and solder is tin with lead or silver. The mix is melted together rather than just glued, so it behaves as one metal.

An amphibian is a cold-blooded animal with moist skin that lives part of its life in water and part on land. Frogs, toads and newts hatch as tadpoles with gills, then change into adults with lungs, and their skin has to stay damp, which is why you find them near ponds and in wet grass.
An ancho is a dried poblano: mild, 1,000 to 2,000 Scoville, raisin-sweet and a little smoky. Two soaked in a sauce for four give colour and depth without heat.

An angiogram is a dye test that shows the arteries: a fine tube goes into the wrist or the groin under local anaesthetic, dye is injected, and X-rays follow it round. It takes 20 to 40 minutes and does not hurt beyond the sting of the numbing injection. You rest with pressure on the puncture for a few hours, go home the same day in most cases, and should keep the arm or leg easy for 24 hours - no lifting, no driving that day.

An ankle sprain wants ice for 20 minutes at a time for the first two days, a support wrap and the foot up when you sit, then gentle movement and a slow return to walking on it. Most settle in two to six weeks, and the swelling can take months. Get it looked at the same day if you cannot put any weight on it, it swells badly, or it looks crooked.

An ankle that keeps rolling or giving way has usually left the ligaments loose after an old sprain, and the fix is strength and balance work rather than a support: stand on one leg with your eyes shut for a minute a day, do heel raises, and a physio can set you a short programme. Get it looked at if it swells up after each turn, locks, or you cannot put weight on it now.

An annual pension statement has four numbers worth finding: the pot's value now, what you and your employer paid in during the year, the charges taken out, and the income the scheme projects at retirement. Check the charge line first, because 1% a year sounds small and takes a fifth of a pot over forty years, and a free Pension Wise appointment will walk through the rest with you if it still does not add up.
An ant carries 10 to 50 times its own body weight, and holds on with feet that grip smooth surfaces, which is why one can walk off with a whole crisp.

An antibody is a protein your immune system makes that sticks to one particular germ or chemical, marking it so the body can clear it, and it stays in the blood afterwards, which is why you usually do not get the same illness twice. That is also how a vaccine works: it shows you the shape first, so the antibodies are ready.

An appliance that trips the power is usually the appliance itself: unplug it, try it in a socket on another circuit, and if it trips again stop using it and get it repaired. Anything that takes the RCD out the moment it is plugged in has a fault to earth, so don't keep resetting the switch to check - that one needs an electrician.

An apprenticeship is a paid job with the training built into the week: most of the time you work, about a fifth of it you study, and there are no tuition fees. They run from GCSE level up to degree apprenticeships in engineering, digital, nursing and accountancy, so one can stand in place of a degree - you earn while you learn and finish with experience and no student debt, but with less choice of where you study. Pay is at least the apprentice minimum wage and more on most schemes.

An apprenticeship is a paid job with training and a qualification, usually one to four years. A traineeship is a short unpaid course - weeks, not years - for someone not yet ready for an apprenticeship, and it's often the step before one.

An aspidistra wants the opposite of fuss: a spot out of direct sun, water only when the compost is dry to the touch, and almost nothing in winter. Brown tips and splitting leaves are dry air or a wet pot rather than hunger, so let it drain and stand it somewhere less dry rather than feeding it.

An asteroid is a lump of rock and metal left over from the birth of the solar system, smaller than a planet and usually irregular in shape. Most circle the Sun in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter; one that enters Earth's atmosphere and burns up is a meteor, and one that lands is a meteorite.

An aubergine keeps about a week in the fridge drawer, in a paper bag or loose, and only 2 to 3 days once it is cut, wrapped on the cut face. It is a warm-weather fruit and the fridge will mark the skin, so a week is the limit rather than a target. One that has gone soft, dull and spongy has dried out: use it in a curry or a dip rather than a bake, and bin one with a brown, wet patch.

An ear that smells, hurts or makes him shake his head is usually an infection or ear mites, and a vet needs to look down it with an otoscope and give drops that match the cause - the wrong drops can burst an eardrum. Don't push cotton buds down it or use old drops from last time, and hold off the bath until it is clear. A head tilt, a swollen ear flap or an ear that is painful to touch wants to be seen the same day.

An ear that aches and feels blocked after swimming is usually swimmer's ear: water sits in the canal and the skin gets sore and infected. Keep it dry for a few days, use painkillers, and let a pharmacist look at it - drops help, but only the right ones, and not if you have ever had a perforated eardrum. See a GP if there is discharge, fever or real pain.

An ear infection usually settles in three to seven days without antibiotics. Give paracetamol or ibuprofen for the pain, and see a GP if there is discharge from the ear, if it is no better after three days, or the same day if there is swelling, redness or tenderness behind the ear.

An easy run or a light session is fine if you feel like it - keep it short, drink water before and after, and eat something first. Skip anything hard: alcohol leaves you dehydrated with a higher resting heart rate, so your usual pace feels twice as hard, and don't take ibuprofen before you run on a hangover.

An eco wash is the long one, three and a half to four hours, because it heats the water slowly and soaks rather than blasts; the standard programme is about two hours and the quick one 30 to 60 minutes. Use eco for a full load and the quick wash for a light one, and skip the pre-rinse if you are running it the same day.

An egg a day is fine for most people: the cholesterol in food moves blood cholesterol far less than saturated fat does, which is the butter you cook it in. An egg gives cheap protein, vitamin D and B12. Two a day is still reasonable for a healthy adult; if you have heart disease or diabetes, ask your GP what suits you.

An egg is one of the cheapest good foods there is: about 78 calories and 6g of protein, with the B12 and vitamin D that people buy supplements for. The cholesterol in food turned out to matter far less than the saturated fat in the diet, so one or two a day is fine for most people. What makes an omelette heavy is the butter and the cheese, not the eggs.

An electrician is usually £40 to £70 an hour, with a call-out of £50 to £100 that often covers the first hour. A new socket or a light fitting is a one-hour job; a fuse board or any work in a bathroom or kitchen needs a certificate, which adds £50 to £150. Ask for the certificate in the quote, because a landlord or a buyer will want it.

An electron is the tiny negative particle that orbits the nucleus of an atom, and it is the one that moves when electricity flows. Its arrangement decides how an atom joins others, which is the whole of chemistry in one sentence.

An element under the water gets hot and the water round it rises, so a current stirs the kettle and it heats from the bottom up. A strip of two metals that bend as they warm cuts the power when steam reaches it, which is why a kettle switches itself off and why limescale round that strip makes one boil on.
An elephant's trunk has no bones at all and around 40,000 muscles, which is why it can pick up a single peanut or lift a tree. Elephants greet by touching trunks.
An emperor penguin can hold its breath for around 20 minutes and dive past 500 metres; most dives are one to five minutes and less than 100 metres.

An empire is one state ruling other peoples and places beyond its own borders, usually taken by force and governed from the centre; a kingdom is one country under a king or queen. Empires rarely last more than a few hundred years, because the parts stop needing the centre.

An empty aerosol can go in the kerbside recycling with the tins in most areas - check the council's list, and don't pierce or crush it. One that still has something in it is not rubbish: it goes to the tip, and a spray paint or a solvent goes to the hazardous waste.

An endoscopy is a thin camera on a tube passed down your throat to look at the food pipe, the stomach and the top of the bowel, and it takes 10 to 20 minutes. Your throat is numbed with a spray and you are usually offered sedation, so the gagging is the worst of it rather than pain; you go home the same day, but not driving if you took the sedation. A sore throat and a bit of wind for a day are normal, and you will be asked not to eat for about six hours before.

An engine that uses a litre every 1,000 miles or so is within what most makers call normal, and many use more than people expect. Beyond that it is worn valve seals or piston rings, or a leak that only shows when it is hot: park over cardboard overnight and look for drips, and check the coolant for an oily film and the exhaust for blue smoke on start-up. Keep it topped up and get it looked at; running it low is what turns a cheap fix into a new engine.

An episiotomy is a cut a midwife or doctor makes at the opening of the vagina during birth, under local anaesthetic, to make room for the baby when it is needed quickly or the tissue is about to tear badly. It is not routine - most births do not need one - and a natural tear is usually preferred where there is time. The cut is stitched, the stitches dissolve, and it is sore for a week or two: keep it clean and dry, change pads often, and take the painkillers you would take for a headache. Ring the maternity unit if the pain gets worse rather than better, if it smells, or if you cannot pass urine.

An equation says two things are equal, and the equals sign is the point: 3x + 4 = 19 is an equation. An expression such as 3x + 4 has no equals sign, so it can be simplified but not solved. Solving an equation means finding the number that makes both sides balance.

An equinox is the day the sun sits over the equator, so day and night are about twelve hours each everywhere: around 20 March and 22 September, which is when spring starts on one half of the planet and autumn on the other.

An escrow account is a holding account run by a third party - usually a solicitor or a specialist escrow firm - that keeps money until the thing it is paying for is done. On a house purchase the deposit sits there between exchange and completion, and on a building job the payment sits there until the stage is signed off, so neither side can walk off with it. Ask who holds it, whose name is on the account, what exactly triggers the release and what happens if the two sides disagree, because money held in a client account at a bank is protected and money in the firm's own name may not be.

An evening of non-stop feeding is cluster feeding, and it is normal in the first weeks: it is not a sign your milk is short, it is how the supply is built. Keep them on, swap sides, and get someone else to take them for an hour once they settle so you can sleep. A baby who is having six or more wet nappies a day and gaining along their line is getting enough - the scales at the clinic settle it better than the length of a feed.

An eviction always needs proper notice and a court order, so do not leave before a court order whatever the letter says. Check the notice is in writing and in the right form: a section 21 needs at least two months and cannot be served in the first four months of a tenancy, and a section 8 has to name the ground and the date. Shelter (0808 800 4444) is free and will check what you have been served; the council's tenancy team and Citizens Advice will too. If you have also fallen behind on the rent, tell them that as well, because it changes what you can ask for.

An excess is the first part of any claim you pay yourself: if the repair is £900 and your excess is £250, the insurer pays £650. Every policy has a compulsory excess and you can usually add a voluntary one on top in return for a lower premium. It applies to each claim rather than each year, so two separate claims mean paying it twice; the schedule says the amount and whether it comes off the payout or goes to the repairer.

An exothermic reaction gives out heat as it happens, so the mixture gets warmer: burning, rusting and the reaction in a hand warmer are all exothermic. The opposite, one that takes heat in and feels cold, is endothermic.

An extra hour or two is usually the good call after a short night. Let the sleep happen, then open the curtains and get some daylight. Keep the rest of the day on the usual times and go to bed at the usual hour tonight: a long lie-in shifts the body clock and makes the next night harder. If the tiredness is there most mornings for weeks, that is worth a GP and a blood test.

An eye test is usually £25 to £45 on the high street, and free on the NHS if you qualify - over 60, diabetic, glaucoma in the family, or on certain benefits. A retina photo or a scan is often offered as an extra £10 to £25. Ask what the test includes and whether the prescription is yours to take away.

An eye test is about 20 to 30 minutes, and longer if you are choosing glasses afterwards. Say at the start if you drive or use a screen all day, because the test and the prescription are read with that in mind.

An hour to three hours, until the numbness has gone - after that you can eat, though keep to soft, cool food for the rest of the day. Chewing a hot or hard meal while you are still numb is how people bite their cheek or burn their mouth.

An hour and a half to two hours takes a phone, tablet or laptop from nearly flat to full, and half an hour on a fast charger gets you about half way. Overnight is fine - a modern one stops charging at 100% - but heat is what ages a battery, so take it out of a thick case and off the radiator.

An immersion is nearly always 3kW, and a full 120-litre tank takes about an hour and a half to two hours from cold; 30 to 40 minutes is enough for a couple of showers. Colder water in winter and a scaled element both make it slower, and turning the thermostat higher does not make it heat any faster - it only makes the water hotter. Leaving it on all night is what the timer is for.

An indoor cat lives about 12 to 15 years, and many reach 18 or more. A cat that goes outside averages a few years less, mostly because of roads, so a cat flap with a curfew or a secure garden is what buys the extra years.

An induction hob makes the pan the heater: a coil under the glass sends a fast-changing magnetic field into the base, which sets up currents in the metal and heats it directly, so the glass around it stays cool enough to touch. It is quicker and more controllable than gas, and the pan must be magnetic - if a magnet sticks to its base, it will work.

An ingrown toenail is a nail edge pressing into the skin at the side: soak the foot in warm salty water for 10 to 15 minutes twice a day, cut the nail straight across rather than down the corners, and wear shoes with room in the toe - and don't cut a V in the middle, which does nothing. See a GP or podiatrist if it is badly painful, if the skin is red, hot or weeping pus, or if you have diabetes or poor circulation: they can take a wedge of nail away, and that is the fix that lasts.

An inkjet squirts tiny drops of ink onto the page from a head that sweeps across it; a laser draws the page with static charge on a drum, dusts it with powder and fuses the powder on with heat. The inkjet dries out if it sits unused, and the laser's powder does not, which is the trade most people are choosing between.

An insect is a small animal with a hard outer skeleton and three body parts - head, thorax and abdomen - with six legs and usually two pairs of wings. Beetles, bees, ants and butterflies are insects; a spider is not, because it has eight legs and two body parts.

An insulator is a material that does not let heat or electricity pass through it easily because its electrons are not free to move. Plastic and rubber insulate electrical wires, and trapped air in foam, wool or double glazing slows heat loss; that is why a woolly jumper keeps you warm and a plastic handle lets you hold a hot pan.

An integer is a whole number - positive, negative or zero - with no fraction or decimal part. So 4, -7 and 0 are integers, while 2.5 and 1/3 are not; the integers are the counting numbers, their negatives, and zero.

An invertebrate is an animal with no backbone: insects, spiders, worms, snails, crabs, jellyfish and squid are all invertebrates. They are most of the animal species on Earth, and many have a hard shell or exoskeleton instead of bones.

An invoice needs seven things: your name and address, the client's name and address, a number of its own (0001, 0002 - never reused), the date, what you did with the dates you did it, the amount with the payment terms on it, and your bank details. Add your VAT number once you are registered, and put the terms in words - "payment due within 14 days of the invoice date" - plus what happens if it is late. Keep the same number series for ever and send it the day the work finishes, not at the end of the month: an invoice sent a fortnight late is paid a fortnight late. A PDF named with the number and the client is enough; a template in a word processor is all most people need.

An invoice is the bill you send after you have done the work: it asks for a set amount by a set date and is your record of the sale. Put your name and address, theirs, your business name and company number or 'sole trader', a number of its own, the date, what you did with quantity and rate, the total, VAT only if you are registered, the payment terms such as 'due in 14 days', and the bank details. A receipt is the other way round - proof of payment after the money arrives - and a quote comes before the work.

An ion is an atom or molecule that has lost or gained electrons, which leaves it with an electrical charge. Table salt is sodium ions and chloride ions held together by that charge, and the ions in seawater are what make it conduct electricity. Your nerves and muscles work by shuffling ions in and out through their membranes.

An itchy ear canal is usually dry skin or a touch of eczema, sometimes a little water or wax left behind. Leave cotton buds, keys and hairgrips out of it: they scratch the skin and pack wax against the drum, which is what keeps the itch going. A few drops of olive oil, or an ear spray from a pharmacist, settles most of it. See a pharmacist or GP if there is discharge, pain, a drop in hearing, or it has been weeks.
And what has actually been said or done so far?

Anger in a child is usually the top of something else - hunger, tiredness, screens off too fast, or a day with no say in it - so name the feeling for them, stay calm yourself, and give the same short limit every time; a child who is shouting needs you quieter, not louder. Pick the moment later, when everyone is calm, to talk about what set it off and what they could do instead, and give them something physical to do with it (run, kick a ball, punch a cushion). Ask the school or the GP for help if it is most days, if someone is getting hurt, or if it has got worse over a few weeks rather than better.

Anger is mostly a physical build-up, so catch it early rather than arguing with it: notice the first sign - jaw, shoulders, a louder voice - and leave the room for five minutes, breathing out for longer than you breathe in. Say "I need a minute" rather than the thing you are about to say. Then look at the fuel: too little sleep, no lunch, four coffees and a hangover will do more to your temper than any argument. If the fuse has been short for weeks rather than days, see a GP: anxiety, depression and a thyroid problem all arrive as irritability, and talking therapy works on anger.
Annoying. Is it every time, or only now and then?

Answer once, in advance, rather than each time it happens: "I'm off tomorrow. I'll pick up anything non-urgent on Thursday morning, and if something cannot wait, call me on this number." Then do not answer the ordinary messages - a reply on a day off teaches people that the day off is available. If it is every week, ask your manager what the on-call arrangement is; unpaid standby is a rota question, not a favour.

Answer the question the report exists for in the first two lines, then the evidence: what you did, what it showed, what you want to happen next. Short sections with headings, one number or example per claim, and a line at the end saying what you need from the reader. Anybody who reads only the first paragraph should still know the answer.

Answer the question in your first sentence, plainly, and let the rest of the essay back it up: "Prisons in the 1800s did more to hide poverty than to fix it." No "In this essay I will discuss" and no dictionary definition — a marker wants to see your answer straight away.

Answer the question in it and leave the tone alone: reply to the work, in two lines, with the dates and the facts, and no apology you do not owe - "Thanks - the report went out on the 4th, so we're clear. Anything else you need from me?" Written politeness beats matching the tone, and a flat reply gives them nothing to quote back. If there is a pattern, keep the emails and say the thing out loud once, in person: "Your last two notes read as though I dropped the ball - was that meant?"

Answer the feeling first and the evidence second: 'That sounds horrible, and I don't think that's true.' Then point at something specific you have seen them do, and praise the effort rather than the result - 'you kept going when that was hard'. If they say it most days for more than a couple of weeks, or stop wanting to go in, tell the teacher and ask what they see; a dip at eight is usually about one lesson or one friend.

Answer a message that asks a question or makes a plan the same day; leave a chatty one as long as you like. What matters is the rhythm: replying in minutes for a week and then disappearing for two days reads as a mood, so keep it steady rather than fast. Waiting three days to seem busy fools nobody and loses the thread.

Answer it once, properly, and then give the same short answer every time: 'I'll tell you if there's news, and I'm not talking about it before then.' Say it warmly and without a reason, because reasons are what they will argue with. Then change the subject to them: a question about their week takes the sting out of it.
Anthony Albanese is the prime minister of Australia: in office since May 2022 and re-elected in May 2025. The head of state is King Charles III, represented there by a governor-general.

Antibiotics do nothing for a cold or flu: those are viruses and antibiotics only kill bacteria. What actually helps is rest, plenty of fluids, and paracetamol or ibuprofen for the aches, plus honey in warm water for a cough; see someone if a fever lasts more than a few days or you are breathless.

Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them growing, usually by attacking something bacterial cells have and ours do not, such as their cell walls. They do nothing for colds and flu, which are viruses, and using them when they are not needed helps resistant bacteria spread.

Anxiety that is worst in the first hour is usually the body waking up rather than a verdict on your day: cortisol peaks about 30 minutes after you get up, and short sleep, low blood sugar and alcohol the night before all push it higher. Eat something within an hour of waking, get outside in daylight before you look at your phone, and leave the coffee until after food; if it is most mornings for a month, or comes with a racing heart or breathlessness, have a GP look at it.

Anxiety is the background feeling - worry and tension over days and weeks; a panic attack is a short, sudden surge that peaks within minutes, with a racing heart, breathlessness and a feeling that something awful is about to happen. You can have either without the other, and both are treatable.

Any shop can print or email another copy, because it can find the sale from the date, the time on the till roll and the last four digits of your card, so ask at the till and say roughly when you paid. If it cannot, a card or bank statement showing the payment is proof of purchase for a return, and a photo of the paper slip in your phone covers most warranties and expenses. Ask for a VAT receipt when you pay if you need to reclaim the VAT, since an ordinary till receipt often has no VAT number on it.

Any temperature in a baby under three months is a same-day call: ring 111 or your GP today rather than waiting to see how it goes, because at that age they are checked over rather than watched. Keep them feeding and in light clothes while you wait. A baby who is floppy, not feeding, hard to wake or has a rash needs 999.
Any time.

Any yolk, grease or water stops them whipping: use a clean dry bowl, separate the eggs while they're cold, then let the whites come to room temperature. A pinch of salt or a drop of lemon helps, and so does beating on a medium speed rather than flat out.

Any bleeding after the menopause needs to be looked at, and the GP will refer you within two weeks for a scan of the womb lining - that is the routine for every woman with it, not a sign that anything is wrong. The usual causes are a dry, thin lining, a polyp or hormone tablets, and most turn out to be harmless. Ring and say the words 'bleeding after the menopause' so you get the right appointment, and go the same day if it is heavy or you feel unwell.

Anyone 18 or over can vote in a general election if they are a British, Irish or qualifying Commonwealth citizen on the electoral register - members of the Lords cannot vote, and EU citizens can vote in local elections only. The register is at gov.uk/register-to-vote, and you have to be on it about 12 working days before polling day.

Anything wholly and necessarily for the work: stock and materials, tools, software and subscriptions, insurance, bank fees, the business share of your phone and broadband, travel between jobs (not the commute), and a share of the heating if you work at home. Keep the receipt and note what it was for. Mileage is 45p a mile for the first 10,000 miles and 25p after that, instead of the running costs. You cannot claim your own wages, a suit you also wear out, or the commute - and if you use simplified expenses for the home you cannot also claim the bills.

Anything with a hazard symbol on it is household chemicals, and the tip's hazardous waste skip is where it goes - most sites take it from householders, and a few councils run set days, so ring before you drive over. Keep it in its own labelled container, never mix two together, and never pour it down the drain or into the bin. A gas bottle goes back to the shop that sells them.

Anything bought online, by phone or by post can be cancelled within 14 days of it arriving, then sent back within 14 days, with the refund due 14 days after that. Bespoke items, perishables and opened hygiene products are the usual exceptions.
Anything comfortable and warm: cinemas run cold, so a jumper and soft trousers or jeans, and shoes you can slip off if you like to curl up.

Anything it can win: fish and shellfish, worms and insects off a ploughed field, other birds' eggs and chicks, chips, and whatever the bin has. A herring gull will drop a shell on a car park to break it, which is the same trick, not a taste for cars.
Anyway means in any case - anyway, I went home. Any way means any method - is there any way to fix it. If you can put 'in any case' there, it's one word.
Apart means separated - we live apart, take it apart. A part means one piece of something - a part of the team, a part of the problem. If you can drop the 'a', it's apart.

Appeal in writing inside the deadline they gave you - often five to seven working days. Keep it to three things: the dates and reason for the lateness (a bus that stopped running, a nursery drop-off), the reason a warning is out of proportion (no prior conversation, everyone else late), and what you will do (a later start agreed in writing, or an alarm and a check-in). Ask a union rep or HR for the policy before you send it. A warning is often quietly dropped when the appeal is calm and factual.

Appealing goes to the DVSA rather than the garage: ask them for the appeal form (VT17) within 14 days of the test, and it costs nothing. Do not have the repairs done before you decide, because an appeal is only worth it while the car is as it was tested - if the fault is real and the argument is only about how serious it is, the cheaper route is to ask the test centre to explain the sheet and then have the work done and the partial retest, which is free within 10 working days.

Appetite usually goes with something rather than on its own: a bug or an infection that has not quite cleared, stress or low mood, or a new medicine - some kill appetite and the leaflet will say so. Meanwhile eat by the clock rather than by hunger: something small every two or three hours, whatever you fancy, with a glass of milk or a yoghurt in between, because you will eat more in small amounts than at one plate. See a GP if it lasts more than a fortnight, if you are losing weight without trying, or if you are also low, sleeping badly or thirsty all the time.

Apples keep for weeks in the fridge, far longer than on the counter, and away from other fruit, because the gas they give off ripens everything beside them. A bruised one is fine: cut the bruise out and use it first.

Apply on the country's own government site, never a paid lookalike, and apply early: an ESTA for the USA is valid two years and should be done at least 72 hours before you fly, while a visa for most countries is a few weeks, so start six to eight weeks out. Check the entry rules for your own passport and any country you change planes in, and keep the approval on your phone and printed.

Apply straight to the college, not through your school: every college has an online form on its own site, and for a September start the deadline is usually the spring before, with places filling from January. You apply before your GCSE results, the offer is conditional on the grades, and you confirm it on results day - so apply to two colleges if you are not sure, and ring admissions the week results come out if anything goes wrong.

Apply to them like jobs, because that is what they are: the vacancies are on the government Find an Apprenticeship service (gov.uk in England, apprenticeships.scot in Scotland, careerswales in Wales, nidirect in Northern Ireland), and big employers also advertise on their own sites with closing dates in the autumn and winter before a September start, so apply months early and to several. They come at four levels: GCSE-level, A-level, higher (the first two years of a degree) and degree, and the degree ones are competitive and want A-levels or a good BTEC. You need English and maths at GCSE for most of them, and if you missed those the employer usually puts you through them alongside the job. Pay is at least the apprentice minimum wage and rises with each year, so check the travel before you accept: a low wage plus a long commute is the thing people regret.

Apply to your council, not the NHS: the qualifying benefits are the higher rate of the mobility part of DLA, or 8 points or more on the moving around part of PIP, plus a few conditions such as being registered blind. You upload a photo, proof of address and the benefit letter, the council may book an assessment, the fee is up to £10 and a badge lasts up to three years and takes about six to eight weeks.

Apply to Student Finance England (or the equivalent in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland) by the end of May before the course starts, and it does not matter whether you have a confirmed place yet. The tuition fee loan goes straight to the university; the maintenance loan is paid into your account in three instalments, and the amount follows your household income, not your grades. You can reapply every year, and you only start repaying the April after you leave, once you earn over the threshold.

Argue your market rate, not someone else's pay: write down what you deliver with numbers, check two adverts for the same title and area, then ask for a meeting about your pay and name a figure. Do not lead with what a colleague earns - it puts them in the room instead of you, and in some contracts you are not meant to know. If the answer is no, ask what would have to be true for a yes and when to come back.

Argue about one decision at a time and not in front of them: pick the thing that comes up most - bedtime, screens, homework - and agree one rule you can both keep, badly if need be. Where you still differ, agree the fallback out loud so the child hears one answer: 'after eight it's the parent who is here.' Take the row somewhere else, after they are asleep, and keep the other person's side of it out of the telling-off.

Argue about two numbers rather than the principle: what has to go out each month for bills, and how much each of you can spend without asking the other. Write both down once, look at them on the same day each month for twenty minutes, and let the rest be each of yours to spend badly - most rows about money are about the pot nobody was given, not about the bills. Bring one thing to the conversation and leave the last ten years out of it.

Around 400mg of caffeine a day is the usual safe limit for an adult, which is about eleven cans of cola at 35mg a can; pregnant women are advised to keep to 200mg. Stop by early afternoon if your sleep is affected, and cut down slowly over a week or two, since going cold turkey can bring headaches and irritability.

Arrange it as ax² + bx + c = 0, then put the numbers into x = (-b ± √(b² - 4ac)) / 2a. If b² - 4ac is positive there are two answers, zero means one answer, and negative means none without imaginary numbers. Try factorising first when the numbers are small: x² + 5x + 6 is (x + 2)(x + 3), so x is -2 or -3.

Arranged overdrafts are charged per day now, so the deepest days cost the most: move a fixed amount onto it every payday and keep spending within what's left. Ask your bank for a repayment plan if the balance is large, and think about a basic account with no overdraft if it keeps happening.

Arrive 45 minutes early the first time: queues at the turnstiles and bag searches are what make people miss kick-off. Take the card you booked with, check whether your stand is seated or standing, and expect to be close to strangers and loud for two hours — that is the point. At half time, either go for food in the first five minutes or wait until the second half starts.

Arrive early, when it is easier to join a small group, and ask people about the thing you are both already at: how they know the host, what they thought of the food. Have three open questions ready and let the other person do most of the talking.

As a rough guide, a one-bedroom flat is about £1,300 to £1,900 a month in outer London and £1,900 to £2,800 in inner London, with a room in a shared house around £700 to £1,100. It swings a lot by borough and by how close you are to a Tube line, so check live listings for the postcode rather than the city average - the ONS Price Index of Private Rents publishes the current figures by borough, and Rightmove or Zoopla will show what is actually available today. Budget a month's rent plus five weeks as a deposit, and check the deposit is protected.

As a sole trader you do not legally need one, and you should still open one: a separate account means every payment in is income and every payment out is a cost, which is most of a tax return done already. Mixing the two is the reason people spend a weekend with a shoebox. Free business banking for 12 to 18 months is normal at the moment, so compare two or three before you pick, and check the monthly fee afterwards and the cost of paying cash in. A second personal account works if no bank will take you yet. A limited company does have to have its own account.
Asafoetida is not hot, but it is ferociously strong - a pinch in hot oil, no more, and it smells of onions and garlic once it has cooked. A quarter teaspoon for a pot for four.

Ask months ahead and bring the plan with you: how long, from when, who covers your work, and how you keep your hand in while you are away. Read the contract and handbook first - some employers hold the job for a set period, and some let you buy extra leave instead. Ask in writing, propose a review date for the return, and get the answer in writing too.

Ask once, plainly, and then leave the door open: "You have not seemed yourself for a couple of weeks - is something going on?" Side by side (in the car, on a walk) is easier than face to face, and a shrug the first time is normal, so ask again another day. Keep the answer small and specific - a walk, one friend round, a lie-in - and do not turn it into a lecture about screen time. If it lasts more than two weeks, or they stop eating, stop sleeping or say they are hurting themselves, ring the GP and ask about CAMHS: that is the route to real help, and asking does not put the idea there.

Ask once, plainly and without accusation: 'I haven't heard from you in a while — are you okay?' Then give it time. People go quiet for their own reasons, and one warm message beats three worried ones.

Ask once, plainly and without an audience: 'I'm sorting my budget this month, when can you pay me back?' A message can be easier than a face-to-face. If money is tight, offer a plan such as a date or a small monthly amount; saying it out loud usually ends the awkwardness, not the friendship.

Ask once, warmly, with a figure and a reason: "I'm delighted about the offer. Given the range for the role and my five years doing X, could we look at 32,000?" Name a specific number, not a range, and ask for the final version in writing. Employers expect the question and very rarely withdraw an offer over one ask.

Ask once, with the thing, the time and what you want, and then leave it: "the bins need to go out before eight - can that be yours?" One reminder the same day is fair; a running commentary is what makes it nagging, and the more it is repeated the less any of it is heard. Then look at what is underneath: if you ask for the same thing every week, the fault is in the agreement rather than in their memory, so make it a rule instead - "you do the bins, I do the laundry" - so nothing has to be chased. Say the things that got done out loud, too, because a house where only the misses are mentioned feels like an audit for both of you.

Ask once, in private, at a calm time, and make it about the thing and not the person: "The telly carries through the wall after eleven - could you turn it down a notch?" Give when it happens, how it lands and what would fix it. Do not knock at midnight while it is loud - the ask that lands is the one made in daylight, and the first ask should sound like a favour between neighbours, because it is.

Ask once, in your own words, and make it about them rather than a list of charges: 'You seem a bit off with me - have I done something?' Then leave room for the answer. If they say nothing is wrong, take it at face value and carry on as normal; most of the time it is their week and not you, and a second and third 'are you okay?' is what makes it awkward.

Ask one person you trust rather than the whole group: 'I felt a bit out of the loop about Saturday, was it a last-minute thing?' Most exclusion is carelessness, not a message, and asking gives them a chance to put it right.

Ask other parents at the school gate first: a sitter vouched for by someone you know beats any app. Then do one evening while you are still in the house, paying them to play while you get on with something, so the first real night out isn't the first time. Leave a written sheet: bedtimes, allergies, the wifi code, your number and a neighbour's.

Ask payroll or HR: digital payslips are usually in the HR or payroll portal, and a paper one is the stub or a PDF they can email. An employer has to keep the record, so they can give you a copy of any month you are missing, and a former employer's HR can usually reissue one. HMRC does not hold payslips, but your personal tax account shows the pay and tax each employer reported.

Ask the module leader or tutor before the deadline, in writing, with the date you need - and ask what the evidence rule is at your place, because it is a form with a name: mitigating circumstances, extenuating circumstances or special circumstances. Send the form and the evidence (a GP note, a letter, a hospital appointment) in one email, and keep a copy. The standard extension is a week or two for a short illness; longer or repeated problems go to the mitigating circumstances panel rather than to your tutor. Ask early: most universities will not accept a claim made after the deadline has passed, and asking costs nothing.

Ask the person who can say yes, not the till: "is there anything you can do on the price?" Have a number and somewhere cheaper to point at, and ask about ex-display or last season's colour. At a market or on a big ticket offer about 10 per cent under, ready to walk away; a shop that cannot move can often throw in delivery instead.

Ask the person who can do your shift first, offer the trade rather than the favour ("I'll take your Saturday if you take my Tuesday"), then get it agreed in writing with whoever writes the rota - a swap the manager has not seen is the one you get blamed for. You must still get 11 hours between shifts, so a night cannot be swapped into a day starting at seven. If a manager refuses, ask which rule it breaks.

Ask the practice or hospital for its complaints procedure and put it in writing: what happened, when, who you saw and what you want. Ask for a written reply and keep copies. Still unhappy? Ask for a deadlock letter and take it free to the NHS ombudsman - PALS at a hospital will help you word it, and private dental work has the free Dental Complaints Service. If someone was harmed, get the records and advice from AvMA before signing anything.

Ask the room something it already knows the answer to, or name the one detail everyone there has seen - "hands up who has been handed a handbag and told to hold it" - then wait a beat before your name. Keep it under ten seconds and make the joke about you rather than anyone in the room, and if nothing comes, open with the strangest real detail of the story instead of a joke.

Ask the school office in advance and put it in writing: a note or an email naming the day, the time and who is collecting is enough for an appointment, and the office logs it as authorised absence. A pupil who leaves on their own should tell their form tutor and the teacher whose lesson they will miss, so nobody marks them absent, and take the work with them. Ring the office the same morning only for something you could not plan, and read the attendance policy before anything that is not medical - an appointment, a funeral and a religious day are authorised, a family trip in term time usually is not, and repeated unauthorised absence is what leads to a fine.

Ask the seller first, in writing, and say what went wrong and what you want - most refunds are done there and it is the step both the card and the bank will ask about. If they will not, go to your card issuer and use the word chargeback: card rules give you 120 days from the transaction, or from when the goods should have arrived, and the issuer reverses the payment while it investigates. A direct debit is faster still - the bank must refund an unauthorised one straight away and a wrong amount the same day - and a payment sent to the wrong account is the bank's recall, which works best in the first hours. Keep every message.

Ask the shop first, in writing, and keep it short: what you bought, when, what went wrong and what you want back. If they will not play, ring your card provider and say you want a chargeback: a debit or credit card payment can be reversed when the goods never arrived, arrived wrong or the seller will not refund, usually up to 120 days from the payment. Anything over £100 on a credit card is stronger than that, because Section 75 makes the card company jointly liable for the whole purchase.

Ask the teacher or the dance school first: for a show they usually name a supplier, sell the costume themselves or keep a rail of spares, and buying the wrong shade of leotard wastes the money. If it is yours to sort, hiring costs less than buying for one night, fancy-dress shops and second-hand marketplaces have plenty a week before, and a plain base layer with two bought accessories reads perfectly well from the audience.

Ask the carrier to bar third-party charges as well as stopping it in the app store: a subscription billed through the phone goes on the bill until the carrier blocks premium-rate and third-party charges, and that block is free and takes one call. Then cancel with the company too, because the carrier only stops the charge reaching your bill and the subscription itself keeps running.

Ask the council's adult social care team for a carer's assessment. It is free, it is about your needs and not theirs, and you can ask without telling them. It takes about an hour, at home or on the phone, and it can bring respite hours, a direct payment you spend yourself, training and a number to ring in the worst moments. Say "I would like a carer's assessment" and get what they agree in writing.

Ask the couple what colours the wedding party is in, then pick something in that family but quieter: navy, sage, burgundy or grey all work, and the one thing to leave alone is white, ivory or cream, which belong to the bride. Comfortable shoes, a dress you can sit and eat in, and something with sleeves if the day runs late. If the couple have a colour scheme or a dress code on the invitation, follow it and let them see the outfit first.

Ask the host what the dress code is, then dress for the kind of party: jeans and a nice top for a house party, something dressier for a bar or a big birthday. Wear the shoes you can stand in for four hours, and a layer that survives a warm room.

Ask the host if there is anything they need, then bring something they can use that night: a bottle of something they drink, a soft drink if you are not sure, or a pudding or cheese for the table. For a housewarming, a plant or a nice tea towel lasts longer than another candle. For a birthday, ask the person or a close friend what they are into, and bring something small and specific rather than another candle.

Ask the lender why in writing: it's nearly always the credit file, the deposit size or the affordability sum. Fix errors on your report, save a bigger deposit and use a whole-of-market broker; don't send several applications at once, because each one leaves a mark for a few months.

Ask the lender before you miss a payment, not after: ring or write, say what has changed and what you can afford, and ask for a payment holiday, a switch to interest-only for a while, or a longer term - mortgage lenders have to offer one of those. Get their agreement in writing. Interest usually keeps building during the break and is added to the balance, and a holiday can be marked on your credit file, so ask what it costs first; for a card or a loan, a payment plan is often cheaper than a holiday.

Ask them to show you how the figure was worked out, in writing, and give a meter reading: an estimate built on last year's use is the usual reason, and the reading fixes it the same day. You never have to accept a figure you cannot afford - ask for a payment plan or to pay for what you use - and if the amount was wrong or taken early the Direct Debit Guarantee makes your bank refund it.

Ask them, on a calm day, what helps when one starts - most people know, and being asked is worth more than being managed. What helps most between attacks is not avoiding the places they happen: the list of avoided things grows, and the fear with it. Panic disorder is treatable, so it is worth a GP conversation: CBT has the best evidence, and an SSRI helps some people alongside it. If the attacks are getting more frequent, or they start avoiding work, shops or travel, say so to the GP rather than waiting. And if one ever comes with chest pain, or it is their first, get it checked rather than assuming panic.

Ask three or four people who have just passed and book a single lesson with the one they liked most - a good instructor is the thing that makes lessons worth the money, and one lesson tells you more than any advert. Look for someone approved by the DVSA (an ADI badge on the windscreen), a quiet manner, and a lesson plan rather than being driven round for two hours. Prices are usually £30 to £45 an hour, and if you are not getting on, change early: it is normal, and a good instructor will not mind.

Ask to go on the waiting list and to be rung if a table frees up, and ask about eating at the bar, which most places allow when the room is full. Ring back at about five in the afternoon: that is when the day's cancellations are known and the tables are released. If it is a birthday or an anniversary, say so - it gets you further than arguing does.

Ask twice in writing, then copy one person above, and make it dated: that is what gets a reply. Send the question again as one email with a single ask and a deadline: "I need the rota signed off by Thursday - can you do it, or tell me what is blocking it?" If nothing comes back in three working days, forward that email to your boss's manager or to HR with one line: "I have asked twice and I need this by Friday, can you help?" Keep a short note of what you sent and when, because a list of dates is what gets acted on if it has to go further.

Ask two people who have managed you - or one manager and one senior colleague - and ask before you hand their name over. Send them the job description and one line about what you want them to stress. A manager from years ago is fine; a friend is not. If nobody has managed you yet, a teacher, a coach or the person who ran the volunteering is the usual choice.

Ask two things before you take a side: why now - smaller, cheaper, the stairs, or to pay for care - and what date they are working to, because those decide everything else. If any of the money is coming your way, get it written down what it is: a gift, a loan or an advance on what you would inherit, and who agreed it. And do the dull paperwork while everyone is well - the will, and who can act on the accounts - before the boxes are packed. The furniture is what starts the rows, so ask early who wants what.

Ask what playtime actually looks like before you fix anything - who they stood with, what they did - because 'no friends' often means one friendship broke, not that there is nobody. Then set up one short playdate at home, ask the teacher to pair them with someone at break, and give them two opening lines to try. If they are still eating lunch alone after a few weeks, tell the school: they can arrange a group without it looking like help.

Ask what the next level looks like in writing, then start doing one part of it now - promotion usually follows evidence, not a request. Bring a one-page case: what you delivered, what you already do that the role needs, and who you have trained. Ask at a planned review, not straight after a good day.

Ask what the plan is rather than giving a verdict: the rent, the deposit, the commute and who else is on the tenancy. Offer the help you can actually give - a guarantor, the first month, a van and a Saturday - and say plainly, once, what you cannot. Let them make the mistake if they are going to make it; a grown child told no digs in. If you think it is really about being unhappy at home, ask that straight and be ready to hear it.

Ask what the range is and when the pay is next reviewed, and get that date in writing. If the pot really is empty, ask for what is not salary — a better title, a training budget, a day a week at home, or a named figure at a review in six months — and look around meanwhile, because a freeze at one firm is rarely a freeze across the market.

Ask what is actually wrong with the job first - the boss, the hours or the work itself - because each one wants a different answer. Then do the money on paper together: what the drop in pay is, how many months you could both cover, and what they would do next. Say your worry once, plainly, and let the decision be theirs; being the one who listened counts for more than being right.

Ask when you book what people wear there: smart casual (smart trousers or dark jeans and a collared shirt or a nice top) covers nearly every restaurant. Shorts and flip-flops are only right somewhere on the seafront.

Ask whoever organised it whether it's drinks in a bar or a sit-down dinner, then go smart casual one notch up: dark trousers or jeans with a nice top, which works whether people dress up or not. Comfortable shoes, because these nights are long.

Ask whoever invited you, or look at photos of the team on the company site. For an interview, go one notch smarter than the job: a shirt and trousers, or a plain dress or blouse, and nothing loud. Clean shoes and a jacket cover most of the doubt.

Ask with a plan, not a preference: which days, how you'll be reachable, what you'll measure, and a three-month trial. Put it in writing after the conversation, and point to the policy or to a colleague already doing it, because the answer is usually easier than people expect.

Ask your network for the unlock code and it is free once your minimum term is up - Ofcom requires them to do it, so nobody should be charging you. Find the request form or the chat in your account (some networks do it in the app) and it usually lands within a couple of days; then put another network's SIM in and follow the on-screen prompt. On an iPhone, Settings - General - About showing Carrier Lock: No SIM restrictions means it is done.

Ask your old network for a PAC code by texting PAC to 65075: it is free, they must send it within a minute, and it lasts 30 days. Give the PAC to the new network when you order the SIM and the switch happens the next working day, usually with only a few hours without service. Do not cancel the old contract first or the number can go with it - the PAC cancels it for you.

Ask your own manager first, before the other team hears it from someone else: "I'm interested in the data team and I'd like to be considered if something opens." Give a reason that is about the work, not about them. Then speak to the other manager, and ask what a handover would look like so your current team is not left short - a transfer people think is tidy is the one that actually happens.

Ask your water company to check the reading and the tariff, and for a free meter if there are more bedrooms than people: that is usually cheaper, and you can switch back within a year. A typical household bill is around £450 a year, about £38 a month, set by your region unless you are on a meter, and on a meter showers instead of baths, full loads and a fixed dripping tap cut the most.

Ask your bank to block gambling payments today, install GamStop to exclude yourself from every UK site for five years, and ring GamCare on 0808 8020 133 — free, 24 hours, they will talk it through without judging. One day at a time, and tell one person who can hold the money with you.

Ask your bank for a chargeback: it reverses a card payment for goods that never came, arrived damaged or were not what was described. Most banks take claims up to 120 days from the payment, and it's the route for debit cards under £100.

Ask your dentist to refer you to an orthodontist and whether it qualifies for NHS treatment: the bite decides that (IOTN), not money, and it is free up to 18 in England and Wales. Privately it is 2,000 to 5,000 pounds, and people wear them 18 months to two years, then a retainer at night or the teeth drift back. New braces ache for three or four days: soft food, paracetamol, and wax on any wire that rubs.
