Ask HMRC for a review first: within 30 days of the decision letter, write to the address on it saying you disagree and why, and include the figures, dates and any evidence - HMRC must look at it again and answer it in writing. If the review goes against you, appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Tax) within 30 days of that answer: it is free, independent of HMRC, and most appeals are settled on the papers or by phone. Ask for the decision to be paused while you appeal so it is not collected in the meantime.

Ask HR in writing which pension scheme you are in and how to join it: if you are 22 or over and earn more than 10,000 pounds a year, the duty to enrol you is theirs, and a flat no is worth challenging rather than accepting. If there really is no scheme, open a personal pension or a SIPP yourself and pay in what you can - the government adds 20% to what a basic-rate taxpayer puts in, and the years already on your national insurance record still count towards the state pension.

Ask - 'could you box up what's left?' is normal, and most places say yes, though here it is their choice rather than your right. Get it into the fridge within two hours and eat it within a day or two, reheating it once until it is piping hot.

Ask about something concrete rather than 'how are you': the thing you are both at, a project you are both near, or what they are doing at the weekend. Keep it light, let them choose how much work to bring up, and have one follow-up question ready so the answer is not a dead end.

Ask about the answer you just got instead of starting a new subject - "how did that go?" or "what was the best bit?" - because a conversation usually dies from answering and moving on, not from having nothing to say. Give a little of yourself so it is not an interview, and when the talk stalls offer something to look at or do: the weather lasts a line, a photo, a menu or a dog lasts ten minutes.

Ask about their day in small pieces rather than 'how are you': what they had for breakfast, who they sat with, what is on the noticeboard. Take in one bit of news from outside - the weather, a grandchild, the garden - and do something side by side instead of talking face to face: a hand of cards, a photo album, the crossword. Ten honest minutes beats an hour of performing, and you can say the kind thing you would say if they were well.

Ask at the till before you pay, because almost no retailer matches a price after the sale. Have the competitor's page open on your phone with the exact model, the price and the date, and check the small print first: most promises exclude marketplace and third-party sellers, sale and clearance prices, membership prices, vouchers and mis-priced listings. Some chains match online prices only against their own website, and a few knock off the difference rather than the whole amount. If the assistant says no, ask for the manager and ask which rule you missed - a written promise on the wall is worth quoting.

Ask at the desk the same day, and name what you want: another room, a clean, or money off the night. Photograph the room before anyone touches it, and put the complaint in an email that evening so there is a date on it and a name on the reply. If the hotel cannot fix it, the booking site or your card is the lever - say the room was not as described and ask for a partial or full refund, then a chargeback if they refuse. The hotel's own complaints address and its country's trade body come after that, not before.

Ask before they go who is taking over your work, and get it in one sentence: "While this is covered by Y, approvals go to Y." Then introduce yourself to that person with a short list of what you own and what is due. If nobody is named, ask HR in writing who your line manager is now - it is an ordinary question, and the answer is what you point at when a review goes wrong.

Ask early, in writing, with the dates and the day you are back: "Could I take 2-9 June, back at work on the 10th?" Offer the handover before they ask for it. Requests usually fail because they arrive in the busy week, not because the time itself is refused.

Ask for one named job, on a named day, in writing: "can you take Mum to the clinic on the 14th?" is a question with a yes or no in it, while "I need more help" can always be answered with "I'm busy". Have the list of what the week actually holds in front of you both - appointments, tablets, shopping, the night she rang three times - because the sibling who does little usually believes they do their share. Then split by whole areas so one of you owns the money and the other owns the hospital, rather than both hovering. If they still will not, ask the council's carers service what you are entitled to on your own, and tell them what you have taken on and that you are at your limit: a sibling who will not help is not something you can fix, but the load on you can be.

Ask for one thing that stretches you rather than waiting to be taught: a piece of the reporting, a supplier call, the job nobody has written down - and say you want to learn it, not just do it. Then ask your manager what the next skill for your role is and who could show you, and put a review date on it. If six months pass with no new work and no answer, the job has stopped teaching you, and that is a reason to look rather than a fault in you.

Ask for ten minutes at a calm time, then say it in one sentence with one example: "when you cancelled on Friday it felt like I didn't matter" lands, while "you always cancel" starts a fight. Say what you want to change rather than what they did wrong, let them answer once without interrupting, and finish by agreeing what happens next time.

Ask for the one thing, with a day on it: 'can I have the grey jumper back before Friday, I want it for the weekend' - one item and one date lands, and 'you always take my stuff' does not. Then agree the rule you can both live with: a drawer or a shelf that is fair game and everything else asked for first, and keep the pieces you care about out of the shared hallway. If it keeps happening, say no once and mean it - 'that one's not up for lending' is a complete sentence, and it does more than a second row about the same jumper.

Ask for the range in one short email before the interview - "Could you tell me the salary range for this role?" - and it costs you nothing: recruiters expect it, and a job that will not give a band is telling you something about how it hires. If you would rather not ask first, leave it to the end of the first interview, when they have met you. Have your own number ready, from what you need to live on and what the same role pays elsewhere.

Ask for the reason and what would make it a yes: "What would need to change for this to be a yes?" Then ask when you can come back with that, and put that date in the calendar. If the no has no reason at all, ask who else can agree it, or when it is worth asking again - and get the answer in writing if it will matter later.

Ask for the refusal in writing with the policy clause they're relying on, then complain formally and quote the wording back. After 8 weeks, or a final response, the free Financial Ombudsman Service can review it, and its decision binds the insurer.

Ask for the slot to be a standing one rather than a one-off: "Can we hold Thursday at 10 for our one-to-one, and if it has to move, let me know the day before?" Then put your two or three points in writing before each one, so a fifteen-minute meeting still covers them, and keep the list on the same email thread. If it keeps getting bumped, reply to the last cancellation with what you were going to raise and ask for it in writing instead - a boss who will not sit down for long will usually answer an email.

Ask for the bill in writing with the dates and amounts, and send your proof of payment — bank statement, reference number — in writing too: a dispute is settled on paperwork, not on the phone. Keep paying what you agree you owe meanwhile, and if it is energy or water, complain to the company first and then to the free ombudsman.

Ask for the formal help first: a dyslexia assessment at university goes through the disability service, and it unlocks extra time in exams, a reader or text-to-speech software, and often a grant for equipment - at school it is the SENCO, and it costs you nothing to ask. For the reading itself, use text-to-speech so the page reads to you while you follow with a finger, take the chapter in 20-minute blocks with the summary read first, and ask for the reading list in advance so you are never reading against a deadline. Being slow at decoding is not being slow at thinking, and the extra time is the standard fix, not a favour.

Ask for the increase in writing, with the date it starts and the reason: a home cannot put the price up whenever it likes. If the council pays part of it, any top-up has to be agreed by you in writing and is voluntary, so ask the council to arrange your care at its own rate instead. Complain to the home first and then the council's adult social care team, and ask about a deferred payment agreement so the house is not sold in a hurry.

Ask for the increase in writing and check the notice: in England and Wales a rent rise needs a section 13 notice with at least one month's notice and cannot normally happen more than once a year, and Scotland has its own rules on rent increases in a tenancy. Then check it against what similar flats nearby are asking, because you can accept it, negotiate it or challenge it at a tribunal if it is above market rent - and start paying the new amount only once the notice is correct, keeping the old letters.

Ask for the interesting work by name rather than waiting to be noticed: "I'd like a go at the reporting - could I take one piece of it next month?" Pick a small piece so a yes is easy, and say what you would drop to fit it in. Then ask for the dull jobs to be shared out rather than defaulting to you, and agree a date to look at it again in three months. If nothing changes by then, the job really is only the boring half, and that is worth knowing before you decide to stay.

Ask for the itemised bill while you are still at the table, not the card slip, and point at the line: 'sorry, we didn't order the garlic bread' is enough and they will reprint it. A service charge you were not told about comes off the same way, because it is discretionary rather than law. If you have already paid, a short email to the manager with the date and the receipt gets it refunded, and a card payment can be disputed if they refuse.

Ask for the itemised bill, or the listing for a holiday let, and dispute the line in writing the same day: a charge has to be something you actually had or agreed to, and they have to show the signed docket or the term you accepted. If it came off the card you gave at check-in, that is a wrong amount your bank can charge back, and somewhere that ignores you is a complaint to the site you booked with.

Ask for the mark scheme, not for a favour: "could I see which part of question 3 lost the marks?" That is a normal request, and a good teacher will show you. Then ask for one example of what a full-mark answer looked like and rewrite that paragraph with it in front of you. If the marks still look wrong against the published scheme, ask the school for a remark in writing rather than arguing in the corridor.

Ask for three written quotes, a public liability insurance certificate and two phone numbers for recent jobs. Never pay cash up front: a small deposit on a card is fine, because a card payment over £100 gives you a claim against the card company too. A quote that names a start date, a price and what is included is the thing that keeps the job straight.

Ask for a private twenty minutes and say it plainly in the first sentence: "I'm not coping with the current load and I want to sort it out before it shows in the work." Then bring two or three specifics - the tasks, the hours, what has slipped - and two things you want changed, because a manager can act on a proposal and rarely on a feeling. Ask what support exists: an employee assistance line, occupational health, flexible hours or a temporary reallocation. Put a short summary in an email afterwards so there is a record, and if nothing changes, that email is what you take to HR.

Ask for a proper one-to-one and name one thing that could be fixed, not the whole job: "the mornings are relentless since Jo left - can we look at the rota" gets an answer, while "I'm unhappy" asks your manager to guess. Take one example and one request, write down what they agree to, and give it a month. If nothing moves, that is your answer about whether to stay.

Ask for a short private meeting and say the thing in your first sentence: "I want to raise something before it gets bigger." Then give one concrete example: what happened, when, and what it cost you or the work - and what you want changed, because a fix is easier to agree to than a complaint. Follow it up in writing ("to sum up what we agreed...") and keep that copy. If it is about how you have been treated, ask HR for the grievance procedure in writing: it has fixed steps and time limits, and they have to follow it.

Ask for a specific example first: "Can you give me a case where that happened?" Then say thank you and write it down without defending - you can disagree later, once you have checked it. Come back a day later with what you will change; that reply is the bit people remember.

Ask for a time rather than for distance: 'an hour after work to myself' or 'Saturday morning on my own' is a request someone can say yes to, where 'I need space' sounds like the start of leaving. Say it is about what you need, not what they did, give the time you will be back, and keep it small enough to happen this week.

Ask for a weekly fifteen-minute check-in and a written definition of done for each piece of work, then say why: "If we agree what finished looks like on Monday, I can run with it and bring you the result on Thursday." Bring one recent example of the checking and the cost of it ("we rebuilt the same slide twice"), not a verdict on them. If it carries on, ask what would have to be true for them to trust the work without checking.

Ask for a bassinet seat at booking if they are under two: it is free on most airlines and gives you a bed and floor space. Feed or offer a dummy at take-off and landing for the ears, pack twice the nappies you think you need, and take a change of clothes for yourself as well as for them.

Ask for a bigger rope in the language of their worry: "Give me the report for two weeks and I'll send you the summary on Friday. If it is wrong, we go back to daily checks." Name one thing you will deliver and one date, then deliver it - hovering usually comes from a manager who was caught out before, and evidence retires it faster than a complaint. If nothing changes, say what it costs: "The checking is taking an hour a day. What would make you comfortable with less?"

Ask for a mandatory reconsideration within one month of the decision letter: ring the number on it, then put the request in writing and ask for the statement of reasons and the evidence used. Add a letter from your GP, employer or landlord if it helps. If it is still wrong, appeal to the tribunal within one month of the reconsideration notice - it is free, and you can ask for a phone hearing.

Ask for feedback in one short email - you want to know what would have made you the stronger candidate - and then send the interviewer five lines: one thing you would add to your answer, and why you still want the job. Do not apologise twice. Most people who get an offer chased one thing they got wrong; a bad hour with a panel is not a verdict on you.

Ask for fifteen minutes and bring the list: "I have these five things due; I can do three properly this week - which matter most?" That hands your boss a decision instead of a complaint, and it makes the trade-off visible. Send a short email afterwards confirming what you agreed, so it is on record.

Ask for fifteen minutes in private and put the decision in the first line, then one reason: "I have decided to move on; my last day would be the 14th." Do not apologise more than once, and do not be drawn into a debate about the money on the day - "I have thought about it a lot" is a complete answer. Then agree what to tell the team and when, and send the same thing in writing so the date is on record.

Ask for it back: a credit balance is your money, and a supplier has to refund it when you ask if the account is closed or after a price change, so ring or email with a final reading and your bank details, and keep the closing bill. If you are still with them, ask for the direct debit to come down instead, because a big credit means you have been paying more than the year needs.

Ask how long they've owned it and why they're selling, whether it's ever been in an accident, what the mileage is, when the cambelt or chain was last done, and whether the service history and V5 are both in their name. Ask to see it at their home rather than a car park: it tells you how the car has been kept, and it's where a private seller's story tends to come apart.

Ask in one short sentence when you sit down or when you order - 'could we have a highchair?', 'no onion in the pasta please', 'a table away from the door if you have one' - and it needs no explanation or apology beyond please and thanks; staff would far rather be asked than find you unhappy later. Kitchens do 'on the side' and smaller portions all the time and neither costs anything, so ask for 'a starter portion of the main' when the menu sells the dish both ways. Tap water is free and comes without a fuss, and the answer to almost all of it is to ask early, because 'we have already started cooking it' is the only real no.

Ask in one short email framed as a business case: the course, the cost, the dates, and the one thing at work it fixes - the report nobody can run, the system only you know. Say what you will bring back and offer to show the team afterwards. If the budget is fixed, ask for half of it, or for the study time instead, and ask again at the next budget round rather than dropping it.

Ask in the store, not the app: on an iPhone use reportaproblem.apple.com within 90 days, and on Android open Play Store > Payments and subscriptions > Budget and order history > Report a problem, within 48 hours. Say plainly that it was a mistake or did not work, and do not spend the money again in the meantime; children's purchases are refunded most readily when you say it was a child.

Ask in writing, with the case in numbers: what you got done from home, how you stay reachable, and the one day a week you would come in for the parts that need a room. Most managers say yes to a trial far more easily than to a permanent change, so ask for three months and a review date, and offer to keep the desk hot for the team days.

Ask in writing, by email, with the dates you want and why: a short line about the weeks you would like off and what you will have finished before you go beats a case about fairness. Before you send it, check the staff handbook for a buy-more-holiday scheme - many employers let you trade up to five days out of salary once a year - and ask what the notice period is. If the answer is no now, ask what would make it a yes next year and get that in writing, or offer to take the days unpaid.

Ask in writing and name what you want: a refund, a repair, or money for the trouble. Once eight weeks pass, or they send a final response you disagree with, take it to the ombudsman for that industry - Financial for a bank or insurer, Energy for a supplier, Communications for broadband and phones, and the Local Government Ombudsman for a council - which is free and needs no lawyer. Keep the date of every call and letter: the timeline is the case.

Ask in writing and name what you want: a refund, a repair, or money for the trouble. Once eight weeks pass, or they send a final response you disagree with, take it to the ombudsman for that industry - Financial for a bank or insurer, Energy for a supplier, Communications for broadband and phones - which is free and needs no lawyer. Keep the date of every call and letter: the timeline is the case.

Ask in writing and make it easy: a short message naming the address, the dates you rented and asking whether they will confirm that rent was paid on time. Landlords usually just verify dates, rent and that the property was left in good order, so you can offer your bank statements or a rent statement alongside it. If they say no or go quiet, an employer or a previous letting agent will do, and a guarantor covers the gap.

Ask in writing for an itemised list of what was taken and why, and say which of the deductions you disagree with. If your deposit was in a protection scheme, use its free dispute service rather than arguing with the landlord; you can also raise it with the council. Photos from the day you moved in are the evidence that wins this.

Ask in writing for an itemised list of what was taken and why, and say which deductions you disagree with. Fair wear and tear - a carpet going thin where you walk, a worktop faded by sunlight - is not chargeable; a burn or a paint mark is. If the deposit went into a protection scheme, use its free dispute service rather than arguing with the agent, and keep the photos from the day you moved in.

Aspirin and ibuprofen set off an attack in the minority of people with asthma who react to them, and nobody knows which they are until it happens. If you have taken them before with no trouble, they are usually fine; if you have ever wheezed after one, or your asthma is bad at the moment, paracetamol is the one to use.

Assume there is something round the next bend - a tractor, a horse or a walker - so drive at a speed you could stop from within what you can see, which on a hedge-lined lane is often 30mph or less. On a single-track road use the passing places: pull in on your left to let oncoming traffic through, and do not park in one. Give horses a wide berth and pass them slowly, watch for mud and slurry on the surface after a tractor, and dip your headlights for oncoming cars at night rather than lighting up the bend.

Asthma is inflamed, twitchy airways: they narrow with a wheeze, a tight chest and a cough that is worse at night, in cold air or on exercise. The preventer inhaler - usually brown, a small dose of steroid - is the one that matters, and it has to be taken every day even when you feel fine; the blue reliever is for symptoms and needing it more than twice a week means the preventer is not right, so book a review with the asthma nurse. Use a spacer with both, take the flu jab, and ask for a written action plan. Ring 999 for an attack where talking in sentences is hard, the reliever is not helping, or the lips look blue.

Astro trainers or moulded boots, shin pads, shorts and a top you do not mind sweating in, plus water. Most places play on 3G astro, so no studs, and a lot of leagues ask for the same colour top for the whole team - ask the organiser before you buy anything. A size 4 ball is the usual one for five a side, and someone always brings one.

At the top of the stairs use a screw-fixed gate, never a pressure-fit one: a pressure gate grips between two surfaces and a determined toddler can push it out of the opening, and the top of the stairs is the one place that matters. A pressure gate is fine in a doorway or at the bottom of the stairs, where it needs no drilling, but check it by hand every week or so as the pads work loose. Measure the opening at its widest and buy a gate whose stated range covers it, and add a banister or newel-post adaptor, or an extension, when one side is a post rather than a flat wall. Look for a gate to BS EN 1930, at least 73cm high, with a door that swings away from the stairs, and no bottom bar across a step because it is a trip.

At 11 to 15 it is a child account in their name with you as the adult on it, and a debit card with no overdraft: every high street bank has one free, while the paid apps charge a few pounds a month for the same thing. At 16 they can open their own account with a full debit card, and at 18 it becomes an adult account, so check it is not one that quietly adds an overdraft. Set a standing order for pocket money on the same day each month, and let them see the balance rather than asking you for it.

At about 5mm of ice, switch it off at the wall and move the food into a cool box: budget two to three hours, or overnight with bowls of hot water inside and the door shut. Most freezers need this once or twice a year. Never chip at the ice, because a knife can pierce a pipe and write the freezer off, and a frost-free one never needs it at all, so ice in one means the door seal has gone.

At least 24 hours' notice in writing and a reasonable time of day, and you can say no to a time that does not suit and offer another - the tenancy agreement can promise more than that but not less, so a clause letting them walk in whenever they like does not stand. An emergency is the exception: a leak, a fire risk or no heating can be seen to without asking, and they have to tell you afterwards. If they let themselves in or turn up unannounced, put it in writing once that you want 24 hours' notice, keep a note of every visit with the date and time, and if it carries on ring the council's tenancy relations officer - they deal with harassment by landlords - or Shelter on 0808 800 4444, which is free. A landlord who keeps a key is not breaking the law, but using it without notice is; do not change the locks without checking your agreement first, because that can be a breach even when they are the ones at fault.

At least 30 hours a week of paid work, and an apprentice under 18 cannot be asked to do more than 40 hours a week or more than 8 hours a day. Everyone still counts the 28 days' paid holiday a year, bank holidays on top if the contract says so, and the off-the-job training - about a fifth of the hours - happens inside your paid time rather than after it. Overtime is allowed if you are over 18 and it is in the contract, and the 48-hour average week limit applies as it does to any job.

Attendance Allowance is for someone over State Pension age who needs help with personal care because of an illness or a disability: about £74 a week if the help is needed in the day or at night, about £110 if it is both (2025-26; the rates move every April). It is not means-tested, so savings and income do not count, it is tax-free, and nobody has to be paid to help you yet. Claim on form AA1 - phone the DWP and they will fill it in with you - and it also unlocks Pension Credit for some people.

Auto-brightness is the usual cause: in Settings > Display it tracks the light in the room, so the screen dims when you step out of the sun. Low power mode is the next thing to rule out: below 20 per cent battery the phone caps the brightness until you charge it. Heat does it too: a phone left in the sun or charging under a pillow dims the screen to cool itself, and it comes back once it is off the charger in a cool place. If it dims while you are holding it and the battery is fine, take the screen protector off and check for a schedule that turns the brightness down at night.

Auto-enrolment is the law that puts you into your employer's pension without you asking: it covers everyone from 22 to state pension age earning more than 10,000 pounds a year, and the minimum is 8% of your pay in total, at least 3% of it from the employer and the rest from you with tax relief on top. You can leave within the first month and get your own money back, and any time after that you can stop paying in and keep the pot - but leaving gives up the employer's 3%, which is a pay cut to get your own money back sooner.

Autumn is when the male house spiders wander about looking for a mate, and a warm room is where the insects are. British house spiders are harmless: a glass and a piece of card is the kindest way to move one out. The cobwebs up in the ceiling corners are worth leaving, since they catch flies and midges.

Avocado is a good food that is easy to overdo: half a medium one is about 150 calories and 15g of fat, nearly all of it monounsaturated, which is the kind that helps cholesterol rather than harming it. It also brings about 5g of fibre and more potassium than a banana per 100g. Half a day is a sensible portion; a whole one on toast is a meal, not a spread.

BBC stands for British Broadcasting Corporation, and the letters it does not have are the interesting part: no advertising, because it is paid for by the licence fee, and a charter that keeps it at arm's length from the government.

BMI stands for body mass index: weight in kilos divided by height in metres squared, with 18.5 to 24.9 called healthy for most adults. It is a rough measure - it cannot tell muscle from fat, so it reads high on a rugby player and low on some older people, which is why waist size is worth knowing too.

BMI is weight in kilos divided by height in metres squared, and 18.5 to 24.9 is the range the NHS calls healthy. It is a crude tool: it cannot tell muscle from fat and it reads badly for very tall, very short or very muscular people, so waist measurement and how you feel matter alongside it. Use it as a rough flag, not a diagnosis, and if you want a real assessment ask the GP or a pharmacist.

BTW stands for by the way, and in a message it does real work: it flags a change of subject that does not need an answer. Anything that does need one is better off without it, since a line starting by the way reads as an aside.

Back pain with numbness around the groin or between the legs, or losing control of your bladder or bowels, needs looking at the same day: ring 111 or go to A&E, and don't wait for it to settle. The sooner it is seen the better it works out.

Back pain in later pregnancy is common: a bump pulls the pelvis forward and the ligaments soften. A support belt, a pillow between your knees at night, sitting with your hips higher than your knees and a pregnancy-safe physio class all help, and paracetamol is the painkiller that is considered safe. Ring your midwife the same day for pain under the ribs, a headache with flashing lights, swelling in the face or hands, or reduced movement.

Back pain is very common in the second half of pregnancy: the weight sits out in front, and the hormone that loosens your ligaments for the birth loosens them everywhere. Paracetamol is the painkiller to use; steer clear of ibuprofen and the other anti-inflammatories unless your midwife or doctor has said they are fine for you. A maternity support belt, flat shoes, a warm bath and sleeping on your side with a pillow between your knees all take the strain off, and your midwife can refer you to a physiotherapist who deals with exactly this. Ring your midwife or maternity unit the same day if the pain comes with bleeding, any waters, a bad headache, blurred vision or swelling in your hands and face, a temperature, stinging when you pass urine, or the baby moving less than usual.

Back the files up first, then tell the two noises apart: a grinding or scraping that follows the fan's speed is the fan bearing, and a fan is £20 to £40 fitted. A regular click or a tick followed by a pause is the hard drive going, which is urgent - copy the files off now and stop using it, because those drives go from clicking to dead with no warning.

Back up first, because a factory reset erases everything: photos, messages, and any account you have not signed out of. On Windows it is Settings > System > Recovery > Reset this PC; on an iPhone, sign out of your Apple ID first or the phone will lock; on Android, Settings > System > Reset. Then sign back in and restore from the backup.

Back it up now, before it gets worse - a screen that blinks black is usually the display connector working loose or a battery that cannot hold its voltage, and both get worse rather than better. Then rule out the cheap causes: take the case off (a case pressing on the sleep button dims it), let it run flat and charge it to full once, and check for a software update. If it only does it in one app, that app is the fault. If it does it in calls and near your ear, it is the proximity sensor, which is normal. A phone that still blinks after a restart wants a repair shop.

Bacon keeps about a week in the fridge once the pack is open, sealed in a bag, and 3 months in the freezer, rashers separated with paper so you can take one at a time. It goes slimy and smells sharp when it is off; the cure keeps it pink long after that.

Badminton is won with the feet: after every shot get back to the middle of the court, and split-step as your opponent hits so you can move either way. Learn the overhead clear hit high and deep to the back line, then the drop shot from the same action, so your opponent cannot read it. Twenty minutes of shadow footwork with a racket in your hand beats an hour of hitting.

Bake salmon fillets at 200C (180C fan) for 12 to 15 minutes, until the flesh just flakes. In a hot pan, 4 minutes skin side down and 1 minute the other way is enough; salmon dries out fast when it's overcooked.

Bake something that is low in sugar by nature rather than swapping in sweeteners: an almond and olive oil cake, a carrot cake made with less sugar and more spice, or berries with cream and a little dark chocolate. Keep the portion small and have it after a meal rather than on its own, and put the fruit and the cream on the plate so the cake slice can be thinner.

Bake a lasagne at 190C (170C fan) for 35 to 40 minutes, until it bubbles at the edges. Made ahead, cover it and keep it in the fridge. Cook it from cold with foil over the top for the first 25 minutes, and give it 15 minutes extra so the middle is hot.

Bake it blind: chill the lined tin for 20 minutes, prick the base, cover it with paper and baking beans, then 15 minutes at 200C (180C fan) and 5 minutes uncovered to dry the base out. Brush the hot base with beaten egg so the filling cannot soak in, and cook a wet filling down first - a quiche or a fruit pie goes soggy from the inside too.

Balance it with salt and acid rather than more of anything sweet: a pinch of salt, a squeeze of lemon or a spoon of vinegar, and a little more of whatever the dish is built on - flour, cream, yoghurt, tinned tomatoes. For a cake that is already baked, serve it with unsweetened cream or fruit, and cut the sugar by a quarter next time: most recipes take it.

Bananas ripen fastest in a paper bag on the counter, especially with an apple; the fridge slows them right down but turns the skin black. Black-spotted skin is a sweet banana, and overripe ones are perfect for banana bread.
Bananas are about 15p to 25p each, so a bunch of five is roughly £1. Loose ones are cheaper than a pre-packed bag, and the ripe ones on the reduce shelf are the bargain.

Bar-chewing is usually a cage too small or bedding too shallow to dig in: a Syrian wants about 100 by 50 cm of floor, a 28 cm wheel it can run in with a straight back, and 15 cm of bedding, and a dwarf a little less. If the cage is big enough it is boredom, so add a sand bath, tubes and paper to shred, and swap the chews weekly. A bare patch on the nose, or chewing that runs for hours, is worth a vet check.

Barefoot is best indoors until they are walking well: it is how the foot learns to grip and balance. Once they walk outside, a first shoe wants a flexible thin sole, a wide toe box and a fastening that holds the heel, so you can feel their toes through it. Pram shoes are decoration only. Check the fit every eight to ten weeks - a thumb's width at the toe - because toddlers grow about two sizes a year.
Bart De Wever is the prime minister of Belgium: in office since February 2025, after seven months of coalition talks. The head of state is King Philippe.
Bats sleep upside down, hanging by their feet, and many hibernate through the winter that way. Hanging upside down means a fall is a drop of a few centimetres, and taking off is just letting go.

Batter keeps 1 to 2 days in the fridge in a jug with a lid, and stir it before it goes in the pan because the flour sinks. One with baking powder in it loses its lift after a day, so use it the same day for pancakes. Crepe batter is better after half an hour's rest, and a batter that smells sour or has grey on top goes down the sink.

Batteries last about 3 to 5 years and cost roughly £70 to £150 fitted, more with stop-start. Match the size and the cold-cranking rating in the handbook, and note that many newer cars need the new battery coded to the car, so a garage is easier than doing it yourself.

Be there before you fix anything: say the plain thing - "that's really hard, I'm sorry" - and then ask what they need today, company or quiet. A fixed offer helps more than an open one ("I'll bring dinner on Thursday", "walk on Sunday?"), and the message tomorrow, when the first day's fuss has died down, is the one they remember. If it has been weeks and they have stopped seeing anyone or stopped eating, say so plainly and help them book a GP appointment.

Be warm and specific rather than general: "I love seeing you and I need Sundays to myself" lands, where "I need space" sounds like a rejection. Offer the thing you will do instead, such as a call on Thursdays or lunch once a month, and keep to it, because a parent given a reliable time to count on stops ringing at random.
Be brief and offer a substitute: "I can't make Tuesday — can we do Thursday, or shall I send a note with my points?" A short reason and an alternative reads as organised rather than rude.

Bean and alfalfa sprouts are the one salad thing to be careful with: they are grown warm and damp, which is exactly what bacteria like, and rinsing does not remove what has got inside the seed. Eat them cooked - stir-fried or dropped into soup for a minute - and if you want them raw, buy a bag that says ready to eat and keep it cold. Pregnant, elderly, or on treatment that lowers your immunity, cook them: the same advice covers a raw mung-bean salad.

Beans, lentils and the cabbage family carry sugars your small intestine cannot break down, so the bacteria in your gut ferment them and give off gas. It is normal, and it settles: rinse tinned beans well, soak dried ones and pour that water away, cook them properly, and add them a little at a time so your gut adjusts over a few weeks.

Beans are optional, and it is a regional thing rather than a rule: Tex-Mex chilli usually has none, and most home versions have kidney beans. If you want them, a 400g tin of kidney or black beans, drained and rinsed, goes in with the tomatoes so it simmers the last 30 minutes - about one tin to 500g of mince, and no longer, because they go floury. Without them, keep the mince at 500g and add an extra onion or a handful of red lentils with the stock so it does not go dry and sharp. Baked beans are the sweet one: they work, but they want less sugar and a splash of vinegar in the pot.

Beat two or three eggs with a pinch of salt and a splash of milk in a mug or a small bowl, add a small knob of butter, and cook on full power in 30-second bursts, stirring properly between each one. Two eggs take about 90 seconds to two minutes in total, and they should come out still slightly wet - they carry on setting as you stir, and a microwave takes them from soft to rubbery in twenty seconds. Salt again at the end, not before. A whole egg in its shell is the one thing to keep out: it bursts, so if you want a fried egg on a plate, break it and prick the yolk first.
Been one of those? Park it for tonight — most of it will look smaller in the morning.

Bees pollinate a large share of the fruit, vegetables and nuts we eat, so losing them would make food scarcer and dearer. You can help with bee-friendly flowers, a shallow dish of water and a corner of garden left a bit wild.

Bees make it: a worker drinks nectar out of flowers into a honey stomach, where enzymes start breaking the sugar down, then passes it to a hive bee who packs it into a wax cell and fans the water out of it until it is too thick to spoil. One bee makes about a twelfth of a teaspoon in her whole life.

Beetroot is ready eight to ten weeks after sowing, at golf-ball size for eating fresh and up to tennis-ball size for storing. Twist the leaves off rather than cutting, so it does not bleed, and lift them before the first hard frost.

Before you buy one, try the cheap fixes: a firm board under the mattress, rotating it, and a pillow between your knees if you sleep on your side. If it's over eight years old or you wake with back pain most mornings, a medium-firm mattress is the usual recommendation.

Before you decide anything, write down what you would want the answer to be if a friend described your week to you - that is usually clearer than how you feel at midnight. Then one honest conversation, with a time on it: what you want to be different, what you will do yourself, and what you will not carry any more. Relate and similar services do this with a third person in the room, and one session is cheaper than a lawyer. If there is shouting, fear, or controlling behaviour in the house, talk to a solicitor or a domestic abuse line first, quietly, because that changes the order you do things in.

Being off sick is not in itself a reason to be sacked, but long or repeated absence is handled as an attendance or capability issue, and that has steps: a meeting, a chance to improve, usually a warning first. Ask for the policy in writing, ask to be referred to occupational health, and take a union rep or a colleague into any meeting. ACAS advises free. Keep every sick note and every letter.

Being puffed after stairs or a run for the bus is usually just fitness: a brisk walk, stairs instead of the lift and two or three short bouts of getting out of breath a week make a real difference in a month or two. Breathlessness that comes on at rest, wakes you at night, or comes with chest pain, a cough for weeks or swollen ankles should be checked by a GP rather than worked through.

Being hit needs dealing with every time, separately from the row about the toy: stop it straight away, say the rule in one sentence ('we do not hit'), and give the same calm consequence you always give, then let them start again. If one child is being hurt often, or is frightened of the other, talk to the school or your health visitor - a pattern that never changes needs another adult in the room.
Being in the dark about something means nobody has told you what is going on. What is it you have not been told?
Belfast has about 350,000 people, and about 670,000 in the wider area.

Believe them first and write down what happened, with dates and names, then ask the school for a meeting with the head of year rather than the class teacher alone. Ask what the school will do and when, and keep checking in with your child; if nothing changes in a few weeks, put it in writing and ask to see the head.

Bend at the hips and knees rather than the waist, keep the load touching you, and brace your stomach as you stand - a weight held out at arm's length puts five times the strain on your back. Feet shoulder-width, one foot slightly forward, and turn with your feet instead of twisting your spine. For a heavy move, take the drawers out first and use a sack trolley, and slide things on a blanket rather than lifting them.

Bend at the hips and knees, keep the load against your body and your feet hip-width apart, and take a sofa or a mattress with a second person on the other end: two people and a strap beat one person and a bad back. If your back has gone since, keep moving gently rather than resting it in bed - most strains ease in one to two weeks - and ring the doctor the same day if you cannot weight-bear, go numb round the groin or lose control of your bladder.

Benedict Cumberbatch plays Sherlock Holmes in the BBC series (2010-2017), with Martin Freeman as Watson. Robert Downey Jr played him in the two Guy Ritchie films, and Jeremy Brett in the 1980s series.

Benjamin Netanyahu is the prime minister of Israel: in office since December 2022, and the longest-serving prime minister the country has had. Israel has a president too - Isaac Herzog - but that job is ceremonial.
Berbere is medium to hot, roughly 3,000 to 5,000 Scoville - a blend of chilli, paprika, fenugreek and warm spices. A tablespoon for four gives an Ethiopian stew its heat.
Berlin has about 3.8 million people, the biggest city in Germany and about eight times the size of Frankfurt.

*Gardeners' Question Time* is the one to start with: three experts answering listeners' questions, so you get the answer to the thing you were wondering about. *Talking Gardens* is the interview version and *The RHS Podcast* the seasonal jobs.
*Happy Valley* is the closest in quality: British, tense, brilliantly acted, and less gory than Line of Duty. *Sherwood* and *Bodyguard* are the other two to try next.

*Hard Fork* (Kevin Roose and Casey Newton) is the weekly one on what the tech companies just did, and it is funny. *Darknet Diaries* is true stories of hacks and the people who did them, and *The Vergecast* is the long argument about gadgets.

*Hidden Brain* is the one to start with: one piece of psychology an episode, told as a story. *The Happiness Lab* is the research on what actually makes people happier, and *Where Should We Begin?* is Esther Perel with one real couple in a single session.

*Home Cooking* (Samin Nosrat and Hrishikesh Hirway) answers listeners' kitchen questions and is the friendliest place to start. *The Sporkful* is about how and why people eat what they eat, and *Gastropod* takes one food an episode and does its history and science.

*Parenting Hell* (Rob Beckett and Josh Widdicombe) is two fathers being honest about how badly it is going, which is the most reassuring thing on the subject. *Happy Mum Happy Baby* is the calmer interview version, one parent an episode.

*The Money To The Masses Podcast* is the plain-English one, *Meaningful Money* for pensions and savings, and *Moneybox* for news you can use. All three skip the jargon and none of them tries to sell you anything.
*The Rest Is History* is the best all-round history podcast, with two hosts who are funny as well as accurate. For true stories, *Casefile* for crime and *This American Life* for real people's lives.

*The Rewatchables* is one film an episode and why it still works, which is the best listen for someone who likes films. *Kermode & Mayo's Take* reviews what is out now, and *You Must Remember This* tells the old Hollywood stories properly.

*Wow in the World* is the best one to start with: science stories with two silly hosts, made for 5 to 8 year olds. *Story Pirates* turns stories children send in into sketches and songs, and *Circle Round* tells a folk tale in fifteen minutes with a proper cast. *But Why* answers the questions children actually ask, and *Smash Boom Best* is two things argued over by comedians with your child as the judge.

Berries are the best fruit for the calories - about 30 to 60 per 100g - and a 80g portion counts towards your five a day, with vitamin C, fibre and the red and purple pigments that give them their colour. Frozen ones are just as good and a lot cheaper out of season. A punnet is two or three portions, so tip half into a bowl rather than eating from the box.

Berries keep 3 to 5 days in the fridge, spread on a plate lined with kitchen paper rather than heaped in the punnet, and only washed when you eat them. Pick out a mouldy one straight away, because it spreads through the lot, and freeze or cook the soft ones instead of binning them.

Best not: raw flour and raw egg are both a real risk, and flour is the one people forget - it can carry E. coli straight from the field. Normal dough is for the oven; if you want to eat it raw, use a recipe with heat-treated flour and no egg.

Better not: cook it in a separate buttered tray, 25 minutes at 180C, because stuffing in a turkey soaks up the raw juices and holds the middle of the meat below a safe heat, so the bird needs about 20 minutes more and the stuffing comes out soggy. If you do stuff it, give the stuffing itself a thermometer read of 74C before the bird comes out to rest.
Bin it, I'm afraid: cooked pasta left out for more than 2 hours isn't worth eating, even if it looks and smells fine. Get leftovers into the fridge within the hour next time and they keep 3 days.
Bin it, I'm afraid: cooked chicken left out for more than 2 hours isn't safe to eat, even if it looks and smells fine. Next time, get leftovers into the fridge within an hour and they'll keep 3 days.

Bin it. Mould, an off smell or a slimy feel in a soup, sauce, stew or a cooked grain means threads and bacteria under the surface where you cannot see them, and heating it through does not make it safe - the opposite of hard cheese. A pot that tastes sharp, fizzes or has bubbles is the same answer with no mould showing.

Bin it if it smells sour or fizzy rather than tangy, or if there is any mould on the surface; a little watery separation on top is fine, so stir it back in. Cream keeps about 5 days once opened, and yogurt a week past its date if it has been in the fridge.
Birmingham has about 1.15 million people, which makes it the second biggest city in the UK after London.

Biting the same cheek or tongue is nearly always a habit that shows up when you are tense or eating fast: slow down at meals, keep the tongue away from the teeth line, and chew gum when you notice yourself doing it. If it happens in your sleep, a dentist can fit a soft guard, and a bite that has changed or a rough tooth or filling is worth checking, because a sharp edge keeps catching the same spot.

Biting at this age is nearly always frustration or teething rather than naughtiness, and the same short script every time is what works: a firm "no biting, that hurts", put the child down or turn away for half a minute, then give your attention to whoever was bitten - a long telling-off teaches nothing and gives the bite attention. Biting peaks between 18 months and two, and drops off once the words come. A teething baby wants a cold teether or a damp flannel from the fridge; a child who bites when tired, hungry or crowded needs the nap or the snack before it starts. Ask nursery to use the same words, so the rule does not change between home and there.

Bitter in a sauce is burnt garlic, a roux or flour taken past golden, or a burnt pan scraped back in; a pinch of sugar, a spoon of cream and a squeeze of lemon take the edge off, but if it tastes of scorched garlic or flour there is no rescuing it. Low heat, garlic in last and stirred for 30 seconds is the fix next time.

Bitter means overcooked or undercooked: halve them and boil 4 to 5 minutes, no more, or roast them cut side down at 200C for 20 minutes. Cut a cross in the stalk end so the middle cooks at the same time as the outside, and finish with butter, lemon or a little bacon - a pinch of sugar in the water does very little.

Bitterness is usually the raw garlic and the pine nuts: toast the nuts, use half a small clove, and stir in a handful of parsley or a squeeze of lemon at the end. Blitz in short pulses, because blending for a long time warms the basil and turns it bitter, and keep it in the fridge under a film of oil for a week.
Black pepper is mildly hot, at the back of the throat, and nothing like chilli: a whole teaspoon of it is gentler than a pinch of cayenne. Freshly ground is far sharper than the dust in a jar.

Black spot is a fungus that overwinters on fallen leaves and splashes up in the rain: pick off every spotted leaf and bin it - never the compost - clear the fallen ones from the soil, and water the roots rather than the plant. Feed it and mulch with compost so it grows away from the spots, and in a bad year spray a rose fungicide when the first spots show.

Black, green, white and oolong are the same leaf, picked and processed differently: black is fully oxidised and malty, green is steamed or pan-fired and grassy, white is the young leaf dried, and oolong sits between green and black. Everything else - peppermint, chamomile, rooibos, fruit - is a herbal infusion rather than tea, so it brews and keeps differently.

Blackthorn is the first: white blossom on bare, spiny hedgerow twigs in March, before its leaves. Cherry plum and wild cherry come next, then apple and hawthorn in May. White flowers on a leafless hedge in early spring is almost always blackthorn; blackthorn has thorny twigs and hawthorn flowers after its leaves are out.

Bleach does not leave a stain, it takes the dye out, so nothing you apply brings the colour back: the only fixes are a fabric pen in a close colour, a patch or embroidery over the spot, or dyeing the whole thing darker. On white cotton it is invisible, so check before you panic. Next time, gloves and an old shirt.

Bleeding after sex is common and usually not serious: dryness or thinning skin after the menopause, a patch on the cervix or a small polyp, or an infection. It is worth a GP appointment rather than a wait-and-see - they can look at the cervix and check your smear is up to date - and it is not something to be embarrassed about, they see it every week. Ring the same week if it is heavy, painful, or there is discharge that smells.

Bleeding does not put pressure back in - it lets air out, and it can drop the gauge a little. Top it up at the filling loop to 1 to 1.5 bar with the system cold, then check it the next day; if it is low again there is a leak somewhere and that is an engineer's job.

Blend or mash soft fruit with a little sugar and lemon - strawberries, mango, berries, or just orange juice - and pour it into moulds or paper cups with a stick in, leaving a centimetre at the top because water expands. Four to six hours in the freezer. A splash of yoghurt or milk makes them creamier, and a spoon of vodka stops them going rock hard.

Blend it far longer than feels sensible - 3 to 4 minutes in a food processor, scraping down twice - and add 2 to 3 tablespoons of iced water while it runs: graininess is under-blending and a paste that is too dry, and rubbing the skins off the chickpeas before you blitz them takes it the rest of the way.

Blitz stale bread, or crush crackers, cornflakes or oatcakes in a bag with a rolling pin. A crumble or a gratin topping takes porridge oats or crushed crisps, and for binding mince or meatballs a slice of bread soaked in a little milk is the classic.

Blitz 50g of basil, 30g of pine nuts, 50g of parmesan, a small garlic clove and a pinch of salt, then pour in about 100ml of olive oil with the motor still running. Rocket or spinach and walnuts stand in for basil and pine nuts, and it keeps a week in a jar under a layer of oil.

Block or tablet salt, dropped into the brine tank and kept above the water line - check it monthly and top it up then, because a family of four gets through roughly one 25kg bag a month. Fill no higher than the top of the brine well, and never use table, cooking or dishwasher salt: the anti-caking agents turn to sludge in the tank.

Block the number in your phone's call log (tap it, then Block) and do not ring it back, because a missed call from an unknown number is often just checking the line is live. In the UK register free with the Telephone Preference Service, and if it keeps happening ask your network to switch on a nuisance-call filter.

Block the first ninety minutes for the work that needs thinking, before the day fills up, and treat it like a meeting in your calendar. For the rest: agree with the team that questions come by message and you will answer in two batches, wear headphones as the sign, and if one person is the source, ask them for a ten-minute slot rather than taking it piecemeal - most interruptions are curiosity, not emergencies, and asking 'can it wait until two?' is a complete answer.

Blocks are not bedded on sand and cement: they go down on 30 to 40mm of sharp sand alone, compacted with a wacker plate, and the joints are brushed full of kiln-dried sand afterwards, so there is no cement to measure at all. For 20 square metres reckon on about a tonne of sharp sand for the bed and two or three 25kg bags of kiln-dried sand for the joints, plus an edge restraint on every open side, which is the part that stops the blocks spreading.

Blood types come from markers on the surface of red blood cells: the ABO system gives A, B, AB or O, and the rhesus factor adds positive or negative. Your type is inherited, and it matters for transfusions because the immune system attacks markers it does not recognise; O negative is the universal red-cell donor, and only a blood test can tell you yours.
Blood is red because of haemoglobin, the iron-containing protein in red cells that carries oxygen. Bright red blood is rich in oxygen; darker blood has given its oxygen to the body.

Blot up what you can without rubbing, then dab with cool water and a drop of washing-up liquid, working from the edge inwards, and blot dry with a towel. Keep going with clean water until the towel comes away clean, and don't scrub: that pushes the wine deeper into the filling.

Blot up as much as you can with kitchen paper, then dab with cool water and a drop of washing-up liquid, working from the outside in so it doesn't spread. Blot dry with a towel and repeat; on a coffee stain, a little white vinegar in the water helps.

Blot what is still wet with kitchen paper and do not rub it, because rubbing pushes the paint into the pile. Emulsion and the water-based satins lift with cold water and a little washing-up liquid worked in with your fingertips and blotted out again; oil gloss and varnish need a cloth damped with white spirit, dabbed from the edge of the mark inwards so it does not spread. Try white spirit on a corner you cannot see first, since on a wool carpet it can lift the dye.

Blot, don't rub, then dab with cool water and a drop of washing-up liquid from the outside in, and dry it with a towel rather than a hairdryer. Use as little water as you can, because a sofa takes days to dry and a damp one smells. A loose cover that unzips is better washed on its own; leather wants a barely damp cloth and saddle soap.
Blot, don't rub, then dab a little hand sanitiser or isopropyl alcohol into the mark with a cotton bud and blot again. Rinse with cold water and wash; hairspray does the same job in an emergency.

Blot it while it is still wet with kitchen roll rather than rubbing, then work a paste of bicarbonate of soda and washing-up liquid into a carpet, a towel or a worktop with an old toothbrush and rinse with cold water; a cream cleaner does the same job on a basin, a bath or a tile. On fabric, cold water and washing-up liquid first and an oxygen bleach soak only if the mark has dried. Heat sets it, so keep it out of the dryer and off the iron until the mark is gone, and if it has dried on a carpet a carpet cleaner will lift the rest.

Blot it while it's wet, don't rub, then work out what you're dealing with. Leather: a barely damp cloth with a little saddle soap, then polish once it's dry. Canvas or mesh: an old toothbrush with washing-up liquid and cold water, rinse by dabbing rather than soaking, and stuff them with newspaper to dry away from a radiator. Never put them in the machine or the dryer, and suede wants a suede brush only, no water at all.

Blot it, don't rub, with kitchen paper, then pour on cold water and blot again, repeating until the water runs clear. A paste of bicarbonate of soda left on it for an hour pulls the rest out; white wine or salt are the old tricks and both work better than hot water.

Blot it at once with kitchen paper, then stretch the fabric over a bowl and pour boiling water through it from a height; that shifts most red wine from cotton. For a delicate or dry-clean-only piece use cold water and a little washing-up liquid and take it to a dry cleaner the same week.

Blue is scattered much more strongly than green, so the green that is scattered arrives mixed with far more blue and the sky reads as pale blue. Violet is scattered even more, but there is less of it in sunlight and our eyes are less sensitive to it, so it never dominates.

Bluetooth is a short-range radio link, about ten metres, that your phone and the other device use to talk directly without a network or a router. They hop channels 1,600 times a second so they do not collide with wifi, and pairing is simply the two agreeing a key once so they recognise each other afterwards.

Blushing is adrenaline opening up the small blood vessels in your face, and it happens when you feel exposed to other people's attention. You cannot stop it on purpose, which is exactly why it makes you more embarrassed, though people read it as honest rather than weak.

Board across the joists, never beside them: 18mm chipboard or loft boards screwed down into the timber, with the joins over a joist. Keep the 50mm gap at the eaves and do not squash the insulation under the boards, because it needs the air to work - if the wool is deeper than the joists, screw loft legs on top and board onto those instead. The ceiling below carries a ceiling and not a floor, so a water tank or a stack of boxes wants a joist under it.

Boil or steam broccoli for 4 to 5 minutes, until a knife goes in with a little bite left. Drain it and run it under cold water if you're not serving it straight away: that keeps it green instead of army-issue grey. Broccoli that has already gone yellow is either overdone or a few days old - it is still fine to eat, so give it 3 minutes next time and use this lot in a soup or a stir-fry rather than on the plate.

Boil the kettle and let it stand for no more than 30 minutes, so the water is still at least 70C - that is what kills the bacteria in the powder. Put the water in the bottle first, then add a level scoop of powder for every 30ml of water, and shake it with the cap on. Cool it under a running tap or stood in cold water, and test a drop on the inside of your wrist before a feed.

Boil them in salted water: 15 to 20 minutes for chunks and 20 to 25 for whole medium potatoes, until a knife slides in with no resistance. Floury potatoes mash best, so steam them dry for a minute, then mash with warm milk and butter and stop as soon as it's smooth: over-beating turns it gluey.

Boil a pan of water with a few slices of lemon or a splash of vinegar for 10 minutes with the window open: that is what clears cooking smells out of the air. Wash the pan, the board and the bin straight away, and leave a bowl of bicarbonate of soda in the fridge overnight if the smell got in there.

Boiled eggs keep about a week in the fridge with the shell on, and 2 to 3 days once peeled, in a covered bowl of water. Raw ones in their shells keep far longer: about three weeks past the date on the box if they stayed cold.
Bola Tinubu is the president of Nigeria: in office since May 2023. A Nigerian president serves four years and can stand for a second term.

Book on Trenitalia, the state operator, or Italo for the other fast line: both sell online and at the machines in the station, and a ticket bought a week or two ahead is much cheaper than one bought on the day. The fast Frecciarossa trains do Rome to Florence in about 1 hour 30, Florence to Venice in about 2 hours, and Rome to Naples in about 1 hour 10, so Milan, Florence and Rome makes a comfortable week. Regional trains are cheap and need no reservation but are slow, and a regional ticket bought at a machine has to be stamped in the small machine on the platform before you get on.

Book six to eight weeks ahead for short-haul and two to four months for long-haul, and be flexible about the day: Tuesday and Wednesday are usually cheapest. Search one way at a time, and check the airport transfer before you commit to a bargain.

Book the room as soon as the date is fixed if it is a weekend, a city or a wedding - four to six weeks ahead is enough for most trips, and three months or more for a popular place in summer or a bank holiday. Midweek and January are where last-minute hunting pays. If a booking site shows less than the hotel's own site, ring the desk: they usually match it, and the direct terms are better.

Book the seat you can sleep in if it is overnight, then treat it as a day with no work in it: water instead of the wine, a proper meal before you board rather than the tray, and stand up every couple of hours to walk to the back. Compression socks and shoes with room in them are worth more than any gadget; an eye mask, earplugs and a spare toothbrush turn the last three hours into a rest. Put a change of clothes, your medicines and a charger in the bag under the seat, and set your watch to the new time when you board.

Book the theory test first at gov.uk - it is £23 and the pass lasts two years - and the practical only after it, because a practical booking needs the theory pass number. The practical is £62 on a weekday and £75 for an evening, weekend or bank holiday, and the test centre slots come up 6 to 24 weeks out by area, so take the first one that has a warm-up lesson the day before rather than holding out for a perfect date. Cancelling or moving it needs five clear working days or you lose the fee; the car has to be taxed, insured for the test and have a second mirror for the examiner, and the licence goes with you.

Book the bag with the ticket rather than at the airport: a checked bag is usually about £15 to £40 each way online and £40 to £65 at the desk, and on a short trip a 10 kg cabin bag with priority is often the cheaper way to take a case. Weigh it at home on the bathroom scales - a few kilos over is charged at the airport rate however you booked.

Book the check-up and say on the phone that you are nervous and have not been for a while - practices hear it every week, and most will give you a longer first appointment, a signal to stop, and no lecture. The first visit is usually a look round and an x-ray, nothing more, and you can agree to one small thing at a time. If it helps, take headphones, agree a hand signal for a pause, and go in the morning when you are less tired. Ring the same week if a tooth is painful, a filling has come out or your gums bleed a lot, because those are quicker to fix early.

Book a bulky waste collection with your council, usually £15-£40 for a roll, or take it to the household waste site yourself - it will not go in the wheelie bin. A fitter who is laying the new one will often take the old one away for a small charge, and a charity shop takes a clean rug. A sound piece is worth keeping: laid upside down under gravel or bark it stops weeds for years.

Book a bulky waste collection with your council - most charge twenty to forty pounds and collect from the doorstep - or take it to the recycling centre, where it is stripped for its springs. Charity shops rarely take one for hygiene reasons, so a free-ad site is the other realistic route if it is clean and you say collection only.

Book direct with a small hotel or guesthouse once you know roughly where you want to be: a phone call often beats the price on the booking site, and it is the cheapest way in small towns. Hostels and apart-hotels win for a week, and a kitchen saves more than a lower nightly rate. Look at the total with tax and breakfast, not the headline.

Book early and ask two questions: the call-out charge and the hourly rate after the first hour, because a weekend call-out is usually about double the weekday one and the quote over the phone is what holds them to it. Ring three local firms from eight in the morning and say what is wrong and when you need someone; the one who can tell you what it probably is on the phone is the one to book. Anything with water coming through is worth a call straight away - turn the stopcock off first - and a smell of gas is the free 24-hour gas emergency line, 0800 111 999, not a plumber.

Book early and compare the total with insurance included, not the headline daily rate. Check the excess and whether your own policy or a credit card already covers it. Pay the deposit on a credit card: it is usually a few hundred pounds or euros held on the card and released when you return the car. Photograph every panel before you drive off, return it full-to-full, and remember that a young or second driver usually costs extra.

Book it like an appointment rather than waiting for it to happen: a standing hour and a half a week, same slot, out of the house or with the phones in another room. Small and regular beats the big night out that keeps sliding, and ten minutes at the end of the day asking about the day - solving nothing - is what most couples are actually missing. Take turns arranging the slot, so it is not one person's project.

Booked online with the ticket, a 23kg bag is usually £20 to £45 each way on a budget airline, and £50 to £65 if you add it at the airport desk. A heavier bag costs more again, so weigh it at home. Compare that with a fare that includes a bag before you book: the cheap headline fare plus a suitcase often costs more than the fare that already has one.
Boots, layers and a waterproof, whatever the forecast says, because you'll be on your feet on grass for hours. Nothing white, nothing dry-clean-only, and nothing you'd be upset to lose.

Both names in full, the date and time written out, and the place with a postcode: then the one thing the guest has to act on - whether there is a meal to choose, whether children are invited - and an RSVP date with a name and a number to reply to. One side of a card is plenty. "Alex and Sam would love you to join them" does more work than three lines of poetry, and "no gifts please" only goes on if you mean it.

Both phones do it for you: on an iPhone, put the new one next to the old and follow the Quick Start prompt; on Android, use the cable or the copy-apps option during setup. Do it while both are plugged in, because moving photos over wifi drains the old phone.

Both, and they do different jobs: a sit up moves the trunk through a range, so it works the front of the core and the hip flexors, and a plank holds the trunk still, which is the job a back has to do all day. If you have time for one, take the plank - it is the one that carries over to lifting and sitting, and it needs no movement to get wrong - and add crunches after it if you want the curl. Two or three sets of a plank you can hold with a straight back beats a hundred sit ups.

Both, for different reasons: something small and mostly carbohydrate one to two hours before gives you the energy for the session, and some protein within a couple of hours after helps the muscle repair. If you only do one, the after matters more for strength training and the before matters more for a long run.

Both are sodium chloride and season the same; sea salt is coarser and less dense, so a level teaspoon holds less of it, and table salt is fine, treated to run freely and has iodine added in the UK. Use table salt in baking, where it has to dissolve evenly.

Both are state schools and free to attend. A maintained school is run by the local authority; an academy is funded directly by the government, sets its own curriculum and admissions, and is run by a trust. For a parent, the practical difference is who you complain to.

Both feet stay on the ground behind the line, and the ball goes back over your head with both hands on it from behind - a foot over the line or a hand that comes round the side turns it over. Plant both feet shoulder width, get some bend in the elbows and throw it flat to a teammate's feet rather than high and looping. The long throw is a run-up and a bigger arch of the back, and it is worth learning only if you can reach the box.

Both mean an insurer wrote the car off instead of repairing it, and both are legal to buy and drive once the repair has been signed off. Cat N is non-structural damage - usually a stolen-and-recovered car, a bump or flood - and cat S is structural damage that was pulled straight again. (Cat A and B are breaker-only and must never go back on the road.) An S car is worth less than an N, both are worth noticeably less than a clean one, and both are harder to insure and to sell on: ask for the damage photos and the repair invoice, have an inspection done, and get an insurance quote on the registration before you commit.

Bottles, teats and dummies all get the same treatment: wash them in hot soapy water with a bottle brush straight after use, because milk left in a bottle grows bacteria fast, then sterilise before the next feed by steam, cold-water tablets or boiling for the time the packet says. Everything the milk touches goes in - bottle, teat, collar and lid - and the NHS says sterilise for every feed until your baby is 12 months old. Wash your hands first, and do not rinse the teat under the tap afterwards. Keep two dummies going, one in the steriliser while the other is in use, and rinse a dropped one rather than licking it.

Boudicca (died about 61 AD) was queen of the Iceni in eastern Britain, who led a revolt against Roman rule after she was flogged and her daughters were assaulted, burning Colchester, London and St Albans. Her army was beaten by a much smaller Roman force, and she died soon after, by poison or illness.

Brackets hold an aside the sentence would survive without: the date of a law, a translation, a word the reader may not know. Read the sentence without it - if the grammar still works, the brackets are doing their job. In British style the full stop goes outside them unless the bracket is a whole sentence of its own.

Braise it rather than boil it: shred it, soften sliced onion in butter, add the cabbage with a chopped apple, two tablespoons of vinegar and a spoon of sugar, a splash of water, then put the lid on for 45 to 60 minutes on a low heat, stirring now and then. The vinegar is not for flavour alone - it is what keeps the colour a deep red instead of a grey-blue, so taste and add more at the end.

Brake dust is the black coating, and the mistake is letting it sit: it is mildly caustic once wet and it eats the lacquer. Use a wheel cleaner made for the job - the acid-free ones are safe on painted alloys - leave it a couple of minutes, then agitate the spokes with a soft brush and rinse. Never use the sponge that touches your paint, and wash wheels last or with their own bucket. A sealant or a wax twice a year makes the next wash a rinse.

Bread people go straight for the pun - Doughlene, Clint Yeastwood, Bread Pitt, Jane Dough - and everyone who asks about it wants the joke, so any name with dough, yeast or rise in it works. The starter does not care, and saying the name out loud once a day is a good reminder to feed it.

Bread is fine: two slices of wholegrain or seeded is about 6g of fibre and a fair base for a meal. The white sliced loaf has less fibre and less staying power, so keep it for toast and make the everyday one wholegrain.

Break the silence with something small and concrete rather than a big talk: a photo with 'saw this and thought of you - how are you doing?' on it, or a practical question about a parent or a house you both care about. Don't relitigate the argument in the first message - the point is a door left open. If they don't answer, wait a few months and try once more, without keeping score.

Breathe out slowly under the water and turn your head to the side to breathe in as one arm comes over, rather than lifting your head forwards. Practise with a float and breathe every three strokes to start; goggles make all of it easier.

Breathe in through the nose and mouth together, into the belly rather than the chest, and let the rhythm follow your steps - two in, two out, then three and three when the pace is easy. If you can only speak a few words at a time, slow down: most breathless running is a pace problem, not a lung problem. Cold air is fine, just warm up first.

Bright light sets off a sneeze in about one person in four: the light triggers the same nerve that starts a sneeze reflex, so looking at the sun or walking out of a dark cinema does it. It is harmless and tends to run in families.
Brilliant. Thanks for telling me.

Bring photo ID - a passport or a driving licence - a copy of your CV, and the certificates for anything the advert asked for; in the UK the right-to-work documents (a passport, a visa or a share code) are often wanted on the day. A list of two referees with phone numbers is worth having as well. Whatever they put in the invitation wins over all of it, so if anything is unclear, email the recruiter and ask.

Bring them in if you can, because a pot freezes from every side: the roots sit above the frost line, so a night that a border shrugs off can see off a plant in a tub. If they are too heavy to move, stand them together against a house wall on pot feet, wrap the pot rather than the leaves in bubble wrap or a sack, and push them under the eaves - grouping them and getting them out of the wind does most of the work. A forecast of 2C or below at ground level is the one to act on, and anything tender left out after that is worth bringing in for good.

Bring three lines: what you did since last time, what you need help with, and one thing you want to be different. It's your meeting, not a report: the middle line is the one that gets you support, and asking for it is what one-to-ones are for.

Britain outlawed the slave trade in 1807 and slavery itself in the colonies in 1833, in force from 1 August 1834. The government paid 20 million pounds to the slave owners, about 40 percent of the state budget, and nothing to the enslaved people.

Broccoli keeps 3 to 5 days in the fridge, loose in a bag or a tub with a sheet of kitchen paper to take the damp. It drinks, so stand the stalk in an inch of water and it holds a couple of days longer. Yellowing florets are old age rather than rot and are fine cooked; a head that smells strong, is slimy or has black patches should go.

Brown pesto is the basil oxidising where the air reaches it, not spoilage: press it flat in the jar and cover the surface with a film of olive oil, and stir a squeeze of lemon through before you serve it. It is still good to eat for a few days if it was in the fridge and smells fine.

Brown tips are usually dry air, hard tap water or a plant that dried right out once: the leaf edges die first because they are furthest from the roots. Snip the brown off with scissors so it stops spreading, water it when the top of the compost is dry rather than in sips, move it off a radiator or a draughty windowsill, and use rainwater or left-out tap water if your water is hard.

Brown to the live pin marked L, blue to neutral N, green and yellow to earth E, and the cable grip clamped over the outer white sheath, not the inner cores - that clamp is what stops the wires pulling out. Strip about a centimetre, twist each core so no strand strays, and shorten the live and neutral so the earth is the last to pull tight if the cable is tugged. The fuse has to match the appliance: 3A for a lamp or a radio, 13A for a kettle or a heater. Never open a moulded plug - if it fails, cut it off and fit a new one.

Brown, crisp tips are usually the water: tap water left to stand overnight, or rainwater, takes the fluoride and salts out that build up at the leaf edges. Dry air and letting the compost go bone dry do the same, so check both and cut the tips off with a clean pair of scissors — the leaf keeps going.

Brown flowers on a hydrangea are almost always thirst, or simply old blooms: it has shallow roots and wants damp soil and shade from the hottest afternoon sun.
