Water it deeply twice a week in dry spells, mulch around the base, and cut the spent heads off so the plant puts its energy into next year's buds rather than seed.

Brown marks are iron rather than the calcium of scale, from a steel screw or fitting, a chip in the enamel, or iron in the water, and the acid that lifts scale lifts rust too: white vinegar or a citric acid paste, left ten minutes and rinsed. Never bleach, because it sets rust into the surface, and never wire wool, which leaves specks of steel behind to rust again. If it keeps coming back, find the steel that stays wet - a screw, a shower rose, the frame of the screen - and dry it or replace it.

Browse first, not grass: brambles, hedge, leaves, bark, weeds and thistles, then hay - about 2 kg of hay a day plus a mineral lick and water. A goat is a browser with a stomach for roughage, so rich grass or a lot of grain makes it ill, and it will strip a garden to the fence line given the chance.

Brush off dry dirt with a suede brush, and for marks rub gently with a suede eraser or a clean pencil eraser. Keep them out of the rain and spray a protector on when they're dry; if they get soaked, stuff them with newspaper and dry them slowly, never on a radiator.

Brush it off and eat the food: a fly that lands for a moment leaves little behind, and the dose is what matters. If it has been walking about on it, cut away that patch or rinse what you can, and tip out a drink it fell into. What is worth avoiding is food a fly has been sitting on for a while, or anything from a bin or off the floor, because flies feed on waste and carry it on their legs.

Budget about £600 for the court fee in England and Wales - £593 to apply, and a further £275 only if a judge has to decide the money - plus £1,000 to £3,000 for a solicitor on a simple, agreed split, or nothing if you do the forms yourselves. If you agree everything, a mediator at a few hundred pounds a session is far cheaper than two solicitors arguing, and the financial consent order that makes the split final is the part to spend money on, because without it a claim on a pension or a house can come back years later. Check whether you qualify for help with the fee before you pay it, and if there is any risk of violence, get advice before you file.

Build a sentence from the first letters (Never Eat Shredded Wheat for the compass), or tie items to places on a walk round your house - the sillier the image, the better it sticks. Mnemonics are good for lists and orders, useless for understanding; use them for the facts you keep dropping.

Bulk-forming ones - Fybogel, Movicol, lactulose - are the ones that can be taken for weeks or months, with plenty of water, because they work like fibre. Stimulant ones - senna and bisacodyl - are for a few days at a time; taken every day they leave you needing them. They do not damage the bowel and they are not addictive in the way people fear, but if you need one most weeks the answer is the diet and a GP visit rather than a bigger dose.

Burning in the middle of the chest that arrives after food, or when you lie down, is reflux: acid washing back up the gullet, not the heart. An antacid or an alginate (Gaviscon and the like) settles it in minutes, and a pharmacy omeprazole taken daily for a fortnight works better if it keeps coming back - smaller meals, three hours between dinner and bed and the head of the bed 10 to 15cm up do the rest. See a GP if it lasts over three weeks or food starts sticking on the way down, and ring 999 instead if the pain spreads to your arm or jaw or comes with sweating or breathlessness.

Butter first, then something sharp or salty on top: peanut butter and sliced banana, mashed avocado with salt and lemon, beans with a dash of Worcestershire, or a tin of sardines on hot toast. Cheese on toast under the grill for 3 minutes is the fastest good one, and a sliced tomato under the cheese stops it going dry.

Butter is churned cream; margarine is refined vegetable oil blended with water and flavouring, made to spread and bake like butter. Butter tastes better and browns better, margarine is cheaper and spreadable straight from the fridge.

Butter is fine in small amounts and is not a health food: about 700 calories per 100g and half of it saturated fat, so a teaspoon on vegetables is 35 calories and a thick spread on two slices is nearer 200. The guideline is 20g of saturated fat a day for a woman and 30g for a man, which is why oil is the better everyday cooking fat and butter is the one for the taste.

Butter keeps 2 to 3 weeks in the fridge and about 4 days in a covered dish on the counter; salted lasts longer than unsalted. It freezes for 3 months, cut into what you use in a fortnight. Rancid butter smells like old paint and tastes sharp, so bin it.

Butter keeps about 2 weeks in the fridge once opened, wrapped so it does not pick up the smell of everything else, and 3 months in the freezer; salted keeps longer than unsalted. It is fine in a dish on the counter for a day or two, and it turns rancid at the surface first, which shows as a darker edge and a cheese smell.

Buttercream or ganache keeps 3 to 4 days in a sealed tub in the fridge, or 2 months in the freezer: thaw it in the fridge overnight and beat it again, because it splits when it is cold. Cream cheese frosting is the short one at 2 to 3 days, and it does not freeze well. Keep an iced cake in a tin rather than the fridge, where it sweats.

Butterflies mostly fly by day and rest with their wings folded up together; moths mostly fly at night and rest with theirs spread flat. Moths also have fatter, hairier bodies and feathery antennae rather than thin ones with a club on the end.

Buy one pair of dark trousers in the size that fits you now and one plain shirt, this week rather than on the morning: those two do more for how you look than an expensive jacket that does not button. Ask for the trousers to be taken up while you are in the shop. Supermarkets and charity shops sell both for under 30 pounds, and a dark pair of unripped jeans and a clean shirt pass everywhere outside law, finance and the civil service. Polish the shoes you already have, take a spare shirt if the day is long, and wear the jacket open or leave it off; nobody is measuring the label, they are looking at whether the shirt is clean and the shoulders sit where they should.

Buy a three- or four-year-old car with a loan if you keep cars five years or more: £12,000 over five years at 7% is about £240 a month, and at the end it is yours and still worth £4,000. Lease or PCP only wins if you want a new car every two or three years and drive under the mileage cap. Compare the total cost, not the monthly: deposit, payments, any final balloon and the excess-mileage charge.

Buy for the first night, not for the shelves: a takeaway voucher for the evening the boxes are still out, a box with loo roll, tea, milk, mugs, bin bags, a corkscrew and a phone charger, or a hot meal you turn up with. A plant, a good bottle or a decent set of tea towels all last longer than another candle, and a voucher for a hardware shop is the unromantic one people are pleased about. Ask first whether they want things or help: an afternoon of unpacking and a trip to the tip is often the present.

Buying one is about £50 to £150, then £5 to £15 a month for the monitoring; renting is usually £10 to £20 a month with nothing up front. Ring adult social care at the council before you buy anything: most run a telecare service (Lifeline, Careline) from about £3 to £7 a week, and a falls assessment can bring that down or make it free. Ask about a key safe too.

Buying online gives you a 14-day right to change your mind from the day it arrives, and you only pay the return postage unless the shop says otherwise; buying in a shop gives you no right to change your mind at all, only the shop's own policy. That is the real difference, not the price. So for anything you might not keep - clothes, a mattress, furniture in a colour you have not seen - order online and check the returns page before you pay. For something you need today, or want to try first, buy in the shop and ask what their returns policy is in writing.

Buying usually wins if you'll stay five years or more, because the deposit, fees and stamp duty take about that long to cancel out. Renting is cheaper for shorter stays and gives you the freedom to move, so the honest answer is how long you plan to stay.

By hand in cool water with a wool wash or a little shampoo, squeeze rather than rub, rinse in water of the same temperature, and dry it flat on a towel away from heat. A wool cycle at 30C with a mesh bag is fine if the label allows it; the dryer never is.

CBT stands for cognitive behavioural therapy: a short talking treatment that works on the loop between what you think, what you do and how you feel, usually six to twenty weekly sessions with something to try between them. It is what the NHS offers first for anxiety and low mood, and in England you can refer yourself to it without seeing a GP.

COPD is damage to the airways and air sacs, almost always from smoking, so breathing out gets slow: breathless on stairs or a hill, a cough most mornings, chest infections that hang on. It cannot be cured but it can be slowed a lot - stopping smoking is the one thing that changes the course, the inhalers work only if they are used every day rather than when it is bad, and pulmonary rehab, a supervised exercise course, does more for breathlessness than any tablet. Get the flu and pneumonia jabs, and ask the GP for a plan for bad days with steroids and antibiotics ready to go. Go to A&E for blue lips, confusion or breathlessness that is suddenly worse than your normal.

Caffeine blocks adenosine, the molecule that builds up through the day and makes you sleepy, so it hides tiredness rather than removing it. Its effect lasts about five hours: have your last coffee by early afternoon, and cut down slowly to avoid headaches.

Caffeine has a half-life of about five hours, so a 4pm coffee is still in your system at bedtime: stop by early afternoon. Cutting down gradually over a week avoids the headaches that a sudden stop brings.
Call 999 or 911 now. Sit upright, stay calm, and if there's an asthma inhaler or an adrenaline pen, use it as prescribed while you wait.
Can't complain. What's on your mind?

Cancel or change it yourself at your bank, in the app or in writing: a standing order is yours to set and stop, so the payee cannot do it for you. Tell whoever you were paying as well, so a bill paid by standing order does not quietly fall behind, and remember there is no Direct Debit Guarantee on one - a wrong payment is not refunded automatically, you have to ask for it back.

Cancel from the place you pay, not from the app: on an iPhone it is Settings > your name > Subscriptions, on Android it is Play Store > Payments and subscriptions. A free trial that is about to renew has to be cancelled at least 24 hours before or it renews, and cancelling a subscription turns off the renewal rather than the access you paid for.

Cancel in writing, by email, and keep the date you sent it: most gyms want a month's notice, so email the branch rather than telling the desk. If a payment went out after you cancelled, ask your bank for a direct debit indemnity, which has to put it back. Joined online? You have 14 days to cancel, and moving away or injury usually gets you out early. If the gym has closed, ask for the unused months.

Cancel in writing and keep the date you sent it: most gyms and clubs want a month's notice, and the contract you signed says how much and whether there is a fee. Email the branch or use their cancellation form rather than telling the desk, then check the next two statements; if they keep charging past your notice date, ask your bank to reverse the direct debit and show them the email.

Cancel in writing first, because the refund follows the cancellation: say the booking and the date, ask what the notice was and what they are keeping. A deposit is normally returned inside the notice they set, on the card you paid with, and a chargeback is what is left if they stop answering - so keep the confirmation and the messages.

Carb loading tops up the glycogen in your muscles, the fuel they run on in the last hour of a long race - the reason a marathoner hits the wall near 20 miles. It only helps for events over 90 minutes: take the last two days easy and eat 8 to 10g of carbohydrate per kilo of bodyweight a day, rice, pasta, bread and potatoes, keeping the fat and fibre low so it does not sit heavy. Drink and salt matter too, and nothing new on race day.

Carbohydrate is not fattening in itself - it has 4 calories a gram, the same as protein and less than half of fat's 9 - and wholegrain versions carry the fibre that keeps you full. What adds up is the fat and sugar that arrives with it (chips, garlic bread, cream sauces), and the portions. Wholegrain carbs are worth keeping.

Carbs in the evening do not turn into fat any faster than carbs at lunch: your body stores what it does not use whenever you eat it. A plate of pasta at nine is only a problem if it is on top of a full day of eating or sits so heavy it spoils your sleep. Try to leave two hours between dinner and bed.
Cardamom is aromatic, not hot: menthol and flowers. Crush the pods just before they go in, because the seeds lose their smell within a day of grinding.
Cardiff has about 370,000 people, and about 1.1 million in the wider south Wales area.

Carer's Allowance is about £83 a week for caring 35 hours or more for someone who gets PIP daily living, Attendance Allowance or DLA middle or higher care. You must be 16 or over, not in full-time education, and earning under about £200 a week after tax. Claim on gov.uk and date it from the day you started, because it backdates three months; earn too much and Carer's Credit keeps your NI record going instead.

Caring is experience and it is written in the words the advert uses: planning and managing a household, appointments and medicines, dealing with doctors, social services and forms, keeping records, staying calm in a crisis, negotiating. Put it on the CV like a job - "Carer, family member, 2019-2023" - with three lines of what you actually did, then one example ready for the interview: a problem, what you sorted out, what changed. Say plainly why you are going back to work now, and leave out any apology for the time it took.

Carpal tunnel is a nerve squeezed where it passes through the wrist: numbness, tingling or pins and needles in the thumb, index and middle fingers, often worst at night and eased by shaking the hand. A wrist splint worn at night from a pharmacy is the first thing and settles most mild cases; if the hand is weak or you keep dropping things, see a GP, because an injection or a small operation stops it getting worse.

Carrots are about 40 calories per 100g and one decent carrot gives you more than a day's vitamin A, as beta-carotene. Cooked with a little fat - butter, oil, in a stew - you absorb more of it than from raw sticks, so both are worth eating. They do not turn you orange unless you eat them by the bagful for weeks, and they are one of the cheapest vegetables there is.

Carrots keep for weeks in the salad drawer of the fridge, in a bag or a lidded tub so they do not dry out, with the green tops cut off because they pull the water out of the root. Bendy ones are still safe to eat and firm up again in a bowl of iced water for half an hour.

Carry it on you, in a zipped inside pocket or a money belt, and not in a back pocket or an open beach bag. Put a photo of the ID page in your own email: it makes a replacement far quicker and it costs nothing. A hotel safe is fine while you are in the room, but keep the passport with you on travel days. If it is taken, report it to the police and go to your embassy for an emergency travel document.

Carry it in your hand luggage rather than the hold, in the original box with the pharmacy label showing your name and the dose, and take a few more days' worth than the trip lasts. A repeat prescription printout or a short letter from the GP answers the customs question without an argument. Ordinary medicines are fine almost everywhere; anything controlled - codeine, strong painkillers, sleeping tablets, ADHD medicines - is worth checking with the embassy of the country before you fly, and a few want a certificate in advance. Insulin and anything that needs the cold goes in hand luggage too, in a cool bag and never against ice. Antibiotics are worth asking the GP about before you go rather than buying out there - some destinations get a standby course for a stomach bug, and it is a prescription, not a souvenir.

Cash or a separate spending card caps the damage: fill an envelope for the week, and when it's empty it's empty. It works because a card makes spending painless, and seeing the money run out is exactly the feedback a budget needs.

Cast on with the long tail, which is the one most patterns assume: pull out a tail about three times the width of the knitting, make a slip knot on the needle, then scoop the thumb strand through the finger strand and put that loop on the needle, over and over until you have the number the pattern asks for. Count them once at the end and, if you are one out, it matters - a stitch lost here shows up as a lop-sided edge fifty rows later.

Castles were built as fortified homes, not just forts: a lord needed somewhere his family could live that also held off raiders and rivals. The Normans brought them to England in 1066, first as quick earth-and-timber mounds, then in stone.

Catch the waiter's eye as they pass and say 'could we get the bill when you have a moment' - short and polite, and it says you are ready without rushing them. Check it before you tap, then pay at the table on the card machine. Say up front if you want it split: most machines take two cards, and it is easier before the slip is printed.

Catch it in the act, interrupt with one short low word - 'ah-ah' or 'no' - and then show him what you do want: the sit instead of the jump, a chew toy instead of the shoe, and praise that. A telling off even a minute later means nothing to a dog, and shouting or a smack teaches him to hide it from you rather than stop. Use the same word every time, keep your voice flat rather than loud, and be quicker to reward the right version than to mark the wrong one.
Catherine Connolly is the president of Ireland: elected in October 2025. The job is largely ceremonial - the taoiseach, Micheal Martin, runs the government.

Cats show affection on their own terms, and the way to be chosen is to stop reaching: sit on the floor, play with a wand toy for five minutes twice a day, and let her come to you and walk away again without being picked up. Offer a finger to sniff, blink slowly at her and look away, and put a treat down rather than holding it out. She may never be a lap cat and that is normal; the cats who do sit on laps are the ones nobody lifted. It can take weeks or months with a shy cat, and a cat who used to be affectionate and now hides from you is a vet question, because pain and thyroid trouble both change a cat's temper.

Cats sleep 12 to 16 hours a day, so a sleepy cat is normal, especially after a big meal or a warm afternoon. What is not normal: a cat that stops eating, hides away, or is floppy when you pick her up, which needs a vet the same day.

Cats are bad at drinking, so encourage it: a wide bowl filled to the brim, a second bowl away from the food, and a running tap or pet fountain. Wet food adds water too, and it matters most for their kidneys.

Cats chew plastic and string for the crinkle and the texture, and it is usually boredom or hunting that has nowhere to go: a wand-toy game before meals, a cardboard box to shred and a chew-safe toy give her something better to do. Keep bags, rubber bands, hair ties, tinsel and string out of reach, because a cat that swallows them can get a linear blockage that needs surgery. If she has swallowed string or tinsel, or is being sick or off her food, ring the vet today rather than watching it.

Cats eat grass now and then and it is mostly harmless: the blades tickle the stomach so she brings up a hairball or settles an upset tummy. Check the grass has not been treated with weedkiller, and see the vet if she is sick every time or off her food.

Cayenne is hot: about 30,000 to 50,000 Scoville, so a quarter teaspoon heats a whole pot. It has little taste of its own, which is why it is the thing to reach for when a dish needs heat and not another flavour.

Cellulitis is a skin infection that turns an area red, hot, swollen and tender and keeps spreading, most often on a lower leg: it needs antibiotics the same day, so ring the GP or 111, and draw a line round the edge with a pen so you can see whether it is shrinking. Get seen urgently if it is on the face or near an eye, if the skin blisters or goes dark, or if there is a fever with shivering and feeling very unwell.

Celsius freezes water at 0 and boils it at 100; Fahrenheit puts the same two marks at 32 and 212, so a Fahrenheit degree is the smaller one. To convert, multiply the Celsius figure by 1.8 and add 32 - body heat is 37C or 98.6F, and a hot day is 30C or 86F.

Change nothing but the aim: same stance, same grip, same speed every throw, elbow up, and a follow-through that finishes with your hand pointing at the target. Practise in blocks - 20 darts at treble 20, then 20 at the doubles round the board, and always finish on a double. If the darts drift, slow the throw down rather than throwing harder; speed is what scatters them.

Change or cancel it at any time: ring the company to move the date or the amount, and if they will not, tell your bank to cancel it, then confirm with the company so the paperwork agrees. The Direct Debit Guarantee means the bank has to refund a wrong payment in full and straight away, so an amount you never agreed is their problem, not yours. If the bill itself went up, send a real meter reading first - an estimated one is the usual cause - then ask them to spread the rest of the year instead of taking it all at once.

Change that password now, and change it anywhere you used the same one, because that is what gets tried next; a password manager makes that ten minutes' work rather than an afternoon. Then check the account's own security page for devices and sessions you do not recognise and sign them out, and turn on two-factor with an app rather than a text if it offers one. If money is involved, ring the bank on the number on your card.

Change the sleep timer, not the lid. On Windows, Settings > System > Power & battery > Screen and sleep: set 'Put my device to sleep after' to Never or 30 minutes, once on battery and once plugged in. On a Mac, System Settings > Lock Screen for the display and Battery > Options for 'Prevent automatic sleeping on power adapter'. On a tablet it is Settings > Display > Screen timeout, or Auto-Lock on an iPad. If it still sleeps while you are typing, the screensaver or the maker's own power app is doing it.

Change the water every three to four months, or after about thirty uses, whichever comes first: a 4 to 6 person tub holds 1,000 to 1,500 litres, so check the level weekly with the hose and the chemicals, and do a full change when the water stops holding chlorine. To empty, hook a hose on the drain valve at the bottom into a drain, or drop a sump pump in, because a tub of chlorinated water kills the lawn and burns a border. Then flush the pipes with a line cleaner, wipe the shell with bicarbonate of soda rather than a detergent, and refill through the filter.

Change the cable and the port first: a tired HDMI or DisplayPort lead loses the signal for a second and the monitor goes to standby, so try the other port and a lead you know works. Then stop the machine sleeping the screen - on Windows Settings > System > Power > Screen and sleep, and turn off the monitor's own power saving in its menu. A monitor that clicks off and shows 'no signal' is the cable or the graphics driver; one that goes black with the power light still on is usually the backlight, which is a repair.

Change the cable first, because a tired HDMI lead loses the picture for a second and the set shows 'no signal': unplug both ends and push them back in, then try the other HDMI port and a lead you know works. Check the input with the remote (Source or Input) so the TV is on the socket the box is in, and if it is a set-top box, aerial or satellite, restart that box at the wall rather than the TV. A set that says 'no signal' while the power light is on is nearly always the cable or the source; a picture that goes and comes back on its own is the cable or a loose aerial.

Change both batteries - two AAA in nearly all of them, with the shape of the tray showing which way round - and check they are the right way round: a remote that needs the button pressed hard is a battery on its way out - then test it: point it at a phone camera and watch the little light on the end through the screen, which shows on a working remote and never does on a dead one. A remote that tests fine but does nothing is usually unpaired (a Bluetooth or voice remote, paired by holding the two buttons the manual names while the TV is on) or it is sending to the box rather than the set. The channel's own app will run the set while you sort it out.

Change a tampon every four to six hours and never leave one in for more than eight, so take it out before bed rather than sleep through with the same one. Use the lowest absorbency that still lasts four hours, wash your hands before and after, and if one has been in longer than that take it out now and watch for a fever, a rash like sunburn, vomiting, dizziness or a sore throat: that is toxic shock syndrome, which is rare but serious, so ring 111 for advice. Contact lenses and retainers have their own limits, and pads rather than tampons are the answer during pregnancy and for the first weeks after a baby.

Change down before the hill rather than on it, into a gear you can turn at about 70 to 80 turns of the pedals a minute: that keeps you seated, and standing up costs more energy than it looks. Sit up with your hands on the tops of the bars so your chest stays open, and breathe in time with the pedal strokes. If the easiest gear is still too hard, a cassette with a bigger bottom sprocket is the real fix.

Change it every three months, or sooner if the bristles splay: a worn brush cleans much less well. Electric brush heads are the same, rinsing it after use and letting it dry upright, and swap it after any illness if it has been in a shared pot.

Changed your mind? Bought online, by phone or by post, you have 14 days from the day it arrives to say so and another 14 to send it back, for any reason, and the refund covers the standard delivery. Bought in a shop there is no automatic right, so it comes down to their policy - take it back with the receipt and the tags on and ask for a refund, and a goodwill credit note is a fair answer if the policy says no.

Charcoal (about 1kg for ten people), a chimney starter and firelighters, long tongs, a wire brush, a tray for the cooked meat, and a meat thermometer. Put a bucket of water or sand beside it; a gas one needs a spare bottle instead.

Charge it for half an hour on a cable you know works, then hold the power button for ten seconds: on an iPhone, press volume up, volume down, then hold the side button until the Apple logo shows. If nothing happens at all, try a different charger and leave it an hour before you assume the worst.

Charles Darwin (1809-1882) was the naturalist whose 1859 book On the Origin of Species set out evolution by natural selection: the individuals best suited to their surroundings pass on their traits. He reached it after five years aboard HMS Beagle, and it is still the basis of all modern biology.

Chase it through the route you applied by, with the reference number and the date the application was received, rather than a general enquiry line. Ask for it to be marked urgent if travel is booked and send proof of the booking. Keep the reference in the email thread so nobody has to start the story again.

Chase it in the order of cheapness: the chainring bolts, the pedal threads (a drop of grease and a tighten), the seatpost and saddle clamp, then the crank bolts. A click once per pedal stroke that only happens when you push hard is usually the bottom bracket, and one that comes when you are out of the saddle is the headset or the stem bolts. A loose crank or headset wears the frame, so find it this month.

Chase it in writing and in steps, because the paper is what wins later: on the day it is due, one short email with the invoice attached and a new date; a week later, a firmer one that says what happens next; after that, a letter before action giving 14 days. Then use the money claim online, which handles claims up to £10,000 for a fee that is added to what they owe. A business debt also carries statutory interest at 8% above the Bank of England base rate from the due date, plus a fixed sum of £40 to £100 depending on the size of the debt - say so in the letter, because it is enough to make most late payers move. Stop doing new work for them the day the first payment is missed, and never hand over the finished work before the deposit.

Cheap is fine if the fit and the sole are right: supermarket own-brands are £10 to £25, and an outlet or the January sales gets a good pair at £25 to £35 rather than £50. Check for a thumb's width at the toe, room across the widest part and a sole you can bend - a school-age child will need the next size in four to six months.

Cheapest is the one you can actually get. If you claim Universal Credit, ask for a social tariff first: BT Home Essentials, Sky Broadband Basics and Virgin Essential are about £15 to £20 a month and need no new line. Otherwise compare the whole 18 months rather than the first-year price, because the price rises partway through and since January 2025 the contract has to tell you the rise in pounds, not a formula, so read that figure in the summary before you sign; a cashback deal through a comparison site is often worth £60 to £100 on top. At renewal, ask for the new-customer price before you switch - it usually works.

Check roaming is on in Settings > Mobile data, and that you have a roaming pass for that country, since most UK networks charge about £2 a day in the EU and much more outside it. Then turn the phone off and on so it re-registers, and set the network selection to automatic in Mobile data > Network selection.

Check the obvious one first: signal, then mobile data off for iMessages and on for MMS, then the message centre number (Settings > Apps > Messages > Message centre). If it is one contact only, their number may now be wrong or blocked; if no text at all will send, restart the phone and try a normal-length text with no picture, because a big photo with weak signal fails silently.

Check the online account and the award letter first: a change of circumstances, bank details that failed or a sanction all stop a payment showing, and the letter says which. Ring the number on the latest letter the same day and ask why, and ask for a hardship payment if there is nothing coming in - it is repayable from future awards. Keep a note of who you spoke to and when.

Check the pack first, because most prawns are sold already cooked: those only need thawing, and a cooked prawn is safe to eat cold once it has defrosted overnight in the fridge. Raw prawns are grey rather than pink, and those have to be cooked all the way through until they curl, turn pink and are opaque in the middle - 2 to 3 minutes in a hot pan or 1 to 2 minutes in boiling water, and you can put them in frozen with a minute or two extra. Thawed prawns keep a day, do not go back in the freezer, and in pregnancy eat only the thoroughly cooked ones. Bin any that smell of ammonia or feel slimy.

Check the phone's own settings before blaming the network: airplane mode off, mobile data on, and Settings > Mobile > Network selection set to Automatic. Restart the phone, then take the SIM out and put it back. If a phone beside it has signal and yours does not, the SIM or the phone is the fault; if neither has any, the network is down.

Check the plug and the socket first, then the fuse in the plug, and press the set's own power button on the side or underneath rather than the remote, because a flat remote looks exactly like a dead television. If the standby light is on but the screen stays black, shine a torch at it: a picture you can just see means the backlight has gone, which is a repair; no light at all usually means the power board.

Check the policy before you spend, because the deadline is the thing people lose money to: most employers want receipts within a month or the tax year. Photograph every receipt the day you get it, put the claim in as one list with the date, the reason and the amount, and use your own car's mileage rate if you drive - 45p a mile for the first 10,000 business miles in the tax year and 25p a mile after that (24p a motorcycle, 20p a bicycle). If a claim is refused, ask for the policy in writing; anything you spend that is wholly for the job and not reimbursed can be claimed against tax. Working at home is the same idea: claim £6 a week flat rate from HMRC without receipts, or the actual extra costs of broadband and heating if they are higher.

Check the pressure gauge (1 to 1.5 bar), the thermostat and the boiler's reset button, and make sure the programmer is on the hour you think it is; a pressure top-up or a reset fixes a lot of no-heat mornings. The checks take ten minutes. In a cold snap, the white condensate pipe outside can freeze and stop the boiler, so pour warm water along it. If it locks out twice, or you smell gas, stop and call a Gas Safe engineer: gas is not a DIY job.

Check the programme first: a 30C or a cold wash never heats much, and many machines have a cold-only option that stops the element coming on. If it is a hot programme and the door glass is still cold after twenty minutes, the element is the usual cause - a cheap part that an engineer swaps in half an hour - and the thermostat that reads the water or the relay on the board are the next two. A machine that heats on some programmes but not others is a board fault, not the element.

Check the programmer first: a light on ADVANCE or ON rather than AUTO is a button pressed by accident, and a room thermostat left high keeps the heating running. If the radiators heat up when the hot water is on, the diverter valve has stuck and wants replacing - about 150 to 250 pounds fitted, and worth doing before winter. A frost stat firing on a cold night is normal.

Check the rate you booked: a flexible rate is free to cancel up to a stated day, usually 24 to 48 hours before, and a saver rate is usually non-refundable - that is why it was cheaper. Cancel in the app rather than by phone so you have the confirmation, and if the hotel cancels on you, ask for a room of the same standard or a full refund plus the cost of a replacement if nothing is left.

Check the signal first: on a phone the call bars are not the data bars, so look at how many show while you are on a call, and if it is one or none, the fix is wifi calling (Settings > Phone > Wifi Calling on an iPhone, Phone app > Settings > Wifi calling on Android) so calls go over your broadband. Then restart the phone, take the case off if it covers the microphone, and clean the microphone hole with a dry brush - a muffled 'can you hear me' at one end is usually fluff, not the network.

Check the silent switch first: the little switch on the left side of an iPhone, or Do Not Disturb and the Focus modes on either phone, which are easy to leave on by accident. Then open the contact and make sure they are not on the block list, and check the ringtone is not set to None and the volume for ringtone is up (Android keeps a separate call volume). If it still goes straight to voicemail, that is the network: ring your provider and ask whether calls are being diverted.

Check the source before the set: press the input or source button on the remote and make sure it is on the socket the box is plugged into, then push the HDMI lead in at both ends and swap it for another one if you have a spare. If the sound carries on while the picture dies, the backlight is the usual fault on a TV; on a monitor it is more often the cable, a sleeping screen saver or the sleep timer. Power it off at the wall for a whole minute before you decide it needs repairing.

Check the thermostat and the programmer first: a timer slipped to water only, a room stat turned down, or flat batteries in a wireless one are the commonest cold houses. Then look at the boiler's pressure gauge (1 to 1.5 bar cold) and top it up at the filling loop, and press reset once. In a cold snap the condensate pipe outside can freeze, so pour warm water along it. If it still will not fire, or you smell gas, that is a Gas Safe engineer.

Check the volume on the phone rather than the headphones first, then unplug and replug the jack or forget the pairing and pair again: a headset that works on another device is the phone's setting (some phones mute Bluetooth and wired separately). If it went quiet in one ear only, the mesh over that driver is blocked with wax - brush it dry.

Check the weight and the cord length before anything else, because the best vacuum is the one you will actually push round the house. A bagged machine holds its suction and suits anyone with allergies; a bagless one is cheaper to run but needs emptying over a bin. A cordless is a quick-clean tool and rarely enough on its own in a carpeted house, so try one for weight and check the filters can be washed.

Check the wheel is sitting all the way home in the dropouts and the quick release or through-axle is shut first, because a wheel half in looks exactly like a rubbing brake. Then loosen the caliper bolts a touch, squeeze the lever to centre the pads on the rim or disc, and tighten them again with the lever held. On discs, a pad that drags after a wheel change usually just needs the pistons pushed back with a tyre lever.

Check the battery before blaming the starter: switch the headlights on and crank, and if they stay bright while nothing turns over, the starter is the suspect. One loud click that repeats is the solenoid or a flat battery, a starter that whirs without turning the engine needs a garage, and a replacement is £150 to £300 fitted.

Check the bin first, because it keeps them for 30 days: Photos > Albums > Recently Deleted on an iPhone, or Photos > Bin on Android, and Google Photos has one too. If they are gone from there, look in the cloud account's own trash on a browser, and stop taking new photos so the space is not reused, because a recovery tool can only get back what has not been overwritten.

Check the box first: if it says modified release, extended release, MR, XL or SR, or that the tablet is film-coated or a capsule, do not crush, split or open it - the whole dose comes out at once. An ordinary plain tablet can usually be broken along the score line, or crushed and taken in water or yoghurt. Ask a pharmacist for the same medicine as a liquid or a dispersible tablet; they do that most days and it costs nothing to ask.

Check them on the Ofsted register first: search "Ofsted registered childcare" and the provider's page shows when they registered, the last inspection and any conditions. A registered childminder has an enhanced DBS check and paediatric first aid, and should show you both. Then ask which days they have room, how many children they already have then, and for two families you can ring.

Check two things before you sell: the trade-in price from the network or the maker, and what the same model with the same storage sells for on a resale site - the private sale is often 20 to 30% more. Say the battery health and any marks honestly, sign out of your accounts and factory reset it in front of the buyer.

Check what your employer pays first: many give six months full pay and half pay after that, and statutory sick pay alone is about £119 a week, so the gap you are insuring is the real question. If you have a mortgage or children and only statutory sick pay, income protection that pays out after 13 or 26 weeks is much cheaper than one that pays from day one, and a fee-free broker will price both. Skip critical illness cover sold alongside a mortgage until you have checked it is not already in the deal.

Check what it actually pays: under about 3% while prices rise means the money buys less each year, whatever the balance says. Move it to an account paying more - a regular saver or a one-year fix beats a branch account - keep three to six months of bills in easy access, and put money you will not touch for five years into a global tracker inside a stocks and shares ISA.

Check your neighbours' bands first: the valuation list is free online, and two identical houses on different bands is the evidence a challenge needs. In England and Wales you have six months from moving in; ask the council which route applies if that has passed. A challenge can raise the band as well as lower it, so ring the council about a wrong bill before you go to the valuer.

Check your operator's own figure the day before, because it is the one that counts: a cruise wants you at the terminal two to three hours before, a ferry an hour with a car and about thirty minutes on foot, and Eurostar asks for 75 to 90 minutes. Boarding closes before departure and a ship or a coach will not wait, so aim to be there early and take a book rather than cutting it fine.

Check Settings > Battery for the app using the most: social and video apps in the background are usually it, so restrict background refresh and turn the screen brightness down. If the phone is two or more years old, have a look at battery health, because a worn battery drains no matter what you switch off.

Check for ice crystals rather than counting the hours: anything still firm and icy can be cooked and eaten or put back, and nothing needs binning for the door alone. What went soft and warm goes in the bin - meat, fish, shellfish, cooked rice and milk most of all - and do not taste it to check. A fridge is the stricter one: milk, cooked meat, cooked rice and leftovers go if the door was open for more than about four hours, while butter, hard cheese, jam and pickles come through it. Melting ice cream is binned whatever it feels like, and a freezer that was open all night is worth running for an hour before you trust the ice.

Check in on the airline's app or website 24 to 48 hours before the flight and the pass appears there with a QR code - that is all most airports need, and it updates itself if the gate changes. Print it at home only if you would rather have paper or your phone battery is a worry, and the airport kiosks will print one either way.

Check in online as soon as it opens, usually 24 to 48 hours before a short-haul flight and up to 72 on some, and save the boarding pass into your phone wallet as well as your email: a screenshot works when the signal does not. Have your passport details to hand. If you are checking a bag, drop it before the airline's cut-off, which is usually 45 to 60 minutes before departure and a full two hours at some airports, and if you would rather check in at the desk, get there about three hours before the flight: the desks close on that same timetable, queue and all.

Check it where they are: whether it is swollen or bruising fast, whether they will use it at all, and whether it looks bent. Ice it for 15 minutes, keep it raised, and give children's paracetamol if their age allows. A limb they will not use or let you move, one that looks bent, or swelling that comes up fast is A&E the same day; a bang on the head with sickness, drowsiness or a knockout is 999.

Checkmate is a king in check with no legal way out: no square to move to, nothing to block with, and nothing that can take the piece giving check. Being in check is not checkmate - you can move the king, block the line or take the attacker, and only if none of those work is the game over. Stalemate is the other ending, and it is a draw: the king is not in check but has no legal move, which is why you never chase a lone king into the corner without giving it a square.

Cheese, chutney and an apple; cream cheese with smoked salmon or cucumber; hummus and something crunchy; butter and a sliced boiled egg with salt and pepper. Anything soft wants something crisp on it, and anything dry wants something wet.

Cheese and beans, tuna mayo, coleslaw, chilli or last night's bolognese: butter and salt first, then the topping, and back in the oven for 5 minutes if you want the cheese melted. A wet filling wants something crisp alongside - a pickled onion, a handful of salad.

Cheese is calorie-dense - about 400 calories per 100g of cheddar - but a portion is only 30g, roughly a matchbox, and it brings calcium and protein with the fat. It is not a food to avoid, it is a food to weigh: grated rather than sliced goes further.

Chemotherapy is cancer drugs that travel through the whole body, given as a drip, as tablets or both, in cycles of a treatment day followed by a few weeks off so the body recovers. The drip itself does not hurt and takes an hour or a few depending on the drugs; a cannula or a line goes in first. The side effects that matter are the ones your team gives you drugs for in advance - sickness, a sore mouth, and above all an infection risk in the week after, so a temperature over 37.5C or feeling shivery is a phone call to the unit the same day, not a wait.

Chewy comes from soft brown sugar and pulling the tray out early: swap a third of the caster sugar for light muscovado, add an extra yolk, and take them out while the middles still look underdone, because they carry on setting on the hot tray.

Chicken is the one to be strict about: a sour or ammonia smell, a tacky or slimy feel, or any change of colour means bin it, and cooking it will not make it safe. Raw chicken keeps 1 to 2 days in the fridge and cooked chicken 3; if it has sat out warm for more than 2 hours, that is enough on its own.

Chicken is lean protein - about 30g in a breast for 160 calories - so it is what you cook it in that matters. Skin off and not fried, it is one of the better everyday meats; the breaded and the deep-fried versions carry the fat.

Children's sight tests are free on the NHS in every part of the UK, and any optician who tests children can do one from about three - younger if there is a squint, a lazy eye in the family, or the child was premature. There is also a screening check at school in the first year. Do not wait for the child to say something: sitting close to the telly, tilting the head, rubbing the eyes or one eye turning are the usual signs.
Chilli oil is as hot as the chillies that went into it - usually medium, around 10,000 Scoville - and the crisp bits are hotter than the oil. A teaspoon over noodles.

Chilli powder is a blend, usually mild to medium with cumin and oregano in it, so the heat depends on the jar - some are mostly cayenne. Taste a pinch on your tongue before you decide how much goes in.
Chilli flakes are medium-hot, around 30,000 to 50,000 Scoville, and they give their heat slowly: a pinch in oil at the start is warmer than the same pinch scattered at the end.

Chilli heat is not real heat: capsaicin switches on the same nerve receptors as a burn, so your mouth reports fire. Milk, yoghurt or ice cream settle it because the fat and milk protein lift the capsaicin away; water and beer just spread it round.

Chillies are ready from late summer: pick green for a milder heat, or leave them on to turn red for the fullest flavour. Cut them with a short stalk and keep picking, because a plant left to ripen stops setting new fruit.

Chisel and plane iron: the bevel is 25 degrees off the flat back, so a honing guide set to 25 and a strip of wet-and-dry on a flat tile does it - 240 grit if the edge is nicked, then 600 and 1200, ten strokes on the bevel, then lay the back flat on the finest paper and pull it back a few times to take the burr off. A blunt chisel crushes the wood and takes more force to steer, so it is the sharp one that is safer. A masonry bit is blunt when the tip is rounded: a few strokes of a diamond file on the wings either side of the point, at the angle they already have, brings it back. An HSS bit filed by hand is slow going and a new one costs a few pounds, so buy a bit rather than an afternoon; a Drill Doctor type jig, about £30, earns its place only if you go through a lot of them. In a utility knife, swap the blade: a snap-off blade is sharper than anything you can dress at home.

Chit the seed potatoes somewhere light and cool, in an egg box, until the sprouts are 2-3cm long, then plant them from late March. A 40-litre bag or a 30cm pot takes three seed potatoes: 10-15cm of compost in the bottom, sit them on it, cover them with another 10cm and water. When the shoots are 15cm above the compost, earth them up - cover all but the top few centimetres with more compost - and keep doing that until the bag is nearly full, because tubers that form near the surface turn green in the light.

Chocolate keeps about a year in a cool, dry cupboard, not the fridge, where condensation brings out a white bloom. The bloom is sugar or fat rather than mould, so it is still fine to eat; a bar that has been warm goes grey and grainy and is only good for melting.

Cholesterol is a waxy fat the body needs for cell walls and hormones, and the liver makes most of it; the rest comes from food. The number that matters most is the LDL ('bad') part, which can clog arteries, and diet, exercise and sometimes a statin bring it down.

Choose on the modules in years two and three, not the course title: read them, and if half of them bore you the course is wrong whatever it is called. Then check the entry requirements against your predicted grades, the contact hours and whether a placement or a year in industry is offered, and the graduate outcomes page for where last year's students went. Go to an open day and sit in one lecture if you can, because a department feels like something on the day. Apply to five with one dream and two safe choices, and keep the one you would be happy at if the grades go wrong.

Choose something short you can actually get through: a poem, a psalm or a few lines from a book they loved, read by somebody other than the closest person if you can. Two readings is plenty for a crematorium slot, five to ten minutes of speaking in all. Read it aloud twice at home first and give the reader a printed copy in a large font; the celebrant or the funeral director will read it for you if nobody in the family can.
Chris Evans plays Captain America: The First Avenger (2011) through Avengers: Endgame (2019).
Chris Hemsworth plays Thor, from Thor (2011) to Thor: Love and Thunder (2022).

Christian Bale plays Batman in the Dark Knight trilogy: Batman Begins (2005), The Dark Knight (2008) and The Dark Knight Rises (2012). Heath Ledger played the Joker in The Dark Knight, and Tom Hardy played Bane.

Chronic kidney disease in a dog is the kidneys losing their filtering slowly, usually found on a blood test in an older dog, and it is managed rather than cured - many dogs live comfortably for a year or two, some much longer. A prescription renal diet is the main thing: lower phosphate and moderate protein, and it works best started early, so ask the vet whether to switch now. Have the blood pressure and the urine protein checked too, because both are treatable and both make it worse; phosphate binders, a potassium supplement and something for sickness are added if needed. Bloods every three to six months, and the weight at home. Ring the vet this week if your dog stops eating, loses weight, is sick, drinks far more or seems dull, and the same day if it has not eaten for a whole day.

Chronic kidney disease is the kidneys slowly losing their filtering over months to years: it is the commonest long illness of an older cat, it is found on bloods rather than by looking, and most cats found early live for years with it. A prescription renal diet - wet food lower in phosphate and protein - is the one thing shown to slow it, and any wet food she will eat beats dry. Have the vet check her blood pressure and her urine protein as well as the bloods, since high blood pressure is treatable and causes the sudden blindness. Bloods and urine every three to six months, and her weight once a month at home. Ring the vet this week if she stops eating, loses weight, drinks and wees far more, vomits or starts hiding away, and the same day if she has not eaten for a whole day or her breath smells of ammonia - not eating is what makes them worse fastest.
Cinnamon is warm and sweet, not hot. The sticks sold cheaply are cassia, which is stronger and slightly bitter - fine in a curry, and worth knowing if a recipe came out tasting of cloves.

Claim the flat rate: HMRC lets you claim £6 a week (£312 a year) for working from home without keeping a single receipt, and you can go back up to four tax years. If you are employed, claim online or with form P87; if you already send a tax return, put it in the employment expenses section. Claim the real extra costs instead (a share of heat, light and broadband) only if they clearly beat £6 a week, and remember an employer allowance up to £6 a week is tax-free and needs no claim at all.

Claim from the shop you bought it from, not the warranty: in the UK the retailer owes you a repair or replacement for up to six years in England, Wales and Northern Ireland (five in Scotland), and a manufacturer's guarantee sits on top of that rather than replacing it. Put it in writing with the order number, the fault and the date, and ask for a repair, a replacement or a refund in that order. Out of warranty, ask anyway: a goodwill repair is common, and the card you paid with may carry its own cover.

Claim it in the room, lightly and factually: "As I put in Tuesday's note, the plan is...". If it keeps happening, one private sentence does more than a meeting fight: "When you presented that, it would help me if you said it came from me." Then put your ideas in writing and copy in whoever decides.

Clamp the head in a vice or hold the axe steady on a block and push a file away from the edge along the bevel, at the angle the bevel already has, until you feel a burr on the far side - then take two or three light strokes on that side to take it off. A file costs a few pounds and does less damage than a bench grinder, which heats the edge and takes the temper out of it; an axe only needs sharp enough to bite, not shaving sharp.
Claudia Sheinbaum is the president of Mexico: in office since October 2024, and the first woman to hold the job. A Mexican president serves one six-year term and cannot stand again.

Clay is a soil and rock material made of microscopic flat particles that pack tightly, so it holds water and feels sticky when wet and hard when dry. Pots and bricks are made from it because it can be shaped wet and keeps that shape when fired.

Clean the mesh on the quiet side with a dry toothbrush, because earwax is the usual culprit, then check the balance in your phone's accessibility audio settings is in the middle. If it is an AirPod, take it out and put it back in the case for ten seconds; if the other one has sound, the earbud is not dead.

Clean the cover and the blades first: a dust-clogged fan in a steamy room is both weak and loud, and the grille usually comes off with a push and the blades wipe with a damp cloth once the isolator is off. A rattle is normally the cover or the backdraught flap in the duct; a buzz or a grind means the bearing has gone, and a new fan is £25 to £60 for the part with about an hour of an electrician. A fan that runs on for ten or fifteen minutes after the light goes off is the timer doing its job and is what actually stops the damp; one that never stops has a stuck timer or a humidistat set too high, and the module is a swap.

Clean the filter at the bottom, wipe round the door seal, and run an empty hot cycle with a dishwasher cleaner or a bowl of white vinegar on the top rack. The problem is usually food and grease sitting in the filter and the door seal. Check the salt and rinse aid too: running out of either makes everything come out cloudy.

Clean the lens: it is a tiny piece of glass that collects fingerprints, and a dry microfibre cloth or a cotton bud with a breath on it is all it needs, never a tissue and never alcohol. Then check the camera app itself is not set to a low resolution, and that the light behind you is not the brightest thing in the frame, because a window at your back is what makes a face go dark and grainy.

Clean around it with a dry soft toothbrush and a puff of air, because grit and dried sweet drink are what wedge them, and never push oil or water in. Work the button gently a few dozen times with the phone off; if it is still stuck or the phone is now stuck in a boot loop, a shop replaces the flex cable for £30 to £70. Until then the on-screen volume slider does the job.

Clean it and let it dry: paint on a dirty or damp fence flakes within a year. Brush or spray a water-based fence stain rather than a film-forming paint, two coats on a dry day above 10C, keeping the bottom of the panel clear of the soil. A shed wants an oil or wood preserver, not a fence stain.

Clear the most expensive debt first - a credit card at 20% beats anything you can earn - then top the emergency fund back up to a month of essentials, and only then look at the pension or a stocks and shares ISA, where a lump sum can go in now and grow. Bonus tax is already taken through PAYE, so there is nothing to declare. Keep a tenth for something you actually want, or the plan never sticks.

Clear the queue first (Settings > Bluetooth and devices > Printers on Windows, Printers & Scanners on a Mac), because a stuck old job makes every new one crawl, and plug the printer in by cable to see whether wifi is the problem rather than the machine. After that it is the file and the setting: a photo or a long PDF takes a minute a page on a cheap inkjet, so drop the quality from Best to Normal and print a few pages at a time.

Clear the screen before you set off, because it is a legal requirement: front demist on, air conditioning on (it dries the air), heat up and the air on fresh rather than recirculate. A clean inside windscreen stops the mist coming back; shaving foam polished off works for a week.

Clear the cache rather than the data: on Android it is Settings > Apps > the app > Storage > Clear cache, and on an iPhone the same space goes by offloading the app (Settings > General > iPhone Storage > Offload App), which keeps your logins. In a browser, clear cached images and files only, and you stay signed in everywhere.

Clear the cupboard the meters are in and take a photo of the readings first, because the old ones go with the fitter. Someone over 18 has to be in, and it takes about an hour per fuel; the gas and electricity go off for a few minutes each. The fitter should leave the in-home display set up and working, and the old meters away - if a display is not showing, ring the supplier rather than living with it.
Clearing your head means stepping away for a bit - a walk, fresh air, no screens - so the thinking gets easier. What is crowding it?

Clearing a blocked drain is usually £80 to £200 with rods or a pressure jet, and a camera survey to find the cause is £150 to £300 on top. Roots and collapsed pipework are the expensive cases. Ask whether the price includes the survey and the waste removal, and if the blockage is in the pipe the water company owns, ring them first because they clear it free.

Click the speaker icon in the corner and check it is not muted and the right device is chosen - a laptop will happily send the sound to an HDMI lead or a headset that has gone away. Then try it with nothing plugged in: if the speakers work, the jack socket is the fault; if not, reinstall the sound driver from the maker's own site.

Clicking, clunking or a catching feeling around a new joint is usually the soft tissue moving over the new parts, and it is common while the muscles are still settling - keep up the exercises the team gave you and mention it at your next check. Ring the ward that did the operation, or 111, the same day if the joint is hot, red or more painful than it was, if you have a fever or the wound is weeping, or if the joint gives way or you cannot put your weight on it.

Clip each pair together or put them in a mesh washing bag before they go in. When one goes missing, check the door seal first: the fold of the rubber is where most singles end up. Then the filter, under the drum paddles, and inside a duvet cover or a trouser leg. Keep the orphans in a bag and pair them up a month later.

Close the tabs you are not reading: each one costs memory, and twenty open tabs will make any machine crawl. Restart the browser, then remove the extensions you do not recognise; a fresh profile or clearing the cache is the next step.

Close the blinds flat and wipe them with a microfibre cloth or a sock over your hand, then turn them the other way and do the back; a vacuum brush does a whole set in minutes. Skip the duster that just moves the dust around.

Close the door on a sheet of paper and pull it out: it should drag, and a note that slides out easily at that spot is a gap. Wipe the seal with hot soapy water and dry it, because a sticky or crumpled seal often shuts fine once it is clean, then check the door hinge has not dropped. A split or hardened seal is a part: the model number is on a sticker inside the fridge, and a new one is usually £20 to £40 and pushes into the channel by hand.

Close every other app that might be holding the camera, then check the permission: on Windows, Settings > Privacy & security > Camera, and on a Mac, System Settings > Privacy & Security > Camera, and switch your app on. A laptop with a sliding shutter over the lens is the other common one. A plug-in webcam: try another USB port and another app before blaming the camera.

Close it with a reason and a warm line rather than fading out: name the thing you have to get to, say one true thing about the time, then go. "I'm going to have to head off - I'm so glad we got to talk" or "I'd better get on, but it was really good to catch up." Have your reason ready in one line because the next question is always why, and don't apologise twice; leaving when you said you would is kinder than drifting about waiting for a gap.

Close it with a reason and a warm line rather than fading out: name the thing you have to get to, say one true thing about the conversation, then go. "I'm going to have to head off - I'm so glad you told me about the job" or "Right, I'd better get on, but it was good to catch up." Give the reason first, because people hear the reason as respect, and keep it about the time rather than the person. If someone is mid-ramble, wait for a full stop and step in with their name; if you are on the phone, stand up and say you have to go. End with something that opens the next time - "next week?", "text me when you hear" - so it reads as a pause and not a brush-off.

Close it with a reason and a warm line, then move: "I'll let you go - it's been really good to catch up." Turning it round to them is the trick, because "I'll let you get back to it" ends the call without anyone being brushed off. In person, say one thing you want to come back to ("I want to hear how the move went - let's get a coffee next week"), then go; a promise to continue is what makes leaving feel friendly rather than rude.

Cloudy glasses and white marks are hard water and rinse aid running out: fill the salt and rinse aid, then run the hottest cycle with a dishwasher cleaner. Glasses washed by hand go cloudy from too much washing-up liquid and water that's too hot, so use less and let them air dry instead of towelling them.
Cloves are warm and very strong, not hot, and two or three in a pot is enough. Too many and the dish tastes of the dentist.

Clumped salt has taken damp, not gone off: break it up with the back of a spoon and it still tastes of salt and works the same in cooking. A few grains of rice or a piece of dry cracker in the jar keeps it running, and a lidded jar in a dry cupboard keeps it clump-free where the paper packet does not.

Cocktail dress code means short dresses or a smart top and skirt for women, and a suit or smart jacket and trousers for men: dressy, but not formal long gowns or full black tie. Heels you can stand in for two hours matter more than height.

Cocoa beans grow in pods on trees in the tropics; they are fermented, dried, roasted and ground, and the fat that comes out with the powder - cocoa butter - is what makes chocolate smooth enough to melt on your tongue.

Coffee beans are the seeds of a cherry that grows on bushes in the tropics, mostly in a band round the equator. The picked fruit is dried, the two seeds inside are removed and roasted, and the roast is what turns them brown and flavours the drink.

Cold milk in a jar with a lid, shaken hard for 30 seconds and then 30 seconds in the microwave, gives a real foam with no machine, and a French press pumped up and down 15 times does the same. Whole milk froths best because the fat holds the bubbles, and stop heating at about 60 to 65C - past that the foam collapses and the milk tastes scalded.

Cold or strong emotion makes tiny muscles pull your hairs upright, which traps a layer of air for warmth and made our furry ancestors look bigger. We have kept the reflex even though we no longer have the fur for it to work.

Cold pasta is best fried: toss it in a hot pan with oil, garlic and whatever vegetables you have, and add a splash of water or passata so it doesn't stick. Or bake it in a white sauce with cheese on top for 20 minutes at 200C.

Cold pizza is fine if it went into the fridge within a couple of hours of arriving: eat it within 3 days, and reheat it to piping hot if you want it hot again - a splash of water in the pan or 10 minutes in a hot oven brings the base back. Pizza left out overnight is the one to throw away.

Cold water only, and plenty of it: hot water sets blood into the fibre. Blot the mark with a cloth wrung out in cold water, work in a little washing-up liquid or a dab of biological detergent, then blot again with clean water. On a mattress, use as little water as you can and dry it well with a towel so the filling does not stay damp.

Cold, dry air narrows the airways, so most people with asthma cough and wheeze more in winter: breathe through a scarf over your nose and mouth for the first few minutes, warm up slowly, and take the blue inhaler ten minutes before cold exercise if your nurse advised it. Keep the preventer going every day, get the flu jab, and see your asthma nurse if you need the blue inhaler more than three times a week - that is the sign it is not controlled.

Cold air does not damage healthy lungs: it is dry and it warms on the way in, so a run or a ride in the cold is fine. Start slower for the first ten minutes, cover your hands and ears, and wear a layer you can tie round your waist. If you have asthma, take your inhaler before you go out and warm up indoors first, and use a buff over your mouth on very cold days.

Cold cooked rice is best fried: hot oil, an egg, soy sauce and whatever veg is in the drawer, 4 minutes. On hot rice, a curry or a chilli ladled over it is dinner, and cold rice with tuna, sweetcorn and mayo is a lunch - the rice wants a day old for either, because fresh rice steams instead of frying.

Cold cream, a cold bowl and a big balloon whisk: whip in a steady circle, keeping the whisk under the surface so you beat air in rather than flick it over the side. Double cream takes 2 to 3 minutes by hand and stiffens just as the trails stop disappearing. Stop a moment before it looks ready, because it goes grainy fast; a splash of milk whisked in rescues one that has gone too far.

Cold does not damage joints, it makes them feel stiffer: muscles and the fluid inside the joint move less freely when you are cold, so an old injury or arthritis aches more in winter. Keep it moving - a walk, a warm shower in the morning, layers over the knees - and see a GP if a joint is hot, swollen, locking or waking you at night.

Cold for a fresh knock and heat for a stiff, old ache. Ice in the first 48 hours of a sprain, a bump or a pulled muscle: a bag of frozen peas or an ice pack wrapped in a tea towel, 15 to 20 minutes at a time, every two or three hours, never straight on the skin and never for longer, because that burns. After that, heat - a hot water bottle, a wheat bag or a warm bath, 15 to 20 minutes - loosens a muscle that has tightened up, so it is the one for a stiff neck or a back that has been bad for days. Never heat a fresh injury, a hot swollen joint or anywhere you cannot feel properly, and do not use either on broken skin. Heat on a sprain after two days is fine; ice on a stiff neck is not. If the joint is hot, very swollen or you cannot use it, that is a look-at-it-today rather than a compress.

Cold hands and feet are usually just circulation: the body pulls blood in from the skin when you are cold. Warm the whole body, not just the hands - gloves, thick socks, a hat, a warm drink - and flex the fingers and toes. White, then blue, then red and painful in the cold is Raynaud's, and keeping the wrists warm helps. See a GP if it is one hand only, or comes with tiredness or weight change.

Coleslaw keeps 3 days in the fridge once it is opened, and homemade 2, because it is the mayonnaise that turns. Keep the tub cold and eat it by the date on it, and bin slaw that smells sharp or has gone watery in the bottom of the tub.

Colic is crying in long bouts, mostly in the evening, that eases off by three or four months; it does not mean anything is wrong. Try simeticone drops (Infacol) before feeds, a clockwise rub of the tummy, bicycle legs, feeds sat upright, and a sling or white noise, one at a time. See the GP the same day for a temperature, green vomit, blood in the nappy or poor feeding. Gripe water is not licensed for babies; simeticone is.

Colleges usually ask for five GCSEs at grade 4 or above, including maths and English, and a sixth form taking A levels often wants a 6 in the subjects you pick - a 6 in maths for maths, for instance. The points people talk about are just that arithmetic: a grade 4 is worth 4, so five grade 4s is 20 points, and each college publishes what it asks for. If English or maths is below 4, most colleges will let you take it alongside the course rather than turn you away, so ring admissions with the exact course and ask.

Combustion is burning: a fuel reacts with oxygen and gives out heat and light, usually leaving carbon dioxide and water. It needs fuel, oxygen and enough heat to start, which is why a fire goes out when you cut off the air.

Coming off is a fall, so check the head first: a bang that knocked them out, made them sick, left them confused or gave them a bad headache is A&E the same day, and so is anything they cannot remember. Most falls land on a hand or a shoulder, and a wrist that cannot take weight or an arm that cannot be lifted across the chest is worth an X-ray today - the collarbone is the break people miss. Grazes want cool running water, a dressing and no scrubbing. Ice a bruise for 20 minutes at a time with a cloth round it, take paracetamol or ibuprofen if you can, and expect it to be stiffer tomorrow than today. A helmet that took the hit is finished, even with no crack you can see.

Command-C copies, Command-V pastes and Command-X cuts - the Command key sits either side of the space bar, where Control is on a Windows keyboard. In a Mac app the same commands are under the Edit menu if you would rather click.

Compare the price per 100g on the shelf label, not the pack size: bigger packs are often, but not always, cheaper. Own-brand staples (rice, pasta, tinned tomatoes, oats) are usually the same product, and the savings there pay for the things you care about.

Compare the reading on the bill with the numbers on your meter first: an estimated reading, often after a supplier change, is the commonest cause of a shock bill, and sending a real reading puts it right. After that it's usually the season (heating), the immersion or a heater left on, or a fridge or freezer seal failing, so read the meter once a day for a week with everything off and see what still ticks up.

Compare the exact model across two or three shops, and check its price history first: a "was £500" tag is often a week old. For appliances the cheapest safe route is usually refurbished or graded stock with a real warranty, or ex-display if you ask. Buy at the end of the season or when a new model lands, and pay by credit card over £100 for the extra protection.

Compare the AER rather than the headline rate, and pick instant access for money you might need and a one or two-year fix for money you won't. Watch for a bonus rate that drops after a year, and keep under £85,000 with one bank so the protection scheme covers all of it.

Compare the APR and the total repayable rather than the monthly payment: £5,000 at 8 per cent over three years comes back as about £5,650, and a longer term lowers the payment while raising that total. Your own bank and a credit union are the cheap end, and a credit union lends on your circumstances rather than a score, so bad credit is not an automatic no. A guarantor helps more than a payday lender, where £300 for a month can cost £90; if you are already behind, StepChange gives free advice before you borrow again.

Compatible cartridges cost a third of the branded ones and work in most printers, so check the model number and buy those online. Before replacing one, take it out and give it a gentle shake and wipe the gold contacts with a dry cloth, which often gets a few more pages out of a cartridge that is only streaky; set the printer to draft or greyscale to make a cartridge last much longer.

Complain to the practice manager first, in writing, and ask for the treatment plan, the notes and an itemised invoice. NHS treatment goes on to the NHS complaints team at your local integrated care board; private treatment goes free to the Dental Complaints Service, which can refund fees within 12 months. Work you did not agree to is not owed, so say so in the same letter, and photograph the tooth before anyone touches it.

Complain to the provider first and ask for a deadlock letter if it isn't fixed; phone and broadband disputes then go free to an independent ombudsman. If the service is unusable and you're in contract, most providers have to let you leave without a fee.

Complain to the shop first, in writing, and keep it to facts: what you bought, when, what went wrong, what you want and by when. Use email or the online form rather than the phone so there is a record, and give them 14 days. If they do not fix it, escalate inside the company - ask for the complaints procedure and the name of the person dealing with it - then go outside: Citizens Advice or Trading Standards for a legal point, the relevant ombudsman for a service, and the small claims track for money you are owed. Card payment is your spare lever: a claim under section 75 over 100 pounds, or a chargeback under it.

Complain to the supplier in writing and ask for a deadlock letter if they will not fix it: after eight weeks, or straight away with that letter, the Energy Ombudsman takes the case free and can order a refund or compensation. Keep the bills, the readings and the dates you called. If a direct debit you did not agree to has been taken, tell your bank as well.

Complain to the bank first, in the app or by phone, and ask for the complaint reference: they have eight weeks to give you a final answer. If they have not settled it by then, or you do not accept what they say, the Financial Ombudsman Service takes it on free and independently, and you have six months from their final answer to go there. Keep the dates, the amounts and what you were told each time. A charge you did not agree to, a fraud the bank refused to refund and a mis-sold product all go the same way.

Complain to the bank in writing first and keep the date: it has 8 weeks to give you a final answer, and often answers sooner. If you are not happy, the Financial Ombudsman Service is free and its decision binds the bank, and you keep the right to go to court instead. A bank closing your account has to give notice and tell you why, unless that would tip off a criminal.

Complain in writing to the rep while you're there and to the company when you're back, and photograph what's wrong: that record is what a claim rests on. A package holiday has to match what was advertised, so a closed pool or a filthy room is a price reduction or compensation, not bad luck.

Complain in writing, say what you want (a refund, a repair, an apology) and give them 14 days. If that fails, ask for a final response or deadlock letter and take it free to the relevant ombudsman; keep every email and reference number.

Condensation comes from warm wet air hitting cold surfaces, so ventilate and keep the place a bit warmer: use the extractor fan, open a window for 10 minutes a day, dry clothes outside or in a vented dryer, and leave the heating on low rather than off and on. A dehumidifier helps in a bedroom that gets it badly.

Condensation is water out of the air landing on a cold surface: the windows and the outer corners are wet in the morning, it clears when the room is aired, and it comes back on cold days. A leak is a patch that grows and stays wet whatever the weather, and rising damp only runs along the bottom metre of a wall, usually with a tide mark. To tell them apart, dry a patch with a hairdryer, tape a square of cling film over it tight and leave it three days: water on the room side of the film is condensation, a wall still wet behind it is water coming through.

Conduction is heat moving through a solid, passed from one particle to the next: a metal spoon left in soup gets hot to the handle while a wooden one does not, because metals carry heat well and wood does not.

Confidence comes after doing, not before, so pick one small uncomfortable thing - asking a question in a meeting, saying one sentence in a group, ringing instead of emailing - and do it until it is ordinary. Prepare the first thirty seconds of whatever frightens you, keep a note of the times it went fine, and measure yourself against yourself last month rather than against the loudest person in the room: the feeling follows the evidence, not the other way round.

Constant throat clearing is usually a drip down the back of the nose, from a cold, an allergy or a blocked nose - or dry air, or reflux, or plain habit. Rinse the nose with salt water or try a steroid spray, and sip water instead of clearing. See a GP if it lasts weeks, if the voice changes, or if you can feel a lump in the neck.

Contact lenses are usually £15 to £35 a month on a supply plan, and the fitting appointment at the start is £30 to £60. Daily disposables cost more per day than monthlies and need no cleaning, and the aftercare visit is often included in the plan. Ask what the plan includes, how often the checks are, and whether you can stop whenever you like.
