Contractions are fine in ordinary writing, emails and anything with a human voice, and they read as friendlier. In formal academic writing most style guides still prefer the full form - write "do not" rather than "don't" and you cannot be marked down for it.
Convection is heat carried by a moving fluid: warm air or water rises because it is lighter, cooler stuff sinks to take its place, and that loop is what heats a room and builds a thundercloud.

Cook one meal and serve it in parts, keeping the sauce, the vegetables and the meat apart, so the parts that are not wanted can be left without it being a scene. Say the thing you actually need once, at a calm moment rather than over the plate: one night a week they cook, or they sort their own dinner on the nights they do not want what is on. Keep a short list of meals you both eat and rotate those midweek, and try anything new at the weekend when nobody is tired. Policing the plate makes a fussy eater worse, and a handful of safe dinners eaten happily beats a row three nights a week.

Cook the pasta 2 minutes short of the packet, mix it with a sauce that is wetter than you think, top it and bake it 20 to 25 minutes at 200C (180C fan) until the top is browned and bubbling. Cover it with foil for the first 15 minutes and the middle stays loose instead of drying out.

Cook the potato on its own in unsalted water and mash it with a little of that water, some of their usual milk or a knob of unsalted butter, and no salt at all: babies under one should have none, and their kidneys cannot deal with it. Keep it smooth and a little looser than yours while they are learning to swallow, and add nothing else until you know they have had it before. Your health visitor is the one to ask about amounts and what to add next, because it depends on the baby's age.

Cook the same sort of dinner as for anyone, with the starchy part smaller and the vegetables bigger: chicken or fish with two veg, a chilli with beans instead of rice, or an omelette and salad. Halve the potatoes, rice or pasta rather than cutting them out, go wholegrain where you can, skip the sugary drinks, and keep pudding small - and ask them what they usually do rather than guessing.

Cook the vegetables or potato first in an ovenproof frying pan until soft, then pour over 6 beaten eggs for a 20cm pan, seasoned and with a handful of cheese if you like. Keep it on a low heat for 3 to 4 minutes until the edges set, then finish it under the grill or in a 180C oven for 8 to 10 minutes until the middle is just set. It takes 6 eggs to feed four, and it is good cold the next day.

Cook two portions and let the second one be tomorrow's lunch or dinner: it is barely more work and it is the whole trick. Buy the smaller packs where they exist, freeze half a loaf and half a pack of mince on the day, and keep eggs, tinned tomatoes, pasta, rice and frozen veg in as the base of a ten-minute dinner. A frying pan and one small pot will do most of it.

Cook meat right through: no rare steak, no pink lamb, and nothing raw or cured unless it is cooked into a hot dish. The worry is toxoplasmosis, which is in raw meat, and salami, chorizo, Parma ham and prosciutto are cured rather than cooked. Well-done steak, cooked chicken, ham from the deli counter and hot dogs heated until steaming are all fine.

Cooked mince keeps 3 days in the fridge in a sealed box, and freezes for 2 to 3 months. Reheat it once until it is piping hot right through, and give it 2 days rather than 3 if it was in a sauce with cream in it.

Cooked pasta keeps 3 days in the fridge in a sealed box, tossed with a little oil so it doesn't clump. Reheat it in the sauce with a splash of water until piping hot, once only, and bin it if it smells sour or feels slimy.

Cooked porridge keeps 2 days in a lidded tub in the fridge: cool it quickly, then reheat it with a splash of milk or water and a stir, because cold porridge sets solid. Porridge left out on the side overnight goes in the bin.

Cooked prawns keep 2 days in the fridge, in a sealed box away from anything raw, and ones from the deli counter keep a day less than a sealed pack. Eat them cold or warm them through in a sauce rather than frying them again, and bin any that smell of ammonia.

Cooked rice keeps a day in the fridge and no longer: cool it within an hour of cooking, box it, and put it in cold. Reheat it once, all the way through until it is steaming hot, and never a second time - the spores that grow in rice left warm are not killed by reheating. Rice that sat out overnight goes in the bin, and so does anything that smells or feels slimy.

Cooked salmon keeps 2 days in the fridge, covered, and it is better cold in a salad than reheated, which dries it out. Cool it within an hour of cooking and bin it after 2 days; smoked salmon keeps 3 days once the pack is open and freezes for a month.

Cooked sausages keep 3 to 4 days in the fridge in a covered box, and freeze for 2 months. Reheat them in a pan or the oven until they are hot right through rather than in a microwave, which leaves the middle cool.

Cooked stuffing keeps 2 days in the fridge and it is the leftover to be strict with, because it has been inside the bird and soaked up the juices: cool it within 2 hours, box it, and reheat it until it is piping hot right through. Stuffing that never went in the oven is a different thing and keeps as long as the bread in it.

Cooked bacon keeps 4 to 5 days in the fridge, wrapped or in a box, and freezes for 2 months. It is already cured, so it lasts longer than other cooked meat: reheat it in a dry pan until it sizzles, and eat it cold within 3 days.

Cooked beans, lentils and chickpeas keep 3 days in the fridge in a covered box, and freeze for 2 months in portions. Reheat them until they are hot right through, and bin any that smell sour or have gone fizzy.

Cooked fish keeps 2 days in the fridge, less than meat: box it once it has cooled, and eat it cold the next day rather than reheating it, because fish goes dry and rubbery the second time. It freezes for a month if you cooked too much.

Cooked food can go back in the freezer once - cool it within two hours, rice within one, and rice should only be reheated once after that. Raw meat or fish turns on where it thawed: on the worktop or in a warm kitchen, cook it and eat it now, because it should not be frozen again - the thaw lets bacteria multiply and freezing does not undo that. Only meat or fish that thawed in the fridge can go back in, a bit drier than before.

Cooking from scratch is usually a fifth of the price: a home-cooked portion costs about £1.50 to £2.50 where a takeaway is £8 to £12, so three swaps a week saves £1,000 a year. The catch is the waste, so plan the week's meals before you shop and cook double on the nights you are already at the hob.

Cool running water now, and stay under it for twenty minutes: that is the part that limits the damage, and a cloth or a soap is not it. While the water runs, take off anything the chemical has soaked into - a sleeve, a watch, a ring. Then get advice and say what the chemical was and how long ago: 111 in the UK, 911 in the US, the poison centre number on the label, and straight to A&E if the skin is white or blistered, if it is a strong acid or a caustic soda, or if any of it reached an eye - an eye wants the water for longer, with the eyelid held open.

Cool the room before you get in, not after: windows open and a fan on for half an hour, then a lukewarm shower and dry off properly. Cotton sheets, one light layer rather than a duvet, and a damp flannel on your neck or feet. Sweating is how your body dumps heat, so give it moving air instead of covering up.

Cool them fast in iced water - an egg peeled warm tears, and the cold sets the white away from the shell - then tap the shell all over and start at the fat end, where the air pocket is, with a teaspoon of the water under the shell to loosen it. A teaspoon of bicarbonate in the pan helps too, and the freshest eggs are the ones that stick, so an egg a week or two old peels more cleanly than one from today.

Cool cooked rice fast and box it: it keeps 24 hours in the fridge, no longer, and you reheat it once until it's piping hot all the way through. Rice left out at room temperature is the one leftover worth being strict about.

Cool it under running water or with an ice pack for ten minutes and put an antihistamine cream on it: a nettle sting is histamine plus tiny hairs, which is why a dock leaf does nothing except cool the skin as you rub it. It settles in a few hours. Get help if the swelling spreads well beyond the sting, or if they feel wheezy, sick or faint.

Cool it: a clean flannel under the cold tap, wrung out, for ten minutes at a time, and an antihistamine if the other eye or the nose is itchy too. Go to A&E or an urgent care the same day if the lid is red, hot and painful rather than just puffy, if the swelling came on fast, if your sight has changed or the eye itself is bulging, or if you have a temperature - that is an infection behind the lid and it needs antibiotics.

Cooled within two hours and put straight in the fridge, cooked chicken, meat, fish and pasta keep two days and cooked rice one, and that is the whole rule - the date on the pack does not stretch it. After that it is a reheat question rather than a keep one: reheat it once, all the way through, until it is steaming hot, and never reheat rice twice. Bin anything that smells, feels slimy or was left out overnight.

Copy the lot onto an external drive or a big USB stick: on Windows open File Explorer and drag the user folder (Desktop, Documents, Pictures, Downloads) across, and the same on a Mac from Finder. If both machines work, a cloud folder does it without a drive - sign in to OneDrive, iCloud or Google Drive on the old one, let it upload, then sign in on the new one. Do the browser bookmarks and passwords through the browser's own sync, and sign out of the old machine before you get rid of it.

Coral is an animal, not a plant: a colony of tiny polyps that build a hard skeleton around themselves, and the reef is thousands of years of those skeletons stacked up. They get most of their food from algae living inside them, which is why they bleach white when the water gets too warm.
Coriander seed is not hot: it tastes of orange peel and hay, and it is the rounded body in a curry powder. Toast it before grinding and the smell doubles.

Cornflour is the quickest stand-in: mix one tablespoon with two tablespoons of cold water, stir it into the simmering sauce and let it bubble for two minutes - it only thickens at a boil. Arrowroot does the same and gives a clearer gloss. With no starch at all, simmer with the lid off until it coats a spoon, or off the heat whisk in a knob of cold butter or a spoonful of cream. A gluten free plain flour blend makes a roux the same way as ordinary flour.

Corporation tax is the tax a limited company pays on its profit: 19% on profits up to £50,000, 25% above £250,000, and somewhere between the two in between. It is worked out on profit, not on what you take out - salaries and pension contributions are costs, dividends are paid from what is left after tax. You file a CT600 with accounts within 12 months of the year end, and pay usually nine months and a day after it. Allowable costs come off first: stock, tools, software, insurance, mileage, and the salary you pay yourself.

Cotton rather than polyester, because it breathes and you wake up less clammy: a t-shirt and shorts or loose pyjama bottoms is plenty, and socks if your feet get cold. A pair of shorts you'd answer the door in is worth having in the summer.

Couch to 5k is nine weeks of three runs a week, starting with 60 seconds of jogging alternating with 90 seconds of walking. Each week the jogging gets longer and the walking shorter, and by week nine you run 30 minutes without stopping. The free NHS podcast tells you exactly when to run and when to walk, which is the bit that makes it work for people who have never run.

Council tax is the yearly bill your council charges on a home, not on the people in it, for the services it runs - bins, roads, libraries, social care and the fire service. What you pay is set by the band your home was put in, A to H in England and Scotland and A to I in Wales, and a band D home in England averages about £2,171 a year, so a band B home pays seven ninths of that. One adult living alone gets 25% off the bill.

Councils collect real trees in the first couple of January weeks and shred them for mulch - check the day on the council's site, and strip the decorations and the stand first. Garden centres often take them back, and one that still has its roots in a pot can be planted out instead.
Count the seconds between the lightning and the thunder: every 3 seconds is about 1 km (5 seconds per mile). If the gap is under 30 seconds, the storm is close enough to be dangerous, so get indoors.

Count the sleep first, because most of it is that: a 5 to 11 year old needs 9 to 11 hours a night, a teenager 8 to 10, and school start times steal it. Then look for the other three - snoring or breathing pauses in the night, a diet short of iron (iron deficiency is the commonest cause of a tired child), and enough to drink. A child who has been tired for more than a month, or who is pale, breathless, losing weight or not growing, should have a blood test, so book the GP and ask for iron and vitamin D.

Count the whole 24 hours, not just the night: a newborn sleeps 14 to 17 hours in stretches of two to four, and a baby of three to twelve months 12 to 16 hours including two or three naps. Wake a newborn for a feed if a stretch goes past about three hours until they are back to birth weight, then let them sleep. Night feeds are still the job at this age, so do not try to stretch the night - back to sleep in an empty cot, room at 16 to 20 degrees, and go by a baby who is feeding and gaining rather than by the clock.

Count the days you actually have (sleep and school nights are not revision), list the topics per subject, and give each topic one block rather than one subject one day: three blocks a day is a real day's work. Put the subject you dread first, in the morning. Leave the last three days for past papers under time, and leave one day empty, because something always slips.

Count up from the price to the note rather than subtracting: on £12.40 out of a £20, add 60p to reach £13, then £7 to reach £20 - so the change is £7.60. Counting up stops at the round numbers on the way, which is why it is easier to do in your head and easier to check: what you counted back plus the price should land on the note.

Courgettes keep about a week in the salad drawer, loose in a paper bag rather than a plastic one that sweats them, and unwashed until you cook them. They go soft at the ends first, and a soft one is still fine grated into a soup, a fritter or a cake; one with slimy skin or mould on the stalk end goes in the bin.

Couscous takes a dressing better than it takes a sauce: lemon juice, olive oil, chopped tomato, cucumber, parsley and feta is a lunch in 10 minutes. It also drinks up the juices of a stew or roast veg, which is why it is served under them.

Cover most of it with cardboard and compost to kill the weeds while you work on one bed at a time, and start with the bit you can see from the gate. Clear, dig and plant that bed this month, then move on; trying to do the whole plot at once is how people give up.

Cover sold alongside something is insurance: you can cancel it and get the premium back within 14 days, and a firm that sold you cover that did not do what you were told owes the money back - complain in writing, then to the Financial Ombudsman, which is free and can order the refund. Check what it excludes before you cancel, because a fault in the thing itself is already the retailer's job.

Cover is for whoever would lose money if you died: a partner, children, a joint mortgage. Check your workplace pension first, because death in service usually pays two to four times your pay already. If someone does depend on you, level term cover of about ten times your income, running until the children are grown or the mortgage ends, is the usual shape, and it costs less than most people expect. With no dependants, savings for a funeral are usually enough.

Cow's milk comes by fat: whole at about 3.5%, semi-skimmed at 1.7% and skimmed at almost nothing, and the fat is what carries the taste in coffee and sauces. Fresh and UHT are the same milk, one pasteurised hotter so it keeps for months unopened. Goat's and sheep's are the other animals, sharper and richer. Plant milks - oat, soya, almond, coconut - are a different drink, and the barista ones are the ones that do not split in hot coffee.

Crack the egg into your hand over a bowl and let the white slide through your fingers, or tip the yolk from one half-shell to the other and let the white fall. Cold eggs separate more cleanly than warm ones, so take them straight from the fridge, and lift a stray bit of shell out with the wet shell itself, which the white will not cling to.

Cracking and fidgeting are how the body burns off a wriggle, so the fix is a quieter outlet rather than sitting still: a stress ball in your pocket, a foot pressed to the floor, or a short walk every hour. It happens most in meetings and while waiting.

Cramp in a run is usually a tired muscle, not a lack of salt: it comes on late in a session and eases when you stop and stretch. Walk, then stretch the calf against a wall for 20 to 30 seconds. To keep it away, build your distance more slowly and drink water with a pinch of salt if you sweat heavily for more than an hour.

Cravings are usually the brain asking for quick energy or a habit cue rather than a nutrient shortage: sugar and salty fat hit the reward system fast, and seeing or smelling food can set one off. Eat a proper meal with protein and fibre first, then wait ten minutes; if you are craving non-food things, get that checked.

Cream goes by the date on the pot more than by any rule of thumb, and once it is open it keeps about 5 days in the fridge, with double cream lasting a few days longer than single. Keep it near the back rather than in the door, where the temperature swings. A little separation is fine and stirs back in; a sour smell, a yellow tinge or any mould means bin it, because cream does not come back.

Crisphead - iceberg - is the crunchy one that keeps for a week and is mostly water. Cos, or romaine, is the upright one with a spine, and it is the one for Caesar. Butterhead - round and little gem - is soft and sweet, and wilts first. Loose-leaf - oakleaf, lollo rosso, frisée - is the curly one to tear into a bowl. Rocket and spinach are leaves sold beside it, not lettuce, and they are peppery or earthy rather than crisp.

Crohn's is inflammation that turns up in patches anywhere from the mouth to the back passage, so it comes in waves: cramping pain, urgent diarrhoea, tiredness and weight loss, sometimes a sore mouth or sore joints. It is not caused by a bad diet and no diet cures it - treatment is steroids for a flare, then azathioprine or a biologic that a gastroenterologist chooses to keep it away, and stopping those because you feel better is how a flare comes back. Ask the GP to check B12, iron and vitamin D. Stop smoking, which makes it worse. Ring the IBD nurse at the first sign of a flare rather than waiting for the clinic, and go to A&E for blood in the stool with a fever and a fast heartbeat.

Crude oil, heated in a refinery until its parts separate by boiling point. Petrol is one of the light fractions taken off near the top, then cleaned and blended, which is why it evaporates so quickly and catches light so easily.

Cruise control holds the speed you set by working the throttle for you: get to the speed, press set, and the car holds it until you touch the brake or clutch, which cancels it. Use it on a motorway in dry weather, never in rain, traffic or on bends, because it will not slow for anything ahead - only the adaptive kind follows the car in front.

Crumbly biscuits have too little fat or too much flour, and the dough was worked too long: weigh the butter properly, rub it in until it looks like breadcrumbs, and stop mixing the moment it comes together. Let them cool on the tray, because they are fragile while hot, and handle the dough as little as you can.

Crumbly bread is usually too little water or too much flour: the dough should be tacky and slightly sticky rather than dry enough to handle, so hold back a little of the flour and weigh it rather than scooping with a cup. Knead until a piece stretches thin enough to see light through it, which is what holds the crumb together, and let the loaf cool on a rack for an hour before cutting, because warm bread tears. If it is also pale and heavy, the oven was too cool or the loaf was under-proved.

Crying is a pressure valve: strong feeling sets off the same nerves that make your breath catch, and the tears are part of that response rather than a sign of weakness. Emotional tears carry stress hormones, and most people feel calmer afterwards.

Cucumber keeps about a week in the fridge, wrapped in a tea towel or a paper bag in the salad drawer: cling film traps the water and that is what makes it slimy. A soft one is still fine cooked, and the cut end dries first, so shave that off.
Cumin is not hot at all - it is warm, earthy and slightly bitter, and it is the smell of a curry rather than the fire in it. A teaspoon for four, fried in the oil for a few seconds first.

Cured meat is not immune: a slimy feel, a sour or musty smell, or grey-green patches means bin it. Ham keeps about 3 days once the pack is open, dry-cured bacon up to a week, and sausages 2 to 3 days.

Curling is nearly always the climate rather than a disease: dry air and a hot windowsill make the edges roll up, and a plant that dried out badly once keeps its new leaves curled. Water it properly and move it off direct sun, then feel under the curled leaves for aphids, which cluster on soft new growth and make it pucker.

Curls want water and conditioner more than shampoo: wash the scalp two or three times a week, put plenty of conditioner through the lengths and squish it in with your head upside down, then rinse it out cool. Dry by scrunching with a cotton T-shirt rather than a towel, add a little leave-in while it is still soaking wet and then leave it alone until it is dry, because touching it is what makes it frizz. A trim every ten to twelve weeks keeps the shape.

Curry powder is mild - it is turmeric, cumin, coriander and fenugreek, and it is not where the heat in a curry comes from. Two spoons in a curry for four is about right, and the heat is added separately with chilli.
Curry leaves are not hot at all: they are citrusy and nutty, and they only give that up when fried in hot oil for a few seconds at the start. Dried ones taste of very little.

Cut saturated fat first, since that is what raises LDL: butter, cheese, fatty and processed meat, pastries and coconut oil. Swap to olive or rapeseed oil, and add oats, beans, nuts and oily fish twice a week, all of which lower LDL or triglycerides a little. Activity most days raises the good HDL. Together that is often 5 to 10%, so if your LDL is high enough for medication your GP will offer a statin, which does more than any diet does.

Cut saturated fat first, because that moves the number more than anything else: less cheese, butter, fatty meat, pastry, biscuits and coconut oil, and swap to olive or rapeseed oil and leaner cuts. Then add the things that help - oats, beans or lentils daily, nuts, oily fish twice a week, and 30 minutes of walking on most days - and get a retest after about three months, since diet alone typically takes 10 to 20 percent off. If you have been given a statin, keep taking it; diet and the tablet work together.

Cut stale bread into cubes, toss them in olive oil with a little salt, and bake at 180C for 8 to 10 minutes until they rattle in the tin - a halved garlic clove in the oil is the whole trick. For breadcrumbs, tear the bread up, blitz it or grate it on the coarse side, dry them in the same oven for 5 minutes, and they keep a month in a jar.

Cut the mitres first, on the ceiling line and not the face, with the piece upside down and back to front in the mitre box as though it were already on the ceiling, and try every cut on an offcut before it goes near the wall. Then adhesive along both the top and the bottom edge in a zigzag, press it up onto a pencil line drawn at the coving's drop, and put a screw into the wall just under the bottom edge for the first metre until the adhesive grabs - the screw head gets filled afterwards. Long walls want a joint cut on a scarf rather than butted, and any gap at the ceiling line is caulk and paint, not more adhesive.

Cut the old silicone out and scrub the joint back to dry, grease-free tile and bath before anything else, because fresh silicone will not stick to the old. Fill the bath with water first, so the bead is made at the weight it has to carry, then run anti-mould silicone along it and smooth it with a wet finger or a tool. Leave it 24 hours before you let the water out, and it will not part from the bath in a month.

Cut the shrub down to about 30cm of stem first so you can see what you are doing, then dig a trench a spade's width outside the stems and cut straight down through the roots all the way round until the rootball rocks. Lever it out with the spade rather than pulling at it, and take the big roots with it - a laurel or a willow left with roots in the ground sends up suckers for years.

Cut the treats first and weigh the day's food on a kitchen scale instead of guessing: a dog should lose about one to two per cent of its body weight a week, so a 20kg dog is about 200 to 400g. Fill part of the bowl with green beans or carrot, and add a walk rather than taking food away. Have the vet weigh him first, because an underactive thyroid and bad joints both look like greed and both need a different plan.

Cut the chilli in half lengthways and scrape out the seeds and the white pith with a teaspoon or the tip of a knife: nearly all the heat sits there, so a chilli with them out is mild and the flesh left behind still tastes of chilli. Wash your hands straight after and keep them off your eyes; leave the seeds in when you want the heat.

Cut the distance and the speed for a week or two: most running knee, shin and ankle pain is too much, too soon, and hip and glute strength work fixes it. Ice after a run and run on softer ground, and see a physio if the pain is sharp, that leg swells up after every run, or it is still there in two weeks.

Cut the food and the cover before you bait: take the bird feeders down or use a seed tray, keep the compost heap closed and stop putting cooked food in it, and clear the long grass and rubbish they are running behind. Then use two lockable bait stations along the wall where you have seen them and check them every couple of days - loose poison is a real risk to cats, dogs and children. If they are in the house, the council's pest control team is usually cheaper than a private firm.

Cut them straight across rather than down the sides, leave a millimetre or two of white, then round the two corners with a file so nothing catches on a sock. Do toenails after a bath, when the nail is soft, and keep them longer than you think: rounding a toenail drives the edge into the skin and gives you an ingrown one. Once a fortnight is plenty, and clippers beat scissors on a thick nail. See a GP if one side is red and painful with skin growing over it, or if a nail has gone thick and yellow.

Cut what starts with the machine - Task Manager > Startup on Windows, Login Items on a Mac - and make sure the disk has about 10% free. If it still takes minutes, the old spinning drive is the fault and a £40 SSD makes the same laptop start in seconds.
Cut cold butter into small cubes and leave it 15 minutes, or grate it; both soften it fast without melting it. Don't microwave it, because butter that's too warm splits a cake mix.

Cut it to what the job actually is: a plain title, three or four real duties, the pay or the range, the hours and the place, and the one thing a candidate must have. Drop the adjectives - "dynamic self-starter" tells nobody anything - and drop any requirement that is not essential, because long lists put people off applying at all. Say whether it is full or part time, whether it can be done from home, and how to apply, in a line each.

Cut it back and stop feeding, then move it against a wall out of the worst of the frost: most summer bedding will not come back, so a spring refill is the honest plan. Empty a basket you are leaving out and stand it dry, or the compost freezes solid and cracks the liner.

Cut it into wedges so the stalk cooks with the leaf, drop it into plenty of boiling salted water and leave the lid off: 5 to 8 minutes for a firm white or green cabbage, 3 to 4 for savoy and spring greens, until a knife goes into the stalk with a little resistance left. Drain it at once and toss it with a knob of butter or a little oil - cabbage left standing in the pan carries on cooking and turns to water.

Cut lettuce about eight to twelve weeks after sowing, in the morning when it is cold and crisp, at the base with a knife, and it will often come again. A lettuce that has started to shoot up a stem has bolted: pick it at once and eat it that day, because it turns bitter.

Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases a gas that irritates your eyes, so they make tears to wash it away. A sharp knife and a chilled onion release less of it, and the root end holds most of it, so cut that last.

Cycling is one of the kinder things for knees: it puts no weight through the joint and builds the muscle that holds it, and most cycling knee pain is a saddle set too low or a gear too big rather than wear. Raise the saddle until your leg just straightens with your heel on the pedal, spin an easier gear, and ease off while a knee is hot or swollen. Pain at the front is usually the saddle; at the back, too high.
Cyril Ramaphosa is the president of South Africa: in office since 2018, and chosen again by parliament in June 2024 after the ANC lost its majority. The ANC has governed since 1994.

DBS stands for Disclosure and Barring Service: the checks that show a criminal record to an employer, for work with children, patients or vulnerable adults. A basic, standard or enhanced check is applied for by the employer, not by you, and the certificate goes to you so you can show it to whoever asks.

DIY stands for do it yourself: the jobs around the house you do instead of paying a trade. The word of warning is the useful part - anything involving gas, a fuse box beyond changing a fuse, or a wall you are not sure is load-bearing is not a DIY job, and the rules on rented homes make some of it your landlord's.

DVD stands for digital versatile disc, and the versatile is the honest part: the same disc holds a film, an album or a computer program. It is the same size as a CD and holds about seven times as much, and a Blu-ray holds about five times more again.

DWP stands for the Department for Work and Pensions: the department that pays Universal Credit, the state pension, PIP and jobseeker's payments, and runs the jobcentre. A letter from it with a date on it needs an answer by that date even if the answer is 'I need more time', because a missed deadline restarts the claim rather than pausing it.
Dairy milk is made by cows, in the udder, from what they eat - mostly grass and silage - and it is about 87% water. A milking cow gives roughly 25 to 30 litres a day, in two or three milkings.
Dan Castellaneta voices Homer Simpson, and has since the first short in 1987 - he also does Grampa, Krusty and Barney.

Dark urine first thing is normal: you have not had a drink for eight hours, so the kidney holds on to water and the waste that is left is concentrated. Drink a glass or two and it should be pale straw within an hour; if it stays dark all day, or looks like tea or cola, or it comes with thirst, tiredness and needing to wee a lot, get it checked the same week.

Dark chocolate is the one to keep in the house if you want chocolate: 70 per cent cocoa is about 600 calories per 100g, so two squares is 120 or so, and it carries iron and magnesium with less sugar than milk chocolate. The heart-health claims come from cocoa flavanols and need far more than a square a day, so treat it as a nicer 120 calories, not a supplement.

Dark marks usually mean the drum or the seal needs cleaning: wipe the rubber door seal with a damp cloth and check the filter, then run an empty 90C service wash with a machine cleaner. Run the load a size smaller than you think; an overfull drum can't rinse properly.

Dates keep 6 months in a sealed jar and a year in the fridge, and past the date on the pack they harden rather than spoil: the soft medjool in a tub go first, and the dry baking ones last longest. Ten minutes in a bowl of hot water brings a hard one back. White crystals on the outside are sugar, not mould.

Dead strings are most of what makes a guitar sound dull. Change them every one to three months if you play often, or the moment they feel rough, look tarnished or stop holding tune. Fit them one at a time so the neck keeps its tension: thread the string, leave two or three windings round the post, tune up to pitch and pull each string gently away from the fretboard a few times, then tune again. Nylon strings take a few days to settle, so expect to retune the first three days.

Deal with the specific work, not the character, and say it once to them first: "When the shift plan is left to me, I end up doing both - can we split it so you take the weekends?" If nothing changes, ask your manager for a short meeting and talk about the work that is not being covered rather than the person, with two recent examples and dates. Ask for a written split of who does what; most of this ends when the responsibility is written down.

Deal with it quickly and in person if you can: say what you did, how it landed for them, and what you will do differently, without a 'but'. A clean apology is short and has no defence in it; most rows cool in a day when someone goes first.

Decaf is ordinary coffee with the caffeine taken out of the beans before roasting, usually by soaking them in water, a solvent or carbon dioxide: a mug has 2 to 15mg against about 95mg in regular coffee, and the taste and antioxidants are much the same. It is the swap to make if caffeine is costing you sleep, without losing the ritual or the afternoon mug.

Decaf is fine in pregnancy: a mug of it has well under 10mg of caffeine against about 100mg in the ordinary cup, so it counts towards the 200mg a day but only just. Keep the total to about 200mg a day - two mugs of instant coffee, one filter coffee, or two to three cups of tea - and let decaf be the cup that is habit rather than need, such as the evening one.

Decide the reason first, in one sentence you could say to the person and to HR: the job is not being done after warnings, the role has gone, or the rules were broken. Check your own policy and the contract before you speak to them, because the order matters - an informal chat, then a meeting with notice, then a letter - and check whether they have the two years' service that makes an unfair dismissal claim possible (it is one year in Northern Ireland; ACAS will tell you free and they are quicker than a lawyer). Book a room with a witness, keep it to the facts and under fifteen minutes, have the notice, the last pay and their holiday in writing on the day, and take their keys and access in the same hour rather than at the end of the week. Do not do it by text, and do not argue: if they are angry, say the decision will be confirmed in writing and end the meeting.

Decide the shape before the menu: a sit-down meal is about £35 to £60 a head catered and a buffet or hog roast about £20 to £35, while doing it yourselves lands near £10 to £15 a head and costs you the day. Work back from the number of guests - 60 people is a caterer's job unless you have a big kitchen and willing help - and ask the venue first, because many barns and halls either insist on their own list or charge corkage and a kitchen fee. Book six to nine months ahead for a summer Saturday, put dietary needs on the reply card, and plan evening food if the day runs past nine: something hot and cheap at 9pm saves a long hungry evening.

Decide first whether you want to stay, because that decides the rest. If you do, the affair has to end and your partner has to hear it from you rather than find it: tell them plainly, answer their questions once, and expect anger. If you are leaving anyway, say that instead of the confession, which only moves the hurt onto them sooner. Couples counselling helps either way, and so does working out what you were looking for before you were looking elsewhere.

Decide in advance what you will do and how long you will stay, and tell people early so nobody is surprised on the day. Have one safe topic and one exit ready ('we need to get the little one home'), and step outside for ten minutes when it heats up.
Defrost chicken in the fridge overnight, on a plate on the bottom shelf, never on the worktop. Small pieces take a few hours, a whole bird a day or two; cook it as soon as it is thawed.

Defrost fish in the fridge overnight, still wrapped, on a plate. If you're short of time, seal it in a bag and sit it in cold water for an hour, changing the water; never defrost it on the worktop. A prawn is quicker, and needs no night in the fridge: cold water for 10 to 15 minutes, or straight into a curry or stir-fry from frozen with two or three minutes extra.

Defrost it when the ice is more than about 5mm thick: switch it off at the wall, move the food into a cool box, and leave bowls of hot water inside with the door shut. Budget two to three hours, or overnight leave it with the door open and towels down. Never chip at the ice with a knife, because a pierced pipe writes the freezer off. The reason is moist air getting in every time the door opens.

Deja vu is a brief misfire in memory: the brain takes in a new scene and, for a second, files it as familiar, often because a similar layout or sound has primed the same circuits. It is common and harmless, especially when tired; if it comes with a seizure, a smell or a feeling of losing time, get it checked.

Delay Repay is the train operators' scheme: on most of them you can claim from 15 minutes late, and some pay from 30. Claim on the operator's own site within 28 days, with the ticket or booking reference and the time you actually arrived, and it comes back as cash, a voucher or a free ticket depending on the operator.

Delete the pairing on both sides and pair again from scratch, then keep the phone in a pocket on the same side as the earbud - a body in the way is the commonest cause of dropouts. Charge the case fully, and if it only happens in one place, look for a busy wifi router or a microwave nearby, since both crowd the same radio band.

Delete the phone from the car's own Bluetooth list and the car from the phone's, then pair again from scratch, and check the phone is allowed to connect automatically. In the car's settings turn off the options that take the audio back (auto-play, media sync), and keep the phone's wifi off if it is trying Android Auto over wifi.

Dengue is a virus spread by daytime-biting mosquitoes in the tropics, and it is not passed from person to person: sudden high fever, a severe headache behind the eyes, deep muscle and joint pain and often a rash, with the fever usually breaking after three to seven days. Take paracetamol only - ibuprofen and aspirin raise the risk of bleeding - drink plenty, and get seen the same day for sickness that will not stop, tummy pain, bleeding gums or nose, or drowsiness, because those are the warning signs of the severe form. It is worth telling any doctor you see where you travelled.

Dentures that will not stay in are a fit problem, and the fix is at the dentist or the clinical dental technician who made them: ask for a reline or an adjustment, which is quick and often free within the first year. Until then a thin smear of fixative - not a thick line - holds them for the day, and taking them out at night gives the gum a rest. A sore spot under a denture usually settles in a few days once you leave them out overnight; one that is still there after a week, or a white patch or lump under the plate, should be looked at rather than filed down at home. A cracked or snapped one can be repaired: take both pieces to the technician rather than gluing it, because superglue makes a proper mend harder.

Depression is most of the day, most days, for two weeks or more, with the pleasure gone out of things you usually enjoy and sleep or appetite changed with it. The next step is the GP: say how long it has been going on and what has changed, and in most areas you can refer yourself for talking therapy without waiting for them.

Describe it to a search instead of reaching for the name: the year, one scene you are sure of, an actor's face. "film where a boy finds a whale, 90s" finds it, and IMDb's advanced plot search takes one detail at a time.
Dessert is the sweet course, and it has two s's because you want more of it. Desert, one s, is sand or the verb to abandon; the stress moves too - DESSert, deSERT.

Devolution is power handed down from Westminster to three parliaments: Scotland's at Holyrood (129 MSPs), Wales's Senedd (60 members) and Northern Ireland's at Stormont (90 MLAs). They make law on health, education, housing and transport; defence, foreign policy and most benefits stay at Westminster.

Dialysis does the filtering job the kidneys cannot: your blood is taken out, run past a filter and put back, either in sessions at a unit - usually three a week, four hours each - or at home overnight. It is not painful, and people read, sleep or watch something through it; the needle going in at the start of each session is the only sharp bit, and a fistula in the arm is looked after carefully for that reason. Between sessions the work is fluids, salt and potassium, and the team sets the limits.

Diffusion is particles spreading out on their own from where there are many of them to where there are few, because they are always moving. A drop of ink colours a whole glass of water without stirring, and the smell of toast reaches the next room the same way. Warmer means faster, which is why tea brews quicker in hot water.

Dig it square rather than round, about twice as wide as the root ball and the same depth as the pot it came in: a round hole makes the roots circle, and a hole deeper than the root leaves the plant sitting in a sump that fills with water. Keep the top soil to one side, rough up the bottom and sides of the hole with a fork so the roots can get out, plant it so the old soil mark sits level with the ground, firm it in with your heel and water it well.

Dig it 60cm deep in the middle with a shelf 20 to 30cm deep and 30cm wide around the edge for marginal plants, and go at least a metre across - a pond shallower than that freezes solid and has nowhere for anything to live. The rim is the part people get wrong: keep it level all the way round, checked with a straight edge and a spirit level before the liner goes in, or the water shows one edge of it. Line it with butyl rather than cheap polythene, leave the liner to settle for a day, then fill it and let it stand a week before anything goes in.

Digital content has to work and be as described, so you can ask for a repair or a replacement first, and a price reduction or your money back if that fails or is not possible. Ask the seller who took the payment, not the platform, put it in writing with the order number, and if they refuse a card payment can go to your bank as a chargeback.

Dip your headlights as soon as another car is in sight - a main beam left on dazzles the driver coming towards you for several seconds - and drop your speed, because you can only stop within the distance your lights light up. Look towards the left edge of the road when someone comes the other way with lights on, so your eyes are not fixed on theirs, and keep the windscreen and mirrors clean inside as well as out, since smears scatter oncoming light into a glare. If you are dazzled, slow down and, if you cannot see, stop where it is safe until the car has passed.

Dissolve about 50g of salt in a litre of cold water - roughly 2 litres for a whole bird - and keep it in the fridge for an hour for every kg, or overnight for a chicken. A big pan or a clean bag works, with something on top to keep the bird under. Dry the skin well before it goes in the oven and add no more salt; a brined bird browns faster, so cover the top with foil for the first half hour.

Diverticulitis is small pouches in the bowel wall becoming inflamed, and it comes on as constant pain low on the left of the tummy, often with a temperature, feeling rough and a change in the bowels. Ring the GP the same day rather than wait it out: uncomplicated cases settle in a few days with rest, fluids and painkillers, and antibiotics only if there are signs of infection. Go to A&E for severe pain, a hard belly, a high temperature or blood in the stool. Once it has settled, fibre, fluids, exercise and losing weight make another attack less likely, and seeds and nuts are not the enemy they were once thought to be.

Divide the monthly fee by the visits you actually make. £40 a month is good value at eight visits (£5 a session) and poor at two (£20), which is usually cheaper as pay-as-you-go or a council leisure card. If you want to keep it, book the sessions in the calendar like appointments - the fee is not the problem, the unused month is.

Divide the top and the bottom by the same number until nothing goes into both: 6/8 divides by 2 to give 3/4, and that is as far as it goes. The number to start with is the highest common factor of the two.

Divide the yearly pay by the hours you are actually paid for: £30,000 over 37.5 hours a week is £30,000 ÷ (37.5 × 52) = about £15.40 an hour, and only the paid weeks count, so unpaid breaks or a term-time contract change the figure. Take-home hourly pay uses the figure after tax and pension, not the salary.
Divide it by 2: half of 46 is 23, and half of 7 is 3.5. For a quarter, halve it twice; for 10 per cent divide by 10, and for 5 per cent halve that.

Dizzy first thing is usually low blood pressure on getting up, low blood sugar after a long night, or not enough to drink: sit on the edge of the bed for a minute, have water and breakfast, and it often settles. If the room spins when you turn over in bed, that is the crystals in the inner ear (BPPV) and a GP or physio can fix it with the Epley manoeuvre. See a GP if you faint, or get chest pain, or weakness on one side.

Do not pay: message them that the phone is blocked and report it to the police as found property, which is free and makes the phone theirs to hand in, not to sell. Lock it from Find My or Find My Device so it cannot be used, tell your network, and change the passwords for the accounts that were signed in on it.

Do not pay: a loan from an unlicensed lender is not enforceable in court. Ring Stop Loan Sharks on 0300 555 2222 (England) or 0800 074 0878 (Scotland) — it is free and confidential, they can stop the demanding, and never hand over a bank card or your ID. Tell someone you trust today, and if you feel unsafe, 999.

Do not reply, and do not use the number or link in the message; forward scam texts to 7726 (free in the UK) and block the sender. If it claims to be your bank, ring the number on the back of your card, and never move money because someone on the phone told you to.

Do not ring the number back: a missed call from a number you do not know is often just checking the line is live, and ringing it can cost you. Block each one in the call log (tap it, then Block) and ask your network for anonymous call rejection, which refuses withheld numbers. Register free with the Telephone Preference Service, and if it keeps up ask the network to switch on their nuisance-call filter.

Do not rush to fix it: "That's rough - I'm sorry. How are you doing?" Then offer the practical thing they will need in a week or two, like a reference, a look over their CV or a name to ring, rather than a plan on the first day. Skip anything that sounds like a lesson - everything happens for a reason, it worked out for the best - and do not ask what they did wrong.

Do not start the engine: even a few minutes spreads the wrong fuel through the pump and injectors and turns a drain into a repair. Leave the ignition off, put it in neutral and push it clear of the pump, then ring the station or your breakdown cover for a drain and flush. That is around 150 to 250 pounds against a few thousand for new injectors.

Do not start iron tablets on a guess: ask a GP for a blood test first, because iron builds up and too much is harmful. If your ferritin is low, ferrous fumarate or sulphate with a glass of orange juice, and a gap of a few hours from tea, coffee and calcium, is absorbed far better; it takes about three months to refill. Black stools and constipation are the usual side effects, and vitamin C helps both.

Do not take a side and do not ask what happened: "I'm sorry - that's a lot. How are you holding up?" Then listen, and offer one thing you can actually do, like a bed for the night or dinner on Thursday. Say nothing about their ex that you might have to take back later, and keep checking in over the next few months, when the visits stop.

Do not use that code and do not read it out to anyone: someone has your number and is trying to sign in to an account of yours or open one in your name. Change the password on the accounts tied to that number, starting with the bank and your email, and check no one has ordered a replacement SIM. If the texts keep coming, tell your network - a SIM swap is the thing to rule out first.

Do not argue with it or take it as a verdict - a child who says that is usually saying "I am angry and this is the biggest thing I have". Answer the feeling and keep the door open: "You can be that cross with me and I still love you - I am here when you want to talk." Then look for what set it off (a rule, a new baby, a change at school, being tired) and fix that rather than the words. If it comes with weeks of withdrawal, no friends, or giving up things they loved, ask the GP or the school about CAMHS - that is a different thing from a row.

Do not click the link: open the company's site or app yourself and check the message there, which is how real banks and delivery firms contact you. Check the sender address carefully, and if you did click, change that password and ring the real company on the number from their website.

Do not laugh the first time, because the laugh is what teaches them it works, and do not make it the biggest thing in the day either: say plainly "we don't use that word in this house" and move on. Give them the word they were reaching for - "say I'm really cross" - since most young swearing is a strong feeling without the words for it. Watch your own mouth for a week, because that is where it came from, and if it is aimed at someone, deal with that, not the word.

Do nothing and you roll onto the standard price, the dearest one, so ring your supplier this week: get one rival's price first, then ask for retentions and say you are out of contract and have a cheaper quote - they usually keep you below the standard price. If they will not move, switch, giving the notice your contract asks for, usually 30 days, and getting the end date in writing: a switch that starts early can carry a fee.

Do one thing you could not do with them in the house and one thing that is only rest, and put the fun one first, because the tidying can wait until Sunday evening. The first night can feel strange and quiet, and that is normal rather than a sign anything is wrong. Make the handover easy on everyone: bags packed the night before, a set time and place, and one short message to the other parent with anything the children will need - keeping it businesslike is what stops the weekend turning into an argument.

Do the one that is the goal of the session first, then the other: lifting first if you are training strength, cardio first if you are training for a run. If you are after general fitness, three of each a week on separate days beats worrying about the order.

Do the paper trail in one afternoon: tell the council tax office for the old and the new address, register with a GP near the new place and ask for your notes to move with you, and read the meters on the day you leave and arrive. Set up a Royal Mail redirect for three months, because it catches the accounts you forget, and take photos of the meters as proof.

Do the paperwork before the objects: find the will, value the house and the accounts, and put every decision in writing to all of you at once so nobody hears it second-hand. For the belongings, draw an order and let each person pick in turn, and photograph what is left - the fights are almost always about fairness, not the thing itself. If it has already turned hostile, try a mediator before a solicitor; it is cheaper and it keeps the family.

Do the safety things this week, not later: a lockable back gate, an alarm on the door, a card in a pocket with your number, and tell the neighbours and the local police what to do if they see them out alone. Ring the council's adult social care line and ask for a carer's assessment and a telecare alarm; wandering usually needs a person checking in during the day, and that is arranged, not improvised.

Do the same thing to both sides until x is on its own: in 3x + 4 = 19 take 4 off both sides to get 3x = 15, then divide both by 3 for x = 5. Undo the adding and subtracting first and the multiplying or dividing second, then put the answer back in to check it.

Do the body first, because this kind of nerves is an alarm, not a thought: breathe in for four counts and out for six for two minutes, which is what actually brings the heart rate down, and it works in a corridor or a loo. Then decide the one sentence you want the room to take away and say that first, in the first ten seconds - the nerves fade once you are talking. Get there early, sit rather than stand about, and take water. The shake shows far less than it feels.

Do the ceiling first and the walls after. Cut in round the edges with a brush and a 2cm band, then roll in strips about a metre wide with a long-handled roller, overlapping the last strip while it is still wet so the edges do not dry into lines. Work away from the window and towards the light so you can see where you have been, and roll the last metre without reloading to feather it out. Put a dust sheet down because a ceiling always drips. Matt emulsion, two coats, and a ceiling that is already white may need only one: if it is a bare or patched ceiling, thin the first coat by about a tenth as a mist coat.

Do the cheap things in order. If it is wireless, fresh batteries or a full charge first, then check the little switch underneath is on and unplug the receiver and put it in a different USB port - a tired port takes the mouse down with it. If it is wired, try another port and another cable before blaming the mouse. When it still does nothing, turn it over: a hair or a bit of fluff over the sensor is the commonest fault of all, so wipe the lens and use it on a plain surface rather than glass or a shiny desk. A mouse that is dead on every port is the mouse, and any cheap one will do while you decide about a repair.

Do the introducing before the birth and keep it small: show the scan picture, let them choose a present to give the baby, and arrange for someone else to hold the baby for the first ten minutes so your older child gets your hands and your hello. Then give them a job that makes being big a promotion - fetching a nappy, choosing the blanket - and expect a few weeks of baby talk or clinginess rather than calling it naughty.

Do the inviting yourself, and make it the same thing each week - a walk on Tuesday, a coffee on Saturday - because a standing date is easy to say yes to and does not need them to suggest anything. Ask specifically and name the day, ring rather than text, and keep asking after a no, since the first answer from someone lonely is often no. Tell them one thing you like about their company so it does not feel like charity, and if it is an older relative, offer the lift as well as the invitation, because the journey is often what stops them. If they seem low for weeks rather than lonely, ask them plainly how they are and help them see a GP.

Do three things with them, once, and the phone calls get shorter: their State Pension forecast at gov.uk/check-state-pension, a free Pension Wise appointment if they are 50 or over, and a list of every pension they have ever paid into, because old employers' schemes are the ones people forget. Then agree who handles what, so it is one conversation instead of a worry every week.

Do it on wifi with the phone on charge: on an iPhone it is Settings > General > Software Update, and on Android Settings > Software update (Samsung: Settings > Software update > Download and install). Take it even when it is just a security patch, because those are the fixes that stop the known holes being used, and leave enough space free - a nearly full phone cannot unpack the update and says it is up to date when it is not.

Do it while they sleep, or with another adult holding them: use a small pair of rounded baby nail scissors or a file rather than adult clippers, and press the finger pad away from the nail so you can see the edge. Cut straight across and leave a sliver of white - too short is what causes sore fingers - and file any sharp corner. Every week or so is plenty for a newborn, more often once they are grabbing; if you nick the skin, press a clean cloth on it for a minute and it stops quickly.

Do it 48 hours before every colour, even a brand you have used before: mix a little of the dye and the developer as the box says, put a coin-sized patch behind your ear or in the crook of your elbow, let it dry and leave it. Red, itchy or swollen means do not use it; a tingle that settles is fine. It matters most in pregnancy and after a reaction to anything else, and a strand test on a hidden piece of hair is the other one worth doing before a bleach.

Do it in person, somewhere private and neutral, and keep it short and about the relationship rather than a list of their faults: 'I've been unhappy for a while and I don't think this is working - I've decided to end it.' Do not offer hope you don't mean, and do not do it by text if you can stand to wait a day. Have the practical bits ready - who moves, the key, the shared account - and expect to feel awful afterwards even when you are sure.

Do it in private, on the effect rather than the judgement: "I think that will cost us the Tuesday deadline - can we check the dates?" Name what you would do instead, and leave one pause for them to think: a boss who is contradicted in front of the team defends the decision, not the facts. If the call is theirs to make and it goes ahead, follow it and put your objection in an email the same day - "as discussed, my concern is x" - so it is on the record without a second argument.

Do less than you want to: play twenty minutes of it rather than the whole hour, and warm up for five with a jog and a few short sprints before the first ball, because the sprint cold is what goes. Boots with grip for the surface, water at the side, and expect to ache for two days afterwards - that soreness is normal and walking helps it. If a joint swells or gives way, or a pain is still there after a fortnight, that is a physio rather than another game.

Dogs and cats don't catch our colds: a pet that is sneezing, has a runny nose or runny eyes usually has an infection of its own, an allergy or a bit of grit, and a cat with cat flu is the one that needs a vet quickly. Keep the water topped up, wipe the eyes with damp cotton wool, and ring the vet if it lasts more than a few days, or straight away if there is a green discharge, a fever, no appetite or noisy breathing.

Dogs hear thunder much more loudly than we do and feel the pressure change, so the fear is real. Give them a small den to hide in, stay calm and don't force them out; background noise and closing the curtains help, and a vet can suggest calming options before the next storm.

Dogs hear bangs far louder than we do and can't tell they are harmless, so plan the night instead of waiting for the first one: walk him before dark, then shut the windows and curtains, put the radio on and let him hide where he likes with something to chew. Stay in with him, don't take him to a display and never tell a frightened dog off; if he panics badly, ask the vet about a calming plan a few weeks ahead and check his microchip details are up to date in case he bolts.
Doing well, thanks — what about you?

Don't pay anyone for it: Citizens Advice, StepChange and National Debtline all give debt advice free, and MoneyHelper is the government's own service. Ring StepChange if there are several debts and you want a plan written to the people you owe; ring National Debtline to work it out yourself with someone on the phone; go to Citizens Advice for a benefit, a bill or a bailiff. Have your income, what you owe and any letters to hand, and ask them to write the plan down.

Don't pick or peel it off - that takes the top layers of the nail with it and leaves it flaky for months: file the shiny surface, soak the nail in acetone for 10 to 15 minutes, then push the softened gel off gently with an orange stick. A salon soak-off is quick and cheap, and a fortnight's break between sets is what lets the nail recover.

Don't pour boiling water on it: the glass can crack and the water refreezes. Spray a de-icer and scrape with a plastic scraper, work the heater and front demist, and clear the whole screen, the mirrors and the lights before you set off, because driving with a peephole is an offence. To stop it coming back, cover the screen overnight with an old towel or a mat, lift the wipers off the glass, and park facing east if you can.

Don't reach for the scissors yet: press ice or a bag of frozen peas on the gum for two or three minutes until it hardens, then work it out with your fingers and a comb, along the hair rather than pulling down it. If it is welded on, massage in a spoonful of cooking oil, olive oil or peanut butter for a few minutes, slide it off and shampoo twice; peanut butter works on chewing gum on anything washable. Only a blob right at the fringe is quicker to trim.

Don't rub it: rinse the eye with milk if you have some, then clean, cool water or saline for ten to fifteen minutes with the lid held open, and blink it through. The burn fades over an hour or so and the redness can last a day. Ring 111 or go to an eye casualty the same day if the pain is getting worse rather than better, if your sight is blurred, or if you wear a contact lens - take it out first. Wash your hands and the knife before you touch your face again, because the oil sits on skin for hours and soap barely shifts it.

Don't rub it - that is what scratches the surface. Blink a few times and let the tears do the first of it, then rinse the eye with clean, cool water or saline for ten to fifteen minutes, with the lid held open, over a sink or in the shower. If it is still there, or it was a piece of metal, grit from grinding or anything that hit the eye fast, or you cannot see properly, go to an eye casualty the same day rather than fishing for it. Never use tweezers or a cotton bud, and take a contact lens out.

Don't set a trap to prove it: at this age most lies are about dodging trouble, so make the truth cheaper than the lie - 'tell me what happened and you won't be in trouble for it.' Talk about the thing, not the character ('the tablet was on after bedtime', not 'you're a liar'), and ask yourself what failing at home feels like. If it is constant and about everything, that is worth a chat with the school about how things are going there.

Don't try to answer the whole of it at once. Write three short lists: what you are good at (the things other people ask you for, not what you would like to be good at), what you would do for free, and what you need money for. Then pick one small experiment that touches two of the three - a course, a volunteering shift, a paid side project - and give it three months, because direction comes from doing rather than deciding. Keep whatever you would happily do again.

Don't try to be the parent yet: be a reliable adult who is not in charge of the rules and let their actual parent do the discipline for a while. Keep the offers small and repeated - a lift, a snack they like, a show you both watch - because loyalty to the other parent is usually what is behind the hostility. Never say a word against their mum or dad in front of them.

Don't try to fix it: say you are sorry, then ask what they need today, company or quiet. Turn up with food and let them talk; the friend who doesn't hand out advice in week one is the one they remember.

Don't: never make a pet sick at home. Salt water, peroxide and fingers down the throat do real damage, and for some poisons being sick makes it worse. Ring the vet or the animal poisons line, say what was eaten and how much and how long ago, and they will tell you whether it needs to come up and how.

Don't: the annual rate can run past 1,000%. Ask your bank about a small overdraft, a credit union for a low-cost loan, and a free debt advice service such as StepChange about grants, payment plans or a breathing space on what you already owe.

Don't: washing raw chicken splashes bacteria over the sink, the taps and anything within a metre, and cooking kills them anyway. Pat it dry with kitchen paper, bin the paper, wash your hands, and cook it right through.

Don't act on it yet: check it through a route you found yourself, the number on your card or bill or the company's own app, and never through a number or link the message gave you, because a scam works by being the only voice you hear. The marks of one are being hurried, being asked to keep it secret, and being asked to move money, read out a code, or pay in a way you would not normally use: a gift card, a payment app, or a transfer to a person. No real bank, tax office or courier asks for any of those. If you have already paid or given details, ring your bank the same day, because some transfers can be recalled and you are not in trouble; keep the message and report it to the fraud service for your country, or forward a suspicious text to 7726 in the UK.

Don't blank them - be brief, dull and busy, which is easier to keep up than avoidance and gives them nothing to push against. Answer in a sentence, ask nothing back, do not laugh at the jokes, and keep your hands occupied or your coat on. "I can't stop, I'm just heading in" works every time, and stepping away while you say it ends the exchange. If it is someone you cannot move away from, sit at the end of the row and arrive a minute late rather than making a thing of it.

Don't cut the mould off a loaf and eat the rest: the threads reach further than the green you can see, so bin it. Warmth, damp and the plastic bag it came in are what mould needs, so a loaf keeps longer in a paper bag or a bin, with half of it frozen sliced on day one. Hard cheese is the exception - cut an inch around the mould and the rest is fine.

Don't feed him for a few hours before a journey, keep the car cool and well ventilated, and cover the seat with a familiar blanket. Short trips to somewhere good, built up over weeks, settle most dogs; ask the vet about travel sickness tablets for long journeys.

Don't force the handle or the key: warm the key in your hand, put a little de-icer in the lock and push the door with the flat of your hand to break the seal round the rubber. Wipe the door seals with silicone spray or vaseline in autumn and they will not stick next time. Never pour hot water on a frozen lock or screen, because it refreezes straight away.

Don't force it, and don't get somebody to walk on your back or wrench it round - the pop you are after is a joint letting go, and a hard twist is how discs and ribs get hurt. What gives the same relief safely is movement: kneel and round your back up and down slowly (cat-cow) ten times, sit back on your heels with your arms stretched forward, then lie on your back and pull each knee to your chest. Standing and leaning back over the edge of an open door with your hands on the frame opens the mid-back too. If the back is sore rather than stiff, treat it as a strain - keep walking, take paracetamol or ibuprofen if you can, and see a GP if it is no better in a fortnight.

Don't force it: rub a pencil point or a little candle wax along the teeth, pull the fabric edges apart and ease the slider back. If the slider has come off one side, zipping it back on from the bottom usually fixes it; otherwise a tailor can replace the whole zip.

Don't ignore a parking ticket: an informal challenge inside 14 days keeps the 50% discount open, and paying in that window gets it. Photos of the sign, the bay and the ticket you bought decide it, so send them on the council's own form, never through a paid appeals firm. If that is refused, make a formal representation within 28 days of the Notice to Owner; the independent tribunal named on the notice is then free and cancels plenty of these.

Don't just cancel it: tell your insurer the date you sold the car and either move the policy to the new one or cancel, and you get the unused months back minus a fee, usually £25 to £50. Send the V5C to the DVLA with the buyer's details on the day, or you stay liable for the tax and the fines.
Donald Tusk is the prime minister of Poland: in office since December 2023, after the October 2023 election. The president is Karol Nawrocki, elected in June 2025.

Drain them the second a knife slides in and let them sit in the colander off the heat for 2 minutes so the steam escapes: potatoes go watery when they sit in their water, and a lid left on traps it back on. Save a splash of the cooking water to loosen mash instead of milk if it still looks wet.

Draw what is in front of you, not from memory: a mug, your own hand, the chair opposite. Ten minutes a day beats a long session at the weekend, one object a day for a fortnight, and use a soft pencil (2B) on cheap paper so you are not afraid of it. Copy one drawing you admire every week and do not rub anything out - the wrong line next to the right one is how you learn to see.

Drawings for an extension are usually £1,000 to £2,500, and a full service is 8 to 15% of the build cost, so a £60,000 extension is £5,000 to £9,000 in fees. A structural engineer's calculations are £400 to £1,000 on top when a wall is coming out. Ask what the fee covers - planning, building regs, and site visits during the build are separate jobs.

Dress one step smarter than the job's everyday clothes on your first day: a shirt or blouse and smart trousers, a jacket if you own one, and closed clean shoes. Look at photos of the team or the office, and keep the trainers and hoodie for after you've seen what everyone else wears.

Dress for standing about outdoors: shorts or jeans and a light top, with a jumper for when the sun goes in. Leave the white things and the dry-clean-only at home, because there's smoke, grass and someone with a ketchup bottle.

Dried or tinned is the first split: dried needs soaking overnight and a hard ten-minute boil, tinned is cooked and ready. After that it is the bean: kidney is the chilli one, cannellini and haricot are creamy and white (baked beans are haricot in tomato), black beans are earthy for Mexican food, and butter beans are the big soft ones. Chickpeas, lentils and split peas are the same family - pulses - and they cook without soaking.

Dried pasta does not need soaking: it cooks in 8 to 12 minutes in salted boiling water, and soaking it first just makes it pale and floppy. If it is cooked pasta you mean, it keeps 3 days in the fridge, and anything that sat out for more than 2 hours gets binned.

Dried pasta keeps about 2 years past the date on the packet in a sealed jar in a cupboard, and longer if it stays dry. Cooked pasta keeps 3 days in the fridge, tossed with a little oil so it does not clump, and reheats once in the sauce.

Dried beans, chickpeas and lentils cost about a third of the tinned price for the same amount on the plate: half a kilo of dried, around £1.20, cooks up to about the same as three or four tins at 70p to 90p each, and a bag of dried lentils is under £2 a kilo where mince is £5 to £7 for 500g, so pulses are much the cheaper protein. Tinned wins when dinner has to be on the table in ten minutes; dried wins if you cook a big pot at the weekend and freeze it in portions.

Dried herbs are fine in anything cooked: use about half the amount of fresh and add them earlier so they soften. Keep fresh for the end, and for salads and dressings where their green taste is the point.

Drink plenty of water, take paracetamol and pee when you need to rather than holding on - most cystitis in women settles in a day or two. See a GP or pharmacy the same day if it lasts over three days, comes with blood, a fever or back pain, or if you are pregnant, a man or a child. Three or more in a year is worth a GP review.

Drink plenty of water, take paracetamol for the sting, and see a GP or pharmacist promptly: a short course of antibiotics clears most of these. Go the same day if you have a fever, back or side pain, blood in your pee, are pregnant, are a man, or it is a child - those need looking at rather than waiting.

Drink water with a little salt and sugar in it, keep eating plain food like toast and rice, and it usually settles in two to three days. See a GP if there's blood, a high fever, or it lasts more than a week, and keep away from others while it's going on.

Drive a long screw into the middle of the cork, leave a few centimetres sticking out and lever it up a little at a time with a fork, pliers or the back of a key. In a pinch you can push the cork in with the handle of a wooden spoon, which is fine if you are drinking the bottle now. Warm the neck in your hands first if the cork is stubborn.

Drop frozen peas into already boiling water and give them 2 to 3 minutes: they're blanched before freezing, so they need no more than that. They're done when they float and taste sweet; longer turns them grey.

Dry rice keeps for years in an airtight jar in a cool, dark cupboard - the date on the bag is a best-before, not a use-by: brown rice is the one that turns, in about six months, and it tells you by smelling of old oil. Weevils or damp and it goes out. Only cooked rice needs the fridge, and that one is worth being strict about: 24 hours and no longer.

Dry rice keeps for years in a sealed jar in a cupboard, and the date on the bag is a best-before rather than a use-by. Cooked rice is the one to be strict about: cool it within an hour, box it, and keep it no more than 24 hours in the fridge - reheating does not kill the spores that grow in rice left warm.

Dry the skin and salt it, keep it uncovered in the fridge for an hour if you can, and roast it on a rack at 200C (180C fan) without basting or covering. Steam is the enemy: a wet bird in a crowded tin comes out pale and flabby.

Dry, tight skin in winter is mostly central heating and long hot showers washing the oils out: short lukewarm showers, pat dry rather than rub, and a thick unperfumed cream within three minutes while the skin is still damp. Cracked hands and heels want a cream with urea or lanolin and cotton gloves overnight. If the cracks bleed or the skin is red and itchy, a pharmacist can give you an emollient.

Dry eyes are usually the tear film breaking up: screens, heating, air conditioning, contact lenses or getting older - and watering is often the same thing, because a dry surface makes the eye produce tears that do not stay on it. A pharmacist's lubricating drop - carbomer or hyaluronic acid - three or four times a day does most of the work, plus the 20-20-20 rule at the screen. Five minutes of warm compress on the lids helps if they are crusty. See an optician if it is painful or you need drops every hour.

Dry heat, not the microwave: 200C for 8 to 10 minutes straight on the oven shelf, or in a covered frying pan on a low heat for 5 minutes - both give you a crisp base again. A microwave heats the water in the sauce and turns the base to leather, so only use it for 10 seconds if you want it warm rather than good.
Dublin has about 590,000 in the city and about 1.5 million in the county, which is roughly a third of the people in Ireland.

Dust them first with a soft brush or the vacuum's brush head, then wipe with a cloth wrung out in warm water and a drop of washing-up liquid, and dry as you go so the water does not sit on the join with the floor. Do the top edge, the front and the groove on the way past. A melamine sponge takes scuffs off, but gently, because the paint film on a skirting is thin. Never wet an MDF one: it swells, and no amount of drying brings it back.

Dust between the fins does more to cut the heat than anything you can do on the outside: run a vacuum cleaner's crevice tool down each gap with the heating off, and a long flexible duster gets the space behind without moving the radiator. For the paintwork plain warm water with a drop of washing-up liquid is enough - skip anything abrasive, which takes the enamel off - and keep water away from the valves and away from an electric one. Once before the heating goes on in autumn, and again in mid-winter if a room is slower to warm than it used to be.

EHIC stands for European Health Insurance Card: the free card that gave state-provided medical care in the EU on the same terms as a local. New applications were replaced by the GHIC after Brexit, and an EHIC already issued still works until the date on it runs out.

EPC stands for energy performance certificate: the A to G rating a home gets when it is sold or let, from how much it costs to heat and how well it holds the heat. A rented home has to reach band E, and a low rating is the best handle for asking the landlord for insulation or a newer boiler.

Ears pop because the air pressure around you changes faster than the pressure inside your middle ear - in a lift, or in a plane as it climbs. Swallowing, yawning, or holding your nose and blowing gently pushes it back into balance; a blocked nose from a cold makes it harder.

Earthworms are most of it: a badger can eat well over a hundred in a night, which is why a lawn full of small conical holes is badger work rather than a pest. The rest is beetles and grubs, slugs, roots, windfall fruit, and now and then eggs or a chick, plus anything a bin bag offers.

Eat something plain you've had before, like porridge or toast with banana, two to three hours before the start, and sip water rather than drinking a lot at once. Nothing new on race day, and go out slower than feels natural.
