Eat in date order first, and after that the food that is on borrowed time: fresh fish and mince within a day or two, then soft fruit, berries and salad leaves, then milk, yoghurt and cream, then hard cheese, butter and cooked leftovers. Where it sits matters as much as the order - cooked and ready-to-eat food on the top shelves, raw meat and fish on the bottom shelf in a box so nothing drips, and vegetables in the drawer. The door is the warmest part, so keep milk out of it, and the top of the door is fine for butter and condiments.

Eczema is dry, itchy, red skin, often in the elbow and knee creases, and it flares with soap, heat and stress. Psoriasis makes thick, silvery scaly patches, usually on elbows, knees and scalp, and it can affect the joints too. Both are treated with emollients and steroid creams, so a GP or pharmacist is the place to start.
Edinburgh has about 510,000 people - smaller than Glasgow, though it is the capital, and the festival more than doubles it in August.

Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay were the first to reach the top of Everest, on 29 May 1953, at the end of the British expedition. Tenzing was a Sherpa climber from Nepal and the two of them stopped about fifteen minutes at the summit.

Egg salad keeps 2 days in the fridge, covered, on a shelf rather than in the door, and no more than 2 hours out at room temperature before it should go in the bin: mayonnaise and boiled egg together is the part that turns. If it has sat out at a picnic since morning, don't risk it.

Eggs are back on the everyday list: the cholesterol in food turned out to matter far less than the saturated fat in your diet, so most people can eat them daily. If you have familial high cholesterol or heart disease, ask your GP - otherwise one or two a day is fine, and they are one of the cheapest good sources of protein.

Egyptians removed the organs, dried the body with salt for about 40 days, then wrapped it in linen with amulets between the layers. They kept the heart, which they believed was weighed against a feather in the afterlife.
Eight arms, and two rows of suckers on each, about 2,000 suckers in all. Each one can taste what it touches.

Eighteen to vote in a general election in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and 16 in Scotland and Wales for the Scottish Parliament and the Senedd. You have to be on the electoral register as well, which is a separate step from turning 18, so register as soon as you can - it takes about five minutes online and closes 12 working days before a vote.

Either dug up as rock salt, laid down by seas that dried out long ago, or dried out of sea water in shallow ponds. Both are the same sodium chloride, and the difference in the shop is the size of the crystal and whether iodine or an anti-caking agent has been added.

Elbow pain on the outside is tennis elbow, an overused tendon, and it settles over weeks to months once you rest from the gripping and lifting that sets it off: a strap just below the elbow and slow strengthening with a light weight help. See a GP if it is no better in six weeks.

Elbows under your shoulders with the forearms flat, feet hip-width: squeeze your glutes and tuck your ribs down so the hips neither sag nor poke up - one straight line from ear to heel - and keep breathing. Twenty to thirty seconds done well beats two minutes with a sagging back; add ten seconds a week and stop the set when the hips drop. A low back that aches during a plank is usually the sag, not a weak back.

Electrolysis is passing a current through a liquid or solution to drive a chemical change that would not happen on its own: it splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, and it is how aluminium is extracted and how metal is plated.
Eluned Morgan is Wales's first minister - Labour, in office since August 2024, and the first woman to hold the job. The Welsh parliament is the Senedd, in Cardiff Bay.

Email the module leader today, before they chase you: say the piece is late, give the reason in one sentence and name the date you will submit. Most places take 10% off a day up to a cap of a pass mark for a few days, and the late penalty is usually shown on your marks breakdown - check your module handbook for the exact rule rather than guessing. If the reason was illness or something serious, ask for mitigating circumstances now: it can remove the late penalty and give you a resit as if for the first time. Silence is the only version where nothing can be fixed.

Emergency tax means HMRC had no P45 or tax code for you yet, so that month is taxed as if it were your only one and none of your tax-free allowance goes against it - the code shows W1, M1 or an X. It usually corrects itself once payroll has your P45 and HMRC sends the right code, so hand the P45 in and check the code in the HMRC app; if it is still an emergency code after the next payslip, ring HMRC and they will tell your employer what to use. Anything overpaid comes back in your pay or as a refund after the tax year ends.
Emma Watson plays Hermione Granger in all eight Harry Potter films (2001-2011).

Emmeline Pankhurst (1858-1928) led the suffragettes, the Women's Social and Political Union, whose window-breaking and hunger strikes pushed the vote for women up the agenda. Some women got the vote in 1918 and all of them in 1928, weeks after she died.

Employees pay 8 per cent of pay between about 12,570 and 50,270 pounds a year, and 2 per cent on anything above that; below 12,570 there is nothing to pay. Your employer pays a separate share on top and it does not come out of your pay. The line on your payslip is the employee part only, so it should come to roughly 8 per cent of what you earn over the threshold - if it is nowhere near, ask payroll to check your category letter.

Empty the Downloads folder and the bin first, then look in Settings > System > Storage (Windows) or Apple menu > System Settings > Storage (Mac) at what is biggest. Videos, old installers and a cloud folder kept offline take most of it; moving those to an external drive is the quickest big win.

Empty the wardrobe, wash or dry-clean everything woollen, then vacuum the drawer and the carpet edge and hang cedar or lavender with the clean wool: moths come back to damp, unwashed wool, so dry storage is what keeps them out. Small holes can be darned or covered with an iron-on patch.

Empty the Sent and Deleted items, then sort by size and delete the big attachments, since a handful of photos can be most of it. If you use IMAP, keep only recent mail on the device, and archive the rest to folders; a free 15GB with Gmail or Outlook is enough once the junk is gone.

Empty it out every time you get home, turn it inside out and wipe the lining with a cloth wrung out in warm soapy water, then leave it open to dry somewhere airy. Sweaty kit goes straight in the wash, not back in the bag, and a sock of bicarbonate of soda left in the bottom overnight takes up what is left of the smell.

Empty it into a cool bag first, then wipe every shelf, drawer and the door seals with hot soapy water and dry them. Clear the drain hole at the back with a cotton bud and warm water, and leave a bowl of bicarbonate of soda on a shelf between cleans: it absorbs smells instead of covering them. Once or twice a year is enough if nothing has spilled.

Emulsion thins with water, about one part to ten of paint; oil-based gloss thins with white spirit at much the same rate. Add it a little at a time and stir until the paint runs off the stick in a steady ribbon. A first mist coat on new plaster is thinner still, about 20 to 30 per cent water. Don't thin to stretch a tin: it covers less, and that is where streaks come from.

Emulsion and other water-based paint lift with warm soapy water: soak the splash for a few minutes, then slide it off with a plastic scraper or a razor blade held almost flat to the glass. Gloss and oil paint want white spirit on a cloth, left a moment to soften, then the same scraper. Work in one direction and keep the blade wet, which is what stops it scratching.

End the day with a two-minute shutdown: write tomorrow's first three things on one list, close the laptop, and do something that marks the change - a walk round the block, changing clothes, the kettle. Keep work email off your phone after a set hour unless you are genuinely on call, and tell people the hour rather than just going quiet. If the work does not fit the day, that is a conversation with your manager about what to drop, not a longer evening.

End the meal the first time it lands on the floor: take the plate away calmly, say 'food stays on the tray', and try again at the next snack. Give one thing at a time and small portions, because a full plate is an invitation to play. Don't pick it up and hand it back - that is the game.

Endometriosis is tissue like the womb lining growing outside it - most often on the ovaries, the back of the womb or the bowel - which bleeds each month with nowhere to go, so periods are very painful, sex hurts and sometimes passing stools hurts. Write down the pain and the days for two or three cycles and take that to the GP: ask straight out for a referral to gynaecology rather than waiting to be offered one, because the delay from first symptom to diagnosis is years. Hormonal treatment (the pill, a progestogen, an IUS) or surgery helps, and it does not always mean you cannot have children.

Envy is usually information: it points at the thing you want, not at a fault in them, so the useful move is to say it plainly to yourself - 'I want that' - and then name the one step towards it that is yours to take this month. Say something warm to them about the thing you envy, because a compliment costs nothing and digs do not; and if it stings every time you see them, see them a little less for now rather than pretending it does not.

Epilepsy is a tendency to have seizures: a burst of electrical activity in the brain that can be a brief blank stare or a strange smell, or a full fit with jerking and loss of awareness. Most people are well controlled on one tablet - lamotrigine, levetiracetam or sodium valproate, chosen by a neurologist - and the three things that keep it that way are taking it every day, sleeping properly and going gently on alcohol. In the UK a first seizure means telling the DVLA and not driving for six months, so check the DVLA rules before you get back in the car. Ring 999 if a fit lasts more than five minutes, if another follows straight after, or if it is a first seizure and they are not coming round.

Equity release takes money out of a home you own without moving: a lifetime mortgage adds the interest to the loan, so the debt grows, and a home reversion sells a share of the house outright at below market value. Nothing is repaid until you die or go into care, which is why the family inherits less. Take advice from someone who does not sell them - it is free and it is required.

Erosion is the wearing away and moving of rock, soil or sand by water, wind, ice or waves: rain washing soil off a bare field, or a river cutting into its banks. The material is then dropped somewhere else, which is deposition, and planting cover or slowing the water is the usual defence.

Escrow is money held by a third party until both sides have done what they promised. In a house purchase your deposit sits with your solicitor until completion, and if the sale falls through it comes back to you; on a building job a stage payment can sit in escrow until the work is signed off. Nobody in the middle can spend it, which is the whole point.

Europe and many other countries use two round pins, the UK uses three square ones, and the US uses flat pins, so take a universal adapter. Check the voltage on your chargers: phone and laptop chargers handle 100-240V fine; hairdryers often don't.

Evening snacking is usually habit plus a lunch that was too small, not greed. Eat a proper lunch with protein and fibre in it, have your evening meal a bit later, then brush your teeth straight after it and leave the kitchen - it is far easier to change the routine than to resist the cupboard.

Evergreen blocks a view all year, and yew, holly or laurel reach 2m in a few years: buy them bare-root in autumn, plant 60cm apart, and put a strip of membrane down so you are not weeding under them. Quicker than a hedge is a fence or a trellis to 2m at the back of a garden (1m is the usual limit at the front, and a listed building or a conservation area wants permission) with a climber over it - ivy, honeysuckle, a climbing rose. Pleached trees on stilts screen an upstairs window in one season, and a sail shade on posts does a patio straight away. Check whose fence it is before you build on it, and ask before taking a hedge down: a boundary hedge is often shared.

Every reader has a free join: in Adobe Acrobat's online Merge Files tool you pick the PDFs in order and download one file, and on a Mac Preview does it by dragging the pages' thumbnails into the first document (View > Thumbnails, then drag). On Windows, open the first PDF, choose Print, select Microsoft Print to PDF and add the other files as extra pages. Number the files first so the order comes out right.

Every six months for the water filter inside the fridge, and most of the ones that have one put a light on the door when it is due. The fridge itself is a different job - once a month for a proper empty-out and wipe.

Every six to eight weeks is plenty for most dogs, and less for a short coat: use a dog shampoo rather than yours, because a dog's skin sits at a different pH. Wet him right down to the skin, lather, then rinse for twice as long as feels necessary - leftover shampoo is what causes the scratching afterwards. Brush the knots out before he gets wet, since water tightens a tangle into felt, and dry him properly and keep him warm after.

Every three to four months for the pillow itself, and every six weeks or so if you sweat at night, sleep with a pet on the bed or wake up sneezing. Two pillows fit in most 7kg machines two at a time; a memory foam pillow is not machine washed at all - sponge the cover and air it. A pillow past its wash is still a pillow past its life: fold it in half and let go, and if it stays folded it is done.

Every two to three months for the inside if you use it most days, and a wipe of any spill once the oven is cool enough to touch: burnt-on grease is what smokes and what takes an hour of scrubbing once it has baked on. The door glass is worth a wipe every few weeks, and the racks come out to soak two or three times a year. A self-cleaning oven wants its pyrolytic cycle about every three months.

Every two years is the usual rhythm, and every year if you are over 70, diabetic or have a close relative with glaucoma. It is free on the NHS for under 16s, over 60s and people with diabetes, and it checks the health of the eye as well as the prescription.

Every two years is the usual answer for an adult, and every year once you are over 70 or if you are diabetic or have glaucoma in the family. In Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland the sight test is free on the NHS; in England it is free if you are under 16, over 60, diabetic, on certain benefits or have a close relative with glaucoma, and otherwise it is usually around £25 - worth it, because the test spots glaucoma and diabetes changes years before you would notice them.

Every two days, and every day in warm weather: fresh water, a rinse of the vase, and a fresh cut on the stems at the same time, because the water clouds from what the stems give off and the stems seal over where they were cut. A drop of bleach or a spoon of sugar is the old trick, and the cut is the part that actually works.

Every week or so if you wear it daily: it touches your neck and hands, and it hangs in the damp air of a bathroom, which is what turns it sour. Most go at 40C on a normal cycle - towelling and thick cotton will take 60C - and skip fabric softener on towelling because it coats the fibres. Dry it right through before it goes back on the hook, and hang it out of the bathroom between wears.

Every couple of months for a shower head in a hard-water area, and every three months or so where the water is soft; a tap aerator is the same job on the same timetable. The test is not the calendar but the spray: the moment the jets start going sideways, take it off and leave it an hour in half water, half white vinegar, or hang a freezer bag of it over the head, then rinse it and run the shower for a minute.

Every dairy ingredient has a straight swap: unsweetened soya or oat milk in place of milk, one for one, olive oil or a dairy-free spread for butter, and soya yoghurt for yoghurt. Where a recipe wants buttermilk, put a tablespoon of lemon juice in 250ml of plant milk and leave it ten minutes. Soya is the one with as much protein as milk, so pancakes, porridge and coffee taste least different with it.
Every day, two words, means each day - I walk every day. Everyday, one word, is the adjective for ordinary - everyday shoes. If you can say 'each day', keep the space.

Exchange is the moment the sale becomes legally binding: after that neither side can simply walk away, and if the seller refuses to complete you can sue for the deposit back and your costs, or press for the sale to go through. Before exchange either of you can pull out for any reason and owes nothing but their own legal fees - which is exactly the window a seller uses to take a better offer, and that is gazumping. So the practical answer is to push to exchange as soon as the searches are back, and to keep the deposit small until then.

Expect bleeding like a heavy period for up to two weeks after a miscarriage, sometimes on and off for three, with cramps that ease over a few days: use pads, and take paracetamol and ibuprofen as the packets say. Ring the ward or your GP the same day if you soak a pad in an hour, pass clots bigger than a 50p coin, feel feverish, or the discharge smells - that can mean tissue is left behind. A pregnancy test at three weeks should be negative; if it is not, ask to be seen.

Expect it, name it, and do not argue them out of it: "it's hard having someone new in the house" lands better than "you love your sister really". Give the older one ten minutes a day that belong to nobody else, let them help with the baby only if they offer to, and blame the baby for nothing they can hear - "the baby needs me" rather than "you'll have to wait". A few weeks of baby talk, wetting or clinginess is a bid for the same attention, not a step backwards, and it usually passes once the visitors stop.

FAQ stands for frequently asked questions: the page, usually at the foot of a website, where the thing you are about to write in has already been answered. Search that page for one distinctive word of your problem before you write, because the answer is often there in two lines and the form takes days.

Fake tan is a dye, usually DHA, that colours only the dead cells on the surface and fades after about five to seven days, so it gives no sun protection; you still need SPF, and the one real risk is breathing in a spray mist - ask for a lotion or mousse, hold your breath or wear the mask, and patch test first.

Familiar, subdued clothes are the thing: black or dark colours, smart and comfortable, and nothing new needed. If the family asked for bright colours or a football shirt, follow that instead, because it's about them.

Faulty goods: 30 days to return them for a full refund, then repair or replacement instead. Bought online or by post: 14 days from delivery to change your mind, and another 14 to send it back, you paying the postage unless it is faulty. In a shop, a change of mind is whatever their policy says, so check the receipt.
Feed birds seeds, fat balls and mealworms, and put out water too; skip bread, which fills them up without much goodness. Once you start in winter, keep going, because they come to rely on that spot.

Feed a sourdough starter equal weights of flour and water, about its own weight, once a day at room temperature. To start one from nothing, mix 50g of wholemeal flour with 50g of water and feed it the same way every day - it takes about a week of that before it doubles reliably. It is ready to bake with when it doubles within 4 to 6 hours and smells of yoghurt rather than acetone.

Feed a kitten kitten food, not cat food, four small meals a day until about six months and then two: wet food plus a little dry suits most, and leave water out in a wide bowl. A kitten should gain weight steadily, so weigh her weekly and ask the vet if she does not.

Feed first, then have the drink: alcohol is in your milk at its highest about half an hour to an hour after a glass and is gone in two to three hours for one drink, and there is no need to pump and dump - that only empties the milk, it does not speed the alcohol up. So an odd glass with a meal is fine, especially if you feed just before it or wait a couple of hours after. Getting properly drunk is the thing to avoid, and so is sharing a bed or a sofa with the baby after drinking.

Feed him before you sit down and give him something to do - a chew on his bed in another room, or a stuffed toy - so your meal is not the interesting part of his evening. Never hand food over from the table, and get everyone in the house to hold the same line: a dog given a scrap once will try every single meal.

Feed houseplants only while they are growing, from March to September: a half-strength liquid feed every two to four weeks is plenty, and none in winter while they rest. Overfeeding is worse than underfeeding - it burns the roots and leaves white crust on the compost - so if the leaves look pale, check the light before you reach for more food.

Feed houseplants from March to September, about once a month at half the strength on the bottle, and not at all in winter: most of them stop growing then, and the food just builds up in the compost. Fresh compost feeds a plant for the first couple of months, so nothing is needed after repotting.

Feel the back of the neck or the chest, not the hands: cool and dry is fine, hot and sweaty means a layer off, and cold and mottled means a layer on and a warmer room. Aim for about 16-20C, a vest and a sleepsuit, and one more layer than you are wearing; no hat indoors. Never a hot-water bottle or electric blanket with a baby, and keep the cot clear of loose bedding.

Feel the compost first: wet and smelly means too much water, so stop watering, let it drain and repot in fresh compost if the roots are brown and soft. Bone dry and light means the opposite, so soak the whole pot in a bowl for ten minutes. If it is neither, check the light and look under the leaves for tiny insects, and give it a few weeks before changing anything else: plants sulk slowly and recover slowly.
Feeling under the weather means a bit unwell - off colour, not seriously ill. What is wrong - sore throat, tired, sick?

Feeling washed out for a week or two after flu or another virus is normal, and it eases faster if you build back up slowly - a short walk, then a bit further - rather than going straight back to everything. Eat properly, keep fluids up and get your usual sleep. See a GP if the tiredness is no better after three or four weeks, or if it comes with breathlessness, a racing heart or feeling low.

Feeling wiped out for a week or two after flu is normal: build back slowly, sleep more than usual, and do not go straight back to full days. See a GP if you are still exhausted after four weeks, breathless at rest, or getting worse rather than better.

Feeling cold all the time is usually real rather than imagined: an underactive thyroid, low iron or a low body weight all do it, and so does being thin, tired or short of sleep. Ask a GP for a thyroid test and a full blood count if it is new or getting worse; meanwhile eat regularly, keep moving and wear a layer more than the people around you.

Feeling flat and tired in January or the dark months is common: less daylight shifts sleep and mood, and most people pick up by March. Get outside within an hour of waking, even on a grey day, keep up vitamin D in winter, and keep seeing people. If it stops you working or eating, or lasts beyond the winter, see a GP: light therapy and talking therapy both work, and it is not something to just push through.

Feet that are always cold are usually circulation: the body pulls blood in from the skin to keep your middle warm, and the feet are the far end of the line. Thick socks, shoes with a real sole and a walk every half hour help more than a hot water bottle. Always cold with tiredness or weight gain is worth a thyroid and anaemia blood test, and one cold foot is a GP question.

Feet that go numb or tingle in bed are usually a nerve being pressed by the position: crossed ankles, sitting on a foot, or a duvet tucked in tight. Change position and move the foot about, and it should come back within a few minutes. If it happens most nights, is there in the day too, or both feet are affected, see a GP for a blood test (B12, thyroid, blood sugar), because a nerve or a vitamin gap is what that pattern usually means; numbness with a new back pain, or a foot you cannot feel at all, is a same-day call.

Feet hip-width with the weight over the middle of your feet, then bend at the hips and knees rather than the back: take the bar (or the box, close in against your shins and no further out) with straight arms, chest up, shoulders slightly in front of it, and set your back flat before you pull. Push the floor away with your legs, keep the weight dragging up your shins, and stand tall without leaning back; lower it by sending the hips back first. A weight you can lift with a flat back is the weight to use - a rounded back is the whole risk.

Felipe VI is the king of Spain: he took the throne in June 2014 when his father Juan Carlos abdicated. The king is head of state but does not run the government - the prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, does.

Fence posts go 1.8m apart, centre to centre, for a standard 1.8m (6ft) panel, and 2.4m for a 2.4m panel - a gravel board and a panel are sold to that width, so measure the panel before you dig. On a slope, keep the tops level and let the bottom of each panel follow the ground, stepped one post at a time rather than raked.
Fennel seed is not hot - it is sweet and aniseedy, and it is half the taste of a sausage. A teaspoon crushed in a curry for four.
Fenugreek is not hot: it is bitter and maple-sweet, and a little goes a long way. The leaves are gentler than the seeds, which turn a dish bitter if they are fried too hard.

Ferdinand Magellan's expedition was the first to sail round the world, but he did not finish it: he was killed in the Philippines in 1521 and Juan Sebastian Elcano brought the one remaining ship, Victoria, home to Spain in September 1522.
Ferdinand Marcos Jr is the president of the Philippines: in office since June 2022. A Philippine president serves one six-year term.

Fifty multiple-choice questions in 57 minutes and you need 43 right, then 14 hazard-perception clips where you click as the hazard develops and you need 44 out of 75. Learn from the official DVSA bank rather than a free app, practise the clips on a big screen, and book the test once practice scores sit in the high forties.

File it now, even if you cannot pay: the £100 penalty for being a day late is charged whatever you do next, and it grows from there - £10 a day after three months, then 5% of the tax or £300 at six months and again at twelve - so the sooner it is in the smaller the bill. Interest runs on any tax unpaid after the deadline. If you cannot pay it, ring HMRC and ask for time to pay: a payment plan is agreed over the phone and it stops the collection letters.

File it today anyway: Companies House fines you automatically and the penalty climbs in bands, so filing now costs no more than filing next week within the same band. For a private company's accounts it is £150 up to a month late, £375 up to three months, £750 up to six, and £1,500 beyond that, and it doubles if you file late two years running. A late confirmation statement is £150, up to £1,500 if it keeps happening. Self assessment is separate: £100 the moment it is late, then £10 a day after three months. If the company cannot pay, the fine is still there, so tell Companies House rather than going quiet.

Fill the middle of the shelf, not the edges: a fan oven runs hottest near the door and the sides, so keep tins in the middle third with a gap of two fingers between them, and turn the tray round halfway through. Give it 15 minutes to preheat and check the dial with a cheap oven thermometer - most ovens are out by 10 to 20C, and an oven that reads 20C low browns the back before the front. If it is always the bottom that catches, the tin is too low or it is a dark one: move it up a shelf, use a lighter tin and drop the heat 10C. If the same side is always pale while the other catches, that is the element or the fan, not your baking.

Fill the bath about 5cm deep with water at 37 to 38C, warm on your wrist rather than hot, and get the towel, nappy and clothes open and ready before you start. Hold the head and shoulders with one arm so they never slip under, wash the face and hair first with plain water, then the body, and keep the room warm. Two or three baths a week is plenty for a newborn. A bath rather than a shower, because a newborn cannot hold their head up to have water poured over it; a shower together is fine once they sit up, head against your shoulder. Their hair needs no shampoo for the first months - plain water, and a hand across the forehead so none runs into the eyes.

Fill a tray or small pot with seed compost, firm it, water it first, and sow on the surface at the depth on the packet - about twice the seed's own size, and barely at all for tiny seed. Keep it at 18 to 21C somewhere light, cover it with a clear lid or a plastic bag until the first shoots show, then take the cover off. Water from below by standing the tray in a little water rather than pouring on top, and move each seedling into its own pot once it has two true leaves, holding it by a leaf and not the stem. Tomatoes, chillies and peppers are started indoors in March and April; hardier things wait until April, six to eight weeks before they go outside.

Fill a freezer bag with white vinegar - half vinegar, half water if the chrome worries you - tie it over the shower head so the nozzles soak for an hour, then rub them with a sponge and poke any blocked holes with a pin. Run it hot for a minute afterwards. Once a month keeps it clear; in a hard-water area, do it every couple of weeks.

Fill first, then sand, then finish: push the filler into the dents and holes, leave it a little proud, and sand it back level with the wood once it is hard. Then sand the whole surface - 120 grit on a block for paint or varnish, 80 to 100 on a filler patch - wipe the dust off with a tack cloth, and put the first coat on. Sand lightly between coats with 180 to 240 grit and wipe the dust off again, because that is what makes the last coat sit flat; leave the final coat alone. On a wall you only need to sand between coats if there is a run or a bit of grit.

Fill in the buyer's details on the V5C, tear off the green slip (V5C/2) and give that to them, then send the rest of the log book to DVLA at SA99 1BA - or do both online with the reference number on the front. Keep the yellow slip: it is your proof you told them. The new keeper needs the green slip to tax the car, and their own insurance from the moment they drive it away, so do the paper at the handover rather than later: until DVLA has the change on record, a parking ticket or a camera fine is still yours.

Fill it to about 5 to 8 cm with water at 37 to 38C - elbow or wrist temperature, which feels neither warm nor cool - and have the towel, nappy and clean clothes within reach before you start, because you never leave a baby alone in water, not for a second. Support the head and shoulders with one forearm, wash with plain water for the first month or so, and keep the room warm since a wet baby loses heat fast. Twice or three times a week is enough for a newborn; top and tail in between.

Fill it with hot water, a spoon of bicarbonate of soda and a splash of vinegar, leave it overnight and wash it as normal in the morning: that lifts the smell out of the plastic where soap alone does not. Dry it with the lid off, and leave a scrunched sheet of newspaper inside - a tub sealed while it is still damp is what keeps the smell in. Lemon juice, or a paste of bicarbonate, does the same job in an hour.

Filtration is passing a mixture through something with holes too small for the solid bits, so the liquid goes through and the solid stays behind: a coffee filter, a sieve in a flour mill, a kidney. It separates a solid from a liquid but not one dissolved chemical from another.

Find out which bit they want to stop before you decide, because a coach who shouts, a team where they never get picked and a child worn out by three clubs are three different problems, and only the last one is solved by quitting. Then ask them to finish the term or the season: stopping mid-way teaches that a hard patch is a way out, and it is usually the point where the fun comes back. If they still want out at the end, let them out, and swap it for something they choose themselves - the aim is a child who still moves, not a footballer.

Find out which bit is the problem before you argue about attendance: the work, one person, the noise at lunch, or the walk in - 'school' is nearly always a cover for one of them. Ask the teacher for a five-minute chat and agree one change you can all see this week. If they are refusing to go at all, ask to speak to the special needs coordinator; it is usually sorted with the school, not with a bigger row at home.

Find the model number on the inside of the flap and look up its reset - on most Hive and Nest units that is a pinhole or a menu option that puts the schedule back to the factory one, and then you set the times again from the app, which is much easier than on the unit. Before you reset, note the two numbers you actually care about: the times you get up and go to bed, and 18 to 20C while you are in.

Find the noisy board and work talcum powder, french chalk or graphite powder into the gaps between the boards - it stops the wood rubbing on the nail. If it still creaks, screw the board down again from above instead of nailing it, and on stairs check the treads are tight.

Find the plasterboard screws instead of hunting for timber: a small magnet run slowly across the wall sticks at each screw, and the screws are driven into the studs, so a line of them is the frame and studs are usually 400 or 600mm apart. A stud finder does the same job for a few pounds, and knocking along the wall for the dull solid note works if the wall is bare. Before you drill anywhere, check for cables and pipes - most run vertically above sockets, so keep to the screw line you found and stay wide of them.

Find the reason before you repaint, or it comes back: feel the patch for damp (a bathroom, a kitchen or a ceiling under a cold roof is the usual one), and press the plaster - if it crunches or sounds hollow it has blown and needs cutting back to sound plaster and filling. Paint flakes off a ceiling most often because an old distemper or silk finish was painted over without a primer, or bare plaster was painted without a mist coat, so scrape back to the firm edge, sand the edge flat, and prime the bare patch before you paint. Then two coats of the same finish, and deal with the steam or the leak, because paint cannot hold on a wet wall.

Find the relight sequence in the boiler's manual first: most modern boilers relight from a reset button, and an older one with a permanent pilot wants the gas knob held in for about twenty seconds once the flame catches. If it will not stay lit, stop there and call a Gas Safe engineer - it is usually the thermocouple, a part that takes ten minutes. Never keep pressing reset, and if you smell gas turn it off at the meter, open the windows and ring 0800 111 999.

Find the water before you treat the wall: a leaking gutter or downpipe, an overflow running, ground above the damp course, or a slow leak near the patch. Feel whether the wall is wet high up (a leak) or only at the bottom (rising damp). Warm it and ventilate it while you look, don't paint over it, and in a rented flat ask the landlord in writing.

Find the way in first: mice follow pipes and cables, so check the gap round the pipework under the sink, the air brick, and any gap wider than a pencil behind kitchen units, and block those with wire wool and filler. Then bait two or three traps along the wall, because mice run against edges, and clear the food source - a sealed bin and nothing left out overnight. Skip poison in a loft if there are pets or children, and the council pest control team is usually cheaper than a private firm.

Find the end date of your minimum term on the bill: out of contract it is 30 days' notice, in contract you owe the rest unless the price went up mid-term or the line does not work. Ask for the cancellation date and the final bill by email, and switch to the new provider the same day. If a payment still goes out after the date they confirmed, ask the bank for the direct debit indemnity.

Find the end date of your minimum term on the bill first: out of contract you give 30 days' notice, in contract you owe the rest unless the price went up mid-term or the service does not work. Ask for the cancellation date and the final bill by email, keep paying by direct debit until that final bill is settled, and ask for a PAC code if you want to keep the number.

Find the first topic you stopped understanding rather than the newest one, because everything after it is built on it: go through the textbook contents or the topic list and mark the last thing that made sense. Then do three things - tell the teacher you have fallen behind and ask which two topics matter most for the next test, spend twenty minutes a day on those two only, and get one session with a classmate who is good at them. Catching up is a short list worked through patiently, not the whole course read again.

Find a club that teaches technique rather than a fitness boxercise class - most amateur clubs run beginners' sessions and lend gloves and wraps for the first few. Go twice a week, expect the first month to be footwork, stance and the basic four punches on your own, and tell the coach you have not boxed before so nobody puts you in to spar. Boots, wraps and your own gloves are the only kit worth buying early.

Fine webbing and leaves that look speckled and dusty mean spider mites, which thrive in hot, dry air. Take the plant to the sink or shower and wash both sides of every leaf, raise the humidity around it - group it with other plants, or stand the pot on a tray of wet pebbles - and wash it again every three or four days for a fortnight, because the eggs hatch in between. A plant that is badly covered is better thrown out than fought for.

Fine, and this is where people cut out more than they need to: feta, halloumi, mozzarella, cottage cheese, cream cheese and all the hard cheeses - cheddar, parmesan, paneer - are made with pasteurised milk, and listeria is the only reason soft cheese is a worry. Check the label says pasteurised if it is a farm shop one; the supermarket tubs always are.

Fingers or toes that go white, then blue, then red when they warm up, or that go numb in the cold, are Raynaud's: keep the hands and feet warm, warm up slowly rather than in hot water, and see a GP this week, because it can be managed and it is sometimes linked to another condition. Numbness down one side of the body, or a hand that is weak or drops things, is 999.

Fingers that go numb in bed are usually a nerve being pressed: carpal tunnel if it is the thumb, index and middle finger, the ulnar nerve if it is the little finger, or the weight of your body on the arm. Shake it out, keep the wrist straight, and try a wrist splint from the pharmacy at night for a couple of weeks; see a GP if it wakes you most nights or the hand is getting weak. Numbness on one whole side, or in both hands and feet, is a same-day call.

First, it is not the end of anything: there are more routes from here than there were before results day. If you have missed a university offer, ring the university yourself today — courses take people who call — and look at Clearing the same afternoon. For school exams, ask about a remark and about resitting in November or next summer; both are normal and neither sets you back a year if you use the time.

Fish rest but do not sleep the way we do: most have no eyelids, so they hover still in a sheltered spot, often at night, with their gills still moving. Some, like sharks, keep swimming the whole time so water keeps flowing over their gills.

Fish take oxygen out of the water with gills: water flows in at the mouth and over thin, blood-rich filaments, where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out. Out of water the filaments collapse and stick together, so the fish suffocates even in air.

Fish and frogs first, then eels, water voles, insects, and in spring ducklings and moorhen chicks. A heron hunts by standing still in the shallows and striking, so a pond with a planted edge and deeper water gives the fish somewhere to hide.

Fish goes off faster than anything else and does not forgive it: it should smell of the sea, so an ammonia or fishy-sharp smell, flesh that stays dented when you press it, or grey gills means bin it. Use it the day you buy it or freeze it that day.

Fish is done at 50 to 55C, or the moment a fork twists a flake and it just separates, and it keeps cooking off the heat, so take it out a touch early and rest it two minutes. Cook it through to 63C for anyone pregnant, elderly or with a weak immune system. A salmon fillet wants 4 to 6 minutes a side in a hot pan or 8 to 12 minutes at 200C, cod and haddock a minute or two more, a tuna steak only 1 to 2 minutes a side so the middle stays pink, and a whole fish 10 minutes per 2.5cm of thickness. Salt it 15 minutes ahead or not at all and keep lemon off it until it is off the heat: both draw water out. Flakes that stay in soft pieces mean it was in long enough, so lift it then rather than waiting for it to look white all through.

Fit it first, because a badly set aid is why most of them get refused: a stick should come up to the crease of the wrist when they stand, and it is held in the hand opposite the bad hip or knee - an NHS physiotherapist or occupational therapist will set the height in ten minutes, and a parent takes that from a professional where they will not take it from you, so ask the GP for a falls or balance assessment. Then make it theirs: a cane they chose the colour of, a shopping trolley, or a frame that lives by the door gets used where a hospital one does not, and a pendant alarm is easier to accept as "so I stop worrying", with a key safe so help can get in. The council's adult social care team sends an OT free of charge, and the same visit fits grab rails by the loo and the stairs. Offer it for the garden and the icy week, not for getting old.

Fit it in a door rather than a wall, and take the door off its hinges first: a door that lies flat is ten minutes with a jigsaw. Mark the template at the height of the cat's belly, drill the four corners, cut between them, and screw the two halves together through the door with the tunnel trimmed to the door's thickness. Watch where the cat already pushes before you cut, keep the flap clear of any panel doing structural work, and in a double glazed door use a glazier - a cut pane has to be replaced, not drilled.

Fitness and touch come back at different speeds, and it is the second one that gets people hurt. Train twice a week for a fortnight before you play any match at all, then a half, then a full one - about six weeks from the first session to playing as you did. If it was an injury that stopped you, the date is the physio's and not the calendar's: the usual guide is a week of easy training for every week you were out, and nothing at match pace until you can sprint and turn without thinking about it.

Fitting a new one is the long job, not the short one: an hour or two for a washing machine or a dishwasher, about an hour a radiator once the system is drained, and a boiler is the big one - usually a full day plus the gas check at the end. Ask when you book whether the price includes taking the old one away, the gas safety check and any making good, because those are the parts that turn a quote into a bigger bill.

Five minutes of walking for each month of age, twice a day, so three months is about fifteen minutes a time and six months about half an hour. Until the vaccinations are done, keep him off the ground where other dogs go and let him play in the garden instead; free running and stairs are the things to hold back on while his joints form.

Five minutes, in two parts: first something easy that gets you slightly out of breath - a brisk walk, a slow jog, skipping, the exercise bike - then a few quick movements through the range you are about to use, like leg swings, arm circles, hip circles and ten bodyweight squats. Start the first set lighter than the rest. Save the long holds for afterwards: stretching cold muscles first does not prevent injury and takes a little power off the session.

Five or six poos a day is normal in a newborn, and so is once a week in a breastfed baby, as long as it stays soft and they are feeding and having six or more wet nappies a day. It should be mustard yellow; green usually only means it went through quickly, and the black-green first poos are normal for a day or two. Ring the health visitor or the GP today for white or very pale poo, blood, black poo after the first few days, watery poo that soaks the nappy, or a baby who feeds less, has a hard tummy, or is floppy or feverish.
Five spice is not hot - star anise, fennel, cinnamon, cloves and pepper - and it is strong, so half a teaspoon for four is the usual amount.

Five substitutions from three stoppage windows in the Premier League and most competitions, plus a sixth in extra time; it was three until 2020. A bench of nine is named, so most of the squad gets a game.

Five things in the first two sentences: full name, age, where they lived, the date they died, and who they leave behind. Then one or two sentences of character - what they did for a living, what they loved, a phrase people will recognise - and the funeral or donation details at the end. Ring the funeral director first: they will word it with you and most put it on their own website free, and a local paper charges by the line.

Five to ten minutes: two or three minutes on the bike, rower or cross-trainer until you are warm, then a couple of light sets of whatever you are about to do - the same movement at half the weight, for 10 reps. That is a warm-up; the long stretches are for afterwards, when the muscles are warm.

Five to ten minutes in an ordinary room: a drink comes off the kettle at about 90C and is comfortable to sip at about 60C, and a splash of cold milk takes it down at once. A wide mug cools faster than a tall narrow one, and standing the mug in a bowl of cold water does it in a couple of minutes - stir it and test it with your lip, not a finger. A lid on the mug keeps the heat in, so take it off if you want it sooner.

Five words a night, not the whole list: look at the word, say it, cover it, write it, then check it, and put the ones she gets wrong to the back of the queue. Say the word in a sentence as you test her, because a spelling she can only write in a list is not learnt yet. Ten minutes is enough, and the night before is for the five she keeps missing, not for the twenty she knows.

Five years at dental school, then a year of dental foundation training in a practice before you can work on your own, so six years from starting to being paid as a dentist. The entry grades are the thing that decides it: A-level chemistry and biology are wanted by most schools, and the UCAT test plus an interview come before any offer.

Five lines that rhyme AABBA, and the rhythm is the whole thing: three beats then three then three on the first two lines, two then two on the short ones, then back to three. Put a person and a place in line one ("A fellow who lived in Peru"), keep line five for the punchline, and read it aloud - if a beat is missing, the joke dies.

Five lines in the first person: what you do, who you do it for, one proof - a project, a number, a place you worked - and how to reach you. Cut the adjectives at the top, because "passionate about stories" tells a reader nothing, and write the sentence you would say if someone asked at a party what you do.

Fix the boundary before the training, because recall never stops a dog getting out. Walk the fence line: 1.2m holds most dogs and 1.8m a jumper, nothing against it to climb, and a gap under a gate is wide enough if his head goes through. Set the mesh 30cm into the ground or run a line of slabs along the base so he cannot dig out. Keep him out of the hall while the front door is open, or put a stair gate across it. Then microchip and a tag with your number, and a long line for recall practice.

Fix a monthly figure you would not miss - one or two per cent of your take-home pay is a common rule - and set it as a standing order so it does not cost a decision every time. Always tick Gift Aid if you are a UK taxpayer: it adds 25% at no cost to you, and higher-rate payers can claim the difference back. Look the charity up on the Charity Commission register first, and prefer ones that publish what share of income reaches the work rather than the fundraising.

Fix a total you can pay for in cash this month, divide it by the people you buy for, and write the cap next to each name before you open a browser. Buy in October, agree a secret santa with the adults, and shop for food from a list in early December: the overspend is nearly always late presents and a trolley filled in a panic.

Fix it to the wall and never through into the floor, because the floor moves and the board will crack or come loose: plugs and screws at 600 mm centres, or grab adhesive with a screw at each end, and keep the screws 10 mm down from the top edge. The two cuts that matter are the corners, so mitre an offcut first and check it against the actual corner - internal corners can be coped instead, which is the back of the profile cut away with a coping saw so it sits over the board it meets and the joint cannot open. Mark the board in place and scribe the bottom to the floor rather than trusting the gap, prime the bare ends and the back before it goes on, then caulk the top edge and fill the screw holes.

Fix it before it grows: turn the garment inside out and darn across the hole with small running stitches, then across them at right angles, in thread close to the colour. A knee or a jeans pocket takes an iron-on patch on the inside, which is invisible and takes five minutes.

Flat pancakes are usually over-mixed or too thin: stir until the flour just disappears, leaving lumps, and use roughly 1 part flour to 1.2 of milk by volume. Resting the batter 15 minutes helps, and a pinch of baking powder makes the thick American ones rise.

Flat means the fizz has gone, or - in a still wine - the fresh edge that made it worth drinking, because the gas and the aromas escape as soon as air gets in. A stopper and the fridge slow that to 3 to 5 days; a vacuum stopper or a squirt of inert gas buys a day or two more. Past that it is cooking wine, and wine that has turned vinegary is a good vinegar.

Flatten them and keep them dry: clean cardboard goes out with the kerbside recycling, cut down to the size your council takes, and tape, polystyrene and any food grease keep a box out of it. More than the bin will take is a bulky collection or a trip to the recycling centre, and removal boxes in good nick go fast on a local free-and-wanted group.

Fleas are not a sign of a dirty house: they come in on the animal and the eggs drop into the carpet, so the house is the part that keeps them coming back. Treat the animal and the house on the same day: a spot-on or tablet from the vet for every pet, bedding washed at 60C, and the carpets vacuumed daily for a fortnight, emptying the vacuum outside, because most of a flea infestation is eggs and pupae in the floor, not fleas on the pet. Only about one flea in twenty is on the animal at any time, which is why one treatment rarely clears it and it takes a few weeks; a pet that is still itchy a week later is a reinfestation, not a failed treatment. Never put a dog flea product on a cat - permethrin, in most dog spot-ons, is deadly to cats.

Floaters are bits of the jelly inside the eye casting a shadow, and one or two that have been there a while are normal with age - they fade as your brain stops noticing them. What is not normal is a sudden shower of new ones, flashes like lightning at the edge of your sight, or a curtain or shadow coming across it: ring an optician or go to A&E the same day, because that is how a detached retina starts and it is fixable if it is caught quickly. Also get your sight checked if the floaters came with a blow to the head.

Florence Nightingale (1820-1910) was the British nurse who reorganised the army hospital at Scutari in the Crimean War, where cleaning, fresh air and proper food cut the death rate. She then set up the first professional nursing school, at St Thomas's in London, and made nursing a trained job.

Florets take 5 to 7 minutes in boiling salted water and a whole head 10 to 15, until a knife slides into the stalk with no crunch left. A tablespoon of milk or lemon in the water keeps it white rather than grey, and salt it properly or it tastes of nothing. Drain it well, because a cauliflower left sitting in its water goes soft and sulky.

Flour, water, salt and yeast. The yeast gives off gas as it feeds on the flour, and the gluten in the flour - stretchy because it is wheat - traps it as bubbles, which is what makes the loaf rise; the oven then sets the structure and browns the crust.

Flour keeps 6 months in a sealed jar in a cool cupboard and a year in the freezer; wholemeal and brown flour go off sooner, 3 months, and smell of old paint when they do. Put a bay leaf in the jar and the weevils leave it alone.

Flowers are optional now: many families ask for no flowers and name a charity instead, so ask them or the funeral director first. If you are sending some, a simple bouquet or wreath from the family and a spray for the coffin are the usual, and a florist who does funerals will know what holds up outdoors and roughly what it costs. A single bunch from a supermarket is fine too, and nobody will mind.

Flowers dropping with no fruit is nearly always pollination: courgettes have separate male and female flowers, and the female one has a tiny fruit behind it that shrivels if no pollen arrives. Pick a male flower, strip the petals and dab it into the centre of a female one in the morning, and leave some male flowers on for the bees.

Flu usually hits hardest for two or three days and is mostly gone in a week, but a cough and a flat, tired feeling can drag on for two or three weeks, and that is normal. Sleep as much as your body asks for, drink more than you think you need, and go back to work or training gently. See a doctor if you are breathless, have chest pain, a fever past five days, or are still exhausted after a month.

Flu is rest and fluids for most people: stay in bed while the fever lasts, drink more than you think you need, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen for the aches at the dose on the pack. Expect two or three bad days and a tired week. Ring a GP or 111 the same day if you are breathless, have chest pain, cannot keep fluids down, or are pregnant, over 65 or have a long-term condition.

Flu is influenza and Covid is the coronavirus, and you can't tell them apart by symptoms - fever, cough and tiredness come with both, so a test is the only way to know. Both are worth staying home for, and both are riskier for the same people.

Flushes and night sweats last about four years on average, and around one in ten women has them for 12 years or more. The years of changing periods before the last one usually start in the mid-forties, the average age of the last period is 51, and symptoms that start early or last long are worth a GP visit - HRT shortens them for most women.

Fly east and your body has to run ahead, so shift your bedtime 30 minutes earlier for a few nights before you go, then get out in morning light at the other end. Skip caffeine after midday there and stay up until at least 10pm local.

Flying west stretches your day, so go to bed an hour later than usual for the last two or three nights before you go, then sleep in a little at the other end and get afternoon daylight. Stay up to 10pm local on night one rather than napping, which is what leaves you awake at 3am.

Flying is usually fine: most airlines take you up to 36 weeks for one baby, and 32 weeks for twins, and some ask for a letter from the midwife from 28 weeks, so check your airline before you book. Drink water, get up and walk every hour or so and wear compression socks on a long flight. Ask the midwife first if you have had bleeding, high blood pressure, pre-eclampsia or twins.

Fog forms when damp air cools to the point where its water vapour condenses into droplets near the ground. Driving in it, slow down and use dipped headlights or fog lights, not full beam: full beam bounces off the fog and makes it worse.

Fold the pillow in half and let go: one that stays folded has gone flat, which for most is after one to two years, hollowfibre sooner than foam. Buy the same loft and firmness again rather than a fancier one, and until it arrives a rolled towel under the neck end fills the gap a flat pillow leaves - two flat pillows stacked do not, they just make the head higher.

Fold a sheet of A5 thick paper in half, press the crease under a book, and write inside before you stick anything on - ink on a finished card is the usual ruin. One bold thing on the front, a cut shape or a photo or thick pen, and three lines inside naming something you did together beats a lot of stickers.

Follow the air path: take the hose off both ends and drop a coin through it, shake the bag or empty the bin, wash the filter (most are washable, and it has to be bone dry before it goes back) and cut the hair off the brush bar. A blocked hose, a full bag or a matted filter is the answer nearly every time, and all three are free to fix.

Food miles are the distance food travels from where it is grown to your plate, and they matter less than most people think: transport is around a tenth of the emissions in a typical shopping basket, while what the food is and how it was made is most of the rest. Air-freighted green beans and out-of-season asparagus are the exceptions worth avoiding; eating less meat and wasting less food cuts far more than buying only local.

Food, water and cover, in that order: a feeder with mixed seed or fat balls, a shallow dish of water with a stone in it, and a shrub or a hedge to bolt into. Put the feeder where a cat cannot sit under it, leave the seed heads on perennials over winter, and skip the tidy-up in autumn - the birds eat the insects in the stems.

Food banks give a few days of free food, and most ask for a referral from a GP, school, Citizens Advice or support worker. Search for "food bank" plus your town, or ring Citizens Advice; some also help with fuel and baby things, and there's nothing to be embarrassed about.

Food first: kitten food, not cat food, four small meals a day until about six months, and water in a wide bowl. Keep her in one warm room to start with a litter tray, a bed and something to hide under, and let her come to you rather than picking her up all the time. Book the vet in the first week: the first jab is due at eight to nine weeks and the second three to four weeks later, worming runs every two weeks until twelve weeks, and a microchip and neutering at about four months. Play with a wand toy rather than your hands, so hands stay boring, and no cow's milk - it gives kittens the runs.

Food in a fridge whose door stayed shut is safe for about 4 hours, and after that the perishables go: milk, soft cheese, cooked meat, cooked rice and leftovers, and anything past its date. Butter, hard cheese, jam, pickles and most fruit and veg come through a warm day, so a full clear-out is not needed.

Foot pain is often the plantar fascia, the band under the arch, worst on your first steps in the morning: stretch the calf against a wall before you stand up, roll the arch on a cold bottle, and wear shoes with a firm sole indoors too. A heel that hurts all day, or a foot that is red and hot, needs looking at.

For most people the cholesterol in food matters much less than the saturated fat in it: an egg a day is fine, and it is the butter, cheese, fatty meat and pastries around the egg that move your LDL. People with diabetes or an inherited high cholesterol are usually advised to keep to about one a day, and it is worth asking your GP if that applies to you. Prawns and liver are similar: fine in normal amounts, not a reason to worry on their own.

For most things, 180C (160C fan, gas mark 4) for cakes, biscuits, a tray of vegetables and a slow roast, and 200C (180C fan, gas mark 6) for chips, roast potatoes and anything you want brown and crisp. Go to 220C (200C fan, gas mark 7) for a fast pizza or a crisp edge, and down to 150C (130C fan, gas mark 2) for meringues and slow bakes.

For one sofa and a bed, hire a man with a van for a couple of hours or borrow a van and two friends; book the van for the whole morning rather than by the hour. Measure the doorways and the stairwell first, because a sofa that doesn't fit costs you the day.

For ordinary documents a cheap mono laser is the one to have: about £100, and its toner costs less per page than inkjet ink and never dries out. An inkjet is the right printer for photos and colour, but only if you print often enough that the ink does not dry out. Whatever you pick, work out the cost per page from the cartridge price and its page count - the cheapest printer is often the most expensive ink.

For science with jokes: *The Infinite Monkey Cage*, a physicist and a comedian on one question in 45 minutes. *Science Vs* takes one claim an episode and weighs the evidence, and *Ologies* is a long friendly interview with a scientist each time. For space, *13 Minutes to the Moon* is the best thing made about Apollo.

For standing all day, prioritise a cushioned sole, room at the toes and a snug heel, and buy at the end of the day when your feet are at their biggest. Two pairs worn alternately last far longer than one.

For the scales, food moves more than exercise does: a hard session burns maybe 300 to 500 calories, and an extra biscuit and a glass of wine take that back. Do both, but take the food loss slowly - a smaller portion of the same meals and fewer liquid calories - and add two brisk sessions a week rather than cutting hard and training hard at once.

For the gym: trainers you only wear indoors, two towels (one for the floor and machines), a water bottle, a padlock for the locker, deodorant and a bag for wet kit. A resistance band and a notebook beat anything else a shop will sell you.

For the juice: lime is the nearest, or white wine vinegar or cider vinegar at half the amount, or a splash of orange juice if the dish is sweet anyway. For the zest: lime or orange zest, or a few drops of lemon essence. Where the lemon is the whole point - lemon drizzle, hollandaise, a lemon tart - a bottle of juice does the job, and nothing else does.

For video editing, gaming or CAD you do need a dedicated graphics card: look for 16GB of RAM (32GB for 4K video) and a screen that covers 100% sRGB. Expect to pay £900 to £1,300, and check the weight before you commit to carrying it.

For work, four things decide it: the fabric, the rise, the length and the pockets. A wool-poly blend or a cotton twill with a little stretch creases less and gives when you sit and stand; a mid rise that sits at the waist stays put through a shift; and the hem should break once on the shoe, so buy the length that fits you - short and petite lengths are sold off the rail and cost no more than a tailor. Check a phone goes in the pocket without pulling, and two pairs of one dark colour is the cheapest way to always have a clean pair.

For an older dog: a warm, soft bed away from draughts, a ramp or a low step for the sofa, shorter and more frequent walks, and a vet check twice a year. Keep its claws short, which is easy to forget when it walks less, and ask the vet about pain relief if it's slow to get up.

For an adult: 200 to 400 mg every four to six hours, at most 1200 mg a day without a doctor's say-so, and always with food. Skip it if you have a stomach ulcer, kidney trouble, asthma that aspirin sets off, or are past 20 weeks pregnant; paracetamol is the safer default. A pharmacist will settle the dose for your case.

For an electric, the whole fix is a headphone amp or an audio interface into your phone - a twenty pound plug-in amp is silent to everyone else. On an acoustic, stuff a cloth or a soundhole cover in the hole, play with a thin pick and a light touch, and put the instrument on a cushion in a small room rather than against a shared wall; a digital piano with headphones does the same for keys.

For anything faulty you're entitled to a full refund within 30 days of buying it, and after that to a repair or replacement. Online orders can go back within 14 days of delivery for any reason if they're unused; in a shop, a change of mind is the shop's policy, not the law.

For 250ml of buttermilk: 250ml of milk with a tablespoon of lemon juice or white vinegar, left 10 minutes to thicken. Plain yoghurt thinned with milk works too, and so does sour cream loosened with a splash of milk.

For a night before an early flight, book an airport hotel with a shuttle and check the first and last shuttle times before you pay - a 4am shuttle that stops at 11pm is the usual trap, and so is a "5 minutes from the terminal" that is five minutes by car on a road with no pavement. A town two or three stops away on the train, or a park-and-fly with the transfer included, is usually about half the price; add up the transfer, the parking and the extra hour and pick on the total. Take the flexible rate if the flight is early, and get the shuttle time in writing.

For a pet, buy the comfort they use every day rather than another toy: a cat wants a warm bed by a radiator, a scratch post tall enough to stretch up on, or a food-puzzle ball; a dog wants a long-lasting chew it only gets on the day, a snuffle mat, or a spare lead for the car. A rabbit or a guinea pig wants a bigger hidey house and a chew stick, and a box with a blanket in it is famously the best present of all. Keep chocolate, grapes, raisins and anything with xylitol away from a dog, and skip the novelty toys they will ignore by Boxing Day.

For a risotto or a rice pudding, don't rinse it: that surface starch is what makes it creamy. For separate, fluffy grains, rinse in a sieve until the water runs clear, which washes the starch off. It was never about hygiene.

For a room with no window, take the plants that cope with low light: pothos, snake plant, ZZ plant, peace lily and spider plant will all hold on, and a bathroom's steam suits a fern. Everything slows down in the dark, so water far less than the label says - every two to three weeks, once the top of the compost is dry - or the roots rot. If there is no daylight at all, no plant will live there: a lamp left on for twelve hours is what keeps one going, and a good fake is the honest answer for a cellar.

For a week: five tops, three bottoms, two layers, one pair of shoes you can walk in and one smarter pair, plus a waterproof, swimwear if there is water, chargers and any tickets. Plan to wash once on day three or four - a hostel or a launderette - and you can halve the clothes. Roll everything, put the first night's things on top, and leave the "just in case" outfit at home.

For a UK student, a taught masters is usually £9,000 to £15,000 for the year - around £8,000 to £12,000 for a classroom subject, £12,000 to £20,000 for a lab one, and an MBA can be £25,000 or more - plus living costs for a full-time year. A postgraduate master's loan from Student Finance covers up to about £12,500 of it, paid in three instalments, and it does not depend on your income. Ask the department about scholarships and fee waivers before you ask a bank, and check whether the course runs part time, because that spreads the cost over two years while you work.

For a box it is length x width x height, so 10cm by 5cm by 2cm is 100cm³. A cylinder is pi x radius² x height, and a sphere is 4/3 x pi x radius³. Put every measurement in the same unit before multiplying.

For a cat or a dog with dandruff, look at food, fleas and baths before a shampoo: a dry flaky coat is usually a cheap diet or winter air, and flea dirt looks like it until a damp tissue turns it red-brown. Brush weekly to lift the flakes, add an omega-3 or fish-oil supplement, and bathe no more than monthly with a pet shampoo. Thick greasy flakes, red or itchy skin, or flakes with hair loss is the vet's call - that is often a mite or a yeast.

For a child, fluid and fibre do most of it: water through the day, fruit, vegetables and wholemeal bread, fewer fizzy drinks, and not too much milk, which is the usual cause. Have them sit on the potty or loo after meals with their feet flat on a stool, praise them for trying, and never force or scold. An adult laxative is not the answer; see the GP if there is blood, real pain, or nothing for two weeks.

For a chip pan or a fryer, fill it no more than a third full and never past half - hot fat rises when the food goes in, and a pan that is too full is the way people get burned. 180C is the temperature for chips: a cube of bread browns in about 30 seconds. Fry in small batches so the fat does not drop, stand back as the chips go in, and never leave the pan.
For a commute: *The Rest Is History* (30 to 50 minutes, always interesting), *The Diary of a CEO* for long interviews, or *Short History Of...* for 40-minute stories. All work with one earbud in.

For a 500g loaf: 10g of salt, 7g of dried yeast and 320ml of tepid water. That is the ratio to remember rather than the grams - 2% salt, a little over 1% yeast and about 64% water by flour weight - so double the flour and double all three. The dough should feel tacky but come away from the bowl; add water a spoon at a time if it is stiff and a spoon of flour if it is sloppy.

For a day on open hills, yes: waterproof over-trousers weigh almost nothing in a rucksack and turn a wet walk into a fine one, and above the treeline the wind makes an umbrella useless. Cheap ones sweat from the inside, so look for taped seams and a long zip up the leg so you can pull them on over boots.

For a family with an older parent, WhatsApp is the easiest: install it, add the contacts, then tap New group, name it and pick the people. Turn on their notifications for that one chat and pin it to the top of their screen, and start by sending a photo so there is something to reply to.

For a first session you need very little: shorts or leggings that stretch, a t-shirt, trainers with a bit of support, a water bottle, a small towel and a padlock for the locker. That is the whole list - no gym turns anyone away for supermarket kit, and the machines are set up for exactly that. Wear what you already own, wash it after each session, and only buy a second set once you know you are going twice a week.

For a first 10k, build up to three runs a week and add about 10% to your longest run weekly, with the last long run a fortnight before race day. If you can run 5k comfortably now, eight to ten weeks is a realistic build.

For a fresh knock, sprain or strain, the first two days do most of the work: rest it from the movement that hurt, ice it for 15 to 20 minutes every few hours with a cloth between the pack and the skin, wrap it firmly and keep it up when you sit. After 48 hours gentle movement beats total rest, and paracetamol or ibuprofen eases the pain. Go to A&E the same day if you cannot put weight on it, a joint looks crooked, or the skin past the injury goes numb, white or cold; see a GP or a physio if it is no better after a week, if it gives way, or if the swelling keeps coming back.

For a holiday read: *The Thursday Murder Club* (funny, short chapters), *Lessons in Chemistry* (warm and clever), or *The Midnight Library* (gentle and quick). All three are easy to pick up and put down.

For football, *Football Weekly* from the Guardian is twice a week, quick and funny, and *The Rest Is Football* is Lineker, Richards and Shearer talking. For cricket, *Tailenders* is the one people who do not like cricket listen to.

For health with the evidence shown: *Zoe Science & Nutrition*, one food or habit an episode with a scientist and a doctor. For sleep, *Nothing Much Happens* reads quiet stories slowly and *Sleep With Me* rambles on purpose, both made to send you off rather than to be listened to.

For healthy kidneys, up to about two grams of protein a kilo a day is not a risk: no study has shown kidney damage in people with normal kidney function, and it does not harm your bones either. Extra protein beyond what your muscles use is simply burned, not stored as poison, and you do not need to force litres of water - drink to thirst. If you already have kidney disease, ask your doctor for a number before you raise it.

Force the app closed and open it again first, then update it in the App Store or Play Store: an app that is behind the phone's software is the usual cause. If it still will not open, restart the phone, then check the phone has storage free (an almost-full phone cannot run apps), and as a last step delete the app and reinstall it, which keeps your account but loses anything saved only on the phone. If the store says the app needs a newer iPhone or Android version, the phone itself is the limit and no amount of reinstalling will fix it.

Force a restart first, because a frozen digitiser is the commonest cause and nothing else works while it is frozen: on an iPhone press volume up, then volume down, then hold the side button until the Apple logo appears; on Android hold the power button for 20 to 30 seconds. Then clean the glass, take off a thick screen protector or a case that presses on the edges, and dry your hands - a damp or gloved finger is not read. A screen that responds in some places and not others has a dead band in the digitiser, which is a new screen, £50 to £120 fitted on a mid-range phone.

Forget the network and rejoin it: Settings > Wifi, tap the network, Forget, then add it again with the password off the router's sticker. If other devices are fine on the same wifi, the phone is the problem, so restart the phone and check it is not set to a static IP by accident; a phone that will not connect at all while everything else does is usually too old for the newer security setting, which the router can be set to WPA2 to fix.

Forgiving yourself is not letting it slide: it is saying what you did plainly, making the amends you can, and then treating the debt as paid instead of re-running the court case every night. Pick the smallest real repair - the apology, the thing you would do differently - do it this week, and say privately that the next time you would act differently. If the same voice keeps going over it months later, that is worth talking through with someone.

Forgiving is not saying it was fine, and it is not trusting them again: it is deciding to stop charging them for it, so the thing stops running your week. Do it as a decision rather than waiting to feel warm about them, and say what you are dropping - 'I am not bringing this up again, and I am not pretending it did not happen.' You can forgive someone and still keep them at arm's length, and nobody is owed the words back until they have said sorry.

Forward the text to 7726 - that is the free number UK networks use for spam - then block the sender and delete it. Never reply, not even with STOP, because a reply tells them the number is live; and never use a link in one, however much it looks like your bank.

Four medium tins a week, or two fresh tuna steaks: that is the limit for an adult, and it is about the mercury rather than the fat. Tuna is the one oily fish that does not count towards the two portions a week - canning strips most of the omega-3 - so it is protein, not a fish-oil dose. If you are pregnant or trying, keep to the same four tins; a child gets about half a tin as a portion.
Four quarters: 10 minutes each in international (FIBA) games, so 40 minutes of play, and 12 each in the NBA for 48. The clock stops on every whistle, so the whole game takes about two hours.

Four things never go down a drain: fat, oil and grease (they cool, set and make fatbergs), wet wipes even the ones marked flushable, anything that swells or sets - rice, pasta, potatoes, flour, eggshells and pastry scraps go down soft and pack hard a metre along - and paint, thinner and the chemicals that go with them. Fat goes into a jar or the bin, wipes and grounds into the bin, rice and peelings into the food waste with a sieve in the plug for the last rinse. A toilet takes the three Ps and nothing else: pee, poo and paper. Soapy water, tea, milk and small crumbs are fine.

Four things: a layer of blubber, feathers packed so tightly that water never reaches the skin, feet and flippers with a heat-exchange that keeps the blood warm, and huddling. In a huddle each bird takes a turn on the freezing outside.

Four thousand characters including spaces, or forty-seven lines - whichever you hit first - and that is one side of A4 in plain prose. Write the draft long, then cut: the sentences that say nothing ("ever since I was young") go first, then any description of the course you can read on the university's own page. Paste it into a character counter rather than guessing, and leave room for the edit.

Four to six weeks, with a test kit telling you when it is done. Ammonia from fish waste and food has to be eaten by bacteria that take weeks to grow, and the tank is ready when ammonia and nitrite both read zero a day after you add a little food: ammonia peaks in the first week or two, nitrite in the third or fourth, and nitrate climbing at the end is the sign it has finished. A bottle of starter bacteria can cut a week or so off. Don't add more than a few small fish at first, and don't change the filter media in that time.
Four 15-minute quarters, so 60 minutes of play, and about 75 minutes all told with the breaks. The clock stops for injuries and for the ball going out, so a close game can run a little past that.

Fourteen lines of iambic pentameter - ten beats a line, da-DUM five times - with either ABAB CDCD EFEF GG (Shakespeare's) or ABBAABBA then a sestet (the older Italian shape). The easy way in is Shakespeare's: three quatrains that each push the idea one step further, then a couplet that turns it, so write the last two lines first.
Frank-Walter Steinmeier is the president of Germany: in office since 2017 and re-elected in 2022. The job is mostly ceremonial - the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, runs the government.
