Freckles are clumps of the brown pigment melanin that your skin makes in response to sun, so they show up most on fair skin in summer and fade in winter. They are harmless, and the fairer your skin the more carefully you need to cover up: sunscreen and a hat stop new ones and protect against sun damage.

Freckles are little patches of melanin, the pigment that colours skin, made by cells that respond to sunlight; people with paler skin and certain genes make more of it, which is why they show up after time in the sun. They are harmless, but a new or changing spot needs checking, and sunscreen keeps them from darkening.

Free ones that work: a walk with a purpose (a park, a canal, the woods, a hill with a view - flask in the bag), a museum or gallery with free entry, the library, or a Saturday market. With kids, add a list of five things to find and a ball. Take snacks and a drink, and the day costs you parking and a coffee.

Free to join: take the card or the form and something with your name and address on it - a bill, a driving licence, a bank statement - to any branch, or join on your council's library website and collect the card there. A card lapses after a year or two without use and renewing it is free at the desk or online; a lost one is a couple of pounds to replace. The same card gets you the ebooks and audiobooks, through the Libby or BorrowBox app with your card number and PIN, and nothing you borrow that way needs returning.

Freeze the card in your bank's app first: most let you unfreeze it, so it costs nothing if the card turns up. Then order a replacement and read through the last few transactions. Report anything you don't recognise the same day; you are usually not liable for spending after you tell the bank.

Freeze the joint account today - either of you can ask the bank to, and it stops more money going out - then open your own current account in the same week and move your pay and your direct debits across. You are both still liable for an overdraft or a joint loan on it, so agree in writing who pays what off and tell the bank in writing that you have separated. Ask Citizens Advice before you sign anything about that debt: it is free and it is the part people get wrong.

Freeze a bottle of water or a small ice pack overnight and put it in the bag with the food, or freeze the sandwich fillings themselves (hummus, cooked chicken, cheese) and let them thaw by lunchtime. A bag with a lining holds the cold far better than a paper one, and the food wants to sit against the cold pack rather than next to it. Rice, cooked meat and dairy are the things to be strict about: over 5C for more than a couple of hours and they are not worth eating.

Freezer burn is the food drying out where air can reach it: the water at the surface turns straight to vapour in the cold, so that patch goes pale, leathery and tasteless. It is safe to eat, just cut that bit off - and pressing the air out of the bag and freezing in portions, rather than a loose bag of loose bits, is what stops it.

Fresh water every day, and properly wash the bowl every day or two rather than just topping it up: a bowl that is only rinsed grows the slimy film that puts a cat off drinking, and a dog will drink from it anyway and then be off his food. Hot water and washing-up liquid, then a rinse, is enough - a dishwasher cycle once a week is easier still. Water bottles for rabbits, guinea pigs and hamsters get fresh water daily too, and twice a day in hot weather.

Fresh water every day, and wash the bowl properly every day or two: hot water and washing-up liquid, then a rinse, because a bowl that is only topped up grows a slimy film on the side and a cat will stop drinking from it. A dishwasher cycle once a week is easier still, and a water bottle wants fresh water daily and a scrub with a bottle brush.

Fresh juice keeps 3 to 4 days in the fridge once it is opened, and a carton's date is for the unopened pack: after opening the vitamin C fades and it starts to ferment, so it is not a thing to keep for a week. Keep it cold, shake it before pouring, and go by the smell - juice that is fizzy or sharp has started to turn. A smoothie keeps about 2 days, and a shop-bought one no longer than its date.

Fresh lasagne sheets need no cooking at all: layer them straight in. Dried sheets made without egg go in dry too, as long as the sauce is wet enough; dried egg pasta is better for 3 or 4 minutes in boiling water first. Either way rest the finished dish 10 minutes before cutting so it holds together.

From an accepted offer, eight to twelve weeks is normal, and a chain adds a few weeks per link. Searches and the freeholder's pack are what drag, not the mortgage offer, so ask the solicitor how the searches are going and agree a target completion date in writing. Nobody is bound until contracts are exchanged, so do not hand in notice on a rented place, and budget for the survey, legal fees and stamp duty.

From a few weeks old, once you both feel well - the common six-week mark is about your own healing, not the baby's readiness, and classes take them from about four weeks. Keep the first dips to 10 or 15 minutes in water near 30 to 32C, and get out when they shiver or their lips go blue; a cool public pool below about 28C is a short splash rather than a session. Hold them so the head stays clear and stay within arm's reach the whole time - armbands and floats are not a substitute for your hands. A wary baby settles faster if you go in with them and let them watch from the edge first.

From 70 the licence is renewed every three years, and it is free. You declare your medical conditions and eyesight each time, and if you only drive a car you do not need a medical unless the DVLA asks. There is no upper age limit and no retest, but you must be able to read a number plate 20 metres away.

Front pads usually last 25,000 to 50,000 miles and rears about twice that, so most cars want a front set every three to five years; town driving with a lot of braking wears them sooner, and motorway miles stretch them. Discs normally go every other pad change, or whenever they are scored or below the minimum thickness in the handbook. A wear indicator light, or a squeal on light braking that stops when you press harder, means book it in now rather than at the mileage.

Frozen peas keep about a year at -18C in a bag that stays shut: they don't go off, they dry out and turn starchy, so a bag from two winters ago is safe but not worth eating raw. Once they have thawed on the counter, cook them and eat them that day rather than freezing them again; a bag that thawed but stayed cold in the fridge can go back in the freezer, though the texture will be softer.

Frozen pizza wants a fully heated oven, not a cold one: 200C (180C fan, gas mark 6) for 12 to 15 minutes, straight on the shelf or a hot tray, until the cheese bubbles and the base lifts. A cold oven gives you a soggy middle and a pale top, and an air fryer does a small one in 8 to 10 minutes at 180C.

Frozen chips want 20 to 25 minutes at 200C (180C fan), turning once; an air fryer does them in 12 to 15 minutes at 200C, shaken once. Fresh-cut chips take 30 to 35. One layer with space between them, and salt when they come out: a crowded tray steams.

Fruit that drops in June and early July is the tree thinning its own crop, and it is normal: it lets go of more than it can carry, and the apples that stay grow bigger for it. If it is later than that, or the whole crop goes, look at water and pollination first - a dry spell in summer, a wet cold week when the bees were out, or a heavy pest year. Water the tree deeply once a week in dry weather, pick up the fallen fruit so wasps and rot do not move in, and let it drop what it wants.

Fruit and a spoon of honey, granola or toasted oats for crunch, and nuts or seeds for texture; a spoon of peanut butter and a little cocoa makes it taste like dessert. Plain yoghurt with chopped cucumber, mint, salt and garlic is a dip instead, and it wants straining first if it is watery.

Fruit juice has as much sugar as the equivalent amount of Coke - about 20g in a 200ml glass of orange juice - with none of the fibre of the fruit and none of the chewing that makes you feel full. One small glass a day with a meal is the usual advice; a smoothie is not much better once the fruit is blended.

Fry them first: whole spices go into a little oil over a medium heat for 30 seconds to a minute, until they smell warm and one or two start to pop, because the oil carries the flavour that water cannot. Ground spices need only 20 to 30 seconds, added with the onion or just before the liquid goes in. Keep the heat moderate and have the next ingredient ready: a spice that darkens has gone bitter and cannot be rescued.

Fry them into a hash: chop them small, start with an onion and a pinch of salt, and let them crisp at the edges before you add anything wet. Roasted vegetables are better through pasta with garlic and a spoonful of the cooking water, and anything soft goes into soup with stock and a blender.

Fry a drained tin in olive oil with cumin and paprika for 8 minutes and they go crunchy enough to eat as a snack or over a salad; mash them with tahini, lemon and garlic for hummus, or simmer them in tomatoes and coconut milk for a curry in 20 minutes.

Frying adds about 50 to 100 calories per portion of oil soaked in, and oven chips have roughly a third of the fat of fried ones. Frying at the right temperature helps: if the oil is hot enough the food steams from inside and takes on less. Once or twice a week is not the problem; it is the rest of the plate that matters.

Full-time nursery is roughly £1,000 to £1,500 a month in England, childminders are usually cheaper, and the help is what brings it down: 15 hours a week free for every three and four year old (30 if both parents work and earn under £100,000 each), plus tax-free childcare, which tops up every £8 you pay in with £2 up to £2,000 a year per child. Ring your council's family information service for the nurseries near you with places and prices, because it varies enormously by area, and ask about the free hours before you compare the monthly figures, since most nurseries spread them over the year.

Full fibre is about £25 to £35 a month for 100 to 500 Mbps, on an 18 or 24 month deal, and it jumps £10 or so once that deal ends - the price on the site is rarely the price in month 25. A social tariff is £15 to £20 a month if you claim Universal Credit or Pension Credit, and most big providers offer one quietly, so it is worth asking. Line rental only comes on top if you keep a landline.

GHIC stands for Global Health Insurance Card: the free card that gives you state-provided medical care in the EU on the same terms as a local, and it replaced the EHIC for new applications after Brexit. It does not cover private treatment or getting you home, so travel insurance is still the thing to buy.

GP stands for general practitioner: the family doctor who sees you first and refers you on to a specialist. You can change practice without giving a reason, and the same-day slots usually go to the people who ring at opening time, so ring rather than walk in.

GPS stands for Global Positioning System: a ring of about thirty satellites, each beaming the time and its own position, and your phone works out where it must be from the difference between those signals. Only the American set is called GPS - Europe's Galileo and Russia's GLONASS do the same job, and your phone listens to whichever it can hear.

GSM is grams per square metre, and it is how heavy a fabric is: a thin t-shirt is 140 to 180, a good everyday tee 180 to 220, a hoodie 300 to 400, and a heavy sweatshirt 400 or more. Towels run 400 to 600 GSM, and bedding 120 to 150. Higher is thicker, heavier and warmer, not automatically better - a 600 GSM towel takes forever to dry outdoors.
Gal Gadot plays Wonder Woman: Batman v Superman (2016), her own film in 2017, and 1984 in 2020.

Gallstones are stones of bile in the gallbladder, and most never cause a problem - they are found by chance and left alone. The pain they do cause is biliary colic: a severe ache under the ribs on the right, an hour or two after a fatty meal, spreading to the right shoulder blade, easing over a few hours. Go to A&E the same day if it lasts more than about five hours, or comes with a fever, yellow skin or a swollen, tender belly. Cutting fat out does not dissolve them; keyhole surgery to take the gallbladder out is the fix.

Games go to 11 and you serve every two points, so a game turns faster than it looks: serve short and low, keep the ball on the table rather than hitting it hard, and step back only when you have to. The basics win club games - a heavy spin serve, a steady block, and returning the serve rather than trying to win the point with it.

Games go to 21 points, and you score on every rally whoever served, so a game is quick; win two games and you win the match. The bit that catches beginners is that the shuttle cannot be hit before it crosses the net, and a serve has to go diagonally and land past the short service line.
Gammon is the cut before it is cooked - a cured hind leg of pork - and ham is what you call it once it's cooked or sold ready to eat. You buy gammon to roast, and ham to put in a sandwich.

Gap insurance pays the difference between what your insurer gives you for a car written off and what you still owe on the finance, so you are not paying for a car you no longer have. It is worth having only while the finance is bigger than the car is worth and you could not clear the rest yourself, and not on a car you own. Buy it from a specialist, not the dealer, who often charges twice as much.

Garage labour is usually £50 to £90 an hour, and a job is priced by the hours the book allows rather than by what the car is worth: a clutch is £300 to £800 fitted, a cambelt £250 to £500, a wheel bearing £150 to £300. Ask for the price in writing with parts and labour split, and get a second quote for anything over £300.
Garam masala is warm, not hot: cinnamon, cardamom, cloves and pepper, ground together. A teaspoon goes in at the end of cooking, where the smell survives; boiled for an hour it tastes of dust.

Garden leave is being paid to stay away from work during your notice period: you are still employed, still on the payroll and still bound by your contract, but told not to come in or to contact clients. You keep your holiday, your notice carries on running, and you are usually not allowed to start another job until it ends, so read the contract or ask HR before you take a new role. It is the usual answer for someone who could take customers or information with them.
Garlic powder is not hot at all - it is savoury and a little sweet, and it burns if it sits in hot oil, so add it with the liquid.
Garlic burns in seconds because it's full of sugar: crush or slice it and add it later than the onion, on a lower heat. If it's already bitter, start again; burnt garlic taints the whole dish.

Geese want grass to graze, a shelter they can walk into and a lot of space, and two at the least. They are good watch animals and very messy, and a gander will chase people in the breeding season, so keep them away from a path small children use.
Get out of the sun, cool the skin with a shower or damp towel, and drink water; after-sun or plain moisturiser helps the sting. Don't pop blisters, and keep it covered until it heals.

Get out of the sun, cool the skin with a shower or a damp cloth, and drink plenty of water; calamine or after-sun takes the sting out. Blisters, shivering or feeling faint need a doctor, and keep it covered for a few days.

Get the reason looked at if it has come on lately: breathlessness, a calf that aches and stops you, or one leg tiring before the other are worth a GP appointment, and a physio can fit a stick or a four-wheel rollator properly instead of guessing. Then build the distance in short bouts rather than one trip: five minutes out and back, twice or three times a day, adding a minute or two a week, and sit down at the far end rather than turning round the moment it aches. Short and often beats one long walk for both legs and confidence, and leaning on a shopping trolley or carrying a folding stick makes the shops doable now rather than after.

Get the ride first: a bus or tram driver will wave you on, station staff let you through a barrier, and a ticket machine or the operator's app takes another card or the phone. In a taxi, the meter and a receipt are what a complaint rests on. Then ring the bank: a daily limit, an offline reader or a block is the usual cause, and a fare charged twice is the operator's to refund.

Get the thinking out of your head before bed: ten minutes with a pen, a list of what is actually worrying you and the first step for each, and a line at the bottom saying what can wait until morning. Then keep the bed for sleeping - if you are still awake after about twenty minutes, get up, sit somewhere dim with something dull, and go back when you are sleepy, so the bed does not become the place you argue with yourself. Same winding-down half hour each night, phone out of reach, and get up at the same time whatever happened, because the wake-up time is what steadies the sleep.

Get the tin and its oil smoking hot, 220C (200C fan), before the batter goes anywhere near it. The batter is 100g plain flour, 2 eggs, 150ml milk and a pinch of salt, rested 30 minutes and poured in cold, about 1cm deep, and then the oven door stays shut for 20 minutes. Flat ones are a cool tin or a batter that was too thin.

Get the fail sheet priced line by line, in writing, and ask which items are the failure and which are advisories they would like to do - a garage will often quote for the lot and only the failure is compulsory. A second quote is normal and free, and the partial retest is free if the work is back within 10 working days. Then weigh it against the car: a bill over about a third of what the car would sell for is the point to ask whether the money is better spent on a replacement, and a garage will tell you what it would buy the car for as it stands.

Get them warm before anything else: dry layers, a hot drink, a blanket and the heating on, and sit with them for a bit. Being cold on its own is usually just the room - an older person sits still and does not feel it coming - but cold with drowsiness, confusion, slurred speech or shivering that has stopped is hypothermia, and that is a 111 call. Ring 999 if they are unconscious or breathing oddly.

Get three firms to look round the place before they quote: an over-the-phone figure is the one that grows on the day. Check they are a British Association of Removers member and ask for goods-in-transit cover in writing, which is what pays if your sofa goes through a window; agree a fixed price rather than an hourly rate, and pay no more than a small deposit up front, never cash.

Get a vet to look at it: most lumps are harmless fatty ones, but one that is firm, growing fast, or bigger than a pea is worth a needle test, and small is the cheapest time to find out. Note the date and the size - a lump on a ruler tells a vet more than a memory does.

Get a 3kW one for speed and 1.7 litres for a family, or a 1 litre one if it is mostly you - a small kettle boiled often costs less than a big one boiled for two cups. A concealed element and a wide lid make descaling easy, a water-level window on both sides saves guessing, and temperature settings are worth it only if you make green tea or filter coffee. Decide stainless steel or glass by looks, then check the minimum fill line: a kettle that needs half a litre before it will switch on wastes water and power.

Get daylight as soon as you can after landing, eat at local meal times, and keep caffeine to the local morning. Sleeping on arrival makes it worse; a short 20-minute nap before 3pm is the most you want.

Get it off today, and get help if you cannot: a finger that has gone numb, cold, blue or black behind a ring needs the ring cut off, so go to A&E or ring 111 and they will tell you where. While you wait, keep the hand raised above your heart and run it under cool water, and do not keep twisting the ring. A jeweller can cut it off for a few pounds if the finger still looks normal.

Get it signed off rather than doing the flue yourself: a Hetas-registered installer, or a fitter whose work building control inspects, is what the regs ask for, and an unsigned stove is a problem when you sell the house as well as a fire risk. Size the stove to the room - roughly 1kW for every 14 cubic metres, and no more, because a big stove turned right down smokes and soots the flue. It needs a non-combustible hearth (12mm of slate or stone is the usual, and 300mm in front of the door), the flue swept and lined if the chimney is old, and a carbon monoxide alarm in the same room, which the law has required for a solid-fuel stove since 2022. In a smoke control area the stove must be DEFRA-exempt, so check that before you buy it.

Get left and off the carriageway if you still can, then hazards on. Everyone out of the doors on the left, behind the barrier, and well back from the car: never stand between it and the traffic, and never change a wheel on a motorway. Leave the warning triangle in the boot. Ring 999 if you are stuck in a live lane.

Getting puffed on the stairs is usually fitness rather than illness, and it improves in a few weeks if you walk a little more each day. Get it checked if it has come on over weeks, if you are breathless sitting still or lying flat, if it comes with chest pain, swollen ankles or a cough, or if it is worse than it was a month ago - that is a GP appointment, not a training problem.

4K means about 4,000 pixels across the screen - 3,840 by 2,160, which is four times the detail of a 1080p set. Whether you see it depends on size and distance - on a 55-inch screen from a sofa it is subtle, and HDR, the brightness and colour range, changes the picture far more.
Ginger is warm and sharp rather than hot like chilli, and the burn fades in seconds. A thumb-sized piece grated into a curry for four is a good amount.

Give the day a shape: same start time, dressed, a real lunch away from the desk, and a walk to end it. Put the phone in another room for one 50-minute block before you open email, and have one call with a colleague a day - the office is what you are missing, so put a bit of it back in the week.

Give the loop a shape instead of trying to switch it off: ten minutes with a pen, one line saying the thing that keeps coming back, one line for what you are actually afraid of, and one line for the next thing you can do about it. Then do that one thing today, because going over a thing feels like working on it and is not: an unanswered message, a question for the doctor, a text that says you are thinking of them. If it is somebody else's illness, ask them what they want rather than deciding for them, and offer something specific - a lift, a meal, an hour on Thursday. If the same loop is still going weeks later, or it comes with no sleep, no appetite or no pleasure in anything, say so to a GP.

Give them the same bottom number first, then add or subtract the tops: 1/2 + 1/3 is 3/6 + 2/6, which is 5/6. Use the lowest bottom both numbers divide into, which is 6 here and 4 for 1/2 + 1/4, then cancel the answer down.

Give them a minute and a way out rather than advice: "Let's grab a coffee" or "Do you want to take five?" Then say nothing and let the silence sit - most people fill it themselves. Don't ask what happened in front of anyone else, and don't promise secrecy you cannot keep; if it is about work, say the one thing you can do ("I'll cover the meeting") and do it. Afterwards treat it as ordinary, not as a thing to mention again, and if it keeps happening, ask them once, privately, whether something at work is behind it.

Give them a fact rather than a reassurance: "I'll text you when I'm on the train" works where "don't worry" does not, because a worry needs something to hold. Ask what exactly they are afraid of, answer that one thing once, and then stop explaining - saying it a second and third time is what teaches them the worry is worth asking about.

Give up on being liked as a project: someone who has decided against you will not be argued out of it, and more effort usually reads as pushing. Be consistently easy to have around - turn up when you said, bring the thing she actually likes, leave on time - and let your partner handle every difficult conversation with her, because it is their mother. You are owed good manners, not affection; if she is rude to your face, one plain sentence said once is the line, and your partner is the one who should be holding it with you.

Give yourself a run-up rather than trying to switch off: the same wake-up time every day, no caffeine after about two, the last hour dim with the phone out of reach, and a cool dark room. Falling asleep is a slope you slide down, so nothing you try harder at helps: if you are still awake after about twenty minutes, get up, sit somewhere dim with something dull, and go back when your eyes are heavy. Counting minutes on the clock is what keeps it going.

Give as much notice as you can - a day is plenty for a table, 24 hours for a haircut, and longer for a big group - and ring rather than not turning up. A call keeps the goodwill and usually the deposit, and a place that knows in time can fill the table.

Give a rescue dog three days to feel safe, three weeks to unwind and three months to trust the routine: keep the first week quiet, no visitors and no long trips, and let him come to you. Feed and walk at the same times, give him a bed he can retreat to, and build up time alone from ten minutes. A confident dog settles in a fortnight, a nervous one takes a couple of months; if he is still hiding or off his food after a week, ring the rescue for help.

Give a very hot pan five minutes before it meets cold water: a thin stainless or aluminium pan can warp, and enamel or cast iron can crack. Warm water first, or fill the sink and set the pan in it rather than running the tap straight onto it. Deglazing on the hob with a splash of stock or wine is fine - it is the cold plunge from a screaming pan that is not.

Give each question the minutes it is worth: one mark is about one minute, so a ten-mark question gets ten. Write the clock time you must move on by in the margin before you start, and move on when it arrives even if the answer is unfinished - a half answer plus the next question beats a perfect first one and three blanks. Read the whole paper first, do the question you know best, and keep the last five minutes for checking names, units and whether every question has an answer.

Give even a four-year-old two jobs that are theirs alone, such as putting shoes by the door and setting out the cutlery. Call them the family's jobs rather than a favour or a punishment, and expect them done badly at first; doing them is the point.

Give it three months before you judge it, and use them: a new role is mostly the parts you did not see, so the first job is to name what actually changed - the admin, the hours, the people problems - because that is what can be fixed. Ask your manager for one specific change "I want to keep two days of the client work" and a review date, and put it in writing. If nothing moves by then, stepping back down is a normal move and not a failure, and asking for your old job back is far easier before you have been in the new one a year.

Give it three or four minutes: the lock holds until the drum has stopped and the water has drained. If there's water inside, run a drain or spin cycle first. When it's empty and still locked, most machines have an emergency release: a small plastic tag or cord behind the filter hatch that you pull down while pushing the door. Don't force the handle, because the catch breaks before the door does.

Give it when the baby is calm rather than hungry, and have somebody else offer it - a baby who can smell milk will hold out for the breast. Warm the teat and use a slow-flow one, hold them fairly upright and keep the bottle level so the milk comes at their pace rather than pouring in. Offer one bottle a day for a week without forcing it, and change the teat, the room and the person holding them before you decide they will not take one. If they are under six weeks old, are losing weight or the nappies are dry, ring the health visitor rather than pushing on.

Give it about 50 pages, or a tenth of the book if it is a long one, and then stop without guilt if you still do not care: there are more books than evenings. Halfway through and dreading it is as clear a sign as you get - put it down, and keep it for a long train journey in case you come back to it. Finishing a book you dislike is not a virtue, and nobody is marking it.

Give it a day before you judge it: paint reads about a shade lighter while it is wet, so a wall that looks too strong tonight has usually settled by tomorrow, and the light you look at it in changes it as much as the paint does. If it is still too dark once it is hard, nothing can be added to a coat to lighten it - so the fix is either one coat of the colour you wanted over the top (a pale colour covers a dark one in two or three coats, and a test patch on a scrap of plasterboard or lining paper will tell you how many before you buy another tin), or a glaze of white emulsion wiped over it while it is tacky to lift it a shade. If the tin was a match to a sample, take a photo in daylight and the tin back to the shop: most will retint or exchange one they mixed wrong. A wood stain that went too dark sands back to bare wood and starts again with a pale one, since stain sinks in rather than sitting on top.
Giving someone the cold shoulder means being deliberately distant with them. Has someone gone quiet on you?

Giving up driving is three jobs, and doing them in this order makes it much easier. First the official side: if the reason is medical, tell the DVLA, because a licence you should not be using is not valid for insurance, and tell your insurer either way. Second, the money: insurance, tax, MOT, servicing and fuel usually add up to enough for a taxi or two a week, so that sum becomes the new travel budget instead of disappearing quietly. Third, the alternatives, arranged before the keys go rather than after: a bus pass, the local dial-a-ride or community car scheme, and a rota of two or three people for the trips that matter, because one lift is easier to ask for than a favour you think you cannot repay. Keep the car a month if you can, so the first week is not also the week you learn the bus.

Glandular fever is the Epstein-Barr virus, and for most people it lasts about four to six weeks, with the tiredness often lingering for two or three months after the sore throat and fever have gone. Rest is the treatment: sleep when you need to, drink, take paracetamol or ibuprofen for the sore throat, and no alcohol while you are unwell because the liver is involved. The one rule people miss is no contact sport, heavy lifting or anything with a risk of a knock for at least four weeks - the spleen is enlarged and can rupture - and your GP may say longer. Sudden severe pain in the upper left of the tummy means A&E. A blood test confirms it, and tiredness that is not lifting after three months is worth a review.
Glasgow has about 635,000 people, and about 1.7 million in the wider Clyde valley. It is Scotland's biggest city.

Glass is sand melted with soda ash and limestone at about 1,700°C, then cooled fast enough that it sets as a liquid instead of forming crystals - which is why you can see through it. It can be melted down and remade indefinitely without losing anything.

Glue ear is fluid behind the eardrum rather than an infection, and it usually clears on its own but slowly: about half of children are clear within three months, and most within a year. Antibiotics and decongestants do not help it. Because the hearing is muffled while it lasts, ask for a hearing test if it has been there three months or more, and see a GP sooner if the child's speech is behind, if it keeps coming back, or if either ear is sore or running.

Gluten is just the protein in wheat, barley and rye, and it is only a problem for the roughly one in a hundred people with coeliac disease, or for a wheat allergy - for everyone else there is nothing to avoid. If bread and pasta leave you bloated, windy or tired, ask the GP for a coeliac blood test before you cut gluten out, because the test only works while you are still eating it. Wholegrain wheat is one of the best sources of fibre in an ordinary diet, so it is worth keeping unless a test says otherwise.

Go out after dark with a torch and pick them off, which beats most products; copper tape round pots and a gritty barrier round seedlings help too. Encourage birds and frogs, and water in the morning rather than the evening.

Go straight to the airline's desk or app before the next one closes: when both legs are on one ticket the airline has to put you on the next available seat, and pay for a hotel and meals if the wait is overnight. On two separate tickets the second one is a no-show and nobody owes you a seat, so ring that airline and ask anyway. Keep every receipt.

Go the weekend after a bank holiday, or in the shoulder season, and book the train three or four weeks ahead with a railcard - it usually costs less than the petrol. Stay one town out from the famous one and travel in: a twenty-minute train is a few pounds and the same room is half the price. Two nights is plenty for a city, so pick one area to walk and one thing to go inside for, and eat the big meal at lunch, when set menus are cheapest. Two nights for two, with travel and a room, is about £250.

Go to whoever writes the rota and make it about the shifts, not about needing the money: say which days you can cover, that you want more of them, and ask to be the first call when someone drops out. A lot of contracts add hours quietly once the manager knows you want them, so ask what it takes to be put on the next rota and get the answer in writing. If you want a permanent increase, ask for that in writing too, and check what your contract says about guaranteed hours.

Go up off the foot opposite your shooting hand - right hand, left foot - and take the last dribble with the outside hand a stride before you jump. Bring the ball up in two hands and let it go softly off the backboard into the top corner of the square, rather than throwing it at the rim. Aim to jump up rather than forward: most missed layups are a jump that was too long and too fast.

Go up slowly: above 3,000m, sleep no more than 500m higher than the night before, and take a rest day every third day. Drink plenty, skip alcohol, and if you get a bad headache with nausea, go down rather than waiting it out.

Go at it dry first and test a hidden corner: a soft pencil rubber or a clean, barely damp cloth with a drop of washing-up liquid lifts most marks off paper, working from the bottom up so drips do not streak. Water is what ruins wallpaper, so keep the cloth as dry as it can be - a washable vinyl paper takes a mild soap, a printed or flocked one usually will not, and a mark that will not lift is better patched or covered than scrubbed.

Go back only if you can say what ended it and something has actually changed since - if the honest answer is only that you miss them, that is loneliness, and it eases. If you do go back, take it slowly and in daylight: meet to talk, keep your own place and your own money for a few months, and say out loud what each of you would do differently. It is worth asking whether you want them or the version of your life you had with them. Trying once to find out is not a mistake; going back to the same argument a second time is the thing to avoid.

Go back to the shop you bought it from with the receipt: the retailer owes you a repair, replacement or refund for up to six years in England and Wales, and a guarantee is in addition to that right, not instead of it. Buying an extended warranty is usually not worth it, since those rights already cover the appliance, and paying by credit card makes the card company jointly liable over £100 under Section 75. A guarantee covers a fault, not damage: a cracked screen or a dropped phone is an insurance claim.

Go back to whoever sold you the ticket - the box office or the agency, not the venue - because their terms decide it, and a ticket is usually non-refundable if you simply cannot go. If the show is cancelled or moved you are owed the face value back, and whether the booking fee comes too depends on the seller; ask for a refund rather than a credit note. If you just cannot make it, some sellers run an official resale or ticket exchange, which gets you more than nothing.

Go by the child's inside leg, not their age: stand them against a wall in shoes and measure from the floor to the crotch, and the saddle should go low enough that both feet are flat on the ground when they sit on it, with their hands on the brake levers. That is different from an adult's bike, where the leg almost straightens on the pedal. A bike whose saddle will not go low enough is too big, whatever the wheel size says.

Go by tog: 4.5 for summer, 9 to 10.5 for spring and autumn, 13.5 for winter, or one 10.5 all year with a 4.5 on top in January. Match the size to the bed - single 135x200cm, double 200x200, king 225x220, super king 260x220 - because a duvet smaller than the bed leaves a cold edge. Down and feather are warmest for the weight, wool breathes and handles damp best, and hollowfibre is the cheap washable one; a synthetic duvet goes in a 9kg drum at home, while down wants a launderette and a tumble dryer with dryer balls to bring the loft back.

Go by what the tooth is doing: a twinge with cold that settles, or a check-up you are overdue, is an ordinary appointment. Ring the dentist today if it aches at night or keeps you awake, if there is swelling in your face or under the jaw, a fever, a lost filling or crown that hurts, or bleeding that will not stop. A tooth knocked right out goes straight back into the socket, by the crown and not the root, and you are seen within the hour; ring 111 for the out-of-hours dental service if your practice is shut.

Go by inside leg, not age: a child should be able to put both feet flat on the ground with the saddle at its lowest. A bike one size up with the seat down is safer than an oversized one they can't control, and balance bikes beat stabilisers.

Go chapter by chapter before you write a line: one sentence per chapter on what changed, then join them into a paragraph that follows the argument or the plot rather than the order of the pages. Keep the ending in - a summary that hides it is a blurb - and put your own one-line judgement at the end, clearly marked as yours.

Go for something shared rather than an object: dinner somewhere she has mentioned, a night away, or a small thing tied to a memory you both have. Write a card that says why, and it will beat anything expensive and impersonal.

Go for time and something used up rather than another object: a meal or a night away somewhere they have mentioned, tickets to something on their list, a lesson in a thing they keep talking about, or a very good version of a daily thing - coffee, olive oil, socks - with a note saying why you picked it. Someone who wants for nothing is short of time and good consumables, not of things.

Go for a canal towpath, a country park or a flat riverside path: wide, level, benches along it and nothing to climb over, which is what a short walk needs. Check the surface and the slope on the site's own page before you set off, because a walk advertised as circular can still hide a stile or a flight of steps, and ring ahead if someone uses a wheelchair - big attractions, National Trust and English Heritage places among them, lend one for free if it is booked a day or two in advance. For someone who tires quickly, plan a there-and-back of half a mile with a seat at the turning point and pace it bench to bench rather than by distance. A stick helps if a hip or knee is the trouble: the handle wants to reach the crease of the wrist with the arm hanging down, it goes in the hand opposite the sore side, and the tip gets a new ferrule once it has gone smooth.

Go for a chocolate cake with no nuts at all: a plain chocolate sponge with cocoa and boiling water, iced with melted chocolate and cream. Check the chocolate and any ready-made icing for 'may contain nuts', and keep the worktop and tin clean if the allergy is serious.

Go in quietly, keep the light off, say the same short thing and walk them back, so waking up gains nothing. Then look at the day: a nap that runs past three, a bedtime too early or too late, a room too warm, or a drink of milk that has become the reason to wake. Hold the same answer for a week before you change anything, because it is the consistency rather than the trick that works.

Go in with one sentence written down: what happened, what you want changed, and who you have already spoken to. Ask for the head of year rather than the class teacher alone, and agree a date they will come back to you, because a meeting with no date is how these stall. If it is about your child being treated unfairly, ask for the school's complaints policy in writing before you go, and take a notebook.

Go in with two questions and one fact: what is my child like in your class, and what is the one thing we should do at home this term. Write the teacher's points down while you are there, because "struggling with fractions" is useful and "needs to focus" is not, and ask what it looks like when it is going right so you know what you are aiming at. If it is about behaviour, ask what happens just before it and what the school does about it, and agree one thing you will try and one thing they will before you leave - then ask for it in an email afterwards, so there is a record.

Go in having written the year yourself: what you delivered, what slipped and why, and what you changed afterwards. Say the bad part first and in one sentence - "the migration slipped six weeks; I flagged it in May and we re-planned" - then spend the time on the fix and on next year. Ask what would make next year a good one in their words, and write down what they say. A bad year handled openly reads as senior; a bad year explained for twenty minutes reads as a problem.

Goats are herd animals, so two at the least: one on its own is a distressed goat. They want a dry shed, a fence they cannot lean on and something to climb, hay and browse all day, a mineral lick, and their feet trimmed every couple of months.
Gochujang is medium, around 1,000 to 2,000 Scoville, and sweet and fermented with it, so the heat arrives after the sweetness. A tablespoon for four.

Going off food is usually the illness, the stress or the medicine rather than the food itself, and it comes back as that settles: small amounts of whatever they fancy every couple of hours, not a plate to finish, and drinks between meals rather than with them. Ask the GP if it lasts more than a fortnight, or if they are also losing weight or drinking very little.

Going often is worth a check rather than a guess: drink water through the day and cut tea, coffee and alcohol for a week to see if it settles. If it carries on, or you are thirsty all the time and passing a lot, see a GP for a blood sugar and urine test, and go the same day if there is blood, a fever or a pain in your back or side.

Going back later is common, and the money is the first thing to check: a full-time degree is three years without a salary, so most people do it part time, one module at a time, or with the Open University. Student finance counts you as an independent student, so your own income decides the loan, and a course can credit what you already know. Do one evening class first, before you commit to three years.
Goldfish need far more room than pet shops suggest: 100 litres plus for one, and a filter and a spare tank for cleaning. A bowl isn't a home for a fish that grows to 20cm.
Good to hear. What was the best bit?
Good. What's the first step you're unsure about?

Gout is uric acid forming crystals in a joint, most often the big toe: it comes on over hours, red, hot, shiny and too sore to bear the weight of a sheet. An attack settles in three to ten days. Start ibuprofen or naproxen with food straight away, rest and raise the foot, and see a GP - colchicine or a short steroid course works if anti-inflammatories are not an option. Once it settles, cutting beer, sugary drinks, shellfish and organ meat off the ordinary week is what keeps it away; repeated attacks are worth a blood test and daily allopurinol to bring the uric acid down. See the GP the same day if the joint is hot with a fever, because that is an infection until proven otherwise.

Grass needs four hours of direct sun a day, so in deep shade it will always be thin: the fix is to take away the shading before you feed anything. Cut back the branches over the lawn or raise the canopy, and mow higher in shade - about 6cm rather than 4 - because longer blades catch what light there is. Feed lightly and water less often but deeply, since shade keeps the soil damp. If it stays bare, sow a shade mix of fescue and bent rather than ryegrass, or give that corner over to gravel, ferns or a bench: a lawn under a tree is a losing fight.

Grass, and mostly grass: a ewe eats about 2 per cent of her body weight in dry matter a day, so 1.5 to 2 kg, plus a mineral lick and clean water. Late pregnancy wants more, and very rich spring grass or a sudden feed change is what brings on twin lamb disease and bloat, so any change is made over a week.

Grass, leaves, shoots, buds, ivy and brambles, and fruit in autumn - a deer browses at the height of a hedge rather than grazing it, which is why the roses are stripped to a line and the buds on your apple tree go first. A muntjac also eats bluebells and birds' eggs.

Grass and silage, in bulk: a dairy cow eats 50 to 60 kg of fresh grass or silage a day and drinks 60 to 100 litres of water. The rumen and its bugs are what break the grass down, which is why a little grain is a supplement and not a diet. Kitchen scraps are illegal to feed to farm animals in the UK, and have been since 2001.

Grass and hay, roughly 2 per cent of its body weight a day in dry matter: a 500 kg horse gets through about 10 kg of hay plus water and a salt lick, and hard feed such as oats or barley is for work rather than the diet. Lush spring grass holds enough sugar to bring on laminitis, so a fat pony is the one to ration.

Grate or blitz it into something wet and strongly flavoured: a grated carrot or courgette in bolognese, chilli, lasagne or a tomato sauce disappears, and a handful of spinach or a few peas blitzed into soup leaves nothing to pick out. Mash takes half cauliflower, and grated carrot or beetroot goes into muffins and a fruit loaf unnoticed. Keep the plain veg on the plate too - hiding gets the vitamins in, but it does not teach anyone to like it.

Gravy keeps 2 days in the fridge, less than the meat does, because it is mostly liquid and it cools slowly in the jug: get it in within 2 hours of making it, standing the jug in a bowl of cold water if it is still hot. Reheat it until it boils right through, and bin any that has sat out on the table all evening.

Green on a potato is chlorophyll, which is harmless, but it comes up in the light alongside solanine, which is not: cut out any green patches, and bin a potato that is green all over or has long white sprouts. Keep them in a dark cupboard rather than on the windowsill, and never eat the sprouts.

Green or purple blotches, a bright line and a growing black patch all mean the panel inside is damaged - a cracked layer, pressure from a case, or liquid that got in - and no setting, reset or software update will clear it. Back up and get your photos off it today, while the screen still responds, because the damaged area usually spreads. A replacement screen is usually £50 to £120 fitted on a mid-range phone and £150 to £300 on a flagship; a repair shop does it in a few hours and your data stays put.

Green poo is almost always food moving through a bit fast, so bile does not get time to turn brown - a stomach bug, a curry, spinach, green food colouring, or iron and some antibiotics. It settles in a day or two on its own: drink plenty, eat simply, and keep taking rehydration sachets if there is diarrhoea too. See a GP if it is still green after a week, if there is blood in it, or if it comes with pain, a fever or weight loss.

Green rhubarb is not a problem: some varieties are green-stemmed (Timperley Early goes pink, Victoria stays greener), and stems that were forced or shaded go redder than the same plant left in the open. Colour is variety and light, not ripeness - pick on stem size, and stop picking by the end of June so the crown can build up for next year. Only the leaves are poisonous, so cut those off and compost them.

Green water is algae feeding on sunlight and on the nutrients in the water, so the fix is to take one of those away: put a water lily or floating plants over half the surface for shade, and plant up the margins so the water has less of the light and the feed it needs. Barley straw in a mesh bag slows blanket weed and is harmless to the fish, and a dark dye does the same job in a pond with no plants in it. Rinse the filter sponges in a bucket of pond water, never under the tap, because the chlorine kills the bacteria that keep the water clear, and clean them a little at a time so the pond never loses its whole filter in one afternoon. Feed the fish what they clear in five minutes, once a day in warm weather, and not at all below 10C, because the food they leave is what turns the water green. For blanket weed, twirl it out with a stick rather than reaching in, and net the leaves out in autumn before they sink, because the sludge on the bottom is next summer's algae.

Grinding means the pads are down to metal: stop driving and get them changed, or you will score the discs too. A squeal is often the wear indicator or glazed pads, and a pedal that feels soft or sinks means air or a fluid leak, which is a garage-now job. Front pads fitted are usually £100 to £200.

Grip the tick as close to your skin as you can with fine tweezers and pull steadily upwards without twisting or squeezing. Then watch the spot: a spreading rash or a fever in the next few weeks means see a doctor and mention the bite.

Grip comes from holding heavy things for time: hang from a bar for 20 to 30 seconds, three times, and carry a heavy bag or a pair of dumbbells in each hand for 30 metres. Add a thick towel round the bar or the handle now and then to make it harder without more weight. Do it twice a week on the end of a normal session, and give it a rest day after - the forearms recover slowly and a strained tendon takes weeks.

Ground spices fade in about 6 months and whole ones last 2 to 3 years: small airtight jars, away from the hob and the light. Sniff a spoonful - if it smells of nothing it will taste of nothing, and toasting what is left brings it back a little.

Ground coffee is at its best in the 2 weeks after opening: keep it in an airtight tin in a dark cupboard rather than the fridge, which is damp and smells of everything else. Beans keep a month, and more than a month's worth is better frozen and ground from frozen.

Group the pots together out of the wind, mulch the compost with gravel or bark, and stand them in a saucer so the water that runs through soaks back up. A big pot dries out far slower than a small one, so pot up rather than watering more, and in a heatwave check them morning and evening - a pot whose roots fill it can want water twice a day.

Guacamole keeps 1 to 2 days in the fridge in a tub with cling film pressed right onto the surface, and the lime in it is what slows the browning. Brown on top is oxygen, not rot: stir it in and it is fine. After two days it tastes flat and watery, so eat it first.

Guinea pigs graze all day, so a hungry one is doing what it is built for: keep hay in the rack so there is always some, and add a mug of leafy greens and a quarter of a pepper a day for the vitamin C they cannot make themselves. Nuggets are a small measured handful, not a bowl to top up. If the appetite is new and the weight is going down, or the teeth look long, that is the vet, because guinea pigs hide illness until they are quite unwell.

Gums that bleed, swell or recede are nearly always plaque left at the gumline rather than brushing too hard: brush twice a day for two minutes with the bristles angled where tooth meets gum, and clean between the teeth once a day - small interdental brushes reach more than floss for most adults, in the size your dentist shows you. Done daily, gums that bleed stop within one to two weeks, and a little blood in the first days is normal. A hygienist removes the hard tartar you cannot brush off, and smokers and people with diabetes should go sooner because the bleeding is easy to miss. Gum that has receded does not grow back, so the point is stopping it where it is. See a dentist if one patch is swollen or tender, a tooth feels loose, or there is pus or a fever.

Gutter clearing is usually £60 to £150 for a house, more for three storeys or a lot of access problems. A repair or a new run of gutter is a separate job, priced by the metre. Ask whether the price includes the downpipes and a check for leaks, and whether they clear up what comes out.

Guy Fawkes (1570-1606) was the Catholic soldier caught in the cellar under the Houses of Parliament on 5 November 1605 with 36 barrels of gunpowder, in a plot to blow up King James I. He was tortured, tried and hanged, and the night is still marked with bonfires.

HDMI stands for high-definition multimedia interface: one cable that carries the picture and the sound together, which is why a television has needed only one lead since about 2005. Both ends are the same plug, so the spare socket on a television is usually the one to use for a laptop.

HMO stands for house in multiple occupation: a house or flat let to three or more people who are not one family and who share a kitchen or a bathroom. A larger one needs a licence from the council, and the council's private renting team is who to ring about fire doors, alarms or overcrowding - not the landlord's own answer.

HMRC stands for HM Revenue and Customs: the tax office, which deals with income tax, National Insurance, VAT and child benefit. It never asks for a password, a payment or a gift card by text or email - that message is a scam - and refunds, tax codes and self-assessment all go through your own account on gov.uk.

HMRC does not text, email or ring about a refund, and a real one asks nothing of you: it arrives as a P800 letter or appears in your online tax account and is paid automatically. Do not use the link or ring the number in the message. Forward the text to 7726, send the email to phishing@hmrc.gov.uk, and check your account by typing gov.uk into the browser yourself.

HPV stands for human papillomavirus: a very common group of viruses passed on by skin-to-skin contact, and most infections clear on their own. The types that cause most cervical cancer are the ones the NHS vaccine guards against, offered at 12 to 13, and the smear test finds the changes years before they become cancer.

HR stands for human resources: the department that holds the contracts, the pay, the holidays and the complaints. The order that works for a problem at work is your manager first, their manager if that goes nowhere, and HR in writing after that, because HR's job is the company's side of the paperwork.

HRT replaces the oestrogen your body stops making, and it is the most effective treatment for hot flushes, night sweats and the broken sleep they cause: a tablet, patch or gel, plus a progestogen if you still have a womb. For most women under 60 the benefits outweigh the risks - the one that rises is breast cancer, about 4 extra cases per 1,000 women taking combined HRT for five years, and a GP weighs that against your own history. It works best started within 10 years of your last period, and it is not a lifelong sentence: many women stop after a few years.

HRT stands for hormone replacement therapy: oestrogen, usually with a progestogen, given to ease hot flushes, night sweats and mood swings of the menopause and to protect bone. It comes as tablets, patches or gel; for most women under 60 the risks are small, and a GP can talk through which type suits you.

Hair gets its colour from melanin, and the cells that make it gradually stop as we age, so new hairs grow in without pigment. Genetics decides when that starts, and stress can speed it up but does not turn a single hair white overnight.

Hair loss is usually a pattern that runs in families: follicles on top of the head shrink under testosterone by-products, so hairs get thinner and eventually stop. Sudden or patchy shedding is more often stress, illness, childbirth, iron or thyroid trouble, so see a GP if it is fast or patchy; minoxidil helps pattern loss but only while you keep using it.

Hairballs are normal a few times a year in a cat that grooms a lot, and the fix is brushing rather than a paste: comb her daily through the moult with a metal comb so the loose hair goes in the bin instead of down her throat, and keep her water and wet food up because a dry diet alone makes them likelier. Retching that brings nothing up, or hairballs more than about once a month, is the vet rather than a remedy: it can be over-grooming from fleas or stress, or something blocking the gut.

Half your take-home on needs (rent, bills, food, transport), 30% on wants (eating out, clothes, subscriptions) and 20% on saving and paying down debt. Take-home, not salary: on £2,200 a month that is £1,100, £660 and £440. If rent alone eats more than half, do not force the split - take the saving 20% out on payday first and fit the rest around it, and start that 20% at £20 if that is what you can do this month.

Half your age as a percentage of your pay is the rule of thumb for a pension started now: 5% at 20, 10% at 30, 15% at 40, and your employer's minimum 3% counts towards it, so someone starting at 30 paying 7% gets to 10% with the employer's share. Aim for 12 to 15% of pay going in altogether once you can, because a pot built late has to work much harder: money paid in at 25 has about four times as long to grow as money paid in at 45.

Half a roast chicken is two more meals: strip the meat off the carcass now, keep it in a covered tub in the fridge for up to 3 days, and use it cold in a salad, or hot in a pie, curry, risotto, soup or sandwiches. Reheat it once, until piping hot all the way through, and simmer the carcass with an onion for stock.

Half a roller of paint, a slow push, and roll the excess off on the tray's ramp before the sleeve touches the wall: a roller splatters because it is overloaded and moving too fast, and paint spins off the top of a sleeve that is turning at the ceiling. Then roll from the dry part into the wet in long strokes with light pressure. The sleeve matters too - short pile for smooth plaster, medium for a light texture, and a long pile holds so much paint that it throws it - and a brand new cheap sleeve spits fuzz for the first wall, so wash it out first or wrap tape round your hand and run it over. Sheet the floor and tape the edges, and any fleck that lands wipes off with a damp cloth while it is wet.

Half fill the kettle with equal parts water and white vinegar, or a sachet of citric acid, boil it and leave it half an hour, then tip it out and boil fresh water twice before you use it again. In a hard-water area do it every couple of months: the scale forms because hard water leaves calcium behind as it boils, and a thick layer makes the kettle slow and puts a scum on the tea.

Halloumi keeps a couple of weeks unopened in the fridge, and about a week once the pack is open if you keep it in its brine or in a tub of salty water: out of the water it dries and goes rubbery rather than off. It also freezes, though it crumbles a little afterwards, and a block that has gone pink or smells sour is past it.

Halve the weights but not quite everything: salt, spices and strong flavours go a little under half, because they do not scale with the rest, and a raising agent like baking powder goes to about three quarters of half, or the bake tastes of it. An egg is the awkward one, so weigh it beaten and use half by weight - about 25g of a large egg. The tin matters more than the time: half the batter in the same tin is a shallow cake that bakes fast and dries, so use a smaller tin and check it early rather than turning the oven down. Doubling is the same in reverse: double the tin's volume, not its width, or bake in two tins.

Hand wash it in cool water with a little gentle detergent, press the water out in a towel rather than wringing it, then reshape the cups and dry it flat or hung by the centre gusset. Heat is what kills the elastic, so no dryer and no hot wash, and fastening the hooks before washing stops it snagging everything else.

Hand, foot and mouth is a virus and clears on its own in about a week: drinks, soft food that does not sting, and children's paracetamol or ibuprofen by weight; a pharmacist can give a mouth gel for the ulcers if they will not drink. Keep them off nursery or school while they are unwell - the spots need no covering, and once they have scabbed they are not infectious. See a GP if they are not drinking, are under three months old, or are no better after a week.

Hand-sewing is three stitches: running stitch, in and out in an even line; back stitch, one back for every two forward, which is the one that holds a seam that takes a pull; and slip stitch, worked inside a fold so it barely shows, which is what a hem wants. Start and finish with two tiny back stitches on the spot instead of a knot, and keep the thread to a forearm's length.

Hand-wash silk in cool water with a drop of shampoo or silk detergent, rinse in water of the same temperature, and never wring it: roll it in a towel and press the water out. Dry it away from sun and heat, and iron it on the silk setting while it is still slightly damp, with a cloth between the iron and the fabric.

Handball is when the ball touches the arm below where the armpit ends: the shoulder and the very top of the arm are fine. It also counts when the arm makes the body bigger, even by accident — which is why defenders tuck their arms behind their backs in the box.

Hands and fingers that go numb, often in bed or after holding a phone, or that cannot be felt at all, are usually a nerve being pressed, most often the median nerve at the wrist (carpal tunnel), which is why the thumb and first two fingers tingle and shaking the hand brings it back. Sleep with the wrist straight - a soft splint from a pharmacy keeps it that way - and take breaks from gripping and typing. See a GP if it starts happening in the day, the hand weakens or wastes, or it is numb all the time.

Hands crossed on your chest or resting at your temples, never laced behind your head and never pulling: pull with your neck and you get a sore neck, not a stronger middle. Press your lower back into the floor, curl your ribs towards your hips and lift only until the shoulder blades clear the floor, then lower slowly. Ten slow ones beat thirty fast: two or three sets of ten, twice a week, is plenty. If a sit up hurts your back, a dead bug or a plank trains the same muscle without it.
Hang the garment in the bathroom while you take a hot shower, or spritz it with water, smooth it flat and hang it somewhere warm. Ten minutes in a dryer with a damp towel drops the creases too.

Hang up, then ring the number on the back of your card, or the one on gov.uk for a tax or DVLA call: no bank, tax office or police force asks you to move money to a 'safe account', pay a bill on the phone, or confirm a PIN, and none of them threatens you with arrest. Report it to the bank's fraud line or Action Fraud, and change your online banking password from a device the caller has not touched.

Hang it on a wide wooden hanger in a steamy bathroom for twenty minutes and smooth it with your hands while it is warm; the steam lifts most travel creases. Never iron leather directly, keep it away from radiators, and a little leather conditioner after the steam stops it drying out at the fold.

Hang it in small bunches, upside down and spread out, somewhere warm, dark and dry with a bit of air moving - a shed, an airing cupboard or a room with the window open - and it is dry in one to two weeks. A low oven at 50C with the door ajar does the same in an hour or two. Strip the leaves or buds off the stems once they crumble, keep them in a sealed jar out of the light, and they hold their flavour for about a year. Lavender keeps its scent better in a paper bag than in a jar, and the buds go into a small cloth bag for a drawer or under a pillow.

Hard water is the reason: it carries dissolved calcium and magnesium, and they are left behind as a chalky scale whenever the water boils away or dries on a surface. Soak the scaled part in half water, half white vinegar, or a spoonful of citric acid in water - boil it in the kettle and leave it an hour, or tie a bag of it round a shower head or tap for an hour - then rinse twice. A filter jug or a scale reducer cuts down how often it comes back.

Hard biscuits are usually baked a couple of minutes too long or worked too much: pull them out while the middles still look slightly soft, because they firm as they cool, and mix just until the flour is in. More butter or an extra yolk keeps them short, and a slice of bread in the tin softens them overnight.

Hard cheese is all fine - cheddar, parmesan, gruyere - and so are feta, halloumi, mozzarella, cottage cheese and cream cheese, because they are made with pasteurised milk. The ones to cook until steaming or leave alone are the mould-ripened and blue ones: brie, camembert, stilton, gorgonzola, and any soft cheese with a rind. Skip anything labelled unpasteurised.

Hard cheese keeps about 2 weeks in the fridge once it is opened and soft cheese about a week. Wrap it in paper rather than cling film, which sweats it, and keep it in the drawer at the bottom rather than the door.

Harden it rather than heat it: sit an ice cube or a bag of frozen peas on the gum for a couple of minutes, then shave it off with an old card or a flat scraper held almost flat, so it lifts rather than smears. On concrete or paving a stiff brush and hot soapy water take the last film; on wood or tile wipe the residue with a drop of oil or a citrus cleaner and rinse, because a blade marks the surface. Don't burn it off - the ash stains, and it is how people melt the thing they were cleaning.
Harden it first: press a bag of ice against the gum for a few minutes, then crack it off with a blunt knife. A little oil or vinegar lifts the last bits from anything washable.

Hardness is calcium and magnesium dissolved in the water, and the only thing that takes it out is an ion-exchange softener plumbed in where the mains comes into the house: it swaps the calcium for sodium, and the salt you put in it is what does the swapping. A jug filter changes the taste and nothing else, and boiling leaves the calcium behind as the scale you find in the kettle. It needs a plumbed feed and a drain, so in a rented flat ask the landlord first.
Harissa is medium-hot, roughly 4,000 to 5,000 Scoville, with cumin and garlic in the paste. A spoon per portion stirred into the sauce at the end.

Have one short conversation, in private, about the effect rather than the character: "When you come in at half nine the phones are already going - what is making the mornings hard?" Ask before you accuse, because childcare, a bus and a second job all look the same from your desk. Then agree one specific change and a date to look at it again, and note the date and what was said. If nothing changes, take the dates to your manager once instead of raising it in the moment - a pattern is a manager's job, a single late morning is not.

Have someone else offer it while you are out of the room - a baby who can smell milk will hold out for the breast - and warm the teat in hot water first. Offer it when they are calm rather than starving, at the same time each day, and give it a week of small tries before deciding it hasn't worked. If they are under six weeks old or losing weight, ring the health visitor rather than pushing on.

Have the chimney swept once a year, before the heating season starts, and twice if it is your main heat or you burn wood - soot and creosote build up out of sight, and a blocked flue is how carbon monoxide gets into a room. A sweep costs about 40 to 80 pounds and gives you a certificate to keep for the insurance; while he is there, ask him to check the cowl and put a carbon monoxide alarm in the same room as the fire.

Have the line ready before the glass arrives: 'Not for me, thanks - I'm on the lime and soda.' Four words, said with a smile, and then ask them something, because a reason at a table is an invitation to be talked round. Keep a soft drink in your hand - people top up a full glass far less - and if a round lands in front of you anyway, leave it or pass it on rather than argue. When someone presses, use the same sentence again, then name it once, quietly and only to them: 'I don't drink - it's boring, but it's easier if you don't buy me one.' Two no's from the same person is not rude; it is what stops the third.

Have a recent bill ready, because the comparison needs your usage in kWh rather than pounds. Then pick a fixed deal and let the new supplier do the switch: it takes about three weeks, your old supplier contacts you rather than the other way round, and there is a 14-day cooling-off period. Check the exit fee on your current tariff first, since that is the only cost a switch can carry.

Have in a spare bed with its own bedding and a nightlight, a small cup and plate, snacks they already like, wipes, a spare towel and the parents' number written down. For a toddler, socket covers, a gate on the stairs and medicines out of reach; a box of bricks, paper and crayons covers most ages. Then ask the parents what they eat, what time they go to bed and whether they need a cot or a bed rail.
Having your hands full means you are as busy as you can be. What is taking all of it?

Hay fever is an allergy to pollen - sneezing, itchy eyes and a runny nose, no temperature, and it comes back at the same time each year. A cold is an infection: a sore throat first, then a blocked nose, gone in about a week.

Hay is the diet, not a topping: give a pile the size of the animal's own body every day, and it should be eaten. Meadow or timothy hay for adults, alfalfa only for growing youngsters and nursing mothers. If yours will not touch it, buy a fresher, greener bag, put it in a rack and a cardboard tube as well as on the floor, and cut the pellets and treats right back, because a pet full of nuggets has no room for hay. Drooling, or no droppings for a day, means the vet today.

Hay is the diet: a pile the size of the rabbit every day, since it wears the teeth down and keeps the gut moving. Add a handful of leafy greens - lettuce, kale, spinach, herbs - and an eggcup of nuggets. Carrot, apple and grapes are treats, because the sugar loosens the droppings, so go easy on cabbage and iceberg lettuce too. Grass is fine unless it has been weedkilled. Change a food over a week, not in a day.

Head shaking, scratching at an ear or a smell usually means an ear infection, which needs the vet rather than cotton buds, because the treatment differs for yeast, bacteria and ear mites. Keep ears dry after walks and swimming, and only use an ear cleaner the vet has approved.

Head the ball with your forehead, not the top of your head: attack it, keep your eyes open, keep your neck firm and head it back where it came from rather than up in the air. For a clearance, jump early and put your shoulders through it, and learn the timing with a soft ball so the head does not do the flinching.

Healthy weight is a range, not a number: a BMI of 18.5 to 24.9 for most adults, which for someone 1.70m tall is roughly 54kg to 72kg. BMI gets it wrong for very muscular people and for older people who have lost muscle, so add a waist measurement - under 94cm for a man and 80cm for a woman is the usual guide. If your weight has changed without trying, that is worth a word with a GP.

Heat and moving air are what dry a paint too fast, so keep the room cool and out of direct sun, shut the window and turn any fan off. Lid the tin and decant only what you will use in ten minutes, because a wide tray is all surface; a smaller tub keeps it workable. Water-based paint can take a splash of water, no more than one part in ten, or a paint conditioner from a decorator's shop. Then work to a wet edge: do one wall at a time in one go, roll into the bit you just did rather than next to it, and do not stop halfway across. A brush or roller you are coming back to in a few minutes goes in a damp cloth or a bag, and a skin on the paint in the tin gets lifted off, not stirred back in.

Heat and sun take it out of you: drink before you're thirsty, stay out of the midday sun, and eat something salty if you've been sweating. Feeling dizzy or confused in heat is a sign to get cool and drink, not to push on.

Heat is in the variety before it is in the size: a jalapeno is mild enough to eat raw, a bird's eye or a scotch bonnet will heat a whole curry, and the same kind varies from one to the next, so taste a sliver before you commit to two. Chop them small and add them early for a rounded heat, or late and sliced for a sharp one; the white pith and the seeds carry most of it, so scraping them out takes the edge off without making it mild. Wash your hands straight after and keep them off your eyes, or wear gloves for the very hot ones: the oil stays on skin for hours and soap barely shifts it.

Heavy periods mean soaking a pad or tampon every hour for a few hours, clots bigger than a 50p coin, or bleeding over seven days; if that is most months, see a GP. Common causes are fibroids, an underactive thyroid and, in your forties, perimenopause. Iron tablets may be needed if you feel tired, and a hormonal coil or tranexamic acid usually lightens things a lot.

Heavy legs by the evening are usually blood and fluid pooling from sitting or standing a long time: walk about every hour, put your feet up above hip height for twenty minutes, and cut back on salt. Compression socks help if it happens most days, and strong calf muscles do more than anything - calf raises and a daily walk push the blood back up. See a GP if one leg is swollen, hot or red, if the heaviness is there in the morning too, or if it comes with breathlessness; and if you are on the pill or just off a flight and one calf is painful, ring 111 the same day.

Hedgehogs eat beetles, caterpillars, earthworms and slugs, and by autumn they need to put on weight before hibernation. To feed one, put out cat or dog food (chicken or turkey, not fish), chopped unsalted nuts and a shallow dish of water, after dark. Never milk or bread, and feed under a slate or in a box so cats cannot get at it.

Helium does not raise your voice: sound travels about three times faster in it than in air, which makes the echoes in your throat ring higher. Your vocal cords move exactly as before, and it wears off in seconds.
Hello {name}! What are we doing today?

Help them shrink it to one question they can answer on a page - not the whole subject, but one thing about it - then one page of notes from one book or site, in their own words. A project is marked on the child's reading and thinking, so doing it for them shows in the writing and they learn nothing: sit beside them, ask what they already know, and hand back the pen. Break it into three sittings - notes, plan, then the poster or slides - and start with the part they are avoiding. If it is a model to build, build it first and write up what happened, because the write-up is the marked part.

Help to Buy in England was an equity loan: the government lent 20% of the price (40% in London) on a new build, interest-free for five years, and new applications closed at the end of March 2023. Nothing replaced it as it was - the help that exists now is shared ownership, First Homes and the mortgage guarantee scheme, and a Lifetime ISA adds 25% to what you save. A Help to Buy ISA closed to new savers in 2019, but an existing one can still be used until 2030. Scotland and Wales ran their own schemes, so check what your country offers now.

Henna is a plant dye that coats the hair instead of lifting it, so it adds warm red and brown and can darken, but it can never make hair lighter. Buy pure henna (lawsonia inermis) and mix it with water and lemon: black henna is not henna at all, it is PPD, and it can scar. Do not bleach or put a box dye over henna, because the metallic salts in some mixes can turn hair green and burn, so strand test first if you plan to.

Henry VIII (1491-1547) was king of England from 1509 and is remembered for two things: six wives and the break with Rome. He wanted his first marriage annulled so he could marry Anne Boleyn, the Pope refused, and in 1533 he made himself head of the Church of England and closed the monasteries. Two of the six wives were executed, two divorced or annulled, one died in childbirth, and Catherine Parr outlived him. His children were Edward VI, Mary I and Elizabeth I, who was his daughter by Anne Boleyn.
Henry Cavill plays Geralt in the first three series of The Witcher (2019-2023); Liam Hemsworth took the part from series four.
Hi {name}. Anything changed since we last spoke?

Hiccups in a baby or a small child are normal and they do not bother them: feed a little more upright, burp them, and the hiccups stop on their own within a few minutes. Mention it to a health visitor or GP if they come with reflux, coughing or trouble feeding.

Hip pain in an adult is usually the joint or the tendon over the outside of the hip bone: keep walking as far as is comfortable, sit with your knees lower than your hips, and take a painkiller before a walk rather than after. See a GP if it hurts when you are resting or at night, or you have started to limp.

Hire purchase is paying for something in instalments while you use it: the lender owns it until the last payment, then it is yours. Most forecourt car finance is this. You can hand the car back once you have paid half of the total, and the rate is fixed, but you cannot sell it before the end without settling it first.

Hire a piano remover rather than a general removal firm: it takes two people who know the handholds, a proper trolley and straps, and a knocked soundboard is a repair bill. Keep it upright and never on its side, take the legs off an upright only if the maker's instructions say so, and let it settle in the new room for a few weeks before it is tuned. Stairs and narrow turns are what make a quote go up, so send a photo of the route when you ask for one.

Hiring is usually the better call for a move: the van comes with insurance and a mileage cap, so a scratch costs you the excess rather than the repair, and you are not relying on someone else's mood or policy.
