A splash of dry vermouth or dry sherry is the closest thing to the wine itself, so half wine and half stock is a good way back. In a risotto, add the stock a ladle at a time either way, and taste for salt at the end.

Leave the carrier out all the time with a blanket and a familiar smelling toy in it, feed her next to it and then inside it, and never tip her in: pick the carrier up with her already in it, or lower her in back feet first. On the day, a towel over the carrier keeps her calmer, and the seatbelt goes through the handle rather than the cat loose in the car. If she panics every time, ask the vet for a plug-in or a short course of a calming supplement before the next appointment.

Leave the dressing on as long as the artist said, then wash it gently with fragrance-free soap and water twice a day, pat it dry and put a thin layer of tattoo balm on. Keep it out of the sun and out of swimming pools for two to three weeks, and do not pick at it: it will peel and flake a week or two in, and that is it healing.

Leave them with her and keep the room warm and quiet: for the first week she does everything, and handling is mostly weighing - a kitchen scale in a box, once a day, written down, because a kitten that is not gaining is the one that needs help. She wants kitten food and water within reach of the nest, and a litter tray she can get to in two steps. Kittens should stay with her until eight weeks, and never leave before then. If she leaves one out, will not settle on it or it feels cold, ring the vet that day; a mother cat that stops feeding them needs the vet too, not a bottle from the kitchen.

Leave a small warm light on - a plug-in night light or the hall light with the door ajar - rather than the room light, so the room still reads as night. Look round the room together before lights out and move whatever makes a shape (a coat on a chair, a streetlight through the blind), then give the same short routine each night and leave before they are asleep; staying until they drop off becomes the thing they need.

Leave earwax alone: it works its way out, and cotton buds push it back and pack it against the eardrum. If it blocks your hearing, a pharmacist can sell you olive or sodium bicarbonate drops for a week; if that does not shift it, a nurse can syringe or microsuction it. Never put anything smaller than your elbow in your ear.

Leave it on: a modern boiler is built to run overnight, and its frost setting fires it only when the house gets cold. What matters is not the hours but the flue and the alarm - a carbon monoxide alarm on the same floor as the boiler, the flue checked at the yearly service, and nothing stacked against the vents or the air brick. An old back boiler or an open flue is the one to ask a Gas Safe engineer about before you sleep with it on. If you mean the heating rather than the hot water, it costs more than switching it off and back on, which is the money question and not this one.

Leave it on low rather than off if it will be cold: 12 to 15C, or the thermostat's frost setting, costs a few pounds a week and is far cheaper than a burst pipe, which is what a hard frost does to a cold house. Turn the water off at the stopcock before you go as well, and hot water can be switched off entirely. For a summer trip, or a house that will not drop below about 5C, off is fine.

Leave it where people look, and where the business will see it: the order page for an online shop (that is the one the seller can answer), Google Maps for a cafe, shop or restaurant, TripAdvisor for a hotel. Three or four lines beat a rant - what you bought, when, what went wrong, and what you want - and give the stars you actually mean, since a 2 with a fair paragraph is read and a 1 with none is not. Post within a week or so while the details are checkable, keep the order number and any photos, and you can edit or delete your own review later from your account.

Leaves are the vegetable, not the meal: add a protein, something starchy and something rich, and dress it while the starch is still warm. Chickpeas or a boiled egg, new potatoes and feta is dinner; tinned tuna, leftover rice and a spoon of mayo is lunch. A plate rather than a side bowl is the portion that fills you, and salt it properly.

Leaves dropping off a houseplant is usually too much water: compost that has stayed wet for a week or more, or a saucer left standing full. Feel the compost - wet means no water for a fortnight, dry means a good soak and a pot that drains. Otherwise it is reacting to a change, cold from a window or a move to a new spot: leave it where it is for a month, since moving it about is what keeps it dropping.

Leaving a modern phone on the charger overnight is fine: it stops at full and the charger trickles nothing. The heat is what wears a battery, so take the thick case off, keep it off the duvet and out of the sun, and if you want it to last longer, use a slow charger rather than a fast one.

Lee Jae-myung is the president of South Korea: in office since June 2025, after winning the snap election that followed Yoon Suk Yeol's impeachment. A South Korean president serves one five-year term.
Leeds has about 810,000 people, the biggest of the Yorkshire cities.

Leeks can be lifted from September and stand in the ground all winter, which is the point of them: dig as you need them, and they will take hard frost. Earth up the stems a few weeks before lifting if you want more white.

Leeks keep about a week in the salad drawer, loose in a bag or standing in an inch of water in a jar, and the green tops go in the freezer for stock. Cut leeks dry out from the cut end first, so keep them whole until you cook them; a leek that has gone slimy at the root is past it, and the layers inside hold grit, so wash them after slicing.

Leg before wicket: the ball hit the batter's leg (or body) when it would have gone on to hit the stumps, and the bat wasn't involved first. The umpire has to think the ball was going on to hit, so a ball pitching outside leg, or a batter who hit it first, is not out.

Legs that feel like jelly for a few minutes are usually one of the ordinary things: a hot day or a hot room, a missed meal, standing still for a long time, a bug you are getting over, a first hard session at the gym, or adrenaline before something you are dreading. Sit down with your feet up for ten minutes, drink a glass of water, and eat something with salt or sugar in it - that is what puts the strength back. Get it looked at the same day if it comes with a weak or heavy arm, a drooping face, slurred speech or numbness down one side (ring 999 for those), if you cannot feel your saddle area or cannot pass urine, if it came on with a bad back, or if one leg has gone weak and stayed weak. Weak legs that come back every few days for weeks are worth a GP check with a blood test, because low iron, low vitamin D and a slow thyroid all do it.
Lemon or lime juice on the cut face slows it down, and cling film pressed right onto the flesh works better than a loose lid. Brown patches are only air damage; cut them off and the rest is fine.

Lemon curd keeps 2 weeks in a jar in the fridge once it is opened, and homemade curd the same, though eat homemade within a week if you did not sterilise the jar. It freezes for 3 months and thaws in the fridge. Curd that has separated, or smells of nail varnish, goes in the bin - the egg in it is what spoils.

Lemons and limes keep a couple of weeks in the fridge in a bag in the salad drawer, or about a week on the counter. A cut half keeps 3 days wrapped cut side down, and a hard one gives more juice after 20 seconds in the microwave.

Lentils and beans are one of the best buys in the shop: a drained tin has around 8g of protein and 6g of fibre for about 120 calories. They count towards your five a day and they keep you full far longer than the same weight of rice.
Leo XIV is the pope: elected in May 2025 and taking the name Leo XIV, after Francis. He was Cardinal Robert Prevost, and he is the first pope from the United States.

Lessons are usually £30 to £45 an hour, and a block of ten is often £270 to £400. Most people need 40 to 50 hours of lessons plus practice, so the total lands around £1,500 to £2,000 with the tests. Ask whether the car is used for the test and what that costs, and whether the instructor is on the official register.

Let the mud dry completely, then brush it off with a stiff brush before you touch water; washing mud while it is wet just pushes it into the fabric. A little washing-up liquid and a soft brush lifts the rest, then rinse and dry away from heat. Cold water only on a kit: hot water sets the mud and the grass stain both, and a wash at 30 with a normal dose of powder takes out what brushing leaves.

Let the mud dry completely, then brush it off with a stiff brush before you touch water; washing mud while it's wet just pushes it into the fabric. A little washing-up liquid and a soft brush lifts the rest, then rinse and dry away from heat.

Let the top 2-3cm of compost dry right out between waterings and water from the bottom for a few weeks: the larvae live in wet compost and dry compost kills them. Stand a yellow sticky trap in the pot for the adults, put a layer of grit on the surface so they cannot lay, and repot into fresh compost if it is bad. A half potato pushed into the soil overnight collects larvae you can throw away.

Let them start with a semi-permanent or a wash-out colour: it fades out in six to eight washes, so a mistake costs a month rather than a year, and it needs no bleach. Read the box together for the 48-hour patch test and do that first, then colour over a basin with gloves and an old towel, and keep anything lighter than two shades of their own colour for a salon - a home bleach on a teenager is what goes orange. Check the school's rule on 'unnatural' colours before you buy, because that is the argument you actually want to avoid.

Let it set, then crack off as much as you can with a knife. Lay kitchen paper over the rest and press it with a warm iron: the paper soaks the wax up, and you change the paper until nothing more comes through. On carpet, spoon some brown paper and iron that instead.

Let it stand 10 to 15 minutes out of the oven before you cut it, which is what sets the layers: a lasagne that runs was cut straight from the oven. Next time reduce the ragu until a spoon leaves a trail and use a thicker bechamel - 50g each of butter and flour to 500ml of milk - with the egg in it.

Let it cool, pour it into a bottle or a tub, and put that in the general waste - never down the sink, where it sets with wipes into a blockage. A little fat can go in the food waste caddy if your council collects one, and a recycling centre takes larger amounts of used cooking oil.

Let it cool and set first: warm chocolate smears further, so lift the solid part off with a knife or a spoon before any water goes near it. Then work a drop of washing-up liquid into the mark with your fingers, rinse from the back of the fabric in cold water, and wash at the temperature on the label. On a sofa, a car seat or a carpet, blot with a damp cloth instead of rinsing, and finish with clean water.

Let it cool in the tin for 10 minutes, until it starts to shrink from the sides, and turn it out then: too hot and it breaks, stone cold and it sticks. Run a thin knife round the edge first, and line the tin with baking paper next time so it cannot grab.

Let it go cold, then rub the soleplate with a paste of bicarbonate of soda and a little water on a damp cloth, or lay a cloth soaked in white vinegar on the plate for half an hour, and wipe it off with a dry cloth - never a scourer or a knife, which takes the coating off. For white flakes and spitting, fill the tank half and half with water and white vinegar, let it steam itself empty over a basin, then run a tank of plain water through; empty the tank after every use so the scale never gets going.

Let it harden completely - a bag of ice on it for 10 minutes speeds that up - then flick it off with a plastic card or a fingernail. For the film that is left, warm it with a hair dryer and blot it up with kitchen paper, or wipe it with a cloth wrung out in hot water and washing-up liquid, then re-polish the wood only where the wax was.

Let it install - most of what arrives is security fixes, and the nagging stops once it is done. Do it when you are plugged in and will not need the machine for half an hour, and back up first if it is a big numbered upgrade. If it keeps coming back without finishing, free up some disk space: an update needs about 20GB to unpack.

Lettuce keeps about a week in the fridge: wash and dry the leaves, wrap them in kitchen paper inside a bag and dress them only at the table, because wet leaves and early dressing are what wilt a salad. Keep the bag in the salad drawer rather than at the back, where it freezes; limp leaves come back in iced water for 10 minutes.

Level it first: the machine must not rock on the floor, so turn the front feet out until it sits flat on all four and lock the nuts. If it is new, the four transport bolts at the back have to come out or the drum is still locked to the frame. After that, an even load stops most of it - mix towels with lighter things rather than washing one heavy item - and check the shipping bolts are the right length for a laminate floor.

Lie with your head on an extra pillow and keep the room cool, then rinse the nose with a saline spray or a salt-water rinse before bed - it clears the swelling rather than just the snot, and it is safe every night. A decongestant spray works for three or four days only, because after that it makes the blockage worse; steam from a hot shower helps for an hour. One side blocked for weeks, bleeding, or a lost sense of smell needs a GP.

Lift new potatoes in June and July, once the flowers open, and maincrops in September and October when the tops have died back. Fork well beside the row so you do not spear them, then leave them on the soil for an hour to dry before storing in paper sacks in the dark.

Lift onions in July and August when the tops fall over and start to yellow: bend the tops down, leave them a fortnight on the soil in dry weather, then store in nets somewhere airy. An onion that is not properly dried is the one that rots and takes the rest of the sack with it.

Lift parsnips from October through to February, and leave them in the ground until after a frost: the cold turns starch to sugar and they taste far better. Fork underneath the root rather than pulling, because a parsnip snaps at the shoulder and the best part stays in the soil.

Lift the slab, scrape off the old bedding and re-bed it on 30 to 40mm of 5:1 sharp sand and cement, tapping it level with its neighbours with a rubber mallet and checking with a straight edge. A slab that rocks after rain is usually a hollow bed or ants. Point the joints with dry sand and cement, not soil, and leave it a day.

Lift the drain cover and clear the gully of leaves and silt with gloves and a trowel, then flush it with a bucket of water. If it's still slow or smells after that, or it's the main sewer, ring your water company: blocked public sewers are usually their job and free to clear.

Lift them out and soak them in the bath or a big sink in hot water with a good squirt of washing-up liquid and a couple of tablespoons of bicarbonate of soda, for an hour or overnight: the burnt-on grease then comes off with a nylon scourer or foil. If they fit, a dishwasher does most of it, and a bin bag with a splash of ammonia left outside overnight lifts the worst without scrubbing.

Lift garlic in July, when the bottom three leaves have yellowed and the rest are still green: stop watering a fortnight before, ease each bulb out with a fork, and dry them somewhere airy for two or three weeks before storing. Left in longer the bulbs split and they keep badly.

Lift it with a spade or two thin chisels and keep the pieces to match the colour, then bed it back on a full layer of sharp sand and mortar rather than four dabs at the corners, which is what lets a slab rock. Tap it down level with its neighbours with a rubber mallet, running a straight edge across the joints, and leave it 24 hours before you brush sand in. A slab cracked in two can be glued with exterior resin, but the crack will always show.

Light tells your brain it is still daytime, so keep the room as dark as you can: a blackout curtain or an eye mask, and turn the lamp off rather than dimming it. If a streetlight gets in, a curtain that reaches the floor helps.

Light clothes and plenty to drink matter more than the number on the thermometer, and children's paracetamol or ibuprofen at the dose on the bottle for their age brings it down. Most fevers are a virus and ease in three or four days. Under three months with any temperature, or a child who is not drinking or is getting worse, needs help the same day.

Light it in layers and move the air with a fan. One bright lamp in each corner beats a single ceiling light, an LED around 4000K reads closest to daylight, and a mirror or pale wall opposite the door bounces it about. For the air, prop the door open with a fan pulling air through to another room, or run a small dehumidifier: a windowless room goes damp before it goes stuffy.

Lightning heats the air along its path to about 30,000°C in a split second, and the air expands violently, making a shock wave we hear as thunder. You see the flash first because light travels far faster than sound.
Limp celery comes back in 20 minutes in iced water, so shave the dry bottom off first: a head keeps 2 weeks wrapped in foil in the fridge, which keeps it crisp where a plastic bag turns it slimy.

Limp leaves are fine to eat: wilting is only water loss, so they are safe once they have had 10 minutes in iced water. Slimy, sour-smelling or brown-and-soft leaves are not safe, and no rinse fixes them, so bin those.

Line the tin with the pastry, prick the base all over with a fork, then cover it with a sheet of crumpled parchment and fill that with baking beans or dry rice. Bake at 200C (180C fan) for 15 minutes, lift the paper and beans out, and give it another 5 minutes to dry the base before the filling goes in. Blind just means baked empty - the weights stop the base rising and the sides slumping.

Line it with a coco mat, or a bin bag with a few holes punched in the bottom, and use a compost that holds water. In a 30cm basket put four or five plants: something upright in the middle and trailing lobelia, petunia, bidens or trailing begonia round the edge. Water it every day in summer and twice on hot days, because a basket dries out faster than anything in the ground, and feed it with tomato feed every fortnight until September.

Linen creases because the fibre has no give, and the fix is water and heat: wash it on a normal cycle at 40C, take it out the moment the machine stops, shake it hard and hang or line dry it. Iron it damp on the hottest setting it will take, or leave it creased and call it the point of linen. A new, stiff piece softens after three or four washes.

Linen is woven from the fibres of the flax plant, which makes it the strongest of the plant fibres and the coolest in heat: it carries water away fast and does not cling. It creases the moment you move and feels stiff when new, and both of those go off with washing - a linen shirt gets softer every wash for years. Wash it at 30 or 40 and never tumble dry it hot, or it shrinks and goes brittle.

Listen to what it does: a click or nothing at all is the battery or its connections, a slow groaning crank is a flat battery, and a fast crank that won't fire is fuel or ignition. Try a jump start first; if that works, the battery or alternator is the problem, not the engine.

Listeria is a bug that is rare but dangerous in pregnancy because it can cross to the baby, and it grows in food kept cold rather than in food left out - soft cheese, pate, smoked fish and cooked meats from a deli are the usual culprits. That is why the advice is to heat leftovers until steaming, wash the veg, and skip those foods. It usually shows as a mild flu-like illness, so mention any fever to the midwife.

Load it so it can be tipped in one go, and put the awkward things on top: a car load usually drives straight in, but many sites ask for proof of address, and a van or a trailer is often booked. Paint, chemicals, gas bottles, batteries and anything with a screen go to a staffed container or to a steward rather than into a skip, so ask at the gate. Soil, rubble and plasterboard are usually limited to a few bags a visit. If you cannot drive it there, the council's bulky waste collection is the other route: usually charged, booked online or by phone, and they take it from the doorstep.

Load less: a third of the bristles wet, half a roller of paint, and lay it off with light strokes in one direction rather than going back over it. A run is too much paint in one spot, so scrape the roller back over the tray's ramp every time and don't reload until it stops giving paint, and keep the brush moving in one direction instead of scrubbing back and forth. When a run has started, brush it out while it is still wet - lay the brush flat and drag the run sideways into the dry paint - then leave it alone: going back over paint as it dries is what leaves the brushmarks. On a ceiling, paint towards yourself and slightly away from the wall so the last stroke is a pulled one, and thin the paint only if it is genuinely thick.

Lochia is the bleeding after birth: heavy red blood for three to five days, then browner and lighter for up to six weeks, coming back a little when you do more - so a bleed still going past six weeks is a GP visit, not lochia. Use pads, not tampons. Ring your maternity unit the same day if you soak a pad in an hour, pass clots bigger than a 50p coin, or the blood smells bad or you are feverish - and 999 or 911 if you are faint, dizzy or flooding.

Lock the frame and one wheel to something fixed in the ground with a D-lock, and take the front wheel or its quick release with you if it is not also locked. Keep the lock off the ground and the bike where people pass, since an angle grinder and a quiet street is how most bikes go. Register the frame number and photograph the bike; it is what gets it back.
London has about 8.9 million people, and about 14 million in the wider area around it. It is the biggest city in the UK by a long way - Birmingham, the second, has about 1.1 million.

Loneliness at the desk is real: the small talk that used to fill the day is gone, and it does not come back by itself. Put one person in the day on purpose - a standing fifteen minute call with someone on your team, a lunchtime walk where you actually speak to someone, and one thing a week outside work with people in it. If the office is an option, take two days and make them the days you like people; if not, tell your manager the team has gone quiet and ask for a weekly call. Weeks of it without lifting is worth a GP.

Long pasta - spaghetti, linguine, tagliatelle - is for thin sauces that coat it. Short shapes - penne, fusilli, rigatoni - hold chunkier sauces, and the ridges and tubes are there to catch them. Filled pasta - ravioli, tortellini - is a meal with its sauce inside. Dried is durum wheat and water; fresh is egg and soft wheat, cooks in two or three minutes, and is richer. Wholewheat is the same shapes with the bran left in, and takes a minute longer.

Long sighted means the near things are the blurry ones: the eye is a little short, or the lens too weak, so light from a page would come to a focus behind the retina and the eye has to pull it forward by straining. That is why small print and phone screens get held further away, and why the eyes ache and the head thumps by evening rather than first thing. An optician sorts it with glasses or contact lenses, and a child who is long sighted can read the board but not a book, so a test is worth it if schoolwork slips.

Long division is the same four steps over and over: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down. Take 492 divided by 4: 4 goes into 4 once (write 1), 1 x 4 = 4, subtract to get 0, bring down the 9. 4 into 9 goes twice (write 2), 2 x 4 = 8, 9 - 8 = 1, bring down the 2 to make 12. 4 into 12 is 3, so the answer is 123. Say each step out loud the first few times, and use real objects for the first example so the place value makes sense.

Long grain, basmati and jasmine rice do not need soaking - rinse it in a sieve until the water runs clear and cook it straight away, and that rinse is what stops it going sticky. Soak when the dish asks for it: about 30 minutes for pilau or biryani, and an hour or two for brown rice, then use a little less water because the grains already hold some. Do not leave raw rice sitting in water overnight on the counter - do it in the fridge if you want to get ahead.

Longitude is how far east or west of Greenwich a place is, measured in degrees up to 180 each way, and it is what sets your time zone. Sailors could find their latitude for centuries before they could find their longitude, which is why accurate clocks were so valuable.

Look up the plainest word in the sentence, not the cleverest: that is the one with a useful choice. Take a word you would say out loud, check it in the dictionary for the sense you mean, and leave the rest alone - a thesaurus makes writing worse when it is used to sound clever.

Look up the base word rather than the ending - 'running' is under 'run' - and read the example sentence before the definition, because the example shows the word at work. Then write one sentence of your own with it the same day: a word you only read is one you lose by Friday.

Look at the pattern, not the last time: three cancellations in a row is a way of holding you at arm's length, and one apology does not answer it. Ask for something firm instead of another vague 'soon' - a day in the diary in the next fortnight - and take the answer as information. If it stays one-sided, match their effort for a while and put your evenings into people who turn up; you do not have to announce it or end the friendship.

Look at the terms on your confirmation, because the notice they ask for is what decides it: most restaurants, hairdressers and garages want a day's notice and will move you to another day free, while a deposit on a table or a slot is usually what buys the first one. Ask in writing with the date, the time and the booking reference, and ring as well if it is within 24 hours - a phone call is what gets a deposit moved rather than kept. If they will not move it, ask what the deposit was held for and whether a friend can take the slot, since a booking nobody used and a table nobody turned up for are not the same thing.

Look at the week before the people: what is due, who is covering it, and what can be moved or dropped, then take one real thing off the list this week and say out loud why you moved it - a team that is flat is usually carrying more than its hours, and a speech about wellbeing does not buy that back. Then ten minutes with each of them, one at a time, and ask which part of the week is heaviest rather than whether they are coping: the one task they dread is the one you can shift, and it is rarely the one you guess. Say no to the next piece of new work with a reason and a date, and go up the chain with the load rather than down it, because a team short of people is a staffing decision somebody above you is paid to make. If someone is signed off, or crying at work, or saying they cannot go on, that is a person to sit with today and a GP appointment to help them book, and if several are off at once treat it as a workload problem before anything else.

Look at the colour before you do anything. A white or creamy film on top, with no fur on it, is kahm yeast and the starter is fine: skim it off, move the jar to a clean one and feed it. Anything furry, or pink, orange, green or black, means mould has gone through the jar - throw it out and start again, because the spores are in the flour and not just on the surface. Wash the jar with hot soapy water before the next one, and keep the sides scraped down so nothing grows on the rim.

Look at the contract first: if it guarantees your hours, a permanent cut is a change to your terms, so put your objection in writing and carry on working as before while you sort it out - ACAS (0300 123 1100) is free and will tell you where you stand. If it says the hours vary, short-time working is allowed, but ask for guarantee pay: a day's pay for each day you are laid off, up to five days in three months.

Look at the digit just after the place you are keeping: 5 or more rounds the last kept digit up, 4 or less leaves it. So 3.456 to two decimal places is 3.46 and to the nearest whole number it is 3. Round once, at the end of a sum, not at every step.

Look at the edge first: a serrated kitchen pair cannot be sharpened at all, and a smooth pair is done with a fine diamond file or a small whetstone, five or six light strokes along the bevelled side only, at the angle the bevel already has, then wipe the burr off with the flat of the stone. A stiff screw is usually the pivot, not the blade: a drop of oil and a quarter turn on the nut frees it. If the two blades no longer meet along their length, a repair shop re-grinds them for a few pounds, which is cheaper than a good new pair.

Look at when and how it is eaten. Ragged holes and slime trails, worst overnight, are slugs and snails: go out with a torch after dark and pick them off, or set a beer trap, and put copper tape round pots. Clean holes in the middle of leaves with the edges left alone are caterpillars - look under the leaves in daylight and pick them off. Tops nibbled to a stump with a clean cut are pigeons or rabbits, so net or cage it. Seedlings cut off at soil level are cutworms or mice.

Look at which switch is down before you reset it: a single breaker is one circuit, a wider switch marked RCD or RCBO is a fault to earth. Unplug everything on that circuit, push the switch fully down and then back up, and if it holds, plug things back one at a time until it trips again - that appliance is the fault. If it will not reset with nothing plugged in, or it is the RCD that keeps going, leave it up and get an electrician. Never tape a breaker up or fit a bigger one.

Look at both feet every day - the soles with a mirror, and between the toes - and never go barefoot, even indoors, because with diabetes a small cut can turn into an ulcer before it hurts. Dry them well, cut the nails straight across, use a moisturiser on hard skin but not between the toes, and have corns and calluses done by a podiatrist. Ring the clinic the same day about any cut, blister or red, hot or weeping patch.

Look for the dishwasher-safe mark on the base or the handle first: it is usually a glass-and-fork symbol, and most stainless steel pans, baking trays and everyday cutlery carry it. Keep out of the machine bare aluminium (it goes grey and pitted), copper, brass, cast iron and carbon steel (they rust or lose their seasoning), and anything with a wooden or glued handle. Most non-stick is better washed by hand, because hot alkaline water wears the coating, knives lose their edge knocking against other cutlery, and a wooden board will crack.

Look for "extra virgin" and a harvest date, not a best-before: oil is a fruit juice and it fades, so the newest pressing tastes best. A dark glass bottle or a tin keeps it that way, and a peppery catch at the back of your throat means the good bitter polyphenols are still there. Spend on the bottle you use raw - dressing, bread, a finished dish - and use a cheaper olive oil or a plain oil for roasting and frying. "Light" on the label means light in taste, not in calories.

Look in the port with a torch: a plug of pocket fluff is why most phones stop charging. Switch the phone off, then dig it out with a wooden toothpick or a dry soft toothbrush, never a pin or a metal clip, and do not use water, alcohol or a can of air. If the plug still feels loose or the port looks burnt, a repair shop swaps it for £30 to £60.

Look in the fridge before you go to the shop: see what is left, then plan the next two dinners around it. Keep the oldest veg at the front of the drawer, freeze bread, milk and any meat you will not use in two days on the day you buy it, and treat the freezer as a pause button rather than a cupboard. A weekly "whatever is left" soup or frittata uses up the odds and ends, and a written list stops you buying a third bag of carrots.

Look it up on the carrier's own site with the number on the counter receipt or the emailed label - not the shop's app, which only shows what the carrier told it. The number is also what a claim rests on, so keep it. If the page has not moved at all for 10 working days, Royal Mail treats the item as lost and the claim starts then.

Loosen the wheel nuts half a turn while the car is still on the ground, then jack it at the marked point, take the nuts off, lift the wheel away and put the spare on. Nip the nuts up in a star pattern, lower it, then tighten properly with the brace. Keep under 50mph on a space saver and check its pressure every few months.

Loosen it with liquid before anything else - a splash of milk, water or juice, then blend again - and add ice last: a smoothie thickens as it stands, so make it a little thinner than you want it, and a spoon of yoghurt or half a banana gives body without the clag.
Lose has one o and means not winning or not being able to find something; loose has two and means not tight. Your trousers are loose, and you might lose them.

Losing weight without trying is a symptom before it is anything else: more than about 5% of your body weight in six to twelve months is worth a GP appointment, and they will check the common causes - thyroid, coeliac, diabetes, low mood - with blood tests. Go now rather than later, and take a note of when it started, how much has gone and any change in appetite, bowels or thirst, because those answers decide what gets tested first.

Ludwig van Beethoven (1770-1827) was the German composer who carried classical music into the romantic age, from the Fifth Symphony to the Ninth and its Ode to Joy. He was going deaf from his late twenties and still wrote some of his greatest music once he could no longer hear it played.
Luis Montenegro is the prime minister of Portugal: in office since April 2024 and re-elected in May 2025. The president, who can dissolve parliament, is Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa.

Lukewarm water and a gentle unperfumed cleanser, morning and evening: warm water and a flannel lift grime and make-up, while hot water strips the oils and leaves the skin tight. Pat dry rather than rub, and put moisturiser on while the skin is still damp; anything that stings is too harsh for a face.
Lying there trying harder doesn't work, sadly. Get up after twenty minutes, something dull and warm, then back to bed.

MOT stands for Ministry of Transport, the department that invented the test in 1960, and the letters have outlived it. The test checks safety and emissions on a car over three years old once a year, and it is the garage that keeps the record - driving without one is a fine, and the car's insurance can be void.

Macadamia nuts are poisonous to dogs: within 12 hours they can bring on weakness, wobbling, tremors and a fever. Ring your vet now, keep the packet and tell them how many he ate; most dogs recover in a day or two with support, but tremors need seeing to.
Magma is molten rock under the ground; once it reaches the surface it is called lava. It forms where rock gets hot enough to melt, and because it is lighter than the rock around it, it rises.

Magna Carta was a charter King John was forced to seal at Runnymede in 1215. It limited the king's power over his barons and is remembered because it put in writing that even the monarch is under the law.

Make the new one first - Gmail or Outlook, both free - then tell the people and the sites that matter: your bank, work, and anyone who emails you often. Keep the old address open for a couple of months instead of closing it, and set it to auto-reply with the new one, because a password reset will still go there.

Make the shape, not the whole outfit: black leggings and a black top read as almost anything, then one thing does the work - a cardboard box for a robot or a rocket, a bin bag and a belt for a cape, a paper plate and elastic for a mask, a stripy top and an eye patch for a pirate. Paint it the night before, not the morning of, and ask the party's theme first. If it is for world book day, check the school's rules, because some ban masks and face paint.

Make the task visible and small: one page, one timer, everything else out of the room. Body-doubling works for a lot of people - study alongside someone, in person or on a video call with mics off. Move between two or three subjects rather than forcing one, and use a paper checklist you tick, because visible progress is the fuel.

Make the vegetarian dish the main for the whole table and put the meat on the side as an extra: a mushroom and lentil lasagne, a chickpea and spinach curry with rice, or a tray of roasted veg with feta and couscous. Nobody gets a plate of sides, and you cook one dinner.

Make the feed within 30 minutes of boiling: the water should still be at least 70C when it goes onto the powder, because that is what kills anything in it. Then cool the bottle under a running cold tap or stand it in a jug of cold water - about 10 to 15 minutes, and shake a drop onto the inside of your wrist to test it. Water that has been boiled once and left to cool is fine for drinking, but make a fresh feed rather than reheating an old one.

Make the first session tiny and today: open the topic list, pick the one you know least, and test yourself on it for ten minutes, because starting is the part that is failing rather than the studying. Then put three short sessions in the week you actually have, each ending with a self-test instead of a reread, and give each one a stopping time so it cannot drift to midnight. Testing yourself is what makes the last day calm instead of terrible; if the exam is tomorrow, pack the bag, read your one-page summary once, and sleep.

Make the gift something you do together: a picnic at the spot of your first date, a small photo book of the year, or a jar of twelve notes with one to open each month. The thought shows in the specifics, not the price.

Make up a bed before they arrive: a sheet, a pillow, a towel on the end of it and a lamp they can reach. Ask ahead about anything that would spoil the stay - a food they cannot eat, a pet allergy, whether they need to be up early - and have the wifi code and a spare key written down. Milk, bread, tea, coffee and something for breakfast covers more than a plan does.

Make a paste of bicarbonate of soda and water, coat the inside (not the elements), leave it overnight and wipe it out with a damp cloth and a little vinegar. It takes some scrubbing but doesn't fill the kitchen with fumes like caustic oven cleaner. The racks soak in hot water with a dishwasher tablet while the paste works.

Make it one resolution, small enough to do on your worst day - ten minutes, not an hour - and tie it to something you already do, like a walk after your morning coffee. Mark the days you did it rather than the streak you broke, and if you miss once, the rule is never to miss twice.

Make it one rule rather than one row: anything borrowed comes back by Sunday, or it is not borrowed again. Say it once, warmly, the next time they ask - 'yes, if it's back Sunday' - and keep the things you actually mind out of reach rather than arguing about them each time. The annoyance is worth naming once: 'it's not the jumper, it's never knowing where it is'.

Make it small, specific and easy to refuse: "Could you water my plants on Tuesday and Friday? No problem if not." Saying what it involves and that they can say no makes people much more likely to say yes.

Make it small and timed: ten minutes, everything off the floor, with a timer they can see, and work alongside them the first few times. Give each thing a home - a box for the lego, a basket for washing - because 'tidy' is impossible when nothing has a place. One zone at a time beats the whole room.

Make it two minutes of something else - a timer, a song, or an app that shows the teeth - and let them have a go first before you finish the job properly. Brush yours at the same time, side by side, and keep it boring rather than a fight: hold them gently and get it done if you have to. Under three they only need a smear of fluoride paste, and a first dentist visit at this age is mostly about liking the chair.

Make it about the driving, not the birthday: a licence renews at 70 and every three years after, and it is a medical condition - eyesight, dementia, a stroke, epilepsy - that has to be reported to the DVLA, not the age. Ask the GP to raise it with his permission, and offer a driving assessment at a mobility centre: an hour in his own car, and it settles the question with evidence instead of an argument. Line up the alternative before the keys go - lifts, a bus pass, a taxi budget - and don't take them yourself.

Make it a question about them, not an accusation: 'You seem a bit off with me — have I done something?' Say it once, in person or on the phone, not in a long message. If they say nothing is wrong, believe them and carry on normally; people often need a day before they can say it.

Male pattern baldness is mostly inherited: hair follicles on top of the head become sensitive to testosterone by-products and shrink, so hairs get thinner and eventually stop. It is not caused by hats, washing or stress alone, and treatments only work while you keep using them.

Malware is software written to do something you did not ask for: a virus that spreads, spyware that watches, ransomware that locks your files until you pay. It arrives as an attachment, a fake update or a program from a site that is not the maker's, so the protection that works is updating the system, keeping to official app stores and never opening a file you did not expect.
Manchester itself has about 550,000 people; Greater Manchester, the whole cluster of towns around it, has about 2.9 million.

Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa is the president of Portugal: in office since 2016 and re-elected in 2021. Unlike most ceremonial presidents he has real power, including the right to dissolve parliament; the prime minister is Luis Montenegro.
Margot Robbie plays Harley Quinn in Suicide Squad (2016), Birds of Prey (2020) and The Suicide Squad (2021). Lady Gaga plays her in Joker: Folie a Deux.

Marie Antoinette (1755-1793) was the Austrian-born queen of France, wife of Louis XVI, who was hated for her spending while the country went hungry, and who was guillotined in October 1793. There is no record of her ever saying that the hungry should eat cake.

Mark both ends before you drill: the rail sits 10 to 15cm above the window recess and 15 to 20cm past each side, so the curtains clear the glass, and check it with a spirit level because a rail two people can see is crooked. Fix into masonry or a timber stud rather than the plasterboard alone - a rail hangs all its weight on two points and pulls downwards - so find the studs with a magnet dragged along the wall, which sticks at the screw heads, or drill and use a masonry plug. Hang the curtains on the rail before it goes up, and use the last eyelet at each end.

Mark a level line one tile up from the lowest point of the wall and work up from a batten screwed along it, because a floor is never level: the cut row goes in at the bottom last. Spread adhesive with a notched trowel over about a square metre at a time, press each tile on with a slight twist, and keep 2mm spacers between them. In a shower or round a bath use waterproof adhesive and grout, leave the grout 24 hours, then wipe the haze off with a damp sponge and seal the corners with silicone rather than grout.
Mark Carney is the prime minister of Canada: in office since March 2025, and his Liberal party won the April 2025 election. He took over from Justin Trudeau, who resigned after nine years.

Mars is about 225 million km from Earth on average, but the gap swings from roughly 55 million to 400 million km as the two planets move round the Sun. That is why a mission leaves only every 26 months, and why radio messages take between 3 and 22 minutes each way.

Martin Luther (1483-1546) was a German monk and professor who in 1517 published 95 arguments against the Church selling forgiveness. Printing spread them across Europe, he was excommunicated, and the movement he started became Protestantism. He also translated the Bible into German, which shaped the modern language.

Martin Luther King Jr (1929-1968) led the American civil rights movement without violence: the Montgomery bus boycott in 1955, the 1963 March on Washington, and the laws of 1964 and 1965 that ended legal segregation and barred the poll tax. He was shot in Memphis in April 1968.

Mash them in rather than serve them whole: beans or lentils blended into a tomato sauce or a shepherd's pie disappear, and peas or sweetcorn folded through rice do too. Put the new thing next to something they already eat, no bargaining and no second dinner, and keep offering it - it can take eight or ten tries before a child accepts a food.

Mash a drained tin of black beans or chickpeas with a grated small onion, a handful of breadcrumbs, a spoon of tomato puree and an egg to bind it - or a flax egg, a tablespoon of ground flaxseed in three of water, left ten minutes - then chill the mix twenty minutes so the patties hold. Shape them 2cm thick and fry 4 to 5 minutes a side, or bake them 20 minutes at 200C (180C fan). Keep them thick and turn them gently: they are softer than beef, and a thin one breaks. A spoon of smoked paprika is what makes them taste of something.

Mash it with the water it cooked in and a fat that is not butter: two or three spoons of the cooking water and two tablespoons of olive oil, or the same of a dairy-free spread, plus a splash of warm oat or soy milk if you want it looser. Work it with a fork or a whisk for a minute rather than a masher - starch and liquid are what make it smooth - and taste for salt, because without butter it wants a little more. A spoon of mustard, horseradish or a soft garlic clove cooked with the potatoes puts back some of the flavour the butter was giving.

Mashed potato keeps 2 days in the fridge, less than the potatoes it came from, because the butter and milk in it turn first. Warm it in a pan with a splash of milk over a low heat and stir, rather than in the microwave on high, which makes it gluey. It freezes for a month and comes back a little looser, so beat a knob of butter through it.

Mask the glass with tape, or cut in at a shallow angle with a 25mm brush and keep the brush lightly loaded so it does not run onto the pane, and paint the frame before the sliding parts. On a sash window do the staff beads and the pulley recess first, then the sashes. Run a knife round the join and open the window a crack while the paint is still soft, or it dries shut; outside wants an undercoat and two coats of gloss on a dry day.
Masoud Pezeshkian is the president of Iran: in office since July 2024. The man with the final say is the supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, and the president runs the government under him.

Match the pillow to how you sleep: on your side you want a firm, high one that fills the gap between shoulder and ear, on your back a medium one, and on your front a soft, thin one so your neck is not cranked up. A pillow that folds in half and stays folded is worn out - most last two to three years, not ten. Memory foam and latex hold their shape, hollowfibre is cheap and washable at 60C, and down is soft but needs plumping; a washable protector keeps whichever you pick clean.

Match it to the age first: a one year old is ready at 6.30 to 7.30pm and needs 11 to 14 hours out of 24, two to five year olds 6.30 to 8pm with 10 to 13 hours, five to eight 7 to 8pm with 9 to 12. Then shift it 15 minutes every three or four nights rather than all at once, and keep the wake-up time fixed: the morning light is what sets the body clock, so open the curtains straight away and get outside before school. The last hour wants to be dim and calm - bath, pyjamas, a story, no screens - and a child old enough to read can have half an hour of looking at books in bed. If a nap is running past 3pm, cap it at 20 minutes or move it earlier; one late nap undoes a week of earlier bedtimes.

Maternity leave is 52 weeks: 26 weeks of ordinary leave, then 26 of additional leave, and you can go back early if you give 8 weeks' notice. You have to take 2 weeks straight after the birth, or 4 if you work in a factory. Only 39 weeks of the 52 are paid. Tell your employer your due date and the date you plan to stop work 15 weeks before the baby is due.

Matt white, or the palest tint of the wall colour, and one shade lighter than the walls if you want a tint at all: a ceiling painted as deep as the walls comes down on you and makes a small room feel lower. White bounces light back into the room, which is why a dark hallway or a north-facing room looks better with a warm white than a cool one, and a sunlit south room can take a cool white. In a kitchen or a bathroom use a moisture-resistant matt emulsion, because ordinary emulsion flakes over the steamy half of the room. Two coats of matt, rolled on a pole in strips, and paint the ceiling before the walls.

Measure round your ribs under the bust, snug, and round to the nearest even number: that is your band size. Then measure round the fullest part, and the difference in inches is the cup - one inch is A, two is B, three is C, four is D. A bra should sit level all the way round with room for two fingers under the band, and nearly all the support comes from the band, not the straps, so straps that dig in mean the band is too big, not the cup too small. Shops size differently, so get fitted once - it is free in most department stores and takes ten minutes - and try the sister size (one band smaller, one cup bigger) if the one you measure is between sizes.

Measure the old cylinder before you buy one: the length each side of the fixing screw, and whether it sits flush with the door or sticks out. Undo the retaining screw on the door edge, put the key in and turn it slightly, and the cylinder slides out; the new one goes in the same way, with the key in it. Fifteen minutes with a screwdriver, the door left open while you work, and about fifteen to thirty pounds for a kite-marked one.

Measure the pole or track, not the window, and add 10 to 20cm either side so the curtains cover the edges when closed. For the length, measure from the pole to where you want them to finish, then double the width for a full gather: one and a half times the width looks skimped.

Measure the distance between the two hinge holes and the shape of the pan before buying, because seats come in round and oval and the holes are not all the same spacing. Most hinges are top-fixing now - a screw you turn from above with an Allen key that pulls a rubber bung tight under the rim - which is a ten-minute job. If the old one is bottom-fixing, the nuts are underneath and behind the pan, so a small spanner and a torch help; put the new seat on with the hinges level and tighten until it stops wobbling, not until it stops moving.

Measure the gap and the doorway before you argue, and take the legs or the door off if that is all that is stopping it: most sofas come apart at the back. Bought online or over the phone, you have 14 days to cancel and they have to collect a bulky item, though they can charge for that if the terms say so; bought in a shop, a return is their own policy, and something made to your measurements has no right to one.

Meat, and plenty of it: a lion averages 5 to 7 kg a day, taken from zebra, wildebeest, buffalo and smaller prey, and it can go several days between kills and then eat 30 kg at one sitting. The lionesses do most of the hunting, and the pride shares the carcass.

Megabits per second is how fast data moves, and the small b is the whole trick: eight bits make a byte, so a 100Mbps connection downloads about 12 megabytes a second - a song in a few seconds, a two-hour film in about ten minutes. Adverts quote megabits because the number is bigger, while file sizes on your phone are in megabytes.

Melt 25g of butter, stir in 25g of plain flour and cook it a minute, then add 300ml of milk a splash at a time, whisking each splash in before the next - that is what keeps it smooth. Simmer it 3 or 4 minutes, season with salt and pepper, and stir in a handful of grated cheese off the heat for a cheese sauce.

Melt it on the lowest heat, in small pieces, and take the pan off as soon as most of it has gone - the rest melts in the warm pan. Butter splits when it gets too hot, because the milk solids cook and squeeze the fat out and it goes grainy and oily: a split batch comes back if you let it cool a little and whisk in a teaspoon of cold water, and simply warming it again will not fix it.

Meningitis is an infection of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord, and it is a 999 call, not a wait: a fever with a stiff neck, a bad headache, dislike of bright light, drowsiness or a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it. Do not wait for the rash, because it can come late or not at all. A baby may only be floppy, feeding badly, grumpy when picked up, or crying high and not settling. Bacterial meningitis needs antibiotics in hospital the same day; the viral kind is milder and most people are over it in a week or two. The routine jabs cover the main bacterial kinds, so the red book is worth checking.

Mention it lightly instead of letting it fester: 'I missed hearing from you on my birthday, did it slip your mind?' Most friends forgot the date, not the friendship, and saying it plainly beats a cold silence. If it becomes a pattern, that is a bigger talk.

Message before your start time, as early as you can: "I'm not well enough to come in today - I'll update you tomorrow." You do not owe symptoms or an apology; do say whether anything urgent needs covering. Follow your workplace's own rule for how to tell them - usually a call on the first day.

Metal is not colder than the room; it conducts heat away from your hand much faster than wood or cloth, so your skin loses heat quickly and reads that as cold. That is also why a metal spoon feels cold and a wooden one does not.
Mette Frederiksen is the prime minister of Denmark: in office since 2019. The head of state is King Frederik X, who took over in January 2024.
Michael Gambon played Dumbledore in six of the eight Harry Potter films, taking over from Richard Harris, who died after the second. Jude Law plays him young in the Fantastic Beasts films.
Micheal Martin is the taoiseach, or prime minister, of Ireland: in office since January 2025. The president, a largely ceremonial role, is Catherine Connolly, elected in October 2025.

Michelle O'Neill is Northern Ireland's first minister - Sinn Féin, in office since February 2024, with Emma Little-Pengelly of the DUP as deputy first minister. The two jobs are always held by the two biggest parties.
Mike Myers voices Shrek, with Eddie Murphy as Donkey and Cameron Diaz as Fiona, in the four films from 2001 to 2010.

Milk, and mostly cow's milk: it is warmed, a culture and rennet go in so the curds set, and the curds are cut, pressed and salted. Roughly 10 litres of milk go into a kilo of hard cheese, which is where the whey drains off to.

Milk curdles when heat or acid makes its proteins clump together: lemon, wine, vinegar or tomatoes, or a hard boil. Add acid off the heat and slowly, keep dairy out of a rolling boil, and stir a spoonful of flour or cornflour into the milk first when you are cooking it into a sauce.

Milk kefir is 1 to 2 tablespoons of live kefir grains in a litre of whole milk in a jar with a loose lid, left out of the fridge for 24 hours and then strained: the grains go back in fresh milk and the kefir goes in the fridge. The grains grow, so give the extra away. With no grains, 2 tablespoons of live yoghurt or buttermilk starts it off, though it stops after a few lots. It keeps a week.

Milky tap water is almost always air: fill a glass, and if it clears from the bottom up in a minute or two it is just bubbles from pressure in the main and it is safe to drink. If it stays cloudy, or runs brown, blue or green, run the cold tap for two minutes and then ring your water company - and drink bottled water until it clears.
Millie Bobby Brown plays Eleven in Stranger Things (2016-2025).

Mince, sausages and burgers have to be cooked grey all the way through to 71C, and a whole steak does not: mincing mixes the bacteria from the outside through the meat, so a rare burger is a real risk in a way a rare steak is not. Out, order it well done; at home, no pink in the middle and the juices run clear. A mouthful of raw mince is very unlikely to do any harm, but a serving of it is a bad idea - cook it through, and see a doctor if you get cramps, fever or diarrhoea in the next few days.

Mint spreads by runners just under the surface, so pulling it up makes it worse. Sink it in a pot with the rim 2cm above the soil, or a bottomless bucket, or grow it in a container away from the bed. In a border already taken over, fork out the runners in spring and again in autumn for two years, and cut the stems before they flower so it cannot seed.

Mint is not grown from seed: buy a plant, or pull up a piece of root with shoots on it in spring or autumn and pot it in fresh compost. Stand it in a pot with the rim above the soil, because a mint in a border takes over, and divide the pot every couple of years when the stems get thin.

Mirrors, Pyrex and drinking glasses are not bottle-bank glass: they are made to take heat, so they melt at a different temperature and spoil the batch. Wrap it so nobody cuts themselves and put it in the general waste, or take it to the tip.

Misting does very little: it lifts the humidity for a few minutes and does not fix brown tips or stop a plant crisping. For a fern or a calathea, group it with other plants, keep it out of draughts and stand the pot on a tray of wet pebbles that the water can evaporate from; for anything else, the odd mist is mostly for you.

Moles are after worms, so a lawn full of molehills is a sign of good soil: flatten the hills, mow the grass back over them and put the soil on a bed, and leave the traps and the mole catcher to a professional, because spring traps and poison are the only things that work and both are regulated. Sonic spikes, mothballs, windmills and chewing gum do nothing. They often move on by themselves once the worms go deeper in a dry spell.

Momentum is mass times velocity, measured in kg m/s, and it is what makes a lorry harder to stop than a bike going at the same speed. Its rule is that the total is unchanged in a collision: two skaters pushing apart, or a cue ball hitting another, end up with the same total momentum they started with - one gains what the other loses. That is why a big airbag spreads the change over longer, so the force on you is smaller.

Morning sickness that is not pregnancy is usually one of four things: an empty stomach overnight (low blood sugar makes people queasy), acid coming up when you lie flat overnight, dehydration, or a medicine taken at night. Try it in that order - a plain biscuit or a glass of water before you get up, the head of the bed raised a few inches or no food within three hours of lying down, and a glass of water before bed. Write down what you ate and drank the night before for a week; the pattern usually names it. See a GP if it has gone on more than a fortnight, if you are losing weight, if you vomit blood or have pain, or if it comes with a bad headache and blurred vision.

Morning breath comes from a dry mouth: saliva slows overnight, so bacteria on the tongue and between the teeth break down food and cells and give off sulphur-smelling gas. Brush and floss before bed, clean your tongue, drink water, and see a dentist if it lasts all day, because gum disease is a common cause.

Morning headaches usually come from the night: too little water, teeth grinding, a hot room, alcohol, or a pillow that puts your neck out. Try water before bed, a cooler room and less booze, and see a GP if it is most mornings, if you snore and wake unrefreshed, or if the pain is worst as you wake.

Moss on a roof wants a scraper rather than a pressure washer: scrape it off dry, let the tiles air, and clear the gutters and downpipes so the rain runs away instead of feeding it. Don't pressure-wash an old roof - it strips the surface and finds leaks you did not have. If it comes back every year on a north-facing slope, a copper or zinc strip along the ridge kills it slowly as the rain washes over it.

Moss on a lawn means shade, drainage or compacted soil, not bad luck: rake or scarify it out, spike the lawn with a fork, and feed the grass so it thickens and takes the space back. Raise the mowing height and cut back whatever is shading it, and in autumn a forkful of grit in the worst spots keeps the surface draining.

Most mouth ulcers heal in 7 to 10 days on their own: rinse with salt water (half a teaspoon in a glass) four times a day, use a soft brush, and a pharmacy gel or lozenge such as Bonjela or Difflam numbs it enough to eat. Skip acidic, salty and very hot food, and see a dentist or GP if one lasts more than three weeks, keeps coming back, or comes with a fever.

Most mouth ulcers heal in a week to ten days: rinse with warm salty water, avoid spicy and acidic food, and a pharmacy can give you a protective gel or a chlorhexidine mouthwash. Anything still there after three weeks, or ulcers that keep coming back, should be shown to a dentist or GP.

Most nappy rash is skin left too long in contact with a wet nappy and with poo, and it settles in two or three days by changing more often - every feed and straight after a poo - and using a thick barrier cream (Sudocrem or a zinc and castor oil cream) at every change, with nappy-off time on a towel. Use plain water and cotton wool rather than perfumed wipes while it is sore, do not use talc, and skip soap and bubble bath. See the GP if it has not improved after three days, if it has blisters or bright red spots with satellite patches (a thrush rash needs an antifungal cream, not a barrier one), or if the baby is unwell or has a fever.

Most night sweats are a hot room, a thick duvet or a fever, so check those first: a cooler room and a lighter duvet settle it often enough. If you wake drenched for weeks with no explanation, or with weight loss, a cough or swollen glands, see a GP, because night sweats are worth checking for an infection, a thyroid problem and, rarely, lymphoma.

Most of the cup is milk: a latte is about five parts steamed milk to one of espresso, so roughly 200ml of milk and a 60ml double shot in a medium, and 300 to 350ml of milk in a large. A flat white is the same coffee with about half of that, 100 to 120ml, and a cappuccino sits between the two at about 150ml - a third of it foam, so ask for it wet if you want more milk and dry if you want more air. A macchiato or a cortado is a splash, 20 to 40ml, and a mocha is a latte with chocolate in it.

Most of the dust in a house is you: skin flakes and the fibres fabrics shed, plus what blows in through the windows and gets walked in on shoes. The big sources are bedding, carpet and soft furnishings, so wash the sheets at 60C every week or two and vacuum properly with a decent filter rather than a quick pass. Open the windows for ten minutes a day and damp-dust from the top down, so what you lift lands on the floor to be vacuumed instead of in the air.

Most of the fade is the wash and the heat, so wash less often in cooler water with a sulphate-free colour-safe shampoo, and keep the hot tools and hot showers off it on the days you can. A weekly purple shampoo keeps blonde from going yellow, and a tinted gloss or a semi-permanent in the same shade every four to six weeks tops the colour back up without a full dye job. Sun, chlorine and a hard-water shower head all take a share too, so a hat and a rinse after swimming are worth the faff.

Most of these are one of four things: it was pruned at the wrong time - a shrub that flowers on last year's wood (lavender, lilac, clematis, peony) loses its buds if you cut it in spring - it is too shaded, it got too much nitrogen and grew leaves instead, or a late frost took the buds. Bulbs that never came up were planted too shallow or too late. Give it sun, a high-potash feed and the right pruning time.

Most ovens reach 180C in 10 to 15 minutes from cold, and a fan oven is quicker than a conventional one, so a 20-minute preheat covers nearly everything. Trust an oven thermometer over the dial - they are often 10 to 20C out.

Most paper is wood: chips are cooked with chemicals until the fibres separate into pulp, and the pulp is washed, pressed and dried into a sheet. Recycled paper skips the tree and goes back to pulp, and most office paper is now a mix of new and recycled fibre.

Most people nod off within 10 to 20 minutes of lights out, and 30 minutes or more is the usual sign of a body clock that is not ready yet: shift your getting-up time earlier slowly rather than going to bed earlier. Lying there clock-watching makes it longer, so get up and do something dull for ten minutes and try again.

Most people pay no tax on savings interest: the personal savings allowance covers £1,000 of interest a year if you are a basic-rate taxpayer and £500 if you are higher rate, and additional-rate payers get nothing. Interest inside an ISA is always tax free, and anything over the allowance is taxed at your income tax rate.

Most people put it up in the first week of December, and the old rule is that it stays until Twelfth Night, twelve days after Christmas. A real tree only holds its needles for about four weeks, so the later you put it up the better it looks on the day - and anything from Advent onwards is normal.

Most people with pneumonia start to feel better three to five days after treatment begins, and are back to normal in about six weeks, though tiredness can linger for months. Get seen the same day if breathing is fast or hard, the lips look blue, or you are confused.

Most people are over the worst of covid in about a week, though a cough and tiredness commonly last two to four weeks and a lost sense of smell can take months to come back. Stay home while you have a temperature. Get help the same day if you are breathless, confused, or your lips or face look blue.

Most phones sold since about 2017 are IP67 or IP68, which means they survive a splash or a dunk in fresh water, not a swim and not the sea, and the seals weaken with age and after a repair. So rain and a wet hand are fine, and the bath, the beach and a hot shower are not; a wet charging port is the commonest way people damage one, so let it dry before you plug it in.

Most phones get security updates for five to seven years from new - an iPhone around five or six, a Samsung flagship about four, a cheap Android two or three - so a phone keeps working well for about four years, and the battery is usually what gives out first. A £50 to £90 battery swap buys two or three more years, which is far cheaper than a new handset.

Most primary homework is 20 to 30 minutes a night by the last years at primary, and about an hour a night in year 7 and up, with a break part way. If a piece runs well past that, write a note to the teacher rather than pushing through it, because homework that takes an hour and ends in tears is usually the wrong homework.

Most pulled muscles settle in two to three weeks: rest it from the movement that hurt, ice it for 15 minutes every few hours for the first two days, then keep it gently moving, because gentle movement after 48 hours heals faster than total rest. Paracetamol or ibuprofen helps, and ease back into exercise rather than stopping. See a GP if you heard a pop, cannot put weight on it, or it is no better after a week.

Most puppies are clean in the house by four to six months, and a determined few take until nine or ten. The way there is frequency rather than a clock: out every hour at eight weeks and every two hours by twelve, and always after waking, eating and playing, plus once last thing at night. Catch the accidents you can - watch for sniffing and circling, take him straight out, praise the moment he goes, and clean any spot with an enzyme cleaner so no smell invites him back. A house-trained dog that suddenly starts needs the vet to rule out a urine infection.

Most puppies manage a whole night at around four months, and none of them at eight weeks: their bladder is small and they need to go out in the night. Take him out last thing and once in the night without playing or talking, keep the room dark, and wake him for that trip rather than waiting for the whine, so he learns the night is for sleeping.

Most repetition is the same point made twice in different words: keep the shorter one and delete the other. Vary how sentences start - if three in a row begin with 'the' or 'I', rewrite two of them - and search the document for your favourite filler ('really', 'just', 'important') at the end, because you will not hear it yourself.

Most sets have a free app that turns the phone into the remote: SmartThings for a Samsung, LG ThinQ for an LG, the Google TV or Android TV Remote app, Roku for a Roku, and the Apple TV Remote in Control Centre for an Apple TV. The phone and the TV have to be on the same wifi, and the TV has to be on. A set with no app needs an infrared blaster or a universal remote instead.

Most shop pesto is not vegetarian: parmesan is made with animal rennet and jars usually use it. Buy one marked vegetarian, or make it with a vegetarian hard cheese, and leave the cheese out altogether for vegan.

Most shoulder pain is a strained or trapped tendon, worse when you reach overhead or lie on that side: keep using the arm as far as is comfortable, warm it before you use it, and do the pendulum swing (lean forward, let the arm hang, circle it slowly) a few times a day. See a GP if you cannot lift the arm at all or it started after a fall.

Most side effects are listed in the leaflet in the box, with how common each one is, and the ones that hit in the first fortnight - sickness, a fuzzy head, tiredness - often ease by weeks two to four. Do not stop suddenly on your own: steroids, antidepressants, epilepsy tablets and anything for the heart or blood pressure can be dangerous to stop, even when they are the problem. Ask the pharmacist today, who is fastest on interactions and can say whether a different brand, dose or timing would suit better, then ask the GP for a review with the list of what changed. Get help the same day for a rash with swelling or trouble breathing, a fast heart with fainting, or new confusion.

Most sinus infections settle in two to three weeks without antibiotics: steam, a salt-water rinse and paracetamol, and give it ten days before expecting a turn. See a GP if it is worse after ten days, if it keeps coming back, or if one side of the face swells or the eye is affected, which wants seeing that day.

Most sixth forms and colleges ask for five GCSEs at grade 4 or above, including English and maths, and then a 6 or a 7 in the subjects you want to take at A level - so check the subject page, not the general prospectus, because the maths and science requirement is usually higher than the rest. If you miss the grades, ask about a level 3 course or a mixed programme, which often lets you move on to A level after a year, and apply early with a backup choice: places are offered from the autumn of year 11, not on results day.

Most small company owners take a small salary up to the personal allowance - about £12,570 - and the rest as dividends, because that mix pays the least National Insurance. Run the salary through PAYE even though the tax may be nil: it is what gives you a year of state pension and counts as your earnings. Dividends come out of profit after tax, need profit to cover them, and need a board minute and a dividend voucher on file. Above about £50,000 of profit an accountant usually finds a better split than the rule of thumb, and pension contributions are the other thing worth asking about.

Most snoring is air whistling through a narrowed throat, so start with what widens it: sleep on your side, keep the last drink to three hours before bed, clear a blocked nose with a saline rinse or a strip, and lose a bit of weight if you have some to lose. If your partner hears you stop breathing or gasp, or you are tired all day, ask the GP about sleep apnoea - that one needs treating and a nose strip will not do it.

Most squeaks come from two dry surfaces rubbing, so the fix is powder or wax rather than a new pair: dust the inside with talcum powder or bicarbonate of soda and rub a little beeswax or candle wax along the tongue and where the upper meets the sole. If it is a rubber sole on a shiny floor, scuff it lightly with sandpaper, and let wet shoes dry slowly with newspaper inside rather than on a radiator.

Most supplements are fine with most tablets: vitamin D, vitamin C, a multivitamin, cod liver oil and a probiotic can be taken alongside blood pressure tablets, statins, levothyroxine and antibiotics. The two that need care are vitamin K, which works against warfarin, and calcium or iron tablets, which want four hours between them and a thyroid tablet. Ask about anything that calls itself a herbal remedy.
Most theatres are smart casual now: trousers or dark jeans and a nice top, with a jacket if it's a big West End or opera night. Nobody minds as long as you're warm and not in shorts.

Most things don't need it: it coats the fibres, so towels stop drying you and gym kit stops wicking. A splash helps stiff jeans or scratchy jumpers; white vinegar in the softener drawer does the same job without the coating.

Most toe pain is a stub, a bruise under the nail or an ingrown edge: soak it in warm salty water, wear shoes with room in them and take paracetamol. A big toe that goes red, hot and swollen overnight, often at night, is gout - that one wants seeing this week, and sooner if you have diabetes and it looks infected.

Most tonsillitis is viral and settles in a week: paracetamol or ibuprofen, plenty to drink, and soft food. Ring 111 the same day if you cannot swallow your own spit, your voice goes muffled or one side swells up, and see a GP if it keeps coming back, because repeated bouts are worth talking through.

Most tools are £10 to £35 for the first day at a hire shop: a breaker or a big drill £15 to £30, a step ladder £10 to £20, a carpet cleaner £20 to £35, a floor sander £35 to £60 and a scaffold tower £40 to £80, and a weekend rate is often the price of one day. The deposit, not the day rate, is the figure that adds up at the counter, usually £50 to £200 and back when the tool comes back clean, and a late return is charged as another day. Ask two shops for the day rate with the damage waiver included before you book.

Most tummy aches in a child are wind, constipation or a bug and settle within a day: drinks in small sips, a warm hot-water bottle on the tummy, and no pressure to eat. Keep them off school for 48 hours after the last bout of sickness or diarrhoea. Ring 111 the same day if the pain is severe and constant, sits in the lower right, hurts more when they cough or walk, or comes with green vomit, blood or a swollen tummy - and do not give them anything for the pain before that is checked.

Most two- and three-year-olds can manage five or ten minutes at the table, so make the meal that short and let them down when it is done rather than fighting for longer. A chair with a footrest does more than anything else - feet swinging in the air make the wriggling worse - and eating at the same time as them gives them something to copy. Give them their own spoon and one thing to hold, and praise the sitting down rather than telling them off for getting up: a child who leaves is offered the plate once more at the next snack, with no fuss.

Most veg keeps about a week in the fridge drawer, and a bit longer than you'd think if it stays dry: keep it in a bag or box, and don't wash it until you use it. Cabbage, carrots and peppers go soft before they go off; mushrooms and salad are the ones that turn slimy, so use those first. Root veg - parsnips, swede, turnips, celeriac - is the longest of all, weeks in the fridge and months somewhere cool and dark, and sprouts and cauliflower are the quick ones: a bag with the air pressed out, and eat them inside a week before they yellow. An opened tin of beans or chickpeas keeps 3 days in a covered bowl in the fridge.

Most verrucas clear up on their own within two years, but a pharmacy treatment is quicker: soak the foot, file the hard skin down with a pumice or emery board, then paint on salicylic acid once a day for up to 12 weeks. Keep it covered in pools and gym showers. See a GP if it bleeds, is very painful, or you have diabetes or poor circulation in your feet.

Most aching joints are ordinary wear and tear - osteoarthritis - and keeping them moving is what helps most: walk, swim or cycle, strengthen the muscles around the joint, and lose a bit of weight if you can, which takes the load off knees and hips. Paracetamol or an ibuprofen gel eases a flare. A joint that is hot, red and swollen, or sore with a fever, needs seeing the same day; see a GP if it aches most days or your hands are stiff for more than half an hour in the morning.

Most adults go from nervous to swimming a length in one course of weekly lessons, which is 10 to 12 weeks. Swimming 25 metres without stopping takes a term, and two terms if you are frightened of the water - lessons twice a week get there faster than once a week, because the water stops feeling strange.

Most antibiotics are fine with a drink. The two that are not are metronidazole and tinidazole, which react with alcohol and leave you flushed, sick and pounding - if the label on yours says to avoid alcohol, keep off it until 48 hours after the last dose. Anything else, a glass with your meal is not a problem.

Most antihistamines are fine with blood pressure tablets - loratadine and cetirizine are the ones that do not make you drowsy. The thing to avoid is a decongestant: pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine, in the tablets and sprays sold for a blocked nose, push your blood pressure up. Buy one that says antihistamine only, and ask about a steroid nasal spray.

Most arm pain is a muscle strain or the ache a day after lifting, and some of it comes down from a sore shoulder or elbow: keep using it as far as is comfortable and take a painkiller if you can. See a GP if the arm is weak or numb, and treat a heavy left arm with tightness in the chest, sweating or breathlessness as an emergency.

Most back pain after a day of lifting or gardening settles within a couple of weeks: keep moving gently rather than resting it, take paracetamol if you need it, and avoid the heavy lifting for a few days. See a GP if you cannot weight-bear, have numbness round the groin or saddle area, or lose control of your bladder or bowels.
