Most back pain is muscular and settles in two to six weeks, and staying active is what helps most: keep walking and carry on with your usual jobs as far as you can rather than taking to your bed, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen if you can. See a GP if it is no better in a fortnight, or today if you cannot pass urine, have numbness between your legs, or it came on after a fall.

Most bad breath is bacteria on the tongue and between the teeth, not the stomach: brush twice a day, clean between the teeth once a day, and gently brush or scrape the back of the tongue. Drink water through the day, because a dry mouth is the other common cause, and cut back on coffee, alcohol and smoking. A mouthwash helps for an hour or so but does not fix the cause, and alcohol-heavy ones dry the mouth further. See a dentist if it persists after a fortnight of that, or comes with bleeding gums, a bad taste, or a tooth that hurts - gum disease and a decaying tooth both need treating rather than covering.

Most beaches allow dogs, but plenty of councils ban them on the main stretch from about May to September, so read the sign where you walk on: it names the beach and the months, and the council's own page lists the rest. Take fresh water, because sea water gives a dog the runs, and go early or late on a hot day as sand and pebbles burn pads. Keep the lead on where birds nest or lifeguards are working, check the tide before he swims, and bag it and bin it.

Most bonsai are outdoor trees kept small, so keep it outside - a windowsill indoors is usually too dry and too warm. Water when the top of the soil is starting to dry, which is most days in summer and every few days in winter: soak it until water runs out of the holes, then let it drain. Feed every two weeks in the growing season, trim the shoots back to two leaves, and give it a cool frost-free spot in winter. Only a tropical one such as ficus stays indoors.

Most cars want a service every 12 months or 10,000 to 12,500 miles, whichever comes first, and an oil and filter change is the part that matters most. A minor service is usually £150 to £250; the handbook's schedule is the one to follow, not the garage's upsell.

Most cats never need a bath, because they keep themselves clean, so do it only for something they got into. Use a cat shampoo, lukewarm water an inch deep in the sink, one hand on the scruff or a towel wrap to keep her calm, and rinse very well; then towel her dry somewhere warm. Two people make it far easier than one, and a smear of butter or a lick treat on the side of the sink buys the ten minutes you need.

Most cats that nag for food are bored or used to being fed little and often, and it is fine to hold the line: weigh the day's food against the amount on the packet for her weight and give it in several small meals or a puzzle feeder rather than leaving a bowl down, because a cat that grazes all day never looks full. A cat that is hungry and losing weight needs the vet, since an overactive thyroid and diabetes both start exactly like that and both are treatable. A sudden new appetite in an older cat is worth a check before you feed more.

Most cats hate being lifted off the ground, so pick her up rarely and briefly: one hand under the chest behind the front legs, one under the back legs, and hold her against you so all four feet are supported. Never lift an adult cat by the scruff - that is for a vet holding a kitten. Put her down the moment she starts to wriggle, and let her come to you on the sofa instead: a cat that is picked up only when she asks starts to allow it. If she used to be fine and now struggles, that is often pain - a bad tooth, a sore back, arthritis - so a change like that is worth a vet visit.

Most cheese is fine, but the hard ones - Parmesan, Grana Padano, Pecorino, and some traditional cheddars - are set with animal rennet. Cheddar, mozzarella and cottage cheese are usually made with microbial rennet, and the Vegetarian Society logo settles it.

Most chest infections clear in about a week to ten days, though the cough can hang on for three or four weeks afterwards. See a GP if you are breathless or coughing up blood, if the fever lasts more than five days, if it is getting worse rather than better after a week, or if you are over 65 or have a long-term chest condition, because those want treating sooner.

Most children's earache is a middle-ear infection after a cold and settles in two or three days on children's paracetamol or ibuprofen by weight alone. Hold a warm flannel against the ear that hurts, and put nothing in it - no oil, no cotton bud. See a GP the same day if there is discharge from the ear or the child is under two, and within a few days if the pain is still there after three days or keeps coming back.

Most companies have a bereavement team: ring them, say the account holder has died and they close the account from the date of death without an early-exit fee, and they can usually stop the bills from that day. Send the death certificate when they ask; with a phone or energy account you can ask them to move the number or the supply to you instead. Sorry you have to deal with this on top of everything else.

Most cooked food freezes well: cool it within two hours, pack it in portions and label the date. Eat it within three months for the best quality, defrost it in the fridge overnight and reheat it once until piping hot. Mashed potato freezes well but goes grainy if you reheat it in a microwave, so warm it through in a pan with a splash of milk. Rice is the one to be careful with: freeze it within an hour of cooking, not the next day.

Most coughs after a cold last two to three weeks and settle on their own: honey in warm drinks, plenty of fluids and a propped-up pillow at night ease it, and cough medicines do little. See a GP if it lasts more than three weeks, you are coughing blood or breathless, you have lost weight, or it came with a fever that will not go.

Most coughs in a child are a cold and settle in two to three weeks; the night ones sound worse because they are lying flat, so prop the mattress a little and sit them up. A barking, seal-like cough that starts at night is croup: take them into cool night air or a steamy bathroom for ten minutes and keep them calm, because crying makes it worse. A spoon of honey helps over one year old, never under. Get help the same day if they are breathing fast, sucking in under the ribs, going blue, or too breathless to feed or talk, and see a GP if the cough is still there after three weeks.

Most countries want six months left on your passport beyond the day you plan to return, and some also want it issued within the last ten years. Check your destination's rule on its embassy site before you book: if you are close to the line, renew first rather than risk being turned away at the airport.

Most creams keep about 30 months sealed and 12 months once they are open, so write the month you opened it on the jar; a cleanser or a serum is roughly the same, and mascara is the short one at three months because the wand picks up bacteria. A cream that has separated, gone gritty or smells sour should go, and anything you would not put on a cut does not belong on your face.

Most cycles are two to three hours on eco and about an hour on a normal 40C cotton wash, and nothing is wrong: eco runs the drum slowly and heats the water slowly so it uses less electricity, which is why the eco label says 3 hours plus. The quick washes are 15 to 30 minutes and are meant for a small, lightly worn load. A cycle that runs longer than the dial says is usually a cold fill taking ages, a blocked filter, or extra rinses switched on, so check the filter and the rinse setting before calling anyone.

Most dishwashers wash at about 50C on eco, 60 to 65C on the normal programme and 70C on intensive, and the final rinse is hotter than any of them. For greasy pans, plastic and anything that was hand-washed badly, use the 60C programme or above: that, with the hot rinse, is what does the cleaning.

Most dogs that seem permanently hungry are simply greedy, and it is no sign that anything is wrong: weigh the day's food on the kitchen scale against the amount on the bag for his weight, split it into two meals, and slow him down with a puzzle bowl or a scatter feed. Go to the vet if the weight is dropping, if he has started drinking a lot, or if the hunger came on with a change of food - worms, a gut problem and diabetes all look like this. Treats come out of the day's food rather than on top of it, which is the usual reason a dog on the right amount keeps gaining.

Most dogs are fine down to about -5C as long as they are moving, so walk a shorter round, keep him on the lead in snow, and skip it in freezing rain. Thin, small, short-haired, old and very young dogs feel it sooner and want a coat below about 5C. Turn back if he shivers, lifts a paw or refuses to walk, and wash the salt off his paws when you are home.

Most dogs eat grass now and then and it is usually harmless, but it often means an upset stomach, boredom or too little fibre. Make sure the grass has not been treated with weedkiller, give a little more fibre and something to chew, and see the vet if it is repeated with vomiting, tiredness or weight loss.

Most evening courses are two or three hours of class a week plus about the same again at home, so plan on one evening and four or five hours a week. Ask for the guided learning hours before you enrol, because the college has to publish them, and check the fee: in England, English and maths up to GCSE are free for anyone who does not already have them, and a first level 2 or 3 qualification is often free if you are under 23 or on a low income. At the open evening, ask what the last group went on to do - that is what tells you whether it is worth the year.

Most fabric curtains and bath mats go in the machine at 40C with a couple of towels and a little detergent, then hang them up to dry. A bath mat is a weekly wash; a fabric curtain every month or two. Plastic liners wipe clean with a cloth and white vinegar; run the fan after showers and mould stops coming back.

Most false alarms are small and physical: a spider or a moth crawling across a sensor, a contact on a door or window that has worked loose, or a dying battery in one sensor chirping for attention. Read the event log on the panel first, because it names the zone that tripped, and check that sensor and its battery before you change anything else. The backup battery in the panel sets a fault of its own once it is years old: replace it, then reset with the code you were given. If it still fires at nothing, ring the alarm company rather than the police. If it goes off while you are in the house and someone could be inside, get out and ring 999.

Most fees charged to tenants were banned in England in June 2019: no admin, referencing, credit check, inventory, guarantor or check-out fee, and the only payments an agent can ask for are rent, a deposit capped at five weeks' rent, a holding deposit of one week, and a default for a late payment or a lost key in writing. Ask for the money back and name the fee; the council's trading standards team enforces the ban.

Most foot pain after running is shoes or mileage: check the shoes are not worn through at the heel, build distance slowly and let blisters drain and cover rather than pop. Pain under the heel that is worst first thing in the morning is plantar fasciitis, and a podiatrist or physio sorts it faster than rest alone.

Most fruit keeps 3 to 7 days in the salad drawer, and it is worth knowing the spread: berries and ripe stone fruit a day or two, apples, oranges and pears a week or more, and anything already cut 3 days in a sealed tub. Bananas, whole melons and tomatoes keep their flavour better out of the fridge.

Most headaches are not serious, and the ones to get checked the same day are: the worst you have ever had, one that comes on like a thunderclap, one with a fever and a stiff neck, one after a bang on the head, one with weakness, slurred speech or a change in vision, or a headache that is getting steadily worse over weeks. Otherwise a GP can look at it in the normal way if painkillers are needed more than a couple of days a week.

Most headaches in a child are tiredness, hunger or not enough to drink, and settle with a glass of water, a snack and a quiet half hour; a regular bedtime and a break from screens stop them coming back. Give children's paracetamol or ibuprofen by weight if it is bad enough to stop them playing, and never aspirin under sixteen. See a GP if a headache wakes them at night, is worst in the morning and comes with vomiting, or keeps coming back; ring 999 for a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade under a glass, or drowsiness, and get any headache after a bang on the head checked the same day.

Most hedges want one cut in late summer, from August, once the birds have finished nesting - it is against the law to disturb a nest in use, so check before you start. Box and privet take a cut in June as well. Trim so the sides slope in slightly at the top: a flat-sided hedge shades its own base and goes bare at the bottom. Leave the sides alone if you are cutting a conifer hard, because most will not regrow from old wood.

Most hotels hold your bags free at reception, both before check-in and after you check out: ask them to tag them with your name and ask what time the desk closes, so you are back before then. Keep the passport, the money and anything you would hate to lose in your day bag rather than the big case, and if the hotel will not help, a station left-luggage desk or a locker is a few pounds for the day.

Most hypos come from a meal that was missed or late, a dose that is now too big, exercise without eating, or alcohol - and drink is the usual reason for one at night, because it stops the liver putting sugar out while you sleep. Carry glucose tablets and keep some by the bed, eat before you drink and test before you drive. If you are having them more than once a week, or waking sweaty with a headache, tell your diabetes team: the doses need looking at, and that is their call to make.

Most jobs are done in one visit: an hour or two on site for a repair, and the wait is usually the part, so if something has to be ordered expect a few days between the first call and the fix. Ask when you book whether the price covers the first hour and whether the part is included, and get the call-out fee before anyone comes out. A boiler swap is the long one - usually a full day, plus the gas check afterwards.

Most loose pan handles are one screw through a bracket: hold the nut on the inside with pliers and turn the screwdriver, then check it again after the next wash, because the heat works it loose again. A riveted handle that has worked loose cannot be tightened back safely, so the pan goes, and until it is fixed lift it with both hands rather than by the handle - a pan of boiling water letting go is a scald to the legs and feet. If the screw has stripped the wood, a slightly longer screw with a washer will bite again.

Most lumps in the mouth are harmless - a mucocele, which is a small blocked spit gland and usually on the lower lip, a bony bump on the roof of the mouth, or a firm lump where a tooth has rubbed. Leave it alone and it often settles in a few weeks. Anything still there after three weeks, or hard, ulcerated, bleeding, growing or painless, needs a dentist or a GP within two weeks: that is the mouth cancer pathway, and it is usually nothing.

Mould on the top of a jam lifts off: take a spoon and the patch plus a good centimetre around it, and the rest is fine if it smells and tastes normal. Bin the jar instead if it is a low-sugar or homemade jam, if the mould runs down the side of the jar, or if it smells fermented - and never spoon it back in.

Move the router up and out in the open, not in a cupboard or behind the TV, and put it as central as the phone line allows. If one room still drops, a mesh wifi system (about £100 for two units) fixes it far better than a repeater, and switching the router to the 5GHz band helps when you are close to it.

Move the whole night earlier ten minutes at a time rather than shouting louder in the morning: someone who cannot be woken at seven is usually not asleep until late. Out of the bedroom for a stretch at night, alarms for everyone, and a shower or breakfast worth getting up for. If it is this hard to wake most days, ask the GP about sleep apnoea, especially if there is snoring.

Move the fridge and freezer upright in a van or on a sack truck, never on their side for more than a few minutes, and let a fridge stand upright for 24 hours before plugging it in, or the compressor oil will not have settled back. Empty and defrost it the day before, tape the doors shut and take the shelves out. Two people and a strap beat one person and a bad back.

Move valuables and medicines upstairs, unplug what you can safely reach and stay out of the water: 30 cm of moving water can float a car. Follow your local flood service, and if they tell you to leave, go early rather than wait to see how high it gets.

Move a shrub while it is dormant, from late autumn to early spring, and on a mild day when the soil is not frozen. Water it the day before, dig out a rootball as wide as the branches spread, lift it onto a tarpaulin rather than by the stem, and replant at the same depth with the roots spread out. Water it weekly through the first summer and do not feed it - new roots come before new growth.

Move it up one pot size, no bigger: roots circling the bottom of the old pot, or water running straight through, mean it is ready, and a pot that is far too big holds water round the roots and rots them. Use fresh compost, tease the roots out a little, and keep it out of direct sun for a week after.

Moving prey it can fit in its mouth: slugs, snails, worms, beetles, flies, spiders and caterpillars, caught with a sticky tongue in about a tenth of a second. Tadpoles eat algae and plant matter instead, so a pond with a few leaves in it feeds them.

Moving you to another hotel, resort or date is a significant change: you can refuse it and take a full refund within 14 days, or accept it and ask for the price difference back plus about 20 to 30 percent of the price for what you lost. Put that in writing to the organiser, not the hotel, and name the Package Travel Regulations; ABTA or the CAA can take the complaint.
Multiply the decimal by 100 and put a % sign on it: 0.35 is 35% and 0.07 is 7%. Going the other way, divide by 100 - so 62% is 0.62 - which is just the decimal point moving two places.

Multiply as if the points were not there, then put the point back with as many decimal places as the two numbers had between them: 0.3 x 0.4 is 0.12. To divide, move both points the same number of places until the number you are dividing by is whole: 1.2 / 0.4 is 12 / 4, which is 3.

Multiply everything inside the bracket by what is outside it: 3(x + 4) is 3x + 12. With two brackets, (x + 2)(x + 3), multiply every pair, then add the like terms: x squared + 3x + 2x + 6, which is x squared + 5x + 6.

Mushrooms are about 20 calories per 100g, so a whole punnet is a portion for under 50: they bring 3g of protein, B vitamins including riboflavin and niacin, and selenium, plus the savoury taste that makes them useful in a meal that is meant to fill you up. The vitamin D some packs advertise comes from being treated with UV light - it is real, but a few minutes in the sun does the same job.

Mushrooms keep about a week in the fridge in a paper bag, never a plastic one, which makes them sweat and go slimy. Don't wash them until you cook them; dry and shrivelled is fine, slimy or smelly is not.

Muslin is a loose woven cotton cloth, for straining and for holding things together: it lines a sieve to catch the fine bits in a stock or a jelly, wraps herbs and spices for a bouquet garni, and goes over a bowl of bread dough or a jug of milk as a cover that still lets air through. It is not the same as a tea towel - it is far looser, so liquid runs through it, and it can be boiled to clean it.
Mustard is hot in a different place from chilli - it burns in the nose and fades in a few seconds. Mixed with water it is hottest; vinegar or hot liquid takes the edge off it.

Mute or unfollow and let the story go stale: every check is a small hit of the same thing, so it keeps the wound open rather than closing it, and the person posting has no idea you are looking. Put the app somewhere you keep it least - off the home screen, logged out on the laptop - and give yourself a rule you can keep for a fortnight. It fades faster than you expect.

Mute it first - leaving is for the chat that is genuinely noise, not for one busy week. If you do go, the quiet exit is the polite one: turn off notifications, leave, and tell anyone who matters in a private message. Only a family or work group needs a goodbye line, and one sentence does it: 'I'm going to hop out of this one, message me directly.'

NHS stands for National Health Service, and the part worth knowing is what the words buy you: care that is free at the point of use and paid for out of general taxation, so nobody is asked for a card or an insurance number at A&E, a GP's surgery or a maternity ward.

NHS dentistry is free for children, anyone under 19 in full-time education, pregnant women and mothers in the year after the birth, and people on certain benefits such as universal credit or income support. Everyone else pays a fixed band per course of treatment - about £27 for a check-up, £75 for a filling and £325 for a crown or a denture - and a check-up is free in Scotland. Ask at the desk which band you are in, because the work in one band is covered by one charge.

NS&I stands for National Savings and Investments: the government's own savings bank, where Premium Bonds and Index-linked Savings Certificates come from. The money is backed by the Treasury instead of a commercial bank, so the compensation limit quoted for banks does not apply to it, and the rates are usually ordinary rather than the best on the market.

Nail biting is a habit that turns up when you are bored, tense or concentrating, so give the hand something else to do: keep nails short and filed, hold a pen or a ring of putty, and try a bitter polish for a month. Many people beat it, and most of the way is noticing the moment rather than forcing it.

Nails grow about 3mm a month, so a full nail takes six months and nothing speeds it up much: keep them filed rather than bitten, use a hand cream or cuticle oil daily, wear gloves for washing up, and take in enough protein and iron. Ridges and white spots are normal; a nail that changes colour or lifts is worth showing a pharmacist.

Name on the top line, house number and street below it, then the town, then the postcode in capitals on its own line: Ms J Patel, 14 Elm Road, Leeds, LS6 2AB. Put your own name and address on the back, and use the full name and title - Mr, Mrs, Ms or Dr - of whoever will open it.

Name the pattern before you name the person: which meetings, how often, and what happens to your work afterwards. Then set one limit you can hold - the hour you stop answering, the one meeting you leave on time - and say it once, in terms of the work rather than their character. Keep a dated note of the cases if it carries on, and take the list, not the grievance, to their manager or to HR. If every Sunday is already ruined by Monday, that is your answer about the job, not about your resilience.

Name the person, say you're sorry, and mention one thing you remember or liked about them: "I'm so sorry about your mum. She made the whole street laugh and I'll miss her. Thinking of you all." Keep it short, avoid 'at least' and any advice, and write it by hand if you can.

Name the thing they did and one thing you noticed about them doing it: "All those late nights paid off - well done, Dr Chen." Skip the advice and the joke, and if the card is from a group, sign the group rather than one person's name.

Name the year, then one thing you are glad about: "Ten years, and you still make me laugh at the worst jokes." A line about a specific time beats anything about forever; if it is someone else's anniversary, keep it to the pair and skip the advice.
Name the baby and one wish: "Welcome to the world, Ada - may you be as loved as you were today." Sign both your names, and if you gave a present, the card is not the place to describe it.

Name the baby if you know the name, wish the parents some sleep, and skip the jokes about their life being over: "Congratulations - she is beautiful. Wishing all three of you a slow, sleepy first month." If it is a second baby, say something about the older one too; nobody else will.

Name what they did and what you noticed: 'The grand opening looked brilliant - I've watched you plan it for a year. Congratulations.' Three lines is plenty, and add something only you could say about them.
Name what you did, say why it was wrong, and don't add a but: "I said I'd call and I didn't, and that left you waiting. I'm sorry." Then say what you will do differently, in one sentence.

Name what happened, own it once, say what you are doing and by when, and leave your process out of it: "I'm sorry - we sent the wrong size twice, and that's on us. The right one goes out today on next-day delivery." One apology is enough; explaining the system reads as an excuse, and asking them to do the work reads as a second failure. If it is a public review, answer in two sentences and move the detail to email.

Name it once without defending yourself - "it can't have felt fair, watching me get that" - and then ask what it was like from where they stood, which is the only thing that shifts it. Arguing the facts never does: a jealous brother is not short of facts, he is short of a hearing. Keep your own good news quieter with them for a while if you want the relationship, and remember you are not obliged to shrink to make anyone comfortable.

Nappies and wipes, three or four babygrows and vests, maternity pads, your own toiletries and a phone charger with a long cable, plus snacks and a water bottle. Pack two bags - a small one for the labour room and a bigger one for the ward - and keep your notes and ID on the top of one, because someone asks for them at the door.

Naruhito is the emperor of Japan: he took the throne in May 2019, when his father Akihito stepped down. The emperor is a symbol of the state and has no political power - the prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, runs the government.

National insurance is the second tax on your pay, and it buys your state pension: you need about 35 qualifying years for the full amount, and gaps are worth checking before you pay anything. Look at your record in your online tax account first - some gaps can be filled cheaply, others are not worth it, and you can usually only go back six years. Class 3 voluntary contributions are about 18 pounds a week per missing year.

Natural nut butter separates because there is nothing in it but nuts: the oil rises and the solids sink. Stir it back in with a knife, from the bottom of the jar upwards, and it comes together in a minute or two. A jar that has set hard mixes more easily if it stands upside down for a day first, and standing it in a bowl of warm water for five minutes softens it without cooking it. An opened jar keeps a few months in the cupboard and longer in the fridge, though cold makes it stiffer to spread.

Natural selection is how evolution works: individuals vary, the ones whose variations suit their surroundings have more surviving young, and those variations become common over generations. It is not a plan or a choice - the environment simply filters what is already there.

Natural is milk and cultures and nothing else, and it is what to cook with. Greek is the same yoghurt strained of its whey, so it is thicker and higher in protein; Greek-style is thickened with milk powder and is cheaper and sweeter. Set is cultured in the pot and stays firm, stirred is smooth. Skyr is strained further still, so it is very thick and very high in protein. Live yoghurt has the cultures still alive, which is the kind that helps an unsettled stomach.
Ncuti Gatwa plays the Doctor, from the 2023 Christmas special on. Before him: Jodie Whitaker, Peter Capaldi, Matt Smith, David Tennant and Christopher Eccleston since the series came back in 2005.

Near the horizon the Moon's light crosses much more air, and the air scatters the blue end of it away, so what reaches you looks orange or red. The same effect reddens a low Sun, and dust or smoke deepens it.

Nearly all of it is made by spinning a generator: gas, coal, nuclear, wind and water all turn the same kind of shaft, and the National Grid carries the result around the country and steps the voltage down through substations to your street. Solar panels are the odd ones out - they make it straight from light, with nothing turning.

Nearly always one of three: an oven running 20C cooler than it says (an oven thermometer pays for itself), too much mixing once the flour went in (stop as soon as no dry flour shows), or old raising agent - bicarbonate and baking powder lose their fizz about six months after opening. Tell me what it did - sank, dry, heavy, burnt - and I will give you the fix for it.

Nearly always one of four things: too thin (simmer it uncovered for ten minutes), too salty (bulk it out with more of what is already in it, not water), caught on the bottom (into a clean pan, without scraping the base), or bland (salt a little, then a squeeze of lemon or a splash of vinegar). Tell me which it is and I will give you the fix for that dish.

Nearly always the air pocket at the fat end: prick that end with a pin first, lower them in on a spoon instead of dropping them, and take them out of the fridge ten minutes before so the shell is not cold when it meets the heat. Keep the water at a gentle simmer rather than a rolling boil, and a splash of vinegar in the pan sets any white that leaks before it trails.

Nearly always the fluff and the water: empty the fluff filter and wash it, pull the condenser out and rinse it under the tap if the machine has one, and tip out the water tank or check the drain hose. On a heat pump or condenser dryer the smell is usually the condenser left damp, so run a rinse cycle and leave the door and the drawer open afterwards. A vented dryer wants the vent hose cleared and the outside flap checked, and once a year wipe the drum and the seal with a hot damp cloth.

Nearly always too little liquid: the food should be at least a third covered, and the pot no more than two thirds full. Cook on low rather than high, keep the lid on (every lift loses about 20 minutes of heat), and add milk, cream or flour in the last half hour, because dairy and thickeners are what catch. A liner or a smear of oil stops the edges sticking, and if it only ever burns round the sides the pot is thin-based and running hot - a tea towel under it or a new pot fixes that.

Nearly every phone is fixable, and every repair is cheaper than a new handset: a screen is £60 to £120 at a local shop, a battery £35 to £70, a charging port £30 to £60. Back it up to the cloud first, then get a quote from a local shop and one from the maker, and check your home insurance excess or a card's purchase protection, which sometimes covers accidental damage.
Nectar is the sugary liquid flowers make to attract bees, butterflies and birds, and it is the payment for carrying pollen to the next flower. Honey is nectar that bees have concentrated.

Nelson Mandela was a South African lawyer and anti-apartheid leader who spent 27 years in prison before becoming the country's first black president in 1994. He shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993 for negotiating the end of apartheid peacefully.

Nerves and gut share the same wiring: adrenaline diverts blood to your muscles and slows digestion, so your stomach feels fluttery or churny. Slow breathing helps because it switches the body back toward rest, and it passes once the moment does.

Nerves before something big are normal. Slow breaths for a minute genuinely help, and so does saying the worry out loud to one person: what is it that the day itself might bring? Cold feet before a wedding, a move or an interview are usually the size of the change rather than a warning about it, so give it a night before you act on it - and if it is a promise you are not sure you want, that is worth talking through properly, with the person if you can.

Nervous sweat comes from glands that open up under stress hormones, and it is the bacteria on your skin breaking that sweat down that makes it smell. Ordinary antiperspirant works better than deodorant for the smell and dampness, because it reduces the sweat itself.

Net the crop and the butterflies cannot land: a fine mesh hooped over the rows from the day you plant, weighed down at the edges, is the whole answer for cabbages and brassicas. Without a net, look under the leaves for the yellow eggs in clusters and squash them, and pick off caterpillars in the cool of the morning, when they sit on the leaf instead of dropping. A plant that has lost every leaf to the lace pattern will usually grow back if you net it now.

Netball is seven a side, and the rule that surprises people is that you cannot move with the ball: catch it, and you have to pass or shoot within three seconds, with one foot planted. Each position is limited to certain thirds of the court, which is why goal shooters barely leave the circle.

Neutering is usually £150 to £300 for a dog and £60 to £120 for a cat, with a bitch or a female cat at the top of the range because the operation is bigger. Many charities run low-cost schemes, and the price usually includes pain relief and a check-up. Ask whether the quote covers a follow-up visit, and most are home the same day and back to normal within a few days.

Never pay the balance: ask in writing for the deposit back within 14 days, saying what was agreed and what was not done. If it is not back, report it to Trading Standards through Citizens Advice and start a Money Claims Online case, which is the same route as any unpaid debt and costs from about £35. A deposit paid by card over £100 can also be claimed from the card company.

Never smash the ice: the shock wave stuns and kills the fish. Float a ball on the surface so it keeps a hole open as it moves, or stand a pan of hot water on the ice until it melts through, and keep a hole open all winter so the gases can get out. Keep the pump and filter running, but turn off any fountain above the water because the splash chills the pond. Stop feeding once the water is below 10C, because the fish stop digesting and the food rots, and they sit together at the bottom where the water sits at about 4C. Net the leaves out in autumn, because a rotting layer on the bottom is what turns the water green in spring.

Never wipe a dry lens: grit on a dry lens is what makes the scratch, so rinse them under a tap first and dry them with a microfibre cloth, not a tissue or a sleeve. Keep them in a hard case rather than a pocket or a bag with keys in it, and take them off with both hands so the arms are not twisted. A coating scratch cannot be polished out, so a cheap case saves a new pair.

Never give a pet human painkillers. Paracetamol and ibuprofen are both dangerous to a dog or a cat, and a single paracetamol can kill a cat; rabbits, guinea pigs, hamsters and birds are poisoned by even less, and aspirin and ibuprofen give a dog stomach ulcers and kidney damage. Pain relief comes from a vet, dosed by weight: ring them today, and say what was given, the pet's weight and how much.

New paint smells for three to five days, and up to two weeks for an oil-based gloss: the solvent has to leave, and warmth with a window open is what carries it away. Air changes do the work, so prop the door and put a fan in the doorway rather than sealing the room up. If a smell is still there after a fortnight, or the room gives you headaches, ventilate harder and see a GP if it goes on, because a lingering solvent smell is a ventilation problem.
New York City has about 8.3 million people - 8.3 million in the five boroughs, and around 19 million in the metro area. It is the biggest city in the United States.
Nice one — tell me how it goes.
Nice — worth doing properly. What would you want sorted out first?

Nice jeans or trousers and a shirt or a nice top: the aim is to look like yourself on a good day, not someone who tried too hard. Ask whoever is organising whether it's a pub night or a sit-down dinner.

Night cramp in the foot or calf is usually a muscle that has been short all day. The fix is stretching before bed: stand facing a wall with the back leg straight and the heel down, hold 30 seconds on each side. When one starts, pull your toes up hard towards your shin and stand up if you can, which ends it faster than waiting. Keep water by the bed and a warm blanket on the leg. See a GP if it is most nights, if you take a water tablet or a statin, or if the calf is swollen, hot or tender - that one is a clot until a doctor says not, so ring 111 the same day.

Nine times in ten the mark that looks like a scratch is metal, sugar or limescale burnt onto the glass: scrape the cold hob with a hob scraper held almost flat, then rub ceramic hob cleaner over it with a cloth, and it comes away. A real scratch - you feel it catch a fingernail - cannot be polished out of a glass top, so a fine one is something to live with and a deep one means a new top, which on a built-in hob is often most of the price of a new one. Never use an abrasive powder or a scouring pad; they make more of them.

Nine times in ten a sagging gate, shed door or cupboard door is a hinge screw that has pulled out of the wood, not the hinge wearing out. Take the weight off the free corner, pack the old screw holes with glued matchsticks or a sliver of dowel and screw back in, or move the hinge 10cm along with longer screws. If the wood round the hinge is rotten or the hinge is torn, fit a new hinge onto sound timber - and if the post moves in the ground, brace or replace the post.

Nine times in ten it is the strings: new ones stretch for a week, so tune up, bend every string a little, and tune again - three or four times the first evening. Old strings go dead and stop holding pitch, so if they are more than a few months old, change them. If one string pings as it slips it is catching in the nut, and a pencil lead scribbled in the slot fixes that tonight. Still slipping with new strings is a worn peg or a tuner screw, which is a shop job.

Ninety seconds to two minutes between sets for most of what you do: long enough to get your breath back and keep your strength, short enough to finish in an hour. Heavy sets of 4 to 6 reps want two to three minutes; a small isolation move or a warm-up set needs 45 seconds.

Ninety seconds in this order: what you do now or did last, one thing you did well that they will care about, and why this job is the next step. Nothing about childhood, and don't walk through the CV line by line - they have read it.

No painkiller on the shelf affects the pill. Paracetamol, ibuprofen, aspirin and codeine do not make it less reliable, and neither does an antacid or a hayfever tablet. The two things that do are rifampicin and rifabutin, and the other is a bad stomach - if you are sick within two hours of a pill or have severe diarrhoea, follow the leaflet in the packet.

No pasta: rice, potatoes or couscous under the same sauce, and a layer of sliced potato does the job of lasagne sheets in a bake. Keep the sauce as it was - it is the part that carries the meal - and the same weight of whatever you use, 75 to 100g dry a person.

No pate and no liver, and that includes vegetable pate: liver is so high in vitamin A that too much of it can harm the baby, and pate can carry listeria. The same goes for cod liver oil and any multivitamin with vitamin A in it - take folic acid and vitamin D instead, and ask the midwife about anything else.

No potatoes: pasta, rice or couscous beside the same dinner, and if it is mash that is wanted, parsnip, celeriac or butter beans mash much the same once they are soft, with butter and a little of the cooking water. Roast potatoes really do want potatoes - nothing else crisps that way - so roast carrots, squash or onions instead.
No problem at all.

No real bank rings to ask you to move money, read out a code, or give your PIN, even when the account is at risk. Hang up, wait a few minutes, then ring the number on the card and check whether anyone tried to contact you. If money has gone, ring the bank's fraud line: some transfers can be recalled and you are not in trouble. Report it to the fraud service for your country.

No rice under a curry or a stew: pasta, couscous, bulgur or a baked potato do the same job, drained and buttered the same way, and a tin of chickpeas or a handful of extra vegetables fills the plate if there is less of any of them than you thought. Keep the portion the same - 75 to 100g dry a person. Risotto, paella and egg fried rice want rice itself, so cook something else instead of swapping them.

No single food is fattening - what decides your weight is the total across the day, so a banana at about 100 calories is a snack, not a cause. The foods blamed most often are the ones that go down fast and leave you hungry: bread, pasta, rice and juice. Eat them with protein and vegetables, or in one sitting rather than all day, and they stop being a problem.

No timetables from me, sorry: they are re-cut every few months and the day's works change them, so I can't see today's - a journey planner has the options door to door: where from, and when do you need to be there?
No worries at all.

No, never on a cut or on broken skin: bleach burns the tissue, kills the new cells and leaves the cut slower to close. Rinse it under cool running water for five minutes, press a clean cloth on it for ten, then cover it. Wash splashes off skin with soap and water. A deep, dirty or gaping cut, or one that will not stop bleeding, wants 111 or a walk-in centre today.

No, not a classic one: Caesar dressing has anchovies and Parmesan, so the dressing and the salad with it are not vegetarian. Vegetarian versions swap the anchovy for capers and use a hard cheese made with microbial rennet.

No, not in ordinary amounts: a cup of tea or coffee is mostly water, and the caffeine in it makes you pass only a little more than the drink gave you, so it counts towards your fluids. The six-to-eight-glasses figure includes them. Strong coffee on an empty stomach can still leave you headachy and jittery, and if you are thirsty water is still the better drink.

No, pasta does not need rinsing: it comes out of the pot already wet, and rinsing cools it and washes off the surface starch that makes a sauce cling. Drain it and toss it straight into the sauce, keeping a mugful of the cooking water to loosen things if it looks dry. The one exception is pasta for a cold salad, where a quick rinse under cold water stops it clumping - then drain it well and dress it while it is still slightly warm so it takes up the dressing.

No, it is not cheaper, for the heating or the hot water: keeping a house warm all day costs more than heating it when you are in it, and it shows on the bill. Every degree the rooms are held at is heat leaking out through the walls, so the timer wins - on an hour before you get up, off half an hour before bed, 18C in the living room and 16C in the bedrooms while you are up. Coming home to a cold house is a comfort problem rather than a cost one, and it is cheaper to warm the room you sit in for an hour than to keep the whole house up from midday. Hot water is the same story: heat the cylinder for an hour morning and evening with a jacket on it rather than leaving the immersion on. The exception is a well-insulated house on a heat pump, which is cheaper held at a steady low temperature than pushed up and down.

No: running does not wear out healthy knees, and long-term studies of runners find no more knee arthritis than in people who do not run. What does cause trouble is doing too much too soon, so build the distance slowly and keep the legs strong with squats, step-ups and single-leg work. If a knee hurts for more than two weeks or swells up, get it looked at rather than running through it.

No: the pop is gas coming out of the fluid in the joint, and the studies that have looked have found no link between cracking your knuckles and arthritis. Forcing a joint can make it sore or swollen, so if one clicks with real pain rather than a clean pop, get it looked at.

No: the white scale is calcium and magnesium carbonate, the same minerals that make water hard, and it is harmless to drink - mains water is tested to the same standard whatever its hardness. What it does do is cost money and taste: a scaled element takes longer to boil, and it leaves a scum on tea and a film on taps and shower glass. Descale the kettle every couple of months in a hard-water area. For a baby's bottle, use unsoftened mains water, boiled once and cooled.

No: washing-up liquid and hand soap lather, and a dishwasher or a washing machine turns a teaspoon of it into foam that comes out of the door and can reach the pump. Dishwasher tablets or powder in the dishwasher, washing powder or liquid in the washing machine, and a splash of hand liquid only for hand washing. If it has already foamed, run the machine empty with a rinse.

No: wet hair does not make you ill. A cold comes from a virus, and being damp or cold only nudges down what your nose fights it with, so nobody catches one from a wet head. What a wet head does do is break the hair, because wet hair stretches and snaps where dry hair gives, and a damp pillow is a night of rubbing. Towel it until it stops dripping, do not rub hard, and a loose braid or a silk-ish pillowcase is enough if you would rather not dry it properly. Dry it if you are going out into the cold with it, for comfort, not for the cold.

No: anything made with unpasteurised milk can carry listeria and campylobacter, so leave the raw-milk cheese and the milk straight from the farm. Pasteurised milk and cheese are fine, and most goat and sheep cheese sold in supermarkets is pasteurised - the label will say so.

No: a plumber, an electrician or a builder quotes a price for the job, and that price is the whole of it. A tip is not expected and can read as odd, so the thing worth doing instead is offering a tea and paying on time.

No: a sunbed gives out mostly UVA, the ray that ages skin and drives melanoma, in doses several times stronger than midday sun, and using one before 35 raises the melanoma risk by around three quarters. Under-18s are banned from them in the UK. A spray tan or a gradual self-tan gives the same colour without the damage.

No: household bleach takes the finish off and lifts the grain into a pale, furry patch, and a board keeps the smell of it. For a real mark, sand the patch and use an oxalic-acid wood bleach from a DIY shop, following the tin. For everyday care, hot water, a scrub of coarse salt, and standing it up to dry does more than bleach ever will.

No - paying for vegetables with pudding teaches a child that the veg is the price and the sweet is the prize, and it stops working the moment the bribe is withdrawn. Give pudding with the meal or after it because dinner is over, whichever mouthfuls were eaten, and keep it ordinary rather than earned. Praise the trying ("you had a go at the carrot") rather than the cleared plate, and a sticker chart for trying new foods does more than any food reward, because it pays for the effort rather than the mouthfuls.

No - paying into a pension is your choice, and all leaving costs is money: your employer's contribution of at least 3% of your pay, the tax relief the government adds to yours, and the growth on both over the decades to retirement. Leaving in the first month gets your own money back; after that the pot stays put and you can rejoin or restart payments whenever you like, so a tight few months is a reason to pause rather than to quit.

No - redundancy pay is for a job that is going, not for you leaving, so resigning gets you your notice and any holiday you have not taken but no statutory redundancy pay. Voluntary redundancy is the exception: if the company offers it and you put your hand up, you get the same package. If you are being pushed towards the door, ask for a settlement agreement in writing and get free advice from ACAS or a union before you hand in notice.

No - scrape the food into the bin and load them. Modern tablets and a 55C or hotter cycle cope with grease and smears, and rinsing first wastes the water and time the machine was bought to save. Soak burnt-on pans and give the filter a rinse weekly; that is the washing up worth doing.

No - and a ham sandwich counts. Since Brexit you cannot take any meat, milk, cheese, butter, yoghurt or cream from Great Britain into the EU, even for yourself, and it is taken off you at the port with a fine. Eat the sandwich before you board. Fish, eggs, bread, cakes, fruit, vegetables and sweets are fine, and powdered baby milk, baby food and pet food for a medical reason are the exceptions. Coming back into the UK you may bring 2kg of meat or dairy per person, so buy the cheese for the trip home rather than taking it out.

No - in England and Wales you can arrange a funeral yourself; nobody has to be paid to do it. What the crematorium or cemetery needs is the paperwork: the death registered, the registrar's green certificate (or the coroner's order if there was a post-mortem), and a signed application form from whoever is arranging it. Ask the crematorium or the council's bereavement office what their form and fee are before you decide, because the fee is the same either way and the director's charge is the part you would be saving. A direct cremation, no service and no mourners, is the cheapest version of the same thing and you can buy it from a director for about a thousand pounds.

No - it is still exercise, just less of it: an hour on an e-bike is roughly half to two-thirds the effort of the same hour on a normal bike, and because it is easier you ride further and more often, so the weekly total usually goes up rather than down. Turn the assist down or off on the flat and you get most of the workout back; leave it on full and it is a gentle ride, which is a great deal better than the car.

No - leave them whole. Pricking lets the fat and juice run out into the pan, so they come out drier, and it is fast high heat that splits a skin, not a skin that went unpricked: cook them at 180C (160C fan) for 25 to 30 minutes, or in a pan on a medium heat, turning them now and then, and let them colour slowly. A thick one that splits anyway is still fine to eat - it has just tightened faster than the inside cooked.

No amount of alcohol is known to be safe in pregnancy, so the advice is none at all. But a drink or two before you knew is very unlikely to have done any harm, and the worry is worse than the drink: most women who had one went on to have a healthy baby. Tell your midwife so it is in your notes, and if stopping is hard, ask for help rather than doing it alone.
No body on this end, so coming along isn't mine, sorry. Say what the day looks like and I'll help with the bits that are words - the list, the timing, what to say.
No body and no birthday — I'm a program, so nothing to age and nothing to wear out.

No for a switch, a socket face, a light fitting or a fused spur, so long as the circuit is off at the consumer unit and the wires go back as they came out. You need one for anything inside the consumer unit, a new circuit, a shower or garden supply, or anything that smells of burning or has scorched a plug. A new circuit or work in a bathroom or kitchen also needs a certificate, so use a registered electrician, get the certificate price with the job price, and agree the whole figure before they come.

Nobody adds to it but you, so it is worth it only as a tax deal: open a SIPP or a personal pension and every £80 you pay in becomes £100 with basic-rate relief (higher rate claims the rest through Self Assessment), and the money grows free of tax until you draw it. Put a fixed share of each invoice aside the day it lands - 10% is a workable start - and keep enough in an ordinary account for a bad month, because you cannot touch the pension until you are 55. Also check your state pension record: 35 qualifying years gets the full amount, and gaps can be filled cheaply.

Nobody can say when a particular earthquake will hit: the rock gives way suddenly and the signs beforehand are unreliable. What we can do is forecast where and how strongly the ground is likely to shake, which is why buildings in earthquake zones are built to flex.

Nobody can settle it. Robert Peary said he reached the North Pole in 1909, but his records were too rough to prove it, and the first party nobody disputes standing there is Ralph Plaisted's in 1968, by snowmobile. The first flight over it, and the first sighting nobody argues with, was Amundsen, Ellsworth and Nobile's airship in 1926.

Nobody can tell you before you go: a walk-in centre sees people in the order they need seeing rather than the order they arrived, so a queue of two hours can move in twenty minutes when something urgent comes in, and a quiet room can still mean a long wait. Ring the centre or look at its own site on the day for the wait it is running, and go early rather than late in the evening. Take a drink, a book and any medicines you take with you, and tell the desk if you get worse while you are sitting there rather than wait your turn.

Nobody knows for certain, and the best evidence points at flies and heat rather than camouflage: the stripes seem to confuse biting flies and help the animal lose heat, and the pattern on each zebra is as individual as a fingerprint.
None of that, no — I'm a program. I'm here to help with yours, though.
None, no: I'm a program, so no kids and no school run.

Norovirus is the winter vomiting bug: it comes on within a day or two of contact, with sudden vomiting and watery diarrhoea, and settles by itself in one to three days. There is no medicine for it - small sips of fluid, little and often, is the whole treatment, and oral rehydration sachets help if you are being sick a lot. Wash hands with soap and water, not alcohol gel, which does not kill it, clean surfaces with bleach, and keep away from work, school or hospital until 48 hours after the last symptom. Ring 111 the same day for a baby, an older person or anyone who cannot keep fluid down, or if there is blood.
Not much on my side. Tell me yours and I'll count it as news.

Not needed for a simple list: bread, milk and eggs. Put one in when 'and' joins two complete sentences (I booked the table, and she drove), or when the list items are long enough that the reader needs the pause: we need the report signed, the photos checked, and the invoice sent.

Not on your own, and not by simply stopping: stopping the rent is a breach of the tenancy, and the arrears are what gets tenants evicted, whatever the state of the boiler. Keep paying and do what does work - report it in writing with dates and photos, and ask the council's environmental health team to inspect, since for a serious hazard they can order the repair. Shelter or Citizens Advice will say free whether yours is one of the rare exceptions; get that in writing before you hold back a penny.

Not on its own: bicarbonate is about four times stronger than baking powder and needs an acid to work. Use a quarter of a teaspoon of bicarbonate with a teaspoon of lemon juice or vinegar in place of each teaspoon of baking powder.

Not over woodchip or any textured paper: the pattern shows through, every seam lifts, and a thinned first coat will not hold it down. Smooth, sound lining paper can be painted with a mist coat (emulsion thinned by about a tenth) and then two ordinary coats, and any bubble or lifted seam comes off before the roller comes out.

Not really: a dock leaf only helps because rubbing a cool, damp leaf on a sting cools the skin and takes your mind off it. Nettle stings are histamine plus tiny hairs, so run the sting under cool water for ten minutes and put an antihistamine cream on it; it settles in a few hours.
Not scared, no. No moods of my own here, and no bad days - but I'm glad to hear about yours.

Not the ordinary Lea & Perrins: Worcestershire sauce is made with anchovies, so it is neither vegetarian nor vegan. Anchovy-free versions exist, and a splash of soy sauce or balsamic does the same job in a stew or a cheese on toast.

Not the service itself: it means opening the case and checking the gas side, and a gas boiler is Gas Safe work by law, so the annual service is an engineer's job at about £60 to £120. Yours is the bit around it: keep the pressure at 1 to 1.5 bar, keep the flue and the vents clear, bleed the radiators - and the warranty usually needs the engineer's service anyway.

Not the bin: batteries are a fire risk in a lorry and in the tip. Most supermarkets and every council recycling centre have a battery box by the door, and button cells and lithium ones go in those too, with the ends taped. Vapes, e-bike and scooter batteries and power banks are the ones that actually start fires, so take them to a shop that sells them or to the tip, never the kitchen bin.

Not with a scourer or wire wool: it takes the coating off in flakes, the pan stops being non-stick, and those flakes are what people find in the food. Use the soft side of a sponge with hot water and washing-up liquid while the pan is still warm, and a wooden or silicone spatula in it. Soak a burnt patch with water and a little bicarbonate rather than scrubbing it.

Not automatically: bank holidays sit inside your 5.6 weeks of paid holiday (28 days for a full-time job), they are not days on top of it, so whether you work them is whatever your contract says. If you do work one you get your normal pay unless the contract or a union agreement promises a premium or a day off in lieu, and there is no law that gives you the day back afterwards. Check the holiday clause before you argue, and if the business closes for the day, that day normally comes out of your leave.

Not bad for you: the calcium and magnesium that make water hard are minerals you get from food anyway, mains water is tested to the same standard whatever its hardness, and the studies find no link between hard water and kidney stones - some find slightly fewer stones in hard-water areas. It is hard because it has come through chalk or limestone, which is why the same country has soft water in the west and hard water in the south east. What it does do is leave a chalky film on taps, kettles and shower glass, lather soap and shampoo less so you use more of them, and feel drier on the skin - a filter jug or a scale reducer is enough for most homes. The one to know about is a baby's bottle: a water softener swaps the calcium for sodium, so make formula with unsoftened mains water, boiled once and cooled.

Not a poison, so no vet for a stolen dinner: a dog living on cat food gets fat and its gut complains, and a cat living on dog food goes short of taurine, which it cannot make itself. Feed them at set times in separate rooms and lift both bowls after ten minutes, and put the cat's bowl up on a worktop or a shelf the dog cannot reach, or behind a microchip cat flap. Feed the cat first, because a cat chased off its food twice stops eating. And if either is on a prescription diet, the other must never share it.

Not for the small jobs: a dripping tap, a loo that keeps running, a blocked trap, a ball valve or a washing-machine hose is an hour with a spanner and a few pounds in parts. Call one when the water will not stop at the stopcock, the leak is under a floor or inside a wall, a joint still weeps after two goes, or the job is a new bathroom or a boiler swap. Fitting an appliance is usually cheaper from the shop that sells it, so ask them first. Then get a fixed call-out price before they come, and say what the fault is doing so the price is for this job and not for a look.

Not for injury, no: strength work and building up slowly are what keep you off the physio's couch, and a stretch before sport takes a little power off it. What the flexibility is worth having is the reach - a high shelf, a shoe, getting up off the floor - and that goes quickly if you stop. Half a minute a side, twice, two or three times a week is enough to keep it.

Not if the packet says gelatin or gelatine: that is made from pork or beef skin and bone, so jelly, marshmallows, jelly babies and most gummy sweets are out. The vegetarian versions set with pectin, agar or carrageenan instead, and they say so on the front.

Not illegal as such: what is checked is that the exhaust is secure, gas-tight and no noisier than the car was built to be, so a hole, a blown joint or a missing baffle fails an MOT and wants mending, while an exhaust that has simply got loud with age is a repair rather than an offence. Making one deliberately louder is where people get caught - it can fail the test and a police officer can ask for it to be put right - so a replacement that stays within the standard noise is the only safe way to get a better note.

Not in one go, no. Councils take arrears in instalments, and the thing to ask for is a payment arrangement you can keep: ring the council tax line, say what is left after rent, food and bills, and ask them to hold any action while it is set up. They will want a breakdown of your income and can turn down an offer that looks too low, but they cannot take it from your wages or benefits until a court has made a liability order.

Not in baking: cornflour has no gluten, so a cake or a loaf will not hold or rise. As a thickener it works, at one tablespoon where the recipe asks for two of plain flour, mixed into cold liquid first.

Not meat or dairy: since 2021 you cannot bring ham, sausages, bacon, cheese, milk or butter into Great Britain from the EU, even for yourself, and a ham sandwich in your bag can be taken off you. Fish, eggs, fruit, vegetables, bread and cake are fine, and the alcohol allowance is its own question. If you are not sure, use the red channel and ask.

Note it down for a fortnight before you decide anything: what was forgotten, when, and whether it was new. Forgetting names, or where the keys went, is ordinary at any age and worse when you are tired, stressed, low or sleeping badly. What is not ordinary is losing the thread of something you have always done - a recipe you know by heart, the way to a place you drive every week, paying the same bill twice - and that is what wants a GP. Book one if it is getting worse, if it came on suddenly, or if it frightens you, and take the notes with you: a GP can check the causes that are fixable, which include low B12, an underactive thyroid, blood pressure, sleep apnoea, depression and the medicines you already take. Going early is not an overreaction; it is how the fixable ones get found.

Nothing new on race day: the socks and shoes you did your long runs in, and dress for ten minutes in - a thin wicking base layer, a warm thin layer over it and a windproof shell you can tie round your waist, a cap for rain or sun, gloves for the first two miles and a waterproof jacket if it is really coming down, because you warm up two or three miles in and one layer fewer than feels right at the door is usually the right count. Vaseline on the nipples and inner thighs, safety pins for the number, a dry top and a bin liner for your bag at the finish, and a warm layer to pull on within ten minutes of stopping, which is when the cold really lands.

Nothing new on the day: the shoes, socks and kit you did your long runs in, plus your race number, safety pins, a bottle, and the gels or sweets you have practised with. Eat the breakfast you have tested, get there an hour early, and set off slower than feels right.
Nothing of that reaches me here. So how are they?
Nothing to report here - what's new with you?

Nothing to worry about: a one-off like that is a sore tummy and a late night, not an emergency. Give them water rather than more juice, keep the next meal an ordinary one instead of cutting it, and brush their teeth before bed. If they are sick once or their tummy aches, that passes on its own - small sips of water and a quiet afternoon is the whole of it. What is worth keeping half an eye on is the everyday rather than the day: fizzy drinks and constant snacking are the ones that matter, and they are the easiest to fence off because they never fill anybody up.

Nothing to do but take a reading: Ofgem moves your supply to a new supplier within days without you doing anything, and any credit balance is protected and comes across with you. Keep the direct debit open until the new supplier writes, take a meter reading and a photo of today's balance, and sign nothing until the switch is confirmed - if the new tariff is worse, you can switch again for free.

Nothing today: leave the blackened leaves and soft stems alone, because a plant that looks dead after a frost often has live buds further down and cutting now tells you nothing. Give it about a fortnight, then scratch the stem or the bark with a fingernail - green underneath means it is alive and can be cut back to just above a live shoot, brown and dry means that part has gone. Water it, keep it out of the next cold night, and don't feed or repot something that is still in shock; new growth is the sign it is worth keeping.

Nothing you do this week makes it hurt less, so do not make decisions in it: no long message, no driving past, no drinking the pain quiet. Tell two people today so you are not carrying it alone, keep the basics going - food, water, sleep, one walk outside - and put the phone in another room at night. It starts to ease in a few weeks, and the first days are the ones to get through rather than fix.

Nothing about your child changed today - the report describes the child you already have, and it is the key to the help rather than a label to grieve. Ask what the next step is in writing: the school's SENCO for a support plan, the paediatrician for what comes next, and your council for an EHCP if school support is not enough. Join one parents' group (the National Autistic Society runs them) - the practical answers, like which haircut works and how to get a dentist appointment, come from people who have done it. Take the report to school yourself; do not wait to be asked.

Nothing fancy for the first day: a named bag with a pencil case (two pens, a pencil, a rubber, a ruler), a water bottle, a packed lunch or the money loaded on the dinner account, and the PE kit the school asked for, in a bag of its own if they can. Label everything, including the coat and the shoes, and put the timetable in the front pocket. Buy the cheap version of each until the school sends its list, then fill the gaps.
Nothing in me gets scared. Curious is the closest I get, and you're the reason.

Nothing is banned: it is the size of the starchy and sugary part that counts. Make half the plate vegetables, a quarter meat, fish, eggs or beans and a quarter potatoes, rice, pasta or bread, wholegrain where you can, because it lifts your sugar more slowly. Fruit whole rather than as juice, cake and sweets after a meal rather than on their own, and sugary drinks swapped for water or diet ones - that swap does more than any one food rule. A diabetic nurse can book you on a free course, DESMOND or X-PERT.

Nothing is compulsory on a pedal-assist bike, so insure it for theft, not for the law: home contents insurance usually covers it at home and often away from home too, so start there and check the single-item limit, because a £1,500 bike is over the typical £1,000 cap and has to be named. A bike policy is £5 to £15 a month and wants a Sold Secure lock. Write down the frame number and photograph the bike.

Nothing left the account, but the company records a missed payment - and on a loan, a phone contract or a tenancy that is arrears. Ring them before they try again: move the date to just after you are paid, ask the bank to waive the fee (they usually do the first time), and keep the account topped up so the retry goes through.
Nowhere, honestly - I don't go anywhere and I don't wait anywhere. How has your day been?

Numbers are rules you can look up, not a talent. A fraction is a part of a whole: the bottom is the size of the piece and the top is how many you have, so 2/3 of 12 is 12 / 3 = 4, then 4 x 2 = 8. To add fractions, make the bottoms match first - 1/2 + 1/3 is 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6 - and a percentage is per hundred, so 10% is the number with a zero knocked off, and 20% off 60 is 12 off, so 48. For times tables, learn 2, 5 and 10 first and double for the 4s and 8s.
Nutmeg is warm and sweet, not hot - a quarter teaspoon in a cheese sauce or a pudding is the usual dose, and more tastes of medicine.

Nuts and dried fruit are safe to soak and nothing spoils while they do it: cover them in water, keep them in the fridge, and they are soft by morning. Almonds slip their skins after a night in water, cashews blend smoother for a sauce, and raisins or dates plump up in warm water in about 20 minutes.

Nuts keep 3 to 6 months in an airtight jar in a cool cupboard and a year in the freezer; shelled or chopped ones go rancid sooner, and walnuts and pine nuts fastest. Taste one: a bitter or soapy taste means the oils have turned, and toasting hides it but does not fix it.

OCD stands for obsessive-compulsive disorder: unwanted, repeated thoughts that arrive on their own, and the rituals done to quieten them, like checking the hob or washing. It is common and treatable - talking therapy, usually CBT with exposure and response prevention, helps most people - so it is worth seeing a GP rather than putting up with it.

OLED stands for organic light-emitting diode: every pixel makes its own light, which is why the blacks are truly black and the panel is thin enough to bend. The organic layer dims as it is used, so a bright static logo can leave a faint mark after years, and that is what the extra price over an LCD buys and costs.

Octopuses is right in English, and octopi is the older Latin-style plural plenty of people still use. The same -uses ending covers viruses, cactuses and walruses; crises and analyses keep the Latin -es.
Of course — go ahead, what's on your mind?

Offer against the sold prices, not the asking price: asking prices are hopes, and the only evidence is what the same sort of house on the same street actually sold for in the last year, which is free on the Land Registry sold-price site and in Rightmove's sold-house filter. If those come out 5-10% under the asking price, that is where to start; if they come out at or above it, offering much under wastes everyone's time. Put the offer to the agent in writing with the amount, the words "subject to contract", your mortgage agreed in principle and your position (first-time buyer, no chain, cash). Move in small steps, 2-3% at a time rather than jumping to your maximum, and treat "we have other interest" as a nudge rather than a fact: ask for it in writing before you pay more for it.
Often not: most halloumi is made with animal rennet, so look for vegetarian on the packet or the Vegetarian Society logo. The vegetarian versions grill and squeak the same way.

Often yes: soak it in lukewarm water with a spoonful of hair conditioner for 15 minutes, then stretch it gently back into shape and dry it flat. Cotton goes back a little, wool and anything with stretch in it goes back most; never put it in the dryer again.

Oil or gas, mostly: the refinery makes small molecules like ethylene and propylene and a chemical plant links them into long chains called polymers. How the chains are built decides whether it ends up as a clear bottle or a washing-up bowl.

Oil the food, not the bars: get the grill hot, brush the bars clean, then brush the meat, fish or veg itself with a little oil and put it on. Leave it alone for three or four minutes - it frees itself once it has sealed - then turn it with tongs rather than a fork, and keep a spray bottle of water for flare-ups.

Oil the hinges: a drop of 3-in-1 or a spray of silicone on each hinge pin, then open and close the door a few times so it works in. If it sticks or rubs rather than squeaks it has usually dropped on its top hinge, so tighten the hinge screws - loose ones let the door drop - and if they spin, push matchsticks dipped in wood glue into the holes and screw back in. Rub a candle or a dry bar of soap on the latch plate or the top edge if that is the part catching.

Oil first, not water: rub a little olive or baby oil into the colour, leave a minute and wipe, then a paste of bicarbonate of soda and washing-up liquid or a cotton pad of micellar water for what is left, and the rest fades in a day or two on its own. On the hands, wash straight away with soap and a nail brush and give the rest a day; dark dye on pale skin can leave a faint mark for a few days, and that is not a burn. A smear of barrier cream round the hairline, and gloves, save the next one.

Oil keeps about a year once opened, often past the date on the bottle if it stays cool and dark: the cupboard rather than beside the hob, with the cap on. Rancid oil smells of crayons or old nuts and tastes of them too, so bin it.

Oily fish is worth two portions a week: the omega-3 in salmon, mackerel and sardines is what the heart and the joints use, and a 140g cooked portion is a serving. Tinned sardines and mackerel count and are the cheapest way to do it; tinned tuna is the lean one, so it gives protein rather than omega-3.

Old-style filament and halogen bulbs are just glass and wire, so they go in the bin. The coiled low-energy ones hold a little mercury: take those to the tip or to a shop that sells them. If one breaks, air the room for fifteen minutes, don't vacuum, and wipe it up with a damp paper towel. LEDs are electronics, so they belong with the small appliances at the tip.

Olive oil splits in two: extra virgin is the cold-pressed first press, peppery and best raw or for low heat, and ordinary olive oil is refined, plainer and fine for frying. Rapeseed is the mild all-rounder and the cheapest British one. Sunflower and vegetable oil are neutral and take high heat, which is what chips and stir-fries want. Sesame is for flavour, a teaspoon at the end, and coconut oil tastes of coconut. Groundnut oil is the one restaurants fry in, because it is neutral and stable when hot.

Olive oil is the best everyday fat you can keep in the kitchen: mostly monounsaturated, and the extra virgin sort brings the polyphenols that are the reason it is worth using raw. It is still 9 calories a gram, so a tablespoon is about 120 calories - the drizzle counts, and a recipe's 'glug' can be three of them. Pour it over a finished dish or bread for the taste, cook with a cheaper oil when the pan is hot, and read 'light' as light in taste, not in calories.

Oliver Cromwell (1599-1658) was the parliamentary general who beat Charles I in the civil war; the king was executed in 1649. Cromwell then ruled as Lord Protector from 1653 until his death, and his son lasted less than a year before the monarchy came back in 1660.

Olives, crushed and pressed: the fruit is ground to a paste and the paste is pressed or spun so the oil separates from the water and the solids. Extra virgin means pressed cold with low acidity; the refined kind is heat-treated and blended.

On the NHS in England a crown is band 3, about £325, and that one charge covers the whole course of treatment; a root canal is band 2 (about £75) on a front tooth and band 3 (about £325) on a back one, and a set of dentures is band 3 as well, so ask which band you are in before any work starts. Privately, expect roughly £500 to £800 for a crown, £300 to £700 for a root canal, £300 to £500 a veneer, £200 to £400 a bridge unit, and £2,000 to £2,500 for an implant including its crown, which is private work only. A written quote is normal, and nobody can price a tooth without seeing it; an NHS crown costs the same whatever tooth it is on.

On the NHS in England a filling is band 1, about £28 for the course of treatment including the check-up, and it is free in Scotland and Wales if you see an NHS dentist there; a root canal is band 3, about £320. A white composite filling often costs more than a silver amalgam one on the NHS and is usually only offered on a front tooth. Privately, expect roughly £60 to £150 for a white filling.

On top of the deposit, budget for stamp duty (nothing on most first homes), legal fees of £1,000 to £1,500, a survey at £400 to £700, a mortgage arrangement fee of £0 to £1,000 if you are not paying it up front in the rate, and £500 or so for removals and the searches. On a £250,000 first home that is roughly £3,000 to £4,000 of costs beside the deposit, and none of it can come from the deposit itself.

On your side is the best default: it keeps the airway open and takes the load off your lower back, and a pillow between the knees keeps the hips level. Front sleeping leaves the neck turned for hours, which is why front sleepers wake with a stiff neck, and on your back snoring and heartburn are worse. The position you can stay asleep in beats the perfect one - and if you wake with a sore neck or back, the pillow is usually the thing to change first.

On Instagram it is Settings > Account privacy > Private account; on Facebook, Settings > Privacy > Who can see what you share set to Friends, and on TikTok, Settings and privacy > Privacy > Private account. Private means new people have to ask to follow you, but it does not hide anything from the people already following, so check that list too.

On Windows, Settings > Privacy & security > Camera, and switch access off for everything or just the apps you do not trust. On a Mac it is System Settings > Screen Time > Content & Privacy. The switch on the machine itself, or a sliding shutter over the lens, is the surest way of all.

On an MOT a fault in the brakes, the steering, the suspension, the structure or a tyre is normally marked 'dangerous', and a dangerous fail means the car must not be driven on the road at all - not even to the garage. Book recovery or ask the garage to collect it, and take it back the next working day, when the partial retest is free. If the sheet says 'major' instead, you can drive it to the garage or to a pre-booked test.

On an Xbox it is Settings > Account > Family settings > Manage family members, and the Xbox Family Settings app does the same from your phone; on a PlayStation it is Settings > Family and Parental Controls, with a 4-digit pass code on the console. On a Switch it is the Nintendo Switch Parental Controls app. Set the age rating, the daily play limit and the spending limit there, and change the console's own pass code so the settings cannot be undone.

On an electric oven the heating element is almost always the fault, and it fails in the way you can see: heat the oven for ten minutes in the dark and look for the element to glow red - a dull patch or a cold half is a broken element, about £20 to £40 for the part and £60 to £90 for an engineer. A fan oven that runs cold is often the fan motor or the thermostat instead. Turn the power off at the wall before you touch anything, and a gas oven that will not light is a gas-safe job, not a DIY one.
