On an iPhone open the call or message, tap the name or number, then Block this Caller; on Android long-press the number in the call log and choose Block. To let someone back in, go the other way: Settings > Phone > Blocked Contacts on an iPhone, or the blocked list in the Phone app on Android, and remove them there. Report scam texts to 7726 in the UK first, and for silent nuisance calls ask your network to switch on call screening, which catches most of them.

On an iPhone press the side button and the volume-up button together; on most Android phones it is power and volume-down, held for a second. The picture goes to Photos or Screenshots, and you can crop it there before sending.

On an iPhone tap the smiley face at the bottom left of the keyboard and swipe along the categories; if it is not there, Settings > General > Keyboard > Keyboards > Add New Keyboard > Emoji. On Windows press the Windows key and the full stop together, and on a Mac it is Control, Command and Space.

On an iPhone use AirPlay from the video or the Control Centre; on Android, use the Cast icon or the Google Home app; a laptop connects best with an HDMI cable. If the TV does not show up, check both are on the same wifi network, which is the usual culprit.

On an iPhone, Screen Mirroring in Control Centre sends the screen to a smart TV, and in a FaceTime or WhatsApp call the share button does it inside the call. On Android it is Cast or Smart View in the quick settings, and Zoom, Teams and Meet each have Share Screen once you are in a meeting.

On an iPhone, Settings > [your name] > iCloud > iCloud Backup and turn it on, then Back Up Now with the phone on wifi and on charge; the date of the last backup is on that same screen, and Settings > [your name] > iCloud > Manage Account > Backups shows what each one holds. Plugging it into a computer and opening Finder, or iTunes on an older machine, makes the same backup on the computer instead of in iCloud.

On an iPhone add Screen Recording to Control Centre (Settings > Control Centre) and tap it. On Android it is in the quick settings tiles on most phones. On a laptop, Windows has Game Bar (Windows and G) and a Mac has Shift, Cmd and 5. Everything saved goes to Photos or the desktop.

On an iPhone go to Settings > Sounds and Haptics > Keyboard Feedback and turn Sound off; on Android Settings > System > Languages and input > On-screen keyboard > Gboard > Preferences, and switch off Sound on keypress. A laptop that clicks out loud is the mechanical keyboard itself, not a setting.

On an iPhone it is Settings > Display & Brightness > Text Size, or Accessibility > Display & Text Size for Larger Text and Bold Text. On Android, Settings > Display > Font size, plus Display size for everything else. Most apps then follow the phone, and in a browser Ctrl and + (Cmd and + on a Mac) enlarges a page.

On an iPhone it is Settings > General > Keyboard, where Auto-Correction and Predictive Text have switches of their own. On Android open the keyboard's settings (Gboard > Settings > Text correction) and turn Auto-correction off. Turning off predictive text as well is what stops whole words being swapped under your thumb.

On an iPhone it is Settings > Mobile Data, and on Android Settings > Network and internet > SIMs (or Connections > Data usage) - the switch at the top turns it off, and wifi carries on working. Switch it off when you are near the end of the month or abroad without a pass, since that is when the charges start, and check the per-app list underneath for the one app doing all the downloading.

On an iPhone it is Settings > Phone > Show My Caller ID, off; on Android open the Phone app > Settings > Calls > Additional settings > Caller ID > Hide number. Type 141 in front of a number to hide it for one call only, and 1470 to show it again. Banks and doctors ignore withheld numbers, so it is worth doing for one call rather than always.

On an iPhone it is Settings > Privacy and Security > Location Services, where you can turn the whole thing off or set each app to Never or Ask Next Time; on Android open Settings > Location > App location permissions and set the ones you do not trust to Don't allow. Leave maps and Find My on, since they are the two you want when a phone is lost, and remember a phone still knows roughly where it is from the network.

On an iPhone it is Settings > Screen Time > Content & Privacy Restrictions: turn it on, then set the age rating for apps, block in-app purchases, and require a passcode for installs. On Android install Google Family Link and approve apps and screen time from your own phone. The one rule that matters is the passcode: use a different one from the phone's own, or a child who can unlock it can turn the limits off.

On an iPhone it is Settings > Sounds & Haptics > Ringtone (and Text Tone for messages), where Tone Store buys one and a song you own can be used for a pound or so. On Android it is Settings > Sound and vibration > Phone ringtone, and a music app can usually set any track as the ringtone from its own menu.

On an iPhone it is Settings > Battery > Battery Health; on Android, Settings > Battery > Battery usage usually shows it, or use an app like AccuBattery. Below 80% of its original capacity is when a new battery is worth it, and it is usually £40 to £70.

On an inside wall of the room you heat most, about 1.4 metres off the floor - roughly eye level - where it feels the same temperature as the middle of the room. Keep it away from radiators, direct sun, a draught from a door or window, and the kitchen's cooking heat, or it reads a temperature nobody is standing in and the boiler works to the wrong number. A hallway is the usual compromise: fine if the hall is a room you actually heat, wrong if it is the coldest place in the house, because then every other room runs hot.

On a metric tape the big numbers are centimetres and the small marks between them are millimetres, ten to the centimetre, so three marks past the 7 is 73 mm. The imperial side runs the other way up: between two inches the longest small mark is the half, the next longest the quarter, then eighths, then sixteenths. Lay the tape flat and read it with your eye straight above the mark, and add the width of the hook if you are measuring to an outside edge.

On a motorway get onto the hard shoulder, put your hazards on, and get everyone out to the left and up behind the barrier before you call anyone. On a smart motorway where the shoulder is a live lane, stay in the car with belts on and ring 999. Then call your breakdown service or insurer. A broken-down car is not worth changing a tyre beside moving traffic for.

On a smart TV it lives in Settings > Accessibility as Subtitles or Captions, and on a Freeview remote press SUBTITLE while the programme is on. Inside an app it is the speech-bubble icon on the player, which only appears once something is playing. If they come back on after you turn them off, the TV's accessibility menu is the one that wins.

On a student visa you can work up to 20 hours a week in term time on a degree-level course, and 10 hours a week if the course is below degree level; outside term time you can work full time. The cap covers every hour you work for anyone, and self-employment, freelancing and a permanent full-time job are not allowed at all. The 48-hour week is an employee's average, not your limit: the visa cap is lower and it comes first.

On a Fire tablet hold the power button and volume-down together for a second, and the picture goes into the Photos app in Screenshots. An ordinary Kindle e-reader cannot take one: there is no screenshot button, so your phone's camera is the way.

On a Windows laptop select what you want, press Ctrl+C to copy and Ctrl+V to paste; Ctrl+X cuts it and Ctrl+Z puts back a mistake. A Chromebook is Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V as well, and a right-click gives Copy and Paste in the menu if the keys are awkward.

On a bus or a coach it travels folded, so have it down and the child out of it before the doors open: a driver can refuse a pushchair that is still open, and the space by the door belongs to a wheelchair user first. On trains and the underground a folded pushchair is free and goes in the luggage rack, and most stations have a lift, so use that rather than the escalator. For a coach trip the buggy goes in the hold - tell the driver at the door so it is not loaded under the luggage.

On a combi boiler, about 20 to 30 seconds is normal: you are waiting for the boiler to fire and for the hot water to travel down the pipe from it. If it is minutes, or the water runs hot then cold, the plate heat exchanger is scaled (a typical 5 to 10 year service item) or the boiler is undersized for two taps at once. If the flow is weak as well, check the isolator under the sink is fully open and unscrew the tap nozzle to clear the scale.

On a combined pill taken every day, about 1 in 100 people get pregnant in a year with perfect use, and about 9 in 100 with typical use - most of those from a missed pill, a stomach bug or another medicine interfering. If you want the most reliable, a coil or an implant is over 99% and needs no daily remembering. On the mini pill three hours late counts as missed, so take it when you remember and use condoms for seven days.

On a computer, put the address in the hosts file or use the router's parental controls so it covers every device in the house; a free filter such as Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 for Families does it in one setting. On a phone, Screen Time (iPhone) or Digital Wellbeing (Android) blocks sites by name, and a browser extension does it for one browser only.

On a huge herb rather than a tree: the plant pushes up a single stem, flowers once and fruits once, and then it is cut down and a shoot from the root takes over. Bananas want heat and rain all year, which is why they come from the tropics.

On a long overnight it buys sleep, and that is usually the whole point: a flat bed and a lounge shower on an eight-hour flight is worth more than on a two-hour hop. On a daytime short-haul it buys a bigger seat and a meal, which is rarely worth the money. Look at premium economy before you decide.

Once opened, a tub of tzatziki or taramasalata keeps about 3 days in the fridge and guacamole a day or two, because avocado browns and sours fastest: the date on the lid is for the sealed pot, so judge it by look and smell after that. Press cling film down onto guacamole to keep the air off it, keep all of them cold, and bin anything that smells sour, fizzes or has mould.

Once or twice a day is plenty for most hair: start at the ends, work up towards the scalp in small sections, and use a wide-tooth comb on wet hair, because wet hair stretches and snaps where dry hair gives. The 100 strokes idea is a myth, since that much brushing only roughens the outside of the hair, and a comb through conditioner in the shower is what actually gets tangles out.

Once the cross is rounded there is no grip, so give it grip or give it something else to hold: press a wide rubber band or a steel-wool pad into the head and turn slowly with real downward force, or tap a slightly larger Torx or Phillips bit in with a hammer for a bite. If the head stands proud, cut a slot with a hacksaw and use a flat blade. Last resorts are pliers on the head, or drilling it out and using a screw extractor.

Once you can run for half an hour without stopping, a 10k takes about ten weeks on three runs a week: one long run that grows by five to ten minutes a week, one easy run, and one with four or five short faster bursts inside it. Take the long run up to about 9km two weeks before the day, then ease off. Keep the weekly increase near 10% and put a rest day after the long one, since the distance is built in the recovery, not in the run.

Once a month, in a warm bath or shower when everything is relaxed, hold each testicle between the thumb and the first two fingers and roll it gently between them, feeling for a hard lump, a change in size or a heavy ache that was not there last month. It should feel smooth and firm, like a peeled egg, with the soft tube at the back. Anything new that is still there after two weeks is a GP appointment; sudden severe pain is the hospital the same day.

Once a month for the filter, the door seal and the spray arms, and a hot empty cycle with a dishwasher cleaner or a bowl of white vinegar on the top rack; the salt and the rinse aid are checked weekly, because running out of either is what makes everything come out cloudy. In a hard-water area the descale wants doing every couple of months as well.

Once a month for a proper empty-out and wipe, with a shelf done the moment something spills. The door seals and the little drain hole at the back are where the smell starts, so they get done every time; a bowl of bicarbonate of soda on a shelf only holds it between cleans.

Once a week pour a full kettle of boiling water down it, which melts the fat and soap that hold the smell, and once a month follow with half a mug of bicarbonate of soda and a mug of white vinegar, leave it 15 minutes and flush it through with hot water. Hair comes out with a bent wire or the trap under the sink, and nothing you pour down will shift it.

Once a week, and twice if the bathroom is shared or there is a toddler in the house: a mat holds every wet footprint, so it goes in at 60C with the towels and comes out the thing that stops the floor smelling of damp. Two mats that take turns is the version that always has a dry one down.

Once a week in the rooms you use every day, and every couple of days in a bedroom, in a room somebody is allergic in, or in a house on a busy road: a soft or slightly damp microfibre cloth holds the dust instead of pushing it about, and a feather duster mostly just moves it to the next shelf. Work from the top down - the tops of the cupboards and the picture rails first, the skirting and the floor last - so what you lift off lands somewhere you are going to vacuum anyway.

Once a week in the rooms you actually use, and twice if there is a pet, an allergy or a crawling baby. Empty the bin or the bag when it is two-thirds full rather than when it is packed, and the filter every month or two - a blocked filter is why a vacuum starts to smell.

Once a year you confirm three things at Companies House: the company's address, its directors and its shareholders. It is not the accounts and not the tax return, and it is due 14 days after the review period ends - the year runs from the day the company was set up. It costs £34 online and takes ten minutes. Miss it and Companies House can fine the company £1,500 and strike it off, so diarise it with the accounts date.

Once a year, yes: a gas boiler service is usually £60 to £120 depending on where you are. It keeps the warranty valid, catches a failing part before it strands you in winter, and landlords are legally required to have one. Book it in late summer, when engineers are quiet and the price is lower.

Once a year for a dog, and a cat the same: the leptospirosis part of a dog's booster has to be every year, while the distemper, hepatitis and parvovirus parts are often given every three years, so ask the vet which you are due. Kennel cough is the extra one worth having if he goes to a groomer, day care or a boarding kennel.

Once a year is the usual answer, sooner if you ride in the wet or cover a few thousand miles: a basic service is £50 to £95, which covers the bearings, the gears, the brakes and the wheels trued, or £120 to £200 for a full strip-down. Check the chain, the cassette, the brake pads and the tyres yourself with a chain checker and a ruler, and ask what the price covers before you book.

Once a day is right for most households: a full load uses less water than washing up by hand, and rinsing the plates first wastes the point of it. Wait until it is full, then run it, and leave the door ajar afterwards so the seals dry out.

Once a jar is opened it lives in the fridge: pesto, sauces and ketchup are usually good for 1 to 2 weeks, pickles, chutney, jam and mustard for months, and the label's once-opened line beats any general rule. Keep the surface under a little oil and bin it if it smells sharp or the lid bulges.

Once a lettuce, a spinach or a herb sends up a stem it has run to seed, and the leaves turn bitter as it does: cut it now and eat what is still good, because it will not come back into leaf. It happens in heat and long days, so next time pick a slow-bolt variety, sow so the crop is ready before midsummer or after it, keep it watered, and shade it in a heatwave. Picking the outer leaves often keeps a plant in leaf longer.

Once every couple of months in a hard-water area and once every six months where the water is soft: the scale is only calcium, but a thick layer makes the kettle slow and leaves a scum on the tea. Half water, half white vinegar or a sachet of citric acid, boiled and left half an hour, then boiled fresh twice and tipped away.

Once every few loads, and after every single one if you dry towels, fleeces or anything else that sheds: pull the filter out, peel the lint off in one sheet, rinse it if the mesh takes a rinse, and let it dry before it goes back in. A clogged filter is the commonest reason a dryer takes two cycles over a load and the back of the machine feels hot, and lint left to build up is what catches light.

One nap a day, at the same time straight after lunch, in a dark quiet room: put them down while they are sleepy rather than asleep, and wake them by three so bedtime still works. An hour is plenty after two - longer than that and the night goes wrong. If they will not settle, walk them back the same quiet way you do at bedtime, and give it two weeks before you decide they have dropped the nap for good.

One on every floor, one in the hallway outside the bedrooms, and one in the room with the boiler or the open fire - the hallway one matters most, because smoke in the stairs is what cuts off the way out. Fit sealed ten-year alarms so there is no battery to remember, and check the test button on each once a month.

One page, newest first, and written for someone who has never done your job: what is running, what is due and when, who to ask about each thing, and the two or three things that go wrong if nobody touches them. Name a person for each item - "the Tuesday invoice goes to Sam" - because a handover that ends in a folder nobody opens is worse than none. Send it the day before you go, offer fifteen minutes to walk through it, and keep a copy: it is also the best evidence of what you carried.

One page, newest first: a two-line profile saying what job you want and what you are good at, then each job or course with one line on what you actually did and a number where there is one. Plain headings, a normal font, no photo or date of birth, and send it as a PDF so the layout cannot move.

One page, one issue, one ask. Say who you are and where you live first, with the full postcode, because an MP can only act for their own constituents; then the problem in three sentences with the dates, then exactly what you want them to do - change a rule, chase a department, or write to a minister for you. Attach copies, never originals, and ask for a reply within four weeks. Address it to the House of Commons, London SW1A 0AA, or find the name and the office email on theyworkforyou.com. A short factual letter gets an answer from a caseworker; a long angry one gets a standard reply.

One page if you have under about ten years of experience, two at most after that: nobody reads page three. Cut anything older than ten years to a single line, and keep the detail where it earns you the interview.

One page is enough for a one-person business, and six lines cover almost everything: who you both are, exactly what you will do and by when, what it costs and when it is paid, what is included and what costs extra, who owns the finished work, and how either of you can end it. Add what happens if they change their mind - a set hourly rate for changes is the line that saves the job - and ask for a deposit of a third or half before you start. A quote they answer with "yes, go ahead" in an email is a contract already, so keep that email; you do not need a solicitor for a job worth a few hundred pounds, only for premises, staff or work that could hurt someone.

One repair is the shop's go at it, not an endless supply: if the same fault comes back, you can refuse another repair and ask for a refund or a price reduction instead, because a repair has to be done properly and within a reasonable time. Send that in writing, list both repair dates and what went wrong each time, and keep the receipts. Within six months of buying, the shop has to prove the fault is not theirs.

One rule, always the same, and a place that is better than the one you are banning: a bed in the corner of the same room, a chew there, and a treat every time he settles on it. A baby gate or stairgate does the kitchen and the stairs without a fight, and closing the door beats saying no twenty times. Nobody in the house should let him up "just this once" - that is what teaches him to keep trying. If he is already in the room, walk him out by the collar without a word and reward him for the bed.

One side not browning means the element on that side has gone, or the wire that feeds it: unplug it, and if you look in while it is cold and one element never glows while the others do, that is the fault. On an ordinary toaster that is a new toaster, not a repair. If it browns at one END instead, the bread is sitting proud of the slots and the elements are fine.
One space after a full stop, not two - the double space was a typewriter habit and word processors already add the right gap. The same goes after a comma and a question mark.

One story, four sentences: where you were and what went wrong, what you chose to do, what actually happened, and how it turned out - in numbers if there are numbers. "A supplier went quiet the week of a launch. I rang their depot instead of emailing, got a half-load for the Tuesday, and we shipped on time." Have two ready, one where you fixed something and one where you got it wrong, and tell the same two all the way through: interviewers compare notes.

One thing she or he actually did for you, named plainly: "Thanks for every school run in the rain." A memory does more than "best mum ever", and if you are not close, a warm two lines and both your names is enough - the present is a separate job.

One to two weeks for a bruise to fade, going purple, then green, then yellow as the blood is cleared. A cold pack for 20 minutes at a time over the first day keeps it smaller, and a bruise that turns up with no knock behind it, or that you keep getting, is worth a blood test.

One tray per cat plus one, in quiet places, scooped daily and washed weekly with unscented soap. If it still smells after that, the plastic has picked it up: replace the tray and the litter, which is cheaper than fighting it. If a litter-trained cat suddenly goes outside the tray, a vet check comes first, because it is often a urine infection.

One antihistamine a day is fine for months on end - through the whole pollen season if that is what it takes - and loratadine and cetirizine are the two that do not make you drowsy. What not to do is take two different ones at once to double the effect; if one at full dose is not enough, add a steroid nasal spray or eye drops, or ask about montelukast. A sedating one such as chlorphenamine is the wrong choice for daytime use.

One big dish that stretches beats several small ones: a chilli, a curry or a pasta bake with bread and a big salad, where the cheap starch and veg do the filling and the meat is the flavour. Chicken thighs, mince, tinned tomatoes, lentils and beans cost far less than prime cuts or fillets, and a slow-cooked shoulder of pork or lamb feeds a table for very little. Ask people to bring the pudding or the drinks and nobody minds.

One big meal does not undo anything - a day of overeating is a few hundred calories over, not a week's worth - so the useful move is to go back to a normal meal at the normal time rather than to skip or punish yourself. If you are bingeing regularly, or making yourself sick or using laxatives, please tell a GP: that is treatable, and Beat (0808 801 0677) will talk it through with you first.

One bush, Camellia sinensis: the leaves are picked, then wilted, rolled and dried, and how far they are allowed to oxidise decides the kind - none for green, all the way for black. Almost every tea in the shop, white, green, oolong and black, comes off that same bush.

One coat of wood stain is usually enough on new wood and two on anything that has gone grey, and a second coat goes on after four to six hours - sooner than that and it lifts the first. Wipe off the excess before it dries, because stain that pools sets patchy.

One easy day between hard sessions is enough, and it does not have to be a day in bed: a walk, a swim or stretching keeps you moving without loading the same muscles. Two hard sessions back to back is the pattern that leaves people sore and stale. Sleep and food do more of the rebuilding than any recovery gadget.

One easy line closes it, and you do not owe anyone more than that: "No - I've just had a big lunch." If it keeps coming, or it is someone who should know better, name it once and flatly: "I'd rather not talk about that." You do not have to explain whether you are trying, whether it happened and did not last, or whether you have decided not to - and you can say exactly that: "that's not something I talk about." Then change the subject to them, which is what most people want anyway.

One emoji, only where the tone is already warm: a thumbs-up or a smile in a work chat is fine, a string of them rarely is. Skip faces in anything to a client, in bad news, and in a first email to someone senior; a plain "Thanks!" or a short "Sounds good" carries the warmth without the risk. Never let an emoji replace the words that say what you mean, and never use a winking one to soften a real complaint.

One fact per card, question on one side, answer on the other, and no paragraphs: "What year was the Battle of Hastings?" not "notes on 1066". Review only the cards you get wrong, in short daily sessions, and make them yourself - writing them is half the memory work. Anki does the spacing for you if you prefer an app.

One idea per paragraph: a sentence that says what it argues, the evidence for it, then a line saying why that matters to the question. Your conclusion should answer the question as asked, not repeat the introduction. If you are stuck, write the paragraphs' first sentences as a list first and check they add up to an argument.
One kid, 13 — noted.
One kid, 13 — good to know. Tell me about them.
One kid, eight — noted.
One kid, eight — good to know. Tell me about them.

Onions, garlic, leeks and chives damage a dog's red blood cells, and cats are affected too. A small taste is usually harmless, but a whole onion or a pile of garlic needs a call to the vet today with the pet's weight.

Online, by phone or by post you have 14 days from the day it arrives to tell them you are cancelling and 14 more to send it back, with the refund 14 days after that. In a shop it is their own returns policy that sets the window for a change of mind - 28 days is common, and often just an exchange or credit note - but a faulty item is different: 30 days to reject it for a full refund, whatever the sign says.

Only rifampicin and rifabutin make the pill less reliable; ordinary antibiotics such as amoxicillin do not, and that old warning has been dropped. What does matter is a bad stomach: if you are sick within two hours of taking a pill, or have severe diarrhoea, follow the leaflet in your packet - usually another pill, and condoms for the next seven days. Ask a pharmacist if you are on rifampicin.

Only the platform can take a review down, and only when it breaks their rules: no proof of purchase, abuse, the wrong business, or a rant about something else. Open the review, use its report button and pick the rule it breaks, and keep a screenshot. If the platform says no, ask once more with the order number as proof of what really happened, and reply once in public with the fix - readers weigh that calm reply more than the complaint. Never offer a refund or a freebie for a good review or a deletion: that breaks the rules itself and can cost the listing its stars.

Only the two shooters can score: goal shooter stays in the attacking third and goal attack works the circle edge with her, and the two defenders - goal keeper and goal defence - are the mirror of them at the other end. Wing attack and wing defence carry the ball through the middle thirds and centre takes the pass-offs, so the positions are really about which thirds you may enter.
Only you can say, and I don't want to guess at it for you. What is making you wonder?

Only a dentist can say whether a tooth needs a filling: they look, and sometimes X-ray, so it is worth going if it hurts to bite or to sweet and cold, if you can see a hole or a dark patch, or if food keeps catching there. The filling itself is done with a local anaesthetic, so it should not hurt beyond pressure and the noise of the drill, and mild cold sensitivity for a few days afterwards is normal.

Only if something relies on it - a care alarm, a fax, or a broadband deal built on the old copper line. Calls do not need one: a full-fibre service carries the phone over the same cable, and a landline is being switched off across the UK anyway. If you keep one it is about £5 to £10 a month on top of broadband, so ask what the package costs without it before you renew.

Only if you struggle to hit the number with meals: a shake is convenient protein, not a shortcut, and food does the same job for less money. If you do buy one, a plain whey or a plant blend is fine - one scoop after training covers 20 to 25g - and the timing barely matters, because the total for the day is what builds muscle. Look for 20g or more of protein a scoop and ignore anything promising to burn fat.

Only if your own policy says so. Many comprehensive policies give 'driving other cars' cover, but it is usually third party only, often limited to drivers over 25, and some policies have dropped it altogether, so check the certificate before you drive. The car also needs its own insurance for someone to drive it, and the owner's permission is not cover by itself.

Only if your contract says weekends, or you agreed to them: a boss asking is a request, not a rule, so check the contract and your written rota first. Even on weekends you are owed 11 hours off between shifts and 24 hours off a week, and if weekends were never in your contract you can ask for time off in lieu or a day off in the week to match. Say it once, in writing: "I can do one weekend a month, but not both days every week - can we agree which?" If the contract does include weekends, ask how the rota shares them out.

Only if it thawed in the fridge: that meat can go back in the freezer, though it will be a bit drier. Anything that thawed on the worktop or in a warm kitchen should be cooked and eaten now - cooking it first is what buys you extra days, not refreezing it raw.

Only if it helps them and they can do something about it. Say the one specific thing, not the verdict - 'the pastry came out a bit dry' keeps it about the pastry, 'your cooking is bad' is about them - and say it once, then let it go. If they cannot change it in five minutes, or they did not ask, find something true you can praise instead: a haircut grows out, but the remark stays.

Only lend what you could afford to lose, and say the amount and a date out loud before any money moves: "I can do £500, back by March." If it's for something essential like a car, a short written note or a standing order saves the friendship later.

Onto is one word when something moves onto a surface - he climbed onto the roof. Keep them apart when 'on' belongs to the verb - we carried on to the next town, hold on to it. If you can't move the 'on' away, it's one word.

Open Activity Monitor (Applications > Utilities) and sort by % CPU, then by Memory: the app at the top is what is eating the machine, and quitting it is the whole fix more often than not. Then check disk space under the Apple menu > System Settings > General > Storage - a Mac under about 10% free slows to a crawl - and turn off what starts at login under General > Login Items. If it has been slow since an update, restarting it once clears the leftovers.

Open the message and hold a finger on the bubble: on an iPhone tap Forward, on Android tap the three dots or More and then Forward, then pick who it goes to. A photo or a voice note forwards the same way, and a long thread is easier to screenshot.

Open the new one first and let the Current Account Switch Service move it: the switch takes seven working days, closes the old account for you and redirects payments for three years. If you would rather just shut it, clear any overdraft and check nothing is due in or out, move the Direct Debits and standing orders yourself, then ask in writing and keep the final statement. A joint account needs both of you to agree.

Open the payslip and check three lines before you say anything: the tax code against your P45 or last payslip, the hours or overtime that were paid, and any deduction you did not agree to. Then ask payroll in writing for a breakdown - "my gross is down 120 on last month, could you tell me what changed?" Keep it about the figures, not the person. Most of these are a wrong tax code or a missed timesheet and are fixed within a week.

Open the seam where the zip goes and press it flat, then pin the zip face down on the right side with the teeth on the seam line and baste it by hand - the basting is what keeps the two sides level, and a zip foot lets the needle run close to the teeth without catching them. Stitch one side, close the zip, check the seam lines up, then stitch the other side and unpick the basting. To replace one, unpick the old zip without cutting the seam allowance and reuse its opening. A zip that slides open behind the slider is the slider worn, so pinch it gently with pliers or fit a new slider; if the teeth have gone, the zip has to come out.

Open the tin most of the way, hold the lid down with your thumb and tip it over the sink with a gap of about a centimetre, so the liquid runs out and the food stays in. Pressing the lid flat and squeezing is tidier still, and the lid laid over a bowl makes a strainer if you want to keep the oil or brine for a dressing. Tuna in water wants a good press before the mayo; chickpeas and sweetcorn want a rinse as well.

Open the windows and run the extractor fan, then simmer a pan of water with a splash of vinegar or a sliced lemon for ten minutes, which clears the air faster than air freshener. Wash whatever was in the oven, and leave a bowl of bicarbonate of soda in the kitchen overnight to take the last of it out of the air.

Open the PDF and press Ctrl and P - Command and P on a Mac - then pick the printer; File > Print does the same. If you wanted a paper copy turned into a file instead, choose 'Print to PDF' in the same menu.

Open the PDF in Word itself (File > Open, choose the PDF) and it converts it to an editable document in one step; Google Docs does the same for free - upload it, right click, Open with > Google Docs, then File > Download > Microsoft Word. Either way a scanned PDF comes through as a picture, so you need an OCR pass (Google Docs and Adobe both do it) before any of the text can be typed over.

Open the air control fully, clear the grate but leave an inch of ash, and lay eight or ten sticks of kindling in a loose criss-cross with a firelighter or a twist of newspaper in the middle. Light it low down and leave the door on the latch rather than shut, so air can get in, and wait until the kindling is properly caught before you add one or two split logs - a big log laid on a small flame is how a fire goes out. Once the fire is going and the glass has cleared, shut the door and close the air down to about a finger's width; that is what stops it burning through a load in an hour. If it smokes into the room on a cold day the flue is cold, so hold a lit twist of newspaper up near the throat of the stove for a minute first. Dry wood and a swept flue are the two things that keep it easy: fit a carbon monoxide alarm in the same room, have the chimney swept once a year, and never use petrol, meths or barbecue fluid to start it, because a sooted flue is what turns a stove into a chimney fire.

Open the bank's app before you argue at the till: a block for an unusual payment is the usual cause and you can lift it there, and you can check the balance and the daily limit while you are in. If the app shows nothing, ring the number on the back of the card - a fraud review only they can clear. Carry a second way to pay while it is sorted.

Open the bonnet and look for the cap with the windscreen-and-spray symbol on it - usually blue, and never the yellow one, which is coolant. Mix screen wash concentrate with water as the bottle says: about one part wash to four parts water in summer, one to one in winter, and neat in a hard frost, because the alcohol in it is what stops the bottle freezing and the smear on a gritty screen. Never use washing-up liquid - it foams, smears and blocks the jets. Fill to the neck, and if the spray is still weak, push a pin into the jet and adjust the aim with a needle.

Open the Clock app and tap Timer: type 10 and press Start, and on an iPhone you can say 'hey Siri, set a timer for ten minutes' instead. A timer keeps running with the screen off and rings over the alarm volume, so turn that up in Settings > Sounds if it is too quiet to hear from the kitchen.

Open the lid with the printer on and wait for the cartridge carrier to slide to the middle by itself - do not pull it, because the print head parks at the edge. Press the old cartridge down and towards you until it clicks free, lift it out, then take the new one out of its packaging and pull the tape off the contacts and the nozzle before it goes in. Slide it in at the same angle until it clicks, close the lid and let the printer run its alignment page. Buy the number printed on the old cartridge (or in the printer's menu), and check the price per page rather than the box price.

Open the mail app and pull the inbox down to refresh it - a phone that has been on battery saver stops fetching quietly, so check that first, then Settings > Mail > Fetch New Data (or the account's sync setting on Android) and set it to Push or every 15 minutes. If the account is also full, mail is refused rather than delivered, so check the storage figure. When nothing has arrived for days, remove the account and add it back: the mail on the server is untouched and the last week comes down with it.

Open windows at both ends of the flat for ten minutes; that shifts more than anything you spray. Then wash the things that hold smell: bedding, cushions, the bath mat, the bin lid. Bicarbonate of soda on the carpet, left an hour and vacuumed, lifts stale air, and a pan of water with lemon peel and a cinnamon stick simmered for ten minutes does the rest. Air fresheners mask it; the fix is finding the source, often the bin, the drain or damp.

Open with your verdict in one sentence, then say what the book tries to do and whether it works: a paragraph on the whole thing, a paragraph for each point you want to make with a quote or a page number, and no more than a few lines of plot. Leave the ending out, and finish with who the book suits, so the reader can decide.

Open with a story about one day at that school, not with a thank-you list, and keep the whole thing to three minutes: the story, what it taught you, then the one sentence you want people to remember. Say it out loud standing up four times before the day, and put the last line on a card in your hand - a rehearsed ending is what makes a speech land.

Open a window, then simmer a pan of water with a sliced lemon or a splash of vinegar for 10 minutes: that clears cooking smells better than any spray. Find the source too, because a lingering smell is usually the bin, the drain or the fridge.

Open a dispute in PayPal's Resolution Centre within 180 days of paying, then escalate it to a claim if the seller does not answer: PayPal decides and refunds from the seller's money. On eBay, use the Money Back Guarantee in your purchase history first, and if the payment came off a card as well, your bank can still do a chargeback.

Open every window, drive with the fan on fresh air (not recirculate) for twenty minutes to clear what is in the air, wipe the glass, dashboard and door cards with warm water and a splash of white vinegar, then shampoo or steam the seats, carpets and headlining and fit a new cabin (pollen) filter, which is behind the glovebox on most cars. That order is the job, because the film on the glass and the soft stuff hold the smoke; bowls of bicarbonate of soda or fresh coffee grounds overnight help a bit, and a car smoked in for years needs an ozone treatment from a valeter.

Open it once you have your place confirmed, because the good ones only run while you are a student: you need your passport or driving licence plus proof of address and the UCAS or university letter. Choose on the interest-free overdraft, not the free railcard: £1,500 to £3,000 is normal in the first year, it usually rises each year and then tapers off about a year after you graduate, when the interest starts. Ask what the rate becomes after that, keep the account for your student loan and your rent, and open a normal savings account alongside it for anything you are not spending.

Order the thing you would not cook at home, and one shared starter for the middle: a main each and a side between two is plenty. Ask what is good tonight - the kitchen knows what came in fresh - and say yes to the dish you cannot quite pronounce.

Order a replacement through the driving agency's site (gov.uk in the UK): about £20, a new photo and it usually arrives within a week, and a change of name or address is free. If it was stolen, tell the police first and keep the crime reference, because a licence in someone else's hands is identity theft - and tell the agency it was stolen rather than lost. You can usually keep driving while a replacement is being processed as long as you have applied and your doctor has not told you to stop.

Order a certified copy from the office that holds the record, not a photocopy of your own: in the UK that is the General Register Office online, about £12.50 for a standard copy with more for a fast one, and it arrives in a few days. Passport and licence applications want the certified version, so keep the one they send you flat in the folder with your other documents.

Order a certified copy from the register office where the marriage was registered, or from the General Register Office online, giving the date, the place and both full names as they are on the day. It is about £12.50 and it comes in about a week; ask for the certified copy rather than the decorative one if it is for a passport or a visa.

Order a fresh turkey to collect on the 23rd or the morning of the 24th, and a frozen one to come out of the freezer 3 to 4 days before for a big bird. Allow 20 minutes per 500g plus 20 at 180C (160C fan), and rest it 30 minutes under foil and tea towels.

Order it about a week before you run out: a GP needs two working days and the pharmacy one or two more. Use the NHS app or the surgery's online service, or drop the slip in at the pharmacy and let them order it. Ask for two months if you are going away; only the GP can restart a repeat that was stopped.

Order it from a butcher or a supermarket a week or two ahead, and collect a fresh bird two or three days before: it keeps fine in the coldest part of the fridge for that long. If it is going in the freezer, buy it now, because a frozen turkey needs 24 hours in the fridge for every 2kg, so a 6kg bird is three days of thawing on its own.

Overcooked pasta has taken on water and lost its bite, so drain it now and stop the cooking under cold water. Toss it straight into a thick sauce - a ragu, a bake, or tomato with a spoon of cream cheese - rather than a thin one it cannot hold, and it will pass. Next time taste a piece a minute before the packet time.

Overnight oats keep 3 days in the fridge in a lidded jar, and they are better after the first night than they are after an hour: 40g of oats to about 100ml of milk or yoghurt, left covered overnight, keeps in the fridge for three breakfasts.

Overwatering is the usual cause: yellow, soft leaves on a plant in soggy compost means stop watering and let the top inch of soil dry out, and check the pot has holes. Yellow lower leaves that are dry and crisp are the other story — that is just age, or a plant that needs feeding.

Own it today rather than letting it curdle into a bigger apology: 'I got your birthday wrong and I feel bad about it - can I take you for dinner this week?' Then book the thing, because a small make-up that happens beats a long sorry that doesn't.

PAYE stands for pay as you earn: your employer takes income tax and National Insurance out of each payslip and sends it to HMRC, so the tax is paid as you go rather than in one bill. Your tax code is what tells them how much to take, so check it on the payslip - a wrong code is the usual reason a wage comes out short.

PAYE is the payroll system: the employer works out income tax and National Insurance from your tax code, takes them off your pay before it reaches you and sends them to HMRC, usually by the 22nd of the following month. That is why a payslip shows a gross figure and the net you actually get. As an employer you register for PAYE before the first payday; as an employee it is already done for you.

PCOS is ovaries that make more testosterone than usual, with insulin resistance behind it: periods that are irregular or stop, acne, hair on the face or chin, and weight that settles round the middle. About one woman in ten of childbearing age has it, and losing 5 to 10% of body weight often brings the periods back on its own. The GP can confirm it with a blood test and a scan; the pill regulates the periods and helps the skin and hair, metformin helps the insulin side, and if you want to get pregnant say so early, because a short course of tablets often restarts ovulation. Ask for a yearly blood pressure and blood sugar check, since the diabetes risk is the part that is easy to miss.

PCP is a loan with a final balloon payment: you pay mostly for the car's fall in value, then hand it back, pay the lump sum, or trade it in. Hire purchase spreads the whole price over the term, and the car is yours after the last payment.

PDF stands for portable document format: a file that carries the layout as well as the words, so a form or a ticket looks the same on any machine. That is why a signature on a PDF counts as a signature on that page, and why editing one is awkward - the page is closer to a picture of a page than to a document.

PIP stands for Personal Independence Payment: the benefit for adults under state pension age who have extra costs from a long-term illness or disability, for getting around or for daily tasks. It is not means-tested, so savings and a job do not rule you out, and the decision rests on an assessment of what you can do, not on the diagnosis.

PIP is paid every four weeks, in arrears, into the bank account, and the day is set by the date on the decision letter rather than a fixed day of the month: the first payment lands a few weeks after the decision and the four-weekly cycle runs on from there. A job and savings do not rule you out, and the decision rests on what you can do day to day rather than on the diagnosis, so anxiety or a bad back counts by how it limits you. There are two parts, daily living and mobility, each at a standard or an enhanced rate, and you can get one part without the other. Tell the DWP as soon as anything changes, because a rise is backdated only to the date they were told, and the rates go up each April - the current figures are on gov.uk.

PMS stands for premenstrual syndrome: the mix of low mood, bloating, tender breasts and tiredness in the week or two before a period, which lifts once it starts. It is common and treatable - regular exercise, less caffeine and the combined pill help some women - so see a GP if it is spoiling a week of every month.

PPI stands for payment protection insurance: a policy sold beside a loan or a credit card to cover the repayments if you lost your job or fell ill. Many were mis-sold, and the free route was a complaint to the lender that sold it - the deadline for new complaints passed in 2019, so a policy sold since then is the one worth reading the terms of.

PS stands for postscript, from the Latin post scriptum, meaning written after: the line you add once the letter is finished and signed. On a keyboard P.S. needs the full stops and PS does not, so write whichever matches the rest of what you are typing.

PTSD stands for post-traumatic stress disorder: flashbacks, nightmares, jumpiness and avoiding places after a frightening event, still there a month on. It is not weakness and it is treatable - trauma-focused talking therapy such as CBT or EMDR helps most people - so ask a GP for a referral rather than waiting for it to pass.

Pablo Picasso (1881-1973) was a Spanish painter and sculptor who invented cubism with Georges Braque, breaking a subject into flat shapes seen from several sides at once. Guernica, his answer to the bombing of the Basque town in 1937, is his best-known work.

Pack what you use least first and give it a date: a one-bed flat is about twenty boxes and two weekends if you do it evenings and one weekend if you take a day off; a three-bed house is two or three times that. Every box labelled by the room it goes to, one first-night box kept out of the van, and anything you have not used in a year goes to the charity shop rather than into a box.

Pack for two changes plus one for luck: four or five nappies, wipes or two damp flannels in a bag, a fold-out changing mat, nappy sacks, a full spare vest and sleepsuit, a muslin and a spare top for you. Add a feed - a bottle with the powder in a pot, or a cover if you are breastfeeding - and a snack and water for yourself. Restock it the moment you get home, because the one day it is empty is the day you are out.

Pack for 2 to 8C, wind and rain: a waterproof coat with a hood, warm layers you can take off indoors, and shoes you can walk a hill in. It gets dark around 4pm in December, so a small torch and plans for the afternoon indoors help.

Pack for 2 to 8C, wind and sideways rain: a waterproof coat, warm layers, and shoes you can walk up a hill in. It's dark by 4pm, so plan indoor things for the afternoon and take a torch for Arthur's Seat.

Pack it the night before, not in the morning: the timetable, then the books for those lessons, then the kit or the letter that has to go back. One pocket for pens, one for paper, one for the phone, and nothing loose at the bottom - a bag you can empty in one look is a bag you stop losing things in.

Pain on the outside of the knee that comes on after ten or twenty minutes of running is usually the iliotibial band rubbing: it is a tracking problem, not a worn joint. Cut the run short at the first twinge rather than running through it, run on flatter, softer ground, and shorten your stride. Twice a day, foam-roll the outside of the thigh and do side-lying leg raises and clams; it settles in weeks if you keep runs short till it does.

Pain at the front of the knee on stairs is the kneecap being pulled off line by weak or tight muscles around it, which is common in new runners and in people who sit all day. Three times a week do sit-to-stands, step-ups and wall sits, and ease off hills and deep squats for a fortnight. See a physio if it swells, locks, or the knee gives way under you.

Pain behind the eyes is usually eye strain or a tension headache: screen breaks, an eye test if you have not had one, and water and a dark room for an hour help most of it. Sinusitis makes the area tender and comes with a blocked nose, and migraine can sit there too. Get seen the same day if it is the worst headache of your life, or comes with a fever and a stiff neck, or with blurred or double vision.

Paint keeps for years if the lid is sealed: wipe the rim clean, press the lid down with a block of wood until it clicks, and store the tin upside down so any skin forms at the bottom rather than on top. Keep it somewhere frost-free, because paint that has frozen is never right again. A tin that has gone lumpy or thick can often be saved: lift the skin off, strain it through a pair of tights or a paint strainer into a clean tub, and stir it well - water-based paint takes a splash of water, oil-based takes white spirit, no more than one part in ten. When it is full of hard lumps, or it smells sour, it is past saving and goes to the tip.

Pale, white or blue gums are an emergency, not a teeth problem: lift the lip and press the gum with a finger - the colour should come back within two seconds, and slower than that means the circulation is struggling. Pale gums go with bleeding inside, shock, a badly upset stomach or, in a cat, anaemia from fleas. Ring the vet now and go in today; keep the animal warm and quiet on the way and do not wait to see if it passes.

Pale and otherwise well - eating, drinking, playing, no temperature - is usually nothing: winter, a growth spurt and a diet low in iron all show in the face, and one blood test at the GP settles it. Pale with a temperature, fast breathing, floppiness, unusual sleepiness or no wet nappies is 111 today. Pale with grey or blue lips, a fit, or someone you cannot wake is 999, and so is pale and clammy with chest pain. Pale with a rash that does not fade when you press a glass on it is 999 too.

Palliative care is treatment that controls symptoms and keeps somebody comfortable when a cure is not the aim - and it can run for years alongside treatment for the illness, so it does not mean care has been given up on. It is about pain, breathlessness, sickness, sleep and worry, it happens wherever the person is (at home, in a hospice, in hospital or in a care home), and the GP or specialist nurse can refer. Asking for it early is the thing that makes the last months better rather than the last weeks.

Pan first, then the oil. A dry pan heats evenly and you can judge its heat with your hand or a drop of water, and oil added to a pan that is already hot shimmers and moves at once instead of sitting in a cold pool. The exception is a marinade, a rub or a cold steak straight from the fridge, which goes into the hot oil rather than the bare pan.

Paprika plus a pinch of cayenne is the closest thing to chilli powder: about four parts paprika to one of cayenne, and smoked paprika if you want the depth back. For flakes, a teaspoon is roughly one fresh chilli, so half a teaspoon of cayenne or a chopped red pepper does the job, and a spoon of sriracha, gochujang or hot sauce adds heat and a little sweetness. Without any of those, black pepper and a little ginger give the bite even though the flavour is different.

Paprika is mild, around 1,000 Scoville - closer to a red pepper than to a chilli. A teaspoon colours a pot and sweetens it more than it heats it, which is why a goulash can take two spoons and still be gentle.

Paracetamol and drink is a liver question and ibuprofen and drink is a stomach one, and a normal dose of either with an occasional drink is fine. Paracetamol's warning is about drinking heavily or daily for years, because the liver handles both, and the ceiling stands whatever you have drunk: no more than 4g (eight 500mg tablets) in 24 hours, with no other paracetamol product on top. Ibuprofen mainly raises the risk of stomach irritation and bleeding, so eat something with it and keep to the lowest dose that works. If you drink heavily every day, ask a pharmacist before taking paracetamol at all.

Paracetamol and ibuprofen are not sedatives and neither is meant to make you sleepy - drowsiness is an uncommon side effect of ibuprofen, so if one does leave you dozy it is worth mentioning to a pharmacist. What does make people drowsy is the codeine in co-codamol, and the sleepy feeling is one of the reasons not to drive on it until you know how it treats you. Pain itself is often what stops people sleeping, so a dose at bedtime is fine.

Paracetamol and ibuprofen are both fine while you are breastfeeding - ibuprofen is the one usually suggested for pain with swelling, taken with food. Avoid aspirin, and go easy on co-codamol and other codeine tablets, which can make a baby drowsy. Check what else is in any cold remedy you take, and a pharmacist will check anything else for free.

Paracetamol and ibuprofen are fine with antibiotics - take them as it says on each packet, and they help with the fever and the aches while the antibiotic gets on with the infection. The one to mention at the counter is warfarin, some antibiotics change how it works, and antacids, which need two hours between them and the antibiotic.

Paracetamol is the one to take for a headache in pregnancy, at the lowest dose that works and for the shortest time - not ibuprofen or aspirin unless a doctor or midwife has told you to. Water, food and sleep do a lot, and a skipped meal, dehydration and caffeine withdrawal are the usual causes. Mention headaches that keep coming back to your midwife, and go in the same day if a bad headache comes with blurred vision or flashing lights, pain under the ribs, swelling of the face or hands, or vomiting after 20 weeks: that combination is the one that has to be checked for pre-eclampsia.

Paracetamol is the one to use in pregnancy: the lowest dose that works, for as short a time as you can. Avoid ibuprofen, especially after 20 weeks, and don't take aspirin unless a doctor has prescribed it for you. For anything else - a headache that keeps coming back, heartburn, a bad back - ask your midwife or a pharmacist, who will check it against your stage.
Paris has about 2.1 million people inside the city limits, and about 11 million in the whole metro area - the city proper is small, and the suburbs are where most Parisians live.

Park facing downhill with the front wheels turned into the kerb, and facing uphill with them turned away from it, so the car rolls into the kerb rather than into the road if it moves. Leave it in first gear facing uphill, reverse facing downhill, and pull the handbrake up hard. On a steep hill put a chock or a brick behind a wheel if you have one, and on an automatic use P, which locks the gearbox.

Parking on the pavement is an offence right across London and in Scotland, and elsewhere only where a traffic order covers that street - so the signs and lines on it, and the council's own parking page, are what decide your road, and that is where to check rather than the country as a whole. Where it is allowed you must still leave the pavement clear enough for a wheelchair or a pushchair, and blocking a dropped kerb blocks someone's drive. A ticket for it is a penalty charge notice, argued in the council's own appeal rather than in a court.

Parkrun is a free, timed 5k every Saturday at 9am in a local park: register once online, print or screenshot your barcode, and turn up ten minutes early for the first-timers' briefing. Walkers are genuinely welcome and plenty of people walk it, so you will not be last on your own. No barcode, no time — but you can still run.
Passed is the verb - I passed the shop, she passed the exam. Past is time before now, or beyond something - in the past, walk past the bank.

Passive aggression is anger shown by what a person does not say: a flat 'fine', a sigh, a joke with an edge, being left out of the group chat, help that quietly stops. Treat it as anger that hasn't found words and name the behaviour once, plainly: 'You seemed annoyed when I said that - did it land badly?' Ask about the thing, not the tone, and don't answer it in kind; matching the silence is what turns a week into a year.

Past it, I'm afraid - bin it. A cooked dish keeps 3 to 4 days in the fridge, and rice only 1, so a dish from last week is well beyond that, and reheating it does not make it safe: the toxins that build up in old food do not all break down with heat and they do not all smell. Scrape it out, wash the box with hot soapy water, and next time freeze the half you will not eat within the three days.

Pasta on its own is about 130 calories per 100g cooked and no more fattening than rice or bread: it is the portion (75 to 100g dry) and what goes on it - cream, cheese, oil - that adds up. Wholewheat pasta has more fibre, and cooling and reheating it makes some of the starch harder to digest, which blunts the blood sugar rise a little.

Pasta cooks fine in a microwave, in a big bowl with plenty of room: cover it with boiling water from the kettle, add a good pinch of salt, and give it 8 to 10 minutes on full power, stirring once at the halfway point so the pieces at the top get turned under. Use a bowl at least twice the size of the pasta, because it foams up over the edge otherwise. Test a piece at 8 minutes - it goes from chalky to mushy quickly - then drain it straight away.

Paste it back rather than strip it: lift the loose edge with a knife, scrape the old paste off the wall behind it with a filling knife, spread a thin even coat of overlap adhesive (border and overlap adhesive) on the wall, press the paper back and smooth it out from the middle with a damp sponge. A bubble in the middle gets a slit with a stanley knife, paste, and the same press. Damp patches that keep coming back are not a paper problem.

Pasteurised milk is fine, and worth drinking: about three servings of dairy a day covers the calcium and iodine a baby needs. The one to skip is unpasteurised milk and anything made with it - some farm-shop milk, and raw-milk cheese - because of listeria. If milk turns your stomach early on, yoghurt, cheese and a fortified plant milk cover the same ground.

Pastry shrinks for three reasons: the dough is warm, it is stretched instead of eased into the tin, or it bakes without a rest. Roll it cold, press it into the corners rather than pulling it, leave a little overhang instead of trimming it flush, and chill the lined tin for 20 minutes before it goes in. That rest is what stops the sides sliding down.

Pastry cracks when it's too dry or too warm: sprinkle on a little cold water, chill it for 20 minutes, and roll it between two sheets of baking paper. Patch any tear with a damp finger before it goes in the oven and nobody will see it.

Pay nothing and do not tap the link: couriers never ask for a small fee by text, and the 1.99 is the hook for your card details. Check the parcel on the courier's own website with the tracking number you were given, forward the text to 7726 and delete it; if you did pay, ring your bank and cancel the card.

Pay or appeal within 14 days: most councils take 50% off if you pay in that window, and appealing inside it keeps the discount open. Photograph the sign, the bay markings and where the car was, then appeal online to the council named on the ticket. If they refuse, the free adjudicator cancels a good share - the Traffic Penalty Tribunal outside London, London Tribunals inside it. Never ignore one: it ends with bailiffs.

Pay in by what each of you earns, not by halves: if one of you takes home 60% of the joint income, that person covers 60% of the bills. Keep a joint account for rent, bills and food, keep your own accounts for the rest, and look at it together once a month rather than arguing over individual receipts.

Pay less rather than stop: your own 5% of pay is what unlocks the employer's 3% and the tax relief, so drop to that before you leave the scheme, and change it back whenever a payslip looks better. Stopping altogether costs you the employer's share and the government's top-up, and it takes a phone call to the payroll team to fix, so a tight few months is a reason to pay the minimum rather than to come out.

Paying by direct debit is the cheapest way for most people: suppliers charge less for it than for cash, card or a prepayment meter, and the Direct Debit Guarantee means a wrong amount has to be refunded in full and straight away. If the monthly figure is more than you can manage, ring and ask them to spread the year's use over twelve months rather than ten, or to move the date to just after payday. Behind on it, ask for a payment plan you can keep up rather than one big catch-up figure, and ask what you are owed: the priority services register if you are disabled, ill or caring for a young child, and the discount schemes for low incomes.

Peanut butter is a decent everyday food: two tablespoons is about 190 calories with 7g of protein and 2g of fibre, and it keeps you full. The catch is the jar - buy one whose only ingredients are peanuts and salt, since the sweetened ones add sugar and palm oil - and use a level tablespoon rather than a spoon over the sink.

Peanuts and nuts are fine in pregnancy, and avoiding them does not prevent an allergy - the old advice to cut them out has been dropped. The exception is if you are allergic yourself, or the midwife or GP has told you to avoid them. Nuts are a good snack: a handful with an apple beats a biscuit at three in the afternoon.

Peas that stay hard are usually old: the sugar has turned to starch and no amount of cooking brings them back. Frozen garden peas need 2 to 3 minutes in boiling water, fresh ones 3 to 5. Marrowfat and other big dried peas want a soak overnight and 40 minutes of simmering, and a quarter teaspoon of bicarbonate of soda in the water helps them soften. Acid is the other culprit - lemon juice or tomatoes in the pan keep peas firm - so add those at the end.
Pedro Sanchez is the prime minister of Spain: in office since 2018, and back in office after the 2023 election. The head of state is King Felipe VI, whose role is ceremonial.

Peeling and flaking a week or two in is the tattoo healing, so leave it alone and do not pick at it. Wash it gently with fragrance-free soap and water twice a day, pat it dry and put a thin layer of tattoo balm on, and keep it out of the sun and out of swimming pools for two to three weeks.

Peg out the footprint with a line and dig off about 10cm, then lay 5cm of compacted hardcore under 5cm of sharp sand and stand the shed on bearers or a grid of concrete blocks at 60cm centres, rather than on slabs in the corners where it will sag - or cast a level concrete pad if the ground is soft. Check the level across both diagonals before the shed goes on, because a base that rocks twists the frame and the doors stop closing within a season. Make the base 5cm bigger than the shed each way and a little proud of the grass, so water runs away from the floor rather than into it.

Penguins live in the southern half of the world: Antarctica, and the coasts of South America, Africa, Australia and New Zealand. There are none at the North Pole; the birds there are puffins, which are not penguins.
Peri peri is hot, 50,000 to 175,000 Scoville, and sharp with lemon and vinegar. A spoon in a marinade for four is a strong heat once it is cooked down.

Pesto freezes better than it keeps: spoon it into an ice-cube tray, freeze it, tip the cubes into a bag, and drop one straight into hot pasta. In the fridge it is good for about a week, best with a film of olive oil over the surface.

Pesto is saltier than it tastes because the parmesan and pecorino carry it, so add a pinch only after the cheese is in. If it has gone too salty, stir through more basil, ground nuts or a spoon of breadcrumbs and finish with a squeeze of lemon; more cheese only makes it worse.

Pet insurance is worth it for dogs and cats in most cases: a broken leg can run to £1,500 or more. If you'd rather self-insure, keep a dedicated savings pot of about £1,000 and check whether your vet does a payment plan.

Petite ranges are cut shorter in the body as well as the leg, so start there rather than on the standard rail - most high-street shops carry one online, and the rise and the sleeves come down with the hem. If something you like has no petite cut, buy it to fit the widest part (hips or shoulders) and have the length taken up: a hem is about £10-15 at a dry cleaner or a local tailor and takes a few days. Turn a trouser cuff up once rather than twice, and check the shoulder seam sits on the bone - if it hangs off the shoulder, no hem will rescue it.

Photograph the damage before you unpack further and tell the retailer the same day: they owe you a replacement or refund, and the courier's insurance is their problem, not yours. Don't sign for anything marked damaged without noting it.

Photograph the inside of the fridge and list what was in it before you clear up: if the appliance broke, the shop owes you a repair or replacement under the same 30-day and six-year rights as anything else, and the spoiled food is a separate loss you can ask them for. Most home insurance also pays for spoiled food after a breakdown or a power cut, usually up to a few hundred pounds with an excess.

Photograph every panel, the wheels, the roof and the fuel gauge before you drive off, and walk round it on video: a hire company that charges for damage later has to show the damage was not there when the car went back. Pay with a credit card, because a charge over £100 gives you a claim against the card company, and ask for the damage report and their photos in writing before you dispute it.

Photograph everything before it is cleared up and tell the tradesman in writing the same day, with the cost of putting it right: most have public liability insurance, and that is what pays. If they are not insured or deny it, your own home insurance may cover it and claim it back from them, and Money Claims Online takes the rest.

Photograph it and complain at reception, or to the host if it is a holiday let, before you unpack, and ask to be moved or cleaned: a room that is not what was advertised is a breach of the booking, so you can ask for a refund for that night, and a partial refund for a spoiled stay. If the hotel will not, claim from the site you booked with and then your card company, quoting what the listing promised.

Photograph it in daylight against a plain wall, and price it against what the same thing actually sold for, not what people are asking. Clothes go on Vinted, furniture and anything heavy on Facebook Marketplace, an odd one-off on eBay as an auction with a low start. Take cash, or a transfer that has cleared, before it leaves your hands: a buyer who sends a courier and overpays is the commonest scam there is.

Photos and video are what fill a phone or a laptop: about 3MB a photo, so 10,000 photos is around 30GB, and video runs from 150MB a minute at 1080p to 350MB at 4K. 128GB is enough for most people who stream their music and television and keep photos in the cloud; take 256GB if you record a lot of video or play big games. A laptop is worth 256GB, and a cheap SD card covers the rest.

Pick one substitute word and use it out loud for a week - 'sugar', 'flip', whatever you can say at work - because the habit is in the sound, not the meaning. It spikes with pain and frustration, so slow your breath for a second before you answer.

Pick one thing and do it every week rather than signing up to three apps: a class, a club, a walking group, or a single app you actually answer. Say early what you are looking for, meet in daylight for something short - a coffee, not dinner - and tell a friend where you will be. Choose something side by side over an interview across a table: an hour of climbing, cooking or walking tells you more about someone than two hours of questions about their job.

Pick pears before they are ripe, from late August, while the flesh is still hard: lift one and twist, and when the stalk parts easily it is ready to finish indoors. A pear left to soften on the tree goes gritty and rotten at the core.

Pick peas from June, when the pods are full but still bright green and snap cleanly, and go along the row every two or three days. Leaving them on the plant stops it flowering, and a pod left too long goes starchy and tough.

Pick strawberries from June, when they are red all over including the tip, and pick with a short stalk in the cool of the morning. A berry that is pale at the tip will not sweeten after picking, and one left to rot takes the rest with it.

Pick the one rule and keep it the same every day: the bed or the sofa is off limits, and he has a better place of his own - a bed in the same room, a chew in it, a treat every time he settles there. Say nothing and walk him off by the collar when he tries it, then praise him on his own bed straight away; a telling-off is still attention, and that is half of why he keeps getting up. Nobody in the house should let him up "just this once", because that is the lesson he remembers. If you would rather he shared the bed, put an old blanket where he likes to lie instead, so the fur and the mud land on that.

Pick the one thing you actually mind and let the rest go: sweets straight after school that ruin tea is worth a rule, a biscuit at eleven is not. Say it as the parents' rule rather than a criticism - 'we're doing pudding only after tea at the moment' - and put the treat where it works, at their house and one at a time. Ask them to be the one who gives it: children remember who said yes far longer than they remember what it was.

Pick the one thing you can already do that people pay for, and sell it in the smallest packet: tutoring a GCSE subject, fixing bikes, editing CVs, dog walks on the way home, weekend cover in a bar or care home. Sell to people you can reach this week rather than building a website, do two or three paid jobs before you spend anything on it, and keep a record of what you earn: £1,000 a year of side income is tax free (the trading allowance), and above that you register for Self Assessment.

Pick the subjects you will still work at on a bad week, then check the entry requirements for two or three courses you might want later, because that is what closes doors rather than the subjects themselves. Keeping one essay subject and one numerical one keeps more options open than people expect. Ask a teacher you trust what they think you would enjoy, not just what you are good at.

Pick the thing that matters most and say it once, calmly, as your own view: 'We do that our way here, and it isn't up for debate.' Let your partner handle their own parent where you can, and praise what works; most of this eases once the limits are predictable.

Pick three rather than one: something to come in to, one to sit with during the reflection, and one to leave to. Ask the funeral director for the crematorium's music list and how long each slot runs, because a favourite album track gets cut off halfway. A hymn works best if people know it; a song works best if it was theirs. If the family are choosing too, give each person one slot and let the funeral director hold the list.

Pick tomatoes from late July as they turn fully red, and take the whole truss in October before the first frost. Green ones left then will ripen on a windowsill next to a banana. A tomato is ready when it gives slightly in the hand and smells of tomato.

Pick two the advert actually asks for and hang proof on each: "I'm the one who keeps a messy project moving - on the last one I turned three spreadsheets into one board and we stopped missing deadlines." Two, said slowly, beats a list of five. "I'm a hard worker" and "I'm a perfectionist" are the two that cost you the room.

Pick your lane on the approach and stay in it: left for the first exit or straight on, right-hand lane for anything past twelve o'clock, and use the left lane again for the last exit. Mirror, then signal left just after the exit before yours, and give way to traffic already on the roundabout - it comes from your right, but on a roundabout the give-way line is the rule, not a right of way. On a mini roundabout you still go round the white circle, not over it, and if you miss your exit carry on round again.

Pick by length and tone rather than by fame: 60 to 90 seconds, one idea, and nothing that makes the couple laugh at each other. A poem works if it is plain and short (Auden's "Funeral Blues" is a funeral poem - be careful), and a passage from a book the two of them love beats a sonnet nobody understands. Read it aloud twice before the day, and tell the registrar what you are reading.

Pick a quiet moment rather than a big one, say it in one plain sentence, and say what you want from them: 'I wanted you to know, and you do not have to say anything back' takes the pressure off and stops it sounding like an ask. Then let them have the next move, and give them days rather than minutes to answer - needing time is not a no. If it goes badly, that is about them and their own week, not a verdict on you.

Pick a calm moment with time after it, sit at their level and give the one fact in a short sentence, then say what stays the same: who picks them up, where they sleep, that you are not going anywhere. Then stop and let them ask; the real questions come later, in the bath or the car, and answering them plainly is the rest of the job.

Pick a calm moment, not the moment it happens, and lead with the decision and the plan: "I've decided to leave my job. I've worked out the money and here is what I suggest." Then let them react without defending yourself - the first reaction is almost always about money, so have a number ready and say what you would do if it is tight. If it is bad news rather than a choice, say what happened in one plain sentence and ask for one thing: "I was let go today. I don't want to solve it tonight, I just need you to know."

Pick a calm time, not the moment a bill lands, and put the numbers on the table: what comes in, what goes out, and what is left. Ask what they want to be true in a year - a deposit, a holiday, less stress - before you talk about cuts, because a shared goal is what makes the figures a plan rather than an accusation. Agree one rule you both keep: a joint account for the bills with a set monthly amount in it, personal accounts for the rest, or everything in one pot, and whichever it is, both of you can see it. Say what you are worried about in plain words ('I am scared about the card bill') rather than about them ('you always spend'). If a debt is already in one name only, say so now: a plan made together is the only kind that survives a bad month. And if money is being hidden or controlled, that is not a budgeting problem - talk to someone you trust and to a free adviser.

Pick a calm, sober moment - a morning, or a walk - and say in one or two sentences what you see and how it lands: "when you have four pints on a Tuesday I don't sleep, and I'm worried about you." Don't use the word alcoholic: they will argue about the label instead of hearing you, and the first talk only has to say it. Ask rather than tell - how they feel about it, what they would want to change - and offer one small concrete thing, like going to the GP with them or doing a dry month together. Expect it to land badly the first time and let it go quiet for a week before you come back to it.
