If they will not hear it from you, say it once to their GP or a service like Drinkline, and remember Al-Anon is for you: living with it is its own weight.

Pick a dish that is good on its own rather than meat with the meat left out: a chickpea and spinach curry with rice, a mushroom and lentil lasagne, or a tray of roasted veg with feta and couscous. One proper veggie main plus the usual sides is plenty, and it is worth asking what they actually eat, because vegetarian covers a wide range.

Picking is a hand habit, so give the hand something else: moisturise so the spot feels different, keep a fidget toy or a ring where your fingers go, and cover it with a plaster for the first week so your fingers stop there. Mirrors and screens are where it starts, so keep them out of reach.

A metal taste in food is usually the pan or the water rather than the food: an unlined aluminium or cast-iron pan with anything acidic, a metal spoon left in a tomato sauce, or a furred-up kettle. Cook acidic dishes in stainless steel, enamel or non-stick, move leftovers out of the pan into glass or plastic, and descale the kettle with a 50/50 mix of water and white vinegar.

A metallic taste is usually harmless and usually has an ordinary cause: gum trouble, a dry mouth, a new medicine (metronidazole and some blood pressure tablets are famous for it), a cold or sinus infection, or pregnancy. Brush and floss and drink water through the day, and see a dentist if your gums bleed; see a GP if it lasts more than a couple of weeks or comes with weight loss or a lasting dry mouth.

A meteorite is a rock from space that has landed on the ground; while it is still burning through the air it is a meteor, or a shooting star. Most are chips off asteroids, and the biggest found weighs about 60 tonnes.

A mezzaluna is a half-moon blade with a handle at each end, and you rock it back and forth across the board: for chopping herbs, nuts and garlic finely without a knife's stopping and starting. It is quick on a pile of parsley and hopeless on anything hard or wet.

A microwave floods food with microwaves, which make water molecules spin and rub against each other, and that friction heats the food. It does not make the food radioactive, and it heats unevenly, so stir or leave it to stand.

A mid-contract rise that was not in the terms you signed is a change you can refuse: tell them in writing within 30 days of the notice that you are leaving, on that date, and you owe nothing after it. A rise written into the contract has to follow the wording exactly, and they must tell you personally in advance, not on the website.

A mid-range three-seater is usually £600 to £1,200, with £300 to £500 at the cheap end and £1,500 upwards for a good frame and fabric. The frame, the filling and the fabric are what the money buys, and delivery, assembly and a stain guard are usually extra. Sit on it in the shop for ten minutes and ask what the frame is made of and how long the cover is guaranteed.

A mid-range kitchen is usually £5,000 to £15,000 fitted, and £20,000 or more with appliances, worktops and building work. Roughly a third units, a third worktop and appliances, a third fitting. Get three quotes on the same written scope and ask what happens if the walls are not square, which is where the price moves.

A midlife crisis is the shake-up people often have roughly between 40 and 55, when the shape of a life stops matching the person in it and the changes come in a rush: a new car, a sudden hobby, a job left, a marriage questioned. It is not an illness and it is not inevitable - the research says most people's wellbeing rises through midlife - but the sense of time running out is real, and it is usually about mortality rather than about youth. The useful move is to name what is actually missing (freedom, friendship, a body that works, work that matters) and change that one thing rather than the whole life at once.

A migraine attack usually runs from four hours to three days, and an ordinary headache from a few hours to a day or two. Get seen the same day for a headache that comes on like a thunderclap, one with a fever and a stiff neck, one after a bang on the head, or one with weakness, slurred speech or a change in vision.

A mile is 1,600m, so 64 lengths of a 25m pool or 32 of a 50m one. A steady front-crawl swimmer takes about 30 to 40 minutes, and breaststroke or a first season 45 to 60. Build up 200m at a time - four lengths more each swim - rather than trying the mile on your first session.

A milk tooth going wobbly from about six is normal - let it come out on its own, and do not tie a string to it or pull it before it is ready. See a dentist if it stays loose for weeks with the new tooth coming up behind it, or if the gum is sore or swollen; a milk tooth knocked right out is not put back, so ring a dentist to check it. If the wobbly one is an adult tooth of your own, that is a dentist this week instead: a tooth of your own that has come loose is usually gum disease, and it is treatable.

A mirror does not swap left and right: it swaps front and back, because it sends the light straight back at you. Your face is nearly symmetrical, so the only thing you notice is that a raised right hand seems to be on the other side.

A mirror is glass with a thin layer of silver or aluminium on the back, and light bounces off that layer at the same angle it arrived - in at 30 degrees, out at 30 degrees, which is why you see yourself where the reflection says you are. The glass only protects the silver, so a mirror that has gone patchy has lost that coating rather than got dirty.

A mixture is two or more substances together that are not chemically joined, so each keeps its own properties: sand and salt, or air, are mixtures. You can usually separate a mixture by filtering, sieving or boiling, which you cannot do with a compound.

A DVT is a clot in a deep vein, usually in the calf: one leg swollen, warm and tender, often with a heavy ache, and it is a same-day job - ring 111 or the GP, because a clot can travel to the lung. Sudden breathlessness, a sharp pain when you breathe in, or coughing blood means a clot may already be there, so ring 999. The GP sorts the scan and the blood thinner; do not rub the leg or wait to see if it settles.

A modern LED set is usually good for 7 to 10 years, which is about 30,000 to 50,000 hours of watching; five hours a night is roughly seventeen years of use, so a set that dies at four is the exception and one that lasts twelve is not unusual. OLED panels fade sooner than LCD ones, and the first sign of the end is usually a band or a patch of colour that stays put. If it does go, the panel is most of the price, so replace rather than repair once it is out of warranty.

A mole is a small cluster of pigment cells, the kind you are born with or that arrive slowly over years, and almost all are harmless. The check is the alphabet one: Asymmetry, a ragged Border, more than one Colour, a Diameter over 6mm, and anything Evolving in size, shape or itch. A new dark spot, or a mole that changes over weeks, wants a GP look rather than a wait.

A mortgage offer usually runs three to six months from the date it is issued, six months being the common one, and the clock starts when the lender sends it rather than when you applied. If the purchase is close but not close enough, ask the lender for an extension before it lapses - most will extend it for a fee or free - and do not exchange contracts on an offer with only days left on it.

A mortgage in principle, also called an agreement or decision in principle, is a lender's written 'we would lend you about this much' before you have found a house. It is based on a soft credit check and your income, it usually lasts 60 to 90 days, and estate agents ask for it because it shows you can actually buy. It is not an offer and not a guarantee: the full application checks the property and the paperwork, and the amount can come out lower. Get one before you start viewing and keep the figure you really need in mind, not the top one.

A musty smell is usually damp rather than dirt: check for a leak or a cold outside wall, air the room properly and dry it out before covering anything up. Don't paint over damp patch, because it comes straight back.

A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in space, either thrown off by a dying star or the stuff new stars are forming out of: the Orion Nebula is a star nursery you can pick out with your eyes as a fuzzy patch below the belt.

A neck that is stiff every morning is usually how you slept rather than anything else: a pillow that keeps your head in line with your spine - not propped up, not flat - and a warm shower first thing loosen it. Move it gently through its range rather than holding still. Get it checked the same day if it comes with a fever, a bad headache, or light hurting your eyes.

A negative split is running the second half of a race faster than the first - 5k in 25 minutes then 5k in 24, say - and it is the mark of a well-paced run rather than a fast one. It works because the first half of a race is where people go too quickly: the effort feels easy for the first two miles, so the pace creeps up, and the last third is paid for at a price. Start five or ten seconds a mile slower than your goal pace for the first third, hold it through the middle, and let the last third come to you.

A negative test this early is worth repeating rather than believing: test again in three days, first pee of the morning, because the hormone doubles every couple of days and an early test can simply be too soon. Plenty else shifts a period - stress, a bug, a bad month of sleep, a change in weight, travel, the pill - so one late period with a negative test is common and usually settles. Ring the GP if nothing comes for three months, if the tests stay negative but you feel pregnant, or if there is pain one side at all.

A new phone battery is about £35 to £70 fitted at a local repair shop, and £45 to £90 from the maker (Apple, Samsung), done in an hour or two. It is worth it when the health figure is under 80% or the phone shuts down at 20%; above that, a full day out of the old battery is usually a matter of apps and brightness.

A new small car starts around £18,000 and a new family car around £28,000, and either loses a fifth to a third of that in the first year, most of it in the first hour. A two or three year old version of the same car is about half the new price, which is why that age is where most people buy.

A new carbon steel wok comes with a factory oil on it: scrub that off with hot water and a drop of washing-up liquid, dry it on the hob, then heat it until it just begins to smoke and wipe a teaspoon of groundnut or rapeseed oil round the inside with kitchen paper - three or four times and it goes dark and glossy. After that wash it with hot water and a soft brush, no soap and never a soak, and dry it on the heat. A wok is not non-stick; it gets closer every time you cook in it.

A new closeboard fence is usually £50 to £90 a metre supplied and fitted, so 20 metres of garden is £1,000 to £1,800. Concrete posts and a trellis or a gate push it up, and taking the old one away is often extra. Ask whether the price includes the posts and the removal of the old panels, and check the height limit before you order.

A new combi boiler fitted in place of an old one is usually £1,800 to £3,000, and £3,000 to £4,500 if the pipework has to change or a tank comes out. A service is £60 to £120 once a year. Get two or three quotes on the same boiler model, because the price is mostly the fitter's day and a cheap boiler with a poor warranty costs more later; ask how long the warranty runs and who honours it.

A new joint that feels loose, gives way or clunks hard when you put weight on it is one to have looked at rather than wait for the next appointment: ring the ward or your surgeon's team and tell them when it started and what it does. Sometimes it is weak muscle around a joint that is fine - the physio can tell you that in one visit - and sometimes the parts need checking, which is why it is a phone call rather than a wait. If it gives way and you fall, or the joint is hot and red with it, treat that as urgent: 111 the same day.

A new lump in the breast should be checked by a GP within a week or two, whatever your age - most turn out to be harmless cysts or fibroadenomas, and breast lumps are common. Go the same day if it comes with skin dimpling, a nipple turning in or bleeding, or a hard lump that does not move. Keep feeling for the other breast so you know what is normal for you.

A newborn feeds eight to twelve times in 24 hours, roughly every two to three hours, including waking them if they sleep past four in the first weeks; by four to six months it is four to six milk feeds a day. Six or more wet nappies and a baby who settles after feeds means they are getting enough, and the midwife's scales settle it better than the ounces. Ask for a same-day appointment if they are too sleepy to feed, have fewer wet nappies, or are still under birth weight at two weeks.

A nibble of plain bread will not poison a rabbit or a guinea pig, but bread is not food for one: it swells in a gut that cannot cope with it and can start the bloat and the not-eating that kill small pets quickly. Take the rest away, make sure hay and water are there, and watch for six hours for a tight belly, no droppings or sitting hunched, which is the vet today. Never give mouldy bread, and dough is an emergency.

A nip or a tot is a 25ml measure, the small end of a pub single; a swig is a mouthful of whatever you are drinking and no measure at all. A shot in a recipe is usually 25 to 35ml, so measure it rather than free-pour.

A no-show usually voids the ticket, so ring the airline the moment you know rather than at the airport: many will move you to a later flight for a fee, and a flexible fare may let you do it free. Check the check-in closing time, which is often 45 to 60 minutes before departure, and see whether your insurance covers the reason you were late.

A no ball is the bowler overstepping the popping crease, throwing instead of bowling, or sending down a full toss above waist height: the batting side gets a run and the ball is bowled again. In one-day and T20 cricket the next ball is a free hit, when a batter can only be run out.

A non-refundable rate usually means no cash back, but ring the hotel and ask to move the date instead: many will with notice, and it costs nothing to ask. If you booked through a site, that site holds the cancellation, not the hotel.

A normal resting heart rate for an adult is 60 to 100 beats a minute, and most people sit between 60 and 80; fitter people run lower, and 50 is normal for a regular runner. Take it properly: sit quietly for five minutes, find the pulse on the thumb side of the wrist, and count for 30 seconds then double it. A rate that stays over 100 at rest, drops under 60 with dizziness or fainting, or is irregular should be checked by a doctor rather than watched.

A normal working day is fine for an adult dog if it gets a proper walk before you go and another when you are back, and someone lets it out at lunchtime on the long days - a dog walker, a neighbour or daycare. What is not fair is a puppy, or ten hours with no break at all. Build the time alone up slowly, and an older rescue that is used to a quiet house often suits a working day better than a puppy does.

A normal cold lasts about a week to ten days, and the cough can hang on for two or three. Rest, fluids and paracetamol are the treatment; see a GP if it's getting worse after a week rather than better.

A normal cotton wash is about two hours and an eco wash three or more, because eco heats the water slowly and soaks; the quick programme is 15 to 30 minutes and is for a small, lightly worn load, and the spin at the end of any of them is only 10 to 20 minutes. If you want it done fast, use quick with a lower spin, and run the long eco one overnight on a full load instead.

A normal credit card charges about 20% to 25% APR, a card for people with a thin file can be 30% or more, and a 0% purchase or balance-transfer deal is the cheap way to borrow for a set time. The representative APR is only the rate at least 51% of accepted applicants get, so check the rate you are actually offered before you apply, and add any annual fee. Paid in full each month, none of it matters - no interest at all.

A nose that runs all the time is usually an allergy - pollen, dust mites or an animal - or a rhinitis that comes from cold air, smoke or a spray, and both behave the same way: a salt water rinse and a steroid nose spray from a pharmacist, used every day for a fortnight, settle most of it, and an antihistamine helps the itchy, sneezy sort. Keep the bedroom dusted and the windows shut when the count is high. See a GP if it is only one side, if there is blood in it, or if it has gone on for months with no cause found.

A numb patch of skin around the scar is normal after a joint replacement and it often stays that way: the small nerves under the incision are cut on the way in, so the skin there feels wooden, tingly or dead to touch, and it usually softens over a year or two rather than meaning anything about the joint. An itchy scar is the same story - healing nerves - and so is a scar that pulls or feels tight. A scar that turns hot, red, weepy or spreads, or numbness that comes on suddenly or spreads up the leg, is the one to ring the ward or 111 about, the same day.

A numb arm is usually a nerve being pressed or stretched: lying on it, a heavy bag on the shoulder, or tight neck and shoulder muscles. Shake it out and change position, and it should ease. If it came on suddenly, or comes with a weak hand, a drooping face or slurred speech, ring 999 now; see a GP if it keeps coming back or the arm feels weak.

A numb lip, tongue or cheek after a filling is the local anaesthetic still working: it fades in two to five hours, and a lower-jaw injection often longer than an upper one. While it lasts, eat soft cool food and chew on the other side, because it is easy to bite your lip or cheek without feeling it, and don't have a hot drink. Ring the dentist if it is still numb the next day, or if there is swelling, a fever or a bitter taste with pus. A face that droops or will not move on one side, or an eye that will not close, is not the anaesthetic - that is 999.

A pacemaker is a matchbox-sized unit under the collarbone with one or two thin leads into the heart: it watches the beat and sends a small electrical pulse when it goes too slow or skips, so the heart keeps a steady 60 or so. Fitting one takes about an hour under a local anaesthetic, the battery lasts 8 to 12 years and is swapped with the whole unit, and a yearly check reads it through the skin.

A package buys you protection and less admin: the flights, the transfer and the hotel are one booking, and if the operator fails you are covered and brought home. Booking it yourself is usually cheaper, especially for a city break where you want a flat rather than a hotel, but you carry the risk - so book the flight on a credit card and check the hotel's own cancellation terms. For a beach week with children, the package usually wins on the day something goes wrong.

A paddling pool holds 300 to 800 litres, so buckets are the hard way: pull the drain plug if it has one, or lift one side and let it run into a drain or a big bucket, or hook a short hose over the lowest edge and syphon it out. Water that has only had children in it can go on the flower beds rather than the lawn, but water with chlorine or soap in it should go down a drain, since it scorches grass. Scrub the inside with hot soapy water, rinse, dry it in the sun and store it folded and dry, because a pool put away wet comes out black and slimy next summer.

A page turner is a book whose plot pulls you through - short chapters, a question you want answered, a twist you did not see - rather than one you admire slowly. The shorthand comes from book reviews because it says nothing about quality: a thriller can be a page turner and so can a good memoir. If you want one, say what you last could not put down and I will find something in the same shape; if you want a specific book, tell me the kind of story rather than the word.

A paid booking is a contract, so the hotel has to put you somewhere comparable at their cost, or give the money back and pay for what the move cost you. Ask for the alternative in writing while you are still at the desk, keep the taxi and phone receipts, and claim from the hotel, then the booking site. Only a real breach - damage, a noise complaint, too many people - lets them end the stay.

A palette knife is the long flexible blunt blade with no edge, for lifting, spreading and levelling rather than cutting: icing a cake flat, lifting a slice off the board, sliding under a fish to turn it. An offset one - the blade stepped down from the handle - is for spreading inside a tin.

A pan that sticks has usually lost its thin layer of baked-on oil: scrub it, dry it on the hob, rub a film of neutral oil over the inside and heat it until it just smokes, then wipe the surplus off with kitchen paper. Twice more and it is slippery again. That works on stainless steel, carbon steel and cast iron. A non-stick pan is the exception - once the coating is scratched through, nothing brings it back, so replace it.

A pan handle gets hot because the metal carries heat up from the base, and the flame licking past the side of the pan makes it worse: keep the gas inside the base so it does not climb the wall, and use a lower heat with a bigger pan rather than a fierce flame under a small one. Hold the handle in a dry folded tea towel or a silicone sleeve, never a wet cloth, because water carries heat straight through to your hand. Turn the handle in over the hob when you are not holding it, so nobody catches it going past.

A panel that came out in the wind is usually a post that has moved, not the panel, so check the posts are upright with a spirit level before you fix it back: a new panel on a rotten post goes over again. Replace a rotted post base with a concrete repair spur, or set a new post 600mm into the ground in Postcrete, and brace it until it is solid.

A panic attack peaks in about ten minutes and cannot hurt you, so the aim is to ride it rather than stop it: breathe out for longer than you breathe in, name five things you can see and four you can touch, and remind yourself it will pass. Don't fight the heart rate - it is adrenaline, not a heart problem. If they keep coming, ask about CBT: it is the treatment with the best evidence, and a GP can refer you.

A pantry or larder is a cool, dark, dry cupboard for the food that keeps: tins, dried pasta and rice, flour, sugar, oil, spices. Cool and dry matter more than size - a shelf by a radiator or a sunny window turns flour and rice stale and brings weevils - so put it on an outside wall away from the cooker. Keep the oldest at the front of the shelf and the new shopping behind it, and write the date on anything you decant into a jar.

A parallelogram is a four-sided shape with both pairs of opposite sides parallel and equal, so its opposite angles are equal too. A rectangle is a special parallelogram with right angles. Its area is the base times the perpendicular height, not the slanted side.

A part that hurts rather than has snapped is usually loose at its joint: tighten the screws or bolts, check the bracket and the glue line, and keep the weight off it until it feels firm. If it moves when you lean on it, treat it as a break - drill out the old glue, fit a wooden dowel or longer screw, and clamp it overnight.

A party wall is a wall, floor or ceiling that two properties share, or a wall that stands on the boundary between two gardens, and it comes with its own law: the Party Wall etc. Act 1996. If you are doing work on one - a loft, an extension, a new chimney breast, digging foundations within three metres of next door - you serve a notice on the neighbour two months before, and a week before for a simple party wall job. If they agree in writing the two of you can go ahead; if they object, each side appoints a surveyor who sets a party wall award saying how the work is done and who pays. Doing it without the notice is the mistake: the neighbour can go to court and stop the job.

A passkey replaces the password with your fingerprint or face, so there is nothing to type or phish: your phone or laptop holds the key and proves it is you. Turn one on wherever an account offers it, and keep the old password as the fallback for now.

A patch about three metres by two is the size most first plots are, and it feeds two people through a summer. Keep the bed no wider than 1.2m, so you can reach the middle from either side without standing on it, and work back from the plants rather than from the area: a tomato wants 45cm each way, a courgette a square metre to itself, and salad leaves 20cm apart. Two of each is plenty in the first year. A raised bed wants twenty centimetres of soil for salad, herbs and dwarf beans, and thirty for carrots, onions and tomatoes.

A patio slab sits on a full bed of mortar, not on sand alone and never on five dabs: 40mm to 50mm of sharp sand mixed 4 to 1 with cement, so about half a cubic metre of sharp sand for 10 square metres - roughly 800kg, most of an 850kg bulk bag - with 5 bags of 25kg cement. Double both for 20 square metres. Mix it stiff enough to hold the slab when you tap it down with a mallet and lay to a string line, and under a patio on soil put 75mm to 100mm of compacted type 1 down first, which is the part that stops it sinking. Sand alone shifts and washes out, which is why patios laid on it go wobbly in a couple of winters.

A patio is usually £60 to £120 a square metre laid, so a small 15 square metre patio is £900 to £1,800, and block paving for a driveway £80 to £150 a square metre. The base and the drainage are what separate a good job from a cheap one. Ask what depth of sub-base they are laying, and whether the price includes the skip and the sealing.

A pawn moves one square forward and takes one square diagonally forward, so a pawn never moves or captures backwards. From its starting square only it may go two squares, and that is what lets the en passant rule exist: if a pawn goes two squares and lands beside an enemy pawn, that pawn may take it as if it had moved one, on that move only. Getting to the far end promotes it to a queen, rook, bishop or knight, and a queen is almost always right.

A pawn shop, or pawnbroker, lends you money against something you leave with them - jewellery, a watch, a musical instrument - and holds it until you pay back the loan plus interest, usually 5% to 10% a month; if you do not, they sell it. You get far less than the item is worth, so it is a short-term fix rather than a way to raise money: a credit union loan or a free debt adviser such as StepChange costs much less if you can wait a few days.

A payday loan is a small, short loan at an enormous rate: £100 for a month can cost £120 to repay, an APR of over 1,000%. The regulator caps it at 0.8% a day and no more than double the original loan in total. If it is food or rent you need, a council crisis grant, a credit union or a repayment plan with the bill is the cheaper route.

A pencil rubber takes most scuffs off a matt emulsion, and a damp sponge with a drop of washing-up liquid takes the rest - rub gently, because the paint comes off with the mark if you scrub hard. For ink or a stubborn scuff a melamine sponge works, but try it low down first: it is a fine abrasive and it dulls sheen and eggshell.
A pendulum is a weight on a string that swings to and fro at a steady rate, which is how clocks kept time for three hundred years: a longer string swings more slowly, and the weight hardly matters.

A period that comes early is common and usually just a short cycle: stress, a bug, a change in sleep or travel, a big drop in weight, or the pill can all bring one on, and the spotting some people get at ovulation a couple of weeks before is often taken for one. Write the dates down for the next two or three - if they stay under three weeks apart, if you bleed between periods or after sex, or if the bleeding is very heavy, that is a GP appointment. If there is any chance you could be pregnant, test anyway: a bleed can happen early on.

A permanent colour cannot be washed out: a colour remover, about ten pounds, shrinks the dye molecules so they rinse away, and it works far better on a fresh job than on one that has been there months. A semi-permanent fades by itself in six to eight washes, faster with a clarifying shampoo and warm water. Neither will rescue hair that has also been bleached, and a salon correction is the honest answer for a big mistake.

A pest controller is usually £80 to £150 for a wasp nest and £100 to £250 for rats or mice, which usually covers two visits and the bait. Bed bugs are the expensive one at £300 to £800 for a flat, sometimes with a second treatment. Your council may do rats and mice cheaper, so ring them first, and ask whether the price includes the follow-up visit.

A pestle and mortar is a heavy bowl and a rounded club for crushing rather than cutting - spices, garlic, herbs, salt - which is why it gives a different, more fragrant result than a blade: the cell walls burst and the oils come out. Dry spices first, then anything wet, then wipe it out with salt and a cloth rather than washing it.

A pharmacy antifungal cream or spray - clotrimazole or terbinafine - clears most athlete's foot in two to four weeks, and keep using it for a week after the skin looks normal or it comes back. Dry between your toes properly, change socks daily, and dust the shoes with antifungal powder. See a GP if it has not cleared in a month, or the skin is cracked, weeping or spreading up the foot.

A phone screen has a grid of transparent conductors carrying a small charge; your finger conducts, so it changes the charge where it touches and the grid works out the spot. That is why a thick glove, a wet finger or a cracked patch misses, because none of them carries the charge the screen expects.

A phone that turns itself off is nearly always the battery: at 20% or 30% it reads the charge wrong and shuts down, so check Battery Health, and a worn battery is £40 to £70 to replace. If it does it at full charge, take the case off and see whether it happens when it is warm, and back it up before a repair. A phone that reboots on its own every few hours can also be an app, so start it in safe mode for a day.

A phone contract runs 12, 24 or 36 months and 24 is the usual one, and a SIM-only deal is the same shape at a lower price: 12 months, or rolling a month at a time. The minimum term is what ties you in, and it is what an early exit charge counts back from. When the term ends the contract carries on at the same monthly price rather than stopping, so ring then - the deals offered to an existing customer are cheaper than the one you are on, and if the handset is fine a SIM-only deal is about half the price.

A phone goes from empty to full in about 1.5 to 2 hours on an ordinary charger, and a fast charger gets to half in about half an hour and finishes in a little over an hour. The last 20% is the slowest part on purpose - it tops up gently to look after the battery - so a phone that seems to stall near full is behaving normally.

A pill box with the days on it, filled at the same time each week, is the fix that works for most people, and a phone alarm set for when you actually eat beats one at a random hour. Ask your pharmacy about a weekly blister pack as well - many make one up for free.

A pinch of food once or twice a day, and only what they clear in two minutes: a fish's stomach is about the size of its eye, and uneaten food fouls the water faster than anything else. Skip one day a week, use flakes or pellets made for the species rather than bread or scraps, and if the water clouds up after a feed, you are feeding too much.

A pinch is what you can hold between your thumb and finger: about 1/16 of a teaspoon, a little under half a gram of salt, and a good pinch nearer one. A dash of liquid is about 1/8 of a teaspoon, and a handful is 30 to 40g.

A piping bag is the cone you fill with icing, cream, choux or meringue mix and squeeze out through a nozzle, so it comes out in the shape you want - a rosette, a line, a swirl. A disposable bag plus a star nozzle covers most of it; a sandwich bag with the corner snipped off does for a swirl.

A pit stop is the stop for fresh tyres: the crew changes all four in about two seconds, and with the drive down the pit lane at the speed limit it costs roughly 20 seconds of race time. Most races are one or two stops.

A plain sponge or fruit cake keeps 3 to 4 days in a tin, and a week in the fridge if it has fresh cream or custard in it. Undecorated, it freezes well for 2 months: wrap it whole, and ice it after it thaws. It goes stale because the starch firms up rather than because it dries out: a tin with a lid, half an apple in it, and 15 seconds in the microwave brings a slice back.

A plain unperfumed cream is the whole job: thicker (an ointment, or a cream in a tub) for dry or flaky skin, a light lotion or gel for oily skin, and one with SPF 30 in it for the morning if you want to skip a step. Put it on damp skin within three minutes of a shower, buy the cheap own-brand - the price is packaging - and a pump is cleaner than a tub you dig your fingers into.

A plant that has gone tall, thin and stretched is short of light, not ill: it is reaching for the window. Move it nearer the light and turn it a quarter turn each week so it grows evenly, then cut the straggly stems back by half - most houseplants send out two shoots from the cut, and the pieces you cut off will root in a glass of water.

A plant that is bare at the bottom, or long and thin instead of bushy, is short of light: the leaves at the top are the ones getting it and the stems below have dropped theirs for want of it. Move it nearer a window out of direct midday sun, turn it a quarter turn each week so it grows evenly, and in spring cut the long leafless stems back by about a third - new shoots come from the joints just below the cut, and bare stems will not leaf up again on their own. To make it bush rather than climb, pinch out the top pair of leaves every few weeks. If it needs to be smaller, take a cutting from the top first.

A plasterer is usually £150 to £250 a day, or £15 to £25 a square metre for skimming: a whole room's walls and ceiling is £300 to £600, and patching a ceiling after a leak is £80 to £150. Boarding over old plaster adds £200 to £400 a room. Ask whether the price includes the boards and the finishing coat, and how long it takes to dry before paint.

A plug, socket or cable that is hot, buzzing, scorched or smells of burning is not safe to keep using: unplug it at the wall, or switch that circuit off, and leave it off. Warm to the touch is normal for a charger; too hot to hold, crackling, brown marks, a fishy smell of hot plastic or a fuse that keeps tripping is not, and that plug or socket needs replacing by an electrician before it is used again. Never open a socket yourself, and do not just change the fuse and carry on.
A poblano is mild, 1,000 to 1,500 Scoville - roasted and stuffed it tastes of smoke and green pepper, not of heat.

A poinsettia is only a mild irritant: the sap makes a cat or dog dribble and feel sick, and it usually settles without treatment. Rinse the mouth with water and keep the plant out of reach. Mistletoe and holly berries are the ones to ring the vet about.

A posset is milk coming back up with a burp, usually within an hour of a feed, and it is what most reflux in a young baby is: the valve at the top of the stomach is still loose. Keep them upright for twenty minutes after a feed, give a little less and burp more often, and keep the milk going rather than swapping it for water, because a baby under a year needs the feed more than the drink. See the GP if it comes up forcefully, is green or has blood in it, or they are not putting on weight; under three months with a temperature, the same day.

A post that has rotted or gone loose at the bottom wants replacing, not bracing: dig it out and set a new 100mm post 600mm into the ground, prop it plumb, and fill the hole with Postcrete poured dry and watered. If only the bottom has gone, cut the post off above the rot and bolt a galvanised repair spur onto the sound timber. Line the new post up with its neighbour before the concrete sets, and stand it on a gravel board or a slate so the base is not sitting in wet soil.

A pot that smells sour or of drains is waterlogged compost going anaerobic, and the roots are already suffering: stop watering, tip out any water in the saucer, and let it dry out for a week or two. If the smell stays, take the plant out, cut away any roots that are brown and mushy, and repot it in fresh compost in a pot with holes.

A pot that has barely grown over a year is usually in the scheme's default fund withdrawn in cash or bonds rather than shares, or paying charges of 1% or more a year that quietly eat the growth - so find the fund name and the total charge on the yearly statement first. Over decades a global shares fund has beaten cash by a wide margin, and a default that is too cautious is the commonest thing wrong with an otherwise healthy pension; switching funds inside the scheme is free and takes ten minutes.

A potato ricer is a press: you fill the hopper with cooked, dried potato and squeeze the handles, and the potato comes out through small holes in threads. That is what makes mash smooth without a machine - no lumps, and, unlike a blender or a food processor, it never overworks the starch, which is what turns mash gluey.

A potato masher is the wavy wire or plate on a handle, for crushing cooked potato, swede, carrot or beans straight in the pan. It leaves a rougher mash than a ricer, which is fine for most things and wrong for a smooth one: add the butter and milk warm, and mash while the potato is hot.

A power bank is worth it if you are out all day: look for 10,000mAh (about two full charges, pocket-sized) and at least 20W output, so it charges quickly rather than trickling. Anker and Belkin are the reliable ones, around £20 to £35; check it has USB-C output for a modern phone, and keep it in your hand luggage on a plane.

A prefix goes on the front of a word and a suffix on the end: un- in unhappy, -ness in happiness, and the base word (happy) is the root. An antonym is the opposite - hot and cold, early and late - which is the other half of what a synonym is, so if the word you want means the same, look for a synonym, and if it means the reverse, an antonym.

A premium bond is a savings bond costing £1 a unit, up to £50,000, where the interest is paid out as monthly prizes instead of a rate: the prize fund is about 4% a year, but most months with a small holding you win nothing, and the smallest prize is £25. The money is safe and available, so it suits savings you might need, not ones you are counting on growing.

A prepayment meter makes you pay before you use the fuel, so it suits a home where credit is the risk, but the standing charge is often a bit higher and you lose the cheapest direct debit tariffs. A supplier can only force one on you for a debt, and only after writing to you, so ask for a repayment plan instead and for the meter to be swapped back once the debt is cleared. You can ask your supplier (or any new one) to swap it for a credit meter once you are in credit and not behind; they cannot charge you for switching away from a prepayment meter if you ask for it after a debt is cleared. If you cannot top up, ring the supplier — they must give emergency credit.

A prescription in England is £9.90 an item, and it is free in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Check the exemptions before you pay, because a lot of people pay and should not: under 16, 16 to 18 in full-time education, over 60, pregnant or with a baby under 12 months, or on a benefit, and some long-term conditions are exempt. If you pay for more than about 12 items a year, a prepayment certificate is about £33 for three months or £115 for a year and covers everything on it. Get one on the NHS website or at a pharmacy counter, and it starts the day you pay, so buy it before the next item rather than after it.

A private car park's 'fine' is a parking charge notice: an invoice from the company, not a council ticket, and ignoring it is how it becomes a court claim. Appeal to the operator inside 28 days with photos and the signs as they were, and if they turn you down they must give you a code for a free appeal to POPLA or the IAS. Overstaying is only chargeable if the signs were clear and the amount is a genuine estimate of their loss.

A private check-up is usually £40 to £80, with a hygienist visit £40 to £70 and a filling £80 to £200. On the NHS in England you pay a fixed band charge set nationally, which covers the check-up and any work in that band, and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own charges. Ask which band your treatment falls in before you agree to it.
A proton is one of the particles in the middle of an atom, carrying a positive charge, and the number of them is what makes an element what it is: one is hydrogen, six is carbon, eight is oxygen.

A proving basket - a banneton - is the bowl a shaped loaf sits in for its last rise. It holds the dough up as it spreads upwards instead of outwards, and its ridges leave the flour rings on the crust. Dust it heavily with flour (rice flour is best, it does not stick) or line it with a cloth; washed and wet, it goes mouldy.

A psychiatrist is a doctor who can diagnose mental illness and prescribe medicine; a psychologist studies and treats the mind with talking therapy and usually can't prescribe. A GP can refer you to either, and which one you need depends on whether medicine is part of the question.

A pulsar is a tiny, extremely dense dead star that spins and sweeps a beam of radio waves past the Earth, so a telescope sees a regular pulse: some tick faster than a kitchen blender. They are accurate enough to be used as clocks.

A pump moves water by pushing it: a spinning impeller flings water outwards into the casing, or a piston shoves it along, and the pressure it builds is what drives the flow. Pumps push rather than pull, which is why air in the pipe stops one lifting water and a pump that has lost its prime has to be filled again.

A pump moves a refrigerant round a sealed loop, and inside the fridge a pipe lets it expand, so it turns very cold and takes heat out of the food. A compressor then squeezes it, and the heat leaves from the coil at the back, because that is where it is dumped - which is why the back feels warm. Cold air is denser, so it sinks - which is why the bottom shelf is the coldest.

A pump sits between the hot and cold supplies and the shower head and gives the water a push, because a low-pressure gravity system only has the height of the tank in the loft behind it. It needs both a hot and a cold feed it is allowed to draw on - a pump on a mains-fed combi does nothing - and the usual reason one goes weak is air or a filter, not the pump itself.

A quadrilateral is a flat shape with four straight sides and four corners, and its angles add up to 360 degrees. Squares, rectangles, parallelograms, rhombuses, trapeziums and kites are all quadrilaterals; a shape with four sides that is not a quadrilateral does not exist.

A quiche is set by its eggs, so leaving them out gives you warm vegetables in a pastry case rather than a quiche. The nearest thing is 300g of silken tofu blended smooth with a tablespoon of cornflour, or 100g of chickpea flour whisked with 250ml of water and a spoon of oil for a firmer, nuttier set: bake either at 180C for 30 to 35 minutes, until the middle still wobbles. If the reason is an allergy, read the pastry label too, because some shortcrust has egg in it.

A quiet corner away from the food and water, and not next to the washing machine or a door that bangs, because a cat will not use a tray where she cannot hear trouble coming. One tray for each floor, somewhere she can leave in two directions rather than a dead end, and never inside a closed cupboard or under a lid: a tray in the dark is where the mess starts.

A quiet day is usually nothing: watch for the next twenty-four hours, and check the basics - is he eating, drinking, weeing and pooing as usual, and any limping, sickness or yelping when you touch him? A pet who is off his food for a whole day, or low and also sick, lame or drinking a lot, should see a vet rather than wait.

A rabbit thumping a hind foot is a warning, not a problem: it has heard something new, and it does it most at dawn and dusk when a rabbit would be out feeding. Look for a fox or a cat outside the hutch and give it a covered box to bolt into; a rabbit that also stops eating or sits hunched up needs the vet.

A rabbit chews because its teeth grow all its life, so hay all day plus apple or willow sticks and a cardboard box give it something better to chew. Then make the wires boring: plastic trunking or a length of hose split down one side over them, tucked behind the furniture, and a pen that keeps the back of the telly out of reach. Chewing the bars means more space and more to do, not less.

A rabbit lives 8 to 12 years, which is longer than most people expect when they buy one for a child. A rabbit on its own in a small hutch usually dies years earlier than a pair with a run and hay all day, so company and space are the two things that matter.

A rain shadow is the dry side of a mountain range: air is forced up the windward side, drops its rain there, and comes down the other side warm and dry. Deserts like the one east of the Rockies sit in a rain shadow.

A ramekin is a small straight-sided dish, for one portion of something baked or set - custard, a souffle, a fondant, potted shrimp, a dip on a plate. The straight sides matter: the contents slide out in one piece and a crust forms all the way up.
A rat lives 2 to 3 years, and they are social, so a pair lives longer and better than one alone. That short life is the hard part of keeping them.

A reading of 140/90 or higher, seen twice at home, is high and worth a GP check: they will confirm it and talk through treatment. Meanwhile cut salt, keep to 14 units of alcohol a week, and 150 minutes of walking a week lowers it by a few points. 180/120 or higher with a bad headache, chest pain or blurred vision is 999.

A real tree drops its needles because it has dried out, so give the trunk a fresh inch cut off the bottom before it goes in the stand and keep the stand topped up with water - a big tree can drink a litre a day in a warm room. Keep it away from the radiator and the fire, and once it is shedding heavily it is past saving: take it down.

A red oil light means stop as soon as it is safe and switch the engine off: it is oil pressure, and driving even a mile can wreck the engine. Check the level once it has cooled; if the level is fine and the light is still on, it needs a tow, not a drive.

A red, watery, gunky eye is usually conjunctivitis or an allergy: cool compresses, lubricating drops from a pharmacist, and no contact lenses until it settles. See someone the same day if the eye is painful, light hurts, your sight has dropped, or the eyeball feels hard - that is a different problem from a sticky eye.

A red, hot, throbbing finger is an infection of the fingertip or the nail fold - a whitlow or paronychia - and warm salty water is what helps it: soak it for ten minutes three or four times a day, keep it clean and covered in between, and take paracetamol for the throb. Don't squeeze it or dig at the nail, because the fingertip is a closed space and pus pushed deeper is worse. See a GP the same day if the redness is spreading past the finger, there is pus, or you have a fever; a red streak running up the arm is 111 today. Have it looked at sooner if you have diabetes.

A referendum is one yes-or-no question put to the whole electorate instead of to parliament - the 2016 vote on leaving the EU, and the 2014 vote on Scottish independence before it. It is not legally binding in UK law, but no government could ignore a clear result, so in practice it settles the question.

A refund must reach you within 14 days of the shop agreeing to it, or of getting the goods back, and it goes to the original payment card. If it's late, send one written chaser with the dates, then ask your card provider for a chargeback.

A refund goes back to the card you paid with, not to a different one, and it still works on a closed card: the money lands in the account behind it, so ring the bank and tell them one is coming. If the account itself is closed they will take it in and pass it on, sometimes for a fee. If it has not arrived 14 days after the shop says it paid, ask them for the acquirer reference and raise a chargeback with your card company.

A relative going quiet is usually nothing more than a busy year. Send something small and specific - a photo, or a plain 'I've missed you, are you around for a call?' - rather than a note about how long it has been. Name a day and a time, because 'we should catch up' keeps nothing happening. If they do not answer, try once more a fortnight later and leave it there.

A remark lands as a verdict because you fill in the meaning in the gap, so put a pause there: ask one plain question ("what did you mean by that?") or check it with someone who was in the room before you decide what it says about you. Then split the fact from the story - "she did not ask me again" is what happened, "she does not rate me" is a guess - and notice where it happens: with one person it is usually about them, with everybody it is worth asking what makes you braced. Being tired or already having a bad week makes everything land harder, so give it a night before you reply to anything you would not want read aloud.

A renewal is a new quote, not a bill, so start three weeks early and compare two or three others: the same cover is often £100 to £200 cheaper elsewhere. For home and motor insurance the renewal price cannot be higher than a new customer would pay for the same cover, so say so in writing if it is. Ring to cancel before the renewal date, and ask for the annual price rather than monthly.

A repair has to be done within a reasonable time: put a deadline in writing, 14 days, and say that if it is not ready you will collect the item and want the repair price back. Keep a copy, and ask for the item back in writing so there is a record of the date. If the shop still holds it after that, a card chargeback or Money Claims Online recovers what you paid.

A repair is usually £60 to £120 including the first hour, with parts on top, so expect £100 to £200 for a common fault. On a machine more than eight years old, compare the quote with a new one: a £150 repair on a ten-year-old machine is often money down. Ask for the call-out charge and whether it comes off the repair if you go ahead.

A repeater halves the speed it repeats and only helps where the signal is weak but present, so put it halfway between the router and the dead room, ideally in line of sight. If the room gets nothing at all, it will repeat nothing, and a mesh system is the better buy.

A reptile is a cold-blooded animal with a backbone and dry, scaly skin. It cannot keep its own body temperature, so it warms up in the sun, and most lay leathery eggs on land - lizards, snakes, turtles and crocodiles are the groups.

A residential home is about £800 a week and a nursing home £1,100 to £1,400, so £42,000 to £73,000 a year, and it swings a lot by area. The council only helps once savings and property are under £23,250, so ask for a financial assessment in writing, and a deferred payment agreement means the house is not sold while you are alive. If the need is health rather than social care, ask the GP about NHS continuing healthcare.

A rhetorical question is asked for effect, not for an answer: "Who could blame her?" It nudges the reader towards the answer you already have, which is why it works well as an opener and badly as a real enquiry.

A rhombus is a four-sided shape with all four sides the same length and both pairs of opposite sides parallel; a square is a rhombus with right angles, and a diamond shape is one too. Its area is half the product of its two diagonals.

A rib that hurts when you breathe in, cough or press it is usually bruised, not broken, and it mends the same way either way: keep breathing normally rather than in shallow sips, take paracetamol or ibuprofen, and press a cushion against that side when you cough. It eases over three to six weeks. Get seen the same day if you are breathless or coughing blood.

A roast vegetable and feta traybake is hard to beat: chop peppers, red onion, courgette and sweet potato, toss in oil, salt and thyme, roast at 200C for 35 minutes, then crumble feta over and give it 10 more. Serve with couscous and a sharp green salad.

A roast is one joint, potatoes, two veg and gravy, and the veg is where you ring the changes: carrots and parsnips roasted round the meat for the last 45 minutes, greens or cabbage steamed, and peas with mint if it is lamb. Add Yorkshire puddings for beef, stuffing and apple sauce for pork, bread sauce for chicken or turkey. Work back from the meat, because the joint rests 20 minutes and that is when the potatoes go up to full heat.

A roasting tin is the deep-sided metal tin that goes in the oven for joints, roast vegetables and traybakes. Metal, not glass, for high heat and for browning; leave a gap between the pieces so they roast rather than steam, and put the tin in the oven while it heats for crisper potatoes.

A roofer is usually £200 to £300 a day, and the small jobs are priced whole: a patch or a few slipped or broken tiles is £150 to £400, a flat roof on a garage £1,500 to £3,000. A whole roof - a full re-roof or a new roof on a three-bed semi - is £5,000 to £15,000, and scaffolding is £800 to £1,500 of that on its own. Ask whether the quote includes the scaffolding, the disposal of the old covering and a guarantee on the workmanship, and get three quotes on the same written description of the job.

A root canal is a tooth saved rather than taken out: the dentist drills in from the top, cleans the infected nerve out of the canals inside the root, and seals them. It takes one or two visits of 45 minutes to an hour and a half, and with modern numbing it feels much like a filling - the pain comes from the infection before the visit, not from the drilling. The tooth is brittle afterwards, so a crown on a back tooth is the usual last step, and some soreness for two or three days is normal.

A routine consultation is 15 to 20 minutes; a procedure, a scan or a dental is longer and the practice will tell you how long when you book. Ask for an estimate before they start, and for the out-of-hours number on the way out.

A roux is equal weights of butter or oil and plain flour cooked together in a pan, and it is what thickens a white sauce, a gravy or a soup: melt 25g of butter, stir in 25g of plain flour and cook it a minute to take the raw flour taste off, then add the milk or stock a splash at a time, whisking. A pale roux thickens most, and the darker you cook it the less it thickens, which is why a brown roux for gravy needs more flour.

A rubber-backed mat slips once the backing is wet, worn or filmed with soap, so the fix is suckers pressed onto a clean dry floor, or a cheap anti-slip underlay cut to size. Wash and dry the tiles first: soap film is what most of these slips come from. If the backing has gone smooth or hard it will not grip again and the mat wants replacing - a slick mat on a tiled floor is how people end up at the hospital with a wrist.

A running bamboo spreads with rhizomes just under the surface, so it is contained rather than pruned: a root barrier of thick polythene or HDPE, 60cm deep and set at a slight angle outwards, all the way round, with the top 2cm left showing above the soil so you can see a rhizome trying to hop it and cut that off. Never dump a dug-out rhizome on the compost heap: it roots.

A runny nose is mostly your body flushing out irritants: the lining makes extra mucus to trap pollen, dust or a virus and wash it away, and it can keep running for a while after the trigger is gone. Clear, watery stuff is usually allergy or cold; thick green mucus is not automatically an infection, but a fever or one-sided pain should be checked.

A runny nose is the lining making extra mucus to flush out a cold or an allergen, so saline spray or a salt-water rinse, steam from a shower and a decongestant spray for up to three days are what settle it. An antihistamine helps if it itches and sneezes too. See a GP if it is one-sided and bloodstained, lasts more than three weeks, or comes with face pain and a temperature.

A sail works like a wing stood on end: the wind crossing the curved side travels further and faster than the wind on the other side, the pressure drops, and the sail is pulled forward. That is why a boat can head towards the wind but not straight into it - you work about 45 degrees off it and zigzag, turning through the wind to gain ground, which is tacking.

A sale does not end your tenancy: the buyer takes the flat with you in it, your agreement carries on and your deposit stays protected. Keep paying the rent to your current landlord until they give you the new owner's details in writing, and keep the receipts. If they want you out for the sale, they still have to give you the notice your agreement and the law require - a sale is not notice - and a court order if you do not leave. Do not sign anything or hand back the keys without advice; Shelter or Citizens Advice will check the notice free.

A sauce in the time they boil: a spoon of peanut butter, soy sauce, a squeeze of lime and some chilli; or fry them with an egg and whatever veg you have plus soy sauce. Sesame oil and sliced spring onion at the end is what makes them taste like the takeaway.

A saucepan is the deep, round pan with a long handle, for anything with liquid in it - sauces, rice, pasta, boiled eggs, milk. Size is the thing people get wrong: a small pan boils over and a big one scorches a small amount, so 16-18cm for one or two people and 20cm for a family.

A saute pan has straight, fairly high sides and a wide flat base: enough floor to brown without crowding, enough wall to hold a sauce or a braise. It is the pan for a risotto, a curry or a chicken joint browned and then finished in the oven.

A scab is a plug of dried blood, platelets and a stringy protein called fibrin that seals a cut while new skin grows underneath it. Leave it alone - it is the dressing - because picking it off reopens the wound and makes a scar more likely, and the itch under it is new skin and nerve endings knitting back. A scab with spreading redness, heat or pus around it is the one to get looked at.

A scale that switches itself off mid-weigh or jumps about almost always wants a new battery, and one that reads a little wrong wants checking against something whose weight you know: a 1kg bag of sugar should read 1kg and 500ml of water weighs 500g. Weigh on a hard, flat surface with the feet clear of the worktop and nothing else touching the bowl. If it is still out by more than a few grams on a known weight, throw it away rather than cooking around it, because every bake after that is a guess.

A school in England can issue a penalty notice for unauthorised absence - one per parent, per child - and it is halved if it is paid within 21 days and rises if it is not, so check the letter rather than assume. Absence the school has authorised for illness is not that, so send a note for every day and keep any appointment letters. If the absences are anxiety rather than defiance, ask for the pastoral lead, the SENCO or the attendance officer before it gets to a notice: support comes before punishment, and a GP can write the letter that makes the school listen.
A scotch bonnet is very hot, 100,000 to 350,000 Scoville, with a fruity, almost apricot taste that survives the heat. One, deseeded, is enough for a family curry.

A scratch in the glass will not polish out, and toothpaste or a jeweller's rouge only turns one line into a hazy patch. Leave a shallow scratch, put a tempered-glass screen protector over it to hide it and stop it spreading, and for a phone price the glass replacement at a local repair shop first - it is usually £30 to £60 and a protector on the new screen is cheaper than a second repair. A bulge or a crack you can feel with a fingernail needs the screen replacing, not cleaning.

A scrum restarts play after a knock-on or a forward pass: the eight forwards of each side bind together and push against the other pack, the scrum-half feeds the ball into the middle, and the hooker strikes it back with a foot. The side that shoves the other back can win the ball against the head.

A sea breeze is the cool air blowing in off the sea on a sunny afternoon, because land heats faster than water, so the warm air over the land rises and the cooler sea air moves in to replace it. At night the pattern reverses as the land cools faster.

A seat belt is a strap that locks: a reel lets it pull out slowly so you can move, and a sprung weight inside catches on a ratchet when the car stops suddenly, so you are held back instead of going forward. An airbag is a cloth bag a chemical charge fills with nitrogen in a twentieth of a second, and it only works with the belt.

A seed waits until it has water, warmth and oxygen, then its stored food fuels the first root and shoot. Once the shoot reaches light, the plant starts making its own food by photosynthesis, so the seed's reserves matter less.

A select committee is a small cross-party group of MPs - or peers - that examines one area, like the Treasury committee or the health committee. They take evidence from ministers, officials and outside experts and publish reports the government has to answer, which is where a lot of the detail a debate never reaches comes from.

A septic tank is an underground tank for a house with no mains sewer: waste flows in, the solids sink and settle, bacteria break them down, and the clearer liquid runs out through pipes into a soakaway in the ground. Nothing goes in it but pee, poo and paper - wipes, fat and bleach are what kill the bacteria - and a tanker has to empty it every year or two. A blocked or smelly one is usually a soakaway that has had its chips.

A series of religious wars from 1096 to the late 1200s, called by the papacy to take control of holy sites in the Middle East. The First Crusade captured Jerusalem in 1099; the rest largely failed, and the trade and ideas that moved both ways mattered as much as the fighting.
A serrano is 10,000 to 23,000 Scoville - two or three times a jalapeño, with a cleaner, greener taste. Half a one is enough for a curry for four.

A set menu is one fixed price for two or three courses chosen from a short list, and it is usually the best value on the board. A la carte is the full list with every dish priced on its own, so you pay for exactly what you want and nothing else. A tasting menu is a run of small courses the kitchen decides, priced per person and taken by the whole table. If you want the cheapest good meal, order the set menu; if there is one dish you really came for, order that a la carte.

A set of tyres lasts roughly 20,000 to 40,000 miles, and 5 to 6 years from the date on the sidewall even if the tread looks fine, because the rubber hardens. Change them when the tread reaches 3mm for wet grip, or sooner if the sidewalls crack. All four together is best; if you replace a pair, put the new ones on the back.

A set dessert like that keeps 2 to 3 days in the fridge, covered, and it is better on the second day than the first. A cheesecake is 3 to 4 days and freezes well in slices; a mousse or a posset is the shortest at 2 days, because it is mostly cream and egg.

A shake or pulse through the pedal or wheel when you brake is usually a warped or worn disc, and a car that pulls to one side under braking has a sticking caliper or a collapsed hose. Either way it is a garage job soon, and the discs and pads on that axle are usually replaced together, about £150 to £300.

A shake that appears at one speed and fades above it is usually wheel balance, about £10 to £15 a wheel to fix. A judder only when braking points to warped discs, and a wobble over bumps is usually a worn bush or a buckled alloy.
A shallot is a small, mild relative of the onion, grown in cloves, sweeter and gentler raw. Use shallots where you want onion flavour without the bite - dressings, sauces, or roasted whole.

A shallow dent in bare wood comes back up with water and heat: wet the spot, lay a damp cloth over it and press a hot iron on for a few seconds at a time, checking as you go. Once the wood has a finish on it a dent cannot be raised, so the repair is filler, sand and a matching wax or varnish.

A shared office line rings for everyone, so the fix is a rota rather than the block list: take turns to answer, put the line on voicemail for the hour you need to concentrate, and give the people who ring most a better way to reach you. If the calls are sales calls to the business, the residential Telephone Preference Service does not cover you - ask the phone provider about call filtering, and never press a number to "speak to someone".

A shark is a fish: gills, cartilage instead of bone, and a tail that swings side to side. A dolphin is a mammal: it breathes air through a blowhole, has a skeleton, feeds its young milk, and its tail moves up and down.

A shine or scorch is flattened or slightly burnt fibre: sponge it with white vinegar, cover it with a pressing cloth and press it dry. A deep brown burn can't be undone, but a mild shine usually fades after a wash.

A shiny or dry patch on the face is usually one area of skin that is oilier or drier than the rest of it, or a little sun damage, and plain care settles most of them: wash with a gentle cleanser, pat dry rather than rub, and use a light oil-free moisturiser twice a day - give it a fortnight before you judge it. Show a pharmacist if it is raised, scaly, itchy or bleeding, because they can tell a harmless patch from one worth checking, and see a GP if it is growing, changing colour or still there after a few weeks.

A shirt is sized by the neck and the chest: measure round the base of the neck where the collar sits, with one finger's room, and round the chest at the widest part under the arms, over a shirt you would wear underneath. A dress shirt is sold by the neck in inches plus the sleeve length - a 15 in neck is about a 38 in chest and a medium in most casual ranges, 15.5 about 40, 16 about 42 - and a casual shirt goes by the chest alone: 36-38 in is a small, 39-41 medium, 42-44 large, 45-47 extra large. Use the shop's own chart, because the same letter is up to two inches different between them, and take the tape over what you would wear it with rather than against bare skin.

A shop holding your goods for repair has to look after them, and if it loses one it owes you what it would cost to replace, not the repair fee: put it in writing with the make, model and what you paid, and ask for their insurance details. If they will not settle, the free route is a letter before claim and then Money Claims Online, from about £35.

A shoulder that stiffens up over weeks until you cannot lift the arm, especially turning it outwards, is usually a frozen shoulder: the capsule around the joint tightens, often for no clear reason. It eases in stages, and most people take 1 to 2 years to get most of the movement back. Keep using the arm as far as it goes, warm it before gentle stretches, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen if you can; a GP can refer you for physiotherapy and give a steroid injection early, which helps most in the painful first stage.

A shoulder that clicks without pain is usually harmless - it is tendon sliding over bone or a bit of scar tissue - and it needs nothing. If it clicks and hurts, catches, or the arm feels weak overhead, see a physio: rotator cuff and shoulder blade exercises fix most of it without an operation, and the sooner you start the quicker it settles.

A shower of five minutes rather than ten saves about 40 litres a time, and a dripping tap wastes around 5,500 litres a year - both are a washer or a shorter timer, not a new bathroom. After those, run the washing machine and the dishwasher only when they are full (a half load uses nearly the same water as a full one), put a water butt on the downpipe for the garden instead of a hose, and drop a cistern bag in an old loo, which saves a litre or two a flush. A water meter is free to have fitted in most of the UK and usually cuts a bill for one or two people, though a big family can pay more on one.

A shower that goes cold after a few minutes is usually the hot water, not the shower: a combi boiler only heats what you draw, so check whether the hot tap is still hot. If the tap is fine, the shower valve is scaled or failing, and cleaning the head in vinegar is the first free test. If the tap runs cold too, look at the boiler: its pressure gauge wants 1 to 1.5 bar while cold, and its fault code when it cuts out says what it is unhappy about.

A shower curtain clings because the hot water makes the air rise, and the rising air drags the curtain in behind it - so the fixes are weight and air. A hem with weights in it, or a magnet at the bottom corners if the tray or bath is steel, holds it down; a curtain that hangs to just below the rim of the tray clings less than a long one that pools; and a curved rail holds the curtain away from you while it hangs. If it still flaps, leave the bathroom door ajar so the room is not sealed, which is often the whole cause in a small bathroom with the window shut.

A shower is usually fine once the dressing is off and the wound is dry and sealed, and most wards send people home with a waterproof dressing so it can happen sooner - but a bath, a hot tub or a swim waits until the wound is fully closed, around two to six weeks, because standing water is where infection gets in. Pat the wound dry rather than rubbing it, leave it open to the air when you can, and put nothing on it - no creams, oils or powders. Ring the ward or 111 if the wound turns hot or red, leaks or smells, or the edges start to open.

A sick day is for not being fit to work, and a head that will not settle counts as much as a temperature does: say "I'm not well enough to come in today" and nothing more - you do not owe a diagnosis, and you do not have to invent flu to be believed. Do not post the day out, and if the same week keeps needing one it is worth telling your manager what is behind it, because a run of odd days looks worse than one honest conversation. If it is longer than a week or two, that is a GP appointment.

A sickness bug usually lasts one to three days, and you can feel washed out for a few days after that. You are most infectious in the 48 hours after it stops, so stay off work or school for two days after the last episode. Take small sips often; ring 111 if you cannot keep any fluid down, there is blood, or a baby is not wetting nappies.

A side or rear window is toughened glass, so a chip or a crack in it is a new pane rather than a repair: a glass company or a mobile fitter supplies and fits it, £60 to £150 for most cars and more for a window with a heated rear element. Give them the registration or the VIN, because the glass is cut to the car. Check the door seals, the central locking and the window motor work before they leave, and cover the gap with plastic and tape rather than driving with broken glass in the door.

A sieve is the round mesh for flour, icing sugar, cocoa and custard: it breaks up lumps and puts air in, which is why a sponge recipe sifts. The mesh is fine, so it also strains small quantities of liquid and seeds; for a big pan of pasta you want a colander, whose holes are large enough for the water to leave in seconds.

A sim holds your number, your contacts and your texts, not photos, so what fills it is old messages. Delete the old texts first, and picture messages go first because they are big. Copy the contacts to the phone itself or to a Google or Apple account so they do not live on the card, then back up the texts you want to keep - a new sim does not bring the old messages with it.

A single pane of ordinary glass is £60 to £120 fitted, and a sealed double-glazed unit is £100 to £250, with a big or toughened one £250 to £500. A broken window boarded up the same day is £100 to £200. Ask whether the frame is sound, because a rotten frame means a whole new window at £400 to £1,000, and check whether your home insurance covers the glass.
A single chirp every minute or so means a low battery: change it now, don't wait. If it's a sealed ten-year alarm, replace the whole unit, and vacuum the dust out of the vents either way.

A single figure only means something with its timing: 4 to 7 mmol/L before a meal and under 8.5 two hours after is the usual target for someone with diabetes, so 7.8 two hours after eating is close to it, and 7.8 before breakfast twice is worth a GP visit. If you have not been diagnosed, one reading cannot diagnose anything - ask for an HbA1c, which averages the last two or three months. Write down the time with the number.

A sinking fund is money set aside a little at a time for a cost you know is coming: £50 a month for a roof, a boiler or a car's tyres. Work out the bill and the years, divide, and keep it in a separate easy-access account so it is not spent. It is the same idea a leaseholder's building fund uses, and it is why a repair is a plan rather than a shock.

A skillet is a frying pan with straight, deeper sides and usually an ovenproof handle, built to take high heat: searing, frying, then going into the oven to finish. In Britain the word is used loosely for a heavy frying pan; the straight side is the part that matters, because it holds the fat and the food in.

A skin abscess is a pocket of pus under the skin, and the treatment is to let it drain rather than squeeze it: hold a warm flannel on it for ten to fifteen minutes three or four times a day, keep the skin clean and dry, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen at the dose on the pack if it is sore. Do not squeeze, prick or cut it, because that pushes the infection deeper. See a GP promptly if it is getting bigger or more painful, if you have a fever or feel unwell, if it is on your face or hand, or if you have diabetes or a weakened immune system - those often need antibiotics or a small drainage. Ring 111 if the redness is spreading quickly, and 999 if you are confused, breathe fast or feel very ill.

A slotted spoon has holes or slots in the bowl, for lifting the solid part out of a liquid and letting the liquid drain back: vegetables out of a pan, olives out of a jar, a poached egg out of the water, skimming the scum off a stock.

A small motor in the handle shakes the head a few thousand times a minute, far faster than a hand can scrub, so it breaks plaque up by vibration rather than by pressure. That is why you guide it slowly along the gumline, and why pressing hard makes it clean worse instead of better.

A small notebook with three or four prompts - the stories you want to tell and two questions to ask - is normal and reads as prepared; reading whole answers off a page does not. Glance at it when they ask something you planned for, then look up and say it in your own words. If there is a test or a presentation they will tell you what is allowed, and asking the recruiter beforehand is fine.

A smart meter sends your readings to the supplier itself, so you stop reading meters, and it comes with an in-home display. An old meter needs reading by you or a visitor. Neither changes what you pay per unit.

A smart meter is the gas and electricity meter that sends your readings to your supplier itself, so nobody has to read it and the bill is based on what you used rather than an estimate. It comes with a small display for the kitchen that shows what you are spending as you use it. It is free from your supplier and it does not change your tariff.

A smart plug goes between the socket and the thing, and you switch it from an app or by voice; it is the cheapest way to make a lamp, a fan or a Christmas tree smart. Check it is rated for what you plug in (13A for a heater, and never for anything that must not be cut off, like an iron or an electric blanket) and that it works with what you already have, Alexa or Google or Apple Home. Around £10 to £20 each.

A smart TV slows down because of its apps and its wifi, not its screen: close what you are not using, uninstall the apps you never open, then unplug it for a minute and let it restart. If menus still crawl, it is usually the wifi - move the router closer or run an ethernet cable - and a £30 streaming stick with a fresh processor beats replacing the set.

A smash is hit steeply down from above your head: get behind the shuttle, meet it high and in front, and snap the wrist through it as you step forward. The drop shot and the net shot are the same action with a slower swing, the first landing just over the net and the second taken close in so the shuttle tumbles over. A smash is the last shot to learn: a weak one hands your opponent the attack.

A smear test checks the cells on the cervix for the changes that can turn into cancer, and it takes about five minutes with a nurse: a soft brush collects a sample and most people feel a scratch rather than pain. The sample is tested for HPV first, and only a positive one goes on to be looked at under a microscope, which is why most results come back normal. It is offered every three years from 25 to 49 and every five years from 50 to 64; an abnormal result usually means a repeat in a year, not cancer.

A smell from a kettle is nearly always scale or water left standing in it: fill it with equal parts water and white vinegar, boil it, leave it half an hour, then boil fresh water and tip it away twice. A new kettle's plastic smell fades after a few boils; a musty one means water has sat in it, so empty it each night. If the taste still comes through, filter the water.

A sneeze is the nose throwing out something that irritates its lining, and what helps depends on which of the two usual causes it is. If your eyes or the roof of your mouth itch, it is an allergy: a once-a-day antihistamine started before you go out, a saline rinse, windows shut in pollen season and a shower before bed. If it came on with a sore throat and a temperature, it is a cold and settles in a few days: paracetamol, water and rest. Don't hold a sneeze in with the nose pinched - it can push air into the ear. See a GP if it is one-sided, bloodstained, or has gone on for weeks.

A sneeze is your nose clearing itself: dust, pollen or a virus irritates the lining and the body blasts air out to shift it. The droplets fly several metres, which is why you catch it in your elbow rather than your hand.
