A sneeze is a reflex that clears the nose: dust, pollen or a virus irritates the lining and the body takes a sharp breath and blasts air out to shift it. The droplets fly several metres, which is why you catch it in your elbow rather than your hand, and bright light makes some people sneeze.

A soapy or chemical taste is too much bicarbonate, because the soda had nothing acid to react with. Use about a quarter of a teaspoon per 100g of flour and give it something sour - buttermilk, yoghurt, lemon or treacle. Sift it with the flour rather than stirring it in at the end, and a squeeze of lemon over a baked one hides most of it.

A soft or slightly damp microfibre cloth, rung out so it is barely wet, and a bucket of warm water with a drop of washing-up liquid: it holds the dust against the cloth instead of pushing it back into the air the way a feather duster does. Go from the top down, the tops of the cupboards and the picture rails first and the skirting boards and floor last, so what you lift off lands somewhere you are going to vacuum anyway, and do the flat surfaces before the ornaments on them. Rinse the cloth in the bucket as soon as it stops picking dust up, work a room a wall at a time rather than round and round, and leave the radiators and the tops of the doors for the same pass - that is where the grey layer builds up first.

A softener that has stopped using salt has usually bridged: the salt has crusted into a solid shelf over the water, so push a broom handle down into the tank - if it will not sink, break the crust up and let it re-dissolve. If the salt is loose, check the bypass valve is shut, set the hardness to your supplier's figure for your area, and clean the brine injector; still hard after that and it needs a service.

A soggy pizza is three things at once: a cool oven, a thin tray and a wet topping. Heat the oven and the tray to its top setting for 20 minutes, roll the base thin and put it onto the hot tray, drain the mozzarella and pat any vegetables dry, and keep the sauce to a thin layer. Bake it high for 10 to 12 minutes, then finish it under the grill for a minute.
A soggy stir-fry is a crowded pan: cook it in two batches over the highest heat you have, dry the vegetables well first, and add any sauce only at the very end off the heat.

A sole trader is one person running a business with no company around them: you and the business are the same, you register with HMRC, file a self assessment and keep what is left after tax and National Insurance. You can trade under your own name or a business name, your accounts stay private, and you are personally liable for the debts - which is the part that matters if the work involves risk. Register as soon as you start earning more than £1,000 in a tax year, keep every receipt, and put a third aside for the bill.

A sole trader is you and the business as one: simplest to run, but you're personally liable for its debts. A limited company is a separate legal person, so your own money is protected if it fails, and in exchange you file accounts publicly at Companies House.

A solicitor is who you deal with directly: contracts, conveyancing, wills, letters, and preparing a case. A barrister is the court specialist who argues it in front of a judge, and a solicitor usually instructs them for you.

A solid fence is a sail, so the wind pulls on the posts rather than passing through: slatted panels, or a gap under the gravel board, let it through. Set the posts 600mm into the ground in concrete, keep the panel out of the soil, and brace the end posts. A trellis strip along the top takes most of the load off a windy corner.

A solvent is the liquid something dissolves in, and the thing that dissolves is the solute: water is the usual solvent, while white spirit and acetone dissolve things water cannot, like paint and nail polish.

A sore tailbone is usually a knock from a fall or hours sitting on a hard chair, and it mends slowly - a few weeks, sometimes a couple of months. Sit on a soft or doughnut cushion, tilt forward a little rather than leaning back onto it, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen; a warm bath helps the muscles around it. See a GP if it is no better after a few weeks, or if there is numbness or bleeding.

A sore throat in a child is nearly always a virus and settles in three or four days: keep the drinks going, give children's paracetamol or ibuprofen by weight for the pain, and don't expect antibiotics, because they do not help most of them. Honey in warm water helps over one year old and never under. Ring 111 the same day if they cannot swallow at all, are drooling, or the throat is so sore they will not drink; ring 999 for a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it, or difficulty breathing. See a GP if it keeps coming back with big red tonsils.

A sore groin is usually a pulled muscle from twisting, kicking or turning quickly: give the sport that set it off a fortnight off, ice it for 20 minutes at a time for the first two days, then stretch and strengthen gently. Get a lump or a bulge that appears when you cough or lift looked at - that is a hernia - and get a sudden severe pain in one side seen the same day.

A sore knee is usually a strain or the kneecap tracking badly: ease off running, stairs and kneeling, ice it for 20 minutes at a time with a cloth round it for the first two days, then keep it moving gently. Get it looked at if it gives way, locks, or you cannot put your weight on it.

A spare set is the first call, then breakdown cover - most policies include a lockout callout - and then a car locksmith, at about 50 to 120 pounds, who opens it with a wedge and a long rod in a few minutes without damage; an ordinary house locksmith often has nothing that fits a car door. Don't break a window unless someone is in danger, and if you must, a door glass is far cheaper than the windscreen or a rear quarter light. If the key is in the ignition with the engine running, stay with the car and do not let the tank run dry.

A spatula is the flat, flexible, blunt tool for scraping and folding - getting every bit of cake mix out of the bowl, folding egg whites in without knocking the air out, easing a fried egg off the pan. A silicone one will not scratch a non-stick pan; the metal sort that turns and lifts food is the fish slice.

A speeding ticket is usually £100 and three points, or a speed awareness course instead at about £100 if you were not far over the limit and have not done one recently. If it goes to court the fine is means-based and up to £1,000, or £2,500 on a motorway, and the points can be more. Pay within the 28 days and tell your insurer: the policy nearly always asks, and finding out later costs more than the fine.

A sphere is the solid round shape where every point on the surface is the same distance from the centre, like a ball or a marble. Its volume is 4/3 times pi times the radius cubed, and its surface area is 4 times pi times the radius squared.

A spider is the wide, shallow wire-mesh basket on a long handle. It lifts food out of boiling water or hot oil - fried chips, blanched greens, a poached egg, a handful of pasta to test - and lets the water or oil run straight back into the pan, without dragging the pan off the heat.

A spinning class is indoor cycling on a fixed bike for about 45 minutes to music: the instructor calls out when to stand, sprint or add resistance, and you turn the resistance knob yourself, so the effort is as hard as you make it. Set the saddle to hip height, take a towel and water, and start with the resistance light enough that you could still talk.
A splash is a loose tablespoon or two, and a drizzle a thin stream over the top: both are meant to be tasted and topped up, so start small.

A spoonful of honey is as good as any over-the-counter cough syrup for a cough or a scratchy throat, and it is the one thing the NHS suggests first: a teaspoon straight, or in a warm drink with lemon. Never under a year old, because of the botulism risk. See a doctor if it lasts more than three weeks or comes with a fever.

A spore is a single cell that fungi, mosses and ferns release instead of seed, and it grows into a new plant if it lands somewhere damp enough. That is why mould spreads through a room as dust, and why moss appears on a wall.

A sports bra is a bra built to hold the breast still rather than shape it, and the amount it holds is graded: low support for yoga and walking, medium for cycling and weights, high for running and anything bouncy. Buy it by the band size rather than the cup alone - it should be snug on the loosest hook with two fingers of room under the band - and replace it when the band has stretched, usually after about a year of regular washing. Wash it cool after every wear, because sweat and elastic do not get on.

A sprained ankle or wrist usually hurts a lot for two or three days and is properly better in two to six weeks; a bad one can take three months. Ice it for 20 minutes at a time for the first couple of days, wrap it, keep it up when you can, and start moving it gently as the pain allows. Get it checked if you cannot put weight on it, it is badly swollen and bruised, or the joint looks out of shape.

A springform tin has a clip on the side: undo it and the ring lifts away from the cake, so a cheesecake or a torte goes out of the tin without being turned upside down. Line the base or the leaky ones drip, and run a knife round the inside before you release the clip, which stops a set top cracking.

A spurt shows in appetite, sleep and shoes before height: a month or two of eating like a horse and sleeping longer is the growth itself. The aches that come with it are usually growing pains, which are real but harmless - both calves or thighs, evening or night, gone by morning, in a child of three to twelve. Rub the leg, use a warm pad, and give children's paracetamol if it wakes them. See a GP if it is one leg only, if they limp or refuse to walk, if there is swelling, a rash or a fever, or if it hurts in the day.

A square number is what you get when a whole number is multiplied by itself: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and so on, because 4 × 4 = 16. It is called square because that many dots make a square grid, and it is always a whole number.

A standard GP appointment is 10 minutes, so it is worth naming the one problem that matters most and what you need from it. If there are several things, say so when you book and ask for a double slot rather than trying to fit them in.

A standing order is yours: a fixed amount on a fixed date, set up and cancelled in your banking app, and the payee cannot create one. A direct debit is the other way round - you give permission and the company takes what it has told you it will, and the Direct Debit Guarantee means the bank must refund an unauthorised one in full. To stop one, tell the bank and the company.

A starter that has stopped rising is usually hungry, cold or both: give it equal weights of flour and water, about its own weight, at room temperature (20 to 25C) and it should double in four to eight hours. If it has gone quiet, feed it twice a day for three or four days without putting it back in the fridge, and use wholemeal or rye flour for one of those feeds, which wakes it faster than white. A dark liquid on top is alcohol, not death: pour it off and feed. Mould - pink, black or furry - is the only one to throw away.

A starter in the fridge will sit for weeks without much harm and months if you feed it now and then: once a week is plenty in the cold, and a grey liquid on top is alcohol, which you pour off. Before you bake, take it out, feed it and let it double at room temperature, and feed it twice a day for two days if it has been in there a while. Going away for a month is fine - feed it thick, spread a spoonful on baking parchment, dry it and it can be woken up afterwards.

A state that began in Anatolia around 1300 and grew to cover the Balkans, the Middle East and north Africa, ruled from Istanbul. It fought alongside Germany in the First World War and broke up in 1922, replaced by modern Turkey.

A statin blocks the liver enzyme that makes cholesterol, so less LDL ends up in your blood: expect roughly a 30 to 50% fall in LDL depending on the dose, with the biggest benefit for anyone who has already had a heart attack or stroke. Muscle aches are the side effect people worry about, and in trials they were about as common on the dummy tablet; if you do get them, try a different statin or a lower dose before giving up, because the benefit is real. Don't stop one on your own: ask the GP or pharmacist.

A station puts the sound onto a carrier wave, varying its strength (AM) or its frequency (FM), and your aerial picks up every wave in the air at once. The tuner keeps the one frequency you want and the circuit turns its variations back into sound, which is why a weak station hisses.

A steady sound is easier on sleep than a screen, because there's nothing to watch. Keep the radio or podcast low and on a sleep timer; if it is a fan or white noise, point it away from your face. If the noise is a neighbour's, earplugs and a heavy curtain take the edge off.

A steady amber engine light means 'get it checked soon' and the car is usually fine to drive gently; a flashing one means stop, because a misfire can wreck the catalytic converter. Before panicking, check the fuel cap is tight and on properly: it is the cheapest cause there is. A garage reads the code for £20 to £50.

A steady front crawl does a mile - 64 lengths of a 25m pool - in about 30 to 40 minutes. Breaststroke, or a first season of swimming, is 45 minutes to an hour, and building up 200m at a time gets there better than trying the mile straight away.

A steady hum is the motor or the pump doing its job, and every machine has one. A hum that is new or louder is usually the machine standing uneven, something loose touching the case, or a filter or drain pump half blocked: level the feet, take the filter out and clean it, and check the drum or spray arm turns freely with the power off. A whine that rises with the speed is a bearing, which is a repair rather than a service.

A steak and kidney pudding is dinner, not afters: line a buttered basin with suet crust (200g self-raising flour, 100g suet, a pinch of salt, water to a soft dough), fill it with beef skirt and kidney tossed in flour, season it hard and add a little stock, then lid it and steam it for three to four hours. Serve it with mashed potato, buttered greens or peas and extra gravy, and turn it out onto a plate with a cloth round the basin. It is better made a day ahead and steamed again, which is how it suits a Sunday.

A stick blender is the wand you put straight into the pan or jug: soup, sauce, a smoothie, all blended where they are, with nothing to pour and one thing to wash. Keep the blade under the surface before you switch on or it spatters, and do not use it on boiling soup in a deep pan without taking the pan off the heat first.

A stitch is a cramp-like pain in the side, from the diaphragm and the ligaments holding it being pulled while you breathe hard - most often in running. Slow down, breathe out fully, and press a hand into the sore spot; it usually eases in a minute or two, and building distance up gradually stops it coming back. Pain that stays after you stop, or comes with vomiting, is not a stitch.

A stitch is a cramp in the sheet of muscle under the diaphragm, and it usually means you are breathing shallowly or ran too soon after eating. Slow down, breathe out hard through pursed lips, and press your fingers under the ribs on the sore side while you walk it off. Leave two hours between a proper meal and a run, and warm up for five minutes before you pick up the pace.

A stock cube is dried concentrate, about one per 450ml of water, and salty. A stock pot is wet ready-made stock in a tub - fresher tasting and less salty - used one pot to roughly 500ml. Either is fine; taste before you season.

A stockpot is the tall, deep pan for a lot of liquid over a long time: stock, a big pan of pasta, a ham hock, a batch of soup. Tall and narrow is the point - less surface means less evaporation - which is the opposite of a wide saute pan.

A stomach ulcer is a raw patch in the lining of the stomach or the first part of the bowel, usually from an H. pylori infection or from ibuprofen and other anti-inflammatory painkillers: a gnawing or burning pain high in the belly, worse when you are hungry or at night. See a GP - a breath or stool test for H. pylori and a course of acid-suppressing tablets clears most of them. Ring 999 for vomited blood or black tarry stools.

A stopover only helps if you can sleep in a bed: a night in a hotel halfway resets you gently, while a four-hour wait in an airport at 3am just breaks the journey. If you are stopping anyway, take the wait in daylight at the far end and set your watch to the destination as you board the last flight, then sleep on that leg if it is night there.

A storage unit is usually £60 to £150 a month for 25 to 50 square feet, which holds a one-bedroom flat, and the first month is often half price. The price creeps up after the intro offer, and insurance is either included or pushed at you on the day. Ask what the rate is in month four, the notice period, and whether you need your own padlock.

A student loan pays the tuition fee and the maintenance money while you study, and it is only paid back through your pay once you earn over the threshold: 9% of what you earn above about £25,000 a year on plan 5, taken like tax and stopping the month your pay drops below it. The fee part covers the whole fee, and the maintenance part is sized to your household income and whether you live at home or away. Repaying early is rarely worth it, because anything left after 30 to 40 years, depending on the plan, is written off.

A suddenly louder exhaust is nearly always a hole or a blown joint: the back box, the flange where two sections meet, or a pipe rusted through, and it booms loudest when you accelerate. It is not an emergency, but fumes can get into the cabin, so keep a window open and never sit with the engine running in a garage. A garage can sleeve or weld a small hole, or fit just that section, for far less than a whole system, and one hanging loose wants doing before it drops off. Down on power too, or the engine light on, means the manifold or a sensor wants a look.

A sump pump sits in a pit at the lowest point of a cellar and switches itself on when water rises in the pit: a float tips, the impeller starts, and the water goes out through a pipe to a drain, a soakaway or the garden. The check valve just above the pump stops that water running back down, so a pit that keeps refilling with the pump switched off is usually the valve, and a pump that runs and moves nothing is usually a blocked inlet or a frozen discharge pipe. Test it twice a year with a bucket of water, and if the cellar floods when the power goes out, a battery or water-powered backup is what covers that.

A supernova is the explosion of a massive star at the end of its life: its core collapses and the outer layers are blown off, briefly outshining a whole galaxy. The iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones were made in stars that ended this way.

A survey is £400 to £700 for a HomeBuyer report and £600 to £1,200 for a full building survey, on a typical house; a flat is at the lower end and a big or old house at the top. The lender's valuation is not a survey and only tells the lender the house is worth the loan. Get the survey before you exchange, and ring the surveyor afterwards to ask what actually matters.

A swirl of cream or yogurt loosens a thick soup, and something crisp on top - croutons, toasted seeds, a handful of crushed crisps - makes it feel finished. A squeeze of lemon or a splash of vinegar at the end lifts a soup that tastes flat, which is usually what it is missing rather than salt.

A tablet is a touchscreen for reading, watching and browsing; a laptop has a keyboard and full software, so it's the one for typing, spreadsheets and real work. If it's your only device for work, get the laptop.

A tan is your skin making extra melanin to shield skin-cell DNA from ultraviolet light, and that is damage, not health: it raises the risk of skin cancer and ageing, so use SPF 30, shade and a hat and skip sunbeds; a fake tan is safer because it colours only the top layer.

A tap that wobbles is held by one nut underneath: get under the sink and tighten the back nut on the threaded shank with a basin wrench or a long spanner, or the fixing plate on a monobloc. Once it is tight, check the two flexible tails have not started to weep. If the nut has pulled the thread through a thin worktop, a repair plate costs a few pounds and spreads the load.

A team that has gone quiet has usually learned what bad news costs, so change that first: say out loud what you will not be annoyed about - a delay told on Tuesday, a mistake that is already being fixed - and what you will, which is a surprise on Friday, then behave that way once, because one calm reaction does more than any speech. Ask for one piece of bad news a week and thank the person who brings it in front of the others. In one-to-ones ask "what is getting in the way" and then say nothing for ten seconds, and put your own mistake on the table before you ask about theirs: a manager who admits one is the only proof that it is safe to speak. Where it is your ideas that keep getting dropped rather than bad news that keeps not arriving, ask for one objection by name - "what would go wrong with this?" - and credit the change to whoever improves it, because a team that has stopped arguing with you has usually decided it is not worth the cost.

A teaspoon of baking powder is a quarter teaspoon of bicarbonate of soda plus half a teaspoon of cream of tartar. Without the cream of tartar, use the quarter teaspoon of bicarbonate and swap a spoonful of the liquid for lemon juice, vinegar or buttermilk, because bicarbonate needs an acid to work. Self-raising flour already carries it - about 2 teaspoons in every 150g - so a self-raising recipe needs none at all.

A tempo run is 20 to 40 minutes at a pace you could just about hold for an hour - "comfortably hard", where talking is possible in short sentences but not a conversation. It trains the point where your body stops clearing lactate as fast as it makes it, which is what makes a race pace feel easier. It sits inside an easy run, once a week, with the warm-up and cool-down done slowly; if you cannot speak a sentence, it is too fast, and if you can chat, it is too slow.

A tent and bags for everyone, plus what small children need on a campsite: a mat each, because they feel every root, warm layers and a hat for the night even in July, and a full change of clothes kept in the car so a wet sleeping bag is not the end of the trip. Take a torch each, wet wipes, a bin bag for wet things, breakfast that needs no cooking, and something to do after dark. Pitch in daylight, close to the toilets but not beside them, and let them run about before bed so they sleep.

A test is the answer, and the timing is the part people get wrong: from the day your period is due, on the first pee of the morning, which has the most hormone in it. A faint second line is still a line. If it is negative and nothing comes in three days, test again, because the hormone doubles every couple of days. Early signs - sore breasts, going off food, tiredness, feeling sick - are not reliable enough to go on either way. If you would rather not be pregnant, a GP or a sexual health clinic will go through the options without pushing you either way, and the sooner you ring the more there is to choose from.

A thesis statement is one sentence that says the claim your essay will prove, and why it matters: "Cheaper public transport would cut city emissions more than electric cars, because most journeys are short." Put it at the end of your first paragraph, make it something a reasonable person could disagree with, and check that every paragraph after it is evidence for that one sentence. If a paragraph is not, either cut it or change the thesis.

A thick, yellow or crumbly nail is a fungal nail infection: a pharmacist can sell you an amorolfine nail lacquer for a mild one, and a GP can prescribe terbinafine tablets when several nails or most of a nail is affected. Either way it takes months, because the damaged nail has to grow out - file it thin, dry your feet properly and don't share clippers. A dark streak under the nail, or a nail lifting off, is a GP check.

A thin skim of filler is hard in about an hour and can be sanded the same day; a deep fill wants overnight, because it shrinks back if the middle is still soft when you rub it down. Rub it with 120 grit on a block rather than with your fingers, and stop when the edge blends into the wall - two thin fills are quicker than one thick one that has to be dug out. Give it a coat of watered-down emulsion before the paint, or the patch drinks the first coat and shows as a dull spot.

A thin skim is ready for a mist coat after two to four days and painted properly after about a week. A backing coat, or a wall taken back to brick, is roughly a week for every 10mm of thickness, so a fortnight or more. The colour is the best gauge - pale, chalky and the same all over means dry, and a patch that is still dark and cool has not finished, which wants a day or two more. Painting it before it has gone pale traps the water and blows the paint within a month.

A throat that is sore or a voice that is rough first thing, then eases through the day, is usually dry air or breathing through your mouth at night: leave a window open or put a glass of water by the bed. A sour taste, heartburn at night or a cough means reflux - raise the head of the bed and eat earlier. A voice hoarse for over three weeks needs a GP look.

A tide pool is the pocket of seawater left behind in the rocks when the tide goes out, and it is a small sheltered world: anemones, limpets, crabs and weed that survive being cut off until the water comes back.

A tight chest has three common causes and they feel much alike. Asthma: a wheeze, a cough at night or with cold air or exercise, which eases with a blue reliever inhaler. Anxiety: a fast heart, tingling hands, and it comes in waves of ten or twenty minutes, often when you are wound up. A chest infection: a fever, a wet cough and feeling rough, which needs seeing if you are breathless or it is going on. Sudden tightness with pain spreading to the jaw, neck or arm, sweating, or breathlessness while sitting still is 999. If it keeps coming back, see a GP and say when it happens - they may give you a peak flow meter or an inhaler to try.

A tiler is usually £150 to £250 a day, or £25 to £45 a square metre for labour: a small bathroom's walls and floor is £500 to £900, and a kitchen splashback £150 to £300. Tiles themselves are £15 to £60 a square metre on top. Ask whether the price includes taking the old tiles off, the adhesive and the grouting, because that is where two quotes differ most.

A tin of paint has to dry out before it can go anywhere. Stir sand, sawdust or cat litter into it, leave the lid off somewhere safe until it is hard, then take it to the household waste recycling centre, where nearly every site takes paint. To keep a part-used tin, wipe the rim, press the lid down with a block of wood and store it upside down so no skin forms. A few inches left is worth offering on Freecycle.

A tired lower back after a run is usually the load rather than damage: cut your distance and pace for a fortnight, keep off the hills, and add glute and core work three times a week - bridges, bird-dogs and dead bugs. An ordinary ache is fine to run through; pain that shoots down your leg, or numbness, is a physio.

A toddler who goes down at seven and is awake again at ten is usually treating bedtime as a nap: push bedtime later by 15 minutes every few days, keep the room dark and the last hour quiet, and make the 10pm wake-up boring - a quick cuddle in the dark, no lights, no play. Ask your health visitor if it is still happening after two weeks.

A tog is how well a duvet holds warmth, not how thick it is: 4.5 is a summer duvet, 9 to 10.5 is spring and autumn, 13.5 is winter, and 15 is for a cold room. Most people are best off with a 10.5 for eight months of the year and a 4.5 for the hot ones, and two duvets - a 4.5 and a 9 - can be poppered together for winter instead of buying a 13.5. Children under one should not have a duvet at all.

A tooth of your own that has come loose on its own is a dentist this week, and today if it hurts or the gum is swollen: it is usually gum disease, which is treatable, and leaving it is what loses the tooth. Do not wobble it, chew on the other side, and if it was knocked in an accident hold it by the crown, put it back in the socket or in milk and get to an urgent dentist or A&E inside the hour.

A tooth that changes colour has usually lost its nerve: a knock cuts the blood supply, the tooth dies and it goes grey or dark over the next few weeks, sometimes months later. It is not an emergency on its own - get it looked at by a dentist within a week or two, and the same day if it aches, if the gum under it is swollen or sore, or if there is a little pimple on the gum, because a dead tooth can go on to abscess and that is what hurts. It will not go back to normal on its own: whitening and scrubbing will not bring the colour back. Do not pull it, even if it has gone loose - a loose tooth comes out when it is ready, and pulling one early tears the gum and can bring infection. A grey milk tooth in a child often needs nothing: the dentist will say whether to watch it or take it out, so the adult tooth underneath is not affected.
A tortoise outlives most of us: a horsfield's or a Hermann's lives 40 to 70 years and some reach far beyond that, so it is a pet to leave in a will rather than a short commitment.

A tracker mortgage follows the Bank of England base rate plus a fixed margin, so base 4.25% with a 1% margin is 5.25%, and the payment moves the month after base changes. It is usually cheaper to leave than a fixed deal and costs less when rates fall, but the payment rises with them, so leave room in the budget for two more rises.

A trade union is a body of workers in the same job or industry that bargains with employers over pay, hours and safety, and it can take a case to an employment tribunal on your behalf. You pay a monthly subscription, often around 1% of pay or a few pounds a week, and what most people join for is the legal cover: a rep beside you in a disciplinary or a redundancy, which your employer has to allow.

A trader can only charge what you agreed, and extra work needs your agreement before it is done: ask for an itemised invoice, pay the agreed amount, and put in writing that you dispute the rest. If the money has already gone, ask for the difference back in writing and give them 14 days, then a card chargeback or Money Claims Online. At a dentist, vet or clinic, ask for the itemised bill and the plan you signed.

A transit-sized van is usually £40 to £80 a day, plus a deposit of £150 to £300 held against damage. Mileage and a young-driver surcharge are the two things that turn a cheap ad into an expensive day, and the excess on the insurance is often £1,000 unless you pay extra. Ask for the total with mileage and the excess before you book, and photograph the van all round before you drive it away.

A trapezium is a four-sided shape with exactly one pair of parallel sides; in the US the same shape is usually called a trapezoid. Its area is half the sum of the two parallel sides times the height between them.

A treadmill is not bad for you: the deck gives a little more than pavement does, and the machine keeps the pace honest. It is a touch easier than running outside because there is no wind or camber, so set the incline to 1% to make it match the road, and run tall rather than holding the handles. The one habit to avoid is the same flat stride every time - put a hill or a faster minute in most sessions.

A trifle keeps 2 days in the fridge, and it is the cream and the fruit that turn rather than the sponge: cover it once it is made and eat it within a day or two. Do not freeze it - the cream splits and the sponge goes watery.

A trivet is the stand that keeps something hot off the table or the counter - a pan, a casserole, a slow cooker's pot. Wooden, cork, stone or metal, all it does is hold the heat away from the surface; a folded dry towel does the same job when the trivet is not there.
A true yam is a rough, bark-like tuber from Africa and Asia, drier and starchier; the orange or white-fleshed "yam" in most UK shops is a sweet potato. If it has smooth skin, it's a sweet potato.

A trust is a legal box: a trustee holds money or a house for someone else and must use it only for them. People use one to keep savings or a house out of inheritance tax or care fees, or to leave money to a disabled relative without handing it over. Most families do not need one, because a will can hold a child's inheritance in trust until 18 - and a trust costs money to set up and run, with its own tax return. Ask a solicitor for a fixed quote.

A tsunami is a series of waves usually set off by an earthquake under the sea, which lifts a whole column of water. Out at sea they are barely noticeable, but they steepen as they reach shallow water; if the sea suddenly pulls back, get to high ground.

A turbine is the jet's opposite: wind pushes the blades, the blades turn a shaft through a gearbox, and a generator turns that spin into electricity. The blades are long and thin because the force goes up with the square of their length, and the machine feathers them out of the wind when it is too strong to use.

A twitching eyelid is usually tiredness, caffeine or stress, and it settles by itself within a few days to a couple of weeks. Sleep more, ease off the coffee, and use lubricating drops if your eyes are dry from screens. See a GP if the twitch spreads down that side of your face, or the eye closes on its own.

A two or three unit mesh system (around £100 to £150) puts one unit where the router is and the others around the house, and the devices switch between them by themselves. Buy the same brand as one set rather than mixing units, and put the middle one roughly in the centre of the house.

A typical household pays about £140-£150 a month for gas and electricity at the price cap, so £200 a month usually means a bigger or older house, electric heating, or a tariff nobody has compared in a while. The figure that decides it is the kWh, not the monthly estimate: the annual use on your bill against the Ofgem typical figures of 2,700 kWh of electricity and 11,500 kWh of gas tells you whether you are using a lot or paying a lot.

A unit is a kilowatt hour - one kW running for an hour - and under the price cap it is about 25p for electricity and 6p for gas, on top of a standing charge of roughly 40-60p a day for each fuel. So a kettle (about 0.1 kWh) costs pennies and an hour of the oven (about 2 kWh) costs about 50p; your own bill has the exact unit rate and standing charge, and those two times your annual use give the yearly figure.

A universal credit sanction cuts your standard allowance for a set number of days: 7 for a first missed appointment, up to 28 for repeats, and 91 days up to three years for leaving a job. Check the letter for the dates it runs between, then ask for a reconsideration if the decision is wrong and a hardship payment if the money has gone: repayable, and there for exactly this.

A used car is about £2,000 to £4,000 for 10 to 15 years old and 80,000 miles or more, £5,000 to £8,000 for 5 to 8 years old, and £9,000 to £14,000 for 3 to 5. Whatever the price, check the MOT history free on gov.uk and keep £500 back for the first repair.

A vaccine shows your immune system a harmless piece or blueprint of a germ, so it can practise making antibodies without you getting ill. If the real germ turns up later, those memory cells recognise it and fight it off fast.

A valuation is 20 to 30 minutes on site, a homebuyer's report two to three hours, and a full building survey four to six. The written report usually follows within a few days, so ask when you will have it before you book, because your lender and your solicitor may both be waiting on it.

A vasectomy is the two tubes that carry sperm from the testicles cut and sealed, so the semen has no sperm in it; it takes about 15 to 30 minutes under local anaesthetic. You are awake, the worst is the numbing injection, and you go home the same day in loose trousers with a bag of frozen peas. Two days of taking it easy, a week before anything strenuous, and it is not instant: you need a sample checked at about 12 weeks and another clear one before you rely on it, so use something else until then.

A venue or caterer can only keep what your cancellation has actually cost them - the staff booked and the date they could not re-let - and they have to try to re-let before charging you, so ask for a written breakdown and the rest of the deposit back. If you cancelled because of something they did wrong, or a reason the contract names, the deposit comes back in full. Then a card chargeback, and Money Claims Online.

A vertebrate is an animal with a backbone: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals are the five groups. The backbone is a column of bones or cartilage that protects the spinal cord, and it lets the animal grow large and move actively.

A vertex is a corner where two or more edges meet: a cube has eight vertices and a triangle has three. The plural is vertices, and in a graph a vertex is a point with lines, called edges, joining it to other points.

A viewing is about what a photo hides. Press the wall behind the bed and under the window for damp, look at the ceiling for a brown ring, run the hot tap and time how long it takes, and ask how old the boiler is. Go back in the evening for noise and parking. Ask what the rent includes - bills, council tax, broadband - whether the deposit goes into a protection scheme, how long the tenancy runs and what the break clause says. Anything promised out loud, a repair or a new mattress, get it in a text or email before you pay.

A virus is a scrap of genetic code wrapped in a protein coat, and it can only copy itself inside a living cell. That is why antibiotics do nothing for a cold or flu: they kill bacteria, which are cells that can grow on their own.

A virus is a scrap of genetic code in a protein coat that can only multiply inside your cells; bacteria are single living cells that can grow and divide on their own. So antibiotics kill bacteria but do nothing for a cold or flu, which are viral.

A vitamin is a nutrient the body needs in small amounts and cannot make enough of, so it has to come from food: vitamin C is in fruit and vegetables, vitamin A in carrots and dairy, and vitamin D is made in skin from sunlight. A varied diet usually covers them.

A voice that has gone is usually laryngitis: the vocal cords are swollen from a cold, or from shouting, singing or a smoky room. Rest it - sip water often and do not whisper, which strains it more than talking does - and steam helps the rawness. It is usually back within one to two weeks. See a GP if it lasts more than three weeks, if you cannot swallow, or if you have a lump in the neck or trouble breathing.

A warranty is a bonus on top of your rights, not a swap for them: in the UK the retailer has to sort out a faulty product for up to six years (five in Scotland). Go to the shop first and keep the maker's warranty as the backup.

A wasp or a hornet in a room: open a window wide and step back - it flies to the light and goes out on its own, and it will not chase you. Do not swat it - a squashed wasp is what stings, and the ones in late summer are only after sugar, so leave a jam jar away from you and it will go there instead. If it is in the car, pull over somewhere safe, open every window and step out until it leaves; a wasp in a moving car is how people crash.

A watch battery is a coin cell, usually a CR2016, CR2025 or CR2032 printed inside the back, and the number matters: a jeweller will fit the right one for a few pounds, and many watch shops do it while you wait. Doing it yourself needs a case-back tool, and a watch with a screw-down back or any water resistance is worth leaving to them, because the seal has to go back clean or it will fog up.

A watt is a rate of energy use: one watt is one joule every second, so a 10-watt LED left on for 100 hours uses one kilowatt-hour, and a unit on your electricity bill is exactly that. Watts are volts times amps, which is why a 2,400-watt kettle on 230 volts pulls about 10 amps. A kilowatt is 1,000 watts, and a kWh is a kilowatt for an hour - the number the meter counts, not the number on the label.

A wave is a moving disturbance that carries energy without carrying the material with it: a sound wave is air particles pushing and pulling, and a water wave is the surface moving up and down while the water stays roughly in place. Light is a wave too, and so is a radio signal.

A weak flow is almost always at the outlet, not in the boiler: unscrew the tap nozzle and soak it in descaler, open the isolator under the sink all the way, and check the stopcock has not been half shut. A combi only gives full flow at one tap at a time, so if the pressure drops when a second tap runs that is normal. If it is weak on every tap in the house, the stopcock or the mains is the place to look, not the plumbing.

A wedding photographer is usually £1,000 to £2,500 for the day, and a family shoot £150 to £400 including some prints. The package matters more than the day rate: ask how many hours, how many edited images, and whether you get the files to print yourself.

A well-fitted heat pump uses about a third of the electricity of panel heaters for the same warmth: a typical three-bedroom house runs one for roughly £700 to £1,100 a year at today's electricity price, against £900 to £1,200 on gas, and the gap widens as gas gets dearer. It needs radiators big enough for a 45 to 55C flow temperature and a well-insulated house to hit that; in a draughty house with small radiators the running cost climbs above gas. Ask the installer for the figure off their own room-by-room design, not the brochure's.

A white water ring or a heat bloom lifts with mayonnaise or petroleum jelly left on overnight, or with a hairdryer held 15 cm away for a few minutes. A cloth laid over a white ring with a warm iron pressed on it for a few seconds at a time does the same job when the first try does not. A dark stain has gone into the wood and wants sanding back and re-oiling, and ink lifts with a little methylated spirit on a cloth, along the grain, before you polish the whole top so the shine matches.

A white composite filling lasts about five to seven years and a silver amalgam ten to fifteen, and a well-looked-after one can go a lot longer. Grinding your teeth, fizzy drinks and a sweet tooth all shorten it; a filling that chips, feels high or hurts to bite wants another look.

A white film on glasses out of the dishwasher is limescale from hard water: fill the salt right up, set the machine's water hardness, and keep rinse aid topped up, because too little leaves water marks and too much leaves a blue smear. In a soft-water area the film is detergent etching the glass, which does not come off - use less powder, a short cycle, and wash the wine glasses by hand.

A whole squash keeps a month or more somewhere cool, dry and dark, and it does not need the fridge. Cut, it keeps 4 to 5 days wrapped in the fridge, seeds scooped out. A squash goes sweeter after it is picked, so a patch of green skin is fine; soft brown patches or a sour smell mean bin it.

A whole cabbage keeps 2 weeks or more in the fridge drawer, and a cut one about a week with the cut face wrapped tight, because it dries from the cut. Keep it whole until you need it and cut out the core. Yellowing outer leaves are fine, slimy or black patches are not.

A whole chicken takes about 24 hours in the fridge, pieces take 8 to 12, and a turkey two to three days. Keep it on the bottom shelf in a bowl, and never defrost meat on the worktop or in the sink - the outside warms long before the middle.

A whole chicken is nearly always the cheaper way to buy chicken: a 1.5kg bird gives about 700g of meat plus a carcass for stock, which is four portions for £4 to £5, where the same weight in breast fillets is £7 to £9. The catch is a third of the weight is bone and it takes 15 minutes to joint. Roast it whole for a Sunday, joint it for a curry or a traybake, and simmer the carcass for stock; buy fillets only when dinner has to be quick.

A whole cut of red meat - a chop, a loin, a shoulder or a steak, whether pork, lamb or beef - can be a little pink in the middle and still be safe if it reaches 63C and rests for a few minutes, but mince, sausages and burgers have to be grey all the way through to 71C. A mouthful of raw pork or lamb by accident is very unlikely to do you harm, but a serving of it is a bad idea: salmonella, E. coli and, rarely, roundworm. Cook it through, and see a doctor if you get cramps, fever or diarrhoea in the next few days.

A whole head takes about 45 minutes at 200C (180C fan): rub it all over with oil, salt and pepper, sit it stalk down in a tray and cover it with foil for the first 25 minutes, then uncover it so the outside browns. It is done when a knife goes in with no resistance. Florets tossed in oil take 25 minutes at the same heat.

A whole house done properly is most of a day for one person: about four hours for a two- or three-bed that has been kept on top of, and the better part of a day if it has not had a deep clean in a year. Work top to bottom and room by room, with the floors and the bathroom last, so nothing gets done twice; the kitchen takes longest because of the grease. If it is only a tidy before people come, an hour and a half in the rooms they will actually sit in is enough, and the doors on the rest can stay shut.

A wicket is the set of three stumps and two bails a batter defends, and taking a wicket means getting a batter out - so ten wickets in an innings is all ten dismissals. The wicket-keeper stands behind it, with the slips beside them.

A will says who gets what; probate is the court's written confirmation that it was the last will and that the executor may act on it. You need it before selling or transferring a house, closing accounts and paying what the estate owes; banks pay out small balances without it, and anything held jointly or in trust usually passes without it. A straightforward estate gets the grant six to twelve weeks after the forms go in.

A window acts like a mirror: it reflects the sky and the trees you have behind you, so a bird flies at what looks like more trees. Put something on the outside of the glass - stickers, tape, a hanging silhouette - because one on the inside does nothing. If the bird is alive and stunned, put it in a box with air holes in a warm, dark, quiet place and leave it an hour or two; most fly off, and one that has not gone by then wants a wildlife rescue or a vet. A feeder within a metre of the window, or past three metres, helps too. It is not a sign of anything.

A window cleaner is usually £10 to £25 for a small house and £25 to £40 for a larger one, inside usually not included, and a four-weekly round is cheaper than a one-off. Gutter clearing is £60 to £150 for a house, and fascia cleaning £100 to £250. Ask whether they use pure water and a pole or ladders, and whether the price covers the frames and the sills.

A wired bell is a circuit interrupted by the button: press it, the circuit closes, and an electromagnet pulls a plunger that strikes a bar - the ding - then lets it drop back on a spring for the dong. Wireless ones skip the wire: the button sends a coded radio pulse to the chime, which is why a nearby bell can answer someone else's push.

A wisdom tooth coming through usually takes a few weeks of aching and swelling at the back of the gum, worst in the late teens and twenties, and it often settles on its own. Rinse with warm salt water three or four times a day, keep the area clean with a small brush, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen at the dose on the pack if it is sore. See a dentist if the gum over it stays swollen and traps food, if the pain spreads to your ear or jaw, if you cannot open your mouth properly, or if there is a fever or pus - that is an infection under the flap rather than teething. A dentist decides whether it has to come out, and most do not.

A wood burning stove is usually £400 to £1,500 for the stove itself and £1,500 to £3,000 to line the chimney and fit it, so budget £2,000 to £4,500 done properly. It has to be fitted by a Hetas-registered installer, or signed off by building control, and only an Ecodesign stove can be sold new now. Ask whether the chimney is yours to use and whether the house is in a smoke control area before you buy: both change what you can fit.

A wound that is infected shows up two or three days after the injury: the redness spreads outwards (more than about a centimetre a day), the skin round it is hot and tender, it swells, and there is pus or a yellow crust, or the pain gets worse instead of better. Soak it in warm salty water for ten minutes twice a day, keep it covered, and do not squeeze it. See a GP the same day for spreading redness or pus; a red streak running up the arm or leg, a fever, or feeling shivery and ill is 111 today, because that is when antibiotics are needed rather than later.

A yawn stretches the jaw and takes a deep breath, and it seems to help cool the brain and shift gears between waking and sleep. Yawning is contagious because seeing or hearing one triggers the same response, more so in people you are close to.

A year is about 365.24 days long, so every four years we add 29 February to keep the calendar in step with the seasons. Century years skip it unless they divide by 400, which trims the last bit of error.

A yellow card is a formal warning. In football two of them in a match mean a red and the player is off, and a straight red carries at least a one-match ban; in rugby a yellow means ten minutes in the sin bin, and a second one is a red too.

A zester takes the coloured outer peel off citrus without the white pith underneath, which is bitter. A microplane does the same job and also rasps hard cheese, nutmeg and garlic into fluff: one tool, a dozen uses. Take only the coloured layer - down to the pith is where the bitterness is.

A zip, a strap, a lining or a wheel is usually a repair rather than a replacement: a cobbler, a luggage repair shop or a pram and nursery repairer puts in a new zip or strap for much less than the thing cost, and a slider that has split often only needs a new slider. If you bought it in the last six months the shop that sold it has to repair or replace it, because the fault is assumed to have been there when it was sold; after that, look at the maker's warranty, because bags, suitcases and prams are often covered for their zips and wheels for several years.

A zip is one file holding several. To open one, double-click it: Windows and macOS both unpack it into a folder beside it, no software needed. To make one on Windows, right-click the folder > Send to > Compressed (zipped) folder; on a Mac, right-click > Compress. A .rar or .7z needs a free app such as 7-Zip.

A&E stands for accident and emergency, the hospital department for what cannot wait: chest pain, bad breathlessness, a bone through the skin, a head injury with vomiting or a collapse. If you are unsure whether to go, NHS 111 will say, and it is worth the call because A&E is the slowest place to be seen for something a pharmacist or a GP could handle.

A Help to Buy ISA was the first-home savings account that added 25% on what you saved, up to £3,000, when the money went on a first home under £250,000 (£450,000 in London). It closed to new savers in November 2019, but an existing one can still be paid into until November 2029 and claimed until 2030. The Lifetime ISA is the one open now.

A 0% balance transfer is worth it when the fee, usually 1-3% of the balance, is less than the interest you'd pay over the same months. Set a fixed payment that clears the balance before the 0% period ends, because the rate jumps to around 20% after it.

A Junior ISA is the usual choice: up to £9,000 a year, tax free, and the money is theirs at 18. A regular saver or Premium Bonds keeps it simpler if you'd rather not lock it away; either way a small standing order you don't notice is what makes it add up.

A 5k is 3.1 miles and a 10k is 6.2 miles; a half marathon is 13.1 miles (21.1 km) and a marathon 26.2 miles (42.2 km). Races are named in kilometres but most runners in the UK and the US talk in miles, which is why the two numbers never look related.

A 7kW home charger tops a typical electric car up overnight, needs a qualified installer and a dedicated circuit, and costs roughly £800 to £1,200 fitted before any grant your country offers. A three-pin plug works but adds only about 8 to 10 miles an hour, so it suits a small daily mileage; an off-peak electricity tariff is what makes home charging cheap, so set the car to charge overnight.

A 100mm (4 inch) square post carries a 1.8m panel, and 75mm round is enough for a light closeboard fence; a gate wants a 125 to 150mm post of its own, not a panel post with a gate hung on it. Buy posts marked for ground contact (UC4) rather than plain treated timber, because a post rots at the soil line, and on an exposed corner a concrete post outlasts wood.

A 13.5 tog duvet is the winter one, 4.5 tog is for summer and 10.5 tog or two thin ones that button together cover the rest of the year. Tog measures warmth for its weight, not how heavy it feels, so a 13.5 tog feather duvet and a 13.5 tog hollowfibre one are equally warm - buy the filling you can wash and dry. For a cold bedroom, a second lighter duvet on top or a hot water bottle at your feet warms you faster than a heavier one over your whole body.

A SIPP is a personal pension you open yourself, with the same tax relief as a workplace one - the government adds 20% to what a basic-rate payer puts in, and higher earners claim the rest back - but nobody adds an employer contribution and you choose the funds. It is the usual answer for the self-employed, and for anyone whose employer adds nothing: a global tracker fund at a total charge under about 0.5% a year is the plain choice. Only pay into a SIPP after you have taken every employer contribution going, because that is free money a SIPP cannot match.

A SORN is free at gov.uk and it means the car is taxed as off the road: no vehicle tax, no MOT needed while it stays off public roads. The car has to be on a drive or in a garage, not on the street, and a SORN ends as soon as you tax it again to drive it. If you are not the registered keeper the DVLA will not take the declaration.

A USB-C plug fits either way up, so there is no wrong way to push it in, and the one lead carries both power and data. On a phone or a thin laptop it is also the charging port, so the same cable charges the phone and, with a small adapter, runs a monitor or copies photos. If nothing happens, flip the plug and try another lead: cheap ones often carry power but no data.

A baby under three months who stops feeding needs looking at today: ring 111 or your GP now rather than waiting for the next feed. Keep offering small feeds and note the wet nappies - it is the count over the day that tells you how they are doing. If there is also a temperature, they are floppy or hard to wake, they have a rash, or the nappies are dry, that is 999.

A baby under three months with a temperature of 38C or more is seen the same day: ring 111 or your GP now rather than waiting, and don't give medicine to bring it down before they are seen. If they are drowsy, floppy, feeding badly or breathing fast, ring 999.

A baby who is feeding, passing wind and happy is rarely constipated, however often they go - a breastfed baby can go several days and be fine. If the poo is hard and pellet-like, offer cooled boiled water between feeds to a formula-fed baby, try bicycle legs and a clockwise rub of the tummy, and move on to pureed fruit once they are over four months. See the GP the same day if the tummy is hard and swollen, there is blood in the nappy, they are vomiting or feeding poorly, or a baby under six weeks has not passed a stool; never give a baby an adult laxative or a suppository.

A baby who is feeding and comfortable is not in trouble after a day or two without a poo, but do not change feeds, water or juice them on your own: ring the health visitor or the GP today. The same day if the tummy is hard or swollen, there is blood, they are vomiting or refusing feeds, or they seem in pain. Never give a baby a laxative.

A back that goes like that is almost always a muscle strain, and it is at its worst in the first day or two: keep moving gently rather than taking to your bed, take paracetamol or ibuprofen if you can, and use a hot water bottle on the tight part. Most settle in two to six weeks. Ring 111 today if you cannot pass urine, have numbness between your legs, or the pain came on after a fall, and see a GP if it is no better in a fortnight.

A baffle is the whole answer: one on the pole under the feeder, or a set of four plastic baffles on the pole, which a squirrel cannot get past because it climbs with a grip. Then give it nowhere to launch from - 2m from a fence, a tree or a shed and 2m off the ground, because a grey squirrel jumps about 2m across and drops further. A caged feeder lets tits in and keeps the rest out, a weight-triggered one shuts under a squirrel, and chilli powder mixed into the seed is ignored by birds and hated by squirrels.

A bag of spinach keeps about 5 days in the salad drawer and a whole unopened bag a week longer, and the date on the bag is the day to finish it by rather than a day it is still good after. Pick out anything slimy before it spreads, don't wash the leaves until you use them, and a bag that has only gone limp is fine wilted into a curry or an omelette.

A bain marie is a pan of simmering water with a bowl sitting in it, so what is in the bowl is heated by steam and never by flame: chocolate melts without seizing, custard and hollandaise thicken without curdling, and a sauce stays warm without catching. The bowl must not touch the water and the water must not boil hard - steam is gentle, a rolling boil splashes and scorches. A heatproof bowl over a saucepan does the same job, and a folded towel under the bowl stops it rattling.

A bake that stays pale is short of heat or short of sugar. Check the oven with a thermometer, because most run 10 to 20C cool, and put it up 10C for the last ten minutes. Milk or egg brushed on top browns it. If the middle is still wet it is underbaked, not pale: give it 10 more minutes under foil.

A bang is a part with play in it, so press and shake each end to find what moves before you buy anything. A loo seat bangs because the rubber bumpers under it have gone hard: tighten the two bolts through the hinges and fit new bumpers, which cost a couple of pounds. A blind bangs on the wall or the window when the bottom rail has nothing to rest against, so shorten the pull cord onto a cleat. A shutter or a gate in the wind wants a hook and eye or a magnetic catch holding it open. Banging in a chimney is birds or a flue that has no cowl on top, a banging pipe is water hammer, which wants the clips tightened and a clip or two more, and a fence or a gate that rattles in the wind wants the post fixing or a second bolt through the hinge.

A barcode is a pattern of bars that a scanner reads back as a number, with a check digit so a misread is caught. A QR code does the same in two directions and holds a whole web address, and it carries error correction - up to about a third of it can be damaged or covered and still scan.

A barometer weighs the air: inside is a sealed metal capsule with most of the air pumped out, and a spring or a column of mercury balances the outside pressure against it. As the pressure rises the capsule is squeezed and the needle climbs, so a falling barometer means a low coming and the weather on its way down too.

A barrier cream with zinc oxide in it is the one to have - Sudocrem, Metanium or Bepanthen all do the same job - and a thin layer at every change is enough once the skin looks pink. Thick white paste is for a sore bottom, not for prevention. If it is still red after three days, or there are spots at the edges, that is usually thrush and needs an antifungal cream from the health visitor rather than more barrier cream.

A basic funeral in the UK is about £4,000 to £5,000 all in, roughly £3,800 to £4,200 for a cremation and over £5,000 for a burial once the plot and the fees are counted, and extras like flowers, cars and a wake come on top. Three things cut it: ask two or three local funeral directors for their full price list (they must give you one), choose a direct cremation at about £1,500 if there is no service wanted, and check whether the person had a prepaid plan or a funeral notice in their will. If you are on a low income, the council's Funeral Expenses Payment covers a bare funeral and can be claimed from the bereavement service; a surviving partner may also get Bereavement Support Payment.

A bath is right at 37 to 38C - the elbow test is the reliable one, because a hand that has been in the water stops being a judge. Run the cold in first and top it up with hot, never the other way round, and never add hot water with a child already in it. For a baby or a toddler it is the same 37 to 38C and only up to the waist when they are sitting, with the cold tap run last, and a bath above 40C is too hot for anyone to sit in for long.

A batter that goes wrong is nearly always one of three: too thick (a splash more milk, until it runs off the whisk in a ribbon), the pan not hot enough (a drop should sizzle the moment it lands, so heat it a minute longer than feels right), or turned too early (wait for bubbles across the top and a dry-looking edge). Resting the batter fifteen minutes fixes half of them, and a pinch of baking powder lifts the thick American ones.

A battery smoke alarm is usually £10 to £25, and £30 or so with a sealed ten-year battery. A mains one with a backup battery is £25 to £40 plus an electrician, and three linked so they all sound together is £60 to £120. Test it monthly and change the battery once a year even if it has not chirped, and ask your landlord about the mains one in a rented flat, since fitting and checking it is their job rather than yours.

A bay that has gone yellow is usually water at the roots - it hates standing wet in winter and drying right out in summer - so check the drainage and water it in a dry spell. If the yellow leaves are on one side and feel sticky underneath, look for bay sucker or scale insects and wipe them off; a pale bay in a pot is often simply hungry, and a liquid feed through the summer greens it up.

A beaver builds a dam to hold the water deep enough that the entrance to its lodge is under the surface, which keeps out foxes, wolves and bears. The pond also means it can swim to food in winter instead of walking over land.

A bench scraper is a flat rectangle of metal with a handle - a pastry chef's third hand. It lifts a sticky dough off the counter, cuts it into portions, scrapes dried flour and dough off the bench in one pass, and carries chopped vegetables to the pan.

A benefit is money from the government because of your circumstances or your income; a tax credit was an older means-tested benefit paid through the tax system, and most people on them are being moved to Universal Credit. If you're not sure which you're on, your award letter says.

A bicycle tyre is about £15 to £35 for a decent one and an inner tube £5 to £8, with a shop fitting them for £10 to £20 on top. Puncture-resistant ones - a Schwalbe Marathon or a Continental Gatorskin - are £50 to £80 the pair and pay for themselves in fewer flats. Take the size off the sidewall (700x25c, or 26x1.75) and match the width to your rim and the riding you do.

A big pot with room to spare: about 5 litres of water for 500g of pasta, so it comes back to the boil quickly and the strands do not stick together. A wide shallow pan or a large frying pan is fine for long shapes if you stir, and easier for a small portion; any deep saucepan works for short shapes.

A bigger voluntary excess does cut the premium, but by less than most people expect: moving from £100 to £250 often takes £20 to £80 off a year, and the next £250 usually saves less again. Ask the same insurer for the quote at two or three excess levels and weigh the yearly saving against what you would pay on a claim, because the excess is what you find on the day. Do not set it higher than you could pay at short notice, and check that a lease or finance agreement does not cap it.

A bike project or a charity that refurbishes them takes one that does not ride: Re-Cycle and most city bike workshops want frames and parts, and a free-ad listing marked collection only clears one in a day. A scrap dealer buys the frame by weight, and the tip takes it with the metal. Charity shops rarely take bikes, so ring the project first.

A biome is a large region with one climate and the plants and animals that go with it: rainforest, desert, grassland, tundra, coral reef. The same biome turns up on different continents, because it is the climate that decides it.

A biopsy takes about 10 to 20 minutes, and the skin is numbed first, so it is a push rather than a pain; you can eat and drive afterwards. A skin one needs a plaster for a day, a prostate or breast one is sore for two or three days and paracetamol covers it. The result is a separate wait of one to two weeks, because the tissue has to be looked at under a microscope.
A bird's eye chilli is hot, 50,000 to 100,000 Scoville - one or two will heat a curry for four, and they are hotter dried than fresh.

A P11D is the form your employer sends HMRC each year to report the benefits in kind - the perks that are not in your pay: a company car, private medical insurance, a cheap loan, a phone or a season ticket. You do not fill it in and you are not taxed by the form itself: the value is added to your income and the tax comes out through your tax code. Keep the copy payroll gives you, check the figure for a car matches what you thought you paid, and if it is wrong ask payroll to correct it rather than ringing HMRC.

A P45 is the form your employer gives you when a job ends: your pay and tax for that job up to your last day, and your tax code. Hand part 2 to your new employer on your first day, keep part 1A for yourself, and keep it safe if you are not going straight into another job, because it is what a tax refund or a self assessment return is worked out from. Without one you go on a temporary emergency code, so tax comes out on the whole of your pay until HMRC sorts it - ask payroll for the P45 in writing if it never arrived.

A P45 is the form an employer gives you when you leave: the pay and tax so far that tax year and the code the next employer needs. Keep it, because the new job asks for it, and without one you can be put on an emergency code and overtaxed until it is sorted out.

A P60 is the one-page summary your employer gives you after 5 April each year: pay, tax paid, and your tax code. You need it for a mortgage, a visa or a tax return. Ask payroll or look in your online payslip portal - employers must give it to you by 31 May. If you have left a job, a P45 is the same idea for the part year, and you hand that to the next employer. If you cannot get one, HMRC can send you the figures.

A P60 is the one-page summary an employer gives you after 5 April: the pay, the tax paid and your tax code for the year just gone. Keep it, because a mortgage, a visa or a tax return can all ask for it, and it is the quickest proof of what you earned.

A black screen at your ear is the phone's proximity sensor working: it turns the display off during a call so your cheek cannot tap anything, and it should come back as soon as you take the phone away. If it stays black after that, or goes black on speaker, the usual cause is a screen protector, a case or a smudge over the top edge of the phone beside the earpiece - lift the protector off and wipe that strip, then restart the phone. Still blacking out after that points at the sensor itself, which is a cheap repair rather than a new phone.

A blackout lining is the fix, and the fitting matters as much as the fabric: hang the track or pole 10 to 15cm above the window and run the curtains 10 to 15cm past each side, so light cannot come round the edges. The light that wakes people is usually the strip along the top, so a pelmet or a blackout blind inside the recess behind the curtains closes it for a few pounds. The same lining is what slows a bright room fading the fabric, so it earns its keep twice.

A blister, cut or sore on a diabetic foot is a same-day job rather than a plaster: ring the GP or your diabetic foot clinic today, and go to A&E if the foot is hot, red, swollen or has a black or weeping patch, because with diabetes an infection can get deep before it hurts. Don't cut a corn, don't use a corn plaster or a hot water bottle, and stay off it and off barefoot floors until it has been looked at.

A blister is fluid trapped under a separated top layer of skin, usually from friction, heat or a burn, and the fluid is serum protecting the new skin underneath. Leave it whole and cover it loosely - popping it invites infection - and if it bursts on its own keep it clean and put a plaster on it. A burn blister bigger than a 50p, or any blister with spreading redness, wants a pharmacist or GP.

A blocked nose in a baby is a cold until something says otherwise: put a drop or two of saline in each nostril and wait a minute, feed little and often because a stuffy nose makes feeding hard, and put them down flat on their back as usual. No decongestants, drops or vapour rub under two. Ring 111 if they are under three months, refusing feeds, or breathing fast or noisily.

A blocked nose is swollen lining and mucus, so the thing that helps is shrinking the lining: a saline rinse or spray, steam from a hot shower, and a decongestant spray from a pharmacist for up to three days (longer and it bounces back). Sleep propped up and drink more than usual. See a GP if it lasts more than three weeks, if one side is blocked with bleeding, or if you have face pain and a temperature.

A blood transfusion is donated blood run into a vein through a cannula, one unit at a time, each taking about two to four hours. It is not an operation: you sit or lie while it drips, and the nurse checks your pulse, blood pressure and temperature before each unit and again at the start of it. Most people have it as a day patient, feel warmer and less breathless within a day, and the main thing to report is a rash, shivering or a sudden fever.

A blown-down panel is usually the panel, not the posts: lift it back between the posts and screw it to the rails through the post, two 65mm galvanised screws per rail, rather than just slotting it in - or fit a new panel of the same width. If boards have come off, feather-edge boards go back on with galvanised nails, each overlapping the last by about 25mm, and check the gravel board the panel sits on first, because a rotted one lets the whole panel drop. If panels keep going in wind, leave a 25mm gap under the panel so the wind passes through instead of pushing.

A blue reliever inhaler holds 100 doses in the small canister and 200 in the bigger one, so at two puffs four times a day a 200-dose one lasts about three weeks, and one puff a day would stretch it to months. Most have a dose counter on the side now, and that number is what to go by rather than the date on the box. A brown preventer at two puffs twice a day runs out in about a month in the same way. Order the repeat before it empties rather than after, because the last puffs are weaker.

A blue gas flame is the clean one: blue means the gas is mixing with plenty of air, so it burns hot and leaves almost no soot. Yellow or orange tips mean it is short of air and burning dirty, which can give off carbon monoxide, so have the hob or boiler serviced, keep the vents clear and put a carbon monoxide alarm nearby.

A board slides because nothing is gripping the worktop, and the fix is a tea towel: wet it, wring it out and spread it flat underneath, and the board will not move - that is what kitchens do rather than anything you buy. A non-slip mat cut to size or a rubber band round each end does the same. If the board is too small to hold both the food and what you have cut off it, a bigger one is the real answer, because a crowded board makes you work with the knife in a rush.

A boil is an infection of a hair follicle - tender and hot, and it comes to a head and drains. A cyst is a closed sac under the skin, usually painless unless it gets inflamed, and it doesn't drain by itself. Neither should be squeezed.

A boil is a churn of big bubbles you cannot stir down; a simmer is a lazy tremble of small bubbles, about 90C against 100C. Stews, sauces and rice want the simmer, because a hard boil toughens meat and breaks the grains, while pasta and potatoes want the boil. When in doubt turn it down until the bubbles just keep coming.

A boiler service is £60 to £120, and a repair is £80 to £250 including the common parts, with the first hour often £50 to £90. Out of hours or a breakdown in winter costs £100 to £150 before parts. Check the engineer is on the Gas Safe register, and ask whether the repair is a fixed price before they start.

A boiler is built for about 10 to 15 years, so at 15 it is at the end of its life even if it is working today - the useful thing now is to have the money ready rather than be without heat in January. Get it serviced, keep the service record, and start collecting two or three quotes in the quieter months, because a combi swap is roughly 2,000 to 3,000 pounds fitted and it is the same job whether you are desperate or not. A modern condensing boiler is around 90 per cent efficient against 70 to 80 for an old non-condensing one, which is the part of the bill you get back; a well-kept boiler that still works does not have to be replaced on age alone, but plan for it rather than wait for the morning it dies.

A bow tie is tied like a shoelace, only in front of your throat. Put it round your neck with one end about 4cm longer, cross the longer end over the shorter, bring it up behind the crossing and through the loop at your neck, and pull it snug: that is the knot, and the short end now stands up as the front loop. Drop the long end over the middle of that loop, push it up through the small gap behind it, and pull through to make the second loop. Tighten both loops together and straighten it. Practise on your thigh first, where you can see it, and give yourself twenty minutes the first time.
A box of cereal is about £2 to £3.50, and the shop's own version of a branded one about half the price. A big bag of own-brand flakes is the cheapest breakfast there is a bowl.

A brick out of a bread machine is nearly always the yeast: check the date, keep it and the salt apart in the tin (salt kills yeast on contact), and use water at 20 to 25C, because hot water kills it just as well. Half a teaspoon of dried yeast to 500g of strong white flour is the other thing to check. If the dough never rose the yeast is dead; if it rose and then fell, there was too much of it or the salt went in with it.

A bridesmaid gets the bride ready and keeps the day moving: arrive early, do up the dress, hold the bouquet and her phone, keep the tissues and the rings with you, and be where the photographer needs you. Before the day it is usually a fitting, the hen do and a hand with the favours or the place cards. A maid of honour is the same job plus the toast, and she holds the bride's things during the ceremony.

A bridge is the section that comes once, usually after the second chorus, and sounds like neither the verse nor the chorus - it is there to stop the song repeating itself before the last chorus, and it often changes key or drops to a quiet moment first.

A bridging loan is short-term money to buy a place before the old one sells: 0.5% to 1% a month rather than a year, so £150,000 over six months costs several thousand in interest and fees. It keeps a chain together when the sale is certain, and the lender wants a dated exit - a sale or a mortgage - so it is the wrong money for a house that is not selling.

A broken yolk is still good: fry it as it is or scramble it, and it tastes the same though it will not look as neat. When you want them whole, crack each egg into a cup first and slide the good ones into the pan, so one broken one does not spoil the rest.

A broker shops mortgages from several lenders for you and is paid a fee or commission. A financial adviser looks at the whole picture - pensions, savings, investments - and is regulated to advise on them. Use the broker for the mortgage and the adviser for the rest.

A broker compares deals across the market and checks what a lender will actually offer you, which matters most if your income is unusual, you're self-employed or your credit file has a mark on it. Many are paid by the lender, so ask upfront whether they charge a fee as well, and use one that covers the whole market rather than a single bank.

A brown or yellow patch on a ceiling is water, and the first job is to find where it comes in rather than paint over it. Look at what is above: a bathroom or a radiator pipe means a leak at the sealant, the trap or the joint, and an outside wall or the roof means it only grows after rain, so note whether it does. Press it with a finger - soft, crumbly plaster or a slow drip means it is live and worth turning the water off; a hard dry ring that has not moved in weeks is an old stain, which you seal with a stain block and then paint. Photograph it with the date and tell the landlord or your insurer in writing, because a patch painted over with no record is one you cannot claim for.

A brown ring inside a mug, a flask or a teapot is tannin stuck to the glaze, and bicarbonate of soda lifts it: a teaspoon of it with a little water into a paste, rub it round with a cloth, or leave the mug filled with hot water and a spoon of bicarbonate for half an hour. A dishwasher tablet in hot water does the same job overnight, and vinegar is a poor third because it barely touches tannin. Do not scour the inside with an abrasive pad, which scratches the glaze and gives the next stain somewhere to grip.

A brush or rubber strip that screws or sticks to the inside of the door is the cheap fix, about ten pounds and ten minutes: measure the gap first. For a bigger gap, a fabric draught excluder on the floor side; a letterbox flap and a keyhole cover cost a few pounds more. That alone makes the room feel warmer. If the draught is not at the door, run your hand round the window frames, the skirting and any old chimney or vent, and fill the gap with a strip, a bead of sealant or a chimney balloon.
