A bubble is a thin film of water with soap holding it together, and it pops when the water drains or evaporates from the top until the film is too thin. Dry air and a dusty surface speed that up, which is why bubbles last longer in a steamy bathroom.

A bucket list is the list of things you want to do before you die - the name comes from kick the bucket. It works better as ten or fifteen things with a date and a rough cost next to each than as a long wish list: one a year is a good pace, and putting the cheapest next keeps it moving. Then tell somebody about the top one, because a list nobody knows about is the one that never happens.

A budgie or parrot screeches for company, so answer it, let it out for an hour or two a day, and put the cage where the family is rather than in a quiet room. Cover the cage at dusk and keep to the same time each night, because a bird that screams at the same hour every evening is usually asking for the cover. Screaming with ruffled feathers or changed droppings is a vet question.

A budgie lives 8 to 12 years, and a cockatiel or a small parrot 15 to 25. Company matters more than anything else: a bird alone in a cage for years usually has a shorter, sadder life than one with a friend and time out of the cage.

A builder is usually £150 to £300 a day for one person, or £200 to £350 for two, and the big jobs are priced as a whole rather than by the day. Scaffolding, skips, and any work that needs building regulations add to it, and a quote should name all three if they apply. Ask for the price with the materials listed separately, and ask what happens if the job runs over, because that is where the total moves.

A builder's skip is usually £150 to £300 for a week, and a permit on a public road adds £30 to £60. Soil, rubble and hardcore cost more than household rubbish because of the weight, and a mattress or a fridge often cannot go in at all without a surcharge. Ask what the price includes and what happens if it is overfull, since a second skip is the usual surprise.

A bunch is whatever you can close one hand round at the stems; a sprig is a single small stem, and a punnet is the little basket soft fruit comes in. None of them is a weight, so go by eye, and add herbs a little at a time and taste as you go.

A bundt tin is the ring-shaped cake tin with fluted sides. The hole up the middle is why the cake bakes evenly - there is no cold, heavy middle to sit raw while the edge dries - and the flutes give more crust. The catch is the shape: butter and flour every groove, tapping the tin as you go, and let the cake sit ten minutes before turning it out, or a third of the crust stays behind. A standard recipe fills a 10-cup (2.5-litre) tin.

A bundt has no flat base for a paper circle, so use a paste instead: mix equal weights of soft butter and plain flour (a tablespoon of each is plenty for a big tin) and brush it into every groove with a pastry brush, getting right into the corners and the central tube. Tap out any loose flour and bake the cake as the recipe says, then let it stand 10 minutes in the tin before turning it out - any longer and the steam softens the crust and it tears. A silicone bundt needs no paste at all, just a light oil.

A burner heats water and a pump sends it round the radiators; the water comes back cooler and is heated again. A combi boiler makes hot water on demand straight from the cold mains when you open a tap, which is why a second tap running drops the temperature, while a system with a hot tank serves two at once.

A bus is the local service, stopping often along a town route and often turning up without a booking; a coach is for longer journeys between towns, with seats booked in advance, luggage in the hold and few stops. In the UK, National Express and Megabus run coaches.

A business plan for a small business is one page, not forty: what you sell in a sentence, who buys it and where they are now, what one sale earns you, what it costs to make or supply it, the fixed costs each month, and the number of sales a month that covers those costs - that last number is the break-even and it is the only part anyone reads twice. Add how you will reach the first ten customers and what money you need before the first sale. Write it in an hour, then change it after a month of selling, because the version in your head is guessing and the version after ten customers is not.

A cache is a copy kept close to hand so the same thing does not have to be fetched twice: a browser keeps the pictures and layout of a page, and an app keeps a little of your data, so the next visit is quick. It is only copies - clearing it never touches your photos, files or saved passwords - and it is the first thing to try on a page that has gone stale or shows yesterday's price.

A cake rises on three things - the air you beat in, the bubbles the raising agent makes, and steam - and when it does not, the culprit is nearly always baking powder past its date (a teaspoon per 150g of plain flour, or use self-raising), the flour beaten in too hard once it went in, or the oven door opened in the first 20 minutes. Cream the butter and sugar until pale and fluffy, fold the flour in with a spoon, fill the tin two-thirds full, and bake at 180C (160C fan) without opening the door.

A cake sinks when it's underbaked, when the oven door was opened early, or when there's too much raising agent; all three make it rise fast and then drop. Bake it at 180C (160C fan) without opening the door for the first 20 minutes, and check with a skewer.

A callout fee pays for the visit, and a trader can only charge for what you agreed and what they did: if you were billed for a repair nobody made, or a second visit for the same fault, ask for that part back in writing and say what you agreed before they came. Keep the invoice and the text that set the price. If they will not move, a card chargeback, and Money Claims Online from about £35.

A callus is thickened skin built where repeated pressure or friction makes the skin protect itself: hands from tools, weights or a guitar, feet from tight shoes. File it gently after a bath and use gloves or better-fitting shoes so it stops coming back, and don't cut it with a blade. A painful hard lump on a foot, or any foot callus with diabetes, is a podiatrist's job.
A calorie is the unit most food labels in the UK still lead with; a kilojoule is the metric one, usually in brackets beside it. One calorie is about 4.2 kilojoules, so 500 kcal is roughly 2,100 kJ.

A calorie is a unit of energy; the calories on food labels are really kilocalories, the energy to raise 1 kg of water by 1C. An average adult needs roughly 2,000 to 2,500 a day, and eating fewer than you burn is what loses weight.

A cambelt is usually due at 5 years or 60,000 to 100,000 miles, whichever comes first, and it is not a job to stretch: if it snaps the engine is often wrecked. Expect £300 to £600 with the water pump, and check the handbook because some cars have a chain that only gets changed when it gets noisy.

A cancellation is your choice of a full refund or a replacement flight, and the airline has to pay the money back within seven days - ask in writing with the booking reference and keep it. You may also be owed 220 to 520 pounds per person if they told you less than 14 days before, unless the cause was extraordinary like weather or air traffic control. Do not accept a voucher if you would rather have the cash.

A cancelled booking means your deposit back in full, and a course that never ran owes the whole fee: ask in writing for it, with the date you paid. Add what you can show you lost on the replacements - the venue, the dress, the caterer - and ask for their insurer's name. If they will not pay, use a chargeback on the card or Money Claims Online, from about £35.

A car needs its first MOT at three years old, then every year. The test covers lights, tyres, brakes, steering, suspension, seatbelts, emissions and the windscreen, and the maximum fee is £54.85 for a car. You can drive to a pre-booked test without a current MOT, but not otherwise. The only exemption for a car is a historic vehicle: over 40 years old, not substantially changed, and taxed in the historic class - the DVLA form for that is free, and without it the car still needs its test.

A car service is usually two to three hours for an interim or a full service, and a major service with plugs and filters can take most of the day. Ask when you book whether they keep the car or you wait, and whether the price includes the MOT if it is due.

A car MOT costs up to £54.85 in England, Scotland and Wales and £30.50 in Northern Ireland, and plenty of garages charge less; the fee is the same whether it passes or fails. Repairs are extra, and you can ask for the price before they start.

A car battery dies from short trips rather than age: a five-minute run never puts back what the starter took, so give it a twenty-minute drive every couple of weeks, or a smart charger once a month through the winter. If there is white fur on the terminals, pour warm water over them, brush it off and smear a little grease on, and check both clamps are tight - a loose one cranks like a flat battery. Most last three to five years, and a garage can test one in five minutes; a slow crank and lights that dim at idle are the signs it is going.

A carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gas your choices add up to in a year, counted as carbon dioxide: heating, electricity, flights, car trips, the food and things you buy. A typical UK footprint is around 10 tonnes a year, and flying and meat are usually the biggest single items.

A career in enterprise software — wouldn't want to call that from here. What decides it is the pay, the hours, and what the day actually looks like rather than what the job is called. The pay scales are published, and asking two people who do it now about a normal week settles more than any article.

A carpenter is usually £150 to £250 a day, or £30 to £50 an hour for small jobs with a one-hour minimum, and a joiner hanging an internal door is £60 to £120 each. Fitted wardrobes and shelving are priced as a whole: £1,000 to £3,000 for a run of built-in wardrobes with the materials in. Ask for the day rate, whether the price is fixed or an estimate, and get the material allowance in writing.

A carpet that ripples or wrinkles has stretched, and the fix is a re-stretch rather than an iron: the pile gives over the years, and a wet clean, a hot radiator or a heavy chair in one spot speeds it up. A fitter lifts the carpet off the gripper along one or two walls, pulls it tight with a knee kicker or a power stretcher and hooks it back on, which is an hour or two of work and far cheaper than a new carpet. One small bubble can be worked towards the nearest wall by hand and taken out the same way, and a bump that comes back after a day means the underlay has gone, not the carpet. A rug that slides on a wooden floor is the other problem: a rubber or felt underlay pad, or a strip of double-sided carpet tape, stops it without marking the boards.

A carpet clean is usually £25 to £40 a room, or £100 to £200 for a whole flat, with stairs and stubborn stains priced separately. A sofa or a rug is £40 to £100. Ask whether the price includes the stairs and a stain treatment, and whether they move the furniture, because two quotes that look different usually differ on those two things.

A carving fork is the long two-pronged fork that holds the joint still while you cut it, so your fingers are not near the blade. The long prongs go in once, at the thick end, and the guard stops the knife sliding up towards your hand.

A casserole dish is the wide, deep, lidded dish for cooking in the oven - stews, braises, a gratin - and it is chosen by what it is made of: enamelled cast iron holds and spreads heat for a long braise, stoneware is cheaper and slower to heat, and glass lets you see the browning but cannot go under a grill that is close to it. It should say ovenproof and give a top temperature; anything without that line stays off the hob and out of a hot oven.

A cat meows at a closed door because she wants through, and the door she can see but not cross is what the noise is about: open it once while she is crying and the crying is what she learns works. Decide when she is allowed through and be consistent - let her through before she starts if you are going that way, and otherwise ignore the meowing and scratching completely. A cat flap or a bell on the door gives her a quieter way to ask.

A cat suits a working day better than a dog: it sleeps through your shift, needs no walk at seven in the morning and is happy with two rooms and a window. Get an adult cat rather than a kitten if you are out all day, or two cats so they have company, and leave something tall to climb and a windowsill to watch. A dog is the better choice if you want the walk and the welcome home more than the quiet.

A cat that stops eating for more than 24 hours needs a vet, especially an older one: cats can get dangerously ill quickly from not eating. Offer warm strong-smelling food and a quiet place, and ring the vet today if she is 12 and off her food.

A cat that stops jumping up or takes the stairs one step at a time is usually in pain from arthritis, which most cats over ten have somewhere. Take her to the vet: there are painkillers made for cats, and a monthly injection does well for many. Put a step or a box beside the sofa and the bed, keep her food and litter on one floor, and a warm bed away from draughts helps the stiffness more than people expect.

A cat that is sick in the car is usually travel sick or frightened, and the two are managed the same way: nothing to eat for three or four hours before you set off, the carrier on the back seat with a familiar blanket over it and facing forward, the car cool, and a break halfway on a long drive. Two or three short trips to somewhere pleasant and back build her up, and ask the vet about a travel-sickness tablet for a house move. Never let her out of the carrier in a moving car.

A cat with its mouth open is not cooling down the way a dog does, so treat it as a warning: move her to the coolest room, water in a wide bowl, a damp towel on the belly and a fan on the floor rather than on her face, and let her lie stretched out on tiles. If the panting carries on after ten minutes in the cool, or comes with drooling, wobbling, gums that look pale or brick red, or a cat that will not stand, ring the vet now - that is heat stroke, not a warm day. A few seconds of panting after hard play is normal and should stop as soon as she rests.

A cat coughing or wheezing is a vet visit, not a wait-and-see: cats hide chest trouble well and a night cough can be asthma, a hairball problem or heart disease. Note how often it happens and whether she is eating, then book her in; take her straight away if she is open-mouth breathing or her gums look pale or blue.

A cat is mostly a routine it can rely on: two meals at the same times, water in a bowl away from the food, a litter tray scooped every day and washed out with plain hot water once a week, and somewhere high to sit. Play with a wand toy for ten minutes twice a day, because a cat that hunts indoors does not hunt the sofa. Then the vet side: a microchip (law in the UK), a yearly check and booster, worming and flea treatment monthly, and neutering at about four to six months. Indoors-only is fine if there is space to climb, and a kitten should stay in until the vaccinations are finished.

A catalyst speeds up a reaction and comes out of it unchanged, so a small amount does the job over and over. It works by giving the molecules an easier route, which means the reaction can happen at a lower temperature. Enzymes are nature's catalysts and the catalytic converter on a car uses metals to turn exhaust fumes into less harmful gases.

A catalytic converter is the box in the exhaust that turns the harmful gases into harmless ones: carbon monoxide, unburnt fuel and nitrogen oxides go in, and carbon dioxide, water and nitrogen come out, over a honeycomb coated in platinum, palladium and rhodium. It has no moving parts and normally lasts the life of the car, but it only works once it is hot, so most of its cleaning happens after the first couple of miles. It is destroyed by a misfire, by burning oil or coolant, and by leaded fuel or the wrong additive, and it is stolen for those three metals - a car that suddenly gets much louder has usually had it cut out, which is a garage job, not something to drive on.

A catchy piece with a simple shape and a repeated phrase loops because the brain predicts the next note and keeps replaying the bit it knows. Chewing gum, singing the song all the way through, or listening to a different familiar song usually breaks it; it is harmless.
A 250g block of butter is about £2.20 to £3, and a tub of spread about £1.50. Own-brand butter is the cheapest, and it freezes well, so buy it when it is on offer.

A 250ml can is about 80mg of caffeine and around 27g of sugar - a coffee's caffeine with a can of Coke's sugar on top - so it is fine occasionally and poor as a daily habit. Not after about 2pm if you want to sleep, never as a mixer with alcohol, and none at all for under-16s, in pregnancy, or with a heart condition.

A chain that skips under pressure is usually worn, and so is the cassette behind it: a chain checker that drops in at 0.5 percent on 11-speed (0.75 on older setups) means replace it now. A single stiff link is the other cause, and it feels like one jolt per turn of the cranks - free it by flexing it sideways. Change the chain before the cassette, because a new chain on worn teeth skips worse than the old one did.

A charge on a house is a note on the title that someone's money is secured on it, so it cannot be sold or remortgaged without paying them. A mortgage is a charge, and so is a secured loan or a charging order after a debt went to court. It comes off the title when the debt is cleared, and the Land Registry shows who holds it.

A charge cycle is a whole 0 to 100% of use rather than one plug-in, so two top-ups from 50% add up to one, and a phone battery is rated for about 500 of them before it falls to 80% of its original capacity - roughly two years of charging once a day. Newer iPhones are rated for 1,000. The count sits under Settings > Battery > Battery Health on an iPhone.

A charger that is warm is normal; one that is too hot to hold, buzzes, smells or has scorched the plug is not, so unplug it and stop using it. Replace it with a branded charger of the right wattage rather than a cheap one, do not charge a phone under a pillow or on a bed, and pull the plug out by the body, not the cable.

A check-up is about 20 minutes. A filling is 30 to 45 minutes, and a crown or a root canal is usually one longer visit or two, so book the morning for one of those and do not plan anything straight after.

A chesty cough is usually a cold that has moved down, and the colour of what comes up does not mean you need antibiotics. Drink plenty, breathe steam from a bowl or a hot shower, prop yourself up to sleep, and give it two or three weeks. A GP the same day if you are breathless at rest, coughing blood, or feel properly unwell with a fever.

A chickpea and spinach curry is easy and filling: fry onion, garlic, ginger and spices, add a tin of tomatoes and a tin of chickpeas, simmer 15 minutes and stir spinach through at the end. Serve it with rice, and check the stock cube is vegan.

A child needs about a gram of protein for each kilo they weigh, so around 20g a day at 20kg - two small portions of meat, fish, beans or eggs. Babies under one get all they need from breast milk or formula, and from six months you add iron-rich foods twice a day: mashed lentils, egg, chicken, yoghurt. Fussy patches are normal; ask your health visitor if the weight chart worries you.

A child who refuses school, or fakes an illness to get out of it, is usually using the only tool they have for a problem they cannot name, so treat it as information: ask which part of the day they would happily go in for, and ask the school for the pattern - which days, which lessons, who is in them. Then get them through the gate for a short day rather than keeping them home, and ask for the pastoral lead or the attendance officer by name. A GP letter helps the school take it seriously, and they can refer on for anxiety if it has been going on for weeks.

A child who stops eating is worth looking at if it lasts more than a day or two, and the same day if they are also drinking less, weeing less, sleepy or floppy, or have a sore mouth or throat - small children slide on fluids before food. Offer small amounts of what they like, little and often, keep water and milk going, and don't make the table a battle. Ring 111 if they are under five or a temperature comes too, and see the GP if it keeps coming back or they are losing weight.

A child who gets them most days is usually one of five things: not enough to drink, a missed meal, too little sleep, a long stretch on a screen, or eyes that need testing. Write down the time of day each one comes on and what they had eaten and drunk - that diary is what a GP asks for first. Never aspirin under sixteen. See a GP about a run like this, and ring 999 for a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade under a glass, or drowsiness.

A child's passport is applied for by someone with parental responsibility, with the child's birth certificate, a photo showing the whole face and a countersignature where the form asks for one. In the UK use the online service and send the old passport if there is one. A child's passport lasts five years, and standard processing takes a few weeks, so do not book flights until it is in your hand.

A childminder looks after other people's children in their own home, usually with one other adult and no more than six children under eight at a time, and is registered with Ofsted (or a CMA in Wales, the Care Inspectorate in Scotland). Expect roughly £5 to £7 an hour in England, more in London, with the free hours for three and four year olds on top - usually cheaper than a nursery day. That home setting is the difference from a nursery: fewer children, one person who knows your child well, and hours that often bend round a shift, but no cover if the childminder is ill. Ask to see the registration certificate and the latest inspection report, ask what a normal day looks like, and check the first-aid certificate and whether they take the tax-free childcare payments, which most registered childminders do.

A chimney sweep is usually £50 to £90 for an ordinary chimney, and £90 to £150 if it is lined, thatched or needs a camera. A wood burner wants sweeping once a year before the season and twice if it is your main heat, and a gas appliance needs a Gas Safe service rather than a sweep. Ask for a certificate, because your insurer may ask for one after a chimney fire.

A chip smaller than a pound coin can usually be repaired for £20 to £40, and many insurance policies do it free because it saves them a new screen. Cover it with clear tape so dirt stays out and get it done before it spreads. A crack in the driver's line of sight fails the MOT.

A chip in china or glass cannot be glued back safely: the glaze is gone at the chip, that spot holds bacteria and it will crack through in a dishwasher. Retire a chipped mug to a pen pot or a plant saucer, and if it was new take it back, because a chip at the rim is a fault the shop has to put right. Never use a cracked one for hot drinks.
A chipotle is a smoked, dried jalapeño, 2,500 to 8,000 Scoville. The adobo it comes in is milder than the pepper itself - one pepper and a spoon of the sauce for a pot for four.

A chipped edge or a gouge in wood is a filler job: press a two-part wood filler or a wax repair stick into it, a little proud of the surface, and sand or shave it flat once it is hard, then colour it with a touch of wax or stain. Keep the sanding to the filler - sanding the finish around it leaves a pale patch you cannot hide.

A chirp every minute or so is the low-battery warning: twist the alarm off its base, swap the battery (usually a 9V, sometimes AA) and press the test button until it sounds properly. Mains-powered alarms have a backup cell that does the same thing, and any alarm over ten years old wants replacing whole rather than mending.

A chromosome is one long tightly wound packet of DNA; humans have 46 of them in most cells, in 23 pairs, with one of each pair from each parent. They are the filing system that lets a cell copy all its instructions without tangling them, and the sex chromosomes are the pair that decides whether you develop as male or female.
A 300g pack of bacon is about £2.50 to £4. Dry-cured costs more than the kind that is pumped with water, which shrinks in the pan, and the 2-for deals are usually the cheapest way to buy it.

A churning or gurgling stomach is usually wind moving through a normal gut, and it is noisier when the gut is empty because there is only gas in there to move. Eat something plain if it has been hours - toast, rice, a banana - chew with your mouth closed, drink water rather than fizzy drinks, and take a ten minute walk, which shifts trapped wind better than anything. Butterflies before something nerve-racking are the same feeling and they pass. See a GP if it comes with pain that keeps coming back, blood in your poo, weight going down, a lump, or more than three weeks of it, and if you are vomiting or cannot keep fluids down, ring 111.

A cleaner is usually £12 to £18 an hour, so a two-hour weekly visit is £25 to £40, and a one-off deep clean of a three-bedroom house is £60 to £120. An agency costs more than someone working for themselves but covers insurance, tax and holidays. Ask what is included (inside the oven and the fridge usually are not), and whether you supply the products.

A click as you press the pedal is usually the brake light switch or a dry pedal bush, a small fix rather than a safety one. A clunk when you let the pedal off is often a worn caliper slide or a loose pad; a knock over bumps is more likely a suspension bush. A click alone is fine for a few days, but have it looked at sooner with grinding or a sinking pedal.

A 330ml can of regular Coke has 35g of sugar, about seven teaspoons, and 139 calories. Diet and zero versions have none, and the newer zero-sugar versions taste much closer to the original than they used to.

A cloudy stock boiled: once it comes to the boil the fat and protein break up into droplets that nothing will settle again, so keep it at the barest simmer with the lid off and skim the grey foam off the top in the first twenty minutes. To clear one that has already gone cloudy, whisk a lightly beaten egg white into the cold stock, bring it slowly to a simmer and let the white rise and set as a raft, then lift it out with the bits trapped in it. Strain through a sieve lined with kitchen paper, and do not stir it while it simmers or the raft breaks up.

A clutch pedal that feels soft, sinks or needs pumping has air or a leak in the hydraulic side: check the fluid level in the small reservoir by the brake one and have the slave or master cylinder looked at. It usually creeps up on you, so book it in before the pedal goes to the floor at a junction.

A clutch replacement is usually £300 to £800 fitted, and towards the top of that on cars with a dual-mass flywheel, because the flywheel often gets done at the same time. A quote in that range is normal; it is cheap only if the garage is not touching the flywheel or the release bearing, so ask what is included.
A coefficient is the number multiplying a letter in an expression: in 3x the coefficient is 3, and in -5y squared it is -5. If a letter stands alone the coefficient is 1, because x means 1x.

A coil in the pad and a coil in the phone make a transformer with a gap - the pad's alternating current makes a magnetic field, and that field drives a current in the phone's coil. It is the same idea as an electric toothbrush charger, and it is slower than a cable because some of the energy leaves as heat.

A colander is the bowl with holes in it, for draining the water off food - pasta, potatoes, rice, berries - which is quicker than lifting them out a spoonful at a time. Its holes are large, so a big pan of pasta water leaves in seconds and a custard runs straight through; the fine-mesh one for flour and icing sugar is a sieve. A metal colander takes boiling water straight from the pan, a plastic one is fine for cold rinsing but softens and stains under a full pan, and the ones with a single handle are for lifting it out of the sink.

A cold mouthful chills the roof of your mouth and the blood vessels there tighten, then widen again; that swing is the stabbing headache behind your forehead. Eat more slowly, or press your tongue to the roof of your mouth to warm it, and it fades in a minute.

A cold sore is the herpes virus: a tingle, then a blister, usually on the lip, crusting over in a week or so, and it's catching. A mouth ulcer is a raw round sore inside the mouth, not catching, often from a knock, stress or a sharp tooth.

A cold that has gone to the chest is usually a chesty cough that lasts one to three weeks: keep drinking, sit in a steamy bathroom, and a spoonful of honey helps a night cough. See a GP if you are breathless or wheezy, coughing up blood, have a high temperature for more than three days, or it is still there after three weeks.

A cold with no fever, and a child who is eating and drinking, is fine for school - a runny nose on its own is not a reason to stay off. Keep her home if she has a temperature, is too tired or clingy to join in, is being sick, or has a cough that leaves her breathless or wheezing. Send tissues and tell the teacher, and let her go back once the fever has been gone for 24 hours without medicine; the cough can hang on for a week or two after that and does not need another day off.

A cold creeps up on you with a runny nose and a sore throat; flu hits fast with a fever, aching all over and real exhaustion. Flu is the one that puts you in bed for a week, and both are treated with rest and fluids at home.

A cold in a child is a virus and runs its course in about a week: drinks, rest and children's paracetamol or ibuprofen by weight if they are miserable, and saline drops for a baby too stuffed up to feed. Cough and cold medicines are not for the under-sixes, and there is no need for anything else up the nose. See a GP if they are breathing fast or working to breathe, are not drinking, get an earache that lasts more than a couple of days, or are no better after ten days.

A collarbone that hurts after a knock usually mends in a sling over four to six weeks, and the pain often eases before the bone has joined: keep the hand and elbow moving gently, sleep propped up a little and take paracetamol. Have it looked at with an X-ray if you cannot lift the arm, the bone looks out of line, or it hurts too much to sleep.

A colloid is a mixture where tiny particles of one substance are spread through another and stay spread: milk, fog, mayonnaise and paint are colloids. The particles are bigger than in a solution but too small to settle like a suspension.

A colonoscopy is a camera on a flexible tube put up through the back passage to look all the way round the bowel, and it takes about 20 to 30 minutes. You are given sedation and pain relief through a cannula, so most people are drowsy and remember little of it, and you go home the same day once you have eaten and been to the toilet - but not driving, so bring someone. Wind and a bloated ache for a day are the usual aftermath, and the bowel prep the day before matters more than anything else: the cleaner the bowel, the more they can see.
A compliment is praise; a complement completes something, like a wine that complements the meal. 'Complimentary' means free, which is why hotel soap is complimentary.

A 40g serving of cereal is one small bowl - check the box, because granola and muesli are heavier per spoon than cornflakes, and most people pour about twice the serving into a normal bowl. For porridge, 40g of dry oats is one portion, which is about four heaped tablespoons or half a mug; it swells to a proper bowl with 250ml of milk or water. If a 40g bowl leaves you hungry by ten, add a banana or a spoon of yogurt rather than more cereal, and if you are measuring granola, weigh it once - a 50g serving can carry 12 to 15g of sugar.
A 400g pack of salad tomatoes is about £1 to £2, and a punnet of cherry ones £1.50 to £2.50. Loose ones are usually cheaper than a punnet, and in August they are half the winter price.
A 400g block of cheddar is about £3.50 to £5, and the same weight of a named farmhouse one £4 to £6. Mature costs a little more than mild, and the deli counter is dearer than the block.

A concrete floor wants an etch and a paint made for it, not gloss: sweep and degrease it first, let it dry, then etch it with a weak acid or a floor etch from the paint shop so the paint has something to grip. Two coats of a garage-floor paint or a two-pack epoxy, rolled in one direction, with 12 to 24 hours between them, and keep feet and tyres off it for two or three days. Fresh concrete needs a month to cure before any of it, and a damp floor needs a damp-proof coat first.

A conductor is a material that lets heat or electricity pass through it easily because some of its electrons are free to move. Metals are the usual conductors - copper and aluminium carry current in wires, and a metal pan conducts heat - while materials that hold their electrons tightly, such as rubber and plastic, are insulators.

A cone has one circular base and a curved side that comes to a point, like a party hat or a road cone. Its volume is one third of the cylinder with the same base and height: 1/3 times pi times the radius squared times the height.

A conservatory is usually £8,000 to £20,000 depending on size and whether it has a solid roof, and an orangery with the same footprint is £20,000 to £40,000. A solid roof and underfloor heating cost more but make the room usable all year. Ask whether the price includes the foundations, the electrics and building regulations sign-off, because those are the three that get left out of a quote.

A constipated cat needs water rather than a remedy: wet food twice a day, a bowl of water away from the food and a fountain if she likes running water, and a few teaspoons of plain cooked pumpkin in her food. A cat that has passed nothing for two days, or is straining in the tray and producing nothing, or is being sick with it, is a vet visit today: a blocked cat is an emergency, and long-standing constipation needs a vet's laxative rather than a human one.

A constituency is the area that elects one MP: 650 of them, roughly 70,000 to 80,000 voters each. The boundaries are redrawn every few years as people move, which is why a seat can change shape or vanish. Your MP is the one for the constituency your postcode sits in.

A consultation is usually £40 to £70, and anything done in it - a jab, a blood test, an x-ray - is on top, so a first visit often lands at £80 to £150. Out of hours is £150 or more before treatment. Ask for the estimate in writing before you agree to treatment, and ask what insurance would have covered, because the cost of a dog or cat is mostly these bills.
A cooked chicken breast is about 30g of protein per 100g, so a 175g breast carries roughly 50g, near a quarter of a day's protein for an adult, at about 280 calories.

A cooked gammon or ham joint keeps 3 to 5 days in the fridge, and sliced ham 3 days once the pack is open. Wrap it so it does not dry out, keep it away from raw meat, and freeze slices for up to 2 months.

A cooking thermometer takes the guesswork out of doneness: 75C in the middle of poultry, 71C for pork and minced meat, 63C for a beef joint eaten pink, and 104-105C for jam at setting point. Take the meat out of the oven to check it, or the reading climbs as the probe goes in, and leave it in for ten seconds rather than a moment.

A cool box only holds the cold you put in it. Freeze a couple of water bottles or ice packs the night before, because they do the work, and pack them around the food rather than on top. Fill the empty space with more cold drinks or a rolled-up towel: a half-empty box warms up fastest. Keep it out of the sun, out of a parked boot that gets hot, and put a towel or a folded blanket over the lid. Open it as little as you can and shut it straight after. Cold drinks and fruit keep all day like that; cooked food, milk and anything with mayonnaise is the one to throw away if it has sat warm for more than about two hours.

A cooling rack is the wire grid that lets air under a cake or a tray of biscuits as they cool, so the base does not go damp and soggy on the worktop. Leave the bake in its tin for ten minutes first, then move it to the rack; a rack upside down over the tin turns a cake out without breaking it.

A cough that only comes at night is worth a vet visit rather than a wait. In an older dog it can be a heart problem or a collapsing windpipe, in any dog kennel cough or a soft-palate problem, and in a puppy it is urgent. Ring today, and go straight in tonight if he is also panting at rest, breathing fast, off his food or pale or blue at the gums.

A cough that lasts more than a day or two needs a vet, and quickly if the animal is flat, off its food or breathing fast; kennel cough is common in dogs and spreads where dogs meet. Don't give human cough medicine, and keep a coughing dog away from others until the vet has seen it.

A cough after a cold often lasts three to four weeks and still settles on its own: sip fluids, take honey (a spoonful, or in a warm drink), and don't bother with most cough medicines, which do little. See a GP if it is still there after three weeks, or sooner if you are coughing blood, getting breathless or wheezy, losing weight, or have a fever that keeps coming back.

A cough is a reflex that clears the airway: a quick breath in, the vocal cords shut, and air is forced out to shift mucus, dust or an irritant. Most coughs after a cold are viral and settle in two to three weeks, and honey in warm water eases the tickle. A cough with breathlessness, blood, chest pain, or one that lasts over three weeks needs a GP.

A council tax band is the valuation bracket your home sits in, A to H in England and Scotland and A to I in Wales, and every band is a fixed fraction of band D, which is the one councils quote: about £2,171 a year in England on average, so a band B home is 7/9 of that and a band H home 18/9. Check your band on the Valuation Office Agency site: if a neighbour in an identical house is in a lower band, you can ask for a review, and a quarter of a million homes have been moved down.

A couple of hours usually, and it starts straight after the service, so a midafternoon funeral means people are moving on by early evening. Three or four hours if it is a pub or a hall people are glad to be in, and the venue will tell you its own last hour. Nobody minds if you leave when you have had enough: staying for a drink and a sandwich is enough to count.

A courgette or squash that rots at the flower end is the same problem as blossom end rot in tomatoes: the fruit cannot pull up enough calcium when watering swings from bone dry to soaked, so the tip goes soft and brown. Water little and often at the base, mulch to hold the moisture, and take the affected fruit off because it will not recover - the plant then puts its energy into the next ones. A high-nitrogen feed makes it worse, so use a tomato feed instead.

A courier that damages your property owes the repair, and so does the shop that booked them: photograph it the same day, write down the tracking number, the company and the van's registration, and send the claim to the delivery company in writing with 14 days to answer. If they stall, chase the retailer who arranged the delivery, and if a van hit your car report it to the police as well as your insurer.

A court's next step is on the paperwork rather than in a general answer, and the office that sent it can tell you where you stand. The reference on the letter is what gets you through - and Citizens Advice will read it with you for free if the wording is unclear.

A cracked panel is not a repair, it is a new panel, and on anything under about £500 that is more than the set is worth: check the price of the same size before you book anything. If it is a line or a band rather than broken glass, power it off at the wall for a minute and check the HDMI lead first, and claim on household accidental damage cover if you have it, which is usually the cheapest way to a replacement.

A cracked cheesecake was overbaked or cooled too fast: bake it until the edge is set and the middle still wobbles, then turn the oven off and leave it inside with the door ajar for an hour so it comes down to room temperature slowly. Sour cream on top hides any crack, and a water bath stops most of them.

A cramp is a muscle contracting hard and not relaxing, which hurts sharply for a minute or so. Stretch it gently, pull your toes up toward you for a calf cramp, and drink water; cramps at night often come with tired muscles, dehydration or low magnesium. Before exercise, warm up and add distance slowly, and see a GP if a cramp comes on every time you walk a set distance, or comes with a calf that is swollen and hot.

A crate is a good den if it's introduced slowly: leave the door open, feed meals inside, and shut it for seconds at a time while you're in the room. Get one big enough to stand up and turn round in, never use it for long stretches, and never as a punishment.

A creamy or egg-thickened soup curdles when it gets too hot or too sharp: keep it under a simmer - small bubbles at the edge, never a rolling boil - and stir the cream, yogurt or egg in off the heat at the very end. Acid does the same, so add wine, lemon or tomatoes early and let them cook down before the dairy goes in, and a pinch of bicarbonate of soda in a tomato soup stops the split. If it has already gone, take it off the heat and blend it smooth with a little cold cream, or whisk in a cornflour slurry and warm it gently.

A credit union is a savings and loan club owned by its members, not a bank: it takes deposits from the people in it and lends only to them, so the interest goes back to the members instead of to shareholders. Loans are capped by law at 3% a month (42.6% APR), which is far below a payday lender and often below a doorstep one, and savings are protected by the same FSCS guarantee as a bank up to £85,000. You join through a common bond - a workplace, a union, a postcode or a church - and findyourcreditunion.co.uk lists the ones open to you.

A crematorium service is usually 30 to 45 minutes including coming in and leaving, and a church service about an hour. A burial adds 15 to 20 minutes at the graveside, and the wake afterwards lasts as long as people stay. Ask the funeral director which slot is booked: the crematorium keeps to it because the next funeral is waiting outside.
A 500g bag of dried pasta is about 75p to £1.50, and a fresh one £2 to £3. Dried is a fifth of the price a portion, and the shape does not change the price much.

A 500ml bottle of water is about £1 in a shop and £2 or more at a station, while a 6-pack of 1.5 litre bottles is about £3 to £4 in a supermarket. Tap water is the same stuff and costs nothing, so the bottle is for the day out.

A crepe pan is a shallow pan with a very low lip and a flat base, so a ladle of batter can be swirled right to the edge instead of running up the side. A good non-stick frying pan of about 20cm does the same job; the thin lip is what makes it easier to get a palette knife under a crepe.

A crumble or a tart keeps 2 to 3 days in the fridge, covered: the topping goes soft before it goes off. Reheat it at 180C (160C fan) for 15 minutes to crisp the top again, and freeze it unbaked for 3 months, then bake it from frozen for 20 minutes longer.

A crumbly cake usually has too much flour or too little fat and egg, or it was beaten on after the flour went in: weigh the flour rather than scooping it with a cup, and stop mixing the moment the last streaks of flour disappear. Take it out a shade early rather than late, because five extra minutes dries a sponge and dry is what crumbles, and cool it in the tin for ten minutes before turning it out. Cut it cold: a cake cut warm breaks the crumb as the knife goes through.

A crystal is a solid whose atoms sit in a regular repeating pattern, which is why it grows flat faces and sharp edges: salt, sugar, quartz and ice from the freezer are all crystals. The pattern decides the shape, so salt makes cubes and snowflakes make six-armed stars.

A cube number is what you get when a whole number is multiplied by itself three times: 1, 8, 27, 64, because 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. It is written 4³ and read as four cubed; a square number is the same idea with two multiplications.
A cuboid is a box shape with six rectangular faces, like a brick or a cereal box. Its volume is length times width times height, and a cube is the special cuboid where all three are equal.

A current account is the everyday one: your pay goes in and the bills, the card and the cash come out, and it comes with a card and direct debits. A savings account pays more interest but has no card and no direct debits, so the two do different jobs.

A cut needs closing properly if the edges fall apart when you let go, if it is longer than about 2cm, if it is on the face, a hand or over a joint, or if it is a bite or has grit in it: go to a walk-in or A&E, ideally within six to eight hours and sooner for a face wound. A clean, straight cut shorter than that holds with a plaster or steri-strips. Press a clean cloth on it hard for ten minutes first so the bleeding stops, and check your tetanus is up to date.

A cut still open after a week or two, or one that keeps scabbing over and breaking down again, needs a GP look rather than more plasters: slow healing is often circulation, diabetes, low iron, or something left in the wound. Keep it clean and covered, and leave the scab alone. Get it seen the same day if it is spreading red, hot, swollen, smelly or weeping pus, or if you have a temperature.

A cut stings because the broken skin leaves nerve endings exposed, and salt, lemon or soap irritates them directly; the sting fades as the cut seals. Rinse it with clean water and cover it, and get help if it is deep, very dirty or will not stop bleeding.

A cut tree drinks about a litre a day, so stand it in a bucket of water, saw a couple of centimetres off the trunk first so it can take water up, and keep the base covered - a trunk that dries seals over and stops drinking. Keep it away from a radiator, a fire and the sunny window, and it will hold its needles for about four weeks instead of one. A Nordmann fir drops far less than a Norway spruce, which is the one that sheds as you bring it in. A potted tree with roots is a different animal: keep it cool and light in a porch or greenhouse, bring it in for no more than a week, and plant it out after Christmas.

A cut avocado keeps 1 to 2 days in the fridge: leave the stone in, press cling film right onto the cut face, and squeeze lemon or lime over it. The surface browns where air gets to it, which is harmless - scrape that bit off. A whole hard one ripens on the counter in 3 to 5 days and then keeps a day or two in the fridge.

A cut is usually £15 to £35 in a salon and £10 to £20 at a barber, with colour from £60 to £150 depending on how much work it is. A senior stylist costs more than a junior, and a dry cut is often cheaper. Ask for the price of the cut and the blow dry separately, because the blow dry is the surprise on the bill.

A cut is 30 to 45 minutes; colour, highlights or a restyle is one and a half to two and a half hours. If it is your first colour at a salon they will want a patch test 48 hours before, so ring ahead and get that done.

A cylinder has two flat circular ends and one curved side, like a tin or a tube. Its volume is pi times the radius squared times the height, and the curved surface is 2 times pi times the radius times the height.
A CV lists what you've done - jobs, education, skills - in a page or two. A cover letter is the short note that goes with it, saying why you want this job and which bits of the CV matter for it.

A cystoscopy is a thin camera passed up the water pipe into the bladder, and it takes about 5 to 10 minutes. It is done with a numbing gel, so it is uncomfortable rather than painful - a sharp sting as it goes in and a strong urge to pass water while it is there - and you can drive yourself home. Expect stinging and pinkish urine for a day or two and drink plenty of water to flush it through; ring the ward if it is bright red or you get a fever.

A damp rubber glove or a squeegee pulled across the fabric gathers pet hair into rolls that lift off easily, and a vacuum with the brush bar down gets the rest. Wash the covers at 40C now and then: hair works into the weave and no brush reaches it.

A damp cloth with a little washing-up liquid takes off most marks, and a melamine sponge used gently with water lifts a scuff without cutting through the paint. Do not scrub hard: the paint film is thinner than it looks, and a shiny patch where you scrubbed shows in the light more than the mark did. If the mark has gone through to the plaster, or the paint has flaked, it is a touch-up rather than a clean, and it needs the same paint in the same finish or the patch shows.

A damp cloth and warm water is enough after a walk: wipe the pads and between the toes, then dry them properly, especially between the toes. Skip human shampoo, check for grit and grass seeds while you are there, and wash the towel rather than the dog if it is only mud.

A damp dishcloth gets sour within a day or two: rinse it, wring it out and let it dry, and put a fresh one out every day. Run them through the machine at 60C with the towels, or microwave a wet one for a minute.

A date they gave you is part of the deal: if it slips, ask in writing for the new date and say you will cancel if that one is missed, and once it passes, or 30 days if there never was one, you can cancel for a full refund including delivery. Keep the message that promised the day, and a thing sold as in stock when it was not is a misleading claim for Trading Standards.

A day or two at most, and it is the avocado, the cucumber and the fresh herbs that turn first: keep it covered, pressed down so no air is on top, and in the coldest part of the fridge. Guacamole is at its best the day it is made, so make what you will eat.

A dealer has to sell a car that is as described, of satisfactory quality and fit to drive: you can reject it for a full refund within 30 days of collecting it, and in the first six months the dealer has to prove the fault was not there when it sold it. Put it in writing and stop driving it if it is unsafe. 'Sold as seen' does not remove those rights, and the Motor Ombudsman is free.

A debit card spends money you already have, straight from your current account; a credit card borrows from the card company and you pay it back later. Use debit for everyday spending and a credit card for big purchases or travel, where the extra protection helps, then clear the full balance each month so it costs nothing.

A decent 6 by 8 foot shed is usually £400 to £900, and a garden office £3,000 to £10,000. The base is the part people forget: a shed on grass or soil will never sit square, so £100 to £200 on a paved or timber base is money well spent. Ask whether the price includes the base, delivery and the treatment, and how thick the timber is - thin boards are the cheap shed's secret.

A decent double mattress is usually £300 to £700, with £150 to £250 at the cheap end and £900 upwards for pocket springs or a good foam. Firmness matters more than price, and a mattress that is too soft is the common mistake. Ask about the trial period and whether the guarantee covers sagging, and take the old one away as part of the deal if you can.

A decibel measures how loud a sound is, on a scale where each extra 10 dB is about ten times the power and roughly twice as loud to the ear: a whisper is about 30, ordinary talk about 60, and 85 or more for long spells can damage hearing.

A decimal is a way of writing a number using place values for tenths, hundredths and so on, with a point after the units: 0.75 means seven tenths and five hundredths, which is the same as 3/4. The digits after the point tell you the place value, so 0.5 is five tenths and 0.05 is five hundredths.

A decorator is usually £150 to £250 a room for walls and ceiling, or £20 to £40 an hour, with paint and materials on top. Emulsion on sound walls is the cheap end; filling, lining paper, gloss woodwork and high ceilings push it up. Ask whether the price includes the paint, how many coats, and who moves the furniture.

A defined contribution pot is usually outside your estate for inheritance tax and goes to whoever you have nominated, so the nomination form matters more than your will - check it is up to date, especially after a divorce or a new partner. If you die before 75 the beneficiaries normally pay no tax on it; after 75 they pay income tax at their own rate as they take it out. A final salary or workplace scheme usually pays a spouse's or dependant's pension instead, and often a lump sum, so ask the scheme for its rules as well.

A dehumidifier takes water out of the air, which is what stops damp, condensation and mould; an air purifier filters dust, pollen and smoke out of it. Damp room, dehumidifier; allergies or a smoky street, purifier.

A dent with unbroken paint in a flat steel door or wing is a job for paintless dent removal: a mobile specialist works the metal back from behind and keeps the original paint, for about 60 to 150 pounds a panel, which is half what a bodyshop charges to fill and spray it. A plastic bumper dent is often pushed back out by hand from behind after warming it with a hairdryer or a bucket of hot water, and a 10 to 20 pound suction puller lifts a shallow dinner-plate dent in a flat panel. If the paint has cracked, or the crease is sharp, the metal is stretched and only a bodyshop will make it right. Claims are rarely worth it - the excess is usually more than the repair, and the premium rises for three years.

A dentist or a hygienist scale and polish first, because most yellowing is staining on the outside, and then whitening works: either a professional kit made for your teeth or a legal-strength high-street one, and expect it to take a couple of weeks. Charcoal and bicarbonate toothpastes scrub the enamel and do not whiten it.

A deposit held on a table or a slot is normal at a busy place, and it is usually refundable if you cancel inside the notice they set - a day or two for most restaurants, longer for a big table. Ask, before you pay, what the deadline is and whether it comes off the bill, and get that in a reply rather than on the phone.

A diaphragm inside moves when sound pushes on it, and that movement is turned into an electrical signal that copies the shape of the sound wave. A condenser mic charges that diaphragm and needs power; a dynamic one uses a coil in a magnet and needs none, which is why a stage mic is the one that can be dropped.

A direct debit lets the company take the money, and the amount can change, which is why bills use it; a standing order is a fixed amount you send on a date you set, which is right for rent, savings or paying a person. You are protected on a direct debit by the Direct Debit Guarantee, so if they take the wrong amount your bank has to refund it in full. Cancel both with the bank, in writing or in the app, and cancel a direct debit with the company too so the paperwork agrees.

A director's loan is company money you take out and do not take as salary or as a dividend, and the company books it as an asset owed back by you. Repay it within nine months of the company's year end or the company pays s455 tax at 33.75% of the balance, refunded when you do repay. Over £10,000 and it counts as a benefit in kind, so it goes on a P11D and you pay tax on the official interest rate you did not pay. The clean way is a dividend declared with minutes, or a small salary.

A dissertation is one long piece of work - usually 8,000 to 12,000 words for a bachelor's and up to 20,000 for a master's - where you answer one question of your own with evidence, rather than showing what you know about a subject. It is marked on the question, the reading and the argument, in that order. Start with a question narrow enough to answer in the word count, then a plan of four or five chapters, then read for that plan only. Book two supervisor meetings before Christmas and take a written note of what was agreed at each one: the students who fall behind are the ones who go quiet, not the ones who ask.

A dog scooting along the floor is usually the anal glands: a vet or a groomer empties them in a minute, so book it this week. Go sooner if he is licking or biting at the area, if there is a swelling beside the anus or blood on the carpet, because an infected gland needs treating rather than emptying. Worms and a mucky back end do it too, so worm him if that is overdue, and if it keeps coming back ask the vet about adding a little fibre - a spoon of bran or tinned pumpkin - to firm the stool up.

A dog that suddenly drinks much more, and wees more with it, needs the vet: diabetes and kidney trouble both start that way, and so does a bladder infection. Note how much he drinks in a day and take a urine sample if you can, keep the water bowl full in the meantime, and do not restrict it.

A dog that loses weight on the same food needs the vet: worms, bad teeth, kidney or liver trouble, diabetes and an overactive thyroid are the usual causes, and some cancers start that way. Weigh him now, take the number with you, and go this week - a dog should not get thin on a full bowl.

A dog walker is usually £10 to £18 for a half-hour walk and £15 to £25 for an hour, less per dog if they walk a group of four or five. Solo walks cost the most, and a walker who is insured and does a first meet-and-greet at your house is worth a pound or two more. Ask what happens on a wet day and how many dogs go out at once.

A dog who paces or seems confused at night is usually in pain or getting muddled, not being naughty: arthritis makes lying still hurt, and an older dog can lose track of where he is in the dark. Book a vet visit and mention the nights, leave a small light on the landing and let him out calmly when he asks. Do not scold him for it, and note how much he drinks, because that points the vet one way or the other.

A dog groomer is usually £30 to £60 depending on the size and coat, with a hand-strip or a matted coat costing more. Ask what happens if your dog is matted, because some charge by the hour to sort it out, and book four to six weeks apart for a coat that keeps its shape.

A dog lives around 10 to 13 years, and where it lands depends mostly on size: small breeds often reach 14 to 16, while the biggest breeds are usually 8 to 10. Kept lean, walked daily and seen by a vet once a year, a dog sits at the top of its range.

A door that slams in the wind wants a holder or a closer, not a shut window: a hook-and-eye or a door holder on the frame keeps it open, and an overhead closer set to slow the last few inches stops it banging shut. Rubber bumpers on the stop take the rattle out of the catch, and a wedge under the bottom holds a door that swings. A front door that rattles is usually the latch plate, and a wrap-around striker plate or a strip of foam behind it stops that.

A door that bangs is a latch that isn't holding or a gap that lets the wind push it: check the strike plate first — a card's thickness of movement is enough, and moving it 2mm further in with a chisel or a file fixes most of them. If it still swings, a hook and eye or a magnetic catch holds it open or shut, and a foam strip on the stop takes the noise out.

A door that drags or will not shut is usually swollen from damp in winter, or has dropped on its hinges because a screw pulled out. Give the season a fortnight first, with the heating on or a dehumidifier in the room, because many free up on their own. If it has dropped, tighten the top hinge screws, or replace them with longer ones. Otherwise take a millimetre at a time off the edge where the paint has rubbed bright, and seal the bare wood afterwards so it does not take in water and swell again.

A doorbell camera that drops off is nearly always the wifi: check the signal at the door with a phone, and if it is weak, move the router or add a mesh point rather than buying a new bell. Then charge or change its battery, since a low one cuts the video first, and power-cycle the chime - most of them rejoin the network within a minute.

A drink with an SSRI is not dangerous in the way people fear, but it makes you drowsier and flattens your mood the next day, and the newer antidepressants mostly say avoid it. With mirtazapine or an older tricyclic the sedation doubles, so one drink is the sensible limit and none in the first fortnight while you are settling on the dose. Never with an MAOI.

A drink helps you fall asleep but breaks it up later: expect to wake around 3am and sleep less deeply. Leaving three hours between your last drink and bed, with water in between, makes a clear difference.

A drop is the smallest amount you can taste, a grating is one pass over the fine side of the grater, and a scattering is a light pinch over the top: all three are to taste, so start small and add more.

A dropped prescription is an emergency: human antidepressants are dangerous to pets even in small amounts. Ring your vet or the animal poison line now with the packet and the strength, and do not wait for symptoms - serotonin poisoning shows up as restlessness, a racing heart and tremors.

A dry microfibre cloth is all a phone screen needs, and a fingerprint-marked one comes up with a single drop of water on the cloth, never sprayed on the screen. On a laptop or TV, use water only: alcohol and kitchen spray take the coating off, and paper towels leave fine scratches.

A dry, flaky scalp is usually dandruff: a yeast that feeds on the oil on your head, so it is not the same thing as dry skin and body cream will not help it. Wash with an anti-dandruff shampoo - zinc pyrithione or ketoconazole, from any chemist - two or three times a week, work it into the scalp and leave it five minutes before rinsing, and give it a month. Do not scratch the flakes off, and keep washing your hair: a scalp left greasy feeds it. If it is red, sore, or hair is thinning in patches, see a pharmacist or your GP.

A duck egg takes about a minute longer than a hen's: 7 to 8 minutes for a runny yolk and 11 for hard boiled, from already boiling water. It is bigger, the white sets firmer and the yolk is richer, which is why it is good in baking and fried; cook it exactly like a hen's egg, cool it under the tap before peeling, and keep it in the fridge like any egg.
A duck is a batter out for nought, and a golden duck is out first ball. It's just slang for zero on the scoreboard — the shape of the 0 looks like a duck's egg.

A dull wooden floor has worn through its finish, not its wood, so clean it with a diluted wood floor soap rather than a polish or a steam mop, then put a maintenance coat of the same hard wax oil or lacquer back on - one coat on the traffic lanes every year or two. Sanding is only for deep scratches; a whole-room sand and re-finish is £20 to £30 a square metre if you have it done.

A dutch oven is a heavy lidded pot - cast iron, or cast aluminium with enamel on it - that goes from the hob to the oven, which is the whole point of it: brown the meat on the burner, put the lid on, and let the oven do the next two hours. The thick walls hold heat and spread it evenly, so it braises without scorching, and the tight lid keeps the steam in. The enamelled ones want no metal utensils; bare cast iron wants seasoning and drying on the hob before it goes away.

A face puffed up by crying is the salt in tears and the pressure of it, and it settles within a few hours. Cold water on a flannel, or a cold spoon held on the puffy places for five minutes, brings it down fastest, and a glass of water and a sit-down help too. If it is only one side, painful, or spreading to your lips or tongue, get it looked at the same day.

A face that has gone numb, drooped or twisted on one side needs 999 now, not a wait and see - it can be a stroke even if it feels mild and even if it is passing. Note the time it started, unlock the door, sit down and stay on the line to the call handler.

A failed lamp is a bulb, and the job is the same all round the car. Change bulbs in pairs, because the other one is usually the same age and about to go. Half an hour with the handbook and a £10 to £20 bulb is normal DIY, though some cars need the battery or the wheel arch liner out. A lamp that looks milky or yellow rather than dark is the plastic lens fogging, not the bulb, and the cloudy-headlight card covers that.

A fan oven usually runs its cooling fan on after you switch off, sometimes for ten or twenty minutes, to pull the heat out of the casing: that is normal and it stops by itself. If it never stops, or starts again while the oven is cold, the thermostat or the fan switch has failed and it needs an engineer, and it is worth switching off at the wall until then.

A fan pulls the room's air over cold coils, and cold air cannot hold as much water vapour, so the water condenses on the metal and drips into the tank while the dried air goes back into the room. It works best with the doors shut and the tank empty, because a machine that fills up stops, and it will not dry a room that is open to the rest of the house.

A fan costs a penny or two an hour; a portable air conditioner is more like 30 to 50p, and a fitted one more again. A fan only cools you, not the room, so put it in front of an open window at night with another window open across the room. A bowl of ice in front of a fan helps in dry heat, not in humidity.

A fault like that is usually a 'major', not a 'dangerous' one: you can drive it to the garage or to a pre-booked test and nowhere else, and taking it back the next working day makes the partial retest free. Read the sheet before you move it; only 'dangerous' means the car must not be driven at all. Put a bulb, a wiper, a number plate or a tyre right yourself in a few minutes; brakes, steering, suspension and anything rusted through are the garage's.

A fault line is a crack in the Earth's crust where the rock on either side has moved, and it is where most earthquakes happen because the two sides keep slipping. The San Andreas fault is the best known.
A ferret lives 6 to 10 years, with the males usually a little longer than the females.

A few spots under a car can be old spillage or a leaking rocker cover gasket, which is cheap; a puddle that comes back overnight needs looking at. Check the dipstick each week and top up, put cardboard under it to see where the drip lands, and get it looked at before it reaches the clutch or the cambelt.

A fire heats the air in the flue, that hot air is lighter than the air in the room and rises out of the top, and the gap it leaves pulls fresh air in at the bottom - that steady pull is the draw. A cold flue has no pull at all, which is why a fire smokes on a cold morning until the chimney warms, and why a room sealed too tight for air to get in makes any fire sulk.

A firewall is a filter on the traffic going in and out of a device or a home network: it lets the answers to what you asked for through and blocks the connections nobody asked for. Your router has one on by default and your computer has its own, so you rarely need to touch it - a program that cannot reach the internet is the one time it is worth looking at.

A first physiotherapy appointment is usually 30 to 45 minutes, because it starts with the history and an examination, and the follow-ups are 20 to 30. Ask what the plan is and how many sessions they expect before you pay for a block, and whether you need to bring shorts or a vest to move in.

A first provisional licence is £34 online, or £43 on the paper form, and renewing the photocard is £14 online, or £17 on paper. The tests are separate: about £23 for the theory and £62 for the practical, £75 at an evening or weekend slot. Book all of it on gov.uk, and do the provisional first - you cannot book a test without the number.

A first touch is a cushion, not a stop: as the ball arrives, take the pace out of it and push it a stride ahead into the space you are about to run into. Kick a ball against a wall 200 times a day with each foot, using the inside and the sole, then have a partner pass at speed. Twenty minutes of wall work a day fixes more first touches than any drill with cones.

A first 5k usually takes 30 to 40 minutes at a jog with walking breaks; the average parkrun time is about 28 minutes, and anything near 25 is quick. Walking the whole way is roughly 45 to 50 minutes, and most races allow far longer than that, so a first one is not something to worry about being slow at.
A first 10k usually takes 55 to 70 minutes, and the average club runner does 50 to 55; under 45 is quick. Walking breaks in the second half cost you less than you would think.

A first half marathon usually takes 2 hours 15 to 2 hours 30, and two hours is a good club standard; under 1 hour 45 is quick. Walking breaks early on cost you very little, and the cut-offs at most races are generous.

A first marathon usually takes 3 hours 30 to 4 hours 45 minutes, and under 4 hours is a good club standard; under 3 hours 30 is quick. Most people run the first half too fast and lose twenty minutes in the last 10km, so aim for even splits and walk the water stations.

A fish sitting on the bottom, or hanging at the surface gulping, is reacting to the water rather than to you, and ammonia is the usual cause: change a quarter of the water now with water of the same temperature that has been dechlorinated, stop feeding for two or three days, and check the filter is running and not clogged. Then test the water - a kit for ammonia and nitrite costs less than the fish does - before you buy any medicine, because a medicine in a tank with ammonia in it kills faster than the disease. On its side, gasping at the top, or with red gills is an emergency: water change now, lights off, no food.

A fish slice is the wide, thin, usually slotted blade with a handle, for lifting things that fall apart - a whole fried fish, an egg, a slice of cake - and turning them without the corner of a spatula digging in. Thin and springy is what you want; a thick one is a burger press.

A fish hanging at the top and gulping is short of oxygen, which is nearly always the water: test ammonia and nitrite with a liquid kit, change a quarter of the water with dechlorinated water at the same temperature, and add an air stone or point the filter outlet at the surface. Do not feed it for a day, and do not do a full clean - the bacteria in the filter are what is keeping it alive. A fish floating on its side or upside down is swim-bladder trouble or already dead, and either way it comes out of the tank.

A fix buys certainty and you pay a little more for it, usually a quarter to half a point over the cheapest tracker, so take the fix if a two point rise would put the payment out of reach and the tracker if you could absorb that and would rather pay less now. Five years is the usual middle: long enough to be worth an arrangement fee of about £999, short enough not to lock you in if you might move. Check the early repayment charge before you pick a length, because leaving inside the fix usually costs one to five percent of what is left on the loan.

A fixed rate stays the same for an agreed term, so the monthly payment is known from the start; a variable rate moves with the lender or the Bank of England and can fall as well as rise. Fixed buys certainty and usually costs a little more; variable is cheaper while rates are falling.

A fixed speed camera measures how fast you cross two buried loops or a radar beam and photographs the plate if you are over the limit; average-speed cameras instead read the same plate at two points and divide the distance by the time, so braking for one camera does not help. The picture and the calibration certificate are what make a ticket stand up, which is why a faulty or obscured plate is not a way out of one.

A flask is two walls of glass or steel with the air taken out of the gap between them, so there is nothing left for heat to travel through: no air to carry it (convection) and almost none to conduct it. The shiny coat on the inside reflects radiant heat back, and the stopper stops heat escaping out of the top, which is why a flask keeps soup hot all day if it is filled right to the top.

A flat patch on one side is common and comes from lying the same way, and it does not affect the brain. Keep putting them on their back to sleep, but alternate the end of the cot they lie at so they turn their head the other way, do tummy time while they are awake several times a day, and carry them upright in a sling more. Most round out once they sit up and spend less time on their back; see the GP if the face looks uneven, if it is not improving by six months, or if the head shape is fixed rather than flattish.

A flat suits a cat well: two rooms and a window are enough as long as there is something to climb and something to hunt. A tall post by the window, a shelf at head height and a windowsill give it the height a garden would, and ten minutes with a toy on a string twice a day tires it out before bed. A bored indoor cat is the one that yowls at night. Keep the windows on catches, the blind cords short and the cables tucked away, check the lease allows pets in writing, and a rescue that has already lived indoors is an easier first cat than a kitten.

A flexible sigmoidoscopy is a camera on a tube into the lower bowel only, about the last half metre, and it takes 10 to 15 minutes - less of a journey than a full colonoscopy. Most people have it without sedation, lying on their side, with some cramping and wind as the tube goes round the bends; you go home straight afterwards and can drive. The bowel prep is usually an enema at the hospital rather than a day of drinking the stuff.

A flexible ticket is the fare that lets you change the date, usually for no fee or a small one, where a cheap fare charges £30 to £70 plus any fare difference to change and often nothing back if you cancel. It is worth it when the date might move: work, a hospital appointment, a family thing. Check whether the fare is changeable or refundable, because they are not the same, and buy the cheaper ticket plus travel insurance when the difference is more than the change fee.

A flickering picture is usually the lead or the refresh rate: reseat or swap the HDMI or DisplayPort cable, try another port at both ends, then set the refresh rate to 60Hz and update the graphics driver. On a TV, turn motion smoothing off and any eco or auto-dimming setting. If it flickers the moment the fridge or the heating clicks on, it is the wiring in the house, not the screen.

A florist bouquet is £25 to £45, a supermarket bunch £4 to £8, and dried or artificial stems sit in between and last years. For a wedding, flowers are usually 8 to 10 per cent of the budget: put the money into the bouquet and the buttonholes, which are in every photo, and use supermarket or dried stems for the tables and the aisle. For a funeral, a wreath or a casket spray is £30 to £100 and a tied sheaf £20 to £40. Buying the same flower in season, from a market rather than a florist, and arranging it yourself the day before is where the saving usually is.

A floury taste means the flour is still raw, and the fix is time on the heat, not more seasoning: simmer it 5 to 10 minutes longer, stirring, so the starch cooks through and loses the raw edge. A roux wants 2 or 3 minutes of bubbling before any liquid goes in, and if the sauce is already made, a splash of stock and a slow simmer takes it out. Milk, butter or cream rounds off what is left.

A food mill is the pan with a crank and a perforated disc underneath, for pureeing and sieving in one go: it pushes cooked apple, tomato or potato through the holes and leaves the skins and seeds behind. Swapping the disc sets how fine it comes out, which is why it makes smoother mash and seedless sauce without a blender.

A foot that has gone numb is usually a nerve being pressed - a tight shoe, a leg crossed over it, kneeling or sitting on it - and the feeling comes back over a few minutes as the pressure comes off. Shake it out, walk on it and change position rather than rubbing it. If it keeps happening, or both feet are numb, it is worth a GP visit for the usual causes: diabetes, a B12 or thyroid problem, a trapped nerve from the back, and narrow shoes. Both feet numb with back pain, or no feeling between the legs with trouble weeing, is the same-day one: ring 111, or 999 if the back has given way. A sudden cold, white or blue foot, or a foot that drags, is 999.

A foul is illegal contact - a push, a hold, or barging into a shooter - and the other side gets the ball, or free throws if it happened while shooting. Five fouls and you are out of the game (six in the NBA), and a team's fouls add up: once it reaches the limit in a quarter, every later foul gives the other side free throws.

A four-pack of yoghurt is about £1.50 to £2.50, and a 1kg tub £2 to £3, which is much cheaper a portion. Greek-style costs more than natural, and the big tub is the one to buy if you eat it every day.
A frame is one game of snooker, and a match is a set number of them: tour finals are usually best of 19 frames and the World Championship final is best of 35, played over two days in four sessions.

A freezer should sit at -18C or colder (0F on an American dial). Most freezers have a dial marked 1 to 5 rather than degrees, so stand a thermometer between two frozen packs overnight: warmer than -18C and you are keeping food for weeks rather than months, and colder is fine, just dearer to run.

A freezer works best about three-quarters full: the frozen food holds the cold, but packed to the door it cannot move air and the food at the front starts to thaw. Freeze flat in bags with the air pressed out and stand them on edge like files, keep the oldest at the front so it goes first, and use the crush to cook from it - a full freezer is a week of dinners if you eat what is in it. A drawer that will not close means it is time for a clear-out, not more squeezing.

A fridge or freezer holds refrigerant gas that has to be taken out by someone equipped for it, so it can never go out with the rubbish. The shop selling you the new one has to take the old one away on a like-for-like basis, often free or for a small fee, and the recycling centre takes it. Take the doors off before it leaves the kitchen if children or pets will be near it.

A fridge comes down to temperature in about 4 hours empty and is steady at 4C after 24, so switch it on, let it run empty, then load it - a freezer wants about 24 hours to hold -18C. A thermometer in a glass of water tells you when it is ready, not the dial.
