A front is the boundary where a warm air mass meets a cold one. On a cold front the cold air pushes under the warm: heavy rain in a narrow band, then a sharp drop in temperature. On a warm front the warm air climbs over the cold: thickening cloud, drizzle, and it turns milder. The rain comes at the front and the clearing is behind it.

A frost-free freezer never needs defrosting by hand: it clears its own frost, so ice building up means the door seal has gone or the vent behind it is blocked. Check the gasket all round the door with a sheet of paper (it should grip), and a new seal is a cheap fix.

A full service usually means leaving the car for the day, and an oil and filter change or an interim service is two or three hours, so ask for a while-you-wait slot if you need the car. Get the price in writing with the parts listed, and have the book or the app stamped, because the service history is what a buyer checks.

A full-time week is usually 37.5 or 40 hours on paper, and the shift shape is what changes the answer. A nurse is contracted to 37.5 hours, worked as three 12-hour shifts a week plus the odd fourth, and a care worker often has the same 12-hour pattern. A teacher's directed hours are about 1,265 a year over 195 days, and the planning and marking on top usually make 45 to 55 hours in term time. A junior doctor's rota averages no more than 48 hours a week. A plumber, electrician or builder is normally 40 to 45 hours plus emergency call-outs. A lorry driver may drive 9 hours a day, 10 of them twice a week, and no more than 56 hours in a week or 90 in a fortnight, with breaks on top. Nobody in the UK may average more than 48 hours a week over 17 weeks unless they have signed to opt out.

A fuse is a short strip of wire that melts before the rest of the circuit does: overload it and the wire heats past its melting point and breaks the circuit, so the wiring and the flex behind the wall never take the heat. Fixing the cause is the point - a fuse that blows twice is a fault, not bad luck.

A garage will take the old one when it fits a new one, and a scrap dealer or a metal merchant buys it by weight, so it is worth a few pounds rather than a trip to the tip - which takes them too. Never put it in the bin or leave it in the garage for years: it holds acid and lead.

A garage has to give you a written estimate and get your agreement before the work, and ask again before any extra job. If it did work you did not agree to, you only owe the price you agreed: write and say which jobs you authorised, ask for the bill to be corrected and for the old parts back. If they will not release the car, the Motor Ombudsman and Trading Standards through Citizens Advice can take it.

A gardener is usually £20 to £35 an hour, and a fortnightly cut of a small lawn is £30 to £50 a visit. One-off clearances, hedges and anything with a skip are priced by the job instead. Ask whether green waste is taken away or left for you, because that is often the difference between two quotes.

A gift card is an unsecured debt of the shop, so if it folds you are near the back of the queue: register your claim with the administrator the same week, with the card and the receipt. If you bought the gift card on a credit card for over £100, the card company is jointly liable under Section 75, and a chargeback can recover a debit card payment from the last 120 days. If the chain is only wobbling, spend it now.

A gigabyte is about a thousand megabytes, and a megabyte is about a thousand kilobytes: a photo is around 3MB, a song 4MB, a downloaded film 1.5 to 4GB, and a terabyte is a thousand gigabytes. Storage and data use the same units - the GB on a phone's box is how much it holds, the GB on a mobile bill is how much it downloads.

A gland that comes up with a cold, a sore throat or a skin infection is doing its job, and it usually goes back down over two to three weeks. See a GP if it is hard or fixed in place, bigger than about two centimetres, still up after four weeks, or comes with night sweats, weight loss or a fever that will not settle.

A godparent is a spare adult for the child: someone who takes an interest in them for years, remembers birthdays, and is there if the parents cannot be. At the christening you stand at the font with the parents, say the promises with them, and get named in the register. Most churches expect a godparent to be baptised, so if you are not, or the promise is not one you can honestly make, say it when you are asked - many parents want a supporting adult rather than a church promise, and a naming ceremony has none of them. The real job is the next twenty years rather than the day: a card and a small present at the christening, and being the person the child can ring when they are older.

A goldfish lives 10 to 20 years in a big enough tank or pond with a filter, which is why the fish bowl is the problem: a bowl with no filter is usually a couple of years at best. Two goldfish want a tank of 100 litres or more.

A grater turns hard food into shreds: cheese, carrot, apple, potato, courgette, nutmeg. A box grater is the four-sided one - coarse for cheese and vegetables, fine for parmesan and zest, and a slicer on one side; a flat or rotary grater is for cheese at the table.

A gratin dish is a shallow, wide ovenproof dish - the opposite of a deep casserole. The point is the exposed surface: a shallow layer means more of the top browns and crisps, which is what a gratin is. A roasting tin will do at a push, if it is deep enough to hold the sauce.

A gravel board is the timber along the bottom of the run, and its job is to hold the panel up out of the wet ground so the bottom rail does not rot: it sits on the soil or in a slotted concrete board, with the panel fixed above it. Set the top of a timber board about 25mm above the ground and leave the panel 50mm clear of it, so air gets between the two. A slotted concrete gravel board lets you slide a rotten board out without taking the panel down.

A griddle is the thick flat plate - a pan, or a slab over the hob - for cooking with almost no fat and no side walls: pancakes, flatbreads, bacon, a steak. It gets very hot and stays hot, so things brown rather than steam; a ridged one leaves the dark lines and lets the fat run away.

A grip pad under it, not a tighter fit: cut a square of that rubbery open-weave shelf liner to sit inside the cushion's seam or under the throw, and it stops dead. A fitted sheet that will not stay is the elastic gone slack, a sheet a size too small, or a deep mattress on a shallow sheet - sheet clips or a strap across the corners will hold it until you replace it. Cotton and linen grip each other better than a smooth polyester, so a rougher cover is the cheap fix.

A growl while he is being brushed or handled is him saying it hurts or frightens him, so stop as soon as he does it and never tell him off for it - a dog punished for the warning goes straight to the snap. Run your hands over him first, because mats behind the ears, a tight collar and a sore ear or hip are the usual causes, and a dog who has always been fine and has just started wants a vet check. If there is nothing sore, go in two-second bursts with a second person feeding him chicken, and for nails do one a day and let a groomer or a vet nurse do the rest.

A growl is a warning rather than a fault, so the first thing is to stop what you were doing, step back and let him come to you - and never tell a dog off for growling, because a dog punished for the warning learns to skip it and go straight to the snap. Then find out what it is about: being picked up or handled, a hand near his food, bed or a stolen sock, or pain. A dog who growls when he is lifted or touched in one place needs a vet first, since a bad tooth, an ear, a sore back or an arthritic hip is the usual reason. If nothing hurts, keep children out of his space, give him a bed he can walk away to, and ask the vet for a referral to a behaviourist rather than a trainer's quick fix.

A grown sibling's jealousy is usually about one visible difference - a house, a partner, a job, or the way a parent treats you - so do not defend your life or list your own hard parts, which reads as scoring points. Name it once, plainly and without blame: 'I know this has not been easy to watch.' Then keep the relationship on ground that is not a comparison, and if every visit turns into digs or competition, make them shorter and more structured. Their envy is theirs to carry; you are not the one who has to fix it.

A guarantor is someone who signs to pay if you stop paying, so they are on the hook for the whole rent or loan, not just a month of it. Letting agents ask for one when your income is under about 30 times the monthly rent. Ask someone who could afford it and would still be talking to you afterwards, and tell them exactly what they are signing.
A guinea pig lives 5 to 7 years, and they do better in pairs because they are herd animals. Hay all day and vitamin C in the food are what keep them going that long.

A habanero is very hot, 100,000 to 350,000 Scoville, and fruity with it. A quarter of one heats a pot for four, and it is worth wearing gloves for a batch: the oil stays on hands for hours and soap barely shifts it.

A habitat is the place where a plant or animal lives, with the food, water, shelter and space it needs: a hedge is a habitat for sparrows, and a pond is one for frogs. Different species are suited to different habitats, and losing a habitat is the biggest threat to many of them.

A hairline crack is fine: cook it and eat it. A crack with a bit of leaked white is usually fine too if it is fresh and you cook it through, but bin it if the shell is dirty from a cracked egg or it has been sitting warm, since the shell is what keeps bacteria out. Keep cracked eggs out of anything raw, like mayonnaise.
A half marathon is 13.1 miles (21.1 km), which is further than a 10k at 6.2 miles and a 5k at 3.1 miles. A first half usually takes 2 hours 15 to 2 hours 30, over twelve to sixteen weeks of training.

A half marathon is 13.1 miles, or 21.1 kilometres: half the marathon distance, which is why the number looks odd. A first one usually takes 2 hours 15 to 2 hours 30, and most plans build up to it over twelve to sixteen weeks.
A hamster lives 2 to 3 years, and a Syrian is at the top of that while a dwarf is usually closer to 2. That short life is normal rather than a sign you did something wrong.

A handbrake that comes up a long way is a stretched cable, adjusted at the balance bar under the car or at the lever, and a garage does it in half an hour for £30 to £60. The cable is only half of it: the rear brake shoes or the caliper mechanism behind it is usually out of adjustment too, which is why the lever crept up in the first place. Until it is done, park it in gear and turn the wheels towards the kerb, and treat it as urgent - a handbrake that does not hold is an MOT fail, and a car that rolls is how people get hurt.

A handyman is usually £25 to £45 an hour with a minimum of one or two hours, so a morning of small jobs is £100 to £150. Jobs that need a certificate - gas, electrics in a bathroom, anything structural - are not handyman work whatever the advert says. Ask for the hourly rate, the minimum charge and whether they take the rubbish away.

A hard avocado is not ripe yet: leave it on the counter for 3 to 5 days, and a paper bag with a banana in it ripens it in half the time. Once it gives to a gentle squeeze, it keeps 2 to 3 days in the fridge. A cut half keeps a day or two with the stone left in, lemon juice on the flesh and cling film pressed right down on it; brown patches are only air and are fine to cut away, but a soft, stringy or sour-smelling one is not.

A hard disk is the older kind of storage: a stack of spinning plates read by a head, which is why it is cheap for a lot of space and why a laptop with one takes half a minute to wake up. It is fine for a photo archive or a desktop; an SSD is what makes an old laptop feel new, and a 1TB hard disk costs about what a 250GB SSD does.

A hardship payment is extra universal credit, up to 60% of your standard allowance for the month, for when a sanction or a delay has left you short of rent, heating or food - and it is taken back out of later awards. Ask in your journal or at the jobcentre the same day, and ask the council about the Household Support Fund meanwhile.

A harness is kinder for a dog that pulls, because it takes the strain off the throat, and it's the safer choice for flat-faced breeds. Use a Y-shaped one that doesn't cross the shoulders, keep a collar on for the tag, and get the fit checked — two fingers should slip under the straps.

A head of celery keeps 2 weeks wrapped in foil in the fridge, which keeps it crisp where a plastic bag makes it slimy. Limp sticks come back in 20 minutes in iced water, so shave the dry bottom off first.

A headache is pain in the head; a migraine is a condition - usually one-sided, throbbing, worse with light or movement, often with nausea or a warning aura, lasting hours. If a headache sends you to a dark room more than once, it's worth asking a GP about migraine.

A healthy dog with a thick coat is fine out in the cold, but thin-coated, short-legged, old and small dogs feel it: a coat that covers the belly and a shorter walk are enough. Towel him dry when you get in, paws and between the toes included, and rinse off grit and salt. Never leave him in a cold car, and keep antifreeze out of reach, because a few licks of it are fatal.

A hearing aid is a microphone, an amplifier and a tiny speaker in your ear: the microphone picks up the room, the electronics boost the frequencies speech lives in and the speaker sends it down the canal louder. Digital ones split the sound into bands and turn down the background to suit the room. It does not give you normal hearing back, so it takes a few weeks of wearing it all day to stop noticing it. NHS aids are free.

A heart attack is a blocked blood supply to the heart muscle - the person is usually awake, with chest pain, and needs an ambulance fast. A cardiac arrest is the heart stopping altogether: unresponsive and not breathing normally, needing CPR and a defibrillator at once - call 999 first.

A heat pump or condenser dryer needs no outside vent at all - the water goes into a tank you empty, or down a hose to the drain - so it can sit in a cupboard or a bedroom. Only a vented dryer needs the duct, and then it wants the hose out through a wall vent or an open window with no kinks and no crushed section behind the machine; a short straight run to outside is the whole job. Never duct one into a loft or a chimney: that puts the damp and the lint back into the house, and fluff round a hot duct is a fire.

A heat pump works like a fridge in reverse - it takes heat from the air or ground outside, which is always warmer than absolute zero, squeezes it to a higher temperature and puts it into your radiators. Because it moves heat rather than making it, a well-fitted one gives about three units of heat per unit of electricity, against one for a bar fire.

A hedge or a wall that shuts out the light is the council's job, not a court's: if it is an evergreen hedge over 2 metres and it blocks your light, you can complain to the council under the high-hedges rules, but only after you have written to the neighbour and kept a copy, and there is a fee of a few hundred pounds. Branches that overhang your side you can cut back to the boundary without asking, though you must offer the cuttings back and you cannot lean into their garden to do it, and you must not cut a tree under a tree preservation order or in a conservation area without checking with the council first. Right to light through an old window is a separate legal claim and a solicitor's job.

A hernia is tissue pushing through a weak spot in the muscle wall: a soft lump in the groin or at the navel that shows when you cough or stand, and a hiatus hernia is the stomach sliding up into the chest and causing heartburn. Most are not urgent, and a GP refers the ones that hurt or keep growing for a small operation. Get it seen the same day if the lump goes hard, tender and will not push back in.

A high reading is usually the moment rather than the heart: a late night or alcohol, dehydration, a hot room, coffee, standing up quickly, a stressful start to the day or an illness coming on will all lift it, and the body's own waking-up hormones lift it too. Sit for five minutes and take it again, because 60 to 100 at rest is normal. A rate that stays over 100 sitting still, or comes with chest pain, breathlessness or fainting, is a doctor's call rather than another reading.

A hinge is two leaves joined by a pin that runs through interlocking knuckles, so one leaf swings on the pin while the other stays screwed to the frame. The whole weight of the door hangs on that pin, which is why a hinge lasts far longer greased than it does dry.

A holding deposit is the small sum - at most a week's rent in England - that takes a place off the market while the landlord checks you. The tenancy deposit is the bigger amount you pay when you sign, and it has to be held in a government protection scheme.

A hole you can feel in a tooth is decay, and it does not fill itself: ring a dentist and have it looked at before it hurts, because a small filling is quicker and cheaper than the root canal or the extraction a deep cavity ends up needing. Until then brush it like the rest - spit rather than rinse after the toothpaste - keep sugary food to mealtimes, and don't poke at it with a fingernail or a pin. Ring the same day if it is painful, if food keeps packing into it, or if your face or jaw swells: a broken tooth with a sharp edge can also be smoothed by a dentist before it cuts your tongue.

A hormone is a chemical messenger made by a gland and carried in the blood to switch something on or off somewhere else: insulin tells cells to take up sugar, and adrenaline gets the body ready for action. Small amounts can have big effects, and each hormone only acts on cells that can receive it.

A horse is built to eat for sixteen hours a day, so a greedy one is usually normal: keep forage in front of him - hay in a small-holed net or a trickle feeder - and split the hard feed so the stomach is never empty. The appetite to worry about is the sudden one: ravenous with weight dropping is worms, ulcers or a tapeworm burden, and a horse that is hungry and off his hay needs the vet. Keep a fat pony off rich spring grass, because laminitis is what the greedy ones get.

A hospice is for controlling pain and symptoms and for supporting the person doing the caring - it is not a place people are sent only to die. Most of what they do is day services, help at home and short stays, and people are usually referred months before the end, which is the whole point: it is easier to sort pain out early than in a crisis. The care is free (charity and NHS funded) and needs a referral from the GP, district nurse or hospital team, so ask for one; you can also ring the hospice and ask what they have, because they answer that question all day.

A hot non-stick pan with butter foaming but not browning, and eggs beaten just enough to mix: pour them in, then push the set edges into the middle and tip the pan so the raw egg fills the gap. Take it off the heat while the top is still a little wet - it finishes cooking in the pan, and that is what stops it sticking and going rubbery.

A hot service wash once a month, the filter and the detergent drawer every couple of months, and the door left ajar between washes - there is no yearly service to book on a washing machine. If it already smells, a 90C wash with a machine cleaner or a cup of bicarbonate of soda is the fix, and the drawer is usually where it started.

A hot water bottle stays warm for four to six hours under the covers, and it is only too hot for the first twenty minutes or so. If you want it gentler from the start, fill it from the hot tap rather than the kettle and wrap it in a towel or a pillowcase - running it under the cold tap for a few seconds does the same. Never fill it with boiling water for a child or an older person, and check the stopper and the rubber for cracks before each winter.

A hotspot is a wifi network your phone makes out of its own mobile data, so a laptop can use the connection: on an iPhone it is Settings > Personal Hotspot, and on Android it is under Network, Hotspot and tethering. It uses your data allowance like any other use, drains the battery quickly, and is worth a password so nobody else joins.

A houseplant drops its open flowers when that flush is simply over, and nothing needs doing beyond cutting the spent stems back to a leaf so the plant puts its energy into leaves and roots instead. Buds that drop before they open are a different thing: that is the plant shedding what it cannot hold, and it is usually one of four shocks - moved to a darker or draughtier spot, dried out or left standing in water, a sudden cold night by a window, or a bowl of ripening fruit nearby, whose ethylene makes buds fall. Pick one thing, put it right, and give it two or three weeks before changing anything else.

A hung parliament is one where no single party has a majority of the 650 seats, so the largest party has to govern with the support of others: the 2010 coalition with the Liberal Democrats, and in 2017 the Conservatives paying the DUP for a confidence and supply deal. The sitting prime minister stays on and gets the first chance to form a government, and if that fails the monarch asks the next party.

A hypo is low blood sugar - shaky, sweaty, confused - and it needs sugar fast. Hyper means high: thirsty, weeing a lot, tired over hours, and it needs insulin and advice. The hypo is the one that has to be treated in minutes.

A hysterectomy is the womb taken out, either through the tummy, through the vagina or by keyhole, and the operation takes about an hour to an hour and a half. You are asleep for it and in hospital for one to four nights depending on the route. Recovery is the long part: two weeks of taking it very easy, six weeks before lifting anything heavier than a kettle or driving on the road, and no sex or swimming for about six weeks. If the ovaries come out too, that is the menopause starting, and it can be managed.

A jacket potato comes back best at 200C (180C fan): split it open, brush the cut faces with oil so they crisp, and give it about 20 minutes, or 8 to 10 if you only want it hot right through. Three minutes in the microwave and then 10 in the oven is quicker and nearly as good; on its own a microwave leaves the skin soft and leathery.

A jacket potato is a good everyday carbohydrate: about 200 calories for a medium one, more fibre than rice or pasta if you eat the skin, and it fills you up. What decides the meal is the topping - beans, tuna, cottage cheese or chilli are fine; a lake of butter, cheese and mayo turns it into the calorie bomb people blame the potato for.

A jacket potato is fine the next day: cool it within an hour, keep it in the fridge covered and eat it within 2 days, skin and all. Reheat it until it is piping hot right through, or cut it up and fry it - a foil-wrapped one left on the side overnight goes in the bin.
A jalapeño is mild to medium, 2,500 to 8,000 Scoville: hot enough to eat raw in slices, and much milder pickled or cooked. The seeds and white pith hold most of the heat.

A jaw that clicks on its own is usually harmless, but if it comes with pain or stiffness it is the jaw joint (TMJ) complaining: eat softer food for a couple of weeks, stop chewing gum and biting your nails, hold a warm flannel against it, and avoid opening wide while it settles. A dentist can check the bite, give you exercises and fit a night guard if you grind. See someone sooner if the jaw locks open or shut, or if it is very painful. Jaw pain with chest pain or breathlessness is an emergency - call 999.

A job nobody came to do is a debt they owe you: put it in writing - what was booked, the date, what you paid - and ask for the money back within 14 days. If they will not pay, a card chargeback, Section 75 over £100, then Money Claims Online for about £35 with no solicitor. Never pay the balance of a job that has not been done, and keep the messages.

A kettle takes water to 100C and switches itself off there, and that switch is the same thermal cut-out on every electric kettle, so there is no hotter setting to find. The outside of a plastic kettle stays much cooler than the water; a steel one gets hot enough to sting, so lift it by the handle.

A kettle cutting out as the water boils, a microwave stopping when the door opens, an oven stopping when its timer ends or it reaches temperature, a washer or dryer finishing at the end of the programme: that is the machine working as designed, and there is nothing to fix. A fault looks different - it gives up part way through a job with work left to do, or it stops sooner each time it is used.
A kilo of frozen peas is about £1.50 to £2 and lasts months. Fresh peas in season are sweeter but cost three or four times as much for a much smaller bag.
A kilo of long-grain rice is about £1 to £2.50 and a kilo of basmati £2 to £3.50. It keeps for months in a cupboard, so the bigger bag is usually the better buy.

A kitchen scale weighs in grams, which is how most baking is written and the only way to be sure of flour, butter and sugar - a cup of flour varies by a third depending on how it is scooped. Put the bowl on, set it to zero, and add each thing in turn.

A kitten goes out a week after her second vaccination, which is usually around four months, and not before, because she has no immunity to anything until then; a grown cat that is vaccinated and chipped can go out now. Microchip first either way (it is the law from 20 weeks in the UK), then let her out hungry, an hour before a meal, so the rattle of the biscuits brings her back. Go with her for the first few trips, keep them short, and keep her in at night: most cats are lost in their first month out, in the dark.

A knee replacement takes the worn surfaces off the end of the thigh bone and the top of the shin bone and puts a metal and plastic joint in their place; the operation takes about an hour to 90 minutes under a spinal or general anaesthetic. Most people are up on it the day after with a frame, in for two to four nights, and the physio starts straight away because the bending is what needs the work. Expect swelling and a stiff, warm knee for weeks, walking sticks for about six weeks, and up to a year before it feels like your own.

A knee that gives way is one to get looked at rather than train through: it usually means a ligament is not holding, or the kneecap is slipping, and a physio can work out which in one visit. Skip pivoting sports and uneven ground until then, and keep the muscles awake with sit-to-stands and step-ups. Ring your GP or a physio this week.
A knob is about a tablespoon, 15g; a dollop is nearer two tablespoons. Both are meant to be judged by eye, since a walnut-sized lump is a knob and you can always add a little more.

A knock-on is losing the ball forward out of your hands, or it bouncing forward off your arm: play stops and the other side gets a scrum where it happened. A forward pass is the same offence thrown instead of dropped.

A ladle is the deep, long-handled spoon with a lip, for moving liquid in useful amounts: soup into bowls, stock into a jug, sauce over a plate. A 100ml ladle is about three tablespoons, which is a handy measure when a recipe says a ladleful.

A laminate worktop is usually £60 to £120 a metre, solid wood £150 to £400, and quartz, granite or sintered stone £250 to £600. Fitting is £200 to £500 for a straight run, and more where it has to be cut round a sink, a hob or a corner. Ask whether the price is per metre or for the length you need, whether cutting and sealing the edges is included, and have it templated on site rather than from your own measurements.

A laptop screen is a replaceable part, so do not replace the machine: a Windows laptop panel is usually £60 to £150 fitted at a local shop, and an Apple one is £150 to £300 through Apple or a good independent. Back the files up before it goes in, in case the screen gets worse while you wait, and check household accidental damage cover first - it often pays for the whole repair.

A laptop if you will be typing - email, essays, spreadsheets, work - and a tablet if it is mostly reading, video, calls and games on the sofa. A tablet with a keyboard costs about what a laptop does and types worse, so make it the only machine only if you truly do not type; a cheap laptop and a 300 pound tablet side by side covers the most ground for the money.

A laptop is good for about four to six years and a tablet for three to five, and the clock starts when the software updates stop rather than when it feels slow: a machine with no security fixes is the reason to change, not the speed. The battery is the exception, since £40 to £80 fits a new one to a laptop and £50 to £120 to a phone, and that alone buys another two or three years. If the case and the screen are still sound, a battery is nearly always cheaper than a replacement.

A late parcel is a broken promise, not a broken item: if it has not arrived by the date you agreed, or 30 days if you agreed none, you can cancel for a full refund, but money for the delay itself comes only with a guaranteed service such as next-day delivery. Claim in writing with the order number and the date it should have come, and ask for the delivery charge back.

A layover, or a connection, is the wait at an airport between two flights, and a stopover is the same thing when it is long enough to leave the airport, usually a night or more. A connection under about two hours on the same ticket is the airline's problem if the first flight is late, so the risk is a tight change, not a long wait. On two separate tickets you are on your own for a missed second flight, so leave three hours or more.

A leak is nearly always a joint or a hole, and it is a dry-day job: a leaking joint at the stop end or between two lengths is cleaned out, dried and sealed with gutter sealant; a hole or crack is covered with a self-adhesive flashing strip pressed on over a clean, dry surface, which lasts a few years. Before any of that, check the downpipe is not blocked - water backing up finds the weakest joint and pours out there - and re-clip a run that has sagged so it falls towards the downpipe, about 1cm in 3 metres. Never do it off a ladder in the wind or on your own: a ladder on wet ground is the fall that puts people in hospital.

A leap year is a year with 366 days and a 29th of February, because a year is really about 365 and a quarter: without the extra day the calendar would slip a day every four years. One correction keeps it exact, since the year is not quite a quarter longer - a century is only a leap year if it divides by 400, which is why 1900 was not one and 2000 was.

A leg of lamb is 25 minutes per 500g at 200C (180C fan), then 15 minutes resting under foil: about 1 hour 5 in total for a 2kg leg pink, 1 hour 25 for well done. Score the fat into diamonds, push garlic and rosemary into the cuts, and put it in a hot oven.

A leg that swells after a hip or knee replacement is not ordinary swelling and it is worth a phone call rather than a wait: a calf that is hot, tight, red or tender, or a whole leg that swells up, can be a clot, and clots are more common in the weeks after this operation than people expect - ring the ward that did the operation or 111 and say when the swelling started. If you are also short of breath, coughing or feeling faint, that is 999. Swelling around the joint itself is the ordinary sort, and that one goes down with ice and the leg raised.

A lemon tart filling is four eggs, 200g of caster sugar, the juice and zest of four lemons and 200ml of double cream, whisked together and poured into a part-baked pastry case, then baked at 150C for 30 to 35 minutes until it is set with a wobble in the middle, because it firms up as it cools and needs no cornflour. Bake it in a loose-bottomed tin you have lined with shop-bought shortcrust if you are short of time, and let it cool completely before you take it out of the tin or the sides will crack.

A lemon gives about 3 tablespoons of juice, 45ml, and a lime about 2, 30ml. A big orange gives about half a cup (120ml) and a small one a third of a cup; a grapefruit gives about two thirds of a cup. So a cup of lemon juice is four or five lemons, and rolling them hard on the counter before squeezing gets a little more out of each.

A lens that feels dry or scratchy is usually the lens itself: take it out, rinse it in the proper solution (never tap water), soak it as long as the maker says and put it back, or start a fresh one for the day. Rewetting drops made for lens wearers help through the afternoon, and heating, screens and air conditioning dry them out more than anything else. Leave the lenses out for a day if the eye still feels gritty. If the eye is red or painful with the lens in, take it out and get it looked at the same day - a red eye in a lens wearer is the one that needs checking quickly.

A levels are exam-based and mostly academic, usually three subjects; BTECs are coursework-based and vocational, and a full BTEC is the size of three A levels. Both get you to university, and a BTEC suits a subject you'd rather do than read about.

A licensed taxi has to run the meter, so a fare that is not on it is a complaint to the council that licenses the car: note the plate or licence number, the time and the route, and complain the same week. A minicab or an app should have quoted the price before you got in, so dispute it in the app first. Keep the receipt, because the council can make the driver hand the money back.

A lichen is not one thing but two living together: a fungus with algae or bacteria inside it, sharing food the algae make from light and shelter the fungus gives. That is why lichen grows on bare rock and why it is a sign of clean air.

A light scratch in the finish lifts with a walnut rubbed along the grain, or a dab of wax polish in the same shade. If a fingernail does not catch on it, the scratch is only in the finish. A white ring from a wet glass is moisture trapped in the lacquer rather than a mark in the wood: a warm iron over a cloth for a few seconds lifts it, and a deep gouge wants a wax filler stick of the right colour, not sandpaper, which takes the finish off round it.

A light whiff while filling up is normal; a strong petrol smell after is not. Do not smoke or start the engine, and check the filler cap is on properly and not cross-threaded. If the smell is inside the car or stays after a few miles, stop and get it looked at, because a leak near a hot engine is a fire risk.

A light year is a distance, not a time: it is how far light travels in a year, about 9.46 trillion kilometres (5.88 trillion miles). Proxima Centauri, the nearest star after the Sun, is about 4.2 light years away, and the Milky Way is about 100,000 light years across.

A limerick is five lines that rhyme aabba, with the two in the middle short: it is a joke in verse. There once was a cloud over Crewe that had far too much rain to do. It rained on the park from morning till dark, and then, just for fun, rained on you.

A lineout restarts play after the ball goes into touch: the forwards of both sides line up in two rows, a hooker throws the ball straight down the middle, and the jumpers are lifted to catch it. The throwing side usually wins their own ball.

A lintel is the beam over a window or a door opening that carries the wall above it, so the bricks do not sit on the frame. Older houses often have a timber one over a doorway and a stone or steel one over a window; a new opening or a wider one needs a steel beam, designed and signed off by a structural engineer. If there is a stepped crack running up from the corner of a window, the lintel is the first thing to check, and it is a builder's job, not a filler job.

A loaf that collapses rose and then fell back, which is a prove that ran too long: the yeast has eaten its sugar and the gluten that held the bubbles gives way when the heat hits it. Shape it and prove it only until a floured finger pressed in leaves a dent that springs back slowly - if the dent stays, it is ready, and if it fills at once it is not. Bake it at 220C (200C fan) and leave the door shut for the first 20 minutes, and cut the water and yeast slightly next time; a loaf that also smells of alcohol went well past ready.

A loan is cheaper for a fixed sum over a fixed time: the rate is set at the start, the monthly payment never moves and 0% card offers usually end before a big balance is cleared. A credit card is the better tool for something you can clear in full each month, because it costs nothing and protects purchases over £100. For £5,000 over two years, compare the loan's APR with a 0% balance transfer fee plus what the card's rate becomes afterwards, and never use a card for cash.

A locksmith is usually £60 to £120 to let you back in during the day, and £120 to £250 at night or at a weekend, with a new lock £80 to £150 fitted. The cheap quote on a van is often the call-out only, with the rest added on the doorstep. Ask for the total price on the phone, before they come out, and pay by card so there is a record.

A lodger lives in the same home as the owner and shares the kitchen or bathroom; a tenant rents a place of their own with a tenancy and has the whole of it. A lodger can usually be asked to leave with reasonable notice, while a tenant needs a court order - so in England the word on the agreement matters as much as the money.

A loft conversion is usually £25,000 to £60,000 depending on the type, and a single-storey extension £1,800 to £2,500 a square metre. A dormer and a bathroom in the roof are the two things that move it most, and structural engineers, party wall agreements and building regulations are all extra. Ask whether the quote is fixed, what it excludes, and who is managing the inspections.

A lumbar puncture is a needle into the lower back to draw off a sample of the fluid around the spinal cord, and it takes about 15 minutes. The skin is numbed first, so the worst is a push and a strange tingling down a leg; you lie flat for an hour or so afterwards and go home the same day. Drink plenty and keep still for the rest of the day - the headache that follows is the commonest problem, and lying flat is what settles it.

A lump on an arm or a leg is usually nothing: a knock leaves a bruise under the skin that takes two or three weeks to go, so carry on using it as normal and ice it for the first day rather than rubbing it. Without a knock, a soft one that moves and is a bit tender is usually harmless, and a hard one that does not move, is growing, or is still there after two weeks needs a GP - the same rule as a lump anywhere else.

A lump that comes up over a few days in the neck, armpit or groin is usually a swollen gland from an infection and settles in two to three weeks. Anywhere else, one that is soft and tender is usually the harmless sort. Anything hard, painless, fixed in place, or still there after three weeks needs a GP, and so does a lump with night sweats or weight loss.

A lump feeling in the throat with nothing there is usually globus, and it is common with reflux, dry air and tension - symptoms that ease when you swallow food, water, or when you stop noticing it, are the reassuring kind. See a GP if it hurts, comes with food sticking, weight loss, a hoarse voice or a neck lump, or if it has not settled in three weeks, because a camera check of the throat is the way to be sure.

A lumpy pillow has usually just bunched its filling: unzip it, pull the filling apart with your hands, shake it down to the corners and bash it flat. If it still lumps, or it folds in half and stays folded when you lay it on your arm, the filling has gone and a new one is the fix - hollowfibre costs about £10 to £25 and a pillow over two years old is usually past it. A duvet that has gone lumpy is the same job, and a wash on a hot cycle with two tennis balls in the tumble dryer evens the filling out again.

A machine that will not stop is waiting for something it cannot do: switch it off at the wall and turn the water off at the valve behind it, then clean the filter behind the kick plate and check the drain hose is not kinked. Set it to drain or spin only and start it again. If it fills even with the water off, the water-level pressure switch has failed, which is an engineer's job.

A machine that bangs or walks across the floor is almost always an uneven load: stop it, undo the tangle, and put a couple of towels in with a single heavy thing like a duvet. If it does it on every spin, take the transport bolts out of the back (they stay in on a new machine and must come out), level the feet so it cannot rock, and check it is not touching a cupboard. A screech or a burning smell means the drum bearings or the belt, which is a repair.

A machine that keeps going wrong is not bad luck, and it is not your job to keep paying for repairs: a repair has to be done properly and within a reasonable time, so when the same fault comes back you can refuse another repair and ask for a refund or a price reduction instead. Put it in writing, list each date and what went wrong, and keep the receipts - within six months of buying, the shop has to prove the fault was not there when they sold it. Past six months, an independent report saying the fault was built in is what wins it.

A mammogram is an X-ray of each breast, taken by pressing it between two plates for a few seconds at a time, four pictures in all, and the whole appointment is about 20 minutes. It is uncomfortable rather than painful - a firm squeeze that stops as soon as the picture is taken - and you can drive yourself home and go back to work. The screening programme calls women every three years from 50 to 70; a recall for another look is common and mostly not cancer, because screening is meant to find the things too small to feel.

A mandatory reconsideration is the benefit office looking at its own decision again. Ask within one month of the decision letter: ring the number on it, then put the request in writing and ask for the statement of reasons. If it is still wrong, appeal to the tribunal within one month of that notice - free, and you can ask for a phone hearing.

A mandoline is a flat board with a blade set at an adjustable height, for slices of even thickness - 2mm potato for dauphinoise, cabbage for slaw - which a knife cannot match for speed. It is also the sharpest thing in most kitchens: use the hand guard, or a cut glove, every time, and stop while there is still a knuckle's width of vegetable left. Wash it straight after, since dried starch glues the blade in place and the next slice slips.

A marathon is 26.2 miles, or 42.2 kilometres, and a half is 13.1 miles (21.1 km), so the full race is exactly twice as far. The odd 0.2 of a mile is there because the 1908 London course was extended to finish in front of the royal box. A half is the obvious first step, and most plans build up to it over about sixteen weeks.

A mat helps the feet and the legs, not the back: it takes the hardness out of a concrete floor, and two or three centimetres of rubber or dense foam does that, while a thin kitchen mat or a gel mat does very little. Stand on it where you actually spend the shift rather than in front of the counter you visit. For the back the fix is movement, not a mat: shift your weight from foot to foot, put one foot on a low step, and sit down for two minutes every hour, because standing still is what a back dislikes. Firm shoes with room in the toe finish the job, and if your ankles swell by the evening, compression socks help more than any mat.

A maul is a ball carrier held up with teammates bound on to him, everyone on their feet; a ruck is the same idea with the ball on the ground. In both, players must stay on their feet, join from behind the ball, and the side going forward gets the advantage.

Pigeons want a loft with perches, a landing board and open sky in front of it, and a pair is happier than one. A pigeon mix, grit and clean water, and out at the same time each day so they learn the way home.

Pilates is the better pick for a weak or sore back and a strong middle - it is slow, controlled work on the deep stomach and hip muscles - and yoga is the better pick for flexibility, balance and winding down. Both are low-impact and fine to start from nothing, so if the choice is still even, take the one whose teacher you liked.

Piles are swollen veins in the back passage: they itch, ache or sting, and often bleed a little when you go. Most settle in a few days. Eat fibre and drink water so you are not straining, don't sit on the loo scrolling, and a pharmacy cream or suppository takes the sting out. See a GP if bleeding keeps up for weeks, if a lump will not go back in, or if it is very painful; dark blood, or blood mixed with the stool, is worth checking sooner.

Pinch the arms in gently at the temples - most plastic frames can be bent a millimetre or two by hand, and that is usually all it takes - then have an optician tighten the screws and adjust the bridge, which they do free in a few minutes. Silicone nose pads or an ear grip stop a pair that keeps sliding, and wash the nose pads with soapy water, because skin oil makes them skate.

Pine nuts are the classic and sunflower seeds or cashews are the usual swap, about the same weight; toast whichever you use first, because raw seeds taste flat and pine nuts turn bitter once they are brown.

Pink chicken in the middle means it is undercooked, so don't eat it. That is a bad sign rather than a taste thing: put it back in the pan or oven until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 74C, and a little pink near the bone in a roast is still fine. A grey, translucent middle is the same thing said another way: it has not come up to temperature yet, so give it another few minutes rather than looking at the colour of the outside.

Pins and needles come from a nerve being squashed, say by sitting on your foot: the signals get muddled, and the tingling is the nerve waking up as the pressure comes off. It usually clears in a minute or two; if it keeps coming back on its own, get it checked.
Plain peanut butter is fine for most dogs in small amounts, but check the label for xylitol, which is poisonous to them. Keep it to a teaspoon as a treat, and skip it if the dog is overweight.

Plain yoghurt or sour cream for a dip or a dressing, loosened with a spoon of water or lemon, and hummus, butter or mashed avocado in a sandwich. To make it from scratch: one egg yolk with a teaspoon of mustard, then 150ml of oil added drop by drop while you whisk, and a squeeze of lemon at the end.

Plain yoghurt is a good buy: about 10g of protein and a third of a day's calcium in a 150g pot. The fruit ones and the children's tubes are the ones with 12g of sugar or more, so buy plain and add your own fruit or a spoon of jam.

Plain flour at twice the amount, whisked into cold liquid before it goes in, or arrowroot at the same amount. Simmer a minute afterwards, but do not boil a cornflour sauce hard, because it thins out again.

Plan the outing around the walking. Go door to door - a taxi, or the bus that stops nearest the door - and make a bench or a cafe the turning point so the trip is two short walks with a sit in between. A four-wheel rollator with a seat means they can rest anywhere, and most big supermarkets, shopping centres and National Trust or English Heritage places lend a wheelchair or a mobility scooter free if you ring a day or two ahead; a Radar key opens the accessible toilets, and going in the morning, before they are tired, makes the most of the day. Two short trips a week beat one long one.

Plan for half the walking and twice the sitting: one or two things a day with a cafe or a bench between them, and a taxi or the hop-on bus for the long hops rather than marching between sights. Check step-free access before you book, because most museums, galleries and cathedrals publish it, ask the hotel for a room near the lift, and book help ahead on trains and at the airport - it is free, UK rail's Passenger Assist takes bookings up to 24 hours ahead and airports usually want 48. A folding wheelchair or rollator can be hired locally for a week for less than a day's car hire, a lot of places let a carer in free, and a folding stool in a bag turns an unplanned stop into a rest. Skip the walking tour and the climb, and book the view from a roof terrace or a cafe instead.

Plankton is the mass of tiny plants and animals drifting in water that cannot swim against the current: the plant sort makes oxygen and feeds everything up to the whales. Half the oxygen you breathe was made by it.

Plant onion sets from mid-March to mid-April, pushing them into firm soil so just the tip shows, 10cm apart with 30cm between rows. Birds pull them out, so a few short sticks or netting over the row saves them. Onions want firm ground: tread the bed before planting, not after, and keep it weeded.

Plant seed potatoes from late March to mid-April, once the soil is workable and no hard frost is forecast: 30cm apart in rows 60cm apart, 10cm deep, with the sprouts pointing up. Chit them on a windowsill first, in egg boxes, for six weeks. Earlies go in first, maincrops by mid-April, and a frost on the young shoots is what sets them back.

Plant strawberries in late summer, August to September, for a full crop the next June - a spring planting gives you a handful the same year and nothing much the next. 45cm apart with the crown level with the soil and the roots spread, straw under the fruit, and replace the plants every three years, when the crop shrinks and virus builds up.
Plant tulip bulbs in November, later than daffodils, which go in from September: a cold spell helps them flower well. Plant them three times their own depth and pointy end up.

Plant for the whole season rather than one week: lavender, oregano and marjoram in summer, buddleia for July and August, sedum and ivy flowers for September. Leave a sunny corner of long grass and a patch of nettles, because that is where they lay, and put out a shallow dish of water with a few stones in it.

Plant garlic cloves in autumn, October to early December: pointy end up, 15cm apart and about 2.5cm deep, in a sunny spot with soil that drains. It needs cold to split into a bulb, which is why autumn beats spring. Water it while it grows and stop a fortnight before you lift it, when the leaves start to yellow, in July.

Plant it while the roots are still damp: stand the pot or the bare roots in a bucket of water for an hour, dig a hole twice as wide as the pot and the same depth, and set the plant so the old soil mark sits level with the ground. Blueberries and cranberries want ericaceous compost and rainwater rather than tap water; currants, gooseberries, raspberries and blackberries are happy in ordinary soil in sun or half shade. Firm it in with your heel, water it well, and pick the flowers off in the first year so the roots get going instead of the fruit.

Plantar fasciitis is the thick band under the arch pulling where it attaches to the heel bone, and the signature is the first steps out of bed hurting most and easing as you walk. It is not a spur or a bone problem, so the fix is load and stretch rather than rest: roll a frozen bottle under the arch for ten minutes, stretch the calf against a wall and off a step twice a day, and do heel raises on the edge of a stair every other day. Buy shoes with a firmer heel and a bit of support rather than flat plimsolls, drop the running mileage for a few weeks, and see a physio if it is no better in six weeks or it hurts at rest.

Plants sense gravity using tiny starch grains inside their cells: shoots grow away from gravity and roots grow towards it. They also bend towards light, which is why a seedling on a windowsill leans that way.

Plants, in enormous quantity: an adult elephant eats 100 to 150 kg of grass, leaves, bark and fruit a day and drinks 100 to 200 litres of water, so it spends 16 hours a day feeding and travels to find it. Its dung is a seed bank, and a forest grows along the paths it makes.

Plants breathe through tiny holes called stomata, mostly on the underside of leaves, which open to take in carbon dioxide and let out oxygen and water vapour. Roots take oxygen from air pockets in the soil, which is why a plant in soggy, airless compost can drown. They do it day and night; in daylight photosynthesis makes more oxygen than respiration uses.

Plaque is the soft, sticky film of bacteria that forms on teeth within hours of brushing, feeding on sugar and making the acid that causes decay and sore gums. Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and cleaning between the teeth once a day shifts it, and once it hardens into tartar only a dentist can scale it off. Blood on the toothbrush is the sign gum inflammation has started.

Plato (about 428-348 BC) was a Greek philosopher, a student of Socrates and the teacher of Aristotle, who founded the Academy in Athens and wrote dialogues such as The Republic. His theory of Forms says the things we see are copies of perfect versions that exist only in thought.

Plenty bakes without eggs: shortbread, flapjack, a fruit crumble, icebox biscuits and most traybakes need none at all. If a recipe wants an egg for binding, a tablespoon of ground flaxseed in three of water stands in for one, and a tablespoon of yogurt or half a mashed banana does the same job in a cake. Add a splash more milk, because egg is liquid too.

Plucking is usually health or boredom, so have a bird vet see it first: mites, a diet of seed alone and a liver problem all cause it. If it is well, the fix is out-of-cage time, company, things to shred, a bath, and ten to twelve hours of sleep in a covered cage.

Plug one corded phone straight into the test socket behind the master socket's faceplate, with the broadband filter out: if there is still no dial tone there, the fault is outside your house and your provider fixes it free. Ring the landline from a mobile to tell the two apart - if it rings but you hear nothing it is the handset, and if it is unobtainable or goes to voicemail it is the line. A total loss has to be repaired within two working days, so report it with that test result and ask for the refund.

Plug your phone into the power bank's output port (usually marked OUT or USB-C) with its own cable, then press the button on the bank: the lights show how much charge is left, two to four of them. If nothing happens, the port may be the input only, so try the other one, and a phone that still says it is not charging usually wants a different cable.

Plug it in with HDMI or USB-C and it usually just works; then press Windows key + P to choose Extend, which gives you two separate screens rather than a copy. On a Mac it is System Settings > Displays > Arrange, and the menu bar follows whichever screen you drag the white bar to. If nothing appears, try the other port and a different cable before blaming the monitor.

Plug it into a USB port and it shows up as a drive in File Explorer or Finder, then drag the files onto it and eject it before pulling it out. A stick that is not seen is usually the port or the format: try another port and look for it under Disk Management on Windows, since some cheap sticks arrive unformatted.

Plums are ready from August, when they colour up and give a little at the stalk end: pick with the stalk on and eat the soft ones first. A plum that comes away at a squeeze is over ripe, and the wasps find those the same day you do.

Plunge it in iced water for 10 to 15 minutes: cut an inch off the stems first if it is a whole lettuce or a bunch, and most of the crispness comes back. Dry it in a tea towel afterwards and keep it in a bag with a piece of kitchen paper, because wet leaves are what made it limp in the first place.

Plunge limp lettuce into iced water for 10 minutes and it comes back crisp; dry the leaves, wrap them in kitchen paper inside a bag in the salad drawer and they keep about a week. Dress them at the table, since wet leaves and early dressing are what wilted them in the first place.
Plurals never take an apostrophe: two apples, the 1990s, CDs. Keep the apostrophe for missing letters (it's, don't) and for belonging (the dog's bowl). If it's plural, leave it out.

Pneumonia is an infection deep in the lungs that fills the air sacs with fluid, so it is a cold or flu that turns into a fever with a wet cough, faster breathing, a sharp pain in one side on breathing in, and feeling properly ill rather than just bunged up. Most chest infections are not pneumonia and settle on their own; the ones that are need a GP the same day, and 999 if there is fast breathing, confusion, or blue lips. A mild case is treated at home with antibiotics and the fever eases in a few days, though the cough can drag on for three to six weeks. Older people, babies and anyone with a long-term lung condition are the ones to ring about early rather than wait.

Point the camera app at it and hold still for a second - a link or a menu button pops up on the screen and you tap it; there is nothing to install. If nothing happens, the code is too close or too dark, so move back a little and add light. Treat a code on a parking meter or a sticker as suspect: a real one is printed, not stuck over.

Point it at the TV and hold the pairing buttons: on most Samsung sets it is the Back and Play buttons together for three seconds, on LG it is the wheel pressed for five, and a Fire Stick remote pairs from Settings > Remotes on the TV. Change the batteries first, and press a button on the TV itself to wake it, because a remote that will not pair is usually a flat pair of AAAs.

Points go 15, 30, 40, game — a point each from deuce is advantage and then game, so you have to win two in a row. Six games wins a set, but you need a two-game lead, so 6-6 goes to a tie-break. Matches are usually best of three sets, and the big men's matches are best of five.

Pop the silicone tips off and wash them in warm soapy water, then dry them completely before they go back on - a cotton bud barely damp with water cleans the mesh, and a dry soft toothbrush lifts the wax out of the nozzle. Wipe the outside with a cloth with a little washing-up liquid on it, keep water out of the charging port and the microphone holes, and replace the tips every few months because the rubber holds the smell.

Pop the jet out, or unscrew it if it is the fixed sort, and soak it in warm water with a drop of vinegar, then push a pin through the nozzle in the direction the water comes out - not against it, which pushes the grit back in. Aim the jet at the middle of the windscreen with the same pin while the bonnet is open, since a blocked jet that is refitted crooked just smears. If every jet is weak at once, the filter in the bottle or the pump is the part, not the nozzles.

Pork is done when the juices run clear where you pierce the thickest part and a thermometer reads 71C: a chop can keep the faintest blush of pink in the middle and still be safe, but not wet, jelly-like meat. A 2.5cm chop takes 4 minutes a side in a hot pan and 5 minutes resting, and a loin joint roasts 25 minutes per 500g at 200C (180C fan).

Pot a red (1 point), then a colour (2 to 7), and put the colour back on its spot; carry on that way until the reds are gone, then take the colours in order. The maximum break is 147: fifteen reds with fifteen blacks, then all the colours.

Pour boiling water or stock over the couscous to just cover it, cover the bowl and leave it 5 minutes, then fork it through with a little olive oil. Never stir it with a spoon: that's what makes it clumpy.

Pour a kettle of boiling water over them, or a jug of water with a good splash of bleach, then wash the bin out, dry it and put a fresh bag in. The flies lay in the food waste rather than in the plastic, so keep wet scraps in a sealed caddy or a bag in the fridge and take it out daily in warm weather; a lid that shuts properly and a dry bin stops it coming back.
Prabowo Subianto is the president of Indonesia: in office since October 2024, after winning the February 2024 election. A president serves five years and can be re-elected once.

Practise the whole thing rather than the bark: put him on a lead, have someone ring the bell or knock, and ask for a sit a few steps back from the door before it opens. Reward the sit, not the silence. Five times a day for a week with a friend and it starts to stick, and give him a mat or a spot to go to when the bell goes. Shouting at the barking, or at the door, makes it worse.

Pregnancy is counted as 40 weeks from the first day of your last period, which is about nine months, and it is dated that way rather than from when you conceived because nobody knows that day. 'Full term' is 37 to 42 weeks, so a due date is a two-week window rather than a day, and the dating scan at around 12 weeks is what sets it if your periods are irregular.

Press the test button once a month and change the battery once a year - the easy date is when the clocks change. Vacuum the dust out of the vents twice a year, and replace the whole alarm every ten years, because the sensor ages. Fit one on every floor and one in the hallway outside the bedrooms.

Press the touchpad-off key first - it is a squashed rectangle key in the top row on most laptops, usually F6 to F9, and an accidental tap turns it off. On Windows check Settings > Bluetooth and devices > Touchpad is on, then plug in a mouse and try; if the mouse works and the pad does not, restart with the laptop plugged in, and if the pad is still dead it is the ribbon cable, which a shop reseats cheaply.

Press the Windows key, Shift and S together: the screen dims, you drag a box around what you want and it is copied to the clipboard, ready to paste. PrtScn copies the whole screen, and Alt+PrtScn copies just the window you are in.

Press the clove on the board with the flat of a knife until it cracks and the skin comes away in one piece; a handful of cloves shaken hard in a lidded jar works too. For a whole bulb, drop the cloves in boiling water for 30 seconds and the skins slip off.
Press Shift, Command and 4 together, then drag a box: the file lands on your desktop. Shift+Command+3 takes the whole screen, and adding Control copies it to the clipboard instead of saving a file.

Press and hold the message and choose More or Delete, then pick the ones you want gone; on an iPhone you can also swipe left on a whole conversation in Messages to delete it all. Deleting only removes it from your phone, so the other person still has their copy, and a backup can bring it back until that backup is overwritten.

Press a low-tack masking tape along the top edge of the skirting, working it down into the join with a fingernail, then cut in with a 2 inch angled brush and brush the last inch slowly towards the tape rather than at it, so the paint is not pushed underneath. Pull the tape off at a shallow angle while the paint is still soft - leave it until the paint is hard and it tears the edge off with it. Anything that does get through: a wet cloth takes emulsion off a gloss skirting straight away, and once it is dry a sharp scraper or a fingernail lifts it without marking the gloss. Masking tape, not parcel tape, and not left on for a week, or it takes the gloss with it when it comes off.

Press Clock once or twice until the hours flash, type the hour, press Clock again for the minutes, then Clock to save; on many models you hold the Clock button for three seconds first. If it will not stay set, the display is probably showing cook time rather than the clock, so press Stop or Clear once. Unplugging it for a minute and plugging it back in resets the clock on most microwaves.

Press it down rather than lift it: condition the lengths, dry it with the brush pointing down and finish with a hot iron flat against the scalp or a drop of serum. Leave the mousse and the dry shampoo alone, because they are what holds hair up, and ask for a blunt one-length cut if it will not stay down, since layers are what make it stand up.

Press it first: wrap the block in kitchen paper, weight it down for 15 minutes, then cube it and toss it in cornflour. Fry in a hot pan with a little oil until golden on two sides, and stir the sauce in off the heat - tofu added to a wet pan steams and stays soft. It is meant to taste of nothing, so it takes on whatever it is cooked with.

Press Ctrl and the Show windows key together - the key with the rectangles on it, where F5 sits - and the whole screen is saved to Downloads. Add Shift and you can drag a box for part of it, and Ctrl+Alt+Show windows takes just the window in front. Screenshots lose the mouse pointer unless you turn it on first.

Pressing the handle lifts a flap and the water in the cistern rushes down, and the shape of the pan carries it round and over the bend, so the lot siphons away in one go. The fill valve then refills the cistern and a float shuts it off - a cistern that keeps hissing is usually that valve, not the flush.

Prey is the animal a predator hunts and eats: a rabbit for a fox, a zebra for a lion. The word is about the role in the food chain rather than the act of hunting: an animal can be prey to one thing and a predator of another.

Prick a whole potato all over and give it 8 to 10 minutes on high, turning it halfway. Chunks or small new potatoes take 5 to 6 minutes with a splash of water in the dish. Let it stand a minute before you cut into it, and use a knife to check it really is soft all through.

Prickly heat is sweat trapped under the skin, so the fix is cooling down: get out of the heat, a lukewarm shower, loose cotton and a fan, and let the skin dry rather than rubbing it. Calamine or a pharmacist's antihistamine settles the itch, and on a baby or a small child ask a pharmacist before using any cream. It fades in a few days; see a GP if it blisters, spreads, or comes with a fever.
Principal means main or the head of a school; principle is a rule or belief - it's the principle of the thing. The school one is your pal: principAL, the princiPAL.

Probability is how likely something is, written as a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain): a fair coin landing heads has a probability of 1/2, or 50%. You find it by dividing the number of ways the thing can happen by the number of equally likely outcomes.

Probably not: Parmesan, Grana Padano and Pecorino are set with animal rennet, which comes from the stomach of a calf or a lamb, so the traditional ones are not vegetarian. Some supermarket versions use microbial rennet instead - the ingredient list or the Vegetarian Society logo is the only way to tell.

Prune roses in late winter, around February when the buds start to swell: cut out dead, thin and crossing stems first, then take the rest back by about a third, making each cut just above an outward-facing bud so the new shoot grows away from the middle. Deadhead through the summer down to the first strong leaf. Climbing roses are the exception - prune those after flowering, not in winter.

Prune apples and pears in winter, when they are dormant and you can see the shape: take out dead, damaged and crossing branches first, then shorten the growth you left by about a third. Plums and cherries are the exception - prune those in June or July, because winter cuts let silver leaf in. A young tree wants a clear centre like a goblet; an old one that has gone mad can be brought back over two or three winters rather than all at once.

Psoriasis is dry, scaly, well-defined patches, most often on elbows, knees and scalp, and it comes and goes in flares. What helps: a plain emollient daily, a steroid cream on a flare for a week or two, some daylight on the patches, alcohol and stress down. It is not contagious and not caused by being unclean. See a GP if it covers a lot of the body, if your joints are stiff or swollen, or if your cream is not holding it.

Puffy eyes in the morning are usually fluid: too much salt or alcohol the night before, broken sleep, lying flat, or an allergy, and it settles a couple of hours after you get up. A cold spoon or flannel on the lids for five minutes, sleeping with your head a little raised, and going easy on salt in the evening is most of the answer; an antihistamine at night helps if they itch. See a GP if the puffiness is on one side, is painful, comes with a red eye, or spreads to your lips or tongue.

Pull over somewhere safe, hazards on, handbrake on. Loosen the wheel nuts a quarter turn before you jack it up, because they will not move in the air. Jack at the handbook's point, swap the wheel, nuts finger tight, lower it, tighten in a star pattern. Keep to 50mph on a spacesaver. A hole in the tread can be repaired; a cut in the sidewall cannot.

Pull over, switch the engine off and let it cool for at least 20 minutes; never open the coolant cap while it is hot, because it will scald you. Once cool, check the coolant level and look for a leak or a split hose; if it overheats again, stop driving and get it recovered, because a warped head is a very expensive repair.

Pull rhubarb from April to the end of June, twisting each stalk out and leaving three on every crown, then stop: the plant needs the rest of the year to build up for next spring. Do not pull any in the first year after planting, and never eat the leaves.

Pull the hair out of the drum and the filter first: a damp rubber glove or a squeegee gathers it into rolls that lift out, and a vacuum with the brush bar down gets the rest. Clean the filter and the door seal, then run a hot 60C service wash with a machine cleaner, because the grease that traps the hair goes with it. Hair in the drum is not a fault, but a filter packed with it is why a machine stops draining.

Pull the hair and soap out of the trap first (a bent wire or tweezers does it), then pour a kettle of hot water down with a spoonful of bicarbonate of soda and vinegar; a plunger over the plughole clears the rest. Skip the chemical cleaner until last, and fill the trap with a hair collector so it does not come back. The reason is hair, soap and grease caught in the trap and the bend.

Pull the loose hair out with a comb or a pencil, then swill the brush in warm water with a little shampoo and let it dry bristles down. Once a month is plenty, and it makes the brush work properly again.

Pull up just before the corner on the left and stop, then look over your left shoulder through the back window and check the right mirror for anything coming. Reverse slowly, slipping the clutch, and steer so the back of the car follows the kerb round the corner in a smooth arc about half a metre out, straightening as it comes; stop before you swing the front out into the road and look again, because the front of the car sweeps wide.

Pull back on a schedule rather than going cold: answer at set times, tell them when you will next be free, and keep the small contact you can manage so they can see you are still there. Clinginess is usually loneliness or worry, so one reliable thing a week ('I'll call you Sunday') settles more than any big talk. If it carries on, say kindly and plainly that you need a bit more space.

Pull carrots from June, thinning as you go, and lift the main crop in October before the first hard frost. They are ready when the shoulder is 2cm across. Twist the tops off before storing, because leaves keep drawing water, and keep them in damp sand in a cool shed.
Pulling someone's leg is teasing them - saying something untrue as a joke, not actually touching their leg. Was someone having you on?

Pump to the range printed on the tyre's sidewall, near the top for a heavier rider or road riding and near the bottom for wet grass or a light rider. Check them with a gauge once a week, because a tyre loses a little air all the time and a soft one gives pinch punctures. If you can squash the tyre against the ground with your thumb, it needs air.

Pumpkins and squash are ready in September or October, when the skin has hardened so a fingernail will not mark it and the stalk has gone corky: cut with a long handle, cure them in the sun for a week, and they keep for months somewhere dry.

Punch every nail head below the surface first, because a proud nail rips the paper and one rip ruins the drum. Then hire a drum sander and an edge sander, and take the whole room in one pass per grit - 40, then 80, then 120 - moving steadily and overlapping each run by half its width, never stopping in one place, because a sander left standing burns a dip into the board. Vacuum between grits and do not skip the 120, which is the grit that takes the scratch marks out; finish with three coats of floor varnish or two of hard wax oil, de-nibbing lightly between coats.

Push the volume all the way up first - on a phone the media volume and the call volume are separate, so music can be loud while calls are quiet. Then take the case off and clean the speaker grille with a dry toothbrush: fluff packed into it is the usual reason a phone suddenly sounds muffled, and it is worth checking Settings > Sounds for a volume limit before you pay for a repair.

Push the grout into the joints diagonally with a rubber float, a square metre at a time, pressing hard enough that the joint is full and flush - a grout bag or a gun is slower and messier on a wall. When it has firmed up, about 15 to 20 minutes, wipe the haze off with a damp sponge wrung out in clean water and change the water often, rather than wiping while it is still wet and pulling the joints open. Leave it 24 hours, buff the film off with a dry cloth, and run silicone down the corners and round the bath instead of grout, because grout cracks where two surfaces move at different rates.

Push it in: a cork that has snapped or dropped into the bottle does no harm to a wine you are drinking tonight, and a clean cork floats. To get it out, pour the wine into a jug through a sieve, fish the cork out and pour it back. A cork stuck in the neck comes out on a long screw turned into it and pulled with pliers.
Put on something short and funny, or text someone you haven't spoken to in a while.

Put the number plate into gov.uk's free 'check the MOT history of a vehicle' page: it lists every test since 2005 with the mileage at each one and the reasons for any failure or advisory. A jump in mileage, a long gap, or the same advisory year after year tells you more about a car than the seller will.

Put the number down in writing before you talk, so the conversation is about the repair and not about who is the bigger person: what it costs to fix, and a plan you can both live with (weekly amounts, or the repair in instalments). Ask for the insurance details once, in a message, and copy nothing to the rest of the family - a row with a sibling gets decided by whoever is not in the room. If they cannot or will not pay, decide what you are prepared to write off and say so clearly, because an unpaid loan you keep raising costs more than the money.

Put the printer on the same wifi as the laptop, from the printer's own panel: hold the wireless button until its light flashes, pick your network by name and type the password - or use the maker's app (HP Smart, Epson Smart Panel, Canon PRINT, Brother Mobile Connect), which walks you through the same thing and then finds the printer for you. The two usual reasons it fails: many printers only take the 2.4GHz band, so pick that network rather than the 5GHz one, and a guest network keeps devices from seeing each other. On the laptop, Settings > Bluetooth & devices > Printers & scanners > Add device (on a Mac, System Settings > Printers & Scanners > +). If it is still not found, print the network test page from the printer's menu and check the network name on it is the same one your laptop is on - the page also gives its IP address, which you can type into the add-a-printer box.

Put the real reasons on the table before the yes or no, because "not now" and "never" are different answers and they have different fixes: money, sleep, work, the age of the child you have, or one of you already doing more than half. Agree a date to decide by, and what would have to be true for each of you to say yes. It is fine to have different answers for a while; what wears a couple down is one person waiting in silence and the other not knowing they are.

Put the request in writing and name the law, because most refusals change at that point: faulty goods must be refunded within 30 days of buying, then repaired or replaced, and a shop's own returns policy cannot take that away. Ask for a deadlock letter or the name of their complaints procedure, then use the ombudsman or resolver scheme for that trade, or the free small claims track for a sum under £10,000. Keep the receipt, the emails and the dates.

Put the router as high and as central as you can, off the floor and out of a cupboard, because a wall and a metre of height cost more signal than any gadget buys back. Then take the signal to the far end: a mesh system with two units beats a repeater, which halves the speed it repeats, and a pair of powerline adapters with a second wifi point is the cheapest fix for a solid old house. Test in the room that is bad, not beside the router.

Put the rule on the car itself: they are a named driver on your policy or they do not drive it, it comes back with the tank where they found it, and a plain 'not this weekend, I need it' is enough when you do need it. Best said before the next ask rather than during it.

Put the tablets where the job happens rather than where they are stored - by the kettle, the toothbrush, the front door - and set a phone alarm with the name of the dose. A weekly pill box from the pharmacy makes a missed day obvious, and a pharmacist can switch you to a once-a-day version or a combined tablet if the timing is the problem. If you have missed a dose, take it when you remember unless it is nearly time for the next one, and never double up; ask the pharmacist about your particular tablet.

Put the transit bolts back in before it travels: they lock the drum, and without them the drum wrecks its own bearings on the drive. The set came with the machine and is usually still taped inside the door or under the lid; a removal firm can supply one. Turn the water off, unscrew the hoses, drain the filter behind the front flap and the water in the pump, and tape the door shut. Once it is bolted it is fine on its side for a short trip, and a tumble dryer travels upright.

Put the two fitted corners inside each other, so the elastic of one corner is tucked into the corner opposite, then lay it flat and fold it in quarters with the elastic inside - it ends up as a neat rectangle instead of a bundle. Flat sheets and duvet covers fold in thirds lengthways first, then in halves, and a duvet cover can go over a hanger or be folded around its own pillowcase. Keep sets together inside one of their own pillowcases so you are never hunting for a matching pair.

Put the veg in a microwave-safe bowl with two or three tablespoons of water, cover it with a plate or cling film with a corner turned back, and cook on full power: green beans and peas 3 to 4 minutes, broccoli and cauliflower florets 4 to 5, carrot batons 5 to 6, from raw.
