Run a descaler through it: fill the water tank with a citric-acid descaler (or half white vinegar, half water), run half of it through the machine with no coffee in it, switch off for 20 minutes, then finish the tank and run two tanks of plain water through after it. Every week, backflush the group head or rinse the pod holder and leave the drip tray and the steam wand wiped - the wand wants a damp cloth straight after the milk, and the portafilter basket comes up clean in hot soapy water.

Run a hot service wash with a washing-machine cleaner, clean the filter and the detergent drawer, and leave the door open between washes. Wash the load at 60C with half the usual detergent: too much soap is often what makes clothes smell.

Run a hot 60C or 90C service wash with a washing-machine cleaner or a cup of bicarbonate of soda, and clean the filter and the detergent drawer while it runs. The smell lives in damp lint and detergent trapped in the seal, the drawer and the filter. The wash itself is about two hours. Leaving the door and drawer open between washes is what stops the smell coming back.

Run a knife round the join first, because paint gluing the frame to the sill is the usual cause: score the line all the way round, then press on the frame and lift the handle. If it is a sash, check the cords - a snapped cord drops the weights and the window wedges. A tap with the heel of your hand and a dry bar of soap on the runners frees most of the rest.

Run it to a bed or a drain, never the road, and let the size decide how: a water butt goes out of the tap at the bottom onto a hose, and a barrel with no tap is tipped on its side or syphoned with a hose kept full of water. A pond is emptied in autumn, not spring, when frogs and newts are in it: net the fish into buckets of pond water, keep the filter media wet in that water, and put the plants in a tray, because it goes back within a day. A swimming pool is 20,000 litres or more, so it is a hired pump and a drain or a tanker, never the garden hose, and never the road drain without asking the council first.
Rupert Grint plays Ron Weasley in all eight Harry Potter films (2001-2011).

Rust is iron in the water or in the enamel itself, and the acid is what lifts it: soak a cloth in white vinegar or lemon juice, leave it on the mark for an hour, then rub with a non-scratch pad and rinse. A rust remover with oxalic or phosphoric acid does the same job faster on a bad mark, and keep bleach away from it, because bleach sets the colour instead of lifting it. If the enamel is chipped where the rust is coming from, dry it and paint the chip with enamel touch-up paint, or the mark returns from the same spot. Do not leave a rusty tin or a wet sponge sitting in the bath: that is usually how a ring gets there.

SIM stands for subscriber identity module: the chip that holds your phone number and the key your network checks before it lets a call through. It is why you can move your number to a new handset by moving the card, and why an eSIM does the same job written into the phone.

SMS stands for short message service: 160 characters was the limit because the signalling channel it hitched a ride on had room for that much, and the limit shaped the way people write. Pictures and long texts go over data instead, which is why a photo is not an SMS even when it arrives in the same app.

SOS does not stand for anything: it was picked in 1905 because three dots, three dashes and three dots is unmistakable in Morse and spells no word that could be misread. It is not an abbreviation, so there is nothing hidden in the letters.

STI stands for sexually transmitted infection: an infection passed on during sex, such as chlamydia, gonorrhoea or HIV. Most have no symptoms, so a test is the only way to know, and testing is free and confidential at a sexual health clinic or by post - nearly all clear with a short course of antibiotics.

Saddle soap on a barely damp cloth, wiped over and left to dry away from the sun, then a thin layer of leather conditioner worked in while the leather is still slightly damp: that is the whole job, and never washing-up liquid, which strips the oils out and is what cracks a seat. No scrubbing either - a soft cloth and patience, and a cotton bud of rubbing alcohol for an ink mark. Condition twice a year, and more often if the car sits in the sun.
Sadiq Khan is the mayor of London: first elected in 2016 and re-elected in May 2024. The job covers transport, policing and planning for the whole of London.

Sale items carry the same rights as full-price ones: faulty means a refund, repair or replacement, and a shop cannot refuse just because the item was reduced. If you simply changed your mind, the shop's own returns policy decides in store; anything bought online gives you 14 days to cancel from the day it arrives, sale or not.

Saline spray or a salt-water rinse clears a blocked nose, and steam loosens it; sleep with your head raised. A nose blocked most days rather than after a cold is usually allergic rhinitis, and a steroid nasal spray from the pharmacy, used every day for two weeks, beats anything by mouth. A decongestant spray works a few days only - longer and the rebound makes it worse. See a GP if it is one-sided or comes with a nosebleed you cannot stop.

Salt the water properly: about 10g, a heaped teaspoon, per litre of boiling water, so a big pan takes a good tablespoon. That is what seasons the pasta itself, since it takes up the salt while it cooks. Add it once the water is boiling so it dissolves fast, and taste the water - it should taste like the sea, not like a mistake.

Salt and vinegar, gravy, curry sauce, garlic mayo, or cheese and chilli: chip-shop curry sauce is the one to try if you want the bag to feel like a treat. A fried egg on top makes it a meal, and mushy peas or a pickled onion cut through the fat.

Salt is the biggest lever most people have: aim under about 6g a day, a teaspoon, which means cooking from scratch and reading the labels on bread, sauces and takeaways. Then 150 minutes a week of walking, cycling or swimming, losing a few kilos round the middle, cutting back on alcohol, and eating more fruit, vegetables, beans and dairy. Together those often take 5 to 10 points off; if your reading is around 140/90 or more on repeated home checks, see your GP, because tablets do more than the lifestyle changes alone.

Salt is the honest swap: about a quarter teaspoon of salt for each tablespoon of soy sauce, with a splash of water so the dish does not dry out. Tamari is the same thing without the wheat, and in a marinade a teaspoon of balsamic or Worcestershire sauce brings back the dark savoury note.

Salt it an hour ahead - a good pinch per side, left uncovered in the fridge - or marinate it 30 minutes to an hour in something acidic: lemon juice, wine, buttermilk or yoghurt. Then cut across the grain in thin slices, which does more for a chewy steak than any marinade, and cook it fast over high heat to no more than medium, or braise it slowly for hours if it is a stewing cut like shin, chuck or brisket. A bash with a rolling pin between two sheets of baking paper works for thin cuts like flank and skirt.
Sambal is medium to hot, 2,000 to 10,000 Scoville depending on the jar, and salty and sour with it. A teaspoon per portion stirred in at the end.

Same time and same table every night, twenty minutes then a break, and the phone in another room — the fight is usually about the phone and the sudden start, not the work. Sit nearby doing your own quiet job rather than over their shoulder, and only help when they ask. If it is still a battle after a week, tell the teacher what you are seeing: homework that takes an hour and ends in tears is usually the wrong homework.

Sand or de-gloss the surface, wipe the dust off, then a stain-blocking primer, then two thin coats of a water-based satin with a light sand between them. Take the doors and handles off if it has them, and let it harden a good 24 hours before anything goes back on: furniture paint that is rushed stays soft and sticks.

Sand the boards back to bare wood, vacuum and tack the dust off, then thin the first coat of varnish as the tin says and brush it with the grain. Three coats, with a light sand and a dust-off between each, and a full 24 hours between coats. A water-based varnish dries clear and does not yellow, so it suits pale wood; an oil-based one stands up better in a hall or on stairs but darkens pine. Keep the room ventilated and leave it two or three days before anything heavy walks on it.

Sand them, wipe the dust off and run masking tape along the carpet, then brush with the grain in long strokes and a light load on the brush so it does not run onto the wall. Two thin coats beat one thick one, and satin or eggshell is easier to wipe than gloss. If you are doing the walls too, do the woodwork first.

Sand a wooden floor back to bare wood, vacuum the dust off, then a primer and two thin coats of floor paint, keeping a wet edge so the overlaps do not show. Ordinary emulsion will scuff off in weeks, so use a paint made for floors, and leave it a full 24 to 48 hours before anything walks on it - a stair run wants that on both sides of each tread.

Sand it dull first: new paint needs a key to grip, so take the shine off old gloss with 120 grit, wipe off the dust, then one coat of undercoat and your topcoat. A water-based satin goes on after the sanding alone and dries in a couple of hours; oil gloss straight onto old gloss is the way to get peeling in a year.

Sand it dull first: new paint needs a key to grip, so take the shine off old gloss with 120 grit, wipe off the dust, then one coat of undercoat and your topcoat. A water-based satin goes on after the sanding alone and dries in a couple of hours; oil gloss straight onto old gloss is the way to get peeling in a year. Brush marks come from too much paint on a cheap brush, so thin it a little if it drags and keep the brush moving one way.

Sausage rolls keep 2 days in the fridge, in a tub or a paper bag rather than cling film, or they go soft. Reheat them at 180C for 8 to 10 minutes to get the pastry crisp again, and eat them hot rather than warm. They freeze well for 2 months unbaked or baked, and the pastry is what goes first: a soggy bottom means it was wrapped while it was still warm.

Sausages are 70/30 lean pork to fat, minced coarse and kept cold: for 1kg of shoulder add 18g of salt, a teaspoon of pepper, a teaspoon of sage and 100ml of iced water, mix it until it is sticky, and stuff it into soaked hog casings - or shape it into patties, which needs no casing at all. Fry a small piece to taste for salt before you stuff the rest. Eat them within 3 days or freeze them.

Say the one thing that stings most, once, as your own feeling rather than a verdict on them: 'When you say that about my job it makes me not want to ring.' If it is about your children, give the decision rather than the argument - 'we do bedtime this way, and it isn't up for debate every Sunday' - and give a short, boring answer to the rest.

Say the one thing that is actually under the argument, once, and without keeping score: 'When we get together it turns into this, and I'd rather it didn't.' Keep it to the last few months, don't relitigate the childhood, and give both of you somewhere to go - a short visit, a walk - so nobody has to win for it to end.

Say the one thing you want for them and keep it light: "Thinking of you - take the time you need and we will save you a seat." No advice, no story about your own operation, and do not say "let me know if you need anything": offer something specific instead, like a lift home or dinner on Thursday.

Say the one thing you would say out loud if they were in front of you, then the specific thing you noticed: "I still think about the way you laughed at the wrong bit of that film." Three or four sentences is enough, no jokes at your own expense and nothing borrowed from a card. Write it by hand if you can, read it once and take out anything you would not say to their face.

Say the thanks and mean that part, in one line, and do not name the thing: "Thank you - it was so kind of you to think of me." If you will use some of it, say how - "the scarf is going straight on tomorrow" - and if you will not, say nothing about it and thank them again later for the thought. Ask for the receipt only from someone close, and only when the thing was expensive: "It's lovely but the size is wrong - could I swap it?" Nobody is owed the truth about a present.

Say the thing you miss rather than a number of minutes, because a limit argued about in the moment is a row about the phone and a request is something they can answer: "I miss talking at dinner" works where "you are on that thing again" does not. Ask for one phone-free slot a day, a meal is the easy one, and put your own phone face down for it, because a rule that covers both of you holds and one imposed on them does not. If the scrolling is new, or they seem flat as well as glued to it, the phone is the symptom and a chat about how they are is the better move.

Say the word allergy rather than preference, name the dish, and ask them to check with the kitchen: 'I'm allergic to nuts - can you check the curry paste?' A server who says they will ask the chef is the answer you want, and one who guesses is the reason to order something else, because the fryer, the chopping board and the sauce are where it hides. For coeliac, ask about the fryer and the bread separately and ask to see the allergen folder, which every UK chain keeps and has to give you.

Say the baby's name if they used one, and say you are sorry: 'I'm so sorry about the baby, I'm here.' Don't look for a reason and don't say 'at least'; bring food, offer a lift and remember any date they mention, because the weeks after matter more than the first conversation.

Say the child's name and class, the dates they were off, and the reason in one line: "Sam, 5B, off Thursday and Friday with a sickness bug - back on Monday." Ask them to mark it authorised, and offer a doctor's note or appointment card if they want one. Email the school office with the dates in the subject line; most schools want a call on the first morning as well as the note.

Say the good news once and let theirs be theirs: 'it's a bit of luck, honestly' leaves them room to be pleased later. Ask about their week before you tell the next part of yours, and keep the friendship off the scoreboard - the friend who is odd about a promotion is often stuck in their own job, and it passes. If it keeps landing as a dig, name it once, kindly: 'that sounded like a jab - are we alright?'

Say what you agree with first, then the one thing you'd change: 'I'm with you on the timeline - what I'd worry about is the testing.' Use 'I think' and 'from what I've seen', keep it to one point at a time, and if it heats up, offer to take it offline.

Say what you can do rather than what you can't: "I can stay until six tonight, but not tomorrow as well." If it is every week, ask what is being dropped instead of absorbing it, and check what your contract says about overtime and pay. Over your contracted hours you can say no: unpaid regular overtime is worth a word with ACAS. Overtime every week is a staffing problem, not a personal failing.

Say what you can do and by when, not what you cannot: "I cannot do the whole thing by Friday, but I can get you the first two sections and the rest on Tuesday" keeps the work and the relationship. Give one plain reason, no apology and no long excuse, and never blame someone else. If the ask is outside what you do, say so once, clearly, and point them somewhere better - people remember being helped more than being told yes. Offer the smaller version at a price you would happily accept, then stop selling.

Say what it's about and what you need in six words or so: 'Invoice 214 — payment date?' or 'Flat 3 viewing Saturday 10am'. Put the action at the front, and don't write 'Quick question' — it tells the reader nothing.

Say yes to the job and the money in the same conversation: "Thank you - I'd like the role. Can we agree the salary for it before I start?" Ask for the band the role pays rather than a figure you invent, and put the date it starts in writing. If they cannot move now, get a review date four to six weeks out with the number in it; extra work taken on a promise is how people end up doing two jobs for one salary.

Say yes to everything small for the first month - lunch, a coffee, the drink after work - because that is where the friendships actually happen, and nobody notices who said yes. Ask people about their own work rather than talking about yours: "how long have you been doing this?" and "what is the bit nobody warns you about?" get real answers. Then pick one recurring thing - a Friday lunch, a walk at the same time - and keep going to it. Friendships at work come from repeated low-effort time, not one good conversation.

Say yes to help with chores and no to long visits: ask people to bring a meal or take the washing rather than sit and be entertained. Keep visits to an hour at first and let your partner or a friend run the door, so you can feed and sleep without hosting.

Say congratulations first and mean it, then ask how she is: "That is such good news - how are you feeling?" Let her set the tone, because the first months are often sick and tired rather than shiny, and ask who already knows before you tell anyone else. Skip your own birth stories and do not ask whether it was planned.

Say it once, plainly, and only what you know yourself: what you saw, where, and not what you think it means - 'I saw Sam with someone else on Friday and I could not sit on it' is enough, and a hint they can miss is no kindness. Then say that you are not going to bring it up again and let them decide, including the decision to stay, or to be angry with you for a while. Keep what you heard second-hand to yourself unless they can check it, and never offer to prove it for them.

Say it once, plainly, in the moment: 'Please don't comment on my weight - it isn't helping.' You do not have to justify it or explain your body, and the flinch is enough reason. If it carries on, give one flat answer and leave the room ('I've said how I feel about that') rather than defending yourself, which keeps the topic alive.

Say it once, about the pattern rather than the last time: "We've cancelled three times now and honestly it's starting to feel like I'm an afterthought. Can we pick a night we'll both keep?" Naming the pattern and asking for one firm date keeps it about the diary, not about her character.

Say it plainly, soon, and about the money rather than about them: "we cannot afford a new phone this month" is a fact a child can hold, where "we are poor" is a worry they carry about with them. Then say what is not changing - their room, their clubs, dinner on the table - and put one small yes next to the no, like a cheaper handset in a few weeks or a treat on Friday. A child who is cross about it is not being ungrateful, so let them be cross without arguing the point; they are taking the news in. If it is a big cut, tell them before they hear it somewhere else, and keep the sums for the grown-ups: what a child needs is the shape of things, not the arithmetic.

Say it plainly, kindly and early - a text the same evening or the next day is not rude, and leaving it unanswered is: "I enjoyed meeting you, but I'm not feeling a romantic connection, so I don't want to lead you on." Keep it about you rather than about them, because "you're not my type" invites an argument and "no spark" does not. No long explanation, no apology for the feeling, and no offer of friendship you do not mean. Then do not reply to the pushback.

Say it plainly and once - "you have not seemed yourself, and I am worried about you" - and then listen without fixing. Ask whether they have thought about suicide: asking does not plant the idea, and it is the thing that opens the door. Practical help is what people remember: a lift to a GP appointment, a walk, a text on a bad day. If they are in danger now, stay with them and call 999 or the Samaritans on 116 123.

Say it while you are still there, politely and once: most places will replace the dish or take it off the bill rather than argue. For a delivery, photograph it and use the app's help page the same day. If a restaurant refuses, a short email to the manager with the date and branch works better than a long complaint.

Say it as soon as you know, not on the day: what slipped, why in one sentence, what you have done, and the new date you can hit. "The figures are not signed off, so the report will be with you Thursday at noon - I have the draft ready and the delay is the audit check." Offer the smaller version if it helps: the summary now, the full pack Thursday. Late and honest beats late and silent.

Say it as a need for a few days rather than a verdict on them, and put a date on it so it cannot sound like leaving: "I've got a lot on and I need a couple of quiet days - I'll ring you Thursday." Do not explain it as their fault and do not apologise for it three times; a short clear ask with a return date is the kindest version, and it gives them something to wait for instead of something to worry about.

Say it as a decision with a date, not as a question you want permission for: 'I've decided to move out, and I'm looking at places from March.' Pick a calm moment, give the plan in two or three sentences, then let them react - surprise, worry and a bit of sulk are normal and are not a case you have to argue. Have the numbers ready (rent, deposit, the date) so the conversation moves to the practical side, and if they take it badly, come back to it a week later rather than settling it that night.

Say it before they notice, in one line and with the time you will be in: "The 8:12 was cancelled - I will be in at 9:40 and I have moved the 9am to 10." Do not offer a long excuse and do not blame the traffic twice; offer the thing that protects the work. If it is the third time in a month, go further and name the fix - a slightly earlier train, a booked slot for the school run - because a pattern with no plan reads as not caring. If lateness is being raised formally, check your contract and any policy first: some employers have a trigger (three in a month) and a hearing after it.

Say it before they have to ask, and bring a number, not just an apology: 'I haven't forgotten the money I owe you. I can't do it all at once, but I can give you some of it this month and the rest by the end of next.' Then do that — a small date you keep is worth more than a big one you miss.

Say it early, to the person who asked you, and keep it about the money rather than about them: 'I'd love to be there, and I can't do the whole thing this year.' Offer the part you can do - the meal, the one night, a smaller gift - and name a number if you have one. Don't invent a reason and don't leave it to the week before: one honest no, said kindly, is much easier to hear than a yes you cannot afford.

Say it early, be honest and offer a concrete alternative: "So sorry, I'm going to have to cancel tonight — I'm wiped out. Can we do Thursday instead? My treat." Don't invent an illness; a plain reason is easier to forgive.

Say it early, before they plan around you: "I'm sorry - I said I'd help, but I'm not going to be able to." You don't owe a detailed reason; if you want to soften it, offer something smaller you can still do ("I can drop the keys round on Friday"). Don't leave it to the last minute, and don't say yes again to be kind - a clear no now is easier on them than a no then.

Say it early, give the reason briefly, and offer the next time: "So sorry, I need to cancel Thursday — work has landed on me. Can we do the week after? I'll book it." One short apology and a new date beats a long excuse.

Say it early and about the work, not your ability: "I haven't been shown how this system works - could someone spend twenty minutes with me, or is there a guide?" Then do the safe part you can and write down each question as it comes, so one conversation answers all of them. In a new job ask for an induction list; if there is none, keep your own note of who to ask for what.

Say it lightly the first time and let them correct themselves: 'Hang on - I haven't told you my news yet.' If it keeps happening, name the pattern once and without a list: 'I love hearing your stuff, and I've noticed I don't get much of a turn - can we swap about a bit?' Most people who talk over you are nervous rather than selfish, and will be embarrassed and better for being told; if nothing changes, match their effort and put the time into people who ask.
Saying you spoke too soon means the thing you just said has already been proved wrong. What happened?

Scan each barcode against the glass and put the item straight in the bagging area, then pay by card at the end - you are doing the scanning, the till still adds it up. Fruit and veg you pick by name on the screen and weigh, and if it says unexpected item, move the bag aside: the assistant's handset clears it in seconds.

Scarlet fever is a strep infection: a sore throat with a rough, sandpapery rash that feels like goosebumps, flushed cheeks and a red strawberry tongue, and it needs antibiotics from a GP the same day - children are usually much better within 24 to 48 hours of starting them. Keep them off school until 24 hours of antibiotics have been taken, give plenty to drink and paracetamol for the sore throat, and get advice if the fever lasts past five days, the rash spreads, or there is earache or swelling in the neck.

Sciatica is the sciatic nerve complaining, usually where a disc or a tight muscle presses on it: a shooting or burning pain from the buttock down the back of one leg, often with tingling or numbness. Most cases settle in four to six weeks without anything done to them - keep moving and walking as much as the pain allows, which is better than bed rest, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen. See a GP if it is not easing after a few weeks, or sooner for a physio referral. Go to A&E the same day if you lose feeling around the saddle area, cannot pass urine, or the leg goes weak - that is the disc pressing on the nerves at the bottom of the spine and needs seeing at once.

Scones spread when the dough is too wet or the butter warmed up: it wants to be a soft, shaggy dough you pat out rather than roll, and the butter cold and cut in small. Handle it as little as possible, pat it to about 3cm thick, and cut straight down with a floured cutter without twisting it, because a twist seals the edges and stops the rise. A dough that is too wet also spreads before the middle sets, so add flour a spoonful at a time until it just stops sticking to the bowl.

Scones are best the day they are made and keep 2 days in a tin, or a day in the fridge. Sprinkle them with water and give them 3 minutes in a warm oven to bring them back; freeze them on the day and refresh from frozen, and bin any with green on them.

Scoop out a mugful of the cooking water first, then tip the pasta into a colander in the sink: that cloudy water is what loosens a sauce that has gone too thick. Shake it once, do not rinse it, and get it back into the warm pan with the sauce straight away, because drained pasta starts sticking to itself within a minute. Never leave it sitting in the colander - it carries on cooking in its own heat and goes soft.

Score round the edge with a sharp knife where the paint has bridged it to the frame - down both sides, across the top, then along the bottom - and it will come free with a push rather than a shoulder. Then sand the paint off the edge and out of the rebate back to the wood, and rub a candle, a bar of soap or a little wax along the edge so the next coat cannot glue it again. If it is still tight afterwards, take a millimetre at a time off the edge with a plane or a sanding block, and prime the bare wood so it does not swell when the room gets damp. A lock or a handle painted over wants scoring round the same way before it will turn.

Score the skin, pour a kettle of boiling water over it, dry it and rub in plenty of salt and a little oil, then roast it at 220C for 30 minutes and 180C after that, without basting or covering it, and if the skin is still soft once the meat has rested cut the crackling off and grill it for 5 minutes on a rack.

Score it all over, soak it, then scrape it: a paper tiger (or a fork) gives the water somewhere to go, warm water with a splash of washing-up liquid needs 10 to 15 minutes to do its work, and a scraper held almost flat lifts the paper without gouging the plaster. A steamer is quicker than a sponge for a whole room, and an old papered room is a weekend's job.

Scrape the sting out sideways with a fingernail or card, wash it and put something cold on it; an antihistamine helps the itch. Get help fast if the person swells away from the sting, struggles to breathe or feels faint.

Scrape up what you can, then rinse in cold water before anything warm touches it - heat sets both the colour and the smell. Wash with a biological detergent at 40C, or soak in cool water with a scoop of biological powder for an hour, and let it dry in the open air rather than on a radiator. For a carpet or a mattress, blot, then use the same cool detergent and water and dry it with a towel and airflow.

Scrape it out and let the pot cool before anything cold touches it, because a hot ceramic pot can crack under cold water, and the pot and lid are then usually dishwasher safe. A crusted pot lifts clean if you soak it overnight with hot water and a dishwasher tablet or a tablespoon of bicarbonate of soda and wipe it with a sponge, with nothing abrasive on the glaze. The base is the part you do not wash: unplug it and wipe it out with a damp cloth.

Scratch the bark on a young twig with a fingernail: green and damp underneath means that branch is alive, dry and brown means it is not, so do three or four round the tree rather than one. Wait until mid-spring before you write it off, because a hard winter, a late frost or a dry summer makes a healthy tree leaf out late or drop its leaves early, and a bud that is plump and firm in late winter is a tree that is still coming back. If most of the scratches are brown, look for the reason before you buy a replacement: waterlogged ground, mulch heaped against the trunk, the root flare buried when it was planted, or a strimmer wound at the base are what kill a garden tree rather than old age.

Scrub the rust off with a paste of bicarbonate of soda and water or a green scouring pad, rinse it and dry it at once. A little rust is not poisonous, but a tray that has rusted through will keep flaking into food: scrub it, rub a film of oil over it and bake it at 200C for 15 minutes to seal it again, and replace it once the metal is pitted. Knives, forks and tins rust because they sit wet, so wash and dry them by hand and never leave them in the sink or put them through the dishwasher.

Scrub the grout with a paste of bicarbonate of soda and water and an old toothbrush, then rinse. For black mould in the grout, use a mould spray and leave it 10 minutes. To whiten grey grout, a paste of bicarbonate and a little white vinegar left on for ten minutes lifts most of it, and an oxygen bleach (the laundry stain remover kind) left overnight takes the rest. Sealing the grout once it is dry keeps it that way for a year or two, and a grout pen is the quick fix if it is only the colour that bothers you.

Scrub it with half a lemon and a big pinch of salt, rinse in the hottest water you have and dry it standing up: that lifts onion, garlic and fish out of wood or plastic. Plastic boards can go through the dishwasher, wooden ones should never.

Scrub it with hot soapy water and a paste of bicarbonate of soda, then stand it in the sun to dry: surface mould comes off wood and the piece is fine afterwards. If the black has gone into the grain or the wood smells musty when it is dry, bin it, because the hyphae go deeper than the surface. Never put wooden spoons or boards in the dishwasher, and oil them monthly so water stops soaking in.

Scrub it back first - sugar soap for grease or nicotine, a light sand for a mark in the wood - then seal it with a stain block: shellac or an aluminium primer, because ordinary undercoat lets the mark creep back through in a month. Two thin coats of block, then your finish. A knot wants the resin scraped out and shellac over it, and rust wants sanding back to bare metal and a rust-killing primer before the topcoat.

Search "dog friendly pubs" and the town name: the listings on DogFriendly and PubsGalore are usually accurate and current. In most British towns the old pubs with wooden floors are the safest bet, and a quick phone call settles it.

Season it in that order: a pinch more salt, then a squeeze of lemon or a splash of vinegar, then something savoury like a stock cube, a splash of soy or a knob of butter. Bland food is nearly always short of salt and acid rather than spice; if you're cutting salt, the lemon and the savoury splash do most of it on their own.
Seasons stay lower case: spring, summer, autumn, winter. Days and months take a capital - Monday, January - and so do holidays, as in Christmas.

Secondhand smoke is a real risk, not a smell: it carries the same tar, carbon monoxide and carcinogens, and living with a smoker raises a non-smoker's lung cancer risk by roughly a quarter and a child's risk of chest and ear infections much more. There is no safe level of exposure, and an open window or a separate room does not clear it - the only thing that works is smoking outside, away from the door.

Sediment is the loose material that settles at the bottom of water or is dropped by wind and ice: sand, mud, grit and bits of shell. Pressed together over millions of years, sediment becomes sedimentary rock like sandstone and chalk.

See a physio if the pain has lasted more than a fortnight, keeps coming back, or comes with numbness, weakness or pins and needles - and you can refer yourself on the NHS without seeing a GP first. If it is a recent strain that is already easing, gentle daily stretching plus some strength work (sit-to-stands, bridges, a short walk) is what a physio would give you anyway.

See a doctor and get the injury on record first, because a claim rests on medical evidence. Then tell the other side's insurer in writing and keep the photos, the witness names and the receipts. Small whiplash claims go through the official claims portal on a fixed tariff, so a no-win-no-fee solicitor costs you nothing to ask about.

Seeds and nuts first - acorns, hazelnuts, beech mast, sunflower seeds - then fungi, buds, shoots and fruit, and a bird feeder is the same food in an easier place. In autumn a grey squirrel buries thousands of nuts one at a time and remembers where most of them are.

Seeds and grain mostly, so a kitchen is a windfall: cereals, crumbs, nuts, chocolate, pet food, and the odd insect. A house mouse eats only about 3g a day and drinks very little, which is why a small spill keeps a family going.

Seeds and grain, then leaves, buds, berries and brassicas - a wood pigeon will strip a cabbage row - and the feral pigeons in town live on scraps and bread. Bread is not good for any of them: peas, oats or bird seed are the better thing to put down.

Seeds fail from cold soil, drying out, or being buried too deep: keep them at about 18-20C, cover the tray with a clear lid until they show, and water from below so the surface stays damp. Compost over them only as deep as the seed is wide.

Self-raising flour has baking powder already in it, about two teaspoons for every 150g of flour; plain flour has none. Cakes and scones want self-raising, bread and pastry want plain - and you can make self-raising by adding the baking powder yourself.

Self assessment is the tax return you file yourself when tax is not taken from a payslip: self-employed earnings over £1,000, rental income, big savings interest or dividends, or income over £150,000. Register by 5 October after the tax year ends, file online by 31 January and pay by the same day; a first late filing is £100.

Sell it back through the seller, not on social media: the box office, the agent's own fan-to-fan resale, or a face-value site, because a ticket sold in a Facebook group can be refused at the door when the name does not match. Most tickets are non-transferable, so read the terms first and ask for a name change in writing if they allow one. Sell at or below face value and keep the sale inside the platform, so the buyer is covered and you cannot be blamed for a ticket that does not scan. An unused advance train ticket can sometimes be changed for a fee instead, which is often worth more than reselling it.

Send one specific message about something only they would get, and suggest a fixed, small plan: a walk, a coffee, a phone call. Friendships drift on busyness rather than on falling out, and one warm nudge usually tells you quickly whether there is still something there.

Send one friendly reminder with the details: invoice number, amount, due date, and a link or the bank details again. "Just a nudge on invoice 214 (£340), due on the 3rd — could you confirm when it's scheduled?" If it's already overdue, add a date you'll escalate on, and keep it in writing.

Send the company the two payment references and ask for the duplicate to be reversed, in writing, with a 14-day deadline. If it isn't back by then, ask your card provider for a chargeback and send them the same evidence.

Send two lines the same day: thank them for the time, and add the one thing you forgot to say that fits the job. Don't re-argue your case or attach anything they did not ask for - the point is to be memorable for the right reason.

Send it to the right department and give them what they need to act on it: the street or address, the date, a photo or reference number, and what you want done - potholes, pavements and street lights to highways, fly-tipping, bins, graffiti and dog fouling to environmental health, a repair in a council house to the repairs line with your tenancy number. Use the online form or email so there is a record, keep a copy and note the date. If nothing happens in ten working days, chase it and ask for it to be logged as a formal complaint; after their final reply the Local Government Ombudsman takes it on free.

Separate the things they share before anything else: two bowls in different rooms, two litter trays and a high place each, so neither cat can be cornered, and a Feliway plug-in in the room they use most. Then feed them on either side of a closed door and swap their bedding, and only put them together when the hissing at the door has stopped - never face to face to sort it out. If a cat that was calm has turned on the other one, take her to the vet first: pain and a bad tooth are what turn a settled cat grumpy.

Separate the beds as far as the room allows and put something solid between them - a chest of drawers, a shelf, a curtain on a rail - so one cannot see the other. Put whichever child wakes first nearest the door, so you can lift them out without passing the sleeper, and settle the one who wakes in the hall or your own room rather than back in the shared room, where the crying wakes the other. Stagger bedtime by 20 to 30 minutes so the older one is asleep before the younger comes in, and give it a fortnight before deciding it will not work.

Sepsis is the body over-reacting to an infection, and the whole danger is how fast it moves. Ring 999 now and say the word sepsis if there is an infection with any of: a fever with shaking chills, new confusion or drowsiness, breathing faster than usual, a lot of pain anywhere, clammy or mottled skin, or no pee all day. It is not a rash illness and it does not need a wound: a chest, urine, tooth or skin infection can start it. Treatment is IV antibiotics in the first hour, which is why the speed matters more than anything else, and most people who are treated early make a full recovery, though tiredness for weeks after is normal.

Sergio Mattarella is the president of Italy: in office since 2015 and re-elected in 2022. The president is head of state and picks the prime minister after an election; Giorgia Meloni runs the government.

Set the posts first: a string line between the two end posts keeps the run straight, then each post goes 600mm deep and 1.8m apart in concrete, braced for a day. The gravel boards go on next and the panels screw through their rails into the posts, one post's worth at a time. Two people with an auger do 20 metres in a weekend; on a boundary, check the deeds and the 2 metre rule before you dig.

Set the clock and the day on the programmer first, because every on and off time you enter is measured from it. Then give each channel two blocks: heating on about half an hour before you get up and off when you leave, then on again before you come back and off at bedtime, and the hot water channel set to a morning and an evening block. Put the room thermostat at 18 to 19C while you are in and 15 to 16C overnight, and let the thermostat do the switching rather than turning the programmer up and down. A combi boiler with a smart thermostat wants the heating channel left on constant, because the thermostat is doing the timing.

Set the flow temperature on the boiler dial to 55 to 60C. That is the temperature of the water going round the radiators, and the lower it is the less gas each hour costs, because a condensing boiler only recovers its waste heat with a cool return. If the house is slow to warm, go to 65C and turn the room thermostat down again rather than going higher than that. A hot water cylinder stays at 60C whatever the heating is set to, so the two numbers are not the same dial.

Set the handbrake, bring the clutch up to the biting point until the bonnet lifts a little, then add a touch more gas and release the handbrake as the car starts to pull - that order is what stops the roll back. On a steep hill use more gas and let the clutch out more slowly, and if it stalls put the handbrake on before you restart. Going up a long hill, change down early: a lower gear holds the speed better than more throttle in a high one. Going down, use the same lower gear to hold the speed and brake gently, rather than riding the brakes all the way.

Set your watch to the time where you are going as soon as you board, and sleep to that clock rather than the one at home. Earplugs and an eye mask do more than any gadget, and skip the wine: it helps you drop off and wakes you at 3am. Book an aisle or window seat, keep the shoes loose, and take the coffee at the end, not the start.

Set a time and a length rather than rationing the calls: 'I'll ring you every Sunday, and text in the week.' Then keep that call and make it good, because the routine is what reassures them. If a call comes at a bad time, answer with one sentence - 'I'm with the kids, I'll ring you at seven' - and do ring at seven.

Set a limit rather than relying on willpower: Screen Time on an iPhone or Digital Wellbeing on Android shows the real numbers and lets you cap the worst app. Keep the phone out of the bedroom and charge it in another room, which does more than any app.

Set it to go out on its own and it stops being something you can forget: a direct debit or standing order, taken the day after payday rather than on the due date, so the money is there before it is wanted. A phone reminder a week before catches the rest, and anything you pay by hand is worth a calendar entry every month. If you have missed one, pay it the same day and ring them: most will move the date, waive the first late fee or set up a payment plan if you ask before it goes further, and one payment a few days late matters far less than a run of them. Then check the statement or the account once a month, because a missed payment shows there first.

Settings > Face ID & Passcode (Touch ID & Passcode on an older one), then Turn Passcode On: choose a six-digit code, and the same screen has auto-lock and Erase Data. The passcode you type after a restart is the one that protects the backup, so keep it somewhere other than the iPad.

Settings > General > iPhone Storage (or Storage on Android) lists what is taking the space, biggest first: it is nearly always photos and videos. Delete the videos you never watch, turn on Optimise Storage so old photos live in the cloud, and offload the apps you rarely open. Most phones can free several gigabytes that way in ten minutes.

Settings > General > iPhone Storage, or Settings > Storage on Android, shows a bar with what is left and a list biggest first. On Windows it is Settings > System > Storage, and on a Mac the Apple menu > System Settings > General > Storage. Keep about 10 to 20% free: below that phones slow down and updates refuse to install.

Settle the terms before the boxes: how long it is for (six months, then a review), what they pay towards bills, what they do for themselves, and what you will not do - the last one said kindly and early. A trial fortnight first, and one written line each about the kitchen, the door and the evenings, saves months of small rows. It is your partner's home too, so the offer has to be theirs as well as yours before you give it.

Shade the table, not the whole garden: a cantilever parasol is the one that works, because its base sits off to the side and the canopy reaches over the table without a pole in the middle. Second is a sail shade on three posts, set so it faces the afternoon sun and angled 20 to 30 degrees, with the fixings tight enough that it does not flap; take it down when it blows hard, because a sail in a gale pulls the posts out. If you have the room, a tree on the west side is the best of all in five years' time - a rowan, an amelanchier or a small crab apple, 3m from the fence.

Shade first: move the hutch or cage out of the sun, and give her a frozen water bottle wrapped in a towel to lie against, a cool ceramic floor tile and a heavy bowl of water as well as the bottle. Rabbits and guinea pigs cannot sweat or pant, so much over 25C is dangerous - brush out the loose fur, wet her ears with cool water, never bath her, and bring her indoors on the hottest days.

Shampoo just the roots, condition only the ends, and finish with cool water. Washing with a harsh shampoo every day makes oil come back faster, so try every other day for a fortnight and it usually settles.

Shared parental leave lets you split up to 50 weeks of the mother's maternity leave, and 37 of those weeks are paid, if you are both eligible. The mother has to end her maternity leave early - after the 2 weeks she must take - and the rest of the leave and pay can then be shared in blocks. It has to be used within the first year after the birth, and you tell your employer 8 weeks before the first block.

Shave the bobbles off with a battery fabric shaver or a cheap razor, then wash the garment inside out on a gentle cycle. Pilling is normal on wool blends and comes from rubbing, not from the jumper being cheap.

Sheep, and sometimes alpaca, goat or rabbit: the fleece is shorn once a year, washed, carded into loose fibres and spun into yarn. Merino is the same sheep bred for a finer fibre, which is why it does not itch.

Shellfish is the leanest protein in the shop: 100g of prawns is about 100 calories and 20g of protein with barely any fat, and scallops and mussels are much the same, with iron and zinc in the molluscs. Prawns carry cholesterol, but that matters far less than the saturated fat in a diet, so it is the mayonnaise, the butter or the breadcrumbs that make a prawn dish heavy rather than the prawns.

Shift it 15 minutes at a time, not an hour: set the alarm a quarter of an hour earlier every three or four days and go to bed a quarter earlier too, or you just lose sleep. Get daylight on your face within half an hour of waking, and keep the new time at weekends or Monday undoes it.

Shifts come as a repeating rota, not a fixed week - three earlies, three lates, three nights and three off is a common one - and your contract or rota policy says which pattern and how far ahead it is published. The law gives you 11 hours off between shifts and 24 hours off a week or 48 a fortnight, averaged. Ask for the rota in writing and write down every swap you agree, and if the pattern is making you ill, ask about a fixed shift.

Shingles is the chickenpox virus waking along one nerve: burning or tingling on one side, then blisters, settling in two to four weeks. Ring the GP today if the rash is new - an antiviral works best within 72 hours. Seen the same day if it is near an eye or the tip of the nose, in pregnancy, or if your immunity is low. Keep it covered, do not burst the blisters, take paracetamol. You cannot pass on shingles, but you can give chickenpox.

Shivering is your muscles twitching fast on purpose: the movement makes heat, which is the body's way of holding its temperature when it is losing warmth faster than it makes it. Shivering with a fever means your temperature is still climbing, so wrap up and drink something warm.

Shop sushi is made to be eaten the day you buy it: keep it in the fridge, eat it within 24 hours and do not leave it out on the side. The rice and the raw fish are what go off, so bin what is left rather than keeping it for tomorrow.

Shop-bought yoghurt that looks grainy has usually been shaken about or chilled too hard in transit: stir the whey back in and eat it, it is harmless. Homemade yoghurt goes grainy when the milk got above about 46C, because the culture and the milk proteins clump: heat the milk to 85C first, cool it to 43-45C before stirring the starter in, and keep it at 43C while it sets - an oven with just the light on, or a flask, holds it steadier than a warm spot that swings.

Shop around about three weeks before the renewal: the same cover is often £100 to £200 cheaper elsewhere, because insurers raise the price for people who stay. Check the excess, the mileage and the named drivers on every quote, since a wrong mileage can void a claim. Do not let it auto-renew before the new policy starts: driving uninsured is a £300 fixed penalty and six points.

Shop early and buy to sizes you can see: the badge items - the jumper, the blazer, the PE top - come from the school or its named supplier and the plain shirts, trousers, skirts and shoes are cheaper in a supermarket, at the same sizes. Go one size up in the jumper and the coat and buy two of the shirts and trousers, because those are what get dirty fastest, and go in the first week of August: by the end of the month the common sizes have gone. Label everything with a laundry marker, shoes and water bottle included, and ask about second-hand rails - most schools have one.

Shops only have to refund an unwanted gift if their own policy says so, so check the receipt: many give an exchange or credit note within 28 days. A faulty gift is different, and whoever bought it can claim a repair or refund.

Shops in the UK have to charge for single-use carrier bags, and the money goes to good causes rather than to the shop, which is why the charge exists at all: it is there to cut how many bags are thrown away, and it works. A bag for life is the cheap way round it - most supermarkets replace it free when it finally splits - and small paper bags for loose fruit and veg are usually free and are not the charge. If you are charged for a bag you did not ask for, say so at the till and it comes off.

Short, sayable and easy to spell is the whole brief: two words, no apostrophes, and nothing you have to explain down a phone. Say 'we are the ...' out loud and get a friend to spell it back after hearing it once, then search it and check it is not another band or a trademark, because a name you cannot print on a poster is not a name.

Short and often beats long: two or three minutes at a time, a few times a day from the first weeks, working up to about an hour a day in total by six months. Put them on a firm flat surface or over your lap or chest, awake and with you there the whole time, and always back on their back to sleep. If they yell, start with a minute straight after a nappy change or a nap, get down at their eye level with a mirror or a toy, and take them up as soon as they are properly upset rather than pushing on: it is time on the floor that builds the neck and shoulder strength for rolling, sitting and crawling, not a test they have to pass. Keep it off a soft bed or sofa where they could roll off or sink in.

Shortbread is one part sugar, two parts butter and three parts flour: for a 20cm round that is 60g caster sugar, 120g butter and 180g plain flour. Cream the butter and sugar, work in the flour without kneading it, press it into the tin, prick it, and bake at 150C (130C fan) for 35 to 40 minutes until it is pale gold rather than brown. It firms as it cools, so cut it into fingers while it is still warm.

Show it once, then watch them do it once, then let them do it alone with you a few feet away: most of what looks like slowness is a step nobody said out loud. Write the five or six steps on one page they can keep, do the same fifteen minutes at the same time each day rather than a long session on Friday, and ask them to explain it back to you before you decide it has not gone in - if they cannot explain it, the teaching missed rather than the learner. Say what "good" looks like with one finished example to copy, and when they get it wrong let them find it before you take the mouse: the fix they make themselves is the one that sticks. Tell them plainly where they are and what good looks like by when, so slow is a fact you both know rather than a worry.

Showering wins on time and water - five minutes with a normal head is about 40 to 50 litres against 80 or so for a full bath - so if it is the water you are asking about, shower and keep it short. Neither is better for your skin; long hot water is what leaves it tight and itchy, so keep it warm rather than hot and pat dry instead of rubbing. If a bath leaves you light-headed, get out slowly and drink some water.

Shred or slice the cold turkey: it is the best part of the bird, and it goes into sandwiches, a salad with mayonnaise and lemon, a curry, risotto or soup for the last two minutes, or a pie under pastry. Keep it in a covered tub in the fridge for up to 3 days, reheat it once until piping hot all the way through, and simmer the stripped carcass with an onion and a carrot for 30 minutes to make stock.

Shred or slice cooked chicken and mix it with mayonnaise, a squeeze of lemon, salt and pepper, then add crunch: celery, red onion, or apple and walnuts. It's better after 20 minutes in the fridge, and keeps 2 days.

Shrink the job until it is almost silly: name the very next physical action — open the letter, put the shoes by the door — and do only that one, for five minutes, with permission to do it badly. Putting things off is usually about the task feeling too big to begin, and it stops the moment you are in it. Decide tonight what tomorrow's first step is, so it is an instruction rather than a choice.

Shrinkage is heat and agitation, so wash cool (30C, or 20C for anything with stretch) on a short cycle, spin it slow, and skip the tumble dryer or use its lowest setting. Cotton and wool shrink most, linen mostly in the length, and a hot wash is what does it; buying a size up never fixes a jumper that a 60C wash has already felted.

Shut the door of the room, put the other pets out, and leave his food and water low down along the skirting, because they follow walls and come out at night. A bucket with a towel in the bottom and a little food in it catches most of them, and a torch along the edges of the fridge and under the sofa finds the rest; no poison and no traps. One out in daylight is usually thirsty, so offer water first.

Shut it down and unplug it, then blow short bursts of air through the side and back vents with a can of compressed air, holding the fan still with a toothpick so it does not spin. A soft brush takes the mat off the grille; if the vents are caked solid, a repair shop will open it and re-paste the processor for about £40.

Shy is a temperament rather than a fault - about one child in five is slow to warm up, and most grow out of the worst of it without being pushed. Tell them what is coming before a new place, arrive early while it is still quiet, stay close for the first ten minutes, and arrange playdates with one child rather than a party; do not call them shy in front of them. If a child talks freely at home but goes silent in some places and cannot get words out at all, that is selective mutism, and it is worth a speech and language referral.

Sigmund Freud (1856-1939) was an Austrian doctor who founded psychoanalysis, the talking cure built on the idea that dreams, slips of the tongue and early childhood shape adult behaviour. Many of his specific theories are now rejected, but therapy as a conversation starts with him.

Sign in on a browser and do it in Account: Netflix is Account > Security > Change password, and the same page has 'Sign out of all devices', which is the part that actually removes whoever else is watching. Do that first if the account is being used by someone else, then change the password, and check the profile list for names you do not recognise.

Sign in at icloud.com/photos on a computer, select the ones you want and press the download arrow at the top - in batches of a few hundred, or the browser gives up. On a Mac, select them in Photos and use File > Export > Export Unmodified Original. To stop new ones uploading, turn off Settings > [your name] > iCloud > Photos on the phone first.

Silkworms, the caterpillars of a moth, which spin a cocoon out of one continuous thread. The cocoons are unwound into a single fibre, which is why silk is smooth and strong where cotton is short fibres twisted together.

Silverfish eat the starch in paper, card, glue and cotton, and they only settle in a room that is damp, so the damp is the thing to fix: ventilate the bathroom, mend the leak, and clear the piles of cardboard and old paper they are living in. They are harmless otherwise - they do not bite and they do not spread anything - and a dehumidifier does more than any spray.

Simmer 1kg of tomatoes with an onion, 100g of sugar, 150ml of vinegar, a teaspoon of salt and a spice bag of cloves, peppercorns and a bay leaf for 45 minutes, then blend it and simmer it down until a spoon dragged across the pan leaves a line. Push it through a sieve and bottle it hot: it keeps a month in the fridge once opened. Tinned tomatoes and half the sugar make a thinner, sharper ketchup.

Single cream is about 18% fat and only pours; double cream is about 48% and whips, thickens and holds its shape. Use single for pouring over a pudding and double where it has to whip or survive being boiled.

Sinusitis is the lining of the sinuses swollen by a cold, so the face aches over the cheeks and eyes, the nose is blocked with thick discharge and the smell goes dull. Most of it is viral and settles in two to three weeks on its own: steam, a salt-water rinse from a pharmacy and paracetamol do more than antibiotics, which are only worth it if it is going on ten days and getting worse or keeps coming back. See a GP if it lasts over ten days or happens more than three times a year, and go the same day if the skin around an eye swells, vision changes or there is a severe headache with a fever.

Sip small amounts of water or a rehydration drink often rather than a glass at once, and eat something dry and plain - toast, crackers, a plain biscuit - before you get up if mornings are the worst. Ginger, in tea or a biscuit, settles some people. Ring a GP if it lasts more than a couple of days, if you cannot keep any fluid down, or if you are pregnant, on new medicine or have a head injury.

Sit or lie down the moment it starts, and stand up in two stages after: sit on the edge of the bed or the chair for a few seconds, then rise. Most light-headedness is the blood pressure dip on standing, low blood sugar, or not enough to drink - so have water and something to eat, and keep your fluids up in hot weather. Crossing your legs and squeezing, or clenching your fists, pushes the blood back up if it happens again. See a GP if it keeps happening, and ring 111 or 999 that day for dizziness with chest pain, a faint, weakness or numbness on one side, a bad headache, or slurred speech.

Sit or lie down for a few minutes with your feet up and your head low, loosen anything tight at the neck, and drink a glass of water - most faintness is a moment of low blood pressure or low blood sugar and passes with that. Eat something if it has been hours since you last did, and stand up slowly for the rest of the day. Ring 999 if you actually passed out and hit your head, if it comes with chest pain, a racing heart, breathlessness or a weak arm or drooping face, or if it happened while driving. Get a GP check soon if it keeps happening, if you are pregnant, or if you have been losing weight or bleeding.

Sit them upright against your shoulder or on your lap facing away, and rub or pat between the shoulder blades for a minute or two; lay them down flat for a moment and sit them up again if nothing comes. Plenty of babies bring up nothing at all and are fine, so stop after a few minutes if they are happy.

Sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of your nose just below the bone for ten minutes without peeking, breathing through your mouth. Spit out any blood rather than swallowing it. See a GP if it lasts over 20 minutes, keeps coming back, or you are on blood thinners.

Sit where the chat cannot start: front row, or beside someone you do not talk to, and ask the teacher to move you, which is a normal request and not a confession. Keep a corner of the page for the things you want to say and hold them to the end of the lesson - most of them keep, and the good ones come back to you. If it is answers blurting out, count to three and write the answer down first; the urge drops once it is on the page.

Sit facing forward, as far forward and as low as you can, look at the horizon rather than a screen or a book, and get fresh air: those four do more than anything you can buy. Eat something plain before you go, not a big meal, and stop when you can. For a child ask a pharmacist which antihistamine suits their age and weight, and give it an hour before you set off, because the doses are not the adult ones.
Sit in the front seat, look at the horizon rather than a screen, and keep the air cool with the window down a little. Eat something plain beforehand, and stop for ten minutes if you feel bad.

Six rounds of ten questions is the shape people finish: a picture round, a music intro round, general knowledge, a round about your own street or family that nobody can revise for, a true-or-false round, and one joker round where a wrong answer costs a point instead of scoring nothing. Teams of four to six, questions short enough to read aloud twice, the hardest round in the middle rather than at the end, and the answers written down as you go.

Six to ten weeks on site for a kitchen once the units arrive, and three to five for a bathroom. The units are the long wait - order them six to eight weeks before you want the work done - so work the order date back from the day you want it finished.
Six to eight sausages are about £2.50 to £4, and a butcher's £4 to £6. The cheapest are mostly rusk and water, so read the meat percentage on the pack.

Six to eight weeks off running is the usual answer for a stress fracture, and the bone decides rather than the calendar. A foot one often gets a walking boot for a few weeks. Keep some fitness with swimming or cycling if that is pain-free, and come back with walk-run: a minute of jogging to two of walking, adding a minute a week. Get it looked at if one small spot is tender to a fingertip or it hurts sitting still.

Six to eight weeks before the day is the usual rule here, and three months if people have to travel or it is a bank holiday weekend, because the invitation is asking for a yes, a meal choice and sometimes a bed. Post save-the-dates six to twelve months out, put the RSVP date three to four weeks before the wedding, and give the venue the final numbers about two weeks ahead. Chasing the people who have not answered is easier if the card names one date and one name to reply to.

Six weeks is the usual guide for getting back to normal: the cut heals in a fortnight on the outside, but the muscle and the layers under it take about six weeks, and the operation itself is 45 minutes to an hour. The first two weeks are for resting and walking, lifting nothing heavier than the baby, and taking paracetamol and ibuprofen regularly rather than when it gets bad. Driving waits for the day you can do an emergency stop without pain - usually two to six weeks - and tell your insurer; do not drive on strong painkillers. Keep the scar clean and dry, let it get air, and expect it to be numb, itchy or puckered for months, which is normal. Ring your midwife, health visitor or GP the same day for a fever, a scar that is red, hot or leaking, smelly discharge, or pain that gets worse not better.
Six apples are about £1.50 to £2.50 and a kilo about £2. Loose ones let you pick the size, and a bag of the smaller ones is usually the cheapest way.

Six hours of direct sun, and shelter from the wind: in shade a sunflower grows tall and thin and then flops. Sow indoors in April or straight outside in May, 2cm deep and 45cm apart, and stake the tall varieties early rather than after they lean. Water and feed weekly once the bud shows, and put a slug barrier round them while they are small, because that is what takes them.

Sixty degrees on the cylinder thermostat is the number to aim for. A stored cylinder is held at 60 to 65C because below about 50C the bacteria behind Legionnaires' disease can multiply in the tank, and a thermostatic mixing valve on the outlet then brings it down to about 48C at the tap so nobody scalds. A combi has no tank, so set its hot water to 50 to 55C - hotter only burns gas and scales the plate heat exchanger faster. If the water comes out warm rather than cold, the setting is the thing to raise; if it starts hot and cools, the setting is fine and the fault is flow rate or a scaled exchanger.

Sixty degrees, with a full dose of non-biological powder: that is the heat that shifts the bacteria, and a cold wash is why nappies come out still smelling. Rinse the poo off into the toilet, keep the used ones in a dry bucket with a lid rather than soaking them, and wash every two or three days - a bag that sits for a week is a smell you cannot wash out. Run a pre-wash or rinse first, then the 60C main wash, an extra rinse at the end, and no fabric conditioner ever, because it coats the fibres and the nappy stops absorbing. 40C is only with a nappy sanitiser added. Line dry where you can and tumble on low for anything stiff. New nappies get one wash before the first use; bamboo and hemp need three or four to reach full absorbency. Wash them apart from your clothes, or with towels at 60C.

Size the wall and let it dry, then cut each drop with an extra 5cm top and bottom, paste the paper (not the wall) and let it soak for the time the roll says, and hang the first drop plumb from a pencil line rather than from a corner. Smooth it outwards from the middle with a paper smoother, and butt the joins rather than overlapping them. A ceiling is the same paper on a bigger job: paper it before the walls, and work away from the window.

Skin gets thin and creases as the collagen and elastin that keep it springy thin out with age and sun damage; smoking and too much sun make it happen much sooner. Sunscreen every day is the one thing that reliably slows it, and moisturiser plumps out the fine lines a little.

Skip swordfish, shark and marlin completely, and keep tuna to two fresh steaks or four medium tins a week: those three are the fish with the most mercury, and tuna is the one people eat most of. Oily fish like salmon, mackerel and sardines is good for the baby's brain - two portions a week, and no more than one of them tuna.

Skip it unless it is cooked until steaming hot: brie, camembert, soft blue cheeses and any mould-ripened cheese can carry listeria, and listeria can reach the baby. Baked camembert or brie in a hot dish is fine because the heat kills it. Hard cheese is a different story - cheddar, parmesan, and the tubs of cream cheese, cottage cheese and mozzarella are all fine, because they are made with pasteurised milk.

Skipping a meal now and then is fine - a busy day, a lie-in, a big late breakfast - and nothing bad happens. What matters is the total you eat and drink across the day, and whether you get so hungry that you raid the cupboard at four. Skipping meals on purpose to control your weight tends to backfire; skipping one because you are not hungry is not a problem.

Sleep for short breaks, shut down when it will be off for more than a day: sleep keeps your open windows and wakes in seconds, and it sips power rather than charging the battery overnight, while a full shutdown clears the memory and installs the updates it has queued. Either way a restart once a week is what keeps a machine feeling new.

Sleep is worth more than the extra hours of cramming: a rested brain recalls what you already know, a tired one does not. Pack your bag and the pens you need, read your one-page summary once, then stop by nine and do something that is not revision. If you really cannot settle, write down the three things you are worried about forgetting.

Sleeping on your side, cutting out alcohol in the evening and losing a little weight fix it for most people who snore, and a blocked nose is worth treating with a decongestant or a steroid spray from the chemist for a couple of weeks to see. A pillow that keeps you off your back, or a tennis ball sewn into the back of a top, does the side-sleeping job. Snoring with gasping, choking or stopping breathing, or daytime sleepiness despite enough hours, needs a GP - that is sleep apnoea and it is treatable.
Sleeping on it means waiting until tomorrow before deciding, so it looks different in the morning. That is usually a good call for a big one. What are you deciding?

Slice floury potatoes about 2mm thin - a mandoline, or a peeler does one at a time - rinse the starch off in cold water, then dry the slices properly on a tea towel: a wet slice steams instead of crisping. Fry at 160C for 3 minutes, until the bubbling dies down, or toss them in a tablespoon of oil and bake at 200C for 15 to 20 minutes, turning once. Salt the moment they come out and cool them on kitchen paper. Dry slices and a steady temperature are the whole trick.

Slice it, salt it for 20 minutes and pat it dry, then cook it in plenty of hot oil until it's deep golden: aubergine soaks up oil like a sponge, so a dry pan and too little fat is what leaves it rubbery. Roasting at 200C for 25 minutes works the same way.

Slice it 1cm thick, pat it dry and fry it in a dry non-stick pan 2 minutes a side until it is golden, or grill it 3 minutes a side. Patting it dry is what gives a crust instead of steam, and turning it once keeps it from going rubbery. It is already salty, so it needs no oil or salt.

Slice it first, then bag it: bread keeps about three months in the freezer and the slices go straight into the toaster from frozen. Freeze it on the day you buy it, because a loaf frozen when it is already going stale thaws out stale.

Sliced ham from a packet keeps 3 to 4 days in the fridge once it is open, in a tub or wrapped in its paper, and a whole cooked ham keeps about a week. Dry-cured ham like Parma or Serrano keeps far longer, a couple of weeks wrapped in the fridge, because the salt is doing the work. Ham that feels tacky or slimy, or smells sour, goes in the bin whatever the date says.

Slow down by about a third for a week and use lined paper: most messy handwriting is speed, not hand shape. Then pick the two or three letters you join badly (r, n, m and your a's) and copy a paragraph a day, ten minutes, saying each letter as you write it. Check the shelf: a pen with a grip you actually hold, sitting up with both feet down and the paper turned slightly. If it is a child, check the grip first - a fist grip or a thumb over the top makes neat writing almost impossible - and use a pencil long enough to reach the table.

Small things they can use lying in bed: a long phone cable and a charged power bank, earphones, a puzzle book or a magazine, a decent lip balm, a light blanket, or a printed photo of the family to put on the locker. Skip flowers on most wards and skip food unless you know the diet. Ask the ward what is allowed before you bring it in, and go when you can stay a while - the visit is the gift.

Small, petrol, and as dull as you can bear: a hatchback like a Corsa, Fiesta, Polo or Yaris with a small engine. Check two things before the car itself - the insurance group, because a 1.0-litre in a low group can cost half what a bigger car costs to insure, and the MOT history on gov.uk for gaps and advisories. Spend under half your budget on the car and keep the rest for insurance, tax and the first repair, and avoid anything modified, since insurers charge more for it.

Small mammals: a tawny owl lives on mice, voles and shrews, with the odd small bird, frog or beetle, and a barn owl is almost all voles. It swallows the prey whole and coughs up the fur and bones as a pellet, which is what you find under a roost.

Smart and modest works for a christening: a dress or smart trousers and a nice top, with a layer you can take off, and shoulders or knees covered for the church. Nothing showy, and flat shoes if you'll be standing or on grass afterwards.
Smart and modest is the safe read: trousers or a skirt past the knee, shoulders covered, and shoes you'd wear to a nice lunch. Take a layer, because old buildings are cold.
Smart casual usually means dark jeans or trousers with a collared shirt or a nice top, and clean shoes: tidy, no tie. If you're unsure, dress one step smarter than you think and ask the host.
Smart casual is plenty: clean jeans or trousers and a nice top, in something you can kneel down and move about in if there are small children there.

Smart jeans or trousers with a top you like is right for nearly any evening out, and a jacket you can take off covers a cold walk home and an over-hot bar. Wear shoes you can walk and stand in, and check the place's own rules if it's somewhere new, because plenty still say no trainers or sportswear.

Smearing and squeaking blades are a sign the rubber has gone hard: replace both front blades once a year, about £15 to £25 for the pair, and clean the glass properly at the same time. Wipers are easy to clip on yourself and the handbook shows the size.

Smell that survives a wash and nappies that have stopped holding a puddle are almost always detergent or fabric conditioner built up in the fibres. Strip them once: a hot wash - 60C, or 90C for plain cotton prefolds - with no detergent at all and a tablespoon of soda crystals, then an extra rinse, and from then on no fabric conditioner and a smaller dose of powder. The other two causes are a wet bucket (a dry one with a lid is what keeps the smell down) and a main wash cooler than 60C, and a bag that sits for a week is a third. Line drying in sun takes the last of the stains out.

Smoke into the room is a cold flue, a blocked one or a pressure problem at the top: hold a rolled-up newspaper torch at the opening for a minute to warm the flue before you light it, and open a window a crack. If it still smokes once the fire is going, stop using it and get the sweep out, because a blocked or cracked flue lets carbon monoxide into the room. Smoke only when it is windy means the chimney needs a cowl, and smoke in a sealed room with an extractor fan running means it needs an air vent.

Smoked paprika is mild too, around 1,000 Scoville - the smoke comes from drying the peppers over oak, not from heat. Half a teaspoon is enough to taste it; more turns a dish bitter rather than hotter.

Smoked salmon keeps 3 days in the fridge once the pack is opened, wrapped tight, and it is cured rather than cooked so the date on the pack matters more than the days. It freezes for a month in portions, though the texture goes softer. Eat it within 24 hours once it is out on a plate, and bin it if it smells sharp or feels tacky.

Smooth it with a tumble-dryer sheet, a little leave-in conditioner or a spritz of hairspray on the brush. Dry air is the cause, so a humidifier or a bowl of water near a radiator helps in winter, and a metal coat hanger or a metal comb run through the hair takes the charge off in seconds when you are out.

Sneezing first thing is usually the nose reacting to the change in temperature, dust mites in the bedding or a dry room, rather than an allergy to anything outside. Wash the bedding at 60C, air the room and try a saline rinse; an antihistamine at night helps if it goes on. Itchy eyes and a blocked nose in spring point to hay fever.

Sniff it and match the smell: yoghurt or beer is a healthy starter at work and nothing needs doing; acetone or nail polish means it has run out of food and is making alcohol, so pour off any liquid on top and feed it twice a day until it smells of yoghurt again; vinegar or a sharp sourness is the same thing further along, so feed it more often than once a day and use a splash of it in a bake rather than a whole loaf.
Snowed under just means buried in work or messages - nothing to do with weather. What is the pile in front of you?

Soak the paint in oil before you touch it. Work cooking oil or mayonnaise through the strand with your fingers, leave it 20 minutes, then comb it out from the ends up and shampoo twice. Emulsion softens in warm water and washing-up liquid alone. Start at the ends so a blob near the scalp is not dragged through the whole length, and cut out what will not come, which on a fringe is the honest fix.

Soak the sticky patch in warm soapy water or dab it with oil (olive, baby, even mayonnaise) and leave it five minutes, then rub it off with your thumb or a cloth. White spirit or rubbing alcohol lifts the last of it from glass and hard plastic.

Soak the stuck fingers in warm soapy water for 15 to 20 minutes and the glue softens enough to roll apart - roll, do not pull, because pulling takes the skin with it. A little cooking oil, or nail varnish remover on a cotton bud for superglue, works on what is left. Do not use a blade or a solvent on broken skin, and if two fingers are really stuck, or glue has gone into a cut or an eye, get seen the same day.

Soak the grill pan and its rack in hot water with washing-up liquid and a couple of tablespoons of bicarbonate of soda, then lift the burnt bits with a nylon scourer. The element above it is not a thing to scrub: switch it off, let it cool, and wipe it with a damp cloth, and leave the self-clean lever for the whole oven.

Soak up what you can, then wash the patch with a warm solution of biological laundry detergent, blot and rinse well; the enzymes in it break down the smell. Never use bleach or ammonia cleaners, which smell like urine to a cat and invite a repeat.

Soak up whatever is still liquid with cat litter, sand or sawdust, sweep it up, then scrub the mark with neat washing-up liquid and a stiff brush and rinse it away from the drains.
