A patch that has dried lifts with a paste of biological washing powder left on for an hour, or a degreaser from a motor shop. Do it soon: oil that has soaked into tarmac stays dark for good.

Soak 250g of dried haricot beans overnight, boil them hard for 10 minutes then simmer for an hour until soft (or start from two tins). Simmer a tin of tomatoes with an onion, a tablespoon of black treacle or brown sugar, a teaspoon of mustard, a splash of vinegar and a pinch of salt for 20 minutes, stir the beans in and bake at 160C (140C fan) for 40 minutes. It keeps 4 days and freezes.

Soak it first, then steam it: four hours or overnight in cold water, drained, spread in a lined bamboo basket or on a cloth over a pan of boiling water, and steamed for 20 to 25 minutes until it is translucent and chewy. It is a different grain from ordinary rice - short, opaque and chalky - and it is never boiled or stirred, which is what makes it a sticky ball rather than a pot of mush. In a hurry, an hour in warm water does the job, and a rice cooker with a sticky-rice setting takes 1 part rice to 1 part water and does the steaming for you.

Soak it in cool water with a scoop of biological washing powder for half an hour, then wash cool on the usual cycle, and check it before it goes anywhere near the dryer: heat sets a wine stain for good. Curtains can go in the machine if the label allows, hung back damp so the weight pulls the creases out.

Soap molecules have one end that grabs water and one that grabs oil and grease, so they surround dirt and lift it off your skin into the water. Washing with water alone leaves the oils behind; the rubbing and rinsing matter as much as the soap.

Socrates (469-399 BC) was a Greek philosopher who wrote nothing and taught by asking questions until a person saw the hole in their own answer, which is still called the Socratic method. Athens tried and executed him in 399 BC for impiety and corrupting the young.

Soften an onion in oil for 8 to 10 minutes, add whatever vegetables you have, cover them with stock by an inch and simmer 20 minutes. Blend it if you want it smooth, and season at the end - a spoon of cream or a squeeze of lemon lifts a plain soup.

Soften a chopped onion in oil with a pinch of salt for 8 to 10 minutes, add the main vegetable - about 700g of squash, carrots, leeks or tomatoes - then cover it with a litre of stock and simmer 20 minutes until everything is soft. Blend it, taste for salt at the end, and add a potato or a handful of lentils if you want it thicker without cream.

Soften it first: hold a cloth soaked in white spirit, petrol or a tar remover on the spot for a minute, then wipe, never a fingernail or a scourer, which lift the lacquer. Tree sap wants warm soapy water and then methylated spirit. On glass use a plastic scraper. Wash the panel and wax it again afterwards, because the solvent strips the wax too.

Soggy chips are a steam problem, so the fix is dry and hot: pat fresh-cut chips dry (rinse the starch off first if you cut them yourself) and put frozen ones in straight from the freezer, then get the oven and the tray properly hot - 200C (180C fan) - and spread them in one layer with space around each chip, because a crowded tray steams instead of crisping. Salt them as they come out and not before, since salt pulls water to the surface. If they still come out limp, cook them twice: 10 minutes at 160C to soften the middle, then 8 minutes at 190C to crisp the outside, with a few minutes resting in between.

Somebody sees where you are because an app on the phone is sharing it, and sharing is the default in the ones people use to keep in touch: Find My on an iPhone and Google's location sharing on Android both keep reporting until they are turned off, and anyone in a family group, a shared account or a live-location message is already watching. Look at who is on the list rather than at the phone: on an iPhone Settings > Privacy & Security > Location Services, and in Google Maps your picture then Location sharing, both show who can see you and for how long, and each name can be removed from there. If nobody is on either list, a shared account or a car's app is the next place to look.

Something slow and ordinary an hour or two before, with water: porridge, toast and egg, or cereal and a banana. A sugary breakfast spikes and drops you by the second hour, which is exactly when the paper gets hard, so keep the sweet thing for the break. Take a bottle of water and a plain snack in, and if the exam is in the afternoon eat a light lunch rather than a big one - a full stomach is what makes people sleepy at 2pm. Keep the coffee you usually drink and nothing more: a double espresso you never have is what sends people to the loo twice in the first half hour.

Something that wicks and doesn't need adjusting mid-set: shorts or leggings and a breathable top, with a sports bra for anything bouncy, and shoes for the work you're doing - cushioned for running, flat and stable for lifting.

Something you can say to a guest out loud and still not name the house: a joke, a film reference, or the flat number with a word after it. Anything with your surname, the road or the flat number in it tells a stranger where you live, and a name that looks like a router brand marks you out as the default password, so keep the password long and random and let the name carry the joke.

Something you can stir through in the time the pasta boils: garlic and chilli warmed in olive oil, a tin of tomatoes simmered 10 minutes with a pinch of sugar, or cream cheese with lemon zest and black pepper. Keep a mug of the pasta water - a splash of it makes any of them cling instead of sitting in the bottom of the bowl.

Something you did not order is unsolicited: you do not have to pay for it and you do not have to send it back, and a bill for it is not owed. Do tell them in writing, keep the parcel unopened where you can, and say you will keep it unless they collect it at their own cost within a date you set - that is decent and it also gives you a record if they later try to charge you.
Something comfortable and a step nicer than you'd wear at home: jeans with a good top, or a dress with flat shoes. Nothing that needs careful handling next to red wine on someone's sofa.

Sore breasts are usually hormonal: both sides tender, heavy or a bit swollen in the week before a period, and easing once it starts. A bra that fits properly - worn at night too if they ache in bed - less caffeine and paracetamol or ibuprofen if you need them are usually enough, and an ice pack or a warm pack over the sore part helps. Pain in one spot that stays put, one breast that is red, hot or hard, a new lump, or any discharge or bleeding from the nipple is a GP appointment within a week or two; a breast that is red, hot and painful with a fever is 111 today, because that is mastitis and it wants antibiotics.

Sorry to hear it - it is a common day and it is not a verdict. Book the next test as soon as the ten clear working days are up, and take the sheet the examiner gave you to your instructor: it lists every fault as a driving, serious or dangerous one, and the serious and dangerous ones are what failed you. Spend the lessons between now and then on those two or three things only, and one extra lesson in the week of the test rather than ten. Most people pass on the second or third go, so a fail is a date, not a verdict.

Sorry - that is a rough one. Ask for the offer in writing and don't sign it on the day: check the redundancy pay, the notice, and any holiday you are owed. Ask whether the role is really going - if it is not, or the process was unfair, a free service like ACAS or Citizens Advice will tell you where you stand. Then ask for a reference and tell your network, because most jobs arrive through people.

Sort the money and the childcare before the feelings, because those two keep the week running: check what you can claim (universal credit, the childcare element), and ask the council about a nursery place. Then build one reliable adult - a grandparent, a neighbour, another parent at the gate - for the evenings you are stuck. Gingerbread and your local family centre both run free groups, and asking early is not a failure.

Sort the pile by what the label says, because the dots are the fibre: one dot is 110C for silk, nylon and anything with elastane, two is 150C for wool and polyester blends, three is 200C for cotton and linen. Iron the cool things first and let the soleplate heat up, press a hidden hem to test before you touch a collar, and steam or a damp cloth on wool and anything dark rather than more heat.

Sort first, digitise second, and keep the paper: tip the lot onto a table and pull out the faces you cannot lose - the ones people will want in fifty years - then photograph each of those on a phone against a plain background, or use a flatbed scanner for the important ones. Store the prints in an acid-free box somewhere dry and dark rather than a hot loft, write the names and dates on the back of the keepers in pencil, and give the duplicates to the cousins who are in them. Digitising takes a phone app and an afternoon, and a box worth keeping usually shrinks by two thirds.

Sort it by size and move the videos off first: on Windows right-click the drive > Sort by > Size, on a Mac use List view and the Size column, and empty the Recycle Bin or Trash, because deleting alone frees nothing. A stick that says it is full while showing almost nothing is often a fake-capacity one from a marketplace - the real size is what h2testw or F3 report - and an old FAT32 stick cannot take a file over 4GB, so format it as exFAT if you move big videos.

Sort lights from darks, empty the pockets and close the zips, then load it so a hand fits flat on top of the pile - a packed drum does not rinse. Everyday clothes: a 30 or 40 degree cotton wash, normal spin, and the detergent dose on the bottle in the drawer. A pod goes in the drum, not the drawer. A wool or silk label gets its own cycle. Run an empty hot wash once a month.

Sound running behind the picture is a setting, not a fault: find Audio Delay, Digital Audio Delay or Lip Sync in the TV's sound menu and add 50 to 100 milliseconds until the lips match. A soundbar or a Bluetooth speaker adds the most delay, and its own A/V Sync setting takes the rest out.

Sound goes through a wall more than people expect: earplugs and a heavy curtain or a bookcase against the shared wall take the edge off, and a fan or white noise masks the rest. If it is the room next door, ask them once at a calm time to turn it down after a set hour; if it keeps happening, keep a short log of the times and your council's noise team can act on it.
Sounds worth doing — I'm here when you want the next step.
Sounds like a good plan. What's the bit you're least sure about?
Sounds like a good way to spend it.
Sounds like good advice. What's stopping you?

Soup keeps 3 to 4 days in the fridge in a sealed pot, and stew or curry the same, and any of them freezes for up to 3 months. Cool a big pot quickly by standing it in a sink of cold water, then reheat only what you are eating, once, until it is piping hot right through.

Sour milk is curdled and unpleasant, not poisonous: it will not give a child the food poisoning that undercooked meat does, and a mouthful or a cup is very unlikely to do anything. Offer water, and watch for vomiting or diarrhoea over the next few hours. Ring 111 if the child is under one, cannot keep water down, or seems unwell rather than just cross about it. Then bin the bottle - the date is about quality, not safety.

Sour cream is about 20% fat and sours with lactic acid, so it splits if you boil it; creme fraiche is thicker, about 30% fat, and can be boiled without splitting. Stir sour cream in off the heat, and use creme fraiche for a sauce that simmers.

Sow parsley, coriander and dill from March to July, 1cm deep, in a pot rather than a seedbed if you only want a windowsill's worth. Parsley is slow - two to three weeks - so keep the pot damp and be patient; coriander bolts in heat, so sow it little and often and pick the leaves young. Tarragon and sage are better bought as a plant.

Sow parsnips from late February to April, and only fresh seed: parsnip seed dies in a year, which is why a saved packet comes up empty. Sow 1cm deep, 15cm apart once thinned, on ground that has not been manured or they fork. They take three weeks to show, so mark the row.

Sow peas from March to early June, 5cm deep in a wide flat trench rather than a single line, 8cm apart, with a net or twiggy sticks up for them to climb. Mice take the seed, so start them in a gutter of compost if a row disappears. Pick pods every couple of days or the plants stop producing.

Sow radishes from March to September, a pinch every two weeks, 1cm deep and 2cm apart after thinning, and they are ready in about four weeks. They are the fastest thing in the veg patch and a good one to sow with children. Dry soil makes them hot and woody, so water them.

Sow runner and french beans from late April to June, once the soil has warmed, 5cm deep and 20cm apart, after the last frost. Broad beans go in earlier, from February to April, in a double row. Beans need a frame or cane wigwam from the start, and water at the base when they flower or the flowers drop.

Sow swede in May to June and turnips from March to August, 1cm deep and 15cm apart once thinned; swede needs the whole summer to swell and is best lifted after the first frost. Club root is the risk in acid soil, so lime the bed the winter before if you have had it.

Sow sweet peas in October for the strongest plants, or February to March under cover, 2cm deep in deep pots so the root runs straight down. Pinch out the growing tip after two pairs of leaves, harden them off, and plant out in April. Keep picking, because once they set seed they stop flowering.

Sow basil indoors from late April to June, half a centimetre deep and barely covered, at 20C or more: it sulks below 10C, so do not put it outside before June and even then keep it out of a cold wind. Pinch the tips out as it grows to keep it bushy, and sow a second pot in July so you have young plants when the first one goes woody.

Sow beetroot from April to July, 2cm deep and 10cm apart, thinning to one plant per station because each seed cluster holds several. Water regularly: beetroot that dries out goes woody. You can start in April under cloche and sow again in June for small roots into autumn.

Sow cabbage, kale and sprouts from March to May for a winter and spring crop, 1cm deep in a seedbed, then plant out 45cm apart once they have five or six leaves. Firm the soil hard around the stem. Net them straight away: pigeons strip a young brassica in a day, and cabbage white butterflies come later.

Sow carrots from late March to July, a few seeds every three weeks rather than one big sowing, 1cm deep and 5cm apart once thinned. They want a light, stone-free soil: stones make them fork. Cover the row with fleece or a mesh barrier, because carrot fly finds them by smell and a barrier is what actually stops it.

Sow chillies indoors in February or March, half a centimetre deep, at 21C or more: cold seed does not come up at all, so a warm windowsill or a propagator is the whole trick. Pot them on as the roots fill the pot, pinch the top out at about 15cm to make a bush, and move them to the sunniest spot in June. Water when the top of the compost is dry and feed weekly with tomato feed once the flowers open; pick green for a milder chilli, or leave them to turn red.

Sow courgettes from late April indoors and plant out in late May or June, once nights are above 10C, 90cm apart: one plant feeds a family. They need sun, rich soil and steady water. Pick them small, at 10-15cm, because a marrow-sized courgette stops the plant producing.

Sow grass seed in September, or early April if you missed it: warm damp soil, weeds not yet up, and enough time to root before winter. Scatter 35g to the square metre, rake it in lightly, and keep it damp for a fortnight with a light sprinkle morning and evening rather than a soak.

Sow leeks from March to April in a seedbed, then move them to their final spot in June at 20cm apart, dropping each one into a dibbed hole and watering it in rather than filling the hole with soil. Spring onions can be sown from March to July, a pinch every three weeks, and eaten small.

Sow lettuce and salad leaves from March to August, a small pinch every two or three weeks for a steady supply, 1cm deep and 20cm apart for hearting kinds. They bolt in heat: water in the morning, shade the row in a hot spell, and pick leaves young. Cut-and-come-again salad is the easiest thing to grow in a pot.

Speak to your school or college on results day, not next month: they can tell you the resit date (usually November for maths and English, the following summer for most others) and whether the university or college will hold your place, which plenty will once they know. If you were a mark or two off a grade boundary, a remark can be worth it, but it can also go down, so ask the exams officer what the risk is. Failing one paper is not failing the year, and a plan made this week beats a summer of dread.

Speed comes from easy miles, not hard ones: run four times a week with three of those slow enough to chat through, and make the fourth the only hard session - 6 x 2 minutes quick with 2 minutes of jogging in between, at a pace where you could manage one more. Add 5 to 10% a week, keep one full rest day, and expect six to eight weeks before the same 5k feels easier. Runners who only go hard stall after a month.

Speed is accuracy first: set a metronome or a drum loop well below the tempo you can just about manage, play the passage clean five times in a row, then add five beats a minute, and drop back the moment it gets sloppy - two weeks of that beats months of playing it fast and wrong. Keep the fretting fingers close to the strings, pick with a small movement from the wrist rather than the whole arm, and practise the hard two bars on their own instead of the whole song. Ten focused minutes a day is plenty; speed comes from the slow repetitions, not from trying harder.

Spend what you could pay off in a couple of months without borrowing, and treat "two months' salary" as an advert rather than a rule - most people spend a good deal less, and nobody who matters is keeping score. Buy where resizing is free, put the money into the band and the cut you can actually see, and add it to your home contents insurance the day you get it.

Spiders spin silk from glands in the abdomen and pull it out with their back legs, laying a frame first and then a spiral inside it. The silk is stronger than steel for its weight, and many spiders hunt without a web at all.
Spiders have eight legs and usually eight eyes, in rows across the front of the head. They have silk glands in the abdomen and spin the web out with their back legs.

Spin comes from the fingers and the wrist, not the shoulder: hold the ball across the seam in the fingers rather than deep in the palm, and as the arm comes over give it a sharp clockwise rip from the third finger so it turns off the pitch. Keep the arm straight and the run-up slow - spin is a skill of the hand, and the slower ball turns more. Practise on a line until the ball lands where you look.

Spin is the bowler turning the ball off the pitch: a leg break turns away from a right-hander, an off break turns in, and a googly is a leg-spinner's ball that turns the other way - it looks like a leg break out of the hand, but the wrist rolls the other way. Batsmen read it off the pitch rather than the hand, because the wrist gives it away late.

Spinach, kale and the other leafy greens are among the best value in the shop at about 25 to 35 calories per 100g: a bag wilted in a pan is one of your five a day and brings folate, vitamin C and vitamin K, plus nitrates that help blood pressure. The iron in spinach is real (2.7mg per 100g) but poorly absorbed, so eat it with something containing vitamin C - lemon, peppers, a glass of juice. One caution: if you get kidney stones, spinach is the leaf to go easy on, because of its oxalate.

Split rent by room if the rooms differ and by income if one of you earns much more, and agree it before you sign rather than after. Put the household bills in a separate account that each of you pays into on payday, with the amounts written down, so nobody fronts the lot and nobody has to ask twice.

Split the pitch into four small squares and put three or four children in each with one ball: everyone touches the ball, nobody can chase the whole crowd. Rotate the squares every five minutes so they meet each other, and finish with a game on a short, wide pitch so there is always someone to pass to.

Split the room rather than the theme: a dinosaurs-in-space party with a dino dig at one table and a rocket build at the other, then one cake with a dinosaur on one side and a rocket on the other. Each child gets to be the theme for half the party, and nobody's idea is dropped.

Split wood - a spoon, a spatula, a rolling pin - is a hygiene problem before it is a broken one: the crack holds food where a wash cannot reach, so bin it if the split goes through or the wood inside has gone dark, and sand it smooth with fine paper along the grain and oil it if the split is only a surface one. Wood is cheap - a new spoon is a couple of pounds - and water and heat are what split it, so never soak one and never put it in the dishwasher. Oil spoons and boards once a month with food-safe mineral oil, not olive oil, which goes rancid.

Split your week in half: five tailored applications, and three conversations with people who might know someone. Most jobs come through a person rather than a portal, so tell ten people you trust exactly what you are looking for. Keep a one-page list of what you sent and when, and follow up a week later.

Split it in late winter or early spring, before the sap rises: a log cut then has the whole summer of sun and wind to dry and is ready for the fire by the autumn. Hardwood such as oak, ash and beech wants about twelve months and softwood about six to nine, and a split log dries roughly four times faster than a whole round - which is the reason to split everything now and stack it, rather than leave the rounds in a heap until you need them.

Split it into chunks of three or four lines and learn the first word of each chunk, because that is what you will forget first. Read the chunk aloud, look away and say it, then add the next chunk and say both; record yourself and listen while walking or washing up. Say the whole thing out loud twice a day and it settles in about a week.

Splitting is water, not disease: after a dry spell the roots take up water faster than the skin can stretch, so the fruit splits, and a heavy feed does the same. Water little and often at the base so the soil stays evenly damp, mulch to hold that moisture, and pick the split ones straight away because they rot where the skin is broken. In a wet spell pick the fruit a little under-ripe rather than leaving it to swell.

Spotting between periods is usually one of four things: the small hormone dip at ovulation, about 14 days before the next period; the pill, implant or coil, especially in the first three months; a harmless growth on the cervix or a patch of it that bleeds easily; or an infection, chlamydia among them. Note the days it happens for two or three cycles, take a sexual health test if you have changed partners, and see a GP if it keeps happening. Ring the GP the same week if you are soaking a pad an hour, it hurts, or it is after sex.

Spread the rice out on a tray or a wide plate and it is cool enough for the fridge in about 20 to 30 minutes - a shallow layer, not a deep pan with the lid on. Get it into the fridge within the hour, keep it no more than a day, and reheat it once, until it is steaming hot all through. Rice left standing at room temperature is the one to bin, because of the spores that survive cooking.

Spread a paste of bicarbonate of soda and water on the glass, leave it twenty minutes and wipe it off with a damp cloth; burnt specks lift with a plastic scraper or a razor blade held almost flat to the glass. Keep caustic oven cleaner off the rubber seal, and wipe the inside of the door too, because most of the brown film sits between the panes.

Spring onions are a fridge thing, unlike the dried onions below: wrap them in a sheet of kitchen paper or a clean tea towel and put them in the salad drawer, where they keep one to two weeks. A bunch that has gone floppy perks up in a glass of cold water for half an hour, roots down, and chopped ones freeze well in a bag for cooking.

Spring bulbs go in from September to November while the soil is still warm: three times the bulb's own height deep, 10cm apart for daffodils and 8cm for crocuses, pointy end up. They need a cold spell to flower, so a mild autumn is fine. Leave the leaves on for six weeks after flowering and they come back every year.

Squash is two players in a room, and you win a point only when you serve: hit the ball above the middle line and below the top line onto the front wall, and let it bounce once on the floor. If it goes out, hits the tin or bounces twice, the point is over. Stand near the T in the middle after your shot - whoever holds the middle wins.

Squeegee the walls and the tray after every shower, which takes twenty seconds and saves most of the scrubbing; once a week spray the walls and tray with white vinegar or a bathroom spray, leave it ten minutes and rinse. A mug of bicarbonate of soda and hot water down the tray keeps the drain sweet, and black silicone wants a mould spray rather than more scrubbing.

Squeeze three lemons into 100g of sugar dissolved in 100ml of just-boiled water, top it up with a litre of cold water and taste it - a pinch of salt makes it taste more of lemon, not less. A squash is the same drink from a bottle of cordial, and a sprig of mint or a sliced lemon in the jug is what a pub does. It keeps two days in the fridge.

Squeeze a leave-in conditioner or a little hair oil through damp hair and dry it on low with the nozzle pointing down the hair. A smooth cotton T-shirt instead of a towel and a wide-tooth comb cut frizz more than most products do.
Sriracha is mild to medium, around 2,000 Scoville - ketchup-hot rather than chilli-hot, and sweet. A spoon per bowl adds heat slowly enough to taste as you go.

Stack it off the ground on pallets or two rails, in a spot that gets sun and wind, and cover the top only - a tarpaulin over the whole pile holds the damp in and turns a drying pile into a rotting one. Keep it a wall's width away from the house so it is not a ladder for mice, and leave air gaps between the stacks rather than one solid wall of wood.

Stairs are fine from the day you get home, one stair at a time with a rail and the crutches in the other hand: the good leg goes up first and the operated leg comes down first - up with the good, down with the bad - and both feet land on each step rather than one leg per stair. Sit down on the bottom step to put the sticks and slippers on rather than bending. If you live alone and the stairs are steep, ask the ward to watch you do a flight before you go home; it is a normal part of the discharge check.

Stale bread is dry, not spoilt: sprinkle it with water and warm it in a 180C oven for 6 to 8 minutes and it comes back close to fresh, and a dry loaf is the right bread for toast, croutons, breadcrumbs or a panzanella. To stop it happening, keep the loaf whole and cut slices as you need them, in a paper bag or a bread bin rather than the fridge, and freeze half of it sliced on day one.

Stalemate is a draw: the side to move is not in check but has no legal move at all, and the game ends level even if they are a queen down. It usually happens with a lone king in front of the enemy king with no square to go to. If you are winning, leave the other king a square or move a pawn, and if you are losing, look for it on purpose - it is half a point from nowhere.

Stammering that starts between two and five is common and about four in five children grow out of it, so don't treat it as a problem in front of them. Slow your own speech, give them time to finish without filling the word in, and ask one question at a time. Ask the GP for a speech and language referral if it lasts more than six months, if they push hard to get a word out, or if there is stammering in the family.

Stand side-on with your front foot behind the oche and your weight on it, keep the elbow up and still, and throw from the elbow rather than the shoulder: same speed, same release, every dart. Practise grouping rather than scoring - twenty darts at the 20 bed, trying to land them inside a hand's width - and finish every session with ten at a double, because doubles win legs.

Stand the seed potatoes in a single layer, eyes up, in a cool bright place - a windowsill in an unheated room, not a warm kitchen - for about six weeks from late January, and rub off all but the two or three strongest sprouts. An egg box or a tray works, and greening is fine; long white spindly shoots mean too warm and too dark.

Stand the bottle in a jug of warm water for a few minutes, or hold it under a warm tap, then shake it and test a drop on the inside of your wrist. Never warm a bottle in the microwave: it heats unevenly and can scald even when the outside of the bottle feels cool. Warm only the feed you are about to give, and do not reheat one that has already been started.

Stand the bottle in a jug of warm water for a few minutes, or hold it under a warm tap, then shake it and test a drop on the inside of your wrist: at about 37C it should feel neither warm nor cold. Don't microwave it - breast milk heats unevenly and hot patches burn a baby's mouth - and never refreeze milk you have thawed or warm up a bottle your baby has already started, because the bacteria from their mouth multiply as it sits.

Stand them up and feel for a thumb's width between the longest toe and the front of the shoe, on the bigger foot - one is always bigger. School shoes are usually outgrown in four to six months at primary age, so check every half term, and never hand them down: the sole has worn to the other child's foot.

Stand them in a rack, spaced so the air gets round, and let them air-dry: a tea towel mostly moves the water about. If you do use one, wash your hands first and change the towel daily, because a damp cloth that sits out is where the germs come from. Glasses dry without streaks if they go in the rack upright and you do not top them up.

Stand up as soon as the alarm goes, before you have thought about it: that heavy, can't-move feeling is sleep inertia and it lifts about fifteen minutes after you are upright. Alarm across the room, curtains open, and the same wake time every day. If every morning is like that with no energy at all, a blood test for thyroid and anaemia is the next step.

Stand with the ball of the foot on a step and let the heel drop slowly for 30 seconds, three times each side, twice a day; keep the knee straight for the calf and bend it for the soleus behind it. Tight calves that come with sharp heel pain or a sudden snap in the back of the leg need looking at, not stretching.

Stand in a warm shower - warm enough to be comfortable, not hot enough to redden the skin - and work from the top down: hair if you are washing it, then the face, then the places that hold sweat, which are under the arms, under the breasts, the groin and between the toes. Plain soap or shower gel on your hands, a flannel or a soft cloth is all it needs, and a rinse of everything afterwards. Dry the folds properly rather than rubbing, and a wash of the face, hands, feet and under the arms is enough on the days in between a full shower.

Stand it on a hard surface so the vents underneath are clear, and blow the dust out of them: a laptop on a duvet or a cushion overheats in minutes. Check the fan is actually spinning, and stop leaving it plugged in at 100% all day if the battery is swelling.

Standard form writes a number as something between 1 and 10 times a power of ten: 4,500 is 4.5 x 10³, and 0.0002 is 2 x 10⁻⁴. Count how many places the decimal point moves, and make it negative when the number is below 1. To multiply, multiply the front numbers and add the powers.

Standing still is what makes it cold, so that is what to dress against: a thermal base layer, a fleece, a windproof and waterproof coat with the hood up, and boots with a thick sole, because the ground takes the heat out of your feet. Cover the neck, ears and wrists, take a cushion to sit on rather than a cold seat, and put a flask in your bag - a hot drink is worth more than an extra jumper.

Standing up quickly lets blood pool in your legs for a moment before your body tightens the vessels and adjusts, so your head is briefly short of blood and you see stars. Get up in two stages, drink enough water, and see a doctor if you actually faint or it happens most times you stand.
Star anise is not hot: it is liquorice-sweet and very strong, so one star in a pot for four. Two and the dish tastes of cough sweets.

Stars twinkle because their light passes through moving layers of air, which bend it slightly this way and that before it reaches your eyes. Planets look steadier because they are close enough to show a tiny disc rather than a single point of light.

Start small and gentle: a piece of fruit, a yoghurt or a slice of toast, then wait twenty minutes before a proper meal. Fat, sugar and coffee on an empty stomach are what make people feel sick, shaky and headachy, so go easy on those and have a glass of water first. If you have gone more than a day without eating, break it over an hour or two rather than in one sitting, and ask a GP first if you take diabetes medication.

Start the new cover before you cancel the old one - being uninsured for even a day is an offence and a gap pushes the next premium up - and cancel from the day the new policy starts. Ring the insurer, or use their app, and ask for the cancellation date and the refund figure in writing: expect a pro-rata refund of the unused months less an admin fee of about £25 to £50, and nothing back if you have claimed. In the first 14 days of a new policy you can cancel for a full refund minus a small fee. Ask for proof of your no-claims years in writing for the new insurer, and remember a policy paid monthly is a credit agreement, so the instalments can carry on after the cover stops - settle it and get the letter.

Start where the animal came from: the breeder usually takes them back, and every breed has a rescue that will. A good rescue home-checks and asks for the vet records, and that is far kinder than advertising online, where the wrong people look. Be honest about the animal's quirks, expect a waiting list because most rescues are full, and say if money or housing is the reason - there is more help than people expect, from pet food banks to a landlord letter.

Start where you can stand up: hold the rail in the shallow end and put your chin in, then your mouth, then blow bubbles with your nose and mouth under for a second, and build it up over a few visits - goggles, and a nose clip if the water up your nose is the worst of it, get most adults past this. An adult beginner class teaches exactly this in the first lesson, and the instructor has seen it a hundred times. With a child it is the same thing at their size: let them watch and splash their own face at bath time, and never hold them under - one dunking sets a nervous swimmer back months.

Start with one room and one deadline: pack the things you use least first, label every box by room and keep one box for the first night - bedding, toilet roll, kettle, mugs, chargers, a torch and any medication. Anything you have not used in a year, sell, donate or bin it now rather than paying to move it; a bag a day from the back of a cupboard gets rid of most of it. Book the van for the whole morning rather than by the hour, and measure the doorways and stairwell before the day. As a guide, a one-bed flat is about twenty boxes and a couple of weekends of packing; a three-bed house is two or three times that.

Start with one true picture rather than a feeling - the chipped mug, the bus you missed - and write it in short plain lines you would actually say out loud. Keep the best line, cut the explaining around it, and stop one line before you want to. Ten minutes with no rhyming is a good first poem.

Start with run-walk: three minutes of easy running, two minutes of walking, five times, three days a week, and add a minute of running each week. Build up for six weeks before you add speed, keep every run slow enough to talk, and expect the first fortnight to feel harder than it looks.
Start with the smallest version of it and see how it sits.

Start with the switch on the wall: an immersion heater has its own fused spur, usually in the airing cupboard, and it trips like any other. If the spur is on, the thermostat is under the round cap on the top of the element - turn it up a little and listen for a click; no click and a tank that stays cold means the element or the stat has gone. That is a drain-the-tank job: the part is about 40-60 pounds and an hour or two of a plumber's time. Where a tank has two elements, the bottom one does the heavy lifting.

Start with the GP or the health visitor, who can refer you on: in most areas that means a parenting programme such as Triple P or Incredible Years, a CAMHS referral if there is anxiety or low mood underneath it, and the school's SENCO if the trouble shows up there too. Ask for the parenting course by name - they work and the wait is much shorter than CAMHS. Keep a two-week diary of what happens just before each flashpoint, because it turns 'out of control' into a pattern, and it makes your request harder to turn down; if anyone is being hurt at home, say so plainly on the phone and you will be seen sooner.

Start with the filter: it twists out of the bottom of the drum, and a rinse under the hot tap with a check for glass or a label in the sump usually fixes it. Then look at the drain hose where it joins the waste under the sink, because a kink or a blockage there leaves exactly that water in the bottom. If it hums and still won't empty with both clean, the drain pump needs swapping, which is a cheap part and a quick job for a repairer.

Start with the fob battery: a coin cell (CR2032 on most cars) behind the cover, two minutes and about £2. If the fob is fine, try the spare, and hold the fob against the start button on keyless cars, which is the emergency way to start. A fob that has lost its coding needs a garage or a locksmith.

Start with the lock: press the door inwards while you turn the handle, and try lifting the handle up, because plenty of doors lock that way and half a turn frees them. If the handle turns loosely and nothing clicks, the spindle inside has gone and that is a locksmith. A door swollen by damp usually frees with a firm push at shoulder height while someone turns the handle, or with a thin card slid in on the latch side; if it will not shut at all, plane a millimetre off the edge that rubs. If it is rented, ring the landlord or a locksmith who quotes on the phone - and if a child or anyone is shut in, ring 999 rather than fight the door.

Start with two short sessions a week and leave a day between them: a chair stand or a slow sit-to-stand for the legs, a wall press or a light band row for the upper body, eight to ten slow reps each, stopping while you still have three or four left in you. Add a little - one rep or one tin of beans - only when the last session left you tired but not wrecked. Muscle comes back at roughly half the speed of the walking, so expect weeks rather than days, and put protein in every meal: a palm-sized piece of meat, fish, eggs, beans or yoghurt, three times a day. If you were in hospital, in bed for more than a few days, or had heart, lung or kidney trouble, ask your GP or the physiotherapist who saw you before you start, and stop and get advice for chest pain, breathlessness at rest, or a swollen painful calf.
Start with whatever has a deadline, if anything does; if nothing does, start with eating something.

Start with 20 minutes of lengths and break each one into two lengths of front crawl with a rest at the wall - technique first, distance later. A one-to-one lesson or an adult improver class is the fastest way to stop getting out of breath, and two swims a week is plenty at the start.

Start with a pharmacist for anything minor: coughs, colds, sore throats, aches, rashes, hay fever, stomach upsets, cystitis, threadworms, and advice on which medicine to buy. They can treat some of it themselves and will say when it needs a GP. Ring 111 when you are not sure and it cannot wait, and 999 for chest pain, breathing trouble or a stroke.

Start with a chickpea or chicken curry built on four things: onion, garlic, ginger and a spoon of curry powder. Soften a chopped onion in oil for 8 minutes, add the garlic, ginger, a teaspoon of curry powder and one of cumin for a minute, then the chicken or a drained tin of chickpeas, a tin of tomatoes and 100ml of stock, and simmer 20 minutes. Stir yoghurt in off the heat at the end, and taste for salt.

Start absurdly small if that's all there is: £5 a week by standing order on payday. Then find the money in the bills, a fresh energy comparison, a cheaper mobile or broadband contract and the subscriptions you forgot about usually free up £20 to £50 a month, and add whatever they save you.

Start aciclovir cream from the pharmacy at the first tingle and keep going for five days: caught early, it shortens the sore. It stays contagious until it has crusted over, so don't share towels, cups or lip balm, and don't pick it. Keep it away from newborn babies, who need a doctor straight away if one appears on them.

Start at the plug: a dead set is usually the fuse in the plug or the socket, so put something else in the socket to test it and, if that works, change the 3A or 5A fuse in the TV's plug. If the standby light never comes on at all after that, the power board is the usual part, and a repair shop will quote £60 to £120 to look at it - against £250 to £500 for a new set, so an older TV is usually not worth repairing.

Start at the programmer: it is usually on a timer that has slipped, or on 'water only' when you wanted heating too. A combi with no hot water but working heating is nearly always low pressure or a stuck diverter valve, so look at the gauge (1 to 1.5 bar cold) and try the reset. If there is a hot water cylinder, look for the immersion switch and the thermostat on the side, and check the little header tank has water in it. Anything inside a gas boiler, or gas you can smell, is a Gas Safe engineer.

Start at around six months with soft food in sticks they can hold themselves - cooked carrot, toast fingers, ripe pear - rather than spooning puree in. Milk is still the main meal until about a year, so treat food as practice: one new thing next to something familiar, and expect most of it on the floor. No honey before one, no whole nuts or whole grapes, and always sit with them while they eat.

Start feeding when the first truss of flowers has set fruit, then weekly: a high-potash tomato feed, diluted as the bottle says, watered onto damp soil rather than dry. Too much nitrogen before that gives you a big leafy plant and no tomatoes, and a plant in fresh grow bag compost usually needs nothing for the first six weeks.

Start further away than you think you need to: a distance where he can see a dog and still take a treat, then let the other dog pass and walk on. Repeat that a few times a week, never let dogs rush up nose to nose on the lead, and stay calm yourself because the lead tightens when you brace and that tells him there is something to fear.
Stationery with an e is paper and pens - remember e for envelope. Stationary with an a is not moving - a stationary car.

Statutory paternity leave is 1 or 2 weeks, taken in one go, and it has to be used within 56 days of the birth. You tell your employer 15 weeks before the due date. It pays about £187 a week in 2025-26, or 90 per cent of your average pay if that is less, as long as you have worked there for 26 weeks. Plenty of employers offer more - check your contract.

Statutory redundancy pay is half a week's pay for each full year under 22, one week for each year from 22 to 40, and one and a half weeks for each year over 41, capped at £700 a week and 20 years, so the maximum is £21,000 and many people get a good deal less. On top of it you are owed your notice or pay in lieu, any holiday you have not taken, and your final wages, and if 20 or more people are going at once there has to be 30 days of consultation. Check the offer against the statutory figure before you sign anything, because a settlement agreement usually pays more in exchange for you giving up the right to claim - take free advice from ACAS or a union first.

Statutory maternity pay is 39 weeks: the first 6 weeks at 90 per cent of your average pay, then 33 weeks at about £187 a week in 2025-26. You qualify if you were on the payroll for 26 weeks before the baby is due and earn at least £125 a week. If you do not qualify, Maternity Allowance pays about the same for 39 weeks. Repaying it only comes in if your contract's own scheme says so.

Stay off while you have a fever, and go back when you have been 24 hours without one and feel up to it: a normal cold with a bunged nose is fine to work through if you can keep away from people who are vulnerable. Rest and fluids get you back quicker than pushing through, and a fever, aches or a chesty cough means wait.

Stay tall and wait: most takers decide their corner early, so watch the standing foot and the hips rather than the ball, and dive late with a strong hand. Keep your weight on the balls of your feet so the first step can go either way.

Stay with them and say it will pass, because it does: an attack peaks in about ten minutes. Sit them down, loosen anything tight at the neck, and breathe out loud with them - out for longer than in, so they have something to follow rather than an instruction. Do not argue with what they are frightened of and do not leave them alone to fetch anything. If they have never had one before, or there is chest pain with it, get medical advice rather than assuming it is panic.

Stay with them if you can, and ask them straight out whether they mean to kill themselves - asking does not plant the idea. Ring 999 or 911 now if they've taken something or are in danger, and a crisis line (116 123 in the UK, 988 in the US) can talk it through with either of you.

Stay behind the barrier, not beside the car, and keep a coat on: the hard shoulder is the most dangerous part of the road. Ring 999 if you cannot get behind the barrier or you are in a live lane, then your breakdown service. Wait for the recovery truck to reach you rather than walking up the verge to a sign.

Staying on the vape beats going back to cigarettes, so if it is the only thing keeping you off tobacco, the win is not to stop. To come off it: drop the nicotine strength a step every two weeks, keep it out of sight rather than in your hand, and set a date instead of drifting down. The hand-to-mouth habit outlasts the nicotine, so keep a straw or gum where the vape used to live. Feeling low or snappy for a week is withdrawal, and it passes.

Step forward far enough that both knees bend to about a right angle: the front knee tracks over the middle of the foot rather than caving inwards, the back knee dips towards the floor without banging it, and the chest stays upright. Push through the front heel to stand up. If the front knee is what complains, take a longer step and a smaller dip; a wobble means the step was too short.

Stephen Hawking (1942-2018) was a British physicist who showed that black holes give off radiation and slowly evaporate, now called Hawking radiation, and whose A Brief History of Time sold millions. He had motor neurone disease from 21 and wrote and spoke through a computer.

Stews, curries, chilli, bolognese, soup, lasagne and shepherd's pie all freeze well and come back the same; cook them a bit under and freeze in portions flat in bags so they thaw fast. Leave out potatoes cooked in a stew, pasta and rice cooked in it, and add fresh pasta, rice or a jacket potato on the day. Cool within two hours, label the date, eat within three months, and defrost in the fridge overnight.

Stick a brush strip or foam seal round the doors and windows, and put a weighted draught excluder at the bottom of the front door. A chimney balloon and a letterbox flap are cheap and stop the worst of it; seal up the gaps before spending money on heating.

Sticky eyes in a child are usually conjunctivitis and clear on their own in a week or two: wipe from the inside corner outwards with cooled boiled water, a fresh bit of cotton wool each time, and wash your hands after. A pharmacist can give chloramphenicol drops if it looks bacterial, and they should stay off nursery while the eyes are weeping. See a GP the same day for a baby under a month, for pain or a change in sight, or if the eyelid is swollen and red.

Stiff buttercream, or cream whipped until it holds a peak, a star nozzle and a steady squeeze: hold the nozzle 1cm above the cake, squeeze, then stop squeezing before you lift away or you get a tail. For a swirl start in the middle and spiral out; a 1M star tip does swirls and roses, a plain round tip is for writing. Chill the icing 15 minutes if it slumps, and practise on a plate first.

Stiff fingers in the morning are usually the small joints of the hands starting to wear - osteoarthritis - and that kind loosens within half an hour of moving them: run warm water over the hands first thing, do gentle finger and thumb circles, and keep using them, because rest is what makes a stiff hand stiffer. Paracetamol helps a sore spell and a pharmacist can suggest an ibuprofen gel. See a GP if the stiffness lasts more than an hour, the knuckles are swollen, or both hands are the same, because that pattern is the inflammatory kind and wants treating early.

Stir 2 tablespoons of soy, 1 of oyster sauce, a teaspoon of sugar and a teaspoon of cornflour into 100ml of water or stock and pour it in when the vegetables are nearly done: it thickens in about a minute. Garlic and ginger go in first, in the oil, before anything wet.

Stir 50g strong white flour and 50g water in a jar and leave it covered at room temperature. Every day throw half away and feed it the same 50g plus 50g. It bubbles within three to five days and is ready when it doubles in 4 to 6 hours, smells of yoghurt and tastes sour: 5 to 7 days in all. Rye or wholemeal flour starts faster; chlorinated tap water can slow it down.

Stir a tablespoon of lemon juice or white vinegar into 250ml of milk and leave it 10 minutes to thicken: that is buttermilk for a recipe. Thinned plain yoghurt or soured cream work too, and milk alone is fine in most pancake and muffin recipes.

Stir a teaspoon of sugar into 100ml of water that is warm but not hot - about 35C, blood heat, because over 45C kills it - sprinkle the yeast on top and leave it 10 minutes. A thick foam across the surface means it is alive and ready to use; if it sinks and sits there, it is dead, and fresh yeast is the only fix. Do this before you weigh anything else: it costs ten minutes and it is the first thing to rule out when a loaf does not rise.

Stonehenge was raised in stages between about 3000 and 2000 BC in what is now Wiltshire, by Neolithic and Bronze Age Britons whose names we don't know. It was a burial ground and a place aligned with the midsummer sunrise, probably for ceremonies.

Stop riding it until it is fixed: with one cable gone the other brake is all you have, and a single brake locks the wheel more easily in the wet. A new inner cable costs a few pounds and a shop will fit one in minutes. It is not hard to do it yourself with a new inner cable and an Allen key, about twenty minutes of threading it through the lever and outer and setting the pads a couple of millimetres off the rim. Tighten the anchor bolt with the barrel adjuster halfway in, pull the brake firmly before you ride, and check the outer for kinks and the lever for a frayed end.

Stop the cycle, unplug it and turn the water off at the valve behind it, and leave it off until the leak has stopped. Water at the front is usually the door seal or the filter cap, water underneath is the pump or a loose inlet or drain hose, so check the hose connections before you call anyone. A leak from inside the machine itself is an engineer's job.

Stop trying to fix who they are and work on the visit instead: shorter, with something to do, and one subject you can both stand. Decide beforehand what you will not be drawn into, answer it once and flatly, then change the subject. Keep one ordinary warm thing in it - 'it was good to see you' - because the aim is a relationship you can survive rather than a verdict on them.

Stop turning it: the piece in the barrel is what the pins are holding, and every extra turn pushes it further in. Put a drop of WD-40 or graphite at the keyway, then grip whatever is proud with needle-nose pliers or thin side cutters, pull straight out rather than sideways, and jiggling the door handle while you pull helps. A short piece just inside can be walked out with the thin blade of a jigsaw or a coping saw slid alongside it. If it is in past the face of the barrel, it is a locksmith: about £60 to £120 to drill and replace the cylinder, and keep the door on the latch until they come. Do not glue anything to it and do not push a second key in.

Stop using it and replace it: a cable with the wire showing, or the plug end split, can shock you or start a fire, and tape does not make it safe again. Unplug it first, buy a branded cable of the same type and wattage rather than the cheapest one on the app, and if the cable is fixed to the plug - a kettle, a lamp, a washing machine - have the lead replaced rather than taping it. To stop the next one fraying, pull it out by the plug and not by the wire, and do not wrap it tightly round the charger or a corner.

Stop using it and stop charging it: a swollen battery is a fire risk, and pressing on it to make it fit is how they catch light. Keep it out of the sun, do not bend or puncture it, and take it to a repair shop or the battery bin at the tip rather than the kitchen bin. A new battery is usually £40 to £70 fitted, and most shops do it the same day.

Stop waiting as the default: give them the time you mean and start without them ('we're eating at seven'), and if you are going out, drive yourself so their lateness stops costing you. Say the pattern once, without the list of times, and let them feel the small consequence - a cold dinner - instead of hearing about it.

Stop asking what is wrong, which a teenager cannot answer at that age, and be around without an agenda: drive somewhere, cook together, sit in the same room. Say what you notice once, without a question mark ('you've seemed flat this week'), then let them come back with it later. If they stop eating, sleeping or seeing friends for a fortnight, ring the GP and say that first.

Stop asking for a few weeks and let them come to it: a refusal is usually about being made to sit, not about the potty. Leave it in the room with them dressed, read a book on the floor beside it, and let them choose a trainer seat on the big loo instead. Go back to nappies without a fuss for a month and try again in the summer, when fewer clothes make it easier; keep the praise for sitting, never for the result.

Stop drinking anything an hour or two before bed, cut the evening cup of tea and any alcohol, and empty your bladder just before you lie down. If you are up two or more times a night most nights, or it is new, see a GP: it can be an infection, an enlarged prostate or diabetes, and it is worth checking rather than just putting up with.

Stop if it is safe and put your hazards on, and keep yourself off the road rather than standing in it. You must tell the police if you hit a dog, horse, cattle, pig, goat, sheep or donkey, and if you cannot find the owner it must be reported; any other wild animal - a deer, a fox, a badger - does not have to be reported. An animal that is alive and hurt is the RSPCA on their animal rescue line, and a dead one in the road is the council's to clear, reported with the location on their website. If you hit it, tell your insurer too, because a deer strike is usually a comprehensive claim.

Stop it and unplug it, and do not run another load until you have looked: a dryer fire starts with lint round the heater or a vent hose full of fluff, and the smell is the warning. Empty the fluff filter and clear the hose. Still there after that? Get an engineer out, and never leave a dryer running while you are out.

Stop lightening it now: hair that feels like chewing gum has lost its protein and cannot be repaired, only managed until it grows out. A protein or bond-building mask once a week, a leave-in conditioner, no heat and no tight bands, and an inch off the ends if they are snapping. Wait four to six weeks before any more colour, and get a salon to do a strand test before the next lift.

Straight from the freezer, 12 to 15 minutes at 200C (180C fan) on a tray, turned once, until the crumbs are crisp and the middle is hot; an air fryer does them in 10 minutes at 190C. Don't thaw them first, or the breadcrumbs slide off. Chips, peas and something sharp to dip them in.

Straight in is fine - a modern fridge copes with a warm pot, and food left on the counter to cool is the bigger risk. Split a big batch into shallow boxes so it drops below 5C within 90 minutes, cover it loosely while it is still warm, and keep it away from the milk and the cooked meat on the shelf below. The rule is cool it fast, not cool it first.

Strap them in every time, crotch strap as well as the waist one, and stay within arm's reach: a child can slide down and out of a high chair in seconds, and the crotch strap is the one that stops it. Keep it off tables and worktops, away from the hob and the kettle, and not against a wall or drawer they can push off with their feet. Once they can climb out of it the high chair is finished - move them to a chair at the table with a cushion so their feet rest on something.

Streaks are an uneven coat, not a bad paint: roll in strips a roller wide and lap the last strip while it is still wet so no edge dries alone, with a light even load rather than pressing the roller dry. Brush slowly, one way, and don't go back over paint that is setting. On a wall already patchy, a second full coat cures it; touching up spots makes it worse.

Stress is too much pressure while you can still see the point of what you are doing; burnout is the exhaustion that comes after months of it, when you have stopped caring and the work feels flat. Stress eases when the pressure does - burnout does not, and usually needs time off and a change, not a better week.

Strike it with the laces, not the toes: plant your standing foot beside the ball, point the toe down, and follow through towards the target so the ball stays low. The power comes from the follow-through and a locked ankle, not from swinging harder.

Strip the leaves off the stalks - the stalks are the woody, bitter part - then boil or steam the leaves for 3 to 5 minutes, until they are soft but still bright. Curly kale takes the 5 and cavolo nero nearer 3. Massage it with oil and salt if it is going in a salad raw, which softens it in a couple of minutes without cooking it. A splash of lemon or vinegar at the end keeps the colour.

Stuff the neck end only and weigh the bird with the stuffing in: use the same 20 minutes per 500g plus 20, so usually 15 to 20 minutes longer. Check the stuffing is piping hot in the middle, not just the meat.

Sublimation is a solid turning straight into a gas without melting first: dry ice does it at room temperature, and so does the ice in a freezer over months, which is why ice cubes shrink. The reverse, gas straight to solid, is deposition.

Sugar-free gum is good for your teeth: the chewing makes saliva, which washes the acid off, and a regular piece holds only about 2g of sugar anyway, so sugar-free is the one to pick. Give it to nobody's dog, though - the xylitol in sugar-free gum is poisonous to them.

Sugar does not go off: white sugar keeps for years, and the date on the bag is a best-before for quality rather than a use-by. Brown sugar sets hard rather than spoiling - a slice of bread or apple in the jar softens it again - and sugar with insects or damp in it goes out.
Sumac is not hot: it is sour and fruity, the taste of lemon without the wet. A teaspoon over a salad or grilled meat at the end.

Sunlight is white, but the air scatters the blue end of it away, so the Sun looks yellow and, low down, orange or red. At sunset the light crosses much more air, which takes out the blue and lets the reds through; dust and cloud deepen it.

Sunscreen keeps about three years unopened and about a year once it is open, so write the month on the bottle when you start it. Out of date it does not turn dangerous, it just stops protecting as the label says: if it has separated, gone gritty or smells odd, replace it, and a bottle that has sat in a hot car all summer is the one to bin.

Supply follows demand, so the fix is more milk taken out rather than more food in: feed or express every two to three hours, let the baby finish one side before you offer the other, and add a night feed if you have dropped one. Skin to skin, feeding lying down and drinking to thirst help; fenugreek, stout and lactation biscuits are not evidence. Ask the health visitor or a breastfeeding counsellor (NCT and La Leche League are free) to watch a feed if the baby is not gaining, has fewer than six wet nappies a day, or feeding hurts - a shallow latch or a tongue tie is the usual reason, and it is fixable.

Support under the arch matters more than cushioning: a shoe with a firm heel counter and a removable insole you can swap for an arch-support one (about £20 to £40 from a pharmacy) is enough for most people with flat feet. A lace-up trainer with a straight shape and a snug midfoot holds the foot better than a slip-on, and if your feet, shins or knees hurt when you walk, or one arch has dropped recently, a podiatrist is worth the visit.
Sure. Tell me what's happening and we'll work it out together.

Surface rust is harmless: scrub it off with a green scourer, dry the tin, and line it with baking paper so the cake never touches the metal. Replace a tin that has rusted right through, or whose coating is flaking into the food.

Swap rather than subtract: use lentils or a tin of beans for half the mince in a ragu, mushrooms for the other half, and chickpeas where a curry had chicken, and nobody at the table notices. Two meat-free dinners a week is easier to keep than a rule; keep the protein up with eggs, beans, lentils, tofu and cheese, which is the part people get wrong.

Swap rather than ban, because the ban is what makes the 9pm trip to the shop happen: keep something you actually like at home that takes two minutes - frozen chips in the oven, popcorn, yoghurt with fruit, toast and peanut butter. Eat protein and fibre at lunch, because a day of white carbs is what makes the evening raid feel compulsory, and do not shop hungry: the aisle is the thing that decides it, not willpower. One takeaway a week, on a day you choose, holds better than none at all.

Swap the cable first and then the brick, in that order, because the cable is the part that breaks: try the charger in another socket and check the light on the brick comes on. If the laptop only runs when plugged in, the battery has failed; a new one is £40 to £80 and a shop fits it in an hour.

Swedes are lifted from October, and are better after a frost, which sweetens them the way it does parsnips; they will stand in the ground into winter. Turnips are quick - six to eight weeks - and are best pulled small, at 5 to 7cm across.

Sweep or vacuum the hard floors every few days and mop once a week, or twice in a kitchen where frying spits and shoes come in: a floor that looks clean still holds the film that makes it dull and sticky. Carpets want a vacuum once a week, more where people walk in shoes, and a deep clean once a year. A doormat halves the work, and wash the mop head or rinse the bucket out after every use, because a dirty mop just moves the dirt around.

Sweep it first, then wash: on block paving or concrete a pressure washer does most of it, keeping the nozzle moving and working down the slope so the dirty water runs off rather than back over what you have done. On decking keep the pressure low and go along the grain, because a hard jet furries softwood. A small patio is quicker with hot water, a splash of washing-up liquid and a stiff brush, then a rinse with the hose. Do it on a dull day so the soap does not dry before you rinse, and keep the spray off plants, open windows and next door's paintwork.

Sweet peppers want warmth and a long season: sow indoors in late February or March, half a centimetre deep, at 20C or more, and pot them on twice before planting out in June in the sunniest, most sheltered spot you have. Water regularly, because a plant that dries out drops its flowers, and feed weekly with tomato feed when the first fruit set. Pick them green, or wait for red, which is sweeter.

Sweet: honey or jam with a spoon of peanut butter, stewed apple with cinnamon, or frozen berries stirred in while it is hot. Savoury: butter, salt and a poached egg, or grated cheese and black pepper - porridge is only oats cooked in water or milk, so it takes either, and the salt is what makes the sweet version taste of something.

Sweetcorn is ready in August and September: peel back a little husk and press a kernel with a fingernail - milky juice means ready, clear means wait, doughy means it has gone over. Cook it within the hour, because the sugar turns to starch fast.
Swifts sleep on the wing, climbing to where they can glide slowly for hours at a time. Some stay airborne for months, and they only land to nest.

Swimwear, flip-flops, a towel and robe if the place does not lend them, a hair tie, a bottle of water, and your own shampoo if you are fussy. Leave the phone in the locker: the pools and steam rooms dehydrate you faster than people expect.

Switch the printer off and on at the wall, then check the queue: on Windows, Settings > Bluetooth and devices > Printers, clear anything stuck, and set it as the default printer. Nine times out of ten it is a stale job in the queue or the wrong printer selected, not a broken machine.

Swollen feet and ankles are ordinary in the last months: the extra blood and the weight of the bump slow the fluid back up your legs. Put your feet up above hip height for twenty minutes a few times a day, keep walking, wear the support tights, and drink normally rather than less. Ring your midwife the same day if it comes on over a day or two, if one ankle or one leg swells on its own, if a leg is hot or sore, or if you have a bad headache, blurry vision or swelling in your face or hands.
Sydney has about 5.3 million people, the biggest city in Australia.
Tabasco is about 2,500 Scoville, sharper and much saltier than sriracha, so a few shakes per plate. It is vinegar-forward: added early it dulls, added at the table it does not.

Tablets taken by mouth start working in about 30 minutes and are at their best at one to two hours; a soluble or effervescent one is quicker, and ibuprofen lysine and the liquid capsules are faster than a plain tablet. Pain that has not shifted at all after two hours, at a proper dose, is a reason to ask a pharmacist rather than to take more sooner than the packet allows.

Tailbone pain is usually from a knock, a long sit or childbirth, and there is nothing to strap up: it settles over a few weeks. Sit on a soft cushion or lean forward onto the fronts of your thighs rather than taking the weight on it, stand up often, and use paracetamol or ibuprofen if you can. See a GP if a fall made it much worse, if you cannot sit at all, if there is numbness, or if it is still there after eight weeks.

Take out the laces and insoles, brush off dry dirt, then scrub with a soft brush, warm water and a little washing-up liquid, or wash them in a pillowcase on a cold cycle. Bicarbonate of soda on a damp old toothbrush is the stronger version for white canvas, and a melamine sponge or whitening toothpaste takes the scuffs off the rubber sole. Dry them in the shade with newspaper inside, because heat and sun turn white rubber yellow, and once it has gone properly yellow nothing brings it back.

Take printed copies of your CV, the letter or email with the address and the time, photo ID, and a pen and a small notebook. Add three questions of your own about the team and what the first six months look like, and the name of whoever invited you so you can ask for them at reception. Put the address in your phone the night before and arrive ten minutes early: nothing you have to hold all morning, no coffee to spill.

Take the money if the rise is permanent: it lifts your pension, sick pay, overtime rate and every future offer, while extra days stop when the job does. Work out what a day is worth first - a day of holiday is about half a per cent of your salary, so five extra days is roughly 2.5% - and if they are offering the days instead of a rise, that is a smaller offer than it looks. The exception is a job that is burning you out: take the days, because nobody gets a good reference for being tired.

Take the smallest break that is really a break, and take it today: twenty minutes out of the house without your phone, or a bath with the door shut while someone else does bedtime. Then lower the bar for the rest of the day - one meal, one wash, no craft - because a worn-out parent does not need a plan, they need an hour. Ask for a fixed hour each week rather than a whole day once: "Tuesday, six till seven" is something another adult can say yes to, and it is the standing hour rather than the big day that keeps you going.

Take the suit, jacket or dress to a dry cleaner and leave the label alone: the dry-clean-only tag means the fabric or the lining will shrink, bleed or lose its shape in water, and no gentle cycle makes that safe. Two or three times a year is plenty for a suit worn weekly; between times, air it overnight and brush it. A silk or wool item marked dry clean only that is really just delicate can be hand-washed, but that is a gamble on a favourite.

Take the surface out of it first: a mouse on glass, gloss or a shiny desk mat reads the movement wrongly, so put a sheet of paper under it and see if it stops. Then a new battery in a wireless mouse, the receiver moved out of a USB 3 port and into one on the front, and a wired mouse tried in the same port - if the wired one is steady, the mouse or its battery is the fault. On a laptop, a thumb or a wrist brushing the trackpad while you type is the commonest cause of a cursor that jumps.

Take the transport bolts out of the back before the first wash: three or four long bolts hold the drum still for the lorry, and leaving them in wrecks the bearings and the drum in one spin. Water off at the valve first, then the blue fill hose onto the cold inlet with its rubber washer, hand tight plus a quarter turn, and the drain hose hooked up at 60 to 90 cm - a grey hose lying in a bowl on the floor will siphon your wash water away or flood the kitchen. Level the feet so it rocks on nothing, then run it empty on a hot wash before the first load, because new machines carry oil and dust in the drum.

Take the basket and the tray out and wash them in hot soapy water - most baskets are non-stick, so a soft sponge rather than a scourer. Wipe the inside of the drawer with a damp cloth and a little washing-up liquid, and use a brush or a wooden skewer to get the crumbs out of the element guard rather than tipping water over the top. Leave it open to dry before it goes back. For the baked-on grease, a paste of bicarbonate of soda and water left on for ten minutes lifts it without scratching; a wipe after every few uses stops it building up.

Take the biggest single line first and halve it rather than cutting it out: bought coffee and lunches are usually the largest and easiest, and going from five a week to two saves more than cancelling a handful of small subscriptions. Set a weekly limit for that one thing and stop when it is gone.

Take the case off and stop charging it while you use it: heat plus charging is what makes a phone hot. Close the heavy games and video apps, keep it out of direct sun, and if it is hot while idle, check Settings > Battery for an app stuck running.

Take the choice out of the moment rather than counting on willpower: put the phone in another room while you get on with something, turn off everything except calls, and charge it outside the bedroom so the first and last hour of the day are phone-free. If you want a handbrake, set a screen-time limit and let someone else hold the passcode, since a limit you can dismiss is not a limit.

Take the cover off and wash it at 60C with a normal detergent and no fabric softener, which coats the fibres and holds the smell in. The foam or filling inside usually cannot go in a machine: hoover it, sponge any stain with warm water and a little washing-up liquid, and let it dry flat in the sun or by a radiator, turned once, until it is dry right through - a bed that is still damp inside smells again within a week. If there have been fleas, wash everything at 60C and vacuum the cracks round the bed as well, because the eggs are not in the bed. Two covers so one is on while the other washes.

Take the difference, divide it by the number you started with, then multiply by 100: 40 to 50 is 10 more, 10 out of 40 is 0.25, so a 25% rise. To add a percentage on, multiply by 1 plus the rate - 80 plus 20% is 80 x 1.2 = 96 - and to take one off, multiply by 1 minus the rate.

Take the door off and lay it flat if you can, and paint the top and bottom edges first so it still fits after. Then the panels, then the frame parts, brushing with the grain. Lightly sand between coats and give gloss about 16 hours to harden before it goes back on its hinges.

Take the front off the thermostat and change the cells: most take two AA or AAA, and the battery cover is either the whole front pulling off its wall plate, as on a Hive, or a small slide-out tray at the side. Use alkalines rather than rechargeables, because a rechargeable cell sits at 1.2V and the unit reads that as low. After new cells give it five minutes to find the hub again, then check the time and schedule, which is what a dead battery loses.

Take the hand if it is offered, once, at the start - an ordinary grip, two seconds - then stop thinking about it: hands in your lap or resting on the table, and look at whoever is speaking. On a panel, answer the person who asked while glancing at the others. Fidgeting reads as nerves only because it is; still hands fix it.

Take the insoles out and let the shoes air overnight, and sprinkle bicarbonate of soda inside to soak up the smell. Wear them on alternate days, wash or replace the insoles, and most trainers survive a cold machine wash.

Take the insoles and laces out, stuff the shoe with newspaper or kitchen roll, and change the paper after an hour; that pulls the water out far faster than air alone. Then leave them in a warm room with a bit of air moving, and most trainers are dry overnight. Keep leather and glued soles off a radiator and out of a tumble dryer, which cracks the leather and softens the glue; a hair dryer on the cool setting is fine for the last damp patch. If they still smell of damp afterwards, sit a sock of bicarbonate of soda in each shoe overnight.

Take the legs off first: cut the skin between leg and body, bend the leg outwards and cut through the joint rather than the bone. Then slice each breast across the grain from the thin end, keeping the knife flat against the carcass, and let the bird rest before you start if you can.

Take the legs off first: cut through the skin between leg and body, bend the leg back until the hip joint pops, then cut through the middle of the joint rather than through bone. Then take the wings off at the shoulder, and cut each breast away from the backbone, following the ridge with the knife tip. A sharp knife and a pair of kitchen scissors for the joints do most of the work, and the carcass goes in the pot for stock.

Take their temperature before anything else: 38C or above is a fever, and rest, plenty of fluids and paracetamol or ibuprofen are what bring it down. Get advice the same day for a fever with a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade under a glass, breathlessness, confusion or not drinking, and ring 999 if they are hard to wake. An older person with a temperature can go downhill quietly, so a hot nan who is also drowsy or muddled is a 111 call rather than a wait.

Take them with a meal: the fat in food helps you absorb vitamins A, D, E and K, and most people find a multivitamin easier on the stomach with breakfast. Iron is better with orange juice than with tea or coffee, which block it. Do not double up - a multivitamin plus a separate one of the same vitamin can push you over the daily limit, so compare the labels.

Take them back to a pharmacy: every pharmacy takes unwanted medicines for safe disposal, and you do not need to explain. Don't flush them and don't bin them - they reach the water supply, and a child or a pet can find them. Leave them in their packet with the label on, and put a used inhaler in with them rather than in the bin.

Take them if they want to come, with one adult whose only job is them: they can sit at the back, leave for the middle part and come back for the end. Tell them what will happen first - who will speak, that people may cry, whether there is a coffin - and let them choose one small job, like carrying a flower or drawing a picture for the order of service. A child who does not want to go should not be made to; staying at home with someone they like, or visiting the grave later, counts just as much.

Take yes for an answer and put a date on it: 'No problem — when do you think you can get me some of it?' A small amount you actually receive is better than a big promise you don't. If it happens twice, say plainly that you need a plan you can rely on.

Take your medicines in their boxes, the admission letter, phone and charger, and loose clothes you can get on one-handed; for a day case add slippers with a back and a named bag for your clothes. Leave valuables at home, and ask the ward what they provide before you pack towels and toiletries.

Take 10 micrograms (400 IU) of vitamin D every day through autumn and winter, roughly October to March: the sun is too low in the sky here for your skin to make it, however grey or bright the day is. From April to September, short spells outside with hands and face uncovered is enough for most people, and oily fish, eggs and fortified cereal help the rest of the year.
