If the screen says 'Not charging' while it is plugged in, the cable or the port is failing; if it says nothing, the charger is. An iPad on a phone charger charges very slowly or not at all, so use the one it came with.

Try a strong decaf, or a rooibos or barley-cup drink if you want the ritual without the caffeine. Green tea or a sparkling water with lemon work too; the slump at 3pm is often dehydration and a walk as much as coffee.

Try a traybake, a stir-fry and a pasta this week: change one of three things and the same dinner comes out new - the shape (traybake, stir-fry, pasta, curry, soup), the carb under it (rice, potatoes, couscous, bread, noodles) or the sauce that finishes it (tomato, yoghurt and lemon, a spice paste, gravy, pesto). Mince is a ragu, a chilli with rice, or a cottage pie. Keep five dinners you can cook without thinking and swap one of those each week.

Try a mattress topper before a new mattress. A 5cm memory-foam or latex one costs about £40 to £100 and softens a firm bed or fills the dip in a soft one. If the mattress is over eight years old, sagging in the middle or you can feel the springs, it is the mattress and a topper only postpones it. A slipped pillow under your knees takes the strain off a sore lower back, and a too-soft bed is worth trying with a board under it first.

Trying for a baby is a wait of up to a year at under 35 and six months at 35 or over: have sex every two or three days rather than saving up, since timing is less exact than the apps suggest, and take 400mcg of folic acid daily. Cut alcohol and smoking right down. See a GP after a year of trying (six months at 35 or over, sooner if periods are very irregular or painful) - both of you, not just you.
Turmeric is not hot: earthy and a little bitter, and too much of it tastes of soap. Half a teaspoon for four is plenty, and it stains a wooden spoon and a white shirt for good.

Turn off the sleep timer first - it is in Settings > General > Timers or System > Time on most sets, and an hour is the factory default on some. Then look for Auto Power Off or Auto Standby in the Eco or Power settings, which switches the set off after four idle hours on many TVs. If it still happens, unplug everything else from the TV (a games console or a Fire Stick can wake it and put it back to sleep) and check the power lead is not in a socket with a timer switch. A TV that clicks off after ten minutes is usually a power board, which a repair shop fixes for £60 to £120.

Turn off wake timers and the things that nudge it: on Windows search for Edit Power Plan > Change advanced power settings > Sleep > Allow wake timers > Disable, and in Device Manager untick 'Allow this device to wake the computer' on your mouse and keyboard. A laptop that lights up in the night is nearly always an update, a mouse nudged by a cat, or the lid sensor. If it still goes flat over a few days while properly shut down, that is the battery and not something waking it, so check its health first.

Turn on the setting rather than watching the number: an iPhone has Settings > Battery > Charging Optimisation, and most Android phones have Protect Battery or a charge limit in Settings > Battery. Between 20% and 80% is the range a lithium battery lasts longest in, and the makers' own optimised charging gets you most of that without any effort.
Turn on the spell checker in whatever you're writing in and read it once more yourself: a checker catches typos but not the wrong word, so its, it's, your and you're still need your eyes.

Turn on wifi calling, which on most networks is Settings > Phone > Wi-Fi Calling: calls then come over your broadband and the signal stops mattering indoors. Keep a mobile call near a window, and ask your network for a signal box - they are free on most contracts if you can show the problem. A repeater you buy yourself only helps if there is at least one bar outdoors.

Turn on automatic backup: iCloud or Google Photos on a phone, and OneDrive, Google Drive or an external drive on a laptop. The rule that saves people is 3-2-1: three copies, on two kinds of storage, with one of them off-site, so a lost phone is an annoyance rather than a disaster.

Turn the numbered head at one end of the radiator down a notch or two - that is the valve that sets the room, and the numbers are roughly 2 for 16C, 3 for 18C and 4 for 21C. A bedroom wants 16 to 18C for sleep, so 2 is usually the setting there, and turning it down is the way to cool a room that a radiator has made too warm. Leave the plain valve at the other end alone; it is the balance for the whole system. Turn it to the snowflake - frost protection, about 7C - in a room nobody uses, and give it until the next morning, because a radiator takes an hour to show a change. If the head does not click and the radiator stays as hot, the pin under it is stuck: take the head off and work the pin free with pliers.

Turn the seat cushions over and swap them round, then look under them: a sofa sags because the foam in the seat cushions has flattened or the webbing across the base has stretched, rarely because the frame has gone. A new seat cushion in 35kg/m3 foam costs about GBP 30 to 60 and does more than anything else; stretched webbing re-tensions with a staple gun, and a 10mm board under the cushion is the five-minute fix.

Turn the stopcock off first, then ring the water company: it is responsible for the pipe up to the boundary stop valve, and most companies give a one-off leakage allowance that writes off the extra water when the leak was hidden, so ask for it by name. A plumber finds and fixes the pipe on your side, and keep the receipt and the photos of the meter.

Turn the thermostatic head on the radiator down to 0 or to the snowflake, which is frost protection rather than fully off, and leave it there: that closes the valve against the room and the radiator goes cold the next time the heating runs. If it has an old wheel valve instead of a numbered head, turn it clockwise until it stops - the same valve a plumber would close - and turn both ends if you are taking the radiator off the wall. Don't shut the valves on a radiator in a room that gets damp or near freezing, because that is the one that needs the frost setting.

Turn the water off at the isolation valve under the cistern, take the lid off and watch where it goes. Trickling down the back of the pan means the flush valve is not seating: feel the rubber seal for grit, and a new flapper is a couple of pounds and clips straight on. Water into the overflow or up the side means the fill valve is too high or its float has gone, so screw the level down and replace the valve if that does not stop it. A button that stays down or does nothing is the button or the syphon under it, and those are a few pounds at a hardware shop and clip in without any plumbing.

Turn the water off at the isolation valve, flush to empty the cistern and sponge out what is left, then undo the nuts on the water connector and the two screws holding the pan to the floor. Lift the pan out with a bag over the outlet, because there is always water in the trap, and scrape the old seal off the waste pipe. The pan connector and the flexible water connector both get replaced with the toilet, never reused: they seal by being crushed once. Sit the cistern on the new pan before you lift it in, push the pan onto a new connector lined up square, screw it down on its own holes and tighten the water nut by hand plus a quarter turn, because a spanner on a plastic nut cracks the china.

Turn the water off first: the stopcock is usually under the kitchen sink, and if water is near a socket or a light, switch that circuit off at the consumer unit. Then stop whatever is running, bail and mop, and get air moving with a fan and an open window - a floor or skirting that stays wet a day warps and grows mould. Photograph it before you clear up, and ring the insurer and whoever owns the building today if it came through the ceiling.

Turn the barrel adjuster on the gear cable a quarter turn at a time while pedalling: one way tightens a shift that is slow to climb the cassette, the other way cures one that jumps past the gear. If that does nothing, the cable has stretched or seized, or the hanger the derailleur hangs on is bent - a bent hanger is common after the bike has fallen over, and a shop straightens it in minutes.

Turn the boiler off at the wall switch (not at the fuse board, you want the pump to run on for a minute first), put a bowl under it and turn the water off at the stopcock if it's more than a drip. A leak from the boiler casing itself is a Gas Safe engineer's job: don't take the cover off, and don't keep resetting it. Water running from the pressure relief pipe outside means the pressure is too high, which needs looking at too.

Turn the flash off and light the room from one side, because a bare flash on glass is just a white rectangle. Rest the phone on something solid, tap the screen to focus on a crisp corner, and stand a little to one side so the window behind you is not the thing in the glass. If bands crawl across the picture, that is the panel's flicker: step back and zoom instead, or film a second and keep a frame.

Turn the hammer off and use a tile bit, or an ordinary masonry bit with the drill on rotary only: the hammer is what cracks the glaze, and porcelain wants a proper spear-point bit. Put a square of masking tape over the spot so the bit cannot skate, mark the hole through it, and start at a low speed and a shallow angle with almost no pressure until the glaze is through, then straighten up and keep a wet sponge or a squirt of water on the bit because the heat is the other thing that splits a tile. Stay at least 2 to 3 cm in from an edge or a corner, and once you are through the tile put the hammer back on for the wall behind it.

Turn the heat down so it is a steady simmer rather than a rolling boil, and leave the lid half on. A wooden spoon laid across the top of the pan breaks the bubbles before they reach the rim, and a splash of oil or a knob of butter in starchy water (pasta, rice) stops the foam building. Fill the pan no more than two thirds and stir once at the start. Milk and tomato sauces catch on the base and then spatter, so stir them and keep them low.

Turn the heat down to medium, add a little more oil, and splash in water whenever they start to catch; stir them every minute or two. Sweet onions want 8 to 10 minutes of gentle cooking — hot and fast is what burns them.

Turn the heat down and add fat: a knob of butter with a teaspoon of oil in a pan that is already hot, then the egg in when the butter foams but has not browned, and a silicone spatula pushing the set edges into the middle. A stainless pan is ready when a drop of water beads and skitters across it; on a non-stick one, no metal tools and no empty pan over a high heat.

Turn the heating off and let the water cool, then close both valves: the thermostatic head to 0 and the lockshield at the other end. With a towel and a bowl under one end, open the bleed valve at the top with a radiator key and let the water out slowly, then undo the valve nut and lift the radiator off its brackets - it is heavy and full of sludge, so two people. Cap or plug both valves before you put the heating back on, and top a sealed system back up to 1 to 1.5 bar.

Turn the heating off and let it go cold, then brush or roller it with a water-based satin, painting in the same colour as the wall if you want it to disappear. An old cast-iron radiator wants a metal primer first. Leave it a day to dry before the heat goes back on, or the paint softens.

Turn the heating off and let it go cold, then close the valve at both ends: the wheelhead on the flow and the lockshield on the return, and count the turns on the lockshield so you can set it back the same, because that is what balances the house. Put a shallow tray and old towels under the bottom union and open the bleed valve at the top to let air in - the water comes out of the nut slowly and it is filthy black, so do it in short goes. Take the bracket off, and when you refit it open the bleed valve and top the pressure up at the filling loop to about 1.2 bar, then bleed every radiator once more. If it is a sealed combi system and the pressure will not hold, that is a plumber's job. For the whole house rather than one radiator, do the same at the lowest drain cock with every bleed valve open, because one radiator holds only a bucket or two.

Turn your month into weeks before you spend anything: add up the bills that come once a month, multiply by 12 and divide by 52, and put that amount aside out of every week's pay into a second account. Rent and the big direct debits come out of that pot, and the rest of the week's money is yours to spend; put a small amount aside on payday before the week starts, because it is much harder on Thursday. Keep one week's wage as a buffer so an early bill never means a borrowed week.

Turn your shoulders as the ball comes and take the racket back with both hands if it is a two-hander, then meet the ball out in front of your front hip with a flat face and swing low to high so the ball lifts. Hold the finish over your shoulder rather than stopping at the ball - the follow-through is where the control comes from. Practise the turn first: most backhands fail on the shoulders, not the arm.

Turn away and fold your arms the moment he jumps, then greet him calmly when all four paws are down: jumping up is how a dog says hello, so attention is the reward that keeps it going. Ask visitors to do the same, and reward sitting instead.

Turn both radiator valves off and put a towel and a bowl under it, then see whether the water comes from the valve nut or the radiator itself: a drip at the nut often stops with a quarter turn of a spanner on the gland, while water from the panel or a rusty seam means the radiator has gone and wants replacing. Don't overtighten a joint that is held by plastic pipe, and if the water is coming through the ceiling, turn the heating off and ring a plumber today.

Turn it off at the wall and shut the water off at the little isolator tap under the sink, then get the water up - a shallow tray and a towel is enough for a slow one. Water at the front of the door is usually the door seal or the filter, so twist the filter out and check the seal for food or a split; water underneath is the inlet or drain hose where it joins the machine or the waste, so check those joints first. Leave it off until that seal or joint is fixed: a leak from inside the machine itself is a repairer's job.

Turn it on in Settings > Personal Hotspot on an iPhone, or Settings > Network and internet > Hotspot and tethering on Android, and set a password before you do. Other devices then see the phone's name in their wifi list. It eats data fast - a laptop update can take a gigabyte - so keep it for the odd hour and plug the phone in, since a hotspot drains the battery quickly.

Turn it over or open it up and see what has gone: a leg that has snapped wants the old glue drilled out, a wooden dowel or a longer screw and wood glue in the joint, clamped overnight. A cracked seat, back or shelf wants a bracket underneath and a screw through the split, and a split frame is usually cheaper to replace than to mend. Take the weight off it until the glue has set.

Turn it over and find the loose joint: usually one leg has worked free of the seat. Squeeze wood glue into the joint, push it home and clamp it - a strap or a rope round all four legs works - and leave it overnight. Tighten any screws and add a bracket if the same joint keeps going.

Tutankhamun (about 1341-1323 BC) was an Egyptian pharaoh who came to the throne at about nine and ruled for around nine years, and whose tomb Howard Carter found almost untouched in 1922. The gold mask and the grave goods are what taught us most of what we know about royal burials.

Twenty minutes under cool running water, starting now, is the thing that decides how it heals - not ice, not butter, not a cream. Take off a ring or a watch and any clothing that is not stuck to it, then cover the burn loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy cloth and keep the rest of the body warm. Paracetamol or ibuprofen helps the soreness. Get it looked at the same day if it blisters, is bigger than the person's palm, or is on a hand, foot, face or anywhere on a child - those go to a walk-in or A&E rather than waiting.

Twenty pounds for a basic cut is normal in most of the UK: £12 to £20 at a barber or a local salon, £25 to £40 for a stylist or in a city centre, and more in London. So it is not too much unless it is a five-minute clipper cut with no wash. What is worth checking is what the price includes - a wash, a dry, a student or a weekday rate - and that the figure you were quoted is the one on the card machine.

Twenty to thirty seconds, twice on each side, at the point of a gentle pull: the first twenty is when most of it gives, and holding for a minute more adds little. Breathe out into it and do not bounce, and do the long holds after the session when the muscle is warm - a cold stretch before sport takes a little power off it without stopping injuries.

Twenty: fourteen wooden lifeboats, two emergency cutters and four collapsible boats, with room for about 1,180 people, barely half of the 2,200 aboard. Every boat that got away went half empty, and that shortage is the reason more than 1,500 people died.

Twenty countries use the euro: Austria, Belgium, Croatia, Cyprus, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia and Spain. Kosovo and Montenegro use it without being in the eurozone, and Denmark has a fixed rate but keeps the krone.

Twenty degrees or a wool cycle at 30, never 40: heat and agitation are what felt wool, so a jumper washed at 40 in an ordinary cycle comes out smaller and thicker. Use a wool detergent, a short gentle cycle with no spin or the lowest one, dry it flat and never in the tumble dryer. If it is only lightly worn, airing it on a hanger does more good than washing it.

Twice a week for the loo, the basin and the shower screen, and once a week for the bath, the tiles and the floor if anyone showers there every day. The grout and the sealant round the bath want doing every couple of months, before they go black rather than after.

Twice a year, after the leaves fall and again in spring: scooped out by hand in gloves from a stable ladder, with the rubbish into a bag rather than down the drain. Then flush each downpipe with a hose to check it runs. If water still spills over the edge on a wet day, the run of the gutter has dropped or the downpipe is blocked at the bottom, not the top.

Twice a year for a duvet in a cover that is washed every week or two, and every couple of months if you sweat at night, sleep with a pet on the bed, or wake up sneezing. Feather and down want a big drum and hours on low heat with dryer balls; a hollowfibre one survives a normal machine and a cool tumble. A duvet is only washed when it needs it, so the honest signal is a slightly musty smell when you shake it out.

Twice in a row above 15 mmol/L is a call to your diabetes team today rather than a wait-and-see, especially with thirst, lots of weeing or a fuzzy head. Drink water, keep taking your tablets or insulin as prescribed, test more often, and check ketones if you use insulin. Sleepy, breathing fast, being sick and unable to keep fluid down is 999 - that is what DKA looks like. One high reading after a big meal is not.

Two minutes is a good length for a reading, and three or four is the outside for a poem or a psalm: two readings is plenty for a crematorium slot, five to ten minutes of speaking in all, with the music and the eulogy sharing the same half hour. Ask the funeral director how long the slot is before you choose, and read it aloud twice at home with a watch.

Two movers and a van are usually £400 to £700 for a local day, and a one-bedroom flat moved locally comes in around £300 to £500. A three-bedroom house is £800 to £1,500, more if there are stairs or a long carry, and packing as well roughly doubles it. Ask whether the quote is fixed or hourly, whether insurance covers breakage, and whether the price changes if the move runs into a second day.

Two or three play sessions a day of ten to fifteen minutes each, with a wand toy that moves like a bird or a mouse, and finish each one with a small meal so the hunt ends in a catch. That is plenty for an indoor cat; a laser pointer should always end on something she can actually pounce on, or it leaves her wound up.

Two or three times a week suits most people: washing more often strips the oil the scalp needs, and washing less leaves it greasy. Very oily hair can take a daily wash, and dry or curly hair does better every three or four days with conditioner on the ends. If your scalp itches or flakes, use a shampoo for that rather than washing more.

Two or three coats, 8 to 24 hours apart for a danish, teak, tung or linseed oil - thin coats, the excess wiped off after half an hour, and the tin's own figure wins. It is dry to the touch in a few hours but not ready for the next coat, and an oil finish soaks into bare wood rather than sitting on it as a film.

Two pens, a pencil, a spare, an eraser, and your photo ID plus the letter with the room and the time on it. A clear bottle of water if the rules allow one, and nothing else in your pockets - a phone switched off still counts as being in the room, so leave it at home.
Two salmon fillets are about £5 to £7, and a whole side £15 to £25. The frozen fillets are often half the price of the fresh counter for the same fish.

Two sentences: your job title and what you actually do in a week, then one thing you have changed or finished. "I am a warehouse team leader - I run a shift of eight, and I have just moved us onto scanners, which cut picking errors." Thirty seconds is plenty; they are testing whether you can be brief and whether the last job taught you anything. Do not walk through your whole career - that is the next question.

Two slots do for one or two people and four for a family, and the slot width matters more than the wattage: look for wide slots if you toast bagels, crumpets or thick-cut bread. Variable browning plus a cancel button is the pair that stops you scraping burnt toast, and a defrost setting is worth having if you freeze bread. A removable crumb tray and a cord that tucks away are the two things you will notice every week; anything over about 1,500W toasts no better than 900W.

Two thin coats beat one thick one, and a base coat stops the colour staining the nail: wipe each nail with remover first so there is no oil on it, paint from the middle of the cuticle outwards in three strokes, and give each coat 10 minutes so it sets instead of smudging. A fresh top coat every other day is what keeps a manicure looking new for a week.

Two things move the needle: fifteen minutes of tactical puzzles a day on Lichess or Chess.com, and playing long games rather than blitz, then looking at where you lost. Learn the ideas behind one opening for white and one for black instead of memorising moves, and always ask what your opponent's last move was threatening.

Two things are worth starting this week, because neither is sent automatically. Whoever looks after you for 35 hours a week or more can claim Carer's Allowance, about £83 a week, and it keeps their National Insurance record going too. There is money for you as well: Attendance Allowance if you are over pension age, PIP if you are younger, neither of them means-tested, and both unlock more on other benefits. Then ask the council for a carer's assessment - it is free, it is about their needs, and it can pay for someone to sit with you so they get an evening back.

Two things feed a hot water tank. The immersion heater has its own switch on the wall, a fused spur usually marked immersion - that is the one to turn off for the electric side. The tank itself is fed from the cold main through a valve on the pipe running into the side or bottom of it, often red or brass, or a lever valve: a lever across the pipe is shut, along it is open. Close that, then open the hot taps to drain it. Let it cool first - a tank full of water is scalding - and leave the wiring alone beyond the switch.

Two to three minutes in the pan: beat two eggs with a pinch of salt, pour them into a hot buttered pan and pull the set edges inwards with a spatula. Add cheese, mushrooms or ham on one half, fold it over and slide it out while the middle is still soft.

Two to four hours between coats of emulsion, and a full day before you push furniture back against it. Gloss and anything oil-based want overnight, wood stain and water-based varnish four to six hours, and an oil-based varnish 8 to 24. Touch it first: hard and not tacky means it is ready, and the tin wins where it disagrees.

Two to four lines under your name, and the first thing anyone reads: the job you do or want, your strongest two pieces of evidence with a number in them, and what you are after next. Write it last, when you know what the CV holds, and aim it at the advert's job title. Skip "hard-working team player" and anything you could say about anybody: "Warehouse team leader with five years on shift, cut picking errors by 12% and now looking for a shift manager role."
Two tyres take about 30 to 45 minutes, and a puncture repair 20 to 30. Most places take walk-ins, but ring first if you need a particular tyre, and check the pressures again a day or two later.

Two years' service is the line: before that you can be dismissed without a reason and without a warning, unless it is for something automatically unfair - pregnancy, whistleblowing, trade union membership, or a protected characteristic. After two years a dismissal needs a fair reason and a fair process, and a warning usually comes before it, so being sacked out of the blue is worth challenging. Gross misconduct - theft, violence, being drunk on shift - is the exception where they can dismiss on the spot. Keep every message, note the dates, and ACAS's free helpline will tell you in ten minutes whether you have a claim.

Two buckets, and the rinse bucket is the one that stops the scratches: soapy water in one, clean water in the other, and rinse the mitt after every panel. Work top down and do the wheels last with their own cloth, because brake dust drags grit across paint. Rinse before the soap dries, dry with a microfibre towel rather than letting it air dry, and do it out of direct sun. A coat of wax twice a year makes the next wash easier.

Two coats of a decent emulsion usually cover a dark wall, and going much lighter than the old colour can need three; sand and wipe the wall down first and do not thin the paint. If the old colour is a strong red or a dark green, ask for a combined primer and undercoat tinted towards the new colour - it saves a coat and stops the old shade grinning through.

Two coats of gloss over an undercoat, a night apart: gloss, eggshell, satin and anything oil-based want 16 hours or more, so a door or a skirting board is a two-day job. Rub it down lightly between coats so the second one grips.

Two coats on bare or patched plaster, and two whenever the colour changes; a pale wall going a pale colour can take one. Leave about two to four hours between coats, and a full day before you push furniture back against it. Touch the wall first: hard and not tacky means it is ready.

Two coats, four to six hours apart for a water-based varnish - and 8 to 24 hours for an oil-based polyurethane, which is what most furniture varnish is, so read the tin before the second coat. Touch it first: hard and not tacky means it is ready, and a second coat on a tacky surface drags the first about.
Two complete sentences can't be held together by a comma alone. Use a full stop, a semicolon, or a comma plus and/but/because: I was late, so I skipped breakfast.

Two dates mean two things: use-by is about safety, so the food goes in the bin after it, even if it looks and smells fine; best-before is about quality, so dry rice, pasta, flour and sugar are fine for months past it, and a tin for years. For anything fresh, smell it and touch it: a sour smell, a slimy surface or mould means bin it, and cooked food is 2 days in the fridge whatever the label said.

Two different claims. Before you travel, a refund is usually allowed less than an admin fee (up to £10) on an unused ticket, and advance tickets are often non-refundable but changeable. For a late train, Delay Repay pays out from 15 minutes late on most operators - claim on the operator's site within 28 days with your ticket and the delay.

Two different diets in one life: a caterpillar eats leaves, and each kind wants its own plant - stinging nettles for peacock and small tortoiseshell, holly for holly blue, buckthorn for brimstone - while the butterfly drinks nectar from flowers such as lavender, buddleia and sedum.

Two fingers on the trackpad and press, or hold Control and click: both give the right-click menu on a Mac. A two-button mouse works as it always did. To make tapping with two fingers enough on its own, turn on System Settings > Trackpad > Secondary click.

Two free registrations cut most of it: the Mail Preference Service for addressed post, and a 'no junk mail' sticker on the letterbox for the leaflets; the Telephone Preference Service for cold calls, though it takes about a month. Email anyone else and say you withdraw consent. Mark email as spam rather than unsubscribing, because that trains the filter on everything from that sender.

Two lines, one about them as a pair: "So glad you two found each other - the way you laugh at the same things is the whole thing." Put both their names on the envelope, and if you are not going, say so warmly in one line and leave it there.

Two lines is plenty unless it is family: "Merry Christmas - hope the year has been kind to you and the next one is better." Add a specific thing you remember from the year for anyone close ("still laughing about the tent"), and for a neighbour or a colleague a plain wish and both your names is the whole job.

Two meals from a 1.5kg bird, three from a 2kg one: four roast portions, then enough stripped off the frame for two more in a curry, a stir-fry or sandwiches - about 600g of cooked meat from 1.5kg, because a third of the raw weight is bone, skin and water. The frame then gives roughly 2 litres of stock, which is a soup or a risotto, and the fat roasts the potatoes.

Tyre noise that grows with speed is usually uneven wear, a cheap aggressive tread or a wheel bearing on its way out. Run a hand round the inside edge of each tyre for scalloped high and low spots, and have a garage spin the wheels to check the bearings.

UCAS tariff points come from level 3 qualifications only, so GCSEs carry none: an A level is 48 points at grade A, 40 at B, 32 at C, 24 at D and 16 at E, and a BTEC Extended Diploma can score more than three A levels. Add them up across everything you have and compare with the course page, which usually prints both the points and the grades it asks for - when the grades are the offer, the points are only the summary.

UCAS is the one form that covers almost every full-time UK degree: you fill it in once, add up to five courses, write a personal statement, and a teacher or employer adds a reference. The fee is about £28. The early deadline is 15 October for Oxford, Cambridge, medicine, dentistry and veterinary science, and the main one is in mid-January. Offers come back between then and May, and you pick a firm choice and an insurance one.

USB stands for Universal Serial Bus: universal because one plug replaced the pile of different ports a computer used to have, and bus because several devices share it. The letter after it is the shape - USB-C is the small reversible one - and the number is the speed, so a blue USB 3 socket copies much faster than a black USB 2 one.

UTI stands for urinary tract infection: bugs in the bladder that cause burning when you pee, going often and a dragging ache low down. Most clear in a day or two with plenty of water, a pharmacy can advise, and see a GP or ring 111 the same day with a fever, back pain, blood, or if you are pregnant, a man or a child.
Ugh, those are fiddly. How long has it been like that?
Ulf Kristersson is the prime minister of Sweden: in office since October 2022, leading a coalition that the Sweden Democrats support from outside it. The head of state is King Carl XVI Gustaf.

Ultra-processed food is the industrial end of the scale: things made mostly from extracts and additives - emulsifiers, colourings, flavourings, sweeteners - that you would not cook with at home, like fizzy drinks, crisps, sausages, ready meals and most breakfast cereal. The evidence is that people eat more of it and put on weight, but the class is broad enough that hummus and wholemeal bread land in it, so judge by the ingredient list rather than the label. Cooking from plain ingredients is the practical answer.

Umami is the savoury taste that makes food taste deep and round rather than just salty: it comes from glutamates, and the everyday sources are soy sauce, fish sauce, miso, tomato paste, mushrooms, hard cheese, anchovies, seaweed, stock cubes and slow-cooked meat. It is what a dish is missing when it is seasoned but still flat, so add a spoon of one of those rather than more salt, and give it a squeeze of lemon or a splash of vinegar to make it show. Parmesan, tomato and mushroom together are why a good ragu tastes bigger than its ingredients.

Under about 120/80 is normal and 140/90 or over at home is high. Salt is the biggest single lever: under 6g a day means watching bread, cheese, ham, stock cubes, sauces and takeaways rather than the salt cellar. Add 150 minutes of walking a week, more fruit and vegetables, at most 14 units of alcohol and a few kilos off if you carry them, and a typical reading comes down about 10 points in a couple of months. A week of home readings, sitting still, is what a GP wants - and never stop a blood pressure tablet to try diet alone.

Under 90/60 is a low reading, and on its own it often means nothing: plenty of healthy people run at 100/60 all their lives. How you feel is what counts - dizzy or black-visioned on standing up, light-headed, sick, confused, or actually fainting means it is too low for you. When it happens, sit or lie down with your feet up, then get up slowly; drink a large glass of water and don't skip meals. A new or bigger dose of a blood pressure tablet, a water tablet, some antidepressants, and dehydration from a bug or a hot day are the usual causes, so ask a pharmacist to go through your medicines. Fainting with an injury, confusion, chest pain or black stools is 999 or A&E.

Underline what the question actually asks, then write down the numbers it gives you and what units they are in. Guess the answer roughly before calculating - if your working is far off the guess, the sum is wrong, not the guess. Draw it if there is any shape, distance or time in it.

Unlimited data means there is no monthly cap to go over, but almost every such plan has a fair-use point - often 20 to 50GB - after which video is slowed or the speed drops for the rest of the month. It is worth having if you stream on the move; check the fair-use figure rather than the word unlimited.

Unopened beer is best within three to six months in the fridge, and drinkable for a lot longer than that; an opened bottle goes flat within a day, so finish it fresh. Keep it upright and out of sunlight, which skunks the flavour faster than age does.

Unplug the router for 30 seconds, plug it back in and give it two minutes to reconnect; that clears most dropouts. If it keeps happening, check the cables are pushed fully in and note how often it drops before you ring your provider.

Unplug it and take the basket out first: most air fryers will not heat with the basket or drawer not clicked fully home, and a few reset when you open and shut the drawer. If the whole thing is dead, try another socket and check the plug's fuse. One that trips the fuse, smokes or sparks is a return, not a repair, so stop using it and ring the shop or the maker while it is still in warranty. Smoke from one that is working is usually oil or crumbs on the element - let it cool and wipe the element and the tray. A new one that smells of hot plastic settles after two or three uses: run it empty at its top temperature for ten minutes with the window open.

Unplug it and tip the crumbs out over the bin, then brush the inside with a dry pastry brush or an old toothbrush: never put water in a toaster. Wipe the outside with a damp cloth once it is cold, and empty the crumb tray every week or so, since that is what smells when it burns.

Unplug it first, then slide a pillowcase over each blade and pull it off with the dust inside, or wipe the blades with a barely damp cloth and dry them, because a wet blade traps dust. Vacuum the grille with the brush tool and wipe the guard with a damp cloth; a ceiling fan gets the same treatment with a step ladder and a cloth over the motor housing so nothing drops into it. Leave it all dry before it goes back on.

Unplug it for 30 seconds first, because a speaker that has lost the wifi usually comes back on its own. If it does not, open the speaker's own app and check the wifi it is meant to be on and set it up again from there - a changed router password is the commonest cause, and it wants a normal 2.4GHz network, not a phone hotspot.

Unripe fruit and veg are safe to eat - hard, sour and starchy rather than sweet, not poisonous - and a day or two on the counter, or in a paper bag with a banana, ripens most of them; cooking does the rest, as fried green tomatoes and green banana show. A green potato is the one exception: that green is solanine, it does not cook out, so bin it.

Unscrew the old head anticlockwise by hand - a cloth round it if it is stiff - and expect a cupful of water out of the hose. Keep the rubber washer that comes out, wrap the thread two or three turns of PTFE tape clockwise as you look at the end, and screw the new head on by hand until it is snug plus a quarter turn with a cloth; no wrench, because a plastic thread cross-threads and splits. The thread on nearly every UK shower is 1/2 inch BSP, so any head in the shop fits - but pick a low-pressure one if the shower runs off a tank in the loft rather than a combi, or the spray will collapse to a trickle.

Until a parcel reaches you it's the retailer's responsibility, not yours: tell them it hasn't arrived and ask for a replacement or refund. If they stall, ask your card provider for a chargeback, and report a "delivered" parcel you never got the same day.

Up to about 11 it is a savings account in the child's name that you run; from 11 most banks open a current account with a contactless card and no overdraft. At 16 they can take it over; at 18 it is theirs alone, so teach the card habits first. A junior ISA is the other half: £9,000 a year, tax-free, locked until 18.

Up to about four cups of coffee a day is fine for most adults, and it is linked to slightly lower risk of type 2 diabetes and liver trouble. Keep it before early afternoon, and go easy if you are pregnant (200 mg, about two cups) or get heartburn.

Urine is yellow because it carries urobilin, a breakdown product of old red blood cells, and the more water you drink the paler it gets. See a doctor if it is dark brown or red, or comes with pain or fever, because those are not just concentration.

Ursula von der Leyen is the president of the European Commission: in office since December 2019, and given a second five-year term from December 2024 after the European elections in June. The commission proposes EU law; the parliament and the member states' governments pass it.

Use mince that is at least 20% fat, shape it loosely without packing it down, and salt only the outside just before it goes in the pan: that is all the binding beef needs. If it keeps breaking up or the meat is lean, mix in an egg and a handful of breadcrumbs and chill the patties 20 minutes.
Use number for things you can count and amount for things you can't: a number of people, a large amount of work. 'Amount of people' is the usual slip.

Use Do Not Disturb rather than switching the phone off: pull down the control centre (or Settings > Focus on an iPhone) and set it to run overnight. Allow calls from favourites only if you want the family to get through, and leave the phone on charge across the room.

Use 'me' after a preposition or when you're the one being acted on: between you and me, she phoned me. Use 'I' only as the subject of the verb: my sister and I went. 'Between you and I' is the mistake people over-correct into.

Use small animal or cat claw clippers and take only the clear hook off the end, well before the pink quick inside the claw - on a dark claw, shine a torch through it or take a sliver at a time. Wrap the animal in a towel with just one paw out, do a couple of claws a day and give a treat after each; a towel and two people make it much easier, and a hamster or a gerbil is worth a vet nurse's hand the first time instead of your own. Rabbits and guinea pigs on soft bedding need their claws doing every six to eight weeks, and a vet nurse will show you once for free.

Use the phone: the Notes app on an iPhone has Scan Document, and on Android the Files app or Google Drive has Scan, both of which straighten the page and make a PDF you can email. Lay the paper flat in good light, hold the phone still above it, and check the edges are in before saving.

Use the phone's own editor: open the photo in Photos or Gallery, tap Edit, then Filters or Adjust > Saturation and slide the colour all the way down. That keeps a copy you can undo, where a black-and-white camera mode throws the colour away.

Use the plain words and the name the child already uses: "[name] died, their body stopped working, and they are not coming back." "Lost" and "gone to sleep" leave a child waiting, or frightened of bedtime. Answer only what they ask, in one or two sentences, and expect the same question again next week: that is how a small child makes it real. Say what stays the same (who looks after them, school, the dog), and let them come to the funeral if they want to, with someone whose only job is them. A pet gets the same straight words, its own name in place of the person's: a small child grieves a pet as hard, and "put to sleep" tells them sleep is dangerous.

Use the same questions, in the same order, with a written scorecard for every candidate, and score each one straight after the interview and before you discuss them with anyone. Take names and schools off the first read of a CV, and have more than one person on the panel. Where someone does not fit the pattern you expected, ask yourself what evidence you would need to see to be sure - that question is usually enough.

Use the Forgot password link on the sign-in screen, or iforgot.apple.com, and reset it with the email address and phone number on the account; a trusted device or a friend's phone can also approve it. Nobody legitimate ever asks for your Apple ID password or a fee to unlock it, so ignore anyone who offers.

Use the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Turn the brightness down to match the room, sit an arm's length from the screen with the top of it at eye level, and get an eye test if headaches keep coming back, because unnoticed short sight is what makes screens tiring.

Use the brightness keys first - the ones with a sun on them, usually F1 and F2 - and if that does nothing, Windows: Settings > System > Display, and turn off Change brightness automatically; iPhone: Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size and turn off Auto Brightness. On a laptop that dims when it comes off the charger, look in Settings > System > Power & battery for Battery saver.

Use the "forgot password" link on the sign-in page and let it send a reset link to the address the account is registered to: it often lands in spam, and the link expires within the hour. Before you reset, look for a saved password in the browser or the phone's keychain, and if the account still will not open, go through the site's own account-recovery page so you know you are on the real site.

Use the dose on the bottle for their age, with the syringe that comes with it rather than a kitchen spoon: at least four hours apart and no more than four doses in 24 hours. Check nothing else you are giving has paracetamol in it - cold remedies often do. Under three months, ask a doctor before giving anything, and a pharmacist will work the dose out by weight for free.

Use the empty time rather than hide it: ask your manager for one thing the team keeps putting off - a tidy-up, a how-to page, the report nobody has time for - and do it properly. Keep a note of what you take on, because "I had nothing to do" is a reason to be cut and "I fixed this" is a reason to be kept. If it lasts months, the job is the problem, and looking is cheaper than waiting.

Use the free current account switch service: pick the new bank, and it moves your direct debits, standing orders and salary, closes the old account and forwards stray payments for three years - seven working days, and the switch guarantee covers any charges if something goes wrong. Compare the new account's overdraft and monthly fee first, because a free account that charges for an overdraft costs more than one with a fee and none.

Use Find My on an iPhone (iCloud.com/find from any browser) or Find My Device for Android: it shows the location, rings it and can lock or wipe it remotely. Ring your network to block the SIM, and change your password for anything the phone was signed into.

Use about three teaspoons of baking powder for each teaspoon of baking soda, and put the acid the recipe counted on - buttermilk, yoghurt, lemon juice - in some other way, or the rise goes flat. That is the easy direction, because baking powder already carries its own acid. The other way round is not a straight swap: bicarbonate is about four times stronger and needs an acid to work, so a quarter of a teaspoon with a teaspoon of lemon juice or vinegar stands in for each teaspoon of powder.

Use an anti-dandruff shampoo with zinc pyrithione or ketoconazole two or three times a week and leave it on the scalp for five minutes. If it's red, sore or no better after a month, ask a pharmacist about a scalp condition rather than buying more products.

Use an antiperspirant rather than a deodorant, put it on last thing at night on dry skin where it works, and choose one with aluminium in it. Loose cotton and a spare shirt help, spicy food and alcohol make it worse, and if you sweat buckets from one place or at night, that is worth a GP visit.

Use a mid-sheen, eggshell or bathroom paint rather than matt emulsion: it shrugs off steam and can be wiped, where matt goes patchy over a bath. Two coats is a day's work for a kitchen or bathroom. Paint does not stop mould on its own, so sort the extractor fan or open a window while you steam.

Use a needle and doubled thread, coming up through the button and down into the fabric, with a pin under the button to leave room for the cloth. Wind the thread round the stitches under the button a few times, then knot it at the back.

Use a plain lip balm with petrolatum or beeswax, reapply often, and stop licking your lips: saliva dries them and makes it worse. Cracked lips are usually from licking them, because saliva dries as it evaporates and takes the lip's own oil with it. Cracks at the corners of your mouth often clear with an antifungal cream from the pharmacy.

Use a plunger with a good seal, and pour a bucket of water in from waist height rather than flushing again. If the water is rising, turn off the stopcock or lift the ball valve so it can't overflow, and never pour chemical cleaner into a blocked toilet.

Use a semicolon to join two full sentences that are closely related: I missed the bus; the next one was an hour away. If a full stop would work, either is fine — a semicolon just says the two halves belong together.

Use a terbinafine cream from the pharmacy twice a day for two weeks, and carry on for a week after the itching stops or it comes back. Dry between the toes properly, wear cotton socks and change them daily, and alternate shoes so each pair dries out; wash socks at 60C. If the skin is cracked, weeping or has not cleared in a month, ask a pharmacist.

Use a transfer app such as Wise or Revolut for a normal amount: you get the real exchange rate and pay a small fee, and it lands in their bank account in a day or two. Compare the fee and the rate together, because a "no fee" transfer usually carries a worse rate, and use your own bank for large sums where you want the paper trail.

Use a big bowl, because it boils up: one mug of rice to two mugs of boiling water, a pinch of salt, a plate over the top, and 10 minutes on full power. Leave it to stand 5 minutes still covered - that is what finishes it - then fork it through from the bottom. Rinse the rice first so the grains stay separate.

Use a dryer sheet or a little fabric conditioner, or rub a damp hand or a metal hanger over the garment before you put it on. Dry clothes slightly less, because over-drying and synthetic fabrics are what build the charge. It is the fabric rubbing on itself in dry air, so nothing is broken: the dryer sheet is the fix, not the machine.

Use a link rather than an attachment: WeTransfer or Google Drive will take 2GB free and email the other person a link that expires. For photos and video between your own devices, a shared album in Google Photos or iCloud does it without any compression.

Use 80g of oil for every 100g of butter the recipe asks for - about 4 to 5 tablespoons in a 20cm cake - and expect a slightly denser, moister crumb. Sunflower, vegetable or rapeseed gives a light plain cake; keep olive oil for a cake with a flavour of its own, like carrot or chocolate, where a good extra virgin is an asset rather than a taste you notice. Skip it where the method creams butter and sugar for air, and in pastry.

Use half the detergent you think you need and skip fabric softener, which coats the fibres and is the usual reason towels go stiff: a cup of white vinegar in the rinse does the softening job. Dry them with airflow rather than crammed on a radiator, and take them out while they are still a little damp so they fluff up.

Usually no. A new appliance is already covered for a year or two by the maker, and your home contents insurance or the card you paid with often extends that for free. On a phone or a laptop the paid plan is really accidental-damage cover, and a cracked screen is £60 to £120 at a repair shop, so the plan only pays if you drop it more than once. Put the price aside instead: for most things it is cheaper to pay a repair than years of cover you never claim on.

Usually no: you repay 9% of what you earn above about £25,000 a year, whatever the balance, and anything left is written off after 40 years - so on an ordinary salary the extra money disappears into a debt you were never going to clear. It only makes sense as a high earner in your forties with a big balance you could clear outright, and even then check the write-off date first. Put the money into the pension match, a house deposit or an emergency fund instead.

Usually not: jarred pesto is made with Parmesan or Pecorino, and both are set with animal rennet. Look for one labelled vegetarian, or make it with a vegetarian hard cheese - the basil, pine nuts, garlic and oil are all fine.

Usually one of four things, and the cheap checks come first. Feel the radiator in the cold room: cold at the top is air, so bleed it; hot at the top and cold at the bottom is sludge; and a thermostatic valve turned right down or stuck shut does the same. Then look at where the thermostat sits - in a cold hall, or near a radiator or a window, it reads the wrong room and stops the heating before the bedrooms get warm. Then the boiler's flow temperature: 55 to 60C suits a condensing boiler, and set much lower than that the radiators never get hot enough on a cold day. If all that is right the heat is leaving - draughts under the doors, an open chimney, the loft hatch, and loft insulation under 270mm - and that is what to spend on next.

Usually three to five working days on a card, and up to 14 days is still normal for online returns once the shop has the item back. Cash comes back at the till straight away, PayPal is often a day or two, and a card refund can take a full statement period to show because the bank holds it after the shop has paid it. If nothing has appeared after 14 days, send the shop a short written request with your order number and the date you returned it, then take it to your card provider, who can raise a chargeback.

Usually yes, and more so as a first cat. An adult rescue comes with a known character, is past the kitten climbing and biting, and settles in a week or two; a kitten is months of work but you shape it from the start. Ask the rescue what it is like with other cats, children and the litter tray, and take the one that comes to you.

Usually yes, and it is the swap most people are glad of: a walk-in shower is easier for anyone with bad knees or hips, safer than stepping over a bath side, and it makes a small bathroom feel bigger. Budget about £1,500 to £3,500 fitted for a straight swap in the same spot, and £3,000 to £6,000+ for a walk-in with a low tray, a wet-room floor and new tiling - the waterproofing and moving the waste are what the money mostly goes on. Ask for the tiling and the waste in the quote, and check the floor will take a level-access tray before you buy one.

Usually yes, if your bill really has a night rate. Economy 7 gives about seven hours overnight at a lower unit rate - commonly around 00:30 to 07:30, but the hours differ by supplier and region and are printed on your bill or meter. A wash is roughly 1 to 2 kWh, so at a night rate of 15p against 25p in the day you save 10 to 20p a load: worth a delay timer on the washing machine and the dishwasher, and it is the same window for an immersion heater or an electric car, where the saving is much bigger. The catch is a higher day rate, so if almost all your use is in the evening a single-rate tariff is usually cheaper.

Usually yes, if it is a full missing year inside the six years you can still fill: one voluntary year costs around 900 pounds and adds roughly 300 pounds a year of state pension for the rest of your life, so it pays for itself in about three years of retirement. Check your record in your online tax account first - some gaps are already covered by credits and cannot be bought - and do not leave it, because the deadline for older years has moved without warning before.

Usually yes: most supermarket feta is made with microbial rennet and says so on the back, while the traditional barrel-aged Greek and Bulgarian sorts use animal rennet, so read the label before you count on it.

Usually yes: nothing in law stops you working two jobs, and what decides it is your contract, which often asks you to get permission or bans working for a competitor. Check the hours clause and the working time opt-out too, because the 48-hour average covers both jobs together. Tell HMRC rather than your boss - your tax-free allowance sits on one job and the second is taxed at basic rate from the first pound, so expect about 20% off it, and if either job brings you below the threshold you may be able to claim some back. Keep the two sets of hours apart on paper: the commonest problem is not the tax but the second employer finding out you are exhausted.
Usually yes: cocoa, milk and cocoa butter are all vegetarian. Check the bar for gelatin in chewy or marshmallow fillings, and remember whey is fine for a vegetarian but not for a vegan.

Usually yes - potatoes and oil - but chip-shop chips can be fried in beef dripping, which is traditional in the north, and a shop that fries them in the same oil as the fish is a no for some people. Ask, or use oven chips and read the packet.

Usually cheaper to buy a whole e-bike than to convert one well: a mid-drive kit with a battery is £600 to £900, most of the price of a ready-made bike, and the £250 front-hub kits are heavy, lurch at the front wheel and load the fork. Convert only a bike you already like, with disc brakes and a steel or solid fork. It must stay a pedal-assist bicycle - 250W, assist stopping at 15.5mph - or it becomes a moped.

Usually a week to a fortnight: the funeral director books the earliest slot the family, the crematorium and whoever leads the service can all do, and a burial is sometimes sooner than a cremation. A coroner's post-mortem, an inquest or waiting for family to travel can push it out to three or four weeks, and the person stays in the funeral home's care until then. Ask for the earliest date they can offer before you agree a day.

Usually it is the wake-up time rather than the bedtime: a lie-in at the weekend, a nap, or coffee after about two in the afternoon keeps the body clock late, and a warm room or a phone in bed finishes the job. Fix the getting-up time first, move the coffee before lunch, keep the bedroom around 18C and dark, and give it a week before you judge it. If it is a worry that wakes you, spend ten minutes before bed writing the list down so your head is not doing it at three. See a GP if it has gone on a month, or if the days are falling apart.

VAT in the UK is 20%: add it by multiplying the price by 1.2, so £80 becomes £96, and take it off a VAT-inclusive price by dividing by 1.2, so £96 is £80 plus £16 of VAT. The VAT on a net price is simply a fifth of it.

VAT is the tax added to most things you buy: 20% of the price before tax, so a £10 item is £12 with VAT. Home energy and some home work is 5%, and most food, children's clothes and books are zero-rated. A price marked "inc VAT" already includes it, so the tax on a £60 bill is £10.

VLOOKUP has four parts: =VLOOKUP(what you are looking for, the table, which column to bring back, FALSE). The thing you look up must be in the first column of that table, and FALSE means an exact match - leave it out and you get nonsense. =VLOOKUP(A2, Sheet2!A:C, 3, FALSE) says: take A2, find it in column A of Sheet2, give me what is in column C. If it gives #N/A the values are not really equal (a number stored as text is the usual cause); if you have a newer Excel or Sheets, XLOOKUP does the same job without the first-column rule.

VPN stands for virtual private network: it makes an encrypted tunnel between your device and a server elsewhere, so the owner of the wifi cannot see which sites you open. It is worth it on hotel and cafe wifi, but it does not make you anonymous - the VPN company can still see and log the traffic.

Vacuum first, then use a weak mix of washing-up liquid and warm water: spray a small patch, work it in with a soft brush, and blot it out with a towel rather than soaking it, because water under the foam is what makes a car smell damp for weeks. Do the whole seat in patches so it dries evenly, and leave the windows open overnight. A leather car seat is the other job - saddle soap and a conditioner, never washing-up liquid - and it has its own answer.

Vacuum it twice, slowly, then work at any mark from the outside in with a little carpet shampoo on a cloth and blot it dry - a carpet that stays damp is what starts a smell. For a whole room or a set of stairs, a hired shampoo machine is worth it once a year, and open the windows while it dries.

Vacuum it, then dab stains with cool water and a little washing-up liquid, and dust the whole surface with bicarbonate of soda for an hour before vacuuming again. Air it by stripping the bed for the morning, and use a washable protector so this is rare.

Vacuum it first, then test any shampoo or foam cleaner on a hidden patch: a carpet wants a carpet shampoo worked in with a brush and rinsed, or a hired machine once or twice a year, and a sofa wants a foam cleaner and a soft brush with as little water as you can manage. Open the windows and dry it with the heating low, because anything left damp smells.

Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman in space, on 16 June 1963, in Vostok 6. She orbited the Earth 48 times over almost three days, and it was another nineteen years before a second woman, Svetlana Savitskaya, flew.

Vapes travel in your hand luggage, never in the hold: the device and any spare batteries in the cabin, and the liquid in the 100 ml bag. Do not use it on the plane or in the terminal, including the toilets, because most airlines treat it as smoking. A few countries ban them completely, so check the arrival country's rules as well as your airline's own.

Varicose veins are valves in the leg not closing, so blood pools and the vein bulges: legs ache and feel heavy by evening, ankles swell in the heat and the skin can itch. They are rarely dangerous. Compression stockings from a pharmacy, keeping the legs up when you sit, walking and losing weight all ease the ache, and if the look of them bothers you the GP can refer you - the usual fix is a day-case procedure, laser or glue or a small stripping, not a big operation. See the GP if the skin over a vein goes brown, hard or weepy (that is heading for an ulcer) or a vein bleeds, and go the same day for a hot, red, swollen leg - that can be a clot.
Venus is the hottest planet, around 465C, and it is hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is closer to the Sun: Venus is wrapped in a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere that traps the heat.

Verrucas and warts usually go on their own within a year or two; a pharmacy salicylic acid paint or patch speeds that up if you file the hard skin first. Don't pick or cut them, cover them at the pool, and see a GP or podiatrist if one is painful, bleeding or spreading quickly.

Visit at drop-off time rather than for a show-round: how the staff talk to a crying child tells you more than any brochure. Ask about the ratios, how often staff leave, how they handle food and naps, and whether you get two settle-in sessions before you leave them. Go with the one where your child walks in without looking back.
Vladimir Putin is the president of Russia: in office since 2000, with four years as prime minister under Dmitry Medvedev in the middle. His current term runs to 2030.

Volleyball starts with the pass: get your feet there early, lock your arms into a platform and let the ball come to you instead of swinging at it - it should go up and to the setter, not forward. A spike is the last touch of three: high approach, arm back, and hit the top half of the ball so it drives down; a dig is the same low platform, absorbing the ball rather than swinging at it. Serve overhand for consistency, and call the ball loudly.

Volleyball is six a side, and each team can touch the ball three times before sending it over - a block does not count as one of them. Every rally now scores a point, sets go to 25 and the deciding fifth set to 15, and you have to be two points clear.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy is the president of Ukraine: elected in 2019. A presidential election is due, but it cannot be held while martial law is in force.

Volume is weight at the roots, so condition only the ends and rinse the roots well, then dry the hair upside down and rough the roots with your fingers: a little mousse or dry shampoo at the roots, lifted away from the scalp as it dries, holds it there. A cut with a few layers gives it something to sit on, and heavy conditioner or a hot iron flat against the scalp takes it straight back down.

Wait until you are on mobile data for banking, or use the bank's own app on 4G: a public network can be imitated, and the padlock on a site does not prove it is the real one. If you must use it, turn off file sharing, stick to sites you typed yourself, and log out when you finish.

Wait a week after the closing date, or two weeks after you applied if there was no date, then send one short email to the person named in the advert: which role it is, when you applied, one line on why you fit, and a polite ask for a timescale. One follow-up is keen and a second is a nuisance, so if that goes unanswered, put the application down and carry on applying - most rejections are a process that stalled, not a verdict on you.

Wait for two dry days above about 10C and get the surface clean and bone dry before you start, because paint on damp timber peels within a season. Then two thin coats rather than one fat one: fence panels want a shed-and-fence stain, a shed or a wooden gate a preservative and a topcoat, and a metal gate a rust primer and a gloss made for metal. Brush or spray along the grain on wood.

Waiting a few more days is fine, but go sooner if you're getting worse instead of better, are short of breath, or can't keep fluids down. A pharmacist can advise on coughs and colds without an appointment, and they're good at saying when a GP is needed.

Waking up tired usually means broken sleep rather than too little: a warm room, a drink in the evening, a snoring partner and a phone in bed all fragment it. Try a cooler bedroom, no alcohol within three hours of bed, and the same wake time every day for two weeks, because that last one is what rebuilds a steady night.

Waking at night is normal for the first months: keep it quiet and dim, feed without chat, and only change a nappy if it needs it. From around four to six months, use the same short wind-down every night and put them down drowsy but awake, with a pat and a shush before picking up; put them on their back in an empty cot for every sleep.

Waking in the middle of the night is normal - the trick is what you do next: stay in bed, keep the room dark, and do not look at the clock or your phone, because that is what teaches your brain to be awake at 3am. If you are awake more than 20 minutes, get up and sit somewhere dim until you feel sleepy. Alcohol, a late meal and a warm bedroom are the usual culprits.

Walk the route to school together before term starts and rehearse the small things: where they line up, who to ask if they are lost, and how lunch works. Then set up one meet-up with a classmate in the first fortnight; a familiar face at the gate matters more than any pep talk.

Walking alone will not do it - what you eat decides most of it - but 8,000 to 10,000 steps a day is a fair target, and the gain is that it burns a little and keeps you from sitting down all day. The quicker half is the plate: a smaller portion of the starch, more protein and vegetables, and no drinks with sugar in. Half a kilo a week is a good rate, and the walking is easier to keep up than a gym plan.

Warm on the outside after a hot wash is normal, so a washer or dryer that is only a little warm and works fine needs nothing. What is not normal is a plug, socket or cable that is hot, a burning smell, a door glass too hot to touch, or the machine tripping the fuse: switch it off at the wall, unplug it and get it looked at rather than using it again. Otherwise give it air - a hand's gap behind and above, the fluff filter clear, and no cupboard door shut on a dryer while it runs.

Warm the cup or the bowl first: fill it with boiling water, leave it a minute, tip it out and then fill up, because a cold mug takes most of the heat out in the first minute. A lid or a tea cosy keeps a drink hot far longer than a bigger pot does, and a flask is the only thing that holds it for hours, so make a smaller pot and top it up. For soup, a deeper bowl keeps the heat in better than a wide shallow one, and warming the bowls with hot water before you serve buys another few minutes.

Warm water with a drop of washing-up liquid and a soft cloth takes fingerprints and greasy marks off a glass top, then buff it dry with a microfibre cloth so it does not streak. A white ring or a chalky bloom is limescale, and a cloth wrung out in white vinegar lifts it without any scrubbing. Skip anything abrasive - cream cleaner, a scouring pad, a melamine sponge - and skip ammonia or glass spray on a coated or tinted top, because both dull the surface for good.

Warm water and washing-up liquid takes water-based paint off skin while it is still tacky, and a soft nail brush lifts it out of the ridges. Oil gloss wants a little white spirit or baby oil on a cloth, then soap, then a moisturiser, because both dry the skin out. Keep white spirit off your face, a cut or a child, and let the last flecks wear off rather than scrubbing at them.

Warm 200ml of milk and melt 20g of dark chocolate into it, chopped small, stirring until it is smooth - a pinch of salt makes it taste more of chocolate, not less. Cocoa powder works too: a teaspoon each of cocoa and sugar made into a paste with a little cold milk first, so it does not go lumpy. Keep it under a simmer, because milk that boils tastes cooked.

Warm 200ml of a plain oil with four sliced chillies and a crushed garlic clove over the lowest heat for five minutes - it should barely bubble, because burnt chilli turns bitter - then let it cool completely before you bottle it. Keep it in the fridge and use it within a fortnight, since fresh garlic and fresh chilli in oil will grow things at room temperature; dried flakes in oil keep far longer, up to three months cold.

Warm 300ml double cream with a vanilla pod or a teaspoon of paste and 100ml of milk until it steams, and beat 4 egg yolks with 60g of sugar. Pour the hot cream into the yolks slowly, whisking, then put it back on a low heat and stir without stopping for 4 to 6 minutes, to about 82C, until it coats the back of the spoon. Strain it into a jug and it thickens as it cools.

Warm a bottle of red with two tablespoons of sugar, a sliced orange, a cinnamon stick, two star anise and four cloves: keep it at a bare shiver for 15 minutes and never let it boil, which takes the alcohol and the fruit out of it. A splash of brandy at the end makes it stronger, and mulled cider is the same drink made with cider and no sugar.

Warm a litre of milk to just below boiling - 85C, or small bubbles round the edge of the pan - then let it cool to about 43C, which is a finger in it feeling warm rather than hot. Stir in 3 tablespoons of live natural yoghurt, keep it at that warmth for 8 to 12 hours in a flask, a yoghurt maker or an airing cupboard, and chill it once it has set; keep 3 spoons back as the starter for the next lot. Long or warm and it turns sour and grainy, cool or short and it stays runny.

Warm is fine, hot is the part to avoid: keep the water comfortable rather than steaming, and get out if you feel light-headed. Hot tubs, saunas and steam rooms are best skipped for the first 12 weeks, because raising your core temperature early on has been linked to problems with the baby's spine. A warm bath, a shower and a swim are all fine right through.

Warmth, damp and the plastic bag it came in are what mould needs, so a loaf in a warm kitchen goes green within days. Keep it in a paper bag or a bread bin, freeze half of it sliced on day one, and never keep it in the fridge unless you only ever toast it.

Wash the bedding at 60C every week and put mite-proof covers on the mattress and the pillows: the mites live in the fabric and feed on skin flakes, so the two things that work are heat and a barrier. Then keep the room cool and aired, damp-dust from the top down rather than dry-dusting, and vacuum the mattress and the carpet with a filter instead of a quick pass; under about 21C and 50% humidity they stop multiplying. Soft toys go in the freezer overnight. Mite sprays and air fresheners do very little, and a 40C wash does not kill them.

Wash the bin with hot soapy water and a splash of bleach, dry it, and put a couple of bicarbonate-of-soda balls or a sheet of newspaper in the bottom. Line it every time and take food waste out daily in summer.

Wash the bite, then cool it with an ice pack wrapped in a cloth for ten minutes and try not to scratch, because scratching is what makes them swell and scar. A pharmacy antihistamine or a hydrocortisone cream eases the itch. Get help if the skin around it spreads red and hot, or you feel feverish or unwell.

Wash the jars in hot soapy water, rinse them, and stand them upside down in an oven at 120C for 15 minutes; fill them while they are still hot. Lids go in a bowl of boiling water for a minute, and a dishwasher on its hottest cycle does the same job.

Wash them two at a time on a hot cycle with a scoop of oxygen bleach and a little detergent, then dry them thoroughly in a tumble dryer with a clean tennis ball to fluff them up. If they stay yellow or smell after that, replace them: pillows last about two years.

Wash them at the hottest the label allows - 60C for cotton - with a scoop of oxygen bleach rather than chlorine, which yellows elastic and poly-cotton. Soak overnight in a bucket of hot water with a scoop of oxygen bleach and a scoop of biological detergent if the yellow is old, then wash as normal. Dry them in daylight: sunlight lifts yellowing better than anything in a bottle, and a white cotton sheet left out for an afternoon comes back visibly brighter.

Wash them at 60C with half the usual detergent and no softener, then get them fully dry within a few hours - a towel that stays damp in the machine or a basket grows the smell in a day. The smell lives in bacteria left in the pile. Hang each one spread out rather than folded over a rail, and if one wash does not shift it, a cup of white vinegar in the rinse will.

Wash them by hand in hot soapy water, working the blades open and closed under the water so the gunk at the pivot comes out, then dry them at once: a dishwasher rusts the pivot and takes the edge off. A pair that is stiff or hard to open is nearly always the pivot rather than the blades, so put a drop of cooking oil or a squirt of WD-40 on it and work the blades open and closed, then wipe the surplus off. If the two blades have started to spread, nip the screw at the pivot up a quarter turn.

Wash them by hand in hot water with a drop of washing-up liquid, rinse, and dry them with a linen cloth held round the bowl rather than the stem: a dishwasher and a hot rinse are what leave wine glasses cloudy and spotted. Marks that will not lift want a soak in warm water with a splash of white vinegar, then the same cloth.

Wash them by hand in lukewarm water with a drop of washing-up liquid, rinse and dry them with a microfibre cloth - but never in the dishwasher or the washing machine: the heat warps the frame and the salt and detergent strip the coatings, so a pair that goes through comes out scratched and loose. Lukewarm, not hot, for the same reason.

Wash twice a day with a gentle foaming cleanser rather than soap, which strips the skin and leaves it making more oil, then use a light oil-free gel moisturiser - oily skin still needs one. Do not scrub or wash more than twice; blot the shine at lunchtime instead, and a niacinamide or salicylic acid product is the one extra step worth adding.

Wash white cotton at the hottest temperature the label allows with a scoop of oxygen bleach, and dry it in daylight, which lifts yellowing. Keep whites out of a dark wash and use a little less detergent so it rinses out.

Wash with warm water and a drop of washing-up liquid, then squeegee or wipe with a cloth and buff dry straight away with a dry cloth or newspaper. Work top to bottom and out of direct sun, which dries the glass before you can polish it.

Wash your hands first so he does not smell of food, and scoop him up in both hands from underneath: a hand coming over the top is a hawk, and that is what a bite is usually about. Let him wake up properly before you touch him - a hamster woken from a deep sleep bites - keep your fingers out of the bars, and give a new one a week to settle before handling at all. Two or three short goes a day with a treat on the palm, and put him down the moment he nips, teaches him faster than one long hold.

Wash and dry it first, then wax one panel at a time in the shade: a thin coat on a foam pad, let it haze, and buff it off before it goes chalky, turning the cloth as it loads up. A paste wax lasts about six months and a liquid one about three, and two coats a year is plenty for a car kept outside. Do not wax in sun or on a hot panel, and keep it off black plastic trim, where it dries white.
Wash dark things inside out, in cold water, on a short cycle, and skip the dryer. Cold and quick is what keeps black from going grey, and washing every few wears is kinder than every wear.

Wash a baby's things at 30 to 40C with a non-bio powder and skip the fabric conditioner, which coats the fabric and can irritate skin; their own load, not with towels, is what keeps the pilling off. New clothes only need one wash before the first wear. For stains, cold water and a little washing-up liquid worked in before the wash lifts most of it, and sunlight on a washed white vest takes out the yellowing.

Wash a cat scratch under running water for five minutes with soap, pat it dry and cover it with a plaster, and do not use antiseptic or alcohol on it. Cat scratches are the ones that matter: watch for swelling, a red line spreading up the arm, swollen glands or a fever over the next two weeks, and see a GP if any of those appear. Get a bite, a deep puncture or a scratch near the eye looked at the same day, and check your tetanus is up to date.

Wash a down sleeping bag in a front-loading machine on a gentle cycle with a down-specific wash, or by hand in the bath, then dry it on low heat with two or three clean tennis balls to break the clumps up: it takes hours and it must be bone dry before it is stored. Never store it in its stuff sack; hang it or keep it loose, which is what keeps the loft.

Wash it on its own on a gentle cycle with a down or technical wash, no fabric conditioner, then tumble dry on low with two or three clean tennis balls until it's completely dry. Shake it out as it dries, or the down clumps and loses its loft.

Wash it under running water for five minutes with soap, pat it dry and cover it with a plaster, and do not use antiseptic or alcohol on it. Cat scratches are the ones that matter: watch for swelling, a red line spreading up the arm, swollen glands or a fever over the next two weeks, and see a GP if any of those appear. Get a tetanus booster if yours is out of date, and see a doctor the same day for a bite that has broken the skin on the hand, a deep puncture, or a scratch near the eye.

Wash it by hand in hot soapy water and stand it up to dry, and rub in food-safe mineral oil or board butter once a month, left on for an hour and buffed off - never cooking oil, which goes rancid. Wood splits because it has been soaked or dishwashered and then dried too fast, and a rough, dry surface is the stage before that. A hairline crack is fine to keep if you sand the edges smooth; a split that will not close harbours bacteria and wants a new one. Keep it out of the dishwasher and it lasts years.

Wash it first with a technical wash rather than ordinary detergent, rinse it twice and then warm it in a low tumble dryer or press it through a cloth with a warm iron: the heat reactivates the water-repellent finish and the detergent is what kills it, so it often beads again with nothing else done.
