If water still soaks in, wash in or spray on a reproofing treatment (about £10 to £20) and rub a seam-sealer stick along the shoulders and the seams under the arms, which are where it goes first.
Wash jeans every five to ten wears, inside out and in cold water, and air them between wears. Spot-clean small marks instead of washing, and skip the tumble dryer if you want them to last.

Wash kit cool - 30C is enough - with a scoop of bicarbonate of soda or a sports wash, no fabric softener at all, and air dry it. The smell is bacteria in the synthetic fibres, not in the sweat: sweat itself has no smell, and a warm wash with softener leaves a film the bacteria live in, which is why kit can smell the moment it gets damp again. Get it out of the gym bag the same day and hang it to dry before it goes in the basket.

Watch the ball onto your foot instead of swinging at it: get side-on, keep your knee over the ball and your toe down, and strike through the middle so it stays low. Start with a ball tossed up and volleyed into a wall, then ask a partner for a low pass to hit first time.

Watch four things: whether they will drink, whether they are still weeing, whether they perk up between bouts, and how they are breathing. A child who is poorly but plays between bouts is usually fine. Limp or drowsy, breathing fast or grunting, a rash that will not fade under a glass, no wee for eight hours, or nothing kept down all day means 111 today, and 999 if they are hard to wake or struggling to breathe.

Water plants pulled up from the bottom, plus grass, grain and the odd insect or snail. Bread is the wrong food: it is empty of much they need and it fouls the water, so grain, oats or shredded greens are the better offering.

Water plants and their seeds, grain, grass, insects, snails and the odd small fish. Bread is the thing to stop giving them: it fills a duck up without feeding it, and it fouls the water. Oats, peas, sweetcorn or bird seed do the job and float while they eat.

Water retention is usually salt and sitting still: cut the salt and processed food for a week, move your ankles through the day, and put your feet up above heart height for twenty minutes in the evening. Warm weather and some medicines (ibuprofen, the pill) do it too. See a GP if one leg is more swollen, if you are short of breath lying flat, or if the skin dents when you press it.

Water the soil the day before: wet soil holds the day's heat and gives it back at night, and dry soil gives back nothing. At dusk, not at midnight, put fleece, an old net curtain or a doubled bedsheet over the plants and take it off in the morning, and push pots together against a house wall and off the ground, because the wall and the slab give out heat all night. In a greenhouse, bubble wrap the glass and cover the plants, and a paraffin heater or a hot water bottle under a cloche does the rest. Most damage shows up two days later as blackened leaves: leave them on until spring because they are insulation, and start watching the forecast from about 5C, which is when the tender things start to go.

Water the clump the day before, then fork it out on all sides and lever it up. Two forks back to back in the middle, pushed away from each other, part most clumps without cutting anything; a spade or an old bread knife does the rest. Shake off the loose soil, cut back the old foliage, and replant each piece at the depth it was growing, then water it in and keep it watered for a fortnight. Divide summer-flowering perennials in spring and spring-flowering ones in autumn, and hostas whenever they are in leaf but not in flower.

Water tomatoes deeply two or three times a week and let the top of the soil dry in between: a little every day keeps the roots shallow. Even watering is what stops split fruit and blossom end rot, and in a pot or grow bag in hot weather twice a day can be right. Water at the base in the morning, not over the leaves.

Water with a can or a bucket - that is allowed under a ban - and leave the hose, the sprinkler, the pressure washer and filling a pool, which are the things a ban usually covers. Your water company says on its site whether one is on in your area and exactly what it covers, and in England and Wales breaking one can mean a fine of up to £1,000.

Water with a meal is fine: it does not dilute your stomach acid enough to matter, and it helps if you eat fast or get constipated. The only thing to watch is filling up on it so there is no room for the food - a glass or two rather than a pint before you sit down. Soup, tea and squash count towards the day the same way.

Water-based emulsion and the water-based satins come out while they are wet: blot what you can with kitchen paper, then hold the mark under cold running water and rub a little washing-up liquid in from the back of the fabric. Oil-based gloss, undercoat and varnish need a rag damped with white spirit dabbed at the mark before the wash, and let it dry between dabs. Wash on the label's temperature and look before you tumble it, because heat sets paint like a dye.

Water alone does no harm to an eye, so if it stings there is soap or shampoo in it: hold the lids open and rinse with cool clean water for about five minutes, blink, and check your sight is clear. Turn the shower down or aim it at your shoulder while you wash your hair, and get the eye looked at the same day if it is still sore, red, or your sight is blurred after the rinsing.

Water an orchid by soaking it: once a week, stand the pot in tepid water for ten minutes, let it drain right through, and put it back - never leave it standing in water, which rots the roots. They come in bark chips and a clear pot so you can see the roots: silvery-grey wants water, green is fine. Ignore the ice-cube trick; cold water on tropical roots does them no good.

Water an orchid by standing the pot in tepid water for ten minutes once a week, then letting it drain: it lives in bark, not compost, so a normal watering can runs straight through. Roots that are silver want water and roots that are green have had enough.

Water an aloe every two to three weeks in summer and once a month in winter, soaking the pot and then letting it dry out completely. Leaves going soft and pale at the base mean the compost has stayed wet.

Water and snacks that do not crumble, so nobody is eating crumbs at 70mph: a refillable bottle each, fruit, and something savoury in a tub. Then a phone cable and a power bank, the breakdown and insurance details, a blanket or a spare layer each, wet wipes and a bag for rubbish, sunglasses, and cash or a card for parking and toilets. Plan a stop every two hours, and put the first night's bag where you can reach it.

Water a monstera when the top 2 to 3cm of compost is dry, which is about once a week in summer and every two weeks in winter. Give it bright light out of direct sun, and don't worry when water drips from the leaf tips for an hour afterwards: that is the plant pushing out moisture, not a problem.

Water a peace lily when the compost is just dry, about once a week, and it will tell you when it wants more by drooping: it picks itself up within a few hours of a drink. It likes a bright spot out of direct sun and brown leaf tips mean the water or the air is hard.

Water a pothos about once a week, when the compost is dry and the leaves are just starting to look limp: it forgives a missed week but rots in a pot that never dries. It grows in almost any light, and a cutting in a glass of water roots in a few weeks.

Water a rubber plant every week to ten days, when the top 3cm of compost is dry, and wipe the leaves so the dust doesn't block the light. Dropping lower leaves one at a time is usually a cold draught or a sudden move.

Water a snake plant every two to three weeks in summer and once a month or less in winter, and only when the compost is dry all the way down. It stores water in its leaves and rots in wet soil, so the surest way to kill one is to water it on a schedule.

Water a spider plant about once a week, when the top of the compost is dry, and let the pot drain. Brown tips are usually tap water or dry air rather than a watering fault: trim them off and stand the pot somewhere less dry.

Water a succulent by soaking the pot and then letting it dry out completely: every two to three weeks in summer, monthly in winter. The leaves going soft and see-through at the base is rot from wet compost, and shrivelled leaves are the sign it wants a drink.

Water a ZZ plant every two to three weeks in summer and once a month in winter. Its thick underground stems hold water, so it survives neglect far better than kindness: yellow leaves that fall off are the sign of too much.

Water a cactus every two to three weeks in summer, and barely at all from November to March. Soak it, let it dry right out, and never leave the pot standing in water: more cacti die of watering than of neglect.

Water a calathea when the top of the compost is just dry, about twice a week in summer, and keep it out of direct sun. Curling leaves and brown edges are dry air: a tray of wet pebbles or a bathroom does more for it than more water does.

Water a fern when the compost is barely dry, which is twice a week in summer, and stand the pot on pebbles in a saucer of water for the humidity. Crispy brown fronds are dry air, not thirst: a bathroom or a kitchen suits most ferns better than a windowsill.

Water a fiddle leaf fig when the top 3cm of soil is dry, which is about every ten days, and let it drain right through. It sulks if it is moved or sits in a draught, and brown blotches on the leaves are usually too much water rather than too little.

Water a jade plant every two to three weeks in summer and once a month in winter, and let the compost dry between waterings. It wants a sunny windowsill and shrivelled leaves mean thirst while soft, dropping leaves mean too much water.

Water a lawn deeply once a week rather than lightly every day: about a centimetre, or twenty minutes with a sprinkler, in the early morning. Grass roots follow the water down, so a weekly soak makes a lawn that shrugs off a dry spell, and in a real drought it is fine to let it go brown and come back.
Water evaporates, rises and cools, and its vapour condenses into tiny droplets that make clouds. Those droplets collide and grow until they are too heavy to stay up, and then they fall as rain.

Water in the bottom of a fridge is nearly always the drain hole at the back: it clogs with bits of food, so push a pipe cleaner or a piece of stiff wire down it and flush warm water through. Ice on the back wall means the fridge is running too cold, so turn the dial up a notch and let it defrost. If the water keeps coming back, check the door seal by closing the door on a sheet of paper - if it slides out easily, the seal is the fault.
Water is unusual: it expands as it freezes, so ice is about 9% less dense than liquid water and floats. That is also why a full bottle left in the freezer can split.

Water is H2O: two hydrogen atoms to one oxygen. It is wet because its molecules pull on each other and on most surfaces, so a drop spreads into a thin film instead of beading up - which is why water creeps along glass and soaked paper, and why it beads on a waxy leaf.

Wear on the inside or outside edge is the tracking or camber, so get a four-wheel alignment, about £30 to £60, after the new tyres. Wear in the middle is too much pressure and wear on both edges is too little, so check them monthly cold. A bald patch on one spot is a locked wheel or a bad shock.

Wear one: it is not the law for adults in the UK, but a helmet is the difference between a bruise and a head injury in the one fall nobody plans for. It does not make you safe from traffic, so ride as if it were not there: take the lane at junctions and never go up the left side of a lorry. It should sit level, two fingers above the eyebrows, with the strap snug enough that you feel it when you open your mouth wide.

Wear the version of your usual clothes that you feel best in, clean and comfortable, and skip anything you'd be tugging at all evening. A jacket over a nice top covers a cold walk and a warm bar, and flat or low shoes leave you free to walk somewhere else.
Wear what you can sit on the floor in: jeans and a soft top with closed shoes, and nothing pale if there's cake and paint about. A cardigan for the hall, because church halls and soft play are cold.
Wear what you can dance in for hours and don't have to hold: dark jeans or a dress with shoes you can stand in. Check the club's own rules first, because plenty still say no trainers or sportswear.

Wear cotton or wool socks and change them daily, wash feet with soap and dry between the toes, and alternate shoes so each pair dries out. If it doesn't settle, a pharmacy antiperspirant for feet is stronger than deodorant.

Wear gloves and keep it off your skin: bird mess can carry germs, so wash your hands after and keep it away from food, a cut or your face. Soak it with hot soapy water, leave it a minute to soften, then scrub with a stiff brush and rinse, rather than scrubbing it dry into the surface. On washing, a hot wash with detergent is enough. On car paint, let a wet cloth sit on it for a minute and wash the panel after - never scrape at it.

Weather ache is real and it is not damage: cold and damp stiffen the muscles round a joint and the joint itself feels thicker, and the drop in pressure before rain is what people notice most. Nothing about it is doing harm, so the answer is warmth and movement rather than rest - warm up before you go out, keep the knees and hands covered, keep walking, and use a warm bath or a wheat bag in the evening. See a GP if one joint is hot, red or swollen, if the ache is there all the time rather than in the cold, or if it is waking you at night: that is worth a proper look, and arthritis that is worse in winter is still worth an appointment to get the treatment right.

Weigh yourself once a week, same time, same clothes, rather than daily: body water swings 2 to 3 pounds a day and daily weighing mostly tells you about salt and hormones. Judge the trend over a month, and use a tape measure round your waist alongside it.

Weigh 4 eggs in their shells and use the same weight of butter, caster sugar and self-raising flour: beat the butter and sugar until pale, add the eggs a spoon at a time, fold in the flour, then split it between two greased 20cm tins. Bake at 180C (160C fan) for 25 to 30 minutes, until it springs back and a skewer comes out clean, and sandwich it with jam and buttercream once it is cold.

Weigh it on kitchen scales, pack it so it cannot move, and write the address on the parcel itself as well as the label. You do not need a printer: most retailers email a QR code you show at a post office counter or a parcel shop, and the shop prints the label there. Keep the proof of postage until the money is back, because a return that goes missing is the sender's word against the shop's without it.

Wet the hair, rub a 10p-sized blob of shampoo between your palms and work it into the scalp with your fingertips, not the ends, for about 30 seconds. Rinse until the water runs clear, put conditioner on the mid-lengths and ends only, leave it a minute and rinse cool. Wash the scalp, condition the hair: that is the whole trick.

What the checkout promised is what you paid for: if it said room of choice, upstairs or inside, a driver who will not bring it in has not finished the delivery, and the seller has to send someone who will or refund the delivery charge. Say it in writing the same day with a photo of where it was left, and do not drag a heavy item yourself - a damage you caused lifting it is the fight you want to avoid.

What the job looks like decides, not the label on the contract: if they say when you start, where you work and what you do, and you cannot send someone else or turn the work down, you are an employee in law whatever the paperwork calls you. That usually means holiday pay, sick pay and minimum wage that were never paid. ACAS will give you a free status check, and HMRC's CEST tool gives a written answer you can keep; put the question in writing to the employer first, so the hours and the control are on record.

What was it, and roughly how much, and how long ago? If it was grapes, raisins, onion, garlic, chocolate, anything with xylitol in it or any of your medicine, ring the vet now rather than watching him - most of those are treatable and much easier early. If it was a bit of plain meat or bread off the table, no harm done.

What you paid for is yours once the work is done, so put the request in writing and give them 14 days: name what you are owed, the date and what you paid. A photographer or a designer cannot keep the files as security for a bill they never sent you, and a surveyor or an architect has to hand over the report or drawings. If nothing comes, a letter before claim and Money Claims Online cost from about £35 and settle most of these.

What changed your mind? If you already said yes to it, say so early and in one short line to whoever is expecting you - a change of heart is easier to take than a silence, and you do not need a reason they will approve of, only the one that is true.

Wheezing that comes on with running, cold air or at night is asthma until proven otherwise: see a GP, who will listen to your chest and may give you a blue reliever inhaler plus a brown preventer steroid inhaler. Use the reliever two puffs through a spacer when tight, and if it is needed more than three times a week the preventer needs turning up. Blue inhaler not lasting four hours, or lips going blue, is 999.

When it keeps to the school timetable and clears at the weekend, it is usually dread rather than a bug: ask what part of the day is worst - the bus, one lesson, lunch, one child, being picked for teams - and take that one thing to the teacher, asking for the pattern of the days. Get them in for even a short day, because staying home makes the dread grow, and keep the morning small and calm. If they are actually vomiting, or losing weight, that is the GP; if the dread goes on past a fortnight, it is the GP and the school's pastoral team together.

Where the water shows tells you which seal has gone. Water on the floor at the base means the wax or rubber seal between the pan and the soil pipe - the pan has to come up, so an hour of a plumber's time. A trickle from under the cistern is the inlet connection or the coupling washer, a quarter turn with a spanner. Water in the bowl that will not stop is the flush valve. Turn the water off at the isolation valve beside the cistern first, dry everything, and watch again - and if you rent, tell the landlord in writing rather than taking the pan off yourself.

Whether that is dear depends on which one and where from: the same thing is a different number in two places and on two days. Two prices, all in, is the comparison - bring them back and I will tell you which one leaves you better off at the end of the month.

Whether a claim is met is the policy's own test: what is included, then what is excluded, then the excess. The insurer is the only one who can apply that to your case, and asking before you spend anything is the cheap way round.

While pregnant, keep caffeine to about 200mg a day: that is two mugs of instant coffee, or one filter coffee, or two to three cups of tea, and cola and energy drinks count too. It is not that a little is dangerous, it is that the baby clears caffeine slowly and lots of it is linked to a lower birth weight. Switch some cups to decaf or water rather than cutting it out, and ask your midwife if you are unsure.

While a boil-water notice is on, use tap water that has been brought to a rolling boil for a minute and then left to cool for anything you swallow: drinking, brushing teeth, washing salad or fruit, making ice, and a baby's bottle. Kettles, pans and cooled boiled water are fine; a water filter is not, and neither is bottled water unless it says it is for a baby. Washing hands, washing up and the loo are fine with ordinary tap water, and cooled boiled water is also what you want for the pets. Notices usually lift after a day or two once the samples come back clear - check your water company's own page for the postcode, and if anyone in the house has had stomach trouble, ring 111 and mention the notice.

Whip the whites in a spotless dry bowl - any trace of yolk, grease or water stops them stiffening - add a pinch of cream of tartar or a drop of lemon, then add the sugar a spoonful at a time once they hold soft peaks and stop the moment the whisk pulls up a stiff point that stands on its own: over-whisked whites go dry and collapse when you fold the sugar in.

Whisk the flour into the meat juices off the heat before adding stock, then simmer it for 5 minutes. If it's already lumpy, pour it through a sieve and push the lumps through with a spoon. Too thin or runny, simmer it uncovered to reduce it, or knead equal butter and flour and whisk that in a little at a time.

Whisk 3 parts oil to 1 part acid - lemon, wine or vinegar - with salt, then add garlic, honey, soy, herbs or yoghurt. Give chicken or fish 30 minutes to 2 hours and tougher meat 4 hours or overnight, always in the fridge; a lot of acid or sugar left on for a day turns meat mushy.
Whisk 3 parts olive oil to 1 part vinegar with a teaspoon of mustard, a pinch of salt and pepper: the mustard holds it together. Make it in a jam jar and shake it, and it keeps a week in the fridge.

White patches in the mouth are usually thrush if they rub off and leave red skin underneath, or a bit of lichen planus if they sit inside the cheeks in a lace-like pattern; both are common, and a pharmacist can sell an antifungal gel for thrush. Anything that does not rub off, bleeds, or is still there after three weeks is a dentist or GP appointment, because a persistent patch is looked at properly.
White pepper is hotter than black, with a farmyard smell that suits soups, congee and Chinese cooking. Use half as much as you would black.

White spirit for oil-based gloss, water for water-based paint, and only a little: about one part white spirit to ten parts paint, stirred in rather than shaken, and no more than about a tenth of water in emulsion or water-based gloss. More than that and the paint stops forming a film, so it dries patchy and the sheen goes. Thin only when the paint is genuinely stiff - a fresh tin that is hard to brush is usually too cold rather than too thick, so stand it in warm water for ten minutes first, and never thin a primer or an undercoat to stretch it, because that is what makes it fail.

White spots the size of grains of salt are whitespot (ich), and it is curable: raise the temperature a degree or two a day to about 26C, add a whitespot treatment from the aquarium shop or aquarium salt at the dose on the bottle, and keep treating for a few days after the last spot goes - the parasite is only killable when it drops off the fish into the water. Test for ammonia first, because a fish in poor water catches it, and don't add new fish until the tank has been clear for a fortnight.

White spots in a nail are usually small knocks to the nail bed while that part of the nail was forming, and they grow out over a few months - not a calcium or zinc shortage, which is what most people are told. Filing the surface will not shift them and nothing needs doing. White lines across every nail, or half a nail white with a darker band above it, is worth a GP look.

White streaks on chocolate are bloom, and it is harmless: either the cocoa butter has melted and set again, or damp has pulled sugar to the surface. It still melts and tastes the same. Keep it in a cool cupboard around 15 to 18C rather than the fridge, which is what causes it.

White vinegar for limescale, glass, the kettle and the shower screen; bicarbonate of soda for scouring a sink or a pan, a smelly fridge and a slow drain; lemon juice and salt for a wooden board and a copper pan. Two rules cover most of it: no vinegar on marble, stone or grout, because the acid eats them, and never vinegar with bleach, because the two together give off chlorine gas. Warm water and washing-up liquid still does most of the work in a kitchen, and the standbys are for the jobs where it does not.

White furry mould on the top of the compost is harmless: it is feeding on dead bits in compost that has stayed wet in still air. Scrape it off, water only when the top of the compost is dry, empty the saucer, and give the room some air - the plant does not need repotting.

Who owns a boundary fence is in the deeds, not in who mows the grass: the title plan marks the owner's side with a T, and where there is no mark it is usually shared, each side looking after the fence on their own side. Almost no property has to have a fence at all, so a neighbour taking down one that is theirs is usually within their rights. If it is theirs you cannot paint it, fix your side of it or hang anything on it without asking, and if it is shared the fair split is half the cost each.

Who carries the risk depends on how you sent it: with the retailer's own returns label or a collection they arranged, the parcel is theirs from the moment it is handed over, so send the proof of postage and ask for the refund within 14 days. With your own courier you carry the risk until it arrives, so claim on that courier's insurance and keep the receipt. Either way do not reorder until they answer in writing.

Whoever sent it knows what happens next and by when, and nothing I say changes a date that is already set. Ring the office named on the letter with the reference to hand; Citizens Advice will go through the wording with you first at no cost.

Whole milk is about 3.5% fat, semi-skimmed about 1.7% and skimmed under 0.5%. Semi-skimmed has roughly half the fat and calories of whole, and the protein and calcium are much the same, so for most adults it is the swap that costs nothing.

Whole prey, swallowed in one: a grass snake takes frogs, toads, newts, small fish, mice and the odd bird's egg, and an adder takes voles, mice, lizards and young birds. It can go days or weeks between meals, then sit still somewhere warm to digest.

Whole seedlings vanishing overnight is slugs or snails, and the answer is a night patrol with a torch plus a beer trap sunk to the rim, not pellets scattered wide. If the tops are cut off cleanly and the plant is left standing, it is a bird or a rabbit, so net the row. Mice take pea and bean seeds out of the ground, and a cloche or some fleece stops them.

Whole fruit is not the same as added sugar: the fibre and water slow it down and one piece is about 60 calories. The only people who need to limit it are those told to by a doctor, and even then it is juice and dried fruit that matter most. Two or three pieces a day is a normal amount.

Whole garlic bulbs keep for months somewhere dry, dark and airy - a basket or a paper bag, not the fridge, where they go rubbery and mould. A clove that has started to sprout is still fine to cook with, and peeled cloves keep about a week in a jar in the fridge.

Wholemeal is the better everyday loaf: the same calories as white, but two to three times the fibre, and the fibre is what keeps you full and helps your gut. Brown bread is not the same thing - it is often white flour with colouring and a little bran added, so look for the word wholemeal or wholegrain on the label. It is worth the swap; it is not worth worrying about when there is only white in the house.

Whom is only for the object of a sentence, and in everyday writing who is almost always fine. Use whom after a preposition, as in 'to whom it may concern' or 'for whom'. If it sounds stiff, rewrite the sentence instead.

Whose name is on it decides who owes it. A bill or account in your name is yours to keep paid whatever you agreed between you, so pay it, then recover their share: send the bills with a date to pay, then a written request, then a money claim online if it is under £10,000. If it is in their name, ring the supplier and get your name off it rather than paying it. A joint account or joint loan keeps you both liable, so agree in writing who pays what, and take the free advice from Citizens Advice before you sign anything.
Whose asks who owns it - whose coat is this. Who's is short for who is or who has - who's coming? If you can say 'who is', put the apostrophe in.

WiFi does not stand for anything: a branding agency made the word up in 1999 as a play on hi-fi, and the Wireless Ethernet Compatibility Alliance liked it enough to buy it. The thing itself is just a short-range radio link, so there are no letters to expand.

Widening a window opening is a builder's job, not a window fitter's: taking out brickwork under a new lintel is structural, where a swap of the same size is a fitter's morning. Ask a builder to price it, and a structural engineer if the wall carries the floor above; in a flat or a conservation area you may need permission too. Cheaper first: a mirror opposite the window and paler walls.

Wifi is just the radio link between your devices and the router; the internet is the connection the router brings into the house. So a wifi problem is your side (distance, walls, an old router) and an internet problem is your provider's line.

William the Conqueror (about 1028-1087) was the Duke of Normandy who won the Battle of Hastings in 1066 and became the first Norman king of England. He had the Domesday Book compiled in 1086 to tax what he had taken, and his castles and French words reshaped England.
William Ruto is the president of Kenya: in office since September 2022. A Kenyan president serves a maximum of two five-year terms.

William Shakespeare was an English playwright and poet, born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564, who wrote about 39 plays including Hamlet, Macbeth and Romeo and Juliet. He worked in London from the 1590s and died in 1616.

Wind them over-under: pinch the plug end, make a loop with one hand, and alternate each turn the other way so the cable lies flat instead of twisting into a spiral. Hold the coil with a Velcro tie or a loose hairband, not a tight elastic band, and put the two earbuds in a small pouch rather than a pocket full of keys. A figure-of-eight with the plugs tucked through is the other tidy way, and short or wireless headphones end the problem altogether.

Windows: plug in an external drive and turn on File History (Settings > System > Storage > Advanced storage settings > Backup options), or let OneDrive copy your Desktop, Documents and Pictures. A Mac: Time Machine with an external drive, set once. Keep the drive in a different room, and once a year try restoring one file, because a backup you have never opened is a guess.

Wipe the outside with soapy water and dry it first, because the cheap fix for a milky lens is a polish: a £10 to £20 headlight kit with 800, 1500 and 3000 wet-and-dry paper, then the polish pad, then the sealing wipe, and half an hour a side. Toothpaste on a rag gets much of it off if the kits are not handy. Water or mist on the inside is a cracked lens or a perished seal, so dry it out and reseal or it will come back, and a lamp too dull to show a clean beam can fail the MOT.

Wipe the surface with washing-up liquid first, then look at what is left. A white, chalky bloom is scale from the water: leave a cloth soaked in white vinegar on it for ten minutes and rinse. A brown or grey mark is metal rubbed off a pan or a tin, and a big pinch of salt on half a lemon, rubbed along the surface, lifts it. A dark ring that will not shift and feels slightly rough is a burn in a laminate top, which no cleaner will take out - and keep abrasive pads off laminate and quartz, because the scratch they leave stays.

Wipe the tray table, the armrest and the seat-back pocket, which are cleaned rarely, and keep your hands off your face: the germs in a cabin come from the surfaces more than the air, which is filtered. Drink water rather than alcohol or coffee, take a window seat away from the aisle, and wear a mask on a packed winter flight, which is the single biggest thing you can do.

Wipe the chain with a rag, put one drop of chain lube on each link, turn the cranks a few times and wipe off what has not gone in. Do it every couple of rides in dry weather and after any wet one, because a squeak is a dry chain and a dry chain wears the gears out fast. Skip the general-purpose oil and the spray that is mostly solvent: it picks up grit and makes a black paste.

Wipe a warm hob with hot soapy water and a cloth, never a hot one and never by pouring water on it. Burnt-on rings on a gas or solid plate come off with a paste of bicarbonate of soda and water left 15 minutes, then scrubbed. A ceramic or induction top wants a scraper for burnt-on sugar and a cream cleaner, with no scouring pad, or the shine goes for good.

Wipe it with hot water and washing-up liquid first, working from the top down, and rinse the cloth often: hot water melts the grease and the soap lifts it. For a film that has been there a while, make a paste of bicarbonate of soda and water, leave it ten minutes and rinse, or use a proper kitchen degreaser on tiles and a splashback.

Wipe leather with a barely damp cloth and a little saddle soap, let it dry away from radiators, then work in a thin layer of leather conditioner while it is still damp. For a stain, dab rather than rub with a drop of washing-up liquid on a damp cloth; a ballpoint mark lifts with a cotton bud of rubbing alcohol. Leather cracks as it dries, so condition it two or three times a year and never scrub or soak it.

Wish them well in the place, not the paperwork: "Congratulations - may the boiler behave and the neighbours be quiet." A small thing for the house instead of a bottle of wine is a good present, and if you are visiting, ask before you bring anything big.

With the engine up to temperature, cold air from the vents is nearly always the coolant level or an airlock in the heater matrix: check the level when the engine is cold and top it up to the mark, then run it with the heater on full and the cap off to bleed it. If the level keeps dropping there is a leak to find, which is the overheating job first. On a car that holds its coolant, the suspects in order are the thermostat stuck open, a blocked heater matrix and the blend flap not moving, which a garage diagnoses in an hour or two.

Without yeast, bread needs a different kind of rise: a soda bread with bicarbonate of soda and buttermilk, or flatbreads and rotis, which need no rising at all. For a pizza or a focaccia today, half a teaspoon of bicarbonate and a teaspoon of lemon juice to 300g of flour will puff it in a hot oven instead.

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756-1791) was an Austrian composer who wrote more than 600 works in 35 years, including The Marriage of Figaro, Don Giovanni and the Requiem he left unfinished. He toured Europe as a child prodigy and died in Vienna at 35.

Woodchip comes off in two goes: lift the top layer dry with a wide scraper first (it comes away in sheets), then score and soak the backing paper for 10 to 15 minutes and scrape that off. Do not wet it before the top is off, or the chips turn to mush and smear across the wall.

Woodlice eat rotting wood and need damp, so drying the damp out is the whole job: fix the leak, clear wet leaves and timber away from the outside walls, and ventilate the room they keep appearing in. They do not damage anything in a dry house and they die within days indoors. Find the wet wood or the damp corner they are living under, and a dehumidifier or a line of salt buys you time while you sort it.

Wool coats should be dry-cleaned once a season, not washed: brush them down, air them and sponge small marks with cold water. Store them clean and dry in a breathable bag with cedar or lavender, because moths come for traces of food and sweat.

Work on it before it dries, dabbing with a cotton bud dipped in nail polish remover on fabric (test on a hidden bit first) or in acetone on hard surfaces. Blot, never rub, and change the pad as it takes up colour. On skin, warm soapy water and a little oil will do.

Work out the area first and then add a tenth: a 2m by 3m floor is 6 square metres, and with 10 per cent for cuts and breakages you want 6.6, so buy 7. A box tells you how many square metres it covers - usually about 1.2 to 1.5 - so divide by that and round up, and for a wall measure the height times the width and take off the door and the window. Order all the boxes at once so they are one batch, keep a spare box for a repair, and for a diagonal or a herringbone layout add 15 per cent instead of 10.

Work out what you need to earn in a year, divide it by the roughly 220 days you can actually bill, and add about a third for tax, holiday and quiet months: that is your floor, not your target. Quote per project but work from that day rate, and ask for a third up front on anything that takes more than a week.

Work out when it happens: a hot, acrid smell after hard braking is the brakes, a slipping clutch smells like burning paper, and a sweet smell with steam is coolant on something hot. A burning rubber smell is usually a belt, and an electrical, fishy smell means stop and get out. If you can't place it, stop somewhere safe and look under the bonnet.

Work out which paint it is first: a heat gun or a chemical stripper lifts old oil gloss in a few minutes, while a water-based paint softens under a warm damp cloth. Sandpaper alone clogs in seconds on a thick layer, so strip the bulk and sand only the last film. Test anything painted before about 1960 for lead - a kit costs a few pounds - and never sand that one.

Work through it in this order: the battery or the charge, the switch, then the wire at the lamp. A rear light that flickers over bumps is a tired battery or a loose contact in the clip, and a dynamo light that dies at low speed is normal until the standlight takes over. In winter a USB light that will not charge is usually a cold battery - bring it in and let it warm up - so keep a spare set charged.

Work top to bottom and dry before wet: dust the shelves and wipe the mirror first, then the sink, bath and shower, and the floor last so nothing drips on what is already done. Ten minutes once a week on the sink, loo and floor is enough; once a month do the boring parts, the grout, the shower head, the extractor fan and behind the toilet. Squeegee the shower and leave the window or fan on for ten minutes after a bath, because that is what keeps the cleaning small.

Work back from the date: book a van or removals six to eight weeks out, and tell the council, energy, water and broadband a month before, because the bills follow you. Box the things you don't use three weeks out, label every box with its room, and pack one bag with a kettle, mugs, loo roll, bedding and chargers for the first night.

Work backwards from the deadline: decide the three or four points that answer the question, put a heading for each, write the middle sections badly and fast, then the introduction and the conclusion last, then read it out loud once. Ask for a short extension today rather than after the deadline and put the request in writing, because most tutors will say yes before the date and almost none can after it. A complete plain answer scores more than a perfect first half, so hand in every section, even thin.
Work a paste of bicarbonate of soda and water, or a little washing-up liquid, into the green and leave it 30 minutes before a normal wash. Check before drying: heat sets a grass stain in.

Work a little matching shoe cream or a drop of olive oil into the scuff with a rag, in circles, and let it dry before buffing with a soft cloth. Shoe trees keep the shape and stop the creases that turn into cracks.

Work down a short list instead of sitting and worrying: the neighbour on each side, then whoever holds a spare key, then the carer or day centre if one visits, because a carer can usually get in. If nobody has seen them, ring the police on 101 and ask for a welfare check on an older person living alone; they do this routinely and it is not a fuss. Tell them how far away you are and what makes you uneasy (a fall last month, the front door left open, a phone that rings out), and if any of that is true, or you are hours away, ring 999 rather than wait for a call back.

Work from the bottom: lift the drain cover or clear the shoe at the foot of the pipe first, then push a drain rod (or a stiff hose) up from there, because that is where the leaves and grit collect. If the pipe still backs up, go up a ladder and clear the outlet at the gutter end, then flush it with a hose from the top. Rod gently, never with a pressure washer down a plastic pipe, and if the water is coming out of a joint rather than the top, the joint has failed rather than the pipe being blocked.

Work from your own mistakes, not a list of hard words: take the twenty words you actually get wrong in texts and emails, and use look-say-cover-write-check on five a day - look at it, say it, cover it, write it, check it. Break long words into syllables as you say them (gov-ern-ment, sep-a-rate), and read your own writing out loud, because most spelling slips are words you can hear. Spellcheck is fine as a check, but read the suggestion before you accept it, or the same mistake survives.

Work it off with soap and water or a little oil, twisting rather than pulling, hand raised above your head for a few minutes first to let the swelling go down. Wind a piece of thread or dental floss under the ring from the finger side and unwind it around the finger past the knuckle, tucking the ring along a loop at a time. Get help the same day if the finger goes numb, cold or blue: A&E or a jeweller can cut it off.

Work it out as a volume: length times width times depth, all in metres. Gravel and slate chippings go down about 5cm deep, or 10cm if a car drives on them, so a 5m by 3m drive at 5cm is 0.75 cubic metres - about 1.2 tonnes, or fifty 25kg bags. Bark and mulch are the same sum at 5 to 7cm over the soil. Topsoil is the deep one: 10 to 15cm for a new bed, and a 20cm fill in a 3m by 1m raised bed wants 0.6 cubic metres. A cubic metre is roughly 1.5 tonnes of gravel and about a tonne of soil or compost, and a builder's bulk bag is about 0.8 of a cubic metre, so check which one the price is for. Turf and grass seed are sold by area instead: measure the lawn and add 5 per cent for the cuts.

Working muscles need more oxygen, so your heart beats faster and harder to move blood round; a fit heart pumps more with each beat, which is why fit people have slower resting rates. Anywhere from 60 to 100 beats a minute at rest is normal for adults.

Working from home as an employee does not change your council tax or need a business rate, so there is nothing to tell the council. It only becomes business rates if part of the home is used mainly for the business - a shop, a workshop with customers calling - and most kitchen-table businesses stay on council tax anyway. Do tell your insurer if you keep stock or see customers.
World War One ended with the armistice on 11 November 1918, at 11am. The fighting stopped on the Western Front that morning, though the peace treaty was not signed until the following June.

Worms are treated rather than cured: most dogs are wormed every three months and cats on the vet's schedule, with a product from the vet, because shop ones do not always cover tapeworm. Roundworm eggs in dog and cat muck can infect people, so clear the garden and the litter tray daily, wash your hands, and keep children away from the tray. If the animal is also being sick, has a pot belly or a dull coat, or if someone in the house has threadworms, say so when you ring - and worm everyone in the house at the same time, because threadworms pass back and forth.
Worry like that is usually mostly 'what if'. Write down what's actually at stake and it gets smaller.
Worth doing. Where are you with it so far?

Worth it only on an outside wall with no cavity insulation: a sheet of radiator foil behind the radiator, shiny side facing the room, pushed back so it does not touch the brackets, gives you a few percent rather than the half the adverts claim. Keep the gap under the radiator clear, because that is where the cold air comes in and the warm air goes out - a shelf or a curtain hanging over the top cancels the gain. Foil on an inside wall, or over a cavity, does nothing at all.

Worth it if the car is old or you drive far: one recovery is £100 to £200, so cover at £40 to £80 a year pays for itself the first time the car will not start. Check whether your bank account, car insurance or a lease already includes it, and keep the number in the car rather than in your phone.

Worth it if you want steps, heart rate and messages without getting the phone out; not worth it if what you really want is a watch that runs for a week. A Garmin or Fitbit goes five days or more and an Apple Watch about one, and an Apple Watch needs an iPhone, so check the pairing before you choose.

Worth it if you work or stream at home, more than one person uses the connection, or you game: a phone hotspot will do for one light user, but its data cap and the delay on a video call show up fast. 5g home broadband sits between the two - no line and no engineer, but check the coverage at your postcode and how it holds up at 8pm before you take a two-year deal. Cheapest full fibre is usually about £25 a month, and a mobile-only household pays about the same in data once two people stream.

Worth it mainly for accidental damage on a Mac or an iPhone: a screen repair is around £100 to £300 without it, and the plan covers two incidents a year with an excess of roughly £25 to £79 depending on the device. Skip it if your home contents insurance or the card you paid with already covers the device; the free one-year warranty covers faults, never drops.

Wrap whole beetroot in foil with a splash of oil and roast at 200C (180C fan) for 1 to 1.5 hours, until a knife slides in, or boil it 40 to 60 minutes. Rub the skins off with a tea towel while they are still warm, and wear gloves unless you want pink hands.

Wrap each plate in paper or a tea towel and stand it on its edge in the box, like records in a crate, never stacked flat: that is what stops them cracking. A crumpled paper or towel cushion in the bottom and on top, small boxes that one person can lift, and FRAGILE written on the sides. Glasses and mugs go upright with paper pushed inside, a mug handle never takes the weight, and wine glasses travel best one inside a sock. A mirror or a framed picture travels standing on its edge too, with card on the corners and tape across the glass in an X so a crack stays put.

Wrist and hand pain is usually an overused tendon or a nerve pressed by the way you grip and type: take breaks, keep the wrist straight rather than bent, and try a support splint from the pharmacy at night. Pins and needles in the fingers that wake you is worth a GP visit.

Write one number above the other and take the digits of the bottom number one at a time: 34 x 26 is 34 x 6 = 204, then 34 x 20 = 680, and 204 + 680 = 884. Each row moves one place to the left, which is the nought on the end, so keep the columns lined up.

Write one as soon as you own a home, have children or are not married to your partner: without a will the law decides and an unmarried partner gets nothing. A simple one is a £20 to £35 form signed in front of two witnesses who are not family and do not inherit, and it needs redoing after a marriage or a divorce because those cancel it. Pay a solicitor £150 to £400 for a house abroad, a business, a second marriage or someone who cannot handle money.

Write one complaint that names what was agreed, what was done and what it cost you, with photos and dates, and a deadline of 14 days to put it right - a builder is a service, so the shop's 30-day refund rule does not apply, and the letter is what gets the money back. Pay nothing more meanwhile, then claim through the small claims court online for anything under £10,000: it costs about £35, needs no solicitor, and most settle before the hearing. A trader who took a deposit and vanished is a police matter too - report it as fraud.

Write one equation under the other and add or subtract them to lose a letter: 2x + y = 7 and x + y = 4 gives x = 3 straight away, then y = 1 from either one. If nothing cancels, multiply one equation until it does. Put both numbers back into both equations to check.

Write the date in full and in one order: 10 March 2025 (British) or March 10, 2025 (American), with no th and no comma in the British form. In a letter, put it above the greeting; the ordinal - the tenth of March - is for speech.

Write the first sentence and the last sentence first, then three points in between, one card each. Practise out loud standing up, once to a person and once to a wall, and print the cards in big letters: looking up at people is what makes a school talk go well, and you can't look up at a phone.

Write three lines before you go: what you delivered, with numbers if you have them; one thing that slipped and what you changed because of it; and one ask - a project, training, a raise or more flexibility. Then ask "what would make this a great year for you?" and close by saying what you need from them.

Write to your MP with your full name and address so they can see you are their constituent, and say what you want them to do: the problem in two or three lines, the reference numbers, and what you have already tried. Email the constituency office or write to the House of Commons - both work, and a letter is kept on file. They can chase a government department, HMRC, the Home Office or the council, and they usually reply in a few weeks; for bins, housing and roads your councillor is the faster route.

Write tomorrow's list down before bed: most of the racing is your head keeping the list for you. Then a slow breathing pattern, in for four and out for six, for a couple of minutes, and get up rather than lie there arguing with yourself if it goes on past 20 minutes.

Write 200 words a day and edit them the next morning, when you can see what is on the page rather than what you meant: cut one sentence and rewrite one. Copy a paragraph you admire by hand once a week to feel how the sentences are built, and read your own work aloud - the place you stumble is the place to fix.

Write down what you actually see, with examples and dates - the meltdown at the same time each morning, the shoes he cannot bear, how long homework takes - because a pattern on paper is what gets taken seriously. Then ask two people in the same week: the school's SENCO, who can start support without any diagnosis, and your GP, who can refer you to a paediatrician or a children's mental health service. Ask what the local waiting list is and whether the GP can refer elsewhere, since in England you can choose the provider. Meanwhile use what helps now: a visual timetable, a warning before a change, movement breaks and short instructions. You do not need the label to make the day easier.

Write down your start and finish each day, in a note or a spreadsheet, in the same minute you finish rather than at the end of the week. Keep your own copy - the system is your employer's record, not yours. Compare the week with your contract: anything past your contracted hours is the thing to raise, and a month of your own dates is what makes it stick. If hours go unpaid, ring ACAS (free) before you raise it, and claim within three months less a day of the shortfall.

Write down for a fortnight what they forget, and whether it is new. Slower recall of names is ordinary; asking the same question within minutes, getting lost on a familiar route, or forgetting something they have always done are not, and want a GP appointment. Take the notes and ask for a memory assessment, and say if they still drive: an infection, low B12, an underactive thyroid, poor hearing and some medicines can all cause a fixable muddle.

Write every cooking time on one sheet and work back from when you want to eat: the bird rests an hour, so it comes out an hour before, and the potatoes go in as it comes out. Shop for the cold stuff two days before rather than on the day, because fridge space runs out, and hand out the pudding, the drinks and the ice to other people.

Write it on the delivery note before you sign, photograph it where it stands, and tell the retailer in writing the same day: something that arrives damaged is not of satisfactory quality under the Consumer Rights Act, so within 30 days you can reject it for a full refund or ask for a repair or a replacement. The courier is the retailer's problem, not yours - your contract is with the shop - and the seller pays for the return of a damaged item. Keep the packaging and the photos until it is settled.

Write it in this order and the marks look after themselves: aim in one sentence, method in numbered steps someone else could follow, results as a table plus one graph with labelled axes and units, then a conclusion that says whether the prediction was right, then an evaluation of what went wrong. Keep the method past tense and passive ('the solution was heated'), put numbers to the precision the instrument allows, and have one paragraph on sources of error with what you would change - that paragraph is the difference between a pass and a good mark. Do the graph and the evaluation first when you are short of time, because they carry the most marks.

Write it in three moves: who the person is and what they want, the thing that gets in the way, and the question the reader will buy the book to answer - all in the present tense and under 200 words. Keep the climax out of it, end on the question rather than the answer, and read it aloud once: a blurb with the names of five characters in it reads like a synopsis.
Writing began around 3200 BC in Mesopotamia, as marks for accounting: quantities of grain and sheep. Independent systems appeared later in Egypt, China and Mesoamerica.
Xi Jinping is the president of China: in office since 2013, and general secretary of the Communist Party since 2012. The party holds the power, and since 2018 there is no limit on his terms.

Yellow or brown outer leaves on a cabbage are just age: peel off the ones that have gone, trim the dried stem end, and the firm head inside is still good - a whole cabbage keeps a month or more in the fridge, and a cut half keeps a couple of weeks wrapped. The one to bin is a head that is slimy or sour-smelling right through, or soft all the way to the middle. If only the outside looks tired, it is a stir-fry or a soup rather than the bin.

Yellow basil leaves are usually too much water and too little sun: it wants drainage, warmth and a sunny windowsill, and it hates sitting in a wet pot. Let the top of the soil dry out, move it somewhere brighter, and pinch the tops to keep it bushy.

Yellow fever is a mosquito-borne virus in parts of Africa and South America, and most people have a fever, headache, muscle ache and sickness for about a week and then recover. A small share go on to jaundice, bleeding and organ failure, which is a 999 emergency, so get seen quickly for yellow skin or eyes, bleeding or vomiting. The vaccine is the protection: a travel clinic gives it, some countries require a certificate to enter, and it needs booking at least six to eight weeks before you fly.

Yellow leaves on a tomato are usually a feeding or watering problem rather than a disease. If the yellow sits between green veins, that is magnesium: water evenly, mulch, and give a tomato feed with magnesium in it. If the lowest leaves go pale and drop off, the plant is short of nitrogen or the roots are waterlogged. Pick the yellow leaves off, feed weekly, and water little and often rather than in floods; brown blotches or black bottoms are a different problem.

Yelp or say "ow" and stop the game the moment teeth touch skin, then turn away for ten seconds before playing again; the puppy learns that teeth end the fun. Give a chew toy instead every time he goes for hands, and if he is over-tired, a nap settles more of it than any training.

Yes on white cement grout: a cup of thin bleach in four litres of water, brushed on, left fifteen minutes and rinsed, kills the mould at the root. Never on coloured or epoxy grout, which it bleaches patchy, and never mixed with a limescale remover. A stiff brush and an old toothbrush do most of the work; a bicarbonate paste lifts the rest.

Yes, most people hate their job some weeks, and the useful question is which part: the manager, the hours, the pay, the work itself or the people. Pick the one thing that would change the most and try the smallest real fix for a month - a conversation about hours, one project swapped, a fixed finish time - because a job that is wrong in one part is often fixable and one that is wrong in all of them is not. Set a date, three months out, to decide with something in hand: an updated CV, two conversations about other work, and a figure you need to earn. Do not quit on a bad Tuesday, and if you dread it every morning or cannot sleep for it, that is a GP conversation and a sick note, not a weakness.

Yes, on a phone with a separate alarm volume the alarm still sounds on silent - the silent switch mutes the ringer, not the alarm. Two things defeat it: the alarm volume itself turned down (on an iPhone it follows the ringer volume, so raise that with the alarm screen open), and Do Not Disturb with alarms allowed off, which is a setting in Focus. Check both tonight by setting an alarm two minutes ahead.

Yes, once, and until it is piping hot all the way through - steam rising and no cold spot in the middle. Keep cooked chicken in the fridge no more than 3 days, don't reheat it twice, and bin it if it has been out of the fridge for more than 2 hours.

Yes, scrape the black off with a knife and eat the rest: it tastes fine, and burnt toast is not dangerous in the way people fear. Very charred bread does carry more acrylamide, so it is not something to make a habit of, but one slice is nothing to worry about. The smoke is the bigger nuisance, so open a window and run the extractor.
Yes, straight from the bag with no thawing: give them a minute or two longer in the pan. Frozen peas are sweeter than fresh ones that have sat about.

Yes, usually by a third to a half, and the older the thing gets the better the saving: furniture, bikes, tools, a pram, kids' clothes and kitchen kit lose most of their value in the first year and then almost nothing. Buy new the things that wear unseen or are used against your body - a mattress, running shoes, a bike helmet, anything with a safety job (a car seat, a life jacket, a smoke alarm) - and buy new where a warranty is what you are really paying for, like a laptop or a washing machine. Check a used phone or laptop's battery health, ask for the age of a washing machine's drum, and never pay before you see it. From a shop, second-hand goods carry the same rights as new ones: 30 days to reject it, then repair or replacement; from a private seller it is buyer beware unless the advert lied.

Yes, weight for weight, and it needs a hand: turkey and chicken mince are leaner than beef, so brown them in a tablespoon of oil and add a splash more stock than the recipe says, or they go dry and chalky. Quorn and soya mince are a straight swap too - use the same volume, add stock, and give them fifteen minutes rather than forty. In a chilli or a bolognese nobody notices.

Yes, with one rule. Raw is the part to skip: cooked prawns, mussels that have opened in the pan, tinned tuna and smoked salmon are all fine in the UK, and so is sushi made with cooked or frozen fish. What to leave alone is raw fish and raw shellfish - no oysters, no raw prawns - because of listeria and norovirus. Cooked fish is good for you and the baby too: salmon, mackerel and sardines are the ones to have, twice a week.

Yes, and about a hundred to two hundred pounds: a pre-purchase inspection from the AA, RAC or a good local garage costs that on anything over about two thousand pounds, and it catches the hidden faults a test drive can't. Book it after you've seen the car and agreed a price in principle, and walk away if the seller won't allow one.

Yes, and it is the sound that does the work: rhymes teach a child that words are made of parts, which is the same skill reading needs. Read one aloud and let them finish the rhymes, keep it to a couple of minutes, and do not ask them to explain it. Silly wins - a poem they can shout is one they will remember.

Yes, and it is usually fine: you get wet either way once you are out, and the rain cools you rather than hurting you. Wear a thin breathable jacket or a cap with a brim so the rain stays out of your eyes, something bright or reflective because drivers see less in the wet, and trainers with grip - wet leaves and painted lines are slick. Rub a little vaseline where your clothes rub, because wet skin chafes. The one thing to stop for is thunder and lightning: head indoors and wait it out. Stuff newspaper in the shoes afterwards and dry them away from a radiator so they keep their shape.

Yes, and it is less of a career event than it feels. Step out for two minutes if you can, breathe out longer than you breathe in, and come back with "sorry, that caught me - where were we?" Nobody remembers the tears as clearly as you do; what sticks is that you came back and finished the meeting. If it keeps happening, tell one person you trust, and get the thing that is causing it looked at - a workload, a manager, or a doctor.
Yes, at three-quarters of the weight, and take a tablespoon or two out of the liquid. Bake 10C cooler than the recipe says, because honey browns faster than sugar.

Yes, a sentence can start with and or but - writers have done it for centuries and it reads naturally in ordinary writing. What gets noticed is doing it over and over ("And then... And then..."), so use it for effect rather than as a habit.

Yes, a tempered-glass one is worth the £5 to £15: it takes the scratches and the knock the screen would, and it is cheap to replace. For a drop, a case matters more than the glass, so get both, and fit the protector in a steamy bathroom so the dust settles out of the air first.

Yes, give it a sand first: 120 grit on a block for painted woodwork and 80 to 100 on a filler patch, with the grain and light enough to take the shine off rather than the paint, then dust it down and wipe it over with a damp cloth. Old gloss has to be keyed or the new coat slides off it, and a filled patch has to be flatter than the wall around it or it shows through. Bare wood wants 120 grit, then 180, and the dust off before the first coat.

Yes, if there is no hand-wash label on it: everyday china, plain glass, stainless cutlery and pans, and plastic that says dishwasher safe. Top rack for lids and thin plastic, and anything that holds water goes face down. Scrape rather than rinse, and leave the wooden spoons, the sharp knives and the cast iron for the sink.

Yes, if you keep running out of memory: going from 8GB to 16GB is the upgrade that shows up most, and it is £30 to £60 if the laptop has a slot you can open. Check the model takes a stick first, because many thin ones are soldered, and a bigger SSD helps more than RAM if the drive is the thing that is always full.

Yes, if it is greasy: a thick layer of grease and burnt crumbs on the base, the door seal or the grill pan is what catches, and it usually starts when a spill or a bit of foil drops onto the element the next time the oven is on. It does not go up on its own, so it is not an emergency tonight: clean the base and the seal when it is cold, keep the grill pan clear, and never leave a grill or a chip pan unattended. If it does catch, close the door, switch it off at the wall and smother the pan with a lid or a fire blanket - never water on a fat fire.
Yes, in anything cold or stirred in at the end: spoon it in off the heat, because yoghurt splits if it boils. It will not whip and it will not thicken a sauce the way cream does.

Yes, it counts. Comics, graphic novels, magazines and audio books all build the same thing a book does - the habit and the vocabulary - and a child who reads what they like reads far more of it than one handed a book they do not. Keep one chapter book alongside it rather than banning the comics, and ask what happened in the story afterwards. For audio books, same idea: the words go in by ear, and a paper copy of the same book helps once they can follow along.

Yes, it is just food: baby rice is finely ground rice, and the jars are ordinary fruit or vegetables cooked soft with no salt or sugar added, so there is nothing in them a grown-up needs to avoid. They are bland on purpose and cost several times what the same weight of rice or fruit does, so finishing a jar is fine and buying them for yourself is not worth it.
Yes: one cube per 500ml of water for a stock-strength base, and half a cube in a small or already salty dish. Crumble it in rather than dropping it whole.

Yes: rice, pasta, noodles, flour and potatoes are vegetarian, and bread almost always is - the exception is lard in some traditional loaves. Egg pasta is still vegetarian, it is only vegan that rules it out.

Yes: they work in different ways, so paracetamol and ibuprofen can be taken together, spaced through the day at the dose on the packet. Skip ibuprofen if you have a stomach ulcer, kidney trouble or are on blood thinners, and ask a pharmacist if you take anything regularly.

Yes: vinegar is the gentler of the two and bleach at about one part to four of water is the stronger, and either kills the mould it reaches on tiles, grout, glass and the sealant round a bath - gloves on, window open, never mixed with another cleaner. On plaster, paint, wood or fabric neither does more than lift the colour, because it cannot get at mould that has grown in, so those want a mould spray, or the sealant cut out and replaced. And it is the damp that brings it back, so that is the part to fix.

Yes: PAYE is the income tax your employer takes out of your pay before it reaches you, worked out from your tax code each payday and shown on the payslip, so the number you are paid is already after it. National Insurance comes off the same way, and a pension or a student loan is listed as its own line. Compare the code on your payslip with your HMRC coding notice (1257L is the standard one): a wrong code is the usual reason PAYE takes too much.

Yes: cool it within the hour, box it while it is still warm rather than hot, and freeze it the same day - cooked rice keeps about a month in the freezer. Reheat it once until it is piping hot all the way through, and do not freeze it again after that.

Yes: a student loan comes off your pay like tax, through PAYE, once you earn over the threshold for your plan - on plan 5 that is 9% of what you earn above about £25,000 a year (£2,082 a month), shown as its own line on the payslip. Only the part above the threshold counts, so a low month takes nothing, and it stops by itself when the loan is paid off. If the figure looks wrong, ask payroll for the plan they have you on: the wrong plan is the usual cause.

Yes: a croissant is flour, butter, yeast, sugar and egg, all of which are vegetarian, though not vegan. Ordinary pastry is vegetarian too, with one exception - some savoury pie pastry still lists lard, so read the packet before you assume.

Yes - one slash about 1cm deep at a shallow angle is what decides where the loaf opens, so it rises where you cut instead of tearing wherever the crust is thinnest. Do it with a wet blade just before the loaf goes in, not before the final prove, or the cut closes up again. A tin loaf needs no slash, because the tin holds the sides and the top is free to rise; a round loaf or a long one on a tray wants one slash along it or a cross on top.

Yes - paracetamol and ibuprofen work in different ways, so you can take both, and alternating them is what people often do for a bad headache, toothache or a bad back. Keep to the box: two 500mg paracetamol up to four times a day, at least four hours apart and no more than eight in 24 hours, and 400mg of ibuprofen three times a day with food. Skip ibuprofen if you have a stomach ulcer, kidney trouble or are on a blood thinner, and read the labels of anything else you take - a lot of cold remedies already contain paracetamol.

Yes - that is what it is built for, and leaving a slow cooker on low while you are out is an ordinary thing to do. Keep it at least half full of liquid so it does not dry out and catch, put the lid on and do not lift it, sit it on a dry worktop with the cord well away from the hot sides, and keep it to about 8 hours on low (4 on high). Cooked food left in it on warm all evening is the one to avoid: cool the food, put it in the fridge, and reheat it once, piping hot.

Yes - Infacol and the other simeticone drops are safe for a baby: simeticone is not absorbed into the body, it just joins the small bubbles of trapped wind into bigger ones that come up in a burp. It is licensed from birth, the box gives the dose as a dropper before each feed, and two weeks is long enough to know whether it is doing anything. Gripe water is the one to skip, because it is not licensed for babies. If the drops make no difference, the things that help are the winding, feeds sat upright and a sling, not a stronger bottle of anything.

Yes - PAYE is the tax and National Insurance coming out of your pay before it reaches you. The employer works both out from your tax code and pays them to HMRC, and what is left is the net figure on your payslip. The tax code is the bit that decides how much: 1257L is the usual one for one job with no benefits, and if it looks wrong, ask payroll to check it rather than waiting for a rebate.

Yes - baking soda and bicarbonate of soda are the same thing under two names: the American name and the British one. Baking powder is the different one, because it has an acid and a starch mixed in with the bicarbonate, so it fizzes on its own and the soda needs an acid such as buttermilk, yoghurt or lemon to do anything.

Yes - being off sick does not stop your job going, but the selection still has to be fair and they should talk to you about it rather than post the letter. Time off for pregnancy, maternity leave, or because you raised a safety or whistleblowing concern is protected, so a redundancy that is really about those is unfair. Keep the sick notes, ask for the reason in writing, and have ACAS or a union rep look at it while the clock is still running.

Yes - a radiator bleed key: a little square or half-moon spanner, about two or three pounds from a hardware shop or a big supermarket, and a cloth under the valve to catch the drips. Some newer valves take a small flat screwdriver instead, so look at the slot before you buy. A quarter turn is enough, and you stop when water runs steadily rather than hissing air.

Yes - a spoonful of yoghurt stirred in at the end is the usual finish: it cools the heat and rounds off a sharp or bitter edge. Take the pan off the heat first and stir the yoghurt into a spoonful of the sauce in a cup before it goes back in, so it does not split; full-fat or Greek yoghurt splits less than low-fat, and a splash of cream or coconut milk does the same job.

Yes - a warm bath 10 to 15 minutes long, an hour or two before bed, is one of the few home things that reliably helps you drop off: the water warms you and the climb back down afterwards is what makes you sleepy. Keep it warm rather than hot, which leaves skin tight and can make you light-headed, and get out slowly if the room spins. The same bath eases aching muscles for the same reason.

Yes - easy to moderate exercise is fine on your period, and it usually helps: moving lifts the endorphins and blood flow that take the edge off cramps. Go by how you feel rather than by the calendar: a walk, a swim or an easy run is fine on a heavy day, and if day one is rough keep it short and gentle and pick it up later in the week. Ibuprofen about half an hour before helps if cramps are the problem. For swimming, use whatever you already use - a tampon or a cup - and change it straight after.

Yes - it stays in this chat. Nothing is written down and nothing carries over, so nobody else reads it and it is gone when we finish. If it is something a person needs to act on, though, tell someone who can.

Yes - keep it to about 200mg a day, which is two mugs of instant, one large filter coffee or two cans of cola, and have it straight after a feed so the level falls by the next one. A newborn clears it much more slowly than a six month old, so if the baby is wakeful or windy, cut back rather than give it up - and tea, cola and chocolate count towards the total too.

Yes for anything on the gas side, and the pressure gauge (1 to 1.5 bar) and the reset button are worth trying first. A Gas Safe engineer's callout is usually £60 to £120, and it is worth paying once a fault repeats rather than for a one-off reset. Note the make and model, the error code and what happens when it cuts out, because that is what turns a second visit into a first fix. If you smell gas, or water is leaking near the electrics, turn it off and call the emergency line.
Yes for cooking, sauces and coffee: it will not whip, but it will not split in a hot sauce either, so it is the safer one to keep in the cupboard.

Yes if you ride more than half an hour: the pad is what stops the chafing and the saddle soreness, and a padded liner worn under ordinary trousers does the same job without the Lycra. Do not wear underwear underneath, because the seams are what rub, and a cheap pad is worse than none - look for a flat, seamless one.
Yes in cakes and biscuits, at the same weight, if it is a block margarine meant for baking. The soft spread in a tub holds more water and gives a wetter, paler bake.

Yesterday's rice makes great fried rice: heat a little oil, add the cold rice and fry it hard for 3 minutes without stirring much, then push it aside and scramble an egg in the gap with soy sauce, peas or whatever vegetables you have.

You need one to work in the UK, and it is free: apply on gov.uk (search "apply for a national insurance number") and send the ID and address proof they ask for, or ring the helpline on 0300 200 3500 if you cannot apply online. It arrives by post in two to four weeks. If you have lost the letter, the number is on a payslip, a P60 or the HMRC app.

You need your licence, insurance and usually a warning triangle, hi-vis vest and breathalyser kit; check whether your insurer covers abroad or you need a green card. An international driving permit costs a few pounds and is worth having in some countries, so check yours before you go.

You owe for damage only if you were careless, and even then only what it actually cost the shop: an accident on its own is not a debt, so you can politely decline to pay. If you do offer, offer the cost price rather than the shelf price, ask for it in writing, and never pay cash on the spot to a member of staff. Retailers can claim on their own insurance, and a shop that threatens the police over a dropped jar is bluffing.

You paid for the lot, so the rest is still owed: photograph the box and the packing slip, then write and say exactly what is missing and ask for it to be sent or for that part refunded. If they will not, ask the card provider to charge back the missing amount, with the order email as proof.

You pay for the care actually given: a cancelled or missed visit comes off the invoice, and the agency has to show the visit log and timesheet it is billing from. Ask for both in writing, name the visits you were charged for and say you dispute that part of the bill. Council-funded care goes to the council's commissioning team; a private agency that will not credit you is a complaint to the Care Quality Commission.

You usually do not need a printer: the retailer emails a QR code, and the Post Office or a parcel shop scans it and prints the label for you. If it is a PDF label, print it at home or at a library, tape it over the old address so the barcode is flat, and keep the receipt with the tracking number until the refund lands.

You usually get 25% of a defined contribution pot tax-free, capped at about £268,275, and every pound after that is taxed as income at whatever rate you are on when you take it - so a big withdrawal in one year can be taxed at 40% even if you are a basic-rate taxpayer in a normal year. Take the tax-free cash in stages, or draw a smaller amount each year, and check the figure before you press the button: providers will tell you what tax they have to deduct. State pension is taxable too, even though nothing is taken out of it when it is paid.

You will get the court's letter with the date, the time and which court, and you do have to go: reply to it, and tell them straight away if the date cannot work. Take the letter and your statement on the day, plan to be there all day even if you are finished by lunch, and tell the usher when you arrive. A solicitor will go through your statement with you before you are called, and when you are in the box you say what you remember and say plainly when you do not remember. Claim the expenses and the loss of earnings afterwards.

You apply to the council where you live, not the one you would like to live in, and join its housing register: most run a website where you bid on the week's adverts, and offers go by band, meaning how urgent your need is, and then by how long you have waited. Most councils also want a local connection, which is living or working in the area or close family there, and the wait without priority is often years, so bid every week and keep the reference. If you are homeless tonight or have been asked to leave within 56 days, ring the council's housing options team the same day and say those words, because that duty is assessed straight away. A housing association's own list is a second, separate application worth making.

You are owed a choice on the spot: a full refund of the ticket, or a new flight as soon as one is available, plus 220 to 520 pounds per person in cash, not a voucher. While you wait the airline pays for meals and two calls, and a hotel if the new flight is the next day. Ask for the reason in writing and keep the boarding pass; if they refuse, complain to the CAA - you have up to six years.

You buy a share, usually 25% to 75%, and pay rent on the rest to the housing association: the mortgage only covers your share, but the rent and the service charge come on top, so ask what both are before you offer. You can buy more shares later (staircasing), and selling is slower because the association finds the buyer. It is worth it where rents are high and you want to stop renting, and it is a bad deal if the service charge is steep or the lease is short - check both, and only use a regulated scheme run by a council or a housing association.

You can only do it in the seconds after sending: Gmail has Undo in the little bar at the bottom (set Undo Send up to 30 seconds in Settings), Outlook has Undo Send in the same way, and Apple Mail has Undo Send if you turn the delay on. After that the honest move is a short follow-up saying you sent it by mistake and please ignore it, which reads far better than hoping.

You can push back, in writing.
