A landlord can only put the rent up by agreement, under a rent review clause in your tenancy, or with a formal notice - in England a section 13 notice, at least a month before it starts for a monthly tenancy, and no more than once a year. If the new figure is above what similar homes nearby are advertised at, say so, name two or three of them, and offer a lower number in writing. A notice can be referred to the rent tribunal (28 days in England, and the tribunal decides the market rent), and it does not apply if your tenancy has a rent review clause instead. Keep paying the current rent while you argue, so the dispute stays about the rise and not about arrears.

You can run every day eventually, but for the first couple of months three or four runs a week is the better deal - the legs get stronger on the days off, and running every day from nothing is how shins start hurting. Keep most runs easy enough to hold a conversation in; a hard run every day is the other common mistake. Add one run a week rather than one every day.

You can take a newborn out from the first day: a pram or a sling, one more layer than you are wearing, and out of direct sun. Keep them out of crowded rooms and away from anyone with a cough or a cold for the first six weeks, and take the pram rather than passing a newborn round a room. Go out after a feed and you get the long sleep for it.

You can usually still change it, and the sooner you ask the easier it is: at school or college, go to the head of sixth form or the exams officer, and a change is normally possible in the first two or three weeks of Year 12 - after that it is their call, and how much you would catch up that decides it. At university, ask your personal tutor or the course leader about transferring to another course at the same place before you think about leaving, which is usually easier than a fresh application through UCAS or Clearing. Changing after a full year costs money as well as time, because student finance does not normally fund a second first year.

You can cut the sugar in most cakes and traybakes by a third to a half and still get a good bake, but not all of it: sugar keeps the crumb soft, browns the crust and holds the structure, so a cake with none bakes pale, dry and crumbly. Leave at least a quarter of what the recipe asks, add a splash of milk if the batter looks stiff, and eat it within a couple of days. Bread needs its teaspoon to get the yeast going, and jam and meringue are set by their sugar, so those cannot be cut.

You can earn up to £1,000 a year from selling or side work before you have to declare it, which is the trading allowance. Above that, register for Self Assessment by 5 October after the tax year ends and file online by 31 January; you pay tax on the profit, not on everything you took.

You can eat well without cooking if you build the plate from the shop: a bag of salad or a punnet of tomatoes, ready-cooked chicken or a tin of tuna or chickpeas, and bread, couscous or a microwave pouch of rice. Frozen veg straight from the microwave is the cheapest half-plate of vegetables there is, and a pot of yogurt with fruit is pudding. The only rule that matters is the half plate of vegetables, and that needs no hob.

You cannot brush garlic or onion breath away, because the smell is not on your tongue: the sulphur compounds are absorbed into the blood and come out on your breath from the lungs, so it fades over about a day whatever you do. What helps is at the meal - milk, an apple, parsley, mint or green tea blunt the compounds before they get into the blood, and cooking the garlic less hard helps too. Afterwards, brush, scrape the tongue, floss and drink water, which is good for the mouth anyway; mints and mouthwash cover it for twenty minutes. If your breath smells of garlic when you have eaten none, that is a dentist or GP question rather than this one.

You cannot choose where fat comes off: sit-ups build the muscle under it, not the layer on top. A calorie deficit shrinks fat everywhere, and where it goes first is down to genetics, so for most people the waist is the last place to change.

You cannot make someone sorry, so ask for the repair rather than the words: say what you needed and what you will do now - "I needed you to say it mattered, and I am not going to keep bringing it up." Ask once, plainly, and let them decide; if it never comes, the useful question is what you want next, not how to get it out of them.

You do not need one as a sole trader if you are happy filing a self assessment, but most people hire one the first year they go self-employed, because they know what you can claim and it takes them an hour; £150 to £400 a year for a simple return is normal. A limited company is a different matter: accounts, a confirmation statement and a corporation tax return are all due every year, so budget £600 to £1,200 and keep the paperwork tidy. Ask two for a fixed quote and check they are on a recognised body, such as ICAEW or ACCA.

You do not need the paper slip. Proof of purchase can be a bank or card statement showing the payment, an order confirmation email, a photo of the receipt or a gift receipt, and a shop that can see the purchase on its own system cannot insist on the paper. For anything faulty your claim is against the shop, not the maker: a full refund within 30 days, then repair or replacement, and in England, Wales and Northern Ireland up to six years to claim (five in Scotland) - a statement from your bank proves it just as well. If you are returning something because you changed your mind, there is no such right in a shop at all, so you are on their returns policy; ask the manager politely what proof they will accept, and if the goods were faulty and they still refuse, say you are going to Citizens Advice and put the claim in writing.

You do not need to buy antivirus for a Mac: keep macOS updated and install only from the App Store or developers you have heard of, which covers nearly all of it. If the machine is already misbehaving, run the free Malwarebytes scan once and delete it again; the paid suites mostly slow the Mac down.

You do not need to close them: a phone freezes an app the moment you leave it, so swiping them away actually costs battery, because the next open starts from scratch. Turn off what really runs in the background instead - Settings > General > Background App Refresh on an iPhone, Settings > Apps > [app] > Battery > Restricted on Android - and start with social, video and map apps. Notifications, location set to Always and auto-sync are the three settings that cost the most.

You do not need to count calories to lose weight, and most people who do stop within a month. What works is changing a few things you can see: no liquid calories, half the plate vegetables, weighing out pasta and rice rather than eyeballing them. If you like numbers, a two-week food diary tells you where the calories actually are, which is more useful than tracking forever.

You do not need a breakup speech: stop being the one who arranges things, answer warmly but briefly when they get in touch, and let it thin out. If they ask you straight whether something is wrong, tell them the truth once, kindly and without a list - "I've felt like I'm the one keeping this going, so I've stepped back" - which is fairer than silence. Go no-contact only if they are unkind to you or you do not feel safe; for a friendship that has simply run out, a slow drift is the kinder ending.

You do not need a degree: schools ask for GCSE maths and English, and a Level 2 or 3 teaching assistant course helps but is often taken after you start. The way in is to apply to several schools and to a supply agency at the same time - supply is paid, gets you known in a few schools, and turns into a permanent post more often than waiting for an advert does. Ask at the school office for the head of support staff, and mention any volunteering with children.

You do not owe anyone an announcement, and a slow fade is a real option: answer less, decline more, and let it settle on its own. If you do want to say it, say it once, plainly and kindly - 'I've realised I can't keep doing this, and I'm going to step back' - with no list of their faults, and expect them to be hurt. Say nothing about it to the friends you share; they should hear it from them, not from you.

You do not have to pay for something you did not order: say so before you pay and ask for it to come off the bill, and a discretionary service charge can come off too. If you have paid already, ask for it back on the card in writing - a refund is due within 14 days - and keep the bill for a chargeback if they refuse.

You do not have to let them in, and they cannot push past you: keep the door shut, ask for their name and the court certificate through the letterbox, and ring the council or the court that issued the warrant the same day. A bailiff needs a warrant to enter, and it covers only that debt. For free advice ring National Debtline on 0808 808 4000 or Citizens Advice before you pay anything.

You do not have a right to work from home, but you do have the right to ask, from your first day in the job. In the UK they must decide within two months, in writing, and talk it through with you before saying no; a refusal has to be for one of eight listed business reasons, such as cost or effect on customers. Two requests a year. If it is turned down, ask which reason applies and appeal in writing, then let ACAS help - a reason with nothing behind it is where employers come unstuck.

You don't need the perfect words: name it in one line ("that sounds really hard"), say you are glad they told you, and offer one concrete thing - a walk, dinner on Thursday - rather than "let me know if you need anything". Then ask what they need today, company or quiet or a distraction, and do that instead of fixing it.

You don't need to: stopping one or two reps short of failure builds about as much muscle and leaves you far less battered, so keep the last rep hard but doable on most sets. Take a set to all-out failure now and then on a machine or a small isolation move, not on squats or deadlifts where form goes first.

You feel it before you see it: stairs and breathing get easier in two to three weeks, and by six weeks you are lifting noticeably more than your first session. The mirror is the slow part - six to eight weeks for a change you can see, about three months for anyone else to notice, and a kilo of muscle a month at best, so judge it on a session you can now finish rather than on the scales.

You get a national insurance number automatically just before your 16th birthday if you live in the UK, and it arrives as a letter, not a card. If it never came or you have lost it, it is on any payslip or P60; failing that ring HMRC and ask them to post it out. If you have just moved to the UK, apply over the phone and you can usually start work while you wait, as long as you can show you have the right to.

You have to tell the DVLA when you move, and it is free. Update the V5C log book online (the address on it is what the police and the fines go to), and update your driving licence too - the two are separate records. You will not get a new V5C in the post for a licence change, so keep a note of the date you did it.

You keep most of it: only the part of your pay above each threshold is taxed at the next rate, so an extra 1,000 costs you 20 to 45 per cent of that 1,000, not of your old pay. Check the first payslip after the rise - the tax code should have gone up with the pay, and if it did not, that is what to query with payroll. A salary calculator gives the exact figure for your own numbers, and pension contributions come off before tax.

You keep building holiday while you work your notice, and you can ask to take it - but whether you get it is your employer's call, because they can refuse leave for business reasons. If they say no, they pay you for the days you have accrued when you leave, so you are not losing them. Ask in writing with the dates, offer the handover for those days, and check your contract for a clause about notice and leave.

You lose very little in a week or two: the fitness you built comes back quickly and rest can even leave you fresher. Real losses start after about two to four weeks off, and even then most of it returns within a few weeks of training again. What drops first is the top end - sprint speed and the pace you can hold hard - not your easy running. Come back at about 70% of where you left off for a week, then build.
You'll have to tell me - I only get what you type. How are they doing?
You'll have to tell me - I only get what you type. How did it go?
You're means 'you are', so 'you're welcome' and 'you're late' take it. Your shows ownership: your coat, your turn. Read the sentence with 'you are' in it; if that sounds wrong, use your.

YouTube: tap your picture > Settings > Autoplay, or on a TV use the Autoplay switch under the video. Netflix: choose your profile > Account > Profile > Autoplay next episode. Spotify is Settings > Playback > Autoplay. Those three cover most of the annoyance; Amazon Prime has Autoplay under the player's settings cog.

Your personal allowance is per person, not per job, so one employer uses it and the second job is taxed at 20% from the first pound. That makes the second payslip look savage while the total is usually right. If the two together still come to less than £12,570, claim the overpaid tax back; if both employers are using a full allowance, HMRC will send a new tax code, and you can ask them to split the allowance if one job is small. Each job has its own National Insurance threshold, so two part-time jobs can pay less NI than one full-time one.

Your phone talks by radio to the nearest mast, and the network passes the connection from mast to mast as you move - nothing is stored in the air. A city mast covers a few hundred metres and a rural one several miles, which is why the same phone is quick in town and slow in a field.

Your phone works it out from three things - the satellites it can see, which give the position to a few metres, the wifi networks nearby, which the phone recognises by the addresses they broadcast, and the masts it is attached to. Indoors, where satellites are blocked, the wifi list does most of the work, which is why it can place you in a building.

Your phone is not secretly recording you to make adverts, but it does track a lot: turn off ad personalisation in Settings > Privacy > Tracking (iPhone) or Ads (Android), and review which apps have the microphone. The ad that seems to follow a conversation usually comes from your location, your searches and the people you are near.

Your phone listens to satellites that each carry an atomic clock and broadcast their exact position and the precise time they sent it. The tiny differences in when the signals arrive from four of them fix your spot to a few metres - the satellites never learn where you are, your phone does the sum. Thick buildings and tunnels block the signals, which is why the arrow jumps there.

Your provisional licence and the theory pass certificate if you have the paper one, and the car you are using, with L plates front and back, insurance that covers a learner, a valid MOT and enough fuel. Take glasses or contact lenses if you need them to drive, and be there ten minutes early - the examiner reads the documents before you move off.

Your results and records are kept by the GP surgery, not by me: most practices put them in their online service or the NHS app a few days after they are filed, and reception can tell you the number and whether anything needs acting on. Take photo ID the first time you ask for online access; a scan report often appears only after a GP has read it, so if you can see the test but not the report, ring and ask.

Your router turns the internet into radio waves and your phone's aerial picks them up, so wifi is only the last few metres - the internet itself arrives at the router on a phone line or a cable. It uses two bands - 2.4GHz gets through walls better, 5GHz is faster but fades sooner, and water, foil-backed insulation and distance all weaken it.

Your body fights infection in layers: skin and mucus keep germs out, white blood cells attack whatever gets through, and antibodies tag specific germs for destruction. Memory cells remember each germ, which is why you rarely catch the same one twice and why vaccines work.

Your browser or phone has them: on an iPhone it is Settings > Passwords, on a Mac Safari > Settings > Passwords, in Chrome the key icon in the address bar or chrome://password-manager, and it asks for your fingerprint or face first. Turn on the password manager built into the phone rather than letting the browser do it, and the list follows you to the next phone.

Your contract does not die with the shop, but there is nobody at the till to serve it: the money comes from your card provider, or from the administrator. Paid by credit card and over £100? Say Section 75; on a debit card, or under £100, ask for a chargeback within 120 days of the payment, with the receipt and the order email. Register as a creditor with the administrator too, which is free but usually pays pence in the pound.

Your council's bin-day page will say: put your postcode in and it gives the day for your street, and that is the only place that is right, because bank holidays and ice move a round by a day or two and the paper calendar on the fridge goes stale. If it says tomorrow, put it out tonight; either way it has to be out by about 6.30 in the morning, so the night before is safest, and it comes back in the same day. If it is missed, report it on the council's missed-bin form that day rather than ringing - it is free and the round usually comes back within two working days.
Your fridge should be between 0 and 5C, with the coldest shelf at the bottom; use a thermometer rather than the dial. Keeping it properly cold is the single easiest way to make food last longer.

Your holiday is paid at your normal rate: what you would have earned on those days, not just basic pay - regular overtime, commission and shift pay count too. Add up what you were paid in the 52 weeks before, divide by 52, and that average week is what a week off pays; irregular hours work the same way. Leave you have not taken is paid out when you leave.
Yvette Cooper is the home secretary - Labour, in office since July 2024. The Home Office covers the police, the borders, immigration and passports.
Za'atar is not hot: it is thyme, sesame and sumac, so it is herby and sour. A spoon over bread or yoghurt, not a source of heat.

e.g. stands for exempli gratia, Latin for for example, and it introduces one of several: a root vegetable, e.g. a carrot. It is not the same as i.e., which rephrases rather than gives an example, and a list of three or four belongs after e.g. too.
e.g. means 'for example' (think 'example given') and i.e. means 'that is' (a restatement). Both take full stops in British style, and both want a comma after them.

i.e. stands for id est, Latin for that is, and it introduces a rephrasing of what you just said rather than a list: the cake was enormous, i.e. it fed eight. People write it when a shorter or plainer version of the same thing helps.
kg is short for kilogram: 1,000 grams, and about 2.2 pounds. A stone is 6.35 kg, which is why a person's weight in kilos is a bigger number than the same weight in pounds.
kph is short for kilometres per hour, the unit on every speedometer outside Britain and the United States. 100 kph is about 62 mph, and 50 kph in town is about 31 mph.

£40 to £90 for the battery itself, and £60 to £120 fitted at a repair shop; the maker charges most, around £120 to £180. Most laptop batteries are held in with screws and a five-minute job on older machines, so a £60 battery and a screwdriver is usually the cheap way to get three or four more years out of it.

£1,200 to £2,000 buys a dependable new one and £2,500 and up buys a lighter motor and a bigger battery, with decent second-hand starting around £600 to £900. What the money pays for is the battery and the motor: a 400Wh or bigger pack and a mid-drive motor are what separate a £2,000 bike from a £1,000 one, and a hub motor with a small pack is the one to avoid on hills. Add £50 to £100 for a lock that takes more than a minute to cut.

mg is short for milligram: a thousandth of a gram, so 1,000 mg is 1 g. A 500 mg paracetamol tablet is half a gram, and the dose on the box is written in these units because the useful amount is too small to weigh in grams.

mph is short for miles per hour: how many miles the thing would cover in an hour at that speed. 30 mph is about 48 km/h, which is why a British speed limit and a European one are never the same number.

tbsp is short for tablespoon: 15 ml in a British, American or Australian recipe, and three level teaspoons. A heaped tablespoon of flour or sugar weighs more than 15 g, so level it off unless the recipe says heaped.

tsp is short for teaspoon: 5 ml, and a third of a tablespoon. A level teaspoon of salt is about 6 g and of sugar about 4 g, which is why a spoon is a safe measure for salt and a rough one for anything you are weighing.
